## Volume front matter

### Series title page

## COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL LIBRARY

of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared with the greatest care from the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscript codices; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched by two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, by which it is immediately possible for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

An extremely accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent similarity throughout the entire work, the modest price, and above all this collection itself, unified, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**FIRST SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Complete works of Saint Prosper

## Preface to the works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine

A new edition of the complete works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine—once the most faithful disciple of Saint Augustine, the most vigorous champion of the doctrine handed down by him, and secretary of Pope Saint Leo the Great—ought to be brought forth with renewed care. This was necessary, first, so that those who cherish Augustine’s heavenly doctrine concerning the grace of God our Savior, and concerning other matters of faith and morals, might be served in some measure by being supplied with a fuller and more corrected text of Prosper, whose works place the whole of Augustine’s own doctrine before the reader in more concentrated form. It was necessary also that something, and perhaps something not useless, should be added to that outstanding edition of Saint Augustine’s works prepared several years ago by highly learned and devout men: namely, by multiplying the books of the man who may be said to have brought to completion, insofar as this was possible, the labor undertaken by Augustine of refuting and instructing the Semi-Pelagians, since he stripped the remaining fragments of the Pelagian heresy of all the weapons which they seemed to have gathered as survivors of the Pelagians’ defeat. Finally—and this was what above all compelled us to undertake the work—it was necessary to obey the explicit instructions contained in the privilege most graciously granted by the most illustrious Chancellor of Gaul, whom vigilant providence keeps ever intent upon the welfare of the entire kingdom and solicitous also for the advancement of literature, especially ecclesiastical literature.

Since, with God’s permission, we have undertaken to apply our care and whatever labor we can to this new edition, we recognize that it is incumbent upon us, according to customary practice, to offer the readers some account of the commendation of the Author, the purpose of his works, and the arrangement and advantages of this edition. Concerning the first two matters, however, much may be read elsewhere: concerning the merits and praise of this most holy and learned Author, in his Life, which will shortly follow this Preface; and concerning the order—or the year in which each work was written—and the subject treated in it, many details, and, if we are not mistaken, sufficient ones, will be found in the preliminary notice placed before each treatise in this volume. One task therefore remains: to explain briefly what we have attempted or accomplished in this edition, after first setting forth something about the older editions that appeared from various places during approximately the last two hundred years.

Accordingly, insofar as we learned from the books that we were able to examine while engaged in this work, the first of all Saint Prosper’s works to begin appearing in print was a volume in what is called octavo, entitled:

*The Book of Saint Prosper on the Grace of God and Free Will, in Defense of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, against the Book of the Presbyter Cassianus, which bears the preliminary title On the Protection of God.*

Also included were:

*Thirteen Chapters of the Decrees of Pope Celestine, for Prosper and Hilary, on the Grace of God, against certain Gallican presbyters who were followers of Pelagius.*

Prefixed to these was Celestine’s Letter to the Bishops of Gaul, which is reproduced on page 259 of this edition. The work was printed at Mainz on 5 September 1524 through the efforts of Nicolaus Carbachius. In his notice to the reader, Carbachius writes that he had decided to publish this little book, which he observed Prosper had been prompted to write when John Cassian attacked the books Augustine—already dead—had written against the Pelagians in defense of the grace of God. Carbachius states that he had decided to publish this little book, found in the library of the Benedictine religious brothers of Mount Saint James, both because the work was more than 1,070 years old, having been written by Prosper in defense of so great a man, and because it contains teachings approved by the authority of the supreme pontiffs Innocent I, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, and Sixtus III, and by the agreement of the sacred councils. He adds that for this reason he had devoted himself more earnestly to the undertaking, so that the mouths of those who in his own age openly proclaimed themselves supporters of the Pelagian heresy might be stopped, and so that they might see that what they taught had long ago been condemned by the ancient interpreters of Sacred Scripture. Thus far Carbachius.

Seven years later, namely in 1531, a smaller-volume edition appeared of the *Sentences Extracted from Augustine by Prosper*. In 1536, the *Books on the Contemplative Life* by Julianus Pomerius—customarily attached to Prosper’s works—were likewise printed in a volume of the same size.

Two years later, another volume of comparable size appeared at Venice, bearing the title:

*Minor Works on Grace and Free Will of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, Bishop of Regium, a most devout man, disciple of the divine Augustine, and highly learned in the divine Scriptures.*

Venice, printed by Bernardinus Stagninus, 1538.

This volume contained:

- Saint Prosper’s Letter to Rufinus;
- *Against the Excerpts of the Januensians*—which others call the Genoese;
- Saint Prosper’s *Book against Cassianus*;
- the Letter of Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage;
- Celestine’s Letter to the Bishops of Gaul;
- the Authorities of the Apostolic See, and so forth;
- Saint Prosper’s Epigrams;
- and, attached to them, the *Poem to His Wife*.

The following year, 1539, Stephanus Gryphius, a printer of Lyon celebrated for the many books he had printed in elegant type, appears to have been the first to undertake the publication of all the works of the divine Prosper, Bishop of Aquitaine and Regium, carefully revised by learned men through collation with ancient exemplars. He wished to dedicate this labor to the Senate and people of Regium. In writing to them, he relates that approximately four years earlier he had undertaken to print in his press the writings of Saint Prosper, their bishop; that he could not immediately accomplish this because the exemplars were both insufficiently accurately copied and incomplete through the absence of several minor works.

> “Therefore,” he adds, “in order to gratify you and serve the interests of students, I thought that the edition ought not to be rushed. Rather, the first effort had to be made to restore the work, if this could in any way be done, to its former brilliance and genuine integrity. Accordingly, by sending letters here and there, I entrusted the matter to friends, both in Gaul and in Germany, especially to those devoted to humane letters, asking them to send me whatever of this author lay hidden among them in ancient libraries, whether mutilated or complete. Among other things, they sent extremely old exemplars together with the minor works that were missing: namely, two in heroic verse, one on the Providence of God and the other *On the Ungrateful* (*περὶ Ἀχαρίστων*); in addition, an Exposition of the final fifty-one psalms. All of these, as I believe, had not been seen by the people of our age. After carefully collating all these materials with one another, I finally succeeded in bringing it about that your Prosper—so holy and so learned a man, who for so many centuries had lain hidden in darkness, having suffered neglect and decay—might come forth into the light wholly brilliant, pure, and complete.”

Thus far Stephanus Gryphius.

From his words it may be inferred that whatever had previously been published was then revised by learned men, although both Celestine’s Letter to the Bishops of Gaul on behalf of Prosper and Hilary and the Apostolic See’s statements on the grace of God and free will were omitted. Other works, however, were added, including those he lists, to which must be added the *Replies to the Chapters of the Gauls* and the *Replies to the Chapters of the Vincentian Objections*. He also had a Life of Prosper, composed by Giovanni Antonio Flaminio of Imola, placed at the beginning. What should be thought of this Life may be read below, in section 11 of the *Life of Saint Prosper*.

In the year of Christ 1565, however, Joannes Sotellus of Montigny, a student of the theological college of Louvain, dedicated a new revision of the works of our Prosper to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Carolus Vander Linden, bachelor of sacred theology and abbot of the Premonstratensian monastery of Parc near Louvain.

In this edition he omitted nothing from the earlier editions and added several other works through his own labor, namely the two *Books on the Calling of the Nations*, which had previously been read ascribed to Ambrose and certain others. He admits that they were falsely attributed to the holy bishop of Milan, but thinks they should be restored to their true author, Prosper:

> “Not only on account of the similarity of style and phrasing, but also because in the library of the Canons Regular of Saint Martin at Louvain, in the library of the Abbey of Cambron, and in the Abbey of Bonneffe near Namur, they are found under the name of Blessed Prosper in the most ancient manuscript exemplars. Certainly,” he says, “that they are not Ambrose’s is clearer from the style than to require any proof; and especially because they were written after the condemnation of the Pelagians—before whose condemnation Ambrose had died—as may be seen in chapter 22 of the first book.”

He likewise considers the letter he added to the virgin Demetrias to be Prosper’s, partly on account of the style and partly on account of the subject:

> “For it is addressed after the condemnation of Pelagius’s heresy, against Pelagius’s own letter on Holy Virginity to that same Demetrias, which is found at the beginning of volume IV in Jerome. That letter does not seem to have existed while Ambrose was still alive.”

We have discussed these matters at sufficient length in the notice prefixed to each work. He also added Prosper’s letter to Augustine concerning the remnants of the Pelagian heresy springing up in Gaul, which had not yet been published among Prosper’s works. He did not omit Celestine’s Letter, together with the statements customarily appended to it, which had been omitted from the Lyon edition. He was also the first to add to all the books of our Prosper, and not without reason, as we shall later explain, the Canons of the Second Council of Orange.

He likewise prefixed a Life composed from his own imagination and partly from his own conjectures, as Labbe judges (*Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 249). In it he explained his opinion concerning each of the works he had edited. Among other things, he decided that the *Poem on the Providence of God* should be removed from Prosper’s works because it is Pelagian in doctrine, whereas Prosper was a fierce opponent of Pelagianism. We have discussed this matter in the notice on page 779.

He published the *Books on the Predictions and Promises of God* as purely and completely as he could, but thinks it can be shown from the dissimilarity of their style and phrasing, and from the silence of Gennadius and Trithemius, that they were written by someone other than Prosper.

In 1576, all the books of Saint Prosper were once again examined in the Douai edition by Joannes Olivarius, who dedicated his edition to Joannes Sarracenus, prior of Saint-Vaast at Arras. In the dedicatory letter, explaining the labor he had undertaken, he boasts that he is sending Prosper’s works, which had not been sufficiently purged in earlier editions, now made more polished and enriched by a substantial addition of variant readings and numerous lacunae, especially by the restoration of one particularly notable omission.

Many corrections and variant readings had been supplied partly by a book collated by the Reverend Prior himself with ancient codices, and partly by a very old volume in the library of Cambron. This contained, written by hand, three books *On the Contemplative Life*, two *On the Calling of the Nations*, and one book of Epigrams. On the basis of this volume, many passages in these works were improved, omissions were supplied, and numerous observations were recorded—observations which, he hopes, would not be rejected even by the keenest judgment of his patron, to whom he willingly submits them.

The edition produced at Cologne in 1630 followed the standard of this latest Douai edition. It is identified as having been printed at the expense of the heirs of Joannes Crithius, under the sign of the Rooster. All the editions printed thereafter, in different years and different cities, likewise followed it. This is sufficient concerning the earlier editions of Saint Prosper’s works. We must now turn to our own.

In preparing it, our purpose and goal were that the edition should appear as complete as possible, extremely carefully corrected, and arranged in the best order.

> **Note:** Here, and wherever a passage from Saint Prosper’s works is cited, the reader is referred to the boldface numbers continuously inserted into the text of our edition.

We also wished to provide readers with some assistance toward a fuller knowledge of the history of the Semi-Pelagian error. We could not make the edition more extensive than by including everything of Saint Prosper’s genuine works, or of works attributed to him, that had hitherto appeared in print.

For this reason we did not neglect the little work first published by Sirmond in 1649 under the title *The Confession of Prosper of Aquitaine, the Tyro*, from the Vatican Library, after the poems of Eugenius and Dracontius. We explained in the preliminary notice to that work, on page 767, what learned men might think of it.

We also included the complete Chronicle, a work omitted by Prosper’s earlier editors. Stephanus Gryphius gives the following reason for its omission in the Lyon edition of 1539: it had been printed among the chronicles of Eusebius and others, and because, owing to its excessive corruption, it seemed likely to weary the reader.

We did not think that any prejudice should arise against our Prosper because something belonging to him had been joined to the fortunes of others. Given the opportunity, it ought to be restored, both for his honor and for the readers’ convenience. Nor should it now be considered so corrupt as it was 170 years earlier, since it has been examined, corrected, and enlarged by learned men from manuscript codices: both by André Duchesne in volume I of the *History of the Franks*, and by Philippe Labbe, who published it complete in volume I of the *New Manuscript Library*. Following Labbe’s edition as the fuller and more corrected one, while not omitting the differences found in other editions, we also collated it afresh with five Colbertine manuscripts.

We likewise corrected each book of this edition according to as many manuscripts as the limits of the time granted to us permitted us to find and consult, as well as according to the more approved editions previously published. We give a list of these below, immediately after the works and before the Appendix to the works of our Prosper.

And so that we might not be accused of having chosen arbitrarily among the various readings of the same passage found in the books, or of having prejudiced the taste of more learned readers, we thought it appropriate to relegate to the lower margin of each page those readings that we had not adopted, so that the learned reader might remain free to use whichever reading he judged preferable.

The entire work may also rightly appear to have been corrected because we took care to distinguish the spurious from the genuine, and the doubtful from the genuine, both by their placement and by their typeface and by a preliminary notice. We have cited the judgments of learned men concerning each work, without prejudging anyone’s opinion by a more confident censure than is warranted.

We established the order of Saint Prosper’s works according to the order in which their composition can be demonstrated, whether from the text of the books themselves, from their subject matter, or from the judgment and testimony of learned men.

For this reason we placed first Prosper’s Letter to Augustine concerning the remnants of the Pelagian heresy springing up in Gaul, etc., as the earliest effort of our Author against those adversaries of grace. We have not been able to find anywhere the letters that he there says he had previously sent to Augustine, or which he rejoices to have received from him.

This is followed by Hilary’s Letter to Augustine on the same subject, written at the same time and sent by the bearer of the former letter.

Both letters received a reply from the holy bishop of Hippo in the two books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, addressed to Prosper and Hilary. We are surprised that no one had previously observed how justly our Prosper could claim these books for himself and how useful, indeed necessary, was the connection they retained with the letters of Prosper and his companion Hilary. We therefore thought that we would not sufficiently serve the devotion and usefulness of students unless we arranged for these books to follow immediately.

It was not appropriate to postpone for long Rufinus’s Letter to Prosper, written while Augustine was still alive. Nor was it appropriate to delay the notable and never sufficiently praised *Poem of Our Prosper on the Ungrateful*, which likewise appears to have been composed at that time, while Augustine had not yet been taken up among the heavenly ones. It was undertaken to vindicate his reputation and doctrine against the murmurs and slanders of the Semi-Pelagians.

For the sake of greater clarity, no one, we hope, will deny the usefulness of adding to this poem both the brief summaries of each passage, which had already been printed in a vernacular translation of the same poem, rendered both in prose and in verse in 1646, and the grammatical and critical notes appended to it by Martin Steyaert, Doctor of Louvain, who died not long ago, in the *Minor Works* published at Louvain in 1703. These notes also clarify the two Epigrams against Augustine’s detractor and the Epitaph of both the Pelagian and Nestorian heresies, which will be discussed shortly.

Those two epigrams likewise ought not to have been separated from the published *Poem against the Ungrateful*, since they are shown to be not much later than it, inasmuch as they imply that Augustine was still alive.

The *Epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian Heresies* is placed after them because of the affinity of its subject matter with the preceding works, although it may perhaps have been written later, namely after the Pelagians had again been condemned together with the Nestorians.

We immediately place after these the *Replies of Prosper to the Objections of the Gauls and of Vincentius*, which had been disseminated against Augustine’s doctrine and our Author’s reputation, as well as the *Replies to the Excerpts and Doubts of the Genoese Presbyters*. We believe that these preceded the return journey of Prosper and Hilary from Rome, although it must not be concealed that some have thought they should be placed after their return. Let the judgment rest with the readers.

Our Prosper returned from Rome to Gaul with his Hilary, armed with that celebrated Letter of Pope Celestine to the bishops of Gaul. It is believed that the *Authorities of the Bishops of the Apostolic See on the Grace of God and Free Will*, customarily appended to it and drawn from ecclesiastical archives, were attached to the letter. This will be discussed below, on page 263 and the following pages.

Armed with these materials, the vigorous defender of Augustine and of the grace he had defended entered into conflict with the Semi-Pelagians of Massilia with still greater confidence. Among them he began to write against Cassianus, the leading figure among the presbyters of Massilia who criticized Augustine.

This man’s *Conferences* had appeared, filled indeed with salutary teachings, but not entirely free from criticism in several places. Among them was read and circulated the Thirteenth Conference, *On the Protection of God*, in which he did not hesitate to publish a new distinction, devised by himself, that detracted not a little from the rights of divine omnipotence and from faith in original sin.

We judged that this conference would not harm sound doctrine—which Saint Prosper everywhere defends—if it were read in that place; indeed, we thought that the contrast with Prosper’s book written against it would shed light upon orthodox doctrine.

Immediately following it is the *Book of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine on the Grace of God and Free Will against the Collator*, that is, against Cassianus, the author of this conference, whom Prosper nevertheless did not wish to identify by name, out of respect and from a desire for peace.

There follow the *Exposition of the Psalms from 100 through 150* and the *Book of Sentences Extracted from the Works of Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo*. There is also a book of Epigrams drawn from the sentences of Saint Augustine.

Since these works reproduce Augustine’s books either word for word or, almost everywhere, by a perfect imitation of his thought, they show that Prosper had been thoroughly practiced from childhood in turning day and night to the books of that most holy Doctor. The time of their composition is established as quite probable in the notice prefixed to each.

There is nothing further to say here about the complete Chronicle beyond what has already been stated above and what will be discussed more fully in its own notice.

It remains only to add that, in correcting it, besides the manuscripts listed above and the editions of Duchesne and Labbe, and the edition contained in volume VIII of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers* of 1677, we also consulted an edition of the same Chronicle corrected by Arnaldus Pontacus, Bishop of Bazas, from twenty-eight manuscripts and eight editions, and illustrated with his own notes. It was printed at Bordeaux in 1604 by Simon Millanges.

Immediately after the Chronicle is read the Second Council of Orange on Grace and Free Will, held, as is believed, in the year 515. It began to be attached to Prosper’s works, with good reason, in the Louvain edition of 1565 and thereafter, because the Fathers of this council defined the doctrine that Saint Prosper had defended against the Massilians. They are also observed to have composed a considerable number of their canons from the very words not only of Augustine but also of our Prosper.

In the final canon they openly rejected and condemned, with the authority of Scripture and the support of ancient definitions, Cassianus’s distinction between two kinds of predestined persons—a distinction that Prosper had so excellently refuted in the book published against him.

These, then, are the certain and indubitable works of Saint Prosper.

The following works we judged should be counted among the doubtful:

- the *Confession*, said to be by Prosper of Aquitaine, concerning which something has been said above;
- the *Poem of a Husband to His Wife*;
- the *Poem on Divine Providence*, which we have divided into chapters for the first time, prefixed a summary of the chapters to the work, and briefly indicated in the outer margin the subjects treated in each section;
- the two books *On the Calling of All Nations*, with summaries both at the beginning and within the body of the work, as they are found in the latest edition of Leo;
- and finally the *Letter to the Holy Virgin Demetrias*, or *Treatise on Christian Humility*, which concludes the series of genuine and doubtful works.

A considerable amount will be found concerning each of them in the notice prefixed to each.

There is no need to say more here about the Appendix, which we have divided into two parts, beyond what is stated in the notice on the books *On the Contemplative Life* and in the notice preceding the book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*. These two books, together with the Pseudo-Chronicle furnished with its own notice, make up the first part of the Appendix.

The second part of our Appendix consists of writings and monuments whose purpose and usefulness in this location are explained at sufficient length in the notice provided there. We also observed there that these writings and monuments would, as we hope, shed light on the reading of Saint Prosper’s works and on the history of the Semi-Pelagians itself.

Finally, immediately after the works themselves and the list of manuscripts used for their correction, we publish an index of subjects, words, places, persons, and noteworthy statements encountered by anyone reading Prosper, together with those works that may be attributed to Prosper with some foundation, though not certainty.

The writings and monuments that make up both parts of the Appendix, however, are relegated to the end of the entire volume.

These are the things that we have either attempted or accomplished in order to promote the public good and to obey commands that it was not permissible to neglect. If anything less correct has been admitted contrary to our intention, may the fair and learned reader graciously pardon it.

But if anything good and useful is judged to have been accomplished by us, may he, together with us, attribute it all to the One from whom comes “every good gift and every perfect gift” (James 1:17), who “teaches man knowledge” (Psalm 93:10), and who, if it pleases him, “makes the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wisdom 10:21).

[Col. 0017]

# Life of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine

## Compiled from his own works and from the books of ecclesiastical writers

### Article One. The praises of Prosper among ancient and modern writers, and the character of his style

[Col. 0017A]

Among those who became champions of the teaching of Blessed Augustine, Saint Prosper claims the foremost place by the excellence of his learning, the weight of his authority, and the renown of his name (Labbe, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 251).

His friend and colleague Hilary—at whose urging Prosper seems to have entered upon this contest—affirms in writing to Augustine that Prosper was distinguished both by his character and by his eloquence and zeal, and therefore worthy of the acquaintance of so great a man (Hilary, Letter to Augustine).

Victorius, who was writing in the year 457, perhaps while Prosper was still alive, calls him a holy and venerable man (Bucher, *Cycle*, pp. 6–7).

The council held at Rome under Pope Gelasius in 494, while approving his writings, calls him a most devout man (Councils, vol. IV, p. 126).

Gennadius himself, although not sufficiently fair to him—since Prosper had fought against Cassianus with too much success—nevertheless acknowledges him to have been powerful in eloquence and, as Gennadius puts it, “scholastic in speech and vigorous in his assertions” (Gennadius, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 84).

Saint Fulgentius (*Book to the Monks*, chapter 30), observing that Blessed Augustine, overtaken by a swift death, had been unable to refute the objections of the Gallican presbyters, notes that his statements were defended in orthodox faith and copious discourse by Prosper, a learned and holy man.

Fulgentius shortly afterward quotes several passages of Prosper:

> “So that all may know,” he says, “what they ought to think concerning the predestination of the saints and of the wicked.”

Fulgentius repeats the same point elsewhere (*Book II*, chapter 1):

> “Thus, although many ordinarily become seriously disturbed by this question—namely, the difference between the predestination of the righteous and that of the unrighteous—they can easily be instructed both by the testimonies of the divine books and by the books of Saint Augustine and the replies of Prosper, a most learned man.”

Of all the material contributing to Prosper’s praise in Gennadius, Marcellinus copies only this material, and not the rest, under the year 463.

Cassiodorus honors him with the title “saint” (*Institutions*, chapter 17), while Bede calls him a rhetorician or orator (*History of the English*, book I, chapter 10). Finally, Photius affirms that he was truly a man of God (*Bibliotheca*, codex 54).

The modern writers agree with the ancients. Among them one may read Trithemius, who testifies that our Prosper “appeared most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular studies, excellent in poetry and prose, eloquent in speech, profound in understanding, subtle in intelligence, vigorous in assertion, and most holy in life and conduct” (Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 32).

Sixtus of Siena says that he possessed a lively and discerning intellect, a concise, elevated, and elegant style of discourse, and was extremely well versed in both divine and human letters; in addition, he was made worthy of admiration by the remarkable holiness of his life (*Sacred Library*, book IV, p. 369).

Scaliger judges him to have been by far the most learned and accomplished man of his age (*Notes on Eusebius’s Chronicle*, p. 8).

Garnerius says that the letters written by Prosper and Hilary to Augustine against the Semi-Pelagians were so admired by later generations that they were appended to the latest works of the great teacher of grace as works equal to them (Garnerius, *On the Notice of Marius Mercator under the Name of Celestine*). He particularly observes in Prosper an exceedingly watchful eye, from which scarcely anything could escape. He adds that his great learning was matched by an equally keen judgment.

[Col. 0018A]

Prosper, according to the testimony of others and of Gennadius (*Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 84), was born in the province of Aquitaine. Hence he is ordinarily called Aquitanus, so that he may more easily be distinguished from other men of the same name.

In what part of that very extensive region, and in what city, he was born is entirely uncertain.

This shows how little weight ought to be given to a certain manuscript codex, and not a particularly ancient one, in the Colbert Library. On the sole authority of this manuscript, the book of *Sentences Extracted from Augustine by Prosper* was corrected by the highly learned editors of Saint Augustine’s works in the Appendix to volume X, part 3 (our *Patrologia*, volume XLV). It contains the statement:

> “This Prosper was an Equitanian” (perhaps instead of “was an Aquitanian”), “a citizen of Toulon, who, having abandoned secular affairs, devoted himself to divine concerns.”

The city of Toulon is situated in the Viennese province of Gaul.

It is equally clear how little attention should be paid to those who, without any supporting argument, call our Prosper “of Regium in Aquitaine,” even though Regium lies far away (Dupin, vol. IV, p. 430).

[Col. 0018C]

Sirmondus presents it as an unquestionable fact that his surname was Tiro (*History of Predestination*, chapter 5, p. 31). We do not know with sufficient certainty whether he found this in some manuscripts, as Bucherius likewise testifies that it is written in his manuscript of Prosper’s Chronicle (*Cycle*, p. 211), and as Vossius also cites it from another manuscript (Vossius, *Latin Poets*, book II, chapter 17).

Alternatively, perhaps Sirmondus confidently judged that a certain poem should be assigned to our Prosper because it is found among his works and is attributed by Bede to Prosper Tiro. See Saint Paulinus, 1685, dissertation 6, p. 136; and *Ecclesiastical Monuments*, volume XIV, note 4.

Anyone can easily judge from his writings that he was by no means unversed in the liberal arts, and especially in poetry—arts which he and Paulinus cultivated with far greater distinction than any other of all those devoted to the Church who gave themselves to this pursuit. But Prosper consecrated them to even holier monuments than Paulinus did. Something in his prose discourse also stands out that suggests a poet: sublimity, force, a sharp and sinewy style; frequent striking formulations; words that seem to submit themselves to the point of his pen. He also affects the reader much more powerfully, whether through the dignity of his expression or through the strength of his solid and unshakable reasoning. Yet the natural beauty of his speech is sufficient for him. He does not summon ornament to his aid—neither words falling into the same sound, nor full and rhythmical measures, nor evenly balanced and melodiously arranged periods, nor, finally, those affected embellishments that Leo and other authors of his age pour forth to the point of satiety. Since he was the leader of those who defended the Catholic doctrine concerning the grace of Christ, and since he was wholly intent on attacking the Church’s adversaries or defending her against their assaults, he adopts a muscular—if one may use that expression—and military style of writing, and weighs matters much more carefully than words. Hence the composition of his discourse is sometimes somewhat obscure. Yet however intricate the matters may be, he very easily illuminates them, and explains them with no less clarity than sharpness. Thus it may truly be stated of Prosper that his discourse is not worked out with such elaborate art, nor distinguished by as many lights of eloquence, as may be found in the writings of certain others; but that it displays far more good sense, intelligence, and force.

It was worthwhile to preface this discussion of Saint Prosper’s style, so that certain works hitherto inscribed with his name might more certainly be withdrawn from his authorship.

## ARTICLE II. Prosper’s Youth and Conversion

[Col. 0019C]

There exists a certain short work entitled *The Confession of Prosper of Aquitaine* (*Bibl. PP.*, vol. VIII, p. 193), or, as others read it, *The Confession of Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine* (Labbe, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 261), edited by Jacob Sirmond from a Vatican manuscript in 1619. It is written with sufficient elegance to be attributed to the great Prosper, although Antelmius (*Dissertation on the Works of Leo*, p. 370) seems scarcely to have detected in it anything sufficiently similar to Prosper’s style or especially consonant with his reputation; and Louis Ellies Dupin (vol. IV, p. 441) confidently declares it unworthy of so great a father. From this confession of Prosper’s, however (below, p. 769 and following), we learn that at the very beginning of his life he was reborn in Christ Jesus and, once the sin of his origin had been forgiven by the merciful Lord, obtained freedom before he understood the slavery imposed by the savage master who held him captive. He blames himself for having neglected to preserve with the care required the substance received from his most munificent Father, and for having surrendered himself wholly to vices, passing first under the authority of the Egyptians and then also under that of the Babylonians, receiving no other price for his ruin than deadly pleasure. What should be inferred from this manner of speaking, together with what Paulinus likewise reports about the first years of his life, is difficult to determine. Yet Salvian’s complaints about the depraved morals especially of the wealthy Aquitanians are well known (*On the Government of God*, book VII, pp. 154, 160), when he accuses them of being, throughout Gaul, first in wealth and likewise first in vices.

However that may be, the man of whom we are speaking, while serving through innumerable changes of the harshest dominations—not by bodily submission but by the anguish of his soul—and while being troubled by degrading duties and by the worse condition of his status, as he himself says (below, pp. 769–770), began to feel shame. As far as the pressing masters permitted, he withdrew into the hidden secrecy of his spirit and heart; and, taking up the volume of the sacred Scriptures, he considered what hope might still remain for him. Once assured by them that God’s mercy is always most ready for those who sincerely repent of a badly conducted life, he groaned, drenched in a heavy shower of tears: he had sold himself to sin after being redeemed by the blood of God, and, in sorrow, was serving those most hostile to him. Then, strengthened and encouraged, he resolved to break the heavy chains by which he was held bound, return to the one by whom he had been purchased for life, ask, seek, and knock at the door of divine mercy. He was ashamed because he was naked in spirit and possessed nothing with which to cover the indecency of his limbs—that is, of his morals—and he was overwhelmed by the disgrace of obscene poverty. He did not dare to appear before so great a household and so great a Father. “Yet,” he says, “is judgment more bearable when one is accused than when one confesses voluntarily; when one is obstinate than when one is pleading; when one is brought before the dread tribunal of God in death than when, before death, one has sincerely returned to the most merciful Father?” Finally, he resolved this within himself:

> However many crosses and disgraces repentance may have,  
> the fire of shame will be lighter than that of Gehenna.

From these words we cannot immediately assert that he meant he had resolved to embrace the hardships of public penance. Nevertheless, if Prosper had adopted such a course, it is likely that some mention of it would have remained in his writings.

Nor, although he was distressed by the loss of the gifts of grace that he had received in Baptism, did he therefore fail gratefully to adore the swift condescension and prompt clemency by which he had been regenerated while still an infant. He was far removed from those who, to excuse the violation of their regeneration, pleaded their immature age and heedless years, forgetful of so great a benefit undeservedly bestowed upon them.

[Col. 0020D]

He seems to indicate that he was then living among a foreign people when he turned to God and began to recover his senses, and that he alone would have been changed had not a Barbarian, having stationed guards, maintained the boundaries of his kingdom. These things could properly and truthfully have been said by him. For no one is unaware of the devastation caused by the Barbarians, gathered from diverse peoples, both throughout Gaul and especially in Aquitaine, at the beginning of the fifth century.

Prosper also complains in the *Poem on Divine Providence*—if that poem is indeed to be regarded as the genuine offspring of Prosper—that his city was destroyed by fire by the Goths, that he himself was captured by the Barbarians, driven along amid their bands, and forced to go on foot. He says that his bishop, together with the surviving remnants of his afflicted and wretched flock, sought some dwelling—or rather, some place of exile (below, p. 787).

## ARTICLE III. Prosper Is Stirred to Piety by the Calamities of His Age and Rebukes the Obstinate Complaints of Certain Persons

The poem attributed by Bede to Prosper Tiro (*Ecclesiastical Monuments*, vol. XIV, note 4) is extant among the works of Paulinus of Nola, and learned men judge it by no means unworthy of him. Although it is exceedingly difficult to reconcile it with this man’s history, nothing in it is found that does not harmonize extremely well with Prosper’s known circumstances. It is attributed to Prosper not only on Bede’s authority but also on that of several manuscript codices. There is only one feature that might give pause: the poem is more ornate and flows more freely than one would expect of Prosper’s work. But why should he not have used a different style of writing at that time, when he had only recently abandoned the literature of pagan authors and the study of secular eloquence, and another when he was concerned solely with overcoming error and employed words of the kind demanded by weighty judgments and firm arguments?

Whoever, finally, the author of that poem may have been, he was certainly bound by marriage, and dedicates the work to his wife (below, pp. 773, 779). Moved both by the perpetual instability of human affairs and by the harshest afflictions of his age, he urges himself to cultivate piety each day with renewed zeal. Many people of that time, crushed by calamities, had become hardened and did not hesitate to accuse God himself in impious language (Salvian, *On the Government of God*, book VII, pp. 152–153). He, however, professes that he had fixed and placed all his hope in God alone, through whose kindness he, an inhabitant of this earth, had become a citizen of another homeland—namely, the heavenly one. He promises that, knowing earthly riches to be held only by a very brief tenure, he will use them as though they were not his own; that he will no longer marvel at them or pursue honors; and that one who enjoys Christ, rich in himself, will never fear raging poverty. With the same disposition with which he will receive prosperity, he will endure adversity, so that he will permit himself neither to be overcome and cast down by evils nor captured and exalted by good things. He will always give Christ his due thanks and celebrate his praises and honor with a remembering mouth (below, p. 775, verse 45 and following; p. 785, verse 15 and following).

After briefly recounting what God did and endured for the sake of human beings, he adds the following (below, p. 777, verse 89 and following):

> What, then, should I refuse to endure for so great a hope,  
> or what could separate me from the Lord?
>
> Apply fire, search my entrails with your hand, torturer:  
> my loosened limbs will escape your punishments.
>
> If I am shut in a blind prison and loaded with chains,  
> free in the ecstasy of my mind I shall approach God.
>
> If the executioner prepares to cut off my neck with his sword,  
> swift death, brief punishment, will find me unafraid.
>
> I do not fear exile: the world is one home for everyone.  
> I despise hunger, if the Lord’s word is food for me.
>
> Yet this confidence in myself does not arise from me.  
> You, Christ, grant me speech; you grant me the ability to suffer.
>
> We dare nothing in ourselves, but we trust in you—  
> you who command those whom you make fight and conquer.

Since his wife was still alive, he urges her to dedicate herself likewise to God, so that, strengthened by mutual assistance, both might fight the enemy more vigorously and successfully. He addresses her as follows (p. 779, verse 115 and following):

> Now, faithful companion, gird yourself with me for this battle,  
> the battle for which God has provided aid to the weak.
>
> Restrain the one who is lifted up by anxiety; comfort the grieving;  
> let us both be an example of a devout life.
>
> Be the guardian of your guardian; repay mutual care.  
> Raise the one who falls; rise through the help of the one you raise.
>
> Let not only our flesh be the same, but our minds also;  
> let one spirit nourish two persons.

The punishments that God, as avenger, was then exacting from the human race were being used by the most wicked people—whom it was necessary to implore forgiveness—to accuse God, not without blasphemy (below, p. 785, verse 15 and following). Abusing the most evident proofs of divine providence in order to attack it, they saw good and innocent people oppressed by the same evils as the guilty, denied that human affairs were governed by God, and fled to a futile kind of power attributed to fate and the stars (below, p. 809, verse 624 and following).

Such blasphemies, which had impelled blessed Augustine to write that great and outstanding work *The City of God*, also gave occasion, in the year 416, for the *Poem on Divine Providence* (p. 785, verse 1 and following). The author of that poem, who everywhere displays a remarkable sense of extraordinary devotion toward God, had been accustomed to exercise his style in various works, both in prose and in verse. But when Gaul had been ravaged for a decade—that is, since the end of the year 406, when the Barbarians invaded it—grief weighed down the man’s sorrowful spirit and had already compelled him to remain silent for the space of an entire year, since he had borne no small share of his homeland’s sufferings (ibid.). Nevertheless, he was eventually moved by the reckless insults of blasphemous people, some of whom boasted that they professed the Christian faith. Stimulated more sharply by the darts of impious tongues than by all the cruelty of the raging Goths, he undertook to vindicate God’s providence with his pen and blunt the insulting voices of its enemies (p. 789, verse 87 and following).

The poem rests chiefly upon this doctrinal principle: through the calamities of this life God punishes the impious, cleanses the good from the filth of sin, kindles the lukewarm, raises them up, and increases and amplifies them with the adornments of virtue (p. 821, verse 902 and following). He then prays God to number him among those whom, when they sin, the Good One reproves and corrects with a father’s scourge, rather than among those whom, once the rod has been removed, he permits to go wherever their will directs and to be carried along by their own desire. In this work one finds many things about divine grace that seem excellently expressed and by no means unworthy of our Prosper. On the other hand, there are certain passages that one can scarcely judge to be consistent with the assertions he later defended so vigorously and successfully. Hence it may be that this work, otherwise appropriate to him, was undertaken before he had devoted sufficiently serious attention to the doctrine of grace [the text here appears corrupt] (Antelmius, *Dissertation on the Works of Leo*, p. 405 and following, and others).

These are the conclusions we have drawn concerning Prosper’s early years from three writings whose authority seemed neither wholly rejectable nor admissible without any doubt. What we shall say hereafter will rest upon works that are certainly and indisputably his.

## ARTICLE IV. He Defends the Doctrine of Grace against the Semipelagians

Whether Prosper migrated from Aquitaine because of the violence of the Barbarians or because of some other circumstance is not entirely clear. It is more certain that, in the year 428 or 429, or perhaps as early as 426, he was brought by God’s providence to Provence, in order to defend and uphold the Christian doctrine of grace clarified by blessed Augustine. Certain men distinguished both by rank and by their reputation for virtue and piety were then weakening that doctrine in those regions (see *Life of Saint Augustine*, §343, vol. XIII of the *Ecclesiastical Monuments*).

Prosper was personally unknown to Augustine and was known to him only through the mind and speech conveyed in letters sent to him and received in return (below, p. 1). But after reading the holy man’s writings and, with God’s mercy shining before him, learning the truth, he defended it with all his strength (p. 6). Thus Hilary, another vigorous defender of the same truth, when writing to Augustine, who was better known to him, dealt with Prosper so that Prosper too might send his own letter to Augustine (p. 18). Hilary considered Prosper worthy both of a fuller acquaintance with the holy bishop and capable of clearly setting forth the error in which the adversaries were entangled, reporting also which matters in these questions were more obscure and difficult to understand and therefore required to be disclosed by the most excellent Doctor through the clearest explanations.

Prosper accordingly complied with Hilary’s request and sent that famous letter, still extant, at the end of 428 or the beginning of 429, professing that he wrote out of devotion to the faith by which the Church lives (p. 1 and following). Moved by the zeal of both men, Augustine wrote two books to them, *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. He may also have sent them certain other letters, which have since been lost (below, p. 23 and following).

It is clear that Hilary was then a layman (p. 18a). Prosper appears to have been a deacon (p. 1a), perhaps because, when speaking of the deacon Leontius, he calls him his brother, and because both Augustine (*On the Predestination of the Saints*) and Celestine name Hilary before him. Yet neither from Hilary’s letter to Augustine concerning Prosper nor from any other ancient writer does it appear that Prosper was distinguished by any ecclesiastical rank (below, p. 25). He himself testifies (below, p. 6) that he was unequal not to the arguments of those who thought perversely about the truth, but to their authority, because many of them greatly surpassed him in the merits of their lives, and some excelled him by having recently attained the highest honor of the priesthood. Today every learned person acknowledges that there is no monument of antiquity from which it can be established that he had any status other than that of a layman. One manuscript states that, after abandoning secular affairs, he devoted himself entirely to divine matters. He belonged, then, to the number of those who, having renounced the world, lived in retirement without binding themselves to any monastery—such men as Paulinus, Pammachius, Sulpicius Severus, and others of the same age, who were included under the designation “monks.” Saint Prosper followed this manner of life.

Nor should we omit what Garnerius piously and prudently observed in his preface to all the works of Marius Mercator (p. 7):

> “I have sometimes observed, not without great admiration, that God, who loves to resist the proud by the hand of the humble, opposed to three heresies—the Pelagian, the Nestorian, and the Massilian—which the Fathers accuse more than the others of pride, first of all laymen, so that, as the Apostle says, he might confound the strong through the contemptible things of the world and, through the weak, overthrow the swollen power of a Pharaoh.
>
> “Certainly the first to oppose the Pelagians was Constantius, a native of Vico [the text reads *Vicano*; this is evidently how it should be read], living in Rome. The first to expose Nestorius’s deceit and reveal it to the clergy, by posting a protest at the church doors, was Eusebius, at that time, as Theophanes calls him, σχολάστικος τῆς βασιλίδος Κονσταντινοπόλεος, “a legal scholar of royal Constantinople,” as Theophanes calls him; or, as Nicephorus reports, a rhetorician; or, as Leontius writes, a forensic judge. Two laymen, Hilary and Prosper, were the first to resist the Massilian presbyters, and they warned Augustine by letters which a later age regarded with such esteem that it joined them, as though their equals, to the final labors of the great doctor of grace.”

Those who opposed the sound doctrine of Christ’s grace were not moved from their position by the authority of the two books that blessed Augustine wrote to Prosper and Hilary; in later centuries they were rightly called Semipelagians. Not only the Roman and African councils (below, p. 89), and all the sons of promise throughout the world who lived outside Gaul, but also very many people within Gaul itself agreed with blessed Augustine’s doctrine (ibid.), in the confession of grace just as in the whole faith, and were nourished by his most salutary disputations for the reception of evangelical and apostolic teaching. Nevertheless, not a few Gauls secretly murmured against the holy bishop, even though the priesthood was then a special portion of the Lord, and, whenever they found ears willing to listen, slandered his writings against Pelagian error, attributing to so devout a man the impiety of pagans and Manichaeans. Thus they attempted to reduce the Church’s cause to such a position that, while affirming that Catholics had not spoken truthfully on behalf of grace, they could persuade people that the Pelagians had been unjustly condemned (below, p. 308).

If these things were true (p. 89 and following), and Augustine had erred in some respect, why did they not resist his preaching, or at least confront in writing the man from whom such a doctrine proceeded? He certainly would not have refused to listen to those who admonished him, insofar as this could be done without compromising the truth. They would indeed have secured great glory for themselves and rendered a great service to the human race if they had recalled Augustine from error. Nor was there any reason to think that an old man of such great prior merit, whose books no one would accept, ought to be forgiven honorably and mercifully.

But the timid censors did not dare openly to profess themselves adversaries of so great a man, knowing that everyone’s judgment concerning him was highly honorable and that there were people ready to defend his reputation vigorously and energetically. They were annoyed that Prosper resisted the things they had asserted, during many conversations, against a man of such outstanding authority. They did not doubt that, if they raised any question on this matter in any gathering of priests or assembly of the people, they would be confronted by hundreds of volumes of the most blessed Augustine. Once these volumes began, after dispersing the darkness of calumnies, to reveal to the hearts of their hearers the most powerful truth of the Christian faith, they would forbid devout and faithful people to accept the bitterness of those who wished to glory in their own righteousness rather than in God’s grace. Thus they were content to gnaw at him by secret detraction, since they did not dare to accuse him openly and steadfastly (p. 87). In addition, they spread the same rumors about his disciples, so that no one would remain whose authority could drive away the errors that they wished the faithful to approve (p. 98).

## ARTICLE V. Saint Prosper Defends His Own Reputation and Augustine’s, and Writes against the Ungrateful

[Col. 0025C]

Rufinus, a friend of Prosper, disturbed by the rumours being circulated about errors rashly imputed to his intimate friend, wrote to him (below, p. 87). Prosper received his letter as evidence of brotherly concern and most sincere charity, and replied at length, setting forth with complete truth everything then being alleged and reported, to excite empty hostility, both concerning Augustine himself and concerning Augustine’s disciples. In many places in this letter he speaks of Augustine as still alive. Since Augustine died on 28 August 430, the letter must necessarily have been written before the end of that year (below, pp. 89, 99). In it he observes that very many peoples were then beginning for the first time to become participants in Christian grace; and indeed, about this time blessed Palladius brought it to the Irish (Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, ch. 3).

Augustine also seems still to have been alive when Prosper exalted him with such magnificent praises in the *Poem against the Ungrateful* (below, p. 126, v. 90 ff.; Mercator, vol. I, p. 101):

> Could the holy council have reached another conclusion,
> whose leader and genius was Aurelius Augustine,
> whom Christ’s grace, watering with a richer horn,
> gave as a light to our age, kindled from the true light.
> For God is his food and life and rest,
> and Christ alone is all his delight;
> Christ’s love is his one love, Christ’s honour his one honour.
> And while he ascribes no good things to himself, God becomes
> all things to him, and Wisdom reigns in the holy temple.
>
> Therefore, among all who have driven mad beasts
> from the holy flock, his diligence is greater,
> his work greater; more excellently it has imbued the whole world.
> For wherever the crafty enemy turned his step,
> and wherever by hidden winding paths he pursued his doubtful course,
> he was anticipated by this man’s encounter, and the snares
> of a thousand paths found no entrance at all.
> And when, shut out, the rage of ravenous wolves
> gnashed its teeth and turned falsehood toward every device,
> so that it could not corrupt the minds of any sheep
> or disturb wavering hearts with oblique complaints,
> God made it so by this man’s mouth: from this man’s mouth
> rivers of books flowed out over all the world,
> which the gentle and humble drink, and which strive to pour
> streams of life-giving doctrine into the fields of their minds.

Led by love for his faithful brethren, he undertook the arduous work in order to kindle devout minds with zeal for truth, drive from them errors increasing through the wicked arts of enemies, and clearly and pleasantly teach [the printed wording is corrupt at this point] that grace is the maker of our merits. He himself expresses this at the opening of the whole poem (below, p. 115, v. 1 ff.):

> The chaste love of the race born in Christ, poured into me from on high,
> bids me exceed my own powers and kindle devout minds in song,
> lest, after the celebrated victory has ended the war,
> unguarded peace relax secure hearts,
> as though no fear remained after the enemy had been crushed,
> and the venomous head of the bruised serpent no longer throbbed.

He entitled his poem *On the Ungrateful*. For no one suffers more grievously from the vice of ingratitude than one who supposes that what are the greatest gifts and benefits of the Saviour’s mercy and omnipotence are located in himself and in the powers of free choice. “This poem, moreover, is the most splendid and the most extensive of all that Prosper published, and there is no other in which the strength and acuteness of his talent shine more brightly. It is a noble work, composed of great thoughts, great feelings, and, finally, magnificent words and expressions, although it treats such a subject as scarcely admits those free and vehement movements which poetry requires” (Antelmius, *Dissertation on the Works of Leo*, p. 417). A man distinguished in the preceding age for exceptional piety rendered that poem into the vernacular, both in verse and in prose. The most learned author of the new *Library of Ecclesiastical Writers* likewise composed a full and copious analysis of it (Dupin, vol. IV, p. 443 ff.).

The Semipelagians, accused by Prosper of being afraid to disclose their views, appear to have wished to repel that charge. One of them either wrote under another name or professed that he intended to write. Prosper forestalled him with a pair of epigrams (below, p. 191), in which he seems to assume, as indubitable, that Augustine was still alive.

[Col. 0026D]

Garnerius seems to cast doubt on their attribution to Prosper (*Mercator*, vol. II, note on the collection of extracts on Nestorius); but he produced no weight at all for his suspicion, nor perhaps could he easily have found any, since Bede is read as citing one of them under the name of Prosper the rhetorician—namely, that which begins with the words, *Against Augustine*, etc. Some suspect that Vincent of Lérins is designated in both places, accusing him of publishing his *Commonitorium* against Augustine under a feigned name in 434. No one was more suitable than Cassian to challenge Augustine in writing; others maintain that he is attacked by the two epigrams. Yet he seems to have published nothing openly against the holy Doctor. His thirteenth Conference, however, was both written and published under his own name in 426, although he propounds in another person the unsound doctrines contained in it (below, p. 310). No one besides him appears to have dared to commit his views to writing before 433. Thus either the writer of whom Prosper speaks was silent for at least several years, complying with Prosper’s admonition; or, if anyone should contend that the work promised and boasted of by the Semipelagians is identical with the thirteenth Conference, he must date the two epigrams now under discussion to 426 and concede that Prosper had already then declared war on the Semipelagians.

[Col. 0027B]

“Prosper’s poems did not restrain the adversaries of grace. For heretics, as Baronius says while dealing with this very matter (*Under the Year 431*), can be refuted because they are light and weak; they cannot confess themselves conquered by truth because they are proved obstinate.” Yet those bishops who had been somewhat moved and troubled by Augustine’s doctrine, among them Hilary, bishop of Arles, had either at last recognized the truth or at least remained silent and quiet, waiting for God to deign to disclose and reveal it to them (Mauguin, vol. II, p. 475). A few presbyters, intent upon discord in the Churches, did not cease to criticize the doctrine of blessed Augustine (below, pp. 260–261). They objected that he said sinners were predestined not only to the judgment due to sins but also to sin itself; and they accused Prosper and Hilary too of preaching what was contrary to truth (Fulgentius, *To Monimus*, book I, ch. 30). They compiled a list of the things which they boasted that they had found condemnable in blessed Augustine’s books, distributed it into fifteen chapters, and prefixed to it the title “of condemnation,” or, as in other manuscripts, “of argument”; in these they ascribed to the holy Doctor a meaning far different from that contained in his writings (below, pp. 260, 203). This could indeed have taken place in 431. For by then the holy man had departed this life, and Prosper in the preface to his response to the Chapters of the Gauls calls him a bishop of holy memory (below, p. 203). Yet Saint Prosper had arisen as his successor in defending the doctrine of grace (Fulgentius, p. 23). Hence, together with him and blessed Jerome, he is numbered among those whom God had established to teach all others what should be believed concerning this subject (Cassiodorus on Psalm L, pp. 171–172).

[Col. 0027D]

And indeed our author willingly displayed both copious speech and a wholly sound faith in defending his master’s words and opinions. He therefore published a work in which he replied to each of the arguments or Chapters of the Gauls (below, p. 204), showing from Augustine himself what his true and sincere meaning was. “Lest anyone,” he said there, “rashly accept this persuasion and suppose that the writings of a Catholic Doctor contain the meaning which those who calumniate him in vain display, I reply to the individual chapters which they have prefixed with the title ‘of condemnation’ (elsewhere ‘of argument’) by a brief and complete confession, departing in no respect from the course of those definitions contained in the holy man’s disputations.” This work is the *Responses to the Chapters of the Objections of the Calumniating Gauls*. Its final two responses are cited by Fulgentius (p. 25), who observes that the objections of the Gauls are directed especially at Augustine’s book *On the Predestination of the Saints*. “You are not unaware,” he says, addressing Monimus, “that in former times certain Gauls objected to that very distinguished work of Saint Augustine which he wrote *On the Predestination of the Saints*, that blessed Augustine, in his assertion of divine predestination, said that sinners were predestined not only to judgment but also to sin; and, because he was overtaken by a swift death, the learned and holy Prosper defended his statements with sound faith and copious speech.” These are the words of Saint Fulgentius at the beginning of chapter 30 of book I *To Monimus*.

## ARTICLE VI. Saint Prosper Replies to Vincent and to the Presbyters of Genoa

The adversaries were no fairer toward the disciple than toward the master. For some, forgetting Christian and brotherly charity (below, p. 217, Preface), strove by every means to injure even his reputation, so greatly that, in their desire to harm, they did not see that they were overthrowing their own. They concocted monstrous falsehoods of certain utterly foolish blasphemies, comprehending them in whatever formulations they could, and carried them about publicly and privately to be shown and pressed upon many people. They asserted that Prosper held such opinions as were contained in the diabolical list, as he calls it.

[Col. 0028C]

Our saint could readily and sufficiently have proved, by subscribing a single anathema, that these things were falsely alleged against him in order to excite hostility. But lest the malice of those who thought themselves injured if men thought well of him should regard the very brevity of that subscription as suspect, he considered it necessary and fitting, both to soften the minds of his calumniators and to instruct those in whose ears anything of the sort had sounded, to set forth as fully and clearly as possible, with the Lord’s help, what he thought of the perverse propositions. He therefore chose, after setting out the sixteen chapters one by one, to place under each of them words expressing his own view and the faith which, against the Pelagians, he defended on the authority of the Apostolic See. Thus those who deigned to devote a little attention to reading these things might clearly recognize that no trace of impious and profane opinions adhered to his heart, and might judge that the blasphemies which they saw condemned in his confession ought to be punished in their inventors. It will be useful to set these matters out here at length from his own words, so that readers may see with what zeal our author rejected wrong doctrines and defended right ones. The date at which this work was completed is wholly uncertain.

The title of this book is *Responses in Defence of Augustine’s Doctrine to the Chapters of Vincentian Objections* (below, p. 229). From this title it appears that a certain Vincent composed this perverse and diabolical list, as Prosper himself does not hesitate to call it. At that time there was in the monastery of Lérins that Vincent whose *Commonitorium*, published against all heresies, is extremely famous.

[Col. 0029A]

Vossius, who maintains that he was hostile to Augustinian doctrine (*On the History of Pelagianism*, book I, ch. 9), relying on reasoning by which it might likewise be proved that Vincent knowingly and deliberately misused Celestine’s letter, judges that these calumnies against Prosper were invented by the same man. Cardinal Henry Noris of the Holy Roman Church (*History of Pelagianism*, book II, ch. 11), and others who believe this Vincent followed Semipelagian doctrines (Antelmius, *Dissertation on the Works of Leo*, p. 419), agree with Vossius on this point.

Those, however, who take a better view of his doctrine—whether they follow Augustine as their guide in what concerns grace, or depart in some measure from his mind—all agree in seeking another Vincent, to whom they may wish to attribute these objections. Baronius holds (Annals, 431), and others follow him (Miraeus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 66; Maugérin, *Vindiciae*, vol. II, p. 448; Labbe, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 252), that they may have belonged to a certain Vincent, whom Gennadius testifies that he himself saw, both a priest and a Gaul, like the Vincent of Lérins (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 80). Nor do we think anything prevents his being that priest Vincent who, in the name of Constantius or Constantianus, probably bishop of Digne, took part in the Council of Riez in 439.

For although Gennadius survived Pope Gelasius, who died in 496, this does not therefore mean that he could not have seen a man who was writing in 430. Since Gennadius is an unstinting praiser of those who, like himself, were not well disposed toward Augustine, he says that this Vincent was trained in the divine Scriptures and possessed a tongue polished by habitual speech and by reading the works of the ancients. He adds that Vincent wrote a commentary on the Psalms, some portions of which Gennadius had read to the holy man of God Cannatus while Vincent himself listened, promising at the same time that, if the Lord granted him life and strength, he would labor with the same devotion over the whole Psalter.

Saint Cannatus is indeed celebrated at Marseille and in other churches of the province on 15 October; but he is said to have been bishop of Marseille, and Guesnay places him in the year 621, whereas the most learned Sammarthani assign him to 480. Guesnay cites nothing concerning him except a life written in a rough style in the time of the counts of Provence, in which he is said to have been the son of the king of Aix, to have succeeded Serenus, and to have been a contemporary of the Iconoclasts. It is, moreover, certain that Serenus was a contemporary of Saint Gregory the Great, as is proved by various letters of that holy pope addressed to Serenus—namely, book V, letter 52; book VII, letter 110; book IX, letter 9; and letter 52 of that same book.

What disturbed the Gallic priests also troubled the Genoese (below, p. 241). But the latter showed themselves wiser and more moderate. For two of them, Camillus and Theodore, when certain things in the blessed Augustine’s books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance* had disturbed them as unusual or insufficiently clear, extracted passages from the course of the discussion and sent them to blessed Prosper, so that they might learn with what understanding and judgment he had received them.

He did not withhold his compliance with their requests—or, as he himself says modestly, with their commands—not as though he possessed more intelligence than they for examining these matters, or as though they ought not rather to have exercised their own abilities in proportion to their capacity for this investigation; and, if some obscurity delayed them, to have hastened to the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends, and from whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding is given. Rather, with the Lord’s help—he who grants wisdom to the little ones—he undertakes briefly to indicate what he thinks about these Chapters together with his holy and learned brothers. He nevertheless asks them not to suppose that, where there was the simplicity of obedience, there was an assumption of learning. These events took place after Augustine’s death.

## ARTICLE VII. Saint Prosper travels to Rome with Hilary. Pope Celestine defends both of them in writing. On Venerius, bishop of Marseille.

The Semipelagians did not cease accusing Prosper and Hilary, and even Augustine himself, of error. In response, they professed that they followed and approved only those things which the most holy see of blessed Peter had established and taught, through the ministry of its bishops, against the enemies of God’s grace.

Prosper and Hilary therefore had recourse to the apostolic see, went to Rome, and brought their complaints before Pope Celestine. He praised their concern for God; and although they considered themselves blessed, since the promised beatitude awaited those who endured persecution for righteousness, the pious pontiff was nevertheless distressed by the affliction of these devout souls—for it was wrong that they should suffer such things—because they were his members.

Moved by this feeling, he sent a celebrated letter to the bishops of Gaul, in which he both offered an outstanding testimony to his judgment concerning Prosper and Hilary and defended Augustine’s reputation in these words:

> We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion on account of his life and merits; nor was he ever touched even by a rumor of sinister suspicion. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that my predecessors always counted him among the best teachers. All therefore held a good opinion of him in common, since everywhere he was held in love and honor.

Accordingly, he orders the bishops to silence the wicked detractors. “Let such men,” he says, “be corrected; let it not be permitted them to speak according to their own will. If matters stand thus, let novelty cease to assail antiquity; let unrest cease to disturb the peace of the churches.”

He further reproves them and charges them with this: while the bishops remained silent, those priests had an opportunity to debate above the bishops. Although it is known that God appointed bishops, not priests, to teach, silence in such matters is not free from suspicion, since truth would come to meet them if falsehood were displeasing.

He adds that he had already said much on these matters when he sent a written response to his brother, that is, to Bishop Tuencius. These words, together with what follows, suggest that the letter to Tuencius dealt rather with questions concerning the grace of Christ than with those who rapidly elevated laymen to the episcopate—a practice about which Celestine also complains here. Nothing else, however, is known to us concerning Celestine’s letter to Tuencius.

That Celestine wrote this exhortation to the bishops—urging them to resist those who disparaged Augustine’s doctrine and reputation—only after the holy Doctor’s death is clear from the words quoted above, “Augustine, a man of holy memory,” and from the words slightly earlier: “Nor can we wonder if those who now dare to attempt such things against the living also strive to scatter the memory of their departed brothers” (p. 262). It therefore belongs to the year 431, or the beginning of 432, in which year Celestine also departed this life.

This letter was very well known among the ancients and, as early as 433 or 434, was cited not only by Prosper in his book *Against the Collator*, in a chapter formerly numbered 42 and now 21. Prosper writes there:

> Through this man, within Gaul, the freedom of malicious speech was taken away from those very men who criticized the writings of Augustine, of holy memory. For, having undertaken the action of those who sought counsel, and having praised with piety the books displeasing to those who were in error, he made clear in holy speech what ought to be thought of their authority. He plainly declared how displeasing to him was the novelty of this presumption, by which certain men dared insolently to rise up against ancient teachers and, with undisciplined calumny, obstruct the preaching of truth—saying, “Augustine, a man of holy memory,” and so forth, as has already been quoted above.

This letter was praised not only by Prosper but also by Vincent of Lérins. Dionysius Exiguus inserted it into his *Code of Canons*. Photius likewise records that Celestine wrote in support of Augustine to the bishops and against those who were restoring the Pelagian heresy.

Celestine’s letter is followed by several collected judgments of Roman pontiffs and of African councils approved by Roman bishops, under the following title: “Authorities of the Former Bishops of the Apostolic See concerning the Grace of God and Free Choice of the Will.” This collection was compiled so that the Semipelagians, who denied that they would follow anything other than what had been judged by the apostolic see, might have no opportunity for contradiction.

It is proved, however, that this collection is separate from Celestine’s letter, both by its style and by the closing clause of the preceding letter. Accordingly, Sirmond excludes it from Celestine’s authorship; others prefer to attribute it either to Prosper—which some agree with him in doing—or to Leo, as P. Quesnell prefers.

Just as it cannot easily be determined, so it is not very important whose hand actually wrote it, since it can readily be judged to have been composed at Celestine’s command and sent to Gaul. For Peter the Deacon and others praise it as part of the very letter itself in their confession of faith addressed to blessed Fulgentius and certain other bishops of Christ, then exiled in Sardinia. “In agreement with these things,” they say, “most blessed Celestine wrote in his letter to the Gauls: ‘For when the bishops of holy peoples…’” These words occur verbatim in chapter 8 of the Collection under discussion, elsewhere chapter 11 of the letter joined to the Collection. It is also cited by Cresconius, by various writers of the ninth century, and finally by all the ancients.

Dionysius Exiguus inserted it into his *Code* among the decrees of that same pontiff. These, therefore, are the very Chapters to which Pope Hormisdas refers Bishop Possessor, so that from them he may learn what ought to be believed concerning grace and free choice. His words may be read in the letter of the fifteen African bishops exiled in Sardinia to John and Venerius, preserved by Fulgentius, no. 18, p. 275:

> Concerning free choice and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church follows and preserves may indeed be abundantly known from the various books of blessed Augustine, and especially those addressed to Prosper and Hilary; nevertheless, explicit Chapters are also contained in the ecclesiastical archives.

The words of the final one of these Chapters have provided learned men with much material for dispute. It deals with the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions at issue, which those who resisted the heretics treated at greater length, and which the author of the Collection, whoever he may have been, neither dares to despise nor needs to affirm.
