Nor should it perhaps be considered especially necessary to inquire with great effort what was intended by a man who did not think it appropriate to disclose his mind clearly; nor may assistance toward explaining a difficult matter be drawn from an obscure passage. It is therefore worth noting that, when several controversies concerning grace arose in the ninth century, no opinion was then rejected by anyone on the authority of this Chapter. Nor, it is said, did the Semipelagians dare to extract from it anything favorable to their errors.

This much, however, is certain from the Chapter itself: it has nothing to do with those matters necessary to ensure that nothing at all is withdrawn from the work and gracious condescension of divine grace. Nor are the words understood to refer to matters contained either in the Collection itself or in the body of the letter, or necessarily connected with them. Nor may one even suspect that these words refer either to the beginning of faith or to the predestination of the saints, concerning which the contest between the Semipelagians and Prosper had been instituted, since it is established that Pope Celestine favored the latter and rejected the former.

If any doubt remained concerning this, it would be entirely removed by Pope Hormisdas, who declares in the passage cited shortly before (Council Records, vol. IV, p. 1332) that the Roman Church derives its doctrine of grace chiefly from those books which Augustine wrote to Prosper and Hilary on the predestination of the saints.

All this may be read, treated both more fully and more accurately, in P. Quesnell’s dissertation on Saint Leo. The same matters have also been handled carefully by Louis Ellies Dupin, a Sorbonne doctor well known for his merits and writings (Dupin, vol. IV, pp. 90–91).

Celestine’s letter (among Celestine’s letters, our volume L) was addressed generally to the bishops of Gaul, but specifically to Venerius, Marinus, Leontius, Auxonius, Arcadius, and Philtanius, or Sillucius. It may perhaps be agreeable to the reader that a few things be noted here concerning them (below, p. 271).

Venerius was not, as some have thought (Dupin, vol. IV, p. 78), bishop of Milan. At that time the bishop of Milan would not have been counted among the bishops of Gaul, and Martinianus occupied the Milanese chair in 431; he had succeeded Marolius, who had been the predecessor of the other Venerius. Rather, as seems more probable, Venerius presided over the Church of Marseille. Gennadius mentions him in chapter 79 of his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*.

For it was chiefly at Marseille that the Semipelagians flourished under the leadership of Cassian. From a certain inscription we learn that Venerius had lived in a monastery together with Rusticus, who was elevated to the see of Narbonne in 430, and that both served as priests at Marseille. He is believed to have succeeded Proculus, the celebrated man who was still alive in 418. No word at all is found in Pseudo-Dexter concerning Paul, whom Guesnay places between the two and praises extravagantly. For this reason the Sammarthani omit him.

In his letter dated 25 July 428, Celestine certainly permits the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne to deal with the case of the bishop of Marseille, who was accused of having been so pleased by the killing of his brother that he had gone out to meet the murderer as he returned from the deed. What this means is not clear to us. Patroclus of Arles was indeed killed, but in 426.

Venerius is named third in order among the Gallic bishops who wrote to blessed Leo in 451; Leo replied to them on 1 February 452. Gennadius states in chapter 79 of his *Catalogue* that Musaeus, a priest of the Church of Marseille, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and refined by the most subtle practice in interpreting them, as well as possessing a scholarly tongue. At the urging of Saint Venerius, bishop, Musaeus copied from the holy Scriptures readings suitable for the festivals of the entire year, together with responsories and portions of the Psalms corresponding to the season and the readings.

“This work,” Gennadius adds, “is judged so necessary by readers in the Church that it removes both their labor and their delay, and implants in the people knowledge, solemnity, and beauty.” It seems to have given rise to the ecclesiastical course of prayers, which was later called the Breviary. Eustachius succeeded Venerius.

Marinus, whom Celestine names immediately after Venerius, may perhaps be the man to whom Boniface wrote in 419. His episcopal see is not indicated. From this one may judge that Venerius, who is placed before him, had been a bishop at least by 419.

Leontius was certainly the famous bishop of Fréjus, who died only in 432.

The Sammarthani mention Auxentius of Nice (Gallican *Christian History*, vol. III, p. 786). But he was later than Saint Valerian, who was still alive in 455.

They likewise record Auxonius of Viviers, who transferred the episcopal see from Alba to Viviers after Alba had been destroyed, as they say, by Crocus the Vandal. Crocus was indeed ravaging Gaul during the reign of Gallienus, according to Gregory of Tours. But there had not yet begun to be any mention of Vandals in Gaul before 407.

Arcadius is believed to have been bishop of Vence, and Philtanius bishop of Apt, since he succeeded Saint Castor before 426.

## ARTICLE VIII. Saint Prosper writes against Cassian.

When Saint Prosper returned to Gaul, fortified, as it is easy to believe, by the letter of Pope Celestine, he was encouraged by the great hope that the weight of so great an authority would suppress all the disturbances. On this occasion, however, he learned how true was the principle that he himself defended with such firmness of mind: unless grace itself works inwardly in souls, whatever support or light may come from elsewhere is vain and fruitless.

Celestine had praised and approved Augustine’s doctrine and faith only in general terms; and because the title of the books for which the pope’s letter had intervened was not stated, nor had he offered a particular or distinct testimony concerning the books Augustine had most recently written, certain men dared to argue that those books were thereby shown not to have been approved, and that the praise bestowed upon Saint Augustine had been given on account of the merits of his earlier writings.

But apart from the fact that such cavilling was pointless and rested on no foundation, Augustine’s disciples would have been satisfied if the Semipelagians, who rejected Augustine’s recently published books, had been content with his earlier writings against the Pelagians and had agreed with what had previously been written in defense of Christian grace. For it would readily have been recognized that their errors were condemned in those works.

But they did not do so. For, as Saint Prosper rightly observes, they knew that everything opposed the Pelagians—or, according to another reading, that everything Pelagian, that is, directed against the Pelagians, opposed them—and that they could gain nothing toward resolving the later questions if they confessed that the truth rested in the earlier writings.

Accordingly, after Celestine’s death in the year of the Lord 432, they did not cease to assail Augustine with calumnies, to proclaim that grace had been wrongly defended by him, and to disturb the peace of the victorious Church, taking up again the weapons of his enemies and reviving the complaints of the condemned, especially the most shameless insults of Julian.

Those who did not cease attacking Augustine’s books written against the Pelagian error with immoderate calumnies were nevertheless such that neither their ecclesiastical rank nor their abilities appeared contemptible. Since they displayed an appearance of piety in their zeal while denying its power in their understanding, they drew many unlearned people to themselves and troubled hearts that lacked discernment of spirits.

This evil grew daily from hidden and insignificant seeds and spread farther and wider from its origin. Saint Prosper was therefore moved to resist their efforts again, so that he might repel the injury inflicted both upon Augustine and upon all the others—especially the pontiffs of the apostolic see, who had made Augustine’s doctrines their own. The result was that he paid more cautious and diligent attention to what ought to be thought of those advocates of a more refined doctrine who were acting as censors of the man under whose leadership the Catholic army had been accustomed for more than twenty years to fight and conquer the enemies of God’s grace.

He undertook to attack the definitions of one man in particular, whom there was no doubt to surpass all the others in the study of the sacred Scriptures. He thought that these definitions ought to be brought into debate for this reason alone: their actual character could not be doubted. They had been written and published in an edition by their author; it was no longer necessary to ask whether they existed, but to demonstrate what they taught.

He does not state the man’s name, but no one doubts that he refers to Cassian, then still alive and already famous throughout the world. Prosper therefore published a book in which, quoting the very words of the thirteenth *Collation* of this man—whose heading is “On the Protection of God”—he refutes all the errors with which it is filled, shows how far it departs from the Church’s doctrines, and how inconsistent the work is with itself.

Concerning this work of our Prosper, Gennadius speaks as follows in his *Catalogue*, chapter 84, under the entry on Prosper:

> “I have also read a book against the little works, with Cassian’s name suppressed. What the Church of God approves as salutary, he denounces as harmful. For in certain matters the opinions of Cassian and Prosper concerning the grace of God and free choice are found to be opposed to one another.”

But what Gennadius says in the first part of this passage concerning the Church’s judgment is futile, since in this matter the Church itself clearly disapproved him. For the Roman Council held, as is generally believed, under Pope Gelasius in 494, approves Prosper’s writings and rejects Cassian’s (Council Records, vol. IV, pp. 1263, 1265).

Cassiodorus too, although by no means sparing in his praise of Cassian, urges his monastic students to read him, while nevertheless warning them that he must be read with the greatest caution in what he says about free choice, for which he had rightly been rebuked by blessed Prosper (Cassiodorus, *Institutions*, chap. 29, p. 245). The same author praises a certain bishop who had corrected Cassian’s books; he himself is also said to have performed similar labor with renewed care (Ado, *Chronicle*, vol. VII, p. 356).

As for Gennadius’s statement, by which he plainly sneers at Prosper for writing against Cassian while falsely claiming that Cassian’s works had been approved by the Catholic Church, Baronius, refuting Gennadius’s passage, asks:

> “What sort of Church of God is this, which approves Cassian’s little works as Catholic? It certainly ought not to be called the Catholic Church, but the Church of the Pelagians.”

Labbe is not pleased if anyone says that the school of his own society favored Cassian against Prosper (*Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 254). In the congregations *de auxiliis*, those debating on both sides agreed without controversy that Cassian’s opinions were rejected and condemned by the Church. A considerable number of canons of the Council of Orange were composed for his condemnation.

Prosper concludes with these words, especially worthy of remembrance (below, p. 369 and following):

> It has been sufficiently demonstrated, as I think, that the critics of Saint Augustine both bring forward vain objections, attack what is right, and defend what is wrong; and that, making an internal war with the weapons of those who have been destroyed, they rebel against divine and human constitutions. Nevertheless, since they have not yet been separated from fraternal fellowship, their intention should be tolerated rather than their correction despaired of. Thus, until the Lord, through the rulers of the Church and the legitimate ministers of his judgments, restores to order the things disturbed by the pride of a few and the ignorance of some, let it be our concern, with God’s help, through quiet and moderate patience to return love for hatred, to avoid the conflicts of fools, not to abandon the truth, and not to contend with falsehood. Let us always ask God that in all our thoughts, in all our wills, in all our words and actions, he himself may hold the first place—he who said that he is the beginning.

## ARTICLE IX. On the other works of Saint Prosper and on his *Chronicle*.

Nothing is recorded anywhere concerning what Prosper did from the year 432, when he wrote against Cassian, up to the pontificate of Saint Leo, which began in 440. During this interval he perhaps composed some of the writings that still survive.

The two heresies of Nestorius and Pelagius had been condemned by the Council of Ephesus in 431 when Prosper wrote a certain epigram, which he called the epitaph of both heresies. They agreed in this respect: one asserted that Christ had attained divinity through his own labor and works, while the other made the same claim concerning the righteousness of the faithful.

Prosper therefore said that the Nestorian heresy, which destroyed grace in the Head, was the mother of the Pelagian heresy, which overturned that same grace in his members. Yet in another sense it ought to be called the daughter, since it appeared only after the Pelagians had been condemned.

John Garnerius denied that this same epitaph had been hung by our Prosper upon the tomb of the two heresies, in chapter 7 of dissertation 7 on the works of Marius Mercator. He maintained that what is offered here is something like a riddle, when one heresy is said to have been both the mother and daughter of the other. He admits that this is ingeniously said, but denies that it is true. He therefore attempts to prove that, from the third century onward, the Nestorian error began to be foreshadowed through the delirious teachings of Paul of Samosata.

He adds that our Poet should be granted pardon all the more readily because Cassian too erred in the same matter and drew Leo the Great, together with many others who later followed their authority, into his opinion.

Despite these objections, Antelmius asserts that this little work belongs to Prosper, in dissertation 9 of the works of Saints Leo and Prosper. He argues that, if Cassian and Leo the Great were permitted to say this while treating the matter seriously, the Poet ought to be forgiven much more readily, since he was not speaking according to the rules of history but was mocking the errors that had been buried, with loosened reins and, as they say, inflated pipes.

This is especially so because Prosper is found to have used this comparison of the two heresies more than once. In the *Chronicle* itself he relates that at Ephesus Nestorius was condemned together with the heresy bearing his name and with many Pelagians who supported the doctrine related to their error. In chapter 21 of his book written against Cassian, he reproaches him with this very joining together of the two errors:

> Through this man, Celestine, the Eastern Churches were also cleansed of a double plague, when he aided Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, with the apostolic sword for the execration of Nestorian impiety; by that same sword the Pelagians too, while they allied themselves with related errors, were again struck down.

Besides these works, Prosper wrote one hundred and six epigrams, which, as the title indicates, present as many sayings and maxims drawn from Augustine (below, p. 615 and following). He first expresses them in prose and then in verse.

Prosper’s character is readily recognized throughout the course of this little work, but especially in the fact that it was compiled from Augustine’s sayings (Antelmius, dissertation on the works of Leo, p. 417–418). He undertook it in order to exercise his mind in sacred speech and nourish his spirit with heavenly bread (below, p. 615, in the Preface):

> “Nor is this the product of our power,” he says, “but this dew is received from him,
>
> who commanded the dry rock to pour forth waters,
>
> so that whatever has entered the heart’s affection
>
> under the guidance of piety,
>
> joyful faith may bring forth in song.”

By placing these words at the beginning, as a kind of prelude to the whole work, he indicates the intention with which he undertook it and declares that whatever is right in it, whatever is found worthy of any praise, he wishes entirely to return to the heavenly fountain from which it flowed.

In one passage (below, p. 651 and following), namely epigrams 65 and 66, he appears to attack the Eutychians, who denied that Christ’s flesh was of the same substance as ours. From this one may reasonably infer that the work was composed around the time of the Council of Chalcedon, held in 451, since Prosper’s life must also be extended further, as we shall see later.

He also published another *Collection of Sentences*, numbering 392, or alternatively 388, drawn from Augustine’s works, both those that still survive and those that have perished. Sometimes it expresses Augustine’s thought rather than reproducing his words. The book is thought to be a kind of theological compendium which Prosper had compiled for his own use, so that the principal elements of Augustinian doctrine might become better known and more familiar to him.

Several sentences from this book were incorporated into the canons of the Second Council of Orange, and very many are cited by Florus under Prosper’s name.

His exposition of the final fifty-one Psalms is likewise almost entirely excerpted from Augustine. He seems to have explained the whole Psalter in the same manner, since, omitting Psalm 107, he refers the reader to what he had said concerning Psalms 56 and 59.

In his treatment of Psalm 144 he expressly denies that there are two persons in Christ. Since Augustine says nothing on this matter in that passage, it is clear that Prosper is refuting the heresy of Nestorius here. On this basis we think the work should be dated earlier than 434.

In this book one finds that vigorous and concise style of expression which is Prosper’s distinctive mark. There too one may readily observe that the holy man was a great disciple of Augustine not only in his doctrine concerning the grace of Christ, but also in every other department.

He also enhanced the reputation of his name through his *Chronicle*, which he extended from the creation of the world down to his own times with a certain pleasing brevity. He followed the *Chronicles* of Eusebius down to the year 326 and those of Jerome down to 378. In it he lists the consuls beginning with the two Gemini and the fifteenth year of Tiberius, which is the year 29 of the common era.

Only the final part of this *Chronicle* survived, namely the portion which Prosper added to Jerome’s work from the year 378 onward. In 1657, however, the complete and finished work was published by Philip Labbe in the first volume of his new *Library of Manuscripts*.

Prosper appears to have undertaken the composition of his *Chronicle* three times and to have prepared, so to speak, three editions of it—in the years 433, 445, and 455. This is inferred from the fact that in several manuscripts a summary of the entire chronology is found there.

Another *Chronicle* is also read, which some attribute to Prosper. They may be granted this much only: that the *Chronicle* is indeed by our Prosper, but was corrupted and falsified by another man, who was both inexperienced and foreign to historical writing and as envious a detractor of Augustine’s praises as Prosper was a devoted admirer of him. This work is sometimes cited under the name of Prosper of Tiro, by which it was first called by some, although unjustly.

Gennadius records in chapter 87 of his *Catalogue* that Prosper composed a Paschal Cycle, after Theophilus, Eusebius, and Hippolytus, but before Victorius—that is, between the years 380 and 457.

If that cycle of eighty-four years was composed in 382, as Bucherius thinks, it cannot in any way have been published by Prosper of Aquitaine, who was still writing in 453. If not, it is sufficiently probable that Prosper—the only man whom Gennadius can be indicating—was the very person whom he had named in the preceding chapter, especially since his *Chronicle* shows that he occupied himself with such computations and mentions that eighty-four-year cycle more than once.

Nor is that cycle well known from any other source. Nevertheless, the Roman Church appears to have used it in the age of Leo the Great. Bucherius, although uncertain, draws his arguments as though he had a full understanding that the cycle belonged to Prosper.

## ARTICLE X. Saint Prosper writes against the Eutychians in support of Saint Leo. His death. He was not a bishop.

When Saint Leo was in Gaul in 440 and was raised to the supreme pontificate, he perhaps brought our Prosper back with him, intending to use his counsel and his pen in giving responses to churches that asked questions and sought advice, just as Damasus had employed Jerome for the same service.

For Gennadius, otherwise not sufficiently fair to Prosper, says:

> “The letters of Pope Leo against Eutyches concerning the true Incarnation of Christ, addressed to various persons, are also believed to have been dictated by him.”

This is generally understood above all of that celebrated letter to Flavian, and the matter is entirely beyond doubt, despite the opposition of Bellarmine and certain others. Marcellinus likewise copies this statement under the year 469.

Prosper may have supplied the arguments and, so to speak, the material of those letters, which Leo then revised and clothed in his own style and language—more graceful and ornate, certainly, than Prosper’s. Yet Prosper may perhaps also have devoted himself to adapting his own style and manner of writing to that of the pontiff whom he served.

For this reason Ado (Annals, 458) and other writers of a later age say that Prosper was a notary, or secretary, of Leo the Great. It is possible that he served him in writing both letters and sermons. Certainly, in a book written by hand more than nine hundred years ago, the fourth sermon for the anniversary of Leo’s elevation to the pontificate bears Prosper’s name, and perhaps others do as well.

From this one may judge that Prosper carried a large share of the work undertaken by Leo the Great against the Pelagians. Ado likewise appears to attribute to Prosper the writings composed by Leo both against the Eutychians and against the Pelagians; nor does Cardinal Norisius contradict this (History of the Pelagian Controversy, book II, chap. 13).

History has not omitted the fact that, when certain people in Rome attempted to revive the Pelagian heresy and dared to make their views on the matter public, Prosper immediately presented pamphlets both to Leo, who was still alive, and to the emperor’s ministers, and succeeded in causing those men’s efforts to collapse empty and fruitless.

From what we have said about Prosper’s *Chronicle*, it is clear that he was still alive in 455. Labbe thinks that he died in the following year because Victorius, writing in 457, calls him a holy and venerable man; but this conclusion cannot certainly be drawn from that statement.

Moreover, Marcellinus mentions Prosper in 463 as though he were still alive. Norisius (History of the Pelagian Controversy, book II, chap. 14) and Bucherius (*Cycle*, p. 144), who wrote extensively about Victorius, do not deny that Prosper lived until that time.

Up to this point we have observed nothing, nor have we learned anything from any ancient author, that would show Prosper to have been superior in rank and order to laymen or monks. Nevertheless, nearly all recent writers claim that he was a bishop, either of Riez in Provence or of Reggio in Lombardy.

If one objects to them that no ancient author calls him a bishop, they reply that this happened because the ancients knew him only through the books he had written before becoming a bishop, and therefore books that did not bear the episcopal title.

But this explanation has no force at all, whether one considers Gelasius, Gennadius, Fulgentius, or even Cassiodorus. All these men were distinguished for learning, and were close to Prosper in age; they could not have been unaware whether a man of such renown was a bishop or not.

As for Victorius, one might perhaps say that he remained silent on this matter because Prosper was not raised to episcopal dignity until after the year 457.

That, indeed, gave rise to this false opinion concerning Prosper’s episcopate: there was another bishop named Prosper, bishop of Reggio in Lombardy—a fact that scarcely seems open to doubt. For the Church of Reggio venerates him as its patron and preserves his sacred body in the celebrated abbey founded by Countess Matilda. It is said, however, that the body was brought there from another basilica in the same city, built by that very man in honor of Saint Apollinaris, and that this transfer took place as early as the time of King Liutprand. Vossius reports his epitaph (*Hist. Pelag.* I.18), which had been composed for inscription on a new tomb erected because the old one had been damaged by the collapse of a tower. He nevertheless states that the epitaph itself may be seen in the Carmelite church. Surius includes a Life of Saint Prosper of Reggio (25 June), written by Flaminius under the impulse of his own imagination and on the basis of mere conjectures, says Labbe (*Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, p. 249). Norisius’s judgment of it is even more severe (*Hist. Pelag.* II.13). He thinks that this Prosper may perhaps have been the author of the book *On the Promises and Predictions*; but there is no particular evidence for this. Flaminius and Ughellus maintain that he was made bishop by Saint Leo and died in the year 456. Perhaps the date of that year was taken from the great Prosper, just as they borrowed his episcopate from the other Prosper. Trithemius, however, assigns as Prosper’s successor Faventius, who sat as bishop of Reggio at the Council of Milan in 451. Ughellus places Elpidius between them. The feast of Saint Prosper is celebrated on 25 June, the day on which the feast of the great Prosper is thought to have been observed.

A feast day is likewise annually kept for Prosper on 24 November, especially among the Canons Regular of the Gallican congregation and at the royal monastery of Saint Victor in Paris. Some regard this as the day of the translation of this Prosper or of the other one.

Those who wished him to have been bishop of Riez were given grounds for their view by the name of Prosper, bishop, who subscribed the Councils of Carpentras and Vaison. They pretended that those councils had been held around the year 442. Since it is now agreed among scholars that they were held in 527 or 529, the Prosper who subscribed them must necessarily have lived much later than the other. Moreover, Maximus presided over the Church of Riez while Hilary of Arles was still alive—that is, before the year 450, indeed before 432 or 433, as we have demonstrated. It is therefore very far from being the case that Prosper, who certainly was still alive in 455, was his predecessor, as Baronius maintains (*Annals*, 466). From Saint Sidonius (*Book* VIII, Letter 25) it is shown that Faustus, who outlived Saint Prosper, succeeded Maximus. Consequently, Prosper cannot have been bishop of Riez.

## ARTICLE XI. On Certain Works Ascribed to Saint Prosper

Nothing more seems necessary to be said either about Prosper’s genuine and certain works or about others which some plausible reason might permit one to attribute to him. What remains is to mention those works which, although it is clear that they were not written by him, were nevertheless published under his name. Nor are they insignificant; rather, they acquired considerable authority in the Church.

Cassiodorus urges us (*Institutions*, chapter 1) to read Saint Prosper with assiduous care, for he comprised three books containing the whole of divine authority in 153 headings, after the manner of the fish which the evangelical nets drew from the stormy depths of this world. There can be no doubt that he was referring to the book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, now divided into five parts. This division had in fact been established by the author himself, who, alluding to the 153 fish mentioned in the Gospel, wished to gather under the same number of headings all the promises of Christ recorded in the sacred books and to demonstrate their fulfillment. Since these promises were given both before the Law and under the Law, but were finally fulfilled under grace, some have consequently thought that the work should be called *The Book before the Law, under the Law, and under Grace*. Cassiodorus cites one passage from its second part under the name of blessed Prosper (*On Psalm XI*). We do not know whether his authority ought to induce us to attribute that work to some Prosper, whoever he may have been. Ludovicus Dupin is certainly closer to this opinion (*vol.* IV, p. 449) than Joseph Antelmius (*Antelmius, Dissertation on the Works of Leo*, p. 363). The eminent Norisius regards the matter as scarcely doubtful (*Hist. Pelag.* II.14), believing that Prosper, the bishop of Reggio, was its author. This much is certain: the work in question is not by Prosper of Aquitaine, whose elegance its author matches neither in style nor in talent. His language is humble, spare, and simple; Prosper’s manner of expression is abundant, rich in strength, vigorous in sinew, and wealthy in aphorisms.

It is sufficiently apparent that the author was African. It should therefore not seem strange that, among the various sects of heretics, he should call the Donatists—and especially the Maximianists—by name; that he should mention Tychonius, the famous Donatist; and that he should report certain unusual events that took place in Africa. He was still a young man and was present at Carthage when Bishop Aurelius dedicated to Christ the famous temple of the Celestial Goddess in that city, perhaps in the year 399. While he and his companions and friends—“as the impatient age of youth carried them everywhere”—were examining each detail with curiosity in proportion to its importance, he testifies that a remarkable and incredible sight was presented to his eyes: namely, the following inscription, written in large bronze letters on the front of the temple:

**AURELIUS THE PONTIFF DEDICATED THIS.**

He was also staying at Carthage in the same year in which Aspar, *vir illustris*, was consul—that is, in 431 or 432 (see the Appendix, p. 193)—and was a witness to a remarkable event, which he carefully narrates. Nor does he pass over in silence a certain man who appeared to be a monk and who, after arriving at Carthage, boasted that he could perform various cures, using oil infused with the bone of some dead person. But when he realized that he had been exposed and that his deceptive arts had been detected, he fled.

The author in question was in Campania when the holy pontiff Leo was overthrowing the Manichaeans and crushing the Pelagians—around the year 443. It seems that he had been expelled from Africa by the Vandals, perhaps when Carthage was conquered in 439, an event he mentions in one passage. More than once he laments the calamities which, in his own time, sins had brought upon peoples, so that sacrifices had been trampled by foreigners and sacred vessels had fallen into the power of barbarian rulers. He was writing during the reign of Valentinian III; but, apparently, Placidia had already died, and therefore the work must have been written after 450 and before 455. In many matters he follows Augustine and sometimes cites his testimony. The Louvain editors, through whose efforts Prosper was published in print in 1565, admit that this book is far removed from Prosper’s phrasing, style, and learning, and that its text has remained corrupt and mutilated in many places. We have tried, insofar as we could, to remedy this defect with the help of the manuscript of Remiremont–Reims and of the early editions.

The books *On the Contemplative Life* were widely praised under the name of Saint Prosper in the ninth century, and indeed as early as the middle of the eighth century, by Chrodegang, bishop of Metz. But the loose and copiously flowing style in which those books were written differs greatly from Prosper’s forceful and compressed eloquence. Jacobus Sirmondus demonstrated with such strong arguments that they must be attributed to Julianus Pomerius, who lived toward the end of the fifth century (*Notes on the Council of Aachen*), that no one today can retain any doubt on the matter.

Men distinguished for intellectual penetration and learning, who have carefully read and examined the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, maintain that they contain nothing inconsistent with the doctrine of Saint Prosper. The books are attributed to him both by the judgment of Hincmar and by the authority of three very ancient handwritten codices. They also contain many statements plainly consonant with what Prosper wrote both in his other works and in the poem *Against the Ungrateful*. The chronology does not conflict with this attribution. Since the books were not composed at the beginning of the disturbances raised by the Semi-Pelagians, and since Gelasius nevertheless praises them as the work of some Teacher of the Church, it remains likely that they were published around the year 440.

Yet the more artfully constructed discourse and the calmer, gentler manner of argument are less compatible with what one finds in Prosper. Accordingly, leaving aside those who gratuitously and wrongly attributed this work to Saint Ambrose—who died long before those controversies arose—it is attributed by some to Hilary, the companion of our Prosper; by others to Saint Prosper, bishop of Orléans, around the year 470. Some think it was written by an African, perhaps one of those who, expelled by Geiseric in 440, reached Italy.

Quesnellus endeavors to show that these books are by Saint Leo, asserting this on the basis of similarity of style (*Leo*, II, p. 358 and following). He maintains that Leo published them before his pontificate, but without putting his name on them. This, he says, caused Gelasius himself not to know that Leo was their author. Antelmius attacked this opinion, which Quesnellus had advanced in an extensive discussion, with an even more extensive study, and sought to restore the books in question to Prosper (*Antelmius, Dissertation on the Works of Leo*, p. 113 and following). Ludovicus Dupin summarized the arguments on both sides, and concluded that there was nothing requiring the books to be attributed to Prosper (*Dupin*, IV, p. 452 and following).

If their style and method of treating subjects are considered, they do appear to belong among Leo’s works; nothing can be produced that would require them to be excluded from his writings. Yet neither can they be assigned to him with any certain argument, since it is established that they appeared without the author’s name, and it could easily have happened that many men then living in Rome and elsewhere had a manner of writing that recalled and echoed Leo’s style. In this state the famous and very widely debated question still stands, and seems likely to remain so for a long time.

The eminent Norisius thought that the author of these books, in explaining matters relating to grace, not only followed a different path from that taken by Augustine and Prosper, but also disagreed with both of them on certain points of the subject itself (*Hist. Pelag.* II.14). Quesnellus replied that the author had in no respect departed from Augustine’s positions, which had been approved and adopted by the Church (*Leo*, II, p. 381 and following). Ludovicus Dupin appears entirely to agree with him; he treated everything contained in this work in a sufficiently comprehensive analysis (*Dupin*, IV, p. 451 and following).

The style of the letter to Demetrias so closely agrees with that of the books *On the Calling of All Nations* that both works may reasonably be assigned to the same author, whether they are attributed to Ambrose or to Prosper. Norisius (*Hist. Pelag.*, II) indeed assigns the letter to Demetrias to Saint Prosper. Yet his authority did not at all persuade others to abandon their earlier judgment; they likewise continued to think that this letter was composed in the same language and style as the books *On the Calling of All Nations* and therefore ought to be attributed to the same writer.

Trithemius writes (*Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 37) that Prosper also wrote several other works: one book of *Letters to Various Persons*; one book *On Illustrious Men*; and one book *On the Captivity of Rome*. It is likely that Trithemius never inspected these books, since he does not give their beginnings, as he does for the others. In any event, he is too recent an authority for anyone to rely on his testimony. He also adds: “He is said to have written several other things as well, but they have not come into our hands.” Since he was therefore unable to conjecture anything about them, we likewise have so far been unable to make any informed guess.

[Col. 0043]

# HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE ON SAINT PROSPER

*(Schoenemann, Historical-Literary Library of the Latin Fathers, vol. II)*

## § I. Life

He is distinguished from other fairly celebrated writers of the same age by the name “of Aquitaine.” Among them was the well-known poet Prosper Tiro, whom Bede mentions and whose surname Sirmondus once ventured to attach to the Aquitanian Prosper himself. Prosper was born in Aquitaine toward the end of the fourth century or at the beginning of the fifth. In what city or place within that extensive province is unknown; and equally unknown are all details concerning his parents, education, and early life.

Nevertheless, from the monuments of his talent that he left behind, it is sufficiently clear that he devoted himself to liberal studies and the arts of a cultivated man, especially poetry. For reasons unknown, he left Aquitaine and established his residence in Provence, where he was certainly living by 428. There he began his controversies in defense of Augustine’s teaching against John Cassian and others who rejected it—mostly priests of Gaul or Provence. A certain Hilary encouraged his devotion to Augustine in this matter. Since nothing further is known about Hilary’s domestic circumstances, he received the name “Prosperian” from this very association with Prosper.

Prosper had already sent letters to Augustine through the deacon Leontius and had received replies from him. Leontius himself had once lived with the teacher of Hippo. In order to bring Prosper into closer friendship with Augustine and reconcile them, he urged Prosper to write to Augustine again with him. This occurred in 428 or 429.

In those letters they explain to Augustine that many monks and priests residing near Massilia regard certain views contained in his writings against the Pelagians as contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to the mind of the Church. They describe the dangers which, as they believe, threaten them because of the blindness or perversity of those men, and explain how they have begun to resist them. Finally, they ask Augustine to strengthen their weakness by the support of his discussions.

Augustine complied with their wishes and sent them his books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. But since both men were burning with such zeal, and yet their opponents could not be moved by frequent disputations and writings, they both went to Rome and accused them before Pope Celestine of slander against Augustine and of heresy. From him, in 431, they obtained that famous letter to the bishops of Gaul in which he severely reproved them for allowing priests to introduce new and undisciplined questions in any manner whatsoever, while showing so little regard for his authority. He urged them to impose silence on such persons and not to permit the memory of Augustine, whom he strongly praised, to be attacked.

Relying on this letter, they returned to Gaul and defended their cause against the Semi-Pelagians with even greater enthusiasm. Prosper in particular began to contend for it in writing, and various works that he produced during this period have survived to our time.

As his reputation for learning and piety spread, some maintain that he was received into the friendship of Leo, then a Roman archdeacon who was renewing friendships between Aetius and Albinus in Gaul; and that when Leo was summoned from that mission to occupy the Apostolic See, Prosper was brought to Rome with him and appointed papal notary. Those who make this claim are indulging in conjecture, the foundation of which has not even been sufficiently established.

For the claim that Prosper was Leo’s notary rests only on later writers and on the highly doubtful testimony of a single Corbie manuscript of Gennadius, although some modern scholars have tried to strengthen it by the similarity of style and thought which they detected between the writings of the two men.

[Note: He is called Leo’s notary by Ado, a ninth-century writer, in his *Chronicle*, and by other authors of later periods.]

The rest of Prosper’s life is uncertain. It is extremely probable that he held no ecclesiastical office.

[Note: Through a fairly common error in manuscript codices and early editions, the title “bishop of Reggio” (the town of Riez in Provence) is often applied to him. The origin of this error is not yet clear.]

We do not know when he died. Nevertheless, it is evident from his *Chronicle* that he was still alive in 453, while others think that they can learn from Marcellinus, under the year 463, that he lived considerably longer and survived Leo.

## § II. Writings

The genuine writings of Prosper, arranged according to the chronological order maintained even by the latest Paris edition, are:

1. *Letter to Augustine on the Remnants of the Pelagian Heresy in Gaul*, etc., written in 428 or 429.

2. *Letter to Rufinus on Grace and Free Will*, written in 429, while Augustine was still alive.

3. *Poem Against the Ungrateful*, written around 429 or 430.

4. Two epigrams against a detractor of Saint Augustine, perhaps written around 430.

5. *Epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian Heresies*, written after the condemnation of Nestorius’s heresy at the Council of Ephesus in 431, when Augustine was already dead.

6. *Replies on Behalf of Augustine to the Chapters of Objections by the Slanderous Gauls*, written around 431.

7. *Replies in Defense of Augustine’s Doctrine to the Chapters of the Vincentian Objections*, perhaps written shortly after the preceding *Replies*.

8. *Replies on Behalf of Augustine to the Extracts Sent from the City of Genoa*, perhaps written at the same time as the preceding works.

9. *A Book on the Grace of God and Free Will against the Collator*, that is, against the book of the priest Cassianus entitled *On the Protection of God*, written around 432.

10. *Exposition of the Psalms from Psalm 100 through Psalm 150*, apparently written before 424.

11. One book of *Sentences Extracted from the Works of Saint Augustine*, perhaps written around 450 or 451.

12. One book of epigrams drawn from the sentences of Saint Augustine, written not long before the Council of Chalcedon, which is known to have been convened in 451.

13. A complete *Chronicle* divided into two parts and ending in the year 455.

We know from the testimonies of Victorius—or Victorinus—Gennadius, Cassiodorus, and Isidore of Seville that Prosper carried this work from the beginning of the world through the death of Valentinian III and the capture of Rome by the Vandals. Thus, insofar as Eusebius and Jerome extended, he abridged their work; the remainder—that is, from 379 to 455—he composed anew. The division of the work itself reflects this difference in his method.

It is likely that he did not complete the whole work in a single effort, but finished it through successive additions and, as it were, published it repeatedly. Some indeed think that he prepared three different editions. They believe that the first ended in the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus, in the year 433, since in that year he gathered together the dates and totals of all the preceding years—a task ordinarily undertaken only at the end of a work, unless some special reason intervenes, and no such reason seems apparent here.

They think that the second edition was enlarged by twelve years and extended to the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nonius, or the year 445, when his common *Chronicle* is usually joined to the chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome. Finally, they suppose that the third edition was extended to the capture of Rome by Geiseric, that is, to the eighth consulship of the emperor Valentinian and the consulship of Anthemius, or the Christian year 455. Copies of both of the later editions still survive.

The following are of doubtful authority:

1. *The Confession*, which is attributed to him.

2. *The Poem of a Husband to His Wife*.

3. *The Poem on Divine Providence*, which is elsewhere attributed to Hilary.

4. The two books *On the Calling of All Nations*, attributed in some manuscripts to Ambrose. Learned men, however, have adopted different opinions concerning their author. Some, such as Erasmus, attributed them to Eucherius; others, including Vossius, to Hilary, Prosper’s associate; Quesnellus assigned them to Leo the Great, while Joseph Antelmius deliberately opposed him and claimed them for Prosper.

They are thought to have been written around 440. The Ballerinii, however, believe that they were composed much later, though still before 496, in their observations on Quesnellus’s second dissertation concerning the author of these books. After comparing the arguments of both sides, they pronounce neither opinion correct and examine carefully and perceptively every consideration that might enter into the debate. Anyone who wishes may consult them in volume II of Leo’s works, pages 662 and following.

5. *A Letter to the Holy Virgin Demetrias*, or *Treatise on Christian Humility*, written around 440. It was formerly published among the works of Ambrose as Letter 84, having first been added by Sotellus to Prosper’s works together with the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, solely because of a certain similarity of style.

The Ballerinii testify, both from the example of the Ambrosian editors and from the manuscripts they themselves examined, that the two short works are never found together in manuscript codices. Quesnellus was the first to attack and seek to overturn this opinion, claiming the work for Leo in his fourth dissertation on the author of this little book. Antelmius rose against him in the book mentioned above, defending Prosper. The Ballerinii, holding the scales between the two sides, understood that they should incline toward neither and therefore judged that the work should be left to an uncertain author. See their observations on Quesnellus’s fourth dissertation, volume II, p. 743 and following. The latest editors of Prosper’s works, however, agree with Antelmius.

6. *Authorities of the Bishops of the Apostolic See of Earlier Times on the Grace of God and Free Choice*, which are commonly placed after Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul. They are thought to have been collected around 431. Dionysius Exiguus was the first to publish them and append them to Celestine’s letter. The Ballerinii demonstrate, chiefly from the testimony of Pope Hormisdas, that Dionysius took them from the Roman archives.

They are nevertheless not by Celestine himself, nor by Leo, as the same scholars established in their observations on the dissertation of Quesnellus mentioned above, volume II, p. 719 and following. Pagius followed and further strengthened Antelmius’s view, which attributes them to Prosper, under the year 431, no. 49. Constantius did the same in his preface to the aforementioned letter of Celestine, and also attempted to discover the occasion of this study. The Ballerinii did not hesitate to add their support to this opinion as well, although they differed from Constantius on certain points. See their observations on Quesnellus’s third dissertation, volume II of Leo’s works, p. 719 and following.

They certainly do not belong to him: the three books *On the Contemplative Life*, which are more correctly marked with the name of Julianus Pomerius; *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, by an uncertain author; and the other *Chronicle*, commonly called the *Pseudo-Chronicle* or the *Chronicle of Prosper Tiro*. It begins with the death of the emperor Valens and proceeds to the capture of Rome by Geiseric.

It has quite a few things in common with the work mentioned above, but many more things different from it. In particular, it is arranged not by consuls but according to the succession of emperors. Pithoeus, who first published it, argued that it was Prosper’s true *Chronicle* and that it reflected his talent. He therefore thought it not unreasonable to regard it as a portion of the larger work which Gennadius testifies that he had read under Prosper’s name, extending from the creation of the world to the capture of Rome by the Vandals. Pithoeus also wondered how it had happened that another chronicle arranged by consuls was appended under Prosper’s name in all editions of Jerome’s *Chronicle*. Labbeus appeared to agree with Pithoeus.

Bucherius and scholars more perceptive than Pithoeus, however, taught that the confused and disordered arrangement of this *Chronicle*, its countless errors against the proper order of chronology, its extremely slight—indeed, almost nonexistent—mention of the Pelagians, and the fact that the only observation it makes about Augustine is that he discussed many subjects in countless books, while saying that the heresy of the Predestinarians—certainly unknown to Prosper—arose from Augustine (Pithoeus dared to foist that claim into Augustine’s books), are each and all arguments proving that the work is unworthy of Prosper and foreign to his talent.

By contrast, the lucid narrative and orderly arrangement of the other *Chronicle*, especially its careful treatment of the affairs of Saint Augustine and the Pelagian heresy, and its mention of both Augustine and Leo only with the greatest reverence, make it clear to everyone that the author was a disciple of Augustine and a defender of his doctrine of grace.

Some therefore thought that this *Chronicle* had been falsely attributed to Prosper in order to bring both him and Augustine into contempt and disrepute. More probable, however, is the opinion also defended by Antelmius: that it was composed without fraudulent intent by a certain Prosper, or by an author of another name; and that, because the copies lacked the author’s name, it was given the name of Prosper, who was publicly known to have written a *Chronicle* in the same period. Alternatively, it may be the genuine *Chronicle* of Prosper, interpolated, abridged, and altered for private use by some Semi-Pelagian, so that it now appears in this form.

Since Antelmius has been mentioned so often here, another of his opinions must not be passed over. He attributed all the writings of Pope Leo to Prosper, as Leo’s notary, and thereby provoked major disputes with Quesnellus. He proposed this opinion in the same book mentioned earlier. Since that work is now very rarely found in libraries, we append its description here:

*Critical Dissertations on the Genuine Works of the Holy Fathers Leo the Great and Prosper of Aquitaine, in which Joseph Antelmius rejects the Chapters on the Grace of God, the Letter to Demetrias, and the two books On the Calling of All Nations, recently attributed to Leo, and restores them to Prosper. Also included, together with his judgment concerning Leo’s celebrated letter to Flavian and other letters to various persons dictated by Prosper in the affair of Eutyches, are other letters, etc.* Paris, published by Dezallier, 1689, quarto.

The author was a native of Fréjus, born in 1648. After completing his studies, he became a canon in his native city. From 1684 onward he was grand vicar and official to J. B. de Verthamon, bishop of Pamiers, and died in 1697. In opposition to Quesnellus’s assertions, he attempted in his first three dissertations to claim the three aforementioned works for Prosper. In the fourth he attacked two of Leo the Great’s letters against the Pelagians: Quesnellus had declared one, addressed to Januarius, authentic, and the other, addressed to Septimius, spurious. Antelmius, however, maintained that the latter was genuine and that the former, addressed to Januarius, was forged.

In the fifth dissertation he defended Gennadius and other ancient writers, who state that Leo’s letter to Flavian in the affair of Eutyches (in Ballerinius, no. 28) was dictated by Prosper, Leo’s notary, against Bellarmine and Labbeus. He also detected unmistakable traces of Prosperian style not only in this letter but in others of Leo’s letters.

Thinking that he likewise recognized no fewer indications of this similarity in Leo’s sermons, he produced various examples in the sixth dissertation, especially from Sermon 4 (Quesnellus’s edition), delivered on Leo’s anniversary, and from the sermons on the Rogations and on Fasting. Investigating the causes of this circumstance, he judged that the chief explanation lay in a custom of that age, when sermons were frequently requested for recitation by other bishops. Gennadius, he notes, testifies that the priest Salvian composed many homilies for bishops and thereby earned the title “teacher of bishops,” not, as is commonly supposed, because he had taught the bishops Salonius and Veranus in their youth.

From this he concludes that the sermons of Leo, the supreme pontiff, were all the more likely to have been requested, and that Prosper, the most learned and eloquent man of his age, may sometimes have supplied them with rhetorical ornament. Prosper, he thinks, served the extremely busy pontiff as adviser in matters of counsel and correspondence, either chiefly or exclusively.

In the following sections he reviews the remaining works attributed to Prosper. In the seventh dissertation he treats the work *On the Promises and Predictions*, which he maintains was falsely attributed to Prosper by Cassiodorus and was written by an author of African origin. He assigns the books *On the Contemplative Life* to Julianus Pomerius and discusses him carefully. He also examines the *Confession of Prosper Tiro*, edited by Sirmondus, which he judges to display scarcely anything sufficiently consistent with Prosper’s style and reputation.

He devotes the eighth dissertation to Prosper’s *Chronicle*, defending it at length against Garnerius in the form in which it commonly exists, but proving that, in the form published by Pithoeus, it has been interpolated and stuffed with additions.

The ninth dissertation examines Prosper’s poems. Antelmius judges the poem *On Providence* to be spurious; leaves the *Anacreontic Poem to His Wife* uncertain; asserts the *Epitaph of the Pelagian and Nestorian Heresies* for Prosper of Aquitaine against Garnerius; and considers the *Poem Against the Ungrateful*, together with Epigram 97 and two other poems against a detractor of Augustine, to be especially genuine. He believes that this detractor was none other than Vincent of Lérins, who in his *Commonitorium* attempted to criticize Augustine’s doctrine as well.

Amid this discussion Antelmius produces a new work of this Vincent, *The Secrets of the Lérins*, indicating that he had devoted himself wholly to arranging and illustrating it. He closes the entire volume with a promise of a complete edition of that work and of all Prosper’s writings.

[Note: This notice is repeated from M.’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, volume I, p. 487. Its authors indicate that they owe it to the *Acts of the Learned of Leipzig*, Supplement, volume I, p. 431. Nevertheless, we have not followed them in every detail. For what they report concerning Antelmius’s opinion on the letters to Septimius and Januarius does not agree with the Ballerinii’s exposition of the same opinion. The Ballerinii, however, refuted both Quesnellus and Antelmius and demonstrated that both letters are genuine; they should therefore be regarded as the better authorities on this matter. See the Ballerinii’s *Admonition on the First Two Letters of Leo*, volume I of Leo’s works, pp. 567–590, where an extensive discussion of both letters and an eighteenth dissertation are appended.]

Quesnellus soon replied to Antelmius with a letter written in French in the *Parisian Journals* of 8 and 15 August 1689. Antelmius did not hesitate to answer him with two further letters to the abbot …, corresponding to the two parts of Quesnellus’s letter, published in Paris in 1690, quarto. Quesnellus, however, allowed himself to be convinced by these no more than by Antelmius’s dissertations, and in the Lyon edition of 1700 he did not retreat by so much as a fingernail from his original opinion.

## § III. Editions

The first work of Prosper to begin being printed among his other writings was the book of *Epigrams*.

[Note: The Paris editors begin their series of printed editions of Prosper with the book against the *Collator*, printed at Mainz in 1524.]

The first edition of the *Epigrams* appeared at Mainz in 1494, quarto; another, without a date, at Turin in the same format; and another at Venice from the press of Aldus in 1501. Close to this came the book *Against the Collator*, issued at Mainz in 1524 and reprinted in Sichardus’s *Antidote* at Basel in 1528; and the edition of the *Sentences Extracted from Augustine*, published at Cologne in 1531.

Not long afterward there appeared the letter to Rufinus and the *Replies to the Extracts from Genoa*, published at Venice by Bernardinus Stagninus in 1538, octavo. Soon afterward, in Gryphius’s Lyon edition of 1539, there appeared the *Replies to the Chapters of the Gauls* and the *Vincentian Objections*, together with the poems *On Providence* and *Against the Ungrateful*.

[Note: Gryphius himself does not indicate that he was the first to publish the *Replies to the Chapters of the Gauls* and the *Vincentian Objections*, although he explicitly makes this claim for the other two short works. Investigate, therefore, whether some earlier edition existed, perhaps seen by very few people.]

With the work of Sebastian Gryphius begins the second period in the editions of Prosper. He was the first to give the title *Works* and declared that he had revised the text by collating ancient manuscripts. The edition was reprinted at Cologne in 1540. In 1565 John Sotellus added to it the letter to Augustine and several short works that do not belong to Prosper.

John Olivarius produced the same edition, cleansed in certain respects, at Douai in 1577. From that time his recension remained in use until 1711, unless Theophilus Raynaudus altered something in the Paris edition of 1671.

In that year, 1711, there appeared in Paris a folio edition which, although not complete in every respect, was far superior to the earlier editions in the apparatus of manuscripts and in the labor and learning of its editor, Jean le Brun de Marette of the Congregation of Saint Maur. D. Mangeant, a member of the same congregation, supervised its publication. From this one may perhaps infer that Lebrun had not yet completed everything when the work was taken from his hands.

A diligent and perceptive reader of the history of those times will easily notice what is lacking, or will be guided to it by the Ballerinii in these passages. Nor, after mentioning this edition, should we pass over in silence the contributions made to the embellishment of Prosper’s works by John Salinasius in 1732 and by P. J. Fogginius in 1758, both at Rome.

It is necessary to make a separate remark concerning the *Chronicle*: three different genuine editions of it exist. The first, commonly called the *Vulgate*, is usually joined to the *Chronicle* of Eusebius and Jerome and extends from the year 379, when Jerome stopped, to the year 445; it was also published by Canisius from the Augsburg manuscript, differing in no small measure from the common text. The second, ten years fuller than the first, was initially published by Duchesne among the contemporary historians of France. The third, comprising the complete *Chronicle* from the creation of the world to the year 455, was presented by Labbe in the *New Library of Manuscripts* in 1657. In all of them, however, the latter portion, from 379 to 445 or 455, varies astonishingly—fuller in some than in others, at one time more diffuse and meager, at another more precise. It is clear that such corruptions must be attributed either to the negligence of copyists or certainly to the deliberate policy of editors. Besides these, a Pseudo-Chronicle was published from manuscript codices by Pierre Pithou in 1588 and again in 1609, and was likewise reprinted by Labbe in the *New Library of Manuscripts* in 1657. Finally, both the genuine *Chronicle* and the Pseudo-Chronicle, with notes and variant readings, were reproduced in the latest Paris edition of Prosper’s works and, with the most learned notes of Basnage, in the new edition of Henri Canisius’s *Ancient Readings* of 1725. Whoever desires more information should consult the *Annals of the Editions*, which we now append.

## FIFTEENTH CENTURY

**1494.** Mainz, printed by Peter Friedberg; quarto. *Epigrams of Saint Prosper, Bishop of Riez, on Vices and Virtues, from the Sayings of Augustine.*

The volume begins immediately on the title page, on its verso, with a preceding eulogy of Prosper from Trithemius. At the end, on folio 22 verso, one reads: “Here end the *Epigrams of Saint Prosper, Bishop of Riez, on Vices and Virtues, from the Sayings of Augustine*. Printed at Mainz by Peter Friedberg. In the year 94 of the Virgin Birth.” This is followed on folio 23 by a poem entitled “A Husband’s Song to His Wife”: “Prosper on the Faith and Morals of Christians and Martyrs, and on the Contempt and Brevity of the Present Life.” That title, however, is inserted only after the first sixteen verses, written in Anacreontic meter. Finally, at the end of this work, on folio 24 verso, there is a commendation by some anonymous person of the author, consisting of seventeen hexameters. From this, the distinguished Braun should be corrected in *Historical and Literary Notes*, part II, p. 260, no. 20.

**Undated.** Turin; quarto. B. Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life and on the Seven Virtues*, with the following little verses added—whether on the same page or on the verso I do not know:

> These Epigrams of Augustine, from sacred sayings,  
> Prosper the rhetorician, joining them in sweet-sounding song,  
> Set forth in hexameter and pentameter verses,  
> Binding them together like a garland of varied flowers.  
>   
> Therefore, reader, who diligently gather them beneath these lines,  
> I ask you to apply attentive ears to the heavenly sounds;  
> For here you will find, if concern enters your mind,  
> What the holy law’s commands chiefly teach human beings  
> To observe, and what to avoid beneath the stars—  
> They who desire to climb to the starry kingdom of heaven.

So that you do not suppose that the books of Julian Pomerius *On the Contemplative Life*, falsely ascribed here to Prosper, are presented, this volume contains nothing other than Prosper’s *Epigrams*. Muratori saw these same verses appended at the end of an ancient manuscript and had them reprinted from it in *Anecdotes*, vol. II, p. 210, [Note: *Literary History of France*, book II, pp. 384–385.] as the authors of the *Literary History of France* testify. From them we further learn that an anonymous Latin commentary was included. When Hamberger sought more definite information about it, he discovered in the Catalogue of the Manuscripts of the Turin Library, among the Latin codices no. 781, e, II, 10, p. 256, a codex of Prosper’s *Epigrams* with a commentary, which may perhaps be identical with this one; but whose it is is no clearer from its subscription than from any other source [Note: Hamberger, *Reliable Notices*, book III, p. 215. The subscription read: “This work was written by Brother Tibaldus de Guerris of Castelnuovo Tortonese, of the Order of Friars Minor, then Bachelor of the convent of Chieri, 12 August 1465.”].

## SIXTEENTH CENTURY

**1501.** Venice, at the press of Aldus; quarto. *The Epigrams of Prosper of Aquitaine on Certain Sentences of the Blessed Aurelius Augustine; together with Aratus’s Poem, the Apostolic History, except for Proba Falconia’s Cento, the Hymns of John of Damascus, and certain little works of Cosmas of Jerusalem.*

In the copy of this book preserved by the Bern Library (*Catalogue*, vol. I, part II), Bongarsius wrote variant readings from manuscript codices beside Prosper’s *Epigrams*.

**1524.** Mainz, at the press of Johann Schöffer; quarto. *The Booklet of Saint Prosper, a Priest of Aquitaine, against the Enemies of the Grace of God, against Cassian’s Collator; and the Letter of Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, against the Pelagians; the Authority of Pope Celestine and of Other Roman Pontiffs concerning the Grace of God, on behalf of Prosper and Hilary, against the Pelagians*—prepared by Nicolaus Carbacchius. *Catalogue of the Paris Library.* [Note: Somewhat differently, but I think more correctly—for the authors of the Royal Catalogue sometimes like to abridge titles and sometimes to add something from the contents of the books—the title is given in the preface to the latest Paris edition as follows: “The Book of Saint Prosper on the Grace of God and Free Will, in defense of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop, against the book of the presbyter Cassian, entitled *On the Protection of God*. Also, thirteen chapters of the decrees of Pope Celestine on behalf of Prosper and Hilary, on the Grace of God, against certain priests of Gaul, followers of Pelagius, etc.”]

Carbacchius had found a copy of this booklet in the Library of the Benedictine religious brothers of Mount Saint James at Mainz.

**1524.** Basel; octavo. *The Little Works of Prosper, Augustine, and Ambrose on Free Will*, from the edition of Johannes Oecolampadius. Baluze, *Library*, vol. II, p. 1001.

I would not dare say whether, besides the book against the *Collator*, anything else of Prosper’s is included. Under Ambrose’s name, no doubt nothing is published here except the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, attributed by many to Ambrose.

**1528.** Basel, at the press of Heinrich Petri; folio. *Prosper of Aquitaine’s Booklet on Free Will against the Collator*, in Johannes Sichard’s *Antidote against All Heresies*, p. 215 ff.

**1531.** Cologne, printed by Johannes Prael; octavo. *Several Sentences, as Aphorisms, Selected from the Books of Saint Augustine and Others, through the Study and Labor of Prosper, Bishop of Riez.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris. See the preface to the Paris edition.

**1533.** Paris; duodecimo. *The Booklet of the Blessed Prosper of Aquitaine against the Enemies of the Grace of God*: added are the letter of Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana; excerpts from the synodal acts against the heretic Pelagius; and Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul concerning the errors of Pelagius. Baluze, *Library*, in the same place. [Note: As I judge, the Mainz edition was reprinted.]

**1534.** Paris, at the press of Antoine Augerelle; duodecimo. *Saint Prosper’s work On Grace and Free Will, to Rufinus, and Responses to the Excerpts of the Genoese.* Baluze, *Library*, in the same place, and the *Tellerian Library*, p. 198b. The authors of the *Literary History of France* state that they saw a copy of this book bearing the year 1533.

**1538.** Venice, printed by Bernardino Stagnino; octavo. *Little Works on Grace and Free Will of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, Bishop of Riez, a Most Religious Man, Disciple of Saint Augustine, and Most Learned in the Divine Scriptures.*

This volume contains: 1. Saint Prosper’s letter to Rufinus; 2. *To the Excerpts of Januensis* (*Genuensis*); 3. Saint Prosper’s book against Cassian; 4. the letter of Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage; 5. Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul and the authorities of the Apostolic See, etc.; 6. Saint Prosper’s *Epigrams* and *Song to His Wife*. Of these, numbers 1 and 2 are here published for the first time. Preface to the latest Paris edition.

**1539.** Lyons, at the press of Sebastian Gryphius; folio. *The Works of the Blessed Prosper of Aquitaine, Bishop of Riez, Corrected and Revised through Collation with Ancient Copies.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

Sebastian Gryphius begins his dedicatory letter to the Senate and people of Riez with an apology: although approximately four years earlier, at their request, he had undertaken the labor of printing all the writings of Prosper, once their bishop, he had not been able to publish them sooner. He attributed this to the fact that some copies had been transcribed insufficiently accurately and that certain incomplete little works were missing.

“Therefore,” he says, “in order to oblige you and serve the convenience of students, I thought the edition should not be rushed; rather, I first had to strive vigorously to restore the work, if it could in any way be done, to its former brightness and genuine integrity. Accordingly, by sending letters here and there, I entrusted the matter to friends, both French and German, especially those devoted to humane letters, asking them to send me whatever of this author lay hidden among them in ancient libraries, whether damaged or complete. Among other things, they sent extremely ancient copies containing the little works that had been missing: namely, two in heroic verse, one on the Providence of God and the other *Περὶ Ἀχαριστῶν* (*On the Ungrateful*); in addition, a commentary on the final fifty-one psalms—all of them, as I believe, unseen by the people of our age. Having therefore carefully collated all these materials with one another, I finally brought it about that this Prosper of yours, a man as holy as he was learned, who for so many past centuries had lain hidden in darkness, suffering decay and neglect, should emerge into the light wholly bright, pure, and complete.”

Thus far Gryphius’s words, quoted from the celebrated letter in the preface to the latest Paris edition. Its authors add, however—using somewhat unclear language here—that, besides the works listed, *Responses to the Chapters of the Gauls* and *Responses to the Chapters of the Vincentian Objections* were newly included. He omitted the complete *Chronicle*, which had been printed among the chronicles of Eusebius and others and which, because of its excessive corruption, seemed likely to weary the reader.

**1540.** Cologne, printed by Hero Alopecius; octavo. *The Works of the Blessed Prosper of Aquitaine, Bishop of Riez, Revised through Collation with Ancient Copies.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris. A reissue of the Gryphian edition.

**1552.** Cologne, at the press of Lambert Sylvius; octavo. *Two Letters of Prosper and Hilary of Arles to the Blessed Augustine, concerning the Remnants of the Pelagian Heresy, Restored to the Text of an Ancient Copy, together with the Dialogue of Honorius of Autun on Predestination and Free Will.* Catalogue of the Bunavian Library, vol. III, p. 208.

**1556.** Basel, from the workshop of Heinrich Petri; folio. *Prosper of Aquitaine against the Collocutor* [sic], *on Free Will*, in Johannes Herold’s *Hæresiologia*, pp. 664–675. He edited it from an ancient Lorsch codex, in which, however, several verses at the end of the book were missing.

**1565.** Cologne, at the press of the heirs of Arnold Birckmann, “at the Fat Hen”; large quarto. *The Works of the Blessed Prosper of Aquitaine, Bishop of Riez, Carefully Purged of Almost Innumerable Errors through the Collation of Ancient Copies by Learned Men.* At the end: “Louvain, printed by Johannes Bogardus.” This place and printer’s notice, with the year 1566 prefixed, undoubtedly indicates this same edition. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

The contents of the preceding edition, according to the list printed on the verso of this edition’s title page, were as follows: *The Work on the Predictions and Promises of God*, by which I do not know when or by whom the number of Prosper’s works was increased; three books *On the Contemplative Life*; the letter to Rufinus; *Responses to the Chapters of the Gauls*, *to the Vincentian Objections*, and *to the Excerpts of the Genoese*; book one against Cassian, *On the Protection of God*; book one of *Sentences Extracted from Augustine’s Works*; book one of *Epigrams from the Same Sentences*; a little work *On Divine Providence*; book one *On the Ungrateful*; and a commentary on Psalms 100–150.

The additions to this edition were numbered as follows: 1. two books *On the Calling of All Nations*; 2. a letter to the holy virgin Demetrias; 3. a letter to the Blessed Augustine; 4. Celestine’s letter on behalf of Prosper and Hilary, insofar as it had been omitted from the Gryphian edition; 5. the canons of the Second Council of Orange.

Of these, number 3 was an entirely new acquisition. Numbers 1 and 2 had previously been attributed to Ambrose and published with his works. Now the former is claimed for Prosper not only because of the similarity of style and diction but also on the authority of manuscript codices; the latter partly because of its style and partly because of its subject matter.

The curator of this edition, Johannes Soteaux (Sotellus) of Montigny, states in his preface to the reader, which begins with the *Life of Prosper*, that he had discovered the books *On the Calling of All Nations* inscribed with Prosper’s name in the oldest manuscripts of the Library of the Regular Canons of Saint Martin at Louvain and of the abbeys of Cambron and Boneffe near Namur.

Concerning the other works, the editor gives the following warning:

“We are not unaware that the books *On the Predictions and Promises of God* are corrupt in many places and, as it appears, mutilated, although not to the extent they seemed when we first received them for reading. But since we had no more correct copies available, we did not wish to alter anything by conjecture. If, because of their lesser learning, some should think that they were written by Saint Prosper when he was still young and just beginning to exercise himself in sacred letters, this is contradicted by the fact that in chapter 38 of the second part the author himself speaks as though he had already passed beyond the years of youth.

“That they certainly do not seem to be Prosper’s is made probable not only because Gennadius and Trithemius, when listing what he wrote, do not mention this work, but also because of the greatest dissimilarity of phrase and style, and because throughout the work the author very frequently employs these sentences as expressions familiar to him: ‘not so much for himself as also for his own,’ and so forth; ‘not so much of the past as also of the present,’ and so forth—expressions which you will nowhere find in the books of the Blessed Prosper themselves. Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that they were written by a man deeply devoted to the writings and books of Saint Augustine. For he cites Augustine’s very words more than once, and we have noted in the margin where they occur in Augustine.

“The book against the *Collator*—which was full of errors and whose order was completely confused, because Prosper’s words were repeatedly printed in it as though they belonged to Cassian—was corrected with the assistance of the learned and outstanding man, Master Johannes Hessels of Louvain, Royal Professor of Sacred Theology at Louvain, just as he supplied a large part of what we have discussed with you thus far, Christian reader.”

In the same preface, he says that he excluded the *Song on Providence* because it is Pelagian doctrine; nevertheless, in the volume itself it is printed in the same order in which it had appeared in the preceding edition [Note: This escaped the Paris editors, because they did not trouble to inspect the book itself.].

Finally, this edition was supplied with very full indexes of subjects and Scriptures, also noted on the title page. Sotellus dedicated it to Charles van der Linden, abbot of the Parc monastery of the Premonstratensian Order near Louvain, in a letter dated at Louvain, from the Minor College of Theologians, on 19 April 1575.

**1577.** Douai, from the workshop of Johannes Bogardus, sworn printer, “under the Golden Bibles”; octavo. *The Works of the Blessed Prosper of Aquitaine, Bishop of Riez, Carefully Purged of Almost Innumerable Errors through the Collation of Ancient Copies.*

The substance of the preceding edition was not increased. But Johannes—I know not which—Olivarius professed in a letter to Johannes Sacracenus, prior of Saint-Vaast at Arras, dated Douai, 13 November 1576, that Prosper’s writings, which had not been sufficiently purged in that edition, were now cleaner and enriched by a considerable addition of variant readings and several lacunae, especially by the supplement of one particularly important lacuna [Note: He says, by way of apologizing for having laid hands on an ecclesiastical writer, that he was occupied only with humane letters and entirely alien to sacred theological study.].

“For,” he says, “many corrections and also various readings were supplied to us partly by the book collated with ancient codices through your exceptional industry, and partly by the very ancient volume of the Cambron Library, which contained three handwritten books *On the Contemplative Life*, two *On the Calling of the Nations*, and one of *Epigrams*. Thus, in these books, many things have been improved, omissions supplied, and numerous matters annotated—things which not even your keenest judgment, to which we willingly submit them, should disapprove.”

For the rest, the entire order of the preceding edition has been preserved here, as have the indexes and even Johannes Sotellus’s preface to the reader.

## SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

**1601.** Ingolstadt, from the Ederian workshop; quarto. Prosper of Aquitaine’s complete *Chronicle*, divided into two parts, together with the latter part—departing considerably from the printed versions—from the Augsburg manuscript; in Heinrich Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, vol. I. See the Basnage edition of 1725.

**1604.** Bordeaux, at the press of Simon Millanges; folio. Prosper of Aquitaine’s *Chronicle from the Death of Valens, etc.*, in Arnaldus Pontacus’s *Chronicles of Three Illustrious Authors, Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper*, pp. 198–210. Notes appear on pp. 760–790.
