**1606.** Leiden, printed by Thomas Basson at the expense of the Commelins; folio. The same portion of the *Chronicle*, in Joseph Scaliger’s *Thesaurus Temporum*, pp. 188–197, and likewise in the Amsterdam edition published by Johannes Janssonius in 1658.

**1609.** Cologne, printed by Arnold Kempensis at the expense of Johannes Crithius; octavo. *The Works of the Blessed Prosper of Aquitaine … Carefully Purged of Almost Innumerable Errors through the Collation of Ancient Copies.* A reprint of Johannes Olivarius’s edition.

**1609.** Paris, from the Nivellian press, at the press of Sebastian Cramoisy; quarto. *The Chronicle of Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine, from the Death of the Emperor Valens to the Capture of the City by Genseric. Now Published for the First Time, Very Different from That Which Has Hitherto Been Appended to the Chronicle of the Blessed Jerome. Also a Fragment from the Chronicle of Victor, Bishop of Tunnuna in Africa, Which He Appended to Prosper’s Chronicle.* In the works of Pierre Pithou, pp. 329–342. Concerning the first edition, of 1588, I have not yet established anything certain.

**1611.** Rome, from the press of the Apostolic Chamber. *The Works of the Blessed Prosper …* (from the edition of Johannes Olivarius). Benedictine excerpts from the Catalogue of the Cordesian Library (Paris, 1643, quarto), p. 73.

**1619.** Paris … octavo. *The Confession of Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine*, now published for the first time from a Vatican codex by Jacques Sirmond, together with the little works of Eugenius, Bishop of Toledo, to which certain poems of Dracontius and other ancient ecclesiastical writers were added. All these were reprinted in the works of Jacques Sirmond, Paris, 1696, vol. II, pp. 913–914.

**1622.** Helmstedt, at the press of the heirs of Jacob Lucius; octavo. *The Sentences of Saint Prosper Collected from the Monuments of the Blessed Augustine*, which is why some call them *Augustine’s Sentences*, separately published for the benefit of lovers of piety and truth, with a very full alphabetical index in which almost all the sentences are recorded.

**1636.** Paris, at the expense of Sebastian Cramoisy; folio. Prosper of Aquitaine’s *Chronicle* … from the edition of the distinguished Pierre Pithou, in Duchesne’s *Contemporary Writers of France*, vol. I, pp. 196–201. Also, the *Chronicle from the Creation of the World*, its latter portion, customarily joined to the chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, much more accurately and fully than in the printed copies, from the manuscript codices of Jacques Sirmond and Pierre-François Chifflet, pp. 201–209.

**1657.** Paris, at the press of Sebastian and Gabriel Cramoisy; folio. *The Complete Chronicle of the Most Illustrious Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine, from Adam to the Capture of Rome by Genseric, King of the Vandals, Divided into Two Parts.*

The first part, from the beginning of the world to the death of Valens, with an annotation of the consuls, is now published for the first time from various handwritten codices. The second part, from the year 379 to 455, is fuller and more accurate in many places than what had previously been published. Also, the *Chronicle* of the same or another Prosper, the Pithou edition corrected in many places through collation with manuscript codices. All in Philip Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscript Books*, vol. I, pp. 16–60.

**1671.** Paris, at the expense of Pierre Variquet; folio. *The Works of the Blessed Prosper, Bishop of Riez*, an edition thoroughly purged of nearly innumerable errors with which the preceding editions abounded; added are the *Heptad of Bishops*, published by Theophilus Raynaud and thereafter reprinted several times, here and now for the final time.

**1677.** Lyons, at the press of the Anissons; folio. *Various Little Works of Prosper … Written in Prose and Verse, from the Revision of Johannes Olivarius; Also the Chronicle of the Same, or of Prosper Tiro, from the Edition of Heinrich Canisius, and the Pithou Chronicle.* In the *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, vol. VIII, pp. 1–203.

**1690.** Paris, at the press of François Muguet; folio. *Apologetic Little Works of Prosper of Aquitaine on Behalf of Augustine and against the Unjust Critics of His Doctrine of Grace and Predestination; Also Prosper’s Book of Sentences from Augustine.* In the third part of the appendix to vol. X of Saint Augustine’s works, prepared by monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur at Saint-Germain-des-Prés; in the Antwerp edition, pp. 110–170.

Included together are: 1. the letter to Rufinus, revised according to a very ancient copy of the Abbey of Saint Remigius at Reims; 2. the book against the *Collator*, corrected from a very ancient Corbie codex and according to the best editions, such as those of Mainz, Louvain, and Antwerp.

**1699.** Utrecht and Leiden, at the presses of François Halma and Pieter van der Aa; folio. Prosper of Aquitaine’s complete *Chronicle*, reproduced according to Labbe’s edition, in Johann Georg Graevius’s *Thesaurus of Roman Antiquities*, vol. XI, p. 269 ff.

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

**1703.** Louvain, at the press of Gilles Denique; octavo. *Prosper of Aquitaine’s On the Ungrateful* (*Περὶ Ἀχαρίστων*), that is, *The Poem on the Ungrateful*, carefully prepared and illustrated with miscellaneous notes by Martin Steyaert, in volume III of Steyaert’s *Little Works or Studies*.

Concerning the author, formerly a doctor of theology at Louvain who achieved great fame among his countrymen, consult Jean-François Foppens, *Belgian Library*, p. 861, where his portrait is also found. This commentary on Prosper’s booklet is a posthumous work. It did not first appear separately but in this edition of his works, which consists of six volumes. All the notes, however, were transferred into the Paris edition.

Accordingly, Jean Albert Fabricius is mistaken if he really asserts that the Louvain edition of Steyaert’s work appeared at Amsterdam rather than at Louvain. For not only do the Benedictines mention it in the *Literary History of France*, but the Paris editors themselves expressly state in their preliminary notice to this poem that it was published at Louvain; indeed, Clericus himself testifies in his preface to the Augustinian appendix that these notes of Steyaert were published at Louvain.

**1703.** Antwerp, at the press of Peter Mortier; folio. *The Poem of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, Περὶ Ἀχαρίστων, that is, On the Ungrateful*, prepared and illustrated by a theologian of Louvain, in the Augustinian appendix, or volume XII of Augustine’s works, prepared by Jean Le Clerc, pp. 1–39.

“Before all else,” says Le Clerc in the preface to this volume, “the poem of Saint Prosper *On the Ungrateful* presents itself to be read. In it he sets forth in verse the doctrine of Saint Augustine, Pelagius, and especially the Semi-Pelagians—indeed, in verses that are not of the highest quality, but are by no means difficult to understand. The learned Louvain theologian had nevertheless illustrated them quite diligently with the notes you see here. Those notes, corrected and enlarged by the hand of a learned man, have been published by us exactly as they were transmitted, without any addition or subtraction.

“They had previously been published at Louvain and bore the name of Martin Steyaert, who was a theologian of that university and died not long ago. He is said first to have belonged to those who defended Augustinian doctrine and then to have crossed over to the opposing side, as is sufficiently clear from various French booklets in which the eloquent theologian of the Sorbonne, Antoine Arnauld, easily the leading representative of the Augustinian party in France, attacked him. Nevertheless, those who transmitted this little work to the bookseller—the purchaser of this appendix—wished Steyaert’s name to be removed. We could not conceal this.”

**1711.** Paris, at the expense of Guillaume Desprez and Jean Desessartz; folio. *The Complete Works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, Disciple of Saint Augustine and First Notary of Pope Saint Leo, Corrected According to Manuscript Codices and Also According to Earlier and More Accurate Editions, Now for the First Time Arranged in Chronological Order, and Enriched with the Complete Chronicle of the Same Author, Extending from the Beginning of the World to the Death of Valentinian III and the Capture of Rome by the Vandals. Prefixed Is the Life of the Same Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, Compiled from His Works and from the Books of Ecclesiastical Writers.*

The editors, Johannes Le Brun de Marette and D. Mangeaut, declare that their purpose in preparing this edition was to make it as extensive, as carefully corrected, and as well ordered as possible, and also to provide readers with some assistance toward a fuller understanding of the history of the Semi-Pelagian error.

Accordingly, they first gathered into it everything genuine by Saint Prosper that had hitherto appeared in print, omitting neither the *Confession*, which he published for the first time, nor the complete *Chronicle*, which all earlier editors had rejected. They then corrected each book of the edition according to the more trustworthy editions and as many manuscripts as, within the limits of the time granted, they were able to discover and collate. For in the royal letters issued on 14 December 1709, by which the booksellers were granted the privilege of printing and reprinting this and other books, there was an order that Prosper’s works be completed within two years.

And lest they be accused of having selected readings of the same passage occurring in different books arbitrarily, or of wishing to prejudice the taste of more learned readers, the readings they rejected were relegated to the lower margin of each page. Nor did they wish to confine their criticism within these limits. They also worked diligently to distinguish spurious and doubtful works from true and genuine ones both by their position and typography and by preliminary notices, while likewise reporting the opinions of learned men concerning each work.

The order of the books is the same in which we listed the individual works above, though various other materials pertaining to them have been inserted, and doubtful works are presented in the same series as certain and genuine ones. A very full index of subjects, names, and notable sayings also refers to them; only afterward is an appendix attached.

Specifically, after Prosper’s letter to Augustine there are inserted Hilary’s letter to the same man and Augustine’s two books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. After the *Responses to the Excerpts of the Genoese* comes a letter of Pope Celestine on behalf of Prosper and Hilary, together with the authorities of the bishops of the Apostolic See concerning grace and the thirteenth conference of John Cassian. After the complete *Chronicle* comes the Second Council of Orange. The remaining works of doubtful authenticity follow in the same order as proposed above.

The appendix contains, in its first part, the three books of Julian Pomerius *On the Contemplative Life*, the book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, and the *Chronicle of Prosper Tiro*. In the second part are various writings and documents whose reading sheds light on the works of Saint Prosper and on Semi-Pelagian history; among these, placed first, is Augustine’s first book *On Rebuke and Grace*, addressed to Valentinus.

The editors devoted no less care to the books presented in the first part of the appendix than to the rest of Prosper’s writings. A special index, prepared with no ordinary care, was also added to the entire appendix. Finally, a distinctive ornament of this edition is the *Life of Prosper*, compiled from his own works and from the books of ecclesiastical writers. It consists of eleven sections and is placed immediately after the preface.

**1725.** Antwerp, at the press of Rudolph and Gerard Westen; folio. *The Complete Chronicle of Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine, Divided into Two Parts.* The first part is published from various handwritten codices; the second from Canisius. The same material from the Augsburg manuscript of the monastery of Saints Afra and Ulrich, together with the Pithou *Chronicle*: all from the revision and with the notes of Jacques Basnage, in the *Thesaurus of Ecclesiastical and Historical Monuments*, or Heinrich Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, arranged according to the order of the centuries. Vol. I, pp. 252–318.

**1732.** Rome, from the press of Antonio de Rossi; octavo. *Some Works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine and Honoratus of Marseille, Illustrated with Notes and Observations by D. Johannes Salinas of Naples, Canon Regular of the Lateran and Lecturer in Sacred Theology, Dedicated to the Most Holy Father Clement XII, Supreme Pontiff.*

This edition of the little works follows the same purpose as the studies of Vincent of Lérins and Hilary of Arles published by him the preceding year: namely, to free these three men from the charge of Semi-Pelagianism. He therefore intended to add a third volume and to demonstrate in a separate dissertation that Vincent, Hilary, and Honoratus did not in fact dissent from orthodox teachers, together with observations he had diligently collected concerning the monastery of Lérins. But death seems to have interrupted his learned reflections.

In this volume he presented several writings of particular importance, from which a judgment could be formed concerning the orthodox doctrine of divine grace: namely, Prosper’s and Hilary’s letters to Augustine, from the Paris edition, with some variant readings drawn from certain Vatican codices; then the poem *On the Ungrateful*, from the same edition, together with a selection of Steyaert’s notes, which are appended there; and finally Honoratus’s *Life of Hilary*, which will be discussed elsewhere.

From the same Paris edition are here reprinted the testimonies of the ancients concerning Saint Prosper, as well as his life compiled from his works and from other ecclesiastical writers, with Salinas’s observations and a chronological synopsis of his works and deeds. This edition was recorded in the *Supplement to the New Acts of the Erudite*, Leipzig, vol. II, p. 17 (1731).

**1740.** Verona; folio. The latter part of Prosper’s *Chronicle*, together with the chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, in Dominicus Vallarsius’s edition of Jerome’s works, vol. VIII, pp. 823–856; in the Venetian edition, vol. VIII, part I, pp. 821–856.

**1744.** Venice; folio. *The Works of Saint Prosper …* I no longer remember where I found this edition recorded. It is undoubtedly a reprint of the Paris edition.

**1758.** Rome, at the press of the Palearini brothers; octavo. *The Complete Works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, Notary of Saint Leo the Great, on the Grace of God and the Free Will of Man and on the Predestination of the Saints.* An extremely carefully corrected edition, prepared with variant readings collected from every source, especially from Vatican manuscript codices, under the direction of P. F. F.

This very handsome edition of Prosper’s little works forms the third part of the *Selected Works of the Holy Fathers on the Grace of God and the Predestination of the Saints*. The editor was Petrus Franciscus Fogginius.

In this volume he included the letters to Saint Augustine and Rufinus; the *Responses to the Chapters of the Gauls*, the *Vincentian Objections*, and the *Excerpts of the Genoese*; the book against the *Collator*; the poem *On the Ungrateful*; the triad of *Epigrams against the Massilians*; and the anthology of *Epigrams from Augustine’s Sentences*—all carefully reproduced from the Paris edition, with not only the variant readings found there but also new ones collected through his own work from Vatican codices.

Moreover, he supplied the poem *On the Ungrateful*, for which he had been unable to find any manuscript copies, as well as the three epigrams commonly appended to it, with continuous scholia drawn from the more extensive notes of Martin Steyaert and the Paris editors. He dedicated the volume to Clement XIII.

**1759.** Rome … duodecimo. *Prosper’s Poem on the Ungrateful and Selected Epigrams.* This is how it is recorded in the Catalogue of the Library of Count Carlo von Firmian, vol. I, p. 53, no. 3027.

## TRANSLATIONS

Apart from the poem *On the Ungrateful*, few of Prosper’s works exist translated into modern languages.

### French

**1647.** Paris, at the shop of the widow Martin Durand; quarto. *Poem of Saint Prosper against the Ungrateful, in Which the Catholic Doctrine of Grace Is Explained and Defended against the Pelagians; Translated into French, in Verse and Prose, with the Verses Placed Beside It, by Louis-Isaac Le Maître de Sacy.* The same translation was reprinted at Paris by Guillaume Desprez and Jean Desessarts in 1717, duodecimo, with the letter to Rufinus and an epitome of the whole Prosperian doctrine concerning grace and free will, drawn from his works.

**1640.** Paris, at the shop of Jean Henault; octavo. *Saint Prosper, On the Calling of the Nations, in Which the Catholic Doctrine of Freedom and Grace Is Declared against the Errors of the Heretics; Translated into French with Reflections, by Father Antoine Girard.*

### Italian

**1586.** Rome; octavo. *Sentences of Saint Prosper on the Promises and Predictions of God, Translated by Giulio Folco*, in *The Miraculous Effects of Almsgiving and Sentences Worthy of Remembrance Relating to It*, collected through the work of Giulio Folco. Argelati, in the place cited below.

### 1751

In Venice, printed by Carlo Pecora; octavo. *The poem of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine on the Ungrateful, or on Grace.* A translation into ottava rima by the abbot Gianfrancesco Giorgetti, dedicated to the most illustrious and most reverend Aluise Foscari, patriarch of Venice and primate of Dalmatia, etc.; with a Dissertation on the Life and Works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, and with philological, historical, and critical annotations.

The Latin text is included. *Novelle Lett. di Firenze*, 1751, 24 September, p. 610; and *Nov. Lett. di Venezia*, no. 44, p. 345; and Argelati, who derived his account from these, in *Biblioteca degli Volgarizzatori*, vol. III, p. 303.

### 1753

In Venice, at the press of Simone Occhi; octavo. *The Thousand Latin Verses of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine against the Semi-Pelagians*, translated into Italian verse by Father Carl’Agostino Ansaldi of the Order of Preachers, among the Arcadians of the Colony of Trebbia, Clomoneo.

This translator also supplied the Latin text and notes in the lower margin. Argelati, in the work cited.

### 1756

In Brescia, printed by Giammaria Rizzardi; large quarto. *A Systematic Investigation of the Text and Thought of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine in His Poem against the Ungrateful.*

Besides the poem *On the Ungrateful*, it also contains two epigrams by Prosper against a detractor of Augustine and an epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies—all in Latin according to the text of the Paris edition, with Latin marginal notes; on the facing page there is an Italian translation, with the same marginal material translated and with critical, historical, and theological notes written in the same language. To these is appended the investigation promised in the title, which, apart from its introduction and conclusion, consists of seventy annotations or chapters. Thus the poems themselves, together with various questions concerning the poet and his genius, [Col. 0062A] as well as the Massilian Semi-Pelagians, are marked as an apparatus to the investigation. The author, Viator of Coccaleo (Viator of Coccaglio), a Capuchin, skillfully addressed his discourse to lovers of Prosper’s doctrine; otherwise, no one could easily say for whom these writings were intended. He dedicated the volume to Cardinal Domenico Passioneo.

### 1760

In Brescia, from the press of Giambattista Bossini; quarto. *The Philosophical . . . Theological . . . Ascetical Spirit of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine in His Epigrams.*

The author is the same Viator of Coccaleo, and the spirit is the same as in the *Commentaries*, but the volume is more substantial. Each Latin epigram is followed by an Italian translation, which is usually extremely lengthy—not treating of the art of the poem or of its meaning, but proceeding from the author’s own ingenuity on the same subject touched upon by the poet [Col. 0062B], as though it were a commentary on the given text. He dedicated the work to Carlo Vittorio Amedeo, Cardinal delle Lanze, archbishop of Nicosia and confessor to the king of Sardinia.

### 1764

In Verona, printed by Agostino Caraltoni; quarto. *The poem of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, secretary of Saint Leo the Great, on the Ungrateful, or Semi-Pelagians, rendered into Italian unrhymed verse by the most reverend Father Don Francesco Maria Ricci, a Roman Benedictine abbot . . . of Monte Cassino.*

Opposite the Italian translation the Latin text is printed, together with annotations and variant readings. But all these materials were taken from the Paris edition. The editor dedicated his translation to Nicolò [Col. 0062C] Antonio Giustiniani, bishop of Verona.

### 1764. Manuscripts from which Prosper’s writings were either first published or subsequently corrected

I. The manuscript codex of the Benedictines of Mount Saint James at Mainz, from which the Mainz edition of 1524 was produced.

II. The aids which Sotellus obtained from manuscript exemplars were few, and have been indicated above by us.

III. John Olivarius mentions only one Cambron manuscript, from which he made numerous corrections in Prosper’s text. But, among Prosper’s genuine writings, it contained only the *Epigrams*; of the others, it contained the books *On the Contemplative Life* and *On the Calling of All Nations*.

IV. The manuscripts of the Benedictine editors of the works of Saint Augustine.

[Col. 0062D] 1. The Corbie codex, from which they corrected the book *Against the Collator*. It had been written approximately nine hundred years earlier. Its title was: *The Book of Saint Prosper for the Preachers of the Grace of God, against the Book of the Presbyter Cassian, Which Is Entitled On the Protection of God.*

2. The Remigius codex, concerning which see below under no. 4.

3. The Colbert codex of the *Sentences Extracted from Augustine*, marked no. 303. It was not especially ancient and contained no more than seventy-six sentences—namely, the first eighteen, then, with the nineteenth omitted, the twentieth, twenty-first, and others selected from the subsequent series. In the printed editions there are three hundred and ninety.

V. The Paris editors had the following manuscripts available:

[Col. 0063A] 1. Codices of the Royal Library of Paris. From one of them they corrected the letter to Augustine and the *Responses to the Chapters of Objections of the Gauls*, as well as the *Sentences Extracted from the Works of Augustine* and, in the Appendix, the two books *On the Contemplative Life*.

2. The Remigian-Reims codex, that is, the codex of the Abbey of Saint Remigius of the Order of Saint Benedict at Reims, from which variant readings had been sent to them. Numerous books were corrected from it, namely the letter to Rufinus, the *Responses to the Objections of the Gauls*, the Vincentian objections, and the Genoese excerpts; the book *Against the Collator*; and the book of *Sentences Extracted from the Works of Augustine*. Nor does the codex from which they received the variants for the book *On Promises and Predictions* appear to have been different from this one, although it may seem strange that an indication of its age was added only to this codex and not likewise to the preceding books. For it is said to be more than eight hundred years old and to have been written in the ninth century through the work of the monks Leutbert and Adelold. But the Benedictine editors of Augustine say similar things about the Remigian codex, with which they collated all the works of Prosper just mentioned, affirming that it was written approximately nine hundred years earlier. Unless, perhaps, this reckoning must be taken in the strictest sense, and the Remigian codex praised in connection with the *Responses to the Chapters of the Vincentian Objections*—said to have been written approximately eight hundred years earlier—is a different codex.

3. The Joly codex, which had formerly belonged to Claude Joly, preceptor and canon of the metropolitan church, and which, through his bequest, had come to the chapter of that church. [Col. 0063C] The editors examined it completely, from beginning to end, and used it for the letter to Rufinus, the *Responses* [Col. 0064A] to the Objections of the Gauls, the Vincentian objections, and the Genoese excerpts; the book *Against the Collator*; the book of *Sentences Extracted from Augustine*; the book of *Epigrams*; the *Confession*; the poem *On the Spouse to His Wife*; and, from the Appendix, the books *On the Contemplative Life* and the *Pseudo-Chronicle*.

4. Codices of the Colbert Library. One was useful for the letter to Rufinus, three for the book of *Epigrams*, and five for the complete and spurious *Chronicle*. In two of them, Prosper’s true *Chronicle* was appended to the chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome; in the other three, the *Pseudo-Chronicle* was appended. Finally, four codices of the same library were collated with the books *On the Contemplative Life* in the Appendix.

5. The manuscript codex of Théodoric, that is, of the monastery [Col. 0064B] of Saint-Thierry near Reims, whose variants for the complete *Chronicle* had been sent to them from that monastery. Besides these, there was also:

6. The Victorine codex of the *Pseudo-Chronicle*, from which Pithou had drawn material; it was examined again for the same book.

VI. Vatican codices, from which Salinasius excerpted variants for the letter to Augustine. Because of the deficiencies of his edition, I have no information about them.

VII. The codices of Foggini. He possessed several Vatican manuscripts of excellent quality. He expressly praises one approximately eight hundred years old, marked no. 558, which had formerly belonged to the Grand Chartreuse and, among other works, contained Saint Prosper’s *Responses to the Chapters of the Gauls*, the Vincentian objections, the Genoese excerpts, [Col. 0064C] the *Epigrams*, and the book *Against the Collator*.

# The First Part of All the Works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, Containing the Genuine Works of the Holy Father

[Col. 0063]

## Notice on the Letter of Saint Prosper to Saint Augustine

Since Saint Augustine had spent the greater part of his life refuting heretics of various kinds, and, after securing for the Church a complete victory over the Arians, Manichaeans, and Donatists, had most recently confronted the Pelagian heresy, hostile to the grace of God, he did not cease vigorously combating it from the year 412 onward in his books *On the Remission of Sins*, *On the Baptism of Infants*, and other works, as opportunity presented itself in subsequent years, until, condemned by several councils of bishops and decrees of the supreme pontiffs, it began to lose its strength and the number of its defenders began to decline.

But in the final years of the most holy Doctor’s life, certain men arose—otherwise Catholic, but either less learned and insufficiently practiced in the Scriptures from which Augustine had drawn his doctrine, or perhaps thinking of themselves less humbly than they ought—who, after reading Augustine’s books, were either disturbed or even scandalized. The disturbances that had arisen among the monks at Hadrumetum in Africa, who obeyed Abbot Valentine, were readily quieted both by the book *On Grace and Free Will* and by another, *On Rebuke and Grace*, whose light dispelled the clouds of doubt that had covered their minds.

Yet another offshoot of the Pelagian heresy created far greater harm to the Church, especially in Gaul. It spread much more widely and struck deeper roots precisely because, at first sight, it appeared less injurious to the grace of Christ the Savior, which it also seemed to magnify to no small degree. Some beginnings of it had appeared with the new teaching of Vitalis, an otherwise Catholic man who, because he had been educated in the Church of Carthage, owed a particular veneration to the teaching of Saint Cyprian, bishop of that city. Augustine nevertheless complained that he had rashly departed from it (*Letter* 217). The holy Doctor did not believe Vitalis to be a Pelagian heretic, but he had heard that he was not so completely orthodox that none of that error had reached him or remained in him. For the Pelagians, as Augustine writes to him there, attribute everything belonging to the faithful and devout life of human beings to free choice of the will in such a way that they think it must be sought from ourselves, not from the Lord. Vitalis, however, did not want the beginning of faith—where the beginning of good, that is, devout, willing also lies—to be a gift of God; rather, he maintained that we possess it from ourselves, so that we begin to believe. He did agree that God grants the other goods of the religious life by his grace to those who already ask, seek, and knock through faith. Augustine refutes this error of Vitalis, which those called Semi-Pelagians also embraced, chiefly on the grounds that the Church offers prayers to God for unbelievers, so that they may be converted, and offers thanksgiving for those same people once converted to the faith; likewise, she offers prayers for believers, so that they may persevere, by God’s gift, in what they have begun to be. This letter to Vitalis appears to have been written after the disagreement among the Hadrumetine monks and the books published to settle it, and should be assigned to the year 426 or 427.

When these later works of Augustine had been disseminated far and wide, there were not a few people at Massilia and elsewhere in Gaul who, through ignorance, persuaded themselves that whatever Augustine had written in his books against the Pelagians concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s good pleasure was wholly contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and the judgment of the Church (see below, in Saint Prosper’s letter to Augustine, no. 2). They thought that this teaching implanted negligence and indifference alike in saints and sinners, because, however they might conduct themselves, nothing other than what God had determined could happen to them. Therefore, even if the doctrine were entirely true, it should nevertheless not be made public, since, although it was not at all necessary, it would produce exceedingly dangerous effects and render the exhortations of those who encouraged others vain and ineffectual.

Their alienation from that Catholic doctrine, from which they drew such offensive consequences, drove them into the celebrated errors of the Semi-Pelagians—a name which they rightly earned. For at first they held better and more orthodox views; but, lacking definite rules and foundations, they shifted their minds and opinions now in one direction, now in another (ibid., no. 6). They thought that the beginning of faith and perseverance to the end were so subject to our power that they were not gifts of God; or that God gave only such perseverance as a person could abandon by his own will (Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, book II, chapter 17, no. 48). There were also those who departed so little from the paths of the Pelagians that they seemed to recognize no other grace than reason and free will, given by the Creator to a person who had merited nothing beforehand (see below, Saint Prosper’s letter to Augustine, no. 4).

Nevertheless, the men who embraced these errors were distinguished among their contemporaries. Through their devotion to every virtue and the reputation for uprightness by which they shone, they had acquired great authority among the simple. Yet no one is more exposed to receiving the impious doctrines of the Pelagians—unless they guard themselves against themselves—than such men; nor are there generally any who more readily abuse God’s gifts by becoming inflated because of them and attributing them to themselves than those who have been heaped with the greatest number of gifts by him.

That plague had seized a large part of the servants of Christ at Massilia, that is, the monks. No one is unaware that John Cassian, who had established the monastery there, propagated this same error in his writings, especially in the thirteenth *Conference*, which he published around the year 426 (see below, Appendix, part II, p. 272), namely, one year after Valentinian III had ordered the Gallic bishops who followed the doctrines of Pelagius to resign and be expelled. Moreover, the error gained considerable authority from the fact that some of those who defended it had recently attained the highest priestly dignity, namely, the episcopate. Hilary himself, bishop of Arles, who had succeeded Honoratus toward the end of 428, was otherwise a follower and admirer of Augustine’s doctrine; nevertheless, he was troubled by matters concerning predestination and raised some complaints about them. On this subject he wished to compare his thoughts with the holy Doctor.

The authority of such distinguished men, so eminent in the Church both for piety and for dignity, made their error more dangerous both to themselves and to others. The reverence owed to them drew the unlearned into imitation and at the same time restrained the tongues of the more knowledgeable in an unprofitable silence. Thus scarcely anyone could be found who would either admonish them or oppose the error they taught, except for a few fearless lovers of perfect grace (see below, Saint Prosper’s letter to Augustine, no. 7). Saint Prosper and a certain Hilary—different from the bishop of Arles—belonged to this number. Prosper was of the lay order, as we shall demonstrate more fully below, in the notice on his letter to Saint Augustine, which follows immediately after the one under discussion.

Saint Prosper, who later succeeded Augustine in the task and labor of defending grace, was an Aquitanian, a scholastically educated man—that is, exceptionally learned—and altogether distinguished in character, eloquence, and zeal, and not unworthy of Saint Augustine’s acquaintance. Although he indicates in some way that he himself belonged only to the lay order, when he admits that he was in no way the equal of the aforementioned Semi-Pelagians, who surpassed him greatly both in the merits of their lives and in the highest priestly dignity (Gennadius, *Catalogue*, chapter 84).

He had never seen Augustine, but had greeted him only through a courteous letter sent by the deacon Leontius, through whom he had also received the holy bishop’s reply. We rightly lament that the letters exchanged between the two men no longer survive. Nevertheless, Prosper, instructed both by his diligent reading of Augustine’s works and by heavenly revelation, recognized that it was utterly perverse to deny predestination and prevenient grace and to say that the beginning of salvation rests with the one who is saved, not with the one who saves; or that the human will produces assistance for divine grace, rather than grace subjecting the human will to itself. Disregarding the hostile efforts of others, he not only remained steadfast in this faith but also defended it against its opponents, using both the works of the holy Doctor and the scriptural testimonies cited there, as well as arguments that he himself derived from the foundations laid by Augustine. He fought with powerful reasoning and those vigorous assertions in which, according to Gennadius’ testimony also, he himself was strong.

At the beginning of this dispute, the Massilians for a time preferred to blame their own slowness rather than condemn a doctrine they did not understand. Indeed, some among them wished to consult Augustine and asked him to give a clearer and more explicit explanation on the subject. But, by the merciful will of God, it happened that the book *On Rebuke and Grace* was brought to Massilia at that time. In that book, the monks of Hadrumetum received such a full and definitive answer to the very issues that were troubling the Massilians that the book seemed to have been written to settle the disturbances of contention that had arisen in Gaul.

When the book was read, those who followed Augustine’s apostolic doctrine drew from it new light and greater resources for defending it. Others, however, whose minds had already been occupied by error and were obstructed by their own darkness, found there nothing but further grounds for offense and a fiercer hatred of the truth. They defended their opinion in the name of antiquity and branded the doctrine of predestination with the stigma of novelty. They said that no one had ever understood the relevant passages of Paul in this way. When asked how they themselves wished to explain them, they admitted that no interpretation that pleased them really occurred to them; but they ordered silence concerning matters whose profundity no one had reached. They produced statements from Augustine’s works composed before the Pelagian heresy, as though these fully agreed with their own opinion. Indeed, they vigorously repeated for themselves everything that Augustine had opposed to them in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*. But what displeased them most was the distinction made there between the grace given to Adam and the grace now given to us. Finally, they did not want the example of predestination to be taken from infants, concerning whom Augustine himself had previously held a different opinion in his books *On Free Will*.

When the defenders of the truth were being pressed by the authority of those whom the spirit of Pelagian impiety so mocked, they were compelled to ask the holy bishop to oppose his own authority to theirs. Hilary wrote him two letters on this matter. The first, now lost, perhaps referred to that offensive formula concerning the preaching of predestination which Augustine says his opponents had brought against him (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, book II, chapter 22, no. 57). In the second, after Hilary had dealt with the complaints of the opponents, he says: “Whatever you may wish or be able to do on behalf of that grace which we, the little with the great, admire in you, we shall receive with the greatest gratitude, as though it had been decreed by an authority most dear and most revered by us.” He also indicates that he had urged Prosper to write on the same matter, and that he was sending Prosper’s letter jointly with his own. These are the letters of Prosper which we present here. At its beginning, Prosper declares that he is writing to the holy Doctor not merely from a desire to greet him, as he had done in a previous letter, but also out of devotion to the faith by which the Church lives.

“For,” he says, “your most vigilant diligence keeps watch over all the members of Christ’s body, and the strength of truth fights against the snares of heretical doctrines. I therefore thought that I need in no way fear being burdensome or importunate to you in a matter that concerns the salvation of many and consequently your piety; rather, I believed that I should be guilty if I did not refer to the special patron of the faith matters which I understand to be exceedingly dangerous.”

After setting forth the considerable virulence contained in those remnants of Pelagian depravity, he adds: “We hope that not only our weakness will be strengthened by the support of your discussions, but that those themselves whom the darkness of this opinion obscures, though distinguished by merit and honors, will receive the clearest light of grace.”

This letter of Saint Prosper was written in the year 428 or 429, during the period when Hilary presided over the Church of Arles, as appears from no. 9. Hilary had been a monk of Lérins before being made bishop of Arles after Honoratus, who died at the beginning of 428 or 429. For Honoratus succeeded Patroclus, who was killed in 426, according to Prosper’s *Chronicle*, and, according to Honoratus of Massilia in the *Life of Hilary of Arles*, occupied the see of Arles for two years.

[Col. 0067]

# Letter of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine to Augustine

[Note: [Col. 0067B] It was written in the year 428 or 429.]

Concerning the remnants of the Pelagian heresy beginning to sprout in Gaul, and concerning the complaints of such men against the doctrine of predestination and grace as explained in Augustine’s works, especially the book *On Rebuke and Grace*.

[Col. 0067A]

**To the most blessed pope, ineffably wondrous, incomparably venerable, most excellent patron, Augustine: Prosper.**

### 1

1. Although unknown to you in face, I have nevertheless become known to you to some extent, if you remember, in mind and speech; for through my holy brother Leontius the deacon I sent letters and received a reply. Even now I dare to write to your Blessedness, not merely from the desire to greet you, as at that time, but also out of devotion to the faith by which the Church lives.

For your most vigilant diligence keeps watch over all the members of Christ’s body, and the strength of truth fights against the snares of heretical doctrines. I therefore thought that I need in no way fear being burdensome or importunate to you in a matter that concerns the salvation of many and consequently your piety; [Col. 0067B] rather, I believed that I should be guilty if I did not refer to the special patron of the faith matters which I understand to be exceedingly dangerous.

[Note: [Col. 0067B] Four manuscripts read *epistulam*, “a letter.” This letter does not survive.]

### 2

Many servants of Christ who reside in the city of Massilia think that, in your writings composed against the Pelagian heretics, whatever you have argued concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose is contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding.

[Note: “Servants of Christ,” that is, monks; the most renowned of them was John Cassian, author of the *Conferences*, later refuted by Prosper himself in his book *Against the Collator*.]

For some time they preferred to blame their own slowness rather than criticize what they did not understand; and some of them wished to request from your Blessedness a clearer and more explicit explanation on this matter. It happened, through the disposition of God’s mercy, that, when certain men in Africa had raised similar questions, [Col. 0068A] you published the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, full of divine authority.

[Note: [Col. 0068B] That is, the monks of Hadrumetum.]

[Note: [Col. 0068B] It is found below, Appendix, part II, p. 221.]

When it was brought to our attention at an unexpectedly opportune moment, we thought that all the complaints of those who resisted would be silenced, because there every question on which your holiness was to be consulted had been answered so fully and completely—as though you had taken special care to settle the matters that had been thrown into confusion among us.

But when this book of your Blessedness had been read, those who had previously followed the holy and apostolic authority of your teaching became much more intelligent and better instructed; whereas those who were obstructed by the darkness of their own persuasion withdrew more hostile than before.

Their violently abrupt dissent must first be feared for their own sake, lest the spirit of Pelagian impiety mock men so distinguished and so outstanding in their devotion to every virtue; [Note: [Col. 0069D] This word is absent from two Royal manuscripts and the Colbert manuscript, but plainly through a scribal omission, as will be clear to the reader of the passage.] and then lest the simpler people, who hold these men in great reverence because of their reputation for uprightness, consider it safest for themselves to accept what they hear asserted by those whose authority they follow without judgment.

### 3

For this is their definition and profession: Every human being sinned when Adam sinned; and no one is saved through his own works, but through the grace of God in regeneration. Yet the propitiation that is offered in the sacrament of Christ’s blood has been set before all human beings without exception, so that whoever wishes to approach faith and baptism may be saved.

Those who will believe, and those who will remain in that faith—which thereafter is to be assisted by God’s grace—God foresaw before the foundation of the world and predestined for his kingdom. He foresaw that, having been called freely, they would become worthy of election and would depart this life with a good end.

Therefore every human being is admonished by divine instructions to believe and hope, so that no one may despair of attaining eternal life, since a reward is prepared for voluntary devotion.

But this purpose of God’s calling—in which, whether before the beginning of the world or at the very creation of the human race, a distinction is said to have been made between those to be chosen and those to be rejected, so that, according to what pleased the Creator, some were created vessels of honor and others vessels of dishonor—both deprives the fallen of concern for rising again and gives the saints an occasion for indifference. For in either case labor is superfluous if neither can the rejected enter by any diligence nor the elect fall away through any negligence.

However they may conduct themselves, nothing other than what God has determined can happen to them; and a course of action cannot remain steady under uncertain hope, since, if the election of the predestining God has determined something else, the striving of the one who acts is vain.

Thus all diligence is removed and the virtues are abolished if God’s decree precedes human wills. Under the name of predestination, a kind of fatal necessity is introduced; or else the Lord is said to be the creator of different natures, if no one can be other than what he was made.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] One Royal manuscript reads, “has been made.”]

[Note: [Col. 0070D] So read two Royal manuscripts and one Colbert manuscript, as well as the recent edition of this letter in volume X of Saint Augustine’s works; other copies read, “And so that.”]

To state their opinion more briefly and fully: whatever your Blessedness opposed to yourself in this book from the perspective of those who contradict you, and whatever you also most powerfully refuted under this question in the books against Julian, all this is proclaimed by these holy men with the greatest insistence as supporting their position.

When we produce your Blessedness’s writings against them, equipped with the strongest and countless testimonies of the divine Scriptures, and, following the form of your arguments, establish something by which they too may be refuted, [Col. 0070A] they defend their obstinacy by appeal to antiquity. They assert that the passages brought from the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans to manifest the divine grace that precedes the merits of the elect have never been understood by any ecclesiastical writer in the sense in which they are now understood.

When we ask them to explain those passages according to whatever interpretations they prefer, they declare that they find no interpretation that pleases them, and they demand silence concerning matters whose depth no one has reached.

At last their entire obstinacy descends to the point that they define our faith as contrary to the edification of those who hear it, and therefore say that, even if it is true, it should not be proclaimed: because doctrines that are dangerously handed down ought not to be accepted, while matters that cannot be understood may be silenced without danger.

[Note: [Col. 0070D] One Royal manuscript reads, “and something else also.”]

### 4

Some of these men depart so little from the paths of the Pelagians that, although they are compelled to confess that grace in Christ precedes all human merits—for if it were given in response to merits, it would be called grace in vain—they nevertheless want the following condition to belong to every human being: that the Creator’s grace establishes each person, who, since he did not yet exist, had previously merited nothing, as a rational being possessing free will. Through the discernment of good and evil, and toward knowledge of God and obedience to his commandments, this grace enables the person to direct his will and to attain the grace by which we are reborn in Christ—namely, through his natural capacity, by asking, seeking, and knocking.

Thus he receives, finds, and enters for this reason: because, having made good use of nature’s goodness, he has merited, through the assistance of initial grace, to attain this saving grace.

They define the purpose of calling grace entirely in this way: God has decreed that no one be received into his kingdom except through the sacrament of regeneration, and that all human beings universally be called to this gift of salvation, whether through natural law, written law, or evangelical preaching. Thus those who wish may become children of God, while those who do not wish to be believers may be without excuse.

For, they say, God’s justice appears in this, that those who do not believe perish; his goodness appears in this, that he rejects no one from life but indiscriminately wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

Here they bring forward testimonies in which the exhortation of the divine Scriptures incites human wills to obey. They think that, because people act by free choice either by doing what is commanded or by neglecting it, it follows that, since the transgressor is said not to have obeyed because he did not wish to obey, the believer likewise must be understood to have been devout because he wished to be.

They hold that each person has as much capacity for good as for evil, and that with equal force the mind can move itself either toward vices or toward virtues: God’s grace supports the person who desires good, while just condemnation receives the person who pursues evil.

[Col. 0071A] 5

When, amid all this, the innumerable multitude of infants is brought before them—infants who, apart from original sin, under which all human beings are born alike into the condemnation of the first man, have as yet no wills and no actions of their own, yet are separated without God’s judgment being absent—some being taken away from the use of this life before discerning good and evil and, through regeneration, received as heirs of the heavenly kingdom, while others, without baptism, pass into eternal death as its debtors, they say that such infants are lost and such infants are saved according to what divine knowledge foresaw they would become in more mature years, if they were preserved until the age of active life.

They do not consider that, although they want God’s grace to be the companion rather than the precursor of human merits, they nevertheless subject it even to those wills which, according to their own fantasy, they do not deny were preceded by grace.

But they subject God’s election to every imaginary merit to such an extent that they fabricate past things that do not exist and future things that will not come to pass; among them, by a new kind of absurdity, things not to be done are foreknown, and things foreknown are not done.

They appear to establish this knowledge of God concerning human merits—according to which the grace that calls operates—in a much more rational way when they come to consider those nations which either in past ages were left to walk in their own ways (Acts 14:15), or even now perish in the impiety of their ancient ignorance, with no illumination of either the Law or the Gospel having shone upon them.

Yet, insofar as a door has been opened to preachers and a way has been made, the people of the nations who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death have seen a great light (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16); those who once were not a people have become the people of God; and those toward whom he once showed no mercy have now received mercy (Hosea 2:24; Romans 9:25).

They say that the Lord foresaw which people would believe, and that times and the ministries of teachers were so distributed to each nation that the faith of good wills was destined to arise.

Nor, they say, is the statement that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4) undermined, since those are without excuse who could have been instructed by natural intelligence in the worship of the one true God but did not hear the Gospel because they would not have received it.

[Col. 0071D] 6. Our Lord Jesus Christ died for the entire human race, and absolutely no one was excluded from redemption by his blood, even if someone passes through this whole life with a mind utterly alien to him, because the sacrament of divine mercy pertains to all human beings. For this reason many are not renewed, because they are foreknown not to have the will to be renewed. Thus, insofar as God is concerned, eternal life has been prepared for all; but insofar as freedom of choice is concerned, it is grasped by those who willingly believe in God and receive the help of grace as a reward for their faith.

Those whose opposition distresses us have committed themselves all the more decisively to this proclamation of such grace, although they previously held better opinions, because, if they confessed that all good merits are preceded by grace and are granted by grace so that they may exist, they would necessarily have to admit that God, according to the purpose and counsel of his will, by a hidden judgment and manifest action, makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. IX, 21), since no one is justified except through grace and no one is born except in transgression.

But they shrink from confessing this and fear to ascribe the merits of the saints to divine action. Nor do they accept that the number of the elect has been predestined and can be neither increased nor diminished, lest the exhortations that encourage unbelievers and the negligent have no place among them, and the command to industry and labor prove superfluous, since effort would be frustrated if election ceased. For, they say, each person can be summoned to correction or progress only if he knows that by his own diligence he can become good, and that his freedom is therefore aided by God if he chooses what God commands.

And so, since in those who have received the time of free will there are two things that effect human salvation—namely, God’s grace and human obedience—they wish obedience to precede grace, so that the beginning of salvation is believed to depend on the one who is saved, not on the one who saves; and they want the human will to procure for itself the help of divine grace, rather than grace to subject the human will to itself.

7. Although, through God’s mercy revealing it and through your blessedness instructing us, we know this to be utterly perverse, we may indeed be steadfast in refusing to believe it, but we are not equal to the authority of those who hold such views. They greatly surpass us in the merits of their lives, and some of them have recently risen above us by attaining the highest priestly office [Note: In the manuscripts, “of the highest.”]. Few, except those fearless lovers of perfect grace, have dared to oppose the disputations of such superiors.

Hence the danger has increased not only for those who listen to them but also for those who are listened to, together with their dignities. Reverence for them either restrains many into useless silence or leads them into thoughtless assent; and what is scarcely challenged by anyone appears to them most beneficial.

Therefore, since in these remnants of Pelagian perversity a measure of no ordinary virulence is being nourished [Note: Two Regius manuscripts and the Colbertinus read, “if in these things.”], if the beginning of salvation is wrongly assigned to human beings; if human will is impiously preferred to the divine will, so that someone is helped because he willed, rather than willing because he is helped; if someone who is originally evil is wrongly believed to begin his reception of good not from the supreme Good but from himself [Note: One Regius manuscript reads, “the correction of good”]; if God is believed to be pleased by anything other than what he himself has granted—then, most blessed pope and excellent father, grant us in this matter, with the Lord’s help, as much of your devoted diligence as you can, so that you may deign to explain with the clearest expositions what in these questions is more obscure and more difficult to grasp [Note: The editions of S. Prosper add here “I beg”; it is absent from the manuscripts].

7–8. First, since many do not think that Christian faith is violated by this disagreement, make clear how much danger lies in their persuasion. Then explain how free choice is not impeded by this grace that works beforehand and cooperates; and whether God’s foreknowledge remains according to his purpose in such a way that the very things that are purposed are to be understood as foreknown; or whether these matters vary according to kinds of causes and classes of persons—so that, because callings differ, in those who are saved without doing anything it may seem that God’s purpose alone is operative, whereas in those who are going to do something good the purpose may stand through foreknowledge.

Or is it rather the case that, uniformly, although foreknowledge cannot be separated from purpose by a temporal distinction, foreknowledge nevertheless rests [Note: One Regius manuscript reads “firmly supported.”] upon purpose in a certain order? And just as there is nothing whatever in any undertaking that divine knowledge has not preceded, so there is nothing good that has flowed into our participation without God as its author.

Finally, explain how, through this proclamation of God’s purpose—by which those who are ordained to eternal life become believers—none of those who ought to be exhorted is hindered, nor given an opportunity for negligence if they despair of being predestined.

We also ask you patiently to bear with our ignorance and demonstrate how this objection may be answered: when the opinions of earlier writers on this subject are reconsidered, nearly all of them appear to have one and the same view, namely, that they understood God’s purpose and predestination according to foreknowledge. Thus, they say, God made some vessels of honor and others of dishonor because he foresaw the end of each person and, under the assistance of grace, foreknew what each person’s will and action would be [pp. 0073C–0074A].

9. When all these matters, and many others that you can see more clearly through a deeper insight as pertaining to this case, have been disentangled, we believe and hope that not only will our weakness be strengthened by the support of your discussions, but that those themselves whose merits and honors are obscured by the darkness of this opinion will receive the most purified light of grace.

For your blessedness should know that one man of outstanding authority and spiritual devotion, the holy Hilary, bishop of Arles [Note: Learned men thought that “Honoratus” should be read instead of “Hilary”; but all the manuscripts that have been examined read “Hilary.” This Hilary, formerly a monk of Lérins, became bishop of Arles after Honoratus, in the year 428 or at the beginning of 429. Honoratus succeeded Patroclus, who was killed in 426 according to Prosper’s Chronicle, and, as Honoratus of Marseille states in his Life of Hilary of Arles, occupied the see of Arles for two years], is in every other respect an admirer and follower of your teaching, and for some time has wished to compare his view with yours in a letter concerning the matter about which he raises a complaint.

But since it is uncertain whether he will do this, or for what purpose he will do it, and since, by God’s grace providing for this present age, the weariness of us all breathes again in the vigor of your charity and knowledge [Note: The editions read “hopes”; one manuscript reads “breathes”], add instruction to the humble and correction to the proud.

It is necessary and useful to write what has been written, lest something be considered insignificant because it is not frequently rebuked. For they think something sound when it does not hurt; they do not feel the wound beneath the skin that has grown over it [Note: The manuscripts read, “because they do not grieve, nor feel the wound covered by skin.”]. But let them understand that what has a persistent swelling will eventually reach the point of incision.

May the grace of God and the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ crown you at all times and glorify you forever as you walk from virtue to virtue, most blessed lord pope, ineffably admirable, incomparably honorable, most excellent patron. [Note: The old Paris edition places two short works here, without any proper justification except perhaps the similarity and near connection of their subject matter, between Prosper’s works: namely, the letter of Hilary of Arles to Augustine and Augustine’s book On the Gift of Perseverance. Since we have already published them among the works of Augustine, volumes II and X (XXXIII and XLIV of our Patrology), the kindly reader is referred there. EDITOR.]

## [LETTER TO RUFINUS]

[Col. 0073]

## NOTICE ON THE LETTER OF ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE TO RUFINUS

Three matters may be investigated concerning the letter to Rufinus: first, who this Rufinus was to whom the letter was sent; second, at what time it was written; and third, on what occasion and under what necessity St. Prosper was compelled to write it.

As for Rufinus and who he was, among the many persons of this name known around that time it is not easy to decide, nor have we so far found anyone who has established the matter with certainty. Certainly he was a friend of our St. Prosper, one of those whom friendship founded upon spiritual charity makes concerned for the salvation of their friends.

Thus, when he had heard confused rumors about the disputes raised against the teaching of St. Augustine and had learned that his very dear friend Prosper was being spoken of unfavorably by many, he feared that the salvation of a soul so dear to him might be endangered. Yet he did not dare condemn him precipitately without hearing him. He therefore thought it better to approach him by letter, since perhaps the great distance between them prevented him from doing so in person, and he entrusted the letter to a mutual friend for delivery.

Unless perhaps you prefer to suppose that he gave the traveling friend the instruction to explain in person, without a written document, the pious concern he bore for his friend. Neither possibility can be established with certainty, but one or the other certainly seems to have occurred on the basis of the opening words of St. Prosper’s letter:

“I received,” he says, “through our mutual friend, signs of your brotherly concern for me, and I gladly recognized the care of your most sincere charity. And lest the malicious rumors, insofar as they cannot withdraw themselves from your ears, should bring you fear or anxiety, I have taken care to free you from every scruple, so far as was possible in an epistolary manner. I have been eager to disclose everything to you with the fullest truth, so that, since you were unable to hear completely what is being spread by our opponents, you may through me personally learn whatever is said and repeated about us to stir up empty hatred.”

Concerning the time when this was written, it may be asserted with certainty that it was composed while Augustine was still alive, but during the final years of so great a teacher. This is made certain by the words of the letter: “The most blessed Augustine, certainly at this time the foremost portion of the Lord’s priests”; and near the end of the letter: “So that the preaching of the foremost man in the Church at this time…” The final years of the holy doctor’s life are clearly indicated by the Gallic detractors and slanderers who accused the works of St. Augustine, especially those whom the reading of his book On Correction and Grace, written around the year 426 or 427 for the instruction and correction of the monks of Hadrumetum, most offended.

Prosper portrays these same men when he adds:

“Amid so many palms of contest and so many crowns of triumph, for the illumination of the Church and for the glory of Christ, by whose radiance he himself has been illumined, certain of our own people—something deeply to be lamented in them—slander him in whispers that are secret but not unknown. Whenever they find ears that are subject and receptive to them, they defame his writings, by which the Pelagian error is attacked, saying that he completely removes free choice and preaches fatal necessity under the name of grace. They add that he wishes two masses of the human race and two natures to be believed, so that the impiety of pagans and Manichaeans may be attributed to a man of such piety.”

He also seems to indicate Cassian’s Thirteenth Conference, which concerns the protection of God, when he says:

“For, wishing to glory in their own righteousness rather than in the grace of God, they are displeased that we resist what they asserted against a man of the highest authority in the midst of many Conferences.”

Since this Conference is read as having been dedicated to Honoratus of Marseille and six others, it is shown to have been written before the year 426, when Honoratus was made bishop of Marseille.

This, then, was the occasion—as has already been suggested—for St. Prosper’s writing the letter: Rufinus had indicated that he was disturbed by the rumors disseminated by the enemies of the teaching of St. Augustine against the reputation of Prosper, Augustine’s disciple, and wished to be freed from this scruple.

Seeking to comply with his friend’s just request, St. Prosper explains more fully what rumors were being spread by the enemies of St. Augustine’s teaching and under what pretext they were not afraid to attack so great a teacher. One of the chief errors of the Pelagians, he says, was that the grace of God is given according to human merits; once they preserved this principle intact, they could easily revive their other doctrines.

At first they had taught that human nature possessed such health that it could fulfill the good through free choice alone. When this was plainly contrary to sound doctrine and the dogma had been rejected by all Catholics, they professed that grace was necessary for beginning, progressing, and persevering in the good. But they understood this confession of God’s grace to mean only that grace was a kind of teacher of free choice: through exhortations, through the law, through teaching, through contemplation of creatures, through miracles, and through external terrors, grace displays itself to the judgment of free choice, so that each person, according to the movement of his will, may find if he seeks, receive if he asks, and enter if he knocks.

From this it followed that grace was given according to human merits, and therefore was no longer grace.

St. Prosper shows that this cunning of the sons of darkness was exposed by the judgment of the Eastern bishops, the authority of the apostolic see, and the vigilance of the African bishops. St. Augustine—whom St. Prosper calls at that time the foremost portion of the Lord’s priests—destroyed it in polemical writings and utterly defeated such a heresy. Nevertheless, certain Catholics in Gaul were found who defamed his teaching and books through malicious rumors, saying that he completely removed free choice and preached fatal necessity under the name of grace, and that he wished two natures to be believed to exist in one human being.

If these accusations were true, such men would oppose him openly and refute the harmful errors in writing; they would not attempt to injure a man by secret whispers. Augustine’s teaching, after all, agreed with the teaching of the Roman Church, the African Church, and indeed all Catholics throughout the world.

These men were driven to such boldness because they were distressed that resistance was offered to what they had brought forward in their Conferences against Augustine’s teaching. Nor was it unknown to them that, if such matters were raised in any gathering of priests, hundreds of volumes by the most blessed Augustine would confront them. Those books abundantly proved that, whenever we have done anything good, we should glory in nothing other than the grace of Christ the Lord, not in the powers of free choice.

Nevertheless, Prosper hoped from the riches of God’s mercy [Ibid., no. 5] that God would not deprive entirely, nor forever, of understanding those whom he then permitted to be deceived by their free choice and to wander from the path of humility.

They were mistaken in this matter [Ibid. and following sections]: they placed the beginnings of virtues and good works in natural possibility; or, if they said that these flowed from grace, they claimed that grace had been preceded by some good work or good will and granted on account of such merit.

St. Prosper carefully overturns this error. From testimonies of Scripture he proves that, after the Fall, no powers for good remain in human beings, not even powers for meriting, without the help of preceding grace; and that human beings can be rescued from the perdition incurred through Adam’s sin only by the gratuitous grace of God’s mercy.

He establishes this by adducing the example of infants who die without baptism and of those nations to which the Gospel of salvation is not yet known to have reached.

Grace, however, does not deny free choice but establishes and reforms it. Left to itself, the human being is sufficient only for evil and falling; grace must heal him, inspiring him to think and act otherwise and teaching him to attribute his restored health not to himself but to his physician (no. 19).

Finally, St. Prosper dispels the cloud of calumnies cast over Augustine’s teaching, by which it was falsely alleged that Augustine introduced fate or a double nature. Prosper insists that Augustine or his disciples never wrote anything close to such errors. Nothing happens to Augustine or his disciples by fate; everything is directed by the ordering of divine providence.

Nor do they posit two natures, one good and the other evil, but only one nature. Although it was created upright, it fell from uprightness through the sin of the first human being and became subject to eternal death. It must be restored through the new creation in Christ, who saves human freedom by restoring it and by preceding it with continual helps.

Prosper concludes the work (no. 20) by exhorting his friend Rufinus to devote himself to learning Augustine’s discussions, if he truly desires to be instructed in sound teaching concerning the grace of God, as it was fitting that he should desire.

[Col. 0077]

## ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE  
[Note: Written while Augustine was alive, around the year 429.]

## LETTER TO RUFINUS  
[Note: The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions of 1630 read here ad Ruffinum, and shortly below Ruffino. The Remigian-Reims and Joliensis manuscripts of the chapter of the metropolitan church of Paris, together with the Lyon edition of 1539, the Venetian edition of 1538, and the third part of the new edition of St. Augustine’s works in the appendix, read ad Rufinum and Rufino.]

### ON GRACE AND FREE CHOICE (C)

[Col. 0077A]

To his most beloved brother in Christ and deservedly venerable Rufinus, Prosper sends eternal salvation [Note: The oldest copy of the abbey of St. Remigius at Reims, mentioned above—which had already been revised by the learned monks of the monastery of Saint-Germain—omits “brother” here, but at the end agrees with the editions and reads “most honored brother.”] [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads aeternam salutem, without the word dicit (“says”).]

### PROLOGUE

1. Through our mutual friend I received signs of your brotherly concern for me, and I gladly recognized the care of your most sincere charity. And lest the malicious rumors, insofar as they cannot withdraw themselves from your ears, bring you fear or anxiety, I have taken care to free you from every scruple, so far as was possible in an epistolary manner. I have been eager to disclose everything to you with the fullest truth, so that, since you were unable to hear completely what is being spread by our opponents, you may through me personally learn whatever is said and repeated about us to stir up empty hatred.

But first the character of the question from which these things arise must be explained to your holiness, so that the falsehood of those who speak against us may become clearer to you and you may see what light they are trying to cover with what darkness.

## CHAPTER I

2. What doctrine the Pelagian heresy undertook to use in destroying the Catholic faith, and with what poisons of impiety it sought to occupy the inmost parts of the Church and the very vitals of Christ’s body, is too well known to require a narrative.

Among its doctrines, however, there is one blasphemy—the most wicked and subtle seed of the others—in which they say that the grace of God is given according to human merits.

For when they first [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits “first”; the other manuscripts retain it.] wished to assert such health [or sanctity] of human nature that it could attain the kingdom of God through free choice alone [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “can attain”]—because, they claimed, it was so fully [Note: The Venetian edition reads “so plainly”] aided by the resources of its own creation that, possessing rational understanding naturally, it could easily choose the good and avoid the evil—and when the works of the will were free in either direction, they said that those who are evil lacked not the ability for good but only the desire for it.

Thus, as I have said, they wished all human righteousness to subsist in natural uprightness and possibility. When sound doctrine rejected this definition [Note: The Joliensis manuscript and the Venetian edition read “definition”], and the view had been condemned by Catholics and later colored by many varieties of heretical deceit [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits the particle “and”], they preserved this device among themselves: they professed that God’s grace is necessary for a human being to begin, progress, and persevere in the good.

## CHAPTER II

3. But in this profession, God’s grace, by revealing it to the vessels of mercy, exposed the deceit by which the vessels of wrath sought to insinuate themselves [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “what deceit”; the Remigianus, “that by deceit”; the editions, “how by deceit.” Shortly afterward the Joliensis manuscript reads “in the vessels of mercy.”].

It was understood—and most beneficially recognized—that they confess grace only in this sense: that it is a kind of teacher of free choice, displaying itself to the judgment of free choice through exhortations, through the law, through teaching, through contemplation of creatures, through miracles, and through external terrors, so that each person, according to the movement of his will, may find if he seeks, receive if he asks, and enter if he knocks [Note: The Joliensis manuscript, together with the Venetian edition, reads “receive”; the other manuscripts read “accept.”] [Note: The Remigian and Joliensis manuscripts read this way. The editions instead read “through the creature, through contemplation”; shortly afterward both manuscripts read “display,” where the editions have “show.”]

For, according to them, the calling of grace itself does this first in relation to us: it warns the judgment of our ability. Grace is nothing other than the law, the prophet, and the teacher, whose common and universal concern throughout the world is directed toward all human beings, so that those who wish may believe, and those who believe may receive justification as a reward for faith and good will.

Thus the grace of God is granted according to human merit; and in this way grace is not grace, because if it is paid out according to merits and is not itself the creator of good things, it is called grace in vain [Note: The Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “and thus”; the Venetian edition, in agreement with the Remigian and Joliensis manuscripts, reads “and in this way.”]

## CHAPTER III

4. When the judgments of the Eastern bishops, the authority of the apostolic see, and the vigilance of the African councils had detected these tricks by which the sons of darkness wished to transform themselves into the likeness of the sons of light, the most blessed Augustine, certainly at this time the foremost portion of the Lord’s priests, destroyed them copiously and beautifully in many discussions contained in books [Note: All the editions read this way. The Remigian manuscript instead reads, “he destroyed them in many extensive and beautiful discussions of volumes.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “he destroyed them in the extensive and beautiful discussion of many volumes.”].

Among the many gifts of God with which the Spirit of truth filled him most abundantly, he also possessed this virtue of knowledge and wisdom from the charity of God: not only to defeat with the unconquered sword of the word this heresy, still twitching in the mutilation it had suffered, but also to defeat many earlier heresies.

Amid so many palms of contest and so many crowns of triumph, for the illumination of the Church and for the glory of Christ, by whose radiance he himself has been illumined, certain of our own people—something deeply to be lamented in them—slander him in whispers that are secret but not unknown. Whenever they find ears that are subject and receptive to them [Note: The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “ears harmful to them”; this is less suitable], they defame his writings, by which the Pelagian error is attacked [Note: The Joliensis manuscript alone reads “his Scriptures”].

They say that he completely removes free choice and preaches fatal necessity under the name of grace. They add that he wishes two masses of the human race and two natures to be believed, so that the impiety of pagans and Manichaeans may be attributed to a man of such piety.

If these things are true, why are they themselves so negligent—not to say so impious—as not to drive such abrupt destruction away from the Church, resist such insane teachings, or at least confront in writing the man from whom such a doctrine proceeds? They would have done great service to the human race if they had recalled Augustine from error.

Unless perhaps these modest men and new censors mercifully and honorably spare an old man of great prior merits and, secure because no one anywhere accepts his books, remain quiet [Col. 0079C] [Note: The Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “and have forgiven.” Rather, the correct reading is “but have recognized.” The Joliensis manuscript adds after “remain quiet”: “although they have not recognized, indeed have recognized,” and so forth].
