Let them recognize, then, that not only the Roman and African Churches and all the children of the promise throughout the various parts of the world agree with this man’s teaching, both in the entirety of the faith and in their confession of grace [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “as in the whole faith”], but also that in the very places where complaint is stirred up against him there are, by God’s favor, very many people who are instructed in the saving teaching of the Gospel and the apostles by his most beneficial discussions and who are daily enlarged as members of Christ’s body, insofar as Christ himself multiplies them.

If we are rightly reproved, why are we not openly and consistently accused? If we ought not to be accused, why are we attacked by hidden detraction?

## CHAPTER IV

5. But who does not know why they mutter these things privately in irritation and remain silent publicly out of deliberation? [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “who does not know”; the Remigianus, “who knows not.”]

For, wishing to glory in their own righteousness rather than in the grace of God, they are displeased that we resist what they asserted against a man of the highest authority in the midst of many Conferences [Note: “The Conferences of the Fathers” refers to those composed by the presbyter John Cassian in the year 426. He dedicated the second group, beginning with the Eleventh Conference, to Honoratus and Eucherius, while they were not yet bishops, since he calls them “brothers” in the preface. Honoratus became bishop of Arles in that year, 426. Because the definitions of the Thirteenth Conference contradict Augustine, St. Prosper first thought they should be resisted by voice and speech, and later, after Augustine’s death, in the written volume called Against the Author of the Conferences].

Nor do they doubt that, if they raise any question on this subject, in every gathering of priests and every assembly of the people they will be confronted by hundreds of volumes of the most blessed Augustine. When these volumes begin to reveal to the hearts of their hearers the most powerful truth of the Christian faith and to flood the minds of those present from the springs of divine eloquence [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “the hearts of those who oppose them”], what believer, what devout person, once the causes of his salvation have been recognized and commended to him, will wish to receive this bitterness of smoky vanity?

For my part, I also hope this from the riches of God’s mercy: that he will not deprive entirely, nor forever, of understanding those whom he now permits to be deceived by their free choice and to wander from the path of humility [Note: The Lyon and Venetian editions read “of humanity”; the others more correctly read “of humility”]. Rather, he delays recalling the one who has advanced farther into the distance so that the work of his grace may be celebrated with greater glory, when he has subjected even the hearts of his opponents—hearts in which danger has arisen from zeal for virtue and peril from moral uprightness.

This is not because anyone ought to be without these qualities, but because their use is most wretched when they are thought to have arisen from natural ability [Note: The Venetian edition alone reads “to be useful”], or to have come from the generosity of grace but through the prior merit of some good work or good will.

## CHAPTER V

6. They indeed support these claims with certain testimonies of Holy Scripture, but they do not assume them reasonably. For in defense of any definition one must bring forward passages that do not yield to the opposing interpretation, by which the definition appears to be contradicted, and that do not abandon the rule to which they have been adapted.

Thus, they say that the following was spoken to those who use free choice:

“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden light” (Matt. XI, 28).

They want this to apply to all human beings who labor in the uncertainty of this life and are burdened with sins, so that those who wish to imitate the gentleness and humility of the Savior and take up the yoke of his commandments may find rest for their souls [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “for their minds”] in the hope of eternal life [Note: The Augustinian edition alone reads “in hope”]. But those who do not wish to do these things are deprived of salvation through their own fault—salvation which, if they had wished, they could have obtained [Note: The Remigian and Joliensis manuscripts and the edition of Augustine’s works read “could have obtained.” The Venetian, Lyon, and Louvain editions read “could obtain”; Douai and Cologne, “could have obtained.”]

But let them also hear what the Lord said to those who use free choice:

“Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5);

“No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI, 44);

“No one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father” (ibid., 66);

“As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wills” (John V, 21);

“No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Luke X, 22).

Since all these statements are unchangeable and cannot be twisted into another meaning by any interpretation, who could doubt that free choice obeys the exhortation of the one who calls only when God’s grace has produced in it the disposition to believe and obey? Otherwise it would be enough merely to warn a person, without also bringing about in him a new will, as it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, 35, according to the Septuagint); and as the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. II, 13).

What good will is meant except that which God has worked in them, so that he might grant the doing of what he had granted them to will?

## CHAPTER VI

7. They also say, to demonstrate the power of free choice, that the centurion Cornelius provides a striking example. Before receiving grace, they say, he feared and prayed to God and devoted himself willingly to almsgiving, fasting, and prayer (Acts X, 2); and for this reason, praised by divine testimony, he received the gift of regeneration.

They do not understand that all Cornelius’s preparation was bestowed through God’s grace (see the Council of Orange below). For when the holy Peter was taught through a vision concerning every kind of animal [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “animals of every kind”] and concerning the baptism of Cornelius, and therefore concerning all the nations, and when he refused as unclean and indiscriminate the food prohibited by Jewish observance, a threefold voice came to him, saying: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts X, 15) [Note: The Venetian edition reads this way; the other manuscripts read “a voice was made, saying”].

By this it is sufficiently and openly shown that all the good works that preceded in Cornelius began through God’s grace for his cleansing [Note: The edition of St. Augustine reads “God’s grace”]. Thus, since the Lord had already granted him this gift, the Apostle did not hesitate to confer the sacrament, lest the beginning of a new and as-yet-unrevealed calling falter, unless it were established through the signs of his preceding zeal that God had been at work in receiving him.

For faith is not possessed by all (II Thess. III, 2), nor do all obey the Gospel (Rom. X, 16). But those who believe are led by the Spirit of God; those who do not believe turn away by free choice.

Therefore our conversion to God comes not from ourselves but from God, as the Apostle says: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” [Note: The edition of St. Augustine omits “and”], “not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II, 8).

## CHAPTER VII

8. Let human weakness acknowledge itself, and let the succession of all generations, condemned in the first human being, acknowledge itself as well. When the dead are made alive, when the blind are illumined, when the impious are justified, let them confess Jesus Christ as their life, their light, and their righteousness; and let the one who boasts boast in the Lord (I Cor. I, 31), not in himself.

Although he was impious, blind, and dead, he freely received from his liberator both righteousness, light, and life. For he was not acting justly and his righteousness was increased [Note: The word “justly” is absent from the Remigian manuscript]; nor was he walking toward God and his course strengthened; nor was he loving God and his charity inflamed. Rather, while he was without faith and therefore impious, he received the Spirit of faith and became righteous.

“The righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17);

“Without faith no one can please God” (Heb. XI, 6);

“Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 23) [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “so that you may understand.”].

Thus he should understand that the righteousness of unbelievers is not righteousness, because nature without grace is defiled.

## Chapter VIII

*Textual notes: [Col. 0082D] The printed editions read “introduced into love for God”; the Remigian and Jolian manuscripts read “introduced; and by love for God,” etc. The Remigian and Jolian manuscripts, with the new Augustinian edition, read “was known”; all our printed editions read “was set aflame.” The Jolian manuscript reads “he himself first loved us,” and shortly afterward, “God first loved us.”*

**9.** For once natural innocence had been lost, humanity, exiled and ruined, walking without a path, entered ever deeper errors; but it was sought, found, and brought back, and was introduced into the way that is truth and life. And through love for God—who first loved the one who did not love him—it was set aflame. As blessed John the Apostle says: “Not as though we had loved God, but because he himself loved us” (1 John 4:10); and again: “Let us therefore love God, because God first loved us” (1 John 4:19). The same Apostle also says: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God; and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love” (1 John 4:7–8).

Blessed Paul agrees with him, saying: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any force, but faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). From what source, then, does this faith joined to love come, except from the source from which he himself shows that it was received, saying: “For to you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29)? This certainly could not happen without great love. And again: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). Without this love, the Apostle testifies that however great the faith and knowledge, whatever virtues, endeavors, and labors may be, they are of no benefit (1 Corinthians 13). For many praiseworthy and astonishing qualities can indeed be found in a person which, without the marrow of love, possess the likeness of piety but not its reality.

## Chapter IX

*Textual note: [Col. 0082D] The words “but whoever was chosen by God was made worthy” are absent from the Jolian manuscript. [Col. 0083D] The Jolian manuscript reads “which we did,” rather than “which we had done”; it reads “makes better from good people,” rather than “it makes them better from good people.”*

**10.** No one was found worthy of so great and ineffable a good; but whoever was chosen by God was made worthy. As the Apostle says (Colossians 1:3): “Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.”

And again, to Timothy (2 Timothy 1:8): “Work with me,” he says, “for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of the world.”

And to Titus (Titus 3:3): “For we too were once foolish and unbelieving, wandering astray and serving various desires and pleasures, acting in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared, he saved us—not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy.”

The grace of God, therefore, makes whomever it justifies not better from good people, but good from bad people; afterward, through progress, it makes them better from good people. It does not remove free will but liberates it. As long as free will existed alone, without God, it was dead to righteousness and lived for sin. But when the mercy of Christ enlightened it, it was snatched from the kingdom of the devil and became the kingdom of God. Yet, in order that it may be able to remain in that kingdom, even this power is not sufficient for itself unless it receives perseverance from the same source from which it received its diligence [perhaps: “its righteousness”].

## Chapter X

*Textual notes: [Col. 0083D] The Venetian edition reads “on her behalf,” rather than “for him.” The printed editions read “replied”; the Remigian and Jolian manuscripts read “had replied.”*

**11.** For even the most ardent faith of Saint Peter himself would have failed in the temptations unless the Lord had interceded for him. The Evangelist makes this clear, saying (Luke 22:31–32): “Jesus said to Peter, ‘Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has asked to sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.’” And again: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Luke 22:40).

And so that it might be more clearly demonstrated that free will can accomplish nothing without grace, the one to whom it had been said, “Strengthen your brothers, and pray that you may not enter into temptation,” and who had replied—certainly from free will—“Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22:33), is told that before the cock crows he will deny the Lord three times.

What else does this mean than that he would fail in faith? Certainly the Lord had prayed for him that his faith should not fail; and he had not prayed in vain, since the one who prayed and the one for whom he prayed had one and the same operation. Yet, so that the man who had made great promises about himself would not appear to stand by free will, he is allowed to be endangered, so that the one without whom no one stands and no one perseveres may look upon him when he is shaken and failing, and restore him.

## Chapter XI

*Textual notes: [Col. 0083D] The Remigiano-Remensian manuscript reads “thought,” rather than “knowledge.” The printed editions read “to the people of Iconium”; two Remigian manuscripts and the Jolian manuscript read “to the Lycaonians,” in conformity with the sacred text. The Remigian codex reads “And indeed, not leaving himself without testimony,” omitting “not.” The printed editions read “their hearts”; the Remigian and Jolian manuscripts read “your hearts.”*

**12.** Some recoil from this confession of the grace of God because, once they have confessed it to be such as it is proclaimed by divine speech and recognized in the working of God’s power, they would also have to confess that, from the whole number of human beings born throughout all ages, a definite and determined number of the people predestined to eternal life exists with God, chosen according to the purpose of God who calls.

To deny this is just as impious as to oppose grace itself. For it is not hidden from common observation how, throughout the ages, countless thousands of human beings, abandoned to their errors and impieties, have perished without any knowledge of the true God. As the words of Paul and Barnabas in the Acts of the Apostles also make clear, when they spoke to the Lycaonians (Acts 14:14):

“Men, brothers, why are you doing these things? We too are mortal human beings, like you, announcing to you that you should turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and everything in them; who in past generations allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without testimony, doing good, giving rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.”

If either natural understanding or the experience of God’s benefits had been sufficient for them to attain eternal life, then even in our own time rational contemplation, the temperateness of the air, the abundance of crops, and the supply of food would save us, since, using nature better, we would worship our Creator because of his daily gifts.

## Chapter XII

*Textual note: [Col. 0084D] The Jolian manuscript reads: “But far be from the minds of the pious. The exceedingly foolish and destructive persuasion does not liberate human nature. Apart from the one mediator . . . no one has salvation.” It omits “without him.” The Remigian manuscript similarly reads: “Human nature does not liberate human nature; apart from the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, no one has salvation.” The Remigian manuscript and Venetian edition read “restored us”; the Jolian manuscript omits: “So he himself restores us, and we do not restore ourselves.”*

**13.** But far be from the minds of the pious and of those redeemed by Christ’s blood this exceedingly foolish and destructive persuasion: that human nature is liberated apart from the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Without him no one has salvation (Acts 4:12).

Just as he himself made us, and we did not make ourselves (Psalm 99:3), so he himself restores us, and we do not restore ourselves. And lest human ability seem able, through works of righteousness, either to pay back the price of this restoration or to repay it after being restored, the riches of God’s goodness poured themselves out at the very beginnings of certain infants—in whom there is neither a preceding choice nor a devotion that follows, neither obedience, discernment, nor will.

I am speaking of those who, as soon as they are born, are reborn and, snatched from this life, are appointed to eternal blessedness; while, nevertheless, an innumerable multitude of infants of the same nature and condition dies without regeneration. Of this multitude there can be no doubt that it has no share in the city of God.

## Chapter XIII

*Textual note: [Col. 0085D] The Jolian manuscript reads: “is set against us concerning what is written, ‘who wills all human beings,’ etc.” It also reads: “if you consider the gift of merits,” rather than “if you consider merit.”*

**14.** And what of the objection that those who do not understand things continually set against us as though it were contrary to this—that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4)?

Are there not among all human beings those who, from past generations down to the present time, have perished without knowledge of God? And if, in the case of adults—which is not rightly said—the evil works they committed by free will were harmful to them, as though the good rather than the bad were liberated by grace, what distinction of merits could there have been between the infants who were saved and those who were not saved? What brought the former into the kingdom of God? What excluded the latter from God’s kingdom?

Indeed, if you consider merit, neither group deserved to be saved; both deserved to be condemned. For when all had been overthrown in Adam’s transgression, unless merciful grace assumed some, justice, without blame, would remain over all.

What the cause or reason for this distinction may be in the secret counsel of God is investigated beyond the capacity of human understanding and is unknown without any diminution of faith. Let us only confess that no one is lost undeservedly, no one is liberated by merit, and that the almighty goodness of the Lord saves all and instructs all in the knowledge of the truth whom he wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

For unless he himself calls, teaches, and saves, no one comes, no one is instructed, and no one is saved. For although teachers are commanded to preach indiscriminately to all human beings and to scatter the seed of the word everywhere, nevertheless neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:7).

## Chapter XIV

*Textual notes: [Col. 0085D] The printed editions read “the word of God”; the Remigian and Jolian manuscripts read “the word of the Lord.” [Col. 0086D] The Jolian manuscript reads “of the Thyatireans.” The printed editions read “the apostles were forbidden to enter”; two manuscripts read as in the text. The source adds: “many in those places, delayed and turned away [perhaps: ‘having been delayed and turned away’] by the Gospel’s postponement.” The Jolian manuscript reads “have begun to share in the faith,” rather than “Christian grace.”*

**15.** Hence, when the apostles began to preach the Gospel to the nations, Scripture records concerning some of those who heard them: “When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as had been preordained to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48).

And elsewhere, when many women were listening to Paul teaching: “A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, a worshiper of God, heard; and the Lord opened her heart to attend to what was being said by Paul” (Acts 16:14).

Again, at the very time when the preaching of the Gospel was being sent to all nations, the apostles were prevented from entering certain places by the one who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Many people in those places would consequently die, delayed and turned away by the postponement of the Gospel, without the knowledge of the truth and without the consecration of regeneration.

Let Scripture therefore state what happened: “As they passed through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:6–7).

What is surprising, then, if at the very beginnings of evangelical preaching the apostles could go only where the Spirit of God willed them to go, when we see that many nations have only now begun to share in Christian grace, while others have not yet touched any scent of this good?

## Chapter XV

*Textual note: [Col. 0086D] The Remigian manuscript reads *Et quid* (“And what?”), before “who changed their hearts?”*

**16.** Should it be said that human wills resist the will of God, and that the character of these people is so savage and intractable that they do not hear the Gospel because their impious hearts are not open to preaching?

And who changed their hearts except the one who fashioned each of their hearts (Psalm 32:15)? Who softened the hardness of this rigidity into a disposition to obey except the one who is able to raise up children for Abraham from stones (Matthew 3:9)? And who will give preachers fearless and unharmed steadfastness except the one who said to Paul: “Do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent; for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, because I have many people in this city” (Acts 18:9)?

I think no one would dare to say that any nation of the world or any region of the earth is to be left without the Church’s tents being enlarged there, since God says to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 2:8). And again: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Psalm 21:28). The Lord himself also says: “This Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14).

Whatever nations, therefore, have not yet heard will hear the Gospel, and as many of them as have been preordained to eternal life will believe (Acts 13:48). For no others will enter into fellowship with Christ’s inheritance than those who before the foundation of the world were chosen, predestined, and foreknown, according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11).

## Chapter XVI

*Textual note: [Col. 0087D] The Jolian manuscript reads “revealed [it] to the saints; and this ignorance did not harm them.”*

**17.** Let us therefore confess the works of the Lord and glorify his mercies, and let us not impatiently endure the fact that we do not know what or how great the vessels of election are.

For in earlier ages also, when it was said of the people of one nation, “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75:2), the future election of the nations was hidden. Later it became known what had not previously been revealed. As the Apostle says: “What was not made known to the sons of men in other generations, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are fellow-heirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 1:11 [as printed]).

And in the Acts of the Apostles: “The believers from the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations” (Acts 10:45).

If, then, the Lord concealed and postponed this counsel of his calling for as long as he wished, and revealed it when he wished, and this ignorance did not harm his saints, why do we think it harmful to our hope if it is concealed in what number and among which people the vessels of mercy are prepared for glory?

Nevertheless, it is certain that all the good will enter the kingdom of heaven, by the gift of God’s grace, and that no evil people will enter it, through the desert of their own wickedness.

## Chapter XVII

**18.** It is exceedingly foolish and inconsiderate for opponents to say that, through this grace of God, nothing is left to free will.

*Textual notes: [Col. 0087D] The Jolian manuscript adds, with the Lyons and Venetian editions and an old Remigian manuscript, “to will differently.” The Venetian edition reads “in the Mediator,” rather than “in the physician.” The printed editions read “full of mercy”; the Jolian manuscript reads “not judging according to pretense.”*

Although, in infants passing through baptism, there is most clearly no work and no desire of their will, and although liberating regeneration sanctifies many who use free will but are turned away from the true God and spend their lives in crimes at the very moment when they breathe out their spirit, nevertheless, if we consider with a pious gaze that portion of the children of God which is reserved for works of piety, shall we not find in them free will not destroyed but reborn?

When free will existed alone and was left to itself, it moved only toward its own destruction. It had blinded itself and could not enlighten itself. But now that same will has been converted, not overthrown, and has been granted the ability to will differently, to understand differently, to act differently, and to place its safety not in itself but in the physician.

For it does not yet enjoy such perfect health that the things which had harmed it can no longer harm it, or that it can already restrain itself by its own healthy powers from what is unhealthy.

Therefore, a person who was evil in free will is made good in that same free will: evil through himself, good through God. God restored him to that original dignity by another beginning, so that he not only forgave him the guilt of evil will and action but also granted him the ability to will and do good, and to persevere in these things.

“For every good gift,” says the Apostle James, “and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). He clearly shows what kind of free will is directed by the human spirit and what kind is governed by God when he says: “If you have bitter jealousy and contention in your hearts, do not boast against the truth and become liars. This wisdom is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. For where jealousy and contention are, there is instability and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, modest, persuadable, full of mercy and good fruits, not judging, without hypocrisy” (James 3:14–17).

Whoever therefore strives for and clings to these virtues is enlightened not by his own wisdom but by wisdom from above: “For the Lord gives wisdom, and from his face come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 1:6 [as printed]). [Note: [Col. 0087D] The Jolian manuscript reads *scientiae*, a different inflection of *scientia* (“knowledge”); it also reads *verissime gloria est* (“is most truly glory”) rather than *verissima gloria est* (“is the truest glory”).] Their truest glory is this: that they glory not in themselves but in the Lord.

## Chapter XVIII

*Textual notes: [Col. 0087D] The printed editions read “men intent on injury [to him] proclaim” (*intenti viri injuriae jactitant*). Two manuscripts agree with the text “are proclaimed to the injury of so great a man” (*in tanti viri injuriam jactitantur*), except that one spells the verb *jacitantur*, rather than *jactitantur*. The Venetian edition has *in tanti viri injuriae*, perhaps for *injuriam* (the genitive form “of injury” in place of the accusative “injury”). The Jolian manuscript reads “teachers and errors,” rather than “errors.” [Col. 0088D] It reads *imbuuntur aures* (“their ears are imbued”), at the passage concerning the people whose ears are being used. The first hand reads *magister gratiae* (“teacher of grace”), corrected by a later hand to *minister gratiae* (“minister of grace”). The Jolian reading is *secunda creationis Christi gratia reformaret* (“might reform [it] by a second grace of Christ’s creation”), differing from *secundae creationis Christi gratia reformaverit* (“has reformed [it] by the grace of Christ’s second creation”). The printed editions read *sperando* (“hoping”); an old Augustinian manuscript supports the preferable *spirando* (“breathing”). The editor substitutes *aspirando* (“breathing upon”) from the Jolian manuscript, perhaps no less well. Earlier editions gave the marginal conjecture *inspirando* (“inspiring”).*

**19.** The things that are irresponsibly proclaimed, with the stupidest falsehood, concerning fate and two masses and two natures, to the injury of so great a man, do not even burden the man himself, since errors of this kind are thoroughly refuted in his books [the Jol. manuscript reads: “teachers and errors”]. Nor do they disturb us, for we execrate such opinions together with their authors (see Augustine, *Book II Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapters 6 and 7, and *Book IV Against Julian*, chapter 8, below, Appendix, Part II).

But let those who can invent such absurdities see how they will free themselves from the disgrace of this falsehood, if they would only devote a little care to learning what that most excellent minister of grace has discussed [in the Jol. manuscript, the first hand has “teacher of grace,” later corrected to “minister of grace”]. Indeed, those who say such things ought to have anticipated every delay in this investigation by producing his books and explaining them, or by pointing out even a small passage which, through at least an uncertain interpretation, the holy man published in a form liable to such an explanation.

But they heard nothing of the kind from us and read nothing of the kind, because we know that nothing happens by fate but that everything is ordered by God’s judgment. We know that all human beings were and are created with one nature, not from two masses or two natures, but from one mass—that is, the flesh of the first human being—and that this nature was overthrown through the free will of that first human being, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:22 [as printed]).

Nor do we know it to be freed in any way from the debt of eternal death unless the grace of Christ’s second creation reforms it according to the image of God [the Jol. manuscript: “reformed it by the grace of Christ’s second creation”], and preserves its free will by acting upon it, breathing upon it, helping it, and going before it all the way to the end [the printed editions had “hoping”; corrected more suitably from an old manuscript in Augustine to “breathing”; “inspiring” would perhaps be no less appropriate].

## Epilogue

*Textual notes: [Col. 0088D] The Jolian manuscript reads “questions or accusations.” Augustine reads “I trust in the power”; the Jolian manuscript reads “therefore trust in the power”; the printed editions read “in the power.” [Col. 0089A] The printed editions read “is torn away”; the Remigian and Jolian manuscripts read “is repelled.”*

**17.** Since, therefore, your holiness perceives—if, indeed, the obscurity of my speech does not stand in the way—that certain people among us complain without reason and that I have woven together all those foolish accusations in order to exasperate and turn away the minds of those whom they wish to persuade of something else [the Jol. manuscript reads: “questions or accusations”], trust, then, in the power of God’s mercy. For this opposition, as in other parts of the world, will likewise subside in these regions, so that the preaching of the supreme man now in the Church may be assisted even by those by whom it is at present resisted [the printed editions read “torn away”; the Remig. and Jol. manuscripts read “repelled”].

But you, my dearest and most venerable brother, if you truly desire to be instructed concerning these questions, as you ought to desire, devote yourself to learning the very disputations of blessed Augustine, so that in confessing the grace of God you may attain the purest and most salutary understanding of evangelical and apostolic teaching.

May the grace of God and the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ guard you at all times and direct you through the way of truth into eternal life.

# Poem on the Ungrateful

## Notice concerning the Poem of Saint Prosper on the Ungrateful

The *Poem on the Ungrateful*, consisting of a thousand verses, has until now been attributed by everyone, without anyone dissenting, to Saint Prosper of Aquitaine. It is indeed a noble work, composed of great judgments, great thoughts, and finally magnificent words and expressions. Its sole aim is that, after exposing the error of the Pelagians, the poet may show the people of Marseille that they press so closely upon the footsteps of such heretics that they ought scarcely to be regarded as anything other than hidden Pelagians.

These are the very words of the most learned censor of the works of Leo and Prosper, in the ninth dissertation, *On the True Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, page 417. He adds the following:

> “This poem, more splendid and more extensive than all the works Prosper published, has always rightly been recognized and celebrated as his genuine offspring. For he sings nothing there in different words or expressions from what is emphasized in his other dogmatic treatises.”

He declares that he considered this poem earlier than several of Prosper’s other writings on the following presumption: poetic play is much more suited to youthful minds than to mature age, and therefore our Aquitanian doctor’s ability may at that time have been more fully stirred and exercised, before, provoked by our countrymen—by which name he usually means the people of Marseille and others from the province—he engaged them vigorously and openly in combat.

After rereading some portion of his poetry, or recalling it to memory, he was almost persuaded that the following verses, especially those in chapter 3 of *On the Ungrateful*, could establish the matter with certainty, while Saint Prosper sings:

> Could the holy council have proceeded to any other end,  
> The council whose leader was Aurelius, and whose genius  
> Was Augustine, whom the grace of Christ, watering him  
> With a richer horn, gave as a light to our age?  
>   
> He was kindled by that light; for God was his food,  
> His life, and his rest, and his sole delight  
> Was the one love of Christ, and Christ’s honor alone.  
>   
> And since he attributed no good to himself, God became for him  
> Everything, and wisdom reigned in his holy temple.

Thus Prosper celebrates his excellent teacher as though he were still alive in this continuous eulogy. Why, then, does he not speak in the same place of other bishops or men eminent in this cause who had already died?

This judgment of the most learned man easily assigns the work to some plausible period—namely, to the time when Augustine was still alive, but the Pelagians had already been condemned, and the first unmistakable murmurs of the Semipelagians of Marseille against certain parts of Augustine’s doctrine had begun to arise: approximately the year 429 or 430.

But although he inclines toward this opinion on the presumption that a work of such weight would be unbecoming to mature years and forgivable only in youth, there are several reasons why we should not agree with him. Those who judge poetic art to be properly suited only to the exercise of immature talents, and to the writing of fables and other amusements, do not assign it its due worth. If they are so disposed toward this exceptional art, they must condemn not only this holy doctor of the Church but also, before him and alongside him, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Paulinus, Alcimus, and countless other men of great renown.

Although filled with the divine Spirit, and superior in gravity and sublimity to those who despise this manner of writing, they rightly did not hesitate to adapt the purest poems usefully to loftier and holier subjects. In this way even the Holy Spirit himself—far be it from us to speak irreverently—is accused, since he wished the greatest mysteries and most sacred oracles in the holy Scriptures to be expressed by his prophets in verse.

Finally, the holy Church of Christ, animated and directed by the same Holy Spirit, would be condemned. Apart from the sacred verses of the Psalms, by which—as we may say with Saint Dionysius—it wished the substance of the divine worship offered by it to God to consist, the Church does not permit any of the hours of prayer consecrated to God seven times a day to be celebrated without hymn verses.

Indeed, it is not difficult to judge that, since poetry is such a sublime form of writing that the ancient poets, finding nothing in nature equal to the majesty and nobility of their style, sought heaven itself in imagination, inventing a new world and new gods and devising extraordinary and prodigious things that might in some measure answer the magnificence of their words and the sublimity of their bold and figurative expressions, Christian religion alone truly provides poetry with what paganism had sought in vain.

For in Christianity innumerable events present themselves in ranks, far more wonderful than the fictions of a wandering imagination. Here, at the very source of truth, there appears a new world, new human beings, heaven joined to earth, human things mingled with divine, God made human, human beings taken up into God, and finally innumerable miracles so unusual and so far above ordinary belief that they could have been made credible only by the singular grace and almighty power of God.

Thus one of the chief errors of the Semipelagians—errors chiefly attacked in this poem—is the claim that human beings can prepare themselves from within for believing such things, even though their will has not first been preceded by the mercy of the Savior and the special movement of the Holy Spirit.

But perhaps we are deceived by this happy expectation, and only very few people will enjoy reading the verses of so eminent a Father—especially since they present material so useful and so important—or will not wish to contemplate in this poem the most sacred doctrines of our faith with such elegance and magnificence, together with that pleasing ingenuity which naturally accompanies poetry, and with no small measure of admiration and chaste delight.

For, unless we are mistaken, there is no reason to suspect that any Catholic will dare to diminish the authority of this excellent poem with the presumption and recklessness of the heretics of our time. These heretics contend that all testimonies brought against them from the verses of the Fathers are completely without force on the sole ground that they wish them to be regarded as poetic amusements.

They must be refuted by the response used by the most learned Cardinal Perronius against the enemies of the Church (*Reply to the King of England*, book V, chapter 20): he shows that this is an entirely empty objection, because there is a great difference between profane pagan poets, whose sole concern was pleasure—the end of their fictions and the chief attraction of this kind of writing—and sacred Christian poets, whose sole desire was truth and edification, and whose writings were held in such esteem by the Church that she did not hesitate to adopt them as part of her offices and prayers.

Add also what the illustrious and most eminent prelate just cited rightly observes in defending Christian poets: what they had compressed elsewhere into concise form, they often expressed elsewhere in continuous prose. The example of Saint Paulinus, who was under discussion there, makes this clear. This consideration applies especially to this poem of Prosper, since he wrote nothing in it that he had not taught in other works written in prose, and especially in his letter to Rufinus.

Beyond this, we believe that something further should be added. Since this poem provides Catholics with a powerful and certain testimony from antiquity against the heterodox, entirely suited to asserting the supreme authority of Saint Peter’s successors over all the Churches of the world, nothing could favor the adversaries of the Holy See more than to give room to the empty opinion that so eminent a work deserves less credence because it is written in verse.

Thus, in this same work, we learn with what reverence and honor the sound doctrine concerning the grace of Jesus Christ must be received—a doctrine which may rightly be called the heart of the Church. We learn how the Roman Church must be regarded, since it is acknowledged to be the head of that doctrine. The fortunes of these two doctrines in this matter are so inseparable that nothing can be asserted against one without immediately harming the other.

But the greater the esteem in which this work ought to be held, and the more deserving it is of the love and veneration of all the pious, the more fitting it was that it should be made so clear and accessible to everyone’s understanding that there would be no one whose faith and edification it could not serve.

For this reason it is presented divided into four parts, not only for the reader’s convenience but also because this division appears naturally to arise from the different kinds of questions treated in it. We wished to place an argument before each part, so that in a single view the matters treated at greater length in that part might be set before the eyes of readers. A general table of the chapters of the whole work is prefixed to all of them.

Nor did we think it useless or unwelcome to readers, in order to promote a fuller understanding of so eminent a work and to demonstrate its complete agreement with the other books of our most holy author, to append the notes of the most learned Martin Steyaert—formerly doctor and royal professor at the University of Leuven—beneath each verse that they might assist.

We have likewise taken care to do the same with the three epigrams that follow this poem, one of which received the title of epitaph.

# Saint Prosper of Aquitaine: ΠΕΡΙ ΑΧΑΡΙΣΤΩΝ

That is, **On the Ungrateful**

Some believe that by the name “the Ungrateful” the enemies of grace in general are meant—that is, both the Pelagians and the Semipelagians—and that this work therefore attacks both groups together. They also observe that the name is used here both in Greek and in Latin for “enemies of grace,” as though meaning “without grace.”

Nevertheless, the most learned man who, a few years ago—namely, in 1703—had this poem published at Leuven with notes, and who was a doctor and royal professor at that university, observes that from the very beginning of the preface it is clear that the author used a general word not in its full breadth but for a lesser species, one that had not yet received any more specific name: namely, for the Semipelagians, among whom and the orthodox the particular question was properly debated—concerning the beginning of good will and faith—which is presented here in paraphrase in the first couplet.

Against these alone, therefore, he directs his pen when, in the second couplet, he says:

> Against the ungrateful, proud in false virtue;

As below he addresses only them, at verse 684 and following:

> You alone, therefore, are querulous, and you alone are **PROUD**;  
> You alone are **UNGRATEFUL**.

Nor does he mention the Pelagians elsewhere in the whole work except in order to conclude, from their condemnation—which both the Semipelagians and the orthodox accepted—what ought to be thought about the remaining question disputed between them, according to the following passage, at verse 223 and following:

> Let us bring forward only what has already happened;  
> So that from those events it may easily be examined  
> What this question is, about which we have long been moving  
> In opposing directions while disputing.

## Poem on the Ungrateful, Divided into Four Parts

*Written, apparently, before August of the year 430, while Saint Augustine was still alive. [Col. 0091A] The term “Ungrateful” is said both in Greek and Latin to mean enemies of grace, as though “without grace.”*

### Preface

> From what source does the origin of holy will subsist,  
> From what source does piety dwell in minds, and from what source faith?  
> Against the ungrateful, proud in false virtue,  
> I have cultivated these themes in a hundred times ten verses.

[Col. 0092A] If you strive to learn these things with tranquil care,

You will be safe, reader, from the opposing storm,

Nor will you be carried away rebelliously from freedom of will,

Nor will you dare deny any gifts of God.

[Col. 0093A] But you will confess that the good things which are yours, [Note: [Col. 0093A] Christ’s working. Or refer this to what follows, so that the construction is: “You will confess that the good things which are yours, Christ working, have been received for merit, but not from merit”; or rather—and this is more in Prosper’s spirit—refer it to Christ himself, so that grace may be commended more magnificently, since even the act of confessing this is itself produced by grace. The same subtlety appears in what the Wise Man says, Wisdom 8:21: “I knew that I could not otherwise be continent unless God gave it”; and this very knowledge was wisdom: to know whose gift it was.] through Christ’s working,

[Col. 0094A] have been received not from merit [Note: [Col. 0094A] “Received”—in place of “accepted,” as often here; at times, admittedly, rather harshly expressed, but evidently part of the idiom of that age, since we read that Hilary, Prosper’s associate, used the same expression in his letter to Augustine: “By the will,” he says, “which is received,” that is, “which is received from God.”] but for merit.

# PART ONE

## ARGUMENT

At the outset Saint Prosper declares that he intends, in this poem, to ward off the impending danger to the Church from the hidden enemies of grace, through whose activity the extinguished heresy of the Pelagians might revive. He then discloses what Pelagius’s doctrine was, and with what zeal it was rejected by the bishops of the Church: condemned by the authority of councils and of the apostolic see, and refuted by the holy doctors—above all by the blessed Augustine, whose industry and illumination in this struggle, as a man of outstanding excellence and enriched by God with more abundant gifts of grace, shone above all others.

But since the most hidden poison of this heresy is again emerging through the Semipelagians, the Pelagians could rightly demand from them that, since they approve the Pelagian position, they should receive the Pelagians back into communion; or they could demand from the Church either that they too be permitted to teach what the Semipelagians teach with impunity within the Church, or that the Semipelagians themselves be expelled together with them.

[Col. 0093B] 115 [Note: [Col. 0093B] PROEM. The reason for writing is indicated, and divine assistance is implored.] [Note: [Col. 0093B] “The race born together in Christ”—that is, the Church, or Christian people, because of their common regeneration through baptism. It should be noted that the proem is thoroughly Christian, just as the work itself is: everything here is sacred, and there is none of that ornamental trifling without which some people think every poem grows cold—wrongly, indeed, since our poet here demonstrates by his own example that something very different is possible, and does so with great magnificence.] The pure love of the race born together in Christ,

Implanted in me from above,

Commands me to exceed my own powers

And kindle pious minds with song.

Lest, after the celebrated [Note: [Col. 0093C] “Victory.” Not over the Ingrates, with whom the contest was still continuing, but over the Pelagians, already condemned throughout the world.] victory, the war completed,

An unwary peace relax our secure minds;

As though, once the enemy had been crushed,

No fear remained,

And the serpent’s mangled head no longer quivered.

Grant me to speak, almighty Father,

Whence the evil’s slumbering inventions may rise again,

And from what very end [Note: [Col. 0093C] “From the very end,” or outcome, of the Pelagian cause—from which Semipelagianism began. We have likewise seen “origin” used above in the sense of “beginning,” in the Preface, lines 1 and following.] a new beginning may bring forth deceit;

And to disclose the malign art by which error, cast down, strives again to rise.

[1] [Note: [Col. 0093C]

## CHAPTER I

The doctrines of Pelagius are set forth. Man would die even if he had not sinned. There is no original sin. Adam’s sin harmed his descendants by imitation, not by propagation. If he wishes, man can rise to the summit of virtue. The will possesses sufficient strength for this, and the necessary knowledge is not lacking, whether through reason and the natural law or through the written law. Grace is offered indiscriminately to all, provided they wish to be baptized, so that, once the sins they had committed voluntarily have been forgiven, they may voluntarily preserve the original innocence they have recovered. Infants are baptized so that God, who made them good by creating them, may make them better by adopting them. No one is excluded from God’s gifts, because each person receives them according to what each merits by his own will.

1. “Satiated.” “Saturated,” as though macerated in it; this is how it was translated into French:

> Soaked in the gall of the dreadful dragon.

This could indeed have been said of every heretical doctrine, but here it is said specifically of that proud Pelagian teaching, because of its great affinity with the sin of the ancient dragon, or devil.

2. “The British serpent.” Pelagius, the founder of the heresy, was commonly called a Briton, as in our Prosper’s Chronicle: “Pelagius the Briton.” He came, of course, from that Britain which we now call Great Britain, but which he himself, in Against the Conferences, chapter 21, calls “the remote island of the Ocean” and “the Roman island.” Some make him a native of the part of the island now called Scotland; others prefer to call him an Englishman. He was so designated to distinguish him from a contemporary who was called Pelagius of Tarentum, as Augustine says in Letter 186, chapter 1.

He is likewise identified in this way by Orosius and Mercator in many passages, and he also seems to be so identified by Jerome when he says that he was “weighed down by the porridge of the Scots,” and elsewhere: “He has the offspring of the Scottish race from the neighborhood of the Britons.” By these words Jerome appears to suggest that Pelagius seemed by race to be a Scot or Irishman, since he possessed the native vices of the Scottish—that is, Irish—region, while he derived his origin from neighboring Britain.

Saint Prosper calls him a serpent because he was extraordinarily skilled in concealment and knew how to wrap his errors in Catholic language. He sent out his disciples, who spoke more openly, in order to test how their statements would be received; he could then approve or disapprove them, according as it seemed more advantageous to him.

3. “Created under compulsion,” that is, created by necessity or condition.

6. “By which life leaves the flesh.” A circumlocution for bodily death, distinguishing it from spiritual death, which occurs through sin. There was no dispute with Pelagius concerning this in the case of the first parents, as Augustine testifies in On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 1, chapter 2, although Gregory seems to have thought otherwise in Register, book 5, letter 14, to Count Narses, and elsewhere.

10. “From the fathers,” that is, from the first parents—unless one prefers to think that Prosper, as usual following his Augustine, was uncertain whether descendants might not also derive guilt from their other intermediate ancestors. There is, however, no trace of this uncertainty in the Church today.

12. “I harmed the form, not the seed”: that is, not by propagation but by example, as the same people teach in Augustine, On Nature and Grace, chapter 9. They did not inherit some fault from him—Adam—from whom they were propagated; rather, all who later sinned imitated him when he first sinned.

13. “Innocent, in the citadel of virtue”: that is, without any sin and therefore in the highest perfection. Augustine treats this argument throughout On the Perfection of Human Righteousness, throughout book 2 of On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, and elsewhere. Jerome likewise begins his Dialogues against the Pelagians with it.

16. “Natural honor,” that is, innate honor, as is said below, verse 880 and following:

> That power  
> In which nature was innocent.

The meaning is that the person who now wishes to do so possesses the same power of free choice for good that the first parents once possessed before the Fall. From this meaning it is clear that the preceding phrase, “of the one who wills rightly,” is governed not by “natural honor” but by free choice, which preceded it.

Further below, verses 230 and following, the same error is expressed as follows:

> And since people are now born such as  
> The father of our race was before guilt,  
> Man can lead a life without sin,  
> If he wishes . . . .

19. “To be renewed at the fountain,” that is, to be renewed by baptism. For the discussion concerns those who have fallen before baptism.

20. “Voluntarily drawn in,” that is, actual and personal sin, since the Pelagians denied original sin.

24. “To be.” This is the reading that should be adopted, not “would be,” as in the Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions. Learned men have noted this, and it is clear from the words that follow, where “to be born” and “to merit” are compared.

28. “And the good of nature,” and so forth: that is, so that the good of sanctification may be added to their natural goodness, so that infants may be holy children of God. Thus the Pelagian Julian says in Augustine.

31. “The promises of the one who calls.” Not eternal rewards, of which there is no discussion here, but the gift of baptism, together with forgiveness that removes guilt—that is, the remission of sins, as expressed above. Understand “the gift of the one who calls” in the same way below, verse 166. You will read this error expressed in the following form at verse 240 and following:

> That the grace of Christ is assigned according to human merits,  
> In proportion as each person has made himself fit for God’s gifts.

] The doctrine which the ancient serpent, sated with the dragon’s gall,

The British serpent vomited in pestilential speech,

117 Claimed that the first humans had been created under this condition:

Whether they transgressed the prescribed commandment,

[5] Or remained guiltless by keeping the law,

They would suffer that death by which life leaves the flesh;

Death which was not brought about by sin,

But fixed by God himself as the companion of created beings.

Thus those born from the fathers had inherited no guilt,

[10] Nor were they now born unlike that origin of the first parents,

[Col. 0095A] Who, having misused their freedom, sinned:

The form, not the seed, harmed their descendants.

But all who were innocent could live

In the citadel of virtue and preserve the beauty innate in the mind,

[15] Since natural honor and the law implanted within the heart

Stand at the disposal of the free choice of one who wills rightly,

As does the law written outwardly.

To those who had fallen, the grace of Christ

Had generally provided a refuge, if they wished to be renewed

[20] In the sacred fountain:

So that, once the guilt it had voluntarily incurred had been dissolved by pardon,

Nature might of its own accord return to its own powers,

And, once cleansed, might preserve the strength

Of which it had been stripped through its errors.

This gift of baptism, however, was so rich,

[25] And so much was conferred upon man in this covenant,

[Col. 0096A] That it suited even little children,

Who were entirely without fault,

So that those born good might become better,

And the goodness of nature might be illumined

By the addition of honor.

119 No one among all, however, was excluded from this gift:

[30] No one was born so by the judgment of God;

Rather, each would merit by his freedom

To receive the promises of the one who calls,

Which are undeserved by those who turn away

But owed to those who are upright.

[Note: [Col. 0095D]

## CHAPTER II

How vigorously the Church rejected the teaching of Pelagius. The apostolic see; the Palestinian council convened at Diospolis in 415, where Pelagius denied his errors with a deceitful heart. At approximately the same time Jerome wrote his Dialogues against the Pelagians. The Pelagians were rejected by Atticus, archbishop of Constantinople; expelled at Ephesus; and driven out of Sicily.

39. “Rome was the first to strike back,” namely through Innocent I, in 417. As Saint Prosper says in Against the Collator, chapter 21, Innocent of blessed memory “struck the heads of the profane error—Pelagius and Coelestius—with the apostolic sword.” Innocent did this by sending two letters to the African synods, the Carthaginian and the Milevitan; these letters are included among Augustine’s letters as numbers 181 and 182. Later Zosimus did the same in 418, in a letter sent to the bishops of the African council on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and received by them on the third day before the Kalends of May.

The expression “first,” however, has given some people grounds for asserting that the Pelagian heresy was proscribed by the apostolic see before any judgment by other bishops. Since learned men do not consider this opinion sufficiently compatible with the history of the Pelagian heresy, different solutions to the difficulty have been proposed.

Some contend that “first” should be understood as priority of dignity, zeal, solicitude, and authority. Others, while freely admitting that the judgments of the Africans and Easterners preceded Innocent’s judgment against the Pelagians—since Coelestius is recorded as having been condemned in 412 at the council of Carthage presided over by Aurelius, and again there in 416, and since in 415 the heresy which Pelagius had pretended to abjure was already recorded as having been crushed at Diospolis—nevertheless point out that Innocent I did not reply until 417, after being pressed by several African letters. In that reply he anathematized Pelagius and Coelestius. This was the first judgment pronounced at Rome against such an error.

They therefore say that the African bishops first condemned the Pelagian error in Pelagius and Coelestius, but that Pope Siricius had long before proscribed the same error in Jovinian, whose disciples the Pelagians were. In this way they attempt to reconcile the various passages of this poem and of other books which at first sight seemed contradictory.

Others again understand priority in time in such a way that they do not separate the decrees of the African councils, the Carthaginian and the Milevitan, from Innocent’s letters, but combine them into a single condemnation of Pelagius.

Finally, some have thought that the matter can be settled briefly by saying that the words “first,” and the “then” that follows shortly afterward, indicate no order other than the order of the narrative. Those who recount several events often insert such markers of sequence to avoid confusion, without intending to assert priority or posteriority.

Indeed, the Author himself sufficiently shows that he has observed no such chronological order here, since he prefers everything to appear to have happened simultaneously, though in different places, as if at one time. “By the same decrees simultaneously,” and so forth.

[Col. 0097B] 41. “Whatever it does not possess.” Thus in On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 2, chapter 16: “Through the primacy of the apostolic priesthood, the fortress of religion was made greater than the throne of power,” namely imperial power. See similar passages in Pope Leo, if these very words are not his, as some learned men suspect.

42. “The rulers of the East.” Our Author is speaking of the Palestinian synod held at Diospolis. Pelagius had been brought there after the Gallic bishops Heros and Lazarus had brought an accusation against him—the former from Aix, the latter from Arles—although both had been expelled from their sees. This appears to have occurred in 415.

At this council Pelagius was heard in the absence of his accusers, who had been prevented by necessary circumstances. He artfully answered each article in the written accusation they had submitted, and so deceived the judges through much dissimulation that, after he had abjured and condemned the errors, he himself was declared innocent and orthodox.

43. “And compelled.” The Palestinian bishops’ synod compelled Pelagius to pronounce judgment against himself and his followers, as stated in Against the Collator, chapter 21.

[Col. 0097C] 51. “The beast.” Pelagius, of course. The Fathers frequently used harsher expressions for obstinate heretics.

52. “Had retained the same meaning.” For, as Augustine says in Against Julian, book 1, chapter 5, “what he denied with his mouth, he preserved in his heart.”

55. “Bethlei.” He inflected the Hebrew word Bethlehem according to a Latin ending, making it Bethleam, hence the genitive Bethlei.

Ibid. “Of illustrious name.” Because of the fame of its reputation, and perhaps also because of the etymology of Jerome’s name, as though it meant “of a sacred name.”

57. “Teacher of the world.” Thus the Roman Breviary says of him on the last day of September: “As to an oracle, questions concerning Holy Scripture were brought to him for explanation from every part of the world.” Pope Damasus and Saint Augustine often consulted him concerning the most difficult passages of Scripture, because of his exceptional knowledge not only of Latin and Greek but also of Hebrew and Chaldaic.

58. “In books,” especially in the Dialogues and the Letter to Ctesiphon.

59. “Dissected.” This is not so much because of the sharpness of his style—for the same Breviary says, “He attacked heretics with the keenest writings”—as because in those books he performed a subtle anatomy of the most cunning heresy and revealed, as the following verse says, its very innermost entrails. He was among those who could investigate its meaning most carefully, as the council of Milevis testified in its letter to Pope Innocent, included among Augustine’s letters as 176, formerly 92.

62. “Good in learned speech,” that is, eloquent in an educated manner. The expression is Virgilian, as in Aeneid 9:

> This man is good with the spear, that one with the far-flying arrow.

Ibid. Atticus is called a priest because at that time this was the proper title of bishops, whereas ecclesiastical usage has now left it to presbyters.

64. “From which,” or “by which”: namely, from or by the city, not from the faith, as one might suppose. The construction is completed by what follows: “They endured the torments of silent rejection,” that is, they were rejected or expelled without being heard.

After the judgment of Zosimus, the Pelagians had also been driven from their sees by imperial decrees. They sent some of their number to Constantinople, where, concealing the impiety of their error, they covered themselves and their cause with a false appearance. In that city, however, Atticus had succeeded blessed John Chrysostom. He was a worthy rival of Chrysostom in the faith and, in this case, brought both his learning and episcopal courage to bear. He rejected their embassy, opposed to them the ancient faith of the Church, and pursued them so vigorously that he did not even allow them permission to remain in the city.

It is not clear who the heretics’ envoys were, except that Marius Mercator identifies Coelestius as their leader. Near the beginning of his Commonitorium he writes: “After some years”—namely, after his condemnation at Carthage, when the deacon Paulinus was his accuser—“under Atticus, bishop of blessed memory, he sought the city of Constantinople; there, being exposed in similar matters, he was expelled from that noble city through the great zeal of that holy man.”

65. The Lyon edition alone reads:

> Although they covered themselves with an outward veil of appearance,  
> They endured the torments of the judgment and silent rejection.

The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, and later editions, read:

> Although they covered themselves with an outward veil of appearance,  
> They had endured the torments of the judgment and silent rejection.

For these readings the most recent editor of this poem, the Louvain doctor and royal professor, wishes to adopt:

> Although they covered themselves with the veil of an outward appearance,  
> They bore the judgment’s silent rejection as a torment.

Thus he conjecturally emends a passage hitherto extremely corrupt, saying that he happened to encounter a modern writer who read it in this way. Since he did not entirely trust that reading, however, he elsewhere proposed the earlier form with “they bore.” He also says that he entirely dislikes the word “and,” which he thinks entered the text to complete an otherwise mutilated sentence, and that, through inept correction, “they bore” was changed from the Virgilian form into “they may have borne” or “they had borne.”

Ibid. “The appearance of judgment.” Tacitus would have said “the semblance of judgment,” but our poet had to serve the meter. Marius Mercator perhaps hints at this appearance of judgment when he indicates that Coelestius appealed from the council of Carthage to the apostolic see, but later, after changing his plan, fled to Constantinople under the appearance of an appeal. Thus the Louvain doctor cited above.

[Col. 0099A] 68. “Ephesus, bright with tumult.” He probably means a popular tumult, since that people was fervent in defense of its ancestral faith, as is shown by their joy at the overthrow of the Nestorian heresy. The present passage should not, however, be understood of the condemnation of the Pelagians at that council, since the council had not yet been convened when this poem was written; it is known to have been convened only after Augustine’s death.

Learned men prefer to place the event near the end of 421. At that time the condemned Pelagians attempted to win over this Church, in which Coelestius had imprudently been raised to the priesthood and where, because of his long residence in the city, he may have enjoyed various advantages. They failed, however: the Ephesians rejected the embassy of the heretics and quickly compelled their envoys to leave the city.

70. “Trinacria aflame, the viperous band,” and so forth. Sicily is famously called Trinacria because of its three promontories. After being driven from the East, the heretics returned toward the West and also landed in Sicily. There they attempted to breathe the poison of their depravity upon the Sicilian people, but through the diligence and courage of the island’s bishops they were rejected and expelled from that land and compelled to cross beyond the sea. This took place approximately at this time.

The passage may also refer to the year 419, when several Sicilian bishops, refusing to subscribe to the condemnation of the Pelagians, were expelled from their sees.]

While mad error spread such things widely

And dragged inexperienced ears along with deadly inventions,

[35] The pious care of the holy Fathers, prepared throughout the world

At God’s prompting, came to their aid,

Destroying the savage enemies with heavenly darts,

Not by unequal movement but by a single accord.

For by the same decrees, simultaneously,

One Spirit thundered. Rome’s apostolic see

[40] [Col. 0097A] Was the first to strike down the approaching plague—

Rome, the see of Peter, which, made the head

Of pastoral honor for the world,

Holds by religion whatever it does not possess by arms.

Nor did the care of the rulers of the East

Shine forth less vigorously. It seized the author

Of the wicked doctrine and bound him by a merciful law

[45] To condemn his invention,

Unless he preferred to be cut off from Christ’s body

And separated from the holy flock.

This judgment may seem gentle,

Indeed excessively tolerant toward evil men;

But holy faith, under that examination,

Overcame the offspring that would arise

From the savage seed.

[50] For divine providence had looked ahead

And taken care that, although the beast,

Avoiding the punishment that pressed upon it,

Retained within itself the same meaning of treachery,

[Col. 0098A] Yet, by condemning its own offspring,

It might itself destroy its proper brood,

Extinguishing with its mouth the evil offspring

That its mouth had produced.

[55] Then Jerome, the guest of Bethlehem,

A man illustrious in name,

Graceful in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin speech,

An example of morals and teacher of the world,

HIERONYMUS, dissected the enemy

In books of outstanding excellence,

And made known the storm by which the darknesses

That had arisen wished to obscure the true light.

[60] Why should I speak of the great care

Which the learned-speaking priest ATTICUS

Displayed in the great city of Constantinople,

When he refuted the envoys of the heretics

By the ancient faith?

From that city the impious hearts,

[65] Although they covered themselves with the veil

Of an outward appearance of judgment,

Had endured the torments of silent rejection.

I pass over how greatly glorious EPHESUS

Was stirred by a righteous tumult,

Not allowing within its own homes

[70] The vessels of wrath,

The breath of disease,

Or the seeds of death to remain;

And how the faith of blazing TRINACRIA

Drove the viperous band from its own shores.

[Col. 0100A] [Note: [Col. 0099B]

## CHAPTER III

The Pelagian heresy was defeated chiefly through the assistance of the African bishops. Praise of Augustine. The victory over the Pelagians belongs above all to Augustine alone. The excellence of Augustine’s books on the grace of God. They are read profitably only by the humble.

72. The Lyon, Louvain, and Douai editions read “ours” (nostrae). Others preferred the reading “our Africa” (Africa nostra), even from a Gallic author, as shortly afterward “our African bishops,” meaning “of our party,” indeed “the glory of our party.” The African bishops were the first to condemn this error, as we have already said, beginning in 412, and they defended their earlier judgment at several gatherings held in the following years. They also wrote several letters to Innocent and Zosimus, by which they secured the judgment of the apostolic see against the enemies of sound faith.

77. “And by the celebrated assembly of the two groups of elders.” Learned men disagree about this double council. Some thought that the two synods meant here were the Carthaginian and Milevitan councils held under Innocent in 416. Through these councils the Pelagians were first struck down, and their decrees were renewed in the primary council of all Africa under Zosimus in 418.

Others note, among the various councils of African bishops collected in the Pelagian case, two that seem more distinguished. One should apparently be assigned to the beginning of November 417, after the arrival of the letters Zosimus had sent in favor of Coelestius. In it they implored Zosimus to leave matters in the condition in which they then stood until he had been more fully informed about the case of Coelestius, who had first been accused before them. This council eventually reached a total of 214 bishops. Prosper states in his Chronicle, under the year 418, that it was held before Coelestius was condemned by Zosimus.

The other council appears to have been held when, after receiving their second, later letter, Zosimus replied to the letter of the African council on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April of the following year with a single, fairly brief response. This letter reached Africa on the third day before the Kalends of May, when the bishops were gathering at Carthage to celebrate another council against the Pelagians. Photius says that this council, held in the basilica of Faustus on 1 May 418, reached 220 bishops, apart from the primates Donatianus and Aurelius.

There is no room for doubt that this was the plenary council of all Africa at which Augustine testifies that he and the other bishops established something against the Pelagian heresy. At it eight or nine canons were enacted, which had formerly been attributed to the council of Milevis and which Baronius thought had been sanctioned in that city in 416.

The Louvain editor and commentator seems to adopt this opinion when he writes as follows. First, he says, we gather from what the present poem, and almost this very chapter, supplies us that those African synods of which Saint Prosper speaks were plenary, as is shown by the words in verse 76, “from all the cities.” They were also numerous, since so many bishops gave judgment in them that the Author could appropriately call them “three hundred” in verse 86. Moreover, the two were in a certain sense one and the same council: they were held in the same city, by the same Fathers, concerning the same matter, and within a very short interval, so that in verses 91 and 184 they are called in the singular “the council,” not “the councils.”

Finally, Aurelius of Carthage presided over both, and Augustine was present at both, as verses 91 and 92 indicate. From this we conclude that the passage is not dealing with the Carthaginian and Milevitan synods held under Pope Innocent, since the subscriptions to the letters of each council to Innocent prove that neither was plenary, neither had so large a number of bishops, and neither included both Aurelius and Augustine, whatever some may have thought.

Once these councils are excluded, what remain except the two Carthaginian councils under Pope Zosimus, which everyone admits? Everything mentioned above fits them remarkably well. Augustine himself indicates that they were plenary in Letter 215 to Valentinus. The number of bishops is also known: Prosper counts 214, or elsewhere 217, whom the poet here, in poetic freedom, calls “three hundred.”

But why linger over many details when the matter can be settled at once? I certainly think that the double council mentioned by the Author here, in verse 77—“by the celebrated assembly of the two groups of elders”—and again in verses 90 and 91:

> Could a holy council proceed to any other end,  
> With Aurelius as its leader, and so forth—

is the same council to which he sends the Pelagians below, in verse 184 and following, and orders them to return to

> The throne of Peter at Rome and lofty Carthage.

That is, he orders them to revisit the council where he had earlier said they were condemned.

Why, then, should we still ask where in the world that council was held, when the Virgilian phrase “lofty Carthage” points to the matter more clearly than a finger? If only equal light and certainty shone upon its decrees or canons! That some were enacted there is suggested by verse 84: “They were established and remain written.” The words below, from the cited book Against the Collator, also suggest this, not to mention Augustine’s already cited Letter 217.

Those decrees or letters have either perished, as did the letter of Zosimus by which they were confirmed, or—and this is what I think more likely—they are the same eight canons on grace which the Second Council of Tours later called “the ancient canons of Milevis.” For that reason some have thought that they were first enacted at some Milevitan synod and later renewed at Carthage. But Augustine’s letter to Valentinus makes no mention of a renewal; rather, it speaks in such a way as to indicate that they were enacted there.

[Col. 0101B] 78. “What Rome approves.” For Pope Zosimus of blessed memory added the strength of his judgment to the decrees of the African councils and, to cut down the impious, armed the right hands of all the bishops with Peter’s sword. Saint Prosper, Against the Collator, chapter 41 in some editions, now chapter 21.

Ibid. “Let kingdoms follow.” The emperor Honorius, following the authority of these councils, issued a law against the Pelagians in 418, according to the French translator of this poem. The Author himself explains the matter in Against the Collator, chapter 21, formerly chapter 41, where he says: “Pope Boniface of holy memory rejoiced in the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors, and against the enemies of God’s grace he used not only apostolic edicts but also royal ones.”

81. “The arts were exposed.” The author of the translation mentioned shortly below understands this as referring to the letters to Innocent and Zosimus, and to the eight canons that seem to have been first enacted by the council of Milevis and renewed by the Carthaginian council under Zosimus.
