Hence the Second Council of Tours, in 570, calls them “the ancient canons of Milevis,” although in the code of the canons of the African Church they are attributed to the Carthaginian council under Zosimus; among them the eight canons on grace hold the first place.

The Louvain commentator, however, writes: “I agree concerning the canons, and also concerning the letter to Zosimus, if this paragraph, from verse 79 through verse 84, is to be understood as referring to synodal matters, as are the preceding and following passages. But because it appears rather to have been inserted parenthetically, and because the Author seems to digress to other events accomplished in the same Church, so to speak, outside the synod—for example, by Augustine and similar disputants—I would believe that these matters should be referred to the private activity of such Africans.

“At least I cannot be induced to believe that the Author is speaking of the letters to Innocent. For he nowhere takes account of the synods by which those letters were written, either because they had not been convened expressly for the Pelagian cause but had learned of it only incidentally and in passing, or because they had instead referred the entire matter to the first see, to which whatever was accomplished in this regard should consequently be attributed.”

86. “And three hundred.” This is poetic, as in verse 187 below: “A thousand elders,” and so forth. In prose Prosper consistently gives the number as 214 priests, or in some places 217. But why did the poet not rather say “two hundred” in the verse, equally poetically and with a number closer to the truth? The round number 300 may have appealed to him chiefly because it had long been consecrated by the Fathers of the first Council of Nicaea. So the Louvain doctor.

Others think that, although 220 bishops did not attend each of these councils, it could easily have happened that three hundred different bishops attended the two councils taken together.

89. “Peace.” One may doubt whether this is used in the phraseology of the Fathers, especially Cyprian, for ecclesiastical communion, to which the following is opposed:

> . . . to be cut off from Christ’s body  
> And separated from the holy flock;

or whether it is used in Virgilian phraseology for pardon, as in Aeneid 3, with several similar passages:

> But they order him to seek peace  
> With vows and prayers.

The fact that it means communion with the Church is suggested by the antithesis that follows:

> . . . those who held what was perverse,  
> Once expelled from the Church.

90. “Could another.” The Louvain editor and commentator suspects that a copyist’s error has occurred here, and that the line could not have been written in this form by someone who later, in verse 484, showed himself not ignorant of meter:

> Or was it from the waters that the divine hand, and so forth?

He therefore suggests either reading “Could another” in the same way, or, at his own risk, “Behold another.” Virgil, who often serves as our Author’s model, would support this; compare the following questions in Eclogue 1:

> Will I ever again, after a long time, see my ancestral fields?

And in the Pharmaceutria:

> Will that day ever come, and so forth?

The same doctor adds that “end” should be understood as outcome or success, not as final cause.

91 and 92. “Aurelius was the leader, and Augustine the mind.” No one doubts that Aurelius of Carthage and Augustine of Hippo are meant. It is not the case, as someone once thought, that both names refer to one bishop of Hippo, whose first name was Aurelius and whose surname was Augustine, and who therefore served simultaneously as both leader and mind of this council.

92. “With a more abundant horn.” Perhaps the fabulous horn of plenty, or Amalthea’s horn, came to mind, especially since the divine Scriptures themselves did not disdain it, as the same Louvain doctor says. But this is mistaken. The Author rather alludes to the horn with which Scripture records that the sacred anointings of kings and priests were once performed. See Gregory on 1 Kings 10, where he weighs its abundance against the scarcity of the little flask with which Saul and other ill-omened rulers are said to have been anointed.

97. “He attributes no good things to himself.” The Louvain doctor writes: “I had thought this was said to provoke the envy of the Ingrates, who attributed many good things to themselves and to their own free will. But when I examine the context more closely, this meaning occurs to me instead: Since he seeks no good of his own—‘He does not seek what is his own,’ says Scripture—neither his own food, nor life, rest, pleasure, or honor, as those goods are enumerated in the preceding verses, God becomes all these things for him: food, life, and so forth. And in him, as in a temple dedicated exclusively to himself, that uncreated Wisdom reigns which will not enter a malicious soul nor dwell in a body subject to sins. Wisdom 1:4.”

98. “He reigns.” From this and other present-tense expressions throughout the paragraph it may be inferred that these words were written while the holy doctor was still alive.

[Col. 0103C] 112. “Which the gentle and humble drink.” The Louvain doctor writes: “He indirectly censures his opponents, who are, by contrast, fierce and proud and therefore find the same Augustinian streams distasteful. For, as another says, one must be gentle and humble in order to delight in Augustine’s teaching concerning grace and be nourished by it to salvation. A mind that is more elevated and insufficiently conscious of its own weakness must necessarily recoil from that teaching and take offense at it.”

You, Africa, pursue the cause of our faith with more ardent zeal,  
and, joining your strength to the throne of apostolic authority,  
you crush the savage entrails of war  
[75] and lay the defeated low across a broad field.

Your gracious bishops have assembled from all your cities,  
and, in a most renowned twofold gathering of elders,  
[Col. 0101A] you decree what Rome approves and what kingdoms shall follow.

Nor is the authority of the councils there displayed alone;  
[80] as though those whom our people could not overcome by reason  
should be crushed by force: the arts have been exposed,  
and the venom of heretical thinking laid bare;  
no argument remains at all  
that learned faith could not dissolve.

What flowed forth from the cataracts  
[85] of the eternal fountain in an overflowing stream  
has been established and remains in writing,  
and has been published in the tongues of three hundred leaders—  
so severe goodness governs its own law—  
that those who wished to return from condemned error  
[Col. 0102A] might receive peace, while those who persisted in depravity were driven away.

[90] Or could the holy Council, whose leader was Aurelius  
and whose genius was Augustine, proceed toward any other end?  
Augustine, whom the grace of Christ, watering him with a more abundant horn,  
[127] gave to our age as a light kindled from true light. For God is his food,  
[95] his life, and his rest; every pleasure for him  
is one love of Christ, and his one honor is Christ’s.  
And because he attributes no good to himself, God becomes for him everything,  
and in his holy temple Wisdom reigns.

Therefore, among all those who drove mad beasts  
[100] [Col. 0103A] from the holy flock, this man’s greater diligence  
filled the whole world with a greater and more excellent work.  
For wherever the cunning enemy turned his step,  
and along whatever winding, uncertain path he moved in concealment,  
he was anticipated by this man’s opposition;  
[105] the ambushes of a thousand roads found no entrance.

And when the fury of ravenous wolves, shut out from without,  
gnashed its teeth and turned lies into every kind of device,  
so that it could not corrupt the minds of any sheep  
or disturb uncertain hearts with crooked complaints,  
[110] God acted through this man’s mouth; through this man’s mouth  
rivers of books flowed out over the whole world,  
[Col. 0103B] and the gentle and humble drink from them,  
striving to send the streams of life-giving doctrine into the fields of their souls.

[Note: [Col. 0103C]

## CHAPTER IV

The heresy extinguished by the Church among the Pelagians began to revive among the Semipelagians. The error of the Semipelagians: that the inclination to will the good is natural to human beings, just as the inclination to will evil is.

116. “Of the mother.” The Church is introduced as a woman whose womb has been so occupied by offspring of a foreign stock—namely, the Pelagian stock—that for a long time she regarded them as her own because of their apparent moral character. —Louvain Doctor.

120. “With the habits of outward respectability.” At the beginning of the book Against the Collations, the Author describes the Semipelagians as displaying an appearance of virtue in their zeal; and in the Letter to Augustine he says that among the more simple-minded there was great reverence for their reputation for probity, no. 2. Near the end of that same letter he says that, famous for their merits and honors, they are darkened by the obscurity of their own opinion. He alludes to the same point below, verse 774 and following.

126. “Of the extinguished doctrine,” etc. Thus, Against the Collations, chapter 6: “Why, by rekindling the ashes of the extinguished doctrine” (the Pelagian doctrine), “do you try to kindle the stench of dying smoke into a renewed flame?”

129. “By the power of natural movement.” —Louvain Doctor. Below, verse 925, he more explicitly calls it “natural mobility”:

> So that the lively mind, by natural mobility …

See, therefore, whether “natural” should also be read here; at least, that is my preference.

130. “That each person can pursue goods as good,” etc. Similarly, Letter to Augustine, no. 6: “Let each person have as much ability for good as for evil, and with equal momentum turn his mind either toward vices or toward virtues.”

131. “By natural endowment.” —Louvain Doctor. It is not easy to say in what sense Prosper generally uses this word here. Rarely does he use it in the ordinary sense, for the power of understanding; but neither does he use it in the sense in which it frequently occurs in good authors, namely, for the character or disposition of each thing. I suspected that it was used for the faculty of willing, and you would not take it wrongly in that sense, at least here; but there are other passages where even that does not fit. I therefore think it is taken broadly enough to encompass, in its meaning, the whole mind—both the part by which it understands and the part by which it desires. It is enough to have noted this once.]

And now, after the storm-cloud of night has been scattered by the whirlwind,  
[115] alas, new wars, new offspring arise in the very womb  
of the peaceful mother. Seeing them grow, she shudders  
to find a discordant shoot rising up,  
and, fearing offspring degenerate from hostile seed,  
in whom, long before, while appearances deceived her,  
[120] the mother’s kindly love had gone astray,  
when the origin of a foreign stock was hidden beneath respectable conduct.

Thus false things take the place of true ones, and, through blind discrimination,  
[Col. 0104A] what lies hidden in its end pleases at first sight; thus, through love of praise,  
the pursuit of virtues is corrupted, and from an honorable  
beginning one generally passes into the vice of arrogance:  
[125] by this some are now shamefully inflated, and they attempt  
to revive the extinguished ashes of a destroyed doctrine,  
[129] while placing free choice and the inclination to will  
in the power of natural movement,  
[130] teaching that each person can pursue good by his own  
natural endowment, just as each has the power to be carried toward evil.

[Note: [Col. 0104C]

## CHAPTER V

Those who hold these views do not differ from the Pelagians and therefore ought publicly to make peace with them.

132. The Lyon edition has *qui non distabis* (“you will not differ”), and in the margin, *tu non distabis* (“you will not differ”).

133. “By no wound of sin.” The Pelagians say this above, verse 10 and following.

> Nor are they now born unlike that one, etc.

136. “Receive it with a part cut away.” —Louvain Doctor. Hence the name “Semipelagians,” from a half-Pelagianism. Before them certain people were called Semi-Arians because they accepted the madness of Arius only in part, supposing—both they and the Semipelagians—that they had acted most prudently if, between the disputing parties, they entered upon some middle way; perhaps they were led by those well-known sayings: “Virtue lies in the mean”; “You will go most safely by the middle way”; “I fly between the two”; “The blessed have held the middle,” and so forth—as though a middle way between truth and error were not itself also erroneous.

140. “To give peace openly.” —Louvain Doctor. If our Saint wrote it this way, kindly accept the lengthening of the vowel in *palam*, especially in an age when the quantity of initial syllables had begun to escape Roman, and still more Gallic, ears. Otherwise read *pacemque palam* (“and peace openly”).

141. “To protect those driven out in any respect.” —Louvain Doctor. I will smooth out this rough passage for you once again, reader. Connect *ulla ex parte* (“in any respect”) not with *pulsos* (“those driven out”) but with *tueri* (“to protect”), and understand the sentence thus: “Is it not safe simply to protect these expelled men in even one article of their doctrine?”

142. “To exclude from the temple”: as they then customarily did to those outside their communion, especially if they had been cut off from it on account of heresy. —Louvain Doctor.

[Col. 0105B] 144. “Join.” An imperative, but ironic. Yet *componere* in the following verse is an infinitive governed by *cupidis*. —Louvain Doctor.

146. “By your law.” —Louvain Doctor. That is, under the conditions you yourself prescribe, as the Pelagians themselves explain in the following chapter. The printed editions joined these words with what follows, *jam parce* (“now spare us”), etc., but without making sense.]

Since you affirm this, in what way will you differ from those  
[Col. 0104B] who say that natural goodness has been touched by no wound of sin,  
and that all people are now born with that light  
which was implanted in the first parents?  
[135] Or do you select certain things, accepting them after cutting away part  
and storing them, cleansed, in your heart?  
Say, then, what you approve in their teaching, and what you reject,  
and what charge you remove from the condemned doctrines.

[140] Or are you ashamed to offer the right hand of peace openly to the enemy?  
Is it not dangerous simply to protect those expelled  
in any respect? Those whom you do not hesitate to exclude from the temple,  
drive away from your heart. A new discord divides you from yourself:  
[Col. 0105A] in your heart you cherish what you suppress with your mouth;  
join them to friendly minds, and let the eager make a treaty with you  
according to your law; now spare your threats  
and bring them into harmony with your agreements.

[Note: [Col. 0105C]

## CHAPTER VI

He introduces the Pelagians addressing the Semipelagians in plaintive language, asking to be received into their favor, since they approve their position.

158. “They are cleansed by the fountain of washing.” This does not mean simply “Let them be baptized,” which the Pelagians never rejected; rather, the emphasis falls on being cleansed, that is, purified from sins. —Louvain Doctor.

159. “While our people.” —Louvain Doctor. Our excellent poet is wholly intent on showing that Pelagius appears to have been condemned in vain if even one of his doctrines—also held by the men of Massilia—remained intact.

172. “Of the good—not for the good,” or “the good,” as others, and the Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read. This is a phrase familiar to good authors, as in Horace, *Satires*, book 1, satire 4: “Forgive me, good sir, I beg.” —Louvain Doctor.]

Behold, after wandering through the ends of the earth, we are here,  
and we begin to fill your ears with tearful complaints:  
“Driven from the world and received in no place,  
[150] wandering at last, we return, encouraged by report,  
and we embrace whatever pleases you. The piety of your doctrine  
has been set forth for us; by denying nothing,  
we dispute nothing. Let us be permitted to join our understanding with yours.

“If you believe that human beings were made immortal, we too believe it;  
[155] that they fell into death by sinning and bound all their offspring  
by guilt and death: let no one be without need  
of the sacred baptism of Christ,  
and let infants also be cleansed in the fountain of washing.

“Provided that the glory of our free choice, and the created light  
[160] implanted at the beginning—which can of its own accord adhere to what is right—  
has remained unharmed, and has not been deprived of those powers  
which, when God created it, every human nature generally received in Adam,  
and provided no one has cause to complain  
of a power of free choice that was not received;

[165] “since, without distinction, whether Law or the grace of Christ,  
wishes to save every human being, and the gift of the One who calls  
has been so appointed that everyone can come to it  
by his own freedom and strength,  
let salvation be the lot of those worthy to be saved  
[Col. 0106A] from the fountain of willing.

[170] “If this is your faith, if this is your doctrine, then, once removed  
the positions we rejected on your example, add us to your holy flocks,  
and at last, good men, defend your own people.”

[Note: [Col. 0105C]

## CHAPTER VII

Those who hold these views cannot refuse fellowship with the Pelagians unless they change their position; nor can they embrace them unless they openly dissent from the Church.

179. “Of the saints to the holy things.” —Louvain Doctor. That is, to the temples, sacraments, and so forth; an allusion to the Holy of Holies of the ancient temple.

181. “The decrees of the Fathers.” —Louvain Doctor. That is, those of the bishops and councils against the Pelagians.

Ibid. “And of the pious kings.” —Louvain Doctor. The emperors Honorius, Theodosius, Constantius, and others, who published edicts against the same people. Hence the Author says of Pope Boniface, *Against the Collations*, chapter 6: “He rejoiced in the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors, and against the enemies of the grace of God he used not only apostolic edicts but also royal ones.”]

If a humbled enemy should lament such things before you,  
what will you reply? With what feeling will what you have learned move you?  
[175] You deliberate, tremble, nod, hesitate, and remain in doubt;  
you turn over the question of where your uncertain judgment should plunge.

It is unjust not to grant peace to kindred minds,  
and to deny those whom one faith and the same wisdom bind  
a common access for the holy ones to the holy things.

[180] But to join an alliance with such people, to violate  
the decrees of the holy Fathers and of pious kings,  
and to despise the laws written in God’s law  
[Col. 0106B] is profoundly hostile, excessively bold, and destructive.

[Note: [Col. 0105D]

## CHAPTER VIII

The Pelagians can bring the same complaints before the bishops of the Church. A speech of the Pelagians, in which they ask that judgment be passed on them, so that either they may be received into the Church and be permitted to teach what the Semipelagians teach, or the Semipelagians too may be driven out together with them.

185. “The council.” Saint Prosper seems to make one council out of two: one in November 417 and another in May 418.

186. “To your hesitant favor,” namely, the favor of the men of Massilia toward the Pelagians, whom they favored, though hesitantly because of the laws.

187. “A thousand elders.” Used for a large number of bishops, from whom the Pelagians would suffer rejection in this proposal of theirs, just as previously they had received a sentence of condemnation.

188. “The whole substance of the wicked heresy,” etc. This is characteristic of the Pelagian heresy and deserves close attention: its various errors are so interwoven with one another by a kind of natural connection, and are so linked one to another, that if you admit one, you are drawn, even unwillingly, into all the rest. Saint Prosper had already observed this in the final chapter of *Against the Collations*: “For it is well known that the deceits of that falsehood are so arranged that, if it is allowed, under the appearance of a correction of the past, to retain some shoot of its root favorable to itself, it can restore itself entirely from a small part of itself.” Here the Louvain Doctor notes a common corruption of the passage, caused by the redundant words *sibi faventium* (“favorable to itself”), or else by the omission of certain other words. As for the matter itself, Pope Leo also notes the character of this heresy in Letter 86 to Nicetas of Aquileia; and our Saint briefly makes the same point elsewhere: if God’s grace is not received in its entirety according to the Catholic faith, it is rejected in its entirety, leaving no place for dividing it in half.

192. “Their ancient arts.” By these Pelagius and Coelestius had tried, as if in competition, to insinuate themselves—Pelagius among the Eastern bishops, Coelestius also among the Romans. —Louvain Doctor.

Ibid. “Will have rejected,” and in the following verse, “will have stood”: these are future-tense verbs. The bishops had not yet rejected the proposal; they are predicted to reject it. The point is sufficiently indicated by the sentence itself, at least since we have finally enclosed in parentheses the preceding verses together with the adverb *olim* (“formerly”), which had previously confused the passage. —Louvain Doctor.

[Col. 0107B] 193. “And the judgment will have stood within its own limits,” that is, the Roman and African decision will have remained fixed. —Louvain Doctor.

197. “To what end,” meaning “how long?” not in the sense commonly expressed by “with what intention?” —Louvain Doctor.

199. “Throughout the whole world,” that is, alone among all human beings. —Louvain Doctor.

201. “If even a syllable of ours differs from yours,” etc. They attempt to diminish their disagreement with the orthodox—as is the disposition of all heretics—as though it consisted only in words and expressions. The printed editions join this verse with the following in this way:

> Whom you cannot endure?  
> If even a syllable of ours differs from yours in speech,  
> We no longer defend ourselves by words …

We have followed Gallus, the learned man who rendered this poem into the Gallic language in verse and prose. —Louvain Doctor.

203. “We seek judgment by example.” Contrary to the usual saying that judgment is rendered not by examples but by laws. They therefore ask that judgment be pronounced on them according to the example of the Semipelagians, so that if the Semipelagians are acquitted, they too may be considered acquitted. The Lyon, Louvain, and Douai editions had *extemplo* (“immediately”), but incongruously. —Louvain Doctor.

Ibid. “With peace remaining.” That is, without prejudice to ecclesiastical communion, as above more than once. Understand *sine bello* (“without war”) in the same way in the following verse. —Louvain Doctor.

204. “Of many.” For the Semipelagians had already been numerous from the beginning, as the Author also testifies in the Letter to Augustine, to such an extent that near the end of that letter he calls the defenders of perfect grace few in comparison with them, especially since the faction relied upon immense power and influence, as he likewise shows. —Louvain Doctor.

205. “Your inventions,” and in the following verse, “your first teachings.” Above, in chapter 1, he calls the first doctrines explicitly stated their “first teachings,” as though they were saying: “Our doctrine is no longer the same as when you first condemned us; look, we have withdrawn from those matters at issue”—namely, those mentioned above in chapter 8, section 2. —Louvain Doctor.

208. “Whatever pleases them”: namely, the Semipelagians, whom you still regard as your own or as belonging to your communion. For now, in chapter 8, they present themselves as ready to subscribe to the whole of their doctrine: “Whatever pleases you,” they say, “we embrace.”

209. “What guilt remains?” etc. The printed editions—Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne—generally read: “What guilt remains, by which it is fitting for us,” etc. This makes *quo* a relative in the ablative and makes it modify *quid culpae* (“what guilt”). We have restored the text as we think the Author wrote it, following Virgil, *Aeneid* 5:

> What end to standing? How long should I be held?

Here the tmesis in *quousque* (“how long”) is clear. —Louvain Doctor. The French translator also followed this sense.

210. “Those things which we,” namely, together with your people, or the Semipelagians; for the discussion concerns doctrines common to both groups. —Louvain Doctor.

213. “Through famous towns,” and in the following verse, “great peoples.” Namely, Massilia, or also other places in Gaul, as Hilary says in his letter to Augustine. Hence the entire faction also acquired the name “Massilians,” and the Author wrote a certain short work against the Chapters of the Gauls. He also responded to the excerpts of the Genoese; but these people were not Semipelagians, as those excerpts indicate. I therefore believe that Italy was free from this stain. —Louvain Doctor.

225. “We are moved.” Gallus, the translator, reads *vocamur* (“we are called”), perhaps not inappropriately, unless the third preceding verse were also closed by the same word. —Louvain Doctor.]

Therefore let them return humbly to Rome, the throne of Peter,  
and to another council at Carthage, and let them repeat  
the same complaints that were here lamented in vain  
to hesitant favor.

But when the vigilant wisdom of a thousand elders—  
[185] long ago having perceived and recognized that the whole substance  
of the wicked heresy is concealed beneath a small part of it,  
from which the full infection of evil is renewed  
and the entire body of falsehood rises again in each of its members—  
will have rejected the enemy employing his ancient arts,  
[Col. 0107A] and sound judgment will have remained within its own limits,  
will not just grief be able to open the hidden things of the heart  
and arouse such wretched complaints  
that they say:

“Fathers, what kind of justice is this in generous hearts?  
[195] To what end, to what end do you persist, severe and strict,  
in closing the whole world to us?  
Are we alone in the whole world whose faith  
is everywhere suspect to you, whom you cannot tolerate  
if even a syllable of ours differs from yours in speech?

[200] “We no longer defend ourselves by words or arguments;  
we seek judgment by example. Whatever the free voice of many  
asserts while peace remains, let that be granted to us without war.  
We do not cherish our own inventions,  
nor do we cling to our first teachings: behold,  
[205] the matter from which the old dispute arose has been cut away;  
we have returned to you, we yield, and whatever pleases them  
we approve.

“What guilt remains? How long are we to be rejected?  
[Col. 0108A] But if even these things, which we regard as pious, are absent  
from the truth, and your own good concern rightly opposes them,  
why are those who teach condemned doctrines held free  
from the hatred and punishment of error, and, safe in famous towns,  
[215] fill great peoples with what we proclaim,  
while we are punished and allowed to stand nowhere?

“You see what care these matters, drawn from the holy senate of bishops,  
would require, and what decrees they would provoke.  
Or because, secure in a concealed fault, you are not censured  
by a synod, nor driven by fear of punishment,  
[220] do you despise the appearance of the threatened terror  
and laugh at these things as dreams full of empty phantoms?

“Therefore, setting aside the outcome of what is to be done  
and the ultimate end, let us bring forward only  
the things that have already occurred,  
[Col. 0108B] so that from them it may easily be examined  
what sort of matter this is,  
about which, in our dispute, we have long been drawn in opposite directions.”

## PART TWO

### Argument

He reviews the principal doctrines of Pelagius, which, even by the admission of the Semipelagians themselves, were condemned by the Church. He then sets forth their doctrine, which has two parts.

The first is that grace is offered by God to absolutely all human beings, since he wills all human beings to be saved. The second is that free choice is responsible for one person embracing grace and another rejecting it, for one persevering and another failing to persevere, because the latter neglected to obtain the assistance of grace—which all are able to do, since enough strength has remained in human nature from the remnants of its original integrity to desire and request God’s assistance.

He refutes the first part, concerning grace offered to all so that they may be saved, both by the example of those unbelievers who have never heard anything about the mysteries of faith and who therefore certainly could not have shared in either grace or salvation, and by this argument: if God wished every human being absolutely, without exception, to be saved, all would be saved, since whatever the Almighty wills is undoubtedly fulfilled.

To refute the second part he does two things. First, he explains how grace works in our minds: not merely by counsel and kindly exhortation, teaching and persuading, but by changing the mind inwardly and, moreover, making it will irresistibly. Then he demonstrates that before that grace—which works in us both to will and to act—no one can prepare himself for grace, because faith, which is given first and through which the other gifts are obtained, is God’s gratuitous gift. Before it, human beings can do nothing by which they may merit it, since even all works of moral goodness are sins unless they arise from the seed of true faith.

[226] [Col. 0109A] [Note: [Col. 0109C]

## CHAPTER IX

The principal articles of the Pelagian heresy which, even by the admission of the Semipelagians themselves, were condemned by the Church: that human beings are born pure from every stain of sin; that anyone can, if he wishes, lead a life without sin; that salvation could have been obtained through the law of Moses; and that grace is given according to merits.

227. “What you recognize.” These words too caused confusion; we have therefore enclosed them in parentheses.

235. See above, verses 42 and 77.

Ibid. “And with the world’s hand.” Gallus interprets this as referring to the secular power of the emperors, specifically the law of the emperor Honorius. Someone else understands it as referring to a general subscription by which people of every order indiscriminately would be compelled to condemn the Pelagians. It was simpler to understand it as the agreement by which the whole world embraced the decree of the African councils against the enemies of the grace of God, as we heard the Author himself say above, at verse 78. If, however, the passage is to be understood of a subscription, I would rather hear the Pelagians, who complain in Augustine, book 4 to Boniface, chapter 8: “They complain that a subscription was extorted from bishops sitting in their own places without a council assembled,” while they say nothing about the other orders. —Louvain Doctor.

238. “At the Council of Diospolis.”

239. “The master himself is said to have said it.” In that synod both the following and the preceding article are presented as having been asserted by Coelestius; but what the disciple had asserted was rightly attributed to Pelagius as the teacher. Pelagius replied to the latter article as follows: “Let those who say these things belong to Coelestius see whether they are Coelestius’s; but I have never held them in this way, and I anathematize those who hold them in this way.” See Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 14. In that book the other matters said here concerning this synod may also be found. —Louvain Doctor.

247. “Cultivated in little books.” Augustine reproaches him for this in many places, especially in *On the Grace of Christ*, and likewise in *On Original Sin*. Moreover, “cultivated in little books” is expressed in the same way as above, “I cultivated in verse.” —Louvain Doctor.]

Among the many things that the arch-heretic handed down to his heresy  
(“what you recognize,” he says), he taught that nature, which was made good,  
is created in everyone altogether without any vices,  
[137] and that the guilt of the first parent harmed no one,  
[230] and that people are now born just as that father of our race  
was before his guilt.

He taught that a human being can pass through life without sin,  
if he wishes, just as the first man, by his own freedom,  
was able not to sin. Surely you would admit that these things  
were condemned by councils and by the authority of the whole world.

[235] The same author also connected with this the claim  
that the law once sent the holy into the kingdom of heaven  
in the same way as grace now sends them.  
You know that this too was destroyed by holy judgment.

[Col. 0109B] Another charge was brought forward: that the master himself had said  
[240] that the grace of Christ is granted according to human merits,  
in proportion as each person has made himself fit for God’s gifts.  
But, seeing that this was far too contrary to faith  
and resisted it too greatly, he said that he did not believe this,  
and that those whose minds held such an opinion deserved condemnation.

[245] From this you see that, although the accused agreed with the judges  
who condemned these teachings and no one could defend them,  
he is nevertheless exposed as having cultivated the same doctrines  
again in his own little books, returning through deception  
to the condemned position.

[Note: [Col. 0110C]

## CHAPTER X

The doctrine of the Semipelagians: Grace invites everyone, and there is no one whom it does not strive to bring to salvation; but each person obeys the one who calls by his own free choice. Grace helps those who wish to be helped, and in them, with the Lord’s assistance, virtues subsequently grow, so that everyone has the ability to persevere; yet it happens through free choice that one person perseveres and another does not.

251. “Grace.” Wisdom is personified in Scripture, especially in Proverbs, Wisdom, Ecclesiastes, and elsewhere; and what is said of it is understood by interpreters indiscriminately as referring to uncreated or created wisdom, depending on the context. I wish only to have noted this concerning grace here, leaving the rest to the varying tastes of readers.

[Col. 0110D] 252. “With you.” The Lyon edition reads *nobiscum* (“with us”); and in the following verse, *nec illum* (“nor him”), whereas the other editions read *vobiscum* (“with you”) and *nec ullum* (“nor anyone”).

257. “By his own judgment.” I think the judgment of the will is meant, as Julian calls it in book 4 *Against Julian*, chapter 4—in other words, free choice. —Louvain Doctor.

260. “With goodness as teacher,” that is, teaching; hence immediately afterward, “He learned by the commandments,” and later, “But for those who have been taught,” etc. As for the expression, Virgil’s *Aeneid* 12 had preceded it: “not by skill as teacher.” —Louvain Doctor.]

Now, since it has been shown what displeased us,  
[250] [Col. 0110A] let it become clear how sound your faith is.

You restrict the grace by which we are Christ’s people  
within this boundary, and assign it this form:  
that it does indeed call everyone and invite everyone,  
passing over no one, striving to bring common salvation  
[255] to all and to absolve the whole world from sin.

But each person obeys the one who calls by his own free choice  
and, moved by his own judgment, extends his mind  
toward the offered light, which withdraws from no one,  
but, desirous of what is right, helps and enlightens the willing.

[260] Hence, with the Lord’s goodness as teacher and helper,  
the pursuit of virtues grows, so that what each person has learned  
[Col. 0110B] [139] through the commandments he may pursue with constant love.

And for those who have been taught, you say that this freedom  
is equally available to all, so that they may complete  
the blessed course by persevering,  
with God granting the desired end and accomplishment,  
[265] God, who is never absent from honest minds.

But because strength is not the same in everyone,  
and the scattered will is drawn by the enticements of various things,  
you say that some freely succumb to vices,  
although they could have turned their steps back from the fall  
[270] and remained steadfast.

[Note: [Col. 0110D]

## CHAPTER XI

He refutes that doctrine—Pelagian in character—that it cannot be said that there is anyone to whom the grace of Christ is not given and whom Christ does not wish to save. He proves this by the example of those who received nothing concerning the mysteries of faith.

[Col. 0111B] 275. “For not even,” etc. See the same argument in the *Response to the Chapters of the Gauls*, chapter 4. —Louvain Doctor.

277. “Of the gift,” that is, of the Gospel, as below, verse 289, “the gifts of salvation.” —Louvain Doctor.

284. “Had absolved.” I admit that the older printed editions have *Absorpserat* (“had swallowed up”), but the sense opposes it; it must be believed that *tenebris absolverat* (“had absolved from darkness”) was written here, as below, verse 881, “and absolve from punishment.” The Louvain Doctor had already indicated this with certainty by conjecture. On the judgment of both authorities, and also following the example of the Doctor, we did not hesitate to restore this word to the text.

Ibid. “Of impiety”: in the sense of unbelief, as not only the sacred books but also secular judgments once used the word. Hence Christians were condemned by pagans who had gone astray as guilty of impiety, or *atheotetos*. —Louvain Doctor.]

Now, since your opinion has been surveyed in summary, as far as possible,  
tell us why you prove that the grace of Christ  
[Col. 0111A] passes over absolutely no human being among all who are born,  
and that it wishes to grant the kingdom and blessed life to every one.  
[275] For even in our own time it is not certain that Christ’s Gospel  
has already been made known throughout all lands;  
not to mention that the beginnings of the gift  
could not have spread through the whole world at once.

It was indeed commanded to be carried to all;  
but what is said to occur at one time does not happen all at once.  
[280] And while the Lord opened access for his ministers,  
and the first fruits increased, there must necessarily have been  
some regions of the earth where grace had not yet

[Col. 0111B] [Note: [Col. 0111C]

## CHAPTER XII

Response of the Semipelagians: those to whom faith was not announced were not fit to receive the gifts of salvation, because the light of nature had been oppressed by vices.

Refutation: those who say this fall into two Pelagian heresies: first, that human nature has not been wounded, since it can desire grace and prepare itself for it; second, that grace is given according to merits.

288. “But not at the same time.” Thus in the Letter to Rufinus, chapter 15: “Must it be said,” he says, “that human wills resist the will of God, and that the character of these people is so fierce and unmanageable that they do not hear the Gospel—that is, that it is not preached to them—because their impious hearts are not open to preaching?” The same passage also admirably closes off that escape. —Louvain Doctor.

290. “To the teachers.” That is, to the preachers. —Louvain Doctor.

291. “Passes through”: not “traverses,” as below, verse 581, but “passes by” or “passes over”; for the discussion concerns the nations whom, as it says below at verse 650,

> Grace neglected, dwelling in the shadow of death.

—Louvain Doctor.

293. “To demonstrate,” etc. The phrase is harsh and does not fit Prosper’s usual ease of expression. I think it must certainly be read *se monstrare* (“to show himself”), so that the sense of the period is this: God wished to offer light to all, and in reality did offer it, by which they could at least recognize the one true God; and he sufficiently showed himself to them. But he would also have offered the light of the Gospel, by which they might learn the other matters pertaining to his worship, had they not, by suppressing that first light through vices, made themselves unworthy of the second. The passage is entirely consistent with the Author’s Letter to Augustine, near the middle: “Since,” they say, “those are without excuse who could have been instructed by natural understanding in the worship of the one true God, and who therefore did not hear the Gospel because they would not have received it.” —Louvain Doctor.

294. “By the first light”: namely, natural understanding, the light mentioned in the cited passage. In the following verse, “the second” means the Gospel, as in that same passage. —Louvain Doctor.

297. “Innate,” rather than “infused,” as others have it; both because below, verse 826, the same reading appears—“now to be born such”—and because *innatum* (“innate”) and *nascentibus* (“for those being born”) correspond neatly here. The earlier editions had noted this in the margin, and the learned translator had already corrected it.

301. “You hold both things at once, with the Pelagians,” namely, both that human beings are born with their original freedom intact and that grace calls those whom it finds worthy of being called by a just examination of merits. They assert the first in the two following verses and the second in the verses that follow. To make this clearer, it will be useful to elucidate briefly these verses, obscure enough in themselves, by a paraphrase. Thus:

Ibid. “Offered to all, for all.” That is, all nations and human beings could by the merit of their own free choice have brought it about that the Gospel was announced to them—namely, by not admitting the hardness of heart and ferocity of conduct that stood in the way, since they had not lost their freedom for that purpose. Thus those who were deprived of hearing the Gospel were deprived of it precisely because they had not, by their own merits, prepared a worthy place within themselves for the Gospel. In this way those who are equal by their natural freedom of choice become unequal through unequal use of that same freedom; and merit belongs to the few, although the natural capacity for meriting belongs to all. —Louvain Doctor.

[Col. 0112D] 302. “To apprehend,” in place of “to attain” (as also at verse 845), is a word of declining Latin that eventually also began to be used in the vernacular for “to learn.” It may incidentally be observed how the Author immediately changes this infinitive, in a phrase familiar to him, into a subject infinitive when, after the intervening verse, he continues: “Nor do they perish without justice,” instead of “to perish.” —Louvain Doctor.]

## CHAPTER XIII

He shows that God’s will to save all is not of the kind they imagined, because not all are actually saved or come to faith, and because whatever God wills is undoubtedly fulfilled.

Response of the Semipelagians: God wishes to save all, yet not all are saved, because some will this through free choice and others do not.

Refutation: it is utterly unworthy that human will should prevent the will of the Almighty from accomplishing what he wills.

[Col. 0113B] 320. “The end of the work.” That is, its success. —Louvain Doctor.

Ibid. “In it,” namely, in free choice, as appears at first sight. But what follows in the next verse, “which he also,” indicates that everything together refers to the human being in the preceding verse. —Louvain Doctor.

321 and following. “He should carry before him the inclination of which,” etc., in the sense in which someone is said to carry before him a torch or a standard. This needed to be noted because of the ambiguity of the word and phrase. —Louvain Doctor.]

But if you nevertheless wish to defend these things by some argument,

## CHAPTER XIV

He shows that, at every time, through the grace and power of God, the very worst hearts—hearts in which no right intention had ever dwelt—have been transformed. Grace does not work merely by teaching, exhorting, and persuading, but by effectively changing the mind and, through omnipotent power, making willing people out of unwilling ones. Neither the Law, nor the preachers of the divine word, nor nature left to itself can accomplish this. Grace causes faith to take root in human hearts, to sprout, grow, ripen, be preserved, and persevere to the end.

338. “By the power of creating.” That is, by the same power and potency with which he once formed it, he now reforms it; hence shortly afterward: “What he made, he remakes.” Doctor Lov.

340. “Praestata.” Doctor Lov. prefers to read “prostrata,” although all editions read “praestata sibi”; that is, they say, “left to itself.” Nor would the reading lack elegance as a form derived from the same root: “Nature, not left to itself, accomplishes this…” Nevertheless, he thinks “prostrata” should be read, both because “prostrata natura” is repeated below, verse 889:

“But nature, once prostrate, in how deep an abyss…”

and because verses 398 and following are read in the same sense:

“No one gives to another, no one to himself; neither the letter of the Law

nor natural wisdom”—and note what he says of nature; he continues—

“which, once driven

headlong, etc.,” which is plainly the same as “prostrata.”

346. “Adolet.” So also in the sixth sentence of the *Capitula Gallica*: “The grace of God does not abolish human choice (freedom), but makes it flourish.”

P. Ramus, commenting on the line “And make the rich vervain flourish”: “*Adole*,” he says, properly means “increase,” and here, by euphemism, is used for “kindle.” Thus our author has perhaps used the word in a somewhat unusual way, but nevertheless properly. Doctor Lov.

347. “To fix a root in the mind.” Virgil had said, *Georgics* 2: “To fix a root in the earth.” Indeed, almost this entire paragraph has been drawn from the *Georgics*. Doctor Lov.

350. “Lest darnel, etc.” Ramus comments on a similar Virgilian line, *Eclogue* 5:

“Unhappy darnel, and barren oats hold sway.”

“Darnel,” he says, “is *zizanion* in Greek and *geraea* in French.” The same verse is repeated in *Georgics* 1:

“Burdocks and thistles, and amid the shining fields

unhappy darnel, etc.”

It harms the eyes, as Ovid testifies, *Fasti* 1:

“And may the fields be free of darnel that damages the eyes.”

Then, in the same verse, he proceeds concerning oats: “Oats are the first defect of grain,” says Pliny, book 18, chapter 17. It is called “barren,” moreover, to distinguish it from cultivated (*sativa*) oats; “empty” is used in the same sense, *Georgics* 1:

“The expected harvest mocked him with empty oats.”

Doctor Lovan.]

But if, having removed the cloud of contention, you will calmly look with me upon what is true,

[325] you will see that the ancient ages are filled with evident examples, and you will recognize in our own time many things

that teach that, by the power of God, the hearts of wicked people have been transformed—

hearts in which nothing upright had ever dwelt, and which bore no sign or perception of righteousness.

[330] 143 For just as now grace attracts savage peoples and barbarous kingdoms,

peoples previously unknown to, or despised by, the new grace of Christ,

[Col. 0114A]

and builds a temple for itself throughout the earth,

so earlier it subdued fierce peoples and rebellious cities,

when piety overcame the hostile hearts that resisted it.

[335] It did not do this merely by kindly counsel and exhortation,

persuading and teaching, as though grace possessed the Law as its rule;

rather, it changed the mind within and re-formed it,

fashioning a new vessel from what was shattered, by the power of creating.

Not the warnings of the Law, not the words of the prophet,

[340] not nature, left to itself, accomplish this; but he who made it remakes it. Let the Apostle traverse the world;

let him preach, exhort, plant, water, rebuke, and persist;

wherever he finds the way opened by the word, let him enter:

[Col. 0114B]

[345] yet it is grace alone—not the teacher, nor the student—

that causes the hearer to advance through these labors,

and makes the young plants grow into weighty fruit.

It is grace that fixes the seed of faith in the mind

and commands a vigorous shoot to emerge from the heart’s bosom.

It preserves and nurtures the ripening crop,

[350] lest darnel, thistles, and barren oats hold sway;

lest wind break it, a torrent carry it away, or heat scorch it;

and lest, when it has lifted itself too joyfully and too vigorously upward,

it fall prostrate in a shameful collapse.

[Note: [Col. 0114D]

## CHAPTER XV

The Semipelagians’ fabricated approval of the Church’s doctrines. They confess that a human being cannot by himself attain or persevere in righteousness or salvation, but contend that, by his own freedom of choice, he assents to God when God calls and exhorts him, and that God follows and completes this human effort.

354. “*Inquis*,” rather than “*inquit*,” as the common editions have it, since throughout several of these chapters the address of the Semipelagian is continuous. Doctor Lovan.

355. “Which, unless, etc.” The same person admits in the *Collator against the Collator*, books 3 and 4, that a person may sometimes, through his own impulses, extend himself toward the desire for virtues, but that he always needs to be helped by the Lord; and that the beginnings of good intentions cannot reach the completion of virtue unless they are directed by God. The latter point is expressed here as follows:

“No one will complete himself

by the powers of nature alone.” Doctor Lovan.

[Col. 0115C]

361. “*Accita*.” That is, “called forth,” unquestionably an improper usage. The French translator renders it quite aptly in prose: “When something has been proposed to him.” Doctor Lovan.

365. “*Consilio*.” The French translator seems to understand this as referring to the great plan and wondrous ordering of our redemption. Hence the rather magnificent rendering:

“When he has made him hear those ineffable means

which a God deigns to use to save the guilty.”

Nevertheless, I doubt whether the proper sense may not be: “By which he had proposed to save the world,” that is, what God wishes from us for salvation. Moreover, *proposuisset* is used in the author’s idiom for *proposuerit*, as above, verse 249, *displicuisset*, and verse 292, *voluisset*. Doctor Lov.

365. “*Cupidam et fidam*.” This seems to refer to the two things that the Massilians had previously required before grace: namely, the desire for holiness and faith; or perhaps only to desire, but to a constant and continuing desire, to which they attributed both grace and perseverance as received gifts.

[Col. 0115D]

Doctor Lovan.

The same place, “*In gaudia*.” The French translator has “rewards,” but approves our common reading, first because, if “rewards” were to be read, the passage would more appropriately have said “toward rewards”; and then, especially, because it seems to refer to the Gospel passage, “Enter into the joy of your Lord.” Hence I think that the preceding expression, where the servant is called faithful, is also represented here by “faithful.” Doctor Lov.]

[365] who will lead the desirous and faithful person into promised joys.”

## CHAPTER XVI

They are refuted. By this doctrine the true grace of Christ is overturned, because grace is placed outside the human mind, as though it merely knocked at the door of the heart without opening it. Thus, on this account, grace does not properly act; free choice does. For when someone is moved in various ways by things heard or read that please or displease him, the resulting movements of the mind ought not to be attributed to what he hears or reads, but to his free choice, which twists and turns itself here and there according to its own inclination. Grace, by contrast, bends the will wherever it wishes, with omnipotent power, and no obstacle delays it. The minister who plants or waters externally by preaching is nothing; God is the one who gives the increase within. The effects of grace in human minds are wondrous. Neither one human being to another, nor anyone to himself, can give the affection by which the heart approaches God; nor can natural wisdom give it. The virtues of those who possess only natural wisdom are false.

368. “Marked off by a fixed boundary.” So above, verses 251 and following: “…this is restrained.” *Limite*, “with you.”

369. “*Clausa fore*,” or “the door,” not “*clausae*,” as some have it. Doctor Lov.

370. “The sense of the flesh.” This refers to verse 361: “…and judgment was opened through the ear.”

374. “*Specie*,” elsewhere *species*, so that it may be the correct form of the verb *exoritur*; but since another noun follows immediately—namely, love, hatred, and so forth—it must here be in the oblique case, like the preceding phrase, “by the voice of one speaking.” Doctor Lovan.

377. “*Auctor*.” On conjecture, with my French translator’s agreement, I had substituted *actor*, so that these three—writer, narrator, and actor—would correspond to the three preceding expressions: “the voice of one speaking,” “the appearance of things acted out that we saw,” and “things that we read.” But a passage of Sallust shed light on the matter and showed that *auctor* can also be used for *actor*, so that nothing need be changed in the common editions. For Sallust, shortly after the beginning of the *Catiline*, distinguishes between the writer and the author of events, calling the author the one who performs them. Doctor Lovan.

379. “*Perceptis*.” Doctor Lovan says that he restored this from older editions in place of *praeceptis*, which the more recent editions had; he wished it to be understood as in *Aeneid* 6:

“I have grasped everything and gone through it beforehand in my mind.”

But, having consulted the older printed editions of Lyons, Louvain, and Douai, we uniformly read *perceptis*. Only the Cologne edition and the later Lyons edition have *praeceptis*. We therefore made no change.

380. “According to his custom.” That is, according to the character and disposition he possesses. Thus Sallust in the *Jugurtha*: “Each takes counsel for himself according to his character; some choose flight, others to take up arms.” Doctor Lov.

385. “Not according to character,” in contrast with verse 290: “While the fierceness of character resists.” Doctor Lov.

389. “*Admoveant*,” as though for knocking and entering, as follows. It is therefore not *admoneant*, as some have it. Doctor Lov.

[Col. 0117C]

401. “And although they possess outstanding qualities, etc.” Thus in the *Collator against the Collator*, chapter 10: “Even if he excels in the most outstanding arts and possesses all human disciplines, he cannot be justified by himself, because he makes bad use of his good qualities; in these, without the worship of the true God, he is convicted of impiety and uncleanness, and by the very means by which he thinks he can defend himself, he is accused.” Doctor Lov.

405. “*Decoris occidui*.” The same phrase is used in the letter to Demetrias, chapter 4, where “transient honors” are mentioned—that is, honors which quickly pass away and perish. In several editions (Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne), instead of *vanamque decoris* they read *unamque*, perhaps through a printer’s error—one that the French translator had already corrected. At least our reading cannot be doubtful, since the meaning demands it absolutely. Doctor Lovan.

408. “It is sin.” This is an apostolic expression, Romans 14:23: “Whatever is not from faith is sin.” Consult the interpreters concerning it. Our author seems meanwhile to qualify it when he adds:

“The same becomes guilt, and barren, etc.”

By this he perhaps suggests that the act itself, performed without faith, need not in itself be sin, since it is often morally—so the schools speak—or officially, good; but that guilt is added only when a person boasts of it otherwise than in the Lord, as unbelievers easily boast of their good deeds. At least Prosper neither understood nor could have understood that all the works of unbelievers are, in the strict sense in which theology speaks today, sins. Doctor Lov. One may consult Augustine, *Against Julian*, book 4, chapter 3, appendix, part 2, page 257, and elsewhere.]

Is this sincere faith? Is this the grace of Christ with you?

[Col. 0115B]

outside the human being, with the mind completely shut against it:

Faith is altogether a gratuitous gift. It does not arise from merit, since every merit arises from it.

413. “*Legentem*,” “the one reading,” instead of “*eligentem electus*,” “the chosen one selecting”; that is, God is the subject. Doctor Lov.

434. “*Limite in ipso*.” Some conjecture that *limine in ipso* should be read, either because that is how it appears below, verse 812, or because Virgil, in the *Pharmacopoeia* and *Aeneid* 10, and Lucretius, book 6, use the phrase in that form. ## CHAPTER XIX

The only thing that can rightly be attributed as merit to people of this sort is that they desired rebirth; but this desire arose from faith, and faith itself arose only from grace. Faith, which is the root of all merits, cannot arise from merit; what is not done from faith is not done well. He overturns grace from its foundations who thinks either that any merit can exist before faith in the false virtues of unbelievers, or that faith arises from freedom of willing rather than from God’s gratuitous gift.

[Col. 0119B]

450. “By a straight road and boundary.” He had read in *Georgics* 2: “By a road cut straight.” The statement has the form of a maxim; for that reason we have distinguished it by its own typography. Doctor Lov.

## CHAPTER XX

The defenders of these errors assign no other beginning of human restoration to God than this: that through the Law and preachers he suggests to the human will what it ought to do. According to this view, the will precedes grace, and grace is like a servant; it performs the function not of grace but of the Law, merely commanding and not giving what it commands. How strongly this doctrine reinforces the Pelagian heresy: it teaches that the beginning of being released, or the will to believe, arises from the natural freedom of choice. Grace, however, is nothing other than law and teaching. From this it follows that free choice was not wounded by sin.

[Col. 0119D]

459. “Of divine things, etc.” He abruptly takes up another argument, which is not unusual for him. Doctor Lov.

461. “To believe Christ’s promises,” instead of “to hope,” just as “to know God” is used for “to believe”; for in this verse the three theological virtues are expressed. Doctor Lovan.

462. “To be common to all,” so that they may possess these things by themselves. “I wished,” says the author, “that the Massilians should hold that it belongs to the condition of every human being that, through discernment of good and evil, he may direct his will toward the knowledge of God and obedience to his commandments, and may arrive at the grace by which we are reborn in Christ, namely, by the natural capacity of asking, seeking, and knocking.” Letter of the author to Augustine, shortly after the middle. Doctor Lov.

464. “By the waters,” that is, of baptism. The Massilians indicate that grace begins only then by the words already quoted: “the grace by which we are reborn in Christ.” Doctor Lov.

467. “Is called a gift,” namely, in Scripture, especially in the apostolic letters, Romans 5 and Ephesians 3, etc. Doctor Lov.

471. “By judgment.” Here there is an explicit judgment of the will. Doctor Lov.

The same place: “Nor is grace now grace.” Not because it is not gratuitous, as in Romans 11 and in the author’s letter to Rufinus, chapter 2, but because, as follows, it acts merely by the right of one who gives admonition; and that belongs not to grace but to the Law.

475. “Of fertile soil.” This is Virgil’s phrase, repeated in *Aeneid* 1 and 3:

“Ancient land, powerful in arms and rich in fertile soil.”

I am therefore surprised that the French translator, together with the common editions, read *gleba*. Columella, however, also said *uberi gleba*, “fertile soil.” Doctor Lov. The Lyons edition has *ubere seu glebae*; Cologne, *ubere seu gleba*; Louvain and Douai, *ubere ceu gleba*.

477. “*Praesulcet*.” It is well known that poets use *sulcare*, “to furrow,” for “to plow”; then infer what *praesulcare* means. Doctor Lov.

The same place: “*Temperet aequor*.” Taken from *Aeneid* 1 and transferred from maritime to agricultural language, with Virgil himself leading the way: he calls the flatness of fields not yet worked by the plow *aequor*, “level ground,” but freshly worked ground *novalis* or *novale*, “newly broken land.” Doctor Lov.

478. “*Satis*.” As in Virgil, *Eclogue* 3: “Sweet is the moisture for the crop.” Doctor Lov.

486. “*Corpore mortis*.” An apostolic phrase, Romans 7:24, meaning “a body subject to death,” and referring not so much to bodily death as to the death of desire and of the members of the Law. Doctor Lov.

490. “*Respondeat*.” That is, “appear” or “be conspicuous,” as below, verse 622: “No signs of choice answer to you.” Virgil also used *respondere* for “to yield” in *Georgics* 2:

“But olive trunks more readily, and vines by their shoots,

yield…”

The reader may decide whether this can shed light on the present passage. Doctor Lov.]

## CHAPTER XXI

And whatever else Pelagius taught, including the following: that a human being can attain salvation by his own righteousness and merit heaven; that many people, by their own virtue, pleased God from the beginning of the world without God’s grace; that the Law was given when human morals had become more corrupt, so that fear alone, held before them, might convert them; and that through the Law what is accomplished through grace was accomplished. When vices grew stronger, grace was added to the Law—not because nature could not attain salvation without it, but so that it might do so more easily. Infants are innocent, and in baptism are washed in body, not in mind.

## CHAPTER XXII

If the Semipelagians do not dare to defend these Pelagian doctrines, they ought also to abandon their own errors and confess that nature has been so wounded that it can never rise through free choice to perform righteousness. Even when it strives to do good, it continually falls back into new lapses.

[Col. 0122C]

524. “*Pelago*.” There is at once an allusion to the name of Pelagius—a play in which even Augustine, as we see, was not displeased—and an insistence upon an elegant metaphor taken from sailors.

526. “*Constanter*.” That is: “Be consistent with yourselves in confessing the wounds of nature”; and, when you admit original sin, do not deny the wounds of difficulty and ignorance which, as Augustine calls them, necessarily follow from it. Doctor Lovan.

528. “*Jaculis superatis*.” The person who rendered this poem in verse and prose had written *jaculis superantis*, based on a conjecture placed in the margin of the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions. Doctor Lov. properly defends the reading *superatis*: there was no need to seek *superantis*, namely “of the devil,” as some of the common editions have, and as the French translator himself has it. It was once considered a bad omen to fight with weapons already defeated; hence Tacitus, *Histories* 3: “Caecina, blaming that rashness which handles defeated weapons…” What, then, if our author took *jacula superata* from this passage? Certainly he drew several other things from that foremost of historians, especially the expression cited above, at the beginning of the work, where he called Britain “the secret of Ocean.” But the statement that free choice is armed for its own punishment with these defeated weapons may perhaps be illuminated by Ramus’s aphorism on Virgil, *Eclogue* 9: “Now, defeated, sorrowful…” Thus, he says, Bremius replied to Sulpicius, who was weighing out gold and asking why he was placing a sword, stripped together with its belt, on the scales: “What else,” he said, “but grief for the defeated?” Therefore, “for punishment” means one’s own grief, since weapons are nothing but a source of grief to the defeated when they are displayed before their eyes. Doctor Lov.]

[525] and take your humble stand with us in a peaceful harbor.

[Col. 0122B]

unable ever to rise,
