## CHAPTER XXIII

If they refuse to confess these things, they cannot deny peace to the Pelagians, with whom in reality they agree. They differ only in words, being compelled to say that through Adam’s sin our body was made subject to death, but that the soul was not corrupted by sin. This amounts to attributing injustice to God and completely acquitting human beings.

537. “*Mercede valescat*.” That is, “let him be healed by a price,” not freely, as those usually do who have nothing with which to pay. Doctor Lov.

542. “*Illaesum*.” I frequently read this in this very work; but *illapsum*, as others have it—Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne—meaning “not fallen,” I do not know where it is found. Doctor Lov. *Illaesum* was already noted in the margins of the older editions, and the French translator and Doctor Lov. inserted it into the text.

544. “The punishment of sin.” That is, bodily punishment, such as diseases and death itself. The subject is a punishment that diminishes nothing in the soul; accordingly, the soul’s wounds, which according to the author necessarily follow original sin, are not under discussion. The author shows that this opinion was not truly taught by anyone, but is proposed to the Massilians only as a foolish paradox to which they must come unless they agree either entirely with the orthodox or openly with the Pelagians. In *Against the Collator*, chapter 9, he says: “Unless perhaps it should be said that punishment, not guilt, passed over into Adam’s descendants—which is in every respect falsely said, and for that reason perhaps is not said. For it is exceedingly impious to think this of God’s justice: that he wished those who were free from transgression to be condemned along with the guilty.” These words sufficiently illuminate the end of this chapter. Doctor Lov.]

Are you ashamed, in your lofty minds, to confess these things,

[535] [Col. 0123A]

lest the sick person seem more contemptible beneath so many diseases?

When nothing remains from the entire inheritance of your ancestors

by which he might deserve a physician’s help and be healed at a price?

Therefore withdraw your steps to the hostile camp,

and add yourselves to those whose ingenuity and deceptive weapons

[540] you mock, brandishing missiles from the same tongue.

Exult in the goods of nature,

and teach that the honor of the mind has stood unharmed

through all the ages.

And lest you expose yourselves completely by a naked doctrine,

[545] say that the punishment of sin proceeds only through the bodily path,

diminishing nothing in the mind.

Acquit those pierced through by the wound from the charge,

and accuse God’s own justice,

which permits the punishment to pass over

while you do not wish the guilt to pass over.

[Col. 0123B]

[Note: [Col. 0123C]

## CHAPTER XXIV

God is not unjust, since, according to the Apostle, all fell in one person. Nor afterward could anyone rise again to life except by the grace of Christ—not even the righteous who lived before Christ.

554. “*Numeratis*,” or *numeravit*, namely, Paul. Both readings make good sense. For the Apostle, in Hebrews 11, composed a splendid catalogue of the righteous of old; and the Massilians were entirely intent on including those people among the examples they alleged had lived righteously without grace. Thus writes the author of the poem *On the Providence of God* among Prosper’s works, as do Faustus of Riez and others. Our author also seems to allude to this above, verses 498 and following:

“Bring forth many

who by their own skill and their own will were holy from the beginning of the world.”

Doctor Lov.]

But God is not unjust: Paul’s clear statement shows—]

[550] The voice teaches that all human beings fell together in one collapse;

[Col. 0124A] In which the entire succession of descendants together was overthrown

And perished, nor does anyone have a means by which he can rise

To life, unless he is born again through the sacred birth.

For all whom you count as righteous from the beginning of time,

[555] There is no doubt that they were saved by this aid, which now the Almighty’s grace

Exercises throughout the whole world more widely.

157

**[Note: Chapter XXV. Not even the righteous who lived before Christ. Grace is entirely gratuitous, since no one does good unless God grants him the ability to do good. Nor can it even be desired unless grace itself makes it desirable.]**

**557.** “As has been said”—namely, above, chapters 21 and 22, [Col. 0124C] and elsewhere. —Dr. Lov.

**563.** “Therefore to the way through the way,” elsewhere printed *pariter*, but ineptly (as had already been observed by the most learned translator). These three things, which it is here said cannot be reached except through themselves, seem to be those same things which the Savior proclaims of himself when he says that he is the way, the truth, and the life. Moreover, *ergo*, whether new or perhaps ancient, is certainly used here and generally afterward in a manner different from common usage. —Dr. Lov.]

**THIS**, as has been said, is not a judge of merits,

For it finds nothing except what is full of evils; and unless it grants

What is good, blind will accomplish nothing well.

[560] That this may be sought by anyone’s effort and desire,

It itself brings about, and it is the guide for all who come to it:

[Col. 0124B] And unless one runs through it, one does not go to it.

Therefore we are carried to the way through the way: without light no one sees light;

To seek life without life is death.

## PART THREE

[Col. 0123]

### ARGUMENT

The arguments and complaints of the Semipelagians are refuted. They chiefly raised two objections. First, that free will was abolished, and that neither punishment was owed to vices nor rewards to virtue if either nature, corrupted by sin, wills nothing but evil, or whatever good a person does must be attributed to grace—and indeed to that grace which gives both willing and running. Saint Prosper replies that this objection overturns faith in original sin, through which the liberty granted to us in Adam was destroyed, and we were subjected to the yoke of ruling desire, by which we are always dragged toward evil, even though we do what we wish. Our will cannot be freed from that servitude except insofar as it is freed by Christ’s saving grace; through this, its original liberty is not abolished but restored. Christ owes this grace to no one, but freely bestows it on whom he wills: as is clear in the case of infants who depart from this life soon after baptism, while so many others perish without receiving baptism, and no reason for this distinction can be given except God’s inscrutable judgment.

Furthermore, the remnants of the Pelagians objected: Unless grace is given to everyone, those whom grace has neglected will not be guilty of sin, since they were not given the power to do what is right. He replies that such reasoning belongs to those who do not acknowledge original sin. For since, according to the Apostle, through the offense of one man the whole mass of humanity fell into a most just condemnation, no one can complain that he is not freed by God’s grace, since all deserved to be abandoned by God, and his justice could not be criticized even if he had freed no one from that destruction. We must not investigate why, from the whole human race, one part is chosen and the other rejected, when the same cause implicates everyone: God has withdrawn that secret from our understanding, just as he has withheld many other matters far less weighty. It is enough to recognize him as the author of all good things and humbly to revere the height of his judgments, which are so unknown and inscrutable to human beings that they cannot be unjust.

[565] [Col. 0123D] **[Note: Chapter XXVI. Objection I of the Semipelagians. By this preaching of grace, free will is taken away, and neither punishments nor rewards are owed to anyone if nature, left to itself, wills nothing but evil; but good works must be attributed not to us but to grace.]**

**567.** “The running of those who run,” etc. Did they then dare to contradict Paul’s most sacred statement, “It is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs”? Or perhaps in this too they followed their teachers, changing the most divine affirmation into an impious question? Augustine indeed bears witness to this concerning the Pelagians; but I do not yet remember having read it concerning the Massilians. It will therefore be our poet’s artifice: he expresses his orthodox opinion in these apostolic words in such a way as to make it appear all the more wickedly mocked by his adversaries. —Dr. Lov.

**568.** “For praise,” in place of “for virtue”; from *Aeneid* I:

> Here too praise has its own rewards.

**570.** “Our labor”—that is, our own labor, by which we anticipate grace. —Dr. Lov.]

Here you bring forward a vain complaint with a deranged heart:

[Col. 0124D] Crying out that every work of the will has been taken away,

[Col. 0125A] If there is no running of those who run, nor willing of those who will,

159 Nor is punishment owed to vices, or rewards to praise,

If either nature, bound over, must will evil,

[570] Or good deeds cannot be ascribed to our own labor.

**[Note: Chapter XXVII. The response. Those who reason in this way agree with Pelagius because, like him, they truly do not acknowledge the fall of the whole of nature in the first human being. An excellent description of that fall. The transmission of original sin. Blindness of mind. Free will was not completely destroyed, but fell and was bound to evil. The will therefore remains free, but it is not good. Wherever it is carried, it rushes and slips.

576.** *Nemore.* A reference to Virgil, *Eclogue* 6:

> Every grove shall sing of you;

He notes that *nemus* properly means a woodland arranged for pleasure. Therefore our holy author aptly called paradise a “woodland of delight” by this name. Alcimus Avitus likewise used *lucus*, I believe because of the pleasantness of the trees celebrated there by Sacred Scripture. —Dr. Lov.

**Ibid.** *Nemore almo.* Gallus had printed *alto*. When I saw it, I was certainly pleased, thinking how fond our author usually is of Virgilian phrasing, since one reads *nemora alta* more than once in Virgil. But soon afterward I noticed that he himself had listed *alto* among the errors [Col. 0125D] of the edition and restored *almo*, which is sufficiently sound. —Dr. Lov.

**581.** *Virosa*, as above in the preface, *virosum caput*. A Virgilian expression from *Georgics* I:

> And the Pontus, poisonous with Castor;

There I certainly do not accept interpreters who take the word in a favorable sense, as though it referred to “Castorean” things and not to the Pontus itself, contrary to *The Pharmaceutria*:

> These poisons gathered for me from the Pontus  
> Moeris himself gave me; the Pontus produces very many.

Moreover, what is said here about poisonous drunkenness and crudity is repeated more fully against the *Collations*, chapter 9: “It drank”—namely, free will at the first transgression—“the poison of all vices, and moistened the whole nature of humanity with the drunkenness of its intemperance”; hence, before it digests its lethal crudity by eating the flesh of the Son of Man and drinking his blood, “memory slips, judgment errs, the gait falters,” etc.—just as happens to drunkards. —Dr. Lov.

**583.** *Carbunculus.* Gallus rightly notes in both versions the allusion to the carbuncle of pestilential diseases; but he did not see what “raw food” meant there, because he did not reflect on the words cited above from the book against the *Collations*. —Dr. Lov.

**587.** *Inque ligatis.* A tmesis, in place of *et in ligatis*, or *illigatis*—that is, “in those who are impeded.” It imitates Virgil’s passage in *Aeneid* X, concerning wounded Mezentius withdrawing from the battle:

> Retreating, useless and bound,  
> He withdrew.

**591.** *And rushing with every kind of mobility.* I prefer this reading with Gallus (we add Lugd., Lovan., Duac., and Colon.) to *viğens*, found in most others. Unless a fall or collapse is mentioned in this half-line, what place is there for the word “rise” in the next? And because, when some place the punctuation mark after *ruens*, the following phrase *in vulnera vulnere* scarcely permits any sound sense, I therefore follow those who punctuated it as we have. What is meant by “every kind of mobility” can now be understood from what was said above on verse 129. What is there called “the power of natural motion” must elsewhere be called “natural mobility,” and here “every kind of mobility”: I mean precisely what the Ingrates explain more explicitly again in verses 459 and following:

> In us, they say, both willing and refusing were created,  
> And liberty was summoned to direct the motion  
> Of our free will wherever it wishes.

Finally, we see that Prosper was also fond elsewhere of that polyptoton, “wound upon wound,” namely above, verse 488, “from wound, wound.” I dimly remember either reading the same or something similar in Virgil, or certainly in another poet of the same class. —Dr. [Col. 0126D] Lov.]

Do those teachers of yours, whose words you belch forth,

Not think and proclaim the same things?

But since a related pride bursts forth in a similar complaint,

The answer is now given both to you and to them.

[575] Once we were the inviolate and exalted image of God

In our first father, while he dwelt in the nourishing woodland

And, obeying the command, guarded himself from one tree.

But after the law of the commandment had been broken, he received

[Col. 0125B] Proud counsel mingled with envy from the fountain;

[580] He collapsed, and all of us fell together when our forefather fell:

For the poisonous drunkenness of sin runs through everyone,

[Col. 0126A] And in the belly of the corrupted heart the raw food,

A carbuncle, seethes on.

From that point the vigor of the mind was blunted,

[585] And it was clothed in dreadful darkness; nor does an inert light

Bear the flashes of divine light. From that point free will, fallen

Along crooked paths, limps; amid blind and shackled efforts

There is motion, and error is not absent. The will remains,

Always loving something toward which it may carry itself,

[590] And deceives itself in a labyrinth, entering the windings of doubtful paths:

It desires vain things, swells with and fears vain things; and, rushing

161 With every kind of mobility, rises from wound upon wound.

**[Note: Chapter XXVIII. It is absurd to think that free will is taken away when it is healed and freed by grace. This thought arises from the same pride that destroyed Adam. Free will cannot heal free will by its own power. But Christ’s grace, which is the tree of life, alone is capable of restoring and renewing the weakened mind and granting it the ability to use its own powers well.

597.** “The ancient inventions of deceit”: namely, the deceit devised by the serpent in paradise; hence the following phrase, “with a viper’s whisper.” There is a continuous allusion here to the events of the deception of our first parents, to which Pelagian deception is compared. The comparison is quite apt: impaired free will is compared with the forbidden tree, grace with the tree of life, the works of grace and free will with the fruits of these two trees, and finally the inner reformation promised by the Pelagian on the basis of free will’s powers with the transformation into gods or angels that the serpent promised through the forbidden tree. —Dr. Lov.

**Ibid.** “Desist from seizing,” etc. He has marked the hissing of the serpentine letter, since a viper’s whisper is being expressed. —Dr. Lov.

**599.** *Praecerpere.* He did not say this casually, rather than *decerpere*. For it more clearly indicates the error of the Pelagians and Semipelagians, who first demand the fruit of free will, to be followed afterward by the fruit of grace. —Dr. Lov.

**603.** “From the despised … life.” Perhaps here too the verse has been disturbed by an excessive concern for inverted rhythm, and the author wrote *de fastidita*. At least in his age the verse called Leonine was still considered defective, while this barbarous and Gothic elegance belonged only to the later Middle Ages. —Dr. Lov.]

You say, then, that this free will, when grace heals it,

Is taken away, and that you think it destroyed when life breathes upon it.

[595] What wonder if, with a raging heart, a frenzied sick man

[Col. 0126B] Loves his disease and drives away the physician? Recognize at last

The ancient inventions of deceit, and desist from again lending

[Col. 0127A] Captive ears to the whisper of the viper.

Do not hastily pluck harmful fruits from the broken

[600] Branches of free will: this food does not restore you,

Nor does that food of angelic beauty nourish your appearance.

But it drags those who hunger for forbidden things and swell with foul bile

Far away from the tree of life that they have despised.

One must eat of this tree’s aid and fruit, so that the weakened mind,

[605] Recovering, may also be able to use its own powers well

And find in Christ what it lost in itself.

**[Note: Chapter XXIX. By Christ’s grace we do not lose but recover the ancient honor of nature. That grace is the beginning of merits in us; these increase all the more as we receive grace more humbly and increase it by receiving it.

614.** “We grow equally through things bestowed.” God furnishes this relationship with new gifts, as Gallus correctly explains. From this gather the meaning.

**615.** “And our good becomes the glory of the giver,” or rather the reverse (for the sentence must be inverted in this way): the glory of the giver, namely God, becomes our good. —Dr. Lov.]

Therefore, whoever you are who have removed the garment of your earthly parent,

You do not lose nature’s ancient honor,

But recover it, acquiring what you previously lacked,

[610] So that these things may be yours, if you use what has been bestowed upon you modestly,

And acknowledge that what you possess has been received by you.

The Father of light is therefore the source of merit; hence whatever has flowed

[Col. 0127B] Into us is the cause of greater goods for us,

While, by ascribing his own gifts to the giver, we too are increased

[615] By these acknowledgments, and the glory of the giver becomes our good.

**[Note: Chapter XXX. It is most clearly seen from infants dying immediately after baptism that grace is not given according to the efforts of human will, but according to God’s good pleasure.

616.** “The judgment of free will.” Above we called and explained this as “the judgment of the will.” —Dr. Lov.]

But you who defend the judgment of free will and merit,

And ascribe the gifts of the One who calls to human efforts,

Distinguish the minds of infants and explain what their

Affections and what movements these little hearts possess.

[620] Give character to the tender ones, and instruct them in the freedom of willing,

Although they can scarcely receive a breath of air and milk.

No signs of free will answer you, nor can you distinguish

Equals by any merits: their nature is one,

And equally they cannot will either good or evil.

[625] Yet from these the merciful grace chooses some

[Col. 0127C] And, born again through baptism, transfers them

Into the eternal kingdom, while leaving many others in death,

Whose origin was similar, from the same wound.

**[Note: Chapter XXXI. Their salvation is not to be ascribed to the merits of their parents, nor their condemnation to their demerits. This is especially clear in twins, one of whom is sometimes baptized while the other dies without baptism, Christ’s mercy alone distinguishing them. By the same mercy faith is granted to others, so that they may do good works and increase in merits to the end.

638.** *Legit*, as very often elsewhere, in place of *eligit*. —Dr. Lov.

**645.** “Rich in wisdom,” etc. Most printed editions indicate in the margin a reference to Wisdom 4, concerning the righteous man who was taken away lest wickedness change his understanding. Whatever the case, “Wisdom” here means uncreated Wisdom, namely God’s providence itself, or, as Gallus seems to have preferred, Christ. —Dr. Lov.]

Nor will you be able to attribute this to the merits of parents:

[630] [Col. 0128A] 163 As though the pious care of the honorable had benefited those to be redeemed

And the alien negligence of others had taken away life;

When you see many born of holy parents

Unable to be saved by any effort of their own,

While others, exposed because of the shameful crimes of their mothers,

[635] Are taken from the filth and, through the font of life,

Delivered to the heavenly court by the care of strangers.

What if you also see this differing end, by which Christ’s grace

Chooses one twin while another perishes, and grants salvation,

In twins? You divide those conceived at the same time

[640] And born at the same time; you cannot put forward

Any movements of free will. The work ceases, merit ceases;

Nothing unequal is produced.

[Col. 0128B] Yet God distinguishes even such persons, so that Christ’s goodness

May shine forth more greatly, for it alone is the cause

[645] Of faith and merit in those who are called; for rich in Wisdom,

He also grants many this: that, by doing holy works,

Their reward may be made a gift at the end of life.

**[Note: Chapter XXXII. Objection II of the Semipelagians. If grace is altogether necessary for doing good, and is not given to everyone, those to whom the ability to do good was not given will not be guilty of sin. Response. By this argument original sin is again denied. For by that one sin alone all human beings are born guilty and worthy of death, even if they add no personal crimes to it.

653.** “They deny”: namely, those who reason in this way. —Dr. Lov.

**658.** “To be expiated by being born.” Dr. Lov.: “The sentence is disturbed; arrange it thus: ‘Yet let this one crime contracted by being born be sufficient for a death to be expiated,’ namely, eternal death.” Gallus, briefly and beautifully:

> It is enough to have been born to deserve death.

] But it is neither rightly nor truly said that those

Who are deprived of the divine gift and whom

[650] Grace has neglected, living in the shadow of death,

Are not guilty of sin because the power to do right

Was not given them. They deny that they fell prostrate,

Bound by the fetter of nature; they do not believe that from one stock

The entire offspring of humanity is born with punishment and guilt.

[655] Whoever does not reject this sees the weight of this guilt,

With an equally powerful mass pressing upon the wretched,

[Col. 0128C] So that even if they heap up no other evils, still this one

Crime is sufficient for a death to be expiated by being born.

[Col. 0129A] **[Note: Chapter XXXIII. Therefore the complaint against God is unjust: that he does not free everyone by grace from destruction, although this destruction was so universally deserved that he could justly have freed no one. It is contrary to reason that those who have been freed solely by God’s kindness should accuse him because he has not shown the same kindness equally to all who were guilty. Reflection on the just abandonment of unbelievers and sinners should move God’s pious and faithful servants to seek their liberation and mercy with humble prayer, since the sinners themselves do not seek it and even take pleasure in their misery. God’s mercy is not to be criticized either by those to whom it has been denied or by those to whom it has been granted.

660.** *Positam impositamque*: understand “justly imposed” and “deservedly imposed”; for *impositam* more strongly expresses punishment and refers to merit or guilt. —Dr. Lov.

**661.** “Are saved from it.” I scarcely doubt that *solvantur* (“are released”) should be read: both because of the greater propriety of the expression and because it is preceded by “which no one resolves by himself.” Finally, because what follows says, “that it might remain unbroken over all the offspring”: it is evidently regarded as a kind of bond, to be broken in those who, by contrast, are released from it. —Dr. Lov.

[Col. 0129D] **669.** “He would have led out for them.” The printed editions (though not Lugd., Lovan., Duac., and Colon.) have *eduxit*, so that *iisdem* is trisyllabic. But our author never used this word as a trisyllable, nor did Virgil. —Dr. Lov.

**670.** “When he does not experience the punishment,” etc. All the editions I have seen have joined these two verses to the preceding ones, including Gallus, who therefore struggles remarkably here to carve out some suitable meaning. Let the reader judge whether we have hit the mark. Dr. Lovan. thinks the passage has been restored by him to a better sense through altered punctuation, as follows:

> When he does not experience the punishment in which he was submerged,  
> How miserably would the one bound by it endure it, unless freed from it?

**673.** *Submissa.* The editions of Lug., Lov., Duac., and Colon., together with more recent ones, read *cum summa prece* (“with the utmost prayer”). But the translator who interpreted this poem in verse and prose had altered it in the manner in which it is read here in the text. Dr. Lov. supports him as follows: Thus above, verse 173, “Humbly submitting such things,” etc.; and the expression is sufficiently Virgilian. Others nevertheless read *cum summa*, but nothing similar to this is found elsewhere in the author, nor do I know whether it occurs in anyone else. I therefore did not even think it worthy of being relegated to the margin.

**675.** “So greatly does error harm,” etc. The reason is given why these people offer no prayers for escape; the same point is repeated in chapter 6. Gallus: “Thus free will loves its sicknesses and regards as health the fact that it does not know itself to be sick, until this first remedy is applied to the sick person,” etc. —Dr. Lov.

**678.** “From where, then,” etc. The common punctuation was so wholly devoid of sound sense here that it even lacked this question. I first restored it by following the meaning, and afterward found that Gallus too approved it. ]

This law, then, which no one resolves by himself,

[660] If we confess that it was justly and deservedly imposed:

Why do we complain that not everyone is saved from it?

For if it remained unbroken over the whole offspring,

We would not complain about all being justly condemned,

Or ask whether what is imposed on the whole is not tolerated

[665] When imposed on a part; and whether it would be better to force

Everything that is owed than mercifully to remit much of the whole?

Who, once removed from the squalid prison, would strike

At the aid of mercy with envy because it had not at the same time

Led everyone out from the same darkness into the true light?

[670] 165 When he does not experience the punishment in which he was submerged,

How miserably would the one bound by it endure it, unless freed from it?

[Col. 0129B] Finally, he then conceives toward him a sympathetic feeling

With a kindly mind, by which, with humble prayer, he may reconcile Christ

To the wretched, who, accustomed to being burdened by night,

[675] Offer no prayers for escape. **SO greatly does error harm**

That it helps one to err; and the contagions of the old disease

Steal in so gently that one loves the condition in which one is sick.

From where, then, does this complaint arise? Such concern does not move

[Col. 0130A] Those for whom their own punishment is not yet painful,

[680] Who believe that they have not been abandoned by the light.

But those who, rescued from darkness, live in the light

Rejoice, and from those who pay what they owe they learn

How much has been forgiven them by the goodness of the One who calls.

**[Note: Chapter XXXIV. But this applies only to those who undermine grace as far as they can, attributing the first cause of distinction between good and evil to free will. We owe it to Christ alone if we think and will anything right.

685.** *Ingrati.* This name and its explanation seem to have been taken from Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 8: “Grace,” he says, “is given freely by God, and by his just judgment in others it is shown what grace accomplishes in those to whom it is given. Let us therefore not be UNGRATEFUL, because, according to the good pleasure of his will, for the praise of the glory of his grace, merciful God frees so many from so deserved a destruction that, even if he freed no one from it, he would not be unjust.” —Dr. Lov.

[Col. 0130D] **686.** *Subsistere.* Dr. Lov. placed *consistere* in the margin, which he had found in the printed editions (perhaps the more recent ones, for it is not present in the older editions before us).

**689.** *Judicio*, in place of “election,” as above. —Dr. Lov.

**690.** “As though equal,” etc. See the end of chapter 6, that is, verses 130 and 131.

**693.** *Britannum.* That is, Pelagius (as above, verse 2), who, when the author wrote this, was excluded—that is, expelled from the Church (as again in verse 406)—and was wandering somewhere, homeless and exiled. Hence also verse 149: “Driven from the world, wandering and received by no dwelling,” and similar passages elsewhere. —Dr. Lov.

**694.** *The little flock.* Luke 2: “Little flock”: small, I say, and therefore timid and distrustful of itself. —Dr. Lov.

**696.** *Recti.* Gallus reads *recte*, which I do not approve; our author does not usually say *recte velle* (“to will rightly”), but rather *recta*, as several times above: “right willing,” “right speaking,” etc. “To think rightly” is, however, also used by the Church in the collect for the Holy Spirit. Let it therefore remain as it is: “If we think and will anything right,” Dr. Lovan. Lugd., Lov., Duac., and Colon. agree with this observation.

**699.** “By which he might be chosen”: namely, by us, as Gallus understood it. But this conflicts with the Gospel statement, “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” For this reason, although the author frequently mentions election, he never means any election except that by which we are chosen by God. Therefore *quo legeretur* means “by which he could deserve to be chosen.” For in truth God chooses merit in us, and chooses us for merit—but for merit that he himself gives. In a word, by which I explain the entire verse: God does not find in us the merit by which he may choose us; he himself creates it, and by creating it chooses us. I am speaking of the election that occurs in time, not of the election by which we were chosen before the foundation of the world. —Dr. Lov.]

You alone, therefore, are complainers, and you alone are proud:

[685] You alone are **UNGRATEFUL**, whom grace burns, because you wish

Every work of the will to depend upon your own will;

And because not all mortals enter the courts of life,

You think it depends so much on themselves

That each person's entering is as much a matter of judgment

[690] As his not entering, as though equal ability

Were available for either, and to will good were as much his own

As to will evil.

Go far away, insane impiety, and take away your wicked arts,

And follow your expelled British author.

We are humble and insignificant, a little flock, and fear

[695] To lean upon lofty things, because our sufficiency

Is from Christ. If we think and will anything right,

We owe it to him who released our bonds,

[Col. 0131A] And restored good in place of evil—not by finding

What he might choose on the basis of merit, but by giving what might be chosen,

[700] So that from what was received there might arise the cause of meriting;

And from gifts, in the act of giving, increasing diligence might climb

Step by step, and God might become one good to all.

**[Note: Chapter XXXV. We must not investigate why, from the whole human race, one part is chosen and the other rejected, although the same cause implicates everyone. Nor does ignorance of this harm us, just as it once did not harm us not to know that all nations would be called to faith. Nor does ignorance now of when the world will end harm us. Nor should we investigate the cause of such great variety in the human race: although everyone has the same nature, one rules while another serves, and so forth. Though the causes of so many manifest variations remain hidden, no one nevertheless accuses God, their author. God rightly willed that the secret of divine predestination remain hidden from us as long as we are in this life.

704.** *Legatur:* again, as often elsewhere, in place of *eligatur*. —Dr. Lov.

**706.** “Nor are they distinguished by merit,” namely, before faith and grace. —Dr. Lov.

**Ibid.** *Munere:* throughout this passage, it means “gift,” not “office,” but it is almost nowhere as ambiguous as here.

**711.** “Not brought forth.” Again, as in verse 746, “not brought forth.” By contrast, above, verse 86, “brought forth by tongues,” and verse 151, “brought forth to us,” etc.; that is, *edita* means “declared” or “manifested,” while *non edita* means “hidden.” —Dr. Lov.

**712.** “Thus, when,” etc. *Letter to Rufinus*, chapter 16: “For in earlier ages, when it was said concerning the people of one nation, ‘God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel,’ the future election of the nations was hidden; and afterward it became known, though it had not previously been revealed, as the Apostle said: ‘What was not made known to other generations,’ etc.” This nevertheless seems to be understood only in the sense that people in former times did not generally know that the nations would someday be called; otherwise it is expressly proved in the book *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 18, that the prophets knew and proclaimed this. —Dr. Lovan.

**714.** “At the end of the world,” not the last day, which is mentioned shortly afterward in verses 7–8, but the time of the New Law, which is the final age of the world. —Dr. Lovan.

**725.** *Procedit*, not *procedat*, as others have it; the sense demands this with the words that follow. Dr. Lov. noted *procedit* in the margins; Lovan., Duac., and Colon. inserted it into the text.

**730.** “It has been given, those.” Dr. Lov. prefers *datum*—“it has been given”—but *illos* (“those”). Others, with Gallus, read: “It has been given,” he says, “to those,” etc. But I cannot approve that intrusive repetition of the substantive verb in the middle and at the end of the verse. Add to this that the author uses the conjunction *ast* in the same way shortly below, verse 736.

**734.** “The cold blood has blocked the breast,” etc. A Virgilian phrase denoting a dull intellect. Thus in *Georgics* II:

> If cold blood should have stood around the breast.

They think there is an allusion here to the teaching of Empedocles, who believed that the soul was blood poured around the heart, as Cicero says in *Tusculan Disputations* I. —Dr. Lov.

**736.** “Frenzy,” namely, of desire; for the people mentioned in the present verse are set against those mentioned immediately before: “whom not even lawful heat,” etc. —Dr. Lovan.]

But why, from the whole stock of the human race,

Is one part chosen to be born again in Christ,

While another perishes, though the same cause implicates everyone,

[705] And they are not distinguished by merit?

We dare not investigate this sufficiently, nor proceed through hidden paths

Or tread remote tracks step by step.

[Col. 0131B] For many things lie well concealed; ignorance of them is beneficial

While gentle faith patiently endures certain matters being delayed

And does not suffer harm from anything unrevealed.

Thus, when from all peoples God cherished one chosen people

With laws, sacred rites, a temple, anointing, and signs,

What had been hidden was revealed at the end of the world;

[715] It did not harm them not to know that all nations would someday be called

Into the eternal kingdom, and that what the hope of that small people then possessed would be bestowed throughout the whole world.

Thus the last day, by which the age of the world is closed,

[Col. 0132A] Has not been given to our knowledge; yet the holy multitude

Does not suffer impatiently from this secret.

The bodily origin of the human race itself—

How many causes does it conceal beneath its varied order?

Although one hand brings everyone forth from the same ferment,

And the elements of the parents do not unite from different origins:

[725] From one clay a varied work proceeds; the craftsman changes the forms

Through his vessels and distinguishes one material

By the right of creation.

Thus the same nature of soul and the same nature of flesh

Enter the world under different conditions.

[730] To these it has been given to rule; those must serve:

These are endowed with beauty, strong powers, and vigorous old age;

169 Those with an unattractive appearance and a weak body;

[Col. 0132B] In these the intellect flourishes, suited to distinguished arts;

The cold blood weighs down the breasts of those others;

[735] Some are not even stirred by lawful heat to beget offspring.

But others cannot restrain their mad frenzy:

A tranquil modesty accompanies this person, gentle and calm,

**[Note: Here the complementary fifth member of the antithesis was missing, as the most learned hand had also noted in my copy of Gallus. Gallus himself supplied it in both versions; we have judged that it should also be supplied in the Latin texts. Whether rightly, you, reader, will see. We have deliberately sought the harshness of the canine letter, just as the author seeks the softness of smooth liquids in the preceding verse, and again earlier in *frenare furorem* he seeks the same harshness. —Dr. Lov.

[Col. 0133B] 741.** “Contains within itself.” Understand this phrase from verse 52 above, where similarly it says, “had held within itself,” etc. —Dr. Lov.

**742.** “Explains by an equitable judgment what has pleased him,” etc. Shortly afterward he says:

> So that, although the appearance of the work is revealed,  
> The rule of the will from which this unequal arrangement comes  
> Has not been brought forth.

Likewise, book I of *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 16: “Piety brings forth the work” (I restore *exserit* in place of *erexit*), “power obscures the cause.” The sense of all three passages is one: by the work and execution itself—which is always most just—God shows what pleases him; but, by the right of supreme power, he conceals from us the reasons for what pleases him. —Dr. Lov.

**750.** “In the body of death.” See above, on verse 486.

**753.** “For the testing … of the pious”: not so that they may examine those things, but rather so that through those things they may be examined and proved by God, namely, how humble and faithful they are. —Dr. Lov.]

[Here supply: “The harshness of this unmanageable disposition presses upon him.”]

With these and a thousand other modes, one seed producing variations,

They enter unequal beginnings and distinct forms.

[740] Yet no one among such conflicting things accuses

[Col. 0133A] The author, who contains within himself the law of this work,

While he explains by an equitable judgment what he has deemed fitting,

And just power obscures the causes of things.

If, therefore, an earthly creation and a race assigned to death

[745] Are produced by such unequal origin,

So that, although the appearance of the work is evident,

The rule of the will from which this unequal arrangement comes

Has not been revealed,

What wonder if the secret of a purpose greater than all

Lies hidden and is withdrawn beneath a lofty decree?

[750] While the empty things of the world flow away, while life is lived

In the body of death, and the struggle of the appointed contest is fulfilled,

God has concealed it from our knowledge as something

Not to be known, and has judged it more useful

[Col. 0133B] To veil certain things for the testing of the pious.

**[Note: Chapter XXXVI. Leaving the knowledge of his secrets to God, let us acknowledge him as the one author of all good things, down to the least beginning of a good will. Those are foolish who think they can resolve, by the willing and refusing of free will, the question that was inscrutable even to Paul: why some rather than others are freed by grace. God’s judgment cannot be unjust merely because it is hidden, since everyone possesses a merit worthy of death, even from the one sin of origin. Nothing leads to life except what is granted by grace.

757.** “Without whom,” etc. He magnificently misuses that fetid half-line from Virgil’s *Georgics* III, addressed to Maecenas:

> Without you the mind begins nothing lofty.

From this it is also clear that *rectum* should be read, as Virgil said *altum*, not *recti*, as several editions had it. —Dr. Lov.

**758.** “To attach the causes to free will,” etc. The expression is Juvenal’s, at the end of *Satire* 3, where one reads *subnectere causas*, although in a very different sense (as our author often borrows from the ancients their phrases but not their meanings in the same way). As for the meaning, it may be taken from a similar passage in chapter 8 of Gallus: “But whoever refers the causes of God’s works and judgments entirely to human wills and actions … and wishes God’s dispensations to vary according to the instability of free will,” etc. —Dr. Lov.]

Therefore we do not press upon closed things, nor with impudent

[755] Curiosity pursue what is hidden. It is enough to behold the works

Of the Almighty and to know the author of all good things;

Without whom the mind begins nothing right. Let insane impiety dare

[Col. 0134A] To attach the causes of divine works to proud free will;

But when we see manifest gifts of God, whose source is one,

[760] The supreme will, it is good for us to tremble with Paul

And humbly suspend our dull impulse before the unconquered throne of Christ,

Whose judgment we declare to be so inscrutable and profound

That we must openly confess it to be wholly truthful and just.

[765] For a single guilt is sufficient to undergo death;

For life there is no merit except what grace has granted.

**[Note: Chapter XXXVII. How much faithful men must guard themselves against the enemies of grace. Whoever attributes his virtues either to himself or to grace as though he had earned it, ceases to advance and falls back while running.]**
767. **A new race.** He is not addressing the Ungrateful—as some have thought, perhaps misled by the word *new*, which is often taken in a bad sense—but the orthodox people of the Church: new, certainly, in comparison with the Jewish people, to whom they are opposed here. — Dr. Lov.

[Col. 0134C] 768. **You are plucked away.** A verb used in place of *you are torn away* (*avelleris*). An allusion is made to Romans 11:17, where the Jewish people are discussed as an olive tree, and the Gentile people as a wild olive. See Augustine’s lucid exposition of that passage in his commentary on Psalm 72. — Dr. Lov.

769. **Of the formed foliage**, namely, of the olive tree, distinguished in contrast with the foliage of the wild olive, as shapeless and imperfect. — Dr. Lov.

772. **Of the proud.** An epithet of the Massilians, and indeed one of their two principal epithets. The other is “Ungrateful”; both occur together above, in the Preface and at verse 684. — Dr. Lov.

774 and following. **Of beauty, none, etc.** Until now the passage had been read:

> [lacuna] the image of beauty may creep in.  
> Do you think that none of these can err?

This is not unlike the very abrupt question above, at verse 459:

> You attribute to divine works, etc.?

Nevertheless, I agree with Gallus that the passage is corrupt; he thinks that this half-line should perhaps be joined to the preceding verse. “I would gladly,” Dr. Lov. continues, “have had the help of the manuscripts with him; but, despite examining even in Rome all the more celebrated libraries, including the Vatican itself, I could not obtain it. Therefore, working on my own, and without Gallus’s objection, I restored the passage so that these two verses cohere, though with the conjunction *ut* understood between them. I also wondered whether perhaps an entire verse was missing, for example:

> Since they are conspicuous in character and approved,

without which, or something similar, the nature of that deceptive image of beauty is not sufficiently indicated.

775. **Though they lead their life upon the cross, etc.** “Where, then,” one may ask, “is that evangelical saying, ‘You will know them by their fruits’?” Certainly, conduct provides some test of doctrine. But our author does not deny this; indeed, he rather confirms it. In removing this mask from the Semipelagians, he does not take the route of saying that conduct contributes nothing to the judgment of doctrine, but another route: he shows that their virtues are not solid, because pride and love of their own praise corrupt them—an attitude which they openly profess in their own doctrine. — Dr. Lov.

784. **Vain.** Another epithet of the Ungrateful, with which he again adorns them above, at verse 493. Meanwhile, some read *various* instead—Lugd., Lov., Duac., and Colon.—so that the passage would move from the particular discussion of the Massilians to a general statement. But since what follows also concerns only the Massilians for the moment, I think *various* is an error. — Dr. Lov. When the French translator noticed this, he corrected it.

788. **Not their foundation.** It is useful to quote in full the passages of Scripture to which the author alludes so seriously and reverently in this paragraph, especially since their marginal annotation would be denser and more confusing than could easily be grasped. At this very verse 788 he refers both to 1 Corinthians 3:11: “For no one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ”; and to Ephesians 2:21: “In whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord”; and finally to 1 Corinthians 10:4: “And the rock was Christ.” — Dr. Lov.

[Col. 0136B] 789 and following. An allusion is made to the foolish man of whom the Savior speaks in Matthew 7:26, who built his house upon the sand, etc. — Dr. Lov.

791. Reference is made to Psalm 117:22, which is also frequently repeated in the Gospel: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” — Dr. Lov.

792 and following. First, reference is made to passages in which Christ is called the cornerstone, such as Isaiah 28:16, Ephesians 2:20, and 1 Peter 2:6; then again to Ephesians 2:14: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall,” etc. — Dr. Lov.

795. The words of Psalm 18:6, “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber,” seem to be mingled with the sense of Song of Songs 1:3, “The king brought me into his chambers,” or, as the Church commonly reads it, “into his bedroom.” — Dr. Lov.

796 and the beginning of the following verse. Reference is made to 1 Corinthians 4:7: “What do you have that you did not receive?” — Dr. Lov.

797 and following. An allusion is made to John 6:44: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” — Dr. Lov.

800. Finally, to John 15:5: “Without me you can do nothing.” — Dr. Lov.

## Part Four

### Argument

He compares the doctrine of the Semipelagians with the Pelagian heresy, showing that they establish the Pelagian dogma more dangerously because they do so more covertly and attractively than Pelagius himself, whom they appeared to condemn. He chiefly destroys their fundamental claim concerning the remnants of the original integrity, which they thought survived in human nature; and he teaches that, so far as the desire for true good is concerned, nothing sound remains in nature. For the wound of the first parent struck the mind so deeply that it cannot even raise its eyes upward or recognize its own calamity. Whatever natural gifts remain to it belong only to the cultivation of temporal life—which is wholly a state of condemnation and punishment—not to the acquisition of eternal life, nor to assistance in virtue, but rather to the increase of pride.

Otherwise, if the former strength and power of ancient freedom remained in us, Christ would have died in vain, since each person’s own will could reconcile him to God. Furthermore, from the ineffable humility of God, by which he deigned to suffer such unworthy things, man ought to recognize the captivity in which he is imprisoned and the disease by which he is afflicted: a captivity and disease from which only the physician’s death could rescue him. For the physician mingled himself with the lowest things in order to insert us into the highest, so that through him we might be able to do whatever we can.

Finally, having condemned the madness of those who argued that the saints would be deprived of the reason for obtaining the crown unless good works were found in them that could be attributed to their own free choice, he concludes the poem with a devout invocation of God, the one fountain of all our goods.

[801] [Col. 0135D] **Chapter XXXVIII.** The Semipelagians condemn Pelagius only verbally, while retaining the most subtle poison of his heresy; and Pelagius would have led countless people astray if he had first coated the cup of his teaching with a little honey. For when at first he concealed his errors less carefully, he deterred many people from them by their very deformity.

[Col. 0136D] 803. **With a few, etc.** Dr. Lov.: “At first sight the entire verse displeased me. For what, I asked, are those sinews stripped from the skin? Perhaps *naevi* [“moles”] should be read instead? Then how could the author have stumbled over *squalida* in order to shorten the first syllable, when above he had so clearly lengthened the same syllable in *squalenti*? Meanwhile it occurred to me that our holy author may have found this shortening all the easier because he perhaps thought that the first syllable of *squaleo* was naturally short but was lengthened by authors when the letter *l* is doubled in the middle.

“As for the sinews, I now understand how they can be said to be removed from the skin: namely, if one takes *skin* to mean the whole outer covering by which the internal organs are concealed, and which includes the sinews, muscles, veins, and so forth—in short, even the skin properly so called. For it must be admitted that our author has spoken imprecisely; but he was imitating Ovid’s passage in *Metamorphoses* 11 concerning the flayed Marsyas, where, as here, skin, sinews, and internal organs are all mentioned:

> The skin, he says, torn away from the upper limbs,  
>   
> and the exposed sinews lie open;  
>   
> you could see the leaping entrails  
>   
> and count the translucent fibers in his breast.”

806. **He did not sweeten, etc.** Here again the softness of honey is expressed by the multiplication of *l*’s; conversely, the harshness of the error’s teacher could scarcely have been expressed more harshly than by the accumulation of those canine letters, *r*. — Dr. Lov.

808. **With bitter taste.** It is read in *Georgics* 2:

> But the unmistakable taste will reveal it, and will torment  
>   
> the mouths of those who test it with a bitter sensation.

Thus many read it in the author’s own age, and this explains the indulgence deserved by the rather unusual expression he uses here: for without doubt he used *taste* familiarly in place of *flavor*. Today, however, following Aulus Gellius, book 1, chapter 12, grammarians commonly read Virgil’s line as:

> He will torment them with a bitter sensation.

810. **Disciples.** The Massilians, to whom he repeatedly attributes Pelagius and Pelagian teachers.

814. **Now.** That is, after so many condemnations and solemn pros criptions—or certainly “now,” since so many shapeless things are seen

> at the very threshold itself.

At least I would judge that the signs mentioned two verses later are none other than these shapeless things, which the Pelagian heresy displayed, as it were, upon its very forehead. Meanwhile, the common editions read *so* in place of *now*, so that it is joined, I think, with *bruised*. — Dr. Lov.

816. **To recognize.** This should be read, not *to acknowledge*, as some do. Although the distinction is slight, it is demonstrated by a verse of Virgil’s *Georgics* 4, from which this line is taken:

> Which now you will be able to recognize by unmistakable signs.

The *now* mentioned in the preceding note may perhaps also have been taken from that passage. — Dr. Lov.

[Col. 0137B] [Note: [Col. 0138B] **Chapter XXXIX.** The Semipelagians deceive more dangerously because they appear to condemn Pelagius while admitting that death and sin are transmitted to all from Adam; that no one can attain eternal life except through baptism; and that infants need baptism in order to be freed from sin. [Col. 0138C] Yet they agree with Pelagius when they say that nature can be carried toward the good by its own powers, as it could before sin, as though it had not been injured by original sin. Indeed, they say that the saints can break the fiercest attacks of the devil by their own powers, with God usefully abandoning his own and leaving them to themselves, lest they have no merits if they do nothing good except what grace works in them.

822. **The first origin.** That is, the first birth according to the flesh, distinguished from the second birth through baptism, mentioned shortly before: “unless reborn from the font.” Unless, however, *the first origin* more simply means that which infants derive from their first parent; hence the following phrase also occurs immediately afterward: “through the ancestral wound.” — Dr. Lov.

824. **That nothing exists, etc.** See the same dogma above, chapter 1, and elsewhere. — Dr. Lovan.

835. **Nor yield to punishments, etc.** For the integrity of natural powers is supposedly so great that, even against the devil himself and his savagery, it can fight unaided all the way to the final tortures. Such is their position in the book *Against the Collators*, chapter 20. — Dr. Lovan.

839. **Lest there be none, etc.** Dr. Lov. writes *nor lest there be none*, etc. “That this was in fact the opinion of the Semipelagians,” he adds, “is clear from several other sources, and from the words of the Collator in the same book, chapter 19, near the end. Speaking there of the centurion’s faith praised by Christ, he says: ‘For it would have had no praise or merit if the Lord had preferred in him what he himself had bestowed’—that is, if he had praised it above others.

“As for the reading found here in the common editions, *nor lest there be none*—though it is not found in the older editions of Lugd., Lov., Duac., and Colon.—and Gallus’s reading *lest*: both are wrong and contrary to Prosper’s and Virgil’s usage. When *ut* or *ne* has preceded, they do not add *ne* again, but *neu*, as if *neve*, just as *seu* is used for *sive*, as if *seve*.”

[Col. 0139B] 841. **If anything by the sense of nature, etc.** The common editions carried this reading as a marginal conjecture. Gallus rightly brought it into the text, replacing the former reading: “just as the sense of nature,” etc. He also correctly understood “the sense of nature” as the natural light and judgment which the Pelagians and their disciples repeatedly claimed to be sufficient—at least together with the written Law, mentioned in the following verse—for a person to will or not will what ought to be done. They teach this above in chapter 1, section 3; again in chapter 29, sections 2 and 3; and elsewhere. — Dr. Lov.

844. **As though only the servants of Christ, etc.** Thus he argues against the *Collator*, chapter 6: “If the will is not to be considered ours because it is formed, governed, ordered, and instructed, then the children of God who are led by the Spirit of God are stripped of freedom; they lose the vigor of the rational mind and are deprived of all praise for voluntary devotion, although the Spirit of wisdom and understanding is given to them,” etc. Thus far the author.

He therefore means Christ’s servants who, according to Scripture, are led by the Spirit of God and to whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding is given, etc. His meaning is as follows: If your doctrine is true—namely, that whatever God works in us is deprived of the praise of virtue—then whatever is done by those who are led by the Spirit of God will also be deprived of the praise of virtue. Yet these people are properly Christ’s servants; and on this account they would be inferior even to pagans, who, according to you, often perform praiseworthy acts. — Dr. Lovan.]

> [Col. 0140A] Thus the mind, whose light came from the highest light,  
>   
> wrapped free choice in darkness; and, abandoning the light,  
>   
> [179] chose, by its own deliberation, to grow black with the darkness of night.  
>   
> Nor can it now voluntarily raise its captive eyes upward,  
>   
> [860] because, when the tyrant stripped it of this also,  
>   
> it lost the ability to know how deeply it lies beneath the wound.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] **Chapter XLI.** If anything remains to man from the remnants of his former state, he falsely considers it sound, and from this alone seizes material for pride.

863. **And the life to be lived.** Gallus reads *the life to be lived* in the ablative, so that the sense is: if anything today remains to man of the happy principles of his first state and of the prudent conduct of the life of this exile. I find this so unacceptable that I would rather retain the common reading in the nominative. Yet even that reading is not without its difficulties: for to what does the following phrase, “this sound thing,” refer—does it refer to all the preceding items, including the prudent conduct of life? Certainly the passage would be smoother as follows:

> It remains for the life of exile to be lived prudently.

Compare above, verse 829:

> for the advantages of present life, etc.

Meanwhile, the reading we have retained, and the common reading, may be defended by the author’s practice elsewhere of placing several things together and then referring what follows to only one of them, usually the first. — Dr. Lov.

865. **To love his own understanding** is said of the wisdom of the world—not in the ordinary sense in which someone is said to love his own opinion, but because he loves and admires his own understanding, that is, his own knowledge. This can be inferred both from what follows and from the remarks above at verse 841. Furthermore, “the wisdom of the world” is an apostolic expression found in more than one passage. — Dr. Lov.

872. **Is exercised in numbers, etc.** In mathematics, in which the human mind takes particular pleasure in itself. — Dr. Lovan.

874. **The various eclipses of the sun, etc.** Dr. Lov. The complete verse is from *Georgics* 2 and is almost taken from Lucretius, book 5. Our author did not insert both poets into this passage so much to imitate the philosopher-poet as to mock them as excessively pleased with themselves in this science. Lucretius can be seen almost everywhere exulting in it with childish enthusiasm; and shortly afterward one hears Virgil exclaiming with remarkable feeling:

> Happy is he who has been able to understand the causes of things.

**In the same place: Various.** Since some thought that various effects of the sun could be identified more easily than various eclipses—“for what other eclipse of the sun is there,” they said, “than the one caused by the interposition of the moon, which is called an eclipse?”—and since they were not familiar with Virgil, they conjectured that the reading should be “various effects of the sun.” Just as familiarity with Virgil ought not to be counted as a fault in a theologian, neither should the familiarity be rejected which even the holy Fathers did not generally disdain.

Apart from the fact that the ordinary eclipse itself is not without variety—one is total, another partial, another universal, another particular, and so on—it should also be noted that certain extraordinary eclipses are not entirely unknown to the sun, though we do not call them eclipses. Thus a famous modern philosopher reports that the sun has sometimes shone for several days, and even months or an entire year, with its light dimmed like that of the moon. He attributes this to the abundance and size of the spots which, by means of the telescope, we observe on the body of the sun, though they do not remain constant in number, size, or shape. He also thinks that these spots cause some fixed stars—which he considers to be so many suns—to disappear altogether. Ovid records in his tales, not without a basis in fact, that this happened to the seventh of the Pleiades, although, in keeping with his purpose, he gives a mythical explanation.

Since Ovid has been mentioned, no one mixed natural phenomena more ingeniously with his tales. He is also the one who, alluding somewhere in the *Metamorphoses*—I do not presently remember the passage—to the various eclipses of our sun, introduces Phoebus growing pale with some strange pallor. He expressly adds that this was not, however, the kind of eclipse caused by the interposition of his sister, thereby suggesting that his decline had other forms and causes as well. — Dr. Lov.]

> For if anything remains to him of the happy principles  
>   
> and of the life of exile prudently to be lived,  
>   
> he considers and loves this to be sound, and nothing higher than it,  
>   
> [865] in the understanding of worldly wisdom,  
>   
> admiring himself as illustrious in countless arts:  
>   
> because he seeks hidden things through lofty conjectures,  
>   
> remembers correctly, understands sharply, and assesses suitably;  
>   
> because he has cultivated the skill of speaking, because through laws he has founded cities  
>   
> [870] [Col. 0140B] and curbed savage customs by reason,  
>   
> so that fear of punishment has contended with love of duty.  
>   
> Now, when he is exercised in numbers, when he seeks to know  
>   
> the courses by which the stars of heaven must be recognized,  
>   
> and seems to know the various eclipses of the sun  
>   
> and the labors of the moon,  
>   
> [875] [Col. 0141A] how beautiful he seems to himself—and how he vanishes in these very things!

[Note: [Col. 0141C] **Chapter XLII.** Nor can anyone ever be led from those remnants to true life. If the power in nature were the same as it was in Adam, each person could reconcile himself to God and free himself from sin. Therefore Christ would have died in vain.

878. **Finally, from these things, etc.** We judged that this excessively abrupt period should be enclosed in parentheses. More specifically, it refers to the remarks at the end of the preceding chapter concerning the science of the stars. That science is so far from being able to lead its possessors to true life that it has even drawn some into idolatry, namely, the worship of those very stars—about which Wisdom 13 complains at length.

Here one may admire the perversity of the human mind, which abuses even the best things so perversely that the most beautiful science—physics, I mean—by which, from the things that have been made, it is so easy analogically to discover the Maker, the Best and Greatest, is made to serve against God himself and falls from it not merely into many religions, as our author notes here, but even into the abyss of irreligion and atheism.

Thus the impious Lucretius with his Epicurus, thus Pliny, and thus other interpreters of nature increased the unhappy number of atheists. Even today a satirist of our age dares to cast the disgrace of the same impiety upon the profession of physicists—or, as he calls them, physicians. Perhaps he does so unjustly; nevertheless, one is ashamed, distressed, and wearied by the human race, since at least the suspicion ought to fall upon anyone rather than upon those who should be furthest removed from this evil.

These remarks may serve to confirm this most prudent and truthful parenthesis of Prosper’s—and they come from one who, lest he be thought hostile to physics, once loved, indeed passionately loved, this Galatea himself. — Dr. Lov.

880. **Unharmed.** Dr. Lov. reads *unharmed* in the masculine. Thus above, at verse 541, we read “the honor of the mind unharmed.” Gallus, however—unless it is a typographical error—has *unharmed* in the plural. We have not changed the older reading, since it is supported by the authority of the older editions of Lugd., Lov., Duac., and Colon., and seemed to us to yield a sound sense.

883. **He might atone for death by dying.** There was no need for the conjectural reading *he might bind*, although this is preferred by Lugd., Lov., Duac., and Colon. The phrase imitates the following passage of Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* 8, in the story of Meleager:

> Death must be atoned for by death.

Or, if only Virgilian diction is valued, the author alluded to *Aeneid* 2:

> They will atone for this crime by the death of the wretched.

]

[Note: [Col. 0142C] **Chapter XLIII.** From the ineffable humility of God, by which he deigned to become both man and miserable in order to redeem man, captive man must recognize the prison in which he was confined and the disease by which he was afflicted. Only the physician’s death could come to his rescue. The things that remain to man after the fall should be held in little esteem. When man turns to God, the change should be attributed to God’s grace as its beginning, rather than to free choice. The fact that man attributes too much to free choice proceeds from that pride which the devil inspired in our first parents.

890. **Of the ruin.** Gallus reads this interrogatively up to this point, together with the editions of Lov., Duac., and Colon. “I would agree,” Dr. Lovan says, “if the verse were *it is oppressed by a mass*, etc., rather than *it may be oppressed by a mass*, unless even then I would prefer to read it as an exclamation. But now I say that there is an ellipsis, and not a particularly troublesome one. Anyone who wishes may supply a passage on the same subject from *Against the Collators*, chapter 9: ‘Does it not become perfectly clear from the singularity of the remedy itself into what profound evil the nature of the entire human race has been plunged by the transgression of the one in whom all sinned?’” — Dr. Lov.

897. **Inviolable anywhere by anyone.** Dr. Lovan reads *ever*. Gallus reads *anywhere*; so also Lugd., Lov., Duac., and Colon. He thinks this was said because the Savior was inviolable unless he himself had willed otherwise.

898. **The destroyer.** Not so much Christ himself as the human race; namely, the devil, who is called a murderer from the beginning in John 8:44. He is said metaphorically to be destroyed because—as also in the Gospel—he is to be cast out, his kingdom destroyed, and his dominion over death taken away. Gallus reads it this way in the prose, better than in the verse, where he understands it of death. — Dr. Lovan.

[Col. 0143B] 908. **Punishment**, and indeed the following verse explains in what sense they have been made miserable. The passage concerns the remnants of the first integrity, with reference to the goods of that original integrity, of which only a tiny portion remains, while the rest have been miserably lost.

In this sense, a small portion of great wealth from which someone has been fined by a ruler on account of a crime could be called his punishment, when he looks upon it and considers how little of so much wealth remains to him—especially if that small portion is of little use to him and serves almost only to his detriment. Such are those remnants: without God’s help they bring man to the end of death, as is said above at verse 403, but not, as is added at verse 877,

> [lacuna] can lead to true life.

911. Gallus notes a manifest gap here. Dr. Lov. had filled it with the verse:

> They raise them to heaven and enjoy the true light.

The insertion is sufficiently elegant; nevertheless, he derives another conjectural restoration from Prosper’s own words, namely from the passage in which he treats almost the same subject—if it is indeed his—in the *Letter to Demetrias*, chapter 14:

> “Just as medical skill enables clouded eyes to see what they do not see, so in sluggish and dull hearts the obscured vision is cleared by the Holy Spirit, and from the true light they receive light for a lamp that had already become dark and failing.”

Accordingly, Dr. Lov. presents the passage as follows:

> Or when dull eyes, at last rescued from long darkness,  
>   
> receive light from the true light.

914. **The power of choosing rightly is absent.** Dr. Lov. That is, the virtue of choosing rightly. Thus above, at verse 651 and following:

> [lacuna] because the virtue of doing what is right  
>   
> has not been given.

915. **The first fathers.** Above, at verse 10, we tentatively explained “fathers” as the first father and mother, since the expression seemed very unusual and without any suitable ancient parallel. This passage removes all doubt; grammarians may judge the phrasing. — Dr. Lov.

920. **Which now, etc.** The words *which* and *serpent* make this verse ambiguous and obscure, for someone could easily take the latter substantivally, while it is not immediately apparent to what the former should refer. At first sight it seemed to me to refer to *desire*. But as I now see it, it refers to *tracks*. Take *serpent* participially, and arrange the construction as follows:

> Through these tracks of the ancient fraud, that serpent—the devil, the sower of death—now again strives to inflame the deceived with a similar fury.

— Dr. Lov.

[Col. 0144C] 925. **Mobility.** As above, at verse 592. It should therefore not be *nobility*, as some have thought. — Dr. Lov.

928. **By a price, not by a gift.** That is, by a due payment, not by a gratuitous gift. — Dr. Lov.]

934. **Of the viper’s cup.** That is, given to them by the serpent. For reference is made to the statements in the preceding chapter. — Dr. Lov.

938. **And now may it be, etc.** Gallus took this as an imperative, joining it with the words above at verse 934 and following: “Let us shake off and confess.” To me it seems a subjunctive, connected with the infinitive immediately preceding, in the manner by which our author frequently links these two moods, so that *now may it be* stands for *now to be*—unless the reading should be *so that it may now be*. — Dr. Lov.

944. **He mingled the highest things with the lowest.** An elegant abuse of the familiar expression among good authors, “to mingle the highest with the lowest,” meaning to turn everything upside down. — Dr. Lov.]
