[945] **[Note: [Col. 0144D]**

## CHAPTER XLV

Those who think that the saints are deprived of the reason for obtaining the crown unless human merits are found in them must be driven far away. The virtue of the devout is not for that reason to be esteemed less, because they receive it wholly from Christ. Nor is the heavenly glory of the saints to be esteemed less, although they have it wholly from God, who is everything in all of them. Still less ought we to find it burdensome to acknowledge that, in this valley of tears, we can do nothing good except by grace. Nor is freedom removed by this; rather, it is restored and redeemed. Thus whatever anyone does rightly is not to be credited to that person, but to the grace of Christ. For God, through grace, bestows not only the fruit of the good work, but also the will and thought to perform it, and the entire sequence of a devout life.

—**Objection of the Semi-Pelagians.** By this preaching of grace, the pursuit of virtue is dissolved.

—**Response.** On the contrary, without grace there is no work of virtue, since the human will by itself can do nothing other than go astray. It is solely by the power of grace that we are made capable and that human minds are kindled to live rightly.

[Col. 0145B] **946. “The reason for taking the crown.”** That is, the basis of merit and reward. See above, on v. 839 and following. Doctor of Louvain.

**947. “Their own good things.”** That is, things belonging to them and accomplished without the help of grace, as above, v. 570:

> Nor can our well-performed deeds be ascribed to our own labor.

Understand *propriis* in the same way shortly below, v. 962, namely, as referring to virtues belonging to them. Doctor of Louvain.

**963. “Pleasing.”** But what are those “pleasing” virtues, as opposed to their own? If Virgil’s usage is consulted, it departs widely from our purpose, where he uses this word at the beginning of *Aeneid* IV:

> Will you even fight against a love that has been approved?

Apart from the fact that it should not be thought that Prosper, in so sacred a matter, had looked to a passage from the *Aeneid* rather than to some passage of Scripture. I therefore think that these “pleasing” virtues are the same as the good works “which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10). They are accordingly called approved because they have been ordered and prepared by the divine good pleasure, so that we might walk in them. Doctor of Louvain.

**966. “Bodily labor.”** That is, the kind of labor carried on in this sorrowful body, amid such uncertainty and fear of falling and sinning. For the men of Massilia seemed to seek the particular excellence of works from the wavering uncertainty of free choice left to itself, which they feared would be removed by the operation of grace. Doctor of Louvain.

**970. “And the smallest work of mortal life.”** That is, someone may say, sin—especially deadly sin. This would indeed be elegant, if the following did not then ensue with evident redundancy:

> Which is nothing but sin.

What, then? The passage is difficult. I prefer to preserve it, together with similar passages, in a theological appendix rather than meditate upon it with God in this poem of Prosper’s; for the present, I shall continue with philological diversions. Doctor of Louvain. —The Lyon edition alone has this passage differently:

> Why are they ashamed, even in this valley of tears,  
> to be mighty through God and to have too much mortal work?  
> Which is nothing, etc.

**972. “Alone”:** when it is alone. Doctor of Louvain.

[Col. 0146B] **The same passage. “They return.”** As though to their native spring, as in Horace:

> Though you drive out nature with a pitchfork, still it will return.

**977. “With freedom redeemed.”** Can freedom, then, be redeemed, or can it ever have failed to be free? Thus, at any rate, Prosper expressly teaches below, v. 995:

> Then the course will become swift …  
> Free freedom, etc.

Two things are therefore to be noted: first, that in Prosper’s meaning there is freedom without grace; second, that through grace freedom itself is further set free, namely, for willing and accomplishing the good, God working in it, as Philippians 2:13 teaches. The holy Fathers contemporary with Prosper are also to be understood in this sense of the freedom—so to speak—of freedom, when they sometimes appear to speak more harshly, as though freedom lost through the first sin were recovered through Christ’s grace. In truth, this is the freedom with which Christ set us free. Galatians 4:31. Doctor of Louvain.

**978. “To whom God, etc.”** This punctuation, belonging to the Gallican translator and supported by the Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, is not at all approved by the Doctor of Louvain. In its place he wishes the passage to be pronounced as follows:

> But with freedom redeemed:  
> For God is its ruler; and from the highest light, light,  
> Life, salvation, virtue, wisdom, is the grace of Christ;  
> By which it runs, rejoices, etc.

He says that the sense changes according to the earlier punctuation: in that arrangement, ruler, light, life, salvation, and wisdom are all spoken of God. “This,” he says, “would displease me less, except that *from the highest light* seems to have to be understood of created light; and therefore that expression, and those that follow, ought rather to be referred to grace.”

**983. “You, the petitions of one asking, etc.”** Thus the Church prays on the ninth Sunday after Pentecost: “Grant what is desired to those who ask, and make them ask for what is pleasing to you.” Doctor of Louvain.

**991. “What does it do, etc.”** The Doctor of Louvain writes *What may it do?* “The Gallican,” he says in his note, “again differs. For he first reads *agit*, ‘it does,’ and then postpones the question mark to the end of the verse. Neither reading, I confess, is especially wrong, or causes any notable loss of meaning.” The Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions have *What does it do?*

[Col. 0147A] **994. “You restore.”** This verb says more than the Gallican understood, for he rendered it by his *ramener*, “to bring back.” The same thought is repeated in Book I of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 8:

> Nor should he disdain to carry on his shoulders the sick woman, exhausted from a long journey through trackless places, and to save her not merely by calling her back, but also by carrying her.

Doctor of Louvain.

**The same passage. “You adorn.”** Just as in the preceding verb, *you restore*, he plainly alludes to the Gospel parable of the shepherd carrying the lost sheep back on his shoulders (Luke 15), so here I think he refers to the father in the same chapter, adorning the prodigal son, who had returned to him, with the first robe. At least the Gallican, more successful in rendering this word than the other, translates it correctly in prose: “If you do not adorn him with your gifts and your graces.” Here too he followed the language of Scripture, in which “to adorn” has the same sense as “to enrich.” Doctor of Louvain.

**999. “Let free choice come forth.”** That is, freedom. For *arbitrium*, “free choice,” is used for freedom itself above as well, v. 622:

> No signs of free choice answer to you.

He desires, of course, that freedom which grace gives, and which, following Prosper’s meaning, we have already called the freedom of freedom itself. Doctor of Louvain.

**1000. “May be able.”** I readily accept this from the Gallican, instead of *they are able*, which the others have. I also willingly record his prose explanation, in which he renders *May the bodily senses be able to do nothing without it* as follows: “May it direct all the movements of our body”—that is, “May they perform no operation of our bodily sensation which it does not produce.” O prayer! Yet only a prayer, unless this mortal nature puts on immortality. Doctor of Louvain.

**The same passage. “Servile work.”** He calls it this when our will, rather than God’s will, is at work in us; that is, when we do evil, or when we boast of our good acts as though they were our own. I infer this from Prosper’s antithesis in the following verse and from Augustine’s words, which will shortly be cited. Doctor of Louvain.

**1002. “Sabbaths.”** With a slight allusion to the eternal Sabbath-rest, he speaks of a Sabbath to be observed in this very life. Our author presents it in the words of his Augustine, *Sentences* 278:

> That perpetual Sabbath was prefigured by the observance and rest of a single day. He observes the perpetual Sabbath who, in hope of future rest, devotes himself to holy works and does not boast of his good acts as though they were his own or as though they were things he had not received, recognizing that the One who works in him is also at rest.**]**

Therefore let those who say that care must be taken lest the saints lack the reason for obtaining the crown be silent,

[Col. 0145A] if their own good things are not found in them.

For those who teach this with excessively swollen impiety,

what else do they wish but to strip us of justice and virtue, and of God—

[950] so that light may not shine in the night,

so that the languid may not return to strength, and the dead may not live?

But let it be our glory to draw these things from the highest fountain of true goods,

and to shine with the light from above and with everlasting splendor;

not to place our hope in the fading bloom of hay.

[955] For just as a branch cannot produce any fruits

unless it remains in the vine, which from the root supplies

sap to the leaves and fills the grapes with must,

so those who are barren of virtues and lack their fruit

will be the perpetual food of fire—those who, having abandoned the vine,

[960] dare to trust in the freedom of their flowing locks

[Col. 0145B] lest they become fruitful through Christ’s abundance;

and believe that they can excel more by their own efforts

than if God were the author of pleasing virtues.

Let them therefore think that they will become vile and deformed

[965] when God will be the single glory of the transformed saints;

nor will the pressure of bodily labor any longer

crush the uncertain, but Christ will always be everything in all.

And if this is beautiful and greater than all else,

why are they ashamed, even in this valley of tears,

to be mighty through God and to have the least mortal work,

[Col. 0146A] which is nothing but sin, by which

freedom is tormented—freedom to which evil deeds alone return?

187 Yet when we direct our mind toward holy actions,

when a chaste mind resists the desires of the flesh,

[975] when we do not yield to the tempter and, harassed

by bitter sufferings, remain with our heart unharmed,

we act with freedom—but with freedom redeemed,

whose ruler is God, and from the highest light, light,

life, salvation, virtue, wisdom: the grace of Christ,

[980] by which it runs, rejoices, endures, takes care, chooses, perseveres,

believes, hopes, loves, is cleansed, and is justified.

For if we do anything right, Lord, we do it with you assisting;

you move hearts; you grant the petitions of the one who asks

[Col. 0146B] what you wish to give, preserving what you have bestowed and creating it,

[985] producing merits from merits and heaping your gifts upon crowns.

Yet it must not be thought that this diminishes care

or dissolves the pursuit of virtues, or causes the work of the mind to grow numb,

because the good things of the saints are yours, and whatever in them

is sound or strong draws its vitality from you—so that the human will

[990] might seem to do nothing, while you accomplish everything:

what does it do without you, except that it wanders far away from you?

It always approaches precipitous paths and, by its own movement,

is about to enter byways, unless you, good Lord, receive,

[Col. 0147A] restore, cherish, protect, and adorn it when weary and sick.

[995] Then the course will become swift, and eyes will see;

free freedom, wise wisdom, just

judgment, strong virtue, and sound ability.

Of this help, Father, may we always be in need:

[Col. 0148A] from it may our free choice come forth; without it may nothing

[1000] of bodily sensation be able to act, so that servile work may rest.

189 And while your will, not ours, is at work in us,

may we keep legitimate Sabbaths on holy feast days.

## [EPIGRAMS]

[Col. 0147]

## ADMONITION ON THE TWO SHORT WORKS THAT FOLLOW

The two epigrams placed below, directed against a detractor of Saint Augustine—whether the same man or different men are acknowledged, equally holding perverse opinions—are assigned to Saint Prosper by the authority both of manuscript and printed codices, and by the testimony of every age. Yet it is not equally easy to determine which of the many adversaries of Augustinian doctrine the author attacks, since the silence concerning his name has hitherto left room for doubt.

That he was Vincent of Lérins, the monk and author of the *Commonitorium*, may be read as demonstrated by several arguments in Anthelmius’s frequently cited Dissertation 9. For in that otherwise truly golden work he is thought chiefly to have intended to cast Augustine’s doctrine under suspicion of novelty.

The matter had previously been noticed and approved, after Vossius, by the most learned men Henry Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 11 of Book II, and Natalis Alexander, *Church History*, volume X, chapter 3, article 7, §7. To their arguments he adds this further piece of evidence: Since it is known from Augustine’s *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapters 3 and 4, that at the beginning of his conversion Augustine expressly taught the position concerning the beginnings of faith and good will, the Massilian Semi-Pelagians used those earlier books as a shield. On every occasion they replied to Augustine’s disciples that in those views they were following Augustine’s own words.

When the defenders of Augustinian doctrine made the strong objection that the holy Doctor’s knowledge had advanced through successive stages of growth, so that in old age he recognized and corrected what he had not known, or had written less skillfully, as a young man, they replied that Augustine’s earlier writings were for that reason more deserving of approval than all others, because antiquity supported them, whereas the later writings could rely on nothing but novelty.

Prosper, however, argued more forcefully in the name of all holy and learned brothers, in his responses to the questions of the men of Genoa—questions proposed especially on these matters. He said:

> For the persuasion of those who recalled this man’s knowledge, built up through so many stages of growth, to the beginnings of his youth, so that what he had thought unskillfully at the beginning of his conversion might offer greater support to heretics than what truth had revealed through his episcopal diligence might benefit Catholics, is understood to be neither just nor reasonable. It is rightly the seriousness of the devout Doctor that marks those who use this prejudice and linger over matters long since renounced, because, although they took care to investigate all his opinions, they did not wish to advance with his learning.

As though attempting to answer them in the *Commonitorium*, Vincent placed that celebrated sentence at the end:

> Teach the same things that you have learned, so that when you speak newly, you do not speak new things.

He then ingeniously presents and resolves the objection of Augustine’s disciples:

> “But perhaps someone will say: Is there, then, no progress in religion within the Church of Christ? Certainly there is, and very great progress—for who is so envious of men and so hostile to God as to try to forbid it? Yet it must be progress in faith, not a change. For progress means that each thing is enlarged within itself, whereas change means that something is transformed from one thing into another. Therefore understanding, knowledge, and wisdom must grow and advance greatly and vigorously, through the stages of individuals and of all people, of one person and of the whole Church, through ages and centuries—but only within their own kind, that is, in the same doctrine, the same meaning, and the same judgment.”

These are Vincent’s words. If his earlier and later statements are twisted against Augustine’s later books, no one can deny that the same statements can be turned against Vincent and his defenders. He presents what follows with such artifice that the more zealously he appears at first sight to attack every other heresy, the more he seems secretly to assail the opinions of the holy Bishop of Hippo.

Yet although those statements unjustly struck at Augustine, they struck down all heresies—both those already past and those still to come—with a single blow. The rest may be read in the learned Censor, if anyone has the leisure; we shall omit further discussion, judging this sufficient.

[Col. 0149]

## SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITAINE

[Note: [Col. 0149A] These three pieces have long since been selected from various epigrams of Saint Prosper and joined to the poem *Against the Ungrateful*, doubtless because of the similarity of their subject. In the first two, John Cassian, the chief of the Ungrateful, appears to be harassed; the third also belongs to the same controversy, for the reason sufficiently indicated in the marginal argument and, as I believe, first demonstrated there. I have, however, reversed their customary order. The order of time seemed to require this, according to which the first pieces were either written or imagined to have been written for the sake of poetic propriety: namely, the first when that writer was only beginning to be said to criticize Augustine’s books and to compose some work against them; the second when that work had already begun to spread. Doctor of Louvain.]

## [EPITAPH OF THE NESTORIAN AND PELAGIAN HERESIES]

[Col. 0151]

## ADMONITION ON THE EPITAPH OF THE NESTORIAN AND PELAGIAN HERESIES

For this epitaph to be fully understood, two aspects of the Nestorian heresy must be considered as its principal heads.

The first concerns the union of the human nature with the divine nature in Christ. Nestorius proclaimed that this union had occurred through mere indwelling, not in a unity of person, so that there were two persons in Christ just as there were two natures, and the Son of God was not the same as the son of Mary.

The second concerns the manner in which Jesus attained that union, whatever its character might be. Nestorius maintained that Jesus had not possessed it immediately at conception, but had acquired it later through his own merits. Thus the old Chronologist, quoted by Liberatus, says the following about the Nestorian heresy:

> In the consulship of Felix and Taurus, Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, attempted to introduce a new error into the Churches, preaching that Christ had been born merely a man and not also God, and saying that divinity had been bestowed upon him according to his merit.

Saint Prosper chiefly has this latter error in view, and in it compares the Nestorian heresy with the Pelagian. He says that the Nestorian heresy was at once the mother and the daughter of the Pelagian heresy.

It was its mother because the error that destroys grace at the level of the head, and that asserts that Jesus attained the dignity of Christ through his own merits—which is the heresy of Nestorius—is the source and origin of the error that overturns grace in the members and asserts that human beings can obtain the dignity of Christians for themselves through their own merits—which is the heresy of Pelagius.

It was its daughter because Nestorius did not publish his heresy until after the Pelagians had been condemned. Thus, although at the threshold of this epitaph he had said that the Nestorian heresy succeeded the Pelagian as though it arose afterward—which is true if one considers its public promulgation by Nestorius—he later says that both arose together, both because of the affinity and kinship between their errors and because, before Nestorius, the Nestorian heresy was contained within the Pelagian.

This is evident from Leporius, a Gallican monk, who, while being a vigorous defender of Pelagian doctrine, also taught the heresy for which Nestorius was later condemned; but through Augustine’s works he returned to a sound mind. Nestorius published his heresy shortly after the condemnation of the Pelagians, around the year 429.

John Garnerius of the Society of Jesus denied that this same epitaph had been attached by our Prosper to the tomb of both heresies, in chapter 7 of Dissertation 7 on the works of Marius Mercator. He claimed that what is presented here is something like a riddle, when one heresy is said to have been both the mother and the daughter of the other. He admits that this is ingeniously expressed but denies that it was historically true. He therefore attempts to prove that, from the third century onward, through the ravings of Paul of Samosata, a path had begun to be prepared for the Nestorian error. He adds that our poet should be forgiven all the more easily because Cassian too fell into the same error and drew his friend Leo the Great, as well as many others who later followed their authority, into his opinion.

Despite this, Anthelmius, in Dissertation 9 on the works of Saints Leo and Prosper, denies that the short work should be taken away from Prosper. He appeals both to the authority of Cassian and of Leo the Great—if they were permitted to discuss the matter seriously, the poet should be forgiven much more readily, since he was not speaking according to the strict rule of history, but wished to mock with loosened reins and inflated cheeks, as the saying goes, among errors already buried—and to the fact that Prosper is repeatedly found using this comparison of the two heresies.

He not only reports in the *Chronicle* itself that at Ephesus Nestorius, together with the heresy bearing his name and with many Pelagians who supported a doctrine akin to his error, was condemned; he also reproaches Cassian with this very comparison of the two errors in chapter 21 of the book written against him:

> Through this man, Coelestine, the Eastern Churches too were cleansed of a double plague, when, in abhorrence of Nestorian impiety, he assisted Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, with the apostolic sword, by which the Pelagians too, while they allied themselves with kindred errors, were again struck down.

The sense in which this affinity between the two is to be understood has already been explained at sufficient length above.

## [RESPONSES ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE TO THE CHAPTERS OF THE GAULS]

[Col. 0155]

## ADMONITION ON PROSPER’S RESPONSES ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE TO THE CHAPTERS OF THE GAULS
The doctrine which Saint Augustine had defended against the Pelagians, the enemies of Christ’s grace, for more than twenty years, being inflamed with truly apostolic zeal and not swerving, as they say, even a finger’s breadth from the principles of the Apostle Paul’s teaching—a doctrine which the pontiffs of the Apostolic See had strengthened by their authority as apostolic and catholic—certain Gallic presbyters did not hesitate to reject. They were not so much overcome by Saint Prosper’s outstanding verses as excessively devoted to their own prejudices, partly through ignorance and partly through excessive confidence in their own intelligence. Consequently, in their effort to bring so lofty a herald of doctrine, together with his doctrine, into hatred among the multitude, they conceived the idea of maliciously tearing certain passages—especially from writings he had published shortly before his death—from the context of his works, reducing them to a little list in words devised to make him odious, and spreading them everywhere among the uneducated populace. His vigorous disciple and defender, striving to resist their wicked efforts, did not delay in adequately defending with a correct explanation, wholly consistent with Augustine’s books, those points which they condemned on the basis of a perverse interpretation. He intended thereby that the faith of the simple should remain safe against the insinuations of wicked speakers, and that the whole authority of that distinguished teacher in the Church should not be deprived of its due veneration; and thus, through God’s working, those hostile censors of Augustine’s works might return to a sounder mind and no longer deviate in any respect from the path of sound and salutary doctrine.

He either could not or did not wish to identify who they were, since perhaps they were ashamed to disclose their names while more willing to publicize their perverse opinions. They were certainly from Massilia, perhaps disciples or followers of Cassian, who excessively emulated the glory of such a man and were deeply offended that the system devised by the ingenuity of their master was not approved by Prosper. In order to render him some service to the best of their ability, they thought that Augustine himself ought to be attacked by them and removed from the authority and faith he had acquired. We may readily believe that this occurred not long after Saint Augustine’s death, that is, about the year 431.

In their effort, therefore, to disparage Augustine’s doctrine through fifteen objections, they direct the first seven against the gratuitous predestination of certain people rather than others; the eighth concerns God’s will regarding the salvation of human beings; the ninth, the extent of Christ’s redemption; the tenth, the dispensation of the Gospel; the eleventh and twelfth, the claim that God was said to be the author of sins; the thirteenth, the purpose of the creation of human beings; the fourteenth, the claim that unbelief is attributed to God; and the fifteenth, the confusion of foreknowledge with predestination. Saint Prosper answers each one as fully as necessary, and then, in as many statements set beneath them, presents to his readers, in a simple exposition, the meanings he had expressed more fully above. Thus it becomes clear to everyone that, concerning the chapters written above, he did not conceal his meaning under any artifice of circumlocution, but openly and freely rejected what was wrong while not denying agreement with what was probable, as he says at the end of the work.

[Col. 0155]

## Saint Prosper of Aquitaine: Responses on Augustine’s Behalf to the Chapters of the Gallic Objectors Who Slander Him

[Note: In the Joliensian manuscript, the title of this book is as follows: “Here begins the book of Prosper’s Responses against the chapters of the Gauls, which they set against the books of blessed Augustine concerning Predestination.”] (C)

### Preface

[Col. 0155A] 203 The doctrine which Augustine, bishop of sainted memory, had asserted and committed to writing for many years against the Pelagians, enemies of Christ’s grace and adorers of free will, seemed to certain people worthy of criticism—either because they did not understand it or because they did not wish it to be understood. They offered this, as though it were a concise means of knowledge, to those who were guided by their judgment: they published in little registers of brief chapters what they boasted they had found condemnable in the books of the aforesaid man.

[Note: The Cologne edition alone reads *aut intelligendo* (“either through not understanding”); immediately thereafter the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read *aut eam intelligere nolendo* (“or through not wishing to understand it”). The Joliensian has alternatively *aut etiam* (“or even”).]

[Note: The Cologne edition, together with the recent edition, reads *praedicarent* (“might proclaim”) in place of *publicarent* (“might publish”).]

[Note: All editions have this reading. The word *decomptores* seems to signify those who entirely adorn and praise free will beyond what they ought. The old Remigianus manuscript had *deceptores* (“deceivers”) in the first hand, but the second hand had *defensores* (“defenders”). We read the latter in the royal and Joliensian manuscripts, and also in the heading of the books *On the Calling of the Nations* below.]

They thereby sought, through such a fabrication, to secure hatred and detestation of the man whom they attacked, and to divert the alarmed reader’s attention from what they had branded with infamy.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “and by detestation of him whom they attacked, to hold them back.” The Joliensian manuscript also has *detinerent* (“to hold back”). The remainder is as in the text.]

Therefore, lest anyone rashly accept this persuasion and suppose that the catholic teacher’s writings contain such a meaning as those who falsely accuse him display, I answer briefly and plainly to each chapter which they have prefaced with a heading of condemnation, without departing at all from the path of those definitions contained in the holy man’s disputations.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read *ostendunt* (“show”) for *ostentant* (“display”).]

[Note: The Remigianus manuscript reads *quae damnationis capitulo* (“which [they marked] with a chapter-heading of condemnation”); the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read *quae damnationis capitulo*. The printed editions read *quae rationis titulo* (“which [they marked] with a heading of argument”).] Thus even an observer of slight diligence may easily notice by what unjust reproaches the memory of the catholic preacher is assailed, and into what sin those fall who, moved by another’s instigation, are more ready to blame a writer of the most celebrated name than to know him.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads, “are more inclined to blame.” The Joliensian has, “are readier.”]

## PART ONE: INDIVIDUAL RESPONSES TO THE INDIVIDUAL OBJECTIONS

[Col. 0157]

### Chapter I

#### Objection

205 That, through God’s predestination, as though through a fatal necessity, human beings are compelled and forced into sins and driven to death.

#### Response

No catholic Christian denies God’s predestination; but many who are not even Christians reject a fatal necessity.

[Note: The word “Christian” is added from the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts; it was absent from the printed editions. It corresponds to “many who are not even Christians.” The Regius manuscript reads “even Christians,” but this seems less appropriate.]

Sin therefore leads to death, but God compels no one to sin. For he has commanded no one to act impiously (Sirach 15:21); and: “You hate, Lord, all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5:7).

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “And the Lord hates all who work iniquity, and he will destroy them,” and so forth. The Joliensian reads: “And the Lord hates all … and those who,” without *perdet* (“he will destroy”). All the printed editions, together with the Remigianus, have the reading found in the text.]

Accordingly, one who proclaims fate under the name of predestination is no more to be approved than one who defames the truth of predestination under the name of fate. The notion of fate is vain and born of falsehood; but faith in predestination is supported by the authority of many holy Scriptures. It is in no way permissible to attribute to it the evil actions of human beings, who have come into an inclination to fall not through God’s ordering but through the transgression of the first father.

[Note: The Joliensian manuscript reads *fulta* (“supported”), without *est* (“is”).]

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads *in improbitatem cadendi* (“into a propensity for falling into wickedness”); another reading is *improbitate cadendi* (“by the wickedness of falling”).]

[Note: The Joliensian manuscript reads: “Concerning the punishment of this man.”]

No one is freed from that punishment except through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, prepared and predestined in God’s eternal plan before the foundation of the world.

### Chapter II

#### Objection

That, for those who are not predestined to life, the original sin is not removed by the grace of baptism once received.

#### Response

Every person who, believing in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is regenerated in baptism is absolved both from the sins he has committed through his own evil will and action and from the original sin he has drawn from his parents.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts reverse the order and read: “He is absolved both from original sins and from the personal sins which he contracted through evil will and action.”]

But one who, after baptism, falls back into unbelief and impious conduct, and who denies that original sin has been cleansed, forms as false an opinion as one who asserts that he will not be condemned to eternal death.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “But for those who will fall back … that original sin had been cleansed,” and so forth.]

For one who departs from Christ and ends this life alienated from grace, what does he fall into except perdition?

[Note: In the Remigianus manuscript an old hand corrected this to *alienatus* (“having become alienated”); the Joliensian manuscript also has *alienatus* in its first hand.]

But he does not fall back into what was forgiven, nor will he be condemned for original sin; nevertheless, because of his final crimes, he will suffer the death that was due him on account of those things which had been forgiven.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “Nor now for original sin.” It has shortly before: “he departs from what was promised.” This seems corrupt.]

Since this was neither hidden from nor unknown to God’s foreknowledge, he certainly never chose such a person, never predestined him, and never distinguished him from eternal perdition as one who would perish.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “He distinguished him from eternal condemnation.” The Regius has “he distinguishes.”]

### Chapter III

#### Objection

207 That those who are not predestined to life, even if they have been regenerated in Christ through baptism and have lived piously and justly, gain no benefit from it; but are preserved only until they fall and perish, and are not taken from this life before that happens.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “That it benefits those who are not predestined nothing, but they are preserved,” and the Joliensian also has *reservantur* (“are preserved”).]

#### Response

There is no doubt that many pass from holiness to uncleanness, from righteousness to iniquity, and from faith to impiety; and it is most certain that the predestination of the children of God and fellow heirs of Christ does not apply to such people.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads *transferre* (“to pass over”), perhaps for *transferri* (“to pass”). Both the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts add *et* (“and”); the Joliensian also reads: “Therefore those who …”]

Those, therefore, who have fallen into evils of this kind and have perished without correction through repentance did not possess the necessity of perishing because they were not predestined; rather, they were not predestined because they were foreknown as going to become such through voluntary transgression.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “because they were predestined.” The words “but for this reason they are not predestined” are absent from the Regius manuscript.]

As for the fact that God did not take them from this life at the time when they were in right faith and good conduct, this must be referred to his hidden judgments, which nevertheless are never unjust. For who does not know that, within the single condition of human mortality, the deaths of those who die vary in unequal endings of life, from the infancy of a single hour to the most advanced old age, and that no one’s soul departs from the body that gives it life either earlier or later than God wills?

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “to the most aged old age.”]

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “from the body which he was animating.”]

If, then, someone abandoned God during the length of his life, he used badly the good which came from God. For longevity is from God alone. And what comes from God is good alone; and what is good is not the cause of evil. Therefore, one does not form a correct opinion who thinks that the prolonger of life is the author of sin for those who will fall, since living long is certainly not sin, but living badly; and this can happen even within a few years.

[Note: The Remigianus manuscript has *prorogatorem* (“the one who prolongs”).]

Therefore, just as good works are to be referred to God, their inspirer, so evil works are to be referred to those who sin. For they were not abandoned by God in order that they might abandon God; rather, they abandoned him, were abandoned, and were changed from good to evil by their own will. 208 And although they had been reborn and justified by him, they were nevertheless not predestined by the one who foreknew that they would become such.

### Chapter IV

#### Objection

That not all human beings are called to grace.

[Note: The word “human beings” is absent from the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts.]

#### Response

It is not rightly said that not all are called to grace to whom the Gospel is preached, even if there are people who do not obey the Gospel—unless we are speaking of those to whom the sacrament of Christ’s cross and the redemption through his blood have not yet become known.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts lack *omnibus* (“to all”).]

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “Even if it were established that …”]

For even if it were established that the whole world had already received the Gospel throughout all nations and in every region of the earth—which was certainly foretold as something that would happen—it would nevertheless not be doubtful that, from the time of the Lord’s resurrection until the present age, there had been people who passed from this life without knowledge of the Gospel.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “of whom it could be said …”]

Of them it could be said that they were not called, because they had not even heard the hope of calling.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “From whom it might be said …”]

But if anyone always maintains this full universality of calling as though, from the Lord’s ascension into heaven, not even a single year had passed in which preaching had not reached everyone, let him consider how he can prove that the Asians were called when the apostles, as it is written, were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word of God in Asia (Acts 16:7); or how he can prove that the Bithynians were called, when those same apostles attempted to go to them and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “into heaven.”]

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “Let him also see how …”]

Let him also consider how he can defend the declaration of Truth itself, which says: “This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14).

[Note: The word “of the kingdom” was absent from the printed editions and is also absent from the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts. It was added by the editors of Saint Augustine’s works from the Remigianus manuscript, and agrees with both the Greek and Latin texts.]

For faith in the word totters—although it is impious to say so—if the world was filled with the Gospel four hundred years ago and the Lord’s coming is still being delayed.

[Note: The Joliensian manuscript reads: “which is unspeakable to say.”]

Finally, let us also consider among Christian peoples the many thousands of infants who passed from this life without baptism and who are nevertheless in some way proved to have been called,

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “Let him also consider …”]

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “How can such people be proved [to have been called]?”]

[Note: Both the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts add: “for whom neither the planter could provide assistance.” Nothing further is added, perhaps because of a copyist’s omission.]

for whom neither the planter could preach nor the one who waters could provide assistance.

### Chapter V

#### Objection

209 That those who are called are not called equally, but some are called in order that they may believe and others in order that they may not believe.

#### Response

If calling is understood only as the preaching of the Gospel, it is not truthfully said that it is preached differently to different people, since there is one God, one faith, one regeneration, and one promise.

But if we look to the effect of planting and watering, one thing was done with those whose outward ears were struck by a bodily voice, and another with those whose inward understanding God opened and in whose hearts he placed the foundation of faith and the fervor of love.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read *Si autem effectus* (“But if the effect”).]

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “another with those.”]

[Note: The Joliensian manuscript reads: “the fervor of love.”]

But it is exceedingly absurd to say that certain people were called in order not to believe, as though calling had become the cause of their unbelief and the preaching of faith had made them unbelievers.

For although the stewards of God’s word are, as it is written, “the aroma of life to life” for some and “the aroma of death to death” for others (2 Corinthians 2:16),

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts add: “the aroma of life to life for some, but for others.” These words were also added by an ancient hand in the Remigianus manuscript. They are absent from all the printed editions.]

they are nevertheless a good aroma of Christ to God when they preach Christ crucified: to the Jews, indeed, a stumbling block; to the Gentiles, foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “But as for the fact that …”]

Thus, the fact that Christ crucified, when preached, was a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles was brought about by the rejection of the human will; but the fact that Christ was the power of God and the wisdom of God to those Jews and Greeks who were called was brought about by the operation of divine grace.

[Note: The words beginning “But the fact that …” had fallen out of the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts.]

### Chapter VI

#### Objection

That free will is nothing in a human being, but that, whether toward good or toward evil, God’s predestination operates in human beings.

[Note: The Joliensian manuscript reads: “predestination in human beings.” The Regius reads: “predestination in everyone.” Both lack the word “of God.”]

#### Response

It is wrongly said that free will is nothing or does not exist; but it is not rightly denied that, before the illumination of faith, it acts in darkness and in the shadow of death. For before it is freed from the devil’s domination by God’s grace, it lies in that abyss into which it plunged itself by its own freedom.

Thus it loves its illnesses and considers itself healthy because it does not know that it is sick, until this first remedy is applied to the sick person: that he begins to know that he is ill and is able to desire the physician’s help by which he may rise.

A person who has therefore been justified—that is, changed from impious to pious—receives, without any preceding good merit, a gift by which he may also acquire merit: so that what has been begun in him through Christ’s grace may also be increased through the exercise of free will; yet never with God’s help removed, without which no one can progress or persevere in the good.

[Note: The Regius manuscript alone reads: “the help of the medicine.”]

But it is utterly foolish to say that God’s predestination operates in human beings toward either good or evil, as though some necessity drove human beings toward both, when in good actions the will must be understood as proceeding from grace, and in evil actions the will must be understood as acting without grace.

[Note: The Joliensian manuscript reads: “it is most impiously said.”]

[Note: In the Regius manuscript alone, the words “but in evil actions …” are absent, apparently through a copyist’s simple omission.]

### Chapter VII

#### Objection

That God does not grant perseverance to certain of his children whom he regenerated in Christ and to whom he gave faith, hope, and love, because they were not distinguished from the mass of perdition by God’s foreknowledge and predestination.

[Note: The Joliensian manuscript reads: “distinguished through the knowledge of God and through predestination.”]

#### Response

Among those regenerated in Jesus Christ, some abandon faith and godly conduct, apostatize from God, and end their lives in impiety. This is demonstrated by many examples, regrettable though it is.

But to attribute the fall of such people to God is a sign of excessive depravity, as though he were therefore the instigator and author of their ruin because he foreknew that they would fall by their own will and, for that reason, did not distinguish them from the children of perdition by any predestination.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read *horum lapsus* (“the fall of these persons”).]

For how could the election foreordained in Christ have had those as its own whom a just condemnation was going to have when they departed from Christ?

[Note: The printed editions read: “the election predestined in Christ,” omitting the words “of those departing.” The passage is restored from the faith of the Remigianus manuscript, although that manuscript initially lacked the word *justa* (“just”), which was later added by an old corrector. The editors of the works of Saint Augustine, from the congregation of Saint Maur, restored it in an appendix through the labor of highly learned men. The word is also present in the Joliensian manuscript. Besides the omission common to the other editions, the Cologne edition reads: “for whom there is no doubt.”]

Since there is no doubt that perseverance in the good until the end is a gift of God,

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “that perseverance in the good until the end is a gift of God.” The Joliensian reads: “that perseverance in the good until the end is a gift.”]

it is clear from the fact that these people did not persevere that they did not possess it. God should not therefore be slandered for not giving them what he gave to others; rather, it must be confessed both that he mercifully gave what he gave and that he justly did not give what he did not give.

Otherwise, just as the cause of falling arises from free will, the cause of standing might also appear to arise from it, although the former is accomplished by human action and the latter is fulfilled by a divine gift.

[Note: The word “arise,” which had fallen out of the printed editions, is restored from the Remigianus and Joliensian manuscripts. In the latter, however, the conjunction “and” before “of standing” is absent.]

### Chapter VIII

#### Objection

That God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only a fixed number of predestined people.

#### Response

If, regarding the salvation of the entire human race and its calling to the knowledge of truth, God’s will is to be asserted without distinction throughout all ages, so that it appears that he has nowhere passed over any human being, then the unfathomable depth of God’s judgments is being challenged.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read *per omnia ista saecula disponenda est* (“is to be ordered throughout all these ages”). The Regius manuscript and the Cologne edition read *neminem hominem* (“no human being”).]

For why did God, in past ages, allow all the nations to walk in their own ways (Acts 14:16), when the Lord chose Jacob for himself (Psalm 135:4), and did not deal in this way with every nation, nor reveal his judgments to them (Psalm 147:20)? Why is it that a people which once was not a people is now God’s people, and that those who once had not received mercy now receive mercy (1 Peter 2:10)? Why is it that where it was said, “You are not my people,” they are called children of the living God (Hosea 2:24)?

[Note: The Remigianus manuscript reads *et hic ubi* (“and here where”); the Joliensian reads *et id ubi* (“and that where”).] And why did Israel fail to obtain what it was seeking, while the election obtained it and the rest were hardened (Romans 9:26; 11:7)?

It is impossible to comprehend these matters, and to inquire into them is dangerous curiosity. Nevertheless, no one is permitted to be unaware that there is no injustice with God (2 Chronicles 19:7). Nor should it be believed that anyone, whether before the Law or during the time of the Law, was justified by any other grace or any other faith than this same grace and faith by which our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the counsel of his will, came at the end of the ages to seek and save what was lost.

But whoever refers the causes of God’s works and judgments entirely to human wills and actions, although he finds no such causes in the adoption or rejection of infants,

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “in the adoption or rejection of infants.”]

and wishes God’s dispensations to vary according to the mutability of free will, declares that God’s judgments are searchable and his ways traceable. What the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, did not dare to approach (Romans 11:33), this person thinks he can disclose and proclaim.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read *non audet* (“does not dare”); the Remigianus reads *non audeat* (“may not dare”).] And—something no less impious—he teaches that the grace by which we are saved is either repaid on account of good merits or withheld on account of evil ones.

Therefore, setting aside the cloud of obscure questions, let us turn toward the breadth of revealed grace and say with the Apostle: “For God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4).

[Note: The Regius reads *ad revelationem nos gratiae latitudine*; the Joliensian also has *ad revelationem* (“to revelation”). The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read *cum Paulo* (“with Paul”); the Regius has this reading again below where the printed editions have *cum Apostolo* (“with the Apostle”). The printed editions read “How does God will?”; the Joliensian reads “When he wills all”; the text was corrected in the appendix to Augustine’s works from the Remigianus manuscript.]

And again let us say with the Apostle: “Who is the Savior of all, especially of the faithful” (1 Timothy 4:10).

And let us hear the Lord saying to his apostles: “Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19).

[Note: We add here “to keep all things,” which the editors of Saint Augustine’s works noted as added by a second hand in the Remigianus manuscript; we read it written by the first hand in the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts. It was absent from all the printed editions, although it is present in both the Greek and Latin texts of the Gospel.]

Let us also hear God’s promise to Abraham: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). And if we are children of the promise, let us not hesitate through unbelief (Romans 4:20), but with our father Abraham let us give glory to God and believe most fully that he is able to do what he has promised (ibid., 21).

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “that God is able to do what he promised.”]

Let us hear David prophesying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Psalm 21:28).

And elsewhere: “All the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him” (Psalm 72:17).

And elsewhere: “All the nations which you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord, and shall glorify your name” (Psalm 86:9).

Because these promises are entirely true and cannot in any respect waver,

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts, and the Cologne edition, read “be changed.” The other manuscripts read “waver.”]

they are fulfilled in those who are saved throughout all the ends of the earth, because God is able to do what he promised (Romans 4:21).

[Note: The edition of Augustine’s works omits the word *Deus* (“God”); the other editions do not. Neither the Regius nor the Joliensian manuscript has *quae promisit Deus* (“what God promised”).]

This, then, is the assumption of the entire human race; this is the adoption of the children of God; this is the fullness of the Gentiles, foreknown and predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “This is Jerusalem … so that its foundations may be …,” instead of the reading found in the others, “so that it may be a founded city.”]

This is Jerusalem, which from beginning to end is built with living and chosen stones (1 Peter 2:5), as a city founded upon Christ Jesus himself, the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:20–21).

Nothing is cast out from these stones, nothing is diminished, nothing is snatched away. For the Truth says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6:37).

And again: “You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them from my hand” (John 10:26–28).

[Note: The Joliensian manuscript reads: “He comes to me”; shortly afterward, where the others have “the one who comes to me,” the Saint Augustine edition and the Cologne edition read “whoever comes to me.”]

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “because you are not of my sheep”; shortly afterward the Regius reads: “They will hear my voice, and I know them, and I give them eternal life.” The Joliensian also has “I give them”; the remainder is as in the text and printed editions.]

[Note: The Regius manuscript lacks the words “and they shall never perish,” and has “snatches them away.”]

God therefore cares for all human beings; and there is no one whom either the preaching of the Gospel, or the testimony of the Law, or even nature itself does not address.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “or nature itself.”]

But let us attribute human beings’ unbelief to human beings themselves, while confessing that human beings’ faith is the gift of God, without whose grace no one runs toward grace.

[Note: See Augustine, Letter 215, from which it appears that three, indeed four, synods were held in Africa.]

And with the two hundred and fourteen priests, whose decree against the enemies of God’s grace the whole world embraced, let us say in a truthful confession, in their own words: “By the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, we are assisted not only in recognizing but also in doing righteousness, in each individual action; so that without it we are able to think, speak, or do nothing belonging to true and holy piety.”

[Note: Earlier editions read: “The grace of God … assists us through each individual action.” Our reading is supported both by the edition of Saint Augustine’s works based on the Remigianus manuscript and by the Joliensian manuscript, as well as by the passage itself, as it appears in *Against the Collators*, chapter 5, and elsewhere.]

[Note: This is the reading in the edition of Saint Augustine’s works, and the passage itself is cited elsewhere in this form. In our printed editions, however, “to have” is added here; afterward the Regius and Joliensian manuscripts have *habere*, perhaps in place of *agere* (“to do”), so that we may say, think, or do.]

Nor should we suppose that these gifts are from God in such a way that, because he is the author of our nature, he appears to have already bestowed them through the act of creation.

[Note: The Regius and Joliensian manuscripts read: “We suppose.”]

For he did indeed give human beings this capacity at the beginning; but we all lost it in the one in whom we all sinned. Hence we need to be renewed in Christ through another creation and another beginning. In him we are a new creation and a new workmanship; and through him, although no good merits preceded and many evil merits did, we are granted to become vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath.

### Chapter IX

#### Objection

That the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world.

#### Response
No human being at all exists whose nature was not assumed in Christ our Lord [Note: [Col. 0164D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “in our Lord Jesus Christ.”]—although he was born in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3), whereas every human being is born in sinful flesh. Thus God the Son of God, having become a participant in human mortality without sin, bestowed this upon sinners and mortals: that those who had become sharers in his birth might escape the bond of sin and death. Therefore, just as for the renewal of human beings it is not enough that Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts add, “the Lord.”] was born a human being, unless they are reborn in that same Spirit from which he himself was born [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Regius manuscript alone reads, “unless we are reborn.”], so for the redemption of human beings it is not enough that the Lord Christ was crucified, unless they die with him and are buried with him in baptism. Otherwise, since the Savior was born in the substance of our flesh and crucified for all of us, it would not have been necessary for us to be reborn and to be grafted into the likeness of his death [Note: [Col. 0165D] The edition of Augustine reads “likeness”; the other manuscripts read “similitude.”] (Rom. 6:5). But since no human being attains eternal life without this sacrament, no one has been saved by the cross of Christ [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “by the cross of Christ”] who has not been crucified in Christ. But [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Joliensis manuscript adds the particle “but.”] no one has been crucified in Christ who is not a member of Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 0165D] On the authority of the Remigianus manuscript there is added, “nor is he a member of Christ’s body.”], and no one is a member of Christ’s body who has not put on Christ through water and the Holy Spirit. For this reason he entered into communion with death in our weakness, so that in his power we might share in the resurrection.

Although, therefore, it is entirely correct to say that the Savior was crucified for the redemption of the whole world, on account of the true assumption of human nature and on account of the common ruin of all in the first human being, it may nevertheless be said that he was crucified only for those whom his death benefited. For the Evangelist says that Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also in order to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:51). He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave the power to become children of God: those who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Regius manuscript alone reads, “from the pleasure of the flesh.”], nor from the will of a man, but from God (John 1:11). The lot of those who are counted among the people of whom it is said, “The world did not know him” (John 1:10), is therefore different from theirs. [Note: [Col. 0165D] In the Remigianus, Regius, and Joliensis manuscripts, the passage reads instead of “The world did not know him”: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The Cologne edition is plausibly read: “Thus it may be said: ‘The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world,’” etc. This interpretation is not harmed if a colon is placed after “said.”]

Accordingly, it may be said: “The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, and the world did not wish to be redeemed,” because the darkness did not receive the light (ibid., 5) [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “the darkness—the Jews—did not receive it.”]; and the darkness did receive it, to which the Apostle says, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

The Lord Jesus himself, who said that he had come to seek and save what had perished, said: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). [Note: [Col. 0165D] This passage, which had previously been mutilated, was restored in the appendix to St. Augustine from the Remigianus manuscript. The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts, consulted later, agree with this necessary restoration and both present the passage in the same form as that printed in the text. In earlier editions the words “But who these sheep are ... these are Israelites” were absent. In the Remigianus manuscript the passage read somewhat differently: “The Apostle Paul explains, saying, ‘Not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are the seed of Abraham ... but the children of promise.’”]

But who these sheep of the house of Israel are, the Apostle Paul explains, saying: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites, nor are all who are the seed of Abraham all children; but ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called’: that is, those who are children of the flesh are not the children of God, but those who are regarded as children of promise in the seed” (Rom. 9:6–7). [Note: [Col. 0166D] The Regius manuscript reads, “Among these, therefore, are those of whom we recalled above that it was said.” The Joliensis reads, “Among these, therefore, are those whom we recalled as having been mentioned above.”]

Among these, therefore, are those of whom we recalled above that it was said: “Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also in order to gather into one the scattered children of God” (John 11:51). For not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles, through him who calls what does not exist as though it existed (Rom. 4:17), and who gathers the dispersed of Israel (Ps. 146:2), the children of God, the children of promise, are gathered into one Church [Note: [Col. 0166D] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read: “But they are also called from the Gentiles, through him ... and are gathered into one Church.” The Lovaniensis, Duacensis, and Cologne editions read “may be gathered.”]. Thus what was promised to Abraham is fulfilled: that all the tribes of the earth would be blessed in his seed (Gen. 12:3). [Note: [Col. 0166D] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “will be blessed.”]

## CHAPTER X

### OBJECTION

That the preaching of the Gospel is withheld by the Lord from some people, lest, having received the preaching of the Gospel, they should be saved.

### RESPONSE

If it can be proved that, ever since the Gospel has been preached, there has been absolutely no one to whom Christian grace has not been announced, then it is not rightly said to have been concealed when it is shown to have been preached. But if [Note: [Col. 0166D] The Remigianus manuscript, corrected by an ancient hand, reads “at some time”; the Regius manuscript has the same reading in its first hand.] people are found in some places to whom the Gospel has not been preached, this cannot be said to have happened without God’s judgment; and it is impious to criticize what cannot be understood.

## CHAPTER XI

### OBJECTION

That God compels people [Note: [Col. 0166D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “a person to sins”; so also at the beginning of the Response shortly below, where the Regius manuscript agrees.] to sin by his power.

### RESPONSE

No Catholic has said or says that God compels people who are living piously and rightly to sin by his power, or that divine power does violence to human innocence so as to drive it from its resolve to live well. These are not God’s works but the devil’s, whose joy is the ruin of the saints. But the Lord lifts up all who fall and raises all who are bowed down (Ps. 144:14), granting them repentance so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they were held captive [Note: [Col. 0167C] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “were held captive.”] for his will (2 Tim. 2:25–26). When, however, we read that some have been handed over by God to their desires (Rom. 1:24), or hardened, or abandoned, we confess that they merited this by their great sins, because crimes of such a kind preceded that they themselves deserved to be made a punishment for themselves, which would also turn their punishment into guilt against them. [Note: [Col. 0167C] The corrected Remigianus manuscript reads this way; so too do the Regius and Joliensis manuscripts in their first hands. All the printed editions read, “so that they themselves should owe the punishments to themselves, which would also turn their punishment into guilt.” The Regius manuscript has “into rectitude,” an obvious scribal error, instead of “into guilt.”] Thus we neither complain about God’s judgment, by which he abandons those who deserve to be abandoned [Note: [Col. 0167C] The Regius manuscript reads, “by which he so abandons them,” etc.; the Joliensis, “because he so abandons them.”], nor fail to give thanks for his mercy, by which he frees those who do not deserve to be freed.

## CHAPTER XII

### OBJECTION

That obedience is withdrawn from some who have been called and are living piously and justly, so that they cease to obey.

### RESPONSE

If God drives a person who obeys him away from piety and makes one who is running well fall [Note: [Col. 0167C] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “one who is living well.”], then he repays good with evil and unjustly punishes what he himself compels to happen. What could be said or imagined more perverse, more insane? But those who think that God’s foreknowledge is the same as his will in every respect are drawn into such an interpretation [Note: [Col. 0167C] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “are drawn into it.”]. His will never wills anything except good, whereas his foreknowledge knows both good and evil. He bestows good things, whether he himself does them or enables us to do them [Note: [Col. 0167D] The printed editions read, “commands.” The reading has been corrected according to the Remigianus manuscript.]; but evil things he did not do at all, nor did he advise or compel them to be done [Note: [Col. 0167D] The Joliensis reads, “But he himself does no evil at all”; and shortly afterward, “he advises or compels.”]. Therefore, he did not withdraw the strength to obey from anyone because he did not predestine that person; rather, he did not predestine that person because he foresaw that he would withdraw from obedience itself. [Note: [Col. 0167D] The Lugdunensis edition does not contain the words “rather, he did not predestine that person.” The Lovanienses and the editors of the later editions declared, by conjecture, that they should be added to the text, with this note: “You will not reject this if you compare Responses 2, 3, and 7 above.” The editors of St. Augustine’s works added the correction from the Remigianus manuscript to the text without indicating doubt. Their correction is confirmed by the authority of the Joliensis manuscript, where we read, with a slight difference: “But he did not predestine him because he foresaw that by that very disobedience he would withdraw from obedience itself.”]

## CHAPTER XIII

### OBJECTION

That some people were not created by God for the purpose of attaining eternal life, but merely to adorn the appearance of the present age and to be born for the benefit of others.

### RESPONSE

We do not fail to recognize that all human beings are created individually by God [Note: [Col. 0168C] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “created.”], and that from this whole human race some are to be condemned with the devil and others are to reign with Christ. Therefore, the fact that even those who will not share in eternal life are created involves no fault on the Creator’s part, since he is the author of nature, not of the defect that nature contracted. Who does not understand that even the condition of such people adorns the variety of this world, when he sees so many benefits of the present life furnished through the studies and works of certain impious people—in the invention of arts, the building of cities, the establishment of laws, and the confederation of peoples? [Note: [Col. 0168C] The Regius manuscript reads, “when he sees.” The Joliensis reads, “in the ordering of peoples.” The Regius has “in consideration,” perhaps for “in confederation.”]

But if it is asked whether divine Providence has conferred some benefit from those whom impious error turned away from true religion for the progress of the saints and the growth of the Church, let the cross of Christ itself be considered first [Note: [Col. 0168C] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “let it first be considered.”]. On it, through the great crime of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0168C] The Regius manuscript reads, “through a great crime.”], God’s merciful will was fulfilled, so that his only Son might be killed for our redemption. Let the glorious endurance of the apostles be considered, as amid the uproar of their persecutors they cried out to God with one voice [Note: [Col. 0168C] The printed editions read “with this disposition”; the Joliensis manuscript more aptly reads “with one voice,” and the Remigianus “with a single voice.”] (Acts 4:27): “For truly, in this city, against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate gathered together [Note: [Col. 0168C] The printed editions read “therefore gathered together”; the Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts, with the edition of Augustine’s works, read “for gathered together,” in accordance with the Greek and Latin biblical text.] with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your counsel predestined to take place.” Finally, let the palms of countless martyrs be considered, to whom a blessed victory was granted over the most savage cruelty of unbelievers.

Let the Apostle also be heard as he trains the Church in perseverance in piety [Note: [Col. 0168C] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “inviting”; the Joliensis then reads, “In no respect, however ... has been granted by Christ.” In the Regius manuscript the passage from “In no respect” through “to you, however, has been granted by Christ, not only,” etc., is absent.]: “In no respect,” he says (Phil. 1:28), “being terrified by your adversaries; which is to them a cause of destruction, but to you of salvation, and this from God. For to you it has been granted on Christ’s behalf not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him.”

[Note: [Col. 0168D] The Joliensis manuscript has this passage as follows: “In these errors also, by which God permitted those who would fight against the Church to arise within the Church, let God’s goodness, consulting our welfare, be recognized. He certainly did not create them, but through them he exercised the diligence of his children in the search for and safeguarding of the truth, as the Apostle says: ‘There must be heresies and schisms,’ etc. The Regius manuscript reads: “God permitted opponents to arise within the Church against the Church ... exercising through them the search for and safeguarding of the truth, as the Apostle says: ‘There must be heresies and schisms,’ etc.”]

In those errors also, which God permitted to arise within the Church against the Church, let God’s goodness, consulting our welfare, be recognized: he did not create or foster them, but through them he exercises the diligence of his children in seeking and guarding the truth. The Apostle says, “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.” But when one looks upon the darkness of the impious and the illumination of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0169C] This is the reading of the Regius and Joliensis manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “the illumination of the children.”], who would not, through this very contrast, become more fervent in giving thanks to God, and learn from the ruin of those who perish into what evils he would fall through free will unless the grace of God came to his aid through our Lord Jesus Christ? [Note: [Col. 0169C] The printed editions read, “in the ruin.” The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “from the ruin”; then, “free will would fall.”]

## CHAPTER XIV

### OBJECTION

That those who do not believe the preaching of the Gospel do not believe because of God’s predestination, and that God determined that whoever does not believe should not believe by his own decree.

### RESPONSE

The unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way generated by God’s predestination [Note: [Col. 0169C] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “comes about.”]. God is the author of good things, not of evil ones. God’s predestination, therefore, is always concerned with good, whether in the recompense of justice or in the gift of grace. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Accordingly, the unbelief of those who do not believe must be attributed not to God’s decree but to his foreknowledge. That foreknowledge did not impose the necessity of not believing merely because it could not be mistaken about the unbelief that was going to occur.

But faith, the works of love, and perseverance in them to the end, because they are bestowed upon a human being through God’s grace, are rightly said to have been predestined, as are also the things that are to be repaid to them [Note: [Col. 0169C] The printed editions read, “and these things also.” The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts read, “and they themselves also.”], on the authority of the Apostle, who says (Eph. 2:8): “By God’s grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, it is God’s gift; not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in good works in Christ Jesus, which God prepared so that we should walk in them.” [Note: [Col. 0169C] The words “in Christ Jesus” were absent from the printed editions. They are restored on the authority of the Joliensis manuscript and the sacred text.]

Therefore, the one who attributes the unbelief of the impious to God’s decree is as much in error as the one who does not confess God to be the author of the faith and righteousness of the saints. For the one who lost what he had received does not recover it from the source from which he lost it; rather, he receives from the one who possesses it what he had received from the one from whom he had lost it. [Note: [Col. 0170C] The manuscript reads, “he receives it from the one who has it.”]

## CHAPTER XV

### OBJECTION

That foreknowledge is the same thing as predestination.

### RESPONSE

Whoever does not distinguish God’s foreknowledge in any respect from his predestination attempts to attribute to God regarding evil what must be attributed to him regarding good. But since good things are to be attributed to God, their giver and co-worker, while evil things are to be attributed to the voluntary wickedness of rational creatures [Note: [Col. 0170C] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “to the co-worker of all things; but evil things ...”], there is no doubt that, without any temporal difference, God both foreknew and predestined what he himself was going to do, or what was to be repaid by a just judgment to evil merits [Note: [Col. 0170C] The Regius manuscript reads, “what, as their author, he was going to bring to completion”]; but that he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, what was not going to have its cause of action from him. Foreknowledge, therefore, can exist without predestination; predestination, however, cannot exist without foreknowledge.

# PART TWO. INDIVIDUAL STATEMENTS ON EACH CHAPTER

[Col. 0169]

Although, then, I believe that a wholly clear and complete answer has been given, insofar as the Lord granted it, to all the objections—whether arising from complaining ignorance or deceitful hostility—let us nevertheless compress the profession of our position into a brief form, so that, under the simplicity of a few words, it may become increasingly clear that what we understand from the chapters written above we do not conceal under any art of circumlocution [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “from the chapters mentioned above.”], but state openly and freely, rejecting what is perverse and not refusing assent to what is probable. [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Regius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “but apply [it] openly and freely.”]

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER I

Whoever, therefore, says that by God’s predestination, as though by a fatal necessity, human beings are compelled and forced into sins and driven to death is not a Catholic. For God’s predestination in no way makes anyone wicked, nor is it in any respect the cause of anyone’s sin.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER II

Likewise, whoever says that the grace received in baptism does not remove original sin from those who are not predestined to life is not a Catholic. For the sacrament of baptism, by which absolutely all sins are washed away, is true even in those who will not remain in truth and therefore are not predestined to true life. [Note: [Col. 0170D] In this statement and in all those that follow, the word “likewise” is absent from the Regius manuscript.]

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER III

Likewise, whoever says that those who are not predestined to life, even if they have been regenerated in Christ through baptism [Note: [Col. 0171D] The printed editions read, “in baptism.” The manuscripts and the Remigianus, together with the edition of St. Augustine’s works, read, “through baptism.”], and have lived piously and justly, receive no benefit from this, but are kept for as long as necessary until they fall, and are not taken from this life before this happens to them—as though the fall of such people were to be attributed to God’s decree—is not a Catholic. For God did not prolong anyone’s period of life so that by living long he would fall and abandon the true faith through his longevity, since longevity itself is to be counted among God’s benefits, by which a person ought to have become better, not worse.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER IV

Likewise, whoever says that not everyone is called to grace, if he is speaking about those to whom Christ has not been announced, cannot be criticized. For we know that the Gospel has been destined for all the ends of the earth, but we do not think that it has already been preached in every region of the earth; nor can we say that the call of grace exists where there has not yet been any regeneration through the mother Church. [Note: [Col. 0171D] This is the reading of the Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts together with the edition of Augustine’s works. The printed editions read, “must not be criticized.”]

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER V
