Likewise, whoever says that those who were called were not called equally, but that some were called so that they might believe and others so that they might not believe, as though anyone’s calling were the cause of his not believing, does not speak rightly. Although faith comes only from God’s gift and the human will, unbelief comes only from the human will.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER VI

Likewise, whoever says that free choice is nothing in a human being, but that God’s predestination operates in human beings either toward good or toward evil, is not a Catholic. For God’s grace does not abolish human choice but restores and strengthens it; it calls and leads it back from error into the way, so that what was perverse through its own freedom may become upright through the action of God’s Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0171D] The Regius manuscript reads, “God’s predestination also is always in the good, which knows either to remit sin, committed by the human will alone, with praise of mercy, or to punish it with praise of justice.”]

God’s predestination, too, is always concerned with good: it knows either to forgive sin, committed by the human will alone, with praise of mercy, or to punish it with praise of justice.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER VII

Likewise, whoever says that God did not give perseverance to certain of his children whom he regenerated in Christ, to whom he gave faith, hope, and love, because they were not separated from the mass of perdition by God’s foreknowledge and predestination—if by this he wishes to assert that God did not want such people to remain in the good things he had granted, and that he himself became the cause of their turning away—holds a view contrary to God’s justice. For although God’s omnipotence could have supplied the strength to stand to those who were going to fall, his grace did not abandon them before they abandoned it. And because he foresaw that they would voluntarily defect, he therefore did not include them in the election of predestination.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER VIII

Likewise, whoever says that God does not want all human beings to be saved, but only a definite number of predestined people, speaks more harshly than one ought to speak about the height of God’s inscrutable grace. For he both wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4), and fulfills the purpose of his will [Note: [Col. 0172D] The Regius manuscript reads, “but [fulfills] the purpose of his will.”] in those whom, having foreknown, he predestined; having predestined, he called; having called, he justified; having justified, he glorified. He loses nothing from the fullness of the Gentiles or from the whole seed of Israel, for which an eternal kingdom was prepared in Christ before the foundation of the world. For from the whole world the whole world is chosen, and from all human beings all human beings are adopted.

Nor can God’s promise in any way waver because of the unbelief and disobedience of many, when he says to Abraham (Gen. 22:18): “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.” What God has promised, he is powerful also to accomplish (Rom. 4:21). Thus those who are saved are saved because God willed them to be saved, while those who perish perish because they deserved to perish. [Note: [Col. 0172D] The Regius manuscript reads, “so that those who are saved may be saved in God, because God willed to save them.” In the Joliensis manuscript the word “God” is absent.]

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER IX

Likewise, whoever says that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world looks not to the power of the sacrament but to the portion of unbelievers. The blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world; excluded from that price are those who either delighted in captivity and did not wish to be redeemed, or, after redemption, returned to the same slavery. For the word of the Lord has not fallen, nor has the redemption of the world been emptied of effect. Although the world did not know God in the vessels of wrath, the world nevertheless knew God in the vessels of mercy, which God, with none of their good merits preceding, rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of his love.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER X

Likewise, whoever says that the preaching of the Gospel is withheld by the Lord from some people lest, having received the preaching of the Gospel, they should be saved can ward off the hostile charge of this objection by appealing to the Savior himself. He did not wish to perform his signs among certain people whom he said would have believed if they had seen his miraculous signs (Matt. 11:21); he forbade the apostles to evangelize certain peoples; and even now he permits certain nations to live outside his grace. Nevertheless, we hold with the firmest faith that the Church is to be extended into every part of the world, and that this age will not end before the Gospel is directed to all the ends of the earth and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:11). [Note: [Col. 0172D] The printed editions read, “that Jesus Christ is ...”; the Joliensis manuscript reads, “that the Lord Jesus Christ is ...,” as in the Apostle’s text.]

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER XI

Likewise, whoever says that God compels people to sin by his power is rightly criticized. For God, who is the author of justice and goodness, and whose statutes and commandments are all directed against sin, must not be thought to compel anyone to sin or to drive anyone from innocence into crimes. If some people are so deeply impious that they are regarded as beyond the remedy of correction, they do not receive increases of wickedness from God; rather, they become worse through themselves. Because of their preceding sins, they deserved to be abandoned by God and handed over to themselves and to their deceivers, so that sin itself might be for them the punishment of sin.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER XII

Likewise, whoever says that obedience is withdrawn from certain people who have been called and are living piously and justly, so that they cease to obey, holds a false opinion about God’s goodness and justice [Note: [Col. 0173C] The Regius manuscript reads, “about God’s goodness and justice.”], as though he compelled the pious to impiety and deprived the good of innocence, when he himself is both the giver and guardian of piety and innocence [Note: [Col. 0173C] The particle “and” is absent from the Regius manuscript and also from the Joliensis, though it appears in the printed editions.]. Therefore, the one who clings to God is moved by God’s Spirit; but the one who withdraws from God ceases to obey by his own will.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER XIII

Likewise, whoever says that some people were not created by God for the purpose of attaining eternal life, but merely to adorn the appearance of the present age and to be born for the benefit of others, would speak more appropriately by saying that God, who is the Creator of all things, does not create in vain even those whom he foresaw would not become participants in eternal life [Note: [Col. 0173C] The Regius manuscript reads, “whom he foresaw.”]. For even in wicked people nature itself is God’s good work, and his justice is worthy of praise in the condemnation of the impious. [Note: [Col. 0173C] The Regius manuscript joins these words to what precedes, and reads, “and justice is worthy of praise in the condemnation of the impious.”]

Nor can the person who says that the world is also adorned by the creation of such people rightly be criticized, or that those who will harm themselves through their own wickedness are born for the benefit of others. For no multitude of impious people, however countless, is unbecoming to the world or useless to God’s kingdom, since even through their offspring comes the generation that is to be regenerated, and through the endurance and love shown toward them the people of God becomes more illustrious [Note: [Col. 0173C] This is the reading of the Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts, the Duacensis and Coloniensis editions, and the more recent editions. The older Lugdunensis and Lovaniensis editions read, “leading.”], learning goodness and patience from him who makes his rain fall upon the just and the unjust and makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5:45).

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER XIV

Likewise, whoever says that those who do not believe the preaching of the Gospel do not believe because of God’s predestination, and that God determined that whoever does not believe should not believe by his own decree, is not a Catholic. Just as faith, which works through love, is God’s gift, so unbelief is not God’s decree. For God knows how to ordain punishments for crimes, not crimes themselves [Note: [Col. 0174C] The Regius manuscript reads, “nor is it consequential,” adding: “so that the predestined person, who lives by the faith granted to him, is punished for what he himself did not commit, while it is just that the non-predestined person should perish in voluntary, not compelled, unbelief.” The Joliensis reads, as do the printed editions, “nor is it consequential.” The rest is as in the Regius manuscript. The Remigianus reads, as do the printed editions, “nor is it consequential,” etc. The printed editions have “in unbelief,” without “in,” which is added by all three manuscripts.]; nor is it consequential that he himself committed what he did not forgive. Therefore, the predestined person lives by the faith granted to him; the non-predestined person perishes in voluntary, not compelled, unbelief.

## STATEMENT ON CHAPTER XV

Likewise, whoever says that foreknowledge is the same thing as predestination mixes these two things together in the case of our good works. For the things we have from God’s gift [Note: [Col. 0174C] The Regius manuscript reads, “are called from foreknowledge.”], and the things that are said to have been foreknown, cannot fail to have been predestined; and the things called predestined cannot fail to have been foreknown. But in our evil works, only God’s foreknowledge is to be understood. For just as he foreknew and predestined what he himself does and what he enabled us to do, so he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, what he neither did himself nor required us to do.

# [RESPONSES ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE TO THE VINCENTIAN OBJECTIONS]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO PROSPER’S RESPONSES, ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE’S TEACHING, TO THE CHAPTERS OF THE VINCENTIAN OBJECTIONS

Again and again, what Christ himself declared in the Gospel is fulfilled in the servants of Christ: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Matt. 10:24). When the Gallic critics of the teaching of St. Augustine—that great and incomparable teacher of the Churches of God—rose up against him with great determination, twisting his sound views into unsound interpretations before the uninstructed populace, our Aquitanian, St. Prosper, a disciple and defender of St. Augustine, opposed reasonable responses to their slanderous objections. But when they resolved to attack Augustine himself by name and to bring him into a reputation for impiety, indeed even for madness, they fabricated new objections based both on Augustine’s statements and on St. Prosper’s responses to their earlier slanders. If they were to be believed, these new objections followed from the former ones. For the most part they coincide with the earlier objections, and they did not hesitate to exaggerate some of them two or three times, in words scarcely different, wishing to increase the number of accusations because they could not vary their meaning (St. Prosper, *Response to the Ninth Objection*). The absurdity of these consequences is so plainly apparent at first sight that, as Prosper himself testifies, they did not realize that, in their desire to injure him by whatever means, they were overturning themselves as they forgot brotherly charity and sought to damage his reputation (the same author, in the preface).

He could easily and sufficiently have refuted such insane accusations and such monstrous falsehoods of blasphemies—falsehoods enough to forfeit all credibility with any prudent judge—by the single subscription of an anathema, falsely cast about merely to arouse hostility against him. But he feared that their malice would regard the brevity of such a most sincere profession with suspicion, and that most of the simpler people, disturbed by the fabrication of what he called a “devilish notice,” would need instruction; it seemed better to mitigate the minds of the malicious opponents by a more extended response.

Our holy Doctor declares that he undertook this task not from his own ingenuity or private authority (Response to Objection 5), but writes with the confidence that he will defend, on the authority of the Apostolic See, both his position and the faith that he had hitherto defended against the Pelagians and continued to defend whenever an opportunity arose. From these words some have thought that these responses came after Pope Celestine’s letter, addressed to the bishops of Gaul on behalf of Prosper and Hilary and especially in support of St. Augustine’s teaching. Others, however, entirely reject this conclusion. For while Augustine was still alive, and before Celestine had written to the Gauls, Prosper brought forward the judgment of the Apostolic See and the Roman Church—both in his letter to Rufinus (chap. 3) and in his poem *Against the Ungrateful* (chap. 2). It is therefore probable that if he had wished to cite so weighty a testimony, and one so favorable to his cause, as could be drawn from that letter of Celestine, he would certainly have presented it more openly and forcefully.

Hence, the opinion held by some [Maug., vol. II, p. 488; Nor., *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chap. 11] that Prosper’s statements in this work concerning the authority of the Apostolic See show that the supreme pontiff commissioned Prosper to undertake the defense of the doctrine of Christ’s grace against the Pelagians is one that we would wish to see supported by arguments as invincible as the authority of the learned men who have favored it. Since learned people do not entirely agree about the time when the later opponents of Augustine and Prosper spread these objections among the public, and consequently do not agree when Prosper again responded to them, we judge it merely probable that, shortly after reading the refutation of the earlier objections, those men hurriedly composed these objections and spread them among the public as quickly as they could. St. Prosper did not delay in answering them with the responses that follow.

We do not fail to recognize that some learned men think that these objections preceded in time those which we published earlier; let the reader judge the matter. It is not surprising, however, that in the work before us our holy man is acknowledged to have responded somewhat more harshly to his adversaries than he had responded in the earlier work. For those presbyters, as Celestine later recognized in his letter to the bishops of Gaul (chap. 1), while even their bishops connived at it, were promoting dissension among the Churches, bringing undisciplined questions forward, and obstinately claiming that Augustine’s disciples preached things contrary to the truth. Deaf to St. Prosper’s earlier responses, they devised arguments that were far worse and more contrary to reason and charity.

Who that Vincent was who, above all others, presented himself as the advocate of the worst cause is not entirely agreed upon among scholars. At that time there was in the monastery of Lérins a Vincent who, in a certain book against all heresies, entitled the *Commonitory*, written around the year 434, subsequently became celebrated in the Church. A certain writer (Vossius, *History of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 9) wished to make him the author of the calumnies spread against Prosper, because he maintained that Vincent had been opposed to the teaching of Saint Augustine. He was led to this opinion by reasoning from the fact that Vincent was judged to have manifestly and deliberately abused Pope Celestine’s letter. Others likewise adopt this opinion, counting this Vincent among the adherents of Semi-Pelagian doctrine (Nor., *History of the Pelagians*, vol. II, chapter 11; Antel., *Works of Leo*, p. 419).

Concerning him Gennadius speaks as follows in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men* (chapter 64):

> Vincent, a Gaul by nationality, a presbyter at the monastery on the island of Lérins, a man learned in the Holy Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in knowledge of ecclesiastical doctrines, composed, for the overthrow of the associations of heretics, a most forceful disputation in polished and clear language—now called the *Commonitory against Heresies*—which he gave the title *Against Heretics by Peregrinus*, concealing his own name. Because he had lost the greater part of the second book, which had been stolen by someone from his manuscripts, he reconstructed it in a single book, first recapitulating its sense in a few words. He died while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning, that is, in the year 448 or the following year.

From this many conclude that he accepted Saint Prosper’s responses and embraced Augustine’s teaching, which was the teaching of the Church, because from that time onward his reputation for holiness did not perish.

The author of the *Critical Dissertation on the Genuine Works of the Holy Fathers Leo the Great and Prosper of Aquitaine* also observes that the work in question—namely, the *Commonitory*—although golden and never sufficiently commendable in proportion to its worth, was nevertheless undertaken with the purpose of casting Augustine’s teaching under suspicion; and he has persuaded himself that this view has now become especially prevalent among scholars (Vossius, *History of the Pelagians*; Henry Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 11; Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. X, article 3, § 7). He supports this opinion more fully by a new argument on pages 411 and 412. To this he adds that, although that Vincent sometimes appears to have directed the judgments of his *Commonitory* with greater ingenuity against Augustine’s teaching itself than against the devices and trickery of the heretics, nevertheless, insofar as they prevailed less against Augustine’s teaching, they were all the more effective against other heresies or sects, whether already arisen or likely to arise in the future. Through a most exalted conversion they were turned into weapons; so that among the principal documents which the ancient Fathers entrusted to the Church against errors and schisms, none was employed more frequently than the *Commonitory*, whose power the Church had always experienced in its more effective assault upon rebels and its more successful conquest of them.

Those, however, who hold a better opinion of the teaching of Vincent the monk of Lérins, a man renowned for holiness and learning, agree in seeking another man of the same name to whom they may assign objections of this kind. Baronius and others of his followers think that the work may be attributed to another Vincent, of whom Gennadius writes in the *Catalogue*, chapter 89:

> Vincent, a presbyter and likewise a Gaul by nationality, trained in the divine Scriptures, possessing a tongue polished by habitual speech and by reading the works of the ancients, wrote a commentary on the Psalms. I heard the holy man of God, Connatus, read some of this work; and Vincent promised that, if the Lord granted him life and strength, he would labor on the whole Psalter with the same devotion.

Nor is there anything to prevent our recognizing this same man as the Vincent who attended the council of Riez in the year 439, perhaps in the capacity of representative of Constantine or Constantianus, bishop of Die (*Councils*, vol. III, p. 1289; *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, p. 554). For although Gennadius survived Gelasius, who died in the year 496, he could nevertheless have been a contemporary of a man who published books in the year 430. This opinion also gains strength from the fact that Gennadius was accustomed especially to praise those whom he knew to be far from favorable to Augustine (chapters 94 and 80), whereas he praises this Vincent very highly in the passages cited above.

[Col. 0177]

# Responses of Prosper of Aquitaine on Behalf of Augustine to the Chapters of the Vincentian Objections (C)

## Preface

[Col. 0177A] 227 Certain men, forgetful of Christian and fraternal charity [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “Christian and fraternal truth.”], strive by every possible means to injure our reputation so greatly that, in their eagerness to inflict harm, they do not see that they are overthrowing their own. For they weave together and collect, in whatever statements they can devise, the monstrous lies of certain utterly foolish blasphemies; and they circulate these publicly and privately, displaying and thrusting them upon many people, asserting that such things are present in our understanding as are contained in a diabolical catalogue.

We could easily and sufficiently prove that these things are falsely spread against us to arouse hatred by subscribing a single anathema—unless the malignity of those who consider themselves burdened whenever we are thought well of would itself regard the brevity of our subscription as suspicious. Therefore, lest an occasion for this complaint be found, 228 we have judged it necessary and appropriate [Note: Remigius Manuscript: “we believe.”]—whether to calm the minds of the slanderers or to instruct those into whose ears something of this kind has been uttered—to disclose fully and clearly, insofar as it can be done with the Lord’s help, what judgment we form concerning these perverse definitions.

Accordingly, after setting out the sixteen chapters one by one, we shall place beneath each one the meaning of our position and the words of the faith which, on the authority of the Apostle, we defend against the Pelagians [Note: Remigius Manuscript: “we set down.”]. Thus those who deign to devote even a little time to reading these words may clearly recognize that no trace of impious and profane opinions has adhered to our hearts; and when they see the blasphemies condemned by our profession, they should judge that their authors ought to be punished.

[Note: [Col. 0177C]

This work was perhaps written somewhat after the preceding responses.

The Remigius codex, written approximately eight hundred years ago, originally had *Vincentiarum* in the first hand; but, corrected long ago by a second hand, it bears *Vincentianarum*—as is also read without correction at the end of the book. The Louvain editors observe that some believe the author of the objections to have been Vincent of Lérins, the man whose *Commonitory* against the profane innovations of heresies survives; it was written around the year 434, or, as the author himself testifies in chapter 42, approximately three years after the Council of Ephesus, held against Nestorius.]

# Book of Responses

[Col. 0177]

## 229 Chapter One

### Objection

That our Lord Jesus Christ did not suffer for the salvation and redemption of all human beings.

### Response

Against the wound of original sin, by which the nature of all human beings was corrupted and killed in Adam, and from which the disease of every form of concupiscence has grown, the true, powerful, and singular remedy is the death of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: Printed editions: “of the Lord Jesus Christ,” omitting *our*, which is found in the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts and in Augustine’s edition]; who, free from the debt of death and alone without sin, died for sinners and debtors of death [Note: Here *of death* is added from the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts and from Augustine’s edition of the work].

230 Therefore, with respect to the greatness and power of the price, and with respect to the one cause concerning the human race, Christ’s blood is the redemption of the whole world. But those who pass through this age without faith in Christ and without the sacrament of regeneration are strangers to redemption.

Since, then, because of the one nature of all and the one cause truly assumed by our Lord, all may rightly be called redeemed, while nevertheless not all have been released from captivity, the proper effect of redemption undoubtedly belongs to those from whom the ruler of this world has been cast out, and who are now not vessels of the devil but members of Christ.

His death was not expended upon the human race in such a way that even those who were not to be regenerated belonged to its redemption; [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “but so that,” omitting *in such a way*] rather, what was accomplished through a single example on behalf of all was celebrated in each person through a singular sacrament. For the cup of immortality, prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed possess in itself the capacity to benefit everyone; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.

## Chapter Two

### Objection

That God does not wish to save all, even if all wish to be saved.

### Response

Since the Truth says (Matthew 7:11), “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?”, how can it be that God, who even saves those of whom it cannot be said that they wish to be saved, does not wish to save some even if they wish to be saved—unless there exist certain reasons about which, although they are unknowable to us, he nevertheless judges rightly, since it cannot be said that he ought to have done anything other than what he did? [Note: Printed editions: “although they are unknowable to us, he nevertheless”; the Joliensis Manuscript reads “although he,” which seems better.]

Once this distinction has been set aside—the distinction which divine knowledge holds within the secrecy of its justice—we must sincerely believe and profess that God wills all human beings to be saved. For the Apostle, whose sentence this is (1 Timothy 2:4), most earnestly commands—and this is devoutly observed in all the churches—that prayer be offered to God for all human beings. Of these, the fact that many perish is the merit of those who perish; the fact that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. For that the guilty person is condemned is the unimpeachable justice of God; but that the guilty person is justified is the ineffable grace of God.

## Chapter Three

### Objection

That God creates the greater part of the human race for the purpose of destroying it eternally.

### Response

God is indeed the creator of all human beings, but no one was created by him for the purpose of perishing, because the cause of being born is one thing, and the cause of perishing another. That human beings are born is the beneficence of the Creator; that they perish is the guilt of the transgressor.

For in Adam, in whom the nature of all human beings was prefigured, all sinned (Romans 5:12), and they are bound by the same sentence which he incurred. Nor are they released from this bond, even if they are free from personal sins, unless they are reborn through the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of Christ’s death and resurrection.

Therefore he is exceedingly impious and unlearned who does not distinguish the defect of nature from the author of nature, from whom whatever must be condemned in each person is entirely alien [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “has been condemned.”]. He creates human beings so that they may be human beings; nor does he withdraw his handiwork from the multiplication of successive generations, since according to the counsel of his good will he will restore in many what he himself made, while punishing in many what he himself did not make.

For just as through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one man many are constituted righteous (Romans 5:19) [Note: *For* is added in the Remigius Manuscript and in Augustine’s edition; it is absent from the others].

## Chapter Four

### Objection

That the greater part of the human race is created by God in order to do, not God’s will, but the devil’s.

### Response

It is wholly insane and contrary to reason to say that God’s will is not done by God’s will, and that the condemner of the devil and his servants wishes the devil to be served. But the Pelagians think that they consequently object this to Catholics, since they deny that Adam’s sin has passed to all: for if original guilt does not bind the first birth, infants are not subject to the devil, nor do they need to be rescued from the power of darkness, since they have never departed from their Creator.

But we, who profess that all perished in Adam—“For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10)—do not say that any human being is created in order to do the devil’s will; and we acknowledge that every unredeemed human being is the devil’s captive. For human transgression could not disturb the order of creation established from the ages; and the sinful creature deservedly suffers the penal dominion of him to whom, having abandoned the true Lord, it voluntarily sold itself [Note: The word “deservedly” is absent from the Remigius Manuscript.]. This slavery is not God’s institution but a judgment, by which the fraud of the deceiving devil became the penalty of sin for the deceived and foolishly credulous human being. No one is rescued from it except through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus; and his gratuitous grace is neither bestowed in return for the evil merits of many nor preceded by the good merits of any.

## Chapter Five

### Objection

That God is the author of our sins, because he makes the will of human beings evil and fashions the substance which, by its natural impulse, can do nothing except sin [Note: Printed editions: “can do nothing except”; the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts: “can do nothing whatsoever except.”].

### Response

The emptiness of this objection also proceeds from that school in which human nature is defended as free from and uninjured by Adam’s sin. Since we assert that all human beings are born guilty of transgression and subject to condemnation [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “subject to the condemnation”], and that they will perish unless they are reborn in Christ, they appear to say that the author of guilt is the same one whom we profess to be the creator of nature.

We utterly reject this understanding. We know that God, just and good, is the creator of the human substance and of its inner and outer senses [Note: In the Joliensis Manuscript the conjunction *and* is absent: “of the inner and outer senses of the human substance,” and so forth], so that whatever belongs to nature is entirely from him, while whatever is contrary to nature is entirely not from him [Note: Printed editions: “is not from him.” The reading is corrected from Augustine’s edition against the Remigius Manuscript].

Sin, however, is contrary to nature, and from it arise death and all that belongs to death. Human beings clothed themselves in these evils when the devil led them, deprived of faith and obedience, away from God’s law into his own promises, and bound all the offspring of their posterity to himself through the condition of a corrupted stock.

Therefore, if anyone is a new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), [Note: So read the Joliensis and Remigius manuscripts and Augustine’s edition, where the preposition *by*—“by the devil”—is added. Printed editions read: “let him be free from the devil and subject to God.” The phrase “free from the devil,” as in Romans 6:20, is in the dative case.] he is set free from the devil and subjected to God, reformed from his deformity according to the image of the one who created him (Colossians 3:10).

Unless this takes place, he remains in the one in whom all die, having no share in the one in whom all are made alive. God, therefore, is not the author of anyone’s sin [Note: The word *God* was absent from the printed editions. It is restored from the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts and from Augustine’s edition], but the creator of nature.

Although nature possessed the power not to sin, it sinned voluntarily and by its own will subjected itself to its deceiver. It is moved in vice not by a natural impulse but by a captive one, until it dies to sin and lives to God. It cannot do this without the grace of God, because it does not recover the freedom which it lost through freedom unless Christ sets it free.

For there is no other name under heaven given to human beings by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12).

## Chapter Six

### Objection

That God fashions in human beings a will like that of demons, which by its own impulse can or wishes nothing other than evil [Note: So read the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts and Augustine’s edition. Earlier printed editions read: “can or wishes.”].

### Response

The whole world, as the Apostle John says, lies in the evil one (1 John 5:19); and the malice of many human beings is like that of demons. To such people the Lord said: “Offspring of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matthew 12:34); and, “You are born from the devil as father, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John 8:44).

But this distinguishes evil human beings from demons: even for human beings, however evil, reconciliation remains possible if God has mercy; whereas for demons no conversion has been preserved for eternity.

Therefore, just as God did not implant in the transgressing angels that will “which did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44), so neither did he implant in human beings this disposition by which they would imitate the devil. “The liar speaks from his own resources” (ibid.), and he will not be free from lying unless the Truth sets him free.

## Chapter Seven

[Col. 0181D]

### Objection

That it is God’s will that a large part of Christians should neither wish nor be able to be saved.

### Response

If this is said of those who, abandoning the piety of Christian conduct and faith, have irrevocably passed into profane errors [Col. 0182A] or damnable ways of life, there is no doubt that those who have such a will do not wish to be saved; and as long as they do not wish to be saved, they cannot be saved.

But it must in no way be believed that such people fell into this despair by God’s will, since the Lord rather raises up all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down (Psalm 144:14). For no one is raised up except by his grace, and no one is strengthened except by his grace.

Therefore God’s will is that one remain in a good will. He abandons no one before he is abandoned, and he often converts many who have abandoned him.

## Chapter Eight

### Objection

[Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “That God did not wish it.”]

That God does not wish all Catholics to persevere in the Catholic faith, but wishes a large part of them thereafter to apostatize.

### Response

The impiety of this blasphemy is not unlike that of the preceding statement. Therefore the response given to that statement may also be given to this one, which differs from it in no respect.

## Chapter Nine

### Objection

That God wishes a large part of the saints to fall from their purpose of holiness.

### Response

The madness of this definition says nothing other than what the preceding objection said. It is therefore astonishing that the objector repeated a third time what it would have been enough to say once. But, as matters stand, he wished to increase the number of his accusations because he could not vary their meaning.

## Chapter Ten

### Objection

That adulteries and the defilements of consecrated virgins occur because God predestined them to fall.

### Response

This is a detestable and abominable opinion, which believes God to be the author of anyone’s evil will or evil action. His predestination is never outside goodness and never outside justice. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10).

Holy Divinity does not institute the adulteries of married women [Note: Remigius Manuscript: “of husbands”] or the defilements of virgins; it knows how to condemn them. Nor does it ordain them, but punish them.

When human beings commit these evils, they serve their own lusts and desires, which they drew from that first stain of voluntary transgression. But when they turn away from evil and do good, the steps of a person are directed by the Lord, and he takes delight in that person’s way (Psalm 36:23).

For this reason the Apostle says: “But we pray to God that you do nothing evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good” (2 Corinthians 13:7) [Note: Printed editions: “to the Lord”; the Remigius Manuscript and Augustine’s edition: “to God,” as in the Apostle].

Therefore God’s predestination neither aroused, nor advised, nor compelled the falls of those who fall, the wickedness of the unjust, or the desires of sinners. Rather, it plainly predestined his judgment, by which he will repay each person according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

That judgment would certainly not exist if human beings sinned by God’s will. It will, however, most manifestly exist; and every person whom the discrimination of divine knowledge has placed on the left will be condemned, because he carried out not God’s will but his own.

## Chapter Eleven

### Objection

That when fathers commit incest with their daughters and mothers with their sons, or when slaves kill their masters, this happens because God predestined it to happen.

### Response

If the devil were accused of being himself the author and instigator of such crimes, I think he could in some measure free himself from this charge and convict the perpetrators of such crimes [Note: The passage is corrected from the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts and Augustine’s edition. Other printed editions read: “he would overcome the perpetrator of such crimes by their own will.”] by their own will. For although he delighted in the fury of sinners, he could nevertheless prove that he had not imposed the force of their crimes upon them.

With what foolishness, then, or what madness, is it declared that God’s counsel must be held responsible for something which cannot be wholly ascribed even to the devil—who, in the crimes of sinners, should be regarded as the helper of their enticements, not the creator of their wills?

God therefore did not predestine any such affairs to happen; [Note: So reads the Remigius Manuscript. Other printed editions read: “nor did he prepare that soul.”] nor did he prepare any soul to live wickedly and shamefully for the purpose of living in such a way. But he was not ignorant that such a person would become such, and he foreknew that he would justly judge him on that account.

And so nothing else can be referred to his predestination except what belongs either to the due recompense of justice or to the undeserved generosity of grace.

## Chapter Twelve

### Objection

That by God’s predestination the children of God are made children of the devil, temples of demons from temples of the Holy Spirit, and members of a prostitute from members of Christ.

### Response

Although God’s predestination is uncertain to us while we move amid the dangers of the present life, it remains immutable with him who made the things that are to come. It neither blinds those whom it has enlightened, nor destroys what it has built, nor uproots what it has planted.

For “the gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Romans 11:29), and “the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

Therefore God’s predestination in no way makes some people, from being children of God, become children of the devil; or, from being temples of the Holy Spirit, become temples of demons [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “become a temple”]; or, from being members of Christ, become members of a prostitute. Rather, predestination makes children of the devil become children of God, temples of demons become temples of the Holy Spirit [Note: Earlier printed editions: “become a temple”], and members of a prostitute become members of Christ.

For he himself binds the strong man and seizes his goods (Mark 3:27), rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them from dishonor into glory (Colossians 1:13).

But those of whom it is said, “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19), went out by their own will and fell by their own will. And because they were foreknown to be about to fall, they were not predestined. They would have been predestined if they were destined to return and remain in holiness and truth.

Accordingly, God’s predestination is the cause of standing for many; it is the cause of falling for no one.

## 237 Chapter Thirteen

### Objection

[Col. 0184B]

That all those faithful and holy people who have been predestined to eternal death, when they relapse into their vomit, appear indeed to do this through their own fault; but the cause of that fault is divine predestination, which secretly withdraws good wills from them.

### Response

The same spirit of blasphemy persists, and the impiety that follows does not depart from the preceding lies. Sound reason utterly rejects it, and sound doctrine unhesitatingly condemns it.

For all who have fallen from faith into unbelief and from holiness into shamefulness, and who have not been purified by any correction before the end of life, are owed nothing other than eternal death. But it is wicked to ascribe the causes of such ruin to God. Although, through his eternal knowledge, he has foreknown what he will repay each person according to that person’s merits, he has nevertheless, by the fact that he cannot be deceived, imposed upon no one either a necessity or a will to sin.

If, then, someone falls away from justice and piety, he is carried headlong by his own judgment, drawn by his own desire, and deceived by his own persuasion. There the Father does nothing, the Son does nothing, and the Holy Spirit does nothing; no act of the divine will intervenes in such a matter. By God’s work we know that many are held back lest they fall, but none are impelled to fall.

## Chapter Fourteen

### Objection

That the large part of those Christian, Catholic, faithful, and holy people who have been predestined to ruin and destruction will not obtain perseverance in holiness from God even if they ask for it, because divine predestination cannot be changed: it has preordained, prepared, and fitted them to fall.

### Response

There is absolutely no predestination of God to transgressing the law, neglecting religion, corrupting discipline, abandoning the faith, or committing any kind of sin. Nor can it happen that through the one by whom a person rises from such evils, that person should fall into such evils.

If, therefore, one lives in holiness, if one advances in virtue [Note: Earlier printed editions: “if one advances toward virtue.” The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts and Augustine’s edition read: “in virtue.”], and if one remains in good pursuits, this is plainly a gift of God, without which no fruit of a good work is obtained.

But if someone withdraws from these things and turns toward vices and sins, God does not send any evil temptation there. He does not abandon the one who is about to withdraw before being abandoned, and he often ensures that he does not abandon—or, if he has departed, that he returns.

Why he retains one person and does not retain another is neither possible to comprehend nor lawful to investigate [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “to examine”]. It is enough to know both that whatever enables a person to stand is from him, and that whatever causes a person to fall is not from him.

## Chapter Fifteen

### Objection

That all those faithful and holy people who have been predestined to eternal death, after they have fallen, are so governed by God [Note: So reads the Joliensis Manuscript. Other manuscripts read: “so that they can neither wish nor be able”] that they can neither be freed through repentance nor wish to be freed.

### Response

This is not said truthfully or wisely. For those who have fallen away from faith and holiness, just as they fell through their own will, do not rise through their own will; and they willingly endure the domination of the desires to which they succumbed.

But if some grieve over their captivity and, judging themselves, flee with a changed heart to the mercy of God, they do not do this without the spirit of divine visitation. “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:10); he gives repentance to countless fallen people so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they were held captive for his will (2 Timothy 2:26).

God deprives no one of the path of correction, nor does he strip anyone of the possibility of doing good. For the person who turns away from God has himself taken away from himself both the will and the ability to do what is good.

It does not therefore follow, as those who make such objections think, that if God has not given certain people repentance, he has taken away their recovery; or that those whom he has not raised up, he has struck down. One thing is to drive an innocent person into crime, which is alien to God; another is not to grant forgiveness to a criminal, which proceeds from the sinner’s own merit.

## Chapter Sixteen

### Objection

That the large part of the faithful and holy people who have been predestined to eternal death, when they say to God in the Lord’s Prayer, “Your will be done,” ask for nothing other than what is against themselves—namely, that they should fall and collapse—because God’s will is that they perish by eternal death.

### Response

The Truth does not say that it is God’s will that the faithful and holy should fall from faith and innocence and perish eternally. Rather, the Truth says (John 6:39): “This is the will of the Father who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but should raise it up on the last day.”

Therefore, whatever the Father has given the Son, the Son certainly does not lose [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “will not lose it.”]. The same Son also says (John 6:37): “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out” [Note: We have restored the words “will come to me, and whoever,” which were absent from all the printed editions, on the authority of the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts. Earlier printed editions read: “Everything that the Father gives me comes to me, and I will not cast it out.”].

But if, through the generality of the call and the abundance of God’s goodness, those who will not persevere have been mixed in with those who will persevere, when these people fall away from piety, they fall away not through God’s work but through their own will. They are not driven to fall, nor are they cast out so that they may depart; yet they are foreknown by the one who cannot be deceived as destined to fall and depart from him.

Therefore, as long as they say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Your will be done,” they do not ask against themselves for something which God will in no way or for any reason do—namely, that they should fall and collapse. That is the work of their own wickedness, and their own freedom will complete it [Note: So reads the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts. Earlier printed editions read: “For this is their wickedness,” and so forth].

Rather, they plainly ask against themselves for what is undoubtedly God’s will: namely, that when the Son of Man comes in his majesty and sits upon the throne of his glory, all the nations should be gathered before him, and he should separate them from one another, placing some at his right hand and others at his left; and that those on his right should hear him say, “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you” [Note: So reads the Joliensis Manuscript. The Remigius Manuscript and Augustine’s edition read: “the kingdom prepared for you”; earlier printed editions: “the prepared kingdom for you”] from the foundation of the world (Matthew 25:34).

Let those on his left also hear: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., verse 41) [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “so that he may separate them.”].

Thus those who will not do God’s will, while asking that God’s will be done, are heard in the matter which is to be done by God’s will [Note: Joliensis Manuscript: “they hear”], so that, as imitators of the devil, they may be judged with the devil. For those who despised God’s will when it invited them will experience God’s will when it avenges.

# Responses on Behalf of Augustine to the Excerpts of the Genuans

[Col. 0185]

## Notice concerning Prosper’s Responses on Behalf of Augustine to the Excerpts of the Genuans

We believe that the excerpts of the Genuan presbyters set out below were produced not with the same intention as the preceding writings—namely, to diminish or defame Augustine’s teaching—but were directed to our Prosper for the sole purpose that the holy disciple of Augustine, as one who shared in that more exalted teaching, remote from the limits of common understanding, might resolve the doubts which they had experienced while reading Saint Augustine’s books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. They indicated that they had discovered in those books certain unusual and less clear points, and asked only that he deign to disclose to them with what understanding or judgment he had received them.

The modesty of those men is evident in this manner of proceeding: although they were priests in a perhaps not insignificant city, possibly among its leading men, they did not hesitate to consult a man who, as seems more probable, was a layman concerning such weighty matters (*In the preface to this work*).

Accordingly, Saint Prosper, repaying such praiseworthy humility, replies that what they had requested from him they ought themselves to have supplied to him by careful meditation upon Augustine’s passages and by confident, extended prayer to the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends (James 1:17), and from whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding is given.

For this reason he undertakes, not as a teacher instructing disciples but as a disciple of truth and a follower of humility and obedience, to obey men of a higher order than himself, trusting in the help of him who grants wisdom to the simple (Psalm 18:8). He begins to explain at greater length the passages which they had excerpted from the two books of Saint Augustine mentioned above, restoring them to their proper meanings through the comparison which he urges everywhere with the preceding and following context of the passages from which they had been taken, and demonstrating that in every case they are sound and whole when freed from perverse interpretation. He humbly asks them not to regard as a presumption of learning what in him was merely the simplicity of obedience.

He accomplishes this admirably, both through the authority of Holy Scripture which he brings forward and, above all, through passages from other works of Saint Augustine, compared with those that had caused their scruple. As elsewhere, he always proclaims the same consistent doctrine: that the wholly gratuitous grace of God, and faith itself, take their beginning from that same grace and mercy of God; that not all good is bestowed indiscriminately upon everyone; and that no good work whatsoever can be performed by anyone unless divine assistance is present.

The learned man wishes the city from which they sent this little book to Prosper to have been not Genoa, the principal city of Italy, which received the surname “the Superb” from its elegant buildings, but Geneva, which is also called Gebenna and Aurelia Allobrogum. It is all the more difficult to agree with him on this point because everywhere those presbyters are found called not Genevans but Genoese.

Finally, if the time when these events occurred is asked, we conjecture that this work and its reply were published shortly after the foregoing works, but certainly after the death of Saint Augustine.

[Col. 0187]

## RESPONSES OF SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITANIA ON AUGUSTINE’S BEHALF TO THE EXCERPTS OF THE GENOESE (C)

[Note: This work was perhaps written at the same time as the preceding works, after Augustine’s death.]

### Preface

[Col. 0187A] To Camillus and Theodore, venerable presbyters, Prosper sends greetings.

[Note: The Remigianus codex of Rheims reads “Theudulo.” The Joliensis manuscript of the Church of Paris reads “Camyllo and Theodulo.” The edition of Saint Prosper’s little works On Grace and Free Will, prepared at Venice in 1538, reads “Camillo and Theodolo.”]

241 In the books of Bishop Augustine, of blessed memory, whose title is On the Predestination of the Saints, certain passages have disturbed your holiness, either because they are unusual or because they are insufficiently clear. You excerpted them from the context of the discussion and sent them to my humility, so that you might learn with what understanding, or by what judgment, I received them [Note: Thus the Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts, together with the edition of Augustine’s works. The printed editions read, “or by what judgment I received them.”]—as though I possessed greater intellectual ability than you for examining these matters; and as though, in this inquiry, you ought not rather to have exercised the measure of your own capacity. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript alone reads, “you ought to have exercised.”]

If some obscurity held you back, you should have hastened to the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends (James 1:17), and from whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding is given. Nevertheless, I will not withhold my obedience to your instructions; and, with the Lord’s help [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “with God’s help.”], who gives wisdom to the simple (Psalm 18:8), I shall briefly indicate what I think with my holy and learned brothers about these chapters, asking you not to regard as doctrinal presumption what is merely the simplicity of obedience. You first presented the following excerpts, in which there are the words of Bishop Saint Augustine.

## BOOK OF RESPONSES

[Col. 0187]

### FIRST EXCERPT

[Col. 0187B]

(Augustine, Book 1 of On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 3.) “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript adds “but,” as found in the passage of the book On the Predestination of the Saints. The printed editions did not contain this particle.]

I carried my reasoning to the point of saying: “Therefore God did not choose anyone’s works, which he himself would give, but chose faith in his foreknowledge, so that he might choose the one whom he foreknew would believe in him, and to that person give the Holy Spirit, so that by doing good he might also attain eternal life.” I had not yet investigated the matter more carefully, nor had I yet discovered what the election of grace was.

### SECOND EXCERPT

[Note: In the Joliensis manuscript, the headings of the Excerpts—or, as the printed editions elsewhere had them, of the Doubts—here and from this point onward read, “Likewise, the words of the same man.” The printed editions read, “In the words of the same man.” The edition in the appendix to Augustine’s works omitted this passage.]

[Col. 0189A]

(The same work.) “Then I added: ‘Therefore, what we believe is ours; but what we do well belongs to him who gives the Holy Spirit to those who believe.’” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript, together with the Lyon, Louvain, and Venetian editions, omits “what”; I certainly would not say it.]

“I certainly would not have said this if I had already known that faith itself is also found among God’s gifts, which are given in the same Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:6).” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “which are given,” as in Augustine’s book. All the printed editions, together with the Remigianus, read “which is given,” and shortly afterward the Joliensis manuscript likewise adds “therefore.”]

“Thus both are ours, because of the freedom of the will; yet both have been given, because of the Spirit of faith and love.”

### THIRD EXCERPT

Likewise, the words of the same man.

(The same work.) “And consequently, what I said afterward—‘For neither can we will unless we are called; and when, after the call, we have willed, our will and our progress are not sufficient unless God both grants strength to those who believe and brings them to the place to which he calls them’—and then added: ‘It is therefore clear that what we do well belongs not to the one who wills or to the one who runs, but to God who shows mercy’—is altogether true. But I said too little about the call itself, which takes place according to God’s purpose; for not everyone who is called receives a call of this kind, but only the elect.”

## RESPONSE TO THESE THREE

Although these three chapters have been separated from the body of the discussion [Note: All printed editions read “from the body of the discussion.” We correct this from the Joliensis manuscript, supported by the Remigianus manuscript and the edition in the Augustinian appendix], and have thereby been made more obscure because they do not cohere with what precedes, what lies between, and what follows, nevertheless, if we understand that the writer is treating one and the same matter throughout them [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “one and the same matter”], we see that he is speaking about those who said that, at the beginning of his conversion, he had held a better opinion, when he thought that the faith by which we are Christians did not come from grace or exist as a gift of God, but came from the human being himself and from free choice; whereas now he was in error because he asserted that faith itself was also God’s gift, and that the saying “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) applied to this as well. They also claimed that he was now wrong to refer Jacob’s election to God’s purpose, since previously he had referred it to foreknowledge.

To this objection he replies that, before he knew the truth of grace and before he was placed over the Church as its ruler, he had erred ignorantly in this opinion. But at the very beginning of his episcopate, when he had been consulted by Simplicianus, bishop of Milan and a man of holy memory, concerning the election of Jacob and the rejection of Esau, he examined with keener diligence the whole question concerning these twins. [Note: Earlier editions, omitting the preposition, read: “he consulted Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, of holy memory . . . .” This has been corrected from the Remigianus manuscript in the edition of Augustine’s appendix and by us from the Joliensis manuscript. It is certain that Augustine did not consult Simplicianus; rather, Simplicianus consulted Augustine, asking him to treat two questions from Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. The second concerned the election of Jacob and the rejection of Esau. See Letter 37, volume 2 of the new edition of Augustine’s works.]

With every power of reasoning, he recognized beyond doubt that no human merits precede the election of grace, and that faith, from which all merits begin, is God’s gift: otherwise grace would not be grace (Romans 11:6) if something for which it is bestowed preceded it. Thus, in the statement “Jacob I loved,” what is given to a human being was shown; and in the statement “Esau I hated” (Romans 9:13), what was owed to a human being was shown.

He carefully recalled this in the second book of his Retractations (chapter 1). When he examined all his opinions with censorial gravity, he rejected the opinion which his detractors choose—the opinion which, before the rise of the Pelagian heresy, he foresaw as friendly to the error that would later arise, but which, after the truth of grace had been revealed to him, he rejected.

What reason, then, is there for us not to approve this confession of such a man? By it he teaches us, through the example of his own correction, to discipline our opinions if we have perhaps adopted them imprudently; and by it he teaches that we receive from God what we are commanded to ask that we may receive. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “and which he teaches.” This appears less correct.]

For if we consider the arguments of Pelagian impiety, what does it strive more earnestly to establish than that God’s grace is given according to our merits, so that, in the very matter in which it confesses grace to be necessary, it weakens grace by attributing it to human will? Anyone who thinks that faith does not belong among God’s gifts falls entirely into this perversity. Or he boasts that he refers faith to God for this reason: that nature was created by him, and that he inserted into it rational freedom, through which each person has it in his own power to believe or not to believe; and that, from this natural good—which he received when he was created, without any preceding merits—he merits the other gifts. [Note: The printed editions read “which he received without any merits.” The Joliensis manuscript, and the edition in the Augustinian appendix based on the Remigianus, read “which he received without any preceding merits,” a better reading.]

Whoever asserts this, I believe, admits with us that human nature was corrupted in the first Adam; nor does he deny that in that fall it lost its virtues, which it cannot possess unless it receives them again through grace. But why does he refuse to admit that faith alone was taken away from that same nature, when, had it not first lost faith, it would not have been deprived of all the other goods? By believing the devil, Adam did not believe God; and when he had been intoxicated with the spirit of pride, his heart departed from the Lord. He became the slave of the apostate while wishing to be free from righteousness.

Since, then, we would not have continence unless God gave it (Wisdom 8:21); nor holy love unless the love of God had been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5); and, finally, no one would have wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11:2), unless the Holy Spirit gave these virtues—how could faith, lost in Adam, be found in any of his children unless that same Spirit, who works all things in all people (1 Corinthians 12:6), infused it into them?

Therefore, if Adam’s descendants did not lose what Adam lost, his sin injured him alone and not the human race. But all sinned in one person (Romans 5:12), and by the desert of transgression all his offspring were condemned. Thus all lost what Adam lost. But he first lost faith; and because we were able to lose it first, we need to receive it first. [Note: The printed editions read “we have faith first to receive.” The Joliensis manuscript, together with the edition in the Augustinian appendix based on the Remigianus, reads “we need to receive it first.”]

Let us therefore welcome this preaching of grace, by which faith is defended as God’s gift; and let us not allow Pelagian error to deceive us in any respect. For, in order to persuade us that grace is owed, it refuses to regard faith as given. [Note: The Douai and Cologne editions omit “neither just nor reasonable.” The other manuscripts retain it.]

Because the persuasion of those who recalled this man’s learning—built up through so many stages of progress and polished through so many years of study—to the beginnings of his adolescence was neither just nor reasonable, so that what he had ineptly thought at the beginning of his conversion might support the heretics more than what truth had revealed to him through episcopal diligence might benefit Catholics, the gravity of the pious teacher rightly marks them as using this prejudice and dwelling on opinions long since rejected. Those who undertook to investigate all his thoughts did not wish to advance along with his learning.

But now let us consider what sort of thing it is that you noted from what follows.

### FOURTH EXCERPT

[Col. 0191C]

(The same work, chapter 5, section 10.) “Not because believing or not believing is not within the power of the human will, but because among the elect the will is prepared by the Lord.”

## RESPONSE

Let us join to this what follows, so that what has been proposed may be clearer as part of a connected discourse. “Therefore this also pertains to faith itself, which is in the will” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript does not contain “which is in the will”], “Who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Many hear the word of truth; but some believe and others contradict it. The former wish to believe, while the latter do not. Who is ignorant of this? Who denies it? But when the Lord prepares the will for some and does not prepare it for others, we must examine what comes from mercy and what from judgment. “What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the others were hardened,” as it is written: “He gave them a spirit of remorse, eyes so that they might not see, and ears so that they might not hear, unto this present day” (Isaiah 6:9). And David says: “Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a recompense to them; let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their back” (Psalm 68:23; Romans 11:7).

[Note: The printed editions read, “Behold mercy and judgment: mercy in the election.” We correct this from Augustine’s book, for by the word “election” he understands the elect, not the act by which God chose.]

Behold mercy and judgment: mercy toward the elect, who obtained the righteousness of God; but judgment in the others, who were hardened. Yet the former believed because they wished to; the latter did not believe because they did not wish to. Mercy and judgment, therefore, took place in the wills themselves. [Note: Thus the Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts, together with Augustine’s edition. Other copies read, “For this election.”]

This election is an election of grace, not of merits. For above he had said: “Thus, in the present time also, a remnant has been saved by the election of grace. But if by grace, then not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:5–6). [Note: The edition in the Augustinian appendix alone reads, “Grace, therefore.”]

The election therefore obtained what it obtained freely. Nothing of theirs preceded which they might first give and which could then be repaid to them. “He saved them for nothing” (Psalm 55:8). But in the others who were hardened, as the passage does not leave unsaid, it happened by way of recompense. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10). Yet his ways are unsearchable (Romans 11:33). [Note: In Augustine’s own book: “Therefore his mercy also is unsearchable,” and so forth. The Remigianus manuscript supports this reading, where the word “unsearchable” occurs, as it is repeated below.]

Unsearchable, therefore, is the mercy by which he freely saves, and the truth by which he justly judges.

What offense do all these things cause in the mind of a pious and Catholic reader? What contradiction do they encounter? Is it false that the will is prepared by the Lord (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint)? [Note: The Remigianus manuscript reads, “That the will is thus prepared by the Lord.”] Are not all who are led by the Spirit of God sons of God (Romans 8:14)? Does nature distinguish one human being from another, rather than grace distinguishing the believer from the unbeliever? Can anyone say that he has something which he did not receive, or boast as though it were his own of something he did not receive—something which, had he not received it, he certainly would not have? Is it doubtful that, when the word of truth is preached, some believe by their will and others do not believe by their will?

But when God has opened the heart of some and has not opened the heart of others, we must distinguish what comes from mercy and what from judgment. After recalling the apostolic statement (Romans 11:7), which he supports with prophetic testimonies—namely, that the righteousness of God which Israel sought but did not obtain was obtained by the election through grace, while the others were blinded by recompense—is it not most truly said: “Behold mercy and judgment: mercy toward the elect, who obtained the righteousness of God; but judgment in the others, who were hardened”? And shortly afterward: “The election therefore obtained freely what it obtained. Nothing of theirs preceded which they might first give and which could then be repaid to them: he saved them for nothing. But in the others who were hardened, as the passage does not leave unsaid, it happened by way of recompense.”

What room is there here for complaint, except among the enemies of grace, who, unless what is given freely is referred to recompense, wish to regard what is repaid as injustice? Furthermore, who has denied what he added from the prophetic words: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10)? Or what he appended from the apostolic meaning: “His ways are unsearchable” (Romans 11:33)? His ways are therefore unsearchable: both the mercy by which he freely saves and the truth by which he justly judges.

It is not therefore the mark of sound minds to criticize these things, or to declare that the unsearchable ways of the Lord—that is, the gifts of mercy and the judgments of truth—are penetrable to Pelagian pride. According to the Pelagians, God’s plan is not hidden, nor is the reason for the divine will concealed, if toward every human being both God’s grace and his wrath arise from merit. [Note: The printed editions read, “as both grace and wrath are deserved.” The Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts, from which the Augustinian edition was corrected, read as in our text.]

After this you set down what is said below.

### FIFTH EXCERPT

(The same work, chapter 8, section 4.) “Faith, therefore, both begun and perfected, is God’s gift. And let no one who does not wish to contradict the most evident sacred Scriptures doubt that this gift is given to some and not given to others.”

## RESPONSE

If someone does not accept this, whose opinion does he appear to hold except that of the person who says: “The faith by which I am justified comes from me; and this good, by which the righteous person lives (Habakkuk 2:4), I did not receive through grace, but possess by nature”?

If faith is not God’s gift, the Church prays in vain for unbelievers, that they may believe; and it is enough to apply to the impious the instruction of the law, concerning which it was said: “If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21). The same can likewise be said of nature.

The Apostle also gives thanks to God in vain for those who received the Gospel (2 Thessalonians 2:12), if, according to the Pelagians, this was not bestowed as God’s gift but is possessed solely by human will. And the same Apostle prays in vain for certain people that they may have peace and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ (Ephesians 6:23), so that the pride of the heretics may now be convicted of saying not only that faith but also peace and love are possessed from oneself.

If these things come from the human being, what prevents him from possessing by himself the other, lesser goods, when he dares to attribute to himself the highest goods, without which the others, however numerous and distinguished, are of no benefit?

The statement “Faith, therefore, both begun and perfected, is God’s gift” cannot rightly be refuted, because the Apostle says the same: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift; not from works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9); and: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29); and again: “Let us run with endurance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:1).

By these and many other testimonies of the divine Scriptures it is recognized beyond doubt that, as this man defined it, faith, both begun and perfected, is God’s gift. And he says that this gift is given to some and not given to others; he does not doubt this at all if he does not wish to contradict the most evident sacred Scriptures. [Note: The Venetian edition reads “does not doubt.”]

We should not think this statement has been made truthfully if all human beings are believers. But when some believe and others do not, and the Apostle says, “Faith is not possessed by all” (1 Thessalonians 3:2), who does not see that those who have faith received it, while those who do not have it did not receive it?

### SIXTH EXCERPT

[Col. 0194B]

(The same work.) “Then he says: ‘Why it is not given to everyone ought not to disturb the faithful person, who believes that from one person all went into condemnation (Romans 5:12), a condemnation unquestionably most just, so that there would be no just reproach against God even if no one were delivered from it. Hence it is clear that great is the grace by which many are delivered, and that those who are not delivered recognize what was owed to them, so that the one who boasts may boast not in his merits—which he sees to be equal to those of the condemned—but in the Lord’ (Romans 11:33).” [Note: The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions have the plural: “those who boast … who see their merits to be equal to those of the condemned … may boast in the Lord.” The Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts, with the Augustinian, Lyon, and Venetian editions, have the singular.]

“Why he delivers this person rather than that one: his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable. It is better for us here also to hear or say, ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ (Romans 9:20), than to dare to say—as though we knew what he wished to remain hidden—that he nevertheless could have willed something unjust.” [Note: The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts read, “we hear,” and do not add “or say.”]

## RESPONSE

If these statements are not rightly made, then God’s judgments are scrutable and his ways traceable; it is not hidden why one person is saved rather than another; and the person who has been found worthy by election, while others perish through their own fault, will boast in himself rather than in the Lord. Thus it will indeed be justice that many are condemned, but it will not be grace that many are delivered. [Note: Thus the Joliensis manuscript. Other copies read, “Let these things be far from us,” and so forth.]

Let such things be far from Catholic hearts; let such impiety be far from us, that we should think anyone is rescued from the power of darkness by his own merits and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God by an adoption that is owed rather than freely given.

Adam perished through a great sin, and in him all perished. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads: “Because, for every human being born under condemnation by birth in his forefather—that is, in Adam—it is owed that he perish.”]

For every person born under condemnation by birth in his forefather, that is, in Adam, it is owed that he perish. And just as we cannot complain that in past ages God allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways, so we would have no just ground for complaint if, together with those with whom we shared a common cause, we too perished while grace was still withheld.

Yet just as grace then rescued a few from the whole world, so now it saves countless people from the entire human race—not according to our works, but according to his purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times (2 Timothy 1:9).

You also appended what he says after discussing many matters.

### SEVENTH EXCERPT

(The same work, chapter 16, section 2.) “It is therefore in the power of the wicked to sin; but that, by sinning, their wickedness should do this or that is not in their power, but in God’s, who divides the darkness and orders it, so that even what they do against God’s will does not come to pass except according to God’s will.”

## RESPONSE

Since this is the clearest truth, I am surprised that it was excerpted among obscure passages, as though the reader’s every hesitation could not have been resolved from the connected context. Consider, then, what follows.

(The same work.) “We read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 4:13 and following) that, when the apostles, after being released by the Jews, had come to their own people and reported how much the priests and elders had done to them” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “and had reported to them how much the priests and elders had done to them”; it omits the words “in truth” below and reads “Pontius Pilate.”], “they all raised their voices together to the Lord and said: ‘Lord, you are the one who made heaven and earth and everything in them, who through the mouth of our father David, your holy servant, said: Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ’ (Psalm 2:2).

“For in truth they gathered together in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed: Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the people of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan predestined to be done.”

If what the Holy Spirit prophesied through the mouth of our father David cannot in any way be understood otherwise than as it was understood by the apostles, and if Herod, Pontius Pilate, and the people of Israel did whatever God’s hand and plan predestined to be done, what inappropriate thing did the remarkable disputant say when he stated: “It is in the power of the wicked to sin; but that, by sinning, their wickedness should do this or that is not in their power, but in God’s, who divides the darkness and orders it, so that even what they do against God’s will does not come to pass except according to God’s will”? [Note: The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts read, “For to will evil is easy for the wicked.”]

For to will evil is very easy for the wicked. There is no doubt that God’s power confines their condemnable will, so that they cannot obtain the result of their desire unless he permits it. No one who has been even slightly instructed in piety is unaware that God makes use, even through the deeds of the wicked, which proceed from their own desire, of wisdom and justice in fulfilling his own purposes and judgments.

He sees this in the best will of God the Father, who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, and which was fulfilled through the worst will of Judas the betrayer and of the Jews. [Note: The printed editions read “the will of the betrayers.” The Remigianus codex, more correctly, reads “the will of the betrayer.”]
