He also sees it in the Gospel pages, where Pilate says to Jesus: “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you and authority to release you?” (John 19:10), and the Lord replies: “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given to you from above.” [Note: The edition of Augustine based on the Remigianus reads “given from above.”]

God therefore divides light from darkness. Yet the darkness is not thereby guiltless because God makes good use of it; he has even ordered their works—that is, the works of the darkness itself—so that what proceeds from them might benefit the children of light. [Note: The printed editions read “their works.” The Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts, and the Augustinian edition based on the latter, more correctly read “the works of the darkness itself,” referring to the darkness. The word also alludes to the darkness by which he understands the wicked, who may be called its children.]

He allows the malice of those wishing to do harm to advance only as far as he knows it will be useful either for disciplining or for testing his saints. Thus even what they do against God’s will does not come to pass except according to God’s will.

[Col. 0196B] Next follows what is found in the second book.

### EIGHTH EXCERPT

(The same work, chapter 14, section 35.) “Will anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow to whom he would give the ability to believe, or whom he would give to his Son so that he would not lose anyone from among them (John 18:9)? If he certainly foreknew these things, he surely foreknew the benefits by which he deigns to deliver us.

“This is the predestination of the saints, nothing else: namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered.” [Note: The Venetian and Lyon editions read: “This is the predestination of the saints, nothing else—namely, foreknowledge.” The Joliensis manuscript likewise has this reading. Other editions read: “This predestination of the saints is nothing other than foreknowledge.”]

“But the others—where are they left except in the mass of perdition, by the just divine judgment? That is where the Tyrians and Sidonians were left, who could also have believed if they had seen those wonderful signs of Christ (Matthew 11:21).” [Note: The Venetian and Lyon editions read “but how.”] “But since it was not given to them to believe, even the means by which they might believe was denied them.”

## RESPONSE

Those who resist these statements are shown most clearly to hold the view that faith is not God’s gift; that grace does not precede free choice but follows it; and that God’s grace is given according to our merits.

For if they confess that something is conferred upon a human being through grace, but that no one receives it except by faith—and that faith itself has not been received—then merit lies in the faith to which a gift is not given but a debt repaid.

Holding this position, they consequently think that those are predestined to eternal life whom God foreknew would become believers through the exercise of free will. Thus the predestination of the elect is nothing other than recompense. Accordingly, among those who have been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things, God does not work faith; nor are there any human merits if God works all things. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits “truly.”]

Truly, those who think this have not received faith—or have lost the faith they had received—by following the most vain Pelagian pride and boasting in themselves, not in the Lord, who works all things in all people (1 Corinthians 12:6): plainly good things, not evil things. If he works all good things, then certainly faith also, without which no one can please God (Hebrews 11:6), and which is the foundation of all the virtues.

What sort of thing is it, then, that although the building belongs to God, and unless the Lord builds the house those who build it labor in vain (Psalm 126:1), these people refuse to let the foundation belong to the building, or wish to begin what the Lord may complete?

The Son of God will therefore not be their beginning; they will not be founded upon Christ Jesus, the cornerstone; nor does the statement “The firm foundation of God stands” (2 Timothy 2:19) apply to them, because they place their entire election upon shifting sand and collapsing ash. [Note: The Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts read “their entire pride.” The Cologne edition reads “their entire rejection,” but incorrectly.]

Let us therefore acknowledge wisely and confess piously that God immutably foreknew to whom he would give the ability to believe, and whom he would give to his Son so that he would not lose anyone from among them; and that, if he foreknew these things, he also foreknew the benefits by which he deigns to deliver us. This is the predestination of the saints: namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s grace, by which they are most certainly delivered. [Note: The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts read “namely, the predestination.”] [Note: “Whoever is delivered” might perhaps be added here. These words are found neither in the manuscripts nor in the earlier printed editions, except in a more recent Lyon edition.]

But all the others who are not delivered—those whom grace has not removed from the general perdition of the human race—we should know were not removed by a just judgment. And from them we should learn what has been forgiven us, since we cannot complain about their condemnation.

For there is no injustice with God (2 Chronicles 19:7), nor does anyone innocent perish under his judgment. As this same distinguished preacher of grace says elsewhere (Augustine, On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 23):

“God certainly repays evil for evil, because he is just; and good for evil, because he is good; and good for good, because he is just and good. He does not, however, repay evil for good, because he is not unjust.” [Note: The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “He certainly repays.”]

He therefore repays evil for evil: punishment for injustice; and he repays good for evil: grace for injustice; and he repays good for good: grace for grace. [Note: Here, and three times in what follows, the printed editions read “how,” whereas the Joliensis manuscript and Augustine read “because he is just”; the same applies to the other parts of this sentence.]

When some perish, let us not doubt that what they perish for is to be attributed to their merits; God could certainly mercifully deliver them if he wished. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript, together with the Lyon edition and others, has this reading.]

And when some are delivered, let us not dare to define that they were worthy to be delivered; God could certainly justly condemn them if he wished. Why he does not deliver everyone, or why he delivers these rather than those [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “rather than these”; the others read “rather than those”], it is neither necessary to ask nor possible to discover. It is enough to know, without investigating the causes of this distinction, that with him from whom no one is condemned except justly and no one is delivered except mercifully, neither mercy removes justice nor justice removes mercy.

Concerning the Tyrians and Sidonians, what else can we say than that it was not granted to them to believe—although Truth itself says that they would have believed if they had seen such signs of miraculous powers as were performed among those who did not believe (Matt. 11; Luke 10:13)? But why this was denied to them, let those who bring accusations say, if they can; and let them show why the Lord performed miracles among those for whom they would not be beneficial, [Note: [Col. 0198D] These words, “and did not perform them among those for whom they would have been beneficial,” omitted in all the printed editions, have been restored from the Joliensis manuscript, and earlier from the Remigianus manuscript in the appendix to Augustine.] and did not perform them among those for whom they would have been beneficial.

Even if we cannot penetrate the reason for what he did or the depth of his judgment, we nevertheless know most clearly both that what he said is true [Col. 0198B] and that what he did is just; and that not only the Tyrians and Sidonians, but also Chorazin and Bethsaida, could have been converted and become believers from unbelievers, if the Lord had willed to work this in them. For no one can regard as false what Truth says: “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:66); and (Matt. 13:10–11): “To you it has been given to know the mystery [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “of the kingdom of God.”] of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given”; and (ibid. 11:27): “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him”; and (John 5:21): “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills”; and (1 Cor. 12:3): “No one can say [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “the Lord Jesus.”] ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

Instructed by these authoritative divine utterances, let us give thanks to God, who has given us the spirit of faith and power, of self-control and charity, of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and of his fear. If he had not given us these goods—he who works all things in all people (ibid.)—we would certainly not possess them within us. Otherwise, along with those who did not know the Lord, or who, although they knew him, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became foolish by attributing this very thing to their own wisdom, and, with their heart darkened, [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “and, with their heart darkened.”] became futile in their thoughts (Rom. 1:21), we would sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, possessing neither a complaint concerning punishment, nor an excuse based on ignorance, nor protection from nature.

[Note: [Col. 0198D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “Now also.”]

Now let us see what sort of thing follows.

## EXCERPT IX

[Col. 0198D] (Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, book III, chapter 16.)

“But,” they say, as you write, “no one can be roused by the goads of correction if this is said in the assembly of the Church, with many people listening: ‘The matter stands thus concerning the definite decree [Col. 0199A] [Note: [Col. 0199D] The printed editions read “knowledge”; the Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts, together with Augustine’s book, read “decree.”] of God’s will: some of you, having received the will to obey, will come from unbelief [Note: [Col. 0199D] The words “from unbelief” are absent from the Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts; they occur in all the printed editions and in St. Augustine’s *On the Gift of Perseverance*.] to faith; or, having received perseverance, will remain in the faith. But the others, who linger in the delight of sins, have not yet risen because the aid of merciful grace has not yet raised you. Nevertheless, if there are any of you who have not yet been called, whom grace has predestined for election, you will receive that same grace by which you may and will be elect; and if there are any of you who obey, if you have been predestined to be rejected, the powers of obedience will be withdrawn from you, so that you will cease to obey.’”

## RESPONSE

I am astonished that Your Holiness was unable to distinguish the objection of those who bring accusations from the person defending grace, and that you applied the words of the detractors to the very man who responds to his detractors. For certain people were wickedly and foolishly proclaiming this about the teaching of the Catholic man: that if someone preached God’s grace in such a way that faith and obedience, together with the other virtues and perseverance in them to the end, were believed to be obtainable only as gifts from God, it followed that he would use such words before the people and, through declarations of this kind, would avoid every exercise of free choice.

Because the most devout teacher had recognized this from the writings of those to whom he was replying, he therefore says, “But they say, as you write”; and later, “When they say these things.” [Note: [Col. 0199D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript; the other printed editions read, “therefore he says.”] From this you could have perceived that he himself was not saying these things, but rather those of whom he said, “But they say, as you write,” and, “When they say these things.” The Apostle likewise says (Rom. 3:8): “As some people slanderously claim that we say, ‘Let us do evil so that good may come.’”

Further below, where he responds to these matters more fully, it is much clearer [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “that these words are not his own.”] that such things were never said by him in this manner, and how greatly he disapproves of this form of preaching. Correcting, cleansing, and amending it, he makes it more tolerable to those who hear it, tempering what is true and cutting away what is false. After much else, he adds (the same work, chapter 22):

“Now, as for what is connected with those words, I wonder whether anyone weak in the Christian people can in any way patiently hear it when it is said to them: ‘And if there are any of you who obey, if you have been predestined to be rejected, the powers of obedience will be withdrawn from you, so that you will cease to obey.’ [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts, together with the Lyon edition, read, ‘the powers of obedience are withdrawn’; previously, the Joliensis manuscript read, ‘you obeyed.’] For what else does saying this seem to be than cursing, or in some fashion prophesying evil?”

After this, when he explained how one ought to speak about these matters before the people, he joined to it words expressing his own thought, saying (ibid.):

“I do not think that the manner which we have said should be used when preaching predestination [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “which should be used in speaking to the people”; Augustine’s *On the Gift of Perseverance* reads, “among the people.”] is sufficient for one speaking to the people, unless he adds this or something similar, saying: ‘Therefore, you ought also to hope for perseverance itself in obedience from the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes down (James 1:17), and to ask for it in your daily prayers. In doing this, you should trust that you are not strangers to the predestination of his people, because he himself also grants this very thing—that you should do it.’ [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, ‘who also grants this very thing.’]

“But let it be far from you to despair of yourselves because you are commanded to place your hope in him, not in yourselves. For cursed is everyone who places his hope in man (Jer. 17:5); and, ‘It is good to trust in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0200D] These words, ‘rather than to trust in man,’ are absent from the Joliensis manuscript.] rather than to trust in man’ (Ps. 117:8), because blessed are all who trust in him. [Note: [Col. 0200D] The printed editions read, ‘because they are blessed’; the Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts, together with the Venetian edition, read, ‘because all are blessed’; the Lyon edition reads, ‘rather than they are blessed.’] Holding fast to this hope, serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling (Ps. 2:11). [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Lovaniensis, Duacensis, and Coloniensis editions add, ‘And holding fast to this hope.’]

“For concerning eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised to the children of promise before eternal times, no one can be secure until this life—which is a time of testing upon the earth—has been brought to completion. But [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts read, ‘he will make us persevere’; the word ‘us’ is absent from the printed editions.] he will make us persevere in him until the end of this life, to whom we say every day: ‘Do not lead us into temptation’ (Matt. 6:13).”

Do you see, I ask, how far this speech differs from the one composed by the malice of the slanderers, who even strove to corrupt through a carefully contrived deception of words the things he says rightly? Concerning this same matter the teacher most rightly says (Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 22):

“It is the mark of a deceitful or inexperienced physician to bind even a useful medicine in such a way that it either does no good or does harm.”

And again, concerning a similar absurdity (ibid.):

“Certainly,” he says, “this is most true; yes indeed, but most reprehensible, most untimely, and most inappropriate; [Col. 0200C] not false in expression, but applied in a manner not beneficial to the health of human weakness.” [Note: [Col. 0200D] Thus the Joliensis and Remigianus manuscripts, together with the editions of Augustine’s works. All our printed editions instead read: “not false in expression, but not applied beneficially to the health of human weakness.”]

It is therefore unnecessary to give an account of matters which we have shown to have been said by others and rejected by him himself—yet in such a way that he allowed nothing true to be taken away from him through the admixture of falsehoods. For although he never spoke so foolishly to the Christian people, and recoiled from what lying detraction most absurdly fabricated, [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “had shuddered at it.”] nevertheless, by his devout and steadfast teaching, he abundantly proved that the Church must preach predestination, in which grace is prepared; grace, in which the effect of predestination exists; and God’s foreknowledge, by which before eternal ages he foreknew to whom he would bestow his gifts. Whoever opposes this preaching is an unmistakable ally of Pelagian arrogance.

But what you placed at the end [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Louvain editors, and those who followed them, observe here in the margin that those to whom St. Prosper replies in this book had included something here that is not printed here, from chapter 14 of Augustine’s *On the Gift of Perseverance*, beginning: “From this it is apparent that some have in their very natural capacity …”] ought to have been joined to the preceding chapter, where mention was made of the Tyrians and Sidonians, because in the body of the book it too is connected with that same matter, without the intrusion of any different discussion. Therefore the response that I appended to the preceding matters can also suffice for these [Note: [Col. 0202A] The printed editions read, “for those matters,” an obvious error corrected from the Joliensis manuscript and already corrected from the Remigianus manuscript in the Augustinian edition.], in which there is no obscurity, provided that concerning faith in predestination and the grace of God—from which comes the origin of all good things and the perseverance of merits—what is held is what the truth possesses.

# [ON THE GRACE OF GOD]

[Col. 0201]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK ENTITLED “AUTHORITIES OF THE BISHOPS OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE OF FORMER TIMES,” ON THE GRACE OF GOD AND FREE CHOICE OF THE WILL

A certain collection of authorities of earlier pontiffs of the Apostolic See concerning grace and free choice is customarily appended to Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, transmitted by Prosper and Hilary. Interspersed in it are also several decisions of African councils on this matter, approved by the Roman pontiffs. There is no doubt that this collection was intended to serve as a response to the Semi-Pelagians, who had professed that they would submit only to decrees of the Apostolic See.

They gave this collection the title: *Authorities [or Opinions] of the Bishops of the Apostolic See of Former Times, Concerning the Grace of God and Free Choice of the Will*. Others also call this little work *The Rules of the Apostolic See*, as it is designated in the final chapter. Finally, in the preface it is called *A Brief Index*, and others cite it under the title *Decrees* or *Pope Celestine’s Letter to the Gauls*; still others call it *The Chapters*, using a more general designation.

This little work is found cited under Celestine’s name at the beginning of the sixth century. For Dionysius Exiguus appended it to that pontiff’s decrees, and around the same time Peter the Deacon and others who had been sent from the East to Rome in the cause of the faith cited it in the eighth and ninth chapters of their book *On the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, addressed to Fulgentius, as a part of Celestine’s letter to the Gauls. Later, Cresconius, an African bishop, ascribed it to the same pontiff at the end of his collection of canons, issued around the year 690. Finally, in later centuries, the Chapters were attributed to Pope Celestine by Florus the Master, who wrote in the name of the Church of Lyons against Scotus Eriugena; by Hincmar of Reims, in *On Predestination*, chapter 22; by Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, in his *Collections*, question 2; by Remigius of Lyons, in *On Three Letters*, chapter 23; by Yvo of Chartres; and by many others.

On the basis of all these testimonies, it seemed abundantly established that this little work should be recognized as Celestine’s. Nevertheless, this opinion is challenged by so many contrary conjectures that we must acknowledge that nearly all critics have now abandoned it.

First, on account of the difference in style from that which appears in Celestine’s letter, it is denied that the work is by the same author. Secondly, as judges there are cited Johannes Vuendelstinus, who published the *Code of Canons and Pontifical Decrees* at Mainz in 1525; Crabius, who transcribed a somewhat moderated judgment of the former in his *Collections of Councils* in 1538; and others who did likewise, Surius in 1551 and Nicolinus in 1581. The most eminent and learned cardinals Antonius Carafa and Caesar Baronius likewise deny it to Celestine. Add to them Franciscus Suárez, *Prolegomena* 6, *On Grace*, chapter 1, section 11; Jacques Sirmond in his notes to volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*; and Gerard Vossius, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 3. The last of these nevertheless thinks that the Chapters are partly Celestine’s and partly those of Gallic disciples of Saint Augustine, because, he supposes, they were collected and presented by these men to Celestine and later published under his name and authority.

Third, if they belonged to Celestine and had been appended by him to his letter to the Gauls, how is it that they circulated for so long without his making any mention of them? Yet he says nothing about them there. Nor would he have attached this conclusion to his letter: “May God keep you safe and sound, most beloved brothers,” which demonstrates the end of Celestine’s letter.

Fourth, when Saint Prosper, attacking the Collator, piles up all the testimonies against him, both of councils and of Roman pontiffs, and presses him with the authority not only of Innocent, Zosimus, and Boniface, but also of Celestine himself, it is impious to suppose that he would have omitted anything from the decrees promulgated by the Apostolic See against the adversaries of grace. Moreover, he mentions only one letter of Celestine, namely the one to the Gauls. Although this letter greatly exalts the authority and teaching of Augustine concerning the grace of Christ, it is entirely silent concerning the specific articles and proofs of his teaching.

Fifth, Vincent of Lérins, priest and monk, praises this same letter of Celestine at great length in the final chapter of his *Commonitorium* against heresies. Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, much later likewise reviews it in his *Bibliotheca*. Yet both pass over the Chapters in equal silence. This suggests that neither had discovered them, at least not as a work of Pope Celestine. Is it also believable that Vincent would have used this letter in defense of the Semi-Pelagian position if he had recognized the Semi-Pelagians as so plainly condemned in the appended Chapters?

Sixth, the author of this compilation neither uses a manner of speaking nor claims an authority that would present him as the supreme pontiff. For although he repeatedly invokes the leaders of the Roman Church—Innocent and Zosimus, for example—he nowhere calls them his predecessors. Furthermore, he speaks throughout in such a way that he reveals himself to be a disciple of the Roman pontiffs and even of other writers, rather than a Roman pontiff. For example: “The most devout Fathers taught us”; “The writings of the Apostolic See taught us”; “They speak against our teachers.” Elsewhere: “The most sacred see of the blessed Apostle, through the ministry of its bishops,” and so forth; “the rulers of the Roman Church”; “the Apostolic bishops.”

Seventh, Dionysius Exiguus provided the occasion for the error when he appended the Chapters to Celestine’s letter. From him came Cresconius, Peter the Deacon, and all the ninth-century writers who fought for the grace of Christ. But if Dionysius’s Codex is examined more carefully, nothing will be found from which it can be established that these Chapters were part of Saint Celestine’s letter. On the contrary, the sequence of the Codex itself and the deliberately introduced marks of separation found in it loudly proclaim that Dionysius’s purpose was to distinguish one from the other.

Whenever he wishes to separate the writings of one pontiff from those of another, he always places this title at the beginning of the first decree or letter: “The decrees of Pope N. begin.” He does not repeat it at the beginning of the subsequent decrees or letters of the same pontiff.

First, this mark of distinction is found at the head of the *Authorities Concerning Grace*: “The authorities of the bishops of the Apostolic See of former times concerning the grace of God begin.”

Second, at the beginning of every letter of the same pontiff, the author’s name is never omitted. But Celestine’s name does not appear at the head of the *Opinions Concerning Grace*. From this it is conjectured either that Dionysius did not know the author’s name or that he deliberately omitted it.

Third, he placed a still greater mark of separation on this writing than on the letters of other pontiffs. For at the end of the Chapters we read this conclusion: “The authorities ... end,” with Celestine’s name omitted everywhere. No similar conclusion, or anything like it, is found at the end of the entire Codex. Thus he seems to have wished to close every path to error concerning these opinions, and to have appended this memorandum to Celestine’s letter for no other reason than that he knew it had been composed on the occasion of that letter and handed over at the same time to Prosper.

Eighth, the ancient Roman Codex, although it collected all the letters of the Roman pontiffs, whether doctrinal or decretal—including those belonging to Pope Celestine—omitted the letter to the Gauls. It can have done so for no other reason than that the letter contained no doctrinal material. But it would have contained a great deal if the Chapters had been part of the letter. Therefore this collection was not recognized as a decree of Celestine in the time of Leo, under whom it is probable that the decrees of his predecessors were inserted into the Codex.

These considerations call into question the force of the arguments previously brought forward in favor of Celestine. Consequently, some critics, seeking an author other than that pontiff, and judging that the work could not be attributed more plausibly to anyone than Saint Prosper, did not hesitate to assign it to him, despite the lack both of ancient testimonies and of manuscript evidence.

They seem to have been led to this opinion, first, by the similarity between the questions discussed by Prosper and those discussed by the author of the Chapters, as well as by the very manner of treatment. Secondly, Hincmar is brought forward as a witness. In the book he wrote *On the Non-Trinitarian Deity*, he cites the decrees of Pope Celestine, by whose commission blessed Prosper defeated and suppressed in Gaul, through the authority of Scripture and the teaching of blessed Augustine, the heresy that had arisen there.

From this, the author of this suspicion devised a distinction between the works which Prosper undertook out of private zeal and those which he wrote by commission of the supreme pontiff. In the former, he supposedly examined more obscure questions at greater length; in the latter, he touched only on very few matters, and those obvious to everyone, lest he depart too far from that brevity which is especially fitting for a profession of faith.

Yet even if it were admitted—as some think—that Prosper was commissioned by the Apostolic See to defend the Catholic Church’s teaching concerning the grace of Christ, this commission would nevertheless be narrowed excessively if it were confined to these few and very brief chapters. On that view it would be almost certain that everything Saint Prosper published concerning grace, at least after his journey to Rome, was issued by him at the direction of the Roman pontiffs, and that the propositions he defended in his books against the Semi-Pelagians were asserted by him almost as articles of faith.

To prove this, they cite a passage from Prosper’s *Responses to the Vincentian Objections*, where he says:

“Having set out sixteen chapters individually, under each one we place an exposition of our position and of the faith which we defend against the Pelagians on the authority of the Apostolic See” (*Preface to the Responses to the Vincentian Objections*).

From this the distinction proposed above disappears. On this matter, the preliminary notice to the aforesaid responses to the Vincentian objections may be consulted.

As for Hincmar, even in the passage cited he does not relate Prosper’s commission to the writing or publication of these Chapters. Rather, he relates it to everything that Prosper wrote or discussed after returning to Gaul. For Hincmar is speaking of those matters in which Prosper defeated and suppressed the heresy in Gaul through the authority of Scripture and the teaching of blessed Augustine.

But the author of the Chapters on grace fights with no argument taken from Scripture and none taken from Augustine’s teaching. He argues solely from the authority of the Roman Church: partly from pontifical decrees, partly from African decrees that the Roman Church had made its own by approving them, and finally from what was contained in its solemn prayers and ceremonies.

On the contrary, in many other passages Hincmar speaks of Prosper’s commission in such a way that he never presents him except in the person of a legate, never writing without the right and authority of a legation. Finally, neither in this passage nor anywhere else does Hincmar attribute the Chapters to Prosper. The Chapters are counted by him among Celestine’s decrees in hundreds of places and praised under that name.

As for what is objected in the earlier argument concerning the conformity of style, concepts, teaching, and even vocabulary with Prosper’s works—and what Anthelmius intends to establish before the reader through extended tables—others, such as Quesnel, likewise establish a similarity between the Leonine style and the character of the Chapters, adducing comparisons from numerous passages. Since both have done this after carefully weighing the works of both authors, the more truthful judgment may perhaps be that, in so short a work, whose parts seem so little connected with one another, nothing certain can be established from style alone.

Finally, Quesnel assigned this same collection to Leo, although he had argued that it belonged neither to Celestine nor to Prosper. He had already asserted that Leo was the author of the two books *On the Calling of the Nations*. He thinks that Leo compiled this brief index—not after he had become pontiff, but while serving as a deacon and ministering to Pope Celestine. In both works, he professes to have detected the same intelligence and purpose, and the same style.

First, both writings have the same aim: to establish precisely what a Catholic ought to believe concerning the mystery of divine predestination and grace, setting aside more obscure questions.

Second, in both works the Semi-Pelagians, rather than the Pelagians, are attacked, but with the same moderation and restraint.

Third, both authors suppress the name and authority of Saint Augustine. This was deliberate, because the Semi-Pelagians reproached Augustine as having exceeded the proper measure in discussing grace.

Fourth, the same argument is drawn from the Church’s prayers—not always in the same terms, but with the same method and structure of expression.

The remaining points may be read in the same editor and annotator of Saint Leo’s works, pages 399–405.

Now, concerning the time and occasion when these Chapters were written, and how they came to be attributed to Celestine and appended to his letter, the following conjecture is permissible.

After the death of Saint Augustine, which occurred in August of the year 430, certain Gallican presbyters, with the connivance of their bishops, rose up with particular vehemence against the writings of the most holy teacher of grace. Prosper and Hilary went to Rome to seek the aid and authority of the Apostolic See.

Celestine was then seated at Rome, and the archdeacon Leo was rendering outstanding service in administering ecclesiastical affairs. After Prosper explained the reason for his journey, he received from Celestine a letter to be delivered to the Gallican bishops. In it, the memory and teaching of Saint Augustine are commended in a remarkable manner and defended against the calumnies of his opponents.

Those Gallican presbyters had attacked Augustine’s teaching chiefly because they believed it opposed the teaching of the Roman See. This was the reason Prosper had gone to Rome, as the pontiff’s letter itself sufficiently indicates. In it, Celestine does only one thing: he teaches the Gauls that there is nothing in Augustine’s writings that differs from the teaching of the Apostolic See; indeed, that Augustine had always been regarded by the bishops of the Roman See as one of the Church’s finest teachers.

Celestine even ordered the archives of the Apostolic See to be carefully searched, so that whatever could serve to repel the arrogance of the Gauls might be brought out and handed over to Prosper, who had gone to Rome for this purpose. It is proved by many indications that this task may then have fallen to Leo, who was still a deacon. From these materials Leo composed this memorial index [Col. 0205] and handed it over to Prosper, together with other writings of the same kind, so that it might be useful to him in refuting the objections of the Massilians.

From all these considerations it seems more probable to us that this memorandum was compiled by Leo, perhaps at Celestine’s command, and entrusted to Prosper’s use. It therefore belongs to the same period as the preceding letter, namely the year 431.

[Col. 0205]

# THE BOOK OF SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITAINE ENTITLED “AUTHORITIES OF THE BISHOPS OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE OF FORMER TIMES, CONCERNING THE GRACE OF GOD AND FREE CHOICE OF THE WILL”

[Note: [Col. 0205A] Collected around the year 431.]

(C, G)*

## Preface

Formerly CHAPTER III.

[Col. 0205A] 271 Since certain people who boast of the Catholic name, but remain attached to the condemned opinions of the heretics, whether through perversity or ignorance, presume to oppose devout disputants; and although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Celestius, nevertheless speak against our teachers as though they had exceeded the necessary measure; and profess that they follow and approve only what the most sacred see of the blessed Apostle Peter has decreed and taught against the enemies of God’s grace through the ministry of its bishops, it was necessary to investigate carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged concerning the heresy that had arisen in their times, and what they had considered ought to be held concerning God’s grace against the most destructive defenders of free choice.

Accordingly, we have joined to them certain opinions of the African councils, which the Apostolic bishops certainly made their own when they approved them. [Note: [Col. 0205A] The Mainz, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read, “when they approved them”; the Augustinian appendix edition, from the Corbeiensis manuscripts and the edition of Leo’s works, and Quesnel’s edition, as in the text.]

Therefore, so that those who have doubts about any point may be more fully instructed, we set forth the constitutions of the holy Fathers in a concise index. If anyone is not excessively contentious, he may recognize that the connection of all the discussions depends upon the brevity of the authorities set out below, and that no reason for contradiction remains if he believes and says, together with Catholics:

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0205]

## CHAPTER I

Formerly CHAPTER IV. That Adam injured all human beings, and that no one can be saved except through the grace of Christ.

[Col. 0205B]

In Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost their natural capacity and innocence, and no one can rise from the depth of that ruin through free choice unless the grace of the merciful God raises him up. Pope Innocent of blessed memory declares this and says in his letter to the Council of Carthage (see among Innocent’s letters, volume XX of our edition):

“For he, having experienced free choice, while using his own goods too heedlessly, fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression, and found nothing by which he could rise from there. Deceived in his freedom forever, [Note: [Col. 0205B] Thus the manuscripts and the Mainz edition of 1524, and in Augustine, volume II, and volume X of the appendix. In the new edition of Leo: ‘he would have lain crushed beneath the ruin of this.’ Other editions of Prosper: ‘he would have lain crushed beneath the ruin.’] he would have remained hidden beneath the oppression of this ruin unless the coming of Christ, in accordance with his grace, had afterward restored him. Through the cleansing of new birth, he purged every former fault by the washing of his baptism.” [Note: [Col. 0206B] In the Corbeiensis manuscripts: “the fault of the past.”]

## CHAPTER II

Formerly CHAPTER V. That no one is good by his own powers except through participation in him who alone is good.

No one is good by himself unless he is granted participation in him who alone is good. The opinion of that same pontiff bears witness to this in the same writings, saying (see above):

“For what judgment should we henceforth form concerning the minds of those who think that they owe to themselves the fact that they are good, and who do not consider him whose grace they receive every day, while they trust that they can attain as much without him?” [Note: [Col. 0206B] The Mainz edition reads, “What should we think of them?” Augustine, volume II: “concerning the right minds of those ...” The fuller passage is given in the note below.]

[Note: [Col. 0207D] This passage is read more fully in Letter 181 among Augustine’s letters, as follows: “But now those who are such receive no grace from God, since without him they trust that they can attain as much as even those who ask him scarcely deserve to receive.”]

## CHAPTER III

Formerly CHAPTER VI. That unless we are continually assisted by God’s grace, we cannot overcome the devil’s snares.

No one renewed by the grace of baptism is capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and [Note: [Col. 0207D] Thus the Corbeiensis manuscripts and the edition of this letter in the appendix to volume X of Augustine; all the Prosperian printed editions and the new Leo read, “and defeating.”] conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he receives perseverance in a good way of life. The teaching of the same bishop confirms this in the same pages, saying (see above):

“For although he redeemed the human being from former sins, [Note: [Col. 0207D] Augustine, volume II, and Leo read, “had redeemed.”] nevertheless, knowing that he could sin again, he preserved many things for his restoration, so that he might also correct him after these sins. He provides daily remedies, [Note: [Col. 0207D] Thus the Mainz edition, in Innocent’s letter in volume II of Augustine’s works, and in volume X of the appendix. The other Prosperian manuscripts add the conjunction *atque* (‘and’). The new edition of Leo, omitting this conjunction, reads: “he who provides daily remedies.”] and unless we rely on them and strive with confidence, we will in no way be able to overcome human errors. For it is necessary that, by whose help we conquer, when he does not help us, by that same one we are again conquered.”

## CHAPTER IV

Formerly CHAPTER VII. That through Christ we make good use of free choice.

That no one makes good use of free choice except through Christ, the same teacher proclaims in his letter to the Council of Milevis, saying (see above):

“Recognize at last, O perverse teaching of most perverse minds, that freedom itself deceived the first human being, so that, while using its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression, and could not be rescued from it unless the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, had restored to him the condition of his original freedom.” [Note: [Col. 0208D] In Innocent’s letter in Augustine, volume II, the passage begins with these words: “O perverse teaching of most perverse minds! Let it recognize at last that the first human being ...”; then follows *fell*, where others read *would have fallen*. The same is found in Leo’s edition, which later has *could have* in place of *could*, and at the end *by his coming* instead of *through his advent*.]

## CHAPTER V

Formerly CHAPTER VIII. That all the merits of the saints are gifts of God.

[Col. 0207C]

That all the efforts, all the works, and all the merits of the saints are to be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him for any reason other than what he himself has given. The authoritative rule of the blessed memory of Pope Zosimus directs us to this view, when, writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says (this letter is not extant): “But we, prompted by God—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—have reported everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.” The bishops of Africa revered this discourse, shining with the purest light of truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man as follows (nor is this letter extant) [Col. 0207D]: “But what you placed in your letter, which you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Nevertheless, prompted by God,’ and so forth, we understood you to have said it in such a way that, with the sword of truth drawn in judgment, you cut down, as if passing swiftly across the course, those who exalt the freedom of human choice against God’s assistance [Col. 0208A]. For what did you attribute to free choice more than the fact that you referred everything to the conscience of our humility, and yet faithfully and wisely saw, and truthfully and confidently declared, that this had been done by God’s prompting?” [Note: The Mainz edition has “as if passing across the course.”] “This is so because the will is prepared by the Lord, and, so that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with fatherly inspirations.” [Note: Printed editions have “may touch the hearts of the faithful.” The reading “touches the hearts of his children,” found more suitably in manuscripts and in the appendix to volume X of Augustine’s works, is preferable.] “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14), so that we neither feel that our free choice is absent nor doubt that, in each movement of the human will toward whatever is good, his assistance is more powerful.

## CHAPTER VI. Also CHAPTER IX. That every holy thought and movement of a devout will is from God

[Col. 0208B]

God works in human hearts, and in free choice itself, in such a way that a holy thought, a devout plan, and every movement of a good will are from God, because through him we can do something good, whereas without him we can do nothing. The same teacher trained us in this confession when, speaking to the bishops of the whole world about the help of divine grace, he said (as above): “What time, then,” he says, “intervenes when we do not need his help?” In all actions, causes, thoughts, and movements, an assistant and protector must be entreated. [Note: In Leo, “causes, thoughts”; the reading is not objectionable.] For it is arrogant that human nature should presume anything for itself, while the Apostle cries out: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). And as he himself says again: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24); and again: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty, but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

## CHAPTER VII. Also CHAPTER X. That the grace of God not only forgives sins but also helps prevent them and enables the law to be fulfilled—not, as Pelagius says, merely making it easier, as though, without God’s grace, it could still be fulfilled, though not easily

We also embrace as proper to the apostolic see what was established in the decrees of the Council of Carthage, namely what was defined in its third canon [Col. 0208D] (see the Appendix, p. 272): “If anyone says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the forgiveness of sins already committed, and not also for assistance so that they may not be committed [Col. 0209A], let him be anathema.”

And again, in the fourth canon: “If anyone says that the grace of God through Jesus Christ helps us not to sin for this reason alone, that through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what we ought to avoid, but does not also grant us that we should love and be able to do what we have recognized ought to be done, let him be anathema.” [Note: The Council of Carthage and Leo’s edition of the works read “through it.”]

Since the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1), it is extremely impious to believe that we have the grace of Christ for the knowledge that puffs us up, but not for the love that builds up, since both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do and loving so that we may do it, so that, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff us up. Just as it is written of God, “who teaches man knowledge” (Ps. 93:10), so it is also written: “Love is from God” (1 John 4:7).

Again, in the fifth canon [Note: Thus the edition in the appendix to volume X of Augustine’s works, from the Corbie manuscripts, and Leo’s edition; the others omit “Again,” reading simply “In the fifth chapter.”]: “If anyone says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason, so that what we are commanded to do by free choice we may more easily fulfill through grace—as though, if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema.” [Note: This wording is found in the Corbie manuscripts and in the Augustinian edition of the works. Other editions, however, read *jubeamur*; and several lines later, “without me, nothing [is] more difficult.” But this is less correct, except that in Leo the earlier reading too is *jubemur*, not *jubeamur*.]

The Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do it only with greater difficulty,” but said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

## CHAPTER VIII. Also CHAPTER XI. That, besides the decrees of the apostolic see, all the prayers of the Church of Christ resound with grace, by which the human race is restored from eternal condemnation

[Col. 0209C]

Besides the inviolable decrees of the most blessed apostolic see, by which our most devout fathers, having cast down the destructive arrogance of novelty, taught us to refer to the grace of Christ both the beginnings of good will, the growth of worthy efforts, and perseverance in them to the end [Note: The Douai and Cologne editions, together with Leo’s works, read “having cast down the destructive arrogance of novelty.”], let us also consider the sacramental prayers of the priests. Handed down from the apostles, they are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in the whole Catholic Church, so that the law of prayer establishes the law of belief.

For when the bishops of holy peoples, carrying out a mission entrusted to one another, plead before the divine mercy, they act on behalf of the human race. With the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith may be granted to unbelievers, that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety [Col. 0209D], that, when the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews, that heretics may recover their senses through reception of the Catholic faith [Note: The manuscripts have “through perfection”], that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed love, that the remedies of repentance may be conferred upon the fallen, and finally that, when catechumens have been brought to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.

The effect of these very things shows that they are not asked of the Lord perfunctorily or in vain [Col. 0210A]. For God deigns to draw many from every kind of error, transferring them, rescued from the power of darkness, into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1:13), and making vessels of mercy out of vessels of wrath (Rom. 9:22). The whole of this is perceived to be so entirely the work of God that thanksgiving and confession of praise are continually offered to God, who brings it about, for the illumination or correction of such people.

## CHAPTER IX. Also CHAPTER XII. That the purifying rite established for those to be baptized also testifies to God’s grace, when unclean spirits are driven from them by exorcisms and insufflations

[Col. 0210B]

Let us not contemplate casually what the holy Church uniformly performs throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not first approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven from them by the exorcisms and insufflations of the clergy. Thus it truly becomes evident how “the prince of this world” is cast out (John 12:31), and how the strong man is first bound and afterward his goods are plundered (Matt. 12:29; Mark 3:27): they are transferred into the possession of the victor, who “led captivity captive” (Ps. 68:19) and “gave gifts to men” (Eph. 4:8).

By these ecclesiastical rules, therefore, and by teachings drawn from divine authority, we have been conformed—perhaps, “confirmed”—with the Lord’s help [Col. 0210C], so that we profess God to be the author of all good affections, works, efforts, and virtues by which one strives toward God from the beginning of faith. We do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good. By this assistance and gift of God free choice is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes sound, and what was imprudent becomes provident.

For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes our merits to be what are actually his gifts, and, for what he has bestowed, he will grant eternal rewards. He acts within us so that we may both will and do what he wills; nor does he permit those things that he has given us for exercise to lie idle within us or to be neglected. Thus we may be fellow workers with God’s grace; and if we see that something in us is growing weak through our own negligence, let us hasten anxiously back to him who heals all our diseases and redeems our life from destruction (Ps. 103:3), and to whom we say daily: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13).

## CHAPTER X. Also CHAPTER XIII. That deeper questions are neither to be despised nor wholly asserted

277 [Col. 0211A]

[Note: These final words of the chapter have provided learned scholars with much material for debate, so that it might be determined what the author of this collection intended by those deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise—questions which he neither dares to despise nor considers it necessary to assert. Perhaps it should not be regarded as especially necessary to investigate with great effort what one who did not think it right to speak openly intended to signify; nor should one think that any difficulty can be clarified from an obscure passage. Hence a learned man observes that, in all the disputes concerning the grace of Christ that arose in the ninth century, no one used this passage to refute any particular opinion, and that even the Semi-Pelagians are never reported to have attempted to draw it over to their side. This article of the work establishes only one thing with certainty: nothing can be extracted from it that diminishes the work of grace. Nor can this passage be used to attack anything established throughout the whole course of this collection, or in Celestine’s letter itself, or anything proved to have a necessary connection with these matters. Nor is there any reason to suspect that this passage concerns the beginning of faith or the predestination of the saints. For the entire dispute between Prosper and the Semi-Pelagians concerned precisely this matter, and it is most plainly evident that Celestine approves Prosper’s teaching in the same way that he rejects the Semi-Pelagians’ positions. If any doubt nevertheless remained concerning the present article, it is dispelled by what Pope Hormisdas declares in his letter to Possessor, cited by the African bishops exiled in Sardinia. Letter 15 among the Fulgentian letters: “What the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and preserves concerning free choice and God’s grace can be known abundantly from Augustine’s various books, especially those addressed to Prosper and Hilary, which are precisely his books on the predestination of the saints.” On this subject, one may consult more extensively both the editor and annotator of the works of St. Leo, vol. II, pp. 407 ff., and the author of the *Bibliotheca nova ecclesiasticorum auctorum*, vol. IV, pp. 90–91.]

But the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise, which those who resisted heretics treated at greater length [278], just as we do not dare to despise, so we do not consider it necessary to assert. For, in order to confess the grace of God, from whose work and gracious favor nothing at all must be removed, we believe it sufficient to affirm whatever the writings of the apostolic see have taught us according to the rules stated above, so that we absolutely do not regard as Catholic anything that appears contrary to the propositions set forth.

# AGAINST THE COLLATOREM

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE BOOK OF ST. PROSPER AGAINST THE COLLATOREM

Among the critics of the doctrine defended by St. Augustine in his books against the Pelagians, especially in his later works, the most distinguished and learned was John Cassian, a presbyter and abbot of Massilia, a city of Gaul that was by no means obscure. As seems most probable, he was born in Scythia Minor, one of the provinces of Thrace, perhaps around the year 350 or 360. He was educated in one of the monasteries near the Bethlehem manger and was moderately well trained in the liberal arts. Prosper acknowledges that Cassian excelled in the practice of debate among those with whom he lived at Massilia. After traveling through Egypt, hearing the distinguished inhabitants of the Egyptian deserts, and himself living for some time as an anchorite, he went to Constantinople, where St. John Chrysostom ordained him deacon and later raised him to the dignity of the priesthood. After visiting Rome in A.D. 405, he returned to Massilia around 415 at the latest. There he built two monasteries, one for men and the other for women, and presided over the former, which has been distinguished from that time to the present by the name of St. Victor.

While living there, at the request of Castor, bishop of the Church of Apt in the Second Narbonensis, he composed the *Institutions*, adapted to govern the monks whom Castor had established. It is clear that he wrote these while the controversies concerning grace were still burning, since even then he is observed to favor Augustine’s doctrine far less than he ought to have done. He had been forestalled by this erroneous principle: that the work of our salvation takes its beginning from us, through the merit of good will, and is afterward brought to completion by God. This means that we distinguish ourselves from ourselves, that we possess something we have not received, and consequently that we can glory not in the Lord but in ourselves. Yet one may reasonably infer that Cassian expressed these views before the judgments issued against the Pelagians by Innocent or Zosimus; after their condemnation he would not have dared to affirm, together with such heretics, that nothing other than the law could be called the help of divine grace.

By the same author and speaker, he also undertook to commit to writing a series of spiritual conferences that he had held with Eastern monks. He dedicated the first ten, after the premature death of his friend Castor, to Leontius, bishop of Fréjus, and to Helladius, who was not yet a bishop. He composed the following seven, persuaded by the prayers of the saints Honoratus of Arles and Eucherius of Lyons, later bishops, in the year 426, somewhat later. In these *Conferences*, besides much that was extremely useful for the instruction of the monks of Lérins, for whose use they were intended, and besides material worthy of the praises with which Cassian has been honored by many learned and holy men, various passages hostile to St. Augustine’s doctrine concerning grace are scattered throughout them, especially in almost the whole of the thirteenth conference.

In this matter Cassian was more dangerously mistaken than in other matters, both because of the dignity of the subject and because of the circumstances of the time. The errors of the Pelagians had first been condemned at Rome in 418 and immediately afterward by many councils of the Eastern regions, whereas he published this thirteenth conference in 426. In it the same error is expressed more specifically, although a sufficiently clear trace of it had already been detected in the third conference.

When a man of such authority as Cassian was putting forward a new dogma in the very heat of the controversies—a dogma which, as Prosper observed, was neither wholly consistent with the heresy condemned by the Church nor entirely in agreement with the doctrine of St. Augustine, who had played the greatest part in the condemnation of the Pelagians—it was altogether impossible that considerable disturbance should not arise. Cassian could not reject the errors inserted into the conference by attributing them to the abbot Chaeremon, whom he had introduced as the speaker, since he testified that he himself embraced and approved them with all his strength. Indeed, when he published the *Conferences*, it was his intention to bring forth his own views through them, while he simultaneously extolled with great praises the doctrine of those whom he pretended to have entrusted with the task of teaching. From other passages too it was sufficiently clear that he approved all the statements of Abbot Chaeremon. He showed this clearly enough by neither rejecting this doctrine nor demonstrating that it could be called into question by even the slightest objection.

Hence it happened that many in our Gaul, especially among the servants of God—a name ordinarily used for monks—who lived at Massilia, rose up against Augustine’s doctrine. There is no doubt that they had been led into error by Cassian’s authority, together with other followers of his. These Massilian monks were distinguished men, outstanding in the pursuit of every virtue. Among most people there was such reverence for the contemplation of their moral excellence that they regarded as completely safe whatever they heard asserted by men whose authority they followed without judgment. Among them Cassian was considered the most learned; he alone had not been afraid to publish his thoughts in writing.

At first they acted more cautiously, preferring to blame their own slowness to understand than to criticize what they had not understood in Augustine’s writings. Some of them even requested a clearer and more explicit exposition of his position on the matter. It later became evident, however, that their darkness arose no less from pride—for those whose virtues are held in high esteem by human beings are especially exposed to it—than from natural ignorance or weakness.

For when a copy of the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, which Augustine had sent in 427 to instruct the monks of Hadrumetum, happened to be brought to Gaul, he answered in that book, as though deliberately, all the objections of the Massilians. Once they should have turned the light shining in that book to their own improvement and dispelled the clouds of all their doubts, they instead blazed forth with greater hatred of the truth than before. Among other objections, they alleged that before Augustine none of the ecclesiastical writers had applied passages of Paul to the meaning of predestination. This objection fits no one better than Cassian, who had been nourished on Greek books, from which the occasion for this objection could most readily have arisen.

For this reason Prosper and Hilary wrote to St. Augustine around 428 or 429, and he replied with the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. It is not clear in what spirit the Gauls received those books; it is clear, however, that the disturbances caused by such disagreements did not immediately cease.

While Augustine was still alive, St. Prosper wrote a letter to Rufinus in which he declared that he hoped this from the riches of God’s mercy: that those whom God was then allowing, through the free choice by which they were deceived, to wander from the path of humility would not be entirely, or to the end, deprived of understanding; rather, God delayed recalling them from their advance into remoter regions so that the work of his grace might be celebrated with greater glory, since he would also subject to himself the hearts of those who opposed him, whose pursuit of virtue had become a danger and whose moral integrity had become a peril. It is reasonably questioned whether this last statement ought not to be understood of Cassian, who was evidently farther from the truth than the others, if not in his dogmas, at least in the manner in which he defended them.

After Augustine had been taken up among the blessed, Prosper and Hilary approached Pope Celestine to present their complaints against certain presbyters who were stirring up dissensions in Gaul against the doctrine of St. Augustine and were not even sparing his reputation. In that famous reply of his, which may be read above, Celestine reproved those who, possessing only the rank of presbyter, did not fear to judge the doctrine of the Church according to their own pleasure and arrogated to themselves an authority belonging only to bishops. Cassian may perhaps have been specifically indicated by these words. This is all the easier to infer because, according to Gennadius, the first among the bishops to whom the letter was addressed was Venerius, bishop of the Massilians.

Yet Celestine’s letter did not calm the disturbances or restore peace to the churches of the provinces. When Xystus, or Sixtus III, was given as Celestine’s successor—according to Baronius, on 26 April 432, or a few months later—it became necessary for St. Prosper once again to undertake in writing the defense of Augustine’s doctrine, which calumnious writings continually sought to bring into hatred. To make clear to everyone into what errors those who opposed so great a teacher were slipping, Prosper undertook to overturn Cassian’s thirteenth conference. Cassian surpassed all Augustine’s opponents in doctrinal importance, and he could not deny the writings he had published. Prosper nevertheless did not wish to designate him by his proper name. Instead, he gave the book the title *Against the Collator*, that is, against the author of the *Conferences*. Cassian is known to have still been alive at that time.

Cassian had taught chiefly that the beginning of good will and faith sometimes arose from God and sometimes from human beings; that the seeds of virtue should be recognized within us; that free choice could naturally incline toward the good; that it was sometimes anticipated by grace, while the gifts of grace were often preceded by its movements. St. Prosper proves that all these positions follow from the doctrines of the Pelagians. From them it follows that grace is given according to human merits and that human nature was not damaged by Adam’s sin. Such errors had long since been proscribed, together with the Pelagian doctrines, in various synods of bishops and in letters and decrees issued against them by the supreme pontiffs. Finally, St. Augustine had torn them out by the roots and scattered them in many writings. For this reason Pope Gelasius counted Cassian’s writings among the apocrypha around the year 494, at a council of bishops held at Rome.

To bring as much light as possible to the distinguished work of our Prosper, therefore, it seemed useful to readers that I should arrange for Cassian’s thirteenth conference itself to precede Prosper’s reply in full. The work will be read without danger—and indeed not without some benefit—if, though otherwise dangerous when read by itself, it is compared with the invincible reply of so eminent a teacher.

[Col. 0213]

# THE BOOK OF ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE ON THE GRACE OF GOD AND FREE CHOICE

[Note: In the very ancient Corbie manuscript, written nearly nine hundred years ago, the title of this little work is: “The book of St. Prosper for the preachers of the grace of God, against the book of Cassian the presbyter, entitled *On the Protection of God*.” In the Joli manuscript, about five hundred years old: “Here begins Prosper’s book against the book of Cassian the presbyter, entitled *On the Protection of God*; that is, against the thirteenth conference, held with Abbot Chaeremon.” The Lyons edition of 1539: “The book of the divine Prosper against Cassian the Collator, on the Grace of God.” The Mainz edition of 1524 and those that followed: “The book of St. Prosper [of Aquitaine] on the Grace of God and Free Choice, for the defense of …,” while the Venetian edition gives it the title *On the Protection of God*.—The book *Against the Collator* was written around A.D. 432.]

# THE BOOK AGAINST THE COLLATOREM, THAT IS, FOR THE DEFENSE OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST THE BOOK OF CASSIAN THE PRESBYTER, WHICH IS ENTITLED *ON THE PROTECTION OF GOD* (C)

[Note: It examines twelve definitions of John Cassian concerning grace and free choice, contained in his thirteenth conference, and teaches that, with the exception of the first, they all disagree entirely with Catholic truth. It demonstrates that Augustine’s critics both raise vain objections, attack what is right, and defend what is wrong; and that, by turning against the Church the very weapons of the already defeated Pelagians, they rebel simultaneously against the divine Scriptures and the ecclesiastical and imperial constitutions.]

## 307 CHAPTER I. The calumniators of St. Augustine’s doctrine bring matters to the point that the enemies of grace are believed to have been unjustly condemned by the Church. Hence arises the greater necessity of refuting them

[Col. 0215A]

Some dare to say that the grace of God, by which we are Christians, was not rightly defended by Augustine, bishop of holy memory, and they do not cease to attack with immoderate calumnies his books composed against the Pelagian error. The domestic malice that murmurs within would deserve no less contempt than the heretical loquacity that barks from outside, unless, once the wolves had been driven outside the Lord’s fold, those who are under the name of sheep should lend them support (Matt. 7:15) [Note: [Col. 0215C] Thus the Corbie, Remigian, and Joli manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions and the appendix to St. Augustine’s works; the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read, after “wolves,” “they should lend support under the name of sheep.”], and unless they were such that neither their ecclesiastical rank nor their abilities appeared deserving of contempt.

For, although they have the appearance of godliness (2 Tim. 3:5), in their zeal for that power whose presence in their understanding they deny, they draw many uneducated people to themselves and trouble hearts lacking discernment of spirits [Note: The Joli manuscript has this reading. The Louvain, Antwerp, Lyons, Douai, and Cologne editions have “lacking the spirit of discernment.” The first Mainz edition, published in 1524 from a manuscript of the Benedictines of Mount St. James, has “discernments of spirits”; the Corbie manuscript and the Venetian edition agree. St. Prosper alludes to 1 Cor. 12:10. The Lyons edition and the Remigian manuscript read the passage differently: “so that neither their rank nor their abilities appear deserving of contempt; for, although they have the appearance of godliness in their zeal … they disturb many … and strive to bring the Church’s cause into such a condition …”], they trouble hearts. They strive to bring the Church’s cause into such a condition that, while asserting that our people had not spoken truthfully in defense of grace [Note: [Col. 0215D] The Joli manuscript, with the Mainz and Venetian editions, adds *fuisse* (“had been”).], they persuade others that the enemies of grace were unjustly condemned. This evil, then, must not be neglected, since it grows daily from hidden and insignificant seeds [Note: The Joli and Corbie manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions and the new edition of Augustine, have this reading. Others have “from corrupt seeds.” The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions place “or small” in the margin.], spreading more broadly and farther from its origin. Rather, we must strive, insofar as the Lord helps, to expose the hypocrisy of these deceitful calumniators. From the very magnitude of the injury which, in one man, they have inflicted upon all, and especially upon the pontiffs of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0216C] In the Joli manuscript the words “that is, blessed Augustine, whom the supreme pontiffs praised” follow “in one man”; but we suspect this to be a mere scribal gloss. The Lyons edition has “upon the pontificate of the apostolic see.”], they are judged by the unlearned and incautious to possess superior knowledge, and by a miserable and perverse success they readily obtain agreement with their falsehood [Note: [Col. 0216C] The Remigian manuscript and the Mainz and Venetian editions read *facili mendacio* (“by an easy falsehood”); the Joli manuscript has *facile* for *facilem*.], because by presumption they have gained reverence for themselves.

For, since they are men of good reputation, it is in no way believed that they could have burst into the outcry of a superfluous complaint through slowness of understanding or rashness of judgment [Note: [Col. 0216C] The Mainz and Venetian editions read “into the then stricter judgment and the outcry of their own complaint.” These words are wholly absent from the Lyons edition; omitting *in*, it reads “at the conclusion of a superfluous complaint.”] [Col. 0216C]; rather, people think that they labored with great intelligence and vigorous zeal [Note: The Lyons edition omits “zeal”], so that, after grasping the arguments of a most subtle writer, a stricter judgment and more penetrating examination might now discover what previously secure favor and careless benevolence had not seen.

### 2. From where, then, did this diligence of such a severe examination arise?

[Note: The Lyons edition has “From where, then, did this judgment arise?”]

From where did this brow arm itself with such a harsh expression [Note: The Augustinian appendix, together with the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz and Venetian editions, has this reading. The Lyons edition has “armed such a brow with such a gloomy countenance”; the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions have “armed itself with the brow of such a gloomy countenance.” The Joli manuscript has “armed itself with the brow of a gloomy countenance.”] that an insidious examiner should weigh the measures of meanings, the weights of expressions, and the numbers of syllables, and presume that he had accomplished something great if he fastened the mark of error upon a Catholic preacher? It is as though some previously unknown work, hidden until now, were being attacked [Note: The Venetian edition has “which had until now.”], rather than the doctrine that is being torn by these bites—the doctrine that scattered the inventions of the new heretics and crushed the devilish swelling of Pelagian arrogance.

More than twenty years have passed since the Catholic army, under this man’s leadership, began to fight against the enemies of God’s grace and to conquer [Note: The Joli manuscript, the Corbie manuscript, the Mainz edition, and the Venetian edition have this reading. Later editions have “more than twenty years”; they omit *sunt quod*. Augustine began to fight the Pelagian heresy in A.D. 412, in the books *On the Merits of Sins* and *On the Baptism of Infants*, addressed to Marcellinus. Prosper’s book therefore appeared more than twenty years afterward, around A.D. 432.]. And I say that it conquers, because it does not allow those whom it has defeated to breathe again, and because, for their destruction, it has written the same sentence with the hand of all the priests [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions and the Augustinian appendix, based on the Corbie manuscript, have this reading. The Lyons edition omits “and,” as do later editions. “It conquers,” I say, because it does not allow what it conquers to breathe, and because, for the destruction of those whom it conquered, it wrote one sentence with the hand of all the priests.].

Driven from the pontificate and deprived of communion, they complain of the success of our victory and arm their tongues against us, having preferred exile from the truth to being citizens of the Church [Note: [Col. 0217C] The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “as though concerning the success of our victory.” The Joli manuscript omits “as though.” The Mainz edition joins the following clause to this one and, for “they complain, they arm,” reads “they complain, they arm”; the Venetian edition does the same, but distinguishes the sense from what precedes by a comma and an initial capital.]. But why do our fellow members and fellow sharers in the grace of Christ [Note: [Col. 0217C] The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “and fellow sharers … defended”; the Joli and Corbie manuscripts, the Augustinian edition, and the Mainz and Venetian editions read as in the text.] complain about the weapons by which the common faith was defended? (See Valentinian’s Constitution, below, Appendix, p. 272.) (See Valentinian’s Constitution, below, Appendix, p. 272.) Why do they reopen the war that has been concluded and weaken the defenses of a peace long secure? Do the victors displease them, while the defeated please them? Are the condemned errors cherished with such insolence that, through hatred of wickedness, our authors and judges are attacked? [Note: [Col. 0217C] The Lyons edition reads only “the authors displease,” omitting the remaining words.]

Or has the standard of these new censors so precisely regulated itself [Note: The Lyons edition has “the standard of new opinions.”] that it asserts none of the things that were cut away and rejects some of those that were defended [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions have “so that it also asserts none of the things that were cut away.” The Joli manuscript has “they assert … they reject.”]? Behold, with the peace of Catholic victory preserved and the reverence due to the indissoluble decrees maintained, we are ready to hear the advocates of a more corrected doctrine and to recognize the lines of the most subtle discernment, cut free from every error [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions have “the most subtle lines.”].

Let what arose from new minds be brought forward [Note: The Joli manuscript has “be brought forward publicly.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read “Let them bring forward,” and then continue as one sentence through “loquacity has intemperately poured forth.” The phrase “of one” is distinguished in the same way in the Louvain edition.] [Col. 0217D].

## CHAPTER II. Why he attacks Cassian’s definitions in particular. Cassian’s first Catholic definition. From whom the definition is later introduced that teaches that many come to grace without grace.

1. And lest we seem to be attacking, in order to obscure the knowledge of the learned, those things which the ignoble and insolent loquacity of fools pours forth immoderately, we shall report chiefly the definitions of one man who, beyond doubt, surpasses all those others in the study of the sacred Scriptures. [Col. 0217C–0218A]

[Note: In the Mainz and Venetian editions, after “we shall report” there follows: “whose decrees ought meanwhile to be brought forward for this reason alone, because whether they are so constituted …” This same wording is also found in the Corbie manuscript, but inserted after “ought to be taken up”; in that codex, before “which alone for this reason,” the particle “also” is prefixed. Elsewhere this indicates that one of the two statements has been adopted from another source. In the Remigius manuscript: “of which elsewhere”; “which alone for this reason ought meanwhile to be taken up for discussion”; “the decrees ought meanwhile to be brought forward for this reason alone.” The Jumièges manuscript has: “whose secrets ought for this reason alone to be brought forward.”]

These too ought meanwhile to be taken up for discussion for this sole reason: that there can be no doubt whether matters stand thus.
