[Note: The Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges manuscripts have “purified.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read: “for they have been written and purified in the edition of their author,” referring to the decrees.] For they have been written and published in an edition by their author; and it is no longer necessary to ask whether they exist, but what they teach must be demonstrated.

Thus, in the book whose title is *On the Protection of God*, a certain priestly man, Cassian, [Note: The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions add “of the order.” It is absent from the Corbie manuscript and from the Mainz and Venetian editions.] who, among those with whom he lives, excels in the practice of disputation, [Note: The Jumièges manuscript, and the Mainz and Venetian editions, read “with whom”; the Lyons edition, “with whom he has dealt”; all the others, “with whom he lives.”] introduces a certain abbot, Chaeremon, discussing the grace of God and free choice. Cassian shows that he has approved and accepted Chaeremon’s opinion in every respect. Consequently, our dispute is no longer with Chaeremon, who might perhaps have refuted such opinions of his own by denying them or dissolved them by correcting them, but with Cassian, who deliberately brought forward such a doctrine as an instrument of the enemies of God’s grace. [Col. 0218B]

2. [Note: The appendix to Augustine, volume X, based on the Corbie manuscript, reads “which nevertheless—that is, Cassian.” All the other editions, together with the Jumièges and Remigius manuscripts, have “which nevertheless,” with “doctrine” understood.] Yet at the beginning of his discussion it does not depart from the piety of truth, and would deserve to be honored with well-deserved praise, had he not, by a precipitous and oblique progress, [Note: The Lyons edition reads “by a gentle progress,” apparently less suitably.] strayed from the uprightness with which he began.

For, after the comparison of a farmer, whose pattern he adapted to that of one living under grace and faith, [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “whose form … of one living”; perhaps, “to one living.”] and whose labor he declared fruitless unless he were assisted in every respect by God’s help, he introduced a most Catholic definition, saying:

“From these considerations it is plainly gathered that not only the beginning of actions but also the beginning of good thoughts is from God: he inspires in us both the beginnings of holy willing and grants us the strength and opportunity to carry out the things we rightly desire” (James 1:17). [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “principles” (*principia*) instead of “beginning” (*principium*).]

“For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, who both begins what is good in us, carries it out, and brings it to completion,” [Note: The Jumièges manuscript adds “as the Apostle Paul also says, ‘for he who gives ….’” These words, “as the Apostle says,” are absent from the Mainz and Venetian editions, in which the sentence continues directly after “brings it to completion”: “and supplies bread for food and causes the fruits of our righteousness to increase.” In the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions the sentence is punctuated somewhat differently: “He who gives seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and cause the fruits of your righteousness to increase.”] as the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 9:10), “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and increase the fruits of your righteousness.”

Here, lest anyone think that nothing remained to be performed through free choice, he added, not unreasonably, an argument to prove that free choice is not taken away by these gifts but rather strengthened—unless a person, having turned back to his iniquities, should prefer to withdraw himself from God’s help. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript, together with the Mainz, Venetian, and Augustinian editions based on the Corbie manuscript, reads “should prefer to turn himself away.” Other codices have “should prefer himself.” The Remigius manuscript, with the Lyons, Mainz, and Venetian editions, reads “having turned back.” This was relegated to the margin in later editions, with the note: “or, if you read it in the masculine gender, add ‘man.’”]

“It is our task,” he says, “to follow humbly each day the grace of God that draws us, or certainly, as it is written, to deserve to hear from Jeremiah, when we resist it with a stiff neck and uncircumcised ears (Acts 7:51): ‘Shall he who falls not rise again? Or shall he who has turned away not return?’ (Jeremiah 8:4). Why, then, has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a contentious turning away? They have hardened their necks and have refused to return.” [Note: The Jumièges manuscript, together with the Mainz, Venetian, and Augustinian editions based on the Corbie manuscript, has this wording. The others read: “And further below.” In some editions the wording concerning “stiff neck” and “uncircumcised ears” is arranged differently: “lest, resisting him with a stiff neck and uncircumcised ears, as it is written (Acts 7:51), we deserve to hear …”; some omit “or certainly.”]

Again, below, after he had taught that every pursuit of virtue requires the grace of God, he added appropriately, saying (*Conference* 13.6):

“All these things, just as they cannot continually be desired by us without divine inspiration, so likewise they can in no way be brought to completion without his help.” [Note: This is the reading of the Jumièges manuscript and the Mainz and Venetian editions. The others have: “so they cannot even be completed.” In the same Jumièges manuscript, the word “saying” is omitted above.]

3. But in the seventh chapter (now chapter 8), wishing to show that the grace of Christ is universal and leaves no human being entirely untouched, nor abandons even those who resist, [Note: Some codices have “any human being.”] he says:

“Divine protection is therefore inseparably present with us, and the Creator’s kindness toward his creature is so great that providence not only accompanies it but also continually precedes it.” [Note: The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions add “always” (*semper*) after “is inseparably present with us.” This word is absent from the Jumièges, Corbie, and Remigius manuscripts and from the Mainz, Venetian, and Lyons editions.]

It may be thought that he called providence a companion for this reason: either because it often does not abandon even those who abandon it, or because it follows all whom it precedes. [Note: The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions add “also.” The Jumièges, Remigius, and Corbie manuscripts, as well as the Mainz and Venetian editions, do not.] He continues:

“When it has perceived in us a certain beginning of good will, it enlightens it, strengthens it, and directs it toward salvation, granting growth to that which either it itself planted or which it has seen arise through our effort.” [Note: The Jumièges manuscript lacks “continually.” The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions add “immediately” (*confestim*), then read “and strengthens it and urges it toward salvation.” The Augustinian appendix likewise has “immediately.”]

Here too he can still say that he meant the beginning of that good will whose beginnings were planted or inspired by God, since salutary efforts can proceed from hearts already enlightened. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “whose beginnings are planted.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read “or which seems to have arisen through our effort.” Some witnesses read “can be said to proceed,” while others read “are said to be able to proceed.” The Augustinian edition has “may be said.”]

These efforts are therefore said to belong properly to the human being himself because he has already received the capacity for good efforts, while their seeds are referred back to their author.

## [Elsewhere, CHAPTER III]

4. But in chapter nine he also added and said: [Note: This is the reading of the Jumièges, Corbie, and Remigius manuscripts and of the Mainz and Venetian editions, except that Mainz has “and says.” The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read: “But in chapter nine he adds and says.”]

“Thus it is not easily discerned by human reasoning how the Lord grants to those who ask, is found by those who seek, and opens to those who knock; and yet again is found by those who do not seek him. It plainly appears among those who were not asking him; all day long he stretches out his hands to a people that does not believe in him and contradicts him, calls those who resist and stand far away (Isaiah 65:1), draws the unwilling to salvation, withdraws from those who desire to sin the opportunity to fulfill their will, and mercifully opposes those rushing toward wickedness.” [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions have: “so that it may plainly appear among those who were not asking him.”]

Here, as though through an inscrutable diversity, a definition is introduced by which it is taught that many come to grace without grace, and that some possess the impulse to ask, seek, and knock through the vigilance of free choice. [Note: The Remigius manuscript reads: “by which it is taught.”] Yet in others this is said to be so blinded by great aversion that it cannot be recalled by any exhortations unless it is unwillingly led by the force of the one who draws it. [Note: The Lyons edition alone reads “throughout the whole,” rather than “throughout all.”]

As though the work of manifold grace were not carried out throughout the souls of all people, so that those who are unwilling become willing; or as though anyone who has already begun to use the judgment of reason could receive faith except by his will. [Note: The Lyons edition alone reads “throughout the whole.” This is evidently erroneous, as appears from the other codices and from the sense of the entire passage.]

Hence it is just as foolish to say that anyone advances unwillingly toward participation in grace as to assert that anyone comes to it without being stirred by the Spirit of God. [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions add: “But what is more foolish than to say that anyone advances unwillingly toward participation in grace?” The other material is omitted in those editions up to “Therefore, quickly.”]

5. The disputant therefore quickly forgot the definition he had stated, and quickly departed from his own position with unstable fickleness. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript and the Augustinian edition based on the Corbie manuscript, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, read “with instability and fickleness he departed.”]

For he had regularly said: “Not only the beginning of actions but also the beginning of good thoughts is from God” (see above, chapter 2, section 2). And lest this be understood as referring to instruction supplied externally, he had carefully added:

“He inspires in us the beginnings of holy willing and grants us the strength and opportunity to carry out the things we rightly desire.” [Elsewhere, CHAPTER IV]

“For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, who both begins what is good, carries it out, and brings it to completion in us.” [Note: The Lyons edition reads “Every excellent gift.” The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions omit “for”: “Every good gift and perfect gift.” The Jumièges and Corbie manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions read as in the text.]

Catholic teacher, why do you abandon your profession? Why, leaving the most serene light of truth, do you roll down into the smoky darkness of falsehood? [Note: The Corbie and Jumièges manuscripts read “smoky”; all the editions read “famous.” Several later editions note “smoky” in the margin as a conjecture.]

What you marvel at in those who ask, seek, and knock—why do you not ascribe to the same grace that is sought? You see good efforts and pious pursuits, and do you doubt that they are gifts of God? [Note: The Lyons edition alone adds “of God.”]

The work of grace may have remained hidden while faith, implanted in thought, was enclosed in secrecy; but once submissive prayer, diligent inquiry, and frequent knocking become visible, why do you not understand from the quality of the work the provision made by the one who inspires it? [Note: The Jumièges manuscript omits “becomes visible”; shortly afterward it reads “why not from the equality of the work.” The other witnesses have the reading in the text.]

## CHAPTER III. Cassian agrees fully neither with the Pelagians nor with the Catholics, since in error he asserts that some are justified by grace and others by law and nature. Cassian’s third definition: that a person has the desire for virtue from himself. Refuted from what he had previously confessed in his first definition.

[Col. 0221C] [Elsewhere, CHAPTER V]

1. And you think that you have sufficiently guarded yourself against the Pelagian calumnies if you grant us in part what ought to be believed concerning the whole body of the called. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript has “inappropriately.”] But you are in full agreement neither with the heretics nor with the Catholics. [Note: The Lyons edition reads “there is complete disagreement.”]

They defend, in all the righteous works of human beings, the beginnings of free choice; we always believe that the beginnings of good thoughts proceed from God. You have discovered some shapeless third position, unsuitable to either side, by which you would acquire neither the agreement of God’s enemies nor remain within the understanding of our own people. [Elsewhere, CHAPTER VI]

How, however, do you fail to see that you fall into that condemned position which, whether you wish it or not, you are convicted of asserting: that the grace of God is given according to our merits, since you affirm that some good work must precede from human beings themselves, on account of which they obtain grace? [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads: “that you, whether you wish it or not, fall into that condemned position.”]

For the faith of one who asks, the piety of one who seeks, and the persistence of one who knocks cannot be regarded as without merit—especially since all such people are said both to receive, to find, and to enter. [Note: The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions add “and to come.” The Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, more suitably read “and to find.”]

In this it is superfluous, indeed impious, to make room for merits existing before grace in such a way that the Lord’s statement would not be entirely true: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44)—[Note: We have judged it necessary to restore these words, absent from all the printed editions, on the authority of the Jumièges manuscript alone, since the sense of the passage requires them.] a statement that could not have been made if anyone’s conversion could be believed to occur without God’s illumination, or if the human will could in any way extend itself toward God without God.

For he draws the person who has been called to the Son; he does not compel one who resists and is unwilling, but makes the unwilling willing, and in whatever ways he can bends the unbelief of the one who resists, so that the heart of the hearer, through the delight in obedience generated within it, rises where it had been pressed down, learns where it was ignorant, trusts from the point where it had distrusted, and wills from the point where it had been unwilling. [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions, after “draws,” omit “not,” reading: “he compels the one who resists and is unwilling, and makes him willing from unwillingness.” The Jumièges manuscript reads: “he draws the one called to the Son who does not resist, and compels the unwilling, if from unwillingness …”; the sentence is incomplete there.]

“For the Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit” (Psalm 84:12). [Elsewhere, CHAPTER VI]

But let us see what follows (*Conference* 13.9):

“But to whom would it be easily evident how the sum of salvation is attributed to our free choice? It is said: ‘If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land’ (Isaiah 1:19). And how is it not ‘of God who shows mercy, not of him who wills or of him who runs’ (Romans 9:16)? What also is the meaning of the statement that ‘God will repay each according to his works’ (Matthew 16:17), and ‘God is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good will’ (Philippians 2:13), and that this is not from yourselves but is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast?” [Note: The Jumièges manuscript has “not easily be evident.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read: “But when it is easily evident …” and continue: “God is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to our good will, and this is not from us.” The Augustinian appendix based on the Corbie manuscript reads “according to your good will.” The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “he renders to each.”]

And the other passages he collected from the Scriptures, as though they contradicted one another in alternating meanings, he gathered together in order to entrust the zeal for grace’s gifts to human effort, dividing all humanity so that some are those whom God’s grace saves, while others are those whom law and nature justify. [Note: The Louvain edition says: “Behold, as though collected from the Scriptures, he collides passages that are apparently opposed to one another in alternating meaning.”]

But the law can command that nothing evil be done; it cannot free anyone from evil. It makes the commandment known, but does not supply the affection for obeying—unless what is “death-dealing” through the command of the letter becomes life-giving through the Spirit of grace. [Note: The Remigius and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, read “which is death-dealing.”]

[Elsewhere, CHAPTER VIII]

2. After this he concludes, saying:

“And thus, in all these matters, both the grace of God and the freedom of our will are in some manner revealed; and because a person can sometimes extend himself toward the desire for virtue through his own impulses, yet always needs to be helped by the Lord.” [Note: “And” is absent from the Corbie and Jumièges manuscripts and from the Lyons, Mainz, and Venetian editions. The latter two read: “because a person can sometimes extend himself toward virtue through his own impulses …”; “he always needs to be helped by the Lord.” The Jumièges manuscript supports this reading.]

Where, then, is what was stated earlier as a regular definition: “Not only the beginning of actions but also the beginning of good thoughts is from God, who both begins what is good, carries it out, and brings it to completion in us” (see above, chapter 1, section 4)?

Here, although you confess that God’s help is necessary for good beginnings, you nevertheless ascribe the very laudable impulses and desires for virtue, once God’s grace has been removed, to bare freedom of choice. Thus good and salutary efforts cannot indeed advance unless God helps, but they can nevertheless begin even if they are not inspired by God. [Note: Most printed editions read “yet they can.” The Venetian edition has “they can nevertheless exist, even if they are not inspired by God at the beginning.”]

## CHAPTER IV. It is proved against Cassian that the desire for healing cannot be possessed without grace. Cassian’s fourth definition: that through the good of nature the beginnings of good wills sometimes arise. Refuted both from his first definition and from the Apostle, whose statement “For willing is present with me” is rescued from a false interpretation.

[Col. 0223C]

1. Then, to define more clearly what a human being possesses from free choice and what he receives from grace, [Note: The Corbie, Jumièges, and Remigius manuscripts and the Mainz, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “what he receives from the grace of God.”] you add and say (*Conference* 13.9):

“For when someone wills, he does not thereby enjoy health, nor is he freed from the disease of sickness according to the desire of his own choice.”

You therefore teach that a human being cannot indeed seize health by himself, but that he has from himself the desire for health; that he comes to the physician solely by his own will, and that it is not also the physician’s work that he comes. As though the soul itself were not sick and, being healthy, could foresee a remedy for its body!

Yet the whole human being, together with the soul itself, fell into the depth of its misery, where it takes pleasure in lying before it receives knowledge of its calamity from the physician, always loving its errors and embracing false things in place of true ones (ibid.). [Note: The Jumièges manuscript omits “its.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read “where he lies,” referring to the human being; the others read “where it lies,” referring to the soul rather than the human being, which was the immediate subject.]

Its first salvation is that it begins to displease itself and to hate the oldness of its weakness; the next is that it desires to be healed and knows by whom it must be healed (see *Response to the Sixth Objection of the Gauls*). [Note: The Jumièges manuscript has “its healing”; the Remigius manuscript, “his healing”; shortly afterward the Mainz edition reads “because he is going to heal the sick woman,” where the Jumièges manuscript has “who heals him by grace.”]

These dispositions precede her healing in such a way that they are implanted in her by the one who is going to heal the sick woman, lest, since they could in no way be present in her in vain, she should rightly appear to be saved by merit, not by grace. [Note: This is the reading of the Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges manuscripts and of the Mainz and Venetian editions. The later editions read: “since these things could in no way be present in her”; immediately afterward the Jumièges manuscript has “so that the human being may rightly appear to be saved.”]

2. Then you add:

“But so that it may become more evident that even through the good of nature, which was bestowed by the Creator’s generosity, the beginnings of good wills sometimes arise—although, unless they are directed by God, they cannot reach the completion of virtue.” [Note: The Jumièges manuscript omits “of virtue,” reading “they cannot reach completion.”]

The Apostle is a witness, saying: “For willing is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good” (Romans 7:18). [Note: This is the reading of the Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges manuscripts and of the Augustinian appendix, Mainz, and Venetian editions. The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “testifies.”]

According to this definition, therefore, you earlier falsely said: “Not only the beginning of actions but also the beginning of good thoughts is from God, who both begins what is good, carries it out, and brings it to completion in us.”

But this can in no respect be false in any part; nor should contrary statements have been brought against it, so that what you rightly professed to begin from grace you would afterward affirm that we possess through the good of nature and through free choice. [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions read “you would confirm.”]

The blessed Apostle did indeed say: “For willing is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good” (Romans 7:18). [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “but he said likewise”; the Mainz and Venetian editions, “but he says the same.”] But he also said:

“Not that we are competent to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5). [Note: The Jumièges manuscript has “from ourselves, as though from ourselves”; the Remigius manuscript, “from ourselves, as though from ourselves personally”; the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, “anything from ourselves personally.”]

And the same Apostle said: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to act according to his good will” (Philippians 2:13). [Note: The later Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions have “and to accomplish” in place of “and to act,” which is found in the Corbie manuscript, the Augustinian appendix, and the Mainz and Venetian editions. The latter two read “in us” instead of “in you.”]

The Apostle is therefore not contradicting himself. But when the good will has been given to us, we do not immediately find the ability to act, unless the one who gave the desire grants its effect to those who ask, seek, and knock.

For this utterance of the one who says, “For willing is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good” (Romans 7:18), belongs to one who has been called and has already been established under grace: [Note: These words, “and already established under grace,” are absent from the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions. They are found in the Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges manuscripts and in the Mainz and Venetian editions.] he delights indeed in the law of God according to the inner human being, but he sees another law in his members, warring against the law of his mind and taking him captive in the law of sin (Romans 7:22–23).

Although he has received knowledge of willing rightly, he nevertheless does not find within himself the power to perform the things he desires, [Note: We emend the text on the basis of the Jumièges manuscript. All the others read “the power of those things which he desires to perform,” which seems less suitable.] until, for the good will he has received, he deserves to find the capacity for virtue that he seeks. [Note: The Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions read as translated. The later editions, after “the good will he has received,” had “deserves to find the one who acts.”]

## CHAPTER V. Cassian’s fifth definition: that contrary positions must be accepted together—the position that says good will is born from grace and the position that says grace depends upon good will. Cassian attributes error to Catholics just as to Pelagians. Refuted from the definitions of the supreme pontiffs and the councils.

[Col. 0225B] [Elsewhere, CHAPTER IX]

1. After this you produce many testimonies by which free choice is shown now to be strong, now weak—as though there were some who, by their own powers, fulfill what others cannot do unless God helps them; [Note: This is the reading of the Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges manuscripts and of the Mainz and Venetian editions. The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “what they cannot do without God’s help.”] or as though a command were given to a human being for any other reason than that he might seek divine help.

You therefore conclude and say (*Conference* 13.11):

“And so these matters are, in a certain sense, mixed and confused indiscriminately, so that among many people there is a serious dispute over what depends upon what: namely, whether God has mercy on us because we have supplied the beginning of good will, or whether, because God has mercy, we obtain the beginning of good will.” [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions read “indistinguishable, mixed, and confused”; a few lines later those same witnesses read “For many, believing each of these things.”]

“For many, believing each of these things and asserting them beyond what is right, are entangled in various errors that contradict one another.”

Behold: as you see it, what had been mixed has been distinguished, and what could not be explained has been resolved. [Note: The Lyons edition alone reads “what had been confused.”]

For you define two mutually opposed errors in which those who do not know what should be held between free choice and grace are entangled. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript and the Lyons edition read: “For you define two mutually opposed errors”; the Lyons edition alone adds: “by which those disputing contentiously between free choice and grace are entangled in what should be held.”]

In one category you place those who say that God has mercy on us because the beginnings of good will have been supplied by us—plainly signifying the followers of Pelagian doctrine, who say that the grace of God is given according to our merits. [Note: The Lyons edition reads: “who say that grace is given according to our merits,” omitting all the intervening material found in the other codices.]

In the other you place those who say that the beginnings of good wills arise from God’s mercy, intending that those who defeated the enemies of grace should be understood. [Note: The Lyons edition alone reads “arise from God’s mercy.”]

If, then, it is an error to ascribe the beginnings of good will to a human being who has not been divinely helped, and it is also an error to confess that “the will is prepared by the Lord,” where are we to be directed so that we may avoid both? [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads: “Where are we to be directed? Let us avoid both.”]

2. “If,” you say, “we follow both, we assent to no error.”

You subject us to two errors and, as you understand them, double perversities: by dividing them, you condemn; by mixing them, you justify.

By this law, by this rule, you will be able to proclaim that those who say that one must always be deceived err just as much as those who define that one must never be deceived (Cassian’s seventeenth *Conference* is being noted here, in which he teaches that it is sometimes permissible to lie); but, so that neither alternative is sinful, both should be followed: for falsehood should neither always be avoided nor truth always neglected. [Note: The Lyons edition alone adds: “since severity should not always be avoided,” omitting the rest.]

Your opinion utterly deceives you. One good cannot be made from two evils; two vices do not produce one virtue; two falsehoods do not make one truth. For things that are rightly equal are not diminished by coming together but increase. [Note: The Lyons edition reads: “For things that are equal are rightly not diminished, etc.” The other editions have “are rightly equal”; Mainz and Venice, “are rightly equal.”]

It was therefore not right that those who assert that the beginnings of good wills are generated by God’s inspiration should be censured by the same judgment as those who think that free choice can suffice for these things without the help of grace. One of these definitions has been overthrown by the Church, the other defended. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “the other defended.”]

Nor does the compact of this new covenant suit them in any way—a compact under which the Catholic position would be more corrupt and the Pelagian more correct. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript omits the particle “which.”]

### [Alternatively, Chapter X]

3. “Many,” you say, “by believing each of these things and asserting more than is just, are entangled in various errors contradictory to one another.” Is it therefore pleasing to you to condemn Catholics with heretics, the victors with the vanquished, and to brand with the mark of error those who drove error from the Church? For according to your judgment—in which you do not wish the beginning of holy and faithful wills to be from God in all human beings (as though you were granting much to grace if you allow it to work this in the minds of some)—Pope Innocent, most worthy of the See of Peter, was in error. When he was speaking about those who glory in free will, he says:

> “For what sound judgment,” he says, “are we henceforth to form concerning the minds of those who think that they owe it to themselves that they are good?”

And again, when writing about the fall of the first man:

> “For once having suffered free will, while using his goods too inconsiderately, he fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression, and found no way by which he could thereafter rise; and, deceived forever by his own freedom, he would have lain crushed beneath the ruin of this fall, unless the coming of Christ had, in accordance with his grace, restored him.”

[Note: The editions of Mainz and Venice read “of the most blessed Peter.”]

[Note: The Lyon edition alone reads “various errors contradictory to one another,” omitting *que*.]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz, Venice, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, read: “you assert that the beginning is not from God in all human beings.” The Lyon edition instead reads: “to have had its beginning from God.”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “the most blessed Peter.”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read: “Can it be that … who think that they ought to themselves.” Venice reads: “who think that it ought to be owed to themselves.” Lyon and the later editions read: “For what sound judgment, he says, shall we henceforth form concerning the minds of those who reckon that it is owed to themselves.”]

[Note: These words, “he is,” are added from Innocent’s Letter 29 in volume II of Augustine’s works. They were absent from the Prosperian manuscripts, except the Venetian edition, which reads: “so that he might be able to rise.”]

[Note: The Corbie and Jumièges manuscripts read: “he would have lain hidden, crushed by the oppression of this ruin.” The Mainz edition reads: “he would have lain hidden, crushed by the oppression of this injury.” Lyon, Douai, and Cologne read: “he would have lain, crushed beneath the ruin of this fall.”]

[Note: The Mainz, Venice, and Cologne editions read “had revealed him,” less suitably. The Lyon edition reads: “unless the divine coming had revealed him afterward by his grace.”]

The Eastern bishops were in error, in whose judgment Pelagius was compelled to anathematize those who say that the grace of God is given according to our merits, in order that he might appear Catholic (see *The Book on the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 14, §§33–35).

The African councils of bishops were in error, for by their decrees they established that both are gifts of God: both knowing what we ought to do and loving it so that we may do it; so that, while love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up, because, as it is written concerning God, “He is the one who teaches human beings knowledge” (Psalm 93:10); and thus it is written: “Love is from God” (1 John 4:7) (Council of Carthage, canons 4 and 5; below, Appendix, p. 272).

[Note: Thus the Rheims manuscript, in agreement with the council’s text. In the Jumièges manuscript the words “he is the one who teaches human beings knowledge” are omitted, as are the words “it is written of him.” The same omission occurs in the Mainz and Venice editions. The Lyon edition reads: “For as it is written concerning God: He is the one who teaches human beings knowledge,” with the rest omitted. Louvain, Douai, and Cologne have the same wording as the text.]

The two hundred and fourteen priests were in error. In the letter which they placed before their constitutions, they addressed the blessed Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See, in these words:

> “We have determined that the judgment pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable bishop Innocent, from the See of the most blessed Apostle Peter, should remain in force until they openly confess that, by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, we are helped not only to know righteousness but also to do it in each of our actions, so that without it we are able to possess, think, say, or do nothing of true and holy piety.”

The holy See of the blessed Peter was in error, when, through the mouth of Pope Zosimus, it spoke in this way to the whole world:

> “Nevertheless, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.”

[Note: The Corbie manuscript and the Lyon edition read “they brought forward.”]

[Note: Thus the Jumièges, Corbie, and Rheims manuscripts. The other codices read: “Thus they addressed the Apostolic See …” The Mainz edition reads “they spoke.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “nothing of true and holy piety.” The Mainz and Venice editions read “nothing of true, just, and holy piety.”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “bishops of Africa”; Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne, “African bishops”; the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, “African bishops.”]

[Note: Thus from the Corbie manuscript, the appendix to volume X of Augustine, and the Mainz and Venice editions. The Jumièges manuscript reads “in the soundness of his judgment”; later editions, “in the soundness of this judgment”; Venice, “in the soundness of this his judgment.”]

The African bishops were in error when, writing back to that same Pope Zosimus and praising him for the salutary soundness of this judgment, they said:

> “But what you placed in your letter, which you took care to have sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Nevertheless, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops,’ we have understood as spoken so that you might, as if passing swiftly by, cut down with the sharp sword of truth those who exalt the freedom of the human will against God’s help. For what have you attributed more freely to free will than the fact that you referred everything to the conscience of our humility? Yet you discerned faithfully and wisely that this had been done at God’s prompting, and you said so truly and confidently. For this reason, since the will is prepared by the Lord, he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations, so that they may do something good (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint). For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God (Romans 8:14). Thus we do not feel that our free will is lacking, and in each movement of human willing toward every good thing, we do not doubt that his help is more powerful.”

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, except that the latter have “to be sent beforehand.” The other codices read “to all.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “the hearts of the faithful.”]

[Note: Several editions read “and of the will.” The Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, as well as the Lyon edition, omit *and*.]

[Note: The Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “and in the faithful teacher.”]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions. Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read “ruinous joints” instead of *rimosasque* (“cracked”).]

Do you see your rules shattered by the solidity of invincible constitutions, and the crooked, cracked joints in the structure of the faith—like the walls of Jericho—falling at the sound of priestly trumpets (Joshua 6:20)?

## Chapter VI

Since the question concerning the origin of holy wills has been clearly settled against the Pelagians, Cassianus argues wrongly, gathering together the weapons of those in error, that free will is taken away by grace, whereas through grace it is rather formed, governed, and set in order.

[Col. 0229A]

### [Alternatively, Chapter XI]

1. [Note: The Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts read “settled”; the Lyon edition alone, “of this fever of yours.”]

For when a dispute arose among our people and the Pelagians concerning the origin of holy wills and the beginnings of faith and love, the contest was brought to an end by no doubtful victory and no uncertain conclusion, so that we should still have to deal with the unjust peace of this covenant of yours. The hostile battle-line has been overthrown; the war is finished; we are victors through him who displayed power in his arm, scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts, brought down the powerful from their thrones, and exalted the lowly; filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty (Luke 1:52–53)—through him who, showing mercy to our fathers, remembered his holy covenant and the oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us, delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, to serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days (Luke 1:71); through him who gave us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord (2 Corinthians 15:57); through him from whom we received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we might know the things granted to us by God (1 Corinthians 2:12).

[Note: The Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “the war has been shattered”; the Rheims manuscript with the Mainz and Venice editions reads “and the oath.”]

Why do you strive to gather up the broken weapons of arguments already reduced to ashes? Why, by warming the ashes of an extinguished doctrine, do you try to kindle the odor of dying smoke into a renewed flame?

### [Alternatively, Chapter XII]

[Note: Douai and Cologne noted in the margin the alternative reading “from free will.” The Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts with the Lyon edition read “the grace of God,” without *ex* (“from”).]

There is no danger to free will from the grace of God, nor is the will taken away when the very power to will well is generated within it. For if it is not to be considered ours because it is formed, governed, ordered, and instructed, then the children of God who are led by the Spirit of God lose their freedom (Romans 8:14); they lose the vigor of a rational mind and are deprived of all praise for voluntary devotion—those to whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord is given (Isaiah 11:2).

[Note: The Lyon edition reads “because those who are led.”]

Indeed, those who think they have no need of these restorations have passed from the habit of their old disease into madness: they reject the remedy, cry out, rave, and resist. But if they are children of the promise, they will rest and be healed.

[Note: The Lyon edition reads “they pass into madness … but if they are children of the promise, they rest and are healed.” The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “they pass into madness, but if they are children of the promise, they will rest and will be healed.”]

## Chapter VII

Cassianus, confusing contradictory definitions, attempts to give color by examples to what he intends: namely, that some can do this through free will without God’s help, whereas others cannot unless God cooperates. He is refuted from the Scriptures, and it is shown that the conversion of Matthew and Paul, as well as of Zacchaeus and the thief on the cross, is equally from grace.

[Col. 0230A]

### [Alternatively, Chapter XIII]

1. But now let us see what the disputant’s sobriety produces. To drive out one vice by another—and to cure error by error—he confused definitions contradictory to one another by a novel art; and, so that he might offer this concoction of his to unsuspecting hearers, he tried to color by examples what he had mixed.

[Note: The words “and to cure error by error” are absent from the Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts and from the Mainz and Venice editions.]

For he says (*Collation* 13, chapter 11):

> “For if we say that the beginning of a good will is ours, what was there in the persecutor Paul? What was there in the tax collector Matthew? One of them, occupied with the blood and punishments of the innocent, the other with public violence and plunder, is drawn to salvation.

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “the other.”] But if we say that the beginnings of a good will are always inspired by the grace of God, what are we to say about Zacchaeus’s faith? What about the devotion of that thief on the cross? By the force of his desire, as it were, imposing violence upon the kingdom of heaven, they anticipated the special summons of vocation.”

2. [Note: The Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts and the Mainz and Venice editions read “good”; Louvain and later editions, “of certain persons”; the Lyon edition, “of these beginnings,” and omits the following words, “from the slower obedience of some,” etc.]

By this dissimilarity of good beginnings, therefore, he attempts to prove that some can do this through free will without God’s help, whereas others cannot unless God cooperates; and he wants this understood from the slower obedience of some and the more immediate consent of others.

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts with the Mainz and Venice editions. Later editions read: “where, after a calm exhortation or a mere report, the teachable hearer embraces true conduct without any hesitation.” The Lyon edition has above, for “As though … works,” “That … works.”]

As though, where hard unbelief is subjected to God and suddenly succumbs to the Gospel which it had long opposed, the right hand of the Most High works the transformation of the person (Psalm 76:11); but where the teachable hearer embraces only a calm exhortation or a mere report, without any hesitation of distrust, the goodness of such a human conversion belongs solely to the will.

As though, indeed, the power of God drew to the Son only those whom he had rebuked by his voice, crushed by punishment, or made to tremble with terror; but applied none of his power to the minds of those who ran toward the promises of their Redeemer with joyful hope and eager desire.

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts with the Mainz and Venice editions. Later editions read “the power of God’s grace draws only those to the Son”; the Jumièges manuscript reads “yet the power of God the Father … has made [them] tremble.”]

But the Truth says: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Therefore, if no one comes unless drawn, all who come in whatever manner are drawn.

[Note: Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read: “all, in whatever manner they come, are drawn.”]

### [Alternatively, Chapter XIV]

The contemplation of the elements, and the perfectly ordered beauty of all that is in them, therefore draws one to God. For “his invisible things, understood through the things that have been made, are perceived from the creation of the world” (Romans 1:20).

The narrators of past events draw the mind of the hearer; by their narration they inflame it with the praises and powers of the Lord, and with his wonders that he performs (Psalm 77:4).

Fear draws: “For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 1:7; Psalm 110:10).

Joy draws, because: “I rejoiced in those things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Psalm 121:1).

Desire draws, because: “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83:3).

[Note: The Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts with the Mainz and Venice editions contain “my.”]

[Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript, from which come the appendix to volume X of Augustine and the Mainz and Venice editions, together with the Rheims manuscript. The Jumièges manuscript reads “Divine readings draw”; Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne, “The delight of reading draws.”]

Delights draw: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 118:103).

And who could perceive or explain through how many affections God’s visitation leads the human mind, so that it follows what it had been fleeing, loves what it had hated, hungers for what it had found distasteful, and, by a sudden and marvelous change, what had been closed to it becomes open; what had been burdensome becomes light; what had been bitter becomes sweet; and what had been obscure becomes clear?

But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). For the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” himself shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6)—that is, in the manifestation of his Son, who is in the glory of the Father.

[Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz and Venice editions read “the narrators of past events,” except that they have *relations* rather than *relators*. The Jumièges manuscript punctuates it this way: “The narrators of past events draw the mind of the hearer. Those who narrate inflame it.” The Rheims manuscript reads: “The knowledge of past events and the narrators of divine works draw.” The Lyon and later editions read: “The knowledge of past events and the accounts of divine works draw and inflame the mind of the hearer.”]

[Note: The Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, read “through which affections.” The Mainz and Venice editions read “by what affection the visitation of God leads a person.” The other printed codices read “through how many affections,” as in the text.]

[Note: The Lyon and later editions read “may be open.” The three manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, read “become open.”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “to make light shine out of darkness; he himself shone … in the face.” The Corbie and Rheims manuscripts also contain the words “in the face.”]

[Note: Thus the Corbie and Rheims manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions. The Jumièges manuscript and the Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “in the bosom of the Father.”]

3. He, therefore, who shone in the heart of Matthew the tax collector and of Paul, then a persecutor of the Church, also shone in the heart of Zacchaeus and in the heart of the thief crucified with the Lord.

Or was the Lord’s voice perhaps idle when he graciously addressed Zacchaeus, who was seeking to see who Jesus was, saying: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must remain in your house” (Luke 19:5)? Did he not thereby prepare the mind of the man whose hospitality he had chosen?

Finally, when everyone murmured because he had entered to stay with a sinful man, and Zacchaeus, already doing penance, having distributed half of his possessions to the poor, promised to restore fourfold whatever he had defrauded, the Lord said: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.” And, so that the cause of this salvation might not remain hidden, he added: “For the Son of Man has come to seek and to save what was lost”—so that, when we recognized that he had been saved, we might know that he had been preceded by the one who sought him.

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts with the Mainz and Venice editions. Other codices read “to see him.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “hurrying, come down.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “had prepared it for himself,” as he had said above, so that the Lord’s voice would have been idle.]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, as well as the Mainz and Venice editions. Other editions read “that he had entered to stay with the man.” The word “to stay” is absent from the Jumièges manuscript.]

[Note: The Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions omit *and* before “Zacchaeus … promising to restore.”]

[Note: The Lyon edition omits these words: “so that we might know that he had been preceded by the one who sought him.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript, in agreement with the sacred text, reads “For [the Son of Man] came to seek and to save”; all the others read “But [the Son of Man] came to save and to seek,” in reversed order.]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions with the Rheims manuscript read “are understood.”]

In the justification of the thief also, even if no signs of grace at work were understood, would we not receive him, together with all believers, as one who had been drawn? For the Lord says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Luke 10:22); and: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

Among them all, that he was either handed over or drawn is also demonstrated by the confession of the thief himself. After he had blasphemed Jesus Christ for some time, he was suddenly changed and said: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “and he says.” The Jumièges manuscript reads “when you come.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript omits the word “Christ.” The Lyon edition reads “afterward he imitated him.”]

But from where did such a diversity of contending words arise in one person? Let the blessed Apostle instruct us and say: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’; and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

Thus we should not doubt that, in the will of the same person, what he blasphemed was from himself, while what he believed was from the Holy Spirit.

Therefore this disputant vainly attempted to adapt to the inscrutable variety of one grace an argument for his definition, so that one portion of the justified might be believed to come to Christ solely through the movements of their own will, while another portion is dragged and compelled against its will. For it is God who works all things in all (1 Corinthians 12:6), whether he wishes to draw some in one way and others in another; and no one comes to him unless he is drawn in some manner.

[Note: Thus the Corbie and Rheims manuscripts and the Mainz and Venice editions; however, these have *truth* instead of *variety*. The Lyon edition, together with the later editions, omits *to* and reads: “he wished to adapt the inscrutable variety of one grace to the argument of his definition.” One later edition reads: “and the enlargement of his definition,” a reading also found in the Cologne edition. The Jumièges manuscript reads: “he wished to adapt the enlargement of his definition.”]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions. The others read “be drawn and compelled against its will.”]

## Chapter VIII

The sixth definition of Cassianus: free will and grace must be received together—that is, in such a way that they are believed to contribute equally to salvation. Divine authorities concerning grace are cited, and the reason is given why the will is not taken away by grace.

[Col. 0233A]

### [Alternatively, Chapter XV]

1. [Note: Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read “he subjoins.”]

After this he adds testimonies from sacred history by which he shows that observance of God’s commandments and the completion of the virtues are to be attributed to divine grace (*Collation* 13, chapter 11)—which we also most readily confess.

After recalling the examples of Balaam, whom God transformed from wishing to curse Israel into words of blessing (Numbers 13), and of Abimelech, who was not permitted to sin against Rebecca (Genesis 26), and of Joseph, sold by his brothers, whose evil intention God turned to good (Genesis 37), he returns to confirm his definition. He removes free will, which he says he joins to grace, from a certain part of the human race, insofar as he can, and assigns it to another part, saying:

> “For these two things—that is, grace or free will—seem indeed to be opposed to one another; but we gather from the reasoning of piety that we ought to receive both together, so that, by taking one of them away from the human being, we may not appear to have exceeded the rule of ecclesiastical faith.”

[Note: The Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “against the Israelites.”]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions. Lyon and the later editions read “against Sarah.” The same event is narrated of Abimelech with respect to Sarah in Genesis 20 and with respect to Rebecca in Genesis 26.]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, reads “turned.”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “that is, grace and free will.” Lyon omits “that is” and, like the others, reads “either grace or free will.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “both agree, and both.”]

[Note: The Douai and Cologne editions read “receive”; they have “we have gathered” in common with Lyon and Louvain.]

2. [Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts with the Mainz and Venice editions. Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne here too read, as in the sequence, “It is the ecclesiastical rule.”]

It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith, as the Apostle proclaims: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). “But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10); and: “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25).

It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may belong to God and not come from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith: “In nothing be terrified by your adversaries, which is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation—and this is from God; for it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:28–29).

It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For God is the one who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

The Lord confirms this rule by saying: “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:66); and: “Everything that the Father gives me comes to me” (John 6:37); and: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5, 16); and: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (Luke 10:22); and: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27); and: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21); and: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17).

[Note: The Corbie and Rheims manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, add here the word “Christ,” which is absent from the others and from the Apostle’s Greek and Latin text.]

[Note: This entire sentence—“It is the rule of ecclesiastical faith: But what do you have …” through “as though you had not received it”—had dropped out of the Lyon edition; it is found in all the others.]

[Note: The Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, add “but,” which was absent from the others. The same manuscripts and the Corbie manuscript read “so that the surpassing power may belong to God,” as in the text; Lyon and the later editions instead read “so that the superiority of the power may belong to God.” The Apostle’s Greek text agrees with the former reading.]

[Note: This entire sentence is again absent from the Lyon edition. Louvain, Douai, and Cologne omit the word “perhaps.” The Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts read “you have been made safe” instead of “you have been saved.”]

[Note: The Lyon edition reads “but for us.”]

[Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript together with the Mainz and Venice editions. The Jumièges manuscript reads “For to you it has been granted on behalf of Christ.” The Rheims manuscript reads “For to you it has been granted by Christ.” Lyon reads “For to you it has been given through Christ.” Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read “Because it has been given to you through Christ.”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “with fear and trembling.” Several codices read “with trembling and fear.” The Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts read as in the text.]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “in you,” as in the Apostle. The other codices read “in us.”]

[Note: The Jumièges and Rheims manuscripts read “from ourselves, as though from our very selves.” Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read “from ourselves, as though from ourselves.”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “the Lord confirms”; below, they read “has been given to him,” omitting “to him.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, reads “will come to me.”]

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript adds here “raises the dead and.” The other codices do not add these words.]

3. By this rule the will is taken away from no human being, because the power of grace works in wills not so that they cease to exist, but so that they become good from evil and faithful from unbelieving; so that those who were darkness in themselves become light in the Lord; what was dead is made alive, what was lying prostrate is raised up, and what had perished is found.

[Note: The Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts with the Mainz and Venice editions read: “and those who were darkness in themselves become light in the Lord; what was dead is made alive, what was lying prostrate is raised up, what had perished is found.” Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read the same wording as the text.]

We believe that the grace of the Savior works this without exception of persons in all human beings who are rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love.

For, as he himself plausibly, but not consistently, defined, we say and defend that not only the beginning of good actions but also of good thoughts is from God: he inspires in us the beginnings of holy willing and grants us the power and opportunity to accomplish the things we rightly desire. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James 1:17)—he who both begins what is good, carries it out, and brings it to completion in us.

If the author of this opinion had remained in it, he would not have exceeded the rule of the Church; nor, while hostile to free will, would he have been ungrateful to God’s grace. When he indicates that one of these two works in Paul and Matthew, and the other in Zacchaeus and the thief, he does not understand that in the former he has taken away free will and in the latter grace.

[Note: The Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, read “every good gift.” The others read “every perfect gift,” as also above, chapter 2.]

[Note: The Lyon and later editions read “offended.” The Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, more correctly read “hostile”—namely, appearing, insofar as he can, to take away free will.]

[Note: The word “of the two” is absent from the Lyon edition. In it, and in Louvain, Douai, and Cologne, “he judges to have been done” is read instead of “he indicates to have been done.” In the same Lyon edition, “free will in the former, grace in the latter” is omitted.]

## Chapter IX

Against Cassianus it is proved from the Scriptures and the definitions of the Church that the beginning of a good will is from grace. The first human being, created without fault and able to persevere in the good if he wished, departed from the good through free will; after sin, nothing remained in him except what pertains to temporal life. The depth of evil into which the whole human nature was plunged by his transgression is considered. Cassianus’s seventh definition—that Adam, after his transgression, received knowledge of evil but did not lose knowledge of good—is refuted.

[Col. 0235C]

### [Alternatively, Chapter XVI]

1. Then he added:

> “For when God sees us turning our will toward the good, he comes to meet us, directs us, and strengthens us. ‘As soon as he hears the voice of your cry, he will answer you’ (Isaiah 30:19); and, he says, ‘Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will rescue you, and you will glorify me’ (Psalm 49:15).”

Who does not see that this doctrine assigns merit to free will, by which grace is preceded and made its servant, repaying what is owed rather than bestowing a gift? This definition was condemned even when Pelagius anathematized it at the synod of the bishops of Palestine.

[Note: The Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts omit “God”; afterward they read “turning the will.” The Mainz and Venice editions likewise omit it.]

[Note: The Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts read “and you will glorify me.” The Mainz and Venice editions read “and you will honor me.”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “that grace precedes and serves each person,” instead of “by which grace is preceded and made its servant.” The Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts and the Venice edition read “serves each person.” The Lyon edition reads “that grace is preceded and serves it.”]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Rheims, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions. Lyon and the later editions read “that one was condemned by Pelagius with an anathema.”]

For in the person who begins to will what is good and desires to depart from iniquity and error, we profess that grace itself is at work. For “the steps of a person are directed by the Lord, and he will delight in his way” (Psalm 36:23); and: “Every person’s way seems right to him, but the Lord directs hearts” (Proverbs 21:2); and: “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord; but how can a mortal understand his ways?” (Proverbs 20:24).

And what the Apostle says: “For you have not received the spirit of slavery again into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

[Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “for when someone begins to will what is good …”]

[Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “Every person’s way seems right to himself.”]

[Note: Lyon reads “And as the Apostle says.”]

[Note: All the editions, together with the Jumièges manuscript, read “in fear.” The Corbie and Rheims manuscripts read “into fear,” in accordance with the Greek *εἰς φόβον* (“into fear”).]

[Note: The word “sons” is absent from the Rheims and Jumièges manuscripts and from the Mainz and Venice editions.]

## [Also Chapter XVII]

### 2.

[The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions read: “he continues.”]

After this he continues and says (Conference 13, chapter 12):

“For God cannot be believed to have made such a human being as would never wish, nor ever be able, to do good. Otherwise, he did not grant him free choice, if he granted him only the ability and desire to do evil, but neither the desire nor the ability to do good.”  

[The Lyon edition reads: “if he granted him only the ability and desire to do evil.” The Corbie, Remigius, and Joliensis manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, read: “if he granted him only evil, so that he should desire and be able to do it, but neither desire nor be able to do good.”]

“And how will that sentence pronounced by the Lord after the transgression of the first human being stand: ‘Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil’ (Genesis 3:22)? For he must not be thought to have previously been such a one as was entirely ignorant of good. Otherwise we must admit that he was formed like some irrational and senseless animal.”

[The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts and the Mainz, Venetian, and Lyon editions do not contain the words “and senseless.” The Joliensis manuscript reads: “he must be believed to have been made like some irrational animal.”]

“That would be utterly absurd and wholly alien to the Catholic faith.”

[The Mainz and Venetian editions read “in every respect”; Lyon, Leuven, and Douai read “altogether”; Cologne reads “suitably,” evidently a typographical error.]

Indeed, according to the judgment of the wisest Solomon, “God made human beings upright” (Ecclesiasticus 7:30), that is, so that they might continually enjoy the knowledge of good; “but they themselves sought out many inventions.” For they became, as has been said, knowing good and evil. Therefore, after the transgression Adam acquired the knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of good, which he had received.

## [Also Chapter XVIII]

### 3.

[The Lyon edition reads: “For upright and wholly ...,” as though this were a continuation of the Collator’s words, but wrongly.]

There can be no doubt that the first human being was created upright and free from every fault, and that in him the nature of all human beings was created together with him. He received free choice in such a way that, if he did not abandon God who was assisting him, he could, because he willed it, persevere in the good things he had naturally received; and, by the merit of voluntary perseverance, attain to that blessedness in which he would neither wish nor be able to fall into a worse condition.

[The Mainz and Venetian editions read: “if he had not abandoned the Lord.” Other witnesses read: “if he did not abandon the Lord.” The Lyon edition reads possent in nobis (“they might be able in us”). The Joliensis manuscript, with the Venetian and Lyon editions, reads perveniret (“might attain”); in place of “to that blessedness,” it has “to the same blessedness.”]

## [Also Chapter XIX]

But by that same free choice, through which he remained good for as long as he wished, he departed from the law appointed for him;

[The Joliensis manuscript reads ab apposita.] nor did he fear the punishment of death announced to him. He abandoned God and followed the devil, rebelling against the Lord his Preserver and obeying his enemy and destroyer.

[The Joliensis manuscript reads “his Savior.”]

“Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him we all perished” (Ambrose, Book 7 on Luke, chapter 15).

Blessed Ambrose said this no less truly than the Truth itself truly says: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished” (Luke 19:10).

[The Joliensis manuscript reads: “For he came.”]

For in the universal ruin of that transgression, human nature lost neither its substance nor its will, but was stripped, by the deceit of the envious one, of the light and beauty of the virtues.

[The Lyon edition reads: “its substance was not taken away.”]

But once it had lost those qualities through which it could attain to the eternal and imperishable incorruption of body and soul, what remained to it except what belongs to temporal life, which is wholly condemnation and punishment?

[Many manuscripts read “of the soul also”; shortly afterward the Remigius manuscript and the Mainz edition add “and punishment.”]

For this reason those born in Adam must be reborn in Christ, lest anyone be found in that generation which perished. For if Adam’s descendants naturally acted in those virtues in which Adam existed before sin, they would not be “by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:3), nor would they be “darkness” (Ephesians 5:8), nor “under the power of darkness” (Colossians 1:13). Finally, they would not need the grace of the Savior, because they would not be good without reason, nor would they be deprived of the reward of righteousness, possessing those goods whose loss deserved to exile the first parents from paradise.

[The Joliensis manuscript adds: “nor would they be darkness.”]

But now, since no one can escape eternal death without the sacrament of rebirth, is it not perfectly clear, from the singularity of this remedy itself, into what profound evil the nature of the entire human race has been plunged by the transgression of him in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12), and that whatever he lost, they lost as well?

He first lost faith; he lost self-control; he lost charity. He was stripped of wisdom and understanding; he lacked counsel and fortitude. By impiously pursuing higher things, he was cast down from knowledge of the truth and from the godliness of obedience; nor did he even retain that fear by which he might have avoided what was forbidden or feared punishment, because he did not abstain through love of righteousness.

[The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts read: “with that fear remaining to him.” The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions omit the negative and read: “because he abstained through love of righteousness.” The Corbie and Remigius manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, read: “because he did not abstain through love of righteousness.”]

Free choice, therefore—that is, the spontaneous desire for what pleases oneself—when it grew weary of using the good things it had received and, as the supports of its happiness became contemptible to it, directed its mad desire toward the experience of transgression, drank the poison of all vices and drenched the whole of human nature in the drunkenness of its intemperance.

[The Mainz and Venetian editions read: “drenched it in its intemperance.”]

Before it digests the deadly indigestion of eating the flesh of the Son of Man and drinking his blood, memory slips, judgment goes astray, and one’s steps falter; nor is it in any way capable of choosing and desiring that good of which it voluntarily deprived itself.

[The Lyon edition and the more recent editions read “slips.” The Corbie and Remigius manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions read “memory totters.”]

For just as it could fall without God’s impelling it, so it cannot rise without God’s lifting it up.

## [Also Chapter XX]

### 4.

It was therefore not rightly said: “For God cannot be believed to have made such a human being as would never wish, nor ever be able, to do good”—as though we were saying that this weakness of the human being was created by the Creator, rather than contracted by the human being as the deserved consequence of sin.

Whoever therefore thinks that it follows that, if free choice is said to have been blinded, the blindness itself must be attributed to the author of nature, wants to persuade us that free choice in Adam’s descendants is as sound as it was in Adam before sin.

[The Joliensis manuscript reads: “which we say is alien to the Catholic faith.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read: “which we say is altogether sufficiently alien to the Catholic faith.”]

We regard this as altogether alien to the Catholic faith. For what has been injured by sin, if that has not been injured from which sin arose?

Unless perhaps it is said that punishment, but not guilt, passed into Adam’s descendants—which is entirely false.

[The Corbie manuscript reads: “which is altogether false.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read: “which is said to be altogether false.” The Joliensis manuscript reads: “which is altogether false.”]

And perhaps it is not said for this reason. For it is exceedingly impious to think this about God’s justice: that he wished those who were free from transgression to be condemned together with the guilty.

[The Joliensis manuscript reads: “to be condemned.”]

Guilt is therefore evident where punishment is not hidden, and participation in sin is demonstrated by participation in punishment, so that what belongs to human misery derives not from the Creator’s institution but from the Judge’s retribution.

## [Also Chapter XXI]

### 5.

That statement was foolishly introduced and contrary to the judgment of all interpreters in order to establish the soundness of free choice. He says:

“And how will that sentence pronounced by the Lord after the transgression of the first human being stand: ‘Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil’ (Genesis 3:22)?”

It is as though the devil had truly promised Adam something, and Adam, by transgressing God’s commandment, had advanced into likeness with God, and God had declared that this had been granted to him.

[The Joliensis manuscript, the Mainz edition, and the Venetian edition read: “that God had declared that what he pronounced had been granted to him”; the two printed editions read “had pronounced.”]

Yet in these words it is rather signified what he did not attain: entering upon the path of pride, he lost what he possessed while coveting what he had not received.

[The Mainz and Venetian editions read “had signified,” that is, God.]

There is no less error in the conclusion of this interpretation, where it says:

“Therefore after the transgression Adam acquired the knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of good, which he had received.”

Adam possessed the knowledge of good when he faithfully kept God’s good and holy commandment and remained righteous in the image of his Creator, without forgetting his law.

But after he sold himself—that is, the image and temple of God—to his deceiver, he lost the knowledge of good, because he lost a good conscience.

[The Corbie, Remigius, and Joliensis manuscripts read “sold”; the later printed editions read “subjected.”]

Righteousness was driven out by wickedness; humility was destroyed by pride; self-control was crushed by desire; unbelief seized faith; captivity took away freedom. No portion of the virtues could remain there, where so great a host of vices had burst in.

For “no one can serve two masters” (Luke 16:13); and, “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34); and, “By whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

[The Joliensis manuscript reads: “he is also its slave.”]

No one serves except with some freedom, and no one is free except with some servitude, as the Apostle says (Romans 6:20): “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness.”

[The Corbie and Joliensis manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions read: “no one is free except with some servitude.” The Remigius manuscript omits the words “and no one is free except with some servitude.”]

“What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life.”

[The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions omit “in those things.” The Mainz and Venetian editions include it. The four previously mentioned editions then read: “But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification.”]

Thus, whoever serves the devil is free from God; but whoever, having been freed, serves God is free from the devil. It therefore becomes clear that a bad freedom could arise from the defect of the human will, but that good freedom could not be recovered without the Liberator’s aid.

## CHAPTER X  
### The passage of the Apostle in Romans 2:14 concerning the Gentiles who do by nature what belongs to the law is explained and defended. A certain wisdom among unbelievers derived from the remnants of nature created by God; yet no movement of good will exists except from the Holy Spirit.

[Column 0240A]

## [Also Chapter XXII]

### 1.
