But lest this calamity of the first human being seem to have passed into his descendants, this teacher intends to prove by the example of the Gentiles how intact the nature of all human beings is in judgment.

[Only the Joliensis manuscript reads: “which the nature of all human beings has felt within itself by its own judgment.” The Lyon edition and later editions add “and says.”]

He adds and says (Conference 13, chapter 12):

“Finally, that the human race did not lose the knowledge of good after Adam’s transgression is most clearly shown by the Apostle’s judgment, when he says (Romans 2:14): ‘For when Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature what belongs to the law, these, although they do not have the law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts alternately accusing or even defending them, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings.’”

[The Mainz, Venetian, and Lyon editions read: “Since the Gentiles … do what belongs to the law.” The pronoun ipsorum (“their”) is absent from the Remigius manuscript and from the Mainz and Venetian editions.]

### 2.

If the Apostle is speaking of those who were called from uncircumcision and, although they were far away, “were brought near” (Ephesians 2:13), believing in him who once did not show them mercy but now shows them mercy (1 Peter 2:10), and who, justifying circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith (Romans 3:30), created both in himself and, having destroyed the wall of hostility between Jews and Gentiles (Ephesians 2:14), made peace in one new human being; concluding all under unbelief so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:22)—

[The Joliensis manuscript adds here: “according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ our Lord.” The Lyon edition reads: “were brought near, believing in him. He who once did not show them mercy, and who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith, created the two in himself. And, dissolving in one new human being both walls of hostility, of Jews and Gentiles, made peace,” etc.]

—if, I say, the Apostle is speaking of those in whose hearts God writes the new covenant with his finger, that is, with the Holy Spirit, so that they may naturally fulfill the fullness of the law and the works of charity, nature having been reformed and renewed, what support does the novelty of this most arrogant opinion receive from this?

For the reconciliation of enemies can be attributed only to the grace of the Mediator. “All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Romans 3:23). Therefore grace is the glory of God, not the merit of the one who has been delivered.

“For who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid?” (Romans 11:35).

[The Joliensis manuscript adds: “And it will be repaid to him?”]

No good work proceeds from the dead, no righteousness proceeds from the ungodly; their entire salvation is gratuitous. Therefore it is the glory of God, so that whoever boasts may boast in the one whose glory he needed.

[The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions read: “their entire salvation is grace.”]

[Column 0241A]

### 3.

But if—as this disputant more strongly wishes to be understood—these words are spoken of those who, alienated from the grace of Christ, established certain practices resembling the commandments of the law by their own judgment, understanding that the customs of cities and the harmony of peoples could not otherwise be maintained than by decreeing rewards for right actions and punishments for sins, as was said by the Wisdom of God herself:

“I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, and I held primacy over every nation; I sought rest in Jacob, and I found it.”

[The Mainz and Venetian editions read “they thought.”]

[The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions read “unless,” but the manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions support “unless also.”]

[The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions omit this authority from the book of Ecclesiasticus. It is present in the Corbie, Remigius, and Joliensis manuscripts and in the Mainz and Venetian editions. The Mainz and Venetian editions read “from Wisdom herself, God.” The Remigius manuscript reads: “I held primacy over every nation.” In the Joliensis manuscript the final words, “I sought rest in Jacob, and I found it,” are absent. Thus—]

Who would doubt that this wisdom remains for the human race, for the usefulness of temporal life, from the remnants of nature created by God?

[The Lyon edition reads: “what remains from nature created by God.”]

For if the rational mind did not retain the power to order even these earthly matters, nature would not have been corrupted but extinguished.

Yet even if it excels in the most outstanding arts and possesses every discipline of mortal learning (Ecclesiasticus 24:7), it cannot justify itself, because it uses its good qualities badly. In these qualities, without the worship of the true God, it is convicted of impiety and uncleanness, and by the very means through which it thinks itself defended, it is accused.

[The Joliensis manuscript reads “in moral disciplines of learning”; the Lyon edition and the Remigius manuscript likewise read “in moral disciplines of learning.”]

Since Paul therefore declares that “no flesh will be justified by works of the law” (Romans 3:20), and since in Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but only a new creation (Galatians 5:6), what is this man doing by furnishing the impious freedom of unbelievers with natural goods and wishing to justify it by its own principles?

[The Lyon edition reads: “what is he doing by wishing to justify by its own principles the impious freedom of unbelievers furnished with natural goods?”]

Why does he declare the nakedness of transgressive knowledge adequate for the renewal of assailed old nature?

[The later editions read “the wretched antiquity”; shortly afterward the Joliensis manuscript reads “the freedom of knowledge.”]

It is as though this knowledge, whether acquired as a remnant from the resources of nature or sought from instruction in the law, could, merely through its apprehension, make us love doing what we know ought to be done; or as though any movement of good will existed except that which is created by the breath of charity poured out through the Holy Spirit.

[The word “acquired” is supplied here by the Corbie, Remigius, and Joliensis manuscripts and by the Mainz and Venetian editions.]

“For without faith it is impossible to please” (Hebrews 11:6); and, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23); and, “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

[The Lyon and later editions add “God”: “it is impossible to please God.” The word “God” is absent from the Corbie, Remigius, and Joliensis manuscripts and from the Mainz and Venetian editions; Augustine sometimes omits it, and it is not present in the Greek wording of the Apostle.]

## CHAPTER XI  
### Free choice possesses neither the will nor the ability to do good except through grace. Why human beings are commanded to do what they do not find possible in their nature. Cassian’s eighth definition: What is evil must not alone be attributed to human nature. Human merits are nothing except from grace.

## [Also Chapter XXIII]

### 1.

After this, in concluding the testimonies by which he wished to prove that those who are called deaf and blind through prophetic rebuke can, by the capacity of nature, open their ears to hearing and their eyes to seeing—although the Lord says of these same people, “I will give them another heart, and I will give them a new spirit; and I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh, and I will give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments and observe my judgments and do them” (Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26)—he adds and says (Conference 13, chapter 12):

[The word “their” is absent from the Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts and from the Mainz and Venetian editions.]

“Finally, to indicate that the ability to do good is present in them, he rebuked them and said: ‘Why do you not even judge for yourselves what is just?’ (Luke 12:57).”

[The Lyon and later editions read “he designated,” followed by: “Rebuking the Pharisees, he said: ‘Why do you not, even of yourselves, judge what is good?’ Our reading is preferred by the Joliensis manuscript together with the Mainz and Venetian editions. The Corbie and Remigius manuscripts agree, except that they read “the Pharisees” instead of “them,” although Christ was addressing the crowds when he said this, not the Pharisees specifically. They also read “what is good” instead of “what is just”; the former, however, conforms more closely to the Apostle’s text.]

He would surely not have said this to them unless he knew that by natural judgment they could discern what is equitable.

Now he ascribes to free choice not only the will to do good but also the ability, as though understanding were demanded from them and righteousness required of them because they could produce these things from the goods of nature without God’s gifts.

[The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, read: “as though it were demanded of him … that he bring forth from the goods of nature.”]

Yet these things are commanded to human beings so that, from the very command by which what they have received is enjoined upon them, they may recognize that they lost it through their own fault.

[The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions add “of God.” The Lyon edition later differs from the others, reading “this which he received is judged,” perhaps for “is indicated.”]

The demand is not therefore unjust because the person is not capable of returning what he owes; rather, from the letter that kills he must flee to the Spirit that gives life and seek from grace the ability he does not find in nature.

[The Joliensis manuscript reads: “unless from the letter.” The Lyon and later editions add “before” at this point; the Corbie, Remigius, and Joliensis manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions do not.]

If he does so, God’s mercy is great; if he does not, the punishment of sin is just.

[The Lyon and more recent editions read “the Lord’s mercy.”]

[Column 0243A]

## [Also Chapter XXIV]

### 2.

Then, bringing the preceding argument to completion, he states a ruling principle, saying (Conference 13, chapter 12):

[The Mainz and Venetian editions read: “he pronounces the principle of the judgment.”]

“Therefore we must take care not to refer all the merits of the saints to God in such a way that we attribute to human nature nothing except what is evil and perverse.”

[The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions omit the pronoun “their.”]

What could any disciple of Pelagius and Coelestius have defined more clearly or explicitly according to their doctrine? They say, “God’s grace is given according to our merits”; and the same people say, “God’s grace is not given for each individual act.” Here, within a single statement, he has combined both blasphemies, saying that we must take care not to refer all the merits of the saints to God in such a way that we attribute to human nature nothing except what is evil and perverse.

He therefore wants there to be many merits proper to human beings, which have not been bestowed by the generosity of grace, and to which certain gifts from above are owed for increasing their natural riches.

He wants us not to receive God’s grace for each individual act, and consequently not always to pray for every good work.

[The Corbie and Remigius manuscripts and the Mainz edition read: “and consequently.”]

[The Lyon edition reads: “And thus he thinks that no merit should be believed to exist among God’s gifts, since the one whom God has always assisted in everything is without merit.”]

It will therefore follow that no merit should be thought to exist in God’s gifts, since the person whom God has always assisted in everything is without merit. Or, if merits are assigned even in those things God bestows, it will also be established that these very merits could have been acquired by one’s own ability.

[The Joliensis manuscript reads “by one’s own power.” The Lyon edition presents the entire passage differently: “Or, if they even speak of there being some merits in those things God bestows, it will also be established,” and so forth.]

And consequently we ought to be assisted in some things so that, through grace, what was not impossible by nature may become more possible.

[The Lyon edition reads: “we ought to be assisted … so that what was not possible may become possible”; this is contrary to the sense of the author and to the authority of the other manuscripts.]

Behold, already within this brief handful of words there is a numerous chain of not merely two but many impieties. If it is examined with the discrimination of painstaking care, it will be shown to be in no respect released from the chain of condemned error.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Cassian’s position is more fully demonstrated: that pious thoughts and holy counsels conceived without God’s inspiration can arise from natural wisdom. Against him, by explaining the passage he misused and by adducing other passages, it is shown that pious thoughts do not arise from free choice without God’s inspiration. Human good will is its own in such a way that it is conceived only when God inspires it. Human conversion, although it does not occur without the human being, nevertheless does not begin from the human being.

## [Also Chapter XXV]

### 1.

But lest we seem to be proceeding by suspicions and probing hidden meanings beyond the words, let what follows show what is added to what we already know.

Therefore, the man who at the beginning of his argument had said, “The beginning not only of actions but also of good thoughts is from God; he both inspires in us the beginnings of holy will and grants us the strength and opportunity to carry out the things we rightly desire,” now, wishing to prove that religious thoughts and holy counsels conceived without any inspiration from God can arise from natural wisdom, sets forth Solomon’s words:

“My father David wished to build a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel. And the Lord said to David my father: ‘Because you thought in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well to have this in your mind; nevertheless, you will not build the house for my name’” (1 Kings 8:17).

Then, to show how this should be understood, the disputant himself adds (Conference 13, chapter 12):

[The Joliensis manuscript omits “the disputant himself.”]

“Was this thought, and this deliberation of King David, good and from God, or evil and from human beings? For if that thought was good and from God, why is its accomplishment denied to the one by whom it was inspired? But if it was evil and from human beings, why is it praised by the Lord? It remains, therefore, that it should be believed to have been both good and from human beings. In the same way we can also judge our thoughts every day. For it was not granted to David alone to think something good from himself, nor are we denied the natural ability ever to conceive or think anything good.”

[The Mainz and Venetian editions read: “lest we should ever be able to conceive anything good.”]

### 2.

This testimony and argument can in no way prove that pious thoughts arise from free choice alone and not from God’s inspiration.

David’s will, which was certainly good, must not be considered to have been not from God merely because the Lord wished the temple to be built not by David himself but by his son.

We must therefore ask from what spirit the impulse of this will proceeded—namely, from that Spirit of God in whom he said:

“If I enter the tent of my house, if I climb onto the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Psalm 131:3).

[Only the Venetian edition reads “of my bed.”]

When the Prophet desired this, he did not fail to understand that the true and perfect temple had to be built by the one who, although he was the Son of God, also became the son of David; and who, seeing the temple built by Solomon, said:

“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” But he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19, 21).

[The Joliensis manuscript alone adds immediately after “the son of David,” omitting the intervening words: “Hence the Evangelist says, ‘But he was speaking about the temple of his body.’”]

Therefore, so that the temple which was being ordained in Christ and in the Church might be prefigured, David’s son, not David, was rightly chosen for its construction.

[The Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions read “for its erection”; the Corbie and Remigius manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions read “for its instruction”; the Joliensis manuscript reads “for its construction.”]

Through the son of a man, the Son of God and man was signified; and through the destructible temple, the incorruptible dwelling was indicated. To construct an image of this, David’s will was approved, but the work was transferred to the one whose person corresponded more closely to that image.

[The words “the Son of God and of a human being was signified” are absent from the Lyon manuscript.]

Thus David’s desire was from God, and Solomon’s carrying it out was from God.

[The Lyon edition adds: “And thus David’s desire was from God, and Solomon’s carrying it out was from God.” That edition, like the older editions generally, spells the name “Solomon” differently in the Latin.]

### 3.

To make this clearer by examples, let us inquire where God did not will something to be done which human beings nevertheless willed to do with God willing it.

The Lord commanded his apostles, saying:

“Go, go forth and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to keep everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19).

[The Lyon and later editions read: “He commanded his apostles.” The Joliensis manuscript and the Mainz and Venetian editions read: “Go and teach.” The same manuscript reads “baptizing them.”]

When the apostles heard this, they certainly did not receive mere words through bodily sounds only in their external ears. Rather, the inextinguishable flame of charity was kindled in their hearts by the power of the living word, and through it they desired most fervently to preach the Gospel of Christ to all nations.

[The Corbie manuscript and the edition of this work in the appendix to volume 10 of Augustine’s works, together with Leuven and the more recent editions, read as above. The Remigius manuscript reads: “But when they were forbidden to speak the word in Asia and were prevented from going to Bithynia.” The Joliensis manuscript reads: “But when they wished to speak the word in Asia and to go to Bithynia, they were prevented by the Spirit of Jesus.” The Mainz and Venetian editions largely agree with the Corbie manuscript and our text, omitting “when they attempted.” The Lyon edition reads: “But why were they forbidden to speak the word in Asia and to go to Bithynia? They were prevented by the Spirit of Jesus.”]

But when they were forbidden to speak the word in Asia and, when they attempted to go to Bithynia, were prevented by the Spirit of Jesus (Acts 16:6–7), did they not have this will from God—that they desired to turn to the faith the hearts even of those whom, by a hidden judgment, God did not then wish to hear the Gospel?

Or when the Church prays daily for her enemies—that is, for those who have not yet believed in God—does she not do so from the Spirit of God?

Who could say this except one who does not do it, or who thinks that faith is not God’s gift?

[The Lyon edition alone adds: “and then, when it is requested for everyone.”]

And yet what is requested for everyone is not obtained for everyone. Nor is there injustice with God, who often does not grant what he has given us to request.

[The Joliensis manuscript reads: “which he has granted to be requested.”]

### [Also Chapter XXVI]

4. Therefore, the good will—namely, that by which one cleaves to God—must neither be denied [Note: The Lyons edition reads, “by which he cleaves to God.”] to be proper to man, nor left unacknowledged as conceived under God’s inspiration. For since no one is good except God alone (Luke 18:19), what sort of good can there be that does not have the Good One as its author?

Human nature, whose creator is God, retains even after the transgression its substance, its form, its life, its senses, and its reason, together with the other goods of body and soul—goods that are not absent even from the wicked and vicious. [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges read this way, as do the Mainz and Venice editions, but in those editions *the perception of true goodness* is absent. Lyons reads, “but not in others.” Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read, “but there is not in them a perception of true goodness.”] Yet through these things it does not possess the perception of true goodness, which can adorn mortal life but cannot bestow eternal life.

For it is not unknown how much the schools of Greece, Roman eloquence, and the inquiry of the whole world, laboring with the keenest studies and the most outstanding intellects to discover the highest good, accomplished nothing except that they “became futile in their thoughts” (Romans 1:21), and that the foolish heart of those who used themselves as their own guides for knowing the truth was darkened. [Note: Lyons reads *ob noscendam*; Louvain and later editions read *ad noscendam*.] [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read, “as much as the Greek school.” The manuscripts of Corbie and Remigius, and the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, read, “however much the school of Greece, however much Roman eloquence,” and so forth. The Jumièges manuscript reads, “and Roman eloquence.”]

If, therefore, someone, ashamed of wretched vanities and deceptive madness, understands that everything he had embraced as light and life is darkness and death, and attempts to withdraw from these things, that turning is not from him, although it is not without him; nor does he strive toward the beginnings of salvation by his own strength. Rather, this is accomplished by the hidden and powerful grace of God, which, removing the ashes of earthly opinions and dead works, stirs up the firebrand (*torrem*) buried beneath the heart and sets it aflame with the desire for truth. [Note: Lyons and later editions read “after the ashes ... had been removed.” The Lyons codex reads *terrorem* (“terror”) where the others read *torrem* (“firebrand”), except Remigius, which reads *scintillam* (“spark”); Jumièges reads “the firebrand of the dead heart.”] It does not subdue a man against his will, but makes him desirous of submission; nor does it drag along one who is ignorant, but goes before one who understands and follows.

For free will remains free—free will which God certainly created together with man—and it is changed from its vanities and desires, into which it had declined by neglecting God’s law, not by itself but by the Creator. [Note: The Lyons edition reads *fluxerat* (“had flowed/declined”).] [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges, and the Mainz and Venice editions, read “which God created for each person.”] Thus whatever in it is restored for the better [Note: The Jumièges manuscript omits “for the better.”] is neither without the one who is healed nor from anyone except the one who heals. We are his new creation and new workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, “which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10).

## CHAPTER XIII

**Cassian’s ninth definition: The seeds of the virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator. This is refuted because original sin overturned them. The virtues are not truly present in the impious, but all their works are unclean. There are no beginnings of virtues or merits in us before grace. Although there are many praiseworthy qualities in the talents of the impious, they are not true virtues. The statement that the Collator had attempted to prove from the apocryphal book of the Shepherd—that even before grace man is equally disposed toward good and evil—is refuted.**

### [Also Chapter XXVII]

1. Let us now see how far the intention of this disputant proceeds. “It cannot be doubted,” he says (Collation 13, chapter 12), “that the seeds of the virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s beneficence. But unless they are aroused by God’s assistance, they cannot advance to the growth of perfection; for, according to the blessed Apostle, neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.” [Note: The words beginning “for, according to the blessed Apostle” and ending “but God who gives the growth” were omitted in the Remigius and Jumièges manuscripts. They are also absent from the Mainz, Venice, and Lyons editions. Moreover, in the Remigius and Jumièges manuscripts, and in the Mainz and Venice editions, the word “God” after “assistance” is absent.]

He also teaches most plainly that freedom of choice toward either side belongs to man, even in the book called the Shepherd, in which two angels are said to cling to each of us—one good and one evil—and that it lies within man’s choice to select which one he will follow. Therefore free will always remains in man, so that he may either neglect or love God’s grace. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads, “by which he may neglect God’s grace.”]

If it cannot be doubted that the seeds of the virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted through the Creator’s beneficence, then only Adam transgressed, and no one sinned in his sin; we were conceived in no iniquities, and our mothers bore us in no sins (Psalm 50:7); we were not by nature children of wrath, nor were we under the power of darkness (Ephesians 2:3); and, since the virtues naturally remain in us, we were born instead as children of peace and light (Colossians 1:13).

Away with the treacherous deception of false teaching from the minds of the faithful. Virtues cannot dwell together with vices. For “what participation,” says the Apostle, “has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6:14).

For God is virtue in the primary sense: for him, to possess virtue is nothing other than to be virtue. When we share in him, Christ dwells in us—he who is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24); faith, hope, love, self-control, understanding, counsel, courage, and the other virtues dwell in us. [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read, “he who is dwells in us,” omitting the word “Christ.”]

But when we withdraw from this good, everything contrary arises in us from ourselves. When beauty departs, what succeeds it except ugliness? When wisdom leaves, what remains except folly? When justice does not rule, what dominates except iniquity? [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read, “when we withdraw from this honor.”]

2. Therefore the seeds of the virtues, implanted through the Creator’s beneficence, were overturned by the transgression of our first parent; nor can they be possessed unless they are restored by the one who gave them. Human nature can be restored to its Maker, [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read, “by its Maker.”] and it is capable of recovering the goods it once possessed, so that through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, it may recover, in that very part of it which remains, what it lost.

What remains to it is the rational mind, which is not virtue but the dwelling place of virtue. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript omits the preposition “from.”] For through participation in wisdom, justice, and mercy, we are not ourselves wisdom, justice, or mercy; rather, we become wise, just, and merciful.

These goods, although our rational faculty is occupied by vices and, when we transgress, an unclean spirit has invaded God’s temple, can nevertheless flow back into that rational faculty through the one who “casts out the ruler of this world” (John 12:31), and who, binding the strong man, seizes his vessels (Mark 3:27). When the spirit of this world has been driven away, he gives the Spirit who is from God, [Note: Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges, with the Mainz and Venice editions, read this way; Lyons and later editions read, “he grants us the Spirit.”] “so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 2:12). But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9).

### [Also Chapter XXVIII]

3. I believe that this man is deceived by plausibility and errs in the appearance of false virtues, since he judges that those goods which can be possessed only as God’s gift are also found in the minds of the impious. [Note: The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “supposes” (*existimat*).] He thinks this because many of them pursue justice, temperance, self-control, and benevolence. They do not possess these things without purpose or benefit, and through such pursuits they gain much honor and glory in this life. But because in these pursuits they serve not God but the devil, although they receive a temporal reward from empty praise, they nevertheless do not belong to the truth of those blessed virtues. [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions omit the word “nevertheless.”]

Thus it is most clearly evident that no virtue dwells in the minds of the impious, but that all their works are unclean and polluted. Their wisdom is not spiritual but animal; not heavenly but earthly; not Christian but demonic; not from the Father of lights but from the ruler of darkness. Even those things which they would not possess unless God gave them, they subject to the one who first departed from God. [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges agree with the Mainz and Venice editions. The Lyons and later editions read, “while through those very things which they would not possess unless God gave them, they are subjected to him,” and so forth.]

4. Therefore, when someone says that the seeds of the virtues are naturally present in every soul without any work of grace, what is he trying to show except that from these seeds certain shoots of merits preceding God’s grace spring up? [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie and Jumièges and the Mainz and Venice editions read, “certain seeds.”]

Finally, so that he might seem to have attributed something to grace, he says: “These seeds cannot reach the growth of perfection unless they are aroused by God’s assistance”—so that God’s assistance is merely exhortation and teaching, while the mind, rich in the seeds of the virtues, uses the capacity it possesses, needing help only to seize the summit of those virtues whose beginnings it knows to be within itself.

### [Also Chapter XXIX]

Therefore, according to him [Note: Lyons and later editions read “according to this man.”], the human soul will be built into a temple of God without receiving the foundation “other than which no one can lay, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). But when does this foundation begin, unless when faith is generated in the heart of the hearer? If faith was naturally present, then something was not begun there but built upon it. [Note: Lyons and later editions read, “built above.”] The unbeliever, therefore, would seem to have had faith before believing, and so would have appeared to be an unbeliever needlessly.

The same can be said of the beginnings of the other virtues: grace ought to increase them because they exist, not give them because they are absent. But all the words of the Holy Scriptures teach us something else.

We read that “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 1:7), and we read that this virtue is God’s gift (ibid. 9:10). “The fear of God,” it says, “has placed itself above all things.” [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads, “He placed the fear of God above all these things.” Lyons reads, “I placed the fear of the Lord above all things.” Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read, “The fear of the Lord placed itself above all things.”]

Blessed is the person to whom it has been given to possess the fear of God (Ecclesiasticus 25:14–15). [Note: Corbie and Remigius read “blessed man”; Louvain, Douai, and Cologne enclosed *man* in parentheses as of doubtful authority; Mainz, Venice, and Lyons omit it; Jumièges reads “blessed male/person.” For “fear of God,” Jumièges, Lyons, and later editions read “fear of the Lord.”] Since, then, the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, what virtue can be possessed without wisdom, for which fear is the beginning? [Note: Lyons and later editions read, “of which fear is the beginning.”]

The blessed Apostle Peter says: “May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the recognition of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has now given us, by his divine power, all things pertaining to life and godliness” (2 Peter 1:2–3). [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “in the knowledge ... all things in us.”] Does he say, “He aroused in us by his assistance the seeds of the virtues which we naturally possessed”? No, he says: “He has now given us all things pertaining to life and godliness.” [Note: This entire phrase is omitted in the Mainz and Venice editions. In the Cologne edition, *collocatum sit* (“has been placed”) stands for *collatum sit* (“has been bestowed”).] [Note: The Lyons edition reads, “whether he gave us the things pertaining to life and godliness,” omitting the rest.]

By saying this, what beginning of virtue did he place in nature that was not bestowed by the one who gave all things? For this reason the blessed Paul also says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

5. Therefore we possess all things pertaining to life and godliness not through nature, which has been corrupted, [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read, “but we received them through nature, which is restored by grace”; the Lyons edition omits this entire clause.] but through grace, by which nature is restored.

Nor should we therefore suppose that the beginnings of the virtues exist in natural treasures merely because many praiseworthy qualities are found even in the talents of the impious. [Note: Lyons and later editions read, “things worthy of praise.”] These qualities certainly arise from nature; but because such people have departed from the one who created nature, they cannot be virtues.

For whatever is illuminated by light is light, and whatever lacks that same light is night. “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). Thus what is thought to be virtue is vice, since what is thought to be wisdom is foolishness. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads, “What is the wisdom of this world? It is foolishness.” The Mainz and Venice editions read, “And so what is thought to be wisdom is vice, since what is thought to be virtue is foolishness.”]

How, then, can those who glory in the seeds of natural virtues—seeds which this man magnifies—submit their virtues to the teaching [Note: Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges, with Mainz and Venice, read substantially as in the text. Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read: “How can it happen that he who thinks himself abundant in the seeds of natural virtues, which he himself boasts to be magnificent ... should submit?” Douai and Cologne give in the margin, “which this man boasts to be magnificent.”] that says, “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise, let him become foolish, so that he may become wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18)? And again: “Since the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21).

What could that presumption of knowledge and wisdom judge more inept and more laughable, unless the Spirit of God has subdued the contempt of the proud and, by the power of his grace, destroyed those arguments which, with canine eloquence, opposed the unknown truth—so that the soil of the heart, furrowed by the seed of the word, may receive it, and God’s cultivation produce fruits worthy of the eternal granaries? [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie and Remigius and the Mainz edition read this way; for *furrowed*, they have “of the furrowed heart.” Lyons and later editions read: “What could that knowledge and presumption of knowledge regard as more inept … than that which is unknown to virtue?” The Jumièges manuscript reads: “What is more ignorant than that wisdom, what more inept and more laughable through presumption, except … the furrowed soil of a heart set aflame by truth?”]

### [Also Chapter XXX]

6. [Note: Corbie and Remigius, with Mainz and Venice, read this passage as follows. Jumièges reads: “But that testimony is of no authority which ... by which he wished to show, between the good and evil angel ... Later, however, he added the rule of his definition.” Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read, “and by which he wished to show, between the contrary persuasions of good and evil ... he added,” and so forth. See above at the beginning of this chapter.] After that testimony of no authority which he inserted into his argument from the little book of the Shepherd, by which he attempted to demonstrate that, between the contrary persuasions of the good and evil angel, every human being is so entrusted to natural judgment and personal discernment that he has no more protection from God than danger from the devil, he added the rule of his definition, saying:

“And therefore free will always remains in man, so that he may either neglect or love God’s grace.” [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie, Lyons, and the later editions read “the definition of his own.” The manuscripts of Remigius and Jumièges, and the Mainz and Venice editions, read “of his definition.”] [Note: Lyons and later editions read, “by which he may.”]

In this statement, even the claim that free will always remains in man is not established in every respect. [Note: Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges read, “that it always remains in man”; Mainz and Venice, “that free will always remains in man”; Lyons and later editions, “that free will always remains in man.”] For many thousands of infants who are received into the kingdom of God, or excluded from the kingdom of God, receive or lose God’s grace without any exercise of their own will; and many who are utterly witless and foolish in every respect are rescued from the bonds of eternal death through the sacrament of regeneration.

Let us nevertheless understand this statement as applying properly to those who are able to use free will. Is this freedom so free that, to the extent that it possesses disgust from itself in order to neglect God’s grace, it possesses from itself an equal measure of delight in order to love it? [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, read, “so that it has from itself only as much …” Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read as in the text. Lyons reads *love* instead of *delight*; Douai and Cologne placed the same reading in the margin.]

Has no breath of midday heat relaxed the icy rigidity of that ancient unbelief in him? Has the torpor of a constrained mind warmed itself from its own cold? [Note: The Jumièges manuscript omits “of ancient unbelief.” Remigius reads, “Has any breath of midday heat relaxed that ancient …?”] And when the Lord says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), did no spark reach the cold heart, and did dead ash of its own accord blaze into the flame of love? [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, read this way. Lyons and later editions read: “so that, when the Lord says … a spark may reach … and may blaze into the flame of charity.”]

Nothing of this kind happened in those lovers of grace—such as was experienced by those who said, [Note: Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read “in these condemners of grace,” with “in these” in the margin. Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges, together with Mainz, Venice, and the older Lyons edition, read “in these lovers of grace”; the Lyons margin proposes that “condemners of grace” may perhaps be read. The reading of the manuscripts and older editions is preferred; this and the immediately following statements are to be understood figuratively, as interrogations.] “Was not our heart burning within us while he was speaking to us on the way and opening the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions add “within us”; the other manuscripts used here do not.]

Nor did that other event occur in the case of Lydia, the purple-seller of the city of Thyatira, who alone among the women to whom the Apostle was preaching there is then shown to have believed. “God,” it says, “opened her heart to attend to what was being said by Paul” (Acts 16:14). [Note: Corbie, Lyons, and later editions read “concerning Lydia.” The same manuscript, together with Remigius and Jumièges, reads “God opened her heart”; others read “the Lord opened her heart.”]

According to this man, free will has such soundness and capacity that it possesses love—which is the chief of all the virtues—not as God’s gift but solely from the will. [Note: Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read, “Either such soundness or capacity, so that …” Lyons has the plural “may have,” agreeing with the manuscripts of Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges and with the Mainz and Venice editions.]

What, then, is restored in the soul by its builder? Or by what abundance of grace will it become more beautiful, if those things are its own without which the things given cannot benefit it? [Note: Lyons and later editions read, “What will be prepared?”]

But the Apostle, who declares that without love neither the working of miracles, nor knowledge, nor faith, nor prophecy, nor the distribution of riches, nor even the endurance of the most savage punishments is beneficial (1 Corinthians 13:2–3), does not remain silent about where love itself is obtained: “Because the love of God,” he says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). And again: “Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 6:23). [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions conform to the Apostolic text: “Peace to the brothers, and love with faith.”]

Let the holy Apostle John also instruct us from where we began to share in this good. “Beloved,” he says, “let us love one another, because love is from God” (1 John 4:7). And lest we suppose that love is said to be from God because this affection for salvation had been planted in human nature, he says shortly afterward: “Not because we loved God, but because he loved us” (ibid. 10); and again: “Let us love God, because he first loved us” (ibid. 19). [Note: The Remigius manuscript, together with Lyons and the later editions, reads, “so that we might be able.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “that this affection for salvation might be here”; Jumièges, “that this affection might be here”; Corbie, “that this leap might be here”; Lyons, “that this effect might here be made sound.”]

Let human need therefore acknowledge that what is rightly said of any good is said much more rightly of the one without whom all good things are of no benefit: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). [Note: This passage is absent from the Jumièges manuscript.]

## CHAPTER XIV

**Cassian undertakes to demonstrate the strength of free will. Cassian’s tenth definition: Job overcame the devil by his own strength, not through the assistance of grace, except insofar as God did not give the tempter greater power than he knew Job possessed virtue to withstand. Cassian’s deception: at the beginning of his discussion he professes the catholic position concerning grace, and later attacks that same position. He gradually descends toward the Pelagian precipices.**

### [Also Chapter XXXI]

1. After this, when he had attributed to man before grace as much as it is most beneficial for him to possess through grace, he added certain things obscurely and confusedly in order to demonstrate the strength of free will. [Note: “However” is absent from Jumièges and the Mainz and Venice editions. Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read, after “a little later,” “as much as was most beneficial for him,” and then “added certain things perplexedly and confusedly.” Mainz and Venice read “adds”; the remainder is as in the text.] [Note: The word “however” is absent from the Jumièges manuscript and from the Mainz and Venice editions. Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne add, after “a little later,” “as much as was most beneficial for him,” and then continue confusedly. Mainz and Venice add this; the remainder is as in the text.]

He wished to fortify with the works he performs through the powers already given to him what he had defined as naturally present in him, so that what he had perfected through God’s assistance might be shown to have begun from the liberty of free will. [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “through the virtues.” The same was added in the margin by Louvain, Douai, and Cologne. Mainz later reads “wishes to unite them”; Venice, “to come.” These editions then read “by the liberty of free will,” whereas Lyons and later editions read “through the liberty of free will.” The three manuscripts read “from the liberty of free will.”]

But let us pass over these matters as tolerable, since we too say that free will, through grace at work, conceived the affection of a good will and the beginning of faith, so that by means of these gifts—which were granted to it without any preceding merit—it might merit what has been promised to the one who is to perform them, always asking from the one who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), the ability to do some good. [Note: Lyons and later editions read “for those who are to perform them.”]

### [Also Chapter XXXII]

Let us return, then, to what he put forward concerning the sufferings of holy Job. For he says (Collation 1, chapter 14):

“We read that divine justice also provided for Job, its most proven athlete, when the devil demanded him for single combat. For if he had engaged the enemy not by his own strength but protected by God’s grace alone, and if, without any strength of his own endurance, supported solely by divine assistance, he had endured those numerous masses and disasters of temptations sought with all the enemy’s cruelty, how could the devil not have more justly repeated against him that slanderous accusation which he had previously uttered: ‘Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not surrounded him, his house, and all his possessions on every side? But take away your hand—that is, allow him to contend with me by his own powers—and see whether he will not bless you to your face’ (Job 1:9–11).” [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “the strength of his wisdom … and endured destruction.” Lyons and later editions read “will he worship God?” The words “and his house” are absent from the Remigius and Jumièges manuscripts and from Lyons.]

But since, after the conflict, the slanderous enemy does not dare to repeat any such complaint, he confesses that he was overcome not by God’s strength but by Job’s.

Nevertheless, we must not believe that God’s grace was entirely absent from him. Grace gave the tempter as much power as it knew Job possessed virtue to resist—not protecting him from the enemy’s attack in such a way as to leave no place for human virtue, but arranging only that the most violent enemy, by making his soul senseless and deprived of judgment, should not weigh him down with an unequal and unjust burden of combat. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads, “and deprived of sense.”]

### [Also Chapter XXXIII]

2. Who would believe that these things were proclaimed by catholics among catholics, unless they read them written down which they had often heard defended in private conversations? [Note: Corbie, Remigius, and Jumièges read *collocutionibus* (“conversations”), as do Mainz and Venice; Lyons and later editions read *colluctationibus* (“struggles”).] Has the sight of understanding become so clouded in all human beings, and has the spirit of knowledge and piety departed from all the children of the Church, that they are not ashamed to thrust such disgraceful lies upon the judgment of their readers? [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “by catholics,” without the preposition *by*. Below, for “conversations,” Lyons and later editions read “struggles”; the Jumièges manuscript does not differ.]

Serious man, learned teacher, truthful master, give us back the catholic definition with which, at the beginning of your discussion, you captured our ears and minds. You had declared in the language of the Church: “The beginning not only of good actions but also of good thoughts is from God” [Note: Corbie and Remigius, with Mainz and Venice, read “the Christian faith, in an ecclesiastical utterance”; Lyons and later editions read “the Christian faith, with an ecclesiastical utterance”; Jumièges reads “the Christian faith, in an ecclesiastical utterance.”] (above, chapter 2, section 2), who inspires in us the beginnings of a holy will and grants the power and opportunity to carry out what we rightly desire.

“For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, who both inspires what is good and carries it out and brings it to completion in us” (James 1:17). [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads *hujus enim* (“for of this”).] By the solidity of this statement you had shattered all the devices of the hostile remnants.

Why, after changing your profession, do you build up what you destroyed and attack what you defended? Why, abandoning the impregnable fortress of truth, do you gradually run down toward the Pelagian precipices? [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads, “with the fortress destroyed.”]

You had defined that the beginnings neither of holy thoughts, nor pious wills, nor good actions are from us, but that all good things are generated in us through God’s inspiration and the assistance of his grace, and brought to progress and perfection. Yet shortly afterward you began attempting to make the gifts of grace equal to free will, so that you might show that human beings could possess from themselves the beginnings which you had assigned to God.

You said (above, chapter 3, section 3): “For sometimes a person can be extended toward the desire for the virtues even by his own movements, although he always needs to be helped by the Lord.” [Note: Lyons and later editions read, “could be extended,” and add, “but always needs to be helped by the Lord.”] And again (above, chapter 4, section 2): “Even through the good of nature, which was granted through the Creator’s beneficence, the beginnings of good wills sometimes emerge; yet unless they are directed by the Lord, they cannot reach the completion of the virtues.” [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads, “reach completion,” omitting “of the virtues.”]

After this, to show that some are preceded by grace [Note: Remigius and the Lyons edition read “unto grace.”] while in the case of others you placed the cause of receiving grace in merits that came first, you said (above, chapter 5, section 1): “It cannot be determined which depends on which” [Note: The Mainz and Venice editions read “both.”]—that is, whether God has mercy on us because we have offered the beginning of a good will, or whether, because God has mercy, we attain the beginning of a good will.

And, so that you would not leave these two rules in ambiguity, you took care to support each with examples which seemed suitable to you: confirming one by the forced conversion of Paul and Matthew, and strengthening the other by the voluntary faith of Zacchaeus and the thief. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript, Lyons, and later editions read “the other.”] You say that their desire was so vehement (above, chapter 7, section 1) that special summonses of their calling anticipated that desire in laying hold of the kingdom of heaven. [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “merits” rather than “summonses.”] [Note: The Jumièges manuscript reads “merits of vocation.”]

Then, as the discussion progressed, in order to reveal the soundness of the inner person (above, chapter 9, section 2), you affirm that Adam certainly conceived a knowledge of evil which he had not possessed, but did not lose the knowledge of good which he had received. [Note: Lyons reads, “the awareness of evil; but that he did not lose the knowledge of good which he had received.”]

When you wished to prove this also by comparison with the impious, you went so far as to proclaim (above, chapter 11, section 2): “We must take care not to refer all the merits of the saints to God in such a way that we attribute nothing except what is evil to human nature.” And lest we believe that this nature had lost any virtues in Adam’s transgression, you defined the souls of all human beings to be naturally as sound as the soul of the first man before sin, saying (above, chapter 13, section 1): “It cannot be doubted that the seeds of the virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted through the Creator’s beneficence.” [Note: Lyons reads “any natures”; Mainz reads “minds” instead of “souls.”]

When your definitions are considered, it is not hidden how far you have departed from the soundness of that position in which, by deceitfully proclaiming what should have been attributed to grace, you wished to win the judgment of catholic ears. Once those ears had been secured by the appearance of your initial profession, the later assertions could easily insinuate themselves if the first had been pleasing. [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie and Remigius, and the Mainz and Venice editions, read “of the preceding profession.”]

## CHAPTER XV

**How much strength Cassian attributes to free will. He thinks that Job overcame the devil in the conflict by his own power. It is proved to the contrary that Job overcame through God’s assistance. The strength of endurance comes only from God’s grace. Cassian’s error is that Job possessed the virtue of resistance from free will, not from grace.**

[Column 0255C]

[Also Chapter XXXIV.] 1. But thus far, lest you seem wholly to depart from the rule you had laid down, you transferred the beginnings of virtues and merits from free will to grace, [Note: [Col. 0255D] So the manuscripts of Corbie, Remiremont, and Jumièges, together with the Mainz and Venice editions. The Lyons edition and later ones read, “you transferred to free will from grace,” so that they have, etc.] so that you confessed that the voluntary movements of good desires could neither advance nor be perfected without God’s help. [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “so that the voluntary movements of good things themselves,” omitting “desires.” The later editions, Lyons and others, shortly afterward read “you permitted,” where the manuscripts and the older Mainz and Venice editions read “you confessed.”] But now, with God removed still farther away and separated from the support of man, you attribute such power to free will [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “you attributed power.”] that it not only steadfastly and calmly accepts the loss of numerous possessions, and the bitter end at once of an entire household, family, and relationships, but also overcomes, by the purpose of bare will, the unspeakable tortures of his own body. And so that there could be no doubt about this when you argue in this way, you set forth the holy Job as an example: he, you say, contended against that conspicuous cruelty of diabolical savagery without God’s protection. You strive to prove this by the argument that the bloodthirsty enemy himself confessed that he had been overcome not by the Lord’s power but by Job’s, since, in the more severe conflict, he did not say that God’s grace had stood in his way—as though that man ought to have been surrounded by heavenly protection in losses and bereavements, but in the torments of his flesh and soul had not needed assistance.

If, therefore, by this greatness of spirit, which the punishment of so many deaths inflicted upon every limb, and upon all his limbs, could not overcome, [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “by which the punishment inflicted upon him,” etc., as in the text. The Mainz edition reads, “by which the punishment inflicted”; the Venice edition, “by which the punishment inflicted … the punishment of deaths he overcame.”] nothing more memorable is found among the triumphs of the saints, nothing more illustrious, [Note: [Col. 0256D] The Corbie and Remiremont manuscripts read, “nothing more within” (Remiremont: “among”) “the palms of the saints,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “and since you assert it”; Lyons reads, “and that.”] and you assert that this endurance rests solely upon human virtue, what praise or merit will remain for free will to obtain amid the pursuits of quiet and peace, since you have crowned it on the basis of its own powers at the end of so great a struggle?

2. I ask you, then: does it seem to you that this man, when he was tested by the sufferings we read of, had the Holy Spirit within him? [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Jumièges manuscript omits “within himself”; it then reads, “knowing that.”] If you say that he had him, it is certain that God, who did not abandon him, helped him. But if you say that the Holy Spirit had departed from him, his prophetic utterance refutes you, for he says:

> For I know that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see; my eyes shall behold him, and not another. This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom.  
> (Job 19:25) [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Mainz and Venice editions add, “he lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” The Jumièges manuscript reads, “my saving God … my hope is laid up,” omitting the pronoun “this.”]

If this is rightly understood as a prophecy concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and his resurrection—he who is the firstfruits of those who sleep—and concerning the hope of redemption laid up in him for all the saints, it plainly appears that God’s grace had not departed from his temple. Even then the Lord had made himself present in this holy man, promising that he would afterward do the same in his apostles and martyrs, when he said:

> When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak; for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.  
> (Matthew 10:19) [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “in his holy one.”]

And when that same holy man was replying to foolish comforters, was he not relying upon God’s help when he said:

> Let the one who is mocked by his friend, as I am, call upon the Lord, and he will hear him.  
> (Job 12:4) [Note: [Col. 0255D] The Cologne edition reads, “not in God”; shortly afterward the Mainz edition reads, “he will call upon God.” The Remiremont manuscript reads, “and he himself will hear.”]

Or did he not know that he possessed what he possessed from him of whom he says: [Note: [Col. 0256D] The Jumièges manuscript reads “from him”; the others, “out of him.”]

> With him are wisdom and strength; his is counsel and understanding.  
> (Job 13:3) [Note: [Col. 0257C] The Remiremont manuscript reads, “strength and wisdom.”]

And of whom he says:

> In whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh.  
> (Job 12:10) [Note: [Col. 0257C] Lyons and the later editions read, “and what he says.”]

And again:

> I wait until my change comes. You will call, and I will answer you; you will stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands. Indeed, you have counted my steps, but you spare my sins; you have sealed up my transgressions as in a bag, but you have healed my iniquity. [Note: [Col. 0257C] The Corbie and Remiremont manuscripts, with the Mainz and Venice editions, read “sparing”; the Jumièges manuscript, “you will spare.”]

Therefore the Lord had not abandoned the one whom he was healing; nor had he withdrawn his help from the one to whom he was applying purifying remedies, by which he might shine more brightly. [Note: [Col. 0257C] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “God had not abandoned him.”]

[Also Chapter XXXV.] 3. For this endurance of sufferings, in which this holy man excelled, the one who said the following was also prepared by the Lord: [Note: [Col. 0257D] The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read, “was prepared.”]

> Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, because you are with me.  
> (Psalm 22:4) [Note: [Col. 0257C] The Mainz and Venice editions omit the words “this endurance of sufferings.” Lyons reads shortly afterward, “in which this spirit shone forth.”]

And likewise:

> The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation.  
> (Psalm 36:39) [Note: [Col. 0257D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “But the salvation of the righteous.”]

The one who both believed in Christ and referred suffering for Christ back to Christ was also prepared by the Lord for this endurance. He said:

> Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces tested character, and tested character produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.  
> (Romans 5:1–5) [Note: [Col. 0257D] Here the Mainz and Venice editions add, “by faith,” which is also found in the Apostle’s text. Lyons and the later editions read, “in this grace”; Cologne, “in this glory.”]

And again:

> Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written: Because of you we are put to death all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter. But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us.  
> (Romans 8:33–37; Psalm 43:22) [Note: [Col. 0257D] Lyons and the later editions read, “we have been considered.” The Jumièges manuscript reads, “and in all things.” The Remiremont manuscript reads, “and in all these things.”]

From whom this strength of endurance came, blessed Peter—and in him the whole Church—learned from the voice of Truth itself, which says: [Note: [Col. 0257D] The Lyons and later editions read, “from which it descended.”]

> Behold, Satan has asked to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail.  
> (Luke 22:31) [Note: [Col. 0257D] The Remiremont and Jumièges manuscripts read, “to sift you.” Lyons and the later editions read, “in tribulation.”]

Whoever, therefore, does not fail in tribulations should not doubt that he is helped by the one to whom the hearts of all the faithful cry out daily:

> Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.  
> (Matthew 6:13) [Note: [Col. 0257D] The Remiremont and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, read, “Do not lead us.”]

For:

> The Lord guards the souls of his saints; he will deliver them from the hand of sinners.  
> (Psalm 96:10) [Note: [Col. 0257D] The Lyons edition and the later editions read, “God guards.”]

4. But when you say that God’s grace should be understood not to have wholly departed from Job because God gave his tempter as much power to test him as he knew Job to possess for resisting, [Note: [Col. 0257D] Lyons and the later editions, together with the Corbie and Remiremont manuscripts, read, “that God gave the tempter as much power to test him.” Lyons omits the word “God”; the Jumièges manuscript adds “and” before “him.”] would you not speak more correctly and truthfully if, where you said, “as much power to resist as he knew him to possess,” you said instead, “as much power to resist as he knew he himself had given him”? [Note: [Col. 0258C] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “you should rather affirm.”]

By correcting that one expression, you would have moderated somewhat the whole glory that you wished to assign to human powers, so that the remarkable patience displayed amid so great an affliction would be attributed both to God’s help and to the free will of man. [Note: [Col. 0258C] Thus the Corbie, Remiremont, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions. Lyons and the other codices read, “the correction of one word … would have tempered.”] But you feared diminishing the praise of human nature if you confessed that virtue had been given to it by God. [Note: [Col. 0258D] The Remiremont manuscript omits the conjunction “and” before “God’s help.”]

Therefore you do not want God to be believed a co-worker in that struggle and victory, but merely a spectator, [Note: [Col. 0258D] The Jumièges manuscript, with the Lyons and later editions, reads, “And so the same [one]”; the Jumièges manuscript reads, “to believe.”] so that whoever you can persuade that such a difficult contest was overcome through the natural capacity of free will will not dare doubt that, in lesser matters, the effects of a good will are much freer, and thus fall into the pit of that condemned opinion which says [Note: [Col. 0258D] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “fall into the pit of that condemned opinion.” The Jumièges manuscript reads, “fall into the law of a condemned opinion.”] that the grace of justification is given to us so that what we are commanded to do through free will we may more easily fulfill through grace—as though, if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commands without it, though not easily. [Note: [Col. 0258D] Lyons and the later editions read, “you will be able to persuade … that he overcame.” The Mainz and Venice editions read, “overcome in so difficult a contest.” Lyons and the later editions omit the word “free” before “will.”]

Since Catholic bishops judged this worthy of anathema, we must use the testimony they used, saying:

> For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do this with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing.”  
> (Council of Carthage, canon 5 or 6; see Appendix, p. 272) [Note: [Col. 0258D] The Mainz and Venice editions alone insert here the Gospel passage, “Without me you can do nothing,” which they repeat shortly afterward with the other codices.]

## CHAPTER XVI. How Cassian endeavors to confirm by the example of the Gospel centurion what he had taught above; his eleventh definition: that there would be no praise or merit if Christ had preferred in a person what he himself had bestowed. Saint Prosper proves the contrary: that praise and merit are not taken away by grace, and that praise and merit are attributed to faith and good works without prejudice to grace.

[Col. 0259A]

[Also Chapter XXXVI.] 1. To these definitions of yours, which you believed fortified by adequate authority, and as though secure of the readers’ agreement, you add:

> God sometimes offers more than is sufficient to test our faith, so that the firmness of believers’ faith may be recognized. [Note: [Col. 0259D] Lyons and the editions following it read, “how weak it is.” The reading is corrected on the basis of the Corbie, Remiremont, and Jumièges manuscripts, as well as the Mainz and Venice editions.]

You illustrate this by the example of the centurion who, when he requested healing for his servant, and the Lord promised that he would go to his house, replied:

> I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed.  
> (Matthew 8:8) [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “when he sought healing.”]

The Lord praised him with such admiration that he declared he had not found such faith in Israel. [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Corbie and Remiremont manuscripts, and the Mainz and Venice editions, read “he replied”; the Jumièges manuscript, Lyons edition, and later editions read “he answered.”]

And with a brief conclusion you almost entirely confirm the Pelagian doctrine, saying: [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Lyons and later editions read, “But with a brief conclusion you almost entirely…”]

> For there would have been no praise or merit if Christ had preferred in him what he himself had bestowed.  
> (Conferences 13.14) [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “if the Lord.”]

So it was falsely written:

> No one can be continent unless God grants it.  
> (Wisdom 8:21)

The Apostle falsely proclaimed, when speaking of the same virtue:

> I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that.  
> (1 Corinthians 7:7) [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Lyons edition and those following it read, “but another in that way.”]

And he who said the following also taught falsely:

> If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, and it will be given to him.  
> (James 1:5) [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Mainz and Venice editions add, “let him ask wisdom from God.”]

Nor was it said truthfully:

> Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.  
> (James 1:17)

And:

> No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.  
> (John 3:27)

Or should we say that all virtues must indeed be counted among God’s gifts, but that a person is praiseworthy in those virtues which he has had from himself, and that merit exists where God’s gifts have not?

According to your rule, then, those who were given not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him have lost both praise and merit; nor do those who glory not in themselves but in the Lord possess true glory. But we rightly hear the prophet saying:

> Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, who makes strong the flesh of his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord.  
> (Jeremiah 17:5) [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “his arm.”]

And we hear the one who says:

> I will love you, Lord, my strength.  
> (Psalm 17:1)

And:

> In the Lord my soul shall be praised.  
> (Psalm 33:3)

And:

> The Lord is my strength and my praise.  
> (Psalm 117:14) [Note: [Col. 0259D] The following words are not found in the Jumièges manuscript.]

Thus we may know most clearly that those in whom are not found the things which, unless the Lord gives them, cannot be possessed have neither any praise nor any merit. [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “in whom these things are found.” [Col. 0260D] This appears less correct.]

2. You thought that the testimony of the praised faith could somehow prejudice the gifts of grace, as though faith, when shown to be praised, were not thereby taught to have been given. The Apostle praises the faith of the Romans, and for this good he gives thanks to God, saying:

> First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.  
> (Romans 1:8) [Note: [Col. 0260D] The word “their” is absent from the Lyons and later editions. The Jumièges manuscript and the Mainz and Venice editions do not read the word “to God.”]

He writes to the Corinthians also with a similar affection:

> I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge.  
> (1 Corinthians 1:4–5)

By giving thanks to God, did he take praise away from believers? Or, by praising believers, did he deny God as the author of their merit?

Let us also hear what he thinks of the faith of the Ephesians:

> Therefore I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, with the eyes of your heart enlightened.  
> (Ephesians 1:15–18) [Note: [Col. 0260D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “in Christ Jesus.” Below, it has “in his knowledge,” together with the Corbie and Remiremont manuscripts; all the editions read, “into his knowledge.”]

These people therefore had faith; they also had works of love, which could neither lack praise nor merit. Yet for these virtues the Apostle never ceases to give thanks to God, knowing that these gifts came from the Father of lights. He openly declares that he asks him to give the Spirit of wisdom and understanding to those to whom he gave faith working through love, so that the Ephesians may know that they received from him what they possess, and from him learn to hope for what they do not possess. [Note: [Col. 0260D] The Lyons edition and the later editions read, “so that from him … they may learn to hope for what they possessed from him.”]

For the Philippians also he gives similar thanks to God, and does not suppress their merit or praise, saying:

> I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine making supplication for you all with joy, because of your fellowship in the Gospel from the first day until now, confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ.  
> (Philippians 1:3–6) [Note: [Col. 0260D] The Lyons and later editions read, “because of your participation.” The Mainz and Venice editions add shortly afterward, “he who began the work in us will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.”]

What cause of human praise or merit is here suspended in God? [Note: [Col. 0260D] Thus the Corbie, Remiremont, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions. Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read, “Is not the cause of human praise and merit suspended here?”] What virtue or piety is excepted that has not flowed from the fountain of grace, when from beginning to end both the commencement and the completion of the good work are attributed to the Lord? [Note: [Col. 0261C] The Jumièges manuscript, with Lyons and the later editions, reads, “and piety.”]

Of his saints it is sung:

> Lord, they will walk in the light of your countenance, and in your name they will rejoice all day long; and in your righteousness they will be exalted, for you are the glory of their strength.  
> (Psalm 88:16–17) [Note: [Col. 0261C] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “to the end.” The Jumièges manuscript adds, “and in your favor our horn shall be exalted.”]

## CHAPTER XVII. How far Cassian, in the propositions refuted above, assists the Pelagians, who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits; yet he accuses them of profane opinion and is proved self-contradictory. Salvation cannot in any way exist except through faith.

[Also Chapter XXXVII.] 1. It must certainly be considered how greatly, in this opinion of yours, you assist those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits—although, so that you may defend yourself beneath the shelter of Catholic faith, you profess them to hold a profane opinion, saying:

> Let no one suppose that we have put forward these statements in order to assert that the whole of salvation rests within the power of our faith, according to the profane opinion of certain people who, attributing everything to free will, define that God’s grace is dispensed according to each person’s merit. [Note: [Col. 0261D] The Jumièges manuscript, Venice, Lyons, and later editions read *existimet* (“suppose”), where the text has *aestimet* (“suppose”). Below, the same manuscript, with the Corbie and Remiremont manuscripts and the Mainz edition, reads *aestimas* (“you think”), where the other codices read *existimas* (“you suppose”).] [Note: [Col. 0261C] Lyons and the later editions omit “yet.”]

But I am greatly astonished that you do not see—or think that others do not see—that you condemn yourself by your own words. For by saying that the centurion, whose faith was praised by the Lord’s voice, would have had no praise or merit if Christ had preferred in him what he himself had given, you have defined that the centurion had not a faith given by God but one of his own, and that grace contributed nothing to its beginnings. You have also established that the cause both of praise and of merit lay in that faith, neither of which he would have possessed if the Lord had bestowed the thing to which both praise and merit are due. [Note: [Col. 0261D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “if the Lord had given it to him”; the others read, “if God had given it to him.” Shortly afterward the same manuscript reads, “the centurion himself.”]

In vain, therefore, to escape the odium of a condemned error, do you deny that the whole of salvation rests within the power of our faith, since salvation cannot in any way exist except through faith. [Note: [Col. 0261D] Lyons and the later editions read, “since salvation can exist only through faith.” The Jumièges manuscript likewise has, “salvation can exist only through faith.”]

For:

> The righteous person lives by faith.  
> (Romans 1:17; Habakkuk 2:4)

Truth says:

> Truly, truly, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.  
> (John 6:24) [Note: [Col. 0261D] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “has life and does not come into judgment, but passes from death to life.” The Jumièges manuscript has the same reading as above, but reads “will pass” instead of “will pass over,” and “into life.” The Remiremont manuscript reads, “but passes.”]

And again:

> This is the will of my Father, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.  
> (John 6:40) [Note: [Col. 0261D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “For this is.” The Corbie manuscript reads, “But this is”; shortly afterward the Corbie and Remiremont manuscripts read, “and I will raise him up.” The other codices have the text as above.]

And again:

> This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.  
> (John 17:3) [Note: [Col. 0262C] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “And again.”]
