Since eternal and blessed life is plainly prepared for this faith—which you honor with merits and praises because you prefer to count it among the goods of free will rather than among the gifts of God—how will you evade this wound by which you strike yourself, declaring profane those who define that grace is dispensed according to human merits, while asserting that those who are faithful by the gift of grace plainly possess neither praise nor merit? [Note: [Col. 0262C] The Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read, “that eternal and blessed life has been prepared.” The Lyons edition reads, “by which you yourself are impaled.”]

Whichever way you turn, you are conquered and bound by yourself. [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Remiremont manuscript reads, “and are overcome.” The Mainz and Venice editions omit “and are convicted.” Lyons and the later editions read, “both convicted and overcome.”] For if merits do not precede grace, and faith cannot exist without merits, faith does not precede grace; and in every respect whatever gives rise to merit is possessed through grace, since it is not possessed before grace. [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “will not precede grace.” The Remiremont manuscript reads, “is possessed through grace.” The Jumièges manuscript, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, reads, “is possessed for the sake of grace.” The same manuscript then reads, “from whose merit it arises”; afterward the Mainz and Venice editions read, “which it does not possess before grace.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Cassian endeavors to mingle incompatible things and divides the faithful into two classes, to which he applies contradictory principles. Cassian’s twelfth definition: in the matter of salvation, God is Savior to some and merely receiver to others. Saint Prosper proves that Christ is the Savior of all who are saved. The disciples of evangelical and apostolic teaching shudder at Cassian’s opinions concerning grace and free will.

[Also Chapter XXXVIII.] 1. Therefore, so that the absurdity of your definitions may not appear self-contradictory, you endeavor to mingle incompatible things, [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Remiremont manuscript reads “incompatibility.”] and with unprecedented presumption establish the unity of the members of Christ’s body in two classes of believers: one, namely, to which belongs what you said at the beginning: [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Lyons and later editions read, “what you said among the beginnings.”]

> The beginning not only of actions but also of good thoughts is from God; he both begins what is good and carries it out and brings it to completion in us.  
> (Conferences 13.3) [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “and also.”]

The other, however, is governed by this rule, according to which you say that the centurion would have had neither praise nor merit if the Lord had preferred in him what he himself had given. [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read, “would have possessed neither praise nor merit.”]

Although you have brought the entire text of your discussion under these two formulas, which cannot possibly be harmonized, you now declare more distinctly and explicitly what you wish to establish, saying:

> From these examples, therefore, which we have brought forward from the Gospel records, we shall be able to observe most clearly that God provides for the salvation of the human race in diverse and countless ways and by inscrutable paths. He kindles the course of some who are willing and thirsting to a greater ardor; others he even compels, though unwilling and resisting. [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “to stir up.”] At one time he helps so that what he sees to be beneficially desired by us may be fulfilled; at another he even inspires the beginnings of the holy desire itself; and he bestows either the beginning of a good work or perseverance. [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “records.” The Mainz and Venice editions omit the words “so that what he sees to be beneficially desired by us may be fulfilled.” The Corbie and Remiremont manuscripts read, “to bestow”; the other codices, “to grant.”]

Hence, when we pray, we proclaim the Lord not only our protector and Savior but also our helper and receiver. [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Remiremont and Jumièges manuscripts, and the Mainz, Venice, and Lyons editions, omit the words “and Savior” and also “helper and.”]

In that he first calls us, and, while we are ignorant and unwilling, draws us to salvation, he is protector and Savior; but in that he customarily brings help to us when we strive, and receives and fortifies us when we flee, he is called receiver and refuge. [Note: [Col. 0263D] Louvain, Douai, and Cologne add here the pronoun “our.” The Jumièges manuscript, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, reads, “and receives us when we flee.”]

2. With this distinction, then, prescribed as you define it, this diversity will exist within one Church: [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Remiremont and Jumièges manuscripts, with the Mainz and Venice editions, read “prescription.”] our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it was said,

> You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.  
> (Matthew 1:21)

And of whom it was said:

> There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.  
> (Luke 1:32; Acts 4:12)

He will be Savior not of all Christians but of some, and receiver of others. Thus only those will be saved whom God has compelled, though turned away and resisting, to receive grace; while those will be received who have anticipated the calling by the ardor of a spontaneous course. To the former a gratuitous gift will be granted, while to the latter a deserved reward will be repaid. [Note: [Col. 0264D] The Cologne edition reads, “the gift of graces.”] The former will possess neither praise nor merit, since they have nothing good except what they received; the latter will abound in glory and grow rich in recompense, since, devoted by their own ability, they offered what they had not received. [Note: [Col. 0263D] Lyons and the later editions read, “to receive”; shortly afterward the Corbie, Remiremont, and Jumièges manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, read “opposed” rather than “turned away.”]

Thus Jesus Christ will find some already liberated and liberate others; [Note: [Col. 0264D] The Corbie, Remiremont, and Jumièges manuscripts read “liberated”; the Lyons edition reads “free.”] and what he says,

> You did not choose me, but I chose you,  
> (John 15:16)

will not apply to everyone, if there are some by whom he was chosen although he had not chosen them. Nor will this apply to everyone:

> No one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father.  
> (John 6:66) [Note: [Col. 0264D] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “who says this.” Lyons and the later editions read, “No one comes to me.”]

if there are some who were able to come to the Son without the Father’s granting it. Nor will this apply to everyone:

> He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into the world.  
> (John 1:9)

if there are some who came into this world in such a way that they were not darkness, or who began to be light in such a way that they did not need the illumination of the true light. [Note: [Col. 0264D] The Mainz and Venice editions read, “They do not need it.”]

Nor should what the Apostle says be understood of all who have been adopted:

> He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.  
> (Colossians 1:13)

if they themselves break their bonds, shake off the yoke of their former captivity, and pass with free eagerness from the dominion of the devil into the kingdom of God. [Note: [Col. 0264D] Lyons and the later editions read, “they break … and pass over.” The Jumièges manuscript reads, “they had broken … had passed over.”]

If these things can be preached within one Church, so that neither opinion yields to the other but each in turn succumbs to the other, it may happen that we accept what the Pelagians hold and the Pelagians accept what we hold. But in this way it will be not so much that they are Catholic as that we are Pelagians—which God forbid. For the mingling of opposites is the abandonment of what is better: when virtue admits vice, it is not vice that is abandoned, but virtue.

3. Christian hearts therefore in no way accept what you have tried to persuade us of: that those who are what they are by God’s grace possess neither praise nor merit; or that, of the one who came to save what had perished, one part of Christians is saved and another merely received. For the disciples of evangelical and apostolic teaching, not thinking lofty thoughts but agreeing with the lowly, shudder at this madness of proud exaltation. [Note: [Col. 0264D] Lyons and the later editions read, “they shudder at the madness of proud exaltation,” omitting “this.”]

Throughout the entire body of the Church, and in each of its members, what was dead has been brought to life; what was captive has been redeemed; what was blind has been enlightened; what had perished has been sought; what had gone astray has been found. [Note: [Col. 0264D] Lyons and the later editions read, “what had wandered.”] Not according to this new division—with some as savior and others as receiver—but Christ is both Savior and receiver of all the faithful everywhere. Nor are those deprived of merit and praise who receive from him the means by which they may merit eternal goods. They become happier in proportion as they possess fewer things that are their own and more things that are God’s. [Note: [Col. 0264D] The Remiremont manuscript reads, “neither merit nor praise.”]

The foolish complaint of the proud does not disturb us, in which they complain that free will is taken away if the beginnings, progress, and perseverance in good things until the end are said to be gifts of God. [Note: [Col. 0264D] The Jumièges manuscript reads, “who complain that free will is taken away”; Lyons and the later editions read, “because they complain that free will is taken away.”]

**THE ASSISTANCES OF DIVINE GRACE ARE THE SUPPORTS OF THE HUMAN WILL.** [Note: [Col. 0265C] The Cologne edition reads, “the supports of divine grace.”]

We pray willingly; and yet God has sent the Spirit into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father.”  
(Galatians 4:6)

We speak willingly; and yet, if what we speak is pious, it is not we who speak, but the Spirit of our Father who speaks in us.  
(Matthew 10:20; Mark 13:11)

We willingly work out our salvation; and yet it is God who works in us both the willing and the working.  
(Philippians 2:13) [Note: [Col. 0265C] Lyons and the later editions read, “the very willing,” etc. The Mainz and Venice editions read, “that very willing and working is God’s, who works in us.”]

We willingly love God and our neighbor; and yet love is from God, [Note: [Col. 0265C] The Remiremont and Jumièges manuscripts read, “but nevertheless.” The Jumièges manuscript also reads, “has been poured out by God,” etc.] poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.  
(1 John 4:7; Romans 5:5)

We profess this concerning faith, concerning endurance of sufferings, concerning marital chastity, concerning virginal continence, and concerning every virtue without exception: if they had not been given to us, they would not be found in us. [Note: [Col. 0265D] The Jumièges and Remiremont manuscripts read, “which, unless they had been given to us.”]

And free will, naturally implanted in human beings, remains in nature, but with its quality and condition changed through the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0265D] The Remiremont manuscript reads, “because of which.” The Jumièges manuscript reads, “not that free will … does not remain.”] He turns that will away from what it perversely desired and converts it to desire what is good for it, so that, made glad by delight, cleansed by faith, raised up by hope, and kindled by love, it might receive a free servitude and cast off servile liberty. [Note: [Col. 0265D] The Remiremont manuscript, together with the Mainz and Venice editions, reads, “with hope set upright.” Lyons and the later editions read, “might lose servile liberty”; the other witnesses more suitably read, “cast off servile liberty.”]

# CHAPTER XIX

Saint Prosper recapitulates Cassian’s twelve definitions, so that it may more easily become clear what those who opposed the defenders of grace thought about grace, and how, by reviving questions from the Pelagian school, they disturbed the peace of the Church.

[Column 0265C]

[Alternatively, Chapter XXXIX] [Note: This is the reading in the Corbeiensis and Remigianus manuscripts, and also in the Mainz and Venetian editions. The Joliensis manuscript reads, “It remains, therefore, from the definitions.” The Lyon edition and the later editions read, “The definitions having therefore been opened.”]

1. From these definitions, then, which we have examined up to this point, passing over certain matters [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has *praemittendo*, omitting *quaedam*. The Cologne edition has *permittendo*.], it is neither obscure nor ambiguous [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis, Remigianus, and Joliensis manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions. Lyon and the later editions read, “nor is it ambiguous.”] what those who oppose grace’s most sincere defenders think about the grace of God [Note: The Corbeiensis and Remigianus manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, read “that they disagree concerning the grace of God.”], and how they disturb the peace of the victorious Church by reviving petty questions from the school of the condemned. If, as we have heard, we were to reopen these questions, the length of our discussion would become excessive. From what has become known through their own writing [Note: The Corbeiensis, Remigianus, and Joliensis manuscripts read, “which have become known from their own writing” (*quae de ipsorum stylo innotuerunt*). The Joliensis alone has *ex his* instead of *de his*. The Mainz and Venetian editions likewise read *ex his*, whereas Lyon and the later editions have, “which have become known to their school.”], however, the devout reader can easily understand to what precipices one comes by these paths, and into what muddy mire of filthy streams one is led, from whose abyss the moisture oozes [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “and into this foul mire of muddy streams, whose abyss’s moisture oozes out” (*et in ista lutulentorum rivorum caenosa molagine*, perhaps for *uligine*). The Lyon edition agrees, reading *moligine* instead of *molagine*; and before *his callibus*—“by these paths”—it has *hisce callibus*, as do some others, while others prefer *hisce collibus*—“by these hills.”].

I consider it necessary [Note: Lyon and the later editions read, “I think.”], before concluding the volume, to arrange briefly and jointly the matters we have shown not to accord with Catholic truth [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits the word “Catholic.”], so that those matters which, because of the responses interposed by us, might escape the reader’s memory may more easily be recalled together [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “may … be more faithfully reviewed together.” The Corbeiensis and Remigianus manuscripts, and the Mainz and Venetian editions, read, “may … be more faithfully traversed.” Lyon and the later editions read, “may escape the readers’ recollection, having been reviewed together by the faithful.”].

## THE FIRST DEFINITION, THEN, STATED:

The beginning not only of actions but also of good thoughts is from God [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has “beginnings” (*principia*)], who inspires in us both the beginnings of holy willing and the strength and opportunity to carry out what we rightly desire. For every good gift and every perfect gift [Note: The Cologne edition reads, “every perfect gift” (*datum perfectum*)] is from above, coming down from the Father of lights: he both begins what is good, carries it out, and brings it to completion in us.

We embrace this very fully and profess it to be Catholic [Note: *Valde*—“very fully”—is absent from the Lyon and later editions, which read *confitemur*—“we confess”—instead of *profitemur*. The Joliensis omits *esse* before *confitemur*.].

## THE SECOND DEFINITION STATED:

Divine protection, therefore, is inseparably present with us. So great is the Creator’s kindness toward his creature that providence not only accompanies it but continually goes before it. The Prophet, having experienced this, confesses, saying: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58:11). When he has perceived in us the emergence of some good will, he enlightens and strengthens it, and urges it toward salvation, granting increase to that which either he himself planted or which he sees to have arisen through our effort.

Here there is already a departure from the preceding definition, and what had been attributed wholly to grace is now assigned in part to free will.

## THE THIRD DEFINITION STATED:

“Except that in all these matters both the grace of God and the freedom of the will are declared, by which a human being can sometimes be extended by his own movements toward the desire for virtues, yet always needs to be assisted by the Lord” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, reads, “because he also needs to be assisted.” The Mainz and Venetian editions have *indigeat adjuvari*—“may need to be assisted.”].

“For no one, whenever he wishes, enjoys health, nor is he freed from the disease of illness according to the desire of his own will.”

As though our physician did not also grant the sick this: that they should desire true health [Note: Lyon and the later editions read, “does not now also grant this … so that they may desire what is true.” The Corbeiensis, Remigianus, and Joliensis manuscripts, and the Mainz and Venetian editions, omit *jam*—“now”—and add *et*.].

## THE FOURTH DEFINITION STATED:

“But so that it may become more clearly evident that, even through the good of nature which has been bestowed by the Creator’s kindness, the beginnings of good wills sometimes arise—although, unless they are directed by the Lord, they cannot reach the completion of virtues—the Apostle is a witness, saying: ‘For willing is present with me, but I do not find the means of accomplishing the good’ (Romans 7:18)” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “to the perfection of virtues.” The same manuscript, a little later, has “Willing is present with me, but accomplishing the good is not.” The Corbeiensis and Remigianus manuscripts, and the Mainz and Venetian editions, read *non possum*—“I am not able”—instead of *non invenio*—“I do not find.” Those editions also omit *pariter enim*—“for likewise”—after *velle*.].

As though the Apostle had a good will from natural inclination and not from the gift of grace, when he declares that even the ability to think comes from God (2 Corinthians 3:5).

## THE FIFTH DEFINITION STATED:

“And so these matters are in a certain way mixed and confused indiscriminately, so that among many people there is a major dispute over what depends on what: that is, whether, because we have supplied the beginning of good will, God has mercy on us, or whether, because God has mercy, we attain the beginning of good will” [Note: Lyon and the later editions add *Dominus*—“the Lord”—after *misereatur nostri*, or read, “because God has mercy.”]. “For many, believing each of these things and asserting one more strongly than is just, have become entangled in various errors contradictory to one another.

“If we say that the beginning of good will is ours, what was there in the persecutor Paul? What was there in the tax collector Matthew? One of them, occupied with the blood and punishments of the innocent, the other with public acts of violence and robbery, is drawn to salvation” [Note: Lyon and the later editions read *trahitur*—“is dragged”—instead of *attrahitur*—“is drawn.”]. “But if we say that the beginnings of good will are always inspired by the grace of God [Note: The word *Dei*—“of God”—is absent from the Lyon and later editions. The Remigianus manuscript reads *per gratiam*—“through grace.”], what shall we say about the faith of Zacchaeus? What about the devotion of the thief on the cross? By their desire exerting a certain force upon the heavenly kingdoms, they anticipated the special summons of their calling.

“It is said that both the one who asserts that good will is born from grace and the one who says that grace depends upon good will are in error. Yet both opinions are judged worthy of acceptance, since the pattern of the one is set forth in Paul and Matthew, and that of the other in Zacchaeus and the thief” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has *dicitur*—“is said”—instead of *decernitur*—“is judged.”].

## THE SIXTH DEFINITION STATED:

“These two things, therefore—grace and free will—seem indeed to be opposed to one another; but we understand, by the reasoning of piety, that both agree and that we ought equally to accept both” [Note: The Lyon and later editions read *utrumque*—“both together”—instead of *utraque*—“both.” The Joliensis manuscript has above, “either grace or free will.”], “lest, by taking one of them away from human beings, we appear to have departed from the rule of ecclesiastical faith.”

As though both were to be received in such a way that in some people the will precedes grace and in others grace precedes the will [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits *hominibus*—“in people.”], rather than in such a way that in everyone the will follows grace. For according to them, if free will is taken away when grace precedes, grace is taken away when free will precedes [Note: Lyon and the later editions read “from grace” and below “from free will.”].

## THE SEVENTH DEFINITION STATED:

“After the transgression, Adam acquired knowledge of the evil which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of the good which he had received.”

Both statements are false. For Adam had already learned, when God warned him, from what evil he ought to beware [Note: The Joliensis manuscript does not have the word “Adam.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read “when he believes the devil” instead of “when he believed the devil.”]; and, when he believed the devil, he forgot in what good condition he had been established. Just as the worst knowledge of evil is to be evil [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “it is evil and perverse”], so the worst ignorance of good is to believe that the good does not exist.

## THE EIGHTH DEFINITION STATED:

“Therefore we must beware lest we refer all the merits of the saints to God in such a way that we attribute nothing except what is evil to human nature.”

As though nature before grace were not under condemnation, were not in blindness, and were not in a wound; or as though those whose merits derive from the same source as their righteousness had not been justified freely [Note: The Lyon and later editions read, “from which their merits arise.”].

## THE NINTH DEFINITION STATED:

“Therefore it cannot be doubted that the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s favor [Column 0268C]; but unless these are aroused by God’s assistance, they cannot reach the increase of perfection.”

As though Adam had lost nothing of spiritual goods by his transgression [Note: Here we restore *bonis*—“goods”—from the Corbeiensis, Remigianus, and Joliensis manuscripts and from the Mainz and Venetian editions], and virtue were not to be given in order to be possessed, but only to be encouraged so that it might more easily attain perfection [Note: The Joliensis manuscript lacks the adverb *facilius*—“more easily.”].

## THE TENTH DEFINITION STATED:

“We also read that divine justice provided for this in Job, its most proven athlete, when the devil demanded him for single combat. For if Job had engaged the enemy not by his own strength but protected only by the grace of God, and if, without any strength of his own patience, supported solely by divine assistance, he had endured those manifold masses and destructions of temptations, sought with all the enemy’s cruelty, how could the devil not have more justly repeated against him that slanderous utterance which he had previously made: ‘Does Job worship God for nothing?’ [Note: The Lyon edition and the later editions read, “worships God” (*colet Deum*).] ‘Have you not fenced him in, and his house, and all his possessions round about?’ [Note: These words, ‘and his house,’ which are read here in the Cologne edition and above in chapter 14, are omitted here in the Corbeiensis, Remigianus, and Joliensis manuscripts and in the other editions.] ‘But take away your hand from him’ [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “take your hand away from him.”], that is, let him contend with me by his own strength, ‘unless he blesses you to your face’ [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads *in faciem*—“to your face”—instead of *absque*—“without”—before *tuam*.].

“But since, after the conflict, the slanderous enemy does not dare to repeat any such complaint, he confesses that he was defeated not by God’s strength but by Job’s. Nevertheless, we must believe that God’s grace was not wholly absent from him, since it granted the tempter as much power to tempt as it knew Job to possess strength to resist” [Note: The Lyon and later editions do not have the word *tentandi*—“of tempting.”].

[Note: The recent editions read, “If God alone knew what Job could do, and did not also grant that he could do it, he was a witness to his patience, not its helper.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “knew only.” The other two manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, have *non ut auxiliator*—“not as a helper”—instead of *non etiam donavit*—“and did not also grant.”]

If God knew only what Job could do, and did not also grant him the ability to do it, he was a witness to his patience, not its helper. And in what respect would the assistance of grace be necessary if that great victory had been won by human strength alone?

## THE ELEVENTH DEFINITION WAS STATED CONCERNING THE FAITH OF THE CENTURION:

The Lord marvels at him and praises him highly, placing him before all those who had believed from the people of Israel, saying: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” [Note: The Cologne edition reads, “For the Lord marvels.”]. For there would have been no praise or merit in him if the Lord had preferred what he himself had bestowed upon him.

An impious understanding—that a person to whom God had given nothing is happier than one to whom he had granted everything.

## THE TWELFTH DEFINITION STATED:

Hence, when we pray, we proclaim the Lord not only our protector but also our receiver. In that he first calls us, and draws us, ignorant and unwilling, toward salvation, he is our protector and savior. But in that he customarily brings help to us when we strive, and receives and fortifies us when we flee, he is called our receiver and refuge.

Only one who does not wish to be saved by Christ can agree with this opinion.

# CHAPTER XX

The errors contained in Cassian’s definitions are collected in summary.

[Alternatively, Chapter XL]

1. These definitions teach, write, and proclaim in published disputations the following: that when Adam sinned, his soul was not wounded, but remained sound in the very faculty by which he sinned, since he did not lose the knowledge of the good which he had received; and therefore his descendants could not lose what he himself had not suffered to be damaged [Note: Some manuscripts read, “nor could his descendants have been able to lose it.”].

They also teach that the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s favor [Column 0269D], so that whoever wishes may, by natural judgment, precede the grace of God and merit his assistance, by which he may more easily reach perfection [Column 0270A]; for no one has praise or merit who, possessing gifts that were given, is adorned not with his own possessions.

They further teach that we must beware of referring all the merits of the saints to God as though human nature itself could do nothing good by itself, since its strength is so intact that it can fight against the devil himself and his savagery, even to the utmost punishments, without God’s assistance.

This possibility is natural in all human beings [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “present in all human beings.”], but not all wish to use the virtues innate in themselves [Note: The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts read, “their inborn virtues.”].

They teach, moreover, that the Creator’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that some, because they come voluntarily, are received by him with praise, while others, because they resist, are dragged unwillingly [Note: The Remigianus manuscript reads, “because they resist”; and shortly afterward, “and therefore, while part of the Church…”]. Thus he is the receiver of those who wish, but the savior of those who do not wish.

And although one part of the Church is justified by grace and another by free will, those whom nature has advanced are more glorious than those whom grace has liberated, because in Adam’s descendants the will is as free for every good work as it was in Adam before sin [Note: Lyon and the later editions read, “as it was in Adam.”].

# CHAPTER XXI

He returns to the defense of Augustine undertaken at the beginning. The Semi-Pelagians chiefly attacked Augustine, casting at him the same accusations that the Pelagians, and especially Julian, had previously made. They must therefore be attacked with the same weapons by which the Pelagians were defeated, namely, the authority of the Church: Innocent overthrew Augustine’s opponents by condemning the Pelagians, and the Palestinian synod, the African councils, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine likewise condemned them. The quibbling of certain people against Celestine’s testimony is refuted. Augustine’s doctrine is shown to be everywhere of the same character. Saint Prosper prays that Pope Xystus may repel the hidden enemies of grace.

[Column 0270C]

[Alternatively, Chapter XLI]

1. Behold the teachers of what doctrine these men are: in order to corrupt the purity of Catholic minds by slandering the defenders of grace [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions read, “by slandering the defenders of grace.”], they tear apart with rabid speech the foremost man of our time in ecclesiastical teaching [Note: The Corbeiensis and Remigianus manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions read *concerpunt*—“tear apart.”], believing that they can tear down every bulwark of authority if they repeatedly strike this strongest tower of the pastoral watchtower with the Pelagian battering ram.

“God’s firm foundation stands” (2 Timothy 2:19); yet these men appropriately fulfill their own role. For it is fitting that those who follow the opinion of such men should imitate their madness. They cannot say anything other than what has been spread abroad by the complaints of the condemned and the most insolent insults of Julian [Note: The Lyon and later editions read, “the most insolent.”]. The shoots of a single seed are alike, and what lay hidden in the roots is revealed in the fruits.

We must not therefore fight these men in a new battle line, nor undertake special combats as though against unknown enemies. Their engines were broken, and they fell together with the allies and leaders of their pride, when Innocent of blessed memory struck the heads of their unspeakable error with the apostolic sword; when the synod of the Palestinian bishops compelled Pelagius to pronounce judgment against himself and his associates [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions read, “exhorted him.”]; when Pope Zosimus of blessed memory added the authority of his judgment to the decrees of the African councils and armed the right hands of all bishops with Peter’s sword for the beheading of the impious; when Pope Boniface of holy memory rejoiced in the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors and used not only apostolic but also royal edicts against the enemies of God’s grace; and when, although he was highly learned, he nevertheless requested the responses of blessed Bishop Augustine against the books of the Pelagians.

2. Hence also Pope Celestine of venerable memory, to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that for the condemned not an examination of judgment but only a remedy of repentance was to be supplied [Note: The Corbeiensis and Joliensis manuscripts and the Mainz and Venetian editions read, “a remedy for the sentence”; in the following line, “not of a case examined.” The Remigianus manuscript reads, “not of an intellect examined.” The Lyon edition reads, “not only an examination of judgment, but a remedy of penance is to be supplied.”], ordered Caelestius, who was seeking a hearing as though the matter had not been examined, to be expelled from the entire territory of Italy. He judged that the statutes of his predecessors and the synodal decrees had to be observed so inviolably that he would in no way permit what had once deserved to be cut off to be reconsidered [Note: The Lyon edition reads, “from him and his predecessors, etc.”].

Nor did he free the Britons from this same disease with less care when he excluded certain enemies of grace, who had occupied only their native land, even from that hidden region beyond the Ocean; and, having ordained a bishop for the Scots [namely, Palladius], while striving to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian land Christian.

Through this man the Eastern Churches also were cleansed of a double plague, when, assisting Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria and the most glorious defender of the Catholic faith [Note: The Remigianus manuscript and the Mainz edition read *ad excusandum*—“to excuse.” This is altogether erroneous. The Corbeiensis and Joliensis manuscripts, together with Lyon and Louvain, read *ad excidendam*—“to cut out”; Douay and Cologne have *ad exsecrandam*—“to execrate”; and the Venetian edition has *ad exstirpandam*—“to eradicate.”], with the apostolic sword to cut out the Nestorian impiety, he also used that sword to overthrow the Pelagians when they allied themselves with errors related to their own.

[Alternatively, Chapter XLII]

Through this same man, within Gaul, freedom of evil-speaking was taken away from those very people who criticize the writings of Augustine of holy memory [Note: The Remigianus manuscript has “of bad eloquence.”]. When he received the action of those who had consulted him and praised the piety of the books which displeased the erring [Note: Lyon and the later editions read, “of those who were consulting him.”], he made clear in holy eloquence what ought to be thought about their authority, explicitly declaring how displeasing to him was the novelty of this presumption, by which certain people dared insolently to rise up against ancient teachers and, with undisciplined slander, oppose the preaching of truth:

> “Augustine,” he says (in Celestine’s letter to the Gallic bishops) [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “For he says, Augustine.”], “a man of holy memory, we have always held in our communion, on account of his life and merits; never did even a rumor of sinister suspicion touch him. We remember that he was once of such great learning that he was always counted, even by my predecessors, among the best teachers [Note: The Venetian edition alone reads “in commendation.” Lyon and the later editions have *praedecessoribus*—“by my predecessors”—and below *senserant*—“had thought.”]. Therefore everyone rightly held the same opinion about him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all.”

[Column 0272B]

364 [Alternatively, Chapter XLIII]

3. Against this trumpet-blast of such illustrious praise, against the dignity of this most sacred testimony, does anyone dare to utter the murmur of a malicious interpretation and cast a cloud of oblique ambiguity over a clear and wholly sincere judgment? Namely, because the title of the books on whose behalf the matter was handled was not stated in the pope’s letter, does it therefore appear that those books were not approved, and that this praise of Saint Augustine [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “of Saint Augustine.”] was bestowed only for the merits of his earlier writings [Note: The Lyon edition alone reads *pro autoramentis*, an obscure expression whose meaning here is not readily apparent.]?

Let this condition remain entirely, let it remain, that the novelty of these books—*On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*—be regarded as rejected if, in the same matter, the antiquity of the same man disagrees with them [Note: The Mainz and Venetian editions read obscurely and confusedly, “whether the antiquity of the same man thinks or may think of the same verdure.”]. Let it be judged either useless or inappropriate if something is found in them that differs from what he composed against the Pelagians [Note: The Joliensis manuscript, together with Lyon and the later editions, adds “and as useless.”].

But, to omit those volumes in which he argued for grace from the beginning of his episcopate, long before the enemies of grace arose, let his three books addressed to Marcellinus (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*) be read. Let the letter to Saint Paulinus of Nola, bishop (Letter 186), be reconsidered [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits “bishop.”]. Let the pages sent to the most blessed Xystus, then a presbyter of the Apostolic See and now its bishop (Letter 194), also be consulted [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “To the blessed man of the Apostolic See … Xystus.” The Corbeiensis, Remigianus, and Joliensis manuscripts write *Sixtus*, while all the editions have *Xistus*. This spelling seems preferable to the learned editor: both because the ancients commonly wrote it that way and because the name *Sixtus*, which has become customary, means nothing in either Greek or Latin.].

Let the distinct volumes addressed to Saint Pinianus (*On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin*), to the comes Valerius (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*), and to Christ’s servants Timasius and James (*On Nature and Grace*) be examined. Let the first six books against Julian be read; also one to Saint Aurelius, bishop of Carthage [Note: Lyon and the later editions add “of Carthage” or “Carthaginian.”], on the proceedings of Palestine; another to the priests Paul and Eutropius, against the questions of Pelagius and Caelestius (*On the Perfection of Righteousness*); and four volumes to Pope Boniface of blessed memory (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*) [Note: The Lyon edition and the later editions read, “let the four books be explained.”].

And if in all these works, and in many others which it would be tedious to enumerate, the same spirit of doctrine and the same form of proclamation came first, let the slanderers recognize that they object in vain that no special or separate testimony was given to these books, since their standard is praised throughout all his volumes [Note: The Lyon edition and the later editions read, “and so”; Louvain, Douay, and Cologne have “in all the works.” Cologne then omits “other,” and ends the phrase with a comma before “let them recognize.”].

For the Apostolic See approves what does not differ from what it has previously recognized together with that which it has previously recognized, and what it joins in judgment it does not separate in praise [Note: The Cologne edition reads *fides*—“faith”—instead of *sedes*—“see.”]. Therefore, let those who reject these recently published books accept the earlier ones, and agree with what was previously written in favor of Christian grace [Note: The word *editos*—“published”—is absent from Lyon and the later editions.].

But they do not do so. For they know that everything is opposed to the Pelagians [Note: Lyon and the later editions read, “they know that the Pelagian teachings are contrary to them.”], and that nothing can support their resolution of subsequent matters if they confess that the truth stands in the earlier writings.

[Alternatively, Chapter XLIV]

4. The perversity of such people must therefore be resisted not so much by the labor of disputation as by the privilege of authoritative testimony, so that no limb of a doctrine long ago struck down may be allowed to rise again [Note: The Lyon edition reads, “so that the doctrines of a body long ago prostrated may allow no limb to rise in the body.”].

For it is well known that the cunning of this falsehood is such that, if it senses that it can preserve for itself, under the pretext of correction, some shoot of its root favorable to it, it will seek to restore its whole body from the smallest part of itself [Note: This obscure passage has been emended here on the authority of the Joliensis manuscript. The Corbeiensis and Remigianus manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, read: “It is well known that the cunning of this falsehood is such that, if it is permitted, under the pretext of correction, to retain for itself some shoot of its root favorable to it, it can restore itself entirely from a small part of itself.” Lyon and the later editions read: “the cunning of this falsehood is such that, if they are permitted, under the pretext of correction, to retain some shoot of their root favorable to them, they can restore themselves entirely from a small part of themselves.”].

For where the whole is no more than a portion, it is not devotion to have given almost everything, but fraud to have retained even the smallest part [Note: The Joliensis manuscript, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions, reads *restituisse*—“to have restored.” The other manuscripts read *retinuisse*—“to have retained”—which is better.].

To prevent this from being achieved by the plots of hypocrites, we trust that the Lord’s protection will bring it about: what he accomplished in Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine, may he accomplish in Xystus [Note: The three manuscripts mentioned above read “in Sixtus.” Xystus, or Sixtus, succeeded Celestine in the year of Christ 431, on April 26.]. And may this be the portion of glory reserved for this shepherd in the guardianship of the Lord’s flock [Note: The Corbeiensis and Remigianus manuscripts read “preserved”; all the others, “reserved”]: just as the former drove away manifest wolves, so may this one drive away hidden wolves [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “drive out … expel.” The Mainz and Venetian editions read “cast away.”].

May that most learned old man’s speech resound in his ears, in which he encouraged his fellow worker, saying:

> “For there are certain people who think that the impieties rightly condemned may still be defended more freely [Note: The Lyon and later editions read, “For there are certain people justly condemned who think that impieties should still be defended more freely.”]. There are also those who enter houses more secretly, and do not cease to sow in private what they now fear to proclaim openly. There are others who have become completely silent, oppressed by great fear, but who still retain in their hearts what they no longer dare to utter with their mouths; nevertheless, through their earlier defense of that very doctrine, they can be well known to their brothers [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has “impiety.”]. Therefore some must be restrained more severely [Note: Lyon and the later editions read, “must be restrained.”], others must be investigated more vigilantly [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis, Remigianus, and Joliensis manuscripts, together with the Mainz and Venetian editions and Augustine’s Letter 194. Lyon and the later editions read, “must be investigated … so that, if they do not fear lest they lose…”]; and others, indeed, must be dealt with more gently but taught no less diligently: so that, even if they are not feared lest they destroy, they may nevertheless not be neglected lest they perish” (Augustine, Letter 19 to Xystus).

# CHAPTER XXII

Conclusion of the work. Although Augustine’s critics have been sufficiently refuted, they must nevertheless be tolerated, and one must not despair of their correction. Meanwhile they must always be loved, but avoided; and God must be asked to hold the first place in all our affairs.

[Column 0274B]

It has been sufficiently demonstrated, I think, that the critics of Saint Augustine both make empty accusations, attack what is right, and defend what is wrong; and that, waging an internal war with the weapons of those already destroyed, they rebel against divine words and human constitutions [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “divine and human ordinances.”].

Nevertheless, since they have not yet been separated from the fellowship of the brethren, their intention should be tolerated rather than correction despaired of. This should continue until the Lord, through the leaders of the Church and the legitimate ministers of his judgments, sets in order those things that have been disturbed through the pride of a few and the ignorance of certain others. With God’s help, our task is to return love for hatred with calm and modest patience [Note: These words, “with calm and modest patience,” are absent from the Joliensis manuscript], to avoid conflicts with foolish people, not abandon the truth, and not fight against falsehood; and always to ask God that in all our thoughts, all our wills, all our words, and all our actions, he himself may hold the first place—he who said that he is the beginning.

For from him, through him, and in him are all things. [Column 0276A] To him be glory forever [Note: The Corbeiensis and Remigianus manuscripts omit *saeculorum*—“of ages”—here, apparently following the reading of the apostolic passage to which Saint Prosper seems to refer. The other manuscripts read, “forever and ever.”]. Amen [Note: In the old Corbeiensis exemplar there follows: “The book of Saint Prosper against the book of the former abbot Cassian, entitled *On the Protection of God*; or against the doctrine of Pelagius and Caelestius, inventors and defenders of the impious doctrine and enemies of the grace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and maintaining the defense of the holy Roman bishops and of holy Bishop Augustine, asserting the truth from his books against the aforesaid heretics. Thanks be to God.” The Joliensis manuscript, however, reads: “The book of Prosper against the book of Cassian the priest, entitled *On the Protection of God*, ends.” Finally, the Mainz and Venetian editions read: “End of the book of Saint Prosper against the book of John Cassian the monk, which Cassian himself entitled *On the Protection of God*.”]. (John 8:23; Romans 11:36).

[EXPOSITION OF THE PSALMS FROM 1 TO 150]

[Column 0275]

## NOTICE CONCERNING SAINT PROSPER’S EXPOSITION OF THE PSALMS FROM 1 TO 150
## On the Excellence of the Davidic Psalms

It is not for us here to say anything prefatory about the excellence of the Davidic Psalms. For, above all other books of Sacred Scripture, the holy Fathers both exalted this book with praises and took care, in expositions and sermons delivered to the people, to make it accessible to the understanding of the less educated. It will suffice here to set before the eyes of readers a passage from Saint Ambrose speaking in the preface to the Psalms:

“Although all divine Scripture breathes the grace of God,” says the holy bishop of Milan, “nevertheless the book of the Psalms is especially sweet. For Moses himself, who set down the deeds of our ancestors in plain speech, when he had led the ancestral people across the Red Sea in a memorable spectacle of wonder, and, seeing Pharaoh drowned together with his forces, raised his mind to greater things—for he had achieved things greater than his own strength—sang a triumphant song to the Lord . . . . . . God therefore takes pleasure in song, not only in being praised but also in being reconciled . . . . . . But David was chosen by the Lord above all for this office, so that what appears rare and pre-eminent in the work of others might shine forth in him as something constant and continuous . . . . History instructs, the law teaches, prophecy announces, correction chastises, morality counsels: in the book of Psalms there is the progress of all, and a kind of medicine of human salvation . . . . In the Psalms, therefore, Jesus is not only born for us; he also undergoes that saving passion of the body, rests, rises again, ascends into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. What no human being had presumed to say, this prophet alone announced; afterward the Lord preached it in the Gospel . . . . The Psalm is the blessing of the people, the praise of God, the people’s acclamation, the applause of all, the speech of everyone, the voice of the Church, the melodious confession of faith, devotion full of authority, the joy of freedom, the cry of gladness, the echo of joy. It moderates anger, banishes anxiety, and relieves sorrow. It is a weapon by night, divine instruction, a shield in fear, a festival in holiness, an image of tranquility, a pledge of peace and concord, like a lyre expressing one melody from diverse and unequal voices. Dawn resounds with the Psalm; sunset echoes the Psalm. The Apostle commands women to be silent in the Church, but they too sing the Psalm aloud with propriety: here it is sweet to every age, here it suits either sex . . . . What a great bond of unity it is for the whole number of the people to come together into one choir! The strings of lyres are unequal, but there is one harmony. The artist’s fingers often err on a very few strings; but in the people the Spirit, the artist, knows no error. The Psalm is the exchange of nightly labor, the reward of divine rest, the instruction of beginners, the strengthening of the perfect. The ministry of angels, the army of heaven, a spiritual sacrifice. Even rocks answer the Psalm: the Psalm is sung, and rocky breasts themselves are softened. We see the exceedingly hard weep, the merciless relent. In the Psalm doctrine contends together with grace. It is sung for delight; it is learned for instruction . . . . What is there that does not present itself to you when you read the Psalms . . . . What, then, is the Psalm, if not an instrument of virtues? The venerable Prophet, playing it with the plectrum of the Holy Spirit, made heavenly sound resound as sweetness upon earth?” And so forth.

Augustine, however, discussing the sacred author of the Psalms in Book XVII, chapter 14, of *The City of God*, says:

“David was a man instructed in songs, who loved musical harmony not with ordinary pleasure but with faithful devotion, and served his God, who is the true God, through it by the mystical representation of a great reality. For the rational and measured concord of diverse sounds, through harmonious variety, suggests the unity of a well-ordered city compacted together.”

Finally, almost all his prophecy is contained in the Psalms. He also testifies, taught by personal experience, to their saving and spiritual efficacy in Book IX, chapter 4, of the *Confessions*:

“What voices I gave you, my God, when I read the Psalms of David, songs of faith, sounds of devotion excluding the swelling spirit, while I was still untrained in your true love . . . . What voices I gave you in those Psalms, and how I was inflamed toward you through them, and kindled to recite them, if I could, throughout the whole world, against the pride of the human race! And yet they are sung throughout the whole world, and there is no one who can hide from your heat,” and so forth.

In his fourth exposition on Psalm XXX he sums up the matter briefly when he says to the people surrounding him and listening:

“If the Psalm prays, pray; if it groans, groan; if it gives thanks, rejoice; if it hopes, hope; if it fears, fear. For everything written here is our mirror.”

These few examples are drawn from many. Saint Prosper, certainly taking them into account, and reducing this work of Augustine among all his works on the Psalms to a kind of concise index, put it to the service of advancing his own progress and that of the brethren who would read it.

Why he did not do for all the remaining Psalms what he did for the last fifty-one is not easy to determine. Perhaps he had in fact completed the whole work, and, through the misfortunes of time, only a third of it was able to reach us. Or, certainly, since he was disposed toward writing books in the same manner as the other holy Fathers and teachers of the Church—never undertaking any work unless charity commanded or necessity urged him, and not being led by any desire to win fame for himself—it is readily believed that he pursued with his pen only those subjects suggested by some definite occasion arising under God’s providence and direction.

The former conjecture is indeed favored by the fact that, warning that he would write nothing about Psalm CVII, he says there:

“Psalm CVII has been passed over because it appears to have been expounded in the last part of Psalm LVI and in Psalm LIX.”

From this no one will doubt that he had written some exposition of the Psalms just mentioned.

Moreover, when, in his discussion of Psalm CXLIV, he expressly attacks that error which fabricated two persons in Christ Jesus—an error about which nothing at all is read in Augustine’s corresponding exposition—it is clear that Prosper said this on account of the already arisen, indeed already condemned, heresy of Nestorius. On this basis we have assigned this Prosperian work to a date no earlier than the year 434.[Col. 0277]

As you read this book, you will readily notice that vigorous and concise eloquence by which Prosper is recognized as having a style of his own. You will also observe that our saint showed himself a disciple of the great Augustine not only in transmitting doctrine concerning Christ’s grace, but also in every other respect.

In reading this work, lest what we are about to say concerning the book of the *Short Sentences* should occur here—namely, that, because of the brevity of certain passages, some readers might complain of obscurity—and because in many places he transcribed Augustine’s very words without alteration, while in others he appears to have followed only the sense of his most holy teacher, substituting different expressions, we, considering the convenience of readers, shall present in the appendix to the second part of our work those passages that seemed to require fuller consultation of Augustine’s own *Expositions*. In the margin of the present work we shall add the note “See,” which will indicate the passage reproduced there.

# The Exposition of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine on Psalms One Hundred through One Hundred Fifty

*[Written, it seems, no earlier than the year 434.]*

## Psalm C

### 371. Psalm 100

**(Verse 1.)** “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” This Psalm is to be understood in its entirety from its first verse.[Note: That is, as Augustine says in the heading of his exposition of this same Psalm: “What this hundredth Psalm has in its first verse, we must seek throughout its whole body.”] We must confess to God that all his ways are mercy and truth (Psalm XXIV, 10), so that, whenever circumstances arising from the truth of things present themselves to our thoughts, we may not be moved to any complaint, but may sing mercy and judgment to the Lord in pious confession.[Note: All our editions—Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne—indeed read “from the truth of things.” Nevertheless, we suspect that “from the variety of things” should be read. Since manuscript codices are lacking, we have changed nothing, although our conjecture is confirmed by what is said shortly afterward: “amid the inequalities of the present life.”]

For resolving all the questions that the foolish wisdom of this world dares to raise against God’s providence, there is an utterly unconquerable principle: it teaches us that, amid the inequalities of the present life, neither is mercy absent from God’s justice nor justice from his mercy. When temporal things have been completed, both will become everlasting through righteous judgment, when glory receives those on the right and punishment those on the left, according to the quality of their deeds (Matthew XXV, 34 and following).

**(Verse 2.)** “I will sing and understand in the blameless way, when you come to me.” “In this confession,” he says, “I shall possess good understanding; and through the blameless way of my conduct I shall perceive you coming to me. Since I cannot be good without you, if what I do is upright, I do not doubt that you are present in me.”

“I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.” True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor another (*Sentences* 1 in the *Book of Sentences*). For “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm X, 6). One cannot walk in the breadth of one’s soul—that is, in the dwelling of one’s heart—when guilt constricts him and a life of unlawful action accuses him there. But a devout and undefiled conscience uses the spaces within itself freely; and, possessing the retreats of its own integrity, it does not wander into alien desires.

**(Verse 3.)** “I did not set a wicked thing before my eyes.” We keep before our eyes the things we love, and our gaze remains fixed upon the things in which the mind delights. Therefore, to turn one’s eyes away from a wicked thing is not to love whatever displeases God.

“I hated those who commit transgressions.” People must be loved so that their transgressions may be hated (*Sentences* 2).[Note: The Cologne edition has “all people must be loved.” The others have “people.”] For it is one thing to love what they have been made, and another to hate what they do.

**(Verse 4.)** “A crooked heart did not cling to me; I did not recognize the malicious person who turned away from me.” “I gave no consent,” he says, “to a crooked heart; and I did not recognize, that is, I did not approve, the malicious person who turned aside from the blameless way, because of his dissimilarity.”

**(Verse 5.)** “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, him I pursued.” It is a good pursuit when it persecutes not the human being but the human being’s sin.

“With the proud eye and the insatiable heart, I did not eat together with him.” Pride is the source of envy, which is never anything but malicious and is not satisfied with the misfortunes of others. Therefore I did not dine with those who took pleasure in such poison, because I abhorred the food of their iniquity, with which they were continually filled. For “blessed are those who hunger for righteousness, because they shall be satisfied” (Matthew V, 6).

**(Verse 6.)** “My eyes are upon the faithful of the land, so that they may consider together with me.” This is the voice of the Lord speaking to his imitators: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX, 28).

**(The same verse.)** “The one walking in the blameless way was ministering to me.” “To me,” he says, not to himself. For many preachers of the Gospel are not sincere: they minister to themselves, seeking their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Philippians II, 21).

**(Verse 7.)** “The one who practices pride did not dwell in the midst of my house.” An unjust person did not dwell in the heart of the righteous, which is his house, because there is always a great distance between them in character.

“The one speaking wicked things did not keep straight before my eyes.” The path of the wicked is not straight, and it is far removed from that way over which the eyes of the Lord preside and by which he comes to his own.

**(Verse 8.)** “In the mornings I was killing all the sinners of the land, to destroy from the city of the Lord all those who practice iniquity.” The Lord announces the day of his judgment, who speaks in the Prophet, since the words at the beginning of the Psalm are said according to the truth: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.”

For, since the time of this age is a time of night, ignorance, and tribulation, and no one knows what end each person will reach, God’s mercy grants an opportunity for repentance and acts in various ways so that the righteous may advance, the fallen may be raised up, and those who have turned away may be converted. But this patience is granted while night still remains. When the day has dawned and all hidden things have been revealed, and the impious have been separated from the company of the righteous (1 Corinthians IV, 5), the wicked will no longer be spared; rather, all the sinners of the land will be killed—in that morning when what each person deserves will be made known.

## Psalm CI

**(Verse 1.)** The title of this Psalm is: “A prayer of the poor man when he was distressed, and he pours out his prayer in the sight of the Lord.” According to Augustine, it reads “he poured out.”[Note: Augustine reads “he poured out.”]

This poor man, therefore, is Christ, who, taking the form of a servant, clothed himself in our poverty. And although he is “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy II, 5), he who is in the humility of the body is the same one who is in the glory of the Father, so that, having assumed their nature, he may also undertake their cause.

**(Verse 2.)** “Hear my prayer, O Lord, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face away from me; on whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me.” “Hear my prayer” is the same as “let my cry come to you.” But the repeated request displays the petitioner’s feeling.

“Do not turn your face away from me” is said on account of the humility of his members. For when would the Father turn away from the Son, or God turn away from Christ?[Note: The Cologne edition reads *avertetur*, “will be turned away.” Lyons, Louvain, and Douai read *averteretur*, “would be turned away.”] Therefore he asks to be heard whenever he is troubled, because the compassion of the head suffers together with every part of the body, and the distress of all, though it varies in places and times, is never without him who has mercy upon all.

**(Verse 3.)** “On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly.” The things requested with good desire are obtained quickly; nor are prayers delayed when they ask for what the one being asked himself wills. The hearing is therefore swift when the prayer itself is heard first; and the one who granted the vow does not delay his help.

**(Verse 4.)** “For my days have vanished like smoke.” The days of the first human being, whom the second assumed, are most fittingly compared to smoke that vanishes in its own rising. And since no one is transferred into the newness of Christ except from Adam’s oldness, the Reformer himself groans in those whom he reforms.

“And my bones have been scorched like a frying-pan.” Those who are stronger in Christ’s body are called bones; by their firmness the structure of all the members is protected. The exceedingly strong bone Paul says: “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians XI, 29).

**(Verse 5.)** “My heart has been struck like grass, and it has dried up.” The whole human race was struck in Adam, from whom universal descent proceeds. Those who are saved in hope through Christ groan because of that wound, not without the miseries of mortality contracted from it (Romans VIII, 24).

“For I have forgotten to eat my bread.” The first human being had received the bread of the word in the law of the commandment. But, taking the forbidden food, he forgot the bread by which he lived; and for this reason his heart dried up like grass that had been struck. Let it now revive and eat the bread that it had forgotten—the one who is already in the body of him who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

**(Verse 6.)** “Because of the voice of my groaning, my bones have clung to my flesh.” “Because of the voice,” he says, “of my groaning”—not because of the voice of the groaning of those over whom I groan, because they do not groan rightly, because they desire carnal things, because they covet bodily things.

But because there are stronger members who care for the weak and do not differ in affection from the head, the bones—that is, the stronger members of the body—are instructed by the voice of my groaning, so that they may cling to my flesh, that is, to my weaker members, according to what is written: “We who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak” (Romans XV, 1).

**(Verses 7–8.)** “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like a night-bird among the walls. I kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.”

Every energetic and devout preacher of the Gospel is found comparable to these three birds that have been mentioned, according to the condition of those to whom he announces the word of truth.

If he speaks to unbelievers, he is in the wilderness, like a pelican; nor does he disdain deserted and uncultivated places, because even in such people the Holy Spirit makes a dwelling for himself.

If he preaches to those who have lost the grace they received, he becomes, in a certain sense, a night-bird among the walls, not abandoning those who are falling, so that they may recover both the stability and the beauty of a well-founded building.

But if he exhorts those who, although they appear faithful, are nevertheless lukewarm and carnal, he becomes like a sparrow among those placed under a roof—that is, those living under the weakness of the flesh—rebuking and urging them to be on the roof rather than under the roof: that is, to have the flesh subject to them, not to be subject to it. For “the one who is on the roof must not come down to take anything from his house” (Matthew XXIV, 17); and “what you hear in the ear, preach upon the roofs” (Matthew X, 27).

But no one carries out the diligence required by these conditions more than the Lord Jesus Christ, the voluntary poor man. Coming to save sinners, he assumed the labors and weaknesses of all. For “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians V, 19): so that the wilderness of the Gentiles might receive knowledge of the truth, and light and stability might be provided to the blinded Jews, ruined by their own transgression.

The one who is the illuminator of darkness says through the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V, 8). Yet he himself, having been killed by the darkness that he loved, kept vigil—that is, rose again—and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof, that is, in heaven, where no one has ascended except the one who descended from heaven (John III, 13), who is “the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Corinthians XV, 20) and “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians I, 18; Revelation I, 5).

**(Verse 9.)** “All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who used to praise me swore against me.” These words signify what happened at the time of the Passion. The Lord is reproached because, although he saved others, he could not rescue himself from punishment (Matthew XXII, 49); and those who had been false praisers conspired in his killing.

**(Verse 10.)** “For I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with tears.” The sacrament of the Savior’s mercy is shown here. He makes even those his members for whom such medicine is appropriate, and joins their cause to his own person, in whom he says that he ate ashes like bread and mixed his drink with tears. Unbelievers, indeed, count this as a reproach, saying that the hope of forgiveness is fuel for sinning.

**(Verse 11.)** “Because of the face of your anger and indignation, for, lifting me up, you dashed me down.” This is the anger that Adam deserved and in which we were all born. Accordingly the Apostle says: “We were by nature children of wrath, as were the others” (Ephesians II, 3)—not by God’s creation, but by judgment.

For this reason we are called by nature children of wrath: it has so taken hold in our very beginnings that, apart from our Lord Jesus Christ, no human nature is free from it.

Humanity was lifted up because it was rational and made in the image of God; but it was dashed down because it forgot its dignity, as it is written: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts” (Psalm LXVIII, 13 and 21).

**(Verse 12.)** “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have dried up like grass.” Through sin I withdrew from the eternal day and by judgment fell into transitory days. And because I dried up like grass, through him who is free among the dead I am saved in hope. For “as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 13, 22).

**(Verse 13.)** “But you, O Lord, remain forever, and your memorial from generation to generation.”[Note: Augustine reads “into generation and generation.”]

“Let the eternal one,” he says, “preserve what is temporal. You have not grown old because I fell.” The one who was present to humble me is himself present to free me, and you do not forget your promises.[Note: The Cologne edition reads “you have held me.” Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Augustine have the better reading, “you have grown old.”]

**(Verse 14.)** “You will arise and have mercy upon Zion, because it is time to have mercy upon her.” What time is this, except the one of which it is said: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians IV, 4–5)?

**(Verse 15.)** “For your servants have taken pleasure in her stones, and they will have mercy upon her dust.” There are many stones in Zion, and many are dust. In the stones there is the joy of the saints; in the dust, compassion.

From Zion come the holy patriarchs, holy apostles, and preachers of the Gospel: all these are chosen and tested stones. The others, however, who are not joined to them, are dust, which the wind will carry away from the face of the earth (Psalm I, 4), unless they recognize themselves and say: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Psalm CXII, 14).

**(Verse 16.)** “And the nations will fear your name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.” Once this foundation has been laid in Zion and this mercy has been shown to its dust, another wall will also come from the nations, fitted to the cornerstone; and the two will be brought together into one, he who “made both one” (Ephesians II, 20).

**(Verse 17.)** “For the Lord has built Zion, and he will be seen in his glory.” The Church grows daily into a temple of God, and the whole body is built up from its head. Jesus Christ will appear in his glory when he comes to judge the world, taking some into the kingdom and thrusting others into punishment, on his right and on his left (Matthew XXV, 33).

**(Verse 18.)** “The Lord has looked upon the prayer of the humble, and he has not despised their petition.” This is the building of Zion and its structure. Thus living stones are fitted together, because the harmony of its beauty is reached only through humility and prayer, through groans and tears.

Otherwise, once the house has been completed and dedicated, the one who arrives by another way will knock in vain.[Note: We think the more correct reading would be “lest the one who comes too late,” although Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne print otherwise. It seems to refer to Augustine’s passage, no. 18, where he says: “When God’s building has been made and the house dedicated, why do you run, seeking too late, asking in vain, knocking fruitlessly, destined to remain outside with the five foolish virgins?”]

**(Verse 19.)** “Let these things be written in another generation, and the people that will be created will praise the Lord.” These things are written in the Old Testament through prophecy referring to the generation of the New Testament—that is, to the people who were to be created in Christ. Of this people the Apostle says: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. And all things are from God” (2 Corinthians V, 17–18).[Note: Augustine reads “all things are new,” as in the Greek and Latin apostolic text.]

This means both old and new things, because through one faith each people received justification.

**(Verses 20–21.)** “For he looked forth from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to release the children of those put to death.” When God looks upon the earth—that is, when he grants his mercy to human beings—the bonds of charity have become so strong that the violence of persecution could not overcome them.

Through fear of God the martyrs overcame fear of the world; and the fetters of faith restrained them from the excess of transgression. The labor of perseverance passed into the freedom of glory, so that groans might be turned into joys and fetters into crowns.

The children of those put to death—that is, of the martyrs—are also released. Inflamed by the same faith, they can be freed from the bonds of worldly desires and say: “You broke my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm CXV, 16–17).

**(Verse 22.)** “So that the name of the Lord may be proclaimed in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem.” Once the bonds of sins have been broken, free charity serves God, and the praise of the Lord is multiplied in Zion—that is, in the watchtower, which is the Church. She does not love present things, but looks toward things to come and rejoices in hope of the promises.

**(Verse 23.)** “When peoples and kingdoms gather together, to serve the Lord.” This came about through the blood of the martyrs and the groans of the prisoners. When those who were in groans and oppression were heard, the Church received in our times the freedom by which the peoples of all nations come together in the unity of faith, and the kingdoms that persecuted Christians are subjected to the yoke of Christ.

**(Verse 24.)** “He answered him on the way of his strength.” Whether Zion or Jerusalem—which is the Church, in which the praise of the Lord is celebrated—she answered the one whom she praises through faith, hope, and charity. To answer his call is to believe and obey, and to walk in his commandments.

“On the way of strength,” because perseverance amid all enticements and labors comes from him.

“Declare to me the shortness of my days.” Everything that ends and passes away is short. Temporal life is short in comparison with eternity. For this reason the Church asks that the shortness of her days be made known to her, so that she may know that she will remain until the end of the age, until those days come that can have neither number[Note: We find *annuntiari* printed in the more recent codices, whereas the four often-cited older editions have *annuntiare*, which seems less suitable. For Augustine, in his second exposition of this same Psalm, no. 9, says that the Church asks God to make known to her the shortness of her days.][Note: All the printed editions indicate in the margin that other books read “nor be diminished.”] nor end.

**(Verse 25.)** “Do not call me back in the middle of my days.” “Do not diminish my days,” he says, until the completion of the age that you promised, until “the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Romans XI, 25) and all Israel is saved.

“Your years are from generation to generation.” From the beginning to the consummation, diverse ages have produced different saints of God. Their justification, however, is only in Christ, through whom there is one generation of all generations, which God makes a participant in eternity, so that, without change, he may be “all things in all” (1 Corinthians XV, 28).

**(Verses 26–28.)** “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all things will grow old like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail.”

True eternity and true immortality exist only in the Deity of the Trinity, for whom being is perpetual. It receives no mutability through beginning, increase, or decline.

Created things, even those to which the Creator has given or will give eternity, will not be entirely without an end, since their end is the very change made for their increase (*Sentences* 3). Therefore the earth that you, Lord, founded, and the heavens that are the works of your hands, will grow old and perish like a garment and a cloak—not so that they cease to exist, but so that they exist differently: through a renewal of substance, not through the destruction of nature.

But you are the same, and you do not pass from one thing into another, because you are the one who truly is. In your glory you can be neither less nor greater. You grant to the children of your servants that they may be able to reach your years, which do not fail.

**(Verse 29.)** “The children of your servants will dwell there, and their offspring will be established forever.” The children of God’s servants are the children of the righteous, the children of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs; finally, the children of the whole Church, which is Christ’s body and the mother of all fathers and all children (Ephesians V, 23; Galatians IV, 26).

These, therefore, will dwell in the eternity of God’s years, and their offspring will be established forever. Their offspring is rightly understood as the work of their righteousness, which ought to precede each person, because that blessedness of eternity does not receive one who is barren and fruitless.

## Psalm CII

**(Verse 1.)** “Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name.” The whole Church together with its head, who is Christ (Ephesians V, 23), is one human being. Its proper duty is at all times to bless the Lord and to exhort itself to praise him, whom it loves with all its strength.

Its inward parts are the reasoning faculty of understanding, the hope of faith, the humility of fear, the strength of charity, and whatever other affections there may be by which the mind is lifted into admiration of its Creator.

**(Verse 2.)** “Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses.” The repeated exhortation teaches that one must never cease blessing God. The blessing will be persevering if no forgetfulness of his recompenses ever steals in.

These recompenses have not been made according to human merits. Condemnation was owed to sinners, but grace was granted to the wicked and salvation to the lost. For “the Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished” (Luke XIX, 10), and he “did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Luke V, 32).

He therefore must be blessed who not only does not punish the wicked, but also returns good for evil and makes them good.

**(Verses 3–5.)** “He who becomes gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases; who will redeem your life from corruption, who crowns you with mercy and compassion; who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.”
