[Note: All the editions have “who was gracious.” But in the explanation shortly afterward, “may he be gracious,” perhaps in both places the intended reading is *propitius fit*, “becomes gracious,” as Augustine reads. Below, “who redeems” is printed, whereas our manuscripts have “who will redeem,” except for the more recent ones.]

The enumeration of God’s recompenses shows by what stages the human soul is saved through grace.

“He who becomes gracious,” he says, “to all your iniquities.” He does not say, “to all your virtues,” for there would certainly be no virtues in it unless forgiveness of sins took place.

So that these sins may not rise again, he says, “He heals all your diseases.” What are these diseases except evil desires, carnal longings, and the illnesses of every kind of vanity?

From this corruption the life of the weak is redeemed, because the body of our death became the body of life itself, so that he might crown us with mercy and compassion, as it is written: “I will have mercy on whom I shall have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I shall show compassion” (Romans IX, 15). Thus we understand that crowns of merits are given through the same mercy through which the merits of crowns were given.

Then it is added: “He who satisfies your desire with good things.” Through these cures the soul has been led to good desires, so that, having despised and rejected carnal and earthly things, it may desire spiritual and heavenly things, because “blessed are those who hunger for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew V, 6).

“Your youth will therefore be renewed like the eagle’s”—that is, you will be changed from oldness into newness and from old age into youth, after the likeness of the eagle, which, having shed its feathers and changed its beak, grows young again with renewed vigor and new strength.

**(Verse 6.)** “The Lord performs mercies and judgment for those who suffer injustice.” The Lord knows that in this life his servants are subjected to labors and injustices. But he wishes them to be gentle and patient, because, just as he is merciful in delivering, so he is just in judging.

When he says to all who suffer injustice, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Romans XII, 19), he does not deny help when he announces vengeance. The Lord therefore performs mercy and also performs judgment. But it belongs to the perfect to desire mercy even for those who have inflicted injustice, rather than to desire vengeance.

**(Verse 7.)** “He made his ways known to Moses, his will to the children of Israel.” It is a great and wondrous mystery that the law was given so that, as sin increased (Romans V, 20; Galatians III, 22), the proud might be humbled, the humbled might confess, and those who confessed might be healed.

These are the hidden ways that he made known to Moses, through whom he gave the law, because sin might not abound, so that grace might abound.[Note: All our editions have this reading. Nevertheless, it might perhaps be better to read “so that sin might abound,” both because what follows is “so that grace might abound,” and because this is indicated in Augustine, where he says: “Because people were unwilling to confess themselves sinners, when the law was added they were made transgressors as well. . . . Sin therefore abounded, so that grace might abound. Therefore, as I had begun to say, since this is the great mystery in the law, it was given so that, as sin increased, the proud might be humbled, the humbled might confess, and those who confessed might be healed: these are the hidden ways that he made known to Moses.”]

The true Israelites understood this grace and, with God revealing it, saw what the rationale of the divine arrangements was and what the purpose of the divine wills had been.[Note: The preposition *a*, “from,” which appears in all our books, might perhaps properly be omitted.]

(Vers. 8.) The Lord is compassionate and merciful, long-suffering [Col. 0286A] and of great mercy. What is so long-suffering, what so abundant [Note: [Col. 0286D] Understand “in mercy,” which is expressed in Augustine.] as God, who in his mercy rains upon the just and the unjust, and makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5:45)? Though despised, he spares; though denied, he spares; and he prefers the sinner’s life to his death. For all the length of his patience is instruction in repentance and an offer of correction; nor are any of his works without mercy, since he provides for human beings both through gentleness and through the scourge (Sentences 4).

(Vers. 9.) He will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant for eternity. Divine goodness is angry for this reason: that it may not be angry (Sentences 5); and in mercy it applies temporal severity, lest it inflict eternal [Note: [Col. 0286D] In the Book of Sentences the reading is *juste inferat* (“may justly inflict”), whereas all the Prosperian editions printed here, omitting *juste*, have *referat* (“may bring back” or “return”).] vengeance.

[Col. 0286B] (Vers. 10, 11, 12.) He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as high as heaven is above the earth, so the Lord has established his mercy over those who fear him. As heaven, he says, protects the earth, so God protects those who fear him. As far as the East is from the West, so far has he removed our sins from us. This is the power of regeneration, which strips human beings of their sins and clothes them with the gifts of grace, so that the old may perish and truth arise. For when their condition has been changed, innocence is established in the East, while sins remain in the West.

(Vers. 13, 14.) As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him. For he himself knows our formation; remember that we are dust. [Col. 0286C] He who deigned to assume the role of father does nothing toward his children except mercifully. Let him chastise those he has adopted rather than abandon those he would disown. He himself knows what he has made us, from what fall and into what condition he has restored us, and how greatly the weakness of earthly dust enfeebles us. God is therefore asked to remember the human condition—that is, to continue having mercy on it. For he himself does not forget; rather, he causes us not to forget his grace.

(Vers. 15.) Man’s days are like grass, and like the flower of the field so he will flourish. Let man not be proud, whose days are like grass that blooms briefly and soon withers; but let man not despair, whose weakness is taken up by God’s power. For the Word became flesh (John 1:14), so that the flower that was perishable in Adam might be eternal in Christ [Col. 0286D].

(Vers. 17, 18.) But the mercy of the Lord is from age to age upon those who fear him, and his righteousness is upon children’s children. Eternal joys are promised to those who fear the Lord. And because fear produces obedience, while obedience to the commandments produces its effects, therefore the righteousness [Col. 0287A] of God—that is, his recompense—is upon children’s children. These are better understood as the offspring of good works than as the descendants of the born; for many just people are known not to have had children, and those who did have them did not all glory in them, or glory in them in every respect. To those who keep his covenant and remember his commandments, so as to do them. A person keeps God’s commandments by heart when he practices what is contained in God’s commands. Nor can he go astray amid the breadth of the precepts, since the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon two commandments (Matt. 22:40).

(Vers. 19.) The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom will rule over all. What else is signified here than the Lord’s descent, his ascent, and the sitting of the assumed human being upon the Father’s throne? To him every knee bows—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of the Father (Phil. 2:10–11).

(Vers. 20.) Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word, obeying the voice of his commands. Those who serve the authority of the Word are mighty in the Word, because they are fulfilled by the power of the one whom they serve.

(Vers. 21.) Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers who do his will. The confession of one who blesses is true when the sound of the mouth is the same as that of the heart. To speak well but live badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself by one’s own voice (Sentences 6). The Lord must therefore be blessed especially by the works themselves, and the conscience must use them in such a way that it glories in them in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31).

[Col. 0287C] (Vers. 22.) Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion. Just as there is no place that is not subject to his dominion, so there is no place in which his blessing ought to cease. Bless the Lord, my soul. The psalm is concluded with the same verse with which it began, so that we may understand that we ought to persevere in God’s blessing. This blessing truly continues if one lives well without ceasing.

## PSALM 103

(Vers. 1.) Bless the Lord, my soul. As in the preceding psalm, so also in this one that follows, this is the voice of the members of Christ’s body. There is one man, whose one heart and one soul are united in one faith, exhorting and stirring himself to the praise of God, so that the Creator may be magnified in contemplation of his creatures. [Note: [Col. 0287D] The editions of Douai and Cologne have “Lord my God.”] Lord my God, you have been exceedingly magnified. Nothing can be added to or taken away from God’s greatness; for what he is, he always is unchangeably. He is therefore magnified not for himself but for us, the more intensely as he makes himself known to our understanding, so that not his glory but our wonder may increase. You have clothed yourself with confession and beauty. The Lord our God clothed himself with confession and beauty—that is, he clothed himself with the Church, which through confession put off ugliness and received beauty. For the confession of sins is itself the adornment of those who do what is right.

(Vers. 2.) [Note: [Col. 0287D] The editions of Douai and Cologne have *circumamictus* (“clothed around”). In Augustine: “clothed around with light as with a garment.” Hence perhaps *lumen* (“light”) should be read here instead of *lumine* (“with light”), the reading preferred by our manuscripts.] You are clothed with light as with a garment. This is his garment, having neither spot nor wrinkle, and made radiant through grace; it is also called light, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

(Ibid.) You stretch out heaven like a skin. If we consider the making of heaven literally, as resembling an extended skin [Note: [Col. 0287D] Perhaps *in similitudine* (“in resemblance”) should be read, with the preceding comma found in the Lyon edition.], a certain swiftness is shown by which the Creator brought forth his work without any delay caused by difficulty. For he said, “Let there be a firmament between water and water,” and it was so (Gen. 1:6). For “by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6). But if we seek to examine the figurative meaning, we find that God stretched out heaven like a skin when we understand Holy Scripture to have been called heaven. He first placed its authority in his Church, as though it were a firmament [Note: [Col. 0287D] Thus the editions of Lyon and Louvain. Douai and Cologne, however, have *cujus auctorem* (“whose author”). Augustine, no. 8: “This authority of Scripture God first placed in his Church.” This supports the earlier manuscripts.], and through the ministry of preachers stretched it like a skin over the whole earth. The name “skin” signifies the mortality of the ministers, while their work remains, through which truth is made known everywhere and the invisibility of God is perceived through the visible elements of written letters (Rom. 1:20).

(Vers. 3.) You shelter its upper parts with waters. This too is correctly understood literally, since God commanded that a firmament be made between water and water, and it was so; part of the waters settled upon the earth, while part was placed above the heaven, removed from our sight and entrusted to faith (Gen. 1:6). According to the figure by which, through divine authority, we have received Holy Scripture as the firmament called heaven—stretched over the whole earth like a skin through the fame of preaching—we should understand the upper parts of heaven to be sheltered by waters in this sense: in this heaven, that is, in the divine words and commands, nothing is more sublime than charity, which surpasses all God’s gifts. For it has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). This outpouring signifies the waters of which it is said, “Let your waters run through your streets; let no stranger share them with you” (Prov. 5:16). [Note: [Col. 0288D] Thus the Lyon and Louvain editions, in conformity with Augustine’s text: “Now understand by the name ‘outpouring’ the waters in the charity of the Holy Spirit. These are the waters of which it is said in a certain Scripture, ‘Let your waters run through your streets.’” The later editions of Douai and Cologne have *aquas sanat* (“heals waters”).] This water—that is, love of God and neighbor—is the proper and distinctive virtue of the devout and holy, whereas the other virtues may be shared by both good and evil people (Sentences 7). The upper parts of heaven are therefore protected by these waters, because the commandment of charity is above all the heavens, that is, above all [Note: [Col. 0289D] The editions of Douai and Cologne have *liberos* (“free persons”). It is better to read *libros* (“books”), on the authority of Lyon and Louvain, supported by Augustine’s passage. Thus: “The commandment of charity is above the heavens, above all books; the books are subject to it, and every tongue of the saints serves it.… It is therefore the higher way, and rightly protects the upper parts of heaven with waters, because you find nothing more exalted than charity in the divine books.”] books. Every tongue and every teaching of the saints serves it. The protection of this water did not burden the heaven of Scripture that was subject to it but suspended it [Note: [Col. 0289D] This is indeed the reading in all our manuscripts. Yet we reasonably suspect that *non onerat* (“does not burden”) ought to be read, on the basis of the sense of the passage itself and the authority of Augustine’s work. For God does not protect in such a way that he is, as it were, supported by the one whom he protects; he raises up the one whom he protects, he does not burden him, and so forth.], because the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon the twofold commandment of charity (Matt. 22:40).

(Ibid.) You make clouds your ascent. This was visibly fulfilled when, in the sight of the disciples, the Lord was received by a cloud and ascended into heaven (Acts 1:9). Speaking of the resurrection, the Apostle also says: “Then we who are alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ, and so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:15ff.). But we must see what those clouds are by which one ascends into the heaven of the divine Scriptures. They are surely the preachers of truth, who raise the hearts of their hearers from earthly thoughts and carry them upward to the sublimity of heavenly understanding. From these clouds, which spread the word of God, the Lord’s vineyard of Sabaoth, which is the Church, is made fruitful, so that, having received rain, it may produce fruit and grapes rather than thorns. Let it not be like the vineyard of which the Lord says through the Prophet: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6); nor like those to whom the apostles said: “We were sent to you, but because you rejected the word of God, we are going to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

(Ibid.) You walk upon the wings of the winds. 384 Literally, this may be understood to signify the speed of the word, which travels everywhere, in that it is said to walk upon the wings of the winds. For we know nothing swifter than the winds, whose speed is signified by the name “wings.” Yet swifter than these is the proclamation of truth, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things gently” (Wis. 8:1). In the figurative sense, souls may appropriately be understood by the name “winds”—not because they are of the same nature, but because they are likewise invisible. Their wings are the two commandments of charity, by which they press toward the Lord. But because God’s love, with which he loved us, is greater and more sublime than our love for him, he is therefore said to walk upon the wings of the winds—that is, upon the love of souls—because God’s love surpasses our love. He himself poured into our hearts, through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, the love by which we love (Rom. 5:5).

[Col. 0289D] (Vers. 4.) You make your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning [Note: [Col. 0290D] All the editions note in the margin that some manuscripts read *flagrantem* (“flaming”); this is also found in Augustine, and Saint Prosper himself suggests both readings shortly afterward.] fire. Literally, we do not doubt that the spirits who are invisible to us are ministers of God and are called angels from the office they perform. “Spirit” is the name of their nature; “angel” is the name of their activity. God therefore also makes these ministers of his a burning or flaming fire, just as we read that fire appeared in the bush, and that fire was sent from above and fulfilled what was commanded through the execution of angelic ministry (Exod. 3:2; Gen. 19:24; Lev. 10:2, and elsewhere). Figuratively, all spiritual people in the Church are called spirits. They become angels when they become preachers and messengers of truth. They are also fire when they burn in spirit and set aflame those whom they exhort. They have a twofold effectiveness: they enlighten souls and burn them, when by the same power they kindle the ardor of virtue and destroy the thorns and thistles of sins.

(Vers. 5.) He founded the earth upon its stability; it will not be moved forever and ever. This statement about the earth—that it will not be moved forever and ever—is asserted with difficulty, since it has been said, “Heaven and earth will pass away” [Col. 0290B] (Matt. 24:35). We can understand its being founded upon its own stability in this way: the force by which it is sustained and maintained is called its stability. Although this power is hidden from us, it is rightly believed to reside in the wisdom and power of the Creator, who established all things in himself, in whom he also created all things (Heb. 2:10; Col. 1:16). In the mystical understanding, we have received the earth as a figure of the Church, whose stability and foundation—the foundation upon which the earth has been founded—is Christ. “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11). Not departing from this foundation, it will not be moved forever and ever.

(Vers. 6.) The abyss, like a garment, is his covering; the waters will stand above the mountains. By the name “earth” we understood the Church to have been prophesied, and, having Christ as its foundation, it will not be moved forever and ever. Nevertheless, it is indicated that it will be so surrounded by the flood of persecutions—foretold under the names of abysses and waters—that it must be covered by the hostile peoples as though by a garment. The persecution will grow to such an extent that oppression by the persecutors will also be raised above the mountains, that is, above the most eminent of the saints.

(Vers. 7.) At your rebuke they will flee; at the voice of your thunder they will fear. This happened when God terrified the nations with the thunder of his rebuke. For the wicked ceased to oppress the Church, and the mountains of God, whose sublimity had been covered by the waters standing above them, recovered their eminence when those same waters receded. When the Lord thundered, the waters feared, and the mountains were stripped of the flood.

(Vers. 8.) The mountains rise up, and the plains descend, to the place that you founded for them. The mountains are the swelling heights of the waters, that is, the waves of persecuting peoples. When they raged, they were mountains; but, rebuked, they became quiet and were made plains, once a place had been founded for them in which they could be restrained. This place is understood as a certain measure of fear, within which the hearts of those who raged have been confined. Thus, even if they still retain the bitterness of their unbelief, they cannot rise above the sweet waters—that is, the faithful peoples—nor can those great and bitter waves return to cover the earth. They have received a limit that they will not cross, and they will not be able to bring a flood upon the Church.

(Vers. 10.) You send springs into the valleys. “The Spirit of God rests upon the humble and quiet” (Isa. 66:2); and, he says, “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:37). The valleys therefore signify humility, which is never without the fountain of grace. Nor is it unusual for those who are mountains because of the greatness of the Holy Spirit to be valleys because of the humility of their own spirit. Thus the Apostle Paul was a mountain when he said, “Not I”; and he had a fountain when he said, “But the grace of my God is with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

(Ibid.) The waters will pass through the midst of the mountains. The mountains are the great preachers, who send forth the waters of truth from the valleys of humility. From this abundance they ascribe nothing to themselves and claim nothing as their own; rather, the outpouring of spiritual streams is common and shared. [Note: [Col. 0291D] We conjecture that *ut de aquis* (“so that from the waters”) ought to be read. Nevertheless, we have not altered the text, since the ancient books are lacking.] Or, “from the waters”: that there be no disagreement among the mountains concerning the waters—that is, concerning preaching—but that peace of agreement and the fellowship of charity make one and common what flows forth.

(Vers. 11.) All the beasts of the forest will drink. We have indeed seen this even in the present creation: the beasts of the forest drink from springs and from streams running between the mountains. But because through things known to all certain hidden realities are signified, the discovery of which delights the pursuits of spiritual people, we understand the Gentiles by “the beasts of the forest,” since the Gentiles are often indicated in Holy Scripture under the name of beasts. Thus the beasts of every kind gathered into Noah’s ark (Gen. 7:2, 14), and the sheet let down from heaven in the vision of the Apostle Peter, full of every kind of animal (Acts 10:13), signify nothing other than human beings of every kind who are to be gathered into the unity of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0291D] This obscure passage, which could not be clarified by the authority of the editions, is restored to full light if the word *bibunt* (“drink”) is added here. This is clear from Augustine’s own passage, Sermon 2, no. 11, which reads: “From those waters passing through the midst of the mountains, in that apostolic teaching flowing in the midst for the sake of the harmony of communion, all the beasts of the forest drink. For they were all in the ark, all in the sheet.” From this it can easily be understood what ought to be corrected or what ought to be understood in the text of our Prosper.]

From these waters, therefore, passing through the midst of the mountains—that is, from apostolic teaching flowing in the midst for the sake of the harmony of communion—all the beasts of the forest [drink]. For they were all in the ark, all in the sheet. These waters are passing through because all teaching that is dispensed in this present time passes away, as the Apostle says: “Knowledge will be destroyed, and prophecy will be abolished. For we know in part and we prophesy in part. But when the perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished” (1 Cor. 13:8ff.).

(Ibid.) The wild asses receive [Note: [Col. 0292D] In Augustine we read, and here we scarcely doubt it should be read, with the preposition *in*: “receive into their thirst,” although the preposition is absent from all our printed editions.] their thirst. By wild asses are named the larger and stronger beasts, which receive from the passing waters as much as they thirst for. For these waters are so sufficient that both small and large animals draw from them as much as they desire. Apostolic teaching is so salutary and life-giving that, according to the capacity of those who use it, it leaves no one without a share of it. Whether small or great, weak or strong, everyone finds in it nourishment and satisfaction (Sentences 8).

(Vers. 12.) Above them the birds of heaven will dwell; from the midst of the rocks they will give their voice. There are certain birds that dwell only upon mountains; under their name spiritual souls are signified, rejoicing in the free air and serenity of heaven, yet having their dwelling and nourishment in the mountains. For the mountains are the prophets, the mountains are the apostles, the mountains are all preachers of truth and every kind of lofty teacher. The spiritual person does not depart from them, but takes food and rest in them. Such birds therefore find in the mountains where they dwell certain rocks—the firm supports of the commandments. For just as that one rock is Christ, the Word of God (1 Cor. 10:4), so there are many words of God and many rocks. From the midst of these they give their voice, and when they resound, the rocks answer and reverberate, as the testimonies of Scripture harmonize with their discussions.

(Vers. 13, 14.) You water the mountains from your upper chambers. These mountains received from above whatever waters they pour forth from their valleys and whatever voices they give from the midst of the rocks. They have been watered by divine grace so that they might abound both in waters and in voices, by which they might fill the thirsty and delight the hearers, producing what was suited to each person according to the measure of his capacity. The earth will be satisfied with the fruit of your works, producing grass for cattle and vegetation for the service of human beings. Let no one glory in his works, as though he possessed from himself what he possesses; rather, “let the one who glories glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31), because what satisfies him is the fruit not of his merits but of grace. The justified earth, therefore, made fruitful by heavenly watering, produces grass for cattle and vegetation for the service of human beings, so that what is necessary may be supplied to the cultivators of the Lord’s fields who sow the seed of the word, and so that those who proclaim the Gospel may live from the Gospel. Those who receive spiritual things owe material things, signified under the names of grass and vegetation. For who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Or who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not receive milk from the flock (1 Cor. 9:11)? Fodder must therefore be supplied for the service of those who preside. For the preachers of the word are both cattle and servants; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet receives a prophet’s reward; and whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water, only in the name of a disciple—amen, I say to you—will not lose his reward (Matt. 10:41ff.).

(Vers. 15.) So that he may bring bread forth from the earth, and wine may gladden the human heart. The earth produces grass so that it may bring bread forth from the earth. The holy peoples, of course, serve those who piously serve them; and, supplying material things, they receive spiritual things from the preachers of the word of God (1 Cor. 9:11), who is the bread that descended from heaven (John 6:41). Through those preachers, who still walk on earth and bear an earthly body—for which reason they too are called earth—a splendid and intoxicating cup is administered (Ps. 22:5), so that the saints, drinking, may be filled with the joy of the Holy Spirit.

So that his face may be made cheerful with oil. A certain grace that exists between human beings, especially useful for establishing holy love, is called oil. It is the divine radiance with which the whole body of Christ is anointed; Christ is principally anointed and is the fountain of this oil. And bread strengthens the human heart. He has made clear what bread he was speaking about. Visible bread satisfies the belly and strengthens the stomach. But this food is the strength of the heart and soul, concerning which the Lord himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41).

(Vers. 16.) The trees of the field will be filled. The trees of the field—that is, the Jewish peoples—will be filled with this grace. And the cedars of Lebanon, which you planted. Not only the humble of this world but also the noble and exalted will be satisfied with this grace. Because of their excellence they are called cedars, but they are cedars planted by the Lord, who has also justified many among the rich and illustrious.

(Vers. 17.) There the sparrows will make their nests; the house of the coot is their leader. In these cedars of Lebanon, which God’s grace plants and satisfies, the sparrows will make their nests. These are those who have chosen humility and, abandoning or selling what they possessed, have kept nothing for themselves in this world. Yet, having been received into the houses and estates of wealthy Christians, they are assisted by the necessities that sustain them. Although they rest in the height of the cedars, they do not use the cedars themselves as their guides; rather, the house of the coot is their leader. The house of the coot, which is a sea bird, is not in holes in the ground or in the branches of trees, but [Col. 0293D] on a rock surrounded by waters. The rock is understood as Christ (1 Cor. 10:4), who offered an example of patience to the humble and the sparrows. He is their strength, so that they are not shaken by the waves roaring around them; and if anything in the cedars of Lebanon causes offense, they may follow the house of the coot.

(Vers. 18.) The highest mountains are for the stags; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs. The stags are the great and distinguished spiritual people who pursue the highest of God’s commandments and dwell in the mountains of Scripture. But those who cannot hold the heights also have a refuge suited to their humility. Although they are bristling and thorny with certain small sins—which is signified under the name of hedgehogs—they too are received by the rock, which, whether in the mountains, the sea, or the valleys, is everywhere the protection of all.

(Vers. 19.) He made the moon for the appointed times. The Lord founded the Church, which passes through temporal things to eternal ones. Although it has been destined for perpetual glory, it is nevertheless subject to changes while it dwells here. The sun knew its setting. Christ recognized his passion. Christ’s setting is Christ’s passion. But does the sun set in such a way that it does not rise? Does the one who sleeps not add that he may rise again (Ps. 40:9)? What else does “He knew his setting” mean (Isa. 53:7) [Col. 0294B] except that it pleased him to die? For he willingly took up the cross and death. And just as what does not please him is outside his knowledge, so he knows and recognizes what accords with his will.

(Vers. 20, 21.) You appointed darkness, and night came to be. When the Lord had suffered, the hearts of the apostles were thrown into confusion by the darkness of fear, and a kind of night came to be there when the one who appeared to be the Redeemer of all was killed. There all the beasts of the forest will pass through; the young lions roaring to seize prey, seeking their food from God. In this night of despair and in this darkness of ignorance, the beasts of the forest—that is, evil spirits—lay in ambush. The young lions are the fiercer demons, raging to seize as their food those whom they find in the darkness of unbelief. Yet they can inflict no harm [Note: [Col. 0293D] Lyon has *nihil noxae* (“nothing harmful”); Douai and Cologne, *nihil noxiae*; Louvain, *nihil noxie*.] upon them unless God permits it. Therefore they ask from him the power to seize, since by his judgment a person is handed over to his enemies either to be chastised or to be tested.

(Vers. 22.) The sun has risen, and they have gathered together; and in their dens [Note: [Col. 0293D] All the editions assign *cubabunt* (“they will lie down”) in the margin as a variant reading. This form is found in Augustine’s exposition of this passage, Sermon 3, nos. 23 and 24.] they will be placed. The sun has risen because the sun had set; that is, Christ, having died, rose again and filled the whole world with the manifestation of his glory. Although darkness persists in the hearts of unbelievers, the Church, over the whole earth, where the sun has risen, is in the light. Therefore those spirits that incite the minds of the impious to persecute Christians do not dare to rage amid the great light of the truth received everywhere. Gathered into their dens, they are confined within the hearts of unbelievers.

[Col. 0294D] (Vers. 23.) A man went out to his work and to his labor until evening. For now, in the peace of the Church, the man of God, serving God’s righteousness, acts freely and goes out securely to works that benefit him, until evening. At the end of the world there will be a certain external darkness of persecution [Note: [Col. 0294D] Thus the Lyon edition. Louvain, Douai, and Cologne have *externa* (“external”), perhaps in place of *extremae* or *extrema* (“extreme” or “final”).].

(Vers. 24.) How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom. This wonder, in which the magnificence of the divine works is marveled at, pertains to both kinds of creation: that is, both to this world and to the Church. For the beauty of temporal things signifies the glory of eternal things, and through visible things those that do not appear are perceived by understanding (Rom. 1:20; Heb. 1:10; 2:10; Col. 1). You made all things in wisdom—that is, they were made in Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God. The earth is filled with your creation. The beauty of the world appears broadly to the eyes and is manifold in its splendor; it bears witness to the wisdom and power of its creator. But we should pay greater attention to that creation of which the Apostle says: “If anyone is therefore a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be” (2 Cor. 5:17). [Note: [Col. 0295D] The more recent editions added the word *omnia* (“all things”), which is absent from the four older ones. We read that Augustine noted here that the word is customarily absent from manuscripts, and we have already observed several times above that it is omitted.] For he came who would renew his work, who would refine his silver, who would fashion his coin. And we see the earth full of Christians who believe in him and, abandoning their former vanity, hasten toward the hope of the new age.

390 (Vers. 25, 26.) This sea is great and spacious; there are creeping things there without number. Although the new creation belongs to the new age, it is nevertheless on pilgrimage in this life and cannot reach its homeland except by sailing through this great and restless sea amid dangers, while the malice of innumerable creeping things lies in wait—that is, amid the assault of many temptations. We must beware lest, while they creep, they secretly insinuate themselves; and we must not withdraw from the wood of the cross, in which this savage sea is to be crossed under Christ’s guidance.

There are small and great animals; ships travel there. In this sea are unbelievers. Amid bitter and barren waters move the small and the great—that is, both the weak and the leading figures of this world. Although they oppose the Christian religion, the passage of our ships is nevertheless safe among them; that is, amid the storms and waves of the sea, with Christ as helmsman, the course of the Churches is safe.

This dragon which you formed to sport in it.

In this great sea, where there are creeping things without number, where there are small and great animals, and where our ships also travel, there is also the dragon. Cast down from the heights to the depths by God’s judgment, he was made the devil from an angel for this purpose: so that the saints might mock his malice and wickedness. Although he has an unceasing desire to cause harm, he cannot inflict more temptations upon anyone than he is permitted to inflict.

(Vers. 27, 28, 29.) All look to you, O Lord, that you may give them food at the proper time. When you give it to them, they gather it. All the creeping things, all the animals, and the dragon himself have no food except what the Lord gives. For although the dragon is always eager to devour, he cannot devour anything except what the just God, distributor of all food, has assigned to him for consumption. His food is earth (Gen. 3:14). Therefore no one who is not earth will be given to him as food—that is, no one who has not surrendered himself to earthly desires and actions.

When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness. But when you turn away your face, they will be troubled. The opening of God’s hand is the revelation of Christ. The hand of the Lord is Christ. “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). To whoever he is revealed, he is opened; and whoever he is opened to is filled with goodness. And so that a person may know that he has received this goodness from above, the Lord sometimes turns away his face. Then the one who seemed full of goodness is troubled, so that through sudden want he may understand that the abundance of good had not come from himself.

You will take away their spirit, and they will fail; and they will return to their dust.

Those who gloried in themselves are taught to become less swollen with pride. The spirit of arrogance is taken away from them, so that they may be turned back into their dust, acknowledging that they are of the earth and repenting that they became proud, in order that they may again be filled with goodness.

(Vers. 30.) Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth. For we are his creation, the Apostle says, created in good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them (Eph. 2:10). From the Spirit of God we have received grace, so that we may live in righteousness. For God justifies the ungodly and renews the face of the earth, creating throughout the whole world a new creation through the Spirit of grace, so that, having put off the old person, we may walk in newness of life.

(Vers. 31.) May the glory of the Lord be forever; the Lord will rejoice in his works. Therefore let glory belong to God, and let God rejoice in his works. For if a human being does anything worthy of praise or joy, it is the work of God and the gift of his grace, who takes away the proud spirit and gives the Holy Spirit.

(Vers. 32.) He looks upon the earth, and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains, and they smoke. These are the works of God as he turns back those who have turned away, so that he may look upon the earth presuming upon itself and relying on its own strength, and make it tremble, and so that it may recognize that this is the cause of its trembling: that God works in himself so that it may be good, whereas, when he turned away, it had failed. [Note: [Col. 0295D] Perhaps, “in it,” namely, in the earth, so that it may be good. But if that earth marked by the noun were to be explained according to the primary sense, he would certainly have said, “he works in it so that it may be good.” Our editions contribute nothing toward resolving this uncertainty.] By the same work the mountains too are touched—that is, certain more exalted and powerful people of this age—and they will smoke, that is, they will give confession to God, and their prayers to the God who touched them will rise like smoke.

(Vers. 33.) I will sing to the Lord during my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist. “I will refer everything,” he says, “to the praise of God, and without end I will praise the Lord in all his works.”

(Vers. 34.) May my discourse be pleasing to him; but I will rejoice in the Lord. The discourse of one who, through humble confession, makes himself known to the God who knows him, and to whom God makes himself known although that person did not know him, is pleasing to the Lord. From such discourse arises delight, because confession—that is, the confession of one who does not glory in himself—advances toward the knowledge of God.

[Col. 0297A] (Vers. 35.) Let sinners fail from the earth, and the wicked, so that they may no longer exist. This seems to be a voice of anger and hatred, but it is in fact one of the greatest charity. For he says the same as above: that the spirit of the proud should be taken away and they should fail, and that the Spirit of God should be sent into them, so that a new creation may come to be, with wickedness failing but substance not perishing. For one who, while impious, has been justified will not be impious, but will be righteous. Bless the Lord, my soul. Let the faithful soul bless God in everything, and let the one who boasts boast in the Lord (I Cor. I, 31).

## PSALM CIV

This psalm is prefaced by *HALLELUIA*, which means “Praise the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0297D] Or rather, as in Augustine at this passage, “Praise God.”] Therefore it begins with praise.

(Vers. 1.) Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name. “Praise,” he says, “the Lord, and call upon him”; for praise, here called confession, must always precede invocation. Proclaim his works among the nations. This is said in the prophet to the evangelists, so that Christ may be proclaimed to the whole world.

(Vers. 2, 3, 4.) Sing to him and sing psalms to him. That is: preach him in word and deed, since one sings with the mouth but plays the psalm with the hands. Tell of all his wonders. Glory in his holy name. “Tell,” he says, “of the works of God by confessing them; and in your works be so praiseworthy that God may be praised in you. Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord, and be strengthened.”

The one who seeks the Lord seeks joy. Let him therefore seek him in such a way that he rejoices and is strengthened not in himself but in God. For by approaching the Lord, ignorance will be illumined and weakness strengthened, receiving both understanding by which it may see and charity [Note: [Col. 0297D] The Lyon edition reads, “by which he may serve.”] by which it may burn with fervor (Sent. 9). Seek his face always. “Face” is used for “presence,” as in “the face of the wind” (Ps. XVII, 43) and “the face of fire” (Ps. LXVII, 3). The presence of God must therefore always be sought, and one must act with persevering zeal so that he who grants himself as present may not depart. In this life faith seeks him, hope finds him, but charity possesses him in eternal life, where love of the true presence is neither diminished nor ended.

(Vers. 5, 6.) Remember his wonders, which he performed, his signs and the judgments of his mouth. You offspring of Abraham his servant, sons of Jacob his chosen one. Since it is a great thing, possible for only a few, always to seek God according to what he says of himself, “I am who I am” [Col. 0297D] (Exod. III, 14), he must at least be sought by the little ones according to what he says: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; this is my name forever” (ibid., 15). Remember, therefore, his wonders, which he performed, you who are the offspring of Abraham and sons of Jacob, whom God chose. If you cannot desire God in a higher way, at least seek his presence according to the things he worked among your fathers.

[Col. 0298A] (Vers. 7.) He himself is the Lord our God; his judgments are throughout all the earth. He showed that those are sons of Abraham who are sons of promise (Rom. IX, 8), saying, “His judgments are throughout all the earth,” because throughout the whole world there had been sons of Abraham, whom the prophetic word now urges to remember the wonders of God.

(Vers. 8–11.) He remembered his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations, which he established with Abraham, and his oath to Isaac. He appointed it for Jacob as a statute, and for Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying, “To you I will give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance.” Through the things that have passed away, the things that will remain are signified; and through the image of the old covenant, the promise of eternal inheritance was confirmed by the word that God commanded for a thousand generations—that is, for all generations. For, so that he might omit nothing empty or incomplete, he used a number of generations that plainly cannot be fulfilled even from Adam himself to the end of the world, until all the generations have come to an end, which are comprehended in the abundant number of a thousand. The word of the command remains—that is, the word of faith, to which eternal inheritance was promised. For when he says, “To you I will give the land of Canaan,” this is not a command but a promise. The command, rather, is that “the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. II, 4), to whom an eternal homeland is promised under the name of a certain land. Since possession of that land is not perpetual, it is certain that another thing is signified.

(Vers. 12–15.) When they were few in number, very few, and sojourners in it—that is, in the land of Canaan—they passed from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people. He allowed no one to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake. Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets. [Note: [Col. 0297D] All our editions have *malignare*; in its place, Augustine’s exposition, as in our Vulgate, reads *malignari*. [Col. 0298D]] “When,” he says, “the fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived in the land of Canaan, they were strangers there before they received it as an inheritance; and although they were very few, they passed unharmed from nation to nation. For God did not permit anyone to harm them, so that the very protection of God seemed to say, ‘Do not touch my anointed ones,’ and so forth.” [Note: [Col. 0298D] The older editions read *dicere videtur* (“seems to say”); later ones read *videretur* (“might seem”), and this is not a bad correction.] Although these words are not found in the historical account, they were nevertheless present in the actual outcome of events, since God was acting in the hearts of foreigners so that his chosen ones might remain unharmed. They were already called “anointed ones” for this reason, even though chrism was not yet in use: they too lived by the faith that was to be revealed in the last times. From the beginning, justification existed for all the saints only in Christ.

(Vers. 16, 17.) And he called a famine upon the land, and shattered every support of bread. He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold as a slave. Through this arrangement it happened that they passed from nation to nation, [Note: [Col. 0298D] Thus the Lyon and Louvain editions, as above, read *ut supra legitur*; Douay and Cologne read *et regno*; later editions read *et de regno*.] from one kingdom to another people. But when it says that he “called a famine,” this must not be understood as though famine were some person, or a substantial and living thing brought about by the command of the one calling it, since famine is nothing other than destruction contracted through deprivation of food. Rather, “called” means “made.” For God calls things that do not exist as though they existed (Rom. IV, 17). They were not called because they existed, but they will exist because they were called—that is, they were commanded to come into existence by him who made the things that will be (Isa. XLV, 11, according to the Septuagint). But in the statement that he sent a man before them, and Joseph was sold as a slave, careful examination is necessary, so that we may see how he makes good use of the evil deeds of human beings, when human beings turn God’s good works into instruments of their own wickedness.

(Vers. 18, 19.) They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul, until his word came; the word of the Lord set him aflame. We do not read that Joseph received fetters, but there can be no doubt about what, although the historical account passed it over, the prophet nevertheless did not suppress. By the iron that he says passed through his soul, we must understand the tribulation of harsh necessity. This tribulation remained until the dreams that had been interpreted by his word were fulfilled, and through them he was commended to the king, so that he might also foretell the future to the king himself (Gen. XLI, 25 ff.). But lest anyone attribute these things to the man rather than to the grace of God, it was fittingly added: “The word of the Lord set him aflame,” so that he too may be understood to have burned with the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0299D] The Lyon and Louvain editions read *feruisse*; Douay and Cologne, *ferbuisse*. Grammarians note that the former is derived from *feruo, feruis*. Hence in Terence’s *Adelphoe*: “I had hoped that youth had by now cooled.”]

(Vers. 20.) The king sent and released him, the ruler of peoples, and dismissed him. He is both king and ruler of peoples: he freed him who was in fetters and dismissed him who was confined.

(Vers. 21, 22.) He appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to instruct his princes as himself and teach wisdom to his elders. [395] The history of Joseph does not even report this, namely, that he imbued the Egyptian elders with spiritual wisdom. But how could it be that so great a man, a worshiper of the one true God, was concerned only with feeding the bodies of the Egyptians and providing for earthly affairs, and did not care to instruct the minds of those who were subject to him as well?

(Vers. 23.) And Israel entered into Egypt, and Jacob was a sojourner in the land of Ham. What is Israel is Jacob; and what is Egypt is the land of Ham. For the nation of the Egyptians arose from the offspring of Ham, son of Noah, among whom the Israelites sojourned. If it is asked how they are said to have passed from one kingdom to another people, when they had not yet received the land of Canaan as a kingdom, it may be understood as spoken by anticipation—that is, by prolepsis—so that what was going to happen is spoken of as though it had already happened.

(Vers. 24.) And he greatly increased his people, and made them stronger than their enemies. The statement briefly made above, “He made his people stronger than their enemies,” begins to explain, as though we had asked how it happened, and continues until the matter is fully described.

(Vers. 25.) And he turned their heart so that they hated his people, so that they might deal deceitfully with his servants. God did not deprave the heart of the Egyptians from what was right. Rather, since they were voluntarily wicked and of such a kind that they could envy the fortunate, he turned them against the Hebrews through the beneficence by which he multiplied his people. By doing good to his own, he stirred the Egyptians to hostility against them—not by making the Egyptians themselves wicked, but by granting the Hebrews good things that would burn the wicked with envy.

(Vers. 26, 27.) He sent Moses his servant, and Aaron, whom he himself chose. [Note: [Col. 0299D] Lyon, Louvain, and Douay read *in quem*; Cologne, with later editions, reads *et quem*. In Augustine, *quem elegit* (“whom he chose”) appears without *in* or *et*.] He placed in them the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Ham. Many things were done without any words, whether by the rod, an outstretched hand, or ashes cast into the sky. But since those things that were done without words were not empty of meanings, just as the words we speak are not, they too are called “words”—not words of voices and sounds, but of signs and wonders. [Note: [Col. 0300D] This passage would be made clearer by the addition of a few words. Since our editions did not help us accomplish this and the manuscripts failed us, we gladly transcribe Augustine’s passage word for word: “But since those things that were done were not empty of any signification, just as the words we speak are not, therefore,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 28.) He sent darkness, and it became dark; and they did not provoke his words. That is, the Egyptians endured Moses and Aaron patiently, hard-hearted though they were, until everything God had determined to do was completed.

(Vers. 29, 30.) He turned their waters into blood, and killed their fish. Their land gave forth frogs in the chambers of their kings. This is said hyperbolically, as though he had turned their very land into frogs.

(Vers. 31.) He spoke, and the swarm came, and gnats throughout all their borders. If it is asked when he spoke, it was in his word before it came to be; and without time it was there, at the time when it was to come to be.

(Vers. 32, 33.) He made their rains hail, and consuming fire in their land. And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and shattered the trees of their borders. This happened through the force of hail and lightning. Hence they also called it consuming fire.

(Vers. 34.) He spoke, and the locust and the grasshopper came, whose number was beyond counting. The locust and the grasshopper are one plague, since one is the parent and the other its offspring.

(Vers. 35.) And it devoured all the grass of their land. [Col. 0300D] Grass is also a fruit, as Scripture customarily speaks, since it also calls the grain crops “grass.”

(Vers. 36.) And he struck every firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their labor. This was the final plague, apart from the death in the Red Sea. Although there were ten plagues, not all are mentioned here, nor are they given in the same order in which they are read in Moses. Prophetic praise is free from the rules governing historical narrative.

(Vers. 37.) And he led them out with silver and gold. The deception by which the Egyptians were tricked into giving silver and gold to the departing Hebrews (Exod. XI, 35) must not be attributed to God’s command or inspiration, but only to his promise, by which he allowed even the carnal to be deceived through this desire. Nevertheless, that fraud has something of justice in it, since in a certain sense it took from the wicked what was owed as payment for many labors. And there was no feeble one in their tribes. This too was a great benefit of God, that during that departure no one was weak in body—not in spirit, of course.

(Vers. 38.) Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them had fallen upon them. It must be understood that this happened when Pharaoh and his army had been overwhelmed by the waters, and the remaining Egyptians could fear that the Hebrews might return to destroy them. Once the Hebrews had departed to more distant places, the Egyptians had reason to rejoice.

(Vers. 39, 40.) He spread out a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night. They asked, and the quail came. It is, of course, flesh. [Note: [Col. 0301D] Augustine says at this passage: “They did not desire quail, but flesh. Since quail too is flesh, and since that psalm does not speak of their provocation, in whom God was not well pleased, but of the faith of the elect ... they must be understood to have asked that it should come, so that the murmuring of those who provoked God might be suppressed.” From this you may understand that in what follows the word *murmura* (“murmuring”) necessarily ought to be substituted for *munera* (“gifts”), which appears in all the editions.] This request was granted not to complainers but to the elect, in order to suppress the murmuring of the carnal. For this psalm does not speak of those in whom God was not well pleased, but of the faith of the children of promise, for whose sake those others too were assisted. And he satisfied them with the bread of heaven—that is, manna.

[Col. 0301C] (Vers. 41.) He split the rock, and the waters flowed; rivers ran through the dry land. Through all these benefits of God, the merit of Abraham’s faith is commended.

(Vers. 42, 43, 44.) For he remembered his holy word, which he spoke to Abraham his servant. And he led out his people with rejoicing, and his chosen ones with gladness. And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of peoples. As though we had asked for whose benefit these things had been given: lest it be thought that this temporal prosperity itself was the highest good, he immediately referred it to something else, where the highest good ought to be sought. [Note: [Col. 0302D] Our editions read, “for whose good these things [were given].” But the sense of the passage in Augustine’s work requires us to correct it without hesitation to, “for what benefit these things were given,” that is, to what end they were given, or for what use they were appointed by God.]

(Vers. 45.) So that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law. It must therefore be understood that God’s servants and the chosen children of promise, imitating Abraham’s faith, receive these earthly goods from the Lord for this reason: not to dissipate themselves in luxury through them, or to grow sluggish through perverse security, but to possess all these things, prepared by divine mercy, in the pursuit of which they might be occupied with the most demanding labors, so that they might be free for the purpose by which eternal good can be acquired. This is: “So that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

## PSALM CV

[Col. 0302A]

### HALLELUIA

(Vers. 1.) Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. These two psalms, CIV and CV, are so closely joined to one another that in the preceding one God’s people are commended in his elect, of whom there is no complaint and with whom the Lord is well pleased (I Cor. X, 5); but in this following psalm those who provoked him within the same people are recalled, although God’s mercy was not absent even from them. These words are spoken from the perspective of those who, having turned back, plead for pardon, and examples are recalled of those in whom the rich mercy of God appeared even toward sinners. This psalm therefore begins, like the former one, “Give thanks to the Lord.” But there it continues, “and call upon his name”; here, “for he is good, for his mercy is forever.” The confession of sins therefore contains the praise of God, because the one who asks forgiveness must pray with hope and with praise of the mercy he believes to be eternal.

(Vers. 2.) Who can speak of the powers of the Lord? Who can make all his praises heard? Who can recount the works of the almighty mercy of God, or bring it about that all his praises are heard? For what is uttered by the mouth and what is done in action must be spoken and performed for the praise of God.

(Vers. 3.) Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times. Righteousness and judgment are so similar and closely related that either may be used in place of the other. Nevertheless, if their proper meanings are to be observed more carefully, the one who judges rightly is said to keep judgment, while the one who acts rightly is said to practice righteousness.

(Vers. 4.) Remember us, Lord, in the favor shown to your people. That is, let us be among those with whom you are well pleased, because God is not well pleased with all of them (I Cor. X, 5). Visit us with your salvation. That is, with your Christ, in whom sins are forgiven and souls are healed, so that they may keep judgment and practice righteousness.

(Vers. 5.) To see the goodness of your chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of your nation. “Visit us,” he says, “so that we may see”—that is, illumine us, so that we may not be blind and outside the goodness of your chosen ones. For the inner eyes see what is right, they see equity, and they desire good things. In this goodness, therefore, make us both see and rejoice in the joy of your people, which is not apart from you, because none of your people rejoice except in you. So that you may be praised with your inheritance. That is, so that all the good things of your inheritance, which you chose and adopted, may be referred to your glory and praise. For those whom you visit with your salvation cannot be praised except in your praise, since you make them praiseworthy.

[Col. 0303A] (Vers. 6.) We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity. This can be understood in two ways: either that their descendants sinned with their fathers, who lived so much earlier, or because they were in their fathers’ loins when those fathers were in Egypt—for Levi too was tithed with Abraham—or because they were imitators through a similar obstinacy and sinned with those whom they reproduced in their own behavior (Hebr. VII, 2).

(Vers. 7.) Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they did not remember the abundance of your mercies. He rebukes both their understanding and their memory. By understanding, they ought to have seen to what eternal good those temporal things were calling them; by memory, they ought at least to have been instructed not to forget the wonders of God, since faithful remembrance of God’s benefits could greatly strengthen them. And they provoked him as they went up to the sea, to the Red Sea. “Going up” is spoken according to the position of the land, such that one speaks of descending into Egypt from the land of Canaan, and of ascending into it from Egypt.

(Vers. 8, 9.) And he saved them for his name’s sake, to make his power known. And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up. No word is recorded as having been spoken by which the sea was dried; therefore the power by which this was done is called a rebuke. And he led them through the depths, as through a desert. Because it had become like a desert through its dryness, where there had been depths.

(Vers. 10.) And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. What price was paid in this redemption? Or is this a prophecy that the event took place as a figure of baptism, where we are redeemed from the hand of the devil at the great price that is the blood of Christ? Hence it was fittingly prefigured more especially by the Red Sea.

(Vers. 11, 12.) And the water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained. And they believed his words, and praised his praise. This is the kind of expression found when one says, “He served this servitude,” or, “He lived such a life.” By “his praise” he meant the praise of God contained in the song of Exodus (Exod. XV, 1).

(Vers. 13.) They quickly acted; they forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel. They hastened to become blessed through temporal things, and desired present things more than future ones, although they ought to have understood from the many benefits bestowed on them that they were being called to some blessedness without end.

(Vers. 14.) They desired desires in the desert, and tempted God in the waterless place. This is the same kind of expression as the earlier “they desired a desire,” just as “they praised a praise.”

(Vers. 15.) And he gave them their requests, and sent satiety into their soul. Here he did not speak of the soul according to its rational nature, but according to that by which the soul makes the body animate. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Perhaps Saint Prosper had written, as it appears in Augustine: “according to that by which the soul makes an animate body an animal,” since he immediately adds “for the sustenance of that animal.” We have nevertheless not altered the text, because our editions did not support the change, and the customary reading was not entirely without meaning.] Food and drink belong to the sustenance of that animal.

(Vers. 16, 17.) And they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. And the earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the congregation of Abiron. [Note: [Col. 0304D] The editions have the simple verb *operuit* (“covered”). I have substituted the compound *superoperuit* (“covered over”), as the following explanation requires.] What is “swallowed” is the same as “covered over”; the cause of both was the same, namely, impious schism.

[400] (Vers. 18.) And fire blazed in their assembly, and flame consumed the sinners. Although even the righteous, including those who live commendably, are not without sin, Scripture customarily calls not people guilty of minor faults but those of many crimes and deep iniquity “sinners.”

(Vers. 19, 20.) And they made a calf at Horeb and worshiped a carved image. And they exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass. God was their glory, if they had awaited his counsel; to him it is said, “My glory and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. III, 4). They changed this glory of theirs—that is, the Lord—into the likeness of a calf that eats grass, so that they might be eaten by the one from whom those who think according to the flesh are eaten. For “all flesh is grass” (Isa. XL, 6).

(Vers. 21, 22.) They forgot God, who saved them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, terrible deeds at the Red Sea. The wonders are the same as the terrible deeds. For there is no wonder without a certain fear.

(Vers. 23, 24.) And he said that he would destroy them, if Moses his chosen one had not stood in the breach before him. He did not say “in the breach” as though Moses were to break God’s anger, but in the plague by which they were to be crushed, in which Moses offered himself for them. It was thus shown how much the intercession of the saints avails with the Lord on behalf of the wicked. He stood to turn away his anger, so that he would not destroy them. And they regarded the desirable land as nothing, and did not believe his words. They could not rightly be blamed for regarding the land as nothing, since we too ought to regard as nothing the temporal kingdom of that land, unless the land called “flowing with milk and honey” (Exod. III, 8) had signified a great sacrament. Because they did not understand or desire this, but established their happiness solely in earthly things, they did not believe the words of God and regarded the desirable land as nothing—that is, the eternal and heavenly land.

(Vers. 25–29.) And they murmured in their tents; they did not hear the voice of the Lord. And he raised his hand against them, to overthrow them in the desert, and to cast down their offspring among the nations, and scatter them among the peoples. And they consecrated themselves to Baal-peor, and ate sacrifices offered to the dead. And they provoked him by their inventions, and destruction was multiplied among them. [Col. 0305A] The anger of justice had been suspended, and vengeance against the sinners delayed. But after they consecrated themselves to idols and ate sacrifices offered to the dead—that is, sacrifices made to dead human beings—and also joined themselves to the fornication of foreign women, destruction was multiplied among them, so that because of the increase of their crimes they might be more severely laid waste. In this devastation Phinehas the priest appeased the Lord, because he killed together the male and female whom he had caught in an adulterous embrace. This was reckoned to him as righteousness, because the Lord saw that he had done it out of love for the whole people.

(Vers. 30–33.) And Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the plague ceased. And it was reckoned to him as righteousness from generation to generation, forever. And they provoked him at the waters of Strife, and Moses was afflicted because of them, because they embittered his spirit. And he distinguished with his lips. Holy Moses, disturbed by the murmuring of the people, did not retain the confidence he ought to have had. He struck the rock with his staff hesitantly, distinguishing this miracle from the others, as though the one who had performed the other miracles could not perform this one also. Therefore he deserved to die before entering the promised land. Nevertheless, even after his death God gives favorable testimony to him as to his chosen one, so that we may understand that he was punished only by deprivation of this inheritance, and not of that eternal inheritance signified by the temporal and earthly possession.

(Vers. 34–36.) They did not destroy the nations, as the Lord had commanded them. They mingled with the nations and learned their works. And they served their carved images, and this became a stumbling-block to them. The fact that they did not destroy the nations and that they mingled with them became a stumbling-block to them.

(Vers. 37–39.) And they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons. And they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan. The historical account does not mention sacrifices of this kind, but no one should doubt that the psalm tells the truth. And the land was slaughtered in blood, and it was defiled by their works. This is a figurative expression by which what contains something is signified by what it contains, as when we say “a bad house” of one in which bad people live, and “a good house” of one in which good people live. [Note: [Col. 0305D] Saint Augustine defends this reading at this passage with these words: “We would think it an error of the scribe, and say that he had written *interfecta* instead of *infecta*, unless we had the benefit of God, who willed that his Scriptures exist in many languages, and, when we examined the Greek manuscripts, saw that it was written thus: *Interfecta est terra in sanguinibus*. In Greek it reads, ἐφονοκτονήθη (“was slaughtered”).”] The land, therefore, was slaughtered in blood, since those who inhabited it were slaughtered in soul and defiled by their works. [402] And they fornicated in their inventions. Their inventions are not called theirs as though they discovered them themselves, with no preceding example to follow; they are called theirs because they imitated them and made them their own.

(Vers. 40–42.) And the Lord was angry with his people in fury. The disturbance of anger does not occur in God, but in ordinary speech the unchanging power of vengeance is called by this name. And he abhorred his inheritance; and he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them. And their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands. When he calls them God’s inheritance, this rejection was not for destruction but for discipline.

(Vers. 43–45.) He often delivered them, but they provoked him by their counsel. A man’s counsel is destructive to the man himself when he seeks what is his rather than what belongs to God. Thus he provokes the counsel of God, who promises himself as their inheritance, so that they may not desire to become blessed through temporal things but through eternal ones. And they were humbled by their iniquities. And he saw them when they were afflicted, when he heard their prayer. And he remembered his covenant, and he repented according to the abundance of his mercy. “He repented” is said because he turned the sentence by which he seemed about to punish them toward mercy—something God does without changing his plan. For although certain of his judgments and works vary in our eyes, nevertheless, before him, who foreknows the outcome of all things, nothing is done by a new arrangement. He made the things that were to be. When, therefore, he repented according to the abundance of his mercy, he did what he had determined to do, granting what he had foreknown he would grant.

(Vers. 46.) And he gave them into the mercies of all those who had taken them captive. This can rightly be referred to all the children of promise, who are redeemed through blood and rescued from the power of darkness, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will (II Tim. II, 26).

(Vers. 47, 48.) Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations, so that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise. Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age—that is, from eternity to eternity. For he will be praised without end by those of whom it is said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). Then what was prayed for at the beginning of this psalm will be perfected: “Remember us, Lord, in the favor shown to your people; visit us with your salvation, to see the goodness of your chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of your nation, so that you may be praised with your inheritance.” For he gathers not only from the nations the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel (Matt. X, 6), but also those that are not from this fold (John X, 16), “so that there may be one flock and one shepherd,” as it is said (ibid.). The Jews, however, count this prophecy as belonging to their visible kingdom, because they do not know how to rejoice in the hope of invisible goods; they will rush into the snares of the one of whom the Lord says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John V, 43).

(Ibid.) And all the people will say—that is, the whole company of those predestined, all the children of promise, who are from the circumcision and, in uncircumcision, a holy nation, a people of adoption—Amen, amen.

## PSALM CVI

[Col. 0307A]

(Vers. 1.) Give thanks to the Lord, for he is gracious, for his mercy is forever. One who has tasted can confess the Lord’s graciousness. For how can someone say that something is sweet when he does not know it? Let him therefore draw near to taste, so that he may be able to bring it up again in confession. His mercy is “forever,” that is, eternal, because those whom he has mercy upon in this time will be eternal.

(Vers. 2, 3.) Let those redeemed by the Lord speak, those whom he redeemed from the hand of their enemies and gathered from the regions—from the east and the west, from the north and the sea. Israel appears to have been redeemed from the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery; but here those are called redeemed who throughout the whole world are freed from the great and extensive Egypt, as through the Red Sea, through baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ. Let Christians therefore speak, those who have been called from the whole world, that the Lord is gracious and that his mercy is forever.

### (Verses 4–8)

They wandered in the wilderness and in a parched land; they did not find a way to a city of habitation. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. [p. 404] He led them by a straight way, so that they might go to a city of habitation. Let them confess to the Lord his mercy and his wonders to the children of men.

These verses are repeated four times in this psalm, and the confession of the Lord’s mercies, made so many times, signifies that [Col. 0307C] each of the redeemed must be delivered from the dangers of four temptations in order to arrive at perfect peace. The first danger is for a person, having strayed from the truth, to remain in the wilderness and error of ignorance, and, deprived of the food and drink of wisdom, to waste away from hunger and thirst. But when, wearied by this struggle, he cries out to the Lord, he is led to the way of faith, by which he may begin to proceed toward the city of rest, and confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.

### (Verses 9–12)

For he satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things. Those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in beggary and in iron. For they embittered the words of God and provoked the counsel of the Most High. And their heart was humbled by labors; they grew weak, and there was no one to help them.

As the first temptation was that of error and hunger [Col. 0307D] in ignorance, so afterward, once someone has recognized the way of Christ and begun to know what he ought to believe and what he ought to do, he is met by the labors of a second temptation. When he wishes to struggle against sins as though by his own strength, he finds himself impeded by the difficulties of desires (*cupiditatum*; the printed *cupidatum* is evidently corrupt; Augustine has “the Lord delivers from distresses and breaks the bonds of difficulty,” while Prosper above speaks of one “impeded by the difficulties of desires”), and unable to walk along the way he has learned because of his fetters. Let him therefore cry out in this affliction as well and ask the grace of God for help, so that, once the bonds of his inability have been broken, [Col. 0308A] he may receive the capacity to act rightly. The Lord could indeed anticipate this of his own accord by removing the obstacles, unless it were useful for a person to experience his weakness and to glory in good works not in himself but in the Lord, so that he may learn to confess to the Lord his mercies, whose gifts he receives [or, perhaps, “whose gift he receives,” meaning “by whose gift he receives them”], so that he may overcome his desires.

### (Verses 13–17)

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he saved them from their distresses. He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds. Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men. For he shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars. He took them from the way of their iniquity; for they had been humbled because of their injustices.

[Col. 0308B] Before they were freed by grace from the dominion of sin, they wanted to establish their own righteousness, ignorant of the righteousness of God (Rom. X, 3). [p. 405] Thus they were humbled through the experience of their inability, and discovered that without God’s help they could do nothing. But a third temptation then takes hold of them, one that produces distaste for the word of God. For often those whom ignorance and desire have not destroyed are killed by starvation, weariness, and the languor of disgust—unless perhaps it is not a danger when there is no delight either in reading or in prayer.

### (Verse 18)
