Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death. Just as it is harmful to the body to be unable to take bodily food, so it is dangerous for the soul to find spiritual delights distasteful (*Sent.* 10). [Col. 0308C] ### (Verses 19–20)

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their corruption.

There is a certain corruption of the mind when wholesome and pleasing things are not loved; therefore it is a great good to be delivered from this evil as well.

### (Verses 21–22)

Let them confess to the Lord mercies and his wonders to the children of men [our older editions here omit the word “his,” which was read above, though Augustine does not omit it]. And let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, and declare his works with rejoicing—not with weariness, not with sorrow, not with anxiety, but with rejoicing.

The fourth temptation remains, and it concerns both those who preside and those who are subject to them. For when a helmsman is hard pressed by a storm, [Col. 0308D] all who sail together are endangered by the same peril, and when the storm has subsided they are saved together in the harbor. Accordingly, the text continues:

### (Verses 23–24)

Those who go down to the sea in ships, carrying on their business upon many waters, saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.

Those whose task it is to govern peoples frequently endure storms of sedition and dissension arising from the depths of the human heart, storms capable of disturbing the ship. [Col. 0309A] They recognize that God permits these things for this reason: so that those who have been tested may become more evident (1 Cor. XI, 19), and so that he himself may be invoked by the faithful in their distress.

### (Verses 25–27)

He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood firm—that is, it remained and persisted, so that those who were troubled might pray more earnestly. And its waves were exalted. They rise up to the heavens and descend to the abysses; their soul languished amid evils. They were troubled and shaken like a drunkard, and all their wisdom was swallowed up [read *absorpta est*. The earlier editions contain an error here; this is how our Vulgate, following Augustine, reads]. Those who sit at the helm and faithfully [p. 406] love the ship recognize the force of this disturbance. For often the Church is shaken by scandals of such a kind that the hearts of those who preside grow faint. And what remains except what follows? [Col. 0309B] ### (Verses 28–31)

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he brought them out of their distresses. He commanded the storm, and it became a calm, and its waves were silent. And they rejoiced because they were silent, and he led them into the harbor of their desire. Let them confess to the Lord mercies [the word “his” is again omitted in all older editions, though it is read everywhere in Augustine] and his wonders to the children of men.

Let them confess to the Lord everywhere and altogether—not our merits, not our strength, not our wisdom, but his mercies. Let him be loved in all our deliverance, he who was invoked in all our affliction.

### (Verse 32)

Let them exalt him in the assemblies of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders.

There is no longer any doubt that all the temptations, afflictions, and deliverances mentioned above take place in the Church. What, then, did the Lord accomplish in this Church except that he resisted the proud but gave grace to the humble (Jas. IV, 6)? [Col. 0309C] He rejected the Jews, who exalted themselves on account of their descent from Abraham and the words of the Law; and, after cutting off the natural branches, he grafted the wild olive onto the olive tree, and chose from all the nations Abraham’s spiritual seed (Rom. XI, 20).

### (Verses 33–34)

He made rivers into a wilderness, and springs of water into thirst; a fruitful land into salt flats [Augustine reads “into salt marshes.” All our books have “in salt marshes”; and ancient authors not infrequently use the sixth case for the fourth]. because of the wickedness of those who dwelt in it.

Because of this proud wickedness, grace abandoned the Jews, and their land became sterile and deserted. For all prophecy, every sacrifice, and all the sacraments there ceased, and passed over to the humility of the nations.

### (Verses 35–36)

He made the wilderness into pools of water, and dry land into springs of water. And he caused the hungry to dwell there.

The works of grace are being recounted: [Col. 0309D] grace was poured out upon nations previously unclean and desolate, and alienated from the worship of truth. And they established a city of habitation.

For he who has been justified by faith now possesses the heavenly Jerusalem willingly [we have no doubt that here *sponte obtinet* should be read *spe obtinet*, “possesses in hope,” if the printed editions supported it. Augustine says, “Meanwhile, he possesses habitation in hope,” because, as he says, “Whoever hears me will dwell in hope”; and the Apostle says, “In hope we were saved” (Rom. VIII, 24)]. [Col. 0310A] ### (Verse 37)

And they sowed fields, and planted vineyards, and produced a harvest of grain.

This gladdens that laborer who says, “Not because I seek a gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. IV, 17).

### (Verse 38)

And he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly; and their cattle did not diminish.

“Cattle” and “sheep” are called those in the Church who walk simply but usefully: [p. 407] not highly learned, but full of faith. Thus God blessed and multiplied both the spiritual and the carnal, so that they were not diminished.

### (Verse 39)

And they became few, and were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and sorrows.

The Catholic Church, in its elect—those foreknown by God, the children of promise, the members of Christ’s body—is not diminished or reduced to fewness, because they truly are [members of it]; or, [Col. 0310B] when they have fallen, they are restored and remain. And they are always many, because none of their number perishes. Those, therefore, who either did not enter into this solidity of eternal multitude, or, although they seemed to have entered, withdrew from it, became few, because they were separated from that unity which endures in manifoldness. For those who are tending toward nonbeing are never many. And what is as subject to fewness as that which is destined for perdition (*Sent.* 11)?

### (Verse 40)

Contempt was poured out upon princes.

These are heretics and schismatics rejected by the Church; and they are therefore more despised because they wanted to be princes. And he led them astray in a trackless place, and not on the way.

Those who were heading toward the city of habitation were directed and led onward; but these, abandoning the holy city—that is, [Col. 0310C] the Catholic Church—were permitted to depart through the trackless wilderness of their error, and were handed over to their own will. For God does not lead astray by the malignity of deception, but distinguishes by the truth of judgment [the sense of the passage and the psalm verse being explained plainly require this reading, rather than the reading of the earlier editions, *malignitates educit*, “he leads out malignities,” an error easily introduced typographically into the first edition and left uncorrected in all later ones]. ### (Verse 41)

And he helped the poor man out of his beggary.

The poor and beggarly man is the one who attributes nothing to himself but expects everything from the mercy of Christ, crying and knocking daily before the Lord’s door, so that it may be opened to him and his nakedness clothed. And he made him like sheep in families [all our editions indicate in the margin another reading, by which *patriam* (“homeland”) is read in place of *familias* (“families”)].

God helped this one poor and beggarly man as though he were one person, and multiplied him into families—that is, he extended one Church, one people, one sheep, across the breadth of the whole world. [Col. 0310D] ### (Verse 42)

The upright will see and rejoice, and all iniquity will stop its mouth.

That chattering iniquity which speaks against unity, convicted by the truth, will close its mouth, having nothing to say. [Col. 0311A] ### (Verse 43)

Who is wise? Let him guard these things and understand the mercies of the Lord.

What will the wise man guard except that [p. 408] he should be poor, not rich—that is, not proud and not puffed up? For by guarding these things he will understand the mercies of the Lord, not his own merits or his own strength, but the mercies of the Lord: the Lord who led the wanderer and needy man onto the way and fed him; who released and freed the man struggling against the difficulty of sins and bound by the fetters of anxiety [Augustine says “the fetters of habit”; all Prosperian editions have “the fetters of anxiety”]; who revived the man languishing from disgust and almost dying, after sending the sweetness of his word [in Augustine, “after sending the medicine of his word”]; who led the man endangered amid the shipwrecks of scandals from the danger of the sea into the harbor of tranquility; who finally established him among that people where he gives grace to the humble (Jas. IV, 6), not among those to whom he resists because they are proud; and made him his own, [Col. 0311B] so that, remaining within, he might be multiplied, not diminished by going outside.

## PSALM CVII

The hundred and seventh psalm has been omitted, because it appears to have been expounded in the final parts of the fifty-sixth and the fifty-ninth [supply “in the final parts.” For Saint Augustine too did not think this psalm needed to be expounded. “For,” he says, “I have already expounded it in Psalm fifty-six and in Psalm fifty-nine,” from whose final parts it is composed. The final part of the fifty-sixth is the first part of this psalm, up to the verse where it says, “And your glory is over all the earth.” From there to the end is the final part of the fifty-ninth. Nevertheless, from these words, unless we are mistaken, it could not properly be inferred that Saint Prosper did not collect from Augustine’s entire work on the Expositions of the Psalms in a shorter style, since certainly, if he had left the psalms just mentioned untouched, he would not have failed to expound this one, which reproduces most of them, with the help of the expositions appended to them]. And so it begins—

## PSALM CVIII

### (Verse 2)

God, do not be silent about my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the deceitful man has been opened against me.

Anyone who faithfully reads the Acts of the Apostles recognizes that this psalm contains a prophecy about Christ. [Col. 0311C] There it is clearly shown that what is written here was prophesied concerning Judas, the Lord’s betrayer: “Let his days be few” (Ps. CVIII, 8), and “let another receive his episcopate” (Acts I, 20). But if we try to understand all those things that are spoken here in an evil sense as referring to one person, the method of interpretation will falter. Everything will therefore become clearer if some things are understood to concern the whole class of Christ’s enemies, among whom Judas holds the first place, while others are understood to concern Judas himself specifically [perhaps, “that one person,” as in Augustine: “that one man”].

The voice, then, is that of the Lord: “God, do not be silent about my praise.” His true and greatest praise is that by which he is proclaimed to be what he is: the only-begotten Son of God. Against him the mouth of the deceitful sinner broke out, when my power was concealed by the flesh of weakness [we suspect that *meae* (“of my”) should be read, or “when the flesh of his weakness concealed him,” or that something else must be supplied. Augustine’s corresponding words are: “This, namely, that he is the only-begotten Son of God, was not apparent, but remained hidden while his weakness appeared, when the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man were opened against him, because the power of this one was concealed”].

### (Verse 3)

They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue.

This was when they praised him as a good teacher [Col. 0311D] with crafty flattery (Matt. XXII, 16). [p. 409] And they surrounded me with words of hatred, [Col. 0312A] and attacked me without cause. Those who had earlier spoken deceitfully afterward raged against me with open words of hatred, without cause, because they had no ground for their hostility except their own iniquity; they were malicious and cruel without any advantage proposed for themselves. ### (Verse 4)

Instead of loving me, they slandered me.

This should not be considered a small matter, because he does not say, “Instead of loving me, they killed me,” but “they slandered me.” For they killed him precisely because they slandered him, denying that he was the Son of God and saying that he cast out demons by the prince of demons (Luke II, 15), and, “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” (John X, 20), and other such things. By this slander they turned away from him those whose conversion he sought; this was more harmful than their preparing [Col. 0312B] to kill him, since he was soon to rise again. But I prayed. He did not say what he prayed for, but we understand it as what he said while hanging on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). [Augustine has *quamquam* (“although”); all our editions have *quam* (“how”).]

How well we understand that he prayed for his disciples, for even before his passion he said that their faith should not fail (Luke XXII, 32), when, fixed to the wood, he did not use his power but offered an example of patience. He did not destroy his enemies by divine power, lest he train us to hasten impatiently to vengeance against those whom we endure as evil, since it is written, “The patient man is better than the strong” (Prov. XVI, 32).

### (Verse 5)

And they repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love.

Although the punishment of the one who suffers is voluntary, this is nevertheless [Col. 0312C] the greatest crime of the persecutors: they repaid goodness with wickedness and love with hatred. Because of this impiety, he begins to prophesy what they will receive, in the form of a wish. God does not desire the punishment of the guilty as though he wished to be sated with vengeance; rather, he arranges what is just with tranquility, so that even the wicked may not be without order (*Sent.* 12).

### (Verse 6)

Set a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.

Although the complaint above concerned many, the psalm now speaks of one, and future vengeance is arranged with one person understood—not because the others will be outside punishment, but because a sentence is rightly pronounced upon the head of the crime, and does not omit from vengeance those who share in the impiety, whom it condemns in their leader.

What, then, is “Set a sinner over him” [Col. 0312D] except that the devil should rule him to whom he himself submitted, and should have at his right hand the one whom he chose? [Col. 0313A] For to each person, whether in good or evil, that will become his right hand which he places before everything else. ### (Verse 7)

When he is judged, let him go forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin.

[p. 410] Judas could not pray through the one whom he sold. Prayer that is not made through Christ cannot merely fail to erase sin; it itself becomes sin.

### (Verse 8)

Let his days be few.

That is, the days of his apostleship. And let another receive his episcopate. That this happened as the prophets foretold is stated in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. I, v. 16 and following).

### (Verses 9–10)

Let his sons become orphans, and his wife a widow. When he himself died, both things happened. Let his sons be wandering and beg. “Wandering,” that is, uncertain where they should go. Let them be driven out of their dwellings. This is what he had said above: “Let them be transferred.”

[Col. 0313B] ### (Verses 11–12) Let the moneylender search out all his property, and let strangers plunder his labors. Let him have no helper, nor anyone who shows mercy to his orphans.

That is, let him have neither a helper nor a protector [Augustine understands this as referring to the protection of his descendants].

### (Verse 13)

Let his descendants be brought to destruction; in one generation let his name be erased.

That is, what has been generated from him should no longer generate, and should quickly pass away.

### (Verse 14)

Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord, and let the sin of his mother not be erased.

If Judas had remained in that to which he was called, neither his own past iniquity nor that of his parents would in any way have pertained to him. But because he did not maintain his adoption into the household of God, and instead chose the iniquity of his ancient lineage [perhaps “chose,” as in Augustine; all editions have “had chosen”], the iniquity of his fathers returned [Col. 0313C] before the Lord, so that he himself too might be punished in him , and the sin of his mother was not erased in him.

### (Verse 15)

Let them be continually before the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth.

He said “let them be before the Lord,” not so that they might oppose the Lord, but so that they might be in the Lord’s sight, lest any forgetfulness of their deserts occur. Let their memory perish in this sense: let their name fail, with no succeeding generation.

But if it is asked whether it is credible that the sufferings of living descendants should pertain to the punishment of the dead, then, setting aside every dispute—for many arise concerning this—we rightly believe that these things, prophesied through the Holy Spirit, happened. And if it can be maintained that the punishment of the living does not torture the dead [the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions incorrectly read *virorum*, “of men”; the Lyons edition reads *vivorum*, “of the living”], [Col. 0313D] nevertheless this condemnation was pronounced against Judas, the most wicked , so that amid his punishments he would become still more miserable through the misery of his own, and would continually grieve the destruction of his descendants.

All these things spoken against Judas are also to be understood as prophesied against the Jewish people. For a sinner has been set over that people—that is, the devil, to whom it submitted—and the same one stands at its right hand, whom it preferred to the Savior. It too will be condemned in the judgment, [p. 411] because, by persevering [Col. 0314A] in impiety, it “treasures up wrath for itself on the day of wrath” (Rom. II, 5) [Augustine has *thesaurizat*, “treasures up”; the editions have *thesaurizet*, “may treasure up”].

“And let his prayer become sin,” because it is not made through “the mediator between God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II, 5), and the priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX, 4). “And let his days be few”: this must be understood of their kingdom, because it did not last long after Christ’s crucifixion. “And let another receive his episcopate,” because they rejected Christ, who had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. XV, 24).

Their sons also became orphans. Of them it is said, “But the sons of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness” (Matt. VIII, 12), and they are rightly understood to have abandoned God the Father [all Prosperian editions read *omisisse* (“to have abandoned”); the appropriate reading, as in Augustine, is *amisisse* (“to have lost”)]. For, as the Truth says, “Whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father” (1 John II, 24).

“And his wife a widow.” [Col. 0314B] The wife of the kingdom may be understood as the people, which, having lost the kingdom itself [Augustine has “having lost that kingdom”], became a widow.

“His sons wandered and begged.” His sons, wandering amid dangers, were defeated; they are shown to beg because there is no doubt that they live by another’s mercy. “Let them be driven out of their dwellings,” he says—and so it happened.

“Let the moneylender search out all his property,” so that their entire life, signified under the name of property, might be investigated, and no remission of any debt—that is, of their sin—might occur, because they rejected the one in whom alone sins are abolished.

“And let strangers plunder his labors”: let the devil and his angels seize the fruits of the works performed for them.

“Let him have no helper.” For by whom can one who does not have Christ be helped?

“Nor anyone who shows mercy to his orphans,” because, [Col. 0314C] having lost God the Father, whose Son they persecuted, they have no one to show them mercy—not for receiving or sustaining temporal life, but for true life, that is, eternal life.

“Let his descendants be brought to destruction,” certainly eternal destruction. “In one generation let his name be erased”: because they were generated, not regenerated, therefore in one generation let it be erased [Augustine has “let them be erased”; all our editions have “let it be erased”].

“Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord,” so that the Lord may repay that people, persevering in wickedness, even for the iniquity of its fathers.

“Let the sin of his mother not be erased.” The sin of Jerusalem, “which is in slavery with her children” (Gal. IV, 25), which kills the prophets and stones those sent to her (Matt. XXIII, 31) [the preposition *in* is better omitted in “the sin of Jerusalem,” as in Augustine; it is present in our editions].

“Let them be continually before the Lord”: [Col. 0314D] let their iniquity and sin not be removed from the Lord’s sight, while God exacts vengeance forever.

“And let their memory perish from the earth.” The earth of God, the field of God, is the Church of God; their memory perishes from this earth because, although they were natural branches, they were broken off because of unbelief (Rom. XI, 20).

### (Verse 16)

Because he did not remember to show mercy.

Whether this refers to Judas or to that people. [p. 412] But it is better understood of the people, which could have remembered [Col. 0315A] through repentance that, after killing Christ, it ought at least not to have raged against his disciples and members.

### (Verse 17)

Because he persecuted a poor and beggarly man.

The Lord did not disdain to become poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty we might be enriched (1 Cor. VIII, 9). He may also be understood as beggarly in that he said to the Samaritan woman, “Give me a drink” (John IV, 7), or in what he said on the cross: “I thirst” (John XIX, 28)—words characteristic of one in need.

And to put to death the one pierced in heart. Compunction of heart, which properly belongs to converts from sins, does not apply to Christ, who alone existed without sin. Therefore, in his members who were doing penance and returning in compunction to their head, he too was pierced in heart, [Col. 0315B] because what was being done in the body was not absent from the head, in which he suffers those who persecute him to the end.

### (Verse 18)

And he loved the curse, and it shall come upon him.

Although Judas too loved the curse by selling and betraying the very author of blessing, that people loved the curse more openly when it said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25).

And he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him. Judas indeed rejected blessing in Christ; but the people rejected it more openly when, to the one who had been enlightened and said, “Do you also want to become his disciples?” it replied, “You are his disciple” (John IX, 27–28). And the blessing was made far from him because it passed over to the nations.

And he put on the curse like a garment—whether Judas or that people. [Col. 0315C] And it entered his innermost parts like water. Thus it is both outside and inside: outside, like a garment; inside, like water. For he has fallen under the judgment of the one who can kill both body and soul in Gehenna (Matt. X, 28).

And like oil into his bones. He shows the impious person or people performing evil with pleasure, delighting in iniquity inwardly like water and outwardly like oil. This action is called a curse because God announces eternal torments to such people.

### (Verse 19)

Let it be for him like a garment with which he may cover himself, and like a belt with which he may always gird himself.

The more evident kind of wickedness is that by which the sinner covers himself as with a cloak and is seen to be covered by that which he also displays proudly before human eyes, concealing evil while exhibiting it. He girds himself with a curse because he undertakes evil not suddenly [Col. 0315D] but deliberately, and learns to do harm in such a way that he is always ready.

### (Verse 20)

This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord.

[p. 413] These are the ones who slander Christ himself [the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “those who slander Christ”; the Lyons edition reads “those who slander Christ, him,” which is not bad if it can be corrected on the authority of a manuscript to mean “saying that he is not the one whom the Law of the Lord and the Prophets foretold”], whom the Law of the Lord and the Prophets foretold.

And of those who speak evil against my soul: they deny that he can rise again, although he says, “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18).

[Col. 0316A] ### (Verse 21)

And you, Lord, Lord, act with me.

Some thought that “mercy” should be understood; some even added it. But the more accurate manuscripts read, “And you, Lord, Lord, act with me, for your name’s sake.” From this it is to be understood that the Son said to the Father, “Act with me,” because the works of the Father and the Son are the same, which may also be understood of mercy [perhaps “concerning mercy”; Augustine has “where, even if we understand mercy”]. For it follows: “Because your mercy is sweet.”

We rightly understand that the Father and the Son together act in the vessels of mercy (Rom. IX, 23). It may also be understood in this way: when he says, “Act with me,” it is as though he had said, “Help me.” The Father helps the Son insofar as God helps the human being, because of the form of a servant. In the form in which he is equal to the Father, he does not need to be helped, because the work of both is one, [Col. 0316B] and their power is equal and inseparable. Need and poverty belong to the weakness he assumed, in which he was crucified.

### (Verse 22)

Deliver me, because I am needy and poor, and my heart is troubled within me.

This accords with what he said as his passion approached: “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. XXVI, 38).

### (Verse 23)

I have been taken away like a shadow when it declines.

Here he signified death itself. For just as night comes from a declining shadow, so death comes from mortal flesh [Augustine has “from mortal flesh”].

I have been shaken off like a locust.

Here we understand the matter more suitably of his members. For the faithful were shaken off—that is, driven away—by persecutors. By the name of locusts he either wished to signify their multitude, or the fact that they passed from place to place.

### (Verse 24)

My knees have grown weak from fasting, [Col. 0316C] and my flesh has been changed because of oil.

“Because of oil,” because of spiritual grace. When his flesh had been changed through the glory of the resurrection, and he had ascended to the Father, he sent the Holy Spirit to anoint believers. Their stability, which had been weakened by the loss of their bread—that is, Christ—as though by fasting, was made strong when they received the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that it would not be overcome in their afflictions, though it had failed in the Lord’s passion.

### (Verse 25)

And I became a reproach to them, through the death of the cross. For Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us (Gal. III, 13).

[p. 414] They saw me and shook their heads. They saw him hanging on the wood, but did not see him rise from the tomb.

[Col. 0316D] ### (Verse 26)

Help me, Lord my God; save me according to your mercy.

This refers both to the head, because of the form of a servant, and to the body, because of the servants. He could also say to the Lord in them, “Help me and save me,” in whom he had said to Saul, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4) [Augustine has *dixit*, “he said”; all our editions have *dixerat*, “he had said”]. When he says “according to your mercy,” he commends gratuitous grace.

### (Verse 27)

And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, [Col. 0317A] Lord, have made it.

He said “let them know” of those for whom, while they raged, he also prayed, because among them were even those who afterward believed in him. The hand of God is Christ, as it is said, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1). This, then, was the hand, and he made it. For “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word became flesh” (John I, 1, 14).

### (Verse 28)

They will curse, but you will bless.

[Col. 0317D] Our editions had, “Therefore there is one,” but this is plainly an error. The passage itself, as it stands in Augustine, shows that it should read, “Therefore it is empty”: the curse of the children of men, who love vanity and seek falsehood, is empty (Ps. IV, 3).

But when God blesses, he accomplishes what he says. Let those who rise up against me be put to shame. Those who think they can prevail against me will be put to shame when I have been exalted above the heavens and my glory has been poured out over all the earth.

But your servant will rejoice—[Col. 0317B] whether at the right hand of the Father, or in his members—now in hope, and afterward forever.

### (Verse 29)

Let those who slander me be clothed with shame; that is, let them be ashamed that they slandered me. But this may be something good for those who have been corrected.

And let them be covered with their confusion as with a double cloak. The *diplois* is a double cloak, by which a double confusion is announced for the enemies of Christ: inward and outward, before God and before human beings.

### (Verse 30)

I will greatly confess to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him.

“I will praise him in the midst of many” may be understood of Christ, because he is present in the Church until the consummation of the age (Matt. XXVIII, 20). One is said to be “in the midst” when chief honor is offered to him.

But if the human heart is understood as his midst, it is most rightly understood that [Col. 0317C] he will praise the Lord in the hearts of many—that is, in the midst of many. For Christ dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. III, 17). Therefore he says, “with my mouth,” that is, with the mouth of my heart [Augustine has “the mouth of my body”], which is the Church.

### (Verse 31)

For he stood at the right hand of the poor man, to save my soul from those who persecuted me.

[p. 415] It had been said of Judas, “And let the devil stand at his right hand”: Judas wanted to increase his riches by selling Christ. Here, however, the Lord stood at the right hand of the poor man, so that the Lord himself might be his riches.

The soul will be saved from those who persecute it if it does not consent to evil with them. It does not consent to them when the Lord stands at the right hand of the poor man, so that he may not succumb through that very poverty—that is, weakness.

## PSALM CIX
[Col. 0317D] **(Verse 1.)** “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.’” When our Lord Jesus Christ was asking the Jews whose son they said the Christ was, and they answered, “David’s,” he immediately replied to them: “How, then, does David in the Spirit call him Lord [Note: [Col. 0317D] Here the word *dicens* (“saying”) is absent in the printed Prosperian editions, though it is omitted neither in Augustine’s work nor in the Gospel text, Greek as well as Latin.], saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies beneath your feet”’?” If, then, he calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son (Matthew 22:43)? The Jews remained silent under this question. They neither acknowledged nor wished to acknowledge that he was both Lord and son of David; and they preferred to be shattered by swollen silence rather than to gain instruction through humble confession.

But we, taught by the Gospel of that very Truth, know that Jesus Christ is both Lord of David, according to the words, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1 ff.), and son of David, according to the words, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

We know him as Lord of David because, “though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped.” And we know him as son of David because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). Thus David himself, seeing this in the Spirit, uttered at the beginning of this Psalm, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.’”

Christ sits at the right hand of the Father after his resurrection from the dead and his ascension into heaven (Mark 16:19). Therefore, precisely because Christ was son of David, he became Lord of David. For that which was born from the seed of David was so honored that, while being his son, it was also his Lord. In accordance with this dispensation, the Apostle also says of Christ: “Therefore God exalted him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:9 ff.).

The Lord sits at the right hand of the Father, and his enemies are placed beneath his feet. For everyone who opposes him will be subjected to him, either through correction or through condemnation. For it is necessary that everyone be beneath his feet, either adopted [Note: [Col. 0318D] Earlier editions read “or virtue.” Later editions rightly corrected this to “or conquered,” as it is found in Augustine’s work: “You were an enemy; you will be beneath his feet, either adopted or conquered.”] or conquered, whether through grace or through punishment.

**(Verse 2.)** “The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion.” Zion is Jerusalem itself; from it the rod of Christ’s power was foretold as being sent forth—that is, the kingdom of his power, which begins with Christians and has no end. For insofar as he is the Word of the Father, of one deity and omnipotence, he has always reigned with the Father. This kingdom, then, which Christ, the man who is mediator between God and human beings, acquires, begins from Jerusalem, because from there the power and authority of evangelical preaching were sent forth into the whole world (Luke 24:47).

“Rule in the midst of your enemies.” You, he says, O son of David and Lord of David, rule in the midst of the pagans, in the midst of the Jews, in the midst of heretics, and in the midst of false brothers. We see this happening daily, until the times of the nations are fulfilled (Acts 3:21). For a partial blindness has occurred in Israel until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel is saved (Romans 11:25), and Christ rules in the midst of his enemies.

**(Verse 3.)** “With you is the beginning on the day of your power.” When those who questioned him asked who he was, the Lord replied, “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:28). That is: “I who speak to you am the Beginning.” The Father, too, is the Beginning, in whom “the Word was in the beginning, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1). Are there therefore two Beginnings, because the Father is the Beginning and the Son is the Beginning? By no means. For just as the Father is God and the Son is God, yet the Father and the Son are not two gods but one God, so the Father is the Beginning and the Son is the Beginning, yet the Father and the Son are not two Beginnings but one Beginning.

“With you, then, is the beginning on the day of your power”—on the day when it will be seen how it is believed. For although, even in the form of a servant, that assumption of our weakness itself is not without divine power, since “your weakness is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25), and you will rule in the rod of your power in the midst of your enemies, nevertheless that day will come when, after all temporal dispensations have been accomplished and brought to an end, you will manifest yourself to your saints and appear to them in that glory in which you are equal to the Father, so that they may see: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power.”

**(Ibid.)** “In the splendors of the saints.” The present life of the saints, although it flourishes through grace and shines through its conduct, is not yet in splendor, because it has not yet been freed from corruption. When Christ, the life of the saints, appears, then they too will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4). Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matthew 13:43), that is, in eternal life.

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” If this is spoken of that generation by which God the Son was begotten from God the Father, “from the womb” signifies “from the secret,” “from what is hidden”—from the Father himself, from the substance of the Father. By “before the morning star,” however, he means before the ages. For by the morning star, as the most brilliant heavenly body, the whole is signified by a part: all the stars that were made for signs, seasons, days, and years (Genesis 1:14). What is “before the morning star” is therefore “before the stars”; and what is “before the stars” is “before the ages,” and thus from eternity.

But if this was spoken in the person of the prophet who says, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand,’” there is no doubt that the birth by which the Lord of David is son of David is signified. David could say this on account of the lineage through which the Virgin Mary descended from his stock: “From the womb I begot you”—that is, from the virginal womb, from the womb to which no man came, in which there was only the mother’s conception, without the seed of a father. It is appropriately said, “before the morning star,” because the Lord was born before the rising of day, as the testimony of the shepherds indicates, who [Note: [Col. 0319D] Thus the older editions, in accordance with Augustine’s text. More recent editions have instead: “who were keeping watch over their flock.”] were keeping watch over their flock (Luke 2:7–8).

**(Verse 4.)** “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.’” If we understand the Savior who was born from the Virgin’s womb before the morning star, then from that point he is undoubtedly a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek. For insofar as the Lord was born from the Father, coeternal and equal with the one who begot him, he is not a priest.

The Lord therefore swore—that is, he promised with a fixed decree. “And he will not repent” means that he will not change his plan, will do nothing else, and will never regret this decision. “You are a priest forever” means that your priesthood does not end; and just as the order of Aaron came to an end, so your high-priesthood will not be changed. Your priesthood will have no end, but, according to the order of Melchizedek—that is, according to the mysteries disclosed through him—it will remain forever.

**(Verse 5.)** “The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings on the day of his wrath.” The prophet’s speech is directed to the very Lord who said, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’” He himself, he says, O Lord, to whom you swore, “You are a priest forever,” is the Lord at your right hand who shattered kings on the day of his wrath—those of whom it was said, “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2:2).

For all such people who hate the Christian name and persist in their impiety have indeed already been shattered, and could not accomplish what they wished; but on the day of wrath—that is, in the retribution of God’s just judgment—they will be utterly crushed.

**(Verse 6.)** “He judged among the nations; he filled the ruins.” Those who rise up in pride and persist in their arrogance will be destroyed in such a way that they will not be rebuilt. Those who do not cease to exalt themselves do not cease to be destroyed. But those who fall and prostrate themselves through humility, so that they may become subject beneath the feet of him to whom the Lord said, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet,” will be restored completely, because the Lord did not condemn these ruins but filled them. This is accomplished in the present age, when Christ brings about the restoration of ruins among all nations.

“He shattered the heads of many in the earth.” In this life Christ shatters and inclines the heads of many, making the proud humble.

**(Verse 7.)** “He will drink from the brook on the way; therefore he will lift up his head.” Just as a torrent gathered from rainwater overflows, roars, runs, and, by running, runs its course to its end, so is the whole course of human mortality. Human beings are born, live, and die; then, as others die, still others are born, succeed them, come after them, and depart [Note: [Col. 0320D] Augustine adds, “and will not remain.” Our manuscripts do not add these words.].

From this torrent, then—from this passing noise, from this mortality—the son of David, the Lord of David, drank, deigning for our sake to be born and to die. He thus drank from the torrent on the way, yet did not stand in the way of sinners (Psalm 1:1). Therefore he will lift up his head, because he was humbled and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. For this reason [Note: [Col. 0321D] “God” is understood, as in Augustine: “therefore God exalted him from the dead,” and so forth.] God exalted him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:8–9 ff.).

# PSALM CX

## HALLELUIAH

**(Verse 1.)** “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart.” Confession is not always confession of sins; the praise of God is also expressed through the devotion of confession. The former mourns; the latter rejoices. The former displays a wound to the physician; the latter gives thanks for health.

“In the council of the upright and the congregation.” Without doubt, of those who will sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28). From their council and congregation every hypocrite will be separated, and every tempter excluded.

**(Verse 2.)** “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his desires.” Search, inquire into, and investigate, if you can, all the desires of the Lord: in all things you will always find that his works are great. For no desire is more powerful than his own will. When he permits something to be done against it, he demonstrates his mercy and his justice.

For just as he wills that a human being not sin, so he wills to spare the sinner, so that the sinner may return and live; and so he also wills to punish the one who perseveres in sins, so that the stubborn person may not escape the power of justice. Thus, whatever you choose, O human being, the Lord will not lack the means by which to fulfill his will concerning you. Whether, therefore, he justifies the ungodly, reproves the sluggish, waits for the one who has turned away, or abandons the one destined for punishment, he is always merciful, always just, always omnipotent.

**(Verse 3.)** “Confession and magnificence are his work; and his justice endures forever and ever.” The magnificence of the Lord toward us is shown in this: that, without any preceding merits, he justifies the sinner who confesses, so that “where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more” (Romans 5:20), through which confession itself was also aroused, so that no one might exalt himself, but “whoever boasts might boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

For both the sinner’s confession and the magnificence of justification are the Lord’s work. With him there is no iniquity, even if we do not comprehend his judgments (Romans 9:18), because his justice endures forever and ever.

[Col. 0321D] **(Verses 4–6.)** “The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders; he has given food to those who fear him.” In every creature of God his wonders are both daily and great. But because habit causes them to be admired too little, the Lord arranged that certain signs and portents should be brought forth at appointed times, so that through unusual and new things human attention might be awakened, and a useful fear of extraordinary events might be nourished in it. To this fear, however, the merciful Lord would give the food of power and life—namely, that incorruptible bread which came down from heaven (John 6:41)—so that the Word of God might be food for human beings, just as food is the food of angels.

“He will remember his covenant forever; he has proclaimed the power of his works to his people.” The Lord has fulfilled his promises. He is the power and strength of the saints, because what is difficult for human beings is easy for God, and he himself works all things in all (2 Corinthians 12:6).

**(Verse 7.)** “So that he may give them the inheritance of the nations”—that is, the inheritance which he prepared for all nations. “The works of his hands are truth and judgment”—that is, so that truth and judgment may be preserved; for the hand works, so that tribulation, distress, famine, nakedness, and the sword may not separate one from Christ (Romans 8:35). [Note: [Col. 0321D] We scarcely doubt that this passage of Prosper’s derives whatever obscurity it possesses from the alteration of a single word and faulty punctuation. Since all the editions agree on the same reading, and no manuscript is available, we have not altered it; but we conjecture that, with a slight change, it should be read: “This means that, so that truth and judgment may be preserved, his hand works”—that is, “so that tribulation, distress,” and so forth, “may not separate one from Christ.”]

**(Verse 8.)** “All his commandments are faithful, confirmed forever and ever.” He who gave the commandments also gave the promises, which he faithfully repays, confirmed eternally and never destined to fail. “Made in truth and judgment.” For this is true and just [Note: [Col. 0322D] The Lyon edition adds the substantive verb “is,” which is lacking in the editions of Louvain, Douai, and Cologne.], that there should be labor here and rest there.

**(Verse 9.)** “He sent redemption to his people.” The citizens and heirs of the heavenly Jerusalem are redeemed from the captivity of this pilgrimage. “He commanded his covenant forever.” His covenant, certainly the new one, which he promised would be eternal—not the old one, whose promises were transitory.

“Holy and terrible is his name.” True wisdom is to know and love God. But one ascends to this degree through fear, because just as his gifts are to be desired, so his judgments are to be feared.

**(Verse 10.)** “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” “Good understanding belongs to all who do it.” The one who has good understanding is the person who does what he rightly understands ought to be done, because understanding without works is such as wisdom without fear (Sentences 13).

“His praise endures forever and ever.” Let no one, therefore, ascribe anything to his own justice [Note: [Col. 0322D] It might perhaps be better to read “will ascribe,” and at the end “will be referred,” on account of the future “will rejoice” placed between them; and because our saint seems to be speaking here of the future state of the blessed, in which honor and glory will be referred eternally to God alone by all the saints.], and let no one rejoice as though in his own merits; rather, all the blessedness of the saints is referred eternally to the praise and glory of God.

# PSALM CXI

## HALLELUIAH

The title of the Psalm is: “The Return of Haggai and Zechariah.” After the overthrow of the temple of Jerusalem and the deportation to Babylon, when the seventy years of captivity had been completed under Darius, they began to prophesy concerning the release from captivity and the restoration of the temple. But because the events then carried out bodily bore indications of future realities, through that release from captivity and restoration of the temple the construction of the temple itself was represented spiritually. Christ is its foundation, and upon him, the cornerstone, the structure of the heavenly building rises, fitted together from living stones, so that from the ancient ruin brought about in Adam a new temple of God might be restored together with the renewal of all nations.

The prophecy of Haggai and Zechariah, whose names are presented in the title of the Psalm, therefore pertains to this temple. Whoever understands this mystery and desires to be made firm in the framework of this building should know that the beginning of his return and renewal is in the fear of God.

**(Verse 1.)** “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly desire his commandments.” The blessedness of the righteous man begins with fear of the Lord and advances toward desire for God’s commandments, through which he becomes God’s temple.

[Col. 0323B] **(Verse 2.)** “His seed will be powerful on the earth.” The Apostle testifies that the works of mercy are the seed of the future harvest, saying, “Let us not grow weary in doing good; for at the proper time we shall reap” (Galatians 6:9). What, indeed, is more powerful than this seed, by whose expenditure the kingdom of heaven and eternal life are acquired?

“The generation of the upright will be blessed”—that is, the works of those who are upright in heart, who are not disturbed by the delay of the promises, nor carnally desire things that pass away, but faithfully and patiently await things that endure.

**(Verse 3.)** “Glory and riches are in his house, and his justice endures forever and ever.” Whoever is such in his house—that is, in his heart, where the temple of God is—has glory and riches, because through an unshakable hope he already possesses what is future, and the kingdom of God is within him (Luke 17:21). His justice endures forever and ever, because it itself is his glory and riches.

**(Verse 4.)** “Light has risen in darkness for the upright in heart.” They rightly direct their heart toward their Lord, rightly walk uprightly with their Lord, because, while they were in darkness, they saw a great light (Isaiah 9:2), and remembered that they had once been darkness but are now light in the Lord (Ephesians 5:8).

“The Lord is merciful, compassionate, and just.” He shows mercy so that he may be merciful, and he is just in his recompense, because he will judge no one without mercy.

**(Verse 5.)** “The good man is gracious, showing mercy and lending.” God does not spew this gracious, gentle, and joyful person from his mouth as something foul-smelling or distasteful. All his graciousness consists in this: that he shows mercy and lends—namely, by forgiving sins and bestowing benefits. These two duties of kindness contain all works of piety, as the Lord says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:32).

**(Verses 5–6.)** “He will order his words in judgment. For he will not be moved forever.” Whoever does these things orders his words in judgment. For deeds are certain words of witnesses, by which he might be defended in judgment [Note: [Col. 0323D] In Augustine: “he will be defended.”]. “For he will not be moved forever”—the one who, separated to the right hand, will hear: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

[Col. 0324A] **(Verse 7.)** “The righteous will be in eternal memory; he will not fear evil report.” He will not fear hearing what is said to those on the left: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

“His heart is prepared to hope in the Lord.” For he did not seek his own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21), and confidently awaits his promises.

**(Verse 8.)** “His heart is established; he will not be moved until he sees above his enemies.” His enemies desired present things; and, when invisible things were promised to them, they said, “Who will show us good things?” (Psalm 4:6). They wished to see the goods of human beings who die on earth; but this man believed that he would see the goods of the Lord in the land of the living (Psalm 26:13).

His heart therefore will not be moved, nor will he be troubled by the transitory prosperity of the wicked, until he sees—not what is below, namely, what his enemies see, but what is above and over his enemies—“what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9; Isaiah 64:4).

**(Verses 9–10.)** “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his justice endures forever and ever.” He scattered visible things in order to acquire invisible things; he gave temporal things in order to receive eternal things.

“His horn will be exalted in glory.” “The sinner will see and be angry.” The sinner is angry—but with whom more than with himself? Yet that repentance is late and fruitless, when he says, “What did pride profit us, or what benefit did the boast of riches bring us?” (Wisdom 5:8). He will gnash his teeth and will not revive, as he would have done if he had repented at the opportune time. But he will gnash his teeth then, when the desire of sinners has perished.

# PSALM CXII

## HALLELUIAH

**(Verse 1.)** “Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord.” This exhortation is addressed not only to childhood but to every age. For the Apostle says to everyone: “Do not become children in your minds, but be infants in wickedness, so that you may be mature in your minds” (1 Corinthians 14:20). What wickedness is meant except pride? For pride, presuming on empty greatness, does not allow a person to walk along the narrow way and enter through the narrow gate (Matthew 7:14). A child easily enters through the narrow way; and therefore no one enters the kingdom of heaven unless he has been converted and become like a child (Luke 13:24).

By the name “children,” therefore, not the age of infants but the humility of souls is addressed, because those who think themselves great and, wishing to establish their own justice, are not subject to the justice of God (Romans 10:3), do not praise the name of the Lord. They are not children; and while they want themselves to be praised, they do not praise the name of the Lord.

**(Verses 2–3.)** “May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever. From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise.” That is, may the name of the Lord always be blessed and praised everywhere.

**(Verse 4.)** “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens.” The majesty of the Lord is not only above all nations; his exalted glory is also above the heavens.

[Col. 0325A] **(Verses 5–6.)** “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the humble things in heaven and on earth?” Through Isaiah the Spirit speaks as follows: “Thus says the Most High, who dwells in the heights, whose name is the Lord Most High forever, who has rest in the saints” (Isaiah 57:15).

Heaven is rightly understood as those who are inhabited by the Lord. Although they are holy and therefore exalted, they are nevertheless humble, and are exalted from nothing other than humility. Thus the Lord dwells on high—that is, in the holy, spiritual, and heavenly ones—and he looks upon the humble, that is, upon those same saints, who never glory in themselves but always in the Lord. For he delights in the exaltation of the humble and in the humility of the exalted.

“In heaven and on earth”—that is, among those whose citizenship is in heaven, although they are clothed in mortal flesh. But if there are other humble ones whom our Lord looks upon in heaven and others on earth, heaven may be understood as those whom, once called and sanctified, he already inhabits; earth, however, as those whom he calls so that he may dwell in them.

A clearer interpretation is obtained if we understand “heavens” to mean those who will sit upon twelve thrones and judge with the Lord (Matthew 19:26), and “earth” to mean the remaining multitude of saints who will be placed at the right hand (Luke 16:9), so that, praised for their works of mercy, they may be received by those whom they made their friends from the mammon of iniquity during the mortality of this life into eternal dwellings.

God looks upon both these and those as humble, because both remember what they were through their own wickedness and what they became [Note: [Col. 0325] The Cologne edition reads “through the glory of God.” Lyon, Louvain, and Douai read “through the grace of God.” Augustine also has this reading here.] through the grace of God.

[Col. 0325C] **(Verses 7–8.)** “He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to place him with princes, with the princes of his people.” Let the exalted, therefore, not disdain to have humble heads under the hand of the Lord. For although the faithful steward of the Lord’s money will be placed with the princes of God’s people (Matthew 19:28), although he will sit upon twelve seats and even judge angels (1 Corinthians 6:3), he is nevertheless raised from the earth as a needy man and lifted from the dung heap as a poor man, because all the exaltation of the saints is God’s gift.

**(Verse 9.)** “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children.” God’s grace made the Church, formerly barren, fruitful, so that she might rejoice in many children (Isaiah 54:1). In her the Lord, who dwells on high and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth, possesses from the seed of Abraham both a lofty holiness, to be placed like the stars in heavenly seats, and a merciful and innumerable multitude, like the sand on the shore of the sea, to be separated from the waves on the left and from impious bitterness.

# PSALM CXIII

## HALLELUIAH

**(Verses 1–3.)** “When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judea became his sanctuary, Israel his power. The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned backward.” The history of past events appears to be recalled, and the manner in which the people of Israel, who are the house of Jacob, were led out from the yoke of Egyptian domination (Exodus 14:22) seems to be brought back to memory.

But through prophetic speech future things are indicated more than past things are recounted. Therefore certain things are said here differently from the way they happened there, so that the prophecy may be understood attentively where the historical account does not correspond. First, we read that the Jordan itself did not turn backward but stood still (Joshua 3:15), at the place from which it flowed down from above. Further, we do not read that the mountains exulted and the hills rejoiced; yet the Psalm adds these things and repeats them all. We must therefore understand that those events were figures of us (1 Corinthians 10:11), and that something different is said about them so that we may recognize the times to which they correspond.

For if we retain firmly in our hearts the grace of God that has been given to us, we are Israel, the seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:29). Abraham was made father not only of a people circumcised in the flesh, but also of all who follow the footsteps of Abraham’s faith, who, while still uncircumcised, believed the Lord, was justified by faith, and was appointed father of all nations (Romans 4:10 ff.; Genesis 15:6). It was said to him, “In you all nations will be blessed” (Genesis 12:3).

Because the Christian people is the true Israel, and Egypt is often set forth as a figure of the whole world, from which one must depart spiritually, just as that people could not reach the promised land unless it was liberated by divine aid, so no one is freed from the bonds of this world except through the grace of God, by a strong hand and an outstretched arm (Exodus 6:1, 6), so that he may be worthy to be a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Therefore all who are Israelites, the house of Jacob and heirs of Abraham according to the promise (Galatians 3:29), recognize that they have come out of Egypt when they renounced this world, and that they have come out from a barbarous people when, through their confession of piety, they withdrew from the blasphemies of impious nations.

Let them question their hearts: has faith circumcised them? Has confession purified them—confession of the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? “Judea became his sanctuary in them, and Israel his power.” For he gave them power to become children of God (John 1:12).

Let each person who once labored under harsh domination, subjected in this world to the works of the devil, now remember how he was freed from the yoke, how, amid the restraints of those who tried to dissuade him and the obstacles of those who resisted, he escaped onto the path of freedom and toward the hope of an eternal inheritance.

“The sea saw and fled,” when the obstacles of the world, shaken by the word of God, gave way. “The Jordan turned backward,” because the one who, turned away from his beginning, abandons his Creator flows like a river into the sea. It is good for him to be turned backward, and, returning to his source, to make the sea toward which he had previously been heading lie behind him. Thus the Jordan is turned backward when those who have received the grace of baptism are converted to the Lord.

**(Verse 4.)** “The mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep.” The faithful stewards of the word of truth—the holy apostles and holy evangelists—are mountains and leaders of flocks. The hills, like lambs of sheep, are those to whom it is said, “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). Of them it is said, “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 28:1). They grow fat on the pastures of the mountains and are guided in exultation under the leadership of the rams.

**(Verses 5–6.)** “What happened to you, sea, that you fled? And you, Jordan, that you turned backward? Mountains, that you skipped like rams, and hills, like lambs of sheep?” What is this, he says, O world? Your obstacles have given way. What is this, that so many thousands of faithful people, throughout the world, renounce this world and are converted? What is this, that you rejoice—you to whom at the end it will be said, “Well done, good servant; because you were faithful in little, I will set you over much” (Matthew 25:21)? What is this, that you rejoice—you to whom at the end it will be said, “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34)?

**(Verse 7.)** “The earth was moved at the face of the Lord, at the face of the God of Jacob.” What is “at the face of the Lord” except “at the presence of him” who said, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20)? He, therefore, moves the earth; he converts sluggish and inert hearts.

**(Verse 8.)** “He turns the rock into pools of water, and the cliff into springs of water.” This is the spiritual rock, that is, Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4), who changed his teaching, which had previously seemed hard and rigid, into many streams. Having sent the Holy Spirit from heaven, he made his word drinkable, the word he had conveyed to his disciples, beginning with Moses and continuing through all the prophets, because it was thus necessary for Christ to suffer (Luke 24:26–27).

**(Verse 1.)** “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.” Grace is proclaimed: the water of regeneration was sent forth from the rock that is Christ, without any preceding merits of human beings, because Christ died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6), so that no one might glory except in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

**(Verse 2.)** “For your mercy and your truth.” These two—mercy and truth—are found joined together almost always in the holy Scriptures. In his mercy God called the ungodly, and in his truth he judged those who refused to come. “Lest at any time the nations say, ‘Where is their God?’” For at the end mercy and truth will be manifested. The ungodly will not say, “Where is their God?” when the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven (Matthew 24:30) and judgment is at hand—when he will no longer be preached as one who must be believed, but will be revealed as one to be feared.

**(Verse 3.)** “But our God is in heaven above, and he has done all things whatsoever he willed.” He is not merely in heaven, where those who worship creation see the sun and moon, but in heaven above, which transcends all heavenly and earthly bodies. Yet he is not in heaven in such a way that heaven could exist without him. For he sustains as needy the things in which he is; he who in heaven and on earth has done all things whatsoever he willed.

This means that he established his voluntary grace among both the higher and lower peoples of his own, so that no one might glory in the merits of works. For whether the mountains skip like rams or the hills like lambs of sheep, the earth was moved at the face of the Lord, so that it might not remain in earthly filth.

**(Verse 4.)** “The idols of the nations are silver and gold.” They also have idols made of bronze, wood, clay, and various other materials; but the Holy Spirit preferred to mention what was precious among them. When someone becomes ashamed of what is dearer to him, he is much more easily turned away from venerating what is less valuable, so that he may understand that even in gold and silver there is nothing other than earth.

**(Verses 5–8.)** “They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see. They have ears, but they will not hear; they have nostrils, but they will not smell. They have hands, but they will not touch; they have feet, but they will not walk; they will not cry out through their throats. Let all who make them and all who trust in them become like them.” Let the ungodly, therefore, see with open and perceptive eyes, and worship with minds that are closed and dead—idols that neither see nor live.

**(Verse 9.)** “The house of Israel hopes in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector.” For hope that is seen is not hope. For what does someone hope for if he sees it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience (Romans 8:24). Yet, so that this patience may endure to the end, the Lord is helper and protector.

**(Verse 10.)** “The house of Aaron hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector.” Therefore, even those who are more exalted and excel at the highest rank [Note: [Col. 0327] It appears that a phrase should be supplied here, as in Augustine’s work, since it is lacking in our editions.], must themselves also run on perseveringly until they grasp that for which they were grasped, and know as they have been known; they are fortified by the Lord’s help and protection.

(Verses 11, 12.) Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord: he is their helper and protector. The Lord remembered us and blessed us. “All,” he says, “who fear the Lord and hope in the Lord are perfected by his assistance.” For we do not anticipate the Lord’s mercy by our merits; rather, the Lord remembered us and blessed us.

(Verses 12, 13.) He blessed the house of Israel; he blessed the house of Aaron. He blessed all who fear the Lord. That is, both the higher and the lower, because both fear the Lord. If, therefore, you ask whom he has blessed—both groups—it is answered: the little ones together with the great; that is, the house of Israel and the house of Aaron.

[Column 0328D]

(Vers 14.) May the Lord add to you—to you and to your children. And so it happened. For there also came children of Abraham raised up from stones (Matt. III, 9); there came sheep that were not of this fold, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd (John X, 16); there came the faith of all the nations, and the number grew—not only of wise leaders, but also of obedient peoples—the Lord adding not only to the fathers but also to their children who would piously follow in their fathers’ footsteps.

[Column 0329A]

(Vers 15.) You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth—as though he were saying, “You are blessed by the Lord, who made you.”

(Vers 16.) The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men. Therefore it was not this visible heaven, filled with lights, that he made you; rather, he made you a much more excellent heaven, in which he prepared a dwelling for himself: namely, the higher and purer minds. In comparison with these, whatever is seen is earth. The little ones in the Church, however, may also be called by the name “earth”; by progressing, they are destined to become heaven, and in this very hope they are nourished with milk by the great.

Yet because they already gather the purity and abundance of wisdom not from a human being or through a human being, but from the Lord himself, they have received the little ones—who are indeed destined to become heaven—so that they may know themselves to be the heaven of heaven.

[Note: Augustine has “so that they may know themselves to be.” “Themselves” is absent from our printed editions.]

Nevertheless, they are still earth, to which they may say, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III, 6). For to those children of men whom he made heaven, he gave earth on which they might labor—he who knows how to provide for the earth through heaven. Let heaven and earth, therefore, remain in their Lord, who made them, and live from him, confessing him and praising him. For if they wish to live from themselves, they will die; as it is written: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Ecclus. XVII, 26).

(Vers 17.) The dead shall not praise you, nor all those who descend into hell. For holy Scripture cries out elsewhere: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3).

(Vers 18.) But we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever.

## PSALM CXIV

### HALLELUIA

[Column 0329C]

(Vers 1.) I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer. Let the soul that is a pilgrim far from the Lord sing this; let that sheep which had wandered sing this (Ps. CXVIII, final verse); let that son who had been dead and rose again, who had been lost and was found, sing this. For what is “I have loved, because the Lord will hear” (Luke XV, 24) except: “I have loved, because I have been placed in this hope, that I may believe myself destined to be heard”? For I do not hope this in vain.

(Vers 2.) Because he inclined his ear to me. Therefore he will hear, because he inclined his ear to me. Now, if we ask from where the soul believed that the Lord had inclined his ear toward it, would it not answer: “Because he first loved us and did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32)? When this was announced to me, how could I not believe that the Lord had inclined his ear to me—he who anticipated me with such great mercy and summoned me with such a great calling? And in my days I called upon him. That is, in the days of my misery; in the days of mortality and transgression, by which I abandoned God and deserved a prison—that is, I received the darkness of ignorance and the fetters of difficulty. In these days, therefore,

(Verses 3, 4.) The pains of death surrounded me; the dangers of hell found me. These will not find me unless I wander away from you.

[Note: According to Augustine: “would not find me.”]

But I was not finding them—that is, I was not paying attention to them. For I loved my deceptions, and, rejoicing in the false prosperity of the world, I was sinking into the true dangers of hell. But when your grace shone upon me, I discovered the causes of my tribulation and pain, and I called upon the name of the Lord.

(Vers 5.) O Lord, deliver my soul—as though he were saying: “Amid both the adversities and the prosperities of this world, I have recognized myself as miserable, because the former oppress me and the latter deceive me. Who, then, will free me from this body of death, except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord?” (Rom. VII, 24). The Lord is merciful and just, and our God will have mercy. Merciful first, because he inclined his ear to me; just, because he makes me recognize what was crushing me; and merciful again, because he brings me to the point where he may be invoked and have mercy.

[Note: “And here it would perhaps be better to have ‘merciful again,’ since Augustine has this, as before and afterward.”]

(Vers 6.) The Lord guards the little ones; I was humbled, and he delivered me. He guards the little ones whom he wishes to make perfect; and those who fell into servitude through pride, he makes free through humility.

(Vers 7.) Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt graciously with you. “Return,” he says, “my soul, because you possess the power of returning from him who has dealt graciously with you.”

(Vers 8.) Because he rescued my soul from death. The soul has been rescued from death even while still surrounded by mortal flesh, when it has been changed from unbelieving to believing. Apart from that perfect and eternal rest from all labors, which the precious death of his saints gains in the sight of the Lord (Sent. 14), the soul that has been rescued from the death of unbelief also has its rest in this life. It refrains not from works of righteousness, but from the practice of iniquity.

Such a soul, which already lives for the Lord and is dead to the world, which is vigilantly intent upon spiritual diligence and rests in the tranquil peace of humility and gentleness—not sluggishly, but quietly—already possesses, as things attained, whatever it patiently awaits in unfailing hope (Sent. 14). Therefore he adds and says: “My eyes from tears, my feet from falling.” These goods belong not to temporal life but to eternal life; nor can they be possessed by those surrounded with mortal flesh, so that they do not weep, groan, or suffer the assault of any temptation. Therefore the hope of the saints—who, according to the fact that they are led by the Spirit of God, are no longer in the flesh (Rom. VIII, 14, 9)—rightly rejoices and gives thanks for what has been promised to them by the truth. Finally, to show that he did not yet possess these things but hoped for them,

(Vers 9.) “I shall please,” he says, “the Lord in the land of the living.” Therefore the one who is still in the land of mortals does not yet please the Lord completely; nor can a person be such in this dying life as he will be in the eternal one.

## PSALM CXV

### HALLELUIA

(Vers 10.) I believed; therefore I spoke. Those who do not speak the truth they believe are as reprobate as those who do not believe the truth they speak. The faith of such a person is perfect who says not merely that he believed, but also that he spoke because he believed. But I was humbled exceedingly. Why did he add “But I,” when he could say, “I spoke and was humbled”? Because a human being who proclaims the truth can be humbled by those who contradict the truth, but the truth itself cannot be humbled; the one who believes it gives it utterance. “I believed; therefore I spoke.”

(Vers 11.) But I said in my agitation: Every human being is a liar. Here “agitation” is understood as fear, for this is the voice of martyrs trembling as torture or death approaches and recognizing that they do not possess the strength to overcome what is inflicted upon them. Thus human weakness is found to be deceitful, since, presuming upon its own strength, it cannot help but deceive. The strength of endurance, however, comes from God, who gives steadfastness to the one who does not fear and restores confidence to the one who is afraid. For he is truthful who says: “When they deliver you up, do not consider how or what you should speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 19–20).

“Agitation” is also said to occur when the mind is not alienated by fear, but is taken up by some inspiration of revelation.

(Vers 12.) What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? In saying this, he declares that something other than what he deserved was rendered to him by the Lord: that is, that he received good things in return for evils. And he asks what he himself should return for the good things; he finds nothing except what the Lord himself has given, and he says:

(Vers 13.) I shall receive the cup of salvation, and I shall call upon the name of the Lord. Who gives this cup except the one who says, “Can you drink the cup which I shall drink?” (Matt. XX, 22). By giving an example of suffering, he bestowed the gift, redeeming their very weakness by his blood; and by providing the price of their imitation, he brought it about that there should be

(Vers 15.) Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints. For the Lord purchased it with his blood, which he shed for servants, so that servants would not fear to shed their blood for their Lord. Yet the death both of the Lord and of the servants would benefit the servants, not the Lord.

(Vers 16.) O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid. As though he were saying: “Many call themselves martyrs, and many profess themselves to be your servants because they bear your name amid vices, heresies, and errors. But because they are outside your Church, they are not sons of your handmaid. I, however, am both your servant and the son of your handmaid.”

(Ibid.) You have broken my bonds; I shall sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise. “You,” he says, “have made me your servant and the son of your handmaid—you who broke the bonds of my captivity. Therefore I owe you a sacrifice of praise, because by your grace I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 10), and in you I have glory in which to glory.
