(Vers 18.) I shall pay my vows to the Lord.

[Note: Saint Prosper passes over verse 14: “I shall pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people.” His most holy teacher Augustine had also passed it over. Perhaps this is because both of them discuss the same matter at the end of the psalm.]

Whoever thinks rightly about what he should vow to the Lord and what vows he should pay should vow himself and pay himself. This is what is required; this is what is owed. “Let the image of Caesar be rendered to Caesar, and the image of God to God” (Matt. XXII, 21). But just as one must see what one offers, so one must also consider where one offers it (Sent. 15).

(Vers 19.) “In the courts,” he says, “of the house of the Lord.” And what is the house of the Lord except his people? Therefore it follows: “In the sight of all his people.” And what is his people except what he adds: “In the midst of you, Jerusalem”? Jerusalem, moreover, is interpreted as “Vision of peace.”

Then what is offered will be acceptable if it is rendered from peace and in peace.

[Note: A more recent edition had corrected the reading to *offertur* (“is offered”), quite appropriately, since all the older editions have *offeretur* (“will be offered”).]

Those who are not sons of this handmaid, however, have loved war rather than peace.

## PSALM CXVI

### HALLELUIA

(Vers 1.) Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples. At the end of the preceding psalm, lest the Jews glory in Jerusalem and even carnal Israel claim this dignity for itself, the beginning of this psalm shows who the Israelites are and in whom Jerusalem is found. Namely, all nations and all peoples who, through imitation of faith, have become children of Abraham and the spiritual seed of Israel (Rom. IV, 12; Gal. III, 7).

[Column 0332C]

(Vers 2.) For his mercy has been confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever. The Lord’s mercy was confirmed over us when the raging mouths of hostile nations yielded before the name by which we were delivered, and when, by believing, they praised the one whom they had blasphemed by denying him. The truth of the Lord remains forever, whether in the things he promised to the righteous or in the things with which he threatened the wicked.

## PSALM CXVII

### HALLELUIA

(Vers 1.) Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Here, however, the confession is not that of penitents but of those praising the Lord, to whom by grace it was granted to be rescued from darkness and from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God (Col. I, 13)—for this reason alone: because God is good and has mercy with a mercy that endures forever.

(Verses 2–4.) Let the house of Israel now say: “For he is good, for his mercy is forever.” Let the house of Aaron now say: “For he is good, for his mercy is forever.” The house of Israel and the house of Aaron are all those who fear the Lord—both the little ones and the great (Ps. CXIII, 12–13).

[Note: Here verse 4—“Let those who fear the Lord now say: ‘For his mercy is forever’”—which was omitted above, seems to be touched upon and explained in passing.]

From these, whether Jews or Gentiles, one people has been formed, joining together into one flock under one shepherd, Jesus Christ (John X, 16). This fellowship has been established by the grace of him who is good and whose mercy is eternal and makes people eternal.

(Vers 5.) In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he answered me in spaciousness. Whoever is in tribulation is in distress; but whoever is heard is received into infinite spaciousness.

(Vers 6.) The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me. The Apostle says that our struggle is not against flesh and blood—that is, against the wicked human being—but against the rulers and authorities of darkness (Eph. VI, 12). And what darkness is meant except that of human beings subject to the devil? Therefore the one who, with God’s help, conquers the devil who incites him does not fear what man can do to him.

(Vers 7.) The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies. Whether they are evil human beings or evil angels, the one whose helper is the Lord will look down upon his enemies.

(Vers 8.) It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. Even if a good person or a good angel helps me, “I will not trust in them,” he says, “but in the Lord, who helps me through them.”

(Vers 9.) It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes. “Princes” may be understood as both human beings and angels; but hope must be placed in neither, because authority comes only from God (Rom. XIII, 1).

(Verses 10–12.) All nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them. They surrounded me on every side, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them. They surrounded me like bees and blazed like fire among thorns; and in the name of the Lord—for I took vengeance upon them.

We understand the Lord himself, the head of the Church, to be surrounded by persecutors, just as bees surround a honeycomb. But mystically it is signified that the gathering pertains to the persecutors, while the honeycomb pertains to believers. For the wicked, not knowing what they were doing, made him sweeter by torturing him, so that we might “taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. XXXIII, 8).

That they “blazed like fire among thorns,” however, is better referred to the whole body of Christ, that is, his people. “All nations surrounded me,” because he was gathered from all nations, and everywhere the fires of persecution blazed against him. But he took vengeance upon his persecutors because, once their wickedness had been extinguished, they became Christians; or because all who stubbornly remained unbelieving—having rejected him when he called them—will experience him when he judges.

(Vers 13.) I was pushed and overturned so that I might fall, but the Lord received me. I was turned about like a heap of sand so that I might fall, but the Lord received me. The persecution of the nations had no place to which it could drive the multitude of the faithful gathered into the unity of faith. Although it harassed and agitated them greatly, it could not tear them away and cast them down, because all believed in him together, and because he received both individuals and the whole body everywhere.

(Vers 14.) The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation. Those whose strength and praise they wish to be in themselves fall. But those whose strength and praise is the Lord do not fall any more than the Lord falls. Therefore he became salvation for them—not because he began to be something that he was not, but because, after turning back, they began to possess in him the salvation that they had not possessed when turned away.

(Vers 15.) The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous. The ferocity of the persecutors could not deprive the saints of their inward joy; nor could the wicked take away the gladness of those whose endurance they were unable to overcome. Hence the Apostle also says: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (II Cor. VI, 10).

(Vers 16.) The right hand of the Lord has shown strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me; the right hand of the Lord has shown strength. Great is the power that exalts the humble, makes the mortal divine, grants perfection from weakness, glory from subjection, and victory from suffering. But because no human being exalted himself, perfected himself, gave himself glory, or conquered—and because he was not his own salvation—he repeats God’s praise in devout confession: “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength.”

(Vers 17.) I shall not die, but live, and I shall recount the works of the Lord. This is the voice of the Church, glorifying not in itself but in the Lord. The persecutors thought that God’s people would be extinguished; but the Church increased, and everywhere Christ is the glory of the martyrs, in whose sufferings the works of the Lord are proclaimed.

(Vers 18.) In chastising, the Lord has chastised me, but he has not delivered me to death. Therefore let the rage of the wicked not imagine that it has accomplished anything by its own strength; it would not have had this power unless it had been given from above. Often the head of a household orders his sons to be corrected by the most wicked servants, while preparing an inheritance for the sons and fetters for the servants (John XIX, 11).

[Note: “Perhaps ‘he prepares’ should be read, as in Augustine.”]

What is this inheritance? Is it of gold and silver, or gems, or estates and pleasant properties? Consider how one enters it, and understand what it is.

(Vers 19.) Open for me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them I shall confess to the Lord. Within the gates of righteousness there is a voice of confession and rejoicing. For blessed are those who dwell in the house of the Lord; throughout ages of ages they shall praise him (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

[Note: Douay and Cologne have “they shall praise you”; Lyons and Louvain, together with Augustine’s edition, have “they shall praise him.”]

(Vers 20.) This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it. This is the gate of that Jerusalem which no uncircumcised person and no unjust person enters, where it is said: “Outside are the dogs” (Rev. XXII, 15).

(Vers 21.) I shall confess to you, Lord, because you have heard me, and you have become my salvation. This confession is one of praise: it does not display wounds to a physician, but gives thanks for the health received to the one who himself is salvation.

[Column 0335A]

(Vers 22.) The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. In order to create the two in himself as one new human being, making peace and reconciling both in one body to God (Eph. II, 15)—namely, circumcision and uncircumcision.

(Vers 23.) This has come from the Lord. For although he would not have been the cornerstone unless he had suffered, he was not made this by those from whom he suffered. For those who were building rejected him; but in what the Lord was secretly building, he made him the cornerstone whom they had rejected. And it is marvelous in our eyes—in the inner eyes of human beings, in the eyes of those who believe, hope, and love.

(Vers 24.) This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. The day on which he gave me salvation; the day on which that Mediator between God and human beings became the cornerstone.

(Vers 25.) O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity. Save me, because it is the day of salvation; make the journey prosperous for those returning from pilgrimage, because you have become the way for us.

(Vers 26.) Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord. Cursed is the one who comes in his own name, whom those who did not receive the Son of God will welcome (John V, 43). We have blessed you from the house of the Lord. This is the voice of the great addressed to the little ones: of those great ones who, as far as they can in this life, touch the Word of God, who is God, with the mind, yet temper their speech for the sake of the little ones.

[Column 0335C]

(Vers 27.) God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us. That Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (I Tim. II, 5), has shone upon us. He is also God, equal to the Father; what he caused to be believed, he caused to be understood.

Establish a festival day with assemblies, up to the horn of the altar. That is, up to the inner house of God,

[Note: In Augustine: “from which we blessed you.”]

where the heights of the altar are; where there is the spiritual sacrifice of perpetual praise; where there is the eternal priest and the everlasting altar. To this altar one must run not lukewarmly or sluggishly, but in full assembly, so that concerning the Son of God, who became flesh for us (John I, 14), we may think no longer humbly according to the flesh, in which he deigned to become like us, but sublimely according to the divinity, which is equal to the Father.

[Note: The printed editions note in the margin, by conjecture, that it may be read otherwise: “let us feel.”]

(Vers 28.) You are my God, and I shall confess to you; you are my God, and I shall exalt you. I shall confess to you, Lord, because you have heard me, and you have become my salvation. These words will not be spoken with a clamor of phrases in that house into which he urges us to enter; rather, love clinging to God itself will be the voice of eternal praise.

(Vers 29.) Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. He closes the psalm with the same words with which he began it, because from beginning to end the confession of God’s praises ought to persevere in us.

[Note: Lyons and Louvain have *psalmus* (“the psalm,” nominative); Douay and Cologne have *psalmum* (“the psalm,” accusative).]

## PSALM CXVIII

[Column 0336A]

### ALEPH

(Vers 1.) Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. They cannot be blessed unless they are undefiled. But they are not undefiled unless they walk in the way; and there is no way except the law of the Lord. Therefore, seeking blessedness, let a person be undefiled in the way and walk in the law of the Lord, which is the way of the blessed—that is, let him not be idle.

(Vers 2.) Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart. Without doubt, those walk in the way of the Lord who search his testimonies. But because many wish to possess knowledge without works, he rightly added, “with their whole heart they seek him.” For God is sought rightly only if he is sought not for the sake of other things, but through all things. The blessedness of those who seek the Lord, however, cannot be perfect amid the labors of this life. Yet those are already called blessed who will certainly become so, because they walk undefiled in the way and, searching the testimonies of the law of the Lord, seek him with their whole heart. They are therefore blessed in hope, because blessedness has been promised to such people.

(Vers 3.) For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways. Here the question arises: since iniquity is sin, and those who walk in the ways of the Lord do not practice sin, how did those saints walk in the ways of the Lord who say, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8)? Therefore they had sin and walked in the ways of the Lord, according to Paul’s statement: “If I do what I do not wish, it is not I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. VII, 15).

Thus those who walk in the ways of the Lord do not practice sin, and yet they are not without sin, because it is no longer they themselves who do it, but sin dwelling in them. They themselves do not do it, however, when they do not give the consent of their will to unlawful desires.

Nevertheless, since all the saints living in the flesh truthfully say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 12), how is it understood that they walk undefiled in the way of the Lord when they must daily ask forgiveness of sins? It is because it is true that those who walk in the way of the Lord consent to no crimes, yet are still troubled by certain stealthy incursions of carnal thoughts. For this reason daily forgiveness is necessary for them, so that they may become undefiled. Indeed, this very request belongs to the way of the Lord; the one who continually asks to be made undefiled does not depart from it.

(Vers 4.) You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly. Whether “exceedingly” is referred to the one commanding or to the one keeping, it is not to be understood as “more than is necessary,” but as “very greatly.” For the divine commandments are greatly given and greatly to be kept.

(Vers 5.) Would that my ways might be directed toward keeping your statutes. “You gave a command,” he says, “and ordered it to be kept; but would that you also grant help, so that, with you assisting me, I may do what I have learned should be done, with you teaching me.”

(Vers 6.) Then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments. “When,” he says, “my ways have been directed by your grace, then, by looking upon your commandments, I shall not be put to shame. I shall be not an unprofitable hearer, but an effective doer.”

[Note: It should certainly be read “I shall be a not-unprofitable hearer,” although all the printed editions have “I seek an unprofitable hearer.” The editions of Douay and Cologne had noted in the margin “I shall be.” That “not unprofitable” should be read seems to be demonstrated by the passage in James I, 23, to which our author alludes: “If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man looking at the face of his birth in a mirror: he looked at himself, went away, and immediately forgot what he had been like; but the one who looks into the perfect law of freedom and remains in it, having become not a forgetful hearer (behold an unprofitable hearer, which the psalmist hopes he will not be if he looks upon the Lord’s commandments), this person will be blessed in his deed.” This is what he means when he says, “Then I shall not be put to shame.”]

(Vers 7.) I shall confess to you, Lord, with an upright heart, when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness. If my path and my heart are made upright, then I shall proclaim you, Lord, and praise you, and confess that this is your work.

(Vers 8.) I shall keep your statutes—that is, I shall do what you command, if you help me. Do not abandon me utterly. This is not to be understood as though he wished to be abandoned in some respect; rather, he asks not to be deserted completely, and specifically asks that divine help never and nowhere withdraw from him.

### BETH

(Vers 9.) By what means does a younger person correct his way? By keeping your words. The question is how a younger person corrects his way, and the answer is that his correction consists in keeping God’s words. But who is this younger person whose correction is being described, when many old people also turn to the Lord through observance of the commandments, however late? Therefore this younger person is rightly understood as the new people, renewed through Christ’s grace, who are corrected from the way of ancient error by keeping the word of faith.

(Vers 10.) With my whole heart I have sought you; do not reject me from your commandments.

[Note: This phrase, “with my whole heart,” is found in the edition of Lyons and in Augustine; it is absent from Louvain, Douay, and Cologne. The exposition of the immediately following verse suggests that it should be added.]

“You caused me,” he says, “to seek you with my whole heart; cause me to remain in your commandments. Help me so that they may be possible for me, and do not reject me from them—that is, do not withdraw your help from me.”

(Verses 11, 12.) I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I might not sin against you. Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your statutes. Why does he still seek to learn the Lord’s words, when he has already hidden them in his heart? He certainly would not have done this unless he had learned them. Why does he add, “Teach me your statutes,” except because he wishes to learn them by doing them and to grasp them through knowledge gained in action, not merely to retain them through ease of speech and the recollection of memory?

(Vers 13.) With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth. “I have kept silent about none of your judgments,” he says, “but have declared them all completely with my lips”—namely, those things that you told me with your mouth, that is, through the proclamation of your words.

(Vers 14.) I have delighted in the way of your testimonies as in all riches. The way of God’s testimonies is Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. II, 3). Therefore the one who sees in him many testimonies of divine love fulfilled toward us, and does not doubt those that are awaited for fulfillment, delights in this way as in all riches.

(Vers 15.) I shall exercise myself in your commandments, and I shall consider your ways. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10); their fullness is found in Christ, in whom the whole Church exercises itself in abundant discussions against the enemies of the Christian faith.

(Vers 16.) I shall meditate on your statutes; I shall not forget your words. I shall meditate for this very reason: so that I may not forget your words. I shall meditate so that I may not forget. For meditation is perseverance in action so as not to forget. Therefore he sought the help of grace, saying, “Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your statutes,” so that what he knew through speech he might also fulfill in action.

### GHIMEL

(Vers 17.) Repay your servant; give me life, and I shall keep your words. There are four kinds of repayment: evils may be repaid for evils, as God will repay the wicked with eternal fire; good for good, as he will repay the righteous with the eternal kingdom; good for evils, as Christ justifies the ungodly by grace; or evils for good, as Judas persecuted Christ through wickedness.

Of these four kinds of repayment, the first two belong to justice, so that evils are repaid for evils and good for good. The third belongs to mercy, so that good is repaid for evils. The fourth God does not know; for he repays no one evil for good. The repayment placed third, however, is necessary first. For unless God repaid good for evil, there would be no one to whom good could be repaid for good (Sent. 16).

Therefore the one who says, “Repay your servant,” and adds, “Give me life, and I shall keep your words,” knows that the righteous person lives by faith, which works through love (Hab. II, 4; Rom. I, 17; Gal. V, 6). And because he was dead through his own injustice, he asks to receive life through God’s grace.

[Note: A more recent edition, together with Augustine, has “would repay”; all the older editions of Prosper have “will have repaid.” Nevertheless, Sent. 16 has “would repay.”]

[Note: We read this in Augustine, and the Apostle’s passage to which Saint Prosper alludes recommends this reading, although all our printed editions, clearly through a scribal error that easily arose, have “through his own righteousness.” Nor do we think that this fits the Apostle’s meaning, when he says concerning the Jews in Rom. X, 3: “For, ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God.”]

which he certainly would not ask for if he did not believe at all—that is, if he did not live at all. But because what he had received for desiring was not sufficient for obeying, he asks that he be given life: that is, that the faith he received be increased in him, so that he may be given life throughout every day, being renewed day by day (II Cor. IV, 16).

(Vers 18.) Uncover my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law. “Give me,” he says, “understanding by which I may look upon the wonders of your law and see the power of your commandments.”

(Vers 19.) I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me. Each person is a stranger wherever he is absent from his homeland (Sent. 17). Therefore this person, enrolled as a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem, professes himself a stranger on earth, because he is certain of the promised inheritance.

But because “human life upon earth is a temptation” (Job VII, 1), he asks that, in a time of tribulation and difficulty, God’s commandments not be hidden from him. These commandments, to be sure, have been placed in the midst of all things and can even be known by the wicked. For who is unaware of the briefest and most complete commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. XXII, 37), and “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (ibid.)? On these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend.

How, then, does this inhabitant of the earth pray that the things hidden from almost no one not be hidden from him? It is because knowing the Lord belongs to few, and consequently the commandment of love is hidden from him, since he loves one thing in place of another; and whoever errs in love of the Lord also errs in love of his neighbor.

[Note: Perhaps “the one who loves something else,” since shortly afterward it says, “and the one who errs.”]

Therefore the one who is a sojourner on earth and does not love earthly things rightly asks that knowledge of God’s commandments be revealed to him, lest he be deceived either in love of God or in love of his neighbor.

(Vers 20.) My soul has longed to desire your statutes at all times. “I have longed,” he says, “to possess the desire for your statutes until the end. For you justify me; your grace makes me just and good. It is mine always to desire this and to delight in this protection of yours. Otherwise I shall not be righteous, if either your grace is lacking to me or pride puffs me up.”

[Note: Perhaps *meum est* (“it is my own”); all the printed editions have *mihi est* (“it is mine”).]

(Vers. 21.) You have rebuked the proud; accursed are those who turn aside from your commandments. This rebuke is to be understood as that which the first parents of the human race deserved by their transgression, turning aside from God’s commandment through the pride [Note: [Col. 0340D] We scarcely doubt that *qua* should be read, not *quam*, as all the printed editions have.] which they had coveted—not what God commanded to be loved, but what the devil, through envy, persuaded them to desire (Gen. III, 5). Every proud person, therefore, is subject to this rebuke, whether by inherited fault or by the choice of the will.

(Vers. 22.) Take away from me reproach and contempt, [Col. 0340A] because I have sought your testimonies. This is the voice of the Church, already loving its enemies and praying for its persecutors (Matt. V, 44). Let every Christian say—let all the members of Christ’s body say—“Take away from me the reproach which I hear for this reason, and the contempt [Note: [Col. 0340D] In Augustine: “by which I am despised for this reason.”] with which I am despised for this reason: because I have sought your testimonies,” that is, your martyrdoms. Thus our enemies may come to honor that for which they despise us, when they understand that those whom they thought ought to be persecuted ought instead to be honored.

(Vers. 23.) Indeed, princes sat and spoke against me. The persecution was therefore severe because princes, sitting—that is, presiding from judicial seats—decreed it; and there is no doubt that this was done both against the Head himself and against his body. But your servant was exercised in your justifications. What sort of exercise this was, the following words show.

(Vers. 24.) For your testimonies also are my meditation, and your justifications are my counsel. Thus Christ’s servant was exercised, contending against his persecutors through love. The counsel of the seated princes was to destroy the martyrs whom they had found; the counsel of the suffering martyrs was to find those enemies who were lost. The former returned evil for good; the latter, good for evil. Why then should it be surprising that the former, by killing, were exhausted, while the latter, by dying, conquered?

## DALETH

(Vers. 25.) My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word. Whoever asks to be given life because his soul has clung to the pavement seems to be asking to be rescued from earthly desires. Yet the preceding words are not such that we should believe that the one who said, “Your testimonies are my meditation, and your justifications are my counsel,” had clung more to an earthly way of life than to a heavenly one. He does not therefore desire to be torn away from the world’s desires or separated from the fellowship of the flesh, but from carnal affections; so that the desire which lusts against the spirit (Gal. V, 17) may be diminished, while the desire which lusts against the flesh may increase through persevering progress. For there is no one whose soul is not weighed down by a corruptible body (Wis. IX, 15) and an earthly dwelling (Sent. 18), until this corruptible body puts on incorruption (I Cor. XIII, 53), and the word of God—by which eternal life is promised—is fulfilled.

(Vers. 26.) I have declared my ways, and you have heard me; teach me your justifications. “I confessed my sins,” he says, “and you heard me; I declared my ways, and you wiped them away. Teach me your ways.” He therefore does not wish to learn the justifications in which he was being exercised, but desires to reach those justifications from the former.

(Vers. 27.) Make known to me the way of your justifications, [Col. 0341A] and I shall be exercised in your wonders. In asking this, he desires to increase still further through progress. There are, however, certain justifications so sublime and wondrous that those who have not experienced them think that human weakness cannot attain to them.

(Vers. 28.) My soul has become drowsy from weariness; strengthen me by your words. I am exhausted, then, through weakness, and I slip back through weariness. Strengthen me by your promises; and through what you have given me, I shall strive to ascend, so that, drowsing in my weaknesses, I may be awakened and stirred by your words.

(Vers. 29.) Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to your law. Let not the law of works, through which sin abounded, lead me, in my weakness, into iniquities (Rom. V, 20). “Have mercy on me,” he says, “according to your law”—that is, according to the law of faith [Col. 0341B] (Rom. III, 27)—so that by your grace I may do what I cannot accomplish by myself [Note: [Col. 0341D] The Lyon edition adds the word *implere* (“to fulfill”), which the editions of Louvain, Douai, and Cologne omit. It is also read here in Augustine.].

(Vers. 30, 31.) I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments. 441 I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not put me to shame. I have chosen the way of truth in which I should run; I have not forgotten your judgments, so that I might run. I clung to your testimonies while I was running; Lord, do not put me to shame. How shall I reach the goal toward which I run, and arrive where I am striving? For it belongs not to the one who wills, nor to the one who runs, but to God who has mercy (Rom. IX, 16).

(Vers. 32.) I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart. The enlargement of the heart is love of the truth [Note: [Col. 0342D] In Augustine’s book: “the delight of righteousness.”]; and this comes about through God’s gift, so that he may be served not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness, when the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5). Therefore this man ran the way of God’s commandments because the Lord enlarged his heart.

## HE

(Vers. 33.) Establish for me, Lord, the law, the way of your justifications, and I shall seek it always. He had already said that, with his heart enlarged, he had run the way of God’s commandments. How then does he now ask that the law be established for him? Only because he speaks as one making progress, and knows that his progress is God’s gift; and, in order to progress more and more, he asks the one from whom he received what he has to increase it. Thus he has both run this way and desires to run it; he has sought and loves to seek, until joy is made perfect without danger of losing what he has gained. In order to grasp that joy, he seeks always.

(Vers. 34.) Give me understanding, and I shall search your law and keep it with all my heart. No one therefore penetrates the height and depth of the law unless he has received understanding. Since the fullness of the law is love (Rom. XIII, 10), and the one who understands the law is the one who carries out the works of its commandments, this man plainly asks that the charity by which God and neighbor are loved be multiplied in him, so that he may possess perfect knowledge of this twofold commandment, on which the whole law and the prophets depend (Matt. XXII, 40), and keep it with all his heart.

(Vers. 35.) Lead me in the path of your commandments, [Col. 0342A] for I have desired it. What he previously called the way of justifications, he now calls the path of commandments. For the way that leads to life is narrow (Matt. VII, 14); and although it is narrow, no one runs in it unless his heart has been enlarged (Sent. 19). But because he is still progressing and still running, he seeks divine help by which he may be led.

(Vers. 36.) Incline my heart toward your testimonies, and not toward avarice. Whoever asks that his heart be inclined toward something desires to desire it more fully and perfectly than he presently does. He was desiring it when he said, “Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it”; and he prays that he may desire it when he says, “Incline my heart toward your testimonies, and not toward avarice.” He therefore prays that he may progress in this very will, and that his heart may be inclined not toward avarice but toward God’s testimonies [Col. 0342B] 442—testimonies which convey and teach this: that God is to be worshiped freely. For if the heart is not inclined toward avarice, we worship God for God’s sake alone, so that the worship of God itself may be the reward. Whoever worships God in order to obtain something other than God himself does not love the one whom he worships, because he desires not God himself but something else (Sent. 20).

(Vers. 37.) Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way. “Turn away,” he says, “my eyes”—not my bodily eyes, whose gaze sees many vanities even unwillingly—but the eyes of my heart, lest they be fixed on vanity, lest they seek human glory, and lest, when they desire some good, they do so not from love of the highest good itself but from love of present advantage and praise. Finally, let them not refer their righteousness more to themselves than to the Lord, nor glory in themselves more than in the Lord. Shuddering at this vanity, he rightly added, “Give me life in your way”—that is, in Christ, who is opposed to vanity and is not only the way but also the life and the truth (John XIV, 6).

(Vers. 38.) Establish your word for your servant in your fear. God’s word becomes stable in our heart when what that word commands is done, and it is torn away when the contrary deed is performed. God’s servant therefore asks that persevering obedience be confirmed in him, so that no impulse of evil action may move him from his steadfastness. This is possessed only through the Spirit and through chaste fear—the fear by which care is taken not to offend love, not the fear by which impiety dreads condemnation.

(Vers. 39.) Take away my reproach, which I have suspected, for your judgments are pleasing. To judge rashly concerning the hidden things of another’s heart is a sin, and to censure someone whose works appear only good on the basis of suspicion is a sin (Sent. 21). This reproach, this fault of suspicion, the man who wishes to be perfect desires to have taken away from him. For God alone is the just examiner of things unknown to human beings, and his judgments are pleasing because they are true.

(Vers. 40.) Behold, I have desired your commandments; give me life in your righteousness. “You made me,” he says, “desirous of your commandments; make me effective as well. Help me to do what you commend; yourself grant what you command. For in myself I had the means by which I might die, but I do not find in myself the means by which I might live, except in you, who have placed all righteousness for your human being in love of you and of neighbor.”

## VAU

(Vers. 41.) Let your mercy come upon me, Lord, your salvation according to your word. What does he ask except that, through God’s mercy, he may do the commandments that he desires, which God commanded [Note: [Col. 0343D] In Augustine: “which he commanded”; the printed editions have “which you commanded.”]? And what is mercy except Christ? And according to what word except according to the word of promise, by which things that did not exist were called as though they existed (Rom. IV, 17)? For those to whom the promise was made were themselves also promised, so that the whole body of Christ may say, “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 10).

[Col. 0343B] (Vers. 42.) And I shall answer those who reproach me with a word, because I have hoped in your words. It is ambiguous whether the sense is “a word for those who reproach me” or “I shall answer with a word”; but in either case it signifies Christ [Note: [Col. 0343D] In Augustine: “it signifies Christ”; our printed editions have: “Christ signifies.”]. For they reproach us with him who is crucified and is for them either a stumbling-block or folly (I Cor. I, 23), not knowing that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I, 14)—the Word who was in the beginning and was with God. But even if the reproachers themselves do not reproach the Word, because it is hidden from them and they do not recognize his divinity, while they despise the weakness displayed by him on the cross, nevertheless let us answer all who reproach us with the Word. For it is not enough to have Christ in the heart unless we confess with the mouth what we believe in the heart (Rom. X, 10). Yet this can finally be done only if the believer’s hope in God’s promises is firm.

(Vers. 43.) And do not take away from me the word of truth altogether; that is, do not let me be so disturbed beneath the scourge of persecution that the confession of truth is entirely taken away from me. For many who failed for a time by denying were later restored through repentance and recovered the palm they had lost. For I have hoped beyond hope in your judgments—that is, because your judgments, by which you correct and scourge me, do not merely take away my hope but increase it, since you correct the one whom you love and scourge every child whom you receive (Heb. XII, 6). Therefore you often permit the one who seemed strong in his own eyes to become weak, so that presumption may be removed and the virtue of perseverance restored through your assistance.

(Vers. 44.) And I shall keep your law always, for ever and ever. Lest the word “always” be understood to refer merely to the whole duration of this life, he added, “for ever and ever.” The law that he desires to keep perpetually is to be understood as love, because it is the fullness of the law (Rom. XIII, 10), and when the other commandments cease, it alone remains forever.

(Vers. 45–48.) And I walked in the breadth, because I sought your commandments. And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame. And I meditated [Col. 0344A] on your commandments, which I loved greatly. And I lifted my hands toward your commandments, which I loved, and I was exercised in your justifications.

The preceding verses contained a prayer in which the help of grace was requested. These verses, however, contain a narrative showing 444 what the grace requested accomplished—as though he were saying: “When I prayed these things, you heard me, and I walked in the breadth,” that is, I walked in love, which has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5). This is the Spirit in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Gal. IV, 6); and therefore it is by this Spirit that he sought God’s commandments. Once received, the Spirit also brings it about that he is sought by asking, seeking, and knocking, so that he may be received more abundantly. Strengthened, therefore, by this Spirit of love, he was not put to shame before kings; he exercised his thought in God’s commandments and loved those commandments greatly. He lifted his hands not toward earthly works but toward heavenly things, and was exercised in God’s justifications.

## ZAIN

(Vers. 49, 50.) Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope; this has consoled me in my humiliation, because your word gave me life. When God is told, “Remember,” the desire of the one praying is expressed—his desire to hasten the fulfillment of the promise; God is not admonished as though the matter had slipped from his memory. “Remember,” he says, “your word to your servant,” that is, fulfill your promise; “in which you gave me hope,” that is, in which you made me hope. “This has consoled me in my humiliation”: namely, this hope of mine has consoled me, the hope given to the humble, as Scripture says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6). “Because your word gave me life”: because it made me hope in you and not fail in tribulation.

(Vers. 51.) The proud acted very unjustly against me; yet I did not turn aside from your law. By the proud he wished persecutors of the humble to be understood—that is, impious persecutors of the godly. Therefore he added, “Yet I did not turn aside from your law,” because persecution compelled him to turn aside from it.

(Vers. 52.) I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord, and I was consoled. “From of old,” he says, “from the time when the human race began, I remembered your judgments” (Ps. XXIV, 10). And because I proved that all your ways are mercy and truth, I received consolation in the assistance of your grace; and even through the vessels of wrath I understood the riches of your glory in the vessels of mercy (Rom. IX, 22–23).

(Vers. 53, 54.) Weariness seized me because of sinners who abandon your law. Your justifications were songs for me in the place of my sojourning. Although he suffered weariness because of the sinners among whom the pilgrimage of this present life detained him, God’s justifications were nevertheless songs for him, because grace consoled him in his pilgrimage.

[Col. 0345A] (Vers. 55.) I remembered your name in the night, Lord, and I kept your law. 445 “Night is [Note: [Col. 0345D] Thus all the Prosperian editions. Since Augustine reads, “Night is that humility where the misery of mortality is found,” we may reasonably suspect that the reading should be “Night is in the misery of mortality,” rather than “Night is forever,” which all the printed editions prefer.] forever”; for the night of mortality is found in the proud who act unjustly; night is found in weariness caused by sinners who abandon God’s law; and finally night is found in this place of pilgrimage, until the Lord comes and brings to light the hidden things of darkness (I Cor. IV, 5). In this night, therefore, a person ought to remember the name of the Lord, so that he may keep his law and refer this very act to the glory of God, since “our help is in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXXIII, 8).

(Vers. 56.) This happened to me because I sought your justifications. Your righteousness, certainly, by which you justify the ungodly (Rom. IV, 5)—not my righteousness, which does not make a person godly but proud. What, then, is the “this” of which he says, “This happened to me”? It is not to be understood as the Law, which Greek expresses with a masculine gender; it is better understood of the night, since he had said above, “I remembered your name in the night.” The night happened to me—that is, so that it might benefit me. For this very humility in this place of pilgrimage, rightly understood as night, benefits those who are profitably exercised in it, so that they may learn not to be proud, on account of which evil humanity was driven into this night.

## HETH

(Vers. 57.) My portion, Lord, I said, is to keep your law. [Note: [Col. 0345D] Understand this by supplying the words found in Augustine: “What does ‘My portion, Lord, I said, is to keep your law’ mean, except that …?”] Unless the Lord is to be each person’s portion when that person keeps his law. But because this does not happen without God’s help, he shows what must be obtained by adding:

(Vers. 58.) I entreated your face with all my heart; have mercy on me according to your word. What he obtained through this prayer, and to what progress he attained, he next shows by saying:

(Vers. 59.) I considered my ways, and I turned my feet toward your testimonies. “I turned,” he says, “my feet away from the ways that displeased me, so that they might go toward your testimonies and have their way there.” But where this text reads, “I turned my feet,” some copies read, “You turned my feet,” so that the matter may be attributed more directly to God’s grace. Whether this or that is the reading, however, there can be no doubt that it is a divine gift, both when we think rightly and when we turn our feet back from error [Note: [Col. 0345D] Louvain, Douai, and Cologne: “and when we think rightly, and our feet …”; Lyon: “when we think rightly.” Likewise, in Sent. 22, where we read *recta cogitamus* (“we think rightly”) instead of *recte* (“rightly”).]. Whenever we do good things, God works in us and with us so that we may act (Sent. 22 and canon 9 of the Second Council of Orange).

(Vers. 60.) I am prepared and have not been disturbed, so that I may keep your commandments. He humbly confesses that, through grace, he has been made steadfast for keeping the commandments.

[Col. 0346A] 446 (Vers. 61.) The ropes of sinners have entangled me, but I have not forgotten your law. The word *peccatorum* (“of sinners”) is derived not from what sins are but from what sinners are. The ropes of sinners are therefore the impediments of enemies, whether spiritual or carnal, who try to entangle the saints—those contending for God’s law even to the point of bloodshed—in various difficulties, by which they sought to drag them back from steadfast endurance as with ropes and cords. But if they entangle the body, they do not entangle the spirit, in which this man has not forgotten God’s law, because “the word of God is not bound” (I Tim. II, 5).

(Vers. 62.) At midnight I rose to confess you, because of the judgments of your righteousness. Midnight is profound tribulation, because he was not afflicted in such a way that he was unable to rise. He rose, however, to confess to God that by his just judgment he had given sinners power to persecute God’s saints—saints whom God’s grace helps so that such exercises may make them more radiant (Sent. 23).

(Vers. 63.) I am a companion of all those who fear you and keep your commandments. This voice is properly to be understood as that of the Head himself. We would not become participants in Christ’s divinity unless he himself became a participant in our mortality. Through this participation, his grace is supplied to us, so that we may fear God chastely and keep his commandments. For this reason the God of human beings, the immortal God of mortals, assumed human nature and, by making it participate in his own, caused the grain to fall [Note: [Col. 0346D] Augustine: “into the earth,” in both scriptural texts.] into the earth (John XII, 24–25), so that, once dead, it might produce much fruit.

(Vers. 64.) Your mercy, Lord, fills the earth. This is so, certainly, in that the ungodly person is justified. To advance in knowledge of this ineffable grace, he adds: “And teach me your justifications.”

## TETH

(Vers. 65.) You have dealt graciously with your servant, Lord, according to your word. “You have caused me,” he says, “Lord, to take delight in the good”—which is certainly your great gift. “According to your word,” that is, according to your promise, so that the promise may be firm for all the offspring (Rom. IV, 16).

(Vers. 65.) Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed in your commandments. He asks that these things be increased in him, [Col. 0346D] and [Note: [Col. 0346D] Augustine has “and perfected”; for since he had already said, “You have dealt graciously with your servant,” how can he say, “Teach me goodness,” except that he wishes God’s grace to become increasingly known to him through the sweetness of goodness?] that God’s grace may perfect them in him more and more, in every sweetness of goodness. God teaches goodness by inspiring love; he teaches discipline by regulating tribulation; he teaches knowledge by imparting understanding. “Because I have believed in your commandments”: that is, I have believed that you commanded them, you who grant that they may be done—not a human being, who, although he can make the commandment known, cannot bestow the gift of obedience [Note: [Col. 0347D] A comma is placed here. In the printed editions it was marked after the word “obedience”; we believe that the altered punctuation gives the clearer sense. Augustine says: “For if a human being commanded these things to me outwardly, would he also help me inwardly to do what he commanded?” Thus the gift of obedience is meant, not the commandment of obedience, which was indicated by the other punctuation.]. Teach discipline by teaching patience; teach knowledge by illuminating understanding, because I believed that you commanded these things, you who are God and who grant to a human being [Note: [Col. 0347D] Augustine: “from which you may make him do what you command.”] the means to do what you command.

(Vers. 67.) Before I was humbled, I transgressed; therefore I kept your word. “Because of the first transgression,” he says, “I was humbled; and lest I should again be humbled, I kept your word.” Thus, through your grace, experiencing punishment proved beneficial, so that I might acquire obedience.

(Vers. 68.) You are good, Lord, and in your goodness teach me your justifications. He truly wishes to do God’s justifications when he wishes to learn them in God’s goodness.

[Col. 0347B] (Vers. 69.) The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me. That is, of those for whom it did not prove beneficial that human nature was humbled after it had transgressed. But I shall search your commandments with all my heart. “However great the iniquity may be,” he says, “love will not grow cold in me” (Matt. XXIV, 12). For this reason I search your commandments as one who loves them, so that by doing them more perfectly I may know them.

(Vers. 70.) Their heart is congealed like milk, but I have meditated on your law. “The heart,” he says, “of the proud has been hardened; but through meditation on your law I have learned that you resist the proud and give grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

(Vers. 71.) It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your justifications. You turned punishment into discipline for me and humiliation into instruction, because I desire to know your justifications in such a way that I may do them. For there is no true knowledge of the good unless it is known in order to be practiced (Sent. 24).

(Vers. 72.) The law of your mouth is good for me, above thousands of gold and silver. This is so that love may love God’s law more than greed loves thousands of pieces of gold and silver.

## IOD

(Vers. 73.) Your hands made me and fashioned me. The hands of the Lord are God’s power, which accomplishes the works of his will, so that we do not imagine anything bodily about God by referring to “hands.” 448 If the plural number causes difficulty, let God’s hands be understood as power and wisdom; both are the one Christ (I Cor. I, 24), who is also called the arm of the Lord (Isa. V, 1). Finally, let God’s hands be understood as the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is also the co-worker of the Father and the Son—provided that no bodily form is perceived in the unchangeable nature of the Godhead (I Cor. [Col. 0348A] XII, 11). What he therefore says, “Your hands made me and fashioned me,” or “formed me,” may appropriately be distinguished so that “made” refers to the soul, while “fashioned” refers to the body, although these expressions are often found used indifferently. This work of God preceded not only the creation of the first human being, in whom all were created according to the principle of generation, but is also completed in the daily creation of each individual human being. For if that operative power of God were to withdraw from this work, everything would perish.

(Ibid.) Give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments. Was human nature created in such a way that it lacks understanding? What, then, does he ask to be given, when he has received it, except that the rational faculty itself, corrupted at the beginning through the fault of sin, must be restored by the gift of grace [Note: [Col. 0348D] The Lyon and Louvain editions have *formandum est* (“must be formed”); Douai and Cologne have *reformandum est* (“must be reformed”). The latter seems closer to Augustine: “Because you formed him, reform him,” so that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in the body of Christ: “Be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Rom. XII, 2), leading into Prosper’s following words.]? For what remains to nature is not sufficient unless it receives from its restorer what it lost. The Lord Jesus therefore, in this psalm, through the prophet, asked that understanding be given, as though to himself, to his body, which is the Church (Eph. V, 23). With him the life of his body—that is, of his people—is hidden in God (Col. III, 3); and he himself suffers need in that same body of his, through what is necessary for his members.

(Vers. 74.) Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your words. The present life of the saints is one of fear and labor, but they possess hope of eternal joy and gladness. Since the Church still fears and does not yet see herself in that kingdom where she will rejoice securely, she is the one who will be seen, because amid present temptations she does not cease to hope in God’s promises.

(Vers. 75, 76.) I know, Lord, that your judgments are righteous, and that in your truth you have humbled me. Let your mercy come, that it may console me, according to your word to your servant. Although the heavy yoke of the sons of Adam lies upon the human creature and weighs it down (Ecclus. XL, 1), I have nevertheless learned that your judgments are righteous and that humanity has been humbled according to truth. Let your mercy therefore come, according to your promise, so that mortal life may receive consolation from present gifts and patiently await the future goods of eternity.

449 (Vers. 77.) Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live. Then I shall truly live, when I no longer fear that I may die. For this is true life, which is spoken of without any qualification, as though living there meant nothing other than living without end and without misery. Because your law is my meditation. This meditation would not reach eternal life unless it were in the faith that works through love (Gal. V, 6). Therefore the person who labors to retain God’s law in memory but does not fulfill it in action does not meditate on God’s law profitably [Note: [Col. 0349D] Lyon has *ut actio teneat* (“so that action may retain”), perhaps a reading of *aut lectione teneat* (“or may retain through reading”). Louvain, Douai, and Cologne note it in the margin as though it were found, or could be read, in place of the following word *actione* (“in action”). It may perhaps better correspond to the first part, so that the sense would be “so that he may retain it through reading,” instead of “retain it in memory,” as those codices have it, in conformity with Augustine, where he says that he had entrusted the whole law to memory.].

(Vers. 78.) Let the proud be put to shame, because they have acted unjustly against me with iniquity; but I shall be exercised in your commandments. Although the proud rage and work iniquity against the saints, the love of the godly nevertheless does not grow cold, nor does it cease from exercising itself in God’s commandments.

(Vers. 79.) Let those who fear you and who know your testimonies turn toward me. No human being can say this except the one who, although he is the God of the universe, took human nature upon himself. Those who fear the Lord and recognize that God’s testimonies, foretold about him by the prophets so long beforehand, have been fulfilled will turn toward him.

[Col. 0349B] (Vers. 80.) Let my heart be blameless in your justifications, so that I may not be put to shame. He returns to the voice of the body—that is, of his members—whose heart is made blameless through the Head of the body itself, that is, through the grace of God, in the bath of regeneration [Note: [Col. 0349D] It might perhaps better be read “in the bath of regeneration,” as Augustine has in this same place: “through the bath of regeneration.” For below Prosper himself says, “regeneration having been granted to us.”], where all past sins have been washed away (Gal. V, 17); through the help of the spirit, by which we desire against the flesh, lest we be overcome by its desire; and through the effect of the Lord’s Prayer [Note: [Col. 0350D] Augustine’s work has “through the effect of the Lord’s Prayer.”], in which we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 12). Thus, with regeneration granted to us and prayer poured forth, our heart is made blameless, so that we may not be put to shame. For this too belongs to God’s justifications, when among his other commandments he enjoins, “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI, 37–38).

## CAPH

[Col. 0349C]

(Vers. 81.) My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have always hoped in your word [Note: [Col. 0350D] Our editions note *supersperavi* (“I have hoped beyond hope”) in the margin as a variant reading, the form that Saint Prosper uses below and that is found in our Vulgate. Augustine says that the Greek also has this word, ἐπήλπισα (*epēlpisa*, “I hoped beyond hope”); some of our translators preferred to render it *supersperavi*, because it undoubtedly expresses more than can be said by the simple verb.]. He does not say, “My soul has failed in your salvation,” but, “My soul has failed for your salvation”—that is, toward your salvation. This is therefore a good kind of failing, for it indicates desire for a good not yet attained but ardently coveted; with this desire all the saints of every age have been inflamed. For just as there have never been lacking those who desired the coming of Christ’s incarnation, so after he ascended into heaven there are not lacking those who long for his manifestation, when he will come to judge the living and the dead. “My soul has therefore failed for your salvation, and I have hoped beyond hope in your word.” For this hope in your promise has caused me both ardently to desire what I do not yet see and patiently to await it.

(Vers. 82.) My eyes have failed for your word, saying, “When will you console me?” In the inner eyes, the same failure is the movement of desire reaching toward God’s words—that is, his promises—whose delays in bringing the hoped-for consolations are long. For even what is brief to the one who comes to help seems long to the one who desires it.

(Vers. 83.) For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your justifications. By the wineskin he wishes the flesh of this death to be understood; by the frost, the heavenly benefit by which carnal desires are restrained, as though numbed by cold. From this it comes about that God’s justifications do not slip from memory.

(Vers. 84.) How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment on those who persecute me? This is also the voice of the martyrs in the Apocalypse (Rev. VI, 10), and the disciples ask the Lord that the day of the end be indicated to them (Matt. XXIV, 3) [Note: [Col. 0350D] Perhaps, “from the Lord.”]. But the former are commanded to exercise patience, while the latter are not shown the hidden determination. In these words of the psalm, therefore, this very inquiry of the Church is rightly understood as having been prophesied.

(Vers. 85.) The wicked have told me delightful tales, but not such as your law, Lord. He says that the wicked told him stories of empty opinions, composed with the pleasing artistry of eloquence [Note: [Col. 0350D] The Lyon edition has “delightful tales, composed with the artistry of eloquence.”]. But he found nothing useful in them, as he does in the law of the Lord, in which all truth is found.

(Vers. 86.) They persecuted me unjustly; help me. “I preferred,” he says, “the commandments of truth to stories of lies, and for this reason lovers of falsehood persecuted me unjustly. Help me, therefore, so that I may be able to contend for the truth until death.”

(Vers. 87.) They almost destroyed me on earth, but I did not abandon your commandments. The slaughter of the martyrs took place while they confessed and preached the truth, which, helped by you, I did not abandon.

(Vers. 88.) Give me life according to your mercy, and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth. The martyrs, helped and given life by God’s mercy, did not deny the truth, which is life; by dying for it, they conquered.

## LAMED

451 (Vers. 89.) Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven. The word remains in the angels who keep the eternal service without failing.

(Vers. 90.) From generation to generation is your truth; you founded the earth, and it remains. After the heavenly Jerusalem, he looked also upon its daughter, the Church, which dwells in this world, and said, “From generation [Col. 0350D] to generation is your truth.” By this repetition he either signified all generations, from none of which God’s truth was absent; or he wished two to be understood: one belonging to the Law and the Prophets, and the other belonging to the [Col. 0351A] Gospel, upon the eternal foundation, which is Christ (I Cor. III, 11). This earth, established upon such a foundation, remains and is not shaken “for ever and ever” (Ps. CIII, 5).

(Vers. 91.) By your ordinance the day endures, because all things serve you. “All things,” namely, those about which he was speaking and which pertain to the eternal day.

(Vers. 92.) Unless your law were my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation. This law is the law of faith, which works through love (Gal. V, 6). By remaining in meditation upon it, he earns the help of grace, so that he does not perish in the humiliation of tribulations.

(Vers. 93.) I will never forget your ordinances, because through them you have given me life. [Col. 0351B] Behold how it happened that he did not perish in his humiliation: through that by which he was justified, he was also given life.

(Vers. 94.) I am yours; save me, Lord, because I have sought your ordinances. I did not seek my own desires, by which I was my own; rather, I sought your ordinances, so that I might now be yours.

(Vers. 95.) Sinners waited for me in order to destroy me; I understood your testimonies.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] Duacensis and Cologne read, “Not this.” Lyon and Leuven are better: “Not here.”]

He was not here afraid of perishing through bodily death, which had to be endured for the sake of truth. Sinners therefore waited for him to consent to their evils; for then they would destroy him. But they did not prevail because he understood God’s testimonies—that is, because, confessing the truth, even if he should die, he would not perish.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] This is how the Lyon edition, the oldest of the others, reads, and with a better sense than the later editions: *oporteret* (“it would be necessary”). Augustine’s words express it as follows: “Because, even if they killed me, while I did not consent to them and confessed your martyrdoms, I would not perish.”]

(Vers. 96.) I have seen the end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad. Whoever understood the testimonies [Col. 0351C] and knew that he had to contend for the truth even unto death did not fail to recognize what blessed end awaited every outcome of the godly. By God’s exceedingly broad commandment, love is to be understood: through it God and one’s neighbor are commanded to be loved. What could be broader than this, since the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon it (Matt. XXII, 40)?

MEM.

(Vers. 97.) How I have loved your law, Lord! It is my meditation all day long. 452 “Thus,” he says, “I have loved the law of faith, which works through love (Gal. V, 6), so that my meditation is all day long—that is, at all times.”

(Vers. 98.) You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandment, because it is mine for ever. “The end of the Law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4), so that he may be justified freely by his grace (Rom. [Col. 0351D] III, 24); the enemies of this man did not believe in him. But this man, who did not seek his own righteousness but that which comes from God, and whom God made wiser than his enemies, found this commandment to be his for ever, because he did not desire temporal rewards in exchange for it. For the reward of the one who loves is the beloved himself.

(Vers. 99.) I have understood more than all those who teach me. He understood more than all teachers, because the Father taught him (John VI). This is difficult to understand as spoken in the person of the Word, unless one is somehow able to grasp that the Son was taught by the [Col. 0352A] Father precisely in being begotten. For from the one from whom he has his being, from that same one he also has his being taught. But when understood in the person of the man in whom he assumed the form of a servant, it is easier to understand that he learned from the Father what he said. In this form people thought that a boy of greater age needed to be taught (Luke II, 42, etc.). Yet the one whom the Father taught possessed a deeper understanding than those who taught. Because your testimonies are my meditation. He therefore understood more than all who taught him because he meditated upon God’s testimonies, which had been foretold concerning him and which he himself knew more fully and fulfilled.

(Vers. 100.) I have understood more than the elders, because I sought your commandments. Your commandments, not the commandments of men (I Tim. I, 7); your commandments, not the commandments of the elders, who, wishing to be teachers of the Law, understand neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions.

[Col. 0352B] (Vers. 101.) I restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your words. This is the voice of the members, not of the Head. For the Savior himself, the body’s Savior, was not assailed by any lusts, so that he would have needed to restrain his feet from the way of wicked desire. He therefore restrains our movements and our appetites, so that we are not drawn into crooked paths by harmful desires.

(Vers. 102.) I did not turn aside from your judgments, because you established your law for me. “I steadfastly believed your judgments,” he says, “because you placed your law in my heart, writing it as with your finger, so that I might love it as a son with chaste fear, rather than fear it as a slave without love.”

(Vers. 103.) How sweet your sayings are to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth. This is that sweetness [Col. 0352C] which the Lord grants, so that our earth may yield its fruit (Ps. LXXXIV, 13), and so that we may do what is good truly well—that is, not from fear of a carnal evil, but from delight in a spiritual good.

453 (Vers. 104.) From your commandments I have gained understanding. This is the voice of Christ’s spiritual members. For the body of Christ rightly says this in those who keep the commandments, because, through that very keeping of the commandments, a richer teaching of wisdom is granted to them. Therefore I hated every way of iniquity. Love of righteousness must hate all iniquity when it increases and is inflamed; and for this reason it obeys God and gains understanding in his commandments.

NUN.

(Vers. 105.) Your word is a lamp for my feet, Lord, and a light for my paths. Here “word” must be understood not as that which is equal to the Begetter and which is the true light illuminating every human being (John I, 8), but as the word that came to the prophets or was preached through the apostles—the word, namely, of Christ, concerning which it is written, “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. X, 17). For the apostle Peter also compared the prophetic word to a lamp, saying, “We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend [Col. 0353A] as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (II Pet. I, 19). What he says here, therefore—“Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths”—is the word contained in all the Holy Scriptures. It is not the Word who is deity, but the word of the deity.

(Vers. 106.) I swore and resolved to keep all the judgments of your righteousness. He called this a “swearing,” namely, what he resolved apart from an oath, because the mind ought to be so firmly fixed on keeping the judgments of God’s righteousness that what he resolved should be virtually an oath.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Augustine has *iuramentum* (“an oath”); our editions have *iuramento* (“by an oath”).]

[Note: [Col. 0353D] We have corrected this from Augustine, as the sense of the passage requires it; our editions, doubtless through scribal error, had *pro ratione* (“instead of reason”), whereas the reading should be *pro iuratione* (“instead of an oath”).]

(Vers. 107.) I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word. Because he swore and resolved to keep the judgments of God’s righteousness, he suffered the greatest persecution. And, lest he fail in so great a humiliation, he asks to be given life according to the word [Col. 0353B] of promise, because in the night of tribulations the promise itself is a lamp for the feet and a light for the paths.

(Vers. 108.) Make acceptable, Lord, the voluntary offerings of my mouth, and teach me your judgments. The voluntary offerings of the mouth which he asks to be approved are sacrifices of praise, offered in a confession of love, not from fear of necessity. He desires to be taught God’s judgments, not because he is ignorant of them, but so that he may advance.

454 (Vers. 109.) My soul is always in your hands, and I have not forgotten your law.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] This is how the older editions after Augustine read. Augustine observes: “Some manuscripts have ‘in my hands,’ but more have ‘in yours’; and this is certainly clear. For the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, in whose hand both we and our words are. Later editions changed it to ‘in my hands.’ But they are refuted by the exposition of the following verse.”]

It is said in this way, as though memory, for not forgetting God’s law, were assisted by being in his hands.

(Vers. 110.) Sinners set a snare for me, but I did not stray from your commandments. How could this be, unless his soul [Col. 0353C] were always in God’s hands?

(Vers. 111.) I acquired your testimonies as an inheritance for ever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] The old Prosperian editions all read this way; the more recent ones had written *haereditate* (“as an inheritance”). Perhaps they did so because this is how it is sung daily from our Vulgate, rather than because the word *haereditate* pleased Augustine more in this passage. Some have interpreted it as *haereditari* (“to be inherited”). The complete sense is therefore better conveyed by either of two expressions: “I possessed as an inheritance” or “I acquired as an inheritance”—not “an inheritance,” but “as an inheritance.”]

“You granted me,” he says, “the desire to be your witness; and that I should not fear dying for the truth is a matter of your inheritance and your grace. This gift is mine for ever, because it contains no temporal glory. Therefore, although I have been afflicted in body, I have nevertheless rejoiced in heart.”

(Vers. 112.) I inclined my heart to do your ordinances for ever, because of the reward. The one who says, “I inclined my heart,” had already said, “Incline my heart to your testimonies” (above, v. 36), so that we may understand this to be at once a divine gift and an act of one’s own will. Let him do this because of the reward, so that, since he pursues God’s ordinances out of [Col. 0354A] love, he may deserve to possess for ever what he loves.

SAMECH.

(Vers. 113.) I hated the unrighteous and loved your law. Whoever loves God’s law shows that, in unrighteous people, he hates what is contrary to the law, not the people themselves (Sent. 25).

(Vers. 114.) You are my helper and my protector, and I have hoped exceedingly in your word. “Helper” and “protector” for escaping evils.

(Vers. 115.) Depart from me, wicked ones, and I will search out the commandments of my God. No one can search out God’s commandments except with a quiet mind. Therefore, so that this devotion may be exercised, the activities of the wicked must be driven away.

[Note: [Col. 0354D] In Augustine’s Sentences the wording is first “so that the religious devotion may be exercised,” and then “the quarrels of the wicked must be driven away.” For Augustine says here that the wicked provoke us to perform the commandments, but draw us away from searching them out—not only when they persecute us or wish to quarrel with us, but also when they obey and honor us, and so forth.]

(Vers. 116.) Receive me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not let me be put to shame in my hope.

[Col. 0354B] Whoever hopes attentively asks to be received more and more by the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0354D] Augustine says: “He asks to be received more and more and to be led to that for which he endures so many hardships; for he trusts that he will live there more truly than in these dreams of human affairs.”]

so that only then, when he has attained those things, he may know that he will live; for present things are more like death than life.

(Vers. 117.) Help me, and I shall be saved, and I will meditate on your ordinances always. “So that I may live, so that I may not be put to shame, so that I may always be engaged in your ordinances: help me,” he says, “and I shall be saved,” because one does not come to your promises without your help.

455 (Vers. 118.) You have brought to nothing all who depart from your ordinances, because their thought is unjust. All works, whether good or evil, proceed from thought. Therefore whoever is unrighteous in heart is brought to nothing when he departs from God’s ordinances through an unjust thought.

[Col. 0354C] (Vers. 119.) I have considered all the sinners of the earth transgressors; therefore I loved your testimonies. Since no one can be called a transgressor except one who violates the commandments of the Law (Rom. IV, 15), the question arises how all the sinners of the earth should be considered transgressors, when it is clear that many of them are sinners without the Law. It is found that all the nations except the people of Israel were outside the Law, but that every human being is held under the law of nature, so that one who does not wish to suffer something knows that he ought not to do it to another.

Although, therefore, the one who is a transgressor not only of the natural law but also of the divine law is much more truly a transgressor, nevertheless no one is a sinner except through transgression, because even the one whom the letter does not condemn is accused by conscience. Children too are rightly counted among these, on account of the bonds of original [Col. 0355A] sin. For they too are shown to belong to that transgression, in the likeness of the transgressor Adam (Rom. V, 14), which was first committed in paradise (Gen. III, 6).

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Augustine has *praevaricationis* (“of transgression”); all our editions have *praevaricatoris* (“of the transgressor”).]

Since, therefore, all had sinned and lacked the glory of God (Rom. III, 23), and salvation was found in no one’s own righteousness, there remained the justification of faith, given by God through the grace of the Savior, to provide assistance. Hence the Apostle says, “Through the Law comes knowledge of sin”—knowledge, not abolition. “But now,” he says, “the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, testified to by the Law and the Prophets” (ibid., 20–21). Rightly, therefore, he added, “Therefore I loved your testimonies,” as though he were saying: “Since the Law—whether given in paradise, implanted naturally, or promulgated in writing—made all the sinners of the earth transgressors, therefore I loved your testimonies [Col. 0355B] that are in your Law concerning your grace.”

(Vers. 120.) Pierce my flesh with nails because of your fear. What does he wish to be understood by these words except what the Apostle says: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14); and again, “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 19)?

(Ibid.) For I feared your judgments. If he has already feared, or was fearing, why did he still pray that God would crucify his flesh because of his fear, unless he wished a fear to be added to him sufficient to mortify carnal desires and affections? It may also be understood in another way: “Pierce my flesh with nails because of your fear, for I feared your judgments.” That is: by your chaste fear, which [Col. 0355C] endures for ever and ever, may carnal desires be restrained in me, desires from which fear of your judgments has held me back.

Since, therefore, I desire to do your will and live rightly, not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness, give me this chaste and free fear, to seek which that tutor, the Law, led me as a child, by which I feared your judgments.

HAIN.

(Vers. 121.) I have practiced judgment and righteousness; do not hand me over to those who harm me. Whoever, through chaste fear of God, has his flesh crucified and, uncorrupted by any carnal enticement, practices judgment and performs the work of righteousness ought to pray not to be handed over to his adversaries—that is, lest, through fear of suffering evils, he yield to his persecutors and commit evils.

From the one from whom he receives victory, so that he is not overcome by the pleasure of desire, he also [Col. 0355D] receives the strength of endurance, so that he is not broken by pain. For of the one of whom it is said, “The Lord will give sweetness” (Ps. LXXXIV, 13), it is also said, “From him comes my endurance” (Ps. LXI, 6).

(Vers. 122.) Receive your servant for good, so that [Col. 0356A] the proud may not slander me. That is: lest they drive me into evil, receive me for good. They slander in pride; defend me in humility, so that the slanders of the proud may not harm me.

(Vers. 123.) My eyes have failed in longing for your salvation and for the word of your righteousness. He says that the eyes of his heart have failed in longing for the word of God’s righteousness—that is, for the promise of Christ—not because the attention of his desiring mind was defeated and collapsed, but because it passed over entirely, with all the ardor of the mind, into expectation of God’s grace. Christ is the righteousness of God, who makes [Col. 0356B] people righteous (I Cor. I, 30).
