(Vers. 124.) Deal with your servant according to your mercy. Certainly not according to my righteousness. Teach me your ordinances. Without doubt, those by which he makes the righteous righteous,

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Augustine has the better reading, “not they themselves,” whereas our editions have “not he himself.”]

not by which they make themselves so.

(Vers. 125.) I am your servant. For things did not go well for me when I wished to be my own master, not your servant. Give me understanding, so that I may learn your testimonies. No one is so intelligent, no one so learned, that he does not need this petition. For no increase of these gifts is ever sufficient in such a way that there does not always remain something desired to be understood and known (Sent. 27).

(Vers. 126.) It is time to act, Lord; the proud have scattered your law.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] The word “the proud,” which is not added in Augustine, appears to have slipped into the text of Scripture from the exposition of the verse itself. We have therefore printed it in a different type, especially since a little below it is not found in Prosper, where this part of the same verse is repeated.]

457 What does “They have scattered your law” mean except that, through the wickedness of transgression, they did not preserve its integrity? Once the Law had been scattered, therefore, it was time for mercy to be sent through the only-begotten Son of God. “The Law came in besides,” [Col. 0356C] so that the trespass might abound (Rom. V, 20); through that trespass the Law was scattered. And at the appointed time Christ came, so that where the trespass abounded, grace might abound still more (ibid.).

(Vers. 127.) Therefore I loved your commandments more than gold and topaz. Grace accomplishes this: that God’s commandments are fulfilled through love, whereas they could not be fulfilled through fear. They are loved more than gold and topaz—that is, more than things regarded as precious on earth—when, in observing the commandments, no temporal reward is sought, but righteousness itself, because nothing is better than that good by which the human being himself is made good.

(Vers. 128.) Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments. Because I adhered in love to those commandments, which are right, so that I too might be right. I hated every way of iniquity. How could it happen that one who loves the right would not hate an unjust way?

[Note: [Col. 0356D] Our editions have this reading; Augustine has “the right [way],” namely, “the way.” If *rectum* (“the right”) is read, understand “commandment,” since above he said, “I adhered to those who are right”—that is, to the commandments.]

PE

(Vers. 129.) Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul searched them out. All God’s works are testimonies to his majesty and goodness, and there is none [Col. 0357A] that ought not to inspire astonishment and wonder. But the testimonies of his Law itself are many wonderful things, whose usefulness and righteousness lie deeply hidden when one asks why the Law was given, since it cannot give life and from it no flesh would be justified before God (Gal. III, 21; Rom. III, 20).

[Note: [Col. 0357D] We suspect that *multo mirabiliora* (“far more wonderful”) should be read instead of what all the editions contain, *multa mirabilia* (“many wonderful things”).]

Rightly, therefore, he searched out this depth, because he understood that through the difficulties of the Law God’s mercy brought this about: that those who could not fulfill the Law might turn to grace; [Note: [Col. 0357D] The Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions note in the margin that some read otherwise, *et divina ope* (“and by divine help”).] but by divine assistance might grasp what they could not attain by their own strength (Rom. III).

(Vers. 130.) The revelation of your words gives light and grants understanding to the simple. This simple person, by searching, understood what the Apostle Paul also understood: that the Law was given although it could not give life, because [Col. 0357B] “Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe” (Gal. III, 22). The revelation of this mystery therefore gives light and grants understanding to the simple. For this secret of grace is disclosed only to the humble and weak, who, fleeing to God’s help, confess that they cannot be justified by their own strength.

458 (Vers. 131.) I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Augustine reads *attraxi* (“I drew in”) and explains it as “he drew in what would enable him to act,” namely, the divine commandments. We therefore scarcely doubt that there is an error in the Prosperian editions, which read *abstraxi* (“I drew away”).]

He desired the divine commandments in order to do them. But the weak had no means by which to do mighty things, nor the simple by which to do great things. He opened his mouth, confessing that he could not do this by himself.

(Vers. 132.) Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name. That is, according to the judgment you exercised upon those who love [Col. 0357C] your name, because, in order that they might love you, you first loved them (I John IV, 19).

(Vers. 133.) Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me. What does he ask except that God, by helping, make it possible for the commandments that he imposes by ordering to be fulfilled?

[Note: [Col. 0357D] In Augustine: “unless that he make the commandments which God imposes, etc.”]

(Vers. 134.) Redeem me from the slanders of men, and I will keep your commandments. “Act,” he says, “by pouring in your Spirit, so that the terrors of men’s slanders do not overcome me and lead me away from your commandments to their evil deeds.”

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Augustine has “their evil deeds”; our editions have “evil deeds.”]

“If you redeem me in this way—by granting me steadfastness and patience amid the persecution of slanderers—I will keep your commandments.”

(Vers. 135.) Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your ordinances. “Make your [Col. 0357D] presence manifest,” he says, “by coming to my aid and helping me; and teach me your ordinances in such a way that learning them may mean doing them.”

(Vers. 136.) Streams of water flowed down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law. The descent [Col. 0358A] of the eyes through the outpouring of tears indicates the humility of the penitent. But why is the failure to keep the Law mourned in this way, unless so that grace might be fulfilled, which removes the sin of the one who confesses and assists the will of the believer?

TZADE.

(Vers. 137–138.) You are righteous, Lord, and your judgment is right. You commanded righteousness—your testimonies—and your truth exceedingly. The same penitential feeling continues, explaining why he ought to have wept so much: because, unless he condemned himself, he would rightly be punished. Great, therefore, is God’s righteousness in both respects, and right is his judgment, by which punishment is decreed for the sinner and justification is not denied to the penitent.

(Vers. 139.) Zeal for your house made me waste away, because my enemies forgot your words.

[Note: [Col. 0358D] Lyon, Leuven, and Douai read this way. Cologne, however, has “My zeal consumes me.” Augustine had read, “My zeal has consumed me,” and adds, “or, as other manuscripts have it, ‘your zeal.’” Some also have “the zeal of your house,” and not “has consumed me,” but “has eaten me up.” This appears to have been imported from another psalm, where it seems to me that it was thought necessary to correct the text: “The zeal of your house has eaten me up” (Ps. LXVIII, 18).]

This zeal is one of love, [Col. 0358B] not envy. Through holy emulation he wishes his enemies to be corrected, grieving and wasting away because they have forgotten God’s words.

459 (Vers. 140.) Your word is exceedingly refined, and your servant loved it. Loving the divine utterance, he burned with such love that he wished even his enemies to be kindled with love of God.

(Vers. 141.) I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your ordinances. Here the meaning of the two peoples is rightly understood: they were also struggling in Rebecca’s womb (Gen. XXV, 22–23), when it was said, not on the basis of works but of the one who calls, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Rom. VIII, 13). This younger one therefore calls himself despised; and for that reason he became greater, because God chose what is low-born and despised, and things that are not, [Col. 0358C] as though they were, so that he might bring to nothing the things that are (I Cor. I, 28)—that is, so that the proud might be destroyed and the humble justified.

(Vers. 142.) Your righteousness is righteousness for ever, and your law is truth. How could the Law not be truth, since through it comes knowledge of sin and it bears witness to God’s righteousness (Rom. III, 20–21)?

(Vers. 143.) Tribulation and distress found me, but your commandments are my meditation. The cruelty of enemies brings tribulation upon this younger one, but does not take away his love. His meditation is upon God’s commandments, from which he returns love to those who hate him.

(Vers. 144.) The righteousness of your testimonies is for ever; give me understanding and life. This younger one, who above understood more than the elders, asks for understanding in tribulation and distress, so that he may understand how contemptible is what can be taken away from him who, neglecting temporal things for the sake of God’s eternal righteousness, hopes for eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0358D] The Lyon edition has *quod et* (“which also”); Leuven, Douai, and Cologne, as in Augustine, have *quod ei* (“what can be taken away from him”).]

KOPH.

[Col. 0359A]

(Vers. 145.) I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, Lord. I will seek your ordinances. The cry of the heart is a silent sound of the voice, a great concentration of thought. With this he cried out with his whole heart and desired that this be granted to him by the Lord who hears him: that he might seek his ordinances, grasping them not only through knowledge but also practicing them in deed.

(Vers. 146.) I cried to you; save me, and I will keep your testimonies. The salvation of the soul brings it about that bodily life is despised for the sake of keeping God’s testimonies, if extreme temptation demands that one contend for the truth even unto death.

(Vers. 147.) I anticipated the deep night and cried out; I hoped in your words. The deep night is the middle of the night, a time [Col. 0359B] unsuited to the affairs conducted during the day. By it is signified a certain obstacle of the present age, which in comparison with the future age is called night, and during which God’s promises are delayed until the revelation of eternal light comes.

In this time of deep night, therefore, the one who vigilantly seeks God’s promises cries to the Lord and anticipates the time of recompense through his desire. This may also be referred to those times when the Church, through prophetic voices, was asking for the coming of Christ and hoping for the fulfillment of the promise that all nations would be blessed in the seed of Abraham (Gen. XII, 3; XXII, 18).

(Vers. 148.) My eyes anticipated the dawn, so that I might meditate on your sayings.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] These two words, “my eyes,” which are lacking in our editions, ought to be supplied. This is proved by their presence both in Augustine and in the text of Scripture; without them it is not clear to what the plural verb “they anticipated” refers.]

The dawn came for the Church when light arose for those who sat in darkness and in [Col. 0359C] the shadow of death (Isa. IX, 2). This dawn was provided by the hope of believers. And it meditated upon the sayings of God that had foretold this light in the Law and the Prophets.

(Vers. 149.) Hear my voice, Lord, according to your mercy, and according to your judgment give me life. First God, according to his mercy, removes punishment from sinners, and afterward, according to his judgment, gives life to the righteous. For it is not without reason that this order is expressed: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Ps. C, 1).

(Vers. 150.) Those who persecute me drew near iniquity, but they have gone far from your law.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Our Vulgate has *iniquitati* (“to iniquity”); Augustine, like the Prosperian editions, has *iniquitate* (“through iniquity”), and adds, “or, as some manuscripts have it, ‘wickedly.’”]

Those who persecute draw near when they proceed as far as tormenting or killing the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0360D] The editions have *pereunt* (“they perish”) in the text. Douai and Cologne have *perveniunt* (“they proceed”) in the margin. Since this is read in Augustine, and is also necessary to the sense, it should be preferred.]

[Col. 0359D] But the nearer they are to those whom they persecute, the farther they are from the law of righteousness.

(Vers. 151.) You are near, Lord, and all your ways are truth. Even in their tribulations, it is the customary confession of the saints to attribute to God the truth that they suffer them deservedly. But one may ask how this saying is to be understood, “All your ways are truth,” since another psalm says, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and [Col. 0360A] truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

If, therefore, we consider all human beings, some of whom are freed by mercy and others condemned by truth, all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. But if we look only upon the saints, these ways are not distinguished. For there mercy and truth are inseparable, and truth comes from mercy and mercy from truth, because the blessedness of the saints derives both from the gift of mercy and from the recompense of righteousness (Sent. 28).

(Vers. 152.) From the beginning I understood from your testimonies that you founded them for ever. What are these testimonies except those by which God testified that he would give an eternal kingdom to his children? The testimonies themselves are therefore founded for ever, because what he promised is eternal; and the foundation of the promise is Christ (I Cor. III, 11), in whom the testimonies of this hope [Col. 0360B] are true. He says that he understood them from the beginning because he speaks in the words of the Church, which arose from the beginning of the human race and was absent from no generation.

RESCH.

(Vers. 153.) See my humiliation and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law. This is the voice of the whole Church and of all the members of Christ’s body. Here, where the Lord is invoked to liberate the humble, we understand no law of God more suitably than that by which it is immovably established that everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled and everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted (Luke XIV, 11; XVIII, 14). The proud person is therefore entangled in evils so that he may be humbled; the humble person is rescued from evils so that he may be exalted.

(Vers. 154.) Judge my judgment and redeem me; [Col. 0360C] give me life because of your word. This is a repetition of the same sense. “Judge my judgment” means “See my humiliation,” and “Redeem me” means “Rescue me.” Nor does “because of your word” mean anything other than “because I have not forgotten your law.” To be given life as a humble person is the same as to be exalted, because the exaltation of the saints is eternal life.

(Vers. 155.) Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your ordinances. Salvation is far from the proud because they have not sought your grace, which alone justifies; and they wished to please themselves not in you for your sake, but in themselves for their own sake.

(Vers. 156.) Your mercies are many, Lord. “Even this,” he says, “that we seek your ordinances belongs to your mercies.” Give me life according to your judgment. For I know that your judgment [Col. 0360D] will not be upon me without mercy.

(Vers. 157.) Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies. This is the voice of the Church in its martyrs, who amid torments and multiplied punishments did not yield to their persecutors. Through their most glorious examples the whole world is illumined. Yet they attribute their victory not to themselves but to [Col. 0361A] God, saying in another psalm, “Unless the Lord had been with us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. CXXIII, 2).

(Vers. 158.) I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away.

[Note: [Col. 0361D] Saint Augustine read, “I saw the senseless.” But he observes that other manuscripts have, “I saw those who did not keep the covenant,” and more manuscripts have this reading.]

Who are those who did not keep the covenant except those who, unable to endure the tribulations of many persecutors, turned aside from God’s testimonies? “When I saw this,” he says, “I wasted away,” grieving that they had fallen from so great a glory. Because they did not keep your sayings.

462 This was not to keep the covenant: not to persevere, and to lose God’s promises.

[Note: [Col. 0361D] Perhaps: “not to keep.”]

(Vers. 159.) See that I loved your commandments. That is fruitful endurance which receives the savagery of persecutors through love of the commandments. Lord, give me life in your mercy. The one whose mercy obtained [Col. 0361B] the palm of victory asks in that same mercy also for life.

(Vers. 160.) The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your righteousness are eternal. The judgments of God’s righteousness are those by which eternal life is pronounced for the righteous and punishment for the wicked.

SCIN.

(Vers. 161.) Princes persecuted me without cause, but my heart was afraid of your words. Earthly kings persecuted Christ’s Church without cause, because they had no reason for persecution: Christians harmed them in nothing, and they could not force Christians to deny the truth. They therefore uttered threatening words and inflicted savage punishments. But your [Col. 0361C] words frightened me more: “Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do; but fear him who has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28). My heart was therefore afraid of these words; and, hoping for an eternal reward, I despised temporal punishment.

(Vers. 162.) I will rejoice over your sayings, like one who finds abundant spoils. Through those very words by which he was afraid, he conquered. For spoils are stripped from the defeated; and abundant spoils were captured when many of the guards themselves, admiring the martyrs’ endurance, believed in the one against whom they had raged.

(Vers. 163.) I hated injustice and abhorred it, but I loved your law. The law is the utterances of God, which he feared in such a way that he loved them; for it followed that he should love justice who hated wickedness. That fear, then, of God’s words, by which he was afraid, was not at variance with love, but feared being torn away from what he loved.

[Note: The printed editions have *velli* (“to be torn away”) in the simple form. The editions of Douai and Cologne had placed *avelli* (“to be dragged away”) in the margin. There is no doubt that this refers to the example Augustine had given: “thus a chaste wife both fears her husband, lest she be abandoned by him, and loves him, that she may enjoy him.”]

(Vers. 164.) Seven times a day I have praised you because of the judgments of your justice. By “seven times” he means “always.” For by this number all the days are reckoned and all times revolve. Thus the Church, overcome by no persecutions, continually praises, amid this day of tribulations, the author of her patience and perseverance; for, when the time had come for judgment to begin from the household of God (1 Peter 4:17), she gloried in all temptations and afflictions, not in weakness but in the crowns of the martyrs.

[Note: So all our printed editions read. Although they yield some meaning, we do not doubt that Augustine himself has the better reading: “She was not weakened, but glorified by the crowns of the martyrs.” It was not difficult for a scribe to change *infirmata* (“weakened”) into another word through the influence of *infirmitate* (“weakness”).]

463 (Vers. 165.) Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them. Is the law itself not a stumbling-block to those who love it? Or is there no stumbling-block of any kind for those who love it? Both statements are rightly understood. For whoever loves God’s law honors even what he does not understand in it, and does not doubt that something great and mysterious lies hidden in the depth which he cannot penetrate. Likewise, whoever loves God’s law, if he does not make it depend upon the changeable customs of human beings, suffers no stumbling-block; for even if people of good profession abandon their purpose, the justice of the law nevertheless endures.

(Vers. 166.) I awaited your salvation, Lord, and I loved your commandments. Before Christ’s Incarnation, all the saints always awaited the same redemption of his. But this prophecy may also apply to the person of those who, since grace was revealed and the Gospel has been preached, love Christ’s commandments and await his coming, so that when Christ appears, “our life, then we also may appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4).

(Vers. 167.) My soul kept your testimonies, and loved them greatly. God’s testimonies are kept when they are not denied. But because even being burned in flames for God’s testimonies is of no benefit without love (1 Corinthians 13:3), he therefore added, “and loved them greatly.”

(Vers. 168.) I kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you, Lord. Often, while God’s commandments are being kept, those who despise the same commandments become enemies, and then it is necessary to stand courageously for God’s testimonies. He says that he did this here because all his ways were before the Lord—as though he were saying: “If you had turned your face away from me, Lord, I would have been troubled, and I would have kept neither your commandments nor your testimonies. But now I have kept both because the light of your presence directed my ways.”

TAU.

(Vers. 169.) Let my prayer draw near before you, Lord; according to your word, give me understanding. The prayer that is received draws near, for “the Lord is near to those who are brokenhearted” (Psalm 33:19); and he gives understanding according to his promise, when he says, “I will give you understanding” (Psalm 31:8).

(Vers. 170.) Let my supplication enter before you, Lord; according to your word, deliver me. He repeated, in a way, what he had asked. For the one who also receives understanding is delivered, lest, through failing to understand, he be overthrown.

(Vers. 171.) My lips will pour forth a hymn when you teach me your statutes. “I will praise the Lord,” he says, “and glory in you when you teach me that doctrine of yours by which you assist me to do what you command.”

(Vers. 172.) My tongue has proclaimed your words, because all your commandments are justice.

[Note: In Augustine: “judgments.”]

He promises that he will become a preacher of God’s words; for although God gives the increase, the ministers of the word must nevertheless both plant and water (1 Corinthians 3:7).

(Vers. 173.) Let your hand come to save me, because I have chosen your commandments. In order that I might proclaim your words, I chose your commandments, and love of the truth made me steadfast. Let your hand, then, come to save me from the hand of the stranger—not in such a way that the persecutor will not destroy the flesh, but in such a way that torments will not overcome the soul.

(Vers. 174.) I longed for your salvation, Lord, and your law is my meditation. There can be no doubt that Christ is the salvation, and the righteous of ancient times most truly confess that they longed for him. The Church longed for him who was to come from the womb of his mother; the Church longs for him who is to come from the right hand of the Father. Meditation on the law nourishes and strengthens this desire, while it proclaims Christ through its testimonies.

(Vers. 175.) My soul shall live, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.

[Note: In Augustine and in Prosper’s more recent manuscripts: *Vivet* (“it shall live”). All the older printed editions: *Vivit* (“it lives”).]

These are the judgments that were due to begin from the household of the Lord (1 Peter 4:17). But the Church has always been helped by them; for, with God granting victory, she grew through her sufferings.

(Vers. 176.) I have gone astray like a sheep that has perished; seek your servant, because I have not forgotten your commandments.

This is the sheep for whose sake its shepherd left the ninety-nine in the mountains, and, while seeking it, was torn by Jewish thorns and scourged (Matthew 18:12; Luke 15:4).

[Note: Later editions had added the conjunction *et* (“and”), which is absent from the older editions. For *vepribus* (“with thorns”) means *verberibus* (“with scourges”), as though he were saying: “with thorns,” that is, “with scourges.”]

But it has been found in part and is still being sought. For in that part in which it says, “I have not forgotten your commandments,” it has been found; but through those who choose, gather, and love God’s commandments, it is still being sought, and through the blood poured out and scattered by its shepherd it is found among all nations.

## PSALM 119

The preliminary notice indicates that the title *A Song of Ascents* begins here. By the name “ascents” an ascent is signified, by which all who make progress are raised from temporal things to eternal things, from earthly things to heavenly things. These same steps belong both to ascent and to descent—not because those who had progressed decline, but because “whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). The chief virtue of the exalted is to suffer with the weak and to bend down toward those who are foolish—that is, toward the little ones as well (Romans 15:1)—so that all may set their minds on the things above (Colossians 3:2), and “a brother assisted by a brother is exalted” (Proverbs 18:19). All the faithful have as the pattern of descent the Lord Jesus Christ himself: while remaining in his glory, in which he is equal to the Father, he assumed the nature and likeness of a servant, so that by the same steps by which he descended to our depths, we might be able to ascend to his heights.

(Vers. 1.) To you, Lord, when I was in tribulation, I cried, and you heard me. Everyone who considers entering the Lord’s way and walking in the divine commandments must begin his labor amid many tribulations (1 Timothy 3:12). Nothing is more useful for him than to seek the help of the one toward whom he is striving, who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

(Vers. 2.) Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue. Those who love this world oppose the religious will of one who has resolved to lead a devout life, and by deceitful words they wish to frighten him away from his holy purpose. It is exceedingly difficult to escape their wicked lips, since they seem to offer advice through a kind of affection and, as though taking pity, to call him back from harsh labor, so that what is in fact a most harmful persuasion may appear to be pious concern.

(Vers. 3.) What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, O deceitful tongue? “Do you wish,” he says, “to climb the steps of the virtues? Do you wish to overcome the fraudulent services of a deceitful tongue? Say what help you desire; or, if you are capable of heavenly instruction, ascend by the very fact that you ask for what is useful.”

(Vers. 4.) The sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with desolating coals. The sharp arrows are the words of God. When they pierce the minds of the faithful, they set hearts aflame; they do not wound them. But so that the mind, transfixed by heavenly love, may be free from every contrary desire, the fiery purification of spiritual coals is sought. Through it, after the gathering of harmful shoots has been laid waste, a salutary desolation may come about in a person, provided his inner self is empty of vices as guests.

(Vers. 5.) Woe is me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar. This groaning belongs to the whole Church and to all the saints, who, contemplating through faith the blessings of their heavenly homeland, sigh amid the adversities of a distant pilgrimage, because spiritual people dwell with carnal people, and those who advance toward heavenly things are burdened by those who pursue earthly things. Hence, according to the Apostle, the one seed of Abraham is divided into two kinds: some belong to Ishmael, the son of the slave woman, and others to Isaac, the son of the free woman (Galatians 4:22). The tents of Ishmael were called Kedar, so that those who are not in the inheritance may be understood not to be in the light.

[Note: We suspect that *longinquae peregrinationis* (“of a distant pilgrimage”) should be read, since Augustine writes: “I have withdrawn far from you; my pilgrimage has become distant.” We think that Saint Prosper was referring to these words here.]

(Vers. 6.) My soul has made a long pilgrimage. To prevent you from understanding a bodily pilgrimage, he said that the soul makes a pilgrimage. The body is absent from a place; the soul makes its pilgrimage through its inclination. Therefore we must take care not to be far from the one to whom we ought to draw near by the ascent of the mind.

(Vers. 7.) With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause. Christian perfection is to be peaceful even with the enemies of peace, through hope of their correction, not through consent to their wickedness. Thus, even if they follow neither example nor exhortation, they may nevertheless have no grounds for hating us (Sentences 29).

## PSALM 120

(Vers. 1–2.) I lifted my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Having entered the way of the virtues, in which there are steps of ascent to the mountains—that is, to the various exalted saints—he raises the eyes of his heart and through them asks help from the God who made heaven and earth: earth, namely, from which he desires to rise, and heaven, to which he hopes to ascend. For who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and regards the humble (Psalm 112:5–6)?

(Vers. 3.) May he not let your foot be moved, nor may he slumber who guards you. The faithful soul itself responds through God’s inspiration and strengthens the one desiring progress against pride, which was the first cause of falling for both angel and human being. May your guardian therefore grant you perseverance in humility, lest you be moved by any exaltation; lest, when you have not maintained watchfulness in standing, the one protecting you appear to fall asleep.

(Vers. 4.) Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel. “If you wish,” he says, “to have a guardian who does not sleep, be Israel”—that is, “one who sees God.” See God first through faith, then, so that afterward you may be able to see him by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). For just as the Lord said to Moses, “You cannot see my face; you shall see my back” (Exodus 33:20, 23), so you too must see what is behind, so that you may be able to see what is first. The first things are: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:2); the things behind are: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 1:14). Therefore, because hearts are cleansed by this faith (Acts 15:9): “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

(Vers. 5.) The Lord guards you; the Lord is your protection over the hand of your right side. Frequent repetition impresses upon the hearer that trust must rest principally in God’s protection. The right side of a human being is love of God and desire for the things that unite one to God; and the hand of this right side is the power God has given to believers, so that they may become children of God (John 1:12), abstaining from left-hand things and clinging to those on the right. Therefore we must trust in the Lord in all things and glory in the Lord, because he himself has given and himself preserves the ability to persevere productively on the right.

(Vers. 6.) By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night. The sun signifies Christ, the true light, and the moon signifies the Church, made light by illumination. Since every stumbling-block by which a person is either weakened or burned arises from two causes—when one errs in confessing the divinity, or when one departs from the unity of the Church—God’s protection ensures that we are not overcome by any temptation in the faith and love that are his gifts.

(Vers. 7–8.) The Lord guards you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul. May the Lord guard your entrance and your departure, from this time forth and forever. The Lord guards from every evil—not so that we suffer no adversity, but so that the soul is not harmed amid the adversities themselves.

[Note: The Cologne edition and later editions have *in ipsis adversitatibus* (“amid the adversities themselves”). In the others, and in the Book of Sentences, *in* is omitted.]

For when temptation is present, there is a kind of entry into what attacks us; and when temptation is completed with a good outcome—that is, without a wound to the soul—we go out from the depth of temptation into eternal rest (Sentences 30). As the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

## PSALM 121

(Vers. 1.) I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord. Every person enlightened by faith and eager for God’s promises rightly exults and rejoices in the things spoken by the prophets, preached by the apostles, and declared in the pages of both Testaments concerning God’s calling, which promises those who love the Lord and their neighbor an eternal dwelling in God’s house.

(Vers. 2.) Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem. Not in that Jerusalem which kills the prophets and stones those sent to it (Matthew 23:37), and which could not stand because of its many impieties, but in that heavenly Jerusalem which is the mother of all the saints (Galatians 4:26), whose children rejoice that they stand. Although they are on the way and are still striving toward it, they nevertheless rejoice as though they had arrived, because firm faith does not doubt that what is hoped for will be attained.

(Vers. 3.) Jerusalem, which is built as a city. “In the courts of that Jerusalem,” he says, “stood the firmness of our faith,” which rises not through a mass of stones but through the solidity of virtues, and is built through the fellowship of the saints, which will never be dissolved. Its participation is in the same thing. It became clear that nothing carnal should be understood concerning the eternal building of Jerusalem, since its participation—that is, its union—is “in the same thing.” What, then, is “in the same thing,” except that which truly and eternally is? The divinity of the Trinity is changed by no variation: it has never not been what it is, receives no dissimilarity, and admits no inequality. Human nature is united to it through the Incarnation of the Word, so that, freed from temporal changes, it may possess unchanging eternity.

(Vers. 4.) For the tribes went up there, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to confess the name of the Lord. The tribes are said to have gone up to the eternal Jerusalem—that is, peoples distributed according to their families. But a part is to be understood from the whole, because in every kind of people some are found righteous and others unrighteous; nor are all either persecutors or disciples of the truth. Therefore, only the tribes of the Lord ascend to the harmony of the heavenly Jerusalem. Faith bears witness to these that they are Israel—that is, “seeing God”—and that they present the gift of grace without the deceit of pretense. For the one who truly ascends is the one who confesses that what he has ascended is not the work of his own effort but a divine gift (Sentences 31).

(Vers. 5.) For there the thrones sat in judgment, thrones over the house of David. The more exalted saints are God’s thrones, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom.” And the Lord says to his apostles: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). Therefore the whole house of David—that is, the whole Church, which in Christ is the seed of David and the seed of Abraham—will come to judgment, when those who sit will themselves be God’s thrones, and through the judgment of those who judge, all lovers of God and neighbor will be taken into the unity of Christ’s body.

(Vers. 6.) Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem, and abundance for those who love you. The prophetic word is addressed to those very thrones of God, and says: “You who are going to judge, through whom the examination of consciences will take place, and who are Jerusalem itself, distinguish the humble from the proud and separate the peaceful from the implacable; let unity and abundance come to those who love you. For those who are at peace with you will abound forever in your riches.”

(Vers. 7.) Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers. Your strength, O Church, O Jerusalem, is love, by which you are both rich and strong. Let the peace of your children be established in this; let the height of your towers abound in this: that, by the very thing through which you are great, those who share in you may increase.

(Vers. 8–9.) For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors, I spoke peace concerning you. For the sake of the house of the Lord our God, I sought good things for you. I became a preacher of your peace, not for my own sake but for the sake of my brothers. I sought not my own honor but the salvation of others; not that my glory might increase, but that your inheritance might be extended. For I would be diminished in your sight if I did not labor for the progress of others.

## PSALM 122

(Vers. 1.) To you I lifted my eyes, who dwell in the heavens. The mind that makes progress and ascends sets its mind on the things above, not on the things upon the earth (Colossians 3:2). Therefore it directs the gaze of its heart where it desires to arrive—not by bodily steps, but by the ascent of those who advance in virtue. The dwelling of God is not to be understood as this heaven that is seen and of which it is said, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35), but as that Jerusalem “which is built as a city” (Psalm 122:3), not only in the exaltedness of the holy angels but also in the glorification of the whole Church, which, founded in Christ, is one temple with the heavenly powers of God.

[Note: We suspect that the preposition *de* (“from/of”) is superfluous, although it occurs in all the printed editions.]

(Vers. 2.) Behold, as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a slave-girl are toward the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. This humility and subjection reveal the nature of the trials: amid the troubles of temptations and the wounds of instruction, the eyes of those who groan are said to be turned toward God until he has mercy and spares them. From his judgment comes whatever is inflicted or commanded or permitted. For just as male and female servants are in the power of their masters and mistresses, so the saints know that the measure of their chastisements depends upon God’s decision.

(Vers. 3–4.) Have mercy on us, Lord; have mercy on us. This is the voice of one being beaten and asking for understanding amid the blows, because this whole life is full of temptations and full of wounds. For we have been filled exceedingly with contempt. And our soul has been filled exceedingly: reproach for those who abound, and contempt for the proud. All who wish to live devoutly according to Christ must suffer reproach from the ungodly and from those unlike themselves (2 Timothy 3:12), and must be despised as foolish and insane because they renounce present goods and promise themselves invisible and future things.

[Note: We emend the text from the Book of Sentences, sentence 32, where what we have printed here is read. All the printed editions at this place in the psalm have *qui praesentia bona sperant* (“who hope for present goods”), a meaning plainly contrary to the author’s intention. Unless perhaps one reads: *qui non praesentia bona sperant* (“who do not hope for present goods”) and promise themselves invisible and future things. The printed editions here read *promittunt* (“they promise”), not *promittant* (“let them promise”). Augustine’s passage, which Saint Prosper seems to have had before his eyes, is as follows: “Those who call happiness what they cannot see with their eyes are mocked, and it is said to them: ‘What do you believe, madman? Do you see what you believe? … Behold, I see what I love and enjoy. You are despised because you hope for what you do not see, and the one who, as it were, possesses what he sees despises you.’”]

But this contempt and mockery will be turned back upon them when their abundance has passed into poverty and their pride into confusion (Sentences 32).

## PSALM 123

(Vers. 1–2.) Unless the Lord had been among us—let Israel now say—unless the Lord had been among us. The body of Christ, which is the Church (Ephesians 5:23), is so distributed that some of its members have already escaped the dangers of tribulations, while others are still being worn down by the same hardships. But because there is one liberator of both the saints who came before and those who follow, there is one rejoicing of all: of those who have already conquered adversity and of those who hope to be delivered from present dangers. Since God’s promise gives firm constancy, they use one song because they are fortified by one help, saying: “Unless the Lord had been among us, the greatness of the persecutions would have overwhelmed us. But with him presiding over our hearts, giving endurance, and bringing victory to completion, may we be the glory of him who dwells in us, not the prey of our enemies.”

[Note: Perhaps the reading is *fimus gloria* (“we are glory”).]

(Vers. 2–4.) When people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. Therefore the whole salvation of the faithful and the whole strength of those who suffer must be referred to God, who is wonderful in the saints (Psalm 67:36); for unless the Lord were in them, human weakness would yield to the fury of the ungodly (Sentences 33). Let Israel therefore speak; let the redeemed people, the regenerated people, the adopted people, say: “Unless the Lord had been among us when people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.” Those are swallowed alive who, overcome by persecution, pass into the fellowship of the ungodly and, through love of a brief life, plunge into the depths of eternal death.

When their fury raged against us, perhaps they would have absorbed us alive. Those are absorbed alive who retain their faith in their conscience but, through fear of punishment, consent to the worship of idols. They live, therefore, while holding to the faith; but while acting against the faith, worshiping what they know to be nothing, they are killed and perish.

(Vers. 5.) Our soul has passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul has passed through intolerable water.

[Note: Or, “without substance.” This is how Augustine read it, and he explains this reading in the same way as Saint Prosper does here at the end.]

The greatness of the danger from which those in whom the Lord was present escaped makes the delivered marvel that, oppressed by so great a temptation, they were not overcome. For this reason the word of uncertainty is used: to show that what could not be conquered by human ability has been overcome. By the force of the waters he signified the fury of the peoples. This water is therefore called “without substance,” because sin has no substance; and “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6), filling it with what will not be and making it needy.

(Vers. 6.) Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us as prey—or as a capture—to their teeth. The faithful soul rejoices not in its own strength but in God’s help. It escaped the snares of the hunters because the Lord rendered every kind of captivity ineffective.

(Vers. 7.) Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare or trap of the hunters is love of this life. Sparrows—that is, all the humble among the faithful—escape its deceptions through the protection of heaven. The snare has been broken, and we have been freed. For “the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:31), and all the enticements of present vanities will be crushed. Then the freed sparrows—that is, the humble—will speak with exultation and joy [the syntax of the printed text after “humble” is uncertain].

(Vers. 8.) Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Therefore those who sought help in the name of the Lord, who created heaven and earth, were rightly not captured by the hunters of this world.

## PSALM 124

(Vers. 1–2.) Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; they will not be moved forever, those who dwell in Jerusalem. Amid the stumbling-blocks of the world and the changing conditions of temporal things, not to depart from the Lord but to remain steadfast in his love and in love of one’s neighbor is so illustrious and sublime that those who stand in this firmness attain the likeness of Mount Zion. They dwell in Jerusalem through faith and hope—not in the earthly Jerusalem, but in that heavenly and eternal one “which is built as a city” (Psalm 122:3). The mountains surround it. By the name “mountains” the preachers of truth are signified, whether angels, apostles, or prophets, who spread below the splendor of truth that they receive from above. And the Lord is around his people. Whatever light there is in the mountains is he who makes the mountains shine; and whatever help comes through ministers belongs to him who works all things in all (1 Corinthians 12:6). This is “from this time forth and forever”: so that they may be transferred from temporal things to eternal things.

(Vers. 3.) For the rod of sinners will not remain over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands toward iniquity. Often in this world sinners attain worldly power, and although they themselves are unrighteous, they are nevertheless ministers of public laws. Their authority must also be honored by the faithful because of the benefit of the discipline that has been established. But if they go so far as to try to turn the righteous away from the worship of the true God, they are owed no obedience and no consent. For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, whose lot is God himself. He will give his righteous ones such perseverance that they will not fear the commands of raging ungodly rulers and will abstain from every work of unrighteous action. Thus rulers must be endured both by peoples and masters by servants, so that temporal things may be borne under the exercise of endurance while eternal things are hoped for. Whatever does not violate the purpose of religious devotion increases the merit of virtue (Sentences 34).

(Vers. 4.) Do good, Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart. Those are upright in heart who do not complain about God’s commands and decrees and are not corrupted by the changing circumstances of temporal things, because it is just to bear with equanimity what the one who will judge has willed to be endured (Sentences 35).

(Vers. 5.) But those who turn aside into obligations, the Lord will lead away with those who work iniquity. He says that the Lord will bring to the judgment of recompense those who entertain impious complaints, depart from the boundary of faith, and pass over into imitation of many crimes, bound by equal bonds of conscience, so that they may experience as avenger the one whom they did not believe to be judge.” Peace be upon Israel. Jerusalem is interpreted as “Vision of peace,” and Israel as “Seeing God.” Therefore, whoever sees God sees peace, and peace is upon the one to whom God is always pleasing and who in nothing disagrees with his will.

## PSALM 125

(Vers. 1.) When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted. This prophetic psalm belongs to the ascent of the steps by which the progress of those who run well increases. Under the name of one city and people, it signifies things that are to be understood of the whole Church. For Zion throughout the world is the body of all the saints, and the city led out from the captivity of Babylon, whose name is interpreted as “confusion.” From Adam onward, the whole human race came under the yoke of servitude (Sirach 40:1), through which all the ages of the world and the universal captivity are turned away from the children of adoption. All who belong to the redemption of Christ’s blood have the joy of consolation in the hope of salvation that cannot be doubted.

(Vers. 2.) Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation. Joy properly belongs to the mind. But because what is conceived in the heart is expressed by the mouth, he said that the tongue itself was filled with exultation, through whose service the mind’s abundance pours itself out in thanksgiving. This can also happen while the tongue is silent, because the inner person too has an invisible mouth and a hidden tongue, with which feeling cries out in a silent sound.

(Vers. 2–3.) Then they will say among the nations: The Lord has magnified what he has done with them. The Lord has magnified what he has done with us; we have become joyful. Among all the nations are citizens of Zion, who are daily freed from the yoke of captivity through the redemption and price of Christ’s blood, and they say: “The Lord has magnified what he has done with us,” for through the magnificence of his grace he has restored us to our heavenly homeland. They are joyful because the true joys of manifest hope are theirs.

(Vers. 4.) Turn back our captivity, Lord, like a torrent in the south. The present life is attacked by many temptations, so that even those redeemed from captivity fear its evils and continually implore the help of the Redeemer. They ask that, on the Lord’s way and through the ascent of the steps, they may have freedom for an unhindered course. As waters bound by ice are released when the south wind blows, so may they, their sins’ ice melted by the Holy Spirit, be carried swiftly toward their homeland like torrents.

(Vers. 5–6.) Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves. All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution (2 Timothy 3:12), and the hardship of holy labors is the cause of tears. But the time of weeping is the time of sowing, because works of love, undertaken to relieve human misery, produce a harvest of eternal joys. For the pious farmers will be crowned with the fruit of good works, and with sheaves of glory—that is, with the merits of their deeds—they will joyfully meet the coming of the Lord and Savior.

## PSALM 126

The title of this psalm is *A Song of Solomon*. It is surprising that a song of ascents should be designated by his name, since it is known that he fell from these steps of the virtues (1 Kings 11:1 and following). But if, when he fell, whatever had been spoken through him were erased, it would be thought that he himself had spoken what the Spirit of God spoke, and those words ought to be rejected as his own. Now, however, with the man’s merit set aside, what was done by God is not silenced, and spiritual teaching is separated from the teacher’s transgression. The authority of the prophecy therefore remains—not human but divine (2 Peter 1:21)—and it shows that the temple of God is built only through his own work.

(Vers. 1.) Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain. It is the voice of the Apostle speaking to the faithful people: “You are God’s building; you are God’s cultivation” (1 Corinthians 3:9). The prophet also uses this voice, declaring that the labor of those who build the house is vain unless the work of building is begun and brought to completion with the Lord’s help. This must certainly be understood of the whole Church, which is Jerusalem: in the joining together of all the saints, one house, one temple, and one city, whose construction rises from beginning to end as the Lord builds. Without his grace nothing is solid, nothing firm, but all things are vain and destined to collapse.

Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it has labored in vain. The entire structure of the holy building progresses through the Lord’s work and stands through the Lord’s protection. For the guarding of a superior is useful when the Spirit of God presides over his people and deigns to guard not only the flock but also the shepherds themselves (Sentences 36).

## (Verse 2)

It is in vain for you to rise before the light. The spirit of presumption is rebuked here: it is futile for him to raise himself by his own strength, since no one can share in Christ’s glory unless he has been a true imitator and lover of his humility. If, therefore, someone wishes to rise before the light and escape the darkness of night, he is deceived. For the disordered desire to excel—which ought to have grown through humility—is plunged into the depths when it is lifted up too hastily.

Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow. When it says, “Rise,” it is an exhortation to cast aside exaltation; but when it adds, “after you have sat down,” it shows that one must first devote oneself to humility, since “whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11). And lest there be any doubt concerning those to whom this merit belongs, it says, “you who eat the bread of sorrow”: that is, you who suffer for righteousness and spend the time of the present life in the tears of tribulations. Thus, as members of the Lord’s body, you may walk the way that the Head has entered, preserving a share in endurance to the end, because your hope in Christ is secure, together with the glory of rising again.

“When he gives sleep to his beloved.”  
[Note: Perhaps “God’s beloved” should be read, as in the text of Scripture expounded by Saint Prosper; and in Augustine: “God grants this when his beloved have fallen asleep”—then, “his beloved will rise,” that is, Christ’s beloved. For all will rise, but not in the manner of his beloved.]

God’s elect are his saints, whose death he makes like the sleep from which Christ rose from the dead. So too will those who are his members rise. Following the light that has gone before them, after the labors of humility, they will enter into a share in glorification.

## (Verse 3)

Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward of the fruit of the womb. The sons of the Lord are the Churches, in whom there is both the reward of fruitfulness and joy in the fruit of their womb. For faith’s womb conceived, carried, and gave birth to them, though they were carried in the womb together with those destined for rejection; afterward they were distinguished according to their own character, when the sleep that the Lord gave to his beloved had ended, so that resurrection might follow their sitting down.

## (Verse 4)

As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the sons of those who have been shaken out. The “sons of those who have been shaken out” are understood as the apostles, the sons of the prophets, whose prophecy had been overshadowed by many coverings, which the preachers of the Gospel opened by shaking them out. Thus the apostles, arising afterward from the prophets, shook out their fathers and, by sifting their secrets, brought them to light. They were like arrows sent throughout all the ends of the earth, from the bow of the Lord’s command.

[Note: All editions note in the margin, as an alternative reading, “they ruminated.”]

## (Verse 5)

Blessed is he who will fulfill his desire from them. He shares in the apostles’ blessedness who desires what they attained by desiring and taught by attaining. His desire is therefore said to be fulfilled from them, because through their imitation one reaches the same joys.

He will not be put to shame while he speaks to his enemies in the gate. Who is it that speaks in the gate except the one who evangelizes in Christ? For Christ himself is the door of those entering God’s kingdom. Their enemies, however, are those who resist the preaching of truth; and while they contradict the divinity of the Lord’s Incarnation, they deserve to be excluded from entering through the gate.

# PSALM CXXVII

## (Verse 1)

Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. Many people of evil conscience fear the Lord, recognizing what recompense is owed for their deeds; but while they remain in sins, overcome by their delight in them, they receive not a remedy from their fear but punishment. Fear, therefore, shares in blessedness among those who walk in God’s ways and fear that they may lose something of the good by which they are made blessed—“rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation” (Romans XII, 12).

[Note: The Lyon and Louvain editions had in the text, “who are in the ways of God,” without the words “in them”; although they warned in the margin that these words should be added to the text, later editors in fact inserted them into the text.]

## (Verse 2)

You will eat the labors of your fruits; you are blessed, and it will be well with you. The prophet has passed from the plural number to the singular because we are all one in Christ: from many members we are made one body, since whether there are many or whether there are individuals, Christ is one—both the head is in the structure and the whole structure is in the head (I Corinthians X, 17, and XII, 12).

It is therefore asked how the one who fears the Lord and walks in his ways is going to eat the fruit of his labors. The answer is found in this: the righteous are nourished not only by the fruits of their labor but also by the very labor by which they strive toward the fruit. Before they receive the rewards of devout labor, the love of endurance becomes for them a share in the pleasure that is to come.

[Note: All the printed editions read this way. But we conjecture that perhaps “the labor of your fruits” should be read, both from the text cited shortly afterward and from the following exposition, and also from Augustine’s work, where he discusses this very reading at length in this same passage and concludes: “For now, the labor of your fruits; afterward, the fruit of labor . . . ‘You are blessed’ concerns the present; ‘it will be well with you’ concerns the future. When you eat the labors of your fruits, you are blessed; when you reach the fruit of your labors, it will be well with you.”]

## (Verse 3)

Your wife is like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house. Since many saints had neither marriages nor children, how are they understood to have shared in this blessing unless the fellowship of these relationships is understood in the body of the whole Church—namely, through that spiritual marriage by which the bride is joined to her husband Christ, that is, to the Bridegroom?

The mystery of this union is signified by many names, so that those who adhere to the Head are called at one time his members, at another mother and brothers, at another wife and children, and at another temple and vineyard. Through these various kinds of relationships, that indivisible unity of faith, hope, and charity is displayed; and whatever is joined to Christ is also bound together with everything else, so that the sides of the whole house may be clothed with the abundance of a fruitful vine.

Your children are like young olive trees around your table. Those who were called by the name of wife are recalled by the name of children, compared with young olives because of the fruit of peace. For they will be called the children of God who make peace and who surround the Lord’s table—the table of the sacraments and of teaching—with unanimity (Matthew V, 9), so that what is received from it may not be violated by any dissension.

## (Verse 4)

Behold, thus will every person be blessed who fears the Lord. The Head and the body, Christ and the Church, are one man; one is Christ, who possesses blessing in his own members and in himself, both receiving it and conferring it.

## (Verse 5)

May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life. This is not a human blessing but a divine one; and incorruptible goods are promised, not of an earthly Jerusalem but of the heavenly Jerusalem. Although temporal advantages too are gifts of God, he does not specifically promise them to the saints, since he bestows them commonly upon the reprobate as well.

[Note: The Douai and Cologne editions, and the editions of the learned, read “and the good”; the Lyon and Louvain editions more correctly read “and the reprobate.”]

The joys of the eternal city are therefore eternal, and the perpetual infinity of its enduring days will neither change nor fall away. There the children of children will be seen—that is, the fruits of holy works and the perpetual rewards of righteousness—all of which are expressed under the name of peace. For all that blessedness of Jerusalem will rejoice in unchanging peace, and the good of all will be what belongs to each one individually (Sent. 37).

## (Verse 6)

And may you see your children’s children: peace upon Israel. Every promise of eternal goods is comprehended under the name of peace, and it belongs especially to those who are Israel, that is, “seeing God.” Of them it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew V, 8).

# PSALM CXXVIII

## (Verses 1, 2)

They often attacked me from my youth. Let Israel now say: “They often attacked me from my youth.” The spirit of prophecy exhorts the Church of God to perseverance, so that it may glory in the persecutions it has overcome in the Lord. From the beginning, the ungodly have raged against the saints who are Israel; but the Church, whether in its youth, in more advanced age, or in the old age of the world, already approaching its end, has been conquered by no oppression and no punishment. Through the sufferings and deaths of its members, crowns and triumphs have continually increased for it.

## (Verses 2, 3)

Indeed, they could not prevail against me. Sinners built upon my back; they prolonged their iniquity. The whole purpose of the wicked against the good is to make them like themselves and lead them away from faith and integrity into agreement with their own iniquity. When they cannot achieve this, they attack the lives of the innocent with insults and accusations, constructing upon their backs a heap of falsehoods. It belongs to the perfection of the faithful both to bear such burdens and the burdens of unjust hatred, even when the wicked prolong their iniquity and do not change through any correction. The persistence of the wicked remains far removed from the innocent, and the upright person is not defiled by any fellowship with them.

## (Verse 4)

The righteous Lord will cut off the necks of sinners. “Sinners” is a general name, which even the saints do not consider wholly foreign to themselves. But one thing is removed daily, while another continually increases. The very form of the punishment shows what sort of sinners are being mentioned here, since the Lord is announced as cutting off not the hands of sinners but their necks. By “necks” is signified the pride of those who do not wish to be reproved in anything and who despise the words of God as though they were ravings.

## (Verse 5)

Let all who hate Zion be put to shame and turn back.  
[Note: The Lyon and Louvain editions read “and let them turn back in reverse.” The Douai and Cologne editions read “let them return.” Augustine reads “let them turn away backward.”]

Those who hate Zion are those who hate the Church and despise God’s commandments. But since they have built upon the back of the Church, what will the Church do except tolerate such people, hoping for their correction, to the end? For what follows will come.

## (Verses 6, 7)

Let them become like the grass of the roofs, which withers before it is pulled up. Of it the reaper does not fill his hand, nor the one who gathers sheaves his bosom. Those who despise God’s utterances and love the world are compared with the grass that grows upon roofs and walls. It withers before the time of harvest, and when it seems to stand, it has fallen. Nor do the reapers—that is, the angels—find anything in them to be brought into the Lord’s barns (Matthew XIII, 39), because whatever lacks the substance of charity will be assigned to the fire.

## (Verse 8)

Nor did those who passed by say, “The blessing of the Lord be upon you.” The proud and empty accomplished nothing in the Lord’s field, nor did they deserve to receive the grace of blessing from those who will pass from temporal things to eternal ones. For all the prophets, apostles, and saints blessed those who lived well in the name of the Lord—not in their own name, but in the name of him whose grace made them what they were and whose promises they proclaimed to the good and faithful.

[Note: The second part of the verse is missing here: “We have blessed you in the name of the Lord.” Nevertheless, it seems to be included in the explanation of the verse itself.]

# PSALM CXXIX

## (Verse 1)

From the depths I cried to you, O Lord; O Lord, hear my voice. Whoever understands the depth of the evils of this life and desires to be rescued from earthly things already belongs among those who advance by the steps of ascent. Such a person desires to be helped by heavenly aid, so that through progress in virtue he may climb from the lowest places to the highest.

One must therefore cry to the Lord with the voice of the desire that hopes, asking him to rescue those who labor not from a single depth but from the many depths of human misery. Even those who have made great progress have, until the end, things from which they desire to be delivered.

[Note: This is an obscure passage, which could not be restored because of a defect in the manuscripts. It may perhaps become clearer with a few changes if it is read as follows: “Although this is the condition of the great and the blessed: that as long as they are in the world they suffer the depths of the worldly sea, whose extremity holds those who are submerged . . . the happier they think themselves.” Augustine’s conjecture seems to give some support to this: “They are very deeply submerged who do not cry from the depths. Scripture says: ‘When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises.’ Now see, brothers, what sort of depth it is in which God is despised. This usually happens to those who are very deeply submerged, who prosper in their iniquities and are sunk all the deeper the happier they appear to be.”]

Although this is the condition of the great and faithful: that as long as they are in the world they suffer the depths of the worldly sea, whose extremity holds those who delight in those very lowest depths, they are all the more miserable the more faithful they think themselves to be.

## (Verses 2, 3)

Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication. If you observe iniquities, O Lord, O Lord, who will endure? Because the one who came to destroy the works of the devil—that is, sins (I John III, 8)—and came to seek what had been lost (Luke XIX, 10), gave hope even to one lying in the deepest abyss, by which he might raise himself toward the help of the Savior.

Therefore, no matter how great the weight of evil habit by which a sinner is oppressed, the form of this psalm provides an example of supplication to follow, so that he may not despair of his liberation. For if divine justice in this life rendered to human beings what they deserve, no one could endure the judgment of retribution. What hope belongs to the one who confesses is disclosed by the words that follow.

## (Verse 4)

For with you there is forgiveness, and on account of your law I have waited for you, O Lord. What is forgiveness except sacrifice? And what sacrifice except the slaughter of that Lamb who took away the sin of the world (John III, 29), and who came to fulfill the law of the Old Testament through the new law of evangelical truth?

The law is the perfection of charity, by which God and one’s neighbor are loved, and through which it is said to the giver of the law, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI, 12). The one who carries out God’s command rightly waits for his promises; nor does the one who forgives the sins of others hope in vain that his own sins will be pardoned (Sent. 38). As the Apostle says, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians VI, 2).

My soul has waited for your word. “The substance of my expectation,” he says, “is Christ; and I am not deceived by the promise of your word, because the one who promised is himself the Truth.”

## (Verses 5, 6)

My soul has hoped in the Lord. From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.

[Note: All our printed editions repeat here “from the morning watch.” Augustine too acknowledges having read these words twice: once at the end of the fifth verse, “My soul has hoped in the Lord, from the morning watch until night”; then at the beginning of the sixth, “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.” He insists upon this repetition when he says: “My soul has hoped in the Lord, from the morning watch until night. What does he mean? Has he hoped in the Lord for one day, and has his whole hope ended? From the morning watch until night, he hoped in the Lord. This watch is the end of night . . . Therefore it must be understood that from this point until night my soul has hoped in the Lord; it must be understood so that we do not think that we need to hope in the Lord for only one day.” And below: “And he returns to that passage: ‘From the morning watch let Israel hope in the Lord.’”]

The hope and expectation of the faithful and of the saints are not enclosed within the end of a single day, since even within the brief periods of this life the risings and settings of many days are often renewed. The virtue of patience must therefore be taken from that morning watch in which the Lord Jesus Christ, in the flesh of our nature, rose from the dead, so that all his members might hope that what had gone before in the Head would also be accomplished in them.

This hope must be frightened by no adversities and darkened by no terrors; it must be guarded bravely until the end of the present life, where a kind of night of death intervenes. Thus all Israel, until it departs from this life, must not cease to hope that what was accomplished in the Lord will also be accomplished in it. This is the distinctive hope of spiritual Israelites, whose desire seeks neither empty nor temporal things. From the morning watch of Christ’s resurrection until the night of its own end, their desire runs and reaches toward the place where Christ has already arrived beforehand.

## (Verse 7)

For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him there is abundant redemption. The confidence of those who hope is the mercy of God. No one ought therefore to doubt that he will obtain the Lord’s promise because he knows himself unworthy to share in it, since confession itself, through a change of conduct and mind, earns forgiveness. And abundant is the redemption of the one who denies none of his gifts to those who have been corrected and breaks all the bonds of captives.

## (Verse 8)

And he himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities. Let no one who approaches the Lord fear any iniquities, provided that he devotes himself to him with his whole heart and ceases to do and desire those things in which he is displeasing even to himself. Let him not say that one iniquity may perhaps be forgiven while another must be punished according to its character. Rather, let him cry from the depths and hope from the morning watch until night, because the Redeemer, who was without sin, poured out his precious blood for the unjust in order to erase all the sins of all who believe in him.

# PSALM CXXX

## (Verse 1)

O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up. I have not entered upon great things, nor upon marvelous things. The truth of holy humility is commended in the person of every spiritual Israelite, in whom the whole body of Christ is displayed. All the children of the Church recognize this voice of the psalm as their own. Their temperance desires nothing of human glory, nor do they wish to boast of marvelous works so as to acquire the price of praise through a display of virtues.

Since no member of Christ’s body can be separated from the grace of God, which he graciously works in any one of the faithful, each person makes his own the good whose accomplishment through another gives him joy.

## (Verse 2)

If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, let my recompense be like that of a weaned child upon his mother. The mind of perfect humility delights fearlessly to bind itself by this resolve, so that it becomes liable to a kind of curse if it wishes to think lofty thoughts and grow proud of any miracles.

Just as it goes badly with an infant not yet capable of solid nourishment if it is taken away from its mother’s breasts, since the substance of its food is in its mother, so, he says, let my soul be recompensed in such a way that, when I am unable to eat the bread of angels, I may lose the drink of my mother’s milk; and when I cannot grasp the things above me, I may be deprived of the good of humility, in which it is more salutary to advance than to be afraid [perhaps: “to swell with pride”].

## (Verse 3)

Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time forth and forever. True Israel, therefore, looking toward what has been prepared for it in the Lord, must establish all its hope in the Lord and set its mind on the things above, not on the things upon the earth (Colossians III, 2). It must not seek temporal glory but eternal glory, lest, while loving deceptive goods, it fail to grasp the true ones.

# PSALM CXXXI

## (Verse 1)

Remember, O Lord, David and all his gentleness. It is fitting for the blessed David that he should wish his gentleness to be remembered before the Lord, since he was most observant of it, and the order of his deeds bears witness to it according to the historical account.

But the prophetic word must be understood in a higher sense, so that these words may refer to that one person who is one man in the Head and in the body, that is, in Christ and the Church. The whole city of God and the entire structure of the saints make full use of these words, offering God the gentleness of the powerful and the humility of the exalted, together with the vow of this purpose: that they may become his tabernacle and temple.

Every faithful soul professes and ratifies this through a kind of unbreakable oath, desiring to be possessed by the Lord forever and to be the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.

## (Verses 2–5)

As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house; if I climb upon the bed of my couch; if I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

In all these words the perseverance of the vow and the fervor of faith are displayed. In order to become a place for the Lord and a tabernacle for the God of Jacob, one must pass from one’s own advantage to the common good, not rest in oneself or drowse amid one’s own pleasures. This is what those do who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Philippians II, 21).

The things that belong to Jesus Christ are not the goods of individual members but of the whole body, and no one lacks goods in which everyone rejoices. A person therefore becomes the Lord’s place and the tabernacle of the God of Jacob when he is fitted into the Church and united to Christ’s body through the spirit of charity. He desires to become blessed nowhere else except in that house of which it is said, “Blessed are all who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXVIII, 5).

## (Verse 6)

Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the forest. Ephrata is a Hebrew name interpreted in Latin as “mirror,” in which an image of prophetic significance has gone before. Through the mirror of prophecy, this seat or dwelling of God was announced, of which it is said, “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata”—that is, in the utterances of the prophets.

“We found it in the fields of the forest”: that is, in the height of the nations, among which there were the thorns of idolatry, the tangled growths of error, and the wildness of uncultivated minds. What we heard from the books of the Jews has therefore been made manifest in the faith of the nations.

## (Verse 7)

We will enter his tabernacles; we will worship in the place where his feet have stood. Those who enter in order to dwell are the same as those whom others enter in order to be inhabited; and those are in the house of God who are themselves the house of God, so that they may truly be in the kingdom of God, to whom it can be said, “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21).

These people therefore worship in the place where his feet have stood, whether they are of that house itself, abiding in the Lord, or of the Lord himself, who is the inhabitant of the abiding house. Just as there is no place of worship except in the Catholic Church, so no one can say, “Lord Jesus Christ,” except in the Holy Spirit (I Corinthians XII, 3).

[Note: The Cologne edition and those that followed it read “the Lord Jesus Christ.”]

## (Verse 8)

Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification. The Church, that is, the body of Christ, says to its Head: “You slept through the disturbance of the cross; arise into the rest of eternity, you and the ark of your sanctification.” Thus the glory of the resurrection may be fulfilled not only in the Head of the members but also in the members of the Head.

These members are the ark of sanctification for God, whether through the truth of the Incarnation or through the election of grace.
