Thus, in the person of the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (I Timothy II, 5), he is understood as both the altar of propitiation, the ark of sacrifice, and the ark of teaching.

## (Verse 9)

Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints rejoice. “When you,” he says, “rise from the dead and go to the Father, let that royal priesthood be clothed with faith, because ‘the righteous person lives by faith’ (Romans I, 17). And having received the pledge of the Holy Spirit, let the members rejoice in the hope of the resurrection that has gone before in the Head.”

## (Verse 10)

For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ. This was said to God the Father by the Church, which begs him to remember his promises concerning the house of David, lest the whole Israelite race perish because of the crime of the ungodly.

Although they have received and continue to receive what they deserve, many thousands of them have nevertheless been justified through faith. From them came the apostles, from them the teachers, from them so many martyrs and the firstborn of the whole adoption. They were chosen so that the grain might be separated from the chaff and a remnant might be saved (Romans XI, 5). For their sake the Lord also prayed on the cross, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34).

## (Verse 11)

The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not repent of it. Just as the name of an oath signifies in God an establishment of unchanging truth, so the term “repentance” indicates a change of judgment. Thus it is said that the Lord does not repent (Psalm CIX, 4), because he has determined never to change. What else does this show than the eternity of his gifts and judgments?

From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne. David, in whom the person of the Head and the body—that is, of Christ and the Church—is present, receives this promise: the fruit of his womb will be placed upon his throne, whose kingdom remains forever (Luke I, 33). He is called the fruit of the womb because the Savior, according to the flesh, is the son of the Virgin mother, conceived not through intercourse with a man but through the Holy Spirit.

## (Verse 12)

If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine that I will teach them, their sons too will sit forever upon your throne. To those who keep the covenant are promised the inheritance of the promises and the blessedness of the eternal kingdom. By this blessedness not only David’s sons but also his sons’ sons will be enriched.

This glory, however, is attained by the seed of faith, not by descent of the flesh; and throughout the world those who are in the faith of the holy Fathers are counted among the heirs with honor.

## (Verse 13)

For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has chosen it beforehand as his dwelling. Zion itself is the Church, and it is the heavenly Jerusalem, toward whose peace those who are still pilgrims hasten. It is the city of God, which in its better part has always remained with its author and awaits the part that is daily recalled from exile by God’s grace, so that the whole may together become the building of its inhabitant.

## (Verse 14)

This is my rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, because I have chosen it beforehand. It is clear with what ineffable love God loves his Church, since he calls his own the rest by which he makes it rest, although no disturbance of labor has ever wearied the unchanging tranquility of the Godhead.

The principal cause of this great gift is shown most fully when he says, “Because I have chosen it beforehand,” in accordance with the Lord’s words in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16).

## (Verse 15)

Blessing her widow, I will bless her; I will satisfy her poor with bread. The whole Church of God, hoping in the Lord and advancing through humility, bears the form of a widow (I Timothy V, 5). Since it does not possess the consolation of this world, it persists in prayer night and day (ibid., 6) and relies upon divine help alone.

The poor are also signified: those of whom it is said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew V, 3 and 6)—with the food of grace and the bread of righteousness, so that they may eat him who says, “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 41).

[Note: All the printed editions read “so that they may lead out.” It is better to read “so that they may eat”; for it is clearly not a question here of leading out bread but of eating it, as is shown by the word “they will be satisfied,” which preceded shortly before. The copyist was evidently misled by a verse from another psalm: “That you may bring bread out of the earth” (Psalm CIII, 14).]

Widowhood and poverty should therefore not be understood only of women deprived of the company of husbands, nor only of those who suffer want, but of all the members of Christ’s body. For one thing is what the labor of necessity endures, and another is what the love of religion chooses.

## (Verse 16)

I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints will rejoice with rejoicing. Salvation—that is, the one who brings salvation—is Christ, with whom everyone who has been reborn is clothed. The Apostle says, “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians III, 27).

The whole Church attains this under the name of priests, because the entire Christian people is priestly. The rulers of the people, however, receive this more fully, since they more particularly bear the person of the high priest and Mediator.

## (Verse 17)

There I will bring forth the horn of David. The horn signifies exaltation—not of those who glory in themselves but of those who glory in the Lord—for the height of horns surpasses the measure of all flesh.

I have prepared a lamp for my Christ: that is, I sent prophecy before him, so that those who were established in the darkness of ignorance might use its light. Hence the blessed Apostle Peter says, “We possess the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (II Peter I, 19). The Lord himself also says of John the Baptist, “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John V, 35).

The saints will therefore rightly rejoice with rejoicing, because they glory not in themselves but in the Lord.

## (Verse 18)

I will clothe his enemies with shame, but upon him my sanctification will flourish. It is clearly signified what is owed to the enemies of Christ’s grace and what glory is prepared in him for the saints, when Christ shines forth in his whole body and “God will be all in all” (I Corinthians XV, 28).

# PSALM CXXXII

## (Verse 1)

Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together. The dwelling is good and pleasant that creates unity among the children of adoption and, beyond bodily and local dwelling, joins brotherly minds together in the peace of faith. This is truly fulfilled when all the members of the faithful come together under the one Head of the whole body of Christ.

## (Verse 2)

Like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron. Through the priest Aaron that priest is indicated who alone fulfilled the sacrament of the true high priest—not in the sacrifice of another kind of being but in the offering of his own body and blood. He is at once priest and victim, the one who makes propitiation and propitiation itself, and the accomplisher of all the mysteries through which he was announced.

Having died, been buried, risen, and ascended into heaven, he exalted human nature above every name and sent the Holy Spirit, whose anointing would penetrate the whole Church. For the blessing flowing from the Head, that is, from Christ, descends not only upon the beard but also upon the edge of his garment, that is, even to the lowest members.

In the beard, which first received the ointment flowing from the head, the apostles and martyrs are signified. In them the power of the Head is prominent both in sacrament and in example.

## (Verses 2, 3)

Which runs down upon the edge of his garment. Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion. The descent of the dew signifies heavenly grace, which is the source of the merits of the saints.

Hermon is said to be interpreted as “exalted river.”

[Note: This is the interpretation found in all the printed editions of Prosper. But in Augustine it reads: “We have an interpretation from those who know that language, the Hebrew language. Hermon is said to be interpreted as ‘exalted light.’”]

This is understood as Jesus Christ, who, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings (Psalm LXVII, 19; Ephesians IV, 8). From him the rain of spiritual gifts comes upon Zion, that is, upon the Church. From the whole structure there arises the fruit of blessings and the strength of virtues.

For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever. The grace of Hermon’s dew descends where, through the unity of charity, there is participation in blessing. Those dwell together who live harmoniously in Christ and who, in loving not only their brothers but even their enemies, keep the command by which they are ordered to pray for their persecutors (Matthew V, 44).

For the Lord died for his enemies (Romans V, 10), making those who imitate his love participants in eternity.

# PSALM CXXXIII

## (Verse 1)

Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. “Now,” he says—that is, in this time of tribulations and hardships, in the time of persecutions and tears—bless the Lord, all who remain with one heart and one spirit in confessing and praising the Lord.

Stand—that is, persevere—in the breadth of faith, hope, and charity.

[Note: The Lyon edition does not add the preposition “in” here; later editions added it.]

## (Verse 2)

In the nights lift up your hands toward the sanctuary and bless the Lord. “In adversities,” he says, “which darken the day of this life, do not fail. Instead, lift up your hands in the work of holiness, so that the blessings uttered by the voice may be seen in the godliness of your conduct.”

## (Verse 3)

May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth. He exhorted many to bless the Lord, but he blesses one person, because he made one from many, so that the whole Church, whose body and soul are one, may receive blessing as one person.

# PSALM CXXXIV
### (Verses 1–2)

Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.

This is a good and useful exhortation, by which his servants are urged to praise the Lord—even though God has no need of this, since his glory can be neither diminished nor increased. But because those who praise him make progress through this service and learn to fear and love the one whom they praise, faithful devotion should persist in confessing the divine virtues, so that observance of the custom may become a sacrifice of the will.

What sort of people the preachers of God ought to be is next shown when it says, “who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” [Col. 0383B]—that is, you who remain tireless in God’s commandments. By the very fact that you stand in the Lord’s house, you give thanks to him who releases the fettered, gives sight to the blind, and raises up those who are cast down (Psalm 145:7–8), and who has given you the spirit of understanding, so that it might kindle you to love and praise him.

### (Verse 3)

Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing psalms to his name, for he is gracious.

The Lord’s praise can neither be expressed more abundantly nor more fully than when he is called “good.” Yet this must not be understood in the same way as the other good things that exist only through him, but uniquely above all else: for one thing is the Good that makes all good things and has no author of its own, and another is that which could not exist unless it had been made. Hence it is said, “No one is good except the one God” (Matthew 19:17).

There is no creature comparable to the Creator. Whatever good a creature possesses is not its own by nature but something received. This supreme and unchangeable Good grants its praisers a share in its graciousness because the Son of God, equal to the Father, became the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). For he is, according to the saying “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), the bread of human beings. By descending to us, through us, he made it possible for us to ascend to him through him; and by drinking the cup of our weakness, he enabled us to taste the cup of his power, so that we might acknowledge and confess that the Lord is gracious.

### (Verse 4)

For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.

All the graciousness of God’s goodness [Col. 0383D] is shown in his grace, because the Lord chose Jacob for himself and made Israel his possession, accepting for himself that household which he would choose and adorn in a special way.

[Note: A later edition reads *accipiens* (“accepting”); all the older editions—Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne—read *excipiens* (“receiving” or “taking aside”). For Augustine says that, although God himself created all the nations, he entrusted the others to angels but appointed this one to be possessed and preserved by himself.]

Although he himself created all the nations, he did not entrust this one to angels as he did the others, but assigned it particularly to his own name. Thus he arranged the mystery of his calling so that Israel’s election would pertain to the salvation of all nations, and so that the children of the promise would come into an eternal inheritance—not through descent from the flesh, but through adoption by regeneration.

### (Verse 5)

For I have learned that the Lord is great, and that our God is above all gods.

This is prophetic contemplation, perceiving the higher mysteries of God’s works. “I,” he says, “have learned how great God is, and that his purpose and plan cannot be explained in any language.” But because the Almighty surpasses every power, and there is no nature over which its Creator does not reign, let the created things through which the wonders of the Creator may be understood be recalled.

### (Verse 6)

The Lord has done everything that he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.

Whatever creatures exist in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses, God made; there is no nature or substance that came into existence without his command. In creating the whole universe of things and forms, however, there was no laborious activity but the reasoning of the will. No time preceded it, and no effect was delayed.

When human beings recognize this power by contemplating the whole world, they should confess that whenever something good arises in the field of their heart, it comes from the work and gift of the heavenly farmer, who deigns by grace to restore those things which he established through nature and which were corrupted through disobedience.

### (Verse 7)

He raises clouds from the end of the earth; he makes lightning for the rain. He brings the winds out of his treasuries.

All these things occur throughout the body of the world through God’s action and by God’s will. They ought certainly to be praised with great wonder, and in them we should understand what God works in human beings themselves, whom he made and remade in his image and likeness.

### (Verse 8)

He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from human being to beast.

The firstborn of human beings are the beginnings of a good and commendable life, which takes its beginning from faith. Therefore, when certain Christians stir up schisms or heresies and attack the Church of God with whatever afflictions they can, they become Egyptians—their name being interpreted as “affliction of the people of God.” They are struck in their firstborn, that is, in their faith, which is extinguished when it deserts the charity of the Church.

This is the worst plague among human beings. The beasts too are struck—that is, those who assume the appearance of wise and learned teachers, as well as those who, because of the cause of their folly and ignorance, can be compared with beasts.

### (Verse 9)

He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.

The names of those against whom the Lord pours out his anger contain nothing of good significance. For *Phare* means “dispersion,” and *Egypt* means “affliction.”

[Note: Lyons and Louvain read “to the Egyptians”; Douai and Cologne read “Egypt,” as does Augustine: “For Egypt itself is interpreted as affliction.” Above, instead of *Phare*, Augustine has, several lines later, “Egypt is affliction, Pharaoh is dispersion.”]

Affliction has dispersion as its king, because those who afflict the Church, being themselves dispersed, afflict others, and first serve their king through their own overthrow.

### (Verses 10–11)

He struck many nations and slew mighty kings: Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan.

The slayings of the kings and nations hostile to the people of God were indeed accomplished as they are narrated. But because the historical text is prophetic, the qualities signified by the names of the persons mentioned are not without symbolic meaning. Through the meanings of their names, the Church may recognize from the slaughter of which enemies it is chiefly saved.

For Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of colors,” and the Amorites are interpreted as “those who make bitter.” Since the “temptation of colors” is nothing other than falsehood—which, in order to insinuate itself more easily, assumes for itself the appearance of truth—what wonder is it if those who make bitter are led on by the imitation of a lying king?

[Note: Perhaps one should read “assumes,” with “falsehood” as its subject; unless “they assume” is intended to refer to “those who make bitter,” of whom the discussion immediately follows.]

For the father of falsehood himself, the devil (John 8:44), disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), and the temptation of colors makes those whom it deceives opposed to the truth. Yet these people are spiritually killed when they die to the devil so that they may live to God, and those who had believed falsehood come instead to believe the truth.

The hands of God, however, because they both cut down and give life, destroy Og the king and his people Bashan. For Og is interpreted as “conclusion,” and Bashan as “confusion.” Such a conclusion blocks the way that leads to the Lord and brings those whom it has intercepted into confusion. It now confines the wicked so that they do not believe in Christ; when Christ appears, they will be confounded unless they are now changed by converting grace.

Canaan, however, is interpreted as “prepared for humility.” This should be understood as the punitive humility prepared for the proud, who are now established not in humility but in exaltation and are predetermined for what is to be repaid to vanity.

### (Verse 12)

And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.

This happens every day: what some lose through their own merit, others acquire through the gift of grace. “For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession” (above, verse 4); and to the one who possesses it is said, “Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown” (Revelation 3:11).

### (Verse 13)

[Note: Augustine has “O Lord,” as in our Vulgate.]

O Lord, your name is forever, and your memorial from generation to generation.

That is, the wonders of your virtues will not cease, and what you have accomplished by signifying it, you will continually accomplish by bringing it to fulfillment. The Lord’s memorial is understood in this: he does not forget his promises, but completely accomplishes what he has promised.

This occurs “from generation to generation,” because one generation of human beings is that in which they are born into the world, while another is that in which they are reborn to God. Yet in both, under the highest judgment of God, the work of nature and the work of grace are fulfilled.

### (Verse 14)

For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be entreated on behalf of his servants.

Apart from the future judgment, the Jewish people have already been judged. What does “judged” mean? The righteous have been separated from it, and the unrighteous have remained. Hear the Lord saying: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

The proud have been blinded, while the humble have been given sight. In this one people, which is generally called both Jacob and Israel—for the house of Jacob and the house of Israel are one person, one nation, one people—the Lord invites some and dismisses others, separating the gentle from the fierce and believers from unbelievers.

The Lord, therefore, will be entreated on behalf of his servants—that is, he will be invoked or besought—and among all nations there will be people possessing Israelite dignity, while the Jews, for the greater part of themselves, will be impious and enemies of the truth. But because spiritual Jacob is taken from every nation, the blindness of unbelief is reproached in the worshipers of idols.

[Note: The Lyons edition reads, “and this in one people.”]

### (Verse 15)

The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.

All people from whatever nation who do not know the true God and resist the Gospel of Christ are worshipers of idols. When they fashion doctrines of falsehood in their hearts, whatever they have fashioned is an idol. And if by reasoning they have fortified anything—

[Note: The Lyons edition reads *munierint* (“have fortified”); Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read *minuerint* (“have diminished”).]

—it appears to be made of silver or gold.

[Note: We think *quia* (“because”) should be read; although the printed editions have *qui* (“who”).]

It is so colored by the arguments and eloquence of human wisdom that it wins reverence for itself through the artistry of its falsehoods. In such inventions, therefore, there are works of human hands: what human error has devised, not what the doctrine of truth has established.

### (Verses 16–18)

[Note: In Augustine, this first part of verse 16 is transferred to after the words “and they will not smell.” The words “They will not cry out with their throat” are also omitted, as is “for there is no spirit in their mouth.” In our Vulgate, no more than the following is read: “They have a mouth, and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see. They have ears, and they will not hear, nor is there spirit in their mouth.” The remaining words found here in Jerome’s Psalter, called the Roman Psalter, were read there; they were subsequently cut out of the Gallican Psalter. The latest editors of Jerome’s works observe that the following verses—from “they have nostrils” to “for there is no spirit”—were transferred into the Roman Psalter from the preceding Psalm 141. Yet Prosper’s brief exposition of them, which follows, scarcely permits us to doubt that he had them before his eyes. Finally, it should be noted that these same words are not read in the Hebrew text of this psalm.]

They have a mouth, and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see. They have ears, and they will not hear; they have nostrils, and they will not smell. They have hands, and they will not work; they have feet, and they will not walk. They will not cry out with their throat; for there is no spirit in their mouth. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.

These words seem properly to be spoken about pagans, but they also include heretics, who, while clinging to falsehoods and following the impious inventions of human beings, have lost every function of rational life.

For what does it mean to have eyes and not see except to dwell in the night of errors? To have ears—

[Note: Something seems to be missing here for the sentence to have its complete meaning. Perhaps one might supply “and not hear, rather than obey the divine…” Thus below: “To have nostrils and not smell, rather than perceive how good…” “To have feet and not walk, rather than follow the grace that calls.” “To have a tongue and not speak, rather than speak the truth.” What follows suggests that the first member of the enumeration should be supplied in this way. Perhaps I may at some point encounter manuscripts that remedy the editors’ omission.]

—and not obey the divine teaching? To have nostrils and not receive the good fragrance of Christ? To have feet and not follow the grace that calls? To have a tongue and not speak the truth? To have hands and be without the work of righteousness? For everything that is not from faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

Liars, therefore, will be conformed to falsehood, and with the teacher in whom they trust they will also be confounded. Yet from among them people are changed every day through the miracles of God. Every day the eyes of the blind are opened, the ears of the deaf are unstopped, the nostrils of the senseless are given breath, the mouths of the mute are loosed, the hands of the paralyzed become active, and the feet of the lame are straightened. Children are raised up for Abraham from stones (Matthew 3:9), and to all these it is said together:

### (Verses 19–20)

House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord.

For all these ranks, which one nation possessed, have been obtained by the whole world through the same faith by which that nation was justified. Abraham, the father of believers, is now found among all nations.

### (Verses 20–21)

You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord. Blessed is the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.

God’s dwelling is not that Jerusalem which fell, but the dwelling in the hearts of the faithful and holy, from which the eternal temple of God is built together with the assembly of the angels who have never departed from the Lord.

The Church therefore blesses the Lord “from Zion,” that is, from the watchtower from which she looks forward to God’s promises coming to pass in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace, where there will no longer be any danger from weakness [Col. 0387C] or any adversity from the tempter.

## PSALM CXXXV

### (Verse 1)

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.

This psalm contains the praise of God and ends each of its verses in the same way, so that whatever works of God are reviewed may be understood to have been accomplished for the purpose of making the eternity of his goodness and mercy manifest.

Although after the judgment at the end of the world—when the living and the dead are to be judged, the righteous being sent into eternal life and the impious into eternal burning (Matthew 25:46)—there will no longer be those who are to be saved by the dispensation of divine grace, it can nevertheless rightly be understood that his mercy will endure forever, the mercy which he bestows upon his holy and faithful ones.

For the blessedness they will attain through God’s mercy will never be assailed by any temptation but will remain unchangeable in eternal peace and glory. Since this work of ineffable compassion was contained in God’s eternal purpose and plan—so that eternal things might be preordained through temporal things—the structure of the whole world and of its elements is wonderfully said to have been established on account of this mercy, for the completion of which the order of all things would serve.

### (Verses 2–3)

Give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy is forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever.

When the name “gods” is found used in a good sense, it must be understood according to grace, not according to nature, as the Apostle says: “For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:5–6).

Those, therefore, who are children of God and through the sacrament of adoption have become sharers in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), possess the gift of this name, because they serve one God and in willing submission serve one Lord.

But the gods of the nations are demons (Psalm 95:5), and because they rejoice that they are worshiped by those who err, they will be condemned with their worshipers to eternal fire.

[Note: The Lyons and Louvain editions read “they will condemn.”]

### (Verse 4)

He alone does great wonders, for his mercy is forever.

The wonders may be understood as having been done by God alone when they were brought about neither through angels nor through human beings, but solely through God’s power. Although he himself works all things in all (1 Corinthians 12:6), he alone established the natures of all creatures—heaven and the heavenly things, earth and the sea, together with everything in them.

This does not mean that the Father did anything without his Son, the Word, or without the Holy Spirit. Rather, the Trinity is one God, who made creatures not through a creature but solely through the power of the Godhead.

What is said in the second clause—“for his mercy is forever”—must be referred to the restoration of the human race, which God’s mercy, through the sacrament of regeneration, restores to eternal life.

### (Verse 5)

He made the heavens with understanding, for his mercy is forever.

The heavens were made with understanding, to instruct that creature which was foreordained to the knowledge of its Creator. “The invisible things of God,” as the Apostle says, “are clearly perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made—his eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:20). The same prophet also says, “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands” (Psalm 19:1).

For the beauty of invisible majesty—

[Note: Something seems to be missing from the first member of this sentence. Perhaps one might conjecture “is inferred from the beauty of visible things,” or something similar.]

—and through the bodily creation the incorporeal Creator is recognized.

### (Verse 6)

He established the earth upon the waters, for his mercy is forever.

It is rightly understood that the earth was founded upon the waters, in that it rises above the waters flowing around it. Thus even in the lowest regions the nature of moisture is found in such a way that a solid element is placed beneath it.

But according to the mystery of the Church, which is celebrated throughout the whole world in the bath of regeneration, this statement is more sacredly understood as referring to the preparation of baptism. Upon baptism the earth of human nature is founded, so that the entire structure of the eternal temple rises from the waters.

### (Verse 7)

He alone made the great lights, for his mercy is forever.

He added “alone” here because the other wonders he is about to mention he made either through human beings or through angels.

### (Verses 8–9)

The sun to rule the day, the moon and the stars to rule the night.

The sun’s brightness is powerful during the day, and the brightness of the moon and stars during the night. Besides the usefulness they provide to the world in their appointed alternation, and besides the beauty by which the ornament of the whole world is increased, they signify spiritual graces.

The chief light of faithful hearts is wisdom, coming from the sun of righteousness itself. The second light is knowledge, which amid the darkness of this world provides, in a certain way, the consolation of the moon. Finally, the gifts of many charisms are rightly compared with the fires of the stars, so that those who walk along a difficult road may never lack heavenly protection.

### (Verse 10)

He struck Egypt together with its firstborn.

There is no part of the world that the sword of truth does not strike, so that all things of greatest importance may be subjected to Christ.

### (Verse 11)

He brought Israel out from their midst.

Every day the holy are rescued from the wicked and from adverse tribulations.

### (Verse 12)

With a powerful hand and an exalted arm.

What is more powerful than the one of whom it is said, “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”

### (Verse 13)

He divided the Red Sea into divisions.

The division of the Red Sea signifies the baptism of Christ, in which divisions occur, so that the same reality may be life for some and death for others: life for the faithful, death for their persecutors.

[Note: Augustine has here, “so that one and the same baptism may be life for some and death for others.”]

### (Verse 14)

And he brought Israel out from its midst.

[Note: Douai and Cologne read *eduxit* (“he led out”); Lyons and Louvain read *educit* (“he leads out”), as in Augustine. The discussion concerns the grace of baptism, which is bestowed daily upon those who are reborn.]

The Lord also leads out his people, renewed through the bath of regeneration.

### (Verse 15)

And he shook Pharaoh and his power into the Red Sea.

The king of sin perishes in the waters, and guilt is shaken off from those who have been baptized.

### (Verse 16)

He led his people through the desert.

He leads us also through the barrenness and sterility of this world, so that we may not perish in it.

### (Verses 17–18)

He struck great kings and slew mighty kings.

Through us also he strikes and kills diabolical and harmful powers whenever he grants victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:57).

### (Verse 19)

Sihon, king of the Amorites.

The Lord strikes through his Church Sihon, whose name is interpreted as “useless shoot,” and the king of the Amorites, whose name is interpreted as “of those who make bitter.”

### (Verse 20)

And Og, who heaps up Bashan—

[Note: Augustine had written in the psalm verse, “And Og, king of Bashan”; then, “the one who heaps up,” which is the interpretation of Og; and “the king of confusion,” which is the interpretation of Bashan.]

—that is, confusion. For what does the devil heap up except confusion?

### (Verses 21–22)

And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.

He also gives those whom the devil possessed as an inheritance to the seed of Abraham, which is Christ (Galatians 3:16).

### (Verses 23–24)

For he remembered us in our humiliation and redeemed us from our enemies.

He redeemed us with the blood of his Only-Begotten.

### (Verse 25)

He gives food to all flesh.

This is the food of which the Lord says, “My flesh is truly food” (John 6:55). It is given to all nations, because none of the faithful who have been reborn is excluded from eating it.

### (Verses 26–27)

Give thanks to the Lord of heaven; give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever.

What is said here, “to the Lord of heaven,” seems to have been said above as “to the God of gods.” And what was added there is also connected here: “Give thanks to the Lord of gods,” so that, even if there are those who are called gods and lords, whether in heaven or on earth, nevertheless for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him. To him let us give thanks, for his mercy is forever.

## PSALM CXXXVI

### (Verse 1)

By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, Zion.

The prophecy of this psalm announces not only what, according to the order of events, properly pertained to the Israelite people, but also what takes place and is fulfilled in the whole Church of God, which exists throughout the world.

All the faithful, who are citizens of Jerusalem and are pilgrims in this present age, appropriately and fittingly use these words, saying what the words of the psalm express. For those who have been justified by faith and saved in hope (Romans 5:1; 8:24) long for their heavenly and angelic homeland, remembering God’s promise. They weep and groan over their earthly dwelling, which in every part of itself is Babylon, and whose rivers are all temporal allurements—whether in conduct or in opinions, whichever each person has chosen—in which nothing is stable or firm, but everything is fluid and leads into the depths of the sea.

Those who set their minds on the things above, not on the things on earth (Colossians 3:2), do indeed sit above the rivers and torrents of the world; yet they are not dragged along by the course of the flowing waters, nor are they mingled with the confusion called Babylon.

[Note: All the older printed editions read *quam interpretatur* (“which is interpreted”); the more recent Lyons edition reads *quae interpretatur* (“which is interpreted”). The phrase immediately added, which expresses “watchtower,” indicates that the text has rightly been emended.]

Instead, remembering Zion, which is expressed by “watchtower,” they direct their gaze toward what God has promised and advance from temporal things to eternal things.

### (Verse 2)

Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.

The citizens of Jerusalem have their instruments: the Scriptures of God, the commandments and promises of God, and a certain meditation upon the age to come. But when they live in the midst of Babylon, they hang their instruments upon its willows.

The trees of Babylon, watered by its rivers yet bearing no fruit, resemble sterile human beings who feed upon worldly allurements and bear no fruit of virtue. No seeds of the divine Scriptures can be implanted in them, because they are not capable of receiving God’s commandments. And rightly, by postponement, what they cannot hear through their folly is suspended in them.

### (Verse 3)

For there those who took us captive asked us for words of songs. And those who led us away said, “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.”

All human beings were taken captive by the devil through the first transgression, because “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). But Jesus Christ redeemed us from this captivity by his blood.

That part, therefore, which willingly serves its captors and delights in the things pleasing to its enemies offers itself as a servant for attacking the redeemed. Through it the devil carries out whatever he dares against the holy, so that he himself may rightly be said to do what he accomplishes through people subject to him.

Pagans, and the impious followers of various doctrines, therefore question Christians about the nature of our religion, the benefit of faith in Christ, and its fruit. Their questioning does not wish to learn the truth but to disturb the hearts of believers.

Therefore our instruments must be withheld from the ears of such people, and the mysteries of our songs and hymns must not be disclosed—

[Note: Lyons and Louvain read “and not the holy thing”; Douai and Cologne read “lest the holy thing…”]

—lest what is holy be given to dogs and pearls be thrown before swine (Matthew 7:6).

When such people wish to instruct themselves in the confession of our faith only in order to bring accusations against it, we should answer with what the psalm says:

### (Verse 4)

How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?

A person devoted to the flesh, devoted to the world, serving vanities, and full of errors is a foreign land. In such a person the sacred seeds—the divine words of the song—cannot be sown, because divine praise is not fittingly celebrated anywhere except in Zion, that is, in the Church.

Therefore, so that through contact with foreigners some forgetfulness of the heavenly homeland may creep in, faith must be confirmed by a kind of oath, and one must say:

### (Verse 5)

If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me.

Our right hand is eternal life; the left is temporal life. The former is full of the hope of blessedness, the latter full of the danger of destruction. Whatever is done for the sake of eternal life is done by the right hand; whatever is desired or done for the sake of transitory joys is left-handed.

The right hand comes into forgetfulness of the left when the love and practice of virtue have prevailed. Therefore this happens to those who depart from Jerusalem through love: their right hand forgets them. Eternal life remains in itself, but they remain in deadly pleasure, embracing evils instead of goods, falsehoods instead of truths, and the left instead of the right.

### (Verse 6)

Let my tongue cling to my throat if I do not remember you, and if I do not set Jerusalem above the beginning of my joy.

“Let me become mute,” he says, “unless I remember you.” For what does someone say, or what sound does someone make, if he does not utter the songs of Zion in praise? The song of Jerusalem is the speech of our tongue.

But the mouth that speaks of flesh and sings worldly things is mute and obstructed, because it delights in the very thing by which it is confounded. The true lover and citizen of Jerusalem therefore binds himself by this law: if he does not set the love of the heavenly homeland above every joy, he will be condemned to undergo this punishment.

### (Verse 7)

Remember, Lord, the children of Edom on the day of Jerusalem.

An Israelite placed among foreigners prays that the Lord may remember that there can be no harmony between the children of Edom, that is, Esau, and the children of Jacob, and that those enmities may remain—enmities already signified by the struggle of the unborn twins in their mother’s womb (Genesis 25:23), and later distinguished by the foreknowledge of the Creator, which said, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (ibid., 30).

Thus all the children of the promise represent Jacob, while by the name Esau the whole party of unbelievers is signified. He therefore asks God to remember how Esau rose up against Jacob (Genesis 27:41), and also to remember the day of Jerusalem’s labors—Jerusalem which endures the pride of the impious—or the day of its happiness, by which it is daily rescued from the slavery of captivity—

[Note: Perhaps one should read *ut* (“so that”) rather than *et* (“and”)—“so that it may be brought to the true goods of the eternal homeland”—or at least *perducitur* (“it is brought”), instead of *perducatur* (“may it be brought”).]

—and brought to the true goods of the eternal homeland.

Those who said, “Lay it waste, lay it waste, down to its foundations.”

It is not enough for the persecutors of God’s people to inflict devastation of some kind; they must also overthrow with savage destruction the faith that is the foundation of the holy structure.

### (Verse 8)

O miserable daughter of Babylon.

She is the same as Babylon, which in its offspring is both mother and daughter: mother by giving birth, daughter by succeeding. She is truly unhappy and miserable, for she is both born and gives birth for destruction.

### (Verses 8–9)

Blessed is the one who repays you with the repayment you made to us. Blessed is the one who takes and dashes your little ones against the rock.

We were all born in Babylon at our first birth, and from our very carnal beginning the confusion of the world received us as little ones. This age did nothing else with us than entangle us in various errors through diverse opinions and diabolical arts.

But God’s grace has rescued countless people from this general evil. Even while they remain amid Babylon’s delights, it already counts them among the citizens of Jerusalem. The one who is blessed—and who makes them blessed—has rescued them from darkness and from the power of darkness, so that they may be children of light and of the kingdom (Colossians 1:13), dashed against the rock, Christ, so that by dying to the world they might live to God: cast down and raised up, destroyed and built, ground into dust and made firm upon the rock, with the rock itself restoring them.

[Note: Only the Lyons edition reads “because the one who is blessed…”]

## PSALM CXXXVII

### (Verse 1)

I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard all the words of my mouth.

The title of the psalm, under the name of David, signifies the one who is from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3). The prophetic confession is directed to him, and it is a confession of divine praise, not of human iniquity.

The word “confession” usually indicates the confession of a penitent; here, however, it reveals the gratitude of one who praises. It is spoken with the whole heart because no other affection is joined to it. Therefore the words of his mouth have been heard. Whose mouth is meant, except the heart, from which the words themselves take their beginning? There the voice of the mind is heard by the ears of God.

(Verses 1–2.) “In the presence of the angels I will sing praise to you. I will worship toward your holy temple, and I will confess your name, because of your mercy and your truth.” If we sing psalms to God spiritually, in true exultation of heart, we sing before the angels, because we savor heavenly things rather than earthly ones; and in this religious service angelic blessedness excels. For carnal desires sing only before human beings, whose minds do not raise themselves above earthly things and who cannot share in the joys of the saints, since they do not worship toward God’s holy temple, which is Jerusalem—at once mother and daughter: mother in the angels, daughter in human beings, to whom it is said, “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. III, 17). Religious confession, moreover, proclaims the truth and mercy of God: truth in judging, mercy in helping. For these are not different ways by which he comes to us, nor different ways by which he raises us to himself.

“Because you have magnified your holy name above us.” The Lord magnified his holy name above all: above Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; above the twelve tribes of Israel, whom, rescued from the yoke of slavery, he brought into the promised land; and above all the nations, from which, as from stones, he daily raises up children for Abraham (Matt. III, 9), “so that at the name of the Lord Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 10–11).

[Note: [Col. 0393D] Perhaps “above all,” as is resumed in the explanation, or “above everything,” as in Augustine and in our Vulgate; although all our printed editions have “above us.”]

(Verses 3.) “On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly.” Why quickly? Because you yourself said, “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. LVIII, 9). Why quickly? Because I do not strive toward different things, nor desire what is superfluous; rather, what you have taught me to ask, that I desire to be granted to me. “You will multiply me in my soul, with great strength.” This is an expressed vow according to desire and cleansed of every carnal longing. If he had said only, “You will multiply me,” some earthly conception might have seemed to be intended; but when he added, “in righteousness,” nothing fuller or more perfect could be requested, since the designation “strength” signifies the highest good.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] In Augustine, here reads “in strength,” as also above [Col. 0394D] in the text of the verse.]

(Verses 4.) “Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, Lord, because they have heard all the words of your mouth.” The Gospel will be preached everywhere (Matt. XXIV, 14); apostolic teaching will be learned everywhere. “For their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5). Let all the kings of the earth, then, confess to you, Lord; and because they have no need to desire higher things, let them praise you for the excellence you have given them, since they can no longer fail to see that their scepters are your gifts.

(Verses 5.) “And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, because the glory of the Lord is great.” In which ways, if not those of which it is said, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10)? Thus, since all God’s works are brought to completion in these, no one may glory except in his glory.

(Verses 6.) “For the Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble, but he recognizes the proud from afar.” Both the humble and the exalted are beneath the Lord’s eyes. But because the humble pleases him, he sees the humble as near; the proud, because he displeases him, he recognizes as far away. And although he is near to those who are troubled in heart (Ps. III, 19), “salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. CXVIII, 155).

(Verses 7.) “If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will give me life.” If, he says, I do not love present things, and if, while reaching toward your promises, I do not cling to earthly allurements, you will give me life and hear me quickly, because temporal things bring me tribulation, while eternal hope invites me. “You have stretched out your hand over the anger of my enemies, and your right hand has saved me.” The protection of your arm, he says, defends me from my enemies; and so that I would not be overcome by adversities, your right hand— which freed me from all things on the left—has accomplished this.

(Verses 8.) “Lord, repay on my behalf.” I, he says, am a debtor and cannot be freed by the terms of my own debt (1 Cor. VII, 21);

[Note: [Col. 0394D] Perhaps *condictione*; nevertheless all the printed editions have *conditione*.] you, Lord, will repay on my behalf, since you owe nothing. You kill death by dying, paying what is mine so that I may follow what is yours. “Lord, your mercy is forever; do not despise the works of your hands.” I seek, he says, that mercy by which you rescue me from temporal things and lead me to eternal things, Lord. “Do not despise the works of your hands”: for whether in the fact that we are human beings, or in the fact that we have been changed and justified from our impiety, we are the works of your hands, by which you both create and renew us.

499. PSALM CXXXVIII

(Verses 1–2.) “Lord, you have examined me and known me. You have known my sitting down and my rising up.” In the prophecy of the psalm, these are the words of the Lord Jesus Christ, who, although according to his divinity he is conformed and equal to the Father (John X, 30), nevertheless, according to the fact that “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14) and assumed the appearance of a servant, will say to the Father, “Lord,” since he is both Father and Lord to him: Father of the form of God, Lord of the form of a servant. “You have examined and known me,” not because he did not know him, but because he had made him known to others. To sit is to be humbled; to rise, to be exalted. Hence the Lord sat in his passion and rose in his resurrection. What you willed, Lord, he says, you approved; and therefore it happened, because it pleased you. But if anyone prefers to receive the voice of the Head as spoken in the person of the body, let him understand it as the confession of penitents, who sit through the humility of repentance and rise through the justification of forgiveness.

[Col. 0395B] (Verses 3–4.) “You have understood my thoughts from afar; you have investigated my path and my limit. And you have foreseen all my ways.” Here let us recognize the voice of that younger son who, after squandering his father’s substance, had departed into a distant land, representing the nations that had declined into the worship of idols, and who at last, coming to his senses, said, “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke XV, 11). When he returned, his father ran to meet him, because he had understood his thoughts from afar. “You investigated my path,” he says, the path by which I departed, “and my limit,” the point to which I came, because you enclosed the deserter everywhere by your presence. Therefore you allowed me to labor along my own ways, so that, if I did not wish to remain miserable forever, I might return to your ways. “For there is no deceit in my tongue.” I confess, he says, that it was useful for me, after departing from you, to be crushed by miseries; for if I had been well without you, perhaps I would not have wished to return to you.

(Verses 5.) “Behold, Lord, you have known all things, the last and the ancient.” The ancient sin by which we fell in our first parents, and the final punishment which, through many labors and under the common condition of mortality, we all pay.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] The Lyons and Louvain editions read “of immortality.” The Douai and Cologne editions read “of mortality,” which is better. Augustine here says, “when we came into this laborious and perilous mortality.”]

“You formed me and placed your hand upon me.” All are formed by God in their mothers’ wombs, under that law which the human race endures deservedly because of its pride: the hand of divine power is placed upon it, pressing down the exalted so that it may raise up the humble.

(Verses 6.) “Your knowledge has been made wonderful because of me; it has prevailed, and I cannot reach it.” My pride and departure, he says, caused my heart to be darkened, so that your judgments could not be open to me. For while I delighted in the freedom of my own power, I became more needy and more vulnerable. This difficulty grew strong from me and in me; through myself I was placed outside the light of your knowledge, to which I cannot return except through you.

(Verses 7.) “Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face?” No place is found for one departing from the Spirit of God that is empty of his presence and power. No one flees his anger except the one who flees to him when he is angry (Sent. 235).

[Col. 0396A] (Verses 8.) “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.” If I rise exalted to heaven, I find you resisting me; if I choose the things beneath me, I experience you pursuing me. For just as it is evil for me to be raised up through presumption, so it is evil to sink down through despair.

(Verses 9.) “If I take my wings in a straight direction and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea.” He is already using good counsel who considers taking his wings—namely, the twofold supports of charity, by which he will fly straight—and dwelling at the ends of the sea, that is, at the end of this age. Thus, with the whole attention of his mind made vigilant by the conclusion of temporal life, he will no longer be occupied by empty desires but will be able to fly away from this age toward God’s promises. But who accomplishes this by his own powers unless the one who commands also helps? Therefore what follows says:

(Verses 10.) “For there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will bring me.” Considering the length of the journey and fearing the outcome of his labor, he adds:

(Verses 11–12.) “And I said, ‘Perhaps darkness will trample me’:” that is, perhaps I will be overcome by adversities and become ever more darkened if I do not reach the end of perseverance. “And night will be illumination in my delights. For darkness will not be darkened by you, and night will be illumined as day; as its darkness is, so also is its light.” The time of my labor, he says, is the time of night, yet the splendor of your grace illumines it. “For your word has become a lamp for my steps” (Ps. CXVIII, 105), so that what had been darkness for me might begin to be delight, because the darkness that is darkened by itself receives light from you. For this reason you scourge those who perform works of darkness: so that, blinded by the pleasure of temporal delights, we may not fail to desire eternal goods. At night you habitually shine upon us and make it like day when, through harsh remedies, you call us to life, so that the father’s scourges may be sweet and the father’s judgment may not be bitter.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] Augustine wrote “the judgment of the judge.” Hence we conjecture that an error may have entered the Prosperian manuscripts, where “the judgment of the father” is read.]

Since both the adversities and the favorable circumstances of this life are not without the temptation by which we are either lifted up or pressed down, both become night if that light is absent which permits us neither to grow proud nor to fall into despair.

(Verses 13.) “For you possessed my reins, Lord.” You, Lord, he says, possess not only my flesh but also my reins; and because you dwell within me, it has come about that some light delights me in the night. “You received me from my mother’s womb.” The one who set apart the apostle Paul from his mother’s womb (Gal. I, 15) also set us apart from the womb of our mother—that Babylon of ours—from which, regenerated into a new life, we rejoice in a new hope, new delights, and new light.

[Note: [Col. 0396D] All printed editions read “from the womb of his mother.” This is an obvious error, which we do not hesitate to correct on the support of Augustine’s reading alone.]

For neither does the prosperity of this age make us blessed, nor does adversity make us miserable, if we love true and lasting goods.

(Verses 14.) “I will confess to you, because you have been wondrously terrible; your works are wonderful, and my soul knows them exceedingly well.” Your miracles of grace, he says, strike terror into me; and from the source of joy comes the cause of fear. For my soul knows how greatly you work to save and what dangers I must avoid lest I perish.

(Verses 15.) “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret.” There is in holy people of God a certain unconquerable strength and undefeated patience, which God secretly formed in them and made hidden, possessing an osseous firmness that is neither corrupted by prosperity nor broken by adversity. Of this virtue another psalm says, “Nevertheless my soul is subject to God, because my patience is from him” (Ps. LXI, 6). “And my substance in the lower parts of the earth.” In this fragile substance of a weak body, he says, which is in the lowest parts of the earth, he seeks the strength that would also grant perseverance to the flesh amid savage tribulations.

(Verses 16.) “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all will be written.” In these words the person of the Head is speaking, now in himself and now in his body, because “the two are one flesh” (Eph. V, 31). He therefore speaks of those whose steadfastness of patience had to be strengthened, so that they themselves might suffer for the Lord, who had faltered in his passion: “Your eyes saw my imperfection.” And because those who had trembled even to the point of despair were crowned, with you looking on, even with crowns of victory, he added, “And in your book all will be written.” Therefore all who are fearful and tremble because of their own weakness should hope for the help of heavenly power, so that charity may not fall away from the place where ability is granted.

“They will wander by day, and there will be no one among them.” Or, as it is found in certain manuscripts, “They will be formed by day, and there will be no one among them.” My imperfect ones, he says, all of whom will be in eternal life, “will wander by day,” that is, they will be troubled in me; and there will be no one among them whom the darkness of fear does not lead even to despair. But if we read, “They will be formed by day,” it should be understood that those among whom no one will be troubled will be formed by day—that is, by the illumination of that vision by which he restored blessed Peter, who was exceedingly fearful, to the remedy of patience through his gaze.

(Verses 17–18.) “But your friends, God, have been greatly honored by me; their authority has been greatly strengthened. I will count them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand.” Those, he says, who wandered by day and among whom there was no one who was troubled have become my friends and exceedingly honorable, and they have held authority over the whole Church. Although they have been counted by me, they will nevertheless be multiplied beyond the sand, because both their number and their glory increase without limit.

“I arose, and I am still with you.” This signifies the time during which he is still hidden at the right hand of the Father, before he is revealed in that majesty in which he will judge the living and the dead. Hence he goes on to say what takes place in the Church throughout this entire intervening time: he formed it hidden, subject to the mixture of good and evil and to all the afflictions of temporal life, while their coming is delayed.

(Verses 19–20.) “If you kill sinners, Lord, men of blood, depart from me. What you say in thought, they will receive in vanity in their cities.” The proud are killed when they are abandoned by God’s grace. To the thoughts of the humble and of those who preserve unity, the Lord says secretly, “Men of blood, depart from me”; and openly, in the manifestation of his judgment, he will say, “I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matt. VII, 23).

[Note: [Col. 0397D] Perhaps one should read “and of those who preserve unity,” although all printed editions have “in unity.” For Saint Augustine here directed his judgment against the Donatists, who, inflated in the name of righteousness, persuaded the people, after breaking the bond of unity, to follow them as though they were more righteous, while blind and ignorant. . . . Among these the wheat of Christ groaned, preserving the bond of unity.]

But who are the men of blood except those who hate their brothers? As John says, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III, 15). These, therefore, withdrawing through pride from the unity of the Church, who, as though offended by the mixture of chaff, abandon the wheat before the winnowing fan of judgment, “will receive their cities in vanity,” that is, they will gather themselves into a rejected association and into empty councils. For whoever does not practice catholic charity is scattered by heretical vanity.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] The Douai and Cologne editors had placed “is not united” in the margin.]

(Verses 21–22.) “Have I not hated those who hate you, Lord, and wasted away over your enemies? I hated them with perfect hatred; they became enemies to me.” Perfect love of the Lord consists in not loving what he does not love, and in hating God’s enemies in such a way that their perversity, rather than their nature, is hateful. For one thing in them is what they themselves do, and another is what the Creator established. This is to hate perfectly—that is, knowingly: neither to hate human beings because of their vices, nor to love vices because of human beings (Sent. 65).

(Verses 23–24.) “Examine me, Lord, and know my heart; question me and know my paths. And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the eternal way.” Scrutinize my paths, he says—that is, test and examine my plans and thoughts, the disposition with which I love the good and the spirit in which I endure the wicked. “And lead me in the eternal way.”

[Note: [Col. 0398D] Here something seems to be lacking for completeness of sense. Perhaps what is found in Augustine himself, or something of it: “What else does he say but, ‘Lead me in Christ’? For who is the eternal way except he who is eternal life? For eternal is he who said, ‘I am the way,’ etc.”]

Unless it is the one who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6), and who is “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II, 5), through whom we have access to the Father and who is the advocate for our sins (1 John II, 1–2).

PSALM CXXXIX

[Col. 0398D]

(Verses 1.) “To the end. A psalm for David himself.” The end must be understood as none other than the one declared by the Apostle when he says, “For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4). Therefore, by its title the psalm indicates from where it will speak; for by saying “for David” it signifies the one who is according to the flesh “from the seed of David” (Rom. I, 3). Thus he is not speaking according to his divinity, by which he is the Creator not only of David but also of visible and invisible natures; rather, according to the flesh he deigned to be David’s son, so that his whole body, that is, the Church, might use the help of its Head, and every member of it might say in his voice:

(Verses 2.) “Rescue me, Lord, from an evil man; deliver me from an unjust man.” He does not wish to be rescued from one evil person only, but from one class of evil people; nor merely from their vessels, but from the prince himself, that is, from the devil himself, who wishes to be freed from injustice. For the Apostle says, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. VI, 12), that is, against the rulers of sinners, over whom presides and dominates the instigator of all wickedness.

The evil man is the same as the unjust man. No unjust person is free from wickedness, and among differing sins the sinner bears one and the same name. Even if someone sins in such a way as to refrain from harming others, nevertheless, by harming himself in whatever manner, he is not innocent.

504. (Verses 3.) “They conceived injustices in their heart; all day long they prepared wars.” Open iniquity is less harmful than concealed iniquity; and that enemy is more treacherous who carries good things on his lips but hides evil in the innermost chambers of his mind. In such secret places nothing is prepared except wars—that is, things are arranged that are hostile and opposed to the good, because continuous wars are waged against every vice by the virtues.

[Col. 0399C] (Verses 4.) “They sharpened their tongue like serpents; the poison of asps is under their lips.” There is no doubt what sort of people are compared to serpents: they creep gently, without noise or sound, but they insinuate themselves harmfully.

(Verses 5.) “Preserve me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner, and rescue me from unjust people who have thought to trip up my steps.” All the wicked, whether hidden or manifest, must indeed be carefully avoided, lest they create danger or inflict harm. But their cunning must be feared above all lest they make us their companions and lead our steps from the straight way into their paths and practices. This is the most savage kind of tripping, when the faithful and devout, abandoning their good purpose, pass over into imitation of the impious.

[Col. 0399D] (Verses 6.) “The proud hid a snare for me, and they stretched ropes into a trap for my feet.” He has briefly described the whole body of the devil by saying “the proud.” For this is why they want to appear righteous although they are unjust, and why they flee nothing so much as confession of sins. Although they are false righteous people, they envy the truly righteous, because they resent having their own simulation exposed by the latter’s sincerity. They therefore do everything by the art of deceit to overthrow the steps of the good and make them their imitators, though they grieve that these are better than themselves, to their own condemnation. The deceits of the wicked are called ropes because, lying in wait for the steps of the upright, they add evil to evil and weave sins together with sins.

(Verses 6–7.) “Beside the paths they placed a stumbling block for me. I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God.’” The paths of the righteous are the commandments of God. The wicked cannot establish stumbling blocks within them, but they stretch their snares beside them and attach things resembling the truth to the true things, so that they may not appear to depart from the law of righteousness. Let us therefore not depart from the paths, and the snares will not harm us. But the one who walks along the way of God’s commandments should say to the Lord, “You are my God.” This voice properly belongs to the righteous, although God is also the God of the wicked. Yet they are not helped by this confession so long as they are subject to the Lord by necessity rather than by will.

(Verses 7–8.) “Receive with your ears the voice of my supplication, Lord, Lord, the strength of my salvation.” Although he might seem correctly to have said, “Receive with your ears my supplication”—that is, not a sound, which animals also possess, but a voice, which belongs to those who hope and live—for sounds belong to the underworld, whereas voices belong only to living things—the great feeling of the one praying is nevertheless shown when he repeats the title “Lord” and professes that the cause of his salvation is not in himself but in the Lord’s strength.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] All printed editions read “rather to say.” But an easy error may have entered where “could have been read” was intended, without any addition and with a slight change of letters. The Douai and Cologne editors had already understood this and noted it in the margin.]

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Perhaps “of those who breathe” would be better read, since Augustine explains “the voice of my supplication” as “the life of my supplication”: not what sounds in my words, but that from which my words live. A voice properly belongs to beings endowed with breath; it belongs to the living. How many, however, supplicate God without perceiving God or thinking rightly about God? They can have the sound of supplication, but they cannot have the voice, because life is absent from it.]

“You overshadowed my head in the day of battle.” The present life, which is wholly temptation, is the day of battle (Job VII, 1), because whether outwardly or inwardly there is never a lack of adversity against which one must struggle. Therefore, laboring in this battle, he rightly asks for the shadowing protection of God’s grace, lest, wearied by the heat of his labors, he wither.

(Verses 9.) “Do not hand me over to my desire, to the sinner.” He therefore said that he was overshadowed in the day of battle so that he would not be burned by the heat of desire. Whoever is overcome by this is handed over to the sinner and subjected to an adverse power. For persistence in evil will leads into a snare, from which the one whose desire is calmed by heavenly protection is delivered. “They have thought against me; do not abandon me, lest perhaps they be exalted.” The thought of those who oppose is fraudulent; but so that it may not harm me, he says, do not abandon me, lest they rejoice at my humiliation.

[Col. 0400D] (Verses 10.) “The head of their circuit; the labor of their lips will cover them.” May me, he says, the shadow of your wings cover in the day of battle. But they will labor to cover themselves with their lie, and this will be the head of their circuitous course. For the enemies of truth will never rest in their inventions. Wishing to cover themselves with their lies, they labor so as to be entangled in labors that cannot be brought to an end, because they will not be able to conceal themselves unless they labor the lie of their lips.

[Note: [Col. 0401D] Thus the Louvain, Douai, and old Lyons editions: “the lie by the labor of their lips.” The more recent Lyons edition: “let them labor with the lie of their lips.”]

(Verses 11.) “Burning coals will fall upon them; you will cast them down upon the earth.” Just as the preaching of Christ’s cross was for some “the fragrance of life unto life,” and for others “the fragrance of death unto death” (1 Cor. II, 16), so these coals are the work of Christ, which can both illumine the faithful and punish sinners. This punishment of the wicked occurs on earth, that is, in this age and in this life: the fire of temporal punishment falls upon them before the eternal fire comes. “They will not endure in miseries.” Overcome, he says, by tribulations they will fall and will not endure, because they will not be corrected by the wounds they deserve but will become worse.

506. (Verses 12.) “The man of a talkative tongue will not be established upon the earth.” The talkative person does not grasp knowledge of the truth; for, always loving to speak, he cannot be instructed. His perverse pursuits therefore will not be established, because ignorant loquacity prefers to teach rather than to learn.

“Evil will hunt the unjust man to destruction.” Evils will come, and the unjust will not endure; when they are overwhelmed by some calamity, they perish. For they do not suffer the evils that befall them for the sake of righteousness; and therefore they will not endure, because in their miseries they can sustain no confidence in a good hope.

(Verses 13.) “I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy and [will act] in the cause of the poor; he shows [it] to the wicked.” The poor are the humble, always sighing with holy desire, who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. V, 3, 6). They will be filled; God does not neglect their cause, and in their glory the wicked will see what they have lost (Wis. V, 3, etc.).

[Note: [Col. 0401D] All the ancient editions have “into the cause of the poor”; a later edition has “the cause of the poor,” as it is read in Augustine’s work. We can scarcely conjecture how the words “he shows to the wicked” entered here, since they are absent from Augustine, from both the Roman and Gallican versions of Jerome, and from the Hebrew text—unless perhaps they came from Augustine’s text, where, after quoting this verse, “For the Lord will execute judgment for the needy and the cause of the poor,” he immediately adds in explanation, “He will show the wicked how he loves the righteous.” Prosper nevertheless seems to refer to this when at the end of his exposition he says that in the glory of the righteous the impious will see what they have lost.]

(Verses 14.) “Nevertheless, the righteous will confess your name; the upright will dwell with your face.” The righteous, he says, will be glorified and enriched with eternal blessedness; yet they will claim none of your works for their own merits. They will confess to you the works of your mercy and attribute all their good to your grace. In this they will dwell with your face, that is, they will possess the eternal vision of your face. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. V, 8).

PSALM CXL

(Verses 1.) “Lord, I cried to you; hear me. Attend to the voice of my supplication when I cry to you.” The prayer of Christ’s body is not separated from the Head, who remains in the nature assumed from his members and makes the whole Church pray, saying through the Lord, “I cried to you”—not with a loud voice but with strong faith. Nor, because you have heard me, will I cease crying out, since my condition in humility is such that, while tribulations do not cease, I always rejoice to be helped.

[Col. 0401D] (Verses 2.) “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands an evening sacrifice.” Every Christian recognizes that this must be understood of the Head himself. As the day declined toward evening, the Lord gave up his spirit on the cross (Matt. XXVII, 50), to be joined again to the body, so that the hope of all the faithful might not doubt that what had gone before in the Head would be fulfilled in itself. Above all burnt offerings, therefore, this sacrifice was offered; the hearts of the saints imitate it when, from the good fragrance of their prayers, an incense-like odor rises to God from the altar (Rev. V, 8; VIII, 3).

Its offering does not occur without that confession which Christ made in the person of his body, saying, “The words of my offenses” (Ps. XXI, 2), so that we might recognize that confession of sins is always necessary for us, since we acknowledge that it is present in us through the voice of the one who assumed us.

(Verses 3.) “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.” Surely the Head needs this protection and fortification? But he pleads the cause of his body and asks for what belongs to the members and will benefit them. For the one who says, “Whatever you did for one of these, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40), and who said to the one persecuting the Church, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4), is himself the one who asks in the person of his own people and says, “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.”

(Verses 4.) “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to excuse excuses in sins, with people who work iniquity.” He therefore asks that a guard be placed over the mouth of the faithful and that it be fortified with the door of restraint, so that it may be neither closed to confessing sins nor open to excusing them. For there are people who do not wish their crimes to be charged to themselves; they attribute the burdens of evil habit to the necessity of nature, defending the crimes of their will by accusing their condition. The man who belongs to Christ’s body does not wish to associate with them, saying, “I will not share with their chosen ones.” That is, I will not join myself to those whom they hold as foremost in these excuses—people swollen with a certain knowledge, defending the cause of crimes as though they were more learned, lest the sins that have been committed appear to belong to human beings rather than to the stars. Thus the name “chosen” is, among the good, a gift of grace; among the wicked, a lie of pride. Even after losing their innocence, they boast in defending the crimes they have committed.

[Col. 0402D] (Verses 5.) “The righteous will correct me in mercy and rebuke me.” The correction of the righteous is not the savagery of hatred but the medicine of charity, which does not praise the delinquent but reproves him. The severe mercy of the righteous is better than the flattering praise of the sinner, concerning which it is said, “But may the oil of the sinner not fatten my head.” Let false praise, he says, not delight the innermost consciousness of my heart, because I would rather be reproved than deceived. For who will boast that he has a pure heart or is clean from sin (Prov. XX, according to the Septuagint), since daily the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V, 17)? Let him know that what he suffers while desiring belongs to himself, but that what overcomes the rebellion belongs to grace.

“For my prayer is still in their good pleasure.” The prayer of Christ—whether the prayer he taught (Matt. VI, 9), or the prayer by which he intercedes for us daily (Heb. VII, 25)—will still please those who think our confession laughable, by which we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12). For this supplication grows strong throughout the whole world; and those who falsely justify themselves will prove that this is true wisdom among human beings: that no one presume upon himself, but that “the one who boasts should boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. I, 31).

508.
