(Verses 6.) “Their judges were swallowed up beside the rock.” Their judges—that is, their teachers, who claim judgment for themselves on the basis of worldly doctrines—are swallowed up if they are compared with the rock, that is, with Christ. They are swallowed up in the sense that they will have no place but will fail in their own vanity, because even if they say something right and true, it belongs not to any human being but to truth itself.

“They will hear my words, because they have prevailed.” The Gospel of truth will be overcome by no persecution. The impious will yield, the talkative will yield, and the abilities of those who oppose will make teachers of Christ’s disciples. Exiles, confiscations, deaths, and the cross itself will not frighten them, because my words will prevail, and through the sufferings of the martyrs the glory of triumphs will multiply.

(Verses 7.) “As the thickness of the earth is broken up upon the earth, our bones have been scattered beside hell.” Through the deaths of the martyrs and the blood of the holy who were slain, whose bones were scattered, the earth has been made rich. Just as fields receive the power of fertility from ashes, dung, and the cheapest refuse, so the whole world has been made fruitful by the blood of Christ’s slain witnesses, so that a harvest of martyrs might grow everywhere, and those who were reckoned for hell might be grafted into heaven.

(Verses 8.) “For my eyes are toward you, Lord; in you I have hoped; do not take away my soul.” Against the savagery of persecutors, a voice is raised to the Lord by those placed in tribulation, lest the cruelty of sufferings overcome the strength of faith. Endurance is therefore requested, so that love of God may be stronger than the magnitude of punishment.

(Verses 9.) “Guard me from the snare they have set for me, and from the stumbling blocks of those who work iniquity.” What was the snare except the persecutor’s voice saying, “If you consent, I will spare you,” so that through the food of present life one might enter the traps of eternal death? And what were the stumbling blocks except the examples of those who fell, whose impious failure weighed heavily upon the endurance of those who persevered?

(Vers. 10.) Sinners will fall into his net—not because his own righteousness has given anyone the virtue of not falling, since the grace of God has crowned many even from among the ungodly with martyrdom; but they are said to be about to fall because this fall also makes sinners of those who seemed to be righteous. I alone am, until I pass over. Christ alone is the strength of the martyrs, for whose sake no one died before he himself died, as he says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32); and, “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, has died, it remains alone; but if it has died, it bears much fruit” (ibid., 24). Before, therefore, he died and, rising again, passed over to the Father, he was alone and had no companions in his passion; afterward they grew from the fruitfulness of the one grain into a multiplied harvest.

## PSALM 141

(Vers. 2.) With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I entreated the Lord. What he said by “I cried,” he explained by saying, “I entreated with my voice”—that is, with inward feeling, not with the voice of the body, but of the mind.

(Vers. 3.) I pour out my prayer in his presence—that is, in the secrecy of the heart, which God alone hears and sees, in which chamber, with the door closed, we are commanded to pray (Matthew VI, 6), lest our innermost places lie open to the tempter. For there are two things by which the inner parts of a human being are especially assailed: love and fear. By these twin movements the mind is either opened or closed. But when what it desires or fears is earthly, it offers the devil an entrance; when, however, it savors the things that are above, not the things that are on earth (Colossians III, 1–2), God is received and the tempter excluded.

I declare my tribulation before him. What was said, “in his presence,” means also “before him”; but the repetition shows how incessantly he does this, and how he does nothing without God, always professing that God is both his helper and his witness.

(Vers. 4.) When my spirit failed within me. This is a confession of humility, [Col. 0403] by which the one who does not fail in tribulation becomes strong.

**Note:** Thus the Lyon edition. The Louvain and Douai editions read, “because he becomes strong”; the Cologne edition, “because he may become strong.”

For he would be conquered who did not acknowledge his spirit to be weak, because the one who is led by the Spirit of God is not puffed up by his own spirit.

And you knew my paths. “Toward what,” he says, “my desire tends, and toward what end all my actions hasten, is not hidden from your knowledge, because you know that my paths are your mercies.” The knowledge of God, however, is the salvation of the one who is known by him; for he does not know God in whom he does not find his works and gifts.

On this way by which I walked, they hid snares for me. The way of all the saints is Christ, in whom those who wish to live devoutly suffer persecution (II Timothy III, 12). For “the cross of Christ is indeed a stumbling block to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles” (I Corinthians I, 23). Those, therefore, who oppose Christ think that they are placing a stumbling block in the way when they reproach Christians with the name of the crucified one. But when they did not frighten the steps of the faithful away from his Gospel, they could place no snares in the way; for falsehood does not lie hidden in truth, nor can darkness lurk in the light. Accordingly, it is spoken according to the intention of those lying in wait: they hid snares in the way, because, though they beset everything nearby with their frauds, they could harm no one walking along the way.

(Vers. 5.) I looked to the right and saw, and there was no one who knew me. The things of God and those that lead to God’s promises are on the right; the mind of the one enduring persecution does not turn away from them. Thus, as he gazes upon these things that are on the right, he sees and receives the rewards promised to those who persevere; he attains steadfastness in endurance and love of God, lest he be overcome. Yet no one knows this intention, because it is impossible for a human being to look into the innermost places of another’s heart. Hence he had rightly said to God, “You knew my paths” (verse 4).

Flight has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul. Surrounded by persecutors, he lost the freedom of flight, which he could have used without sin if, while faith remained, his limbs had clung to the punishments. But since in the purpose of his mind he fears falling more than punishment, flight has perished from him who prefers to endure every form of savagery rather than yield. He said, moreover, in view of the multitude of his persecutors, that there was no one who sought his soul, because, apart from God’s gift, no human consolation can offer anyone such protection that faith may remain unharmed amid pressing evils.

(Vers. 6.) I cried to you, Lord; I said, “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living.” He shows from where he endured the greatness of his tribulations: namely, because both here his entire hope is God and in the future his entire reward is God, who will be “all in all” (I Corinthians XV, 28).

[Col. 0405C] (Vers. 7.) Attend to my supplication, because I have been humbled exceedingly. Deliver me from those who persecute me. The humiliation is excessive, and the persecution excessive; only God’s protection overcomes its force. He can indeed grant the saints that their adversaries have no power over them, but he grants something more marvelous by enabling them to overcome every suffering. In persecutors, however, we must beware not only of human hatreds, but much more of the hostility of evil spirits, who secretly attack God’s righteous through the activity of their servants. Of them the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, and powers, and the rulers of this world of darkness” (Ephesians VI, 12). And whom do the wicked have as their ruler, except the devil, while the faithful have none but Christ?

How have they grown strong against me? This is the voice of the Church lamenting that the number of the ungodly has greatly increased, that iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold (Matthew XXIV, 12).

(Vers. 8.) Lead my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name. All distresses and confinements of troubles make a prison, because they constrict the soul and take away its freedom. But the very habitation of the body may be understood as a prison—not because what God made is evil, for he created all things good (Genesis I, 31), but because “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” (Wisdom IX, 15). He desires his soul to be led out not from the body, but from the corruption of the body, so that no necessity of mortality may hinder his confession of God’s praise.

The righteous await me until you repay me. The whole psalm is concluded by the voice of the head, to whom what his members suffer is attributed, and in whom the whole Church will be glorified. It awaits the author of blessed rewards, who says to the Father: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24).

## PSALM 142

(Vers. 1.) Lord, hear my prayer; listen with your ears to my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness. The title of the psalm indicates the passion of Christ, for he is the true David, who in himself and in his own people endures the persecution of false brothers and false sons.

**Note:** The title of this psalm is: “For David himself, when his son was persecuting him.”

Therefore both the head in the body and the body in the head cry out to God—that is, the Church in Christ and Christ in the Church. And when, in prayer, he asks to be heard in God’s righteousness, he expresses God’s grace in a wondrous confession, lest anyone suppose that his prayer is received on account of his own righteousness. Whatever good he deserves is from God, and a sinner cannot do good unless he has been justified by the one who justifies no human being except through the forgiveness of sins.

(Vers. 2.) And do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no living person will be justified in your sight. He quickly made clear why he did not wish to compare himself with divine righteousness and feared being judged by God: “Because no living person will be justified in your sight.” How could I presume upon innocence, when I must be convicted by you of injustice? Or what good of my own could I claim, when I possess nothing that you have not given?

I therefore dread being examined and fear being judged, because no one living in this mortal flesh can truthfully say that he does not bear the contagion of sin, since even the chief rams of Christ’s sheep are commanded to pray in such a way as to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI, 12).

**Note:** The printed editions had “of righteousness,” an obvious scribal error, since the sense of the passage demands otherwise and the words seem to correspond to Augustine, who says: “Let us not litigate; I do not want to have a case with you, so that I may put forward my righteousness and you may convict me of my iniquity.”

(Vers. 3.) For the enemy has persecuted my soul; he has humbled my life to the ground. They have placed me in dark places, like the dead of the ages. This is appropriately understood both of the body and of the head: the devil persecuted the soul of Christ, and Judas the soul of the Master. The same devil remains to persecute the body of Christ, nor is Judas absent, succeeding in false brothers.

For what does any adversary do to us except cause us, once heavenly hope has been abandoned, to fall to the earth? Against them we must therefore keep watch, so that we may be able to say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III, 20).

What, then, is meant by “They have placed me in darkness, like the dead of the ages,” more suitably than in the Lord, who alone was free among the dead (Psalm LXXXVII, 6) and was “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah LIII, 12)? He was the one who could properly and uniquely say: “In me no iniquity has been found” (Psalm XVI, 3).

**Note:** This word seems superfluous to us here, although it appears in all the printed editions.

(Vers. 4.) My spirit was distressed within me. The Lord is recognized when he says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew XXVI, 38). In that sorrow we too were present, because that sadness belonged to our nature, and our old self was crucified on the cross together with him (Romans VI, 6).

**Note:** Following Augustine, the later Lyon edition reads, “was crucified together with him on the cross,” whereas the earlier Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read, “was crucified together with him to the cross.”

My heart was troubled within me. This disturbance was voluntary, and in him alone remained the purpose of his mercy. The others withdrew, not understanding the mystery of his great compassion and not believing that he would rise again, even though he was being subjected to passion and death.

(Vers. 5.) I remembered the days of old, and I kept the eternal years in mind, and I meditated on all your works.

**Note:** These words, “and I kept the eternal years in mind,” appear to have been transferred here from Psalm LXXVI, verse 6. They are absent from Augustine at this point and from the scriptural text of this psalm. Yet Saint Prosper may perhaps refer to them when, in his exposition of the verse, he says, “and the remembrance of all times.” Hence it may be conjectured that this part was inserted here by him.

This remembrance of the days of old, this recollection of all times, and the contemplation of God’s works in them, belongs not to the sense of the head but to that of the body. For what has ever been unseen by the author of all things, with whom both past things are present and future things are already accomplished?

Thus, through the voice of the members, God’s grace is proclaimed, and the Church’s tongue confesses the works of God’s mercy. Reviewing the succession of the whole age, she finds that nothing subsists except by God’s providence and goodness, and that all things were created by him, renewed in him and through him, because “the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Corinthians V, 17).

I meditated on the works of your hands. And I stretched out my hands toward you. “My meditation,” he says, “by which I saw that every good thing flows from your goodness, and that whatever in us can please your righteousness is the work of your doing, strengthened me to place all my hope in you and to seek from you in all things the nourishment of your dew.”

(Vers. 6–7.) My soul is like land without water before you; hear me swiftly, Lord; my spirit has failed. “Let the dryness of my soul,” he says, “thirst for you, because it desires to be watered by you. You have kindled the heat of my heart so that I may ask to be heard swiftly.” For my spirit has failed, so that your Spirit may fill me; and you have made me poor in spirit so that you may grant me what you promised to the humble, whose is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew V, 3).

Do not turn your face away from me, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit. When you turned your face away from me, I was troubled and became like land without water. Since, then, you awakened desire, restore your presence, lest, with your face turned away from me, I become like those who descend into the pit.

And who are these, except those of whom it is said: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises them” (Proverbs XVIII, 3)—that is, he is not converted? Descending into this depth, they fall into the pit of eternal misery because through stubborn pride they have lost the remedies of confession and repentance.

(Vers. 8.) Make me hear your mercy in the morning, because I have hoped in you. “Let the light of your mercy,” he says, “arise within me, and let what I have believed come to pass, so that the hope conceived through hearing may be fulfilled.” Make known to me, Lord, the way in which I should walk. Let your truth be my guide, and let your grace direct my steps, because I have lifted up my soul to you—not presuming on myself, but asking you to help me.

(Vers. 9.) Deliver me from my enemies, Lord, because I have fled to you. He desires to be rescued from those enemies through whom even human hatreds are stirred up—that is, from the devil and his angels, who are “the rulers of darkness” (Ephesians VI, 12) and instigators of the ungodly. Fleeing from them, he takes refuge with the Lord, lest he follow the example of the old human being, who, troubled by an evil conscience, hid himself from the face of the Lord.

**Note:** The Cologne edition reads *humana odio*; the more recent Lyon edition, *humano odio*; the older Lyon edition, Louvain, and Douai editions, *humana odia*.

(Vers. 10.) Teach me to do your will, because you are my God. “Fill me,” he says, “with the affection of your grace, so that I may will what I know you will, and so that nothing may be present in my work except what is in your will.” I ask this because you are my God, who works all things in all people (I Corinthians XII, 6).

(Vers. 10–11.) Let your good Spirit lead me into a right land. For your name’s sake, Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness. Your good Spirit will rescue me from every error and lead me into the right land, which is the region of the living (Psalm CXIV, 9)—not on account of my merit, but for your name’s sake, because your mercy is the cause of every gift bestowed upon me.

(Vers. 11–12.) You will lead my soul out of tribulation, and in your mercy you will destroy my enemies. And you will destroy all those who trouble my soul, because I am your servant. How great is the dignity, how great the blessedness, of being God’s servant, to whom such things are granted without any preceding merit!

## PSALM 143

The title of the psalm touches upon the history of the deed by which Goliath, a mighty warrior, is recognized as having been overcome by the young David in single combat (I Samuel XVII, 4).

**Note:** In Augustine the title of the psalm is “For David himself, against Goliath”; in the Vulgate, “A psalm of David against Goliath.” Jerome writes it in the former way in the Roman translation and in the latter way in the Gallican.

But Goliath also signifies the devil, and David indicates Christ, who is also understood in his body, that is, the Church (I Corinthians XII, 27), because the members are in no way separated from the head. The psalm must therefore be understood in such a way that we recognize historical actions as figures of spiritual realities, and refer David’s victory, by which he struck down Goliath, to the Lord himself, who is from the seed of David (Romans I, 3), and to all his members.

**Note:** The Cologne edition has *Goliat*, whereas the earlier editions and Augustine himself write *Golias*, here and in what follows.

(Vers. 1.) Blessed is the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war. This is the voice of the members of Christ’s body, for whom divine help is always necessary to overcome Goliath, so that both hands and fingers may be taught, whether for battle or for war. The hands signify the fullness of every work; the fingers, however, signify a certain division of labors, so that all strength may pertain to carrying on wars, while the various kinds of battles pertain to the different parts of the mind’s virtues.

Accordingly, the Apostle makes clear with what weapons and defenses Christ’s soldiers are equipped, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in one Spirit, to another kinds of tongues, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually as he wills” (I Corinthians XII, 8ff.).

With these fingers, therefore, whether in war or in battle, Christ’s body fights and casts down every enemy, whether visible or invisible, by the throw of a stone—that is, by the solidity of Christ.

(Vers. 2.) My mercy, my refuge, my protector, and my deliverer. We rightly and truthfully say to the Lord, “My mercy,” because he not only has mercy on us, but also makes us [mercy], so that there may be no judgment without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy (James II, 13).

**Note:** We suspect that the reading should be *makes merciful*, although all our printed editions have *makes mercy*. In Augustine we read at this very place: “You provide me with mercy, and you exist as merciful in me; or have you granted me that I too should be merciful? For the enemy is overcome by nothing so much as when we are merciful.”

He is a refuge from whom weakness receives restoration and awareness.

**Note:** Perhaps the reading should be “and confidence.”

He is a supporter who grants the one fighting that he may not fall. He is a deliverer who grants the one engaged in combat that he may not be wounded. For this reason he adds and says: “My protector, and in him I have hoped, who subdues my people beneath me.”

This seems to have been spoken by the voice of the head: “Who subdues the people beneath me”—that is, “You subject the Church to me through faith.” By the voice of the body, however, it may be understood as referring to any spiritual warrior who confesses that, through the help of grace, the rebellious people of desires and the movement of carnal longings have been subjected to the law of his mind.

(Vers. 3.) Lord, what is a human being, that you have made yourself known to him; or the son of a human being, that you regard him? Human dignity is great: he was created by God so as to know his creator, and was valued so highly that God’s Only-Begotten would pour out his blood for his redemption.

**Note:** Perhaps the text should read, “was created so as to know his creator, and was valued so highly that …”

(Vers. 4.) A human being has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow. Forgetful of his own nature, the human being was changed by voluntary transgression into the likeness of vanity, so that he who had been made for eternal things might exist among vanities—that is, among things that perish and do not endure—and that his days might pass like a shadow.

In comparison with eternal things, temporal things are indeed vain; nor are those things true which either cease to exist or lose what they are. Great, then, is God’s goodness and love toward human beings: he calls such a person to know him, considers him worthy to redeem at so great a price, and leads him out from the shadow of vanity. For “he who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things?” (Romans VIII, 32).

(Vers. 5–7.) Lord, bow your heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and they will smoke. Flash your flashes and scatter them; send out your arrows, and you will trouble them. Send your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from many waters.

The heavens are the preachers of truth who declare the glory of God (Psalm XVIII, 2). Through their bending down, and through their endurance of sufferings, the flashing of the Gospel becomes known to the world, and the lightning of miracles illuminates the hearts of believers. The mountains—that is, all who are elevated and swollen with pride—when God’s grace touches them, will smoke; and, kindled, they will send forth the vapor of their hearts with tears of confession.

God’s arrows are the words of God. By them the proud are scattered, and the unsound are struck so that, being rightly wounded, they may be healed. This is done through God’s hand sent from on high, because the arm of God (John XII, 38), which is Christ, became human, does not abandon the members of his body, and rescues his Church from many waters—that is, from unbelieving peoples, whether attacking from outside or lying in wait within.

(Vers. 7–8.) From the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. From whose hand did the Lord rescue the humility of David—that is, the humility of Christ’s body—if not from the hand of foreign sons?

All unbelievers are foreigners and are not counted among the adoption of God’s sons. Their mouth speaks vanity, because their tongue is alien to the confession of truth. Their right hand is iniquity, because they rejoice in unjust things and delight in crooked things as though they were right.

**Note:** Here the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions add the preposition *in*, which is absent from the Lyon edition.

(Vers. 9.) God, I will sing a new song to you; on a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing praise to you. The new song is the song of grace, of the new human being, and of the New Testament, sung on the ten-stringed instrument—that is, in the ten commandments of the Law. For singing is perfected in love; love is the fullness of the Law (Romans XIII, 10).

(Vers. 10.) You are the one who gives salvation to kings—that is, because you touch the mountains and they smoke, so that, humbled, they may submit to you with a confession of satisfaction. You are the one who redeems David your servant. Whoever is the body of Christ is not without the name of David, and for him there is a struggle against Goliath.

(Vers. 11.) Rescue me from the evil sword. It would not have been enough for him to say merely “from the sword” unless he had added “evil,” because there is certainly also a good sword, of which the Lord says: “I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew X, 34). The evil sword is the one that separates from Christ; the good sword is the one that cuts away from the world.

And rescue me from the hand of foreign sons, who use the evil sword. “The teeth of the sons of men are their weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm LVI, 5). Therefore the foreign sons are the evil sword; they are the many waters. For this reason he adds the same words he had said earlier, so that he may make more clearly known of whom he is speaking: “Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” What vanity the foreign sons speak, and what their right hand of iniquity is, the following words demonstrate.

(Vers. 12–14.) Whose sons are like young plants firmly established from their youth. Their daughters are arranged and adorned like the likeness of a temple. Their storerooms are full, overflowing from one thing into another. Their sheep are fertile, abundant in their offspring; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passage through it, and no cry in their streets.

This abundance and prosperity is common to the wicked and the good. But by the wicked it is held in the right hand, whereas by the good it is reckoned in the left—not because these things themselves are not also gifts of God, but because heavenly and eternal things surpass earthly and temporal things. And just as the saints use present things as though they did not use them (I Corinthians VII, 31), and possess them as though they did not possess them, so the foreign sons, who establish their right hand in transitory goods and slippery happiness, are not accused because of their wealth but blamed for their perverse love of things that can be lost.

Its vanity and iniquity consist in this: they do not savor, through faith, hope, or love, the things that are above (Colossians III, 2), but love frail and fleeting rewards, which they abandon and by which they are abandoned.

(Vers. 15.) They called the people blessed who have these things. Full of vanity, empty of faith, armed with iniquity, and alienated from the portion of the eternal inheritance, they went so far as to call the people blessed who have these things. But let the sons of promise say: Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.

## PSALM 144

[Col. 0411D]

(Vers. 1.) I will exalt you, my God and king, and I will bless your name forever and ever. The whole psalm is woven together with the praise of God. Since the title of the psalm announces the praise of David,

**Note:** Namely, “Praise to David himself,” or “Praise of David.”

it clearly shows that the one being proclaimed is the one who, according to his deity, is Lord and creator of David, and who, according to the fact that “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14), is the son of David. He is not two persons, but one Christ (Romans IX, 5), “who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans I, 25).

His praise, therefore, must be continued even in the present age, and it will remain in eternity. Whoever is alien to this duty in the present age will not enter the future joys of praising God.

(Vers. 2.) Every day I will bless you, and I will praise your name forever and ever. There is no doubt that the praise of God also belongs to the present life, since God’s blessing is appointed to be celebrated every day, without being hindered by the changing variety of circumstances. Whether a day is spent joyfully amid prosperity or sadly amid adversity, one must never cease from praising God. For the one who is never tempted is never tested, and it is better to be exercised through tribulation than to be punished through prosperity.

[Col. 0412B] (Vers. 3.) The Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness. His praise is concluded by no end, since no limit to his greatness is found, and whatever the one praising him may be able to conceive is insufficient in proclaiming him. Since he is always greater than every praise, let him be praised without end. From this very fact let a human being receive hope of eternity, because the one who never ceases to praise the Lord will never cease to exist.

(Vers. 4.) Generation and generation will praise your works, and they will declare your power. The repeated mention of generation signifies the entire human race, which from its beginning to its end rationally understands the author of the universe through contemplation of created things (Romans I, 20). From those things that it is possible to see, and in which there is such abundant material for wonder, it judges those things that cannot be seen. And he surpasses every reach of the mind; the one who thinks that what he understands is sufficient forms an inadequate conception of him.

By one generation, however, the first life of mortals may be signified; by the other generation, the resurrection may be understood, because it too is called regeneration, according to what was said: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty” (Matthew XIX, 28).

He is therefore praised in this age and will be praised much more in the age to come. For if those now fettered do this, how much more will those who are crowned do so?

**Note:** The Cologne codex calls it “generation”; and below likewise, “in the generation.”

(Vers. 5–7.) They will speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness, and they will recount your wonders. They will speak of the power of your awesome deeds, and they will recount your greatness. They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they will exult in your righteousness.

True praisers of God praise all his works and judgments, and they marvel at all his deeds in such a way that he who made them is more marvelous still, because whatever is found praiseworthy in creation returns to the glory of the one who works all things in all people (I Corinthians XII, 6).

Hence even his awesome deeds are filled with the honor of praise: he neither flatters nor threatens. If he did not flatter, there would be no correction.

**Note:** This passage appears to be mutilated in some respect in all the printed editions. The deficiency is supplied both by Sentence 70 below and by Augustine, *On this Psalm*, no. 8: “If he did not flatter, there would be no exhortation; if he did not threaten, there would be no correction.”

The ministers of God’s utterances will therefore proclaim both his mercy and his justice. Just as they will not be silent about the eternal kingdom, so they will not be silent about the eternal fire,

**Note:** We emend the text on the basis of Augustine, as the sense of this passage requires; all the printed editions, through an obvious error, have “the perpetual kingdom,” although it is immediately said that this must be avoided.

so that, established on the way by which one advances toward recompense, people may know what they ought to choose and what they ought to avoid.

But how will they recount God’s greatness, which has no end, unless they will always proclaim that its limit cannot be found? No one is a more eloquent narrator of ineffable things than the one who confesses that the things he speaks are inexplicable.

“These narrators of your greatness,” he says, “will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness,” because you have not forgotten us and make us remember you. Sound doctrine therefore pours forth and causes to be poured forth this teaching about the abundance of divine sweetness: all good people should know that they are ruled by God’s grace, guarded by God’s grace, and by that same grace are granted the ability to rejoice in it.

(Vers. 8–9.) The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful. The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works. God’s mercy and grace, goodness and patience, are declared everywhere; and let no one despair, let no one presume.

**Note:** Perhaps the text should read, “so that no one may despair.”

For just as he is gentle in kindness, so he is just in vengeance. Nothing is lost through his patience: the one who turns to him experiences him as kind, while the one who becomes hardened experiences him as severe. His mercies are over all his works because, in those who will be saved, he condemned what belonged to another.

(Vers. 10.) Let all your works confess to you, Lord, and let your saints bless you. Whatever exists in the universe, from the highest to the lowest, is certainly God’s work. Although only rational and intellectual creatures are moved by affection for divine praise, it is not without reason that all his works are urged to confess God, because nothing is so small or so distant from perception that the Creator is not marvelous in it.

When angels and human beings confess and praise him, the innumerable parts of the world, its forms and natures, continually proclaim their author. By their usefulness and beauty they provide immense material for those who praise him, and they seem to praise while they are themselves worthy of praise: what they cannot speak, they cause not to be silent.

**Note:** The Douai and Cologne editions, along with the more recent editions, read “to express.”

(Vers. 11–12.) They will speak of the glory of your kingdom, and they will speak of your power, so that they may make your power known to the sons of men, and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom. Every form, power, and beauty of creation is God’s kingdom, because he himself is the author and Lord of diverse things.

Yet those things that have not yet been revealed are distinguished from those that are seen; and from the beauty of visible things we understand how greatly superior they are and in what glory those things excel that are more particularly called the kingdom of God. Hence we say every day: “May your kingdom come” (Matthew VI, 10). No heart can conceive its greatness, glory, or beauty; but because it is promised and therefore believed, it is sought with the most certain desire until it arrives.

(Vers. 13.) Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion is in every generation and lineage. The repetition of “generation” indicates both the present age and the future, because the resurrection is also called a generation, having created the saints for the incorruption of blessed eternity.

The Lord is faithful in his words and holy in all his works. The Lord has promised many great things. Some things that were believed he has fulfilled; some he has kept in store to be fulfilled, so that expectation might be secure, strengthened by the power of all that has already been received.

**Note:** We believe the text should read “so many things received,” not “so many commands,” as the printed editions have, because shortly before it said, “some things he has fulfilled as matters of faith.” Augustine likewise says: “He has still promised certain things and has not given them, but let him be believed because of the things he has given.”

(Vers. 14.) The Lord strengthens all who fall and raises up all who have been cast down. “The righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked will become weak amid evils” (Proverbs XXIV, 16). The saints therefore fall in one way, and unbelievers in another. The passage now recalls the latter, none of whom is strengthened by the Lord.

They seem, in a certain sense, to have fallen when they lack all temporal things, are despised by the powerful of the world as dishonored and poor, and are counted among the most rejected. But “God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

(Vers. 15.) The eyes of all hope in you, and you give them food at the proper time. Just as a good physician knows with what food a sick person should be fed and at what time, so the Lord refreshes his servants at the proper time with health-giving nourishment. With the ineffable kindness of his knowledge, he distinguishes what suits each person, so that the submission of the faithful may profit from everything he judges should be applied to them, whether harsh or gentle.

Thus, though sick, they murmur in nothing, but receive every kind of treatment from the author of their salvation with an even temper, saying what the Savior himself deigned to say for the instruction of our patience: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will. Father, let your will be done” (Matthew XXVI, 39, 42).

(Verse 16.) You open your hand and fill [Note: All our printed editions have “every soul” in the text; but they note “every living creature” in the margin, and Augustine cites it thus. It is also read in Jerome, in both versions, although the most learned editors observed in the latest edition that some manuscripts read, “you fill every soul with blessing.”] every soul with blessing. Whatever blessing anyone obtains comes from God’s generosity, because no one would desire it unless, to stimulate that very desire, he opened the hand of his goodness.

(Verse 17.) The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. “All the ways of the Lord,” he says, “are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10): whether he is more severe or more gentle toward us, since even when he plans scourges, he chastises in order to spare.

(Verse 18.) The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth. Many do not call upon the Lord in truth, desiring something other than him; from such people he is far away, because what they desire is contrary and remote from his will. But if they desire what the just and good God commands, he is altogether near to those whom he has inspired with such affections; and he fulfills the will of those who fear him, because what belonged to the Lord has begun to belong also to his servant.

(Verses 19, 20.) He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him; he will hear their prayers and save them. The Lord preserves all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners. Which sinners does he mean except those who persevere in their sins and daily dispute against God? But the right-hand party, which has no fellowship with the left-hand party because they have always been pleased with all God’s judgments, declares what it will do forever and says:

[Col. 0415B] (Verse 21.) My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name forever and ever.

## PSALM 145

[Note: The psalm’s title is “Hallelujah, of Haggai and Zechariah.” In Prosper, nothing is discussed concerning verse 1.]

(Verse 2.) Praise the Lord, my soul; I will praise the Lord during my life, I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist. The holy and spiritual soul itself urges itself to praise the Lord: by its more excellent part it stimulates what is lesser within it. For it is not one soul that speaks and another to which it speaks. Alternatively, this may be the voice of the flesh, which receives both life and understanding from the soul and cannot, apart from the soul, either desire or reject anything. Since the soul’s activities are of two kinds, and by one function it is raised toward the Lord while by another it is inclined toward the flesh, if it serves the spirit well, it presides well over the flesh; and through that part which clings to God, it invites even what clings to the body toward higher affections. Thus, by rational authority, it grants its subjects only as much as suffices for salvation, lest it be diminished by failing to be subject to God.

The mind, therefore—the soul’s highest part—continually stimulating itself in all its efforts, says, “Praise the Lord, my soul.” It does not say this because it fails to do as much as it can, but because, recognizing that what it can do through the weakness of its corruptible body is little, it longs to advance toward that perfect and eternal praise. Mindful of its present condition, in which it does not find the strength for its desire, it answers, as far as it can accomplish this by itself, saying, “I will praise the Lord during my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist.” For although we are now strengthened by faith, hope, and charity, we are not free from tribulations, scandals, and sorrows; and amid the countless obstacles of mortality, [Note: Perhaps, if “and” is omitted, it would read better: “we do not fulfill the duties of eternal life.” Augustine seems to suggest this by these words: “Your soul answers you: I praise as much as I can—weakly, faintly, feebly. Why? Because as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord.”] we do not fulfill the duties of eternal life. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things” (Wisdom 9:15).

In my life, therefore, which no sickness weakens and no poverty makes restless, I will praise the Lord with the full freedom and strength of my being; and I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist, [Col. 0416A] because just as my existence will be eternal, so my praise in the Lord will be eternal.

(Verse 3.) Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. Those who boast in the protection of princes and the support of human beings put their trust in vanity. God alone is the one from whom salvation must be hoped for and from whom it is rightly expected, since he himself has no need of it. What the son of man is, however, is briefly shown in what follows.

(Verse 4.) His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts will perish. Everything, therefore, that is done in this world is temporal and transitory; and no one can truthfully promise another what he cannot provide for himself, since he is mortal. When his spirit has been released and his earthly flesh has returned to its earth, whatever he planned and whatever he thought perishes.

(Verses 5, 6.) Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them. “Blessed,” he says, “is the person whose helper is God”—not the god whom human ignorance invents for itself, but the God of Jacob, who made Jacob himself Israel, so that by faith and understanding he might behold the author of the universe.

(Verse 7.) He preserves truth forever; he executes judgment for those who suffer injustice. He has commended both fearing God and loving him: fearing him, because he has condemned those who do evil by his truth; loving him, because he has crowned those who labor for justice with mercy.

(Verses 7–9.) He gives food to the hungry. The Lord releases those in chains. The Lord makes the blind wise. The Lord raises up those who are cast down; the Lord loves the just. The Lord protects strangers. God’s providence has appointed and supplies nourishment for all living creatures; but to human beings he provides not only earthly food but also spiritual nourishment, which is received by those who desire it. To them it is said, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

Such, then, is the release of those in chains: they escape the chains of mortality through the eternity of adoption. Such too is the illumination of the blind, who become wise from being foolish. Such also is the raising up of those who are cast down: those who have prostrated themselves in voluntary humility are lifted to the height of heavenly things. The Lord loves the just, because he himself is their righteousness; and he protects strangers, for he makes all nations one in Christ and turns stony hearts into sons of Abraham (Matthew 3:9).

(Verses 9, 10.) He will receive the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the way of sinners. The Lord will reign forever, your God, O Zion, from generation to generation, forever and ever. [Note: The words “forever and ever” are not found in the Hebrew text or the Latin text of this psalm, nor in Augustine at this place. In Jerome’s Gallican edition they are absent, but in the Roman edition they are read in place of the preceding words, “from generation to generation.”]

God does indeed help those orphans who remain defenseless after their fathers’ deaths, and God protects all widows. But here we better understand as orphans and widows those who have no protection or consolation in this world, but whose hope is in the Lord their God. [Note: Up to this point, the printed editions, after “the Lord their God,” placed a comma and began a new sense with the words, “Therefore their soul.” But a reader who examines the passage carefully can easily see that this resulted from faulty punctuation. The author also alludes to what was said above, at verse 5: “His hope is in the Lord his God.”]

Therefore the soul that does not trust in temporal goods but is a stranger in this world, desiring a heavenly Father and a heavenly mother, is rightly called an orphan and a widow. Until it sees both its Father and its bridegroom, it now appears to be far away. But the way of sinners will be destroyed when the activities of all iniquities have come to an end, and the vanity of those who walk in broad ways will plunge into eternal punishments.

When evils rush toward this end, what will the city of Zion hear, and what will the city of God attain? “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). For you, O Zion, will be an eternal kingdom in the Church of the Lord your God; and while he reigns, you will reign without end.

## PSALM 146

(Verse 1.) Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; praise is pleasing to our God. [Note: The Lyon edition punctuates it as: “Praise the Lord, for he is good; and praise is a pleasing psalm to our God.”] It is good to praise the Lord and to sing psalms to the glory of God—not merely with the voice, which cannot sing without interruption, but much more through the harmonious ordering of a rational life, which must never be omitted. For in the conduct of God’s spiritual servants, whatever is done at home or abroad is his praise, since one lives by his teaching and gift in such a way that every action is worthy of God’s praise. The Apostle says, “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Those who do this are never silent from God’s praises, and from their good works praise is always pleasing to God.

(Verse 2.) The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersed of Israel. The construction of Jerusalem, which is built as a city (Psalm 121:3), rises through peace; peace gathers all Israel into the solidity of unity. Therefore neither should the voice be separated from works nor works from the voice; and the praise expressed by the voice should proceed from a good conscience. For the structure is not firm if, in the ministry of praise, the heart and voice do not produce one sound (Sentences 6).

(Verse 3.) He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. Behold how the dispersed of Israel are gathered, so that those broken in heart may be healed, for “God will not despise a broken and humbled heart” (Psalm 50:19): humility heals what pride wounded. The binding up of wounds signifies the variety of remedies that the supreme physician applies mercifully and wisely, because many wounds do not have one single cure.

(Verse 4.) He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name. It is not especially praiseworthy in God that the stars of heaven are numbered, since the hairs of people’s heads are numbered (Matthew 10:30). This saying is therefore more worthily understood of those stars which, in God’s Church, shine to console the night of the present age through the example of good conduct and the light of heavenly teaching. To them the Apostle says, “In this crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding the word of life” (Philippians 2:15). God numbers these stars, chosen for eternal glory, and calls them by name from among all nations. “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19), and they will not be counted among those to whom it is said, “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke 13:27).

(Verse 5.) Great is the Lord, and great is his power, and there is no measure of his wisdom. Many things in nature are great, and the power of many natures is great. But in comparison with God nothing is truly called great, nothing truly powerful; in him alone there are true greatness and great power. All excellence therefore has its limits, and every nature exists within the measure assigned to it. But God, by the greatness of his glory, surpasses all things, and the omnipotence of his wisdom cannot be contained by any number. For “from him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36).

(Verse 6.) The Lord receives the meek, but he humbles sinners to the ground. No one approaches the knowledge of God unless humble and meek [perhaps read: “unless humble”]; they believe even what they do not yet understand and await the revelation of hidden things. The Lord receives them to be instructed and makes them capable of his teaching; he has exercised and kindled their desires by delight [perhaps “expansion”]. But he humbles sinners to the ground—those sinners, certainly, who lack meekness for attaining the understanding of the Scriptures and despise as superfluous and vain what they cannot examine inwardly. God sinks their stubbornness into earthly things when he hands them over to folly, so that those who rejected the grace of illumination may undergo the punishment of blindness.

(Verse 7.) Sing beforehand to the Lord with confession; sing psalms to our God on the lyre. Those who desire understanding of the mysteries must begin with confession, so that, accusing themselves and attributing their darkness and [Col. 0418D] slowness to themselves, they may receive a ray of heavenly light. Their confession must not be fruitless: let them sing psalms to God on the lyre, that is, with a certain conscience of good works, so that by acting they may merit the mercy they seek by confessing, and may rightly distribute what they rightly offer.

(Verse 8.) [Note: Augustine has: “He prepares rain for the earth.” So too do both versions of Jerome, in agreement with the Vulgate and the Hebrew text. From this one may infer that Saint Prosper altered this text while writing it in a spiritual sense.] He covers the heavens with clouds; he sends rain of graces down upon the thirsty earth. For this reason God obscured the prophetic sayings: so that their shadowing might prepare rain; and the rain might bring forth fruit and cover what was clear.

He produces hay on the mountains and grass for the service of human beings. The usefulness of spiritual rain makes not only valleys but also mountains fertile. “Hay on the mountains, and grass for the service of human beings.” The mountains are understood as those more exalted among worldly people, who are often so enriched by those above them that the heights of the mountains are fertile from the same source that makes the valleys fruitful. God’s grace therefore produces hay on the mountains: powerful and wealthy people, having received the seed of charity, provide what will benefit the poor and supply grass for the service of human beings, who render the service of their devotion to God and to the Church.

(Verse 9.) He gives their food to the beasts and to the young of ravens that call upon him. By the name of beasts and cattle is signified the multitude of the common people, who are not deprived of necessary food. While sharing in spiritual things, they become ministers to those concerned with bodily things, so that the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled: “Who feeds a flock and does not partake of the flock’s milk?” (1 Corinthians 9:7).

The dispensation of God’s mercy therefore extends not only to the Israelite race but also to the offspring of all nations. Their fathers, venerating idols, bore the figure of ravens, pursuing what was dead and unclean; their young—that is, their children—call upon the true God and are fed with the nourishment of the Holy Spirit. While their parents did not call upon God but remained in their hardness, their descendants believed what the past had not known.

(Verses 10, 11.) He will not have pleasure in the strength of a horse, nor is a man’s encampment pleasing to him. The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy. The proud elevation of arrogance is indicated by the strength of the horse, and this is always hateful to God. Lofty and magnificent tents also reveal the swelling pride of riches; God approves nothing in them, for “he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Those who please him are the meek and poor in spirit, fearing the Lord so that they may hope in his mercy. That fear is useful which is raised up by hope, not sunk down by despair.

## PSALM 147

(Verse 12.) Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion. Since the names of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah are placed at the beginning of the psalm’s title, [Note: This title is found among the Greek interpreters.] and there is no doubt that they were captured with their people in Babylonia (1 Esdras 6:14), and that they foresaw the restoration of that city and announced it as it came to pass, the exhortation of the psalm is understood to concern the whole Church. All citizens and children of Jerusalem in the present life are to recognize that they are bound by a kind of captivity and to receive consolation from the hope of future freedom.

No saint can pass through the present time without labors and troubles. They feel themselves to be in a kind of captivity when scandals arise (Galatians 5:17) and, while disagreements remain [Note: The editions of Douai and Cologne have “in the spirit”; the better reading, in the Lyon and Louvain editions, is “between the spirit.”] between spirit and flesh, they do not do everything they wish (Romans 7:15) and suffer many adversities. The prophetic voice therefore rightly exhorts Jerusalem itself, in hope of future goods, to the praise and glory of God, so that with the holy angels, whose undivided fellowship it will attain, it may rejoice in the joys of eternal peace.

(Verse 13.) For he has strengthened the bars of your gates. The enclosure of Jerusalem and the strengthening of its bars indicate the security [Note: The Douai and Cologne editions have “unchangeable.”] of unchangeable joys, because no evil will have access to its goods, nor will any of the just fear being excluded from them. He has blessed your children within you. Outside Jerusalem there is no blessing, because no one is sanctified unless united to the Church, which is Christ’s body.

(Verse 14.) He has established peace within your borders and satisfies you with the fat of wheat. [Col. 0420B] No wars disturb the city enclosed within the boundaries of peace, nor does anything restless afflict it, since nothing in it is contrary to God’s will. But lest the tranquility of this peace be disturbed by any need, unfailing abundance of bread is supplied to it, so that the food of righteousness may be present at the feast, as it was previously present in desire. For “blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

(Verse 15.) He sends his word to the earth; his speech runs swiftly. The sending of the Word is Christ’s incarnation. As his Gospel runs through the whole earth, all nations are called, the grace of God going before the faith of believers. Nothing is swifter than God’s knowledge and work: he both knows and has made what is future, and what has not yet arisen is already ordained in his presence.

[Col. 0420C] (Verse 16.) He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes. These things do indeed serve to enrich the earth according to the surface meaning of the letter, since falling clouds [Note: Perhaps “snows.”] have the appearance of fleeces, and the dew of mists is scattered no differently from ashes, by which the earth is made fertile. But in these things the works of God’s grace are understood more sublimely. The fleeces of snow signify the calling of the nations, which flows together to produce Christ’s garment, the Church, and is woven entirely into one fabric, having neither spot nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27), but remaining in that purity which shines with eternal glorification. Thus it belongs to the structure of which it is said, “The Lord is clothed with light as with a garment” (Psalm 103:2). For this reason it was fitting that the garment of Christ transfigured on the mountain is read to have shone like snow (Matthew 17:2).

The mist indicates the darkness of ignorance, which flees for refuge to the ashes of repentance. No one can be called just before the calling, since the Son of Man did not come to choose the just (Matthew 9:13), but to save sinners and the ungodly (1 Timothy 1:15).

(Verse 17.) He sends his crystal like pieces of bread; who can stand before his cold? Snow hardened in ancient times is transformed into crystal. This signifies the stony hearts of unbelievers, bound by the frost of excessive antiquity, which have received no warmth of the Holy Spirit. But God’s grace is so powerful that it makes such age-old ice grow hot through heavenly fire and causes those hardened by crystalline cold to become warm through his breath. Thus even those who did not know the food of life begin to distribute the bread of the Word, as happened in blessed Paul (Acts 9:1 and following), who, although he had been a persecutor of believers, became a preacher of the Gospel.

Who, however, can stand if Christ has not freed him from this cold (Luke 12:49)? He came to cast fire upon the earth and to rouse to the fervor of faith what had grown numb through the frost of unbelief.

(Verse 18.) He will send his word and melt them; his spirit will blow, and the waters will flow. The hardness of unbelievers is dissolved by the word of evangelical preaching, so that what was said elsewhere may come to pass: “He struck the rock, and the waters flowed” (Psalm 104:40). When the Spirit blows, the warmth of charity is sent forth, so that rivers may water the thirsty earth and a fountain of water spring up in dry hearts unto eternal life (John 4:14).

(Verse 19.) He announces his word to Jacob, his righteousnesses and judgments to Israel. That is, he gives understanding to those who are called and justified, because all the chosen from whatever nations are called Jacob and Israel. They learn that all God’s judgments are just, and that nothing is done by him for which human ignorance could offer an excuse, because there would also be abundant causes of retribution even against the just [Note: Thus the Lyon and Louvain editions; better than “causes of faults,” found in the Douai and Cologne editions], unless he tempered his justice with mercy.

(Verse 20.) He has not dealt so with any nation, and he has not revealed his judgments to them. God did not wish the height of the riches of his wisdom (Romans 11:33) to be apparent to any nation, nor were the secrets of his judgments open to any people. But from all nations there is one nation, one people, which understands that it is freed from eternal destruction not by its own merits but by God’s grace. Each believer is a minister of God’s mercy, so that what has been done in them may also be done in others, and all dispersion may flow together into unity.

## PSALM 148

(Verse 1.) Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. The people of God, whose way of life is in heaven (Philippians 3:20), and whose hope is in the Lord their God (Psalm 145:5), belonging to the Jerusalem above and already rejoicing in the eternal fellowship of the holy angels, exults in the Spirit of God and kindles all creation to praise its Creator. This is not because irrational and senseless things can praise God by their own confession, but because nothing in the whole universe, from the highest to the lowest, fails by the harmony of its nature to bear witness to the power of its maker.

This entire praise properly belongs to two kinds of creatures, angelic and human. From consideration of the whole world they conceive this devotion, so that the very material of praise is said to praise God along with God’s praisers. Since heavenly beings therefore hold primacy in this duty, it is rightly said first to them that they should glory in the Lord because of the excellence of their dignity and beauty.

(Verses 2–5.) Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. Nothing in the heavenly height is not beautiful and worthy of wonder. Since all things join in praising their Creator, they are not told to rise into the confession of divine praise as though those below were ceasing; rather, the inspired human being shows that what they do pleases him and that by the hope of faith he delights in what he too will be raised toward through God’s promises and exhortations.

Since the Lord Jesus Christ is the Word of God, he is in no way distinguished from the Father’s praise. The psalm says, “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” Whatever God says, he says through the Word; and the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3) carries out the command of the one who speaks.

(Verse 6.) He established them forever and ever; he gave a command, and it will not pass away. Everything created for heavenly blessedness has received the fullness of its duty, so that it may remain in the praise of God. Human nature is also joined to this work, which is why the Apostle says, “Think on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth. Seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1–2). It is therefore right that every spiritual person joins himself to the devotion of heavenly beings and praises the Creator in contemplating the whole creation, so that, according to his measure, he may already do what he will do without end.

(Verses 7, 8.) Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses; fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind, which accomplish his word. By the name of earth are called the things that are near the earth; and whatever appears in this cloudy air—moist in dew or rains, frozen in snow and hail, turbulent in storms, or fiery in flashes of lightning—is included under the names of earth and abyss. None of these is subject to chance movements; each and every thing serves his laws, and he works according to the causes of hidden reason, as he wills, through all things and in all things. [Note: The Cologne edition has “for indeed”; the others have “each and every thing.”]

[Col. 0422D] (Verses 9, 10.) Mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds. None of these was not made in great wisdom (Psalm 103:24); therefore some are mentioned, so that the Creator of the universe may be proclaimed in all things.

(Verses 11, 12.) Kings of the earth and all peoples; princes and all judges of the earth; young men and virgins, elders with the younger, let them praise the name of the Lord. Among human beings there is diversity of rank, difference of sex, and dissimilarity of merits; but in God’s praises every order and every age has one common material. For the whole Church in Christ is one body, and whatever any part rightly does, the whole fullness rightly claims as its own.

(Verses 13, 14.) For his name alone is exalted. His praise is above heaven and earth, and he has exalted the horn of his people. [Note: The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions note in the margin that “is” may perhaps need to be supplied.] He is above all and the creator of all; and whatever is praiseworthy in the universe is the praise of one Creator, which the very beauty of created things confesses in its manifold adornment. The honor of his saints therefore comes from him, and the horn of his people exalts them, because he who has granted great things by nature himself gives greater things by grace.

A hymn to all his saints, the sons of Israel, the people drawing near to him. A hymn is a song by which God is praised, and it is used by all his saints and all the sons of Israel—not those who boast vainly in carnal descent, but those who, born through the faith by which Abraham pleased God, are true sons of Israel (Romans 9:7–8), drawing near to God through him who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6).

## PSALM 149

(Verse 1.) Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is in the Church of the saints. Those who praise the Lord well sing a new song, living not in the oldness of the flesh but in newness of spirit, so that God’s praise may be celebrated in the Church of the saints, which agrees with itself in faith, conduct, and charity. Without this equality there is no sweetness among singers, nor is there harmonious music where faith and life disagree.

(Verse 2.) Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the sons of Zion exult in their king. The true Israelites are the sons of Zion, or Jerusalem, for both are names of one city (Hebrews 12:22), which consists of angels and human beings journeying from a distant exile toward the same fellowship through faith, hope, and charity. Therefore let the one who believes in hope rejoice in hope, because God is both the creator, redeemer, and ruler of the new people. [Note: Perhaps “let him believe in faith”; all the printed editions have “let him believe in hope.”]

(Verse 3.) Let them praise his name in the choir; let them sing psalms to him on the tambourine and lyre. The name “choir” signifies the harmony of those praising; unless their voices are consonant, they cannot please. Rational song, therefore, whose entire melody consists in faith and charity, must disagree neither in conduct nor in confession. Let it use the lyre and tambourine well, loving God and loving one’s neighbor; let the hands in the tambourine and lyre agree with the voice; and let what is sung by the mouth be fulfilled in works. In the stretching of the tambourine and strings the crucifixion of the flesh is understood, because the more tightly the strings are stretched, the more sharply they sound.

[Col. 0424A] (Verse 4.) For the Lord takes pleasure in his people, and he has exalted the meek for salvation. What is as kind as the Lord is toward his people, whom he deigns to turn back when they have turned away, receive when corrected, help when fighting, and crown when victorious? He will grant exultation to the humble, and the meek are raised up from the very place where the proud are pressed down.

(Verse 5.) The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice upon their couches. The exultation of the saints is not in riches, honors, or any earthly prosperity, but upon their couches—that is, in a good conscience. Yet they attribute this not to themselves but to God’s grace, lest they be among those who please themselves in human beings; rather, they are among those who glory in Christ.

(Verse 6.) [Note: The Lyon and Louvain editions have “The exultations of God.” Augustine also reads it thus here, as does Jerome in the book of Psalms translated according to the Hebrew truth. But the Douai and Cologne editions, like our Vulgate, have “The exaltations of God.” Jerome likewise wrote this in both versions corrected once and again from the Greek interpreters. That Saint Prosper wrote this form too is suggested by his exposition, where he says, “They exalt him,” and so forth.] The exaltations of God are in their throats, and two-edged swords are in their hands. Giving thanks to God for all their progress, they exalt him and refer to him whatever they know to be pleasing to him. They hold in their hands the words of God, which are a two-edged sword (Revelation 1:16), effective both for dividing carnal affections and cutting away sins (Hebrews 4:12).

(Verse 7.) To execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples. The power of the word, by which the hearts of unbelievers are struck, has been given not only to those who preside but also to all disciples of the truth, who can correct those who err and recall the wandering by their rebuke.

(Verse 8.) To bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron chains. If the powerful of the world, kings, and nobles do not fear God, whom will they fear? Yet the Gospel of Christ is preached to them, and they are struck by the two-edged sword. Judgment is announced to them, and when they hear of the eternal punishments of those on the left, they are bound and receive the fetters of wisdom (Sirach 6:25), beginning with [Note: Perhaps “fear,” because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110:11), and fear seems to be implied throughout the exposition of this verse, although all the printed editions have “love”; Augustine says, “You begin with fear and are perfected toward wisdom.”] love, so that hard commands may soften the will, and what seemed harsh to those who turned away may become pleasing to those who obey. [Note: The Douai and Cologne editions have “and may be”; the Lyon and Louvain editions have “and becomes.”]

(Verse 9.) To execute upon them the written judgment: this glory belongs to all his saints. The glory of all the saints is that the whole world be subjected to God and to the divine laws, whose justice is uniformly written everywhere and obeyed with equal observance. For this purpose they exercise the power of the Spirit among all nations, so that everywhere a new song may be sung and every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11).

## PSALM 150

(Verses 1, 2.) Praise the Lord in his saints. To confess grace belongs to praising the Lord in his saints, since they are holy through his sanctification. Hence it is said in another psalm, “God is wondrous in his saints” (Psalm 67:36), so that whatever virtues and merits exist in them may all be referred to God’s glory.

Praise him in the firmament of his power. Praise him in his mighty deeds; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness. All these instruments of God’s praises are the saints themselves, through whom the many-toned sound of harmonious confession is sent forth to God. Therefore God is praised in all their duties, because every movement of those who sing is animated by the Spirit whom they proclaim.

(Verse 3.) [Note: The Lyon and Louvain editions have “They praise” here and in the following verse; Douai and Cologne have “Let them praise.” The latter is closer to “Praise him,” which appears in Augustine and in all manuscripts of the sacred psalm text, in every verse and in all of Jerome’s editions. The word may have been inserted into the text by Prosper while he was expounding the psalm.] Let them praise him with the sound of the trumpet, because of the supremely excellent proclamation of the Gospel in Christ. “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5). Let them praise him on the lyre and harp—that is, through things above and things below, as the one who made heaven and earth. Let heavenly things praise him with the lyre and earthly things with the harp, because that hollow wood upon which the extension of the strings resounds is held above in the lyre and below in the harp.

### (Verse 4)

Let them praise him with tambourine and choir. Just as, after the likeness of a tambourine—which is made from a dry and stretched hide—the perceptions of mute flesh are adapted to the confession of God, and, after the likeness of a choir, the company of singers may agree in every modulation—[Note: Perhaps “agrees,” or else the preceding *et* should be changed to *ut*]—so that nothing different from him to whom the song is sung may be perceived.

Praise him with strings and organ—that is, with any musical instrument that can sound either by striking or by blowing.

### (Verse 5)

Let them praise him with well-sounding cymbals. This occurs when each person is honored by his neighbor, not by himself. But when it is said, “Praise him with cymbals of jubilation,” it is clearly shown that throughout all musical works not bodily sounds but movements of the soul are signified. For no reasoning permits jubilation to exist in cymbals unless the cymbals themselves are transferred to the movements of the soul. When the mind cannot express in words the praises of God it has begun, its wonder becomes like jubilation, which marvels in a sound that is not contained within any articulations of syllables.

Therefore, let nothing be conceived outside the saints themselves, to whom the praise of God is enjoined, nor let anything base be understood in spiritual offices. And because to be wise according to the flesh is death, let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia.

## [SENTENCES]

### NOTICE ON THE BOOK OF SAINT PROSPER’S SENTENCES EXCERPTED FROM AUGUSTINE

Such was Saint Prosper’s inclination toward Augustine and toward each part of the teaching handed down by him in various books, and such was his zeal, that, having resolved from childhood to follow almost this one author and teacher, he procured all Augustine’s writings with as much diligence as he could and, with an application scarcely capable of being surpassed, imbued the inner chambers of his mind with them.

But lest the memory of so many and such great matters steal away from him—or rather, so that the heavenly rules of that most holy bishop might serve him as a mirror and assist him in directing each step of his life—he collected what he had read written at greater length and had meditated upon with diligent care into a kind of summary and into brief sentences, for the sake of aiding and renewing his memory. In this work he is found to have provided wonderfully not only for his own advancement but also for the benefit of everyone else. For those who have read Augustine’s works rejoice that his teaching is displayed to them, as it were, in a single view; while those who are still inexperienced and unpracticed in them, and who would be deterred by their length, are kindled by this brief tablet of such lofty and solid teaching to undertake a diligent reading of them.

In this book he seems chiefly to have collected what would promote moral edification, although he did not pass over quite a few matters—especially toward the end of the book—concerning the chief and more hidden mysteries of our religion and faith.

Since, however, many of these sentences are so brief that something might seem lacking for a fuller understanding among certain readers, the very passages in which the same matters are written in a more expansive style, and from which these brief sentences have been excerpted, are indicated in the margin. We thought these passages should be supplied in the second part of the Appendix, so that the reader might not in any way be deprived here of the benefit of consulting them, whether through lack of access to the other books or through reluctance to consult them.

The most learned Benedictine monks of Saint-Germain, editors of Saint Augustine’s works, noted concerning this work in the third part of the Appendix to volume X, on page 323, that the printed copies contain three hundred and ninety sentences. They stated that the first thirty-seven, together with a few others interspersed among the rest, had been excerpted from Prosper’s own Commentaries on the Psalms, but that the remaining sentences came from Augustine’s works. Since, as they prudently add, we sometimes discover that the words of that holy teacher have been altered, “we judge it best to advise readers to inspect those passages in which Augustine’s thought is expressed more fully than his wording.” We provide this indication by placing the word **SEE** opposite sentences of this kind.

The Colbert manuscript numbered 323—the only handwritten exemplar of this book that we have been able to find, and not itself very old—contains seventy-six sentences, no more: namely, the first eighteen; then, with the nineteenth omitted, the twentieth and twenty-first, and others selected from the subsequent series. It has this prefatory annotation:

“Prosper was an Aquitanian, a citizen of Toulouse, who, abandoning secular affairs, devoted himself entirely to divine concerns. Selecting certain sentences from blessed Augustine, he composed this book,” and so forth.

Several sentences from this book are included among the canons of the Second Council of Orange; and very many are cited under Prosper’s name by Florus, or the so-called Vulgate Bede, on Paul. The forger of the decretal letters of Zephyrinus, Callistus I, and other Roman pontiffs also made use of some of these sentences.

Thus far the most learned men, to whom the multitude of students is indebted on so many accounts.

When these same most learned men arranged for Prosper’s Book of Sentences to be printed again at the end of volume X of Saint Augustine’s works, they observed that in some books the sentences were numbered eighty-eight, while in others they were numbered ninety in addition to the three hundred.
