Since they did not identify the origin of this variation, we, after examining the matter, have noticed that it arose because in the earlier Augustinian editions two numbers were marked twice, while in others they were numbered 336 and 337—those of Lyon, Louvain, and Douai—and in still others 340 and 341—those of Cologne and the editions later than it.

We, however, having been permitted, besides that Colbert manuscript, to consult two others—both through men most ready to confer this benefit on all students and through our own efforts—namely, one Remigian manuscript, belonging to the archmonastery of Saint Remigius at Reims of the Order of Saint Benedict, and another from Juilly, which had formerly belonged to the distinguished man Claude Joly, precentor and canon of the Church of Paris, and which, through his bequest, has now become the property of the venerable chapter of that same church, judged that the number of sentences could be increased to 392. We have nevertheless noted the numbers of the earlier editions, lest this alteration create any inconvenience for readers.

Finally, since it may be inferred from what will be said below in the notice prefixed to Saint Prosper’s Epigram that these poems were composed by him around the time of the Council of Chalcedon, held in the year 451, and since it is not difficult to observe that they contain, for the most part, the same sentences as those found here, enclosed within the limits of concise expression, we judge that this Book of Sentences too was composed around the same time and, as seems probable to us, preceded that work.

## ONE BOOK OF THE SENTENCES OF SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITAINE, EXCERPTED FROM THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE  
[Note: Probably written around the year 450 or 451.] (C)

### I. What true innocence is  
[Note: The Juilly manuscript: “Concerning true innocence.”]

True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor another, since “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.” And no one sins against another before sinning against himself.  
(Augustine, on Psalm 100, 2; Prosper, on the same psalm.)

### II. Concerning the people who should be loved

People should be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved; for it is one thing to love what they have become and another to hate what they do.  
(Augustine, on Psalm 100, 5; Prosper, on the same psalm.)

### III. Concerning true eternity

True eternity and true unchangeableness exist only in the divinity of the Trinity. For in it, what is is being, and being is perpetual. Since its nature has no beginning, needs no increase, and admits neither an end nor any change. [Note: The Remigian-Reims and Juilly manuscripts have “immortality,” as it is read in the exposition of Psalm 101 and noted in the margin of all the editors.] [Note: The Remigian manuscript has “is always”; the printed editions note in the margin “is perfect.”]

Creatures, even those to which God has given or will give eternity, are not wholly free from every end, because they are not outside change: they have as their end both temporal institution, local movement, and the very change by which they are made to increase. [Note: The Remigian and Juilly manuscripts add “even here,” as is read in the exposition of the psalm cited in the margin; all our printed editions lack this word here.]

### IV. Concerning the patience of God

The patience of God, by which he spares the one who is despised and also spares the one who is denied, and prefers the sinner’s life to his death, is instruction in repentance and an offer of correction. For none of his works is without mercy, since he provides both forgiveness and the scourge for human beings. [Note: The old Cologne edition reads somewhat differently: “The patience of God is great, by which, etc.; it is instruction in repentance and an offer of correction, for no work of Christ is without mercy, since, etc.” The Juilly manuscript omits *also* after “spares” and prefers another reading. The Remigian manuscript has “does not spare when denied … for it is instruction.” In the margin of the Louvain edition and later editions we read: “Instruction in repentance is an offer of correction”; this is also the reading of a manuscript kept at Louvain in the Carthusian monastery.]

### V. Concerning God’s punishments  
[Note: The Juilly manuscript: “Concerning God’s acts of vengeance.”]

Divine goodness is especially angry in this age so that it may not be angry in the age to come; and in mercy it applies temporal severity so that it may not justly inflict eternal punishment. [Note: The Remigian and Juilly manuscripts lack “in this age” and “in the age to come”; these words are also absent from the exposition of Psalm 102.]

### VI. Concerning the true praise of God  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “Concerning true confession, or praise.”]

The confession of one who blesses is true when the sound of mouth and heart is the same. To speak well while living badly is nothing other than condemning oneself by one’s own voice.  
(Prosper, on Psalm 102, 21.)

### VII. Concerning the virtue of charity

[Note: The Juilly manuscript: “The charity of God,” as is read in Prosper’s exposition of the same psalm.]

Love of God and neighbor is the proper and distinctive virtue of the devout and the saints, whereas the other virtues may be shared by both good and evil people.  
(Augustine, on Psalm 103, 3; Prosper, on the same psalm.)

### VIII. Concerning apostolic teaching

Apostolic teaching is so health-giving and life-giving that, according to the capacity of those who use it, it leaves no one without a share in it. For whether they are little or great, weak or strong, they find in it what may nourish them and what may satisfy them. [Note: Thus the Juilly manuscript. The old Cologne edition reads “so health-giving and life-giving.” The manuscript agrees with the exposition of the psalm. The Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and later Cologne editions read “is health-giving and life-giving.”] [Note: The Remigian manuscript has “leave no one behind,” as in the exposition of the psalm.] [Note: The edition of the Sentences in Augustine’s Appendix, based on the Colbert manuscript, reads “from which they may be nourished and from which they may be satisfied.” The old Cologne edition reads “from which they may be nourished, from which they may be satisfied,” as in the exposition of the psalm. The Lyon and later editions read “from which they may be nourished and from which they may be satisfied,” omitting *and* in the first occurrence.]

### IX. Concerning seeking God

The person who seeks God seeks joy. Let him therefore seek in such a way that he rejoices not in himself but in the Lord. For by approaching God, his ignorance is illumined and his weakness strengthened, and he is given both understanding by which he may see and charity by which he may burn. [Note: The pronoun “his” is added from the Colbert manuscript and Augustine’s Appendix edition. The Remigian manuscript and the editions lack it, although it corresponds to the same pronoun shortly afterward in all the manuscripts. The Juilly manuscript reads “By approaching the Lord, and his ignorance is illumined,” instead of “By approaching God.”]

### X. Concerning spiritual distaste

Just as it is harmful to the body not to be able to receive bodily food, so it is dangerous to the soul to loathe spiritual delights.  
(Prosper, on Psalm 106, 18.)

### XI. Concerning the ends of good and evil  
[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “How liable it is to tend toward nonbeing.” The Lyon edition and the Remigian manuscript likewise read “sometimes.” Others more correctly read “never,” as in the exposition of the psalm.] [Note: The Juilly manuscript has “who perish” instead of “who tend toward nonbeing.”]

There are never many who tend toward nonbeing. For what is as liable to fewness as what is destined for destruction?  
(Prosper, on Psalm 106, 39.)

### XII. Concerning the tranquillity of God’s punishment  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “That God does not desire the punishment of the guilty.”]

God does not desire the punishment of the guilty as though he wished to be satiated by vengeance; rather, he calmly decrees what is just and disposes all things with a right will, so that even the wicked may not be disordered.  
(Prosper, on Psalm 108, 5.)

### XIII. Concerning good understanding

He possesses good understanding who correctly understands what must be done and does it. Otherwise, understanding without action is like wisdom without fear, since it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “who correctly understands what must be done, does it.” The Remigian manuscript: “understands what must rightly be done,” and so forth, as do the other manuscripts.] [Note: The Juilly manuscript adds “since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” The Remigian manuscript reads “since wisdom is in the beginning.”]

### XIV. Concerning the rest of one who still lives in the flesh  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “of those who are living.”]

The soul that has been rescued from the death of unbelief has its rest even in this life. It does not withdraw from works of righteousness, but from the practice of iniquity, so that, living for God and dead to the world, it may rest in the calm tranquillity of humility and gentleness. [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “already in this life.” The exposition of the psalm: “even in this life.” The same Juilly manuscript omits *itself* before “withdraws,” as does the exposition of the psalm.] [Note: All the printed editions read “pleasing.” The Juilly and Corbie manuscripts, from which Augustine’s Appendix edition was produced, read “calm.” The exposition of the psalm has “in quiet tranquillity.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 114, 8.)

### XV. Concerning making vows to God  
[Note: The Juilly manuscript omits “to God.”]

Whoever rightly considers what he should vow to God and what he should fulfill by making a vow should vow and return himself. This is required; this is owed. “Let Caesar’s image be returned to Caesar, and God’s image to God.” (Luke 20:25.) But just as one must consider what one offers and to whom one offers it, so one must also consider where one offers it, because there is no place for true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church. [Note: Thus the Remigian manuscript, which has *bring* instead of *offer*, perhaps through error. The Colbert manuscript and Augustine’s edition, after the old Cologne edition, read “what and to whom you offer.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 115, 8.)

### XVI. Concerning justice and grace

There are two forms of the recompense of justice: when either good is returned for good or evil for evil. There is a third recompense, that of grace, when through regeneration evil is forgiven and good is repaid. Thus it is shown that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.

But God knows nothing of that recompense of the ungodly by which evil is repaid for good. For if he did not repay good for evil, there would be no one to whom he could repay good for good. [Note: Thus the Colbert manuscript and Augustine’s Appendix edition. In the exposition of the psalm: “He repays no one evil for good.” Nevertheless, all the printed editions read “are restored,” while the Remigian and Juilly manuscripts read “they restore.”] [Note: The Remigian manuscript: “to whom they might repay.”]  
(Augustine, Sermon 7 on Psalm 118; Prosper, on the same psalm, 17.)

### XVII. Concerning the citizens of the heavenly homeland

Everyone who belongs to the heavenly city is a stranger in the world; and while using temporal life, he lives in a homeland not his own. There, amid many enticements and many deceptions, it belongs to few to know and love God—those for whom the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes (Psalm 18:9)—so that they are not deceived either in love of God or in love of neighbor. [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “for whom it is made.”] [Note: The Colbert manuscript and Augustine’s Appendix edition: “are not deceived in love.” The exposition of the psalm has the same reading, while all the other manuscripts have “are deceived in charity.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 19.)

### XVIII. Concerning overcoming the desire of the flesh

There is no one whose soul is not weighed down by a corruptible body and an earthly dwelling (Wisdom 9:15). But one must strive so that the desires of the flesh may be overcome by the vigor of the spirit, and so that the inner person, who always feels that he is resisted, may always expect divine assistance. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “one must strive … always for the divine.” The Juilly manuscript: “may seek to be helped.” All the others: “may await help.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 25.)

### XIX. Concerning the narrow way of life  
[Note: The Juilly manuscript: “Concerning the narrow way,” omitting “of life.”]

Narrow is the way that leads to life (Matthew 7:13); nevertheless, one does not run along it except with an enlarged heart. For the path of the virtues, along which Christ’s poor walk, is broad for the hope of the faithful, even if it is narrow for the vanity of unbelievers. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “for faithful hope.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 35.)

### XX. Concerning the reward of the Christian religion  
[Note: The Juilly manuscript does not have the word “Christian.”]

God must be worshiped with such affection and desire that the worship of him itself is the reward. For whoever worships God in order to obtain something else more than God does not worship God, but that which he desires to attain.  
(Augustine, Sermon 11 on Psalm 118, 6; Prosper, on the same psalm, 36.)

### XXI. Concerning things hidden from judgment

To judge rashly the secrets of another’s heart is a sin, and it is unjust to criticize someone whose works are seen to be nothing but good on the basis of suspicion. For, since those things which are unknown to a human being are concerned, God alone is the just judge, who is also the true observer. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “whose works are not seen, except as good … since God alone is judge, because he is just and a true observer.” The Remigian manuscript: “Since, of the things that belong to human beings and are unknown, God alone is the just judge, who is the observer of truth.”]  
(Zephyrinus, Letter 1; Prosper, on Psalm 118, 39.)

### XXII. Concerning God’s assistance

It is a gift of God when we both think rightly and restrain our feet from falsehood and injustice. Whenever we do good, God works in us and with us so that we may act. [Note: The Remigian manuscript: “from the falsehood of injustice.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 59; Canon 9 of the Second Council of Orange.)

### XXIII. Concerning the sufferings of the saints  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “from evils.”]

By the just judgment of God, sinners are often granted power to persecute his saints, so that those who are helped and guided by the Spirit of God may become more illustrious through the exercise of hardships. [Note: The Colbert manuscript and Augustine’s Appendix edition: “so that those who …”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 62.)

### XXIV. Concerning knowledge of the good  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “and action.”]

There is no true knowledge of the good unless it is grasped for the purpose of being practiced. For one does not meditate profitably upon the law of God if one labors to retain in memory what one does not fulfill in action. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “but uselessly.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 71, 77.)

### XXV. Concerning love of the law  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “among human beings.”]

Whoever loves the law of God proves that, in unrighteous people, he hates what is contrary to the law, not the people themselves. [Note: The Remigian and Juilly manuscripts: “in all unrighteous people.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 113.)

### XXVI. Concerning examining God’s commandments  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “without quarrels.”]

No one can examine God’s commandments unless the mind is at peace. Therefore, so that religious study may be exercised, the quarrels of the wicked must be driven away.  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 115.)

### XXVII. Concerning progress  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “always” here.]

No one is so learned, no one so instructed, that he does not need heavenly illumination. For no increase of divine goods is so complete that there does not always remain something which the rational mind desires both to understand and to do. [Note: The Remigian manuscript: “for those things are not so …” The old Cologne edition: “no things are so.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 125.)

### XXVIII. Concerning God’s twofold work  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “of mercy and truth.”]

If we consider all human beings together, some of whom are saved by mercy and others condemned by truth, the ways of the Lord as a whole—that is, mercy and truth—are distinguished by their respective ends.

But if we look only upon the saints, these ways of the Lord are not distinguished. For there mercy is inseparable from truth, and truth from mercy, because the blessedness of the saints arises both from the gift of grace and from the recompense of justice. [Note: The Juilly manuscript lacks the word “of the Lord.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 151.)

### XXIX. Concerning the observance of peace  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “with the wicked.”]

It belongs to Christian perfection to be peaceful even with the enemies of peace, in hope of correction and not in agreement with wickedness. Thus, even if they follow neither the example nor the exhortation of love, they nevertheless have no grounds for hating us. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “if they follow neither the example nor the exhortation of discernment.” The Juilly manuscript: “neither by example nor by the exhortation of love.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 119, 7.)

### XXX. Concerning God’s protection  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “in temptation.”]

The Lord guards us from every evil—not so that we suffer nothing adverse, but so that the soul is not harmed by adversities themselves. For when temptation is present, a kind of entry is made into that which attacks us; and when the temptation is brought to a good end—that is, without a wound to the soul—we depart from the depth of temporal labor into eternal rest. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “and when, with a good end—that is, without a wound—the temptation of the soul is brought to completion.” The Juilly manuscript: “and with a good end.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 120, 7.)

### XXXI. Concerning God’s assistance  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “Concerning God’s gift in the ascent to Jerusalem.”] [Note: The Remigian manuscript: “They do not ascend to fellowship with the heavenly Jerusalem of the Israelites unless they confess,” and so forth.]

No one ascends to fellowship with the heavenly Jerusalem unless he professes with his whole heart that his ascent is not the result of his own work but is a divine gift.  
(Prosper, on Psalm 121, 4.)

### XXXII. Concerning the world’s hatred of Christians  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “Concerning hatred.”]

All who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer reproaches from the ungodly and those unlike them, and must be despised as foolish and insane because they surrender present goods and promise themselves invisible and future things. But this contempt and mockery will be turned back upon the ungodly when their abundance has passed into poverty and their pride into shame. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “in the present.”] [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “seek for themselves.”] [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “upon them”; the Remigian manuscript: “in them,” perhaps instead of “upon them.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 122, 3.)

### XXXIII. Concerning the patience of the faithful  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “Concerning patience, in what it consists.”]

The whole salvation of the faithful and the whole strength of patience must be referred to him who is wondrous in his saints. For unless the Lord were in them, human weakness would succumb to the fury of the wicked.  
(Prosper, on Psalm 123, 5.)

### XXXIV. Concerning due obedience

Subjects must bear rulers, and servants their masters, in such a way that temporal things are endured through the exercise of endurance and eternal things are hoped for. For the merit of virtue is increased by the fact that one’s resolve does not violate religious devotion. [Note: The Colbert manuscript and Augustine’s edition: “the merit.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 124, 3.)

### XXXV. Concerning enduring the world’s variation  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “Not complaining about God’s arrangements.”]

Those who are upright in heart do not complain about God’s commandments and ordinances, because it is just to accept with equanimity everything that the one who will judge has willed to be endured. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “has willed.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 118, 4.)

### XXXVI. Concerning the building up of God’s house

Every structure of a holy building advances as God works, and stands as God guards it. For the protection of superiors is useful when the Spirit of God presides over his people and deigns to guard not only the flocks but also the shepherds themselves. [Note: The Colbert manuscript: “with God cooperating”; below, “is protection” or “is order.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 126, 1.)

### XXXVII. Concerning eternal joys

The joys of the eternal city are eternal, and the unending perpetuity of its abiding days will neither change nor pass away. For those who possess unchangeable peace will possess as a common good whatever will also belong to each individual. [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “and of the days that endure.” The Remigian manuscript: “and of the enduring days.” Afterwards.] [Note: The old Cologne edition: “the infinite perpetuity … whose common good will also be whatever belongs to each individual.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 127, 5.)

### XXXVIII. Concerning the law of charity

The law of Christ is the perfection of charity, by which God and neighbor are loved, and through which it is said to the Lawgiver, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). For the person who fulfills God’s commandments rightly awaits the promise of God, and the person who forgives the offenses of others does not hope in vain that his own sins will be forgiven. [Note: The Juilly manuscript adds “to God” here and, after several words, “who fulfills his commandment.”]  
(Prosper, on Psalm 129, 4.)

### XXXIX. Concerning God’s commands

God commands nothing for his own benefit, but for the benefit of the one to whom he gives the command. Therefore he is truly Lord: he does not need a servant, whereas the servant needs him.  
(Augustine, Letter 138 to Marcellinus, no. 6.)

### XL. Concerning God’s timeless knowledge  
[Note: We emend from the Juilly manuscript, in which the meaning of the following sentence is better presented than in the others, where “concerning temporal knowledge” is read.]

What is new in time is not new to God, who created time and possesses all things without time, distributing them according to the variation of their respective times. [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “to him who …”] [Note: The Cologne edition adds “of all things.”]  
(Augustine, same letter, no. 7.)

### XLI. Concerning God’s providence

The unchangeable reason contains the arrangement of changeable things. In it, things that do not occur simultaneously in time are simultaneously present, because times do not run simultaneously. [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “the unchangeable arrangement.”]  
(Augustine, same letter, no. 8.)

### XLII. Concerning the impunity of sinners

Nothing is more wretched than the happiness of sinners, by which their punitive impunity is nourished and their evil will, like an inward enemy, is strengthened. [Note: The Remigian manuscript: “because …”]  
(Augustine, same letter, no. 14.)

### XLIII. Concerning the letter of the law  
[Note: The Cologne edition adds “without life.”]

The letter of the law, which teaches that one must not sin, kills if the life-giving Spirit is absent. For it causes sin to be known rather than avoided, and therefore causes it to increase rather than diminish, because transgression of the law is added to evil desire. [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “to be known,” as in the passage of Augustine cited in the margin. Our other manuscripts read “to know,” which does not correspond well with “to be avoided.”]  
(Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, chapters 5 and 14.)

### XLIV. Concerning law and grace

The law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. For it was not through any fault of its own that the law was not fulfilled, but through the fault of the wisdom of the flesh. That fault had to be exposed through the law and healed through grace.  
(Augustine, same work, chapter 19.)

### XLV. Concerning God’s promise

God promises what he himself brings about. For he does not promise while someone else brings it about; that would no longer be promising but foretelling. Therefore it is not from works but from him who calls (Romans 9:12; and 4:4), lest the result belong to them rather than to God, and lest the reward be reckoned according to grace rather than according to debt; for then grace would no longer be grace.  
(Augustine, same work, chapter 24.)

### XLVI. Concerning the faults of the faithful and the good works of unbelievers

Just as certain venial sins, without which this life is not lived, do not prevent the righteous from attaining eternal life, so some good works, without which the life of even the worst person is scarcely found, contribute nothing to the impious person’s eternal salvation.  
(Augustine, same work, chapter 27.)

### XLVII. Concerning the effect of an evil will  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “Concerning an evil will and power.”]

When an evil will receives the power to accomplish what it desires, this comes from God’s judgment, with whom there is no injustice. For he also punishes in this way, and it is not unjust because it is hidden. Otherwise, the unrighteous person does not know that he is being punished until he has unwillingly felt manifest punishment; then he recognizes how great an evil is what he willingly perpetrated. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “to accomplish what he desires; it comes from his judgment … how great an evil is what he willingly perpetrated.”] [Note: The Remigian manuscript: “until he has felt manifest punishment unwillingly; then he recognizes how great, etc.”]  
(Augustine, same work, chapter 31.)

### XLVIII. Concerning pride  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “in good works.”]

All vices have force only in evil deeds; pride alone must also be guarded against in rightly performed deeds.  
(Augustine, On Nature and Grace, chapter 27.)

### XLIX. Concerning the unequal use of fortune  
[Note: The old Cologne edition: “Concerning equal use.” The Juilly manuscript: “Concerning the use of prosperity and adversity.”]

It makes a very great difference what use is made either of things that are prosperous or of things that are called adverse. For the good person is neither lifted up by good things nor broken by evil ones; the wicked person, however, is punished by this kind of misfortune because he is corrupted by prosperity. [Note: The Juilly manuscript: “of this world.”]  
(Augustine, The City of God, book I, chapter 8.)

### L. Concerning the death of the saints  
[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “good.” The Juilly manuscript: “That one who has lived well cannot die badly.”]

A death preceded by a good life must not be considered evil. For nothing makes death evil except what follows death. Therefore those who must necessarily die should not be greatly concerned about what may happen to them as they die, but about where they are compelled to go by dying.  
(Augustine, same work, chapter 11.)

### LI. Concerning purity, which one does not lose unwillingly  
[Note: The Cologne edition: “Concerning purity of soul, while the body is oppressed.”]

Thus bodily holiness is not lost when the holiness of the soul remains, even when the body is oppressed; just as bodily holiness is lost when purity of soul has been violated, even when the body remains untouched.  
(Augustine, same work, chapter 18.)

### LII. Concerning the courage of endurance

That person must rightly be called greater in spirit who chooses to endure a troubled life rather than flee from it, and to despise human judgment—and especially popular judgment, which is generally enveloped in the darkness of error—in preference to the light and purity of conscience. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “especially that which is popular.”]  
(Augustine, same work, chapter 22.)

### LIII. Concerning free servitude and servile dominion  
[Note: The Cologne edition: “Concerning free servitude under a servile master”; perhaps “and servile dominion.” The other manuscripts: “Concerning the humility of the righteous,” which is less suitable.]

Whatever evil unjust masters inflict upon the righteous is not punishment for crime but a test of virtue. For even if the good person is a slave, he is free; but the wicked person, even if he rules, is a slave—not of one human being, but, what is more serious, of as many masters as he has vices. [Note: The Cologne edition: “Whatever evil some master inflicts … For even the good person, if he is a slave, etc.” The Juilly manuscript: “even if he is wicked.” The Juilly manuscript begins: “Whatever evil is inflicted upon the righteous.”]  
(Augustine, The City of God, book IV, chapter 5.)

### LIV. Concerning the offering of vows

No one would rightly make a vow to the Lord unless he received from the Lord what he was to vow.  
(Augustine, The City of God, book XVII, chapter 4; Canon 11 of the Second Council of Orange.)

### LV. Concerning the essence of the Godhead

Every substance that is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God. Therefore there is no difference in the Godhead of the Trinity, because whatever is less than God is not God.  
(Canon 12 of the Second Council of Orange.)

### LVI. The kind of people God loves

God loves us as we shall be through his gift, not as we are through our merit.

### LVII. Concerning God’s timeless work  
[Note: All the other manuscripts, except the Juilly manuscript, have “Concerning the temporal.” Its reading seems more suitable to the sentence, in which the order of times is said to exist timelessly in God.]

The order of times exists timelessly in the eternal wisdom of God, and nothing is new with him who made the things that are to come.

### LVIII. Concerning the chief cause of all things

The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily and spiritual movements. For nothing occurs visibly and sensibly that is not either commanded or permitted from the invisible and intelligible court of the supreme ruler, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments, of graces and recompenses, in this vast and immeasurable commonwealth of the whole creation.  
(Augustine, On the Trinity, book III, chapter 4.)

### LIX. Concerning the devil’s pride and Christ’s humility  
[Note: At this point the Colbert manuscript adds the sentence “Concerning the ends of evil and good”: “If you wish to know in which part of reality you should be placed, examine what you fear and what it is that you love.” It is taken from Prosper’s Book of Epigrams, chapter 59.]

The proud devil led the proud human being to death; humble Christ restored the obedient human being to life. For just as the former, lifted up, fell and cast down the one who consented to him, so the latter, humbled, rose and raised up the one who believed.  
(Augustine, On the Trinity, book IV, chapter 10.)

### LX. Concerning spiritual increase
In spiritual matters, when the lesser cleaves to the greater—as the creature cleaves to the Creator—the lesser becomes greater than it was, while the greater does not; and this is what it means to be greater: to be better. For the creature that cleaves to the Creator becomes greater not in bulk but in virtue (Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book VI, chapter 8).

### LXI. On the ineffable excellence of the Godhead

The surpassing excellence of the Godhead exceeds not only the capacity of our customary speech [the text reads *visitati*, probably an OCR error for *usitati*, “customary”], but also that of our understanding. For God is thought more truly than he is spoken of, and is more truly than he is thought. It is no small part of knowledge, however, if, before we are able to know what God is, we are able to know what he is not (Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book VIII, chapter 2).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “Not a small part … if, before we are able to know,” etc. Augustine’s book likewise reads: “For it is not a small part of knowledge … if, before we can know what God is, we can already know what he is not.”]

### LXII. On true blessedness

All the blessed possess what they want, although not all who possess what they want are immediately blessed. Those who either do not possess what they want or possess what they do not rightly want are immediately wretched. Right willing, therefore, even when it has not obtained what it desires, is nearer to blessedness than wrong willing, even when it has obtained what it desires (Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book XIII, chapter 5).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “without having obtained it.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “which desires … what it desired.”]

### LXIII. What it means to be with God

Great is the misery of a human being who is not with him without whom he cannot exist. For whoever exists is certainly not without him; yet if that person does not remember him, understand him, or love him, he is not with him (Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book XIV, chapter 12).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “What it means for them to be with God.”]

### LXIV. On the incarnation of the Word of God

The divinity of the Word, equal to the Father, became a participant in our mortality—not from what was his, but from what was ours—so that we too might become participants in his divinity, not from what is ours, but from what is his (Augustine, *Commentary on Psalm 118*, sermon 16, no. 6; and sermon 19, no. 6).

### LXV. How the wicked are to be hated

Perfect hatred is that which lacks neither justice nor knowledge: that is, you should hate neither human beings because of their vices nor love vices because of human beings. Accordingly, in the wicked we rightly hate wickedness and love the creature, so that nature is not condemned because of vice, nor vice loved because of nature (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XIV, chapter 6; Prosper, on Psalm 138:22).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “On hating wicked people.”]

### LXVI. On the labor of those who fabricate lies

The fabrications of falsehood are difficult and laborious. But one who wishes to speak the truth does not labor; for the good are more at peace than the wicked, and the words of truth-tellers are liberating, whereas the inventions of deceivers are not (Augustine, on Psalm 139, no. 13).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “of those who deceive.” The Colbertinus and Joliensis manuscripts, together with the appended edition of Augustine and all printed editions in the margin of the book, read *veridicorum* (“of truth-tellers”); although in the text they have *veracium* (“of the truthful”).]

### LXVII. On the divine Scriptures

The depths of the mysteries in the Holy Scriptures are good: they are covered so that they may not become cheap; they are sought so that they may exercise us; and they are opened so that they may nourish us (Augustine, on Psalm 140, no. 1).

[Note: The Joliensis and Remigius manuscripts omit *autem* (“but”); it is likewise absent from Augustine’s text.]

### LXVIII. On the Lord’s prayer

When the Lord Jesus Christ prayed with bloody sweat, he signified that the sufferings of the martyrs would flow from his whole body, which is the Church (Augustine, on Psalm 140, no. 4; and on Psalm 85, no. 1).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript adds the pronoun *suo* (“his own”), corresponding to Augustine’s *ejus* at the later passage. The old Cologne edition reads, “On Christ’s prayer in blood.”]

### LXIX. On receiving the sacraments

The unworthy person receives the sacrament of piety to his own judgment. For what is good cannot be beneficial to one who receives it badly (Augustine, on Psalm 142, no. 16).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “On the sacraments as received by the wicked.”]

### LXX. On praising God

One who praises God for the miracles of his benefits should also praise him in the terrors of his punishments. For he both entices and threatens. If he did not entice, there would be no exhortation; if he did not threaten, there would be no correction (Augustine, on Psalm 144, no. 8; Prosper, on the same psalm, section 5).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “Now he entices, and now he threatens.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “For he neither entices nor threatens,” with *non* (“not”) placed where it is not wanted and with *non minatur* (“does not threaten”) as in Prosper’s and Augustine’s texts. The Joliensis manuscript reads *Deum* (“God”) where the others have *Deo* (“to God”). The old Cologne edition reads, “On the praise of God, in benefits and threats.”]

### LXXI. On hastening conversion

The remedies of conversion to God must not be postponed by any delay, lest the time for correction be lost through tardiness. For he who promised forgiveness to the penitent did not promise tomorrow to the one who delays (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 11).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “in the remedy.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “remedies of correction.”]

### LXXII. On humility in prayer

The person who rightly and properly calls upon God accuses himself, not God, in all the evils he suffers; and in the good things he does, he does not praise himself but God. For just as God rejects the person who defends his sins, so he receives the person who confesses them (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 12).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “in good things and evils.”]

### LXXIII. On wonder at creatures

The structure of the world is wonderful, but its Maker is more wonderful. A person who turns away from the Creator is wrongly occupied with created things; and if he cleaves to the higher, he will trample the lower, lest what he has loved contrary to nature be turned into punishment (Augustine, on Psalm 145, no. 5).

[Note: The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “from the Maker”; the same reading is entered in the margin of all printed editions except the old Cologne edition. The old Cologne edition reads, “if he clings to him.”]

### LXXIV. On the disordered soul

The rational soul, placing lower things above higher ones, cannot govern what it used to govern, because it did not wish to be governed by the one by whom it had been governed (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 5).

[Note: The old Cologne and Lyons editions read *voluit* (“it wished”), an obvious error in light of the context and Augustine’s book.]

### LXXV. On the punishment of sin

The body of our flesh was an adornment for us; we sinned, and consequently received fetters, so that the whole course of human action might be impeded by the bonds of mortality (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 17).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “in shackles.”]

### LXXVI. On the manner of singing psalms

The person whose works agree with his voice sings rightly in praise of God. For when the song ends, the voice falls silent; but a life persevering in good deeds never ceases to proclaim the glory of the one whom it rejoices to have working within it (Augustine, on Psalm 146, no. 2).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “remaining.” The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts, since nearly all printed editions had *psallentium* (“of those singing psalms”). The old Cologne edition reads, “On those who sing psalms with work and voice.”]

### LXXVII. On fear

Everything that is feared is reasonably avoided. God is to be feared in such a way that one flees from him to him (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 20).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “so that we may flee for refuge.” The Colbertinus manuscript adds, “It is useful for the prudent to avoid worldly adversities,” the beginning of Prosper’s epigram 73. The old Cologne edition adds, “right fear.”]

### LXXVIII. On rightly ordered concern

Just as misplaced security drives a person into danger, so rightly ordered concern produces security (Augustine, on Psalm 147, no. 5).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “and security.”]

### LXXIX. On virginity

Virginity of the flesh is an undefiled body; virginity of the soul is incorrupt faith (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 10).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “of body and soul.”]

### LXXX. On the proper measure of possessions

We shall be shown to possess many unnecessary things among our resources if we retain only what is necessary. For nothing satisfies those who seek vanities, and the person who uselessly possesses things that would benefit the poor is, in a certain sense, a keeper of what belongs to others (Augustine, sermon on Psalm 147, no. 12; Prosper, on Psalm 144, section 5).

[Note: The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts read *probabimus* (“we shall prove”), rather than *probabimur* (“we shall be shown”). The old Cologne edition reads, “Against superfluities.”]

### LXXXI. On thoughts

Our ears are related to our voices just as God’s ears are related to our thoughts. Good thoughts cannot issue in evil deeds, because action expresses what is conceived in the heart (Augustine, on Psalm 148, no. 2).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “so our thoughts are related to God’s ears.” The old Cologne edition adds, “directed toward God.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “perform evil works”; the Remigius manuscript, “carry out evil works.”]

### LXXXII. On the new song

Just as the old song of the old person belongs to temporal things, so the new song of the new person belongs to eternal things; and each person sings according to the way he lives. The new song is the song of faith that works through love (Augustine, on Psalm 149, no. 1).

### LXXXIII. On true humility

The true humility of the faithful is to be proud of nothing and to murmur at nothing; to be neither ungrateful nor querulous, but in all God’s judgments to give thanks to God and praise him, whose works are all either just or kind.

### LXXXIV. On those who despair

Very wretched is the person who does not hope in God and promises himself good fortune from himself, since by the very fact that he does not seek God’s help he has fallen away from all hope of true salvation (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 33*, sermon 2, no. 13).

[Note: The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts add, “in God,” and below read, “seeks.”]

### LXXXV. On riches

Those who are rich through iniquity are in great poverty; they do not possess the riches of justice or the treasures of wisdom. But those who serve the Lord acquire goods that cannot perish (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 15).

[Note: The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “not possessing.” All printed editions read, “do not possess.”]

### LXXXVI. On true goodness

It is not enough to abstain from evil unless one does what is good; and it is little merely to harm no one unless one strives to benefit many (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 19).

### LXXXVII. On the impunity of evil

A sinner who sins is not for that reason unseen by the Lord merely because punishment for the wrongdoer is delayed; rather, judgment is more severely directed against the person to whom even correction is denied (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 21).

[Note: The Remigius and Joliensis manuscripts read, “when he sins.” The old Cologne edition reads, “against whom wrath is unleashed.”]

### LXXXVIII. On the benefit of humility

One does not approach the height of God except through humility; and the submissive person whom God draws near to is far removed from him when exalted (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 23).

### LXXXIX. On burial

Just as costly funerals benefit rich sinners nothing, so poor saints are harmed neither by inexpensive nor by nonexistent burials (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 25).

### XC. On rightly ordered joy

The person for whom Christ is joy can never be deprived of his delights. For the joy that rejoices in the eternal is eternal rejoicing.

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On useful joy.”]

### XCI. What joins a human being to God

With respect to God, who is everywhere, we are not near or far by place but by our actions, because just as unlikeness separates us from him, so imitation joins us to him (Augustine, on Psalm 34, no. 6).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “We are either near or far,” and shortly afterward the old Cologne edition reads, “just as it separates us.” It also reads, “What it means for a person to be near God.”]

### XCII. On the good struggle

It is a weakness of human nature to take pleasure in sinning in mortal flesh. But a disciple and lover of virtues must not grant peace to this desire; he must declare war on it (Augustine, on Psalm 35, no. 6).

### XCIII. On the hope of the faithful

Do not be frightened, Christian, that what has been promised is delayed. Although the promise is hidden, prayer must nevertheless persevere in hope. Exercise yourself in works; grow in virtues. As the constancy of faith is tested, the glory of the reward increases.

### XCIV. On the times of evil

Every period of evil is brief. For what is as fleeting as that which tends toward not existing?

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “What is so fleeting?” The other manuscripts omit the verb *est* (“is”). The old Cologne edition adds the word “of evils.”]

### XCV. On the increase of charity

The capacity for charity always grows, becoming greater through use and richer through generosity.

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “The charity of ability.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On charity.”]

### XCVI. On the end of evil

The wickedness of the evil must perish, either by its own judgment or by the sentence of God. For no iniquity endures when correction or condemnation brings it to an end.

### XCVII. How one cleaves to God

The person who cleaves to God and always does his will is never abandoned by his indweller. Even if he suffers certain harsh and adverse things, he is not forsaken but tested.

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “always doing God’s will.”]

### XCVIII. On justice

The whole principle of justice is that evils be avoided and good things done. This pattern of conduct must be maintained amid every kind of adversity, because the only thing never lost is what is devoted to the work of piety.

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads, “what is devoted through works.”]

### XCIX. On endurance

Let present evils be endured until the promised blessedness arrives. Let the faithful endure the unbelieving, and let the uprooting of the weeds that have sprung up among the wheat be postponed. However violently the wicked rage, the cause of the righteous is better even in this present time: the more fiercely they are attacked, the more gloriously they are crowned (Augustine, sermon 3 on Psalm 36, no. 17).

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads, “and let the uprooting of the weeds among the garden’s wheat be postponed.” All editions had previously punctuated the passage as, “Let the uprooting be postponed, however violently the wicked rage. Better even is …” The appended edition of Augustine first adopted the present punctuation, which seemed more suitable.]

### C. What a cry to God is

A cry to God is the heart’s intention and the ardor of love, because one always asks for what one always desires. This is not hidden from God, since what proceeds from him returns to him (Augustine, on Psalm 38, no. 14).

### CI. On confessing sin

Confession of sin is good if healing follows. For what benefit is there in uncovering a wound without applying medicine? (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 24.)

[Note: The old Cologne and later editions read, “for the sinner.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “his wound.”]

### CII. On perfection

In this life, which is wholly a time of testing, even among the most exalted saints that perfection is not attained beyond which no further ascent remains.

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads in the title, “On the ascent of progress” (perhaps for “of perfection”).]

### CIII. On the labors of the present life

While the course of the present life is being run, even if the person whose outer self is being corrupted and inner self renewed makes great progress, it is nevertheless necessary, so long as he remains subject to the condition of death, for him to endure the labors of old age (Augustine, on Psalm 38, nos. 8–9).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “whose exercise corrupts the outer person.” Near the end the Remigius manuscript has “labor,” singular, rather than “labors.” The Joliensis manuscript reads in full, “On the progress of the present life.”]

### CIV. That the human being is the image of God, now subject to vanity

The human being is indeed the image of God; the person who walks in the paths of justice strives toward the likeness of his Maker. Yet while living in this life, he encounters the disturbances of vanity (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 11).

[Note: The old Cologne edition omits the latter part of the title. The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the human being made in the image of God.”]

### CV. On divine instruction

The first grace of the divine gift is that it instructs us to confess our humility and makes us recognize that, if we do anything good, we can do it through him without whom we can do nothing (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 18).

### CVI. That the whole life of unbelievers is sin

The entire life of unbelievers is sin, and there is no good apart from the supreme good. For where recognition of eternal and unchangeable truth is absent, virtue is false, even when conduct is at its best.

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “even among the best moral conduct.”]

### CVII. On the spiritual foundation

Just as the foundation of a bodily structure lies below, so the foundation of a spiritual structure lies above. An earthly building begins from the earth; a heavenly construction grows from a beginning that comes from above.

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On heavenly and earthly construction.”]

### CVIII. That remembrance and forgetfulness do not apply to God

God is said to remember when he acts, and to forget when he does not act. For forgetfulness does not apply to God, since he is in no way changed; nor does remembrance, since he forgets nothing (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 87*, no. 5).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “and how.” The Joliensis manuscript presents the whole title differently: “How it should be understood that God forgets.”]

### CIX. Who sees God’s miracles

Those people see God’s miracles to whom they are beneficial. For what is not understood, or from which no progress is made, is not seen (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 10).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “How God’s miracles can be seen.”]

### CX. On joining mercy and truth

Let truth not take mercy away, nor mercy hinder truth. For if, out of mercy, you judge against truth, or if, as though rigidly attached to truth, you forget mercy, you will not walk in the way of the Lord, in which mercy and truth have met one another (Augustine, sermon 1 on Psalm 88, no. 25).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “On mercy and truth encountering each other.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “How mercy and truth should be understood.”]

### CXI. On Christ’s temptation and imitation

Christ’s temptation is the Christian’s instruction. For disciples must be imitators of their teacher, not in performing miracles, which no one demands, but in preserving humility and patience, to which the Lord invited us by his own example (Augustine, sermon 1 on Psalm 90).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “not in miracles.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “Christ’s temptation is instruction for Christians,” and near the end, “to which he invites us.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “and patience, to which God invites us by his example.”]

### CXII. On desire and charity

Just as desire is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all good things (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 8).

### CXIII. On the Christian’s joy

The proper cause of a Christian’s joy is not the present age but the future one. Temporal things must therefore be used in such a way that they do not harm eternal things, so that, on the road along which pilgrims walk, what pleases may be what leads to the homeland.

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “and how.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “What is the proper cause of joy.” The Cologne and later editions read, “the proper cause of joy.” The old Cologne edition has, “let this please,” in a favorable sense.]

### CXIV. On the Sabbath

A person celebrates the Sabbath badly if he abstains from good works. Idleness from wrongdoing, however, should be perpetual, because a good conscience makes the spirit not restless but tranquil (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 91*, no. 2).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “makes the mind tranquil.”]

### CXV. That good should be done with joy

When you do something good, do it cheerfully. For if you do something good sadly, it becomes more a matter of what is done to you than of what you do (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 91*, no. 5).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “That good should be done with joy.” The old Cologne edition reads, “What good should be done with joy.”]

### CXVI. That it is not people, but the perversity of people, that should be avoided

If good people do not adopt the ways of the wicked, there is a great separation even among those who live together. Therefore it is not people—who can be corrected by the example of better people—but the wickedness of people that must be avoided.

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On fellowship.” The Cologne edition reads, “On the cohabitation of good and evil.”]

### CXVII. That sins should be avoided not from fear of punishment but from love of justice

God approves that innocence by which a person becomes innocent not through fear of punishment but through love of justice. For whoever does not sin out of fear, although he does not harm the person whom he wishes to harm, nevertheless harms himself greatly; and although he abstains from the evil deed, he is still guilty in will alone (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 93*, no. 1).

[Note: The old Cologne edition omits “of punishment” and “of justice.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “What true innocence is.” Similar statements may be found in Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapters 8 and 14; *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 57; and *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Book II, chapter 9, and Book III, chapter 4. The more recent Cologne and later editions read, “by the impulse of punishment.” The Remigius manuscript shortly afterward reads, “may be innocent.”]

### CXVIII. On humble confession and proud boasting

In evil deeds, confession is better than proud boasting in good deeds (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 15).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the Pharisee and the publican,” although this statement seems to have taken its occasion from the story of both. The title used here has been substituted for the older one.]

### CXIX. That the wickedness of the unrighteous benefits the good

Through the wickedness of the evil person the good person is scourged; and through the servant the son is corrected (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 25).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the correction of discipline.”]

### CXX. On the perseverance of the faithful

Just as night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not obscure the minds of the faithful who cling to the firmament of Holy Scripture (Zephirinus, Letter 1; Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 93*, no. 29).

[Note: The title in the Joliensis manuscript is “On worldly iniquity,” which is found in the other manuscripts and has been restored here.]

### CXXI. On the human being’s own capacity

A human being has ample capacity of his own for sinning; but for doing good he is not sufficient for himself unless he is justified by the one who alone is just (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 98*, no. 7).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “How what is good can be done.”]

### CXXII. On contrary ways of life

It is a great labor for the good to endure contrary ways of life; whoever is not troubled by them makes little progress. For the iniquity of another torments the just person to the extent that he has departed from his own (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 12).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “How the good ought to endure the wicked.” The old Cologne edition adds “for the good” to the title. It reads, “the iniquity of another’s sin.”]

### CXXIII. How one approaches or withdraws from God

One approaches God or withdraws from him not through distances between places; likeness makes a person near, and unlikeness makes a person far away. It is an immense misery to be far from that good which is everywhere (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 99*, no. 5).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “What it means to cleave to God.”]

### CXXIV. On true freedom

Service to God is always free, for it is not necessity that serves him but charity (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 7).

### CXXV. On endurance

The person who refuses to endure anyone because he thinks he is making great progress thereby shows, through this very refusal to tolerate others, that he is making little progress instead (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 9).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “On enduring people.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On tolerating no one.”]

### CXXVI. From where our good comes

All the good that we possess comes from our Maker. But if what is in us is what we ourselves have made, we shall be condemned for it; if it is what God has made, we shall be crowned for it (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 15).

[Note: All the manuscripts had previously read, “On the supreme artificer,” but the reading of the Joliensis manuscript, adopted here, seemed clearer.]

### CXXVII. On the incarnation of the Word

The Word of God, through whom all things were made, predetermined the time when he would assume flesh; he did not yield to time when he was changed into flesh. For a human being approached God; God did not withdraw from himself (Augustine, Letter 137, no. 10).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the Word of God,” in a more general sense. The Remigius manuscript reads, “he did not approach in time,” and below, “in which he would be seen in the flesh.”]

### CXXVIII. On faith and understanding

Faith opens a way for understanding; unbelief closes it (Augustine, on the same passage, no. 15).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “Faith opens understanding.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “Faith opens hearing to understanding.” The Joliensis manuscript’s title is, “On attaining understanding.”]

### CXXIX. On pride

The very vice by which the human being was first conquered is the one he conquers last. For when he has overcome all sins, there remains the danger that a mind conscious of doing good may glory in itself rather than in the Lord (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 7*, no. 4).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the defeated human being,” a title that seemed more suitable than the older one. The old Cologne edition reads *superatur* (“is overcome”), and later *nihil conscia* (“conscious of nothing”) instead of *bene conscia* (“conscious of doing good”). The Joliensis manuscript reads, “when it has overcome all vices.”]

### CXXX. On the perfection of desires

The end of anxieties is the fulfillment of desires; and each person strives and labors toward this, to reach what delights him. It is therefore characteristic of the wise person to desire what makes him good, not to love what deceives him (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 9).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “The end of anxieties is the attainment of desires,” and later, “which makes one blessed.” The Remigius manuscript and the old Cologne edition read, “It is characteristic of the wise person.” The Joliensis manuscript’s title is, “On the attainment of desires”; the old Cologne edition reads, “On perfection.” This latter reading may not be inappropriate if the end of the statement is considered.]

### CXXXI. On the two gifts of grace

Just as there are two functions of medicine—one by which sickness is cured, and another by which health is preserved—so there are two gifts of grace: one that removes the desire of the flesh, and another that enables the soul to persevere in virtue (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 10).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript inserts, “On the two functions of medicine,” or something similar.]

### CXXXII. On the end of labor

Human labor cannot come to an end unless a person loves what cannot be taken away from him (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 16).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “What must especially be loved.”]

### CXXXIII. On the harm caused by iniquity

It is impossible for iniquity to harm the just person against whom it is directed before it harms the unjust heart from which it proceeds (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 17).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “That iniquity harms itself before others.”]

### CXXXIV. On visible and invisible miracles

A visible miracle calls a person toward illumination; an invisible miracle illuminates the one who, having been called, comes. Therefore the person recounts all God’s miracles who, believing in visible things, passes over to understanding invisible things (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 9*, no. 2).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “visible and invisible.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the visible and invisible miracle.”]

### CXXXV. On those who flee from the devil

The cause of those who flee from the pursuing devil is better than that of those who follow him when he leads, because it is more advantageous to have him as an enemy than as a leader (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 4).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “and those who participate.” The title in the Joliensis manuscript is, “On the devil’s persecution.” The old Cologne edition reads, “than to have him as a participant.”]

### CXXXVI. On depraved desires

All depraved desires are gates of hell, through which one goes to death. Whoever rejoices in having attained what he desired ruinously and in enjoying it submits to death’s dominion (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 14).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “What the gates of hell are.” The old Cologne edition reads, “what will perish.”]

### CXXXVII. On flattery

The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. For it is pleasing to do those things in which one not only fears no reprover but even hears a praiser (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 21).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the vice of flattery.” It and the old Cologne edition read, “a praiser is heard”; earlier editions read, “the listener is praised.”]

### CXXXVIII. On the badly disposed mind

A mind conscious of wrongdoing, when it seems to itself to suffer no punishment, believes that God does not judge. Yet to abuse God’s patience and fail to understand the kindness of the one who spares is already a great condemnation (Augustine, on the same psalm, no. 23).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the malignity of a perverse mind.”]

### CXXXIX. That nature precedes vice

In a creature that sins by its own choice, nature precedes vice. Vice is so contrary to nature that it cannot do otherwise than harm nature. Therefore turning away from God would not be a vice unless it were more fitting for the nature whose vice it is to be with God (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XI, chapter 17).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the creature that sins by its own choice.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “so that, unless it harmed nature, it would not be a vice.” After this the old Cologne edition reads, “unless it harmed nature”; “for turning away from God would not be a vice unless it were a vice of some nature, for which being with God would rather be appropriate.”]

### CXL. On wicked angels and human beings

God would not have created any angel or human being whom he foresaw would become evil unless he likewise knew for what useful purposes he would employ them, and thus adorn the order of the ages, as though it were a most beautiful poem, even by means of certain very beautiful contrasts (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XI, chapter 18).

[Note: The old Cologne edition adds “evil” to the title. The Joliensis manuscript has a different title: “On God’s foreknowledge.” The Colbertinus, Remigius, and Joliensis manuscripts, together with Augustine’s editions, read “for what useful purposes he would employ them,” both in *The City of God* and in the appendix. Prosper’s printed editions read, “he would commend them.” The Joliensis manuscript has “unless he had known” rather than “unless he knew.” The old Cologne edition reads, “and would adorn the order of the ages, as though it were a most beautiful poem, even from certain very beautiful contrasts.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “would display.”]

### CXLI. On the creation of the creature

Three things in particular about the creation of the creature ought to have been made known to us: who made it, through what he made it, and why he made it. “God said,” it says, “Let there be light, and there was light; and God saw that the light was good” (Genesis 1:3). If, then, we ask who made it: God. If we ask through what he made it: he spoke, and it came to be. If we ask why he made it: because it is good. No author is more excellent than God, no art more effective than God’s Word, and no cause is better than that a good thing should be created by the Good (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XI, chapter 21).

[Note: The old Cologne edition does not contain the following: “If, then, we ask … because it is good.” Nor is it found in Augustine’s *City of God*. The Joliensis manuscript’s title is, “On the creation of light.”]

### CXLII. On good and evil love

There is a love by which what ought not to be loved is loved; and the person who loves the other love, by which what ought to be loved is loved, hates this love within himself. Both kinds can exist in one person, and this is good for a human being: as the love by which we live well increases, the love by which we live badly should diminish, until it is healed perfectly and everything by which we live is transformed into good (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XI, chapter 28).

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “which he loves.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “who loves that which ought to be loved.” The Lyons and later editions read, “in one human being”; the Colbertinus, Remigius, and Joliensis manuscripts, Augustine’s appended edition, and the old Cologne edition read, “in one person,” as in *The City of God*. The Remigius manuscript reads, “be consumed.”]

### CXLIII. On the good of the creature

The good of a rational or intellectual creature, by which it is blessed, is none other than God. This good is not from the creature itself, since it was created from nothing, but from the one by whom it was created. When the creature attains this good, it becomes blessed; when it loses it, it becomes wretched (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XII, chapter 1).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “That there is no true good except God.”]

### CXLIV. On the defect of nature

Vice cannot exist in the supreme Good, nor can it exist except in something good. Therefore only good things can exist somewhere; evil things alone exist nowhere. For even those natures that have been corrupted from the beginning by an evil will are evil insofar as they are vicious, but insofar as they are natures, they are good (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XII, chapter 3).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “On the true and highest good, and on some good.” The old Cologne edition reads, “To some … And those things that have been corrupted by the vice of an evil will … but insofar as they are truly [natures], they are good.” Augustine’s *City of God* likewise has “from the vice of an evil will,” and several manuscripts note in the lower margin that the words “and sound” occur at the beginning; all our manuscripts except the old Cologne edition display the present text.]

### CXLV. That there is neither idle repose nor laborious activity in God

It is not right to believe that God is affected differently when he rests and when he works, because he should not be said to be affected as though something occurred in his nature that had not existed before. For whatever is affected suffers, and everything that suffers is changeable. Therefore one should conceive in God neither idle repose nor laborious activity, because he knows how to act while resting and to rest while acting. And when something in his works is said to be earlier or later, this must be referred not to the one who acts but to the things made. For his will is eternal and unchangeable, and it is not altered by changing plans; in it, whatever has preceded or follows in the creation or ordering of things exists simultaneously (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XII, chapter 17).

[Note: Earlier printed editions used the more general title, “What should be believed.” The Joliensis manuscript supplied the title substituted here. The Remigius manuscript adds the pronoun “his” and reads, “what is earlier and later … is to be referred to what has been made,” rather than “to the things made.” The Joliensis manuscript reads, “in his works what is said to be earlier and later.”]

### CLVI. That God alone is Creator

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “That every creature was created by God.”]

No nature, however slight, may be believed or called a creator by anyone except God the Creator. [Note: [Col. 0447D] The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts lack “by anyone” (*ab aliquo*). But a little later they read *adhibent* (“apply”) for *adhibeant*. The same Joliensis manuscript initially writes *minimae creaturae* (“of the least creature”) instead of the other witnesses’ *minimae naturae* (“of the least nature”). The old Cologne edition reads: “But if angels . . . nevertheless they are not creators of living beings, just as farmers are not [creators] of crops,” etc.] For even if angels, when commanded or permitted, apply their activity to things that are generated in the world, they are no more creators of living beings than farmers are creators of crops and trees (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XII, chapter 24).

**CXLVII.** [Note: Earlier editions: “On the first origin of death.” The Joliensis manuscript: “On the first bodily death.” For a fuller sense, we have added the word “and” and “second.” By the first bodily death Augustine understands that by which the soul is separated from the body, from which Prosper derived his interpretation; by the second, that death which is punitive and without end, which, as he says elsewhere, holds the unwilling soul in the body.] **On the first and second bodily death.**

Of the first bodily death it may be said that it is good for the good and bad for the bad. The second, without doubt, just as it belongs to none of the good, so it is good for no one (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XIII, chapter 2).

**CXLVIII. On the death of the godly.**

The death even of the godly is the punishment of sin. But it is called good for them for this reason: they make good use of it, 564 since for them it is an end to temporal evils and a passage to eternal life. For just as injustice makes bad use not only of evils but also of goods, so justice makes good use not only of goods but also of evils. [Note: [Col. 0447D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “so justice makes good use not only of goods but also of evils,” a reading which seems to come closer to the passage in *The City of God*.] (Augustine, ibid., chapter 5).

**CXLIX. On martyrs who have not been baptized.** [Note: [Col. 0448C] The Remigianus and Corbey manuscripts, and the edition derived from the latter, read “not yet” (*nondum*). In *The City of God* the reading is also “not” (*non*), as in all our other manuscripts.]

Those who die in confession of Christ without yet having received the washing of regeneration receive as much benefit toward the abolition of their sins as they would if they had been cleansed in the baptismal font (Augustine, ibid., chapter 7).

**CL.** [Note: We have taken this title from the Joliensis manuscript, since it seemed more appropriate to the following sentence than the title found in earlier editions, “That every sin is a lie.”] **That one must live not according to man but according to God.**

When a human being lives according to himself, not according to God, he is like the devil, because the angel too had to live not according to the angel but according to God, so that he might stand in the truth and speak truth from God, not falsehood from himself. [Note: [Col. 0448D] Thus we emend the text from the Joliensis manuscript, the old Cologne edition, and the work itself cited in the margin; the other editions read *de suo mendacio* (“from his own lie”), as do also the appendix to Augustine and the Colbertinus and Remigianus manuscripts.] Hence it is not without reason that every sin is said to be a lie, because one does not sin except by a will that is contrary to the truth—that is, to God (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XIV, chapter 4).

**CLI.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On human affection.” Earlier editions: “On the differing will of affections.” We have expressed a clearer title from the opening words of the sentence.] **On the diversity of human affection.**

The diversity of human affection arises from diversity of will. If the will is corrupt, affection will be restless through perverse [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “movements.” This is quite acceptable, since Augustine in that book says, “it will have perverse movements.” All the others: “morals.”] habits; but if it is upright, human affection will be not only blameless but also praiseworthy (Augustine, ibid., chapter 6).

**CLII.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the restoration of free choice.”] **On true freedom of the will.**

The choice of the will is truly free when it does not serve vices and sins. It was given by God, and once lost it cannot be restored except by the One who was able to give it. Hence Truth says, “If the Son sets you free, [Note: The word “then” is absent from the Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts and from our Vulgate, although it is present in the Greek text of John 8:36.] then you will truly be free” (Augustine, ibid., chapter 11).

**CLIII.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “How we ought to have our hearts above.”] **That the heart must be directed toward God.**

[Col. 0448C] It is good to have one’s heart above, but not toward oneself, which is pride; rather, toward God, which is obedience. Yet by desiring more, a person becomes less: while trusting that he is sufficient for himself, he falls away from the One who truly suffices for him (Augustine, ibid., chapter 13).

**CLIV. On the blessed life.**

565 The blessed life is not possessed if it is not loved. But if it is loved, [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “it is not possessed.” The old Cologne edition: “it is not therefore possessed.” The text is better as printed here, as it is read in the chapter of *The City of God*.] it is possessed; and it must be loved more excellently than all other things, because everything else that ought to be loved must be loved for its sake. Since no one can be blessed unless he loves it as it deserves to be loved, [Note: The Joliensis manuscript, as in *The City of God*: “as it is worthy.”] it follows that he must desire it to be eternal; and it will then truly be blessed when it has no end (Augustine, ibid., chapter 25).

**CLV.** [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript. All the others: “That God alone is good,” or “God alone is good.”] **That no one becomes good except from evil.**

Not all the wicked indeed progress so as to become good; nevertheless, no one is good except from evil (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XV, chapter 1).

**CLVI.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript completes the title of the others: “On the citizens of the earthly city.”] **On the citizens of the earthly and heavenly cities.**

Nature corrupted by sin produces the citizens of the earthly city, who are vessels of wrath. Grace, freeing nature from sin, produces the citizens of the heavenly homeland, who are vessels of mercy (Augustine, ibid., chapter 2).

**CLVII.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “How God’s anger is to be understood.”] **On the anger of God.**

[Col. 0449B] The anger of God is not a disturbance in him, but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted upon sin. His thinking and reconsideration concerning things that are to be changed is an unchangeable rational ordering. For God does not repent of any deed of his as a human being does (1 Kings 15:29); rather, his judgment concerning everything is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “right foreknowledge.” The old Cologne, Lyons, and Louvain editions: “presence.” The reading is better with the Colbertinus, Remigianus, and Joliensis manuscripts, in agreement with Augustine: “foreknowledge.”] (Augustine, ibid., chapter 25).

**CLVIII.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the enemies of the Church.”] **On those who persecute the Church.**

The enemies of the Church may be blinded by any error or corrupted by wickedness. If they receive power to afflict her bodily, they exercise her patience; if they oppose her merely by holding evil opinions, they exercise her wisdom; and, so that even enemies may be loved, they exercise her benevolence—for God works all things together for good for those who love him (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 1).

**CLIX. On the end of good and evil.**

The end of good is not that by which it is consumed so that it no longer exists, but that by which it is perfected so that it is complete. The end of evil is not that by which it ceases to exist, but that to which it proceeds by continuing to do harm. Hence there is one supreme good and another supreme evil: the former is that for whose sake other goods are to be desired, while it is desired for its own sake; the latter is that for whose sake other evils are to be avoided, while it is itself [Note: Earlier editions: “for the supreme [evil],” which has no proper sense. We correct it from the Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts and the old Cologne edition, in accordance with Augustine’s text at the place cited in the margin.] for its own sake (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVI, chapter 11).

**CLX.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the nature of good.”] **On nature.**

566 There is a nature in which no evil exists, or even can exist. But there cannot be a nature in which no good exists (Augustine, ibid., chapter 13).

**CLXI. On equanimity of spirit.**
