Equanimity of spirit is better than bodily health; and it is more fitting that an unjust person should grieve in punishment than that he should have rejoiced in wrongdoing. [Note: All our printed editions had “the just person.” It is corrected from the Remigianus manuscript and *The City of God*; it had already been corrected from the Colbertinus manuscript in the supplementary edition of Augustine, volume X.] (Augustine, ibid.).

**CLXII. On the commandment of charity.**

In the commandment of charity a human being finds three whom he should love: God, himself, and his neighbor. And because the person who loves God does not err in loving himself, it follows that he should advise his neighbor to love God, since he is commanded to love his neighbor as himself (Augustine, ibid., chapter 14).

**CLXIII.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On domestic peace.” The Cologne edition, under the usual title “On harmony and obedience,” adds “of those who command and those who are subject.”] **On harmony and obedience.**

Domestic peace is the ordered harmony of those living together in commanding and obeying. Those who provide care command—for example, a husband his wife, parents their children, masters their servants. Those for whom care is provided obey—for example, wives their husbands, children their parents, servants their masters. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “But in the house of the righteous, living by faith … while dwelling as a stranger … but by the benefit of providing care.”] But in the house of the righteous person who lives by faith and is still a stranger to that city, even those who command serve those whom they seem to command. For they command not from a desire to dominate but from the duty of providing care, not from the pride of ruling but from the benevolence of providing for others (Augustine, ibid.).

**CLXIV. On [Note: The Joliensis manuscript adds “name and” (*nomine et*).] the condition of servitude.**

The name and condition of servitude were generated by guilt, not by nature; and the first cause of this subjection is sin, because, as it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” Hence the condition of one who serves a human being is better than that of one who serves his own desire (Augustine, ibid., chapter 15).

**CLXV.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On true heads of households.”] **On those placed over others.**

True heads of households advise their subjects, as sons, to worship and win the favor of God, desiring to come to the heavenly home where the duty of commanding will not be necessary. Until that place is reached, fathers ought to bear more patiently the fact that they command than servants the fact that they serve. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “those who rule … those who serve.”] (Augustine, ibid., chapter 16).

**CLXVI.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “How honor is to be understood.”] **On governing the people.**

A position of superiority, without which a people cannot be governed, should indeed be held and administered as is fitting; nevertheless, it is sought improperly. Hence the love of truth should seek holy leisure, [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “should seek.” All the others: “seeks.” In *The City of God* both forms occur, “seeks” and “undertakes,” in the indicative. The old Cologne edition: “Therefore let holy leisure seek; let the necessity of love undertake the direction of truth,” and so forth.] and the necessity of love should undertake just business (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVI, chapter 19).

**CLXVII. On the life of the soul.**

Just as that which makes the flesh live does not come from the flesh but is above the flesh, so that which makes the soul live a blessed life does not come from the soul but is above the soul; for just as the soul is the life of the flesh, so God is the blessed life of the human being (Augustine, ibid., chapter 25).

**CLXVIII.** [Note: The old Cologne edition: “On the pardon from which the blessed life is established.” Others: “On pardon.” The Joliensis manuscript: “On human justice.”] **On human justice.**

Our justice, although it is true because it is directed toward the true end of good, is nevertheless in this life such that it consists rather in the remission of sins than in the perfection of virtues. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “Yet it is not so great in this life that it consists rather through the remission of sins than through faith in virtues.”] (Augustine, ibid., chapter 27).

**CLXIX.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the struggle with vices.”] **On complete peace.**

As long as vices are resisted, there is no complete peace, because both those that resist are defeated in a dangerous battle, and those that have been conquered do not yet triumph in secure leisure but are still held down by anxious rule (Augustine, ibid.).

**CLXX. On the first and second death.**

The first death drives the unwilling soul from the body; [Note: [Col. 0451D] The old Cologne edition reads “takes away” (*tollit*); the Remigianus manuscript, “drives” (*pellit*).] the second holds the unwilling soul in the body. Both deaths have this in common: the soul suffers from its own body what it does not want (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXI, chapter 3).

**CLXXI.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the hidden works of God.” Others: “On unknown causes.” We have added “of the works of God” from the earlier words of the sentence.] **On the unknown causes of God’s works.**

[Note: Thus the Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts. The printed editions omit the preposition “in.”] In the unknown causes of divine works we know something, since we know that the Almighty does not act without reason, although the weak human mind cannot explain the reason (Augustine, ibid., chapter 5).

**CLXXII.** [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript. Other codices: “On negligences.”] **On false confidence.**

In vain does a person promise himself after this body what he neglected to acquire in this body (Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 110).

**CLXXIII [formerly CLXXII]. That it benefits a person nothing to do good unwillingly.**

No one [Note: In the Joliensis manuscript, these words, “No one unwillingly,” and so forth, form a new sentence, prefixed by the title “That it benefits a person nothing to do good unwillingly.” In the other codices these words had merged with what precedes into a single sentence.] does good unwillingly, [Note: The old Cologne edition: “does good.”] even if what he does is good, because the spirit of fear benefits nothing where the spirit of charity is absent (Augustine, *Confessions*, book I, chapter 12).

**CLXXIV [formerly CLXXIII].** [Note: The title of the Joliensis manuscript seemed more appropriate than that found in the other codices, “On human society.” It also represents Prosper’s meaning more fully than “On loving God,” which the other codices preferred.] **On obedience.**

[Col. 0452A] Just as within the powers of human society the greater power is placed over the lesser for the purpose of obedience, so God is placed over all (Augustine, *Confessions*, book III, chapter 28).

**CLXXV [formerly CLXXIV]. On true love.**

Blessed is the person who loves God, a friend in God, and an enemy for God’s sake. For he alone loses no beloved person, to whom all are beloved in Him who is never lost except by one who abandons him. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “who never leaves you first unless he is abandoned.”] (Augustine, *Confessions*, book VI, chapter 9).

**CLXXVI [formerly CLXXV].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “That God alone cannot be corrupted or changed.”] **On things that cannot be corrupted.**

It is clear that the things that are corrupted are good: they could be corrupted neither if they were supreme goods, since supreme goods would be incorruptible, nor if they were no goods at all. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “If they were good, they could not be corrupted; and if they were not good, they could not be corrupted, because, if they were supreme goods, they would be incorruptible.” The old Cologne edition: “Nor, if they were not good, could they be corrupted; for even if they were supreme goods, they would be incorruptible.”] But if they were no goods at all, there would be nothing in them to corrupt (Augustine, *Confessions*, book VII, chapter 12).

**CLXXVII [formerly CLXXVI].** [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript. All the others: “On the unchangeable God.”] **That God made all creatures good.**

Since God, unchangeably good, made all creatures good, and since no nature whatsoever was created except by him, there is no substance of evil: for what has no God as its author does not exist. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “There is no substance that does not have God as its author.”] Therefore the vice of corruption is nothing other than either a desire or an action of a disordered will. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “Therefore”; all the others: “thus.” The old Cologne edition, omitting “thus”: “For what has no God as its author is nothing other than the desire or action of a disordered will.”] (Augustine, ibid.).

**CLXXVIII [formerly CLXXVII].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On spiritual taste.”] **That justice is hateful to the wicked.**

Just as food that is pleasant to the healthy is a punishment to an unhealthy palate, and light in which an unimpaired eye delights is hated by diseased eyes, so God’s justice displeases the wicked. If they were subjected to it, they would not be disturbed. [Note: The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts: “they would not be diminished.” The same reading was noted in the margins by all the editions.] (Augustine, ibid., chapter 15).

**CLXXIX [formerly CLXXVIII]. On the sickness of the soul.**

The sickness of the soul is rational: it occurs when, delighted by inferior goods, it desires superior goods in part and in part does not desire them. Therefore it is divided into two wills; [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “and since neither one is complete, it is not.” This passage is made clearer by Augustine’s chapter, which reads: “And therefore there are two wills, because neither of them is complete, and what is present in one is absent from the other.”] and though it is one, it is not whole: what is present in one is absent from the other (Augustine, *Confessions*, book VIII, chapter 9).

**CLXXX [formerly CLXXIX]. On the kindly person.**

[Col. 0453A] 569 It ought to be insufficient for a kindly person merely not to arouse or increase the hostility of others by speaking evil; rather, he should also strive to extinguish it by speaking well. [Note: The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts: “should have striven.” The other codices: “should strive.” The former is supported by the passage from the *Confessions* cited in the margin.] (Augustine, *Confessions*, book IX, chapter 9; Celestine I, letter 1).

**CLXXXI [formerly CLXXX].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the blessed life.”] **On the hateful nature of truth.**

The blessed life is joy in the truth, which is God. Yet truth is hateful to many, and they do not wish to hear it teaching; and, although they do not wish to be deceived, they want their own lies to appear to be truth. They are justly repaid in this way: they themselves do not escape truth, while truth escapes them (Augustine, *Confessions*, book X, chapter 23).

**CLXXXII [formerly CLXXXI].** [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript. All the others: “On strong endurance.”] **On endurance.**

No one loves what he endures, even if he loves to endure; for strong endurance is one thing and secure happiness another. The labor of battle and the blessedness of victory do not belong to the same time (Augustine, ibid., chapter 28).

**CLXXXIII [formerly CLXXXII].** [Note: In the Joliensis manuscript the meaning is fuller than in the others, which have “On abundant poverty.” The old Cologne edition adds “in speech.” In the chapter cited in Augustine, the subject is summarized as “The difficult search for truth.”] **On the poverty of human understanding.**

Human understanding is often abundantly poor in speech because inquiry speaks more than discovery, and petition is longer than attainment (Augustine, *Confessions*, book XII, chapter 1).

**CLXXXIV [formerly CLXXXIII].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has a fuller sense than the others, which read “On eternity.”] **On the true eternity of God.**

The true eternity of God is that he alone possesses immortality, since he is changed by no form or movement and is not subject to a temporal will. For a will that is one thing at one time and another thing at another is not immortal (Augustine, ibid., chapter 11).

**CLXXXV [formerly CLXXXIV]. On not despairing of sinners.**

One must not despair of the wicked; rather, one should pray for them more earnestly so that they may become good, because the number of the saints is always increased from the number of the ungodly (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 39, section 8).

**CLXXXVI [formerly CLXXXV].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On true peace.”] **How peace is to be sought from God.**

When seeking peace from God, let a person be at peace with himself, [Note: [Col. 0453D] The Remigianus manuscript reads, “be at peace with yourself” (*sis tibi*); this is also the reading in Augustine’s cited work.] lest one thing be present in the profession of his mouth and another in the secret place of his heart. For it is of no benefit that the truth is in the heart if the voice says what is false; truth must both be believed and spoken (Augustine, ibid., section 16).

**CLXXXVII [formerly CLXXXVI].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On true patience.” Others: “Let the just person not grieve”; “the just person” may perhaps be the better reading.] **That one who is justly chastised should not grieve.**

A person should not complain when he suffers some adversities in matters that he rightly possesses; for through the bitterness of inferior things he is taught to love better things, lest a traveler journeying toward his homeland love the inn as his home. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “a better thing.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 40, section 5).

**CLXXXVIII [formerly CLXXVII].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On true repentance.”] **That the sinner should displease himself.**

The person who displeases himself runs well toward the remission of sins. For before the just and merciful Judge, the one who accuses himself is excused (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 41, section 12).

**CLXXXIX [formerly CLXXVIII]. On seeking aids [Note: These two words, “in peace,” are added in the old Cologne edition. The Joliensis manuscript: “On the providence of peace.”] in peace.**

In the tranquillity of peace one must grasp the teaching of wisdom, which is difficult to recognize amid the whirlwinds of tribulations. Nor are aids in adversity easily found unless they were sought in peace (Augustine, ibid., section 16).

**CXC [formerly CLXXXIX]. On the double altar [Note: The old Cologne edition supplies the word “double.” The Joliensis manuscript: “How one ought to approach the altar.”] of God.**

He reaches the invisible altar of God, to which no unjust person draws near, who approaches this present altar having been justified. For there he will find his life if here he has discerned his case (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 42, section 5).

**CXCI [formerly CXC].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the true and perfect end.” All the others: “On the Law.” The meaning will be fuller if it is read, “On the end of the Law,” from the opening words of the sentence.] **On the end of the Law.**

The end of the Law is Christ, in whom the law of righteousness is not destroyed but fulfilled. For all perfection is in him, beyond whom the hope of faith and charity has nowhere further to extend (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 45, section 1).

**CXCII [formerly CXCI]. On the punishment of a bad conscience.** [Note: We take the word “punishment” from the Joliensis manuscript. Others had only “On a bad conscience.” The Joliensis manuscript: “On the punishment of conscience.”]

No punishments are heavier than those of a bad conscience. When God is not possessed within it, consolation is not found. Therefore the Deliverer must be invoked, so that the one whom tribulation has exercised toward confession may be led by confession to pardon. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “in which God is not possessed, consolation, and so forth.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 45, section 2).

**CXCIII [formerly CXCII].** [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript, and indeed better and more clearly than the reading found in all the others, “On the sick person.” The old Cologne edition alone has “On the sick person who kills the physician.”] **On the true remission of sins.**

[Note: Thus it is read in the Corbey and Joliensis manuscripts and in Augustine, volume IV and volume X, appendix. In the Prosperian codices: “What is a more serious sin for the sick person than killing the physician?”] What sin is more serious for the sick person than killing the physician? But if this is forgiven in baptism, what is not forgiven? (Augustine, ibid., section 4).

**CXCIV [formerly CXCIII].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “How the word ought to be heard.”] **On ruminating on the word of God.**

The hearer of the word [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “of the word of God … of animals.” The Remigianus manuscript also writes “of animals,” and afterward, “which from this …”.] ought to be like the animals that are called clean because they ruminate: he should not be sluggish about thinking over what he has received in the belly of his heart. When he hears, he should be like one eating; but when he recalls what he has heard to memory, he should be like one ruminating. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “are called clean … which they receive in the belly of the heart.” The old Cologne edition: “and should not be reluctant to think about these things.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 46, section 1).

**CXCV [formerly CXCIV].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the rule of the soul.” Others: “On the rational soul.”] **On the rule of the soul.**

571 The rational soul is the mistress of its body; but it will not rule what is beneath it well unless it has served God, who is above it, in complete submission through charity. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “has submitted itself.”] (Augustine, ibid., section 10).

**CXCVI [formerly CXCV].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On mercy and truth.” Perhaps the fuller reading would be, “Whence mercy and truth come to a human being.”] **On the mercy of God.**

As the earth awaits rain and light from heaven, so a human being ought to await mercy and truth from God (Augustine, ibid., section 15).

**CXCVII [formerly CXCVI].** [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript. Others: “On the good sons of the Church.”] **On distinguishing the good and the wicked.**

The good sons of the Church should rejoice that divine justice is not mistaken in distinguishing them. But they must not rashly divide those who have been gathered, because it is theirs to wish to gather, while it belongs to the Lord to separate (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 47, section 11).

**CXCVIII [formerly CXCVII].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “How earthly substance is to be possessed.”] **On earthly love.**

The master of the things he possesses is the one who is ensnared by no desire. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “is deceived by nothing.”] For the person bound by love of earthly things does not possess them but is possessed by them (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 48, sermon 1, section 2).

**CXCIX [formerly CXCVIII]. On the eternal inheritance.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “eternal.” Others: “of Christ.”]

The inheritance in which we are coheirs with Christ is not diminished by the multitude of sons, nor does it become narrower through the number of coheirs. It is as great for many as for few, as great for each individual as for all (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 49, section 2).

**CC [formerly CXCIX].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On earthly prosperity and adversity.”] **On happiness.**

Happiness should never be secure, because prosperity is more dangerous for the soul than adversity is for the body. Prosperous circumstances corrupt first, so that they may find adversity to break. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “which may break them.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 50, section 4).

**CCI [formerly CC]. On the remedies of repentance.**

The first salvation is to avoid sin; the second is not to despair of pardon. For the person who does not have recourse to the remedies of repentance before the merciful Judge destroys himself forever (Augustine, ibid., section 5).

**CCII [formerly CCI].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the hidden life of the saints.”] **On the hidden goods of the saints.**

The good lie hidden because their good is hidden. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “nor is it visible or bodily.”] What they love is neither visible nor bodily, and their merits are established in concealment just as their rewards are. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “in secrecy.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 53, section 3).

**CCIII [formerly CCII].** [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “How enemies are to be loved.”] **On the enemies of the good.**

[Col. 0456A] 572 No good person has an enemy except evil. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “which is permitted for this reason.”] This evil is permitted to exist either so that it may be corrected or so that through it a good person may be exercised. Therefore one must pray for enemies, so that either their conversion may be obtained or an imitation of divine goodness may be found in us (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 54, section 4; Celestine I, letter 1).

**CCIV [formerly CCIII].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the resurrection.”] **On the vigor of Christian faith.**

The vigor of Christian faith is initiated at three times: evening, morning, and midday. In the evening, the Lord was on the cross; in the morning, in the resurrection; at midday, in the ascension. The first concerns patience in the One who was killed, the second life in the One who was raised, and the third the glory of the majesty of the One seated at the Father’s right hand (Augustine, ibid., section 18).

**CCV [formerly CCIV].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the testing of the righteous.”] **On the purification of the elect.**

[Col. 0456B] For this reason people are driven by tribulations, so that the vessels of election may be emptied of wickedness and filled with grace. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “People are refined by tribulations.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 55, section 13).

**CCVI [formerly CCV].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On free choice.”] **On the good things that no one loses unwillingly.**

A person may unwillingly lose temporal goods; but he never loses eternal goods unless he is willing. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “will lose.”] (Augustine, ibid., section 19).

**CCVII [formerly CCVI].** [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “On the end of the perfected.”] **On the end of the faithful.**

The end of the faithful is Christ. When the intention of the one who runs reaches him, there is nothing more that he can find, but he has in whom he ought to remain (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 56, section 2).

**CCVIII [formerly CCVII]. On sadness.**

The sadness of one who suffers injustice is better than the joy of one who commits injustice (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 56, section 14).

**CCIX [formerly CCVIII].** [Note: The manuscript: “With what caution sins should be recalled.”] **On past sins.**

The mind must be recalled from remembering past things with a certain pleasure, lest, when desire steals upon us, we return in our hearts to Egypt (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 57, section 10).

**CCX [formerly CCIX].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “Truth must be loved so that we may be conquered by it.”] **On truth.**

It is good to be conquered by truth. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “For correction, let truth prevail over you.”] For correction, let truth prevail over the willing person; [Note: The old Cologne edition: “over the unwilling.” The Joliensis manuscript: “let truth prevail over the unwilling; for it will overcome both the willing and the unwilling.”] indeed, it will overcome even one who is unwilling (Augustine, ibid., section 20).

**CCXI [formerly CCX].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “That sins cannot go unpunished.”] **On the impunity of sins.**

Sins, whether small or great, cannot go unpunished, because they are punished either when a human being repents or when God takes vengeance. [Note: The old Cologne edition adds here, “in judgment.” The Joliensis manuscript: “with God taking vengeance”; others: “judging.” The former is supported by the cited passage from Augustine.] But divine vengeance ceases if human conversion comes first. For God loves to spare those who confess and not to judge those who judge themselves (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 58, sermon 1, section 13).

**CCXII [formerly CCXI].** [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript, whereas others have “On the miserable person.”] **On God’s mercy preceding us.**

No miserable person is freed from whatever misery unless he is preceded by the mercy of God (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 58, sermon 2, section 11; canon 14 of the Second Council of Orange).

**CCXIII [formerly CCXII].** [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript. All the others: “On the remedies of tribulations.”] **On the effect of supplication.**

The person who faithfully supplicates God for the necessities of this life [Note: The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts: “of this life.”] is both mercifully heard and mercifully not heard. For the physician knows better than the sick person what is useful for the weak. But if he asks for what God both commands and promises, what he requests will certainly happen, because charity receives what truth prepares. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “Charity receives.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 59, section 7).

**CCXIV [formerly CCXIII]. On the progress of the good through temptations.** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the progress of the faithful through temptations.” Others only: “On the progress of the good.”]

The progress of the faithful does not occur without temptation. No one comes to know himself except through the test of examination, and no one will be crowned unless he conquers; nor will anyone conquer unless he has fought. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “without the test of examination”; and shortly afterward, “unless he has conquered … unless he has fought.”] But who fights unless he has an enemy and resists temptation? [Note: The old Cologne edition: “Nor will he fight unless he has an enemy.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 59, section 2).

**CCXV [formerly CCXIV].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the prophecies of the prophets.”] **On prophecies being fulfilled.**

He is foolish who does not believe the proclamations of the prophets concerning the few things that remain, when he sees so many things fulfilled that did not yet exist when they were proclaimed as destined to be fulfilled. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “when they were being proclaimed.”] (Augustine, exposition on Psalm 62, section 1).

**CCXVI [formerly CCXV].** [Note: The Remigianus manuscript: “On the worship of idols.”] **On idols.**

Those who worship idols are like those who see empty things in dreams. But if their soul awakens, it understands by whom it was made and does not worship what it itself made. [Note: The Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts: “it will not worship”; and earlier the Joliensis manuscript: “If the soul is awake.”] (Augustine, ibid., section 4).

**CCXVII [formerly CCXVI].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “On the truth of the resurrection.”] **On human bodies.**

All the parts of our body, whether torn apart, putrefied, or even burned, are dissolved into certain ashes; they cannot perish for God. For they pass into the elements of the world from which they were taken by the hand that holds all things. [Note: The old Cologne edition: “separated”; and at the end of the sentence, “which gives all things.”] (Augustine, ibid., section 6).

**CCXVIII [formerly CCXVII].** [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “How one should thirst for God.”] **On good thirst.**

Those who thirst for God ought to thirst with their whole substance—that is, with both soul and flesh—because God gives the soul its bread, that is, the word of truth, [Note: The Joliensis manuscript: “and the necessities of the flesh.”] and God provides what the flesh requires, because the same One feeds both, who made both. [Note: Several printed editions and the Cologne manuscript: “he himself makes [both].” We correct this from the Remigianus and Joliensis manuscripts and the old Cologne edition, with Augustine saying at the cited place, “the one who made both things himself feeds both things.”] (Augustine, ibid., section 7).

**CCXIX [formerly CCXVIII].** [Note: The old Cologne edition usefully adds the words “in leisure and action.” The Joliensis manuscript: “With what diligence God should be contemplated.”] **On the meditation of the faithful in leisure and action.**
Whoever, when free and at rest, does not think about God, how will he be able to think about him amid many activities and laborious affairs? Therefore, when he has leisure, let the faithful person meditate on the things of God [Note: [Col. 0458D] Ms. Jol., “while he has leisure”] and seek the substance of doing good, lest he fail in action (Augustine, same place, no. 15).

## CCXX [Elsewhere CCXIX]. The evil of dissimulation.

[Note: [Col. 0458D] Ms. Jol., “On the evil of dissimulation.” Others, “On simulated innocence.”]

Pretended innocence is not innocence; pretended equity is not equity. Rather, the sin is doubled, since it contains both iniquity and dissimulation (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 63, no. 11).

## CCXXI [Elsewhere CCXX]. The punishment of the soul that abandons justice.

[Note: [Col. 0458D] Thus Ms. Jol. Others, more generally, “On light.”]

[Col. 0458B]

The soul that withdraws from the light of justice, the more it seeks what it may find contrary to justice, the more it is repelled from the light of truth and plunged into darkness [Note: [Col. 0458D] Ms. Jol., “what it may find”; and shortly afterward, Ms. Remig., “and into darkness”] (Augustine, same place).

## CCXXII [Elsewhere CCXXI]. The two cities.

Two cities throughout the whole world are formed by two loves: Jerusalem is formed by the love of God; Babylon, by the love of the world. Therefore, let each person ask himself what he loves, and he will discover from where he is a citizen (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 64, no. 2).

## CCXXIII [Elsewhere CCXXII]. That God’s commandment is easy for one who loves.

[Note: [Col. 0458D] Thus Ms. Jol. Others, “On God’s commandment.”]

Every commandment of God is easy for one who loves. The saying, “My burden is light” (Matthew [Col. 0458C] 11:30), is understood in no other way than because he gives the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5), so that by loving we may do freely what one who does it from fear does slavishly [Note: [Col. 0458D] The old Cologne edition: “for what one does from fear, he does slavishly”; and the mind is not rightly disposed when it would prefer, if it were possible, that what is right not be commanded]—nor is he a friend of what is right when he would prefer, if it were possible, that what is right not be commanded (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 67, no. 18).

## CCXXIV [Elsewhere CCXXIII]. Love.

Love is the fullness of the law, because the law is fulfilled through love, not through fear (Romans 13:10). For the commandments of justice are carried out insofar as the spirit of grace gives assistance (Augustine, same place, no. 24).

## CCXXV [Elsewhere CCXXIV]. Good works.

There are no good works except those performed through faith and love [Col. 0459A], because either one without the other produces no fruit of virtue (Augustine, same place, no. 41; and *On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 26).

## CCXXVI [Elsewhere CCXXV]. Adam’s fall and the conversion of the faithful.

[Note: [Col. 0459C] Ms. Jol., “On Adam’s change.” Perhaps better, “On opposed changes.” For a fuller understanding of the following sentence, we add “and the conversion of the faithful,” on the authority of our text.]

Adam was changed from what God had formed, but for the worse, through his own iniquity. The faithful, however, are changed from what iniquity had produced, but for the better, through the grace of God. That change, therefore, was the change of the first transgressor; this change is the change of the right hand of the Most High (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 68, sermon 1, no. 2; and canon 15 of the Second Council of Orange).

## CCXXVII [Elsewhere CCXXVI]. Temporal pleasures and punishments.

In the present life temporal pleasures are sweet and temporal tribulations are bitter. [Col. 0459B]

But who would not drink the cup of tribulation, fearing the fire of Gehenna? And who would not despise the sweetness of the world, yearning for the goods of eternal life (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 68, sermon 1, no. 3)?

## CCXXVIII [Elsewhere CCXXVII]. The Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0459C] Ms. Jol., “On the unity of the Trinity.”]

In the divine Trinity there is such unity of substance [Note: [Col. 0459C] Ms. Remig., “substance and unity”] that it maintains equality and admits no plurality (Augustine, same place, no. 5).

## CCXXIX [Elsewhere CCXXVIII]. That evil has no nature.

[Note: [Col. 0459D] Ms. Joliensis, “That evil has no nature.” The old Cologne edition, “That evils are created.” This does not seem correct unless read with the negative particle.]

Everything was made through the Word, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3). Since, therefore, all natures were made through the Word of God, iniquity was not made through him, because iniquity is no substance. Sin is not a nature but a defect of nature, desiring [Col. 0459C] what does not belong to its proper order [Note: [Col. 0459D] Ms. Remig., “Since indeed.” Ms. Jol., after a short interval, “were made”; and below, the old Cologne edition, “desiring it.”] (Augustine, same place).

## CCXXX [Elsewhere CCXXIX]. What was taken from the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0459D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. Others, “On the iniquity of the devil.”]

Through his iniquity the devil was bound [Note: [Col. 0459D] The old Cologne edition, “having been conquered.” “Having been bound” is better, for it alludes to Matthew 12:29: “No one enters a strong man’s house and plunders his goods unless he first binds the strong man.” The same note occurs below: not what he possessed as his own, but what he had seized as another’s. For when Christ took from his great house what had perished there, he did not commit theft but recovered stolen property. The reading of the others is supported by what Augustine says in the margin at the cited passage: “The Lord answers you: these vessels had perished from my great house; I did not commit theft, but recovered what had been stolen”]—not what he possessed as his own, but what he had seized as another’s. For when Christ took from his great house what had perished there, he did not commit theft but recovered stolen property (Augustine, same place, no. 9).

## CCXXXI [Elsewhere CCXXX]. The depth of iniquity.

The depth of iniquity then closes a person in when he lies not only immersed in sins but [Col. 0460A] also, wishing to defend them, loses access to confession [Note: [Col. 0460C] The old Cologne edition: “the iniquity of depth”; and near the end, “loses confession and the access to confession.” These readings are found in no other manuscript] (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 68, sermon 2, no. 1).

## CCXXXII [Elsewhere CCXXXI]. That God is merciful in tribulations.

[Note: [Col. 0460C] Thus Ms. Joliensis. In others, “On God’s help.”]

When God permits or causes us to be afflicted by some tribulation, he is merciful even then. For by arousing faith and postponing help, he does not refuse assistance but stirs desire [Note: [Col. 0460C] Ms. Joliensis, “he stirs desires”] (Augustine, same place).

## CCXXXIII [Elsewhere CCXXXII]. Christian rich people.

[Note: [Col. 0460D] Ms. Joliensis correctly adds the word “rich.”]

Christian rich people, if they are true Christians, are altogether poor. In comparison with the heavenly goods they hope for, they count all their gold as sand, because each person has his riches where he finds delight (Augustine, same place, no. 14).

## CCXXXIV [Elsewhere CCXXXIII]. Abraham’s faith.

[Col. 0460B]

Abraham’s faith is Abraham’s seed. Therefore, those who belong to the likeness of faith belong to the promise of the heirs (Augustine, same place, no. 21).

## CCXXXV [Elsewhere CCXXXIV]. Perseverance in goodness.

[Note: [Col. 0460D] Ms. Joliensis, “On the progress of the faithful.”]

Let no member of the faithful, however much he may have progressed, say, “It is enough for me.” For whoever says this remains and has become stuck on the road before the end; he will not persevere to the end [Note: [Col. 0460D] Ms. Jol. and the old Cologne edition, “who has not persevered”] (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 69, no. 8).

## CCXXXVI [Elsewhere CCXXXV]. That every place is in God.

[Note: [Col. 0460D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. All others more generally, “On God.”]

There is no place in God [a corrupt reading; the note conjectures either “Every place is in God” or “There is no place without God”], nor is there anywhere to flee from him except to him. Whoever wishes to escape the one who is offended should flee to the one who has been appeased [Note: [Col. 0460D] We suspect that the reading should be, “Every place is in God,” or “There is no place without God,” both from the title in Ms. Joliensis and from Augustine’s own text: “If I choose another place for myself, I cannot be safe. Choose, human being, if you find one more secure.” Therefore, there is nowhere to flee from him except to him. “If you wish to escape him when angry, flee to him when appeased”] (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 70, sermon 1, no. 5).

## CCXXXVII [Elsewhere CCXXXVI]. The two lives.

[Note: [Col. 0460D] Ms. Joliensis, “That there are two lives.”]

[Col. 0460C]

There are two lives: one is that of the body, the other that of the soul. As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. Just as the body dies if the soul abandons it, so the soul dies if God abandons it [Note: [Col. 0460D] The old Cologne edition, “if Christ abandons it”] (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 70, sermon 2, no. 3).

## CCXXXVIII [Elsewhere CCXXXVII]. From whom a person receives well-being.

[Note: [Col. 0460D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. Others, “On the human being.”]

From the one from whom a person has existence, with him he has well-being [Note: [Col. 0460D] Ms. Joliensis, “from him he has it.” In Augustine, “with him,” as in the other manuscripts] (Augustine, same place, no. 6).

## CCXXXIX [Elsewhere CCXXXVIII]. Obedience.

[Col. 0461A]

God clearly and perfectly demonstrated how great a good obedience is when, having placed the human being in paradise, he prohibited him from something that was not evil [Note: [Col. 0461C] Mss. Remig. and Joliensis, “prohibited him from the tree”]. There, only obedience could win the palm [Note: [Col. 0461C] Ms. Remig., “obedience alone”]; disobedience alone fell under punishment [Note: [Col. 0461C] Mss. Remig. and the old Cologne edition, together with some more recent manuscripts, “fell into punishment.” Mss. Jol. and Colb., with the editions of Lyon, Leuven, Douai, Cologne, and the Augustinian Appendix, “incurred punishment.” Augustine, in the Psalms, has “found punishment”] (Augustine, same place, no. 7).

## CCXL [Elsewhere CCXXXIX]. The instruction of the good through the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Thus Ms. Jol. Others, “How the good are instructed.”]

577

Sometimes God instructs the good through the wicked, and through the temporal power of those who are to be condemned he disciplines those who are to be liberated (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 73, no. 8).

## CCXLI [Elsewhere CCXL]. Confession.

In the presence of God’s mercy, the confession of the penitent has very great power: by confessing, it makes the offended one favorable [Col. 0461B], while by denying it does not make him ignorant (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 74, no. 3).

## CCXLII [Elsewhere CCXLI]. That one should not glory in knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Ms. Jol. adds, “That one should not glory.”]

It is the virtue of the humble not to glory in knowledge, because it is common to all. Just as the use of light is common, so is participation in truth [Note: [Col. 0461D] On the authority of Mss. Remig. and Jol., we add the word “use”] (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 75, no. 17).

## CCXLIII [Elsewhere CCXLII]. How bodies are governed.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Ms. Joliensis, “Let him not care about royal power.” This is not unreasonable if one examines Augustine’s words at the cited passage: “Do not place before your eyes, through a desire to rule, the vast provinces over which you may extend your kingdoms; rule the earth that you bear.” Hence the same manuscript gives this sentence the title, “How we should not care about royal power,” and in the text reads “he knows” instead of “he may know.”]

He does not lack royal power who knows how to command his own body rationally. He is truly the ruler of the earth who governs his flesh by the laws of discipline (Augustine, same place, no. 18).

## CCXLIV [Elsewhere CCXLIII]. The one who fears punishment and the one who loves justice.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Other manuscripts, “On punishment and justice.” The remainder is supplied by Ms. Joliensis.]

As far as outwardly performed works are concerned, [Col. 0461C]

both the one who fears punishment and the one who loves justice do nothing contrary to the commandment. Thus they are equal in hand but unequal in heart; alike in action but unlike in intention (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 77, no. 11).

## CCXLV [Elsewhere CCXLIV]. What is to be worshiped.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Ms. Joliensis, “A person worships what he loves.” Perhaps the better reading in the others is, “How God is to be loved,” rather than, “What is to be loved.”]

A person worships what he loves. Since God is found to be greater and better than all things, he must be loved above all things, so that he may be worshiped (Augustine, same place, no. 20).

## CCXLVI [Elsewhere CCXLV]. A right heart.

[Note: [Col. 0462C] We add the word “right.” Ms. Jol., “On seeking God.”]

The heart is right with God when God is sought for God’s sake (Augustine, same place, no. 21).

## CCXLVII [Elsewhere CCXLVI]. The good will of the just toward the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0462C] We have thought these words should be added for a fuller meaning. Ms. Jol., “On the benevolence of the just and the vengeance of the wicked.” Perhaps the better title in both is, “How the just rejoices in the vengeance of the wicked.” At the end of the sentence Ms. Jol. has “can convert many” without the word “this.”]

[Col. 0462A]

It is benevolence, not malice, when the just person rejoices that vengeance has overtaken the wicked. For he does not take pleasure in the sinner’s destruction, since he wished the sinner to be corrected, but in God’s justice, by which he knows that many can be converted (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 78, no. 14).

## CCXLVIII [Elsewhere CCXLVII]. Simulated peace with an enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0462D] Ms. Joliensis, “On overcoming evil with good.” Others, “On dissimulation,” namely, of love toward an enemy or peace with an enemy.]

He does not overcome evil with good who is good on the surface but evil within: sparing in action, raging in heart; gentle in hand, cruel in will (Augustine, same place).

## CCXLIX [Elsewhere CCXLVIII]. Love and fear.

[Note: [Col. 0462D] The old Cologne edition, “On the work of love and fear.”]

Love and the fear of God lead to every good work; love and fear of the world lead to every sin. [Col. 0462B] Therefore, in order to embrace the good and avoid evil, one must discern what ought to be loved and what ought to be feared (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 79, no. 13).

## CCL [Elsewhere CCXLIX]. Whom misfortune does not break.

[Note: [Col. 0462D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. The others, “On happiness.”]

No misfortune breaks the person whom no prosperity corrupts (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 83, no. 3).

## CCLI [Elsewhere CCL]. How the rich person is poor before God.

[Note: [Col. 0462D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. Others, “On the rich poor.”]

The rich person who is such that he despises in himself whatever it is from which pride is usually inflated is poor before God [Note: [Col. 0462D] Ms. Remig., “whatever exists.” Thus Augustine in the cited Psalm] (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 85, no. 3).

## CCLII [Elsewhere CCLI]. The stages of piety.

[Note: [Col. 0462D] Ms. Joliensis, “On the stages of ascent to God.” The old Cologne edition, “On ascent to God.”]

The stages of ascent to God are affections of piety. Your way is your will: by loving, you draw near; by neglecting, you withdraw [Note: [Col. 0462D] Ms. Joliensis, “by despising, you withdraw”]. Once established on earth, you are joined to God if you love whatever things are dear to God [Note: [Col. 0462D] The same manuscript near the end, “if there are things dear to God”; others, “because the things that are dear to God”] (Augustine, same place, no. 6).

## CCLIII [Elsewhere CCLII]. Requests contrary to God.

[Col. 0462C]

When God is asked for something wrongly [Note: [Col. 0462D] Ms. Joliensis, “When something evil is requested, God”; and in the body of the sentence, “something evil,” where the other manuscripts have “something wrongly”], he is angered by giving and shows mercy by not giving (Augustine, same place, nos. 8–9).

## CCLIV [Elsewhere CCLIII]. Lying.

It is incredible that a person does not lie in order not to be caught when he lies in order to catch another (Augustine, *Against Lying*, ch. 4).

## CCLV [Elsewhere CCLIV]. Also on lying.

Although everyone who lies wishes to conceal what is true, not everyone who wishes to conceal what is true lies. Often we conceal what is true without deceiving, but by remaining silent [Col. 0463A] [Note: [Col. 0462D] Ms. Joliens. and the old Cologne edition, “true things,” as in Augustine. Other manuscripts, “the truth.” The old Cologne edition, “we conceal”]. For the Lord did not lie when he said, “I have many things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12) [Note: [Col. 0463C] Thus, following Augustine in this book, Mss. Remig. and Jol. Other manuscripts have, “when he says”] (Augustine, same work, ch. 10).

## CCLVI [Elsewhere CCLV]. The first and the second human being.

[Note: [Col. 0463C] Thus Ms. Joliensis. Others, “On free will.”]

In the first human being it became clear what human choice could accomplish toward death; in the second, what God’s assistance could accomplish toward life. For the first human being was nothing but a human being; the second human being, however, was God and human being. Sin, therefore, is committed when God is abandoned; justice is not achieved without God (Augustine, *Letter to Dardanus*, ch. 9, no. 30).

## CCLVII [Elsewhere CCLVI]. The letter of the law.

The letter of the law, which teaches that one must not sin, kills if the life-giving Spirit is absent. For it makes a person know sin rather than avoid it, and therefore causes it to increase rather than [Col. 0463B] diminish, because transgression of the law is added to evil desire [Note: [Col. 0463D] Ms. Joliensis, “For it makes known ... rather than guard against,” as in the book of Augustine from which the sentence is taken] (Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 5).

## CCLVIII [Elsewhere CCLVII]. God’s commandment and fear.

If God’s commandment is carried out from fear of punishment, not from love of justice, it is carried out slavishly, not freely—and therefore it is not carried out at all. For a fruit is not good if it does not proceed from the root of love [Note: [Col. 0463D] The old Cologne edition, “proceeds from love.” Ms. Remig., “proceeds from the root of love”] (Augustine, same work, ch. 14).

## CCLIX [Elsewhere CCLVIII]. That God’s law is according to nature.

[Note: [Col. 0463D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. Other books, “On the law.” The old Cologne edition, “On the law in nature.”]

God’s law is according to nature, and when human beings do what belongs to the law, they do it naturally, having overcome the defect that had not removed the law’s protection from nature [Note: [Col. 0463D] Mss. Remigianus and Joliensis have this passage differently: after “they do it naturally,” they add, “having overcome the defect that had removed the protection of the law from nature.” Augustine’s words at the cited passage are: “Therefore human beings naturally do what belongs to the law; those who do not do this fail to do it because of their own defect. Through that defect the law of God has been erased from their hearts; and thus, when the defect has been healed and the law is written there, they do naturally what belongs to the law.”]. When, through grace, God’s law is written in hearts [Note: [Col. 0463D] Ms. Jol., “is inscribed”] (Romans 2:14), what belongs to the law is done naturally [Col. 0463C]—not because grace has been anticipated by nature [Note: [Col. 0463D] In Augustine, “because grace has been denied”], but because nature has been restored through grace (Augustine, same work, ch. 27).

## CCLX [Elsewhere CCLIX]. Glory to be sought only in God.

[Note: [Col. 0463D] Ms. Joliensis, “That we should not glory in what we possess as though we had not received it.”]

No one should glory in what he appears to possess as though he had not received it [Note: [Col. 0464C] Ms. Joliensis, “in that which”], or think that he received it for this reason: because the letter appeared outwardly, either to be read or to sound so that it might be heard. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing (1 Corinthians 4:7; Galatians 2:21). But if he did not die for nothing, then, “Ascending [Col. 0464A] on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:19) [Note: [Col. 0464C] Mss. Remigianus, “he captured”; and below, “For either he does not truly possess.”]. From him, therefore, comes whatever anyone possesses. But whoever denies that he has received from him either does not possess it, or what he possesses will be taken away from him (Augustine, same work, ch. 29; canon 16 of the Second Council of Orange).

## CCLXI [Elsewhere CCLX]. What the human being lost through disobedience.

[Note: [Col. 0464C] Thus Ms. Joliensis. Others, “On the human being and pride”; others, “On human pride.” The old Cologne edition, “On the pride of disobedience.”]

The human being had been made immortal but wished to be God. He did not lose what he was as a human being [Note: [Col. 0464D] Ms. Remig., “But because he wished to be mortal” (perhaps “immortal”)]; rather, he lost what he was as an immortal. And from the pride contracted through disobedience, punishment of nature arose [Note: [Col. 0464D] Ms. Joliensis, “and from the disobedience of pride.”].

## CCLXII [Elsewhere CCLXI]. The praise and reward of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Ms. Joliensis supplies “and reward.”]

The praise of faith is to believe what has not been seen; its reward will be to rejoice in attaining what has been believed.

## CCLXIII [Elsewhere CCLXII]. Why the Wisdom of God came to human beings through the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Ms. Jol. adds the word “of God” to the title “On Wisdom” found in the other manuscripts. The old Cologne edition, “On wisdom in contemplation.” Perhaps it could be stated more fully: “Why the Wisdom of God came to human beings through the flesh,” or, “Why the Wisdom of God became incarnate.”]

[Col. 0464B]

Just as milk passes only through flesh in order to nourish the little child who cannot eat bread, so, unless the Wisdom of God—which is the bread of angels—had deigned to come to human beings through the flesh, no one could approach the contemplation of the divinity of the Word. Since, therefore, light could not be grasped by darkness, the light itself assumed the mortality of darkness and, through the likeness of sinful flesh, gave participation in the true light (Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 33, sermon 1, no. 6).

## CCLXIV [Elsewhere CCLXIII]. Good reputation.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Ms. Jol., “On the fragrance of a good reputation.”]

Good fragrance is a good reputation. Whoever possesses it through works of good life, while following Christ’s footsteps, in a certain way bathes Christ’s feet with the fragrance of precious ointment [Note: [Col. 0464D] Thus Mss. Remig. and Jol., in conformity with Augustine’s text at the passage cited in the margin. Other manuscripts, “which each person draws ... while he follows Christ,” etc.] (Augustine, book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 12).

## CCLXV [Elsewhere CCLXIV]. What is rightly loved.

[Col. 0464C]

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. Other manuscripts, “On desire.”]

There is no difficulty in lacking something except when there is desire in possessing it. Therefore, only that is rightly loved which can never be lost to good effect (Augustine, same work, ch. 18).

## CCLXVI [Elsewhere CCLXV]. Foolish eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Other manuscripts, apart from Ms. Jol., “On the eloquence of foolishness.”]

Whoever overflows with foolish eloquence is all the more to be guarded against because the hearer takes all the more pleasure in him in matters that it is useless to hear, and believes that the person he hears speaking elegantly is also speaking truthfully [Note: [Col. 0464D] Ms. Remig., “the eloquence of foolishness.”] (Augustine, book 4 of *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 5).

## CCLXVII [Elsewhere CCLXVI]. The disposition of good minds.

[Note: [Col. 0465C] Ms. Joliensis, “On the natural character of minds.” Others, “On the mind.” From the text of the sentence we add “good” to the former.]

[Col. 0465A]

The clear mark of good minds is to love truth, not words, in the words of those who speak. For what good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish to open? Or what harm is a wooden one if it can, when we seek nothing except that what is closed be opened [Note: [Col. 0465C] Ms. Remig., “if it can open it.”] (Augustine, same work, ch. 11).

## CCLXVIII [Elsewhere CCLXVII]. The sinner is to be loved and not loved.

[Note: [Col. 0465C] Thus Ms. Joliensis. The others, “On the sinful human being.”]

No sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is to be loved; but every human being, insofar as he is a human being, is to be loved for God’s sake, while God is to be loved for his own sake. From God all who love him receive both what they are and the fact that they love him (Augustine, book 1 of *On Christian Doctrine* [Col. 0465B], ch. 27).

## CCLXIX [Elsewhere CCLXVIII]. That Christ is the first way to God.

[Note: [Col. 0465C] Ms. Jol., “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” Others, “On the immutable good.” We have taken our substituted title from the cited book of Augustine as a fuller one.]

581

The Lord says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” That is: through me one comes; to me one arrives; in me one remains. For when one arrives at him, one also arrives at the Father, because the one who is equal to him is known through the one to whom he is equal. The Holy Spirit overcomes and binds us together [Note: [Col. 0465D] Thus Ms. Jol. and the Augustinian book cited in the margin. The others, “glues us together”], so that we may remain without end in the highest and immutable good (Augustine, same work, ch. 34).

## CCLXX [Elsewhere CCLXIX]. That the one who is deceived is better than the one who lies.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Thus Ms. Jol. Others, “On lying and deception.”]

We find many who wish to deceive, but no one who wishes to be deceived. Since one knowingly does this while another unknowingly suffers it, it is sufficiently clear that, in one and the same matter, the person who is deceived is better than the one who lies, since it is better to suffer iniquity than to commit it (Augustine, same work, ch. 36).

## CCLXXI [Elsewhere CCLXX]. The love of eternal or temporal goods.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Ms. Jol., “What distinguishes temporal and eternal things.” The old Cologne edition, “On loving eternal goods and temporal goods.”]

The difference between temporal and eternal things is this: a temporal thing is loved more before it is possessed, but becomes worthless when it arrives [Note: [Col. 0465D] Ms. Jol. adds “something,” which is found in Augustine; the others do not add it. The same manuscript later has “let it be held ... the soul,” instead of the other manuscripts’ “it is held ... the mind.”]. For nothing satisfies the soul except the true and certain eternity of incorruptible joy. An eternal thing, however, is loved more ardently once attained [Col. 0466A] than when desired. No one esteems it more highly than it actually is, so that it may become less valuable because it had been hoped for more greatly [Note: [Col. 0465D] Ms. Jol. has “as it stands,” as in Augustine at the passage cited in the margin. Other manuscripts, “has about itself.”]. But its excellence there is so great that love will attain far more than either faith believed or hope desired [Note: [Col. 0465D] Mss. Rem. and Jol., “has attained.” Jol. later, “believes ... desires.”] (Augustine, same work, ch. 38).

## CCLXXII [Elsewhere CCLXXI]. Spiritual hunger and spiritual disgust.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Earlier editions had “and fasting.” “Disgust” is better, since the sentence distinguishes it from hunger. Ms. Jol., “On those who seek and do not seek the truth in Scripture.” The old Cologne edition, “On spiritual hunger and fasting in Scripture.”]

Those who do not find in the Holy Scriptures the truth they seek [Note: [Col. 0466C] Ms. Remig., “the love they seek”] suffer hunger. Those, however, who do not seek what they have readily available waste away from the languor of disgust. The danger is equal for both, since blindness takes the food of wisdom away from the former and hunger takes it away from the latter (Augustine, book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 6).

## CCLXXIII [Elsewhere CCLXXII]. The sufferings of the godly.

[Note: [Col. 0466C] Earlier editions had “of sinners.” The editions of Douai, Cologne, and those later than them noted “of the godly” in the margin. The latter reading is better, as the text of the sentence suggests. Ms. Jol. has as its title the opening words, “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy,” etc.]

The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the [Col. 0466B] future glory that will be revealed in us [Note: [Col. 0466D] Mss. Remig. and Jol., “for the future,” as in Augustine; others, “for the glory that is to come”] (Romans 8:18).

582

Let the world rage and roar, reproach us with its tongues, flash with weapons: whatever it does, how much will that be compared with what we are to receive [Note: [Col. 0466D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. The old Cologne edition, “how little will it be compared with that”; the others, “how little will it be compared with that which.” Augustine, “what will it do compared with what we are to receive?” The reading of Ms. Jol. seemed closer to this]? I weigh what I suffer against what I hope for. I feel the one; I hope for the other. Yet what is hoped for is incomparably greater than what is inflicted [Note: [Col. 0466D] The old Cologne edition, “than what is taken away.”]. Whatever it is that rages against the name of Christ, if it can be overcome, it is bearable; if it cannot, it makes progress by attaining the reward more quickly [Note: [Col. 0466D] Ms. Joliensis, “if it can be overcome.” This is the word in Augustine, although some manuscripts there also have “overcome”]. The end of temporal evil passes into the reception of eternal good (Augustine, sermon 279, *On the Apostle Paul*, no. 4).

## CCLXXIV [Elsewhere CCLXXIII]. Love.

Since the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon the two commandments of love, how much more does the Gospel, through which the Law [Col. 0466C] is not abolished but fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0466D] The editions of Douai and those following it have “the greater it is” written in the margin; and shortly afterward, Ms. Jol., “but it is fulfilled”], and of which the Lord says, “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another” (John 13:34) [Note: [Col. 0466D] The old Cologne edition, “that you love one another”]? For love renews human beings. Just as wickedness makes them old, so love makes them new.

## CCLXXV [Elsewhere CCLXXIV]. The scourges of God.

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Up to this point the editions had “On the scourge.” Ms. Jol., “On God’s scourges.” The earlier Cologne edition also added the word “God.”]

When God chastises the human race and afflicts it with the scourges of loving correction, he exercises discipline before judgment and generally loves the one whom he scourges (Proverbs 3:12), not wishing to find anyone whom he must condemn [Note: [Col. 0466D] Ms. Remigianus, “he chooses”; Ms. Joliensis, “he does not choose.” The same reading can be found written in the margin of the book in the Lyon edition and in all editions printed later, including volume 10 of the Augustinian Appendix]. [Col. 0467A]

Yet he scourges the just and the unjust alike, because no one can boast that he has a pure heart or is clean from sin (Proverbs 20:9). Thus, even the crowns of the just come from the grace of his mercy [Note: [Col. 0467C] Mss. Remig. and Joliensis, “from his graciousness,” omitting the word “mercy.”].

## CCLXXVI [Elsewhere CCLXXV]. The sufferings of the faithful.

[Note: [Col. 0467C] Ms. Joliensis, “On the labor of the godly.”]

The labor of the godly is exercise, not condemnation. Nor should we be troubled when some holy person undergoes grievous and undeserved sufferings, if we have not forgotten what the Just One of the just and the Holy One of the holy endured. His suffering surpasses all sufferings, because no creature can be compared with the author of the universe.

## CCLXXVII [Elsewhere CCLXXVI]. Original sin.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Ms. Remig., “On the misery of the human race.”]

[Col. 0467B]

The misery of the human race, from which we see no human being free from birth until death, would not pertain to the just judgment of the Almighty [Note: [Col. 0467D] Ms. Remig., “to the just judgment of God Almighty”] if there were no original sin (Augustine, book 1 of *Unfinished Work against Julian*, no. 3).

## CCLXXVIII [Elsewhere CCLXXVII]. God’s providence at work.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Ms. Remig., “On the omnipotence of the Creator.”]

The omnipotence of the all-sustaining Creator [Note: [Col. 0467D] For the word “all-sustaining,” the editions of Douai and Cologne, together with more recent editions, note “omnipotent” in the margin. Augustine used both terms at that passage: “the power of the Creator and the strength of the omnipotent and all-sustaining one.”] is the cause of existence for every creature. If this power ever ceased to govern the things it created, the form and nature of all things would collapse together. Therefore, when the Lord says, “My Father is working until now,” he shows a certain continuation of his work, by which he both sustains and governs all things together [Note: [Col. 0467D] Ms. Joliensis, “by which all things together ... to the end.”]. In this work his wisdom also continues, of which it is said, “It reaches mightily from end to end and orders [Col. 0467C] all things sweetly.” The Apostle likewise holds this view when, proclaiming God to the Athenians [Note: [Col. 0467D] Ms. Joliensis adds “God,” a word also found in Augustine’s book], he says, “In him we live and move and exist.” If he were to withdraw his work from created things, we could neither live, move, nor exist. Therefore, God is to be understood as having rested from all his works in such a way [Note: [Col. 0467D] Ms. Joliensis, “so that he would create no nature.” Thus it is read in Augustine’s work: “so that he would create no new nature thereafter.” Other manuscripts of ours, “so that he would no longer create any new creature”] that he would no longer create any nature, not in such a way that he would cease to sustain and govern what he had created (Augustine, book 4 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 12).

## CCLXXIX [Elsewhere CCLXXVIII]. Observance of the Sabbath.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Thus Ms. Joliensis. Other books, “On the true Sabbath.”]

[Col. 0468A]

Once the observance of the Sabbath, which was symbolized by resting for one day, has been removed, the person who is devoted to holy works in hope of future rest observes an everlasting Sabbath. Nor does he glory in his good acts as though they were his own [Note: [Col. 0467D] Ms. Jol. adds the preposition “in,” as in Augustine’s book], or in things he has not received [Note: [Col. 0468C] Ms. Remig., “and in those things which ...”], knowing that the one who works and rests at the same time works within him (Augustine, same work, ch. 13).

## CCLXXX [Elsewhere CCLXXIX]. God’s rest.

The rest of God, for those who understand it rightly, is that in which he needs the good of no one [Note: [Col. 0468C] We emend the text on the basis of Ms. Joliensis, which agrees with Augustine’s text at the cited passage. Other manuscripts of ours, “which.”]. Therefore, our rest is also secure in him, because we are blessed by the good that he is, not by the good that we are [Note: [Col. 0468C] Ms. Jol. adds “also”; Ms. Remig. likewise has, “and therefore our rest in him is also certain, because we are blessed.” The old Cologne edition, “is in God,” where others have “is in him.” Mss. Remig. and Jol., together with Augustine, add “we.” The same Ms. Jol. and Augustine later read, “not himself by the good”; at this point other manuscripts of ours have, “not himself by that.”]. For we too are some good from him, who made all things very good, and made us among them. Yet there is no good thing besides him [Col. 0468B] that he himself did not make. Accordingly, he has no need of any alien good, since he does not need the good that he made [Note: [Col. 0468D] Ms. Jol., “no alien good.”] (Augustine, same work, ch. 16).

## CCLXXXI [Elsewhere CCLXXX]. The beginning of time.

[Note: [Col. 0468D] The old Cologne edition, “When the creature was made, time began through movements.” Ms. Jol. omits “when it was made” and begins, “Through the movements of creatures.” The same manuscript also has “times” a second time, as does Augustine. The others have it only once.]

584

Through the movements of created things, times began to run. Hence it is useless to seek times before creation, as though times could be found before time. For if there were no movement, whether of a spiritual or bodily creature, by which the future would succeed the past through the present, there would be no time at all [Note: [Col. 0468D] Ms. Jol., “there would be no time whatsoever.”]. But a creature could not move if it did not exist. Therefore, time began from the creature rather than the creature from time. Yet both come from God. For from him, through him, and in him are all things (Romans 11:36) (Augustine, book 5 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* [Col. 0468C], ch. 5).

## CCLXXXII [Otherwise CCLXXXI].  
[Note: [Col. 0468D] Other editions: “all things are governed by God’s will.” The Joliensis manuscript: “That even the most contemptible things are governed by divine providence.”]

### That even the most contemptible things are governed by divine Providence

When the Savior says that not one sparrow falls to the ground without God’s will, and that he himself forms and clothes the grass of the field, which shortly afterward is to be cast into the furnace (Matthew 10:29; 6:30), [Note: [Col. 0468D] The old Cologne edition confirms this reading.] does he not confirm that divine Providence governs not only this whole part of the world assigned to mortal and corruptible things, but even its cheapest and most contemptible elements, lest we suppose that those things whose causes we cannot comprehend are disturbed by random movements (Augustine, same work, chapters 21 and 22)?  
[Note: [Col. 0468D] The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis supply the complete word *totam* (“the whole”), which the Prosperian editions lacked, although it is found in the cited passage of Augustine.]

## CCLXXXIII [Otherwise CCLXXXII].  
[Note: [Col. 0469C] Thus the Joliensis manuscript, which nevertheless reads *in spiritalibus* (“in spiritual things”). Other manuscripts: “On the rational soul.”]

### The rational soul ought to be raised toward spiritual things

The rational soul ought to be raised toward those things that excel most greatly in the nature of spiritual realities, so that it may have understanding of the things above, not of the things upon the earth (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 6, chapter 22).  
[Note: [Col. 0469C] In Augustine’s book: “which excel most greatly in the nature of spiritual things.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0469C] All our printed editions read *sapiant* (“may have understanding”); the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, following Augustine, read *sapiat* (“may have understanding”). The old Cologne edition reads: “It ought to be governed [or, perhaps, raised] toward those things which excel the nature of spiritual things, and which have understanding of the things above.”]

## CCLXXXIV [Otherwise CCLXXXIII].  
[Note: [Col. 0469D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. Others: “On natural miracles.”]

### That nothing is done contrary to nature in miracles

God, the creator of natures, does nothing contrary to nature in miracles; nor is what is new with regard to custom opposed to reason. Therefore, things unfamiliar to us seem contrary to nature, because the course of nature has become known to us in another way; but they are not contrary to God, for whatever he has made is nature (Augustine, same work, chapter 13).  
[Note: [Col. 0469D] The Joliensis manuscript together with the old Cologne edition reads *consuetudini* (“to custom”). Others read *consuetudine* (“by custom”).]  
[Note: [Col. 0469D] The Joliensis manuscript: “The unfamiliar seem contrary.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0469D] The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis: “This is nature, namely, what he himself made.” The old Cologne edition: “Since what he has made is nature.”]

## CCLXXXV [Otherwise CCLXXXIV].  

### On the unchangeable order of God’s works

It is credible that every body can be changed into every other body; but it is absurd to believe that any body can be changed into a rational soul. For God is omnipotent in such a way that he never overturns the ordinances of his own reason (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 7, chapters 12 and 20).  
[Note: [Col. 0469D] The Joliensis manuscript: “That every body can be changed into another, but never into a soul.” The old Cologne edition: “On the unchangeable transformation of the soul into a body.”]

## CCLXXXVI [Otherwise omitted].  
[Note: [Col. 0469D] In the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, following the preceding sentence 285 [otherwise 284], the title is: “That it is natural for us to wish to live.” The following sentence is attached: “It is natural for us to wish to live, but living badly is no longer a matter of nature, but of a perverse will, which punishment justly follows.” It is drawn from book 7, chapter 27, of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. It was absent from all the editions.]

### That it is natural for us to wish to live, but not to live badly

It is natural for us to wish to live, but living badly is no longer a matter of nature, but of a perverse will, which punishment justly follows (Augustine, same work, chapter 27).

## CCLXXXVII [Otherwise CCLXXXV].  
[Note: [Col. 0470C] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. Others: “On merit,” as in the old Cologne edition; or “On the merit of the will,” as in the other manuscripts.]

### How a human being is illuminated by God’s presence

Just as air does not become luminous by the presence of light because it was made luminous, but becomes luminous—since, if it had been made luminous rather than becoming so, it would remain luminous even when the light was absent—so a human being is illuminated when God is present, but immediately becomes dark when he is absent. One departs from him not through intervals of place, but through the turning away of the will (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 8, chapter 12).  
[Note: [Col. 0470C] The Remigius manuscript adds this word immediately here; it is also found in Augustine’s cited passage.]

## CCLXXXVIII [Otherwise CCLXXXVI].  
[Note: [Col. 0470D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the usefulness of serving God.” The old Cologne edition: “On the usefulness to a human being of obeying God in matters unknown.”]

### We must obey God

It is greatly useful for a human being to serve God even when the reason for God’s command is unknown. By commanding, God makes useful whatever he wishes to command. There is therefore no reason to fear that he may command something that will not be beneficial. Nor can one’s own will fail to fall upon a human being with the weight of a great ruin if, by exalting itself, it places itself above the will of its superior (Augustine, same work, chapter 13).

## CCLXXXIX [Otherwise CCLXXXVII].  

### On the excellence of human nature

How excellent a good human nature is appears especially from the fact that it has been granted the ability to cleave to the nature of the highest and unchangeable good. If it does not wish to do so, it deprives itself of the good, and this is evil for it; hence, by God’s justice, punishment also follows.

For what is so unjust as for one who has deserted the good to fare well? Sometimes, however, the evil of having lost the higher good is not felt while the lower good that was loved is possessed. But divine justice requires that one who by his will lost what he ought to have loved should lose with pain what he loved, and that the Creator of natures should everywhere be praised. For even the fact that the loss of a good causes pain is still a good. If some good had not remained in nature, there could be no pain over any good that had been lost as punishment (Augustine, same work, chapter 14).  
[Note: [Col. 0470D] The Joliensis manuscript: “He abandoned … is praised.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0470D] The manuscripts of Remigius, Lyons, and the later editions read *in poenam* (“as punishment”); the Colbertinus and Joliensis manuscripts, the old Cologne edition, and the appendix to volume 10 of Augustine read *in poena* (“in punishment”); indeed, this is also the reading in the cited book itself.]

## CCXC [Otherwise CCLXXXVIII].  
[Note: [Col. 0470D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the desire and power to do harm.”]

### On the power to do harm

The desire to do harm can arise perversely from each person’s own mind. But power is only from God, and this too follows from his hidden and profound justice, because there is no injustice with God (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 11, chapter 4).  
[Note: [Col. 0470D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript follows Augustine. The Remigius manuscript together with the old Cologne edition reads: “and this [power] is from his hidden and profound justice”; other manuscripts read: “and this is from his hidden and profound judgments.”]

## CCXCI [Otherwise CCLXXXIX].  
[Note: [Col. 0470D] The Joliensis manuscript and the old Cologne edition add “How great” and include it in the other books.]

### How great and excellent a good God is

How great and excellent a good God is is also clearly shown by this: no one who departs from him fares well. Those who rejoice in deadly pleasures cannot be without fear of pain; and those who do not feel at all the evil of their desertion because of a greater stupor of pride are nevertheless seen by others who know how to discern these things to be weighed down by how great a misery. Thus, if they do not wish to receive the medicine by which such things are avoided, they may serve as an example by which such things can be avoided (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 11, chapter 5).  
[Note: [Col. 0470D] The old Cologne edition: “how great their misery is.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0471D] This agrees with Augustine’s text in the edition appended to volume 10 of his works. The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis read: “by which they may be guarded against.” All the other editions, after the word “medicine,” read: “they may serve as an example of things that can be avoided.”]

## CCXCII [Otherwise CCXC].  
[Note: [Col. 0471D] The Joliensis manuscript: “That one creature is good, another better.”]

### That no creature is evil by nature

Just as true reason teaches that the creature which is not at all attracted by what is illicit is better, so that same reason teaches that the creature which has the power to restrain illicit pleasure so greatly that it rejoices not only in other lawful and rightly performed acts, but also in the restraint of that very perverse pleasure, is good (Augustine, same work, chapter 7).  
[Note: [Col. 0471D] The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, following Augustine, read “at its restraint,” since “to restrain” was stated above. All the others read “at its coercion.”]

## CCXCIII [Otherwise CCXCI].  
[Note: [Col. 0471D] The Joliensis manuscript: “That the works of the Lord are great, sought out in all his wills.”]

### On the great works of the Lord

Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills. He foresees those who will be good, and creates them; he foresees those who will be evil, and creates them; offering himself to the good for enjoyment, lavishing many of his gifts even upon the evil; mercifully forgiving and justly punishing; likewise mercifully punishing and justly forgiving; fearing nothing from anyone’s evil; needing nothing from anyone’s justice; seeking no advantage for himself from the works of the good, and providing even through the punishments of the evil for the good (Augustine, same work, chapter 11).  
[Note: [Col. 0471D] The Remigius manuscript reads “also mercifully”; and below, “even from the goods of the evil.” The old Cologne edition reads: “offering himself to the good for enjoyment, lavishing many of his good things … but providing for the good.”]

## CCXCIV [Otherwise CCXCII].  
[Note: [Col. 0471D] The Joliensis manuscript and the old Cologne edition add “and envy,” or “envy.”]

### On pride and envy

Since pride is love of one’s own excellence, while envy is hatred of another’s happiness, it is readily apparent what arises from what. For by loving his own excellence, a person envies those who are his equals because they are his equal; those below him, lest they become his equal; or those above him, because he does not become their equal. Thus every proud person is envious, but no one becomes proud by being envious (Augustine, same work, chapter 14).

## CCXCV [Otherwise CCXCIII].  
[Note: [Col. 0471D] This follows the Joliensis manuscript, which reads: “How the divinity dwells bodily in Christ”; and the title of the other books: “On the fullness of divinity in Christ.”]

### How the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ
