The fullness of divinity is said to dwell bodily in Christ, not because divinity is a body, but because the sacraments of the Old Testament are called shadows of what was to come. By comparison with shadows, the fullness of divinity is said bodily to dwell in Christ because everything that was figured in those shadows is fulfilled in him; and thus, in a certain manner, he himself is the body of the preceding shadows—that is, he himself is the reality of those figures and signs (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 12, chapter 7).  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] The Remigius manuscript: “a shadow of what was to come.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] The Joliensis manuscript and the old Cologne edition read “in those shadows.” Our other books lack the preposition *in*, although it is found in Augustine.]  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] The more recent Cologne edition, together with the later editions, reads: “he himself is the reality.”]

## CCXCVI [Otherwise CCXCIV].  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the piety of action in this life.”]

### On overcoming vices

Pious action in this life consists in worshiping God, fighting by his grace against inward vices, and not yielding to them when they incite or compel us even toward what is illicit; and, whenever one does yield, asking for pardon with a religious and devout disposition, and asking for God’s help so as not to yield. But in paradise, if no one had sinned, the pious action of overcoming vices would not exist, because it would be the continuation of happiness not to have vices (Augustine, *Unfinished Work in Answer to Julian*, book 1, section 70).  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] The Remigius manuscript omits here the preposition *in*, which is found in the other manuscripts of Prosper and in the appendix to volume 10 of Augustine, though not in the book cited in the margin.]  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] The old Cologne edition reads “thoughts,” rather than “when they incite or compel.”]

## CCXCVII [Otherwise CCXCV].  

### On the courage of pagans and Christians

The courage of pagans is produced by worldly desire, but the courage of Christians is produced by the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts—not through the exercise of the will, which comes from us, but through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Augustine, same work, section 83; canon 18 of the Second Council of Orange).

## CCXCVIII [Otherwise CCXCVI].  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. In the others: “No vice can exist except in something good.”]

### That no evil exists except in something good

There can be no evil except in something good, because it can exist only in some nature; and every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good (Augustine, same work, section 114).  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] Thus from Augustine’s book in the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis. All the others read: “insofar as it is nature, is good.”]

## CCXCIX [Otherwise CCXCVII].  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the reward and glory of good works.”]

### Grace is preceded by no merits

A reward is owed to good works if they are performed; but grace, which is not owed, precedes their performance (Augustine, same work, section 133; canon 18 of the Second Council of Orange).

## CCC [Otherwise CCXCVIII].  

### On circumcision and baptism

Circumcision of the flesh was commanded by the law, because nothing could signify better that original sin would be removed through Christ, the author of regeneration. Every human being is born with a foreskin, just as every human being is born with original sin. The law also commanded that the flesh be circumcised on the eighth day, because Christ rose on the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth day after the Sabbath’s seven days. And the circumcised man begets a child with a foreskin, transmitting to him what he himself has already lost; similarly, one who has been baptized transmits to the son whom he begets in the flesh the guilt of original sin, although he himself has already been freed from it (Augustine, *Unfinished Work*, book 2, section 73).  
[Note: [Col. 0472D] In Augustine: “from which he himself has been absolved.”]

## CCCI [Otherwise CCXCIX].  
[Note: [Col. 0473C] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. Others: “On the first and second Adam.”]

### On the first and second human being

The first human being, Adam, died long ago in such a way that nevertheless, after him, the second human being is Christ, although thousands of human beings arose between the first and the second. Therefore it is clear that everyone who is born from that succession of descent belongs to the first, just as everyone who is reborn in him through the abundance of grace belongs to the second. Hence the entire human race is, in a certain sense, two human beings: the first and the second (Augustine, *Unfinished Work*, book 2, section 163).  
[Note: [Col. 0473C] The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis: “succession of descent.” In Augustine: “who is born from him through a succession of descent,” although elsewhere *ex illa* (“from that”) is read. The Prosperian editions: “who is propagated from that succession.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0473D] The Remigius manuscript: “through the granting of grace.”]

## CCCII [Otherwise CCC].  

### On the judgments of God

God’s judgments must in no way be compared with human judgments. We must not doubt that he is just even when he does what seems unjust to human beings (Augustine, *Unfinished Work*, book 3, section 24).

## CCCIII [Otherwise CCCI].  
[Note: [Col. 0473D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On regeneration.”]

### On the birth of the righteous

The righteous person is born from God, not from human beings, because he becomes righteous by being reborn, not by being born. Hence those who have been regenerated are also called children of God (Augustine, same work, section 51).  
[Note: [Col. 0473D] The Joliensis manuscript: “not from a human being.” The same reading occurs in the cited book of Augustine.]  
[Note: [Col. 0473D] We change *renati* (“born again”), found in our editions, on the authority of the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis; although the latter, following the Leuven edition, has written “otherwise, regenerated” in the margin.]

## CCCIV [Otherwise CCCII].  

### On the condition of human nature

Although human nature is evil because it has been corrupted, it is not itself evil, because it is nature. For no nature, insofar as it is nature, is evil; rather, it is wholly good, without which good no evil can exist, since vice cannot exist except in some nature. Nevertheless, a nature can exist without vice, whether it has never been corrupted or has been healed (Augustine, same work, section 206).  
[Note: [Col. 0473D] The words “evil: because vice cannot exist except in some nature” are supplied from the Remigius manuscript and Augustine’s text, although they have fallen out of the other manuscripts. The Joliensis manuscript has only: “No vice can exist.”]

## CCCV [Otherwise CCCIII].  

### On the death of sinners

It is a just judgment of God that each person should perish through his own sin, although God does not create sin; just as he did not create death, and yet he kills the one whom he judges worthy of death. Hence it is written: “God did not make death”; and it is written: “Death and life are from God.” Anyone who distinguishes divine judgments from divine works plainly sees that these two statements are not contrary to each other, because it is one thing not to have established mortality in creating, and another to punish the sinner in judgment (Augustine, *Unfinished Work*, book 4, section 32).  
[Note: [Col. 0473D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript follows Augustine’s book. Our other manuscripts read “perceived.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0473D] We add the words “God did not make death,” and “it is written,” on the authority of the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, which present the cited passage of Augustine more fully.]

## CCCVI [Otherwise CCCIV].  

### On the punishment of sin

God indeed made the world and absolutely all bodies. But that the corruptible body should weigh down the soul, and the flesh lust against the spirit (Wisdom 9:15), is not part of the preceding nature in which the human being was created, but is the consequence of punishment upon one condemned (Augustine, same work, section 67).  
[Note: [Col. 0474C] Thus the Joliensis manuscript, in agreement with Augustine’s text and the appendix to volume 10 of his works. Although our other manuscripts place “the punishment of sin” in the text, they indicate in the margin the word “of one condemned.”]

## CCCVII [Otherwise CCCV].  
[Note: [Col. 0474D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. The other manuscripts: “On the good creation in every nature.”]

### On the good creation of the human being

However many vices may disgrace any nature, its creation is always good. For just as the creation of the body is good even when a person is born diseased, and the creation of the mind is good even when a person is born foolish, so the creation of the human being himself is good when he is born subject to original sin (Augustine, same work, section 115).  
[Note: [Col. 0474D] Duacensis, Cologne, and the more recent editions read *morbidum* (“diseased”). Since Augustine’s passage both in the *Unfinished Work* and in the *Sentences*, as well as our other manuscripts, reads *morbidus*, we have thought that this should likewise be written, since “a human being” can easily be understood: indeed, a few lines later the expression “of the human being himself” occurs explicitly, although the Joliensis manuscript omits it before the word “human being.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0474D] Augustine reads: “subject to the contagion of original sin.”]

## CCCVIII [Otherwise CCCVI].  
[Note: [Col. 0474D] The Joliensis manuscript: “That some parents aggravate original sin and some lessen it.”]

### On the abolition of sin

Just as certain parents aggravate original sin, so certain parents lessen it; but no one removes it except the one of whom it was said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” For him no good of a human being is impossible, and no evil is incurable (Augustine, same work, section 132).

## CCCIX [Otherwise CCCVII].  
[Note: [Col. 0474D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the mercy of God.”]

### On the grace of God

When someone is freed from that mass of the first human being, to which death is deservedly owed, this belongs not to human merits but to the mercy of God. For there is no injustice with God: he is not unjust either in remitting what is owed or in exacting it; and indulgence is gratuitous where vengeance could have been just (Augustine, letter 186, to Paulinus, chapter 6, section 16).

## CCCX [Otherwise CCCVIII].  

### No one can be saved except by God’s mercy

Human nature, even if it had remained in the integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. Therefore, since without God’s grace it cannot preserve the salvation it received, how can it recover without God’s grace the salvation it lost (Augustine, same letter, chapter 11, section 37; canon 19 of the Second Council of Orange)?  
[Note: [Col. 0474D] The Remigius manuscript reads “cannot,” as in Augustine’s letter. Others read “could not.”]

## CCCXI [Otherwise CCCIX].  
[Note: [Col. 0474D] The Joliensis manuscript: “That every sinner is without excuse.”]

### No excuse belongs to the sinner

Every sinner is without excuse, whether because of the guilt of origin or because of the additional guilt of his own will—whether he knows or is ignorant, whether he judges or does not judge. For ignorance itself is unquestionably a sin in those who were unwilling to understand; but in those who were unable to understand, it is the punishment of sin. Therefore, in both cases there is no excuse, but just condemnation (Augustine, letter 194, to Sixtus, chapter 9, section 27).  
[Note: [Col. 0475D] The Remigius manuscript: “in both.”]

## CCCXII [Otherwise CCCX].  

### On those who are led by the Spirit of God

There is no doubt that being led is greater than being governed. For one who is governed does something, and is governed so that he may act rightly; but one who is led is scarcely understood to do anything himself. Nevertheless, the grace of the Savior accomplishes so much in our wills that the Apostle does not hesitate to say: “As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the children of God.” Nor can free will do anything better in us than commend itself to the one who cannot do evil (Augustine, *On the Deeds of Pelagius*, chapter 3).  
[Note: [Col. 0475D] The Joliensis manuscript: “That being led is greater than being governed.”]

## CCCXIII [Otherwise CCCXI].  
[Note: [Col. 0475D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. The others: “On the resurrection.”]

### What it means to be delivered from this body of death

To be delivered from this body of death, with every sickness of the desire of the flesh healed, is not to receive the body for punishment, but for glory (Augustine, book 1, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 11).

## CCCXIV [Otherwise CCCXII].  
[Note: [Col. 0475D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the good things that God does in a human being.”]

### A human being can do nothing without God

God does many good things in a human being that the human being does not do; but a human being does nothing that God does not enable the human being to do (Augustine, book 2, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 8; canon 20 of the Second Council of Orange).

## CCCXV [Otherwise CCCXIII].  

### On true righteousness

The righteousness by which the righteous person lives by faith, since it comes from God to the human being through the Spirit of grace, is true righteousness. Although it may rightly be called perfect in certain righteous people insofar as this life permits, it is nevertheless small in comparison with that great righteousness which the equality of the angels possesses. The one who did not yet possess that righteousness, because of the one that was already present, called himself perfect; and because of the one that was still lacking, imperfect. But clearly, this lesser righteousness produces merit, while the greater produces the reward. Hence whoever does not pursue the former does not attain the latter (Augustine, book 3, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 7).  
[Note: [Col. 0475D] The old Cologne edition: “which Paul, who did not yet possess.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0475D] The Remigius manuscript: “the lesser made merit … the greater becomes the reward.”]

## CCCXVI [Otherwise CCCXIV].  
[Note: [Col. 0475D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. Others: “On Christ’s mortality according to the flesh.”]

### Christ alone, without sin, underwent the punishment of sin

The catholic faith knows concerning the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, that for us he deigned to undergo death—that is, the punishment of sin—without sin. For just as he alone was made the Son of Man so that through him we might become children of God, so he alone accepted punishment without evil merits, just as through him we receive grace without good merits. For just as no good was owed to us, so no evil was owed to him. Therefore, commending his love to those to whom he was going to give life that was not owed to them, he willed to suffer for them a death that was not owed to him (Augustine, book 4, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 4; canon 2 of the Second Council of Orange).  
[Note: [Col. 0475D] The word “good” was absent from the Leuven, Douai, and recent Cologne editions. It is restored on the authority of the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis and of the old Cologne and Lyons editions, in agreement with Augustine’s text.]

## CCCXVII [Otherwise CCCXV].  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. Others: “On nature and grace.”]

### Grace does not come from nature

Just as the Apostle most truly says to those who wished to be justified by the law and therefore fell away from grace, “If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21), so it is most truly said to those who think that the grace commended and received by the faith of Christ is nature: “If righteousness is through nature, then Christ died for nothing.”

For the law already existed here, and it did not justify; nature already existed here, and it did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing: so that through him the law might be fulfilled—he who said, “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17)—and so that nature, lost through Adam, might be restored through him who said that he had come to seek and save what had perished (Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 13; canon 21 of the Second Council of Orange).

## CCCXVIII [Otherwise CCCXVI].  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On faith.”]

### On mercy and judgment

To be able to have faith, just as to be able to have love, belongs to human nature; but to have faith, just as to have love, belongs to the grace of the faithful. But when the will to believe is prepared by the Lord for some people and is not prepared for others, we must distinguish what comes from his mercy and what comes from his judgment. For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10). Yet “his ways are unsearchable” (Romans 11:33). Therefore unsearchable are the mercy by which he freely delivers and the truth by which he judges justly (Augustine, book 1, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapters 5 and 6).  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis and the old Cologne edition read “just as to have love.” The same Remigius manuscript reads: “grace belongs to the faithful.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] The Joliensis manuscript: “is prepared … is prepared.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] The Remigius manuscript: “For his ways are unsearchable.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] The Remigius manuscript and the old Cologne edition: “Unsearchable: the mercy that freely delivers and the truth that …” The same Cologne edition reads: “which freely delivers, and the truth which …”]

## CCCXIX [Otherwise CCCXVII].  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript. Others: “On giving assistance.”]

### On raising the fallen

No one raises another to the position in which he himself stands unless he descends somewhat to the position in which the other stands (Augustine, letter 11, to Nebridius, section 4).  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] The Joliensis manuscript, following Augustine’s cited letter, reads “anyone”; the other Prosperian manuscripts read “anything.”]

## CCCXX [Otherwise CCCXVIII].  

### On despising worldly glory

Only the person who has declared war on it knows what power the love of human glory has to do harm. For if it is easy for anyone not to desire praise while it is withheld, it is difficult not to take pleasure in it when it is offered (Augustine, letter 22, to Aurelius, section 8).  
[Note: [Col. 0476D] The old Cologne edition, together with Augustine’s cited letter, reads “If it is easy for anyone.” The other manuscripts read “even if it is easy for anyone.”]

## CCCXXI [Otherwise CCCXIX].  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On contempt for the world.”]

### On relinquishing temporal goods

The person who despises not only as much of the world’s wealth as he was able to possess, but also as much as he wished to possess, despises all the world’s riches. In this matter one must beware lest pride creep in. For it is more useful to hold earthly wealth humbly than to relinquish it proudly (Augustine, letter 31, to Paulinus, section 5).

## CCCXXII [Otherwise CCCXX].  

### On restraining anger

No angry person thinks that his anger is unjust. Therefore one must quickly return from every indignation to the gentleness of meekness. For a persistent emotion easily turns into hatred of the person whom one does not quickly forgive (Augustine, letter 38, to Profuturus, section 2).

## CCCXXIII [Otherwise CCCXXI].  

### On law and grace

The one who gave the law also gave grace; but he sent the law through a servant, while with grace he himself descended. Thus, because the law reveals sins but does not remove them, those who wish to carry out the law by their own strength, yet are unable to do so, are compelled to turn to grace, which removes both the sickness of inability and the guilt of disobedience (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 3, section 2).  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] The Joliensis manuscript: “shows sin”; and immediately afterward the Remigius manuscript: “did not remove it.”]

## CCCXXIV [Otherwise CCCXXII].  

### On the Sabbath

The Christian observes the true Sabbath by abstaining from servile work—that is, from sin—for “whoever commits sin” (John 8:34) “is the slave of sin” (Augustine, same work, section 19).  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] The old Cologne edition, following Augustine’s passage, adds “himself,” which is absent from our other manuscripts.]

## CCCXXV [Otherwise CCCXXIII].  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] The Joliensis manuscript: “Sin comes from us; righteousness comes from God.”]

### On the things that belong properly to human beings

No one possesses anything of his own except falsehood and sin. But if a human being possesses any truth or righteousness, it comes from that fountain for which we ought to thirst in this wilderness, so that, sprinkled by it as though by drops, we may not fail along the way (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 5, section 1; canon 22 of the Second Council of Orange).

## CCCXXVI [Otherwise CCCXXIV].  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the inseparable work of the Father and the Son.”]

### On the inseparable work of the Father and the Son

What the Father does together with Christ, Christ does; and what Christ does together with the Father, the Father does. The inseparable love, majesty, and power do nothing separately, just as the Lord himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) (Augustine, same work).  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] The old Cologne edition inserts here “nor does he act separately,” and afterward omits “majesty” and “power,” which are found in the other books and in Augustine.]

## CCCXXVII [Otherwise CCCXXV].  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the grace of regeneration.”]

### Whom the sacrament of baptism benefits

The grace of regeneration is not diminished even by those who do not preserve its gifts, just as the brilliance of light is not polluted by unclean places. Therefore, you who rejoice in having received baptism, live in the holiness of the new human being; and, holding the faith that works through love, possess the good that you do not yet possess, so that the good you do possess may benefit you (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 6, section 16).  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Lest by living badly you lose the faith that works through love, possess it.” The Joliensis manuscript, after “holiness,” omits the conjunction “and” and reads “holding.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] Douai and Cologne, together with the more recent editions, indicate *ave* (“hail”) in the margin.]

## CCCXXVIII [Otherwise CCCXXVI].  
[Note: [Col. 0477D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript; the others: “On truth.”]

### How Christ is the truth

Christ is the truth in such a way that everything in Christ is understood to be true: the true Word of God, God equal to the Father; a true soul, true flesh, true human being, true God; a true birth, true passion, true death, and true resurrection. If you say that any one of these is false, corruption enters; worms of lies are born from the serpent’s poison, and nothing will remain whole. For wherever there is the corruption of some falsehood, there the integrity of truth will not exist (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 8, section 5).  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] The Remigius manuscript: “everything truly.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] The Remigius manuscript: “of this falsehood.”]

## CCCXXIX [Otherwise CCCXXVII].  

### On love

How great is love? If it is absent, the other things are possessed in vain; if it is present, all things are possessed (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 9, section 8).  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] The old Cologne edition: “So great is love.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] Augustine says here “all things are rightly possessed.” The word “rightly” is omitted in Augustine’s manuscripts.]

## CCCXXX [Otherwise CCCXVIII].  

### How Christ left his Father and mother

Christ left the Father because, although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6). This is what it means that he left the Father—not because he abandoned or departed from the Father, but because he did not appear to human beings in the form in which he is equal to the Father.

He left his mother by leaving the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, and cleaving to the Church, which he gathered from all nations.  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript together with Augustine at this place. Our other manuscripts read “to be equal to God.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis: “For this is what it means to leave.” The same Joliensis manuscript reads “or departed.”]

## CCCXXXI [Otherwise CCCXXIX].  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] The Joliensis manuscript: “Just as Eve came from Adam, so the Church comes from Christ’s side.”]

### On the comparison of the first and second Adam

Adam sleeps so that Eve may be made; Christ dies so that the Church may be made. While Adam slept, Eve was made from his side; when Christ died, his side was struck with a lance so that the sacraments might pour forth, by which the Church might be formed. Hence the Apostle rightly calls Adam himself a type of the one to come. For just as all die in Adam (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:22), so all will be made alive in Christ (Augustine, same work, section 10).  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] The Joliensis manuscript: “Adam slept.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] Thus the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, together with Augustine’s passage in the Gospel of John. All the others, including the appendix to volume 10, read “while Adam slept.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] The Joliensis manuscript, as in Augustine’s cited passage: “is struck.” Others: “is pierced.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0478D] The Joliensis manuscript: “by which the Church might be made.”]

## CCCXXXII [Otherwise CCCXXX].  
[Note: [Col. 0479D] The Joliensis manuscript: “What will the human being become, for whose sake God became human?”]

### On the Incarnation of the Word

God became human. What will the human being become, for whose sake God became human (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 10, section 1)?

## CCCXXXIII [Otherwise CCCXXXI].  

### On the two births of human beings

One birth is from earth, the other from heaven; one is from flesh, the other from the Spirit; one is from eternity, the other from mortality; one is from male and female, the other from God and the Church. But each of these two births is singular. For just as the womb cannot be repeated, so baptism cannot be repeated (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 11, section 6).

## CCCXXXIV [Otherwise CCCXXXII].  
[Note: [Col. 0479D] The Joliensis manuscript: “That God is invisible.” This comes close to the sense of the sentence, for which we add “in God” for greater clarity.]

### On the diversity of goods in God

If you consider visible things, bread is not God, water is not God, this light is not God, clothing is not God, and a house is not God. For all these things are visible, and each is a distinct thing. What is bread is not water; what is clothing is not a house; what these things are is not God. They are visible, whereas God is everything for you that you rightly desire; and the variety of all good things is poured forth from one fountain. For when he gives his gifts, he gives himself under the various names of his gifts (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 13, section 5).  
[Note: [Col. 0479D] The old Cologne edition: “If you attend to visible things.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0479D] All the printed editions read “this house.” The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, and Augustine’s passage in the Gospel of John, do not contain the pronoun “this.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0479D] The Remigius manuscript: “flows forth.” The old Cologne edition: “is poured over.”]

## CCCXXXV [Otherwise CCCXXXIII].  
[Note: [Col. 0479D] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the soul desiring bodily things.”]

### On the soul and the intellect
Anima desiring carnal things is compared to a woman who has no governing husband, namely the intellect, by whose wisdom she ought to be guided—not as though it were something other than the soul, but because a certain hidden vision [Note: The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis read, “and that it is the soul’s eye.”] belongs to the soul. For just as the external eyes [Note: The manuscript of Remigius reads, “certainly belong to the flesh.”] are something belonging to the flesh, so the mind is something belonging to the soul, excelling within it through participation in divine reason. And then it presides well over all its movements [Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “over its movements”], when it is irradiated by the light from above, so that within it there may be the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (Augustine, *Tractate 15 on John*, no. 19).

### CCCXXXVI [also numbered CCCXXXIV]. On the place of prayer

[Col. 0480A]

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “When you are about to petition, you seek …”]

If, when you are about to petition God, you seek a suitable and holy place, cleanse your inward parts and, driving every evil desire from them, prepare for yourself a secluded place in the peace of your heart. If you wish to pray in a temple, pray within yourself; and always conduct yourself in such a way that you may be God’s temple. For God hears there where he dwells (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 25).

### CCCXXXVII [also numbered CCCXXXV]. On the bodily senses and the judgment of the mind

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On the inner person.”]

The bodily senses report bodily things to the heart. [Note: The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis read, “and the capacity of all is not the same.” The printed editions read, “and the capacity of all is not identical.”] Their capacities are not all the same: for what is seen is not perceived from the same source as what is heard; nor is flavor received from the same source as odor. Nor are these servants sufficient, without the sense of touch, to distinguish smooth and rough, hot and cold, wet and dry. But the mind judges incorporeal things by its own sense alone, and reaches all their variations in a single movement. Whatever discernment [Note: The manuscript of Remigius reads, “of distinctions.”] it rationally discovers between good and evil, just and unjust, is the effect of a single intention [Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis. Others read, “it is an affection of a single intention.” The manuscript of Remigius reads, “for it is the effect of a single intention.”]. Thus the image of God appears where there is one and the same thing by which the mind can do as much as it can [Note: So read the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis; the others read, “which the mind is able to do.”] (Augustine, *Tractate 18 on John*, nos. 9–10).

### CCCXXXVIII [also numbered CCCXXXVI]. On the life of the Son of God

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis asks, “How is the Son said to have life in himself?”]

[Note: So read the manuscript of Joliensis and the old Cologne edition. The others read: “The Son of God, as God, has life in himself, as the Father has it; he did not acquire it by participation, but by being born.”]

The Son of God is said to have life in himself, as the Father has it—not acquiring it by participation, but by being born. For the Father, who is life, begot Life; and there is no difference in any respect between the essence of the begetter and that of the begotten. Since the Son is thus from the Father, there is coeternal equality—not one person, certainly, but one Godhead [Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “so that, being coeternal, there is not one person but one Godhead.”] (Augustine, *Tractate 19 on John*, nos. 12–13).

### CCCXXXIX [also numbered CCCXXXVII]. Why the Son, and not the Father, is said to be the one who will judge

[Note: So the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On judgment.”]

[Col. 0480C]

Although the Father never departs from the Son, it is nevertheless not the Father but the Son who is said to be present for judging the living and the dead. For there neither the Godhead of the Father nor that of the Son will be seen, but that form of the Son which he united to himself through the sacrament of the incarnation. Therefore the judge will be that very one who stood beneath a judge; that very one will judge who was judged, so that the wicked may see the glory of the one whose gentleness they attacked [Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “whose gentleness they attacked.” Remigius reads, “in whose gentleness they attacked.” Other copies have “they raged”; in the margin they read, “they attacked.”]. Thus the judge will appear in a form that can be seen both by those whom he will crown and by those whom he will condemn. The Father, however, will not appear, because he did not put on the form of a servant. But he gave the power of judgment to the Son, who also became human [Note: The manuscript of Remigius reads, “because he also became human, he gave it to him”] (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 16).

### CCCXL [also numbered CCCXXXVIII, before CCCXXXVI]. How we are to do the will of God and our own

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis. The others read, “On the will of God,” as does the old Cologne edition; or, “On the will of God and of man,” as do the remaining copies.]

People do their own will, not God’s, when they do what displeases God. But when they do what they wish in such a way as to serve the divine will, although they willingly do what they do, it is nevertheless the will of the one by whom what they wish is both prepared and commanded (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 19; canon 23 of the Second Council of Orange).

### CCCXLI [also numbered CCCXXXIX, before CCCXXXVII]. On the Father’s teaching through the Word

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On the Word of God.”]

If the Father teaches the one who hears his word, ask [Note: The manuscript of Remigius reads, “His Word, which is Christ, you will find his Word,” omitting the rest.] what Christ is, and you will find his Word: “In the beginning was the Word,” not “In the beginning God made the Word,” just as it says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” For the Word of God is God, not a creature; nor was it made among all things, but through it all things were made. Therefore, so that a human being established in the flesh might be able to approach the teaching of such a Word, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (Augustine, *Tractate 26 on John*, no. 8).

### CCCXLII [also numbered CCCXL, before CCCXXXVIII]. On the flesh of Christ

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On the body of Christ.”]

The flesh of Christ is the life of the faithful, provided that they do not neglect to be his body. Therefore, if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ, let them become the body of Christ; for no one lives by the Spirit of Christ unless he is the body of Christ (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 13).

### CCCXLIII [also numbered CCCXLI, before CCCXXXIX]. Who eat the body of Christ

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “Who receive and who do not receive the body of Christ.”]

[Col. 0480B]

He receives the food of life [Note: The old Cologne edition adds, “and drinks the cup of life”] and drinks the cup of eternity who remains in Christ and in whom Christ dwells. For the one who is at odds with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he daily and indiscriminately receives the sacrament of so great a reality, to the judgment of his own presumption [Note: The manuscript of Joliensis adds, “nor does he eat the flesh of Christ”] (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 18).

### CCCXLIV [also numbered CCCXLII, before CCCXL]. On the happiness of the wicked

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On the false happiness of the wicked.”]

Worldly wisdom would have it that God never allows those who are evil to be happy [Note: The manuscript of Remigius reads, “which, certainly, God will not allow.” Others, omitting the word “God,” read, “he will not allow.” The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “he does not allow it”; and this is not wrong, since Augustine says, “God never allows this.”], but the wicked are therefore thought happy when they have what they want, because they do not know what happiness is [Note: After Augustine, “they do not know” would be the better reading. The editions of Douai, Cologne, and later editions indicate this in the margin, if the manuscripts of Prosper supported it] (Augustine, *Tractate 28 on John*, no. 7).

### CCCXLV [also numbered CCCXLIII, before CCCXLI]. On the change of heart

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “That it is one thing to move from place to place bodily, and another to move in the heart.”]

To move bodily is one thing; to move in the heart is another. One moves bodily who changes place by bodily movement; one moves in the heart who changes one’s affection by a movement of the heart. If you love one thing now and loved another before, you are not where you were (Augustine, *Tractate 32 on John*, no. 21).

### CCCXLVI [also numbered CCCXLIV, before CCCXLII]. On chrism

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “That the name ‘Christ’ comes from chrism.”]

The name “Christ” comes from *chrism*, that is, from anointing. For every Christian is sanctified in order to understand that he is not only a participant in priestly and royal dignity, but is also made a fighter against the devil (Augustine, *Tractate 33 on John*, no. 3).

### CCCXLVII [also numbered CCCXLV, before CCCXLIII]. On the light

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On inner darkness.” Others read, “On the light”; we have added “true” to them.]

[Col. 0482B]

Let us follow Christ, the true light, so that we may not walk in darkness. The darkness to be feared is the darkness of conduct, not of the eyes; and, if of the eyes, not of the external eyes but of the interior ones [Note: We supply these two words, “but of the interior ones,” on the authority of the single manuscript of Remigius–Rheims, because they are written in the margin of the cited passage in Augustine and are necessary to the sense of the sentence]. From these one distinguishes not white from black, but just from unjust (Augustine, *Tractate 35 on John*, no. 1).

### CCCXLVIII [also numbered CCCXLVI, before CCCXLIV]. That Christ is true God and true man

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On the incarnation of the Word.”]

597 The catholic faith believes and proclaims the Lord Jesus Christ to be both true God and true man. Both are written, and both are true. Whoever asserts Christ to be God only denies the remedy by which he was healed. Whoever asserts Christ to be man only denies the power by which he was created [Note: The old Cologne edition reads: “and denies the power by which he was created, and denies the remedy by which he was healed … Christ is God; Christ is also man. Christ is equal to God, equal to the Father, one with the Father; Christ as man is the Son of the Virgin, taking mortality from a human being, but not iniquity.””]. Therefore let the faithful and upright soul accept both: Christ is God, and Christ is man. What kind of God is Christ? Equal to the Father, one with the Father. What kind of man is Christ? The son of the Virgin, taking mortality from humanity, but not taking iniquity (Augustine, *Tractate 38 on John*, no. 2).

### CCCXLIX [also numbered CCCXLVII, before CCCXLV]. On the sending of the Word

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On the sending of the Son.”]

[Note: The manuscript of Remigius and the old Cologne edition read, “The Lord was sent by the Father.” The same Cologne edition continues, “and for the invisible Godhead to come into this world was the same thing as to appear.”]

The Lord Christ was sent by the Father; he did not depart from the Father. His mission was the incarnation, and for the invisible Godhead to come into this world was the same thing as to appear. If it were quickly grasped, there would be no need for it to be believed, because it would be seen. Therefore it is grasped by believing; unless it is believed, it is never understood [Note: We add the words “because he would be seen” from the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis and from Augustine’s own text in the *Gospel of John*. They are absent from the other Prosperian manuscripts. The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “Therefore, by believing, what is not grasped”—perhaps “believed”—“is never understood”] (Augustine, *Tractate 38 on John*, no. 7).

### CCCL [also numbered CCCXLVIII, before CCCXLVI]. On the faith of the Father and the Son

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On the Father and the Son.”]

[Col. 0483A]

In order that the Father and the Son may rightly be believed, the Son himself must be heard when he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). For with two words two heresies are cut down at once. By saying “one,” he struck Arius; by saying “are,” he overthrew Sabellius. For he would say neither “are” of one person nor “one” of different persons [Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “it would be said.” The manuscript of Remigius reads, “he cannot say ‘are’ of different things”] (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 9).

### CCCLI [also numbered CCCXLIX, before CCCXLVII]. On God and the man Jesus Christ

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “We must recognize both in Christ: one by which … and one by which the Father is greater than he.”]

We must recognize both in Christ: the manner in which he is equal to the Father and the manner in which the Father is greater than he. The one is the Word; the other is flesh. The one is God; the other is man. Yet Christ is one, God and man (Augustine, *Tractate 37 on John*, no. 10).

### CCCLII [also numbered CCCL, before CCCXLVIII]. On the unity of the divine Trinity

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “How many may be one heart and one soul, and on the unity of the Trinity.” The old Cologne edition reads, “On the unity of love.”]

Human beings are undoubtedly many souls and many hearts; but if through faith and love they cling to God, they all become one soul and one heart [Note: Thus we read in the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis. The printed editions read, “but when they cling to God through love and faith.” The old Cologne edition continues, “they become one soul and one heart,” and several lines later, “so that the undivided Trinity is one God, one light, and one principle.”]. If, therefore, the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5), makes such unity out of many souls and many hearts, how much more certainly and firmly does an eternal and unchangeable unity remain in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, where the undivided Trinity is one God, one light, and one principle (Augustine, *Tractate 39 on John*, no. 5)?

### CCCLIII [also numbered CCCLI, before CCCXLIX]. How the Father taught the Son

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On the Father’s teaching to the Son.”]

The Father did not teach the Son as though he had begotten him unlearned and imparted knowledge to one who did not know. Rather, timeless teaching is timeless essence; and to be taught by the Father is the same as to be begotten by the Father. For in the simple nature of truth, being and knowing are not two different things, but the same [Note: Other copies read, “but the very same.” The manuscript of Remigius reads, “but this very same,” in accordance with Augustine]. (Augustine, *Tractate 40 on John*, no. 5).

[Note: Earlier editions read, “but temporal teaching is timeless essence.” The text has been altered to “timeless teaching,” as the manuscript of Remigius presents it; the manuscript of Joliensis likewise has “timeless teaching is timeless essence.” This evidently alludes to Augustine’s words in the cited passage, written in the margin: “The Father spoke incorporeally to the Son, because the Father begot the Son incorporeally.”]

### CCCLIV [also numbered CCCLII, before CCCL]. On faith and truth

[Col. 0484A]

Faith always precedes vision. For we believe in order to know; we do not know in order to believe. Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you have believed (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 9).

### CCCLV [also numbered CCCLIII, before CCCLI]. On the good fragrance of Christ

The good fragrance of Christ is the preaching of truth [Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “he takes that fragrance into life”]. By this fragrance the one who serves and conforms to the Gospel through good conduct [Note: The manuscripts of Joliensis and Remigius read, “through good conduct,” instead of “through good works,” which the others have; they nevertheless first indicate the alternative in the margin] gains life; but the one whose life disagrees with what he speaks well incurs death. This condition also binds hearers: when right preaching is heard by some through unbelief unto death, it is received by others through faith unto salvation (Augustine, *Tractate 50 on John*, no. 8).

### CCCLVI [also numbered CCCLIV, before CCCLII]. On the capacity to believe

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On the faith of Christ.”]

Faith in Christ means believing in the one who justifies the ungodly; believing in the Mediator, without whom no one is reconciled to God; believing in the Savior, who came to seek and save what had been lost; believing in the one who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). But the one who, ignorant of the righteousness of God by which the ungodly is justified, wishes to establish his own righteousness does not grasp this faith; rather, through it he is convicted in his pride [Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “by which he is convicted.” It omits the words “Such people,” through the end of the sentence, which are found in Augustine and the other copies]. For those who think such things are hardened and blinded by their own exaltation, because, by denying the grace of God, they are not helped (Augustine, *Tractate 53 on John*, no. 10).

### CCCLVII [also numbered CCCLV, before CCCLIII]. On true love

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On love.”]

[Col. 0484C]

Whoever possesses love, which comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, loves God and neighbor as himself. For the lover of God is a lover of himself; and whoever does not love God does not love his neighbor, because he does not love himself. For the sake of this love, the hatred of the world must also be endured patiently. For it is necessary that the world hate us when it sees us hate what it loves [Note: The manuscript of Remigius reads, “what he loves”] (Augustine, *Tractate 87 on John*, nos. 1–2).

### CCCLVIII [also numbered CCCLVI, before CCCLIV]. On the twofold meaning of “world”

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On the two classes of human beings.”]

Two classes of human beings are designated under the single name “world.” For just as the wicked are called “the world,” so the holy are called “the world.” Thus, although the whole world is divided against itself both in hatred and in love, we are commanded both to hate it and to love it: when it is said to us, “Do not love the world” (1 John 2:15), and when it is said, “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44), so that, while we detest their iniquity, we may desire their salvation (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 4).

### CCCLIX [also numbered CCCLVII, before CCCLV]. On avoiding the glory of knowledge

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On the condition of the learner and the teacher.”]

To avoid the temptation of vainglory, the condition of the learner is better than that of the teacher [Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “the condition of the learner rather than that of the teacher”]. For truth is heard more safely than it is preached. When teaching is received, humility is preserved; but when disputation is pleasing, it is scarcely possible that the speaker should not be struck by at least a little boastfulness (Augustine, *Tractate 57 on John*, no. 2).

### CCCLX [also numbered CCCLVIII, before CCCLVI]. On the praise by which God proclaims himself

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “That God does not exalt himself by praising himself.”]

It is dangerous for a human being to be pleased with himself, since he must beware of becoming proud. But however much God praises himself, he does not exalt himself, the Most High, nor does he wish to appear greater in majesty than he is. When he speaks to human beings of his power, he does not do this so that he himself may be more glorious, but so that they may become better and more instructed. It benefits us to recognize our Creator and to submit to the one who is above all, lest, concerning the one whose nature we cannot comprehend, we should be able to think what he is not [Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “so that concerning the one whose nature we cannot know, we may be able, and so forth.” The manuscript of Remigius reads, “lest concerning the one … what he is.” Most printed editions read, “lest concerning the one … we may be able to think what he is not.” The editions of Douai and Cologne, together with later editions, read, “lest concerning the one … we may be able to perceive what he is not.”] (Augustine, *Tractate 58 on John*, no. 3).

### CCCLXI [also numbered CCCLIX, before CCCLVII]. On the remission of sins

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On the progress of piety through the forgiveness of sins.”]

[Col. 0485C]

Christian observance reaches the progress of perfect piety chiefly through mutual forgiveness of sins [Note: The manuscript of Remigius reads, “progress”], since the Lord gives us an example of his goodness. For if he in whom there was absolutely no sin intercedes for our sins, how much more ought we to pray for one another concerning our own? A person who cannot be entirely free from sin ought indeed to embrace this gracious condition: by forgiving the offenses of others, he washes away his own [Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “who is not entirely able to be without sin”] (Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 5).

### CCCLXII [also numbered CCCLX, before CCCLVIII]. On the fulfillment of the desires of the righteous

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On the eternity of the saints.”]

The satisfaction of the desires of the righteous [Note: The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis read, “to the satisfaction”; all the others read, “to the fellowship.” The former is better, since it reflects Augustine’s words: “He will lead them to that end which is sufficient for them, where their desire will be satisfied with good things.” A few words later, Douai and the recent Cologne edition read, “all in all those things”; the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, and the old Cologne, Lyon, and Louvain editions, more appropriately read, “all things”] will then lack nothing, when God is all in all of them (1 Corinthians 15:28). Those reach this blessedness who die to this age before the separation of the soul from the flesh [Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “the soul from the flesh.” The others omit the preposition “from”], and in whom there are not found desires [Note: Remigius reads, “desires”; Joliensis, “they will be found in desires”] that only the love of God overcomes, so that iniquity suffers what it chose, while justice enjoys the good that it loved [Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “and so that it may therefore enjoy the good”] (Augustine, *Tractate 65 on John*, no. 1).

### CCCLXIII [also numbered CCCLXI, before CCCLIX]. On confessing the man Jesus Christ

Whoever confesses Christ as God in such a way as to deny that the same Christ is truly human—possessing, united to himself, the nature of our flesh and soul—Christ did not die for him, because Christ died according to his humanity. Such a person is not reconciled to God through the Mediator. For there is one God and one Mediator between God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5) [Note: Thus the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, following Augustine at the cited passage. The Louvain and later editions read, “and there is one.” The old Cologne edition reads, “For there is one God and one.”]. He is not justified through Christ, because just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one human being the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). He will not rise in the resurrection of life [Note: So, together with Augustine, read the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis. The printed editions read, “at the resurrection”], because death came through a human being and the resurrection of the dead through a human being. For as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ (1 Corinthians 15:21–22) [Note: The manuscripts of Remigius read, “will be made alive.”]. Nor should anyone defend himself by the example of blessed Peter, who both accused and washed himself with many tears (Matthew 26:75) [Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “Let no one defend himself”], so that the Church might follow its leader not by imitating his denial but by imitating his repentance (Augustine, *Tractate 66 on John*, no. 2).

### CCCLXIV [also numbered CCCLXII, before CCCLX]. On eternity

[Col. 0486C]

Among certain eternal things there may be some difference; eternity itself, however, is without diversity of measure. For the many dwelling places signify, within one life, various degrees of merit. But when God is all in all, there will also be equal joy amid unequal brightness [Note: We emend this from the Douai edition, as required by the sense and by Augustine’s wording in the passage observed by Saint Prosper: “No one is excluded from the kingdom because of the one denarius.” Other copies read “through joy,” which does not fit the immediately preceding phrase, “amid unequal brightness.”], so that what each possesses may be common to all. For through the bond of love no part of the body will be alienated from the glory of the head (Augustine, *Tractate 67 on John*, no. 2).

### CCCLXV [also numbered CCCLXIII, before CCCLXI]. On faith

The faith of those who are going to see God believes what it does not see; for if it sees, it is not faith. Merit is gathered for the believer [Note: We have written “is gathered” in place of “is promised,” which appeared in earlier editions, on the authority of the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, and because all editions from the old Lyon edition to the latest indicate this in the margin; it is also found in Augustine’s passage], while the reward is given to the one who sees (Augustine, *Tractate 68 on John*, no. 3).

### CCCLXVI [also numbered CCCLXIV, before CCCLXII]. That God is merciful when he does not grant the requests of the wicked

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On a contrary petition.”]

A person who would use badly what he wishes to receive does not receive it because God has mercy [Note: The manuscript of Remigius reads, “what he would have received.”]. Therefore, if someone asks God for something by which he would be harmed if his request were granted, he should fear all the more that God, who in mercy could refrain from giving it, may give it in anger [Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “what he could give in mercy”] (Augustine, *Tractate 73 on John*, no. 1).

### CCCLXVII [also numbered CCCLXV, before CCCLXIII]. On Christ’s twofold love for those who love him

[Note: Other editions have the title, “On love”; we have thought it advisable to add some things for greater clarity. The manuscript of Joliensis has as its title, “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father,” and so forth.]

The Lord says, “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” [Note: The manuscript of Remigius here inserts the words, “What does ‘I will love’ mean, and ‘I will manifest myself’?”] What does “I will love” mean? Is he saying that he will love him only then and does not love him now? Far from it. How could the Father love us without the Son, or the Son without the Father? [Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis, in conformity with Augustine’s text at the cited passage. The old Cologne edition reads, “Since they work inseparably, how are they loved separately?” perhaps for “how do they love separately?” Other copies read, “Since they work inseparably, how do they love separately?”]. Since they work inseparably, how do they love separately? Rather, “I will love him” is directed toward what follows, “and I will manifest myself to him.” “I will love and manifest”—that is, I will love for the purpose of manifesting myself. For now he loved us for the purpose that we should believe and hold to the commandment of faith [Note: Remigius reads, “the commandment of faith.” The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “the commandment of faith,” as does Augustine. The others read, “his commandment,” although they mark “the commandment of faith” in the margin]; then he will love us for the purpose that we should see and receive that vision itself as the reward of faith. For now we too love by believing what we shall see [Note: The manuscript of Joliensis adds, “what we do not see.” The others, like Augustine, read as in the text]; then we shall love by seeing what we believed (Augustine, *Tractate 75 on John*, no. 5).

### CCCLXVIII [also numbered CCCLXVI, before CCCLXIV]. On the vine and its branches

[Note: Up to this point the title was “On the branches of the vine.” The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “How the branches are in the vine.”]

The branches are in the vine in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine, but receive from it the source of their life. Thus the vine is in the branches so as to supply them with vital nourishment, not to receive anything from them. Consequently, for the disciples both to have Christ remaining in them and to remain in Christ benefits the disciples, not Christ. For when a branch is cut off, another can sprout from the living root; but the branch that has been cut off cannot live without the root (Augustine, *Tractate 81 on John*, no. 1; canon 24 of the Second Council of Orange).

### CCCLXIX [also numbered CCCLXVII, before CCCLXV]. On the measure of human righteousness

[Note: The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “On what is written, ‘Do not be excessively righteous.’”]

[Col. 0488A]

It is divinely said, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7:17). This does not censure the righteousness of the wise, but the pride of the presumptuous [Note: Thus the manuscript of Remigius and the appendix to the printed edition of Augustine, in accordance with the same passage in the *Gospel of John*. The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “For there is no righteousness.” The other copies read, “For it is not.”]. Whoever therefore becomes excessively righteous becomes unjust through that very excess. But who makes himself excessively righteous except the one who says that he has no sin [Note: We add the word “excessively” from the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis. Augustine says, “For he makes himself very righteous who says that he has no sin.”] (Augustine, *Tractate 95 on John*, no. 2)?

### CCCLXX [also numbered CCCLXVIII, before CCCLXVI]. That only the divine substance is truly simple

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On simplicity.”]

No substance, even that of an incorporeal creature, is truly simple if its being is not the same as its knowing; for it can exist without knowing [Note: The manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis read, “and without knowing.”]. But the divine substance alone cannot do so, because it is identical with what it possesses [Note: Only the old Cologne edition adds here the word “substance,” which is understood from what precedes in all the others]. Accordingly, it does not possess knowledge in such a way that the knowledge by which it knows is one thing and the essence by which it is another; rather, both are one, although it should not be called “both,” since it is most truly simple and one.

The Father has life in himself; nor is he other than the life that is in him. And he gave the Son to have life in himself: that is, he begot the Son, who himself also was life [Note: Other copies read, “who himself is life.” The manuscript of Remigius, following Augustine in the *Gospel of John*, reads, “who himself would be life.”]. Thus we must understand what is said of the Holy Spirit: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16:13), so that we may understand that he is not from himself. For the Father alone is not from another. The Son was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father [Note: The manuscript of Remigius adds here “and from the Son,” and below, “from those from whom he proceeds.” Since these words are found neither in the other copies nor in Augustine’s tractate itself, they appear to be additions by a scribal copyist. This is especially so because in the same tractate, though after much intervening material, the holy Doctor explicitly undertakes to prove that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son.]. The Father, however, was neither born from another nor proceeds from another. Yet human thought should not therefore encounter any inequality in that supreme Trinity, because the Son is equal to the one from whom he was born, and the Holy Spirit is equal to the one from whom he proceeds (Augustine, *Tractate 99 on John*, no. 4).

### CCCLXXI [also numbered CCCLXIX, before CCCLXVII]. How “was,” “will be,” and “is” are to be understood of God

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the other books read, “On the timelessness of the Godhead.”]

Although an unchangeable nature does not admit of “was” and “will be,” but only “is”—for it truly is, because it cannot be otherwise than it is—nevertheless, because of the changing times in which our mortality and our mutability exist, we do not speak falsely when we say “was,” “will be,” and “is” [Note: Remigius reads, “that it was, will be, and is.” Joliensis reads, “and was, and will be, and is,” with the words arranged as in Augustine’s tractate. Other copies have “and was, and is, and will be.” Thus, following Augustine’s cited passage, the manuscript of Joliensis has “in the past”; Remigius has “in the past tense”; others have “in the past.”]. It was in past ages, is in the present, and will be in the future. It was, because it was never absent; it will be, because it will never be absent; it is, because it is always. For it does not perish with the past as though it no longer existed; nor does it slip away with the present as though it did not remain; nor will it arise with the future as though it had not existed. Therefore, although human speech varies according to the sequence of times, the words of any tense are truly said of the one who could not, cannot, and will not be able to be absent from any time.

The Holy Spirit therefore always hears, because he always knows; and for him to know and to hear is the same as always to be. But for him always to be is to proceed from the Father. No one can say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life. Accordingly, just as the Father, having life in himself, gave the Son also to have life in himself [Note: Thus read the manuscripts of Remigius and Joliensis, in accordance with Augustine’s cited passage. Other Prosperian copies read, “so he gave the Holy Spirit to have life”], so he gave the Holy Spirit life to proceed from him, just as he also proceeds from him (Augustine, *Tractate 99 on John*, nos. 5, 9).

### CCCLXXII [also numbered CCCLXX, before CCCLXVIII]. That loving God is a gift of God

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read, “On the love with which we love God.”]

It is altogether a gift of God to love God. The one who loved without being loved first gave himself to be loved. We were loved when we were displeasing, so that something might arise in us by which we would become pleasing. For the Spirit of the Father and the Son pours love into our hearts, and with the Father and the Son we love him [Note: Remigius, together with Augustine’s *Tractate on John* and the canon of the Council of Orange, reads, “pours out.” All our other copies read, “poured out.”] (Augustine, *Tractate 102 on John*, no. 5; canon 25 of the Second Council of Orange).

### CCCLXXIII [also numbered CCCLXXI, before CCCLXIX]. On the peace of Christ

[Col. 0489C]

The peace of Christ has no temporal end, and it is the perfection of every pious intention and action. For its sake we are imbued with his sacraments; for its sake we are instructed by his wondrous works and words; for its sake we have received his Spirit as a pledge [Note: Remigius reads, “we receive his Spirit as a pledge.” The manuscript of Joliensis reads, “we received his Spirit as a pledge,” as does Augustine in the cited *Tractate on John*. Our other books read, “we received the pledge of the Holy Spirit”]; for its sake we believe and hope in him and, insofar as he grants it, are kindled with love for him. Finally, for its sake we endure every tribulation courageously, so that in it we may reign happily without tribulation. For true peace creates unity (1 Corinthians 6:17), since “the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (Augustine, *Tractate 104 on John*, no. 1).

### CCCLXXIV [also numbered CCCLXXII, before CCCLXX]. That all time has been ordered by God

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Joliensis; the others read more generally, “On times.”]

604. Every time has been ordained by him who is not subject to time. For whatever was destined to occur at the successive times possesses in God’s wisdom [Note: For *efficaces* (“effective”), we restore *efficientes* (“productive”), which the Remigius and Joli manuscripts and the cited passage of Augustine’s Gospel commentary have; indeed, all editions after the old Lyon edition noted the latter in the margin, although they printed *efficaces* in the text.] producing causes, in which there are no times. Therefore, one must not believe that the hour of the Lord’s Passion came under the pressure of fate, but rather by God’s ordering. For [Note: The old Cologne edition reads, “For the necessity of fate did not cause it.”] no necessity of the stars brought the cross upon Christ; nor did the stars compel the creator of the stars to die—he who, being timeless with the Father, chose the time when he would die in the flesh just as he chose the time when he would be born of his mother [Note: Augustine expresses this in the Gospel commentary with these words: “with the Father, from whom he was born without time.” The Remigius manuscript reads: “who is timeless with the Father, chose the time in which he would die in the flesh and the time—or perhaps, ‘the manner’—in which he would be born of his mother.”] (Augustine, cited above, no. 2).

### CCCLXXV [Elsewhere CCCLXXIII, before CCCLXXI].  
[Note: The Joli manuscript reads: “On the order of these words: ‘that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.’] On the unity of the Trinity.

[Col. 0490B]

In the statement, “Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), the order of the words is: “that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the only true God.” The Holy Spirit is consequently understood as well, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, as the substantial and consubstantial love of both. For there are not two gods, the Father and the Son; nor three gods, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; rather, the Trinity itself is one and only one true God. Yet the Father is not the same as the Son, nor the Son the same as the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the same as the Father or the Son. For there are three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but the Trinity itself is one God (Augustine, *Tractates on John* 105, no. 3).

### CCCLXXVI [Elsewhere CCCLXXIV, before CCCLXXII].  
[Note: Thus the Joli manuscript. Others, more generally: “What the Father gave the Son.”] That the Father gave all things to the Son by begetting.

Whatever God the Father gave to God the Son, he gave by begetting. For the Father gave the Son those things without which the Son could not be, just as he gave him existence. For how could he give words to the Word, in whom he ineffably spoke all things? (Augustine, *Tractates on John* 106, no. 7).

### CCCLXXVII [Elsewhere CCCLXXV, before CCCLXXIII].  
[Note: Thus the Joli manuscript and the old Cologne edition: “On the guardianship by which God preserves his own.” Others: “On God’s guardianship, by which he preserves his own.”] On God’s guardianship over us.

We must not understand God’s guardianship over us in a merely physical manner, as though the Father and the Son guarded us in turn, with their alternating guardianship preserving us—so that one should succeed the other when the other departed. For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is one true [Note: The Remigius and Joli manuscripts, following Augustine’s commentary on John, add “and blessed,” which the other witnesses omit.] and blessed God, guard us together.

But Scripture does not lift us up unless it first descends to us. As the Word became flesh and descended [Note: The Remigius and Joli manuscripts read “in order to lift us up,” as does Augustine; others read “in order to raise us up again.” The old Cologne edition reads “in order to raise us up.”] in order to lift us up, he did not fall in order to lie there. If we have recognized him descending, let us rise with him who lifts us up; and let us understand that when he speaks in this way, he distinguishes him as to persons [Note: The Joli manuscript, together with Augustine’s commentary on John, reads “him.” Others read “it.”] without separating the natures [Note: The Joli manuscript reads “not separating the nature.”].

### CCCLXXVIII [Elsewhere CCCLXXVI, before CCCLXXIV].  
On the grace of God, by which every human merit is preceded.

[Note: The Joli manuscript: “On the saying of the Lord, ‘Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.’”]

If we consider the nature in which we were created, since Truth created us all, who is not from the truth? Yet not everyone receives from Truth itself the ability to hear the truth and believe it, with no preceding merits whatsoever, lest grace cease to be grace. For if he had said, “Everyone who hears my voice is from the truth,” he would have been thought to be called “from the truth” because he obeys the truth. But he does not say this. Rather, he says: “Everyone who is from the truth hears my voice” (John 18:37). Accordingly, he is not from the truth because he hears its voice; rather, he hears because he is from the truth—that is, because this gift has been bestowed upon him by the truth. What else does this mean than: by Christ’s gift, he believes in Christ? (Augustine, *Tractates on John* 115, no. 4).

### CCCLXXIX [Elsewhere CCCLXXVII, before CCCLXXV].  
On the love with which we ought to love God.

Whoever loves himself and not God does not love himself; and whoever loves God and not himself truly loves himself. For whoever cannot live from himself certainly dies by loving himself. [Note: The Remigius manuscript adds here: “Therefore he does not love himself who loves himself in order not to live”; these words are found at this place in Augustine’s works on the Gospel of John but are absent from the other manuscripts.] Therefore, he does not love himself who loves himself in order not to live. But when the one from whom he lives is loved, he loves himself more by not loving himself—that is, by refusing to love himself so that he may love the one from whom he lives [Note: The Remigius manuscript reads “when he is loved.”] (Augustine, *Tractates on John* 123, no. 4).

### CCCLXXX [Elsewhere CCCLXXVIII, before CCCLXXVI].  
[Note: The Joli manuscript reads: “How the Father acts toward the Son through the Son.”] On the undivided work of the Father and the Son.

Whatever it is that the Father ought to do toward the Son is done only through that same Son: toward him, certainly, because he is the Son of Man and was made among all things; but through him, because he is the Son of God, and through him all things are made by the Father (Augustine, *On the Trinity* I.7, and *Against the Arian Sermon* VII.11, no. 9).

### CCCLXXXI [Elsewhere CCCLXXIX, before CCCLXXVII].  
[Note: Thus the Joli manuscript, which also adds “what the Apostle says.” Others: “On the subjection of the Son.”] How the Son will be subject to the Father.

606. It is not astonishing to say that the Apostle teaches that even in the future age the Son will be subject to the Father, when he says: “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him” (1 Corinthians 15:27). For the human form will remain in the Son, and in this form the Father is always greater.

Nevertheless, some have thought that the Son’s subjection at that time should be understood as the transformation of his human form into the divine substance, as though whatever is changed and transformed into another thing is thereby subjected to it. But the Apostle may be understood to have said that even then the Son would be subject to the Father precisely so that no one would suppose that his human spirit and body would be consumed by some transformation: so that God may be all things, not merely [Note: The Joli manuscript reads “in that human form.”] in that human form, but in all things (ibid., 28), when the glory of the Head fills the whole body (Augustine, *On the Trinity* I.8; *Against the Arian Sermon* 27; and *Against Maximinus the Arian* II.18).

### CCCLXXXII [Elsewhere CCCLXXX, before CCCLXXVIII].  
[Note: Thus the Joli manuscript. Others read: “That nothing in any creature is left disordered by the Creator.”] That all good things are from God.

Whatever good things there are, whether great or small, cannot exist except from God. For what is greater among created things than an intelligent life? Or what can be less than a body? However much these things decline and tend toward nonexistence, some form nevertheless remains in them, so that they exist in some manner. Whatever form remains in a declining thing comes from that form which does not know decline and does not permit the movements of declining or advancing things to exceed the laws of its numbers [Note: Our manuscripts commonly read “of that form.” The Remigius manuscript and the appendix to volume X of Augustine read “of the form in them,” in accordance with the passage cited in the margin.].

Whatever, therefore, is observed to be praiseworthy in the nature of things—whether it is judged worthy of little or great praise [Note: Thus the Joli manuscript, following Augustine at the place indicated here. Others read “whatever is worthy of praise.” The preposition had somewhat disturbed the meaning of the passage.]—must be referred to the most excellent and ineffable praise of the Creator [Note: The Remigius manuscript reads “of the Founder.”] (Augustine, *On Free Will* II.17).

### CCCLXXXIII [Elsewhere CCCLXXXI, before CCCLXXIX].  
[Note: The Joli manuscript reads: “That God compels no one to sin, although he foresees that he will sin.”] That God’s foreknowledge does not compel anyone to sin.

God compels no one to sin; yet he foresees those who will sin by their own will. Why, then, should the just God not punish what he foreknows without compelling it to occur?

For just as no one compels past events to have happened by remembering them, so God does not compel future events to occur by his foreknowledge. And just as a human being remembers certain things he has done, yet does not do everything he remembers [Note: Augustine has “has done” here; all our manuscripts read “does.”], so God foreknows all things of which he himself is the author, yet he is not the author of everything he foreknows. Of those things whose evil author he is not, he is the just avenger (Augustine, *On Free Will* III.4).

### CCCLXXXIV [Elsewhere CCCLXXXII, before CCCLXXX].  
On knowing creatures that are not seen.

The human soul is naturally joined to the divine principles on which it depends. When it says, “This would be better done than that,” if it speaks truly and sees what it says, it sees it in those heavenly principles. Let it therefore believe that God made what it has recognized, by correct understanding, ought to be made by him [Note: Thus the Remigius and Joli manuscripts, as well as Augustine’s book *On Free Will*. Other manuscripts of Prosper read “what it recognizes to have been made.”], even if it does not see this among created things.

For even if it could not see the sky with its eyes, yet concluded by true reason that something of this kind ought to be made, it ought to believe that it had been made [Note: Thus the Remigius and Joli manuscripts, in agreement with *On Free Will*. The other Prosper manuscripts read “ought to have been made.”], although it had not seen it with its eyes. It would not discern by thought that it ought to be made unless it did so through those principles by which all things were made. But what is not there no one can see by true thought any more than it exists [Note: The Joli manuscript reads “than know it.” Augustine, in *On Free Will*, reads “than it is true.”] (Augustine, ibid., 5).

### CCCLXXXV [Elsewhere CCCLXXXIII, before CCCLXXXI].  
[Note: The Joli manuscript reads: “Who are worthy, and who unworthy, of mercy.”] By what remedy human wounds are healed.

What is more worthy of mercy than a wretched person, and what is more unworthy of mercy than a proud wretch? [Note: The Remigius manuscript reads “than a proud wretch.”] [Note: The Remigius manuscript reads: “From him it came about [lacuna] through whom all things were made.”] Thus it came about that the Word of God, through whom all things were made and whom all angelic blessedness enjoys, extended his mercy even to our misery; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

For in this way a human being, not yet equal to the angels, could eat the bread of angels, if that very bread of angels deigned to become equal to human beings. Nor did he descend to us in such a way as to abandon them. Rather, he remained wholly with them and wholly with us: inwardly nourishing them through what he is as God, and outwardly instructing us through what we are [Note: The Duac, Cologne, and later editions read “not outwardly admonishing.”], making those fit through faith whom he will nourish equally through vision [Note: The Joli manuscript, following Augustine’s book at this passage, omits the conjunction “and,” which is found in the other manuscripts] (Augustine, ibid., 10).
