### CCCLXXXVI [Elsewhere CCCLXXXIV, before CCCLXXXII].  
[Note: Thus the Joli manuscript. Others less suitably read: “That no defect of nature comes from its author.”] That every defect is contrary to nature.

There is no doubt that every defect is contrary to nature, even to the nature of the thing whose defect it is. Therefore, since in anything nothing is condemned except its defect, and it is a defect precisely because it is contrary to the nature of the thing whose defect it is [Note: The Remigius and Joli manuscripts read “is contrary to nature,” omitting “of the thing whose defect it is.” The final three words are enclosed in double brackets in all printed Prosper editions, as though added to this passage. Nevertheless, they are found in Augustine’s own text, from which this statement was taken.], no one rightly condemns the defect of anything unless that thing’s nature is praised. For what displeases us in a defect is only that it corrupts what pleases us in nature (Augustine, ibid.).

### CCCLXXXVII [Elsewhere CCCLXXXV, before CCCLXXXIII].  
[Note: The Joli manuscript reads: “On the ignorance and difficulty of sinners.”] On the punishment of sin.

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads: “Every sin belongs to the soul. There are two punishments.”] Every sinful soul suffers two punishments: ignorance and difficulty. Through ignorance error depraves; through difficulty torment afflicts. But to approve falsehoods in place of truths, so that one errs unwillingly, and, while the resistance of the bonds of the flesh opposes one, to be unable to abstain from illicit works, is not the nature with which the human being was established, but the punishment of one condemned [Note: The Remigius manuscript reads “the prison … cannot”; the old Cologne edition, “and, by resisting the resistance of the carnal bond”; the Joli manuscript, “by the opposition of the carnal bond.”] (Augustine, ibid., 18).

### CCCLXXXVIII [Elsewhere CCCLXXXVI, before CCCLXXXIV].  
[Note: The Joli manuscript reads: “On the diversity of commands”; another Joli reading: “On variety.”] On the variety of remedies.

Just as the art of medicine, while remaining the same and in no way changing in itself, nevertheless changes its prescriptions for the sick because our health is changeable, so divine providence, although entirely immutable in itself, comes to the aid of changeable creation in various ways. According to the diversity of illnesses, it commands or forbids different things [Note: Augustine reads “on some occasions he commands one thing, on others another”; a few of our manuscripts read “different things.”], so that it may lead back and strengthen what is failing—from vice, where death begins, and from death itself—to its own nature and essence, that is, away from nothingness, toward which it is tending (Augustine, *On True Religion* 17).

### CCCLXXXIX [Elsewhere CCCLXXXVII, before CCCLXXXV].  
[Note: Thus the Joli manuscript. Others read: “On the first transgression of the human being.”] On the soul’s first defect.

The first defect of the rational soul is the will to do what the highest and innermost Truth forbids. Thus the human being was expelled from paradise into this age: that is, from eternal things to temporal things, from abundance to need, from firmness to weakness.

Not, therefore, from substantial good to substantial evil—for no substance is evil—but from eternal good to temporal good; from spiritual good to bodily good; from intelligible good to sensible good; from the highest good to the lowest good. There is, then, a certain good which the rational soul sins by loving, because it has been placed below the soul. Therefore, sin itself is evil, not the substance that is loved through sin (Augustine, *On True Religion* 20).

### CCCXC [Elsewhere CCCLXXXVIII, before CCCLXXXVI].  
[Note: Other editions read “On the teacher,” etc. The Joli manuscript reads: “On the law of all the arts, which is truth.”] On the truth that is the law of all the arts.

Although the law of all the arts is entirely immutable, the human mind, which has been granted the ability to see such a law, can nevertheless suffer the changeability of error. It is therefore sufficiently clear that above our mind there is a law called truth.

Nor can there now be any doubt that the immutable nature which is above the rational soul is God, and that there are the first life and the first essence where the first wisdom is. For this is that immutable truth which is rightly called the law of all the arts and the art of the omnipotent Craftsman.

Thus, when the soul perceives that it does not judge the form and movement of bodies according to itself, it must at the same time recognize [Note: The Joli manuscript reads “acknowledge,” following Augustine’s *On True Religion*; others read “recognize.”] that it surpasses in nature the nature about which it judges, while that nature according to which it judges surpasses the soul, and the soul cannot in any way judge it (Augustine, ibid., 30–31).

### CCCXCI [Elsewhere CCCLXXXIX, before CCCLXXXVII].  
[Note: The Joli manuscript reads: “How authority and reason incite one to learn.”] How the heart is urged toward learning.

[Col. 0496A]

We are necessarily led to learning in two ways: by authority and by reason. In time, authority comes first; in the matter itself, reason comes first. For one thing is what is given precedence in action, and another what is valued more highly in desire.

Since, then, “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Proverbs 1:7), and humility is the path to sublime things, let human ignorance proceed by faith, so that faith may deserve to see what it believes (Augustine, *On Order* II.9).

### CCCXCII [Elsewhere CCCXC, before CCCLXXXVIII].  
[Note: This final sentence is absent from the Remigius and Joli manuscripts.] On not being proud of riches, and so forth.

[Note: The old Cologne edition reads: “Of riches, flowers, and the nobility of ancestors,” etc.] You boast and exult in your riches, in the nobility of your ancestors, in your homeland, in the beauty of your body, and in the honors bestowed upon you by human beings. Look at yourself, because you are mortal, because you are earth, and because you will return to earth.

Look around at those who before you shone with similar splendors. Where are those whom the power of fellow citizens once surrounded? Where are the unconquerable emperors? Where are those who organized assemblies and festivals? Where are the splendid drivers of horses [Note: All editions after the old Cologne edition record in the margin the alternative “nourishers”?]? The commanders of armies, satraps, tyrants? [Note: The old Cologne edition reads: “Are not all now dust? Are not all now ashes? Is not the memory of their life contained in a few lines?”] Are not all of them dust? Are not all of them ashes? Is not the memory of their life contained in a few bones?

Look at the tombs and see who is servant and who master, who poor and who rich. If you can, distinguish the captive from the king, the strong from the weak, the beautiful from the deformed. [Note: The old Cologne edition reads: “Remember this, then, and never exalt yourself.”] Remember nature, then, and never exalt yourself. You will remember it if you look at yourself.

# EPIGRAMS

## PREFATORY NOTICE ON THE BOOK OF SAINT PROSPER’S EPIGRAMS DRAWN FROM THE SENTENCES OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

There are more than one hundred epigrams, each preceded by a subject drawn from selected sentences of Augustine; one might therefore judge them to be Prosper’s solely on that account. Yet throughout the entire series our author is so intent on explaining or defending the doctrines of divine grace, and so accustomed to revising his earlier formulations, that he reveals himself in every line of the work and could be recognized among thousands, even if all manuscripts everywhere, all editions, and every age did not attribute the work to him.

Joseph Antelmius, so often mentioned, gives precisely this judgment of the work in Dissertation 9, *On the Poetry of Saint Prosper*, among the *Critical Dissertations on the Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*.

The fair and prudent reader will readily judge with what purpose and with what benefit he attempted this. He will understand that the man, intent in all things upon his own and others’ edification, had one aim: that the principal portions of the sentences published in the preceding book should not merely be usefully taken up for the exercise of poetic talent, but that through this kind of writing they might also cling more firmly to the mind and be more pleasantly entrusted to memory, especially by those who care for the elegance of poetry. The sharpness and power of poetry touch human minds more strongly and affect hearts more effectively, adding genuine and enduring usefulness to its innate sweetness, in accordance with the poet’s saying:

> He has won universal approval who has mingled the useful with the sweet.

Or rather, when poetry is taken up for teaching spiritual wisdom, it rightly claims for itself the words said of wisdom itself in Wisdom 8:8: “She teaches moderation and prudence, justice and courage, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life.” And below: “Her companionship has no bitterness, but joy and gladness.” And further below: “Immortality is in kinship with wisdom, and in friendship with her there is good delight.” All these things truly belong only to that wisdom which shines forth in the works of the saints.

[Col. 0497] Our most holy poet clearly indicates that this was his purpose in such a work in the Preface placed before all the following Epigrams, when he first says:

> While it pleases me to exercise my mind in sacred speech,  
> and to feed my spirit with heavenly bread,

he says that he wished to pluck certain flowers, as from a meadow, and weave them into distinct little verses, so that each epigram might sing of its own subject and each part correspond to its title.

Whatever of righteousness or whatever worthy of praise is found there, he wishes and strives to return entirely to the heavenly fountain from which it had flowed. He says so again in the following lines, singing with the fullest expression of grateful feeling:

> This dew is not the work of our power; from him it is received,  
> who commanded waters to split the dry rock.

When, however, Saint Prosper seems in Epigrams 65 and 66 to attack the Eutychians, who refused to acknowledge Christ’s body as consubstantial with our body, he writes:

> Hence the Word was joined to flesh and received death,  
> yet neither mingles with the body nor is doubled.  
> Thus, with power from above increasing human nature,  
> the human being might be light in the true Light.  
> When he absorbed the strength of death in a draught of life,  
> what had been mortal became eternal.

More fully, in the following Epigram 66:

> Whoever thinks contrary to the eternal plan  
> and denies that the Word remains in our flesh,  
> seeks to dissolve the work of divine compassion  
> and wishes to strip the world of its hope.  
> For who will save anyone from the coming wrath,  
> and who will be free from the crime of the first human being,  
> if the divinity of the Word has not been implanted in our flesh,  
> or if Christ was the shadow of a counterfeit body?  
> What child was born from the untouched womb of the Virgin?  
> What nature grew through years and was increased by food?  
> In what offspring did Abraham believe the Father of the world?  
> What descendant of his sanctifies all things?  
> What royal lineage is at once priestly?  
> Who is at once David’s Son and Lord?  
> What one Redeemer has deigned to bring aid  
> to slaves of sin and those bound in death’s fetters?  
> He received the flesh of our race together with death  
> and set our flesh against the enemy, so that he might conquer for us.  
> Having put off the flesh, he struck down the ruling enemy,  
> so that the ancient spoil might win a new palm.

From all this one may readily infer that the work was written not long before the Council of Chalcedon, which is known to have been convened in the year 451, since it is otherwise certain that Saint Prosper survived until the time of that council.

# ONE BOOK OF THE EPIGRAMS OF SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITAINE, DRAWN FROM THE SENTENCES OF SAINT AUGUSTINE (C)

## Preface

615.

> While it pleases me to exercise my mind in sacred speech,  
> and to feed my spirit with heavenly bread [Note: Three Colbert manuscripts and a more recent Cologne edition read “soul”],  
> I was pleased to pluck certain flowers, as from a meadow,  
> and weave them into distinct little verses,  
> so that each epigram might sing of its own subject,  
> and each part correspond to its title.  
> This is not the work of our power [Note: All printed editions read “This is not our work.” One Royal manuscript, three Colbert manuscripts, one Theodoric manuscript, and the Joli manuscript read “This is not the work of our power.” The same reading was indicated in the margin by the Louvain and later editions. The expression is also used by Virgil in the same sense, meaning “help” or “strength”: *Aeneid* IV, “It is not in our power,” and elsewhere, “They rely on their own strength, needing no help from us.”], but this dew is received from him,  
> who commanded the dry rock to pour forth waters.  
> Thus, whatever has come into the heart’s affection  
> under the guidance of devotion, let joyful faith bring forth in song.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0499]

### I. What true innocence is

[Col. 0499A]

True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor another. For whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul. And everyone sins first against himself before sinning against another.

> Perfectly good and truly innocent is the person  
> who does nothing harmful to himself or anyone else.  
> For whoever plans to injure another  
> first strikes himself with his own weapon.  
> And even when the opportunity should perhaps not present itself [Note: Later editions substituted *subitura* for the reading *non paris mensurae* found in earlier ones. The old Venetian and Louvain editions read *secuta facultas*; the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, *secutura facultas*. The later manuscripts do not differ from them.],  
> he nevertheless bears an unmistakable wound in his heart’s inward parts [Note: The Theodoric manuscript reads: “He bears no doubtful wound in the heart’s inward parts.”].  
> Nor does the perverse mind escape the guilt of the crime it has committed;  
> the mere fact that it wished to do harm has harmed it greatly.

### II. On loving human beings

Human beings must be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved, because it is one thing to love what they have been made, and another to hate what they do.

> Whoever does not despise the honor of his own nature  
> should love in every human being what he recognizes as his own.  
> Yet concord must avoid wicked ways,  
> and there must be no treaties of peace with vices.  
> For what the hand of the supreme Craftsman made is one:  
> whatever was created by a good author is good [Note: The Joli manuscript reads “by God, the author.”].  
> Let no divine creation be despised in anyone;  
> let only the evil pursuits added to it be displeasing.

### III. On true eternity

True eternity and true immortality exist only in the divinity of the Trinity. For in it, being is perfect, since its nature lacks a beginning and needs no increase. Just as it admits no end, so it admits no change.

Created things, however, even those to which God has given or will give eternity, are not wholly free from every end, because they are not beyond change. They possess an end, a temporal establishment, a movement in place, and a change made for their own increase.

> Truly eternal is God alone, creator of all,  
> the life living in itself remains what it is.  
> This is the Father; this is the Father’s Word; this is the gracious Spirit [Note: Three Colbert manuscripts and the Theodoric manuscript read “this too,” or “this and.” At the end of the pentameter, five manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “one and the same together,” while other editions read “one and the same of the three.”];  
> their nature is one and the same together.  
> In this there is nothing begun or increased [Note: Seven manuscripts read “nothing here”; the Venetian edition agrees. All others read “nothing subject to this.”],  
> nothing mutable that undergoes the laws of time or number.  
> Its power precedes the past and surpasses the future;  
> it receives nothing variable and contains nothing mortal.  
> For among the things which Wisdom made as she willed,  
> perpetual life has indeed been granted to many [Note: The Venetian edition reads: “Life, indeed, has been granted perpetually to many.”].  
> But whatever can be more or less than itself  
> dies, at some limit, to what it had been [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “to that very thing which had been”; the Joli manuscript reads “to the very thing by which it had been.”].  
> Thus nothing made changeable is eternal.  
> And God, who surpasses all things, is always the same [Note: Thus seven manuscripts. The Venetian edition reads “and everything that surpasses”; all others read “what remains above all things.”].

### IV. On God’s patience

God’s true patience is that by which he spares the one who is despised and the one who denies him [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “he also spares the one who denies him”; another, together with the Joli manuscript, reads “he spares the one who denies him.”]. It prefers the sinner’s life to his death; it is instruction toward repentance and an offer of correction. None of God’s works is without mercy, since he both benefits a human being through forgiveness and through the scourge.

619.

> The patience of the highest King long postpones many things,  
> suspending the scales of equitable judgment.  
> While mercy spares the deeds that deserve punishment,  
> it grants a period in which a human being may cleanse himself from crime.  
> At last human beings continually commit wicked crimes;  
> yet he grants time so that crimes may perish, not human beings [Note: Two Colbert manuscripts, the Cambron manuscript, and the Joli manuscript read “so that crimes may perish, not human beings.” In them the two following verses are absent.].  
> Sometimes he chastises with a paternal heart [Note: Three manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “with a paternal heart”;],  
> lest fierce blows quickly destroy the guilty.  
> Thus, through God’s goodness, the world is not empty of mercy,  
> and there is nothing that does not draw us toward forgiveness.  
> When the King himself takes thought for those to be saved, even anger  
> serves as a physician caring for wounds through wounds [Note: Three manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “and he cares”; the Lyon edition reads “so that he may care.”].

### V. On God’s vengeance

[Col. 0500C]

Divine goodness is angry in this age chiefly so that it may not be angry in the future; in mercy it applies temporal severity, so that it may not justly inflict eternal punishment.

> When God strikes sinners with anger displayed,  
> he acts so that human beings may know what they deserve.  
> For while the periods of mortal flesh are passing,  
> the scourges themselves bring help to the wretched.  
> Thus brief vengeance brings harmful crimes to an end,  
> so that the punishment due may not hold the guilty forever.

### VI. On true praise of God

[Note: The Cambron manuscript reads “On true confession.”]

Confession is true when it blesses God and the sound of the mouth is the same as that of the heart. To speak well and live badly is nothing other than condemning oneself with one’s own voice.

> True praise is uttered to the Lord by the praying mouth  
> if what flows from the voice is held in the heart’s depths.  
> It benefits no one to speak good things in words alone  
> unless a devout mind possesses what the tongue speaks well.  
> For to speak correctly while living wickedly is pitiable;  
> the recognized rule of justice condemns the evil.

### VII. On the virtue of charity

[Note: The Cambron and Theodoric manuscripts read “On the love of God and neighbor.” The Theodoric manuscript adds “and on the virtue of love of God.”]

The love of God and neighbor is the proper and distinctive virtue of the devout and the holy, while the other virtues can be shared by both good and wicked people.

[Note: Six manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *dilectio*, “love.” Other printed witnesses read *charitas*, “charity.”]

> Many good qualities of the saints are shared by many;  
> even in the wicked there is plainly something right.  
> But the devout portion, striving toward the summit of virtue,  
> surpasses the merit of all works through the love of God [Note: Six manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “surpasses”; the others read “conquers,” together with one Colbert manuscript.].  
> Through it he loves every human being as himself [Note: The Venetian edition reads “may love.”],  
> wishing for others what he himself desires.  
> Therefore, whoever lacks these twin wings of virtue  
> has no means by which to fly to the kingdom of heaven.

### VIII. On apostolic doctrine

621. Apostolic doctrine is so health-giving [Note: Five manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “and so life-giving”; one Colbert manuscript reads “as life-giving as it is.”] and so life-giving that, according to the capacity of those who use it, it leaves no one without a share [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “without experience of it.”]. For whether they are small or great, weak or strong [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “whether they are great or small.”], they find in it both what will nourish them and what will satisfy them.

> To drive the world out of its foul darkness,  
> God kindled the light of apostolic teaching.  
> It suits every mind and every age,  
> moistening the little ones with milk [Note: Four manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “the little ones”; other editions read “children”; Lyon reads “small children,” in place of “little ones.”], feeding the strong with bread.  
> Neither age, nor sex, nor circumstance resists it [Note: The Douai and Cologne editions note in the margin the alternative “neither understanding.”];  
> it cares for all, nourishes all, justifies all, gives life to all.  
> Take what Wisdom has placed upon the great table [Note: The Colbert and Joli manuscripts add “and” here],  
> and learn to be nourished by delicacies of many kinds.

Of which one part is the whole feast, and from whatever benefits each person,  
From that he receives the life which one faith brings forth.

## IX. On Seeking God

Whoever seeks God seeks joy. Let him seek Him, therefore, in such a way that he rejoices not in himself but in the Lord. For, by drawing near to God, ignorance is illumined and weakness strengthened; understanding is given him, by which he may see, and love, by which he may serve.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Two Colbertine manuscripts, with the Venetian edition, read: “to the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 0502D] In the Book of Sentences we read: “by which he may burn [with zeal].”]

[Col. 0502A] Desiring to know God, he seeks to rejoice and live,  
If he knows the true and highest God and loves Him.

He wishes to ascribe to Him whatever he rightly understands, desires, and does;  
Without Him, the glory of the flesh will be dust.

Therefore the Author does not abandon anyone in regard to His gifts,  
And the Lord makes Himself manifest through His work.

As a wealthy guest He dwells in those innermost chambers  
Which rejoice that they are adorned with what He Himself has given.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] All printed editions have *hoc se cuncta* in the verse. Lovanium, Douay, and Cologne indicate in the margin *comta*, a word which, on the authority of seven manuscripts, we have substituted. We believe it signifies that those inner chambers, or hearts, are inhabited by God because they rejoice that they are adorned—that is, embellished—with this gift, which God Himself has given, rather than thinking that they possess it from themselves.]

## X. On Spiritual Disgust

Just as it is harmful to the body to be unable to receive bodily food, so it is dangerous for the soul to disdain spiritual delights.

As mortal bodies lose their own life  
If they cannot take bodily food,  
So souls perish unless they are nourished by the delights of reason;  
[Col. 0502B] lacking the bread of the eternal Word, they perish.

For what will drive dreadful disgust far away  
When the mind refuses to satisfy itself with God Himself?

## XI. On the Ends of Good and Evil

[Note: [Col. 0502D] Thus one Colbertine manuscript and the Joliensis. The Remigius manuscript has, “On Good and Evil Men.” Others have, “On the Ends of Evils and Goods.”]

There are never many who are moving toward non-being. For what is so subject to scarcity as that which is destined for destruction?

[Note: [Col. 0502D] The Regius manuscript reads: “who do not tend toward being.”]

To be truly and properly belongs to God; whoever clings to Him  
623 Will always be in the light of the eternal kingdom.

For those who reject righteousness strive toward non-being,  
And move toward nothingness, unable to be anything.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] Five manuscripts read: “nor can they be nothing.” Others read: “and nothing.”]

Therefore their portion cannot appear great,  
Those of whom none will be found among the number of the saints.

But truly great, and many without end, will remain  
[Col. 0502C] Those whose perpetual glory will be in Christ.

## XII. On the Tranquility of God’s Vengeance

God does not desire the punishment of the guilty as though He wished to be sated with vengeance. Rather, He determines what is just with tranquility and orders it with a righteous will, so that even the wicked may not be disordered.

No punishment of wretched culprits delights God,  
Nor does avenging anger move the tranquil One.

For the Almighty’s righteous and tranquil will  
Establishes whatever ought to be decreed.

Thus the King’s judgment will be open to no complaints  
When the due order justly receives the wicked.

[Note: Seven manuscripts, together with the Venetian edition, have “the wicked”; others have “the guilty.”]

## XIII. On Good Understanding

He has good understanding who does what he rightly understands ought to be done.

[Note: The Regius manuscript has: “He rightly understands what ought to be done and does it.” The Venetian edition has: “He understands what ought rightly to be done, and does it.”]

Otherwise understanding without works is such as wisdom without fear, since it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

[Note: [Col. 0503C] Thus four manuscripts and the Venetian edition. The rest read: “since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”]

He sees fully every depth of the Lord’s writings,  
[Note: Four manuscripts have: “He who fulfills by good deeds the words known.”]  
He who fulfills by good deeds the words he has learned.

For he strays too far from the meaning of instruction  
If he flees from doing what he took care to learn.

[Note: Other printed editions have *ascensu doctrinae* (“by the ascent of instruction”). The reading has been corrected from five manuscripts.]

## XIV. On the Rest of One Still Living in the Flesh

[Note: [Col. 0503C] Three manuscripts read: “of those living.”]

The soul that has been rescued from the death of unbelief already has its rest in this life, if it abstains not from works of righteousness but from the practice of iniquity, so that, living for God and dead to the world, it may rest in the peaceful tranquility of humility and gentleness.

[Note: Four manuscripts and the Venetian edition add “also.” From these, the Cambrai manuscript continues after a few words: “which does not come from works.”]

Rest has also been given in this life to many saints,  
Whose souls the perishing world does not hold;

No doomed desires weary them,  
And Christ is their every good and their every honor.

They use earth as though it were heaven; they despise what is fleeting;  
Their God is what they believe, what they love, and what they desire.

[Note: The Theodoricus manuscript alone has “pleasing.”]

## XV. On Vowing to God

Whoever carefully considers what he should vow to God and what vows he should fulfill should vow himself and give himself. This is what is demanded; this is what is owed: “Let Caesar’s image be rendered to Caesar, and God’s image be rendered to God.”

[Note: The Regius manuscript has: “Let him vow himself wholly.”]  
But just as one must consider what and to whom one offers, so one must also consider where one offers it.

[Note: Four manuscripts have: “what you offer and to whom you offer it.” Another Colbertine manuscript has: “one must also consider this in the Sentences.”]

For there is no place for true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.

625 Whoever wisely considers in his heart what he should vow to the Lord,  
Let him prepare and vow himself entirely.

For no offering of the mind can be presented  
Greater upon the altar,  
Nor does any sweeter fragrance issue from Christ’s temple  
Than when a person brings libations of chaste conduct  
And makes sacred offering from the gift of virtues.

[Note: The word “person” is absent from the Joliensis manuscript.]

Yet let the one who renders vows to the Thunderer know  
That there is one place for divine worship,  
Which the true Church provides throughout the world,  
And without which no merit of righteousness exists.

## XVI. On Justice and Grace

There are two forms of recompense belonging to justice: when either good is returned for good or evil for evil. There is a third recompense, that of grace, when evils are forgiven through regeneration and good things are repaid. Thus it is made clear that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript and the Venetian edition have: “are mercy.”]

But God does not recognize that recompense of the wicked by which they return evil for good; for unless He returned good for evil, there would be no one to whom He could return good for good.

[Note: Two manuscripts have “are restored.” The Regius has: “by which they restore evil to the good.”]  
[Note: Three manuscripts have: “For unless.” The Venetian edition has: “For unless God.”]  
[Note: The Regius manuscript has: “there would be no one to whom they could return good.”]

The reward of righteousness is twofold: either when He returns good to the righteous,  
Or when He fittingly returns evil to the wicked.

But the grace of Christ, which saves all,  
Without weighing merit, washes away every evil.

Renewing all who believe through holy baptism,  
It gives good things, that it may give better things to the good.

## XVII. On the Citizens of the Heavenly Homeland

Everyone who belongs to the heavenly city is a stranger to the world; while using this temporal life, he lives in a foreign homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0504C] Three manuscripts and the Venetian edition read: “a stranger to the world.”] There, amid many enticements and many deceptions, knowing and loving God belongs to few—those for whom the Lord’s commandment becomes clear, illuminating the eyes, so that they are not deceived either in love of God or in love of neighbor.

[Note: Six manuscripts and the Venetian edition have this reading. Others have: “for whom the Lord’s commandment is luminous.”]  
[Note: The Regius manuscript has: “so that they are deceived neither in love of God nor in love of neighbor.” The Venetian edition has: “so that they are deceived neither in charity toward God nor in love of neighbor.”]

Called to the heavenly homeland by Christ, who redeems,  
He lives as a guest of passing time.

As he does not make his way to the promised rest by his own resources,  
He suffers many dangers on the worldly road,

Which now, besieged by adversities, now full of prosperity,  
Either breaks the fearful or binds the doubtful.

While running among these snares toward true joys,  
The world will not possess him, for Christ will be his way.

[Note: Three manuscripts have: “not by what is his own.”]  
[Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts and the Cologne edition have: “not full.”]  
[Note: The Joliensis has “the lukewarm.”]  
[Note: Five manuscripts have this reading. All printed editions have: “toward the joys of life.”]

## XVIII. On Overcoming Carnal Desire

There is no one whose soul is not weighed down by corruptible flesh and an earthly dwelling. Yet one must strive so that the desires of the flesh may be overcome by the strength of the spirit, and that the inner person, who always feels resistance within himself, may always expect to be aided by divine assistance.

There is no soul that is not burdened by mortal flesh,  
Nor one that does not groan beneath bodily condition.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] Seven manuscripts and the Venetian edition read: “Nor is there one”; others read: “nor one that.”]

627 But to strengthen what is weak and restrain what rebels  
Is the rightful and proper work of the mind, its mistress.

She must temper the law of nature with equal moderation,  
And subject every harmful thing to her own scepters;

She must seek help and strength from the Lord, so that she may overcome herself  
And not herself stir up her own impulses.

[Note: Five manuscripts have *jus naturae* (“the right of nature”). This perhaps designates natural inclinations arising from the weakness of corrupted nature. Other codices have *vis naturae* (“the force of nature”).]  
[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has: “so that the mind may not.”]

For she will be able to restrain no movements of her servant  
Unless she is always strong through the love of Christ.

[Note: Four manuscripts have “no movements.” Others have “no one.”]

## XIX. On the Narrow Way of Life

[Note: The Joliensis has: “On the Narrow Way.” The Theodoricus has: “On the Narrow and Constricted Way.”]

[Col. 0505A]

Narrow is the way that leads to life.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript adds “eternal” here.]

Yet no one runs along it unless with an enlarged heart, because the path of the virtues on which Christ’s poor walk is spacious for the hope of the faithful, even if narrow for the vanity of unbelievers.

The way of truth is narrow, leading to the halls of life,  
And the mind’s path does not admit the joys of the flesh.

Earthly pleasure walks in broad spaces,  
But lofty virtue seeks the heights by a narrow boundary.

Yet these paths, which the world’s vanities dread,  
Are open plains to magnificent minds.

The step is exceedingly difficult through hard and lofty places,  
But what faith is glad to endure commends it.

[Note: The Lyon edition and later editions have in the margin: “through rough places.”]  

[Note: The Regius manuscript has: “earthly desire.”]

## XX. On the Reward of the Christian Religion

God must be worshiped with this disposition and this desire: that the worship of Him Himself should be its reward. For whoever worships God in order to obtain something else more than God does not worship God, but what he longs to attain.

With this devotion of desire God must be worshiped,  
So that God Himself may be the whole reward of righteousness.

For whoever hopes to be blessed by another gift  
Does not love what he seeks, but what he desires to possess.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript has: “He does not love the one whom he seeks.”]

## XXI. On Not Judging Hidden Matters

It is a sin rashly to judge the secrets of another’s heart; and it is unjust to condemn someone whose works appear only good on the basis of suspicion. For God alone is the just judge of those things unknown to human beings, and He is their true observer.

[Note: The Venetian edition has: “of those works.”]

It is malicious to condemn in anyone what is not known,  
Especially when the things known are good.

Let ears not be readily opened to harsh rumors.  
What it is beneficial not to know, let it not be pleasing to believe.

[Col. 0505C] Let secrets be left to God, who, if anything is concealed,  
Examines it and needs no informers.

[Note: Three manuscripts have “indicators.”]

## XXII. On God’s Assistance

It is a divine gift when we both think rightly and restrain our feet from falsehood and injustice.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] The Theodoricus manuscript reads: “when we think rightly.”] For whenever we do good, God works in us and with us so that we may work.

629 Without doubt God is our ruler and author  
When with our whole affection we perform what is good.

From the appearance of works the heart’s inward things will shine forth:  
What spirit nourishes a person’s mind within?

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript has *agat* (“may do”). Other printed editions have *Quive ... alit* (“or who nourishes”). Five manuscripts have *Quidve ... alat* (“or what may nourish”).]

For the Holy One makes holy, and light arises from light;  
No one becomes good without the Good.

[Note: Printed editions generally have “without God.” All our manuscripts and the Venetian edition have “without the Good,” namely, the good Spirit.]

## XXIII. On the Sufferings of the Saints

By God’s just judgment, sinners are often given the desired power to persecute His saints, so that those who are aided and guided by the Spirit of God may become more illustrious through the exercise of hardships.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] The word “desired” is absent from three manuscripts, the Venetian edition, and the Book of Sentences.]

That the wicked are often permitted to rage against the saints,  
And that the evil can frequently harm the good,  
Does not happen without God’s will: by these very battles He tests the hearts of His own, which are to be glorified.

The palms of the virtues grow, and the crowns grow;  
The world’s battles are changed into God’s peace.

[Note: Three manuscripts have “are despised.” One manuscript has “are conquered.” The Lovanian and later editions had written both readings in the margin.]

## XXIV. On Knowledge of the Good

There is no true knowledge of the good unless it is understood for the purpose of being practiced.

[Note: Five manuscripts and the Venetian edition have: “For it is useless.”]

For one does not meditate profitably on the law of God who strives to retain in memory what one does not fulfill in action.

[Col. 0506B] He knows the law and learnedly holds the commands of the Almighty  
Who, practicing what he knows, loves what he practices.

It is not enough to roll the Lord’s command upon one’s tongue:  
He remembers the law who remembers its work.

## XXV. On Love of the Law

Whoever loves God’s law shows that among all wicked people he hates what is contrary to the law, not the people. He hates those who despise the law as a lover of the law does,

He does not hate the people,  
But condemns what they do.

[Note: The Venetian edition, omitting *sed* (“but”), has: “He condemns what they do.”]

## XXVI. On Examining God’s Commandments

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript has: “On Observing.”]

A quiet mind alone can examine God’s commandments.

[Note: The Regius manuscript has: “Unless the mind is quiet, it cannot examine God’s commandments,” and so forth.]

Therefore, so that religious devotion may be exercised, the quarrels of the malicious must be driven away.

The quiet can examine the law in some measure  
If their hearts are free from noise and empty of disturbance.

[Col. 0506C] Therefore, so that the mind intent upon holy studies may be aided,  
Let divine love overcome the battles of the flesh.

[Note: Three manuscripts have “quarrels.”]

For the temple of the Lord grows through sacred silences,  
And the house that will not fall is built quietly.

[Note: Three manuscripts have “is built.”]

## XXVII. On Making Progress

[Note: The Regius manuscript and the Venetian edition have: “No one is so learned, and no one is.”]

No one is so educated, no one so learned, that he does not need heavenly illumination. For no increase of divine goods is sufficient in such a way that something does not always remain which the rational mind desires to understand and to do.

[Note: The Joliensis has: “so are any divine increases sufficient.” The Regius has: “and to perform.”]

The inner chambers of the Lord’s teaching, in this present time,  
Are fully accessible to no human being.

[Col. 0507A] There is always something remaining for the saints by which they may grow;  
And the glory of the perfected is a beginning.

Let virtue give birth to virtue, let light proceed from light,  
And let every palm make a further step.

For why should the mind not eagerly seek what God offers,  
Since He Himself gave it the capacity to ask rightly for it?

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “the palm of a human being.”]

## XXVIII. On God’s Twofold Work

If we consider all human beings together—some saved by mercy, others condemned by truth—the ways of the Lord as a whole, that is, mercy and truth, are distinguished by their end. But if we look only upon the saints, these ways of the Lord are not distinguished. For there mercy and truth are inseparable from one another, because the blessedness of the saints comes both from the gift of grace and from the recompense of justice.

[Note: The word “of the Lord” is absent from three Colbertine manuscripts, the Joliensis, and the Venetian edition. After several words, the Venetian edition, together with one Colbertine manuscript, has: “it is always of the gift of grace and of the recompense.”]

In all things the Almighty’s work is twofold.  
Everything He does is either justice or mercy.

[Col. 0507B] These descend together upon the earth from the citadel of light,  
So that neither good may be absent from either part.

And since we all need the help of the Merciful One,  
Grace always precedes justice,

Condemning the proud, saving those who have been justified,  
Whom God has increased both by gifts and by merits.

## XXIX. On Maintaining Peace

It belongs to Christian perfection to be peaceable even with the enemies of peace, in hope of their correction, not in agreement with their wickedness; so that, even if they do not follow either the example or the exhortation of love, they may nevertheless have no grounds for hating us.

[Note: [Col. 0507D] The Joliensis manuscript reads: “on account of which.”]

Among the holy, harmony of peace is beautiful in conduct,  
When one agrees and is well-pleased with many.

[Note: Thus reads the Cambron manuscript, which alone seemed to us to fit both the sentence prefixed to the epigram and the context itself. The Regius manuscript has: “Yet the bonds of love must be restrained in this way.” Two Colbertine manuscripts have: “Yet these things must be tolerated in this way.” The Joliensis has “Yet,” and then continues with the Lyon and later editions, which read: “Yet only these things must be tolerated,” and so forth.]

Yet the bonds of love must not be restrained in such a way  
That this peace is granted only to the good.

Let a just will also be extended toward the unjust,  
And let benevolent wishes despise no person.

Not so that they may be joined to the vices of wicked friendships,  
But so that they may serve as medicine for depraved minds.

If this peace of ours does not calm troubled hearts,  
Let our tranquility nevertheless not be able to perish.

## XXX. On God’s Protection

[Note: The Theodoricus manuscript has: “On Guarding the Soul.”]

The Lord guards us from every evil—not so that we suffer nothing adverse, but so that the soul is not harmed by those adversities. For when temptation is present, that which attacks us makes a kind of inroad; and when temptation is brought to a good end, that is, without a wound to the soul, one emerges from the depth of temporal labor into eternal rest.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript has: “not so that.”]  
[Note: The Douay and Cologne editions have “by those who oppose us.” The Theodoricus has “by the adversities themselves.”]  
[Note: The Joliensis has “is consumed.”]  
[Note: Both the Theodoricus and the Venetian edition have “thus.” The Regius has “and thus.”]

### 633

Often indeed the Lord drives away every adversity  
So that no wound can touch a person.

But then the hand of the Almighty is more wondrous,  
When the evils inflicted do not overcome the afflicted.

Let the Guardian be praised, who gives virtue to the one who endures,  
Lest outward fury corrupt what is inward.

For no crown may be hoped for by one who does not fight;  
The end possesses the palm by which glory is won.

[Note: The Regius has: “Let the guardian of virtues be praised, giving to the one who endures,” and so forth.]

## XXXI. On God’s Assistance

No one ascends to fellowship with the heavenly Jerusalem unless with all his heart he professes that his ascent is not his own work but a divine gift.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript has: “confess.”]

As you make your way toward the heavenly homeland, recognize the One who calls you,  
By whose aid you advance if you run well.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “eternal.”]

[Col. 0508B] For if you believe that by your own virtue you can climb  
To the heavenly places, you will fall, driven from above to the depths.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “if you believe.” At the end of the following verse the Cambrai manuscript has “you rush” or “you fall.”]

## XXXII. On the World’s Hatred of Christians

All who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer insults from the ungodly and those unlike themselves, and must be despised as foolish and insane because they abandon present goods and promise themselves things invisible and future. But this contempt and mockery will be turned back upon them when their abundance has come to poverty and their pride has passed into disgrace.

[Note: The Theodoricus manuscript has: “they abandon [present goods], but promise themselves invisible things that will come.”]  
[Note: The Regius and Venetian edition have: “when their abundance has come to poverty and their pride has passed into disgrace.” Four other manuscripts have “they abandon ... they promise.”]

The wicked part of the world is hostile to the portion of the devout,  
Nor can it tolerate minds unlike its own:

It laughs at those unwilling to use present riches  
And hoping that what has been entrusted to them can be given to them.

[Note: The Joliensis has: “But these insults from the people must be despised by the saints.”]

But these insults, which peoples foolishly hurl  
At hearts alien to God, must be despised by the saints.

[Col. 0508C] For from this spectacle our hope becomes more certain than anything,  
Because God is what He promises: whatever we believe.

[Note: Three manuscripts have: “whatever we believe is, God is.” One Colbertine manuscript has: “whatever we believe is, the Lord is.”]

## XXXIII. On the Patience of the Faithful

The entire salvation of the faithful and the entire strength of their patience must be referred to Him who is wondrous in His saints; for unless God were in them, human frailty would succumb to the fury of the ungodly.

When a steadfast soul is broken by no adversities,  
And the strength of faith remains undefiled,

Let strong patience know that the Lord is present within it,  
And attribute to His gift the fact that it has stood.

For if someone attributes not falling to his own strength,  
By that very belief in his standing he has fallen.

[Note: The Theodoricus has: “By this very fact by which he thinks he stands,” and so forth.]

## XXXIV. On Due Obedience

[Col. 0509A]

Thus both rulers by peoples and masters by servants must be endured, so that temporal things may be borne under the exercise of patience and eternal things hoped for. For what does not violate the religious purpose increases the merits of virtue.

[Note: Three manuscripts have: “the merits of virtue.” One Colbertine has: “the gift of virtue.” Others have: “the merit of virtue.”]

635 Whatever the world’s good order rightly demands must be rendered,  
Provided it does not violate the purpose of devout faith.

No authority is to be despised by the gentle and holy:  
It is right to serve kings and masters,

So that it may benefit Christ’s servants unto true honor  
To have loved the good and endured the wicked.

## XXXV. On Enduring the World’s Variety

Those right in heart do not complain about the commandments of God or the arrangements of the world, because it is just to accept with equanimity everything which He, who will judge, has willed to be endured.

[Note: Two manuscripts and the Venetian edition add “of the world.” The Cambrai manuscripts have “of it.”]  
[Note: Three manuscripts and the Venetian edition have “has willed to endure”; others have “has willed to be endured.”]

[Col. 0509B] While the times of changing things run their course,  
And while the world is worn down by its own movements,

It is the part of the righteous to suffer adversity and endure it modestly,  
And nowhere to provoke God with a complaining voice.

By His judgment no unjust person will be spared,  
And everlasting glory will receive the righteous.

## XXXVI. On the Building of God’s House

The whole structure of a holy building progresses as God cooperates with it, and stands as God guards it. For the guardianship of those placed in authority is useful when the Spirit of God presides over His people and deigns to guard not only the flocks but also the shepherds themselves.

[Note: Two manuscripts have: “as God works.” This is also the reading in the Book of Sentences.]  
[Note: Four manuscripts and the Venetian edition have: “the order of those placed in authority.”]

When living stones are joined by the bond of peace,  
And one house comes together in equal numbers,

The Lord’s work shines forth: He builds the whole hall,  
And gives effect to the devout efforts of human beings.

[Note: Four manuscripts have “and its completion.”]

[Col. 0509C] The structure of their perpetual beauty will remain  
If the Author perfectly protects and governs it.

[Note: The Theodoricus has: “If He protects it when completed.” The Joliensis has: “If it is complete.”]

## XXXVII. On Eternal Joys

The joys of the eternal city are eternal, and the perpetual infinity of its abiding days will neither vary nor pass away, because its inhabitants will enjoy unchangeable peace, and the good of all will also be the good of each individually.

[Note: The Joliensis has: “of those people, all of whom.”]

The joys of eternal life will always be what they are:  
For God Himself will be the cause of rejoicing.

Nor will differing wills produce various movements.  
There will be one light in all and one love,

And in the highest goods there will be a happy experience,  
Which will neither wish to increase nor fear to diminish.

[Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts have *quod erunt* (“which they will be”); the second hand has *quod sunt* (“which they are”).]

## XXXVIII. On the Law of Love

The law of Christ is the perfection of love, by which God and one’s neighbor are loved; and through which it is said to the Lawgiver: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” For the one who fulfills His commandment rightly awaits God’s promise; nor does the one who forgives the sins of others hope in vain that his own sins will be forgiven.

True love of Christ is the true keeping of the law,  
637 And the one who loves people fulfills God’s commandments.

By forgiving their faults, people release themselves from their own crimes,  
And by granting this to others, they provide for themselves.

Let sinner forgive sinner, and let him reconcile  
The Lord to himself on equal terms.

His judgment depends upon our own judgment,  
What we sow we reap; what we give we receive.

## XXXIX. On God’s Commands

God commands nothing for His own benefit, but for the benefit of the one to whom He gives the command. Therefore He is truly Lord, who does not need a servant, and of whom the servant has need.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has: “He is the true God.” Two manuscripts have: “but the servant needs Him.”]

[Col. 0510B] God does not command anything for His own benefit,  
Nor does the true Lord need a servant’s service.

The one who serves is increased by His commands,  
And whoever neglects His authority becomes less.

For God, the almighty and all-sustaining power,  
Loses nothing that is His and receives nothing perishable.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript and the Cambrai have: “He receives nothing perishable.” The Regius has: “He receives nothing changeable, receives nothing perishable.” Another Colbertine and the Cambrai have: “He Himself is the highest and everlasting good.”]

He never lacked what He possesses, giving whatever will benefit the one who receives it,  
And receiving nothing except what He has given.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has: “May it benefit, and receiving,” and so forth.]

## XL. On God’s Timeless Knowledge

[Note: Thus the Joliensis. Others have: “On Temporal Knowledge,” with some adding “of God.” The Cambrai has: “On God’s Foreknowledge of Future Things.”]

What is new in time is not new with God, who created time and possesses all things without time, distributing them in their several times according to their varying ages.

[Note: Four manuscripts and the Venetian edition have “with Him.” Two manuscripts and the Venetian edition, in accordance with the Book of Sentences, have “according to their variety.”]

If something unusual is brought forth by passing time,  
The world calls it strange and considers it new.

But no order of things is unknown to the Author of things,  
Who sees whatever all the ages bring,

Which turn their great ranks in no uncertain motion.  
Yet they stand and flow under God’s judgment,

So that nothing exists anywhere in nature  
Which He does not regulate by His own will.

## XLI. On God’s Providence

God’s unchanging reason contains the arrangement of changing things; there, without time, those things are simultaneously present which do not occur simultaneously in time, because times do not run simultaneously.

[Note: The Regius manuscript and the Venetian edition have: “The arrangements of changing things”; the Venetian edition has “the arrangement.” After a little more, three manuscripts and the Venetian edition have: “an unchanging reason contains,” omitting “of God.”]  
[Note: Two manuscripts have: “where all things are simultaneously without time.” The Venetian edition has: “where all things are simultaneously without time.”]

God’s eternal law governs all things by a stable command,  
Nor does He change His purpose with changing time.

Just as the one God is simultaneously present in every place,  
So He holds the limits and measures of time with Himself.

[Note: Seven manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions instead have: “the limits of things.”]

He perceives neither lateness nor haste in the order of things,  
For all things done and to be done stand before Him simultaneously.

### 639

## XLII. On the Impunity of Sinners

[Note: The Theodoricus has: “On the Happiness of Sinners.”]

Nothing is more wretched than the happiness of sinners, by which a punitive impunity is nourished and the evil will, like an inward enemy, is strengthened.

Whoever rejoices that he can use sins successfully  
Is exceedingly unhappy in his prosperity.

While depraved will attains its wretched effects,  
It is always farther from the true light.

Drawing strength from its poisonous habit,  
And embracing its own bonds of death in love.

Let the world’s empty pleasures rather fail,  
And let necks be subjected to the pious yoke that must be borne.

Let care for healing descend into the decaying fibers,  
So that friendly health may drive away the seductive disease.

[Note: Three manuscripts have: “So that it may drive away the causes of the disease.” One Colbertine manuscript has this written in the margin of the printed edition.]

## XLIII. On the Letter of the Law

[Col. 0511B]

The letter of the law, which says that one must not sin, kills if the life-giving Spirit is absent. For it causes sin to be known rather than avoided, and therefore causes it to increase rather than diminish, because transgression of the law is added to evil desire.

[Note: Four manuscripts have: “which teaches.” The Theodoricus has “to give life.”]  
[Note: The Venetian edition has: “To know ... rather than to avoid.” Two manuscripts have: “To be known ... rather than to be avoided.” Others have: “To know ... rather than to be avoided.”]  
[Note: The Regius and Venetian edition have: “causes it rather to increase.”]

The law is an index of sin, condemning it by forbidding it;  
Unless the Spirit cleanses the heart, it destroys.

For no one is innocent through fear of punishment alone  
Who does not love the holy and just command.

Yet the law does not confer this affection; grace does:  
It makes one willing to do what the letter of the law commands.

[Note: Five manuscripts together with the Venetian edition have “this affection.” Others have “the effect.”]

## XLIV. On Law and Grace

The law was given so that grace might be sought, and grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. For it was not fulfilled through any fault of its own, but through the fault of the wisdom of the flesh—a fault that had to be shown by the law and healed by grace.

[Note: The Venetian edition adds “of Christ.” The Joliensis has: “because it is a fault.” The Regius has: “For it was not through its own fault that it was not fulfilled ... and through grace.” The Theodoricus has: “but through the fault of the wisdom of the flesh.”]

The wisdom of the flesh does not serve the law’s commands,  
Nor can it overcome the impulses of sin.

But because the wavering mind suffers the evils of an ailing body,  
We are compelled to seek divine help.

The law therefore makes Christ’s grace be sought,  
By which the difficult commands of the law can be accomplished.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “so that no longer”; other codices have “and no longer.” Five manuscripts have: “the carnal sense”; only the Venetian edition has: “carnal senses.”]

And then carnal senses can no longer overcome  
Those whom the Author of the just law Himself assists.

## XLV. On God’s Promise

[Note: Six manuscripts and the Venetian edition have: “What God promises, He Himself does.” The same Venetian edition continues: “For He Himself does not promise and another do something else ... Therefore people do not become good from their own works, but from God who calls, so that goodness may not be theirs but God’s.” The Regius has: “which would no longer be promising. Therefore people do not become good from their own works, but from God who calls, so that their goodness may not be theirs but God’s”—and then continues: “and the reward may not be reckoned according to what is owed, but according to grace.” The rest is lacking in this manuscript. Another Colbertine also has: “so that their goodness may not be theirs.” The Joliensis and Cambrai have: “from the one who calls it comes.” The Theodoricus has: “people are not justified by works, but from ... so that their justification may not be theirs and not God’s.” Other printed editions have the text as above, as does the Book of Sentences, and also Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 19.]

What God promises, He Himself does. For He does not promise something and another perform it, which is no longer to promise but to foretell. Therefore it is not from works, but from the One who calls; otherwise it would be theirs, not God’s, and the reward would be reckoned according to what is owed rather than according to grace—and thus grace would no longer be grace.

641 Whatever the Almighty God promises, He Himself accomplishes,  
Nor does He fulfill His own work through external powers.

Hence secure faith hopes for what it believes, and loves  
The Author who will accomplish what He promises.

[Note: All manuscripts and the Venetian edition have this reading. The others have: “He will accomplish it.”]

For if the Lord does not perform what He promises,  
But merely foresees human choice,

These things must be called not His gifts but predictions—  
As though anyone could be good from himself, without God.

Because piety does not accept this and it contradicts the truth,  
Let grace not restore; let grace justify.

Thus in all who are called it fulfills its gifts,  
So that for those whose guide it is, it may itself become their companion.

## XLVI. On the Sins of the Faithful and the Good Deeds of Unbelievers

[Col. 0512B]

Just as certain venial sins do not prevent the righteous from eternal life—sins without which this life is not lived—so certain good works do nothing for the wicked toward eternal salvation, though without them the life of even the worst person is found only with great difficulty.

As certain slight stains upon the splendor of the devout—
[A] greater number, which renders virtues void,

Cannot withstand the gifts of eternal life,

Nor does a slight fault obscure great merits:

So the impious often carry some measure of good,

Which is easily overwhelmed by the mass of great evil.

Nor does it profit the wicked to have understood something right,

If they have not worshiped the true [Note: [Col. 0512D] The Joliensis manuscript and the Venetian edition: “and holy.” Five manuscripts: “holily.”] and supreme God.

There is therefore one faith, one hope, and one love,

By which a person becomes just and blessed.

For the good things that remain to the wicked from nature’s endowment

[Col. 0512C] Increase the weight of sin; they do not lessen it.

## XLVII. On the effect of an evil will

When an evil will receives the power to accomplish what it desires, [Note: [Col. 0512D] The Regius manuscript: “It comes from God’s just judgment.”] it comes by God’s judgment, with whom there is no injustice. For he also punishes in this way, [Note: [Col. 0512D] Two manuscripts: “nor does he therefore act unjustly.” The Venetian edition: “nor is it therefore unjust.”] and not unjustly merely because the punishment is hidden. Moreover, the wicked person does not realize that he is being punished until, through manifest punishment, he unwillingly perceives how great is the evil that he willingly committed.

When the power desired for sin is granted to the unjust,

So that an evil mind may perversely accomplish what it desires,

[Note: [Col. 0512D] Three manuscripts: “It is the great anger of God by which he also punishes many in this way.”] It is God’s great anger, by which he punishes many in this way,

So that they perish through the crimes in which they exult.

For, when nothing hinders illicit daring,

Punishment secretly grows with prolonged guilt.

And one should fear more that the scourges may not spare the one who errs

Than that what he has wished to do harmfully should not come to pass.

## XLVIII. On pride

All vices are effective only in evil deeds; pride alone must also be guarded against in [Note: [Col. 0513C] Two manuscripts: “in rightly performed deeds.” One Colbertine manuscript: “in all deeds”; the same manuscript has in the margin: “in rightly performed deeds.”] rightly performed deeds.

643 Every kind of vice has force only through its own act,

And each sin bears its own distinctive form.

Pride alone is armed with countless weapons;

To it even good deeds can provide strength.

## XLIX. [Note: [Col. 0513C] The Joliensis manuscript: “On the use of prosperity and adversity.” The Theodoric manuscript: “Of opposites.”] On the unequal use of fortune

It makes a very great difference what use is made either of those things [Note: [Col. 0513C] Two Colbertine manuscripts and the Theodoric omit “called” here; one adds “of things favorable.”] called prosperous or of those called adverse. For the good person [Note: [Col. 0513D] The Camberon manuscript adds “person”; and below, “but the wicked person is already corrupted by this sort of misfortune … than by the prosperity of this world.” The Venetian edition alone: “by the misfortune of this world.”] is neither exalted by temporal goods nor broken by evils; the wicked person, however, is punished by this sort of misfortune because he is corrupted by prosperity.

[Col. 0513B] In worldly matters the use is not the same for everyone,

Nor do all endure all things with equal dispositions. [Note: [Col. 0513D] Two Colbertine manuscripts: “They bear them in their minds.”]

[Note: [Col. 0513D] One Colbertine manuscript: “For pleasant things do not inflate the good.”] For pleasant things do not inflate the good, nor do harsh things break them.

Rather, the true joys of unconquered faith sustain them.

But the lover of earth and of hay that blooms only briefly,

Whether he lacks what he desires or enjoys it, is wretched.

## L. [Note: [Col. 0513D] In the Joliensis manuscript: “That the one who has lived well cannot die badly.”] On the death of the saints

A death preceded by a good life should not be considered evil. For nothing makes death evil except what follows death. [Note: [Col. 0513D] Four manuscripts: “Therefore, etc.”; then the Camberon manuscript: “For people who must necessarily die.”] Accordingly, those who must necessarily die should not be greatly concerned with what happens in order that they may die, but rather with where they will be compelled to go by dying.

Everything benefits the good, whom death itself also makes blessed,

So that they may take up the beginning of their rewards.

[Col. 0513C] That end, therefore, is evil which punishment will follow,

And which will be the gateway to perpetual suffering.

Not that end in which tears and all labors will be consumed, [Note: [Col. 0513D] Earlier editions, together with a few manuscripts, read “are taken up” or “will be taken up.” Three Colbertine manuscripts more suitably read “are consumed,” or the Joliensis manuscript “are consumed.” The Camberon manuscript gives both readings.]

So that all traces of the former evil may perish.

## LI. On the purity that [Note: [Col. 0513D] Three manuscripts: “which the soul does not lose.” One Colbertine manuscript: “which the soul does not lose unwillingly.”] is not lost unwillingly

Thus bodily purity is not lost while purity of mind remains, [Note: [Col. 0513D] The Venetian edition: “in an oppressed body”; and below: “in an untouched body.” The Joliensis manuscript instead reads: “with purity of soul … purity of soul.”] even when the body is violated; just as bodily purity is lost when purity of mind has been violated, even when the body remains untouched.

An unharmed mind loses nothing when the body has been violated, [Note: [Col. 0514C] Four manuscripts: “when the body has been violated.”]

The wounds of the flesh do not stain one who is unwilling.

A will not joined to the deed does not incur the crime of the act:

To will the crime harms more than to endure it.

Yet everything thus returns to the inner chambers of the heart,

So that often the mind is guilty without the body.

While, separated from the untouched body, that which has been removed from it

The mind alone conceives and inwardly carries out through hidden movements. [Note: [Col. 0514C] Seven manuscripts: “Since that which …”; in the same verse, five manuscripts read “has been removed.”]

## LII. On the fortitude of endurance

That person must rightly be called greater in spirit who chooses to bear a troubled life rather than flee from it; [Note: [Col. 0514C] Thus three manuscripts, together with the Venetian edition and the sentence above, 52. Two manuscripts: “loves to bear.” Other editions: “is able to bear.”] 645 and who despises human judgment—especially popular judgment, which is usually enveloped in the darkness of error—in comparison with the light and [Note: [Col. 0514D] The Regius manuscript and the Venetian edition: “and purity of mind.”] purity of conscience.

One who is able to lead a life burdened by adversity,

And wishes rather to endure evils than flee them,

Has a much greater spirit than one who, trembling, fears to bear

The unjust judgment of the ignorant crowd. [Note: [Col. 0514D] Five manuscripts: “The unjust judgment of the ignorant.”]

For an upright mind, conscious of its own pure heart,

Shines all the more brightly the more it is worn down.

## LIII. On the humility of the just [Note: [Col. 0514D] One Colbertine manuscript: “of the saints.” The Camberon manuscript: “On the usefulness of the just.” The Theodoric manuscript: “On the malignity of servants.” The Joliensis manuscript, before sentence 53: “On free servitude and servile dominion.”]

Whatever evil unjust masters inflict upon the just is not punishment for a crime but a test of virtue. For the good person, even if he is a slave, is free. The wicked person, even if he reigns, is a slave—not the slave of one master, but, what is more serious, of as many masters as he has vices. [Note: [Col. 0514D] Three manuscripts: “of one person.” The Regius manuscript: “nor is he the slave of one master”; then, “he is the slave of as many masters.”]

Whenever the unjust rule over the just who are oppressed,

It is not punishment inflicted as a penalty for merit;

Rather, the virtue of faith grows under such testing,

Nor does a servile yoke burden free hearts.

Only the sinner is badly enslaved; though he may enjoy

An extensive kingdom, he is a wretched servant indeed,

When a carnal mind, subject to a tyrant who dominates too greatly, [Note: [Col. 0514D] The Theodoric manuscript: “carnal.”]

Devotes itself to as many scepters as it has vices.

## LIV. On the offering of vows

No one would rightly make a vow to the Lord unless he received from him what he was to vow. [Note: [Col. 0514D] The Venetian edition: “to God.” Three manuscripts and the editions apart from the Venetian: “will receive.”]

The best vows are vowed to God, whose gift they themselves are.

That which comes from above is worthy to return there.

## LV. On the essence of the Godhead

Every substance that is not God is a creature; [Note: [Col. 0514D] The Regius manuscript: “and whatever is a creature is not God.”] and whatever is not a creature is God. Therefore there is no distinction in the divinity of the Trinity, since whatever is less than God is not God.

There is one omnipotent nature, which created all things,

And gave to everything its being precisely as it is.

[Col. 0515A] [Note: [Col. 0515D] The Venetian edition, together with the Theodoric, two Colbertine, and Regius manuscripts: “Whatever is less.” The Joliensis manuscript: “Whatever is less than this.”] Whatever is less than God is not God. The Word born from the Father,

And the Spirit who is of them both, is God.

Since the essence of the three is one and the same,

It can never be either greater or lesser.

## LVI. What sort of people God loves [Note: [Col. 0515D] The Camberon manuscript: “Whom God loves.”]

God loves us as we shall be through his gift, [Note: [Col. 0515D] The Venetian edition: “as we have been made by his gift, not as we have been made.” The Regius manuscript agrees.] not as we are through our own merit.

We are loved by the Lord as we are formed by him,

Not as we have come to be through our own merits.

May he sanctify, teach, plant, water, cultivate, and adorn us:

647 And make us forever what pleases him.

For nothing in a human being is worthy to be loved,

Unless the good author perfects his own work.

## LVII. On God’s timeless work

The order of times exists without time in God’s eternal wisdom, [Col. 0515B] and no works are new with him, [Note: [Col. 0515D] The Venetian edition: “Nor are any works new with him.”] who made the things that are to be. [Note: [Col. 0515D] The Theodoric manuscript: “the things that are going to be.”]

In the supreme Craftsman there is, without time, an order of time,

And the sequence of things does not change in God.

Everything is always simultaneously present to the eternal Author,

With whom whatever will be is already present in the order of created things.

## LVIII. On the primary cause of all things

God’s will is the first and supreme cause of all corporeal and spiritual movements. For nothing happens visibly and perceptibly that is not either commanded or permitted by the invisible and intelligible court of the supreme ruler, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments, graces and recompenses, in this vast and immeasurable commonwealth of the whole creation.

God is the origin of the world, by whom all things are moved,

And the things which the Author permits or commands are carried out. [Note: [Col. 0515D] Thus all our manuscripts. The editions read “the Author acts.” One Colbertine manuscript: “Whatever the supreme Author commands or permits is carried out.”]

Hence arises the unchanging order of changing things,

Serving the laws of the eternal Craftsman.

Each will proceeds toward its own ends,

Nor is the just Judge absent from the differing merits:

[Note: [Col. 0515D] One Colbertine manuscript has, in place of the following two verses:

“And caring for the humble, driving away the proud,

Exalting the submissive, despising the haughty.”

In the other Colbertine manuscript only the latter of these verses is found.] Guiding hearts, granting strength, forgiving sins,

Gentle toward the submissive, implacable toward the haughty.

Thus neither punishment receives anyone as evil, nor glory anyone as just,

Except together with the praise and honor of God.

## LIX. On the ends of good and evil

God approves that innocence by which a person becomes innocent not through fear of punishment but through love of justice. For one who does not sin out of fear, although he does not harm the person whom he wishes to harm, nevertheless harms himself greatly; and, while abstaining from an unjust deed, remains guilty in will alone.

If you wish to know where among things you should be placed,

Examine what you fear and what it is that you love.

[Col. 0516A] For all are born with these two sources of movement,

And their shoots answer to their own beginnings.

[Note: [Col. 0516D] The Joliensis manuscript: “For whatever …”; in the same verse the Regius manuscript reads: “which he has counted for himself at this time.”] And whatever each person has considered good for himself in this age,

That he will receive by the judgment of the supreme King.

## LX. On the Christian’s joy

For a Christian, the proper cause of rejoicing is not the present age but the future. Temporal things must therefore be used in such a way that they do not harm eternal things: as on a road along which travelers journey, what pleases should be what leads to the homeland.

May the origin of the fleshly human being not draw

The angelic citizens and those reborn as members of Christ

Back to the old human being.

649 The world indeed produces many good things for our use,

And the fruitful earth serves us with her full abundance.

But for guests of earth, called above the stars of heaven,

The palm of virtue is to disdain the sun’s allurements. [Note: [Col. 0516D] The Regius manuscript: “the blandishments of the sun.” In the following couplet the Theodoric manuscript reads: “And now of the present …”; “The road itself is not [a snare] for travelers.”]

[Col. 0516B] And thus to pass through the span of the present life,

So that it itself may not become a snare for travelers.

For those who refuse to bear labor for the highest things,

The lowest things will receive them, greedy as they are for earthly things.

## LXI [Alias LX]. On the ineffable excellence of the Godhead [Note: [Col. 0516D] The Camberon manuscript: “of God.”]

The transcendence of the Godhead surpasses not only the capacity of our customary speech [Note: [Col. 0516D] The Camberon manuscript and the Venetian edition: “customary.”] but also the power of our understanding. For God is thought more truly than he is spoken, and he is more truly than he is thought. [Note: [Col. 0516D] Earlier editions: “It is no small …” Four manuscripts: “It is no small part of knowledge,” as in the sentence above, 61.] It is no small part of knowledge if, before we can know what God is, we can know what he is not.

There is indeed no mind living in mortal flesh

That can behold God with complete knowledge.

Yet the Author is displayed through the wondrous signs of his works,

And all created things sing of their Ruler. [Note: [Col. 0516D] The Camberon manuscript: “all things sing.”]

Although the glory and praise of God

Conquer and surpass the powers of speech and the strength of the mind,

We nevertheless rejoice in the duty of heart and mouth,

And it delights us to have bowed before so great a good.

From this let the power of faith arise, from this the flame of love:

What lies hidden exercises us; what surpasses us restores us. [Note: [Col. 0516D] One Colbertine manuscript, the Venetian edition, and the Lugdun edition: “restores.”]

## LXII [Alias LXI]. On the devil’s pride and Christ’s humility

The proud devil led the proud human being astray into death; [Note: [Col. 0516D] The Joliensis and Camberon manuscripts: “led [him] down.” In sentence 59: “led [him] through.”] the humble Christ led the obedient human being back to life. For just as the former, lifted up, fell and cast down the one who consented, so the latter, humbled, rose and raised up the believer.

A death-bearing angel, exalted excessively by the honor of his nature, [Note: [Col. 0516D] Three manuscripts: “immoderately.”]

Cast down the human being from the place where he himself fell.

But Christ, taking pity on the one deceived by the malign one’s fraud,

Granted him the power to return to life in himself:

If he takes care not to serve under the terms of the proud enemy,

And strives to follow the form of his humble Lord.

Remaining God in the Godhead of the Father, creator of all,

He is true man, born from the holy Virgin.

Thus, taking our body from his Mother’s body,

He might be God, the source of the assumed flesh:

In him, reborn through the bath [of baptism], [Note: [Col. 0517D] One Colbertine manuscript: “reborn through superior power.”]

The new people will receive a heavenly beginning. [Note: [Col. 0517D] Two manuscripts: “received.”]

Retaining nothing of the first human being, but filled with the second,

To be glorified in the splendor of their head. [Note: [Col. 0517D] Five manuscripts: “and of the head”; other codices: “in the head.”]

## LXIII [Alias LXII]. On true blessedness

[Note: [Col. 0517D] The Camberon, Joliensis, and two Colbertine manuscripts: “All who have what they want are not immediately blessed. Those, however, are immediately wretched who either do not have what they want, etc.”] All the blessed have what they want, although not all who have what they want are immediately blessed. 651 Those, however, are immediately wretched who either do not have what they want or have what they do not rightly want. A right desire, therefore, is nearer to blessedness, even when it has not obtained what it seeks, than a wrong desire, even when it has obtained what it coveted. [Note: [Col. 0517D] The Regius manuscript: “even if it has not attained it.”] [Note: [Col. 0517D] Four manuscripts: “even if it obtains what it coveted.”]

A fulfilled desire is not always truly happy,

Since the desires of the unjust are often evil. [Note: [Col. 0517D] Four manuscripts: “since the desires of the mind are often evil.”]

Therefore, one who desires what is right, even if he has not attained it,

Is good because he persists in willing what is good.

But the wicked person, if he does not possess in deed what he bears in his mind,

Is as wretched as if he obtained what he desires.
