## LXIV [Alias LXIII]. [Note: [Col. 0517D] The Camberon, Theodoric, two Colbertine, and Joliensis manuscripts: “What it is to be with God.”] What it is to be with God

Great is the misery of a human being who is not with the one without whom he cannot exist. For he is undoubtedly not without him in whom he exists; [Note: [Col. 0517D] The Venetian edition: “For if he is his …”] and yet, if he does not remember him, understand him, or love him, he is not with him.

Everything that exists anywhere is enclosed by the majesty of God:

Without it, nothing can stand or exist.

If a human being rightly serves him, he clings closely to him;

If he recoils, he lives in miserable exile.

Thus the Lord distinguishes all things in just order,

So that the highest things may be prepared for the good and the lowest for the wicked.

## LXV [Alias LXIV]. On the Incarnation of the Word of God

The divinity of the Word, equal to the Father, became a participant in our mortality, [Note: [Col. 0517D] The Regius manuscript: “not from its own fault, but from ours … but from his own gift.” One Colbertine manuscript: “from our gift”; and at the beginning, “The true divinity,” where others have “the divinity of the Word,” although another hand has written “of the Word.” The Theodoric and Joliensis manuscripts read “from his own,” instead of “from his own gift.”] not from its own but from ours, so that we too might become participants in his divinity, not from our own but from his.

The almighty Father, the Son born, and the gracious Spirit—

In three persons, one equal Godhead—

Made it possible for the human race, overthrown by the malign one’s fraud,

To return to life by this path:

So that Christ, the Redeemer of our nature and our cause,

Might become mortal without diminishing what he was;

And, through the form of a servant, might empty the tyrant’s rights,

And conquer death by innocent death. [Note: [Col. 0517D] In the margin of books from the Lugdun edition onward: “unjustly.”]

Hence the Word inserted into flesh and receiving flesh,

Neither confounds himself with the body nor duplicates himself:

Thus, with the nature of the human being enlarged by heavenly power,

Man might be light in the true light.

Who absorbed the powers of death [Note: [Col. 0518D] Thus four manuscripts, two of which have *obsorbuit* for *absorbuit*. The Camberon manuscript: “because he absorbed [them] through the draught of life.” All the editions: “through the draught of life.”] through the draught of life,

What had been mortal became eternal.

## LXVI. On the same subject [Note: [Col. 0518D] In all the manuscripts that came to us, a new title or sentence is lacking here. Some indicate a distinction from what precedes. In the Camberon manuscript the title is “On the same subject.” We have supplied the title and sentence that seemed to us more fitting in the book of Saint Prosper’s *Sentences*. The same was done for epigrams 59 and 60.]

The Catholic faith believes and proclaims the Lord Jesus Christ to be both true God and true man. For both have been written, and both are true. Whoever asserts Christ to be God only denies the medicine by which he was healed. Whoever asserts Christ to be man only [Col. 0518B] denies the power by which he was created. Therefore, faithful and upright soul, accept both. Christ is God, and Christ is man. 653 What sort of God is Christ? Equal to the Father, one with the Father. What sort of man is Christ? The Virgin’s son, possessing mortality from a human being but not possessing iniquity.

Whoever thinks contrary to the eternal plan

And denies that the Word remained in our flesh,

Seeks to undo the work of divine compassion

And desires to strip the world of its hope.

For who will save anyone from the coming wrath?

Or who will be free from the crime of the first human being?

If the divinity of the Word has not been joined to our flesh,

[Note: [Col. 0518D] The Joliensis manuscript: “And Christ.”] Or was Christ the shadow of a false body?

Who is the child born in the untouched Virgin’s womb? [Note: [Col. 0518D] Thus four manuscripts together with the Venetian edition. Others, together with the remaining editions: “Who was born …”]

What nature grew through the years and was increased by food?

In what offspring did Abraham believe himself to be the father of the world?

[Col. 0518C] Or whose seed is it that sanctifies all things?

[Note: [Col. 0518D] Four manuscripts: “Who is of royal lineage.”] What lineage is at once royal and priestly?

[Note: [Col. 0518D] The Camberon manuscript: “And who is the same.” The Joliensis manuscript: “Who is the same David, both son and Lord.” Prudentius and Sedulius lengthened the first syllable of *David*; Fortunatus shortened it.] Or who is at once David’s son and Lord,

Who deigned to bring one Redeemer’s aid

To the servants of sin and those bound by death’s fetter?

He received the flesh of our race together with death,

And set it against the enemy so that he might conquer for us,

Then, stripping off the flesh, struck down the ruling enemy:

So that he might win a new palm from his clothed spoil.

## LXVII [Alias LXV]. [Note: [Col. 0518D] The Theodoric and Joliensis manuscripts and two Colbertine manuscripts: “With what hatred evil people should be regarded.”] With what hatred the wicked should be hated

Perfect hatred is that which lacks neither justice nor knowledge: that is, one should neither hate people on account of their vices nor love vices on account of people. Thus we rightly hate wickedness in the wicked and love the creature, so that nature is not condemned because of vice, nor vice loved because of nature.

A wise mind, desiring what is right and loving what is honorable,

Judges certain people worthy of its hatred.

Yet it does not drive them entirely from its fellowship, knowing

To distinguish their erring nature from their vices. [Note: [Col. 0519D] Thus five manuscripts together with the Venetian edition. Others: “their wandering nature.”]

Thus it shows indulgence toward its own kind, wishing

That sins be cut away and crimes condemned, not people.

## LXVIII [Alias LXVI]. [Note: [Col. 0519D] Five manuscripts: “On the labor of those who deceive.”] On the labor of fabricating lies

The fabrications of falsehood are difficult and laborious. But one who wishes to speak the truth does not labor. For good people are more at ease than wicked people, and the words of truthful people are more direct than the inventions of deceivers.

[Col. 0519B] Deceivers are always tormented by bitter cares,

And an evil mind never possesses the joys of peace.

While, trembling, it fashions slippery lies through contrived invention, [Note: [Col. 0519D] The Regius manuscript: “Trifles.”]

It consumes all its time in the practice of evil. [Note: [Col. 0519D] One Colbertine manuscript: “the evil of the heart in its craft.”]

But a simple mind, free from deceit and wickedness,

Loves nothing unjust and carries nothing hostile.

The follower of truth will possess serene light,

Since the liar is his own night and pain.

## LXIX [Alias the second part of LXVI]. On the same subject

655 Called from the valley of night to the homeland of life, [Note: [Col. 0519D] The Venetian edition and five manuscripts: “from the valley of night.”]

Climb by the steps of virtue along the road of light.

A steep and narrow path leads to the heavens;

A declining and broad road leads to death:

Along it the deceptive wisdom of the proud world walks,

And, mocked by its own inventions, falls;

While it pursues the evil pleasures of bodily sensation,

It wanders blind and far from the true light:

Nor is it helped by being adorned with the appearance of false virtues.

The mind that does not know the truth loses whatever it does.

Let the wise person therefore know God, and with all his innermost being

Love him, and in loving him love himself also.

Let him be good and just, [Note: [Col. 0519D] One Colbertine manuscript: “let him be true.”] truthful and kind;

Let him be the form, mirror, light, and image of God.

Made new in Christ and now stripped

Of the old flesh, let him leave the worthless earth behind in mind.

[Note: [Col. 0519D] The Camberon manuscript: “And of the sacred temple.”] Wherever he is placed as a part of the sacred temple,

Whatever is in the body of the Head will be great.

## LXX [Alias LXVII]. [Note: [Col. 0519D] Two Colbertine manuscripts and the Camberon manuscript: “On the usefulness of the divine Scriptures.” The Theodoric manuscript: “On the profundity of the divine Scriptures.” The Joliensis manuscript: “On the humility of the divine Scriptures.”] On the divine Scriptures

The depths of God’s mysteries in the holy Scriptures are good: they are concealed for this reason, lest they become cheap; they are sought for this reason, that they may exercise us; they are opened for this reason, that they may nourish us. [Note: [Col. 0519D] The word “of God” is absent from two manuscripts and from sentence 67 of the book of *Sentences*.]

Although in the sacred books, which you labor to know,

[Col. 0520A] Many things, reader, are closed and obscure to you,

Nevertheless, do not cease to keep watch with holy zeal.

Delayed gifts exercise your mind.

The fruit produced by a longer hope is more welcome;

What is offered without effort is of lesser value.

The mind is also delighted by mysteries that are concealed:

He who gave you the desire to seek will add the power to find. [Note: [Col. 0520D] One Colbertine manuscript adds: “so that you may find.”]

## LXXI [Alias LXVIII]. On the Lord’s Prayer

When the Lord Jesus Christ prayed with a bloody sweat, [Note: [Col. 0520D] Three manuscripts and the Venetian edition: “Our Lord.”] he signified the passions of the martyrs that would flow from his whole body, which is the Church.

Christ, preparing to bear punishment and approaching death,

And to implant unconquerable faith in his own,

As he poured out bloody drops from his body in prayer,

The Lord’s sweat was the price of the world.

[Col. 0520B] Nor could the harshness of the cross terrify the willing one,

For it was to be the glory of the flesh that would reign.

But that blood promised equal honors to the saints,

To the martyrs who would arise throughout the whole body.

657 For when the sacred harvest has filled the world,

The whole crop will come from this one seed.

## LXXII [Alias LXIX]. On receiving the sacraments

An unworthy person takes the sacrament [Note: [Col. 0520D] Four manuscripts and the Venetian edition: “of the supreme piety.” One Colbertine manuscript, shortly afterward: “an unworthy person.”] of piety to his own judgment. For what is good cannot benefit one who receives it badly.

Great protection comes from being nourished by the sacred offering,

If no sins oppress the heart of the participant.

For whoever takes what is good but does not shun what is evil

Doubles the weight of sin upon himself.

## LXXIII [Alias LXX]. On praising God

Let the one who praises God for the miracles of his benefits praise him also for the terrors of his punishments. For he both entices [Note: [Col. 0520D] The Camberon and Theodoric manuscripts: “For indeed.” One Colbertine manuscript: “For he does not entice, nor does he threaten.” The Joliensis manuscript: “Now he entices, and now he threatens.” The Venetian edition: “For now he entices in himself, and now he threatens.” The Regius manuscript: “For now he entices, and now he threatens.”] and threatens. If he did not entice, there would be no exhortation; if he did not threaten, there would be no correction.

The one who praises the Lord for the world’s creation,

And proclaims the Craftsman in the appearance of things, [Note: [Col. 0520D] The editions, apart from the Venetian: “in appearance.” More suitably, “in the form,” from the Venetian edition and five manuscripts.]

Let him also praise him as he threatens eternal death and flames,

And fear the judgment of the just King.

Let hope have no doubt concerning the promises; the King will give everything

That he has prepared, and grace will be greater than merits,

[Note: [Col. 0520D] The Theodoric manuscript: “But let the guilty hasten.”] If the guilty hasten to break the bonds of sin,

Before the day of death, while there is opportunity for forgiveness.

## LXXIV [Alias LXXI]. On hastening conversion

The remedies of conversion to God must not be postponed through any delay, [Col. 0520D] lest the time for correction be lost through tardiness. For he who promised pardon to the penitent did not promise tomorrow to the one who delays.

Turning to upright conduct [Note: [Col. 0520D] The Camberon manuscript: “to holy conduct and right living.” The same appears in one Colbertine manuscript.] and living in holiness,

Let him hasten in Christ toward what he desires.

Let the obstacles of empty things yield to virtue,

Lest sluggish faith lose the time of its hope.

What good does it do to prolong the causes of sickness indefinitely?

Why does today’s salvation await an uncertain tomorrow?

We know that pardon must not be denied to those who have corrected themselves,

But the final day is known to none of us.

## LXXV [Alias LXXII]. On fear [Note: [Col. 0521C] The Camberon manuscript adds “of God”; two Colbertine manuscripts and the Theodoric manuscript add “right.”]

Everything that is reasonably feared is avoided: [Note: [Col. 0521C] The Camberon manuscript: “Thus God is to be feared.”] God is to be feared in such a way that one flees from him to him.

It is useful for the prudent person to avoid worldly adversities,

And, foreseeing what must be avoided, to flee it. [Note: [Col. 0521C] The editions: “what must be avoided.” More suitably, most manuscripts omit *est* (“is”).]

But when, on account of the merit of sin, the hand of the Almighty,

Enclosing the guilty person everywhere, constricts him,

One safe refuge is God himself for the one who fears,

[Col. 0521B] 659 From whom, if he has departed, he should return lest he perish. [Note: [Col. 0521C] Three manuscripts: “refuge.”]

For turning back to the Lord is the surest life,

And seeking peace from the one offended is the only salvation.

The one who terrifies spares; the one who strikes himself heals.

If you wish to live, submit yourself to the one whom you fear.

## LXXVI [Alias LXXIII]. On virginity [Note: [Col. 0521C] The Camberon manuscript adds: “of soul and body.”]

Virginity of the flesh is an untouched body; virginity of the soul is incorrupt faith. [Note: [Col. 0521D] The Camberon and Regius manuscripts: “The body is … the faith is …”]

Virginity of the flesh is possessed in an untouched body;

Virginity of the soul is faith kept undefiled,

Without which care for bodily chastity is of no benefit;

But devotion of mind increases both goods.

## LXXVII [Alias LXXIV]. On the proper manner of possessing

We shall prove that we possess many superfluous things among our resources if we retain only what is necessary. For nothing is sufficient for those who seek empty things; and one who uselessly possesses things that would benefit the poor is, in a certain sense, a holder of what belongs to others.

The love of possessing without measure is a great sin,

As is desiring more than is sufficient for life.

For what clothes us, what feeds us, what cares for our health—

If the mind is free from empty things—does not burden us.

Therefore, if anything remains beyond what use requires,

Let it benefit the weak and help the needy.

For whoever greedily stores away what should not be spent, [Note: [Col. 0521D] Thus four manuscripts; the Venetian edition seems to agree, where we read “to be distributed” instead of “to be spent.” Other editions: “to be disposed of.” The Regius manuscript: “to be sought.”]

What he gives to no one, he has stolen from the poor. [Note: [Col. 0521D] Two Colbertine manuscripts: “What he gives to no one.”]

## LXXVIII [Alias LXXV]. [Note: [Col. 0521D] The Theodoric manuscript: “On the poverty of the rich.” Two Colbertine manuscripts and the Camberon manuscript: “On the distinction of riches”; likewise the Joliensis manuscript, which through a scribal error has *divinorum* (“of divine things”) instead of *divitiarum* (“of riches”).] On riches

[Note: [Col. 0521D] In this sentence there is remarkable variation among the manuscripts. The Lugdun edition and those following it, as in the text, agree with sentence 85 above. The Theodoric and one Colbertine manuscript read: “The rich are in great poverty who do not possess the riches of justice and the treasures of wisdom.” The other Colbertine manuscript, the Joliensis, and the Camberon read: “The rich in justice are poor and do not possess the treasures of wisdom.” The Venetian edition has the same words, but arranged differently.] Those who are rich in iniquity are in great poverty: they do not possess the riches of justice or the treasures of wisdom. But those who serve the Lord acquire goods that cannot perish. [Note: [Col. 0522C] One Colbertine manuscript and the Theodoric: “serve God.” The Camberon: “seek those good things.” One Colbertine manuscript: “which cannot perish for them.”]

When the wicked person rejoices in earthly riches,

He does not know that he is wretched for lack of true goods.

For what is there that, in a single moment of time,

He could not lose through the condition of worldly things?

[Note: [Col. 0522C] The Regius and Theodoric manuscripts and the Venetian edition: “Although.”] Whoever is allowed to have everything spared him when adversities cease

Must nevertheless be made poor by the law of death.

But the goods of the just, exposed to no losses,

Fear neither enemies, thefts, fires, nor the sea.

Wisdom keeps its own wealth unharmed,

[Col. 0522B] Nor do peace and faith lose their reward. [Note: [Col. 0522D] This verse, which in all the others is read as the third from last, is the final verse in the Camberon manuscript.]

The whole substance of the virtues always remains safe;

No one can seize Christ’s gifts against their will.

## LXXIX [Alias LXXVI]. On true goodness

It is not enough to abstain from evil unless one does what is good. [Note: [Col. 0522D] The Camberon manuscript: “unless he does it.” The same manuscript and the Regius later read “strives.” The Venetian edition: “unless it is striven for.” The others, as above in the text.] And it is little merely to harm no one unless you strive to benefit many.

Certainly worthy of praise is the one who leads a blameless life

And avoids whatever he knows will harm him. [Note: [Col. 0522D] Four manuscripts: “whatever he knows will harm him”; the Venetian edition: “whatever will harm him.”]

But devotion is not content to be confined within this limit,

Nor is it enough for the just to have abstained from forbidden things. [Note: [Col. 0522D] Thus one Colbertine manuscript and the Camberon. Others: “for the just.”]

The greater concern for goodness is to relieve the hardships of one’s brothers

And to bring desired aid to the sorrowful:

To feed the hungry, clothe the naked, free the bound, [Col. 0522C]

Reconcile those who are at odds with one another,

And to bring forth with a devout heart whatever consolations

Wretched human beings seek, insofar as possible. [Note: [Col. 0522D] Five manuscripts: “These things.” Other codices: “This, insofar as it is possible.”]

So that one who truly desires what is right and is truly kind,

May flee what is evil and do what is good. [Note: [Col. 0522D] The Camberon manuscript: “And what is right.”]

## LXXX [Alias LXXVII]. [Note: [Col. 0522D] Two Colbertine and the Theodoric manuscripts: “On the impunity of the sinner.” The Joliensis manuscript: “On evil impunity.” The Camberon manuscript: “On the impunity of sinning.”] On the impunity of evil

When a sinner sins, the Lord does not fail to see him merely because punishment for his wrongdoing is delayed; rather, a more severe judgment is decreed against the one to whom even correction itself is denied. [Note: [Col. 0522D] The Venetian edition alone: “For that reason he is not seen by the Lord”; and after several lines, two Colbertine manuscripts: “correction is denied.”]

The transgressor rejoices, having obtained sin without punishment,

If the penalty due to the guilty person is not imposed.

As though the Thunderer were offended by no human crimes,

Or as though anything escaped the knowledge of the Most High.

But a more severe anger must then be feared by those greedy for forbidden things,

When the scourges of justice hold themselves back.

For what disease will not gain mastery over the one

To whom heavenly medicine now refuses its aid? [Note: [Col. 0523D] The Theodoric manuscript: “To whom true medicine …”]

## LXXXI [Alias LXXVIII]. On rightly ordered joy [Note: [Col. 0523D] In the first hand of the Joliensis manuscript: “useful”; in the second: “right.” The Camberon manuscript adds “which is possessed in Christ.”]

The one whose joy is Christ can never be defrauded of his delights. For that joy which rejoices in an eternal good is eternal exultation. [Note: [Col. 0523D] Three manuscripts: “is eternal, however.”]

They make people almost happy and always blessed—

The joys born from the true and highest good.

[Col. 0523B] For the brief and perishing pleasure drawn from the world’s riches

Contains the seeds of perpetual death.

Do not be willing to subject your mind to empty things, [Note: [Col. 0523D] Five manuscripts: “to attach.”]

Or burden your eager mind with poisonous nourishment. [Note: [Col. 0523D] The Regius manuscript: “to burden with cares.”]

Let a pure and wise heart be nourished by the fruit of virtue,

And let the love of Christ reign in our breast,

So that, once filled with him, it may never be emptied of him.

Eternal streams of the eternal fountain will be.

### 663 LXXXII [Otherwise LXXIX]. What unites a human being to God

We are either far from or near to God, who is everywhere, not by places but by actions; for just as unlikeness separates us from him, so imitation unites us to him.

[Note: Four manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “imitation unites us.”]

[Note: Seven manuscripts read: “The whole God fills the whole fabric of the world.”]

God fills and encompasses the entire compass of the world,

Nor does he cease to be present to anyone in any place.

He is far, and very remote, from whoever lacks

The light of sincere faith;

But if that person shines by his rays, once night has been driven away,

Filled with divine light, he will himself be light.

Therefore it is not necessary to traverse the circuit

Of the earthly globe or the trackless seas,

In order that the ruler and creator of all things may be approached—

He whom the devout mind always possesses in the temple of the heart.

Whoever, unlike him, withdraws into a grim wilderness,

Is nevertheless as near to him as he is like him in the merit of his life.

### LXXXIII [Otherwise LXXX]. [Note: The Camberon manuscript reads “every”; the Venetian edition has the same reading.] That the whole life of unbelievers is sin

The whole life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the supreme Good. For where the knowledge of eternal and unchangeable truth is absent, virtue is false, even in the best conduct.

[Note: Two manuscripts and the Venetian edition read: “False also is virtue in the best conduct.” Another Colbertine manuscript reads: “False also there is virtue.”]

Although much remains to a human being after the first wounds,

Which can give this life the distinction of praise,

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript alone reads differently:

“If the spring of faith is present to distinguished talent and love of uprightness, etc.”]

Yet if, along with distinguished talent and love of goodness,

The spring of faith is absent, watering the submissive heart,

The useless sprout of every crop withers,

And false honor does not enjoy the true light.

For when God is unknown, and virtue is not believed—

That virtue which by true skill advances toward the highest good—

The mind, obstructed by empty things and weighed down by things that perish,

Is not permitted to strive toward the heavenly kingdoms.

Wisdom of the world wanders through every path,

And adds darkness to what it carries on without light.

### LXXXIV [Otherwise LXXXI]. On the Sabbath

[Note: Four manuscripts read “On the observance of the Sabbath.”]

[Col. 0524B]

He observes the Sabbath badly who abstains from good works. Rest from wickedness, however, ought to be perpetual, because a good conscience makes one not restless but tranquil.

[Note: Three manuscripts and the Venetian edition add “the mind.”]

He does not keep the legal Sabbaths with proper worship

Who believes that an act of piety is forbidden on them.

No day fails to condemn the deeds of wicked people;

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads: “All times accord with justice.”]

All times accord with justice.

Nor are holy periods of rest corrupted by virtues:

Let hearts be free only from sins.

### LXXXV [Otherwise LXXXII]. On true freedom

Servitude before God is always freedom; one serves him not from necessity but from love.

No freedom or power is better or greater

Than to serve God, whom love serves well.

A willing disposition friendly to authority is placed without a yoke:

It thrives through affection and does not groan under command.

### LXXXVI [Otherwise LXXXIII]. On pride

[Note: Four manuscripts add: “which the good conquer last.”]

The vice by which the human being was first overcome is the last that he conquers. For when he has conquered all sins, the danger remains that a mind conscious of doing well may glory in itself rather than in the Lord.

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “this is conquered last”; the Theodoric manuscript, “this last is conquered”; two Colbertine manuscripts, “they conquer it last.”]

The final battles assail the one whom the malicious deceiver

First drove into death by fraud.

[Note: This is the reading in all our manuscripts except the Rogius manuscript, which has “prepared” for “completed”; we suspect, however, that it may be read otherwise: “For him this prepares the final battles.”]

When, therefore, he has taken lofty palms and glorious crowns

And has subdued the enemy beneath his feet,

He may wish to assign the triumph to his own virtue,

Not to the Lord, whose gift and work it was.

In this one thing he always conquers who is not conquered:

When the Lord deigns to extend his hand, no one falls.

### LXXXVII [Otherwise LXXXIV]. On loving God

[Note: This title is found in the Cambrai manuscript. We have added the maxim from the Book of Sentences, no. 135, since it seemed more appropriate. Its heading there was “On the end of labor.”]

Human labor cannot come to an end unless one loves what cannot be taken away from him.

You who wish to overcome the labors of a precarious life,

Love what the true lover always possesses.

Hostile dangers press upon earthly possessions;

Battles rage over losses and over gains.

Nothing is quiet amid carnal desires,

Nor is there peace for the anxious, nor restraint for the covetous.

The mind is safe in God alone; if it is unwilling to leave him,

It will never be without the eternal Good.

### LXXXVIII [Otherwise LXXXV]. On the vice of flattery

The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. For it is pleasing to do those things in which one not only does not fear a reprover but even hears a praiser.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “The tongue binds.”]

The flattering tongue heaps up the sinner’s vice

And binds him, delighted by his crime, with praise.

While honor, ill-advised, flatters the guilty person,

There is no concern to restore the fallen person’s health.

Let the voice of a correcting friend be free,

[Note: The Theodoric manuscript reads “of a reprover.”]

And let it not permit blind poisons to spread through the inward parts.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads: “Do not believe the one praising harmful things.”]

Nor should the sick person, believing the doctor’s deceptive words,

Love the wounds of the praised and harmful disease.

### LXXXIX [Otherwise LXXXVI]. On martyrs who have not been baptized

[Note: Four manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “who have not yet.” One manuscript reads “who have not.”]

Those who die in confession of Christ without having received the washing of regeneration obtain for the abolition of their sins as much benefit from this as if they had been washed in the baptismal font.

[Note: The Regius manuscript and the Venetian edition add here “the outpouring of blood.”]

If, dying to the world, he is reborn through the divine font,

And the one buried in water becomes new in life,

[Col. 0525C]

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “They have not been deprived.”]

They have not been deprived of Christ’s holy baptism,

For whom the very outpouring of their blood was a font.

Whatever the mystic form of the sacred washing conveys,

The glory of martyrdom has fulfilled all of it.

### XC [Otherwise LXXXVII]. On forgiveness, which even the righteous need

[Note: These words, “which even the righteous need,” are added from four manuscripts. They were absent from the other codices. The Theodoric manuscript reads: “On our righteousness.”]

Our righteousness, although it is true because it is directed toward the true end of the good, nevertheless in this life is so frail that it consists rather in the remission of sins than in the perfection of virtues.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “Yet such is the frailty in this life that…” The Regius manuscript reads: “Yet such is the frailty of human life that it consists rather in remission.”]

Great indeed is the excellence found in many holy people,

Whose minds the grace of heaven nourishes with dew.

But while the mind suffers certain afflictions of a sick body,

And external things stir up warfare within,

Victory is never won in a battle so complete

That a human being can enjoy true peace in security.

Contagions spread amid discordant impulses,

And the very joys of virtue contain a wound.

[Note: Six manuscripts and the Venetian edition arrange the verse in this way. In others: “So that long experience may make it known to all.”]

So that long experience may make it known to all,

That in this age there is no complete righteousness,

Unless the Lord, in his mercy, washes away the sins of his people;

And, while giving the gifts of virtues, also gives forgiveness.

### XCI [Otherwise LXXXVIII]. On the unknowable causes of God’s works

[Note: Three manuscripts read “On unknowable things.” In others the title is either absent or reads “On unknown causes.” We have added “of God’s works” from the preceding words of the maxim, both here and in the Book of Sentences, no. 171.]

Although the causes of divine works are unknown, we know something when we know that the Almighty does not act without reason, even when weak human understanding cannot give an account of that reason.

It is not possible for human intellects

To know the hidden causes of divine works.

Yet the person who knows that God has willed many things to remain hidden

Does not contemplate what is concealed without some insight.

A mind imbued with faith learns all things at once in him,

And through the appearance of created works

[Note: Other printed editions read “receives the maker.” Four manuscripts read *suspicit*, that is, “beholds and recognizes.” For the invisible things of God are understood and beheld from the creation of the world through the things that have been made; Romans 1:20.]

Beholds the maker,

Forming shapes, places, times, and movements for things

According to their measures, numbers, and weights.

[Note: Four manuscripts read “lest intrusive concern labor over what is closed off.” Others read “nor intrusive concern.”]

Let no intrusive concern labor over what is closed off,

For it is granted to us to know and possess all things in Christ.

### XCII [Otherwise LXXXIX]. On not despairing of sinners

[Note: The Theodoric manuscript reads “of the wicked.” The Joliensis reads: “That one must not despair of sinners.”]

One must not despair of the wicked; rather, one must pray for them more earnestly, so that they may become good. For the number of the saints has always been increased from the number of the ungodly.

[Note: The Theodoric manuscript reads “of sinners.”]

Just as care for healing must be provided to those oppressed by disease

As long as life remains in the sick body,

So pious prayers must be applied to the wicked,

Burdened by the great mass of their vices.

So long as it is possible for the hearts of the wicked to be changed,

May love of the light shudder at the stray paths of night,

And, once they have been converted, may the grace of Christ give them a new mind,

By which, through justification, people become good.

### XCIII [Otherwise XC]. On seeking aids in peace

[Note: Three manuscripts read “On tranquility.” A fourth adds “of peace.” Another reads “On the providence of peace.” The others read “On seeking aids,” to which we have added “in peace,” taken from the title of the preceding maxim.]

The teaching of wisdom must be embraced in the tranquility of peace; it is difficult to recognize it amid the storms of tribulations. Nor are aids easily found in adversity if they have not been sought in peace.

While the dangers of the world do not disturb the mind,

While no battles press upon the day of peace,

It is fitting to exercise faith with divine weapons

And to anticipate every threat by counsel.

Wisdom will fill a mind tranquil and free from cares,

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “may fill.”]

And will be a guest in a peaceful heart.

For what has not been conceived in a quiet heart

Cannot be acquired amid a savage storm.

### XCIV [Otherwise XCI]. On the good that no one loses unwillingly

[Note: Five manuscripts read “On the good that no one loses or gives up unwillingly”; one reads “receives.”]

A person can unwillingly lose temporal goods; but no one loses eternal goods unless he wishes to.

Every good formed from the world and produced by time

Can be lost under any condition.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads: “Although [lacuna] he is stripped.” The Theodoric manuscript also has “he is stripped.”]

And although vigilant care resists losses,

A person is nevertheless often stripped of his own possessions.

But the goods that are truly good are not held by any end;

Whoever always desires to possess them always possesses them.

Nor can force be inflicted upon a will supported by Christ,

For love persevering in him conquers all things.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “a will submitted to Christ.”]

### XCV [Otherwise XCII]. On remedies for tribulations

When someone faithfully petitions God concerning the needs of this life, he is mercifully heard, and mercifully not heard. For the physician knows better than the sick person what is useful for the sick person. But if he asks for what God commands [and promises], it will certainly come to pass. For love receives what truth prepares.

[Note: Six manuscripts and the Venetian edition do not have “and promises” here. It is found in the Book of Sentences, maxim 213.]

Amid the conflicting evils of worldly life,

[Note: Five manuscripts have “often”; other books have “indeed,” and end the sense with a comma at the end of this verse.]

By which the Lord’s people are often chastised,

Those who suffer beneath the varied ruin of storms

Should know that the righteous bear God’s scourges.

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “that they justly bear.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “and to him.”]

And they should entreat him with every groan and lament,

That he may help the afflicted with the aid he knows appropriate.

For the sick person will not be healed by his own decision,

Nor will he himself prescribe laws to the physician.

Let the right hand of salvation search the sick inner chambers,

And lift the inward parts weighed down by grievous disease.

[Note: The Regius manuscript and the Venetian edition read “wash.”]

Established evils cannot be driven away without pain:

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “evils accustomed to being repelled.”]

But bitter things renew what sweet things have harmed.

Let there be repentance for one’s ways, and, with vices banished by virtue,

Let the court of God reject the reign of sin.

The pious scourges of the righteous King lead toward forgiveness.

Brief anger will give the upright enduring joys.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads “the pious scourges of the King through blows.”]

### XCVI [Otherwise XCIII]. On the internal war

[Note: We add the title from the Theodoric, Joliensis, and two Colbertine manuscripts. In the Cambrai manuscript it is “On the same subject.” We have taken the maxim from the Prosperian collection, since it was thought especially suitable.]

The devout activity of this life is to worship God, to fight against inward vices in his grace, and not to yield to them when they incite or compel us even toward unlawful things; and, whenever one does yield, to ask with religious devotion for forgiveness and for God’s help not to yield. But in paradise, if no one had sinned, the pious activity of conquering vices would not exist, because it would be the state of blessedness to have no vices.

Wars and dangers are never absent from the good,

And the pious mind always has someone with whom to contend.

What delights the flesh is harmful to the holy heart;

The body wages battles against the law of the mind.

Enemies strike from outside with various impulses;

Within there is a civil and social evil.

So that the world’s allurements and vices may be resisted,

The strength of the bodily human being must be mortified.

But what mind will keep its servant under righteous authority,

So that the tamed flesh may rule in its duties,

Unless it serves the exalted King in proper submission?

How will what was made willing by him become strong from him?

[Note: Two manuscripts, together with the Venetian and Lyon editions, read “so that from him.”]

### XCVII [Otherwise XCIV]. That evil has no nature

All things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made. Since, therefore, every nature was made through the Word of God, iniquity was not made through him. For iniquity is no substance, and sin is not a nature but a defect of nature, which desires what is not according to its order.

The one almighty God founded all things through the Word;

No nature of evil was created by him.

And what the rich wisdom of the Word did not make

Has no place in the constitution of things.

Therefore vices have no substance and no life

That might give vitality to the body and to its own matter.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “or to its own matter.”]

But when freedom departs from the right order

And good things do not preserve their proper measure,

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “It is in the defect of guilt.” One Colbertine manuscript reads “The wandering movement is in the defect of guilt.”]

The wandering movement toward what is contrary lies in guilt and vice,

And evil consists in having abandoned the true way.

If anyone hastens to return to it with his whole heart,

There will be no error concerning the boundary he neglected;

The entire punishment of the destroyed sin will perish,

As God restores what was created to its original integrity.

[Note: Seven manuscripts read “of the sin that has been destroyed.” All printed editions read “belonging to the debtor.”]

### XCVIII [Otherwise XCV]. On prayers contrary to God

[Note: Three manuscripts lack the word “to God.”]

When something evil is requested, God shows anger by granting it and mercy by not granting it.

When God does not grant effect to wicked prayers,

He grants much by refusing what would cause harm.

He does not wish those who err in their desire to sin by the deed;

If angered, he would permit what, when calm, he forbids.

Let the suppliant learn to rejoice in a fortunate refusal,

And begin to drive from his mind what he desired.

Let him recognize that God spares him when, about to fall,

He deserved not to be heard, lest he fall.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “in a fortunate rejection.”]

### XCIX [Otherwise XCVI]. On the judgments of God

[Note: Three manuscripts add “which are not to be compared with human judgments.”]

The judgments of God are in no way to be compared with human judgments. We must not doubt that he is just, even when he does what seems unjust to human beings.

Human judgment, which must often be mistaken,

Does not always receive the rule of justice.

But the Lord’s power is equitable and true in all things,

And nothing remote from his sight lies hidden.

Let such a judge be praised, feared, and loved—

One who truly remains just and good—

Calling back those who have turned away, remitting everything to those who turn back,

And, by granting forgiveness to the wicked, making them good.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads: “Calling back those who have turned away,” and begins the following pentameter: “And granting forgiveness to the wicked.”]

Therefore let a mind ignorant of the truth not boldly condemn

What has pleased the judgment of the supreme Judge.

Rather, let ignorance submit itself to the just King,

Who can never will what is not good.

[Note: The Theodoric manuscript reads “unless he can will good things.”]

### C [Otherwise XCVII]. On restraining anger

[Note: Three manuscripts read “On restraining wrath.” The Joliensis alone reads “On anger.”]

No angry person thinks his own anger unjust; therefore one must quickly return from every indignation to the gentleness of meekness. For a persistent emotion easily turns into hatred of the person whom one does not quickly forgive.

No one fails to judge the impulses of his own mind equitable,

And people think that what they want is well intended.

Therefore the mind must be quickly recalled from anger to peace,

Lest time give strength to savage hatreds.

Let forgiving hearts pardon the offenses committed against them,

For no one exists who does not need forgiveness;

Remembering this amid the vanities of the world,

We both grant it and ask it in every matter.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “all people think that what they want is good.”]

### CI [Otherwise XCVIII]. On the end of the saints

Worshiper of justice, lover of divine peace,

Whom blessed life calls to the highest good,

Strive steadfastly to climb the right-hand paths,

Despising the harmful level road of the left.

It is safer to endure the harsh labors of the world

And to suffer the fierce battles of the hostile enemy

Than to submit a mind conquered by flattering obligations

And place a captured neck beneath a servile yoke.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “a bound mind.” Others read “a conquered mind.” The Cambrai manuscript reads:

“Than to submit a mind conquered by vanities to empty things.”]

The use of honor does not last long in the setting sun,

And false joys flow away with rapid decline.

Therefore the wise person will consider the end of his own age,

And will see where the road on which he travels will lead.

For those entangled with the world share in the world’s ruler;

But for Christ’s servants, Christ will be their glory.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “for they are dying,” and later “it is not far away,” with which the final reading of the Cambrai manuscript agrees.]

### CII [Otherwise XCIX]. On chastising the desires of the flesh

Among bodily sensations and dying limbs,

The mind suffers much from the flesh as its dwelling place—

The flesh, seeking what is contrary to the life by which it lives,

Wishes to dissolve the law of the mind by its own law.

But let the prudent leader learn to bridle the rebellious servant

Under the authority of the eternal King;

And, receiving true light from the light above,

Let him drive the night of sin from the dwelling of the heart.

[Note: Six manuscripts read “learns”; in the second following verse they read “drives away.”]

For since God created all things good, and the region of our exile itself

Is beautiful in its own adornment,

Hearing, sight, taste, touch, and smell

Rejoice in having whatever is pleasing supplied from every side.

And the use of the present moment becomes harmful to a human being

If inferior things bind him, captivated by their allurements.

Therefore let the wise mind strive toward the citadels above,

And accustom itself to become blessed by the highest goods.

Receive even now the delights of the promised kingdom;

Hold fast, by virtue and faith, what you desire to be.

[Note: The Regius and Cambrai manuscripts read “by virtue and faith.”]

Do not think that you are running fruitlessly toward an uncertain hope;

Look upon the first fruits of your nature in Christ.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “the members of your nature.”]

If you do not doubt that you have been taken up by him,

You will always be the whole human being in the body of the Head.

Only be willing to observe at the teacher’s command,

For he who says it by word anticipates it by aid.

[Note: Four manuscripts read “what he does by word”; one of these reads “advances by help.”]

### CIII [Otherwise C]. On the height of faith, hope, and charity

[Col. 0530C]

[Note: Three manuscripts read “measures.”]

In the Godhead there are no degrees, measures, or times;

And, what is the same thing, there is neither greater nor lesser.

Let bodily masses and forms depart far away;

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads “depart.”]

Supreme virtue has no boundaries or distances.

[Note: This is the reading in the manuscripts and the Venetian edition; in the others: “What the Father is, that is the Word of the Father, and likewise that of both.”]

What the Father is, the Word of the Father is at the same time, and what belongs to both is

The Spirit. He is one God, and there is one faith:

Through it the hope of true goods climbs

The lofty path with fiery love.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads “with known love”; the Venetian edition, “with unknown love.” Two manuscripts read “through whom.”]

And, having tasted beforehand the sweetness of heaven’s dew,

It rejoices to be nourished by apostolic teachings.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads:

“Whoever does not wish to incur unworthy cares.” Cambrai and three Colbertine manuscripts read “Therefore whoever”; the Joliensis reads “Whoever, therefore.”]

You, then, who do not wish to incur unworthy cares,

Beware of being entangled in empty and perishable things.

The brevity of mortal life requires little;

The use of a short span of time needs only a few things.

[Note: The Theodoric manuscript reads “Willing to be.”]

If you wish to be, desire to rejoice, and seek to know hidden things,

Seek what is highest, so that low things may not hold you.

[Note: Four manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “the final things.” Others read “the lowest things.”]

Delight in God the King; be in heavenly things,

And hold by love what you pursue in hope.

Let no trace of the first human being remain in you,

Nor let the image of the new person bear the form of the old.

Rejoice, recognizing that you have been reborn in the flesh of the Word;

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “If you are part of him.”]

If you are his part, Christ will be your portion.

He, so that you would not choose the evil joys of the world deserving condemnation,

Made himself for you the way to the promised kingdom.

### CIV [Otherwise CI]. On confessing the one God

What the Father does with Christ, Christ does; and what Christ does with the Father, the Father does: inseparable love, majesty, and power do nothing separately. As the Lord himself says, “I and the Father are one.”

Since the Father is always in the Word, and the Word in the Father,

[Note: Six manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “and the Spirit of the Word and of the Father is one”; other codices read “and the Spirit of the Word and of the Father is the same.”]

And the Spirit of the Word and of the Father is one,

So you must not doubt concerning the three Persons,

But confess one God, as learned faith teaches.

The Word, begotten in the Father’s heart, creates and rules all things,

Yet nothing is done by him apart from the Father.

For the movement of both is one, and the reason for willing is one;

Their power is equal, their Spirit the same, their love one.

### CV [Otherwise CII]. On the same subject

[Col. 0532A]

The Son of God, God, did not come to have life in himself as the Father has it by participation, but by being born. For the Father, who is life, begot life; and the essence of the one who begets and of the one begotten differs in nothing, since the Son is from the Father in such a way that there is one co-eternally equal Godhead, though not one Person.

[Note: The Regius and one Colbertine manuscript, along with the Venetian edition, read: “Thus the great God is.” Another Colbertine manuscript reads: “He is the great God.” The Joliensis reads: “This is the great God.”]

Thus God is great: he is sufficient from himself and remains in himself,

For it is his highest and proper nature always to be what he is.

For true light shines from true light,

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “supreme” (perhaps “from supreme light”) for “true.”]

So that, recognizing the Begotten, one may know the Unbegotten.

The Godhead of the three is one, and there is one essence belonging to all.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads “belonging to all,” that is, to the three Persons; the others, “from one.” Four manuscripts read: “The Spirit is the same with the Word and the Father.” One manuscript reads: “The same with the Word.”]

The Spirit of the Word and of the Father is also the same.

[Note: One manuscript reads “The same as the Word.”]

There is no separate work and no unequal power;

In all things there is one beginning, not three.

[Note: The Joliensis reads “not three”; all the others read “there are three.”]

### CVI [Otherwise CIII]. On seeking God perseveringly

[Col. 0532B]

Let no believer, however much he may have advanced, say, “It is enough for me.” For whoever says this has remained behind and become stuck on the road before the end, since he will not persevere to the end.

When the devout mind labors, overcome by the praise of God,

Rejoice that so great a work conquers you so well.

And recognize that you have drawn some strength from heaven,

If what you desire and understand is not enough for you.

Seek the good without end, and persist once you have found it:

Let such desires have no limit in seeking.

For whoever thinks that he needs no gift at all,

No longer wishing to grow, loses what he has acquired by growing lukewarm.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “When the devout mind labors, overcome in the praise of God”; others read “labors.” Four manuscripts read “if what you desire”; the others “what you desire.” Five manuscripts read “seek the good without end, and persist once you have found it”; the others “seek the good without end, and persist in the good once found.”]

## [THE COMPLETE CHRONICLE]

[Col. 0531]

## PREFACE TO THE CHRONICLE OF SAINT PROSPER

So that no portion of the works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine may be lacking from this edition—which we wish to publish, insofar as possible, both as corrected and as extensive as possible—it remains to present, among the genuine and indisputable labors of our author, the Chronicle or Chronicles (for the ancients cite that work under both forms), marked with his name. Until now, everyone, with very few exceptions, has regarded this book as the genuine offspring of Prosper.

The arguments of those few learned men who preferred to assign this work to someone other than our Aquitanian are solidly refuted by the recent, most learned critic and champion of the works of the holy Fathers Leo and Prosper, Antelmius (Dissertation 8, “On the Chronicle or Chronicles of Saint Prosper,” p. 371), whom we have mentioned more than once. In the first place, the testimonies of the ancients assert that Prosper was the author of the Chronicle. They are men of great name, witnesses—so to speak—beyond all exception, whom one cannot suspect of having been deceived by a spurious title.

The first to appear in chronological order is to be listened to with all the greater attention because, by the name of our Aquitanian, he reveals himself as a countryman and fellow citizen; by his study and profession, as a chronographer or calculator of times; by his age, as a contemporary; and finally, by his deeds and associations, as most probably connected with Saint Prosper by acquaintance and familiarity. He is Victorius, or Victorinus, who, at the command of Pope Leo, for whom Prosper served as adviser and secretary, and under the supervision of Hilary, then a deacon of the Roman Church and later pope, composed the Paschal Cycle with the greatest care in investigation.

In his preface to Hilary he speaks as follows:

“After reviewing the trustworthy histories of the ancients—namely, the Chronicles of the blessed Eusebius of Caesarea … and the prologue, and consequently those things which were added to these same Chronicles by the presbyter Jerome of holy memory, through whom they are also shown to have been translated into the Latin language; and also those things WHICH WERE SUPPLIED BY THE HOLY AND VENERABLE MAN PROSPER, down to the eighth consulship of the Emperor Valentinian and the consulship of Anthemius—I found that from the beginning of the world to the Flood … From the time of this Ninus, public writers of events began to exist.

“Therefore the venerable man Eusebius mentioned above began his history from this point in his Chronicles, wishing the reliability of his industry to be weighed also by the contemporary narration of worldly annals, and seeking even the writings of the gentiles as witnesses to the truth he had professed. He was content to explain past ages through the sacred books, revealing only in summary the succession of generations in retrospect from the text of the prologue and at the same time comprehending the fullness of the work in a recapitulation by years.

“THE VENERABLE MAN PROSPER, following his outline, composed these same matters in the same Chronicles with equally remarkable brevity, so that their beginning would commence from the origin of the world.”

Thus Victorius of Aquitaine, who declares that in this difficult work he followed no other guides than Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper—whom he calls holy and venerable, and also venerable man—uses a designation by which, or by a similar one, our Aquitanian is identified among the ancients. Therefore no one should suspect that Victorius intended to indicate anyone other than his fellow countryman …

After Victorius of Aquitaine we place Gennadius of Marseille. Just as that earlier author, superior in age, lends authority to his assertion, so the testimony of this second author, who about forty years later carefully reviewed the catalogue of illustrious men, lends it strength: he expressly identifies Prosper of Aquitaine as the author of the Chronicles and as the opponent of the Massilians. And lest anyone suspect that this had slipped out of him by chance, he repeats the same point in two notable passages.

For, not content, when speaking of Prosper in chapter 84, with having assigned to him as the first fruit of his genius the work of the Chronicles in these words:

“He is said to have composed many works, among which I have read a CHRONICLE entitled with his name, containing the history from the creation of the first human being, in accordance with the testimony of the divine Scriptures, down to the death of the Emperor Valentinian and the capture of the city of Rome by Genseric, king of the Vandals”—

as though, I say, it had not been enough for him to hand this down, and as though he had foreseen the doubts of posterity and hastened to forestall them, two chapters later, while speaking of the already praised Victorius, he presents the following statement reflecting his view:

“He composed the Paschal course with the greatest care in investigation, after the four earlier men who had composed it: namely Hippolytus, Eusebius, Jerome, AND PROSPER.”

Nor should these matters be passed over here. For when we hear Gennadius asserting that he read Prosper’s Chronicles, containing the history from the creation of the first human being in accordance with the testimony of the divine Scriptures, and that Prosper carried them down to the death of Valentinian, we must recall that Victorius has already established that Prosper, following the outline of Eusebius—who likewise began his history or chronological calculations from the beginning of the world—“composed these same matters in the same Chronicles with equally remarkable brevity, so that their beginning would commence from the origin of the world,” and that he further continued them to the consulship of the Emperor Valentinian.

Since these statements fit together with such remarkable agreement, it is now certain and established for us that Gennadius had no other Chronicles supplied to him than those used by Victorius himself, and that those Chronicles ultimately bore their true, not spurious, author: for the work is found with the same design in the possession of both highly diligent writers.

After the calculator and historian, let us bring forward a writer commendable for both pursuits, Cassiodorus Senator. Although he alone might perhaps claim as much authority as others arrogate to themselves, he ought nevertheless to be heard before later witnesses because he was nearly Prosper’s contemporary, was familiar with Gennadius’s labors, and was himself the compiler of another Chronicle. He could not repeatedly fail to handle and take up again Prosper’s labors; consequently, from this need to distinguish the work, he ought to have acquired a greater and stronger opportunity for recognizing its offspring.

He writes in chapter 17 of *On the Institution of Divine Literature*:

“Saint Prosper also carried his CHRONICLE from Adam down to the time of Genseric and the plundering of Rome.”

And as we were proposing to pause with these three testimonies, a fourth presents itself to our view—one so distinguished and venerable that his assertion seems unable to be passed over without injury either to him or to the rights of our Prosper and ourselves. This is another illustrious chronologist and historian, namely Isidore of Seville, bishop in Baetica after Leander his brother, toward the end of the sixth century. In book VI, chapter 17, of his *Etymologies*, we read this assertion:

> Hippolytus, bishop, was the first to compose the Paschal cycle, in the time of the emperor Alexander. After him, the most approved authors—Eusebius of Caesarea, Theophilus of Alexandria, Prosper also, an Aquitanian by nation, and Victor—published multiple cycles, enlarging the calculations of the same feast.

This is the statement of a careful writer who, in the good faith of his own age, freely adopted and confirmed what had been held in the preceding century concerning these *Chronica*; so that we need not be further concerned to bring forward other later witnesses. For we have also omitted from the preceding authorities Victor of Tunnuna, a bishop in Africa, who states that he carried on his history from the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius the Younger, where Prosper left off—which, in any event, means that he did not possess Prosper’s final and more complete copy. John, abbot of Biclaro, who continued Victor from Justin the Younger, where the other had stopped, does not fail at the beginning of his work to praise Eusebius, Jerome, and likewise Prosper, a religious man, as well as Victor of Tunnuna. We shall not pursue these matters further.

From these things, then, it is clearer than midday light that Prosper of Aquitaine committed to writing *Chronica* which highly learned contemporary writers used in ecclesiastical affairs, and that other discerning men subsequently reproduced and commended them in their genuine outlines, without fear of the charge implied by the title of a spurious work.

Since it is sufficiently clear from what has been said that Prosper wrote the *Chronica*, and that they, marked by no fault of spuriousness, were known in their pure and genuine form to contemporary and nearly contemporary authors, it will readily be acknowledged as certain that the *Chronicon* circulated under Prosper’s name, and presented below by us, is itself the work composed by the Aquitanian—not something wholly different from it. Indeed, the Prosper who wrote this *Chronicon* is in no way different from the Prosper who wrote against the Collator and the Massilians. This is sufficiently demonstrated by the agreement of nearly all learned scholars. It will moreover remain unshaken when the few and slight difficulties discussed by the author cited above, in Dissertation 8 of the works of Saints Leo and Prosper, have been examined: they arise from two or three chronological errors which either ought not to be regarded as errors, or which Prosper himself could easily have admitted, or which perhaps entered from no other source than scribal copyists. Nevertheless, some, moved by these considerations, have chosen to adopt a contrary opinion. If we attempted to report these matters here, the limits of our notice would become longer than propriety allows.

Furthermore, when we assert above that Prosper carried his *Chronicon* from the beginning of the world, this must not be understood as though he had proposed to prepare a new work according to the calculations of a new and more exact chronology. Rather, in arranging the same *Chronicon*, he wished to show himself nothing more than an epitomator of Eusebius, as Victor is found to have admirably confirmed, in the words quoted above:

> The venerable man Prosper, following the sequence of Eusebius, composed these same matters in these *Chronica* with the same remarkable brevity, so that their beginning might start from the origin of the world.

These words explicitly attest and prove that the Aquitanian compressed these same *Chronica* of Eusebius with remarkable brevity. The work itself of Prosper demonstrates the same thing. For, as Sirmond aptly observes in chapter 5 of his *History of Predestination*:

> This *Chronicon*, insofar as it extends together with the supplement of Jerome, is a mere epitome of the Eusebian *Chronicon*; hence it is sometimes called the *Epitome of the Chronicles*, or excerpts from the *Chronicles*: for Prosper excerpted everything from it, except that he inserted in his own places the consular fasti, which the earlier work lacked, from the baptism of Christ—or, as he himself calls it, from his manifestation—and also wove together from his own material the remaining events down to the end of the work.

Nevertheless, although he assumed merely the role of an abbreviator and wished, in the first part of his *Chronicles*, to abridge Eusebius and Jerome, he did not always press so closely upon their footsteps that he never departed from them or composed phrases and members of periods from his own resources; indeed, he sometimes substituted other chronological calculations. Therefore, it must always be regarded as a valuable addition to the integrity of ecclesiastical history that this monument, preserved for so long amid the thickest darkness, has finally reached us unharmed and without diminution.

As for the other part of the *Chronicon*, which Prosper himself continued after Jerome completed the continuation drawn from Eusebius, there is no need to point out that Prosper illuminated it with various additions. The published copies, each more extensive than the next, clearly show this; they were certainly transcribed from manuscripts, and the copies discovered later carry the history down to the year 455—that is, to the Vandal sack of the City—whereas other copies had placed its ending eleven years earlier, under the consulship of Theodosius Augustus XVIII and Albinus.

The *Chronicon of Saint Prosper*, enlarged by ten years, was first published by the very learned Duchesne in volume I of the *History of the Franks*. [Col. 0535] The Reverend Father Labbe, S.J., subsequently published the same work complete in the first volume of his *New Library of Manuscripts*. Here we have followed Labbe’s edition as the fuller one, without, however, omitting the differences of the other editions wherever it seemed necessary.

Finally, we read that a man most skilled in ecclesiastical matters observed that Saint Prosper brought his *Chronicon* back to the anvil, as the saying goes, three times, and—if one may speak in this way—published it three times: namely, in the year 433, again in 445, and finally in 455. This is inferred from the fact that several books contain a certain abridgment of the entire chronology down to the year 433. The Scaligerian edition, however, presents it down to 445, at which point it ends the whole *Chronicon*, together with all the others that preceded Duchesne’s edition. Indeed, Victor of Tunnuna, who supplemented Prosper’s *Chronicon*, observes that it ended in the year 444. Yet in the manuscripts used by both Duchesne and Labbe, the work extends to the Roman catastrophe under Genseric, with Valentinian VIII and Anthemius as consuls—that is, to the year 455. Victor, who wrote two years after Gennadius, and Cassiodorus likewise affirm that it extends this far. Moreover, Marius, bishop of Avenches or Lausanne, when he undertook to supplement Prosper’s work, testified to the same thing. Hence one may infer that the limits of Prosper’s *Chronicon* should finally be assigned to the year 455.

[Col. 0535]

# The Complete *Chronicon* of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine

[Note: In Labbe, volume I of the *New Library of Manuscripts*: “The most illustrious man, Tiro Prosper,” etc. This name is also found in one Colbert manuscript and several others.]

[Note: Ending in the year of Christ 455.]

**Divided into Two Parts.** (C)

## First Part: From the Origin of the World to the Death of Valens

With an annotation of the consuls from the death of Christ.

[Col. 0535A] 685 Adam, when he was 230 years old, fathered Seth.

[Note: It will suffice to mention once what Arnaldus Pontacus, formerly bishop of Bazas, observed in his notes on the *Chronicon* of Eusebius, and what had previously been observed in several Colbert manuscripts: in reckoning the years from the creation of the world, Eusebius followed chiefly the edition of the Bible according to the Seventy Interpreters, as he himself explains around the year 547. Josephus himself does the same, although he was a Jew. Hence we see that the ancient Fathers, both Greek and Latin, and the Catholic Church itself, both in ecumenical councils and in martyrologies, followed Eusebius’s calculation, abandoning the Hebrew reckoning. Once this is observed, every difficulty that might arise on reading that Adam fathered Seth in his 230th year will disappear, since the Hebrew text and the Vulgate version state that this occurred in his 130th year. The same judgment should be applied to the numbers of the subsequent generations.]

Seth, when he was 205 years old, fathered Enos.

Enos, when he was 190 years old, fathered Cainan.

But Cainan, when he was 165 years old, fathered Malaleel.

[Note: Labbe’s *Chronicon* reads “Jared” here instead of “Malaleel,” and omits the following generation, which we have restored on the authority of a Colbert manuscript and the edition of the Eusebian *Chronicon* prepared and annotated by Pontacus, since it is not omitted in the Hebrew text or in the Latin version.]

Malaleel, at the age of 65, fathered Jared.

Jared, when he was 162 years old, fathered Enoch.

[Note: Besides the Hebrew text and the Vulgate, one Colbert manuscript and the edition of the Eusebian *Chronicon* published by Pontacus support this number, 162. Labbe’s *Chronicon* had 212.]

Enoch, when he was 160 years old, fathered Methuselah.

[Note: The Colbert manuscript and Pontacus’s *Chronicon*, together with the Hebrew text and the Vulgate, have 65.]

Methuselah, when he was 297 years old, fathered Lamech.

Lamech also, when he was 292 years old, fathered Noah.

[Note: Thus the Colbert manuscript and Pontacus’s *Chronicon*, together with the Vulgate and Hebrew text. Labbe has 188.]

686 He was 500 years old when he fathered three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

[Col. 0536A] After another hundred years, when he fathered Shem, the flood occurred, when he was 600 years old.

To establish the reliability of the chronology, these generations are traced again from the beginning, with the number of years assigned to each. For the posterity of Cain the fratricide was not worthy to be counted with the people of God. But when sin had spread more widely and most of the good had mingled themselves in marriages with foreign women, the crime of unlawful association deserved to be expiated by the flood. Only the righteous Noah, with his wife, his three sons, and an equal number of daughters-in-law, was preserved for the restoration of the human race.

Thus from Adam to the flood there were 687 ten generations, and 2,242 years.

[Note: According to the Hebrew number, 1,656; the Eusebian *Chronicon*.]

After the flood the following generations succeed.

Shem, son of Noah, when he was 100 years old, fathered Arphaxad in the second year after the flood.

[Note: One Colbert manuscript has “102 years”; another Colbert manuscript has “100 years.”]

Arphaxad, when he was 135 years old, fathered Cainan.

[Note: From this point onward one Colbert manuscript agrees with the Vulgate and the Hebrew text. The Pontacian Eusebian *Chronicon* agrees with the preceding text except in a few places: Serug at 79 years instead of 130, and Nahor at 89 years instead of 79. Another Colbert manuscript agrees in every respect with the readings found in the text.]

[Col. 0537A] Cainan, when he was 130 years old, fathered Shelah.

Then Shelah, when he was 130 years old, fathered Eber.

Eber also, when he was 134 years old, fathered Peleg.

At this time, to disrupt the construction of the proud tower, languages were divided, and the dispersion of the nations throughout the world took place.

Peleg, when he was 130 years old, fathered Reu.

Reu also, when he was 132 years old, fathered Serug.

Serug, when he was 130 years old, fathered Nahor.

Then Nahor, when he was 79 years old, fathered Terah.

Terah, at the age of 70, fathered Abraham. When Abraham was 75 years old, he was warned by a divine utterance to leave his land and his father’s house and cross over into the land of Canaan. At that time the promise was made to Abraham that he would become the father of nations.

From the 75th year of Abraham, in which the beginning of the promise occurred, to Moses and the exodus of the Hebrew people from Egypt, 430 years are found.

Thus from the flood to the first year of the promise there are 1,166 years; from Adam, 3,398 years.

[Note: From the patriarchs’ years listed above—the years in which each fathered children—the sum from the flood to the promise made to Abraham comes to 1,145 years; according to the notes on Eusebius’s *Chronicon*, the total is 1,147. From Adam the number is calculated as 3,412.]

Abraham, at the age of 90, fathered Ishmael by the slave woman Hagar. From Ishmael came the Ishmaelites, later called Hagarenes and finally Saracens.

At this time Abraham, justified by the faith through which he believed that all nations would be blessed in his offspring, received the commandment of circumcision. Until the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, it was the bodily sign of the promise; it passed over into the spiritual sacrament of true circumcision of the heart.

Abraham, in the hundredth year of his life and the twenty-fifth year of the promise, fathered Isaac by the free woman.

688 Isaac, when he was 60 years old, fathered twins. The elder was Esau, also called Edom, from whom came the Idumeans.

At this time Inachus reigned at Argos. His daughter Io, whom the Egyptians called Isis, was honored by them with divine worship.

Jacob followed, later called Israel, from whom came the Israelites, who are now the Jews.

[Col. 0538A] It was the 86th year of the promise.

[Note: Two Colbert manuscripts, together with Pontacus’s edition, have 90 years.]

From Jacob’s first year to Joseph’s accession to power in Egypt there were 121 years.

In the fifteenth year of this period, which was the hundredth year of the promise, Abraham died at the age of 175.

At this time, as the Greeks report, Jupiter united with Niobe, and from that intercourse was born Apis, whom they call Serapis.

Thus Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were earlier than Serapis.

At this time Messana, also called Mamertina, was founded.

Jacob, in his 78th year, went down to Mesopotamia and served Laban for seven years.

Jacob, when he was 92 years old, fathered Joseph. When Joseph was 17, he was sold by his brothers, in the 109th year of his father Jacob.

Isaac died in the 180th year of his life, leaving his son Jacob 120 years old.

At this time Memphis was founded in Egypt by Apis.

Joseph ruled Egypt for 80 years. When the 26th year of his rule was underway, Jacob died at the age of 147, prophesying about Christ and the calling of the nations.

In the ninth year of Joseph’s rule, which was the second year of the famine, Jacob entered Egypt with his sons.

Joseph himself died in the 110th year of his life. The Hebrews’ servitude in Egypt lasted 164 years.

[Note: It seems that “years” should be supplied. In place of 164, Eusebius, both in Pontacus’s edition and in five Colbert manuscripts, gives only 144, as follows: “Joseph died in his 110th year. After his death the Hebrews served the Egyptians for 144 years.” But all the years during which the Hebrews were in Egypt were 215, counted from the time when Jacob with his sons descended into Egypt. Therefore Joseph died in the 71st year after their entry. On this Pontacus remarks: “Some reject so many years, considering it incredible that that people should have served for so long a period and, oppressed by such harsh servitude, could have multiplied so greatly that they led out of Egypt six hundred thousand armed men, besides women and children. Nevertheless, since Augustine, in book II of his *Questions on Exodus*, question 47, after discussing much on this matter, finally concludes: ‘Therefore that calculation which Eusebius followed in his *Chronological History* is supported by clear truth; there is no reason, after rejecting the authority of so great a man, to depart from Eusebius’s opinion.’”]

In the twentieth year of this servitude, Atlas, a distinguished astrologer, was considered the brother of Prometheus.

In the sixty-fifth year of this servitude, which was the 350th year of the promise, Aram fathered Moses when he was 70 years old.

At this time Epidaurus was founded, and the temple of Delphic Apollo was built by Erisichthon.

In the 77th year of the Hebrews’ servitude, Haemon first reigned in Thessaly.

In the 80th year, Phorbas gained possession of Rhodes.

689 In the 82nd year, Hercules overcame Antaeus in a wrestling contest.

In the 87th year, Trochilus is said to have been the first to yoke a four-horse chariot.

In the 90th year, Xanthus, son of Triopas, founded Lesbos.

In the 100th year, Cecrops reigned in Attica. Under him the olive was born on the Acropolis, and the Atticans were called Athenians from the name of Minerva, who is called Athena in Greek.

[Note: The distinguished Pontacus remarks in his notes: “I conjectured,” he says, “that one should read either ‘first in Atta’ or ‘first in Acte,’ instead of ‘on the Acropolis,’ since it is established from Pliny, Herodotus, Hyginus, and others that the olive first arose in Attica, or in the region of Acte; and since what follows concerns Athens. Yet, because I had the support of no manuscript, I left the text intact. Either reading can be tolerated. For that citadel was in Acte.”]

In the 113th year, the Curetes and Corybantes founded Cnossus. They invented a rhythmic and coordinated dance in arms.

Moses, in the 80th year of his life, after 430 years had been completed from the beginning of the promise, became leader of the Hebrew people on their journey from Egypt, giving them the law in the wilderness for 40 years.

At this time Corinth was founded; it had previously been called Ephyra.

In the fifth year of this period, Aaron, the brother of Moses, was appointed the first high priest among the Hebrews.

At this time the temple of Delphic Apollo was built by Erisichthon.

[Col. 0539B] Up to this point the five books of Moses contain the events of 3,700 years according to the Seventy Interpreters.

[Note: The Pontacian edition of Eusebius’s *Chronicon*, together with his five Colbert manuscripts, has 3,730.]

After Moses died, Joshua was appointed leader. He held the chief command for 27 years and distributed the land of the Palestinians among the Jews by lot.

At this time Eleazar assumed the high priesthood among the Hebrews.

After Joshua’s death, foreigners held the Hebrews subject for eight years; these years are joined to the period of Othniel, according to Jewish tradition.

At this period Phinehas was high priest among the Hebrews.

Thus all the years of Othniel are reckoned as 40. He himself was from the tribe of Judah.

After Othniel the Hebrews were subject to foreigners for 18 years; these are joined to the period of Ehud, according to Jewish tradition.

Thus all the years of Ehud, the judge from the tribe of Ephraim, are reckoned as 80.

At the end of this period Amphion reigned at Thebes.

Deborah, with Barak, ruled for 40 years. Of these, 30 were years during which, after Ehud’s death, 690 foreigners held the Hebrews subject.

[Note: In five Colbert manuscripts of Eusebius’s *Chronicon* and in Pontacus’s edition, the number is 20 years.]

Deborah was from the tribe of Ephraim, while Barak was from the tribe of Naphtali.

In the seventeenth year of this period, Ilium was founded by Ilus.

Gideon, from the tribe of Manasseh, ruled for 40 years, including seven years during which foreigners held the Hebrews subject, according to Jewish tradition.

At this time Tyre was founded. The Argonauts lived in these times. Cyzicus was founded at this time. Orpheus the Thracian was famous.

[Col. 0539D] Abimelech, son of Gideon, ruled for three years.

These were also the times of Hercules.

[Col. 0540A] Tola ruled for 26 years. [Or 22, according to another manuscript.]

[Note: In Eusebius, 22 years, or 23 according to the Hebrews. The latter figure, “23,” is absent from four Colbert manuscripts but is found in another and in Pontacus’s edition.]

To this period are assigned the war of the Lapiths and Centaurs, the reign of Priam after Laomedon, Medea in Colchis, the death of Androgeus, and the story of the Minotaur.

Jair, from the tribe of Manasseh, ruled for 22 years.

In this period Agamemnon reigned at Mycenae and Menelaus at Lacedaemon.

In the sixth year of these reigns the Tyrians founded Carthage.

This period included Atreus reigning at Argos, as well as Phaedra and Hippolytus.

[Note: In Eusebius’s *Chronicon*: “After Jair the Ammonites brought the Hebrews under their power for 18 years”; in Pontacus’s edition, 8 years. These years are joined to the periods of the later judges according to Jewish traditions.]

Jephthah ruled for six years.

[Note: In one manuscript of Eusebius’s *Chronicon* is added: “Jephthah, in the book of Judges, says that from the age of Moses to himself 300 years are reckoned.”]

Esbon ruled for seven years.

[Note: Other manuscripts have “Ibzan.”]
