This was the time of the rape of Helen and the Trojan War.

Labdon ruled for 18 years.

[Note: In another version, eight years.]

In the third year of his rule, Troy was captured.

In Labdon’s eighth year, Aeneas reigned among the Latins for three years.

[Note: In Eusebius’s *Chronicon*: “After Labdon foreigners brought the Hebrews under their power for 40 years”; these years are joined to the periods of the later judges according to Jewish tradition.]

Samson ruled for 20 years.

In his third year Ascanius, son of Aeneas, founded Alba.

Ascanius reigned among the Latins for 37 years, or 38.

After him Silvius, the posthumous son of Aeneas, ruled for 27 years.

[Note: In another version, 29 years.]

From him the Alban kings were called Silvii.

Eli the priest ruled for 40 years.

[Note: The manuscripts and the editions of Eusebius’s *Chronicon* observe that “40 years” is found in the Hebrew book, but 20 in the Septuagint interpretation.]

After Eli the priest died, the Ark of the Covenant was possessed by foreigners.

Samuel and Saul ruled for 40 years.

Saul, the first king of the Hebrews from the tribe of Benjamin, was in the ninth year of his reign when Aeneas Silvius began to reign among the Latins for 31 years.

[Col. 0540C] After him Latinus Silvius reigned for 50 years.

691 From the beginning of Moses’ leadership to the rise of David’s kingdom there were 439 years.

David, from the tribe of Judah, was the first to reign for 40 years. At that time Abiathar was distinguished as high priest; Gad, Nathan, and Asaph were prophesying.

Solomon, son of David, ruled for 40 years. He began to build the temple at Jerusalem and completed it in eight years. At that time Zadok was distinguished as priest of the Hebrews.

In the fortieth year of Solomon’s reign, Sextus Albanus Silvius began to reign among the Latins for 38 years.

Rehoboam ruled for 17 years.

[Col. 0540D] After Solomon’s death the kingdom of the Hebrews was divided by rebellion. Those who were in Samaria were called Israel; Jeroboam was the first to reign over them.

[Col. 0541A] Rehoboam, son of Solomon, reigned in Jerusalem with two tribes subject to him. These were called Judah, after the king of the Jews from the tribe of Judah.

At this time among the Latins Aegyptus Silvius, the seventh, reigned for 23 years.

In the seventh year of Jeroboam’s reign, Shishak, king of Egypt, fought against the Jews and plundered the temple.

Abijah ruled for three years. Abimelech was distinguished as high priest of the Hebrews; Ahijah, Shemaiah, Jemoded—also called Iddo—and Hanani were prophesying.

Asa the righteous ruled for 41 years.

Jehoshaphat the righteous ruled for 25 years. Among the Hebrews, Obadiah, Jenozias, and Micah were prophesying.

[Note: In Eusebius’s *Chronicon*: Jehu and Uzziah.]

In the twelfth year of this reign, Capys Silvius reigned among the Latins for seven years.

Then the ninth, Compartus Silvius, reigned for five years.

[Note: In Eusebius’s *Chronicon*: Carpentus Silvius.]

Joram ruled for eight years. At that time Elijah and Elisha were prophesying.

Osias ruled for one year. Jonadab, son of Rechab, was distinguished.

[Note: The Vulgate calls her Athaliah, 2 Kings 11. Saint Prosper follows the reading of Eusebius, whom Pontacus says it is not unusual for our Bibles—both Hebrew and Latin, and sometimes even Greek—to diverge from. He expressly teaches this in book X of *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, where, listing all the kings after Ahaziah, he records Athaliah: “Athaliah, seven years.” Theophilus, in book III, after Ahaziah names Gothoniel, with no mention of Athaliah. In Eusebius’s *Chronicon*: Oded.]

Gotholiah, the mother, ruled for seven years.

At this time Homer the poet was famous in Greece.

Joash ruled for 40 years. In these times Jehoiada was a distinguished high priest among the Hebrews; he alone after Moses lived for 130 years. At this time the prophet Azariah was killed; the prophet Zechariah 692 also was murdered by King Joash.

Among the Latins, the twelfth, Aremulus Silvius, ruled for 19 years. After him Aventinus Silvius reigned for 37 years; from him came the name of the Aventine Hill. After him, the fourteenth, Procas Silvius, ruled for 26 years. After him, the fifteenth, Amulius Silvius, ruled for 43 years.

Amaziah ruled for 29 years.

Azariah, also called Uzziah, ruled for 52 years.

In the sixth year of his reign, the kings of the Assyrians came to an end, their empire being transferred to the Medes.

Among the Hebrews, Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, and Jonah were prophesying when Uzziah’s twenty-first year was underway.

In his forty-ninth year the first Olympiad was established: the Eleans held a five-year contest, with four intervening years left vacant. They called this period an Olympiad, after its founder Iphitus.

Jotham ruled for 16 years. Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, and Joel—also called Jobeth—were prophesying.

Ahaz ruled for 16 years.

In the fifth year of this reign Romulus founded Rome and began to reign.

In the eleventh year of King Ahaz, the ten tribes of the Hebrew people, called Israel and occupying the region of Samaria, were defeated by Sennacherib, also called Shalmaneser, king of the Chaldeans. They were transferred to the mountains of the Medes after the kingdom had been in Samaria for 250 years.

[Note: Pontacus, in his notes, p. 346, observes that the words “also called Shalmaneser” are absent from not a few manuscripts, at least in the text. The Colbert manuscripts vary: one names only Sennacherib, another only Shalmaneser, while three others name both. Since, if both names are retained, Sennacherib and Shalmaneser seem to be confused as two persons—although Shalmaneser is read to have been Sennacherib’s father in Tobit 1, and in 2 Kings 17 the ten tribes are said to have been transferred by Shalmaneser while the tribe of Judah remained intact, whereas Sennacherib is said to have come against all the fortified cities of Judah, captured them, and surrounded Jerusalem with a siege in Isaiah 36, Ezekiel 14, and 2 Kings 18, between which events there was doubtless a considerable interval—he replies that Eusebius makes no mention of the siege of Jerusalem, but merely says that Shalmaneser was also called Sennacherib and led Israel into exile. Hence he argues that it is preferable, with Saint Thomas on Isaiah 20, to say that Shalmaneser had six names and was also called Sennacherib. Jerome had already observed, in his commentary on chapter 36, that some thought Shalmaneser was called by many names; this is not foreign to the sacred language, in which the same names are often shared by father and son.]

Sennacherib sent Assyrians as settlers to guard the region of Judea. They became imitators of the law of the Jews and were called Samaritans, which in Latin means “guardians.”

Hezekiah ruled for 29 years. Under him Isaiah and Hosea were prophesying among the Hebrews.

Romulus first recruited soldiers from the people, and one hundred noble old men. Because of their age he called them senators; because of their care for the state, fathers.

At the same time Syracuse and Catana were founded in Sicily.

Manasseh ruled for 55 years.

At the beginning of his reign, Numa Pompilius was reigning among the Romans for 41 years, after the senate had reigned for one year following Romulus.

Amon ruled for 12 years.

[Note: Eusebius’s *Chronicon*: Amon, according to the Septuagint interpretation, for 12 years; according to the Hebrews, for two years.]

[Col. 0542C] At the beginning of this reign Tullus Hostilius was in the seventeenth year of his rule at Rome, and he reigned for 32 years.

Josiah ruled for 32 years. During his reign Chelcias was distinguished as high priest of the Hebrews, and Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and the woman Huldah were prophesying.

[Note: Four Colbert manuscripts support the number 32; the Vulgate counts 31, while Pontacus’s edition, together with one Colbert manuscript, has 22.]

Among the Romans Ancus was reigning. He founded the city of Ostia and reigned for 23 years. After him Tarquinius Priscus reigned for 37 years.

[Col. 0543A] Josiah, king of the Jews, was killed in battle against Necho, king of the Egyptians.

Thales of Miletus is recognized as the first philosopher of physics.

In the twenty-first year of Tarquinius Priscus, Massilia was founded.

Jehoahaz ruled for three months.

Jehoiakim, also called Eliakim, ruled for 11 years. In his third year Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylonia, captured Judea. After bringing many of the Jews under his power, and having already seized part of the temple vessels and made Jehoiakim tributary, he returned victorious to his homeland.

Jehoiachin, also called Joatham or Joachim, ruled for three months.

In Babylon Ananias, Daniel, Azariah, and Mishael were distinguished.

Nebuchadnezzar, coming a second time against Judea, seized Jehoiachin and carried him away with him.

[Note: That this refers to Jehoiachin is established from the Colbert manuscripts, the Eusebian *Chronicon*, and Pontacus’s edition. There the statement “In Babylon Daniel, etc.” is placed after the account of the captivity of the Jews.]

Zedekiah ruled for 11 years.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, captured Jerusalem and burned the temple, which had stood from the beginning of its construction for 342 years.

[Note: In Eusebius’s *Chronicon*, four Colbert manuscripts, and Pontacus’s edition, the number is 442; in one manuscript, 342.]

The captivity of the Jews lasted 70 years, reckoned up to the second year of Darius.

Among the Romans, after Tarquinius Priscus, Servius reigned for 34 years. Tarquinius Superbus succeeded him and reigned for 35 years. In the twenty-fifth year of his reign, Aggaeus, Zechariah, and Malachi were prophesying among the Hebrews, with Jesus son of Josedech as high priest.

At this time the philosopher Pythagoras was famous.

From David to the seventy years of the captivity of the Jews, 555 years are reckoned.

From the seventieth year of the captivity of the Jews, 33 years of Darius, king of the Persians, are reckoned.

In the tenth year of his reign the royal government among the Romans came to an end; that power had remained with them for 240 years. From then on, under Brutus, the Romans began to have consuls, then tribunes of the people and dictators, and again consuls held the republic for 464 years—or 444—up to Julius Caesar.

Xerxes reigned for 20 years. He was the son of Darius, and during his time Sophocles and Euripides were famous. 694 Herodotus, the writer of histories, also belonged to this period.

After Xerxes, Artabanus reigned for seven months.

[Col. 0543D] Artaxerxes ruled for 40 years.

During his reign Ezra the priest was distinguished among the Hebrews. In his time the high priest was Eliakim, also called Eliasib, son of Joachin, son of Jesus, son of Josedech.

Empedocles and Parmenides, Zeno and Heraclitus were celebrated philosophers. At that time Poricides was a historian, Cratinus a comic poet, and Aristarchus a tragedian.

In the twentieth year of Artaxerxes’ reign, Nehemiah the Hebrew, the king’s cupbearer, came from Babylon into Judea with the permission of his lord, and in the thirty-second year restored the walls and the city. If anyone counts from this time the seventy weeks written by Daniel, amounting to 490 years, he will find them completed in the reign of Nero, under whom the siege of Jerusalem began and, two years later, in the reign of Vespasian, the city was captured.

At this time Hippocrates the physician and Socrates the philosopher were distinguished.

Xerxes ruled for two months. Plato was born.

Sogdianus ruled for seven months; one year is included in this reckoning.

Darius, surnamed Nothus, ruled for 19 years, or, in another account, 18.

Dionysius exercised tyranny in Sicily.

The Romans sent envoys to the Athenians to request their laws; from these the Twelve Tables were compiled.

[Col. 0544B] Artaxerxes Mnemon, son of Darius and Parysatis, ruled for 40 years.

In the fifteenth year of his reign the Senonian Gauls occupied Rome, except for the Capitol.

Aristotle, in the eighteenth year of his life, became a student of Plato.

Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, ruled for 26 years.

At the beginning of his reign Camillus defeated the Gauls who had made war upon the Romans.

At the same time Alexander, son of Philip, was born.

The same period also produced the famous orator Demosthenes.

Arses, son of Ochus, ruled for four years.

At this time, when a census was conducted at Rome, 160,000 citizens were found.

[Col. 0544C] Among the Jews Jaddus was distinguished as high priest.

Darius, son of Arsames, ruled for six years.

At that time, among the Romans, the consul Manlius Torquatus had his son beaten with rods and struck with the axe because he had fought the enemy against orders.

At this time Alexander, son of Philip, began to reign. In the sixth year of his rule he overthrew the Persian kingdom and founded the city of Alexandria in Egypt.

695 Appius Claudius Caecus was famous among the Romans. He brought in the Claudia aqueduct and paved the Appian Way.

The Romans subjugated the Samnites.

**Alexander**, after the end of the Persian kingdom, reigned for seven years. In the thirty-second year of his life he died at Babylon.

The kingdom of the Alexandrians arose; Ptolemy, son of Lagus, obtained it and ruled for 40 years. In the fourth year of his reign, after Jerusalem and Judea had been brought under his power, he transferred many captives to Egypt. At that time Onias, son of Jaddus, was distinguished as high priest of the Jews.

The Hebrew history of the Maccabees therefore begins its reckoning of the Greek kingdoms at this point. But these books are not received by the Hebrews among the divine Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0544D] On similar words of Eusebius, see Pontacus in his notes, p. 446. Since, in the Church, before the Third Council of Carthage, all the books of both the Old and New Testaments were not received as canonical by all Churches at one and the same time and with the same degree of certainty . . . . . Hence, in Eusebius’ time, there was no agreement among all, especially among the Greeks, concerning the two books of the Maccabees. They are therefore not to be rejected from the Catalogue, any more than the Book of Esther, which Eusebius likewise does not receive among the divine Scriptures; Athanasius in the Synopsis, Gregory of Nazianzus in On the Genuine Scriptures, Amphilochius rightly, in Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 26, and other Greeks follow him in this, nor any more than the Apocalypse or Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews. Just as the Latin custom did not receive the latter among the canonical Scriptures, so neither did the Greek Church receive the Apocalypse, as Jerome says in his letter to Dardanus. But after the Church, in that Third Council of Carthage—which Augustine attended—established, in chapter 47, a list or canon of the sacred or canonical books, thereafter the two books of the Maccabees, like the others, were regarded by everyone as divine and canonical. Hence Augustine, Book VIII of The City of God, chapter 36: “The Jews do not regard the books of the Maccabees as canonical, but the Church does,” and so forth. To this may be added the authority of the Council of Trent, session 4, in the decree on the canonical Scriptures.]

[Col. 0545A] The Romans defeat the Marsi, Hernici, and Peligni.

During these years Seleucus founded the cities of Antioch, Laodicea, Apamea, Edessa, Beroea, and Pella, in which he granted citizenship to the Jews whom he had transferred there. Seleucus gained possession of Babylon.

In the twenty-fifth year of Ptolemy’s reign, Simon, the high priest of the Jews, son of Onias, was distinguished.

When a census was conducted at Rome, 270,000 citizens were found.

Eleazar, the brother of Simon, assumed the high priesthood among the Jews; Simon’s son Onias, because he was still a child, had been unable to succeed his father.

At that time Beneventum and Ariminum were founded by the Romans.

Ptolemy, also called Philadelphus, reigned thirty-eight years. [Col. 0545B] He permitted the Jews who were in Egypt to be free, and, sending votive vessels to Eleazar, the high priest of Jerusalem, arranged for the divine Scriptures to be translated from Hebrew into Greek by the Seventy Interpreters. He placed them in the Alexandrian Library, which he had assembled for himself from every kind of literature.

A silver coin was first struck in the City in the thirteenth year of this reign. In the twenty-fourth year of this reign, however, the Romans defeated the Carthaginians in a naval battle and captured one hundred cities of Libya.

After Eleazar, his uncle Manasseh assumed the Jewish high priesthood. After him, Onias, son of Simon the Just, was regarded as a distinguished high priest; because he failed to pay the customary tribute to Ptolemy, he provoked him to anger. [Col. 0545C] But Josephus, a man of distinction among his own people, was sent by the Jews as an envoy to Ptolemy. Because he had won the king’s friendship through the many services he rendered him, he was appointed governor of Judaea and the neighboring regions. 696

When the Parthians withdrew from the rule of the Macedonians, Arsaces was the first to reign; from him the Arsacids received their name.

Ptolemy Euergetes reigned twenty-six years.

During this period Simon, son of Onias, was regarded as a distinguished high priest of the Jews. Under him Jesus, son of Sirach, composed the Book of Wisdom, which they call the *Panaretos*.

The poet Ennius was born at Tarentum.

Rhodes was shaken by an earthquake, and the Colossus fell.

About 40,000 Gauls were killed by the Romans.

[Col. 0545D] Ptolemy Philopator reigned seventeen years. The Jews were defeated, and 40,000 of their armed men were killed.

The Romans, meanwhile, subjugated Capua and Sicily.

[Col. 0546A] Antiochus, king of Syria, after defeating Philopator, took Judaea for himself through Ptolemy.

Ptolemy Epiphanes reigned twenty-four years. He appointed Scopas commander of the army, captured Judaea, and took many cities of Syria. The Second Book of the Maccabees contains the events of this period.

At this time, when the Romans demanded Hannibal from Antiochus through envoys—Hannibal had joined Antiochus after being defeated by Scipio—Hannibal fled from Antiochus to King Prusias of Bithynia. When he was also demanded from Prusias through Flaminius and was about to be handed over, he drank poison and was buried at Libyssa in Bithynia.

The comic poet Caecilius flourished.

Ptolemy Philometor reigned twenty-five years, or thirty-five. In the fourth year of his reign, Hyrcanus, son of Josephus, the governor of Judaea, [Col. 0546B] went to Ptolemy and was received by him with honor. But his brothers, after beginning a revolt against him, became the cause of great disasters for the Jewish people.

Aristobulus, a Jew by nationality and a Peripatetic philosopher, became distinguished. He wrote commentaries on Moses for Ptolemy Philometor.

At the same time Antiochus Epiphanes, having withdrawn from the territory of the Ptolemies—which he had suddenly invaded—because he was intimidated by the command of the Roman Senate, came to Judaea. There he entrusted the high priesthood to Jesus and Jason, the brother of Onias. After expelling Jason, he appointed Onias, surnamed Menelaus, as his successor. Thus, because of the dignity of the priesthood, sedition arose among the leaders, and the seeds of enormous misery began to sprout.

[Col. 0546C] The Samaritans and Jews of Alexandria disputed, before Ptolemy as judge, over the honors to be offered by each side to its own temple, and the Jews prevailed. 697

In the twentieth year of that same reign, Judas Maccabaeus, after the death of his enemy Alcimus, was appointed to the priesthood and leadership by the unanimous favor of all the Jews. Having assumed this dignity, he sent envoys to Rome and obtained by decree of the Senate that the Jews should be regarded as friends and allies of the Romans. Judas also expelled from Judaea the commanders of Antiochus, who had attacked the Jewish law with great profanation; after cleansing the Temple of the images of idols, he restored the ancestral religious observances to his fellow citizens after three years.

The poet Ennius died and was buried in the monument [Col. 0546D] of the Scipios on the Appian Way.

Judas Maccabaeus, after exercising the high priesthood for three years, was killed while fighting against the commanders of Demetrius.

[Col. 0547A] Terentius of Carthage, a writer of comedies, died.

Pacuvius the tragedian was held in high esteem. He was the grandson through his daughter of the poet Ennius, and lived at Rome while he practiced painting and sold his plays; later he moved to Tarentum and died nearly ninety years old.

After a census was conducted at Rome, 332,000 citizens were found. [Note: [Col. 0547D] The manuscripts of Eusebius vary in this calculation. In one, the number is 222,000; in another, and in Pontacus’ edition, 322,000; in two others, 334,000; in another, 335,000; and in Pontacus’ edition [the number is as above].] At this time Carthage was brought under Roman rule by Scipio.

Ptolemy Euergetes reigned twenty-nine years.

Jonathan, the high priest of the Jews, was killed by Trypho, and Simon, Jonathan’s brother, was appointed to the priesthood. After Simon was killed, his son John succeeded him. Waging war against the Hyrcanians, he acquired the name Hyrcanus, and by decree of the Senate was enrolled by the Romans [Col. 0547B] among their friends. He also captured Samaria after a siege and leveled it to the ground; later, when Herod restored it, he wished it to be called Sebaste in honor of Augustus.

Attalus, when he died, [Note: [Col. 0547D] The manuscripts of Eusebius add here, “of his own kingdom.”] left the Roman people as his heir.

Ptolemy Physcon, also called Soter, reigned twenty-seven years [Elsewhere, seventeen].

In the eighth year of this reign Cicero was born at Arpinum, his mother being Helvia and his father belonging to the equestrian order; he was descended from the royal family of the Volsci.

Three years later Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus was born.

In the seventeenth year of this reign, Gaius Marius, in his fifth consulship, defeated the Cimbri near the Rhône. After killing 200,000 of them, he captured 80,000 and celebrated a triumph over them together with Catulus.

[Col. 0547C] Jugurtha was captured while fighting against the Romans. A slave war again broke out in Sicily. The Thracians were defeated by the Romans.

Aristobulus, son of Jonathan (John), was both king and high priest, and was the first among the Jews to assume the insignia of a diadem. After him Jannaeus reigned, surnamed Alexander; while also administering the high priesthood, he ruled his fellow citizens with the utmost cruelty. 698

Ptolemy, also called Alexander, reigned eight years.

Philip was reigning in Syria. The Roman commander Gabinius captured him, after Antiochus had already fled to the Parthians and subsequently surrendered himself to Pompey. Thus Syria passed into Roman control.

J. Pomponius of Bologna was regarded as a distinguished writer of Atellan plays.

[Col. 0547D] At this time the poet T. Lucretius flourished. Driven mad by a love potion, he killed himself with his own hand.

Plotius Gallus was the first at Rome to teach Latin rhetoric.

Ptolemy, son of Cleopatra, reigned eight years.

Sallust, the writer of histories, was born at Amiternum among the Sabines.

After a census was conducted at Rome, 463,000 persons were found. [Note: [Col. 0548D] Three Colbertine manuscripts have 464,000; one has 414,000.]

[Col. 0548A] P. Terentius Varro was born in the village of Atax in the Province of Narbonensis. At the age of thirty-five he learned Greek literature.

Ptolemy Dionysius reigned thirty years.

From the sixth year of this reign, Alexandra, also called Selene, the wife of Alexander, reigned for nine years in Jerusalem. During her period, confusion of affairs and various disasters oppressed the Jews. Soon afterward, when Jerusalem was captured by Gnaeus Pompeius and the Temple was opened as far as the Holy of Holies, the Jews became tributaries of the Romans; Hyrcanus was appointed high priest over them, and Antipater, son of Herod the Ascalonite, was made governor of Palestine.

M. Porcius Cato was recognized as a Stoic philosopher.

What Sallust writes concerning Catiline took place during this period.

In the tenth year of the reign of Ptolemy, Virgil Maro was born in the village called Andes, near Mantua, during the consulship of Pompey and Crassus.

Seven years later the satiric and lyric poet Horace Flaccus was born at Venusia to a freedman father.

The consul Crassus was captured at Carrhae together with his son.

Pompey, having been named commander, captured Lusitania and certain islands in the Ocean.

Cleopatra reigned twenty-two years, of which only two are to be counted, because Roman empires arise continuously. From this point their periods are to be reckoned from Gaius Julius Caesar, who was the first among the Romans to hold sole power; from him the Roman rulers were called Caesars.

[Col. 0548C] Caesar crossed the Rhine, ravaged the Germans, and subjugated the Gauls. 699

The beginning of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey.

From this point the Roman reigns are recorded continuously, and Gaius Julius Caesar was the first of all to rule among them.

Gaius Julius Caesar, the first, [Note: [Col. 0548D] The manuscripts of Eusebius’ Chronicle and Pontacus’ edition add seven months.] reigned four years and six months.

Pompey, defeated and fleeing, was killed by the eunuchs of the Alexandrian king.

A decree of the Senate and of the Athenians was sent to the Jews, who had requested friendship through envoys.

Cleopatra entered the City with royal retinue.

Antony decreed that the month Quintilis should be called July, because Julius had been born in it.

[Col. 0548D] Cassius, after capturing Judaea, plundered the Temple.

On the Ides of March, Gaius Julius Caesar was killed in the Senate house.

Caesar Augustus, also called Octavian, reigned fifty-six years. [Note: [Col. 0548D] In Eusebius’ Chronicle six months are added.] From him the Roman kings were called Augusti.

Ovidius Naso was born among the Peligni.

Cicero was killed at his Formian villa by Herennius and Popilius.

Antony began a war against Augustus.

From the Taberna Meritoria across the Tiber, oil burst out of the earth [Col. 0549A] and flowed all day without interruption, signifying the grace of Christ among the Gentiles.

Antiochus, after being defeated by Augustus, returned to his friendship through the intervention of the Senate.

Herod, son of Antipater the Ascalonite and of Cypros, an Arabian woman, received from the Romans the rule of the Jews. Near the time of Christ’s birth, in his reign, the kingdom and priesthood of Judaea—which had previously been held through successions of lesser rulers—were destroyed, fulfilling the prophecy that speaks through Moses as follows: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a king from his thighs [Note: [Col. 0549D] The manuscripts of Eusebius’ Chronicle read, “nor a leader,” as in our Vulgate and in the Hebrew.], until the seed [Note: [Col. 0549D] In Eusebius this word, “seed,” is omitted.] comes, to whom it has been reserved, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10).

At this point as well Christ, whom Daniel records, reached his appointed end. For until Herod there were *christs*, that is, priests [Col. 0549B] who were kings of the Jews. They began to rule from the sixty-fifth Olympiad, and from the restoration of the Temple under Darius until Hyrcanus and the 186th Olympiad, with 484 years having elapsed in between; Daniel also indicated these years when he said: “And you shall know and understand: from the beginning of the word concerning the restoration and rebuilding of Jerusalem until the rule of Christ, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks” (Daniel 9:25).

These sixty-nine weeks, during which *christs*—that is, priests consecrated through anointing—reigned, amount to 483 years, up to Hyrcanus. When the last of all of them had been captured by the Parthians, Herod, son of Antipater, received from Augustus and the Senate a Judaea that had no connection with him; his sons ruled after him, until the final captivity of Jerusalem, [Col. 0549C] with high priests no longer being appointed from a succession of priestly stock, nor serving God with the perpetuity of life according to the law of Moses. Certain obscure men, and at other times others, some serving for a single year or for only a little longer, bought the priesthood from the Roman emperors.

The prophet Daniel also foretells all these things, saying: “And after the seven weeks and the sixty-two weeks, the anointing shall be destroyed, and judgment shall not be in it; and the people of the coming leader shall destroy the Temple and the sanctuary, and they shall be cut down in the flood of war” (ibid., 26). And in what follows he says: “Upon the Temple shall be the abomination of desolations, and until the consummation of time an end shall be imposed upon the desolation” (ibid., 27).

Sallust died four years before the Battle of Actium.

Vinius Maximus acknowledged his master, who had been designated quaestor, and took him away.

The course of the moon according to the Romans was discovered.

Cleopatra and Antony killed themselves, and Egypt became a Roman province.

Caesar was called Augustus; from him the month Sextilis received the name August.

When Augustus was offered a monarchy, he refused it.

[Col. 0550A] Augustus made Calabria [Cantabria] and the Gauls [Gallaeci] tributary.

Tiberius, sent by Augustus, occupied Armenia.

The Cantabrians, who were attempting a revolution, were crushed.

Augustus adopted Gaius Agrippa as his son.

Tiberius made the Vindelici [Note: [Col. 0549D] The books of Eusebius’ Chronicle read, “and those who bordered on Thrace,”] and the neighboring peoples of Raetia Roman provinces.

In the seventeenth year of Augustus’ reign, when a census was conducted at Rome, 4,174,000 Roman citizens were found. [Note: [Col. 0550D] In two Colbertine manuscripts the number is 1,544,000.]

In the twenty-fourth year of Augustus’ reign, Tiberius celebrated a triumph over the Pannonians whom he had captured.

In the twenty-fifth year of the same reign, Virgil died at Brundisium and was buried at Naples, two miles from the city.

[Col. 0550B] Herod, raising Samaria—which had long been lying in ashes—from its foundations, called it Augusta, that is, Sebaste, in honor of Augustus. At Paneas he built what is called the Panion. He also founded Caesarea in Caesar’s name; it had previously been called Strato’s Tower. He also killed Hyrcanus, who had once been high priest of the Jews, after Hyrcanus had returned from Parthian captivity, as well as his son, who had succeeded his father in the priesthood. He most cruelly killed his sister, whom he had taken as his wife, together with her two sons, already young men, and the mother of his murdered wife, his mother-in-law. 701 He also killed the husband of his sister Salome; and when he had given her to another man in marriage, he killed that man as well. He also killed the scribes and interpreters of the divine law in a similar crime.

[Col. 0550C] Augustus condemned his daughter Julia to exile after discovering her in adultery; he adopted Tiberius and Agrippa as sons.

Judas the Galilean urged the Jews to rebel.

In the forty-fourth year of Augustus’ reign, Quirinius was sent to Judaea by decree of the Senate and recorded a census of the people and their possessions.

In that same year Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was born in Bethlehem of Judaea.

All the years from the beginning of Abraham up to the birth of Christ from Mary are reckoned as 2,018 or 2,015. [Note: [Col. 0550D] Three Colbertine manuscripts have 2,014. Two more reliable ones from the same library have 2,015, as does Pontacus’ edition of Eusebius’ Chronicle.]

When Herod learned from the report of the Magi about Christ’s birth, he ordered all the infants in Bethlehem to be killed. Two years later he himself died miserably, but deservedly, from dropsy and from worms swarming throughout his body.

Archelaus was appointed by Augustus in Herod’s place—and his brothers Herod, Antipater, Lysias, and Philip became tetrarchs—for nine years.

Tiberius Caesar brought the Dalmatians and Sarmatians under Roman power.

The Athenians, who were attempting a revolution against the Romans, were crushed.

[Col. 0551A] In the fifty-third year of his reign, Augustus conducted a census at Rome with his son Tiberius and found 9,370,000 persons. [Note: [Col. 0551D] A single Colbertine manuscript reads “and 60,000.” In other manuscripts this census is assigned to the fifty-fifth year of Augustus, and in others to the fifty-fourth.]

Two years before his death the orator Messala Corvinus lost his memory so completely that he could scarcely put a few words together.

Archelaus was exiled to the Gallic city of Vienne in the ninth year of his reign. After him Herod was tetrarch for twenty-four years.

Tiberius made Drusus his partner in the kingdom.

Tiberius, the third, reigned twenty-three years. In the fifth year of his reign thirteen cities collapsed in an earthquake.

In the fourteenth year of the same reign Pilate was sent as governor of Judaea.

Herod founded Tiberias and Livias.

[Col. 0551B] Tiberius summoned many kings to himself by flattering promises, but never sent them back; instead, he converted their kingdoms into provinces.

John, son of Zechariah, preaching to the Jews in the desert beside the Jordan River, testified that Christ, the Son of God, was present among them.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself from this point announced the way of salvation to the peoples, proving by signs and mighty works that what he said was true. 702

Drusus Caesar died by poison.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] In Eusebius’ Chronicle this entry, together with the following one, is assigned to the eighteenth year of Tiberius, after Christ’s Passion.]

Josephus testifies that around this time, on the day of Pentecost, the priests of the Jews first perceived disturbances in the places of the Temple and certain sounds; afterward a voice burst forth from the sanctuary saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

[Col. 0551C] The same Josephus writes that in that same year Pilate, the governor, secretly placed images of Caesar in the Temple during the night.

Thus, up to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the years are calculated as follows: from the restoration of the Temple, which took place in the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, 548 years; from Solomon and the first construction of the Temple, 1,060 years; from Moses and the departure of Israel from Egypt, 1,516 years. [Note: [Col. 0551D] In Eusebius’ Chronicle, 1,539.] From the first year of the promise, 1,572 years; from the year in which Abraham was born, 2,047 years. [Note: [Col. 0551D] In Eusebius, 2,044.] From the Flood to Abraham’s first year, the most eloquent Eusebius reckoned 942 years. From Adam to the Flood, 2,242 years. Therefore, all the years from Adam up to the fifteenth year of Tiberius [Col. 0551D] Caesar amount to 5,360 or 5,228 years. According to the text of Genesis and the reckoning of the historian Africanus, however, 129 additional years are found.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Philip Labbe reports that another reading of this passage is found in certain manuscripts, in the Supplement, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, p. 22, namely: “Some say that Jesus Christ suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius. They derive an argument for this from the Gospel of John, in which, after the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the Lord is understood to have preached for three years. But because the more usual tradition holds that our Lord was crucified in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, during the consulship of the two Gemini, we shall, without prejudice to the alternative opinion, begin the succession of the following consuls from their respective consulships, while retaining the chronological annotations belonging to each ruler.]

Some believe that our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, that is, during the consulship of the two Gemini. In that year, according to the indisputable authority of the evangelist Luke, it is clear that he was baptized and began to preach the Gospel of the heavenly kingdom. According to the Gospel of John, we know that the Lord attended the feast of the Jews’ Passover three times, so that it appears that the third was the Passover which the true Lamb consecrated with his blood.

Accordingly, we begin the consuls from the Manifestation of the Lord, that is, from the consulship of Rufinus Geminus and Rubellius Geminus; but we assign the third consulship after them to the Lord’s Passion, following what tradition and reason have handed down.

THE ANNOTATION OF THE CONSULS BEGINS, [Note: [Col. 0552D] The Supplement, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, adds: “from the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ,”] TOGETHER WITH THE HISTORY.

[Col. 0552B] During the consulship of Rufinus Geminus and Rubellius Geminus.

During the consulship of Vinicius and Longinus.

During the consulship of Sulpicius and Sulla.

James, who was regarded as the brother of the Lord, was appointed the first bishop of the Church of Jerusalem. 703

During the consulship of Priscus and Vitellius.

During the consulship of Gallus and Nonianus.

During the consulship of Gallienus and Plautianus.

Pilate spent the sacred treasury—which the Jews call *Corban*—on an aqueduct at Jerusalem and thereby provided the seeds of a second revolt. From this time innumerable calamities oppressed the Jewish people.

[Col. 0552C] During the consulship of Proculus and Nigrinus.

During the consulship of Julianus and Asprenates.

During the consulship of Publicola and Nerva.

When Pilate reported the Christian doctrine to Tiberius, Tiberius referred the matter to the Senate so that it might be received among the other sacred observances. But when, following the Senate’s decision, it had been resolved that the Christians should be expelled from the City, Tiberius threatened their accusers with death by an edict.

During the consulship of Caesar and Julianus.

Gaius Caesar Caligula, the fourth, reigned three years and ten months.

During the second consulship of Caesar and Saturninus.

During the second consulship of Saturninus and Venustus.

During the consulship of Tiberius and Gallus.

[Col. 0552D] At this time Pontius Pilate, falling into many calamities, killed himself with his own hand.

When Caligula had ranked himself among the gods, he ordered Petronius, the governor of Syria, to place a statue of him at Jerusalem under the name of Jupiter Optimus Maximus. Moreover, throughout the entire Roman world, statues, images, and altars of Gaius Caesar were being consecrated in the Jews’ synagogues.

During the consulship of Crispinus and Taurus.

Many members of the nobility were killed by Gaius.

Gaius was killed in the palace by his own guards.

Claudius, the fifth, reigned thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-eight days. He was the uncle of Drusus, who has a monument at Mainz.

During the consulship of Vinicius and Cornelius.

During the consulship of Asiaticus and Silanus.

The apostle Peter, after first founding the Church of Antioch, departed for Rome, where, preaching the Gospel, he remained bishop of that city for twenty-five years. [Col. 0553B]

During the second consulship of Tiberius and Vitellius.

The beginning of the first cycle.

During the second consulship of Vitellius and Publicola.

Evodius was the first bishop appointed at Antioch.

During the consulship of Verinus and Gallus.

During the consulship of Vetere and Nervilianus.

After a census was conducted at Rome, 6,864,000 or 6,844,000 citizens were found. [Note: [Col. 0553D] In Eusebius’ Chronicle the number is “after 6,800,000, 44,000.”]

704 The reckoning of the Paschal cycle began with these consuls, continued for eighty-four years, and then returned to the same rule.

During the consulship of Claudius and Orfitus.

[Col. 0553C] Under the governor of Judaea, Cumanus, during the days of Unleavened Bread, so great a revolt arose at Jerusalem that, when the people collapsed at the exits of the gates, 34,000 Jews perished. [Note: [Col. 0553D] Eusebius counts only 30,000.]

The prophecy of Agabus, who had foretold in the Acts of the Apostles that a famine would occur throughout the whole world, was fulfilled under Claudius.

Thrace, which had remained under kings until this point, was reduced to a province.

During the consulship of Silanus and Silius.

During the third consulship of Tiberius and Antoninus.

During the second consulship of Silanus and Antoninus.

During the consulship of Marcellinus and Aviola.

Among them was a certain Egyptian false prophet who, gathering many to himself, was crushed by Felix’s army in the very attempt to accomplish great things, in accordance with what is said to Paul in the Acts of the Apostles: “Are you not the Egyptian who, some days ago, stirred up and led out into the desert the four thousand men?”

During the consulship of Nero and Vetere.

During the second consulship of Nero and Piso.

During the third consulship of Nero and Messala.

During the fourth consulship of Nero and Cornelius.

Festus succeeded Felix. In the presence of King Agrippa, the apostle Paul, bound and sent to Rome, was to give an account of his religion before Festus.

Nero was so luxurious that he bathed in cold and hot perfumes and fished with golden nets, which were hauled in by purple ropes.

During the consulship of Pius and Turpilianus.

During the consulship of Marbinus and Gallus.

During the consulship of Crassus and Bassus.

Nero defeated everyone in playing the lyre.

[Col. 0554C] During the consulship of Celsinus and Apuleius.

Lightning struck before Nero’s dining table.

After the evangelist Mark, Anianus was the first bishop appointed over the Church of Alexandria.

705 During the consulship of Capito and Rufus.

During the consulship of Silius Italicus and Turpilianus.

During the consulship of Silvanus and Otho.

During the consulship of Vespasian and Titus.

During the second consulship of Vespasian and Titus.

During the third consulship of Vespasian and Nerva.

To see a likeness of burning Troy, Nero set fire to a very large part of the city of Rome.

[Col. 0554D] Musonius and Plutarch were regarded as distinguished philosophers.

THE FIRST PERSECUTION. [Note: [Col. 0553D] The illustrious Pontacus notes two matters worthy of attention here. First, the author calls this persecution against the Christians the first, or says that Nero was the first to initiate it. He is referring not only to the first universal persecution, or the persecution of the nations—for the persecution narrated in Acts 18 was particular, occurring in Judaea and Samaria and being carried out by Jews—but also to the first bloody persecution. Hence Tertullian writes elegantly in *Scorpiace*, chapter 14: “Nero was the first at Rome to stain the emerging faith with blood.” For, according not only to Suetonius but also to Luke himself in Acts 15 and 18, Claudius had previously expelled Christians from the City together with the Jews. Second, the author may perhaps be speaking of the persecution that occurred in this year not so much to indicate its beginning or initiation as to use the occasion to record the martyrdom of Peter and Paul. For it is certain from Tacitus, Book XV, that Nero’s persecution began in the tenth year of his reign, on the occasion of the burning of the city of Rome, so that he might eliminate, through the tortures and punishments of Christians, the rumor of that fire and extinguish the hatred that everyone had consequently conceived against him.]

Nero was the first who, beyond all his crimes, also carried out a persecution against the Christians, in which the apostles Peter and Paul gloriously perished at Rome.

After Peter, Linus first governed the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0555D] Three manuscripts of Eusebian chronicles have twelve years; two others, together with Pontacus’ edition, have eleven.] for twelve or thirteen years.

Vespasian was sent by Nero as commander of the army to subdue the Jews.

During the fourth consulship of Vespasian and the third of Titus.

Vespasian, after defeating the Jews in two battles, drove them back to the walls.

Ignatius was appointed the second bishop of Antioch.

When the Senate was seeking Nero for punishment, he fled from the Palace and killed himself at the fourth milestone from the City.

Vespasian, the seventh, reigned nine years, nine months, [Col. 0555B] and twenty-two or twenty-nine days.

During the fifth consulship of Vespasian and the fourth of Titus.

After Nero, Galba seized power in Iberia, Vitellius in Germany, and Otho at Rome. But Galba was beheaded at Rome in the seventh month; Otho died by his own hand at Bebriacum [Note: [Col. 0555D] Two Colbertine manuscripts have Vetriacum; three others, Metriacum.]; Vitellius was killed by Vespasian’s commanders and thrown into the Tiber.

Vespasian was proclaimed emperor by the army in Judaea. Entrusting the war to his son Titus, he set out for Rome through Alexandria.

During the sixth consulship of Vespasian and the fifth of Titus.

Titus, after Judaea was captured and Jerusalem destroyed, killed 600,000 men. Josephus writes that 1,100,000 perished from hunger and the sword, and that another 100,000 captives were publicly sold. [Col. 0555C] The reason such a multitude was found at Jerusalem was that the Feast of Unleavened Bread had brought them there: Jews from every nation flocked to the Temple and were shut up in the city as though in a prison. For they had to be killed on those days on which they had crucified the Savior. 706

Thus the entire period is calculated up to the second year of Vespasian and the final destruction of Jerusalem. From the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and the beginning of the evangelical preaching, forty-two years. From the captivity that they suffered under Antiochus, 229 years. [Note: [Col. 0555D] In Pontacus’ edition of Eusebius’ Chronicle, 239; five Colbertine manuscripts likewise have 239, one of which has 43 instead of 42 above.] From the second year of Darius, under whom the Temple was rebuilt, 580 or 590 years. [Note: [Col. 0555D] In Pontacus’ edition of Eusebius’ Chronicle, 591; one Colbertine manuscript has the same. Four others have 590.] From the first construction of the Temple under Solomon to its final destruction under Vespasian, 1,103 years. [Note: [Col. 0555D] Three Colbertine manuscripts have 1,102.]

[Col. 0555D] During the seventh consulship of Vespasian and the sixth of Titus.

During the consulship of Commodus and Rufus.

[Col. 0556A] Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samos, Cilicia, Commagene—which had previously been free under kings and allied rulers—were reduced to provinces.

During the eighth consulship of Vespasian and the seventh of Titus.

During the ninth consulship of Vespasian and the eighth of Titus.

During the consulship of Silvanus and Verus.

During the consulship of Domitian and Messalinus.

During the second consulship of Domitian and Rufus.

Vespasian died at his own villa near the Sabines in the sixty-ninth year of his life. [Note: [Col. 0555D] A single Colbertine manuscript has sixty-four.]

Titus, the eighth, reigned three years and two months. [Note: [Col. 0555D] The manuscripts of the Eusebian chronicles assign Titus two years and two months; Pontacus, eight months.]

Titus, son of Vespasian, was highly eloquent in both languages and of such great goodness that, when one day at dinner he remembered that he had done nothing for anyone that day, he said: “Friends, today I have wasted a day.”

During the third consulship of Domitian and Sabinus.

During the fourth consulship of Domitian and the third of Rufus.

Titus built the Amphitheater at Rome and, at its dedication, killed 5,000 wild animals.

During the fifth consulship of Domitian and Dolabella.

Cletus was appointed the second bishop of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0555D] Four Colbertine manuscripts call this Roman pontiff Anacletus. The oldest of all, a single manuscript, calls him Cletus. Concerning him, see Pontacus’ note, pp. 584–585. See also the authors who argue against the view that a single person was designated under both names: Valesius, note on Eusebius, p. 49, column 1; Cotelerius, note on the Apostolic Constitutions, p. 300; Natalis Alexander, volume I, p. 515; and others.] and served twelve years.

Titus died of illness in the villa where his father had died, in the forty-second year of his life.

Domitian, the ninth, Titus’ younger brother, reigned fifteen years and five months.

During the sixth consulship of Domitian and the fourth of Rufus.

Domitian’s wife was called Augusta.

Domitian prohibited the making of eunuchs; he expelled mathematicians and philosophers from Rome.

707 During the consulship of Flavius and Trajan.

Domitian sent many senators into exile and celebrated triumphs over the Dacians and Germans.

During the second consulship of Trajan and Glabrio.

Quintilian, the rhetorician of Calagurris, was distinguished at Rome.

During the eighth consulship of Domitian and Saturninus.

During the consulship of Silvanus and Priscus.

[Col. 0556D] Domitian prohibited the planting of vines in cities. [Note: [Col. 0556D] Suetonius gives the reason for this edict throughout Italy and the provinces: Domitian believed that, because of excessive zeal for vineyards, the fields were being neglected. Hence Pontacus conjectures in his notes, p. 594, that instead of *in urbibus* (“in cities”), one should perhaps read *in orbe* (“throughout the world”), unless the expression is understood to mean “in the fields near cities.” Vineyards generally lie next to cities and inhabited places. Philostratus gives another reason in his *Life of Apollonius*: quarrels, fights, and killings arose from drunkenness.]

During the consulship of Asprenates and Clement.

[Col. 0557A] Apollonius of Tyana and the philosophers Euphrates were regarded as distinguished.

Domitian was so arrogant that he ordered golden and silver statues of himself to be erected in the Capitol.

During the ninth consulship of Domitian and Clement.

Many nobles were killed, and more were driven into exile.

During the consulship of Fulvius and Vetere.

During the second consulship of Nerva and Rufus.

During the consulship of Senecio and Palma.

THE SECOND PERSECUTION. After Nero, Domitian was the second to persecute the Christians. Under him the apostle John was exiled to the island of Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse, which Irenaeus interprets.

Domitian ordered that those who were of David’s lineage be killed, so that no remnant of the Jewish kingdom might remain.

**TRAJAN XI** reigned eighteen years and seven months [Note: In Eusebius, nineteen years and seven months; in some manuscripts [Col. 0558D], six months]. Trajan was made emperor in Agrippina in Gaul; he was born at Italica in Spain.

Four cities of Asia and two of Greece were destroyed by an earthquake.

[Col. 0558A] Trajan celebrated a triumph over the Dacians and Scythians.

**THE THIRD PERSECUTION.** When Trajan was conducting a persecution against the Christians, Simon, son of Clopas, who held the episcopate in Jerusalem, was crucified; Justus succeeded him.

Ignatius also, bishop of the Church of Antioch, was brought to Rome and handed over to the beasts. After him Eron was appointed the third bishop.

**UNDER CELSUS AND CRISPINUS.**

**UNDER ASTA AND PISO.**

Pliny the Younger, while governing a certain province and having killed very many Christians during his magistracy [Col. 0558C], was terrified by their multitude and asked Trajan what ought to be done. He reported that, apart from their obstinacy in refusing to sacrifice and their gatherings before dawn for singing to a certain Christ as God, nothing else was found among them. Moreover [Note: [Col. 0558D] Five Colbert manuscripts and the Chronicle of Eusebius read, “for establishing discipline”], they were said to prohibit murder, theft, adultery, brigandage, and similar offenses among their members. Moved by this, Trajan replied in a rescript that this class of people should not be sought out, but that those brought before the authorities ought to be punished.

**UNDER MESSALA AND PEDO.**

Alexander presided as the fifth bishop of the Roman Church for ten years.

**UNDER AEMILIANUS AND VETUS.**

**UNDER NIGRINUS AND APRONIANUS.**

[Col. 0558D] Pliny the Younger of Novocomum, a distinguished orator, perished while visiting the region near Vesuvius; and three cities of Galatia were destroyed by an earthquake.

After Justus, Zachaeus assumed the fourth episcopate of the Church of Jerusalem; after him came Tobias as the fifth, succeeded by Benjamin as the sixth, then John as the seventh, Matthias as the eighth, and, in Matthias’s place, Philip as the ninth.

**UNDER CLARUS AND ALEXANDER.**

**UNDER HADRIAN AND SALINATOR.**

[Col. 0559A] **UNDER HADRIAN II AND RUSTICUS.**

**UNDER SERVILIANUS AND FULVIUS.**

At this time the Jews who were in Libya and Egypt, and those at Cyrene and in the Thebaid, stirred up great rebellions against their neighbors.

When the Jews in Alexandria rebelled [Note: [Col. 0559D] In Eusebius, both in five Colbert manuscripts and in Pontacus’s edition, “of Mesopotamia” or “Mesopotamia”], the emperor Trajan ordered Lusius Quietus to drive them from the province. Quietus drew up his forces against them and killed countless thousands of them; for this reason the emperor appointed him governor of Judaea.

The Jews destroyed the city of Salamis in Cyprus.

Trajan died at Selinus, or, as others report, at Seleucia in Isauria, in the sixty-fourth year of his life [Note: [Col. 0559D] The printed edition of Eusebius’s Chronicle and two Colbert manuscripts have sixty-three; three manuscripts have seventy-three]. His bones were placed in a golden urn and set beneath a column in the Forum, and he alone of all the emperors was buried within [Col. 0559B] the City.

**HADRIAN XII** reigned twenty-one years. He was born at Italica in Spain and was the son of Trajan’s cousin.

**UNDER VERO AND AUCURINUS.**

**UNDER AVIOLA AND PANSA.**

The Senate enrolled Trajan among the gods, and Hadrian remitted the remaining taxes owed by the cities, publicly burning the tax records and making many of the cities free from those taxes themselves.

Hadrian captured the Jews when they rebelled against the Romans for the second time.

[Col. 0559C] Justus was ordained the fifth bishop of Alexandria.

The river Cephissus flooded Eleusis; Hadrian joined its banks with a bridge and spent the winter at Athens.

**710. UNDER VERO AND AMBIGUUS.**

**UNDER GALLICANUS AND TITIANUS.**

After Philip, Seneca was appointed the tenth bishop of Jerusalem; after him came Justus as the eleventh, Levi as the twelfth, Ephres as the thirteenth, Joseph as the fourteenth, and Judas as the fifteenth. All these bishops, until the destruction that Jerusalem suffered under Hadrian, had been from the circumcision.

Nicomedia collapsed in an earthquake, as did much of the city of Nicaea; Hadrian supplied public funds for their restoration.

The end of the first cycle and the beginning of the next.

Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and our philosopher Aristides published books composed in defense of the Christian religion.

Serenus Granius, a man of outstanding nobility, sent a letter to the emperor, saying that it was unjust for the blood of innocent people to be handed over to the outcries of the mob, and for people to be made guilty without any crime, solely on account of their name and sect. Moved by this, Hadrian wrote to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that Christians were not to be condemned without charges of crimes. A copy of this letter survives down to our own time.

**UNDER AUCURINUS AND SERGIANUS.**

**UNDER TIBERIUS AND SILANUS.**

Telesphorus was ordained the seventh bishop of Rome and served for eleven years.

Cornelius was placed over the fourth episcopate of the Church of Antioch.

**UNDER SERGIANUS II AND VERO.**

Eumenes presided as the sixth bishop of Alexandria.

**UNDER POMPEIANUS II AND COMMODUS.**

[Col. 0560B] **UNDER LAELIUS AND ALBINUS.**

The Jews took up arms and devastated Palestine, while Taenius Rufus governed the province; Hadrian sent him an army to suppress the rebels.

**UNDER CAMERINUS AND NIGER.**

Basilides, a heresiarch, lived in Alexandria; the Gnostics took their name from him. Basilides differed from Simon’s doctrine in this respect: he believed that there were 365 heavens, the number of days contained in a year. Hence he also commended as a kind of holy name the word **ABRAXAS**, because, according to Greek reckoning, the letters of this name add up to the same number. The Gnostics were so called from their presumption of superior knowledge; some call them Borborites, as though “filthy,” because of the extreme obscenity that they are said to practice in their mysteries. They hand down doctrines filled with the most fabulous inventions. They say that the substance of souls is the nature of God; and in their doctrine they are also said to hold that there is a good God and an evil God [711].

Barcochebas, the leader of the Jews, killed those who refused to provide him with assistance against the Roman army, employing every kind of torture. The Jewish war that was being waged in Palestine brought the affairs of the Jews to an end, when they had been completely crushed. From that time they were also deprived of permission to enter Jerusalem: first by the will of God, as the prophets foretold, and afterward by Roman prohibitions.

**UNDER ANTONINUS AND PRAESENS.**

At Jerusalem, Marcus was appointed the first bishop from the Gentiles [Col. 0560D], since those who had been from the Jews had ceased.

**UNDER ANTONINUS II AND PRAESENS II.**

**UNDER SEVERUS AND SILVANUS.**

Aelia was founded by Aelius Hadrianus. On the front of its gate, through which we leave for Bethlehem, a boar was carved in marble, signifying that the Jews were subject to Roman authority.

Hadrian died at Baiae when he was more than sixty years old.

**ANTONINUS TITUS**, surnamed **PIUS**, XIII, reigned with his sons Aurelius and Lucius for twenty-two years and three months [Note: Pontacus’s edition has twenty-three years and three months. One Colbert manuscript has twenty-three years; the others read as in our text].

[Col. 0561A] **UNDER RUFINUS AND TORQUATUS.**

Hyginus was ordained the eighth bishop of Rome and served for four years.

**UNDER TORQUATUS II AND HERODES.**

**UNDER AVIOLA AND MAXIMUS.**

Antoninus was called “Father of His Country.”

[Note: In other manuscripts, which Philippe Labbe states that he had before him, this passage is expressed as follows: “Valentinus the heresiarch and Cerdo, Marcion’s teacher, came to Rome. Valentinus said that there were two principles of the nature of things, Depth and Silence. From these arose thirty aeons. He called Depth the Father of Christ, who had a spiritual or heavenly body and had taken nothing from the nature of the Virgin mother, but had passed through her like a stream, without the reality of human flesh. They also deny the resurrection of the flesh and promise salvation only to the spirit or soul. Cerdo likewise asserted two principles, one good and the other evil, and denied that the God of the law and the prophets was the Father of Christ. He said that Christ was neither born from a woman nor possessed flesh, and that he neither truly suffered nor truly died. He also rejected the resurrection of the flesh and decreed that the Old Testament should be despised”] Valentinus the heresiarch and Cerdo, Marcion’s teacher, came to Rome. Valentinus fabricated many fables about the nature of things, asserting that there had been thirty aeons, that is, ages, whose beginning was Depth and Silence, and he also called Depth the Father. The Cerdonian doctrine, however, teaches two mutually opposed principles, and says that the lord of the law and the prophets is not the Father of Christ and is not a good God but a just one, whereas the Father of Christ is good. From these two, as though from a union, he says that Understanding [Col. 0561B] and Truth arose, and that they produced eight aeons. From Understanding and Will, he says, the Word arose, producing ten aeons. Further, from the Word and Life, he says, Man arose, and the Church produced twelve aeons. Thus eight, ten, and twelve make thirty aeons, having their beginning from Depth and Silence. Christ, sent by the Father—that is, by Depth—brought with him a spiritual or heavenly body. He took nothing from the Virgin Mary, but passed through her as through a stream or conduit, without taking any flesh from her. He also denies the resurrection of the flesh, asserting that through Christ only the spirit or soul receives salvation [712]. He says that Christ himself was neither born from a woman nor possessed flesh, and that he did not truly die or suffer anything, but merely pretended to suffer. Some say that in their two principles they thus speak of two gods, one of whom is good and the other evil. They deny the resurrection of the dead and despise the New Testament.

Marcion also, from whom the Marcionites were named, followed Cerdo’s doctrine, adding that there were not merely two principles but three: one good, another just, and a third evil. Although some believe that the author of the third principle was a certain Sirenus rather than Marcion.

**UNDER ANTONINUS III AND AURELIUS III.**

**IN THE THIRD CONSULSHIP OF ANTONINUS III AND AURELIUS III.**

After Marcus, Cassianus assumed the seventeenth episcopate of Jerusalem; Publius the eighteenth; Maximus the nineteenth; then Julianus the twentieth; next [Note: In Eusebius’s Chronicle, Gaianus] Grajanus the twenty-first; Symmachus the twenty-second; then Caius the twenty-third; Julianus the twenty-fourth; and after him Capito the twenty-fifth.

[Col. 0562C] Antoninus Pius died at Lorium, in his villa twelve miles from the City, in the seventy-second year of his life [Note: Pontacus’s edition, together with four Colbert manuscripts, has seventy-seven; another Colbert manuscript likewise has seventy-two] [elsewhere, seventy-seven].

**M. ANTONINUS**, also called **VERUS**, and **L. AURELIUS COMMODUS**, XIV, reigned nineteen years and one month.

**THE TWO AUGUSTI.**

These men were the first to administer the empire jointly with equal authority, whereas up to this time there had been only one Augustus at a time.

[Col. 0562D] **THE FOURTH PERSECUTION.** When persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Poeonius suffered martyrdom [Note: Eusebius has Pionius or Pyonius]; written accounts of their passions are also in circulation.

[Col. 0563A] In Gaul also very many were killed for the name of God; their contests, preserved in books, continue down to the present day.

**UNDER APRONIANUS AND PAULUS.**

**UNDER CETHEGUS AND CLARUS.**

The emperor Lucius died of apoplexy in the ninth year of his reign, or, as some think [Note: The manuscripts of Eusebius’s Chronicle have eleven], the tenth, between Concordia and Altinum.

[Col. 0563B] Melito, an Asiatic bishop, presented the emperor Antoninus with an Apology on behalf of the Christians.

Apollinaris of Hierapolis, an Asiatic bishop, is regarded as distinguished.

At the same time Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, was famous, as was Pinytus of Crete, a most eloquent man.

At this time the false prophecy called the Cataphrygian movement began, with Montanus as its author and Prisca and Maximilla as its mad prophetesses [Note: In the books of Eusebius’s Chronicle, Priscilla]. The name of the error was derived from the province of Phrygia, because its originators first appeared there and lived there, and even now have communities in those same regions. They assert that the coming of the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord had come upon themselves rather than upon the apostles. They regard second marriages as fornication; and therefore they say that the apostle Paul permitted them because he knew in part and prophesied in part, for “the perfect” had not yet come. They rave that this perfection came upon Montanus and his prophetesses. They are said to practice deadly sacrifices. For they are said to make what they call their Eucharist from the blood of a one-year-old child, which they extract from his entire body by means of tiny puncture wounds, mixing it with flour and making bread from it. If the child dies, he is regarded as a martyr; but if he lives, as a high priest.

[Col. 0564A] **UNDER SEVERUS AND HERENNIANUS.**

[Note: In other manuscripts examined by Philippe Labbe, this passage is fuller. “The heretic Tatian is recognized, from whom the Encratites took their name. They condemn marriage and define it as equivalent to fornication and every kind of depravity; they do not admit into their fellowship either a man or a woman bound by marriage. They follow certain emanations of the ages from the fables of Valentinus. They deny the salvation of the first man”] Tatian the heretic became known; from him the Eneratites took their name. Their doctrine is to admit into their communion only those who practice continence, and those who have renounced the world in such a way that they possess nothing of their own.

[Note: The following passage is found there in a more expansive form: “Bardesanes, the founder of another heresy, became known. Although Bardesanes had for some time been eminent in the faith, he afterward passed over into the errors of Valentinus, although he did not follow all of Valentinus’s teaching”] Bardesanes, too, the author of another error, became known at the same time; he fell partly into the heresy of Valentinus.

**UNDER ORPHITUS AND MAXIMUS.**

**UNDER SEVERUS AND POMPEIANUS.**

When the army of the emperor Antoninus was overcome by thirst in the region of the Quadi [Note: More is said about this rain, sent by divine power in response to the prayers of Christians, by Orosius, book VII, chapter 15; Eusebius, book V, chapter 5, who copied it almost word for word from Tertullian, *Apology*, chapters 5 and *To Scapula*; Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 12; Justin, in his *Apology*; the Deacon, book X; Dio, who attributes this rain to magical arts; and Capitolinus, who says that it was obtained by Antoninus’s prayers to God. Xiphilinus reports that the legion was therefore called **Κεραυνοβόλον**, that is, “thunderbolt-bearing” or “lightning-striking.” It is clear from the emperor’s own letters to the Senate that this occurred in the fourteenth year of Antoninus, in which he speaks of the great victory obtained through the prayers of Christians. These letters are found from the Vatican Library in Onuphrius, *Fasti*, p. 350; they identify Antoninus as holding tribunician power for the twenty-eighth time. Coins and ancient inscriptions, however, show that he held tribunician power for the fifteenth time in the year when he himself assumed the empire. This is Pontacus’s note], rain was sent by divine power; while, in contrast, lightning pursued the Germans and Sarmatians and killed very many of them. Letters of Marcus Aurelius, a most serious emperor, survive in which he attests that the thirst of the Germans was dispelled by rain granted through the prayers of Christian soldiers [Col. 0564B].

Some learned men think it is the place now called Petronilla in Austria, where the ruins and site of the camp are visible].

**HELVIUS PERTINAX XVI** reigned six months. Although he was more than seventy years old and was serving as prefect of the City, he was ordered by a decree of the Senate to assume the empire.

Victor assumed the thirteenth episcopate of Rome and served for twelve years; considerable works on religion by him are extant [Note: The negative particle is absent from the Eusebian manuscripts].

Pertinax refused when the Senate urged him to make his wife Augusta and his son Caesar, declaring that it was enough that he himself was ruling unwillingly.

Pertinax was killed in the palace through the crime of Julianus the jurist, whom Severus afterward killed at the Milvian Bridge.

**SEVERUS XVII** reigned eighteen years. He was born in the town of Leptis in the province of Tripolitania and was the only Roman emperor from Africa down to the present day. In honor of Pertinax, he ordered himself to be called Pertinax.

**UNDER SEVERUS III AND ANTONINUS.**

At this time there was a Jewish war and a Sarmatian war [Note: The books of Eusebius’s Chronicle, except for one Colbert manuscript, read “Samaritan” or “Samaritan war.” Pontacus comments: “The common reading, which is more genuine, is that in which it is called Samaritan,” and it is followed, besides other copies, by the *Contractor*, Vincentius, and Antoninus. As for the claim that Severus declared war on the Sarmatians, no one, so far as I know, has written it. A most learned man says that he has never found a Jewish war waged by Severus. Yet he could have noted it here]. Severus was called Parthicus, Arabicus, and Adiabenicus from the names of the peoples he subdued.

When a question arose among the bishops of Asia as to whether, according to the law of Moses, the Passover should be observed on the fourteenth day of the first month, Victor, bishop of Rome; Narcissus of Jerusalem; Polycrates; Irenaeus; Bachylus; and very many other pastors of the churches published in writing what had seemed probable to them. Their memory has survived down to us.

[Note: These words are added in our edition from the *Auctuarium* that Philippe Labbe appended to the Eusebian and Hieronymian Chronicle.] At this time Sabellius is said to have existed. [Col. 0567B] His error is that, in the divine Trinity, he asserts that the one whom he calls the Father is the same as the Son and the same as the Holy Spirit. Hence the perpetrators of this impiety are rightly also called Patripassians: by holding this view, they are convicted of asserting that the Father suffered the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he endured for the salvation of the human race.

At this time Origen seemed distinguished at Alexandria. [Note: The following material is found added to the passage in the *Auctuarium* of Philippe Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova.] He attempted, through his great eloquence, to establish certain perverse doctrines, composing books entitled **Περὶ Ἀρχῶν** (*On First Principles*), in which, besides many things opposed to sacred teaching, he also asserts [718] that the entire rational creation will undergo a change: not only the souls of the impious, but the devil himself as well, is to be restored through a long purification to the dignity of his origin, with successive cycles always passing from good to evil and from evil to good [Col. 0567D]. Since this alternation cannot fail to be perpetual, the wretched will in turn become blessed and the blessed wretched.

**UNDER GALLUS AND VOLUSIANUS.**

**UNDER VOLUSIANUS II AND MAXIMUS.**

Novatus, a presbyter of Cyprian, came to Rome and joined Novatian and the other confessors to himself, because Cornelius had received repentant apostates. From him the heresy of the Novatians took its origin. Because of the purity that they arrogate to themselves with extreme pride, they wish to be called Cathari, “the Pure.” They do not admit second marriages [Note: We have substituted the words “they do not admit; they deny reconciliation to penitents,” found in copies reproduced in the *Auctuarium*, volume I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, for the nearly similar wording previously read, “denying and not admitting penitents to repentance”], and they deny reconciliation to penitents.

Demetrianus was appointed the fourteenth bishop of Antioch [Note: He is numbered thirteenth in Pontacus’s edition and in one Colbert manuscript; in others he is called the fourteenth].

Lucius held the twenty-first episcopate of the Roman Church for eight months [Note: One Colbert manuscript has seven months]. After him, Stephanus became the twenty-second bishop and served for three years. Letters of Cyprian to both men are extant.

Gallus and Volusianus set out from Rome against Aemilianus, who was attempting a revolution in Moesia, and were killed at Interamna [Note: In Eusebius, “at the Forum of Flaminius,” or, as others think, at Interamna].

Aemilianus was killed in the third month after seizing the tyranny.

Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, and Asia were ravaged by the Goths. The Quadi and Sarmatians occupied the Pannonias. While the Germans held Spain, Tarraco was stormed. The Parthians, holding Mesopotamia, invaded Syria.

[Col. 0570B] Paul of Samosata departed from the preaching of all the others and revived the heresy of Artemon. This heresy asserts that Christ did not always exist, but proclaims that his beginning was when he was born from Mary, and regards him as nothing more than a man. Photinus was also an advocate of this error. Through his more vigorous zeal, he achieved the result that the followers of this impiety were called Photinians rather than Paulinians [Note: In the *Auctuarium* of volume I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, from manuscripts: “This heresy first belonged to Artemon, but through more effective cunning Paul of Samosata gained the leadership in it. Later, with the addition of the renegade Photinus, it happened that their disciples were more famously called Photinians than Paulinians. The Council of Nicaea decreed that these people were to be baptized in the Catholic Church. Hence it must be believed that they did not possess the rule of baptism”]. The Council of Nicaea decreed that these people were to be baptized in the Catholic Church. Hence it must be believed that they did not possess the rule of baptism.

Domnus was appointed the sixteenth bishop of Antioch in Paul’s place.

Claudius defeated the Goths while they were devastating Illyricum and Macedonia. For this reason a golden shield was placed for him in the Senate House, and a golden statue on the Capitoline.

Claudius dies at Sirmium; his brother is Quintillus.

[Note: [Col. 0570D] In the Chronicle of Eusebius, both in the printed edition and in the Colbertine manuscripts, the wording is different after this: “He dies at Sirmium. Quintillus, the brother of Claudius, [was made emperor] by the Senate,” etc.; nor is the word “Claudius” repeated.]

Claudius was proclaimed Augustus by the Senate, but on the seventeenth day of his reign he was killed at Aquileia.

AURELIAN, XXIX, reigns five years and six months.

VALERIAN AND BASSUS.

At Antioch, Timaeus is appointed the seventeenth bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0570D] Three manuscripts read “Timotheus”; another, “Timotheus or Timaeus”; another, “Timaeus,” as does Pontacus’s edition.]

Aurelian recovered the Gallic provinces after Tetricus betrayed his army at Châlons.

[Col. 0570D] QUIETUS AND VOLDUMIANUS.

Zenobia is defeated at Immae, not far from Antioch. After her husband Odaenathus had been killed, she had held the empire of the East. In this battle the commander Pompeianus, surnamed Francus, fought against her with the greatest courage.

[Note: [Col. 0570D] Four Colbertine manuscripts read “Timas.” Then, instead of “Odaenathus,” all the manuscripts of Eusebius have “Odenathus,” or “Denathus.”]

TACITUS AND PLACIDIANUS.

Eusebius, bishop of Laodicea, is held in distinction.

Aurelian, celebrating a triumph at Rome, was preceded by Tetricus and Zenobia. Tetricus later became Corrector of Lucania, while Zenobia grew old in the city in the highest honor; from her, even today, the Zenobia family at Rome takes its name.

AURELIAN AND CAPITOLINUS.

At Rome, FELIX assumes the episcopate as the twenty-fifth bishop and holds it for five years.

AURELIAN II AND MARCELLUS.

When Aurelian had begun a persecution against us, lightning fell beside him and his companions; and not long afterward he was killed on the old road between Constantinople and Heraclea, at Coenophrurium.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] Xilander, the translator of Cedrenus, says that the place was called “New Fortress” in their language. Pontacus, in his notes, p. 658.]

TACITUS, XXX, reigns six months. After he was killed in Pontus, FLORIAN, XXXI, secured the empire and reigned for eighty-eight days.

After Florian was killed at Tarsus, PROBUS, XXXII, reigns six years and eight months, or, according to another reckoning, four.

PROBUS AND PAULINUS.

Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, learned in the disciplines of the philosophers, is celebrated in extensive writings.

The insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose, having as its founder a certain Persian called Manes. It would take too long in this work to explain their impieties, sacrileges, and indecencies. It is enough to know that they assert two principles opposed to one another and coeternal, and two natures, namely, that of good and that of evil. They have no true understanding of Christ. They say that his birth from Mary according to the flesh, his passion, and his resurrection were mere appearances and were not accomplished as they are proclaimed. They reject the Old Testament and the Prophets, and suppose that the author of those Scriptures was not the good God but the ruler of an evil nature. From the New Testament they accept those things which they think agree with the apocrypha. They deny the resurrection of the flesh, condemn marriage, regard adulterous intercourse as lawful, and believe that the baptism of regeneration contributes nothing. Their sacred rites are as abominable as their morals.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] In the Appendix to volume I of Labbe’s New Manuscript Library: “Among the Manichaeans, a certain Manes was the author of a most deranged doctrine. Among them two principles are proclaimed, namely, the good and the evil; their natures have always existed opposed to one another and coeternally. From their conflict they have fabricated monstrous tales and empty falsehoods, promising their disciples purification through sacrilegious rites, in which there is nothing except the accursed filth of an obscene alliance. They do not accept the Old Testament, corrupting the evangelical truth in every respect.” [Col. 0572D]]

At Alexandria, Theonas presided as the fifteenth bishop.

Probus is killed by a military uprising at Sirmium, in the tower called Ferrata.

CARUS, with his sons CARINUS and NUMERIAN, XXXIII, reigned for two years.

CARUS AND CARINUS.

CARUS II AND NUMERIAN.

Carus of Narbonne, after laying waste the entire region of the Parthians and capturing Cocha and Ctesiphon, their most renowned cities, died after being struck by lightning while he had pitched his camp above the Tigris. Numerian, while being carried in a litter because of an eye ailment, was killed by the treachery of his father-in-law Aper. Carinus, for his part, was defeated in battle near the Margus and perished.

DIOCLETIAN, XXXIV, reigned twenty years.

DIOCLETIAN AND ARISTOBULUS.

MAXIMUS AND AQUILINUS.

Diocletian takes HERCULIUS MAXIMIAN into partnership in the government. After crushing the mass of peasants who had given their revolt the name of the Bacaudae, he restored peace to Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0572D] Three Colbertine manuscripts read “Bagaudae.”]

Carausius assumed the purple and seized Britain.

DIOCLETIAN II AND MAXIMIAN.

MAXIMIAN II AND JANUARIUS.

Constantius and Galerius Maximian are admitted to the government.
