To unite them also by marriage alliance, Diocletian gave Constantius Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculius, as wife, while he gave Galerius his own daughter Valeria. To strengthen these marriages, he compelled both men to divorce the wives they had previously had.

BASSUS AND QUINTIANUS.

DIOCLETIAN III AND MAXIMIAN III.

TIBERIANUS AND DIO.

HANNIBALIANUS AND ASCLEPIODOTUS.

DIOCLETIAN IV AND MAXIMIAN III.

Diocletian was the first to order that he be worshiped as a god and that gems be set into his clothing and footwear. Before him, emperors were greeted in the manner of judges and differed from private dress only by a purple cloak.

[Note: [Col. 0572D] In Eusebius’s Chronicle, both in the printed edition and in five Colbertine manuscripts, the word is “were saluted.”]

CONSTANTIUS AND MAXIMUS.

TUSCUS AND ANULINUS.

At Rome, MARCELLINUS assumes the episcopate as the twenty-eighth bishop and holds it for nine years.

[Note: [Col. 0572D] One of the Colbertine manuscripts reads “Marcellianus.” Nevertheless, the other reading is more generally accepted, as Pontacus observes in his notes on Eusebius’s Chronicle, where he immediately adds: “It is surprising that Eusebius passes over Marcellus, when he speaks of only one Marcellinus; but perhaps he was deceived by the similarity of the names. Nevertheless, from Augustine, Letter 165 (now 53), Optatus, book II, the martyrologies, and all the historians, it is clear that Marcellinus and Marcellus were two different men. I will not conceal, however, that the Lodun manuscript reads as follows under Diocletian’s twelfth year: ‘Marcellianus assumed the episcopate of the Roman Church for eight years; Marcellus, for three years.’ In other manuscripts only the name Marcellinus or Marcellianus is given, and nine years are assigned to him. If you wish to place this Marcellinus’s elevation to the ecclesiastical office in Diocletian’s ninth year, you may cite O., Vi., and Mar.; if in the tenth year, Fa. and the printed editions; if in the eleventh, Pi.; and finally, if in the twelfth, Fux., Peta., and Lo. (these are the manuscripts which he had before him); I follow the latter. For in this way the fifteen years of the preceding pontiff Caius or Gaius will be more easily established, as well as the nine years which must be placed between him and Eusebius, his successor. Moreover, you will depart less from the eminent men Baronius and Onuphrius, who date the beginning of that see from Diocletian’s thirteenth year.” [Col. 0573D]]

DIOCLETIAN V AND CONSTANTIUS II.

At Jerusalem, Zabdas is ordained the thirty-seventh bishop.

MAXIMIAN IV AND MAXIMINIAN II.

FAUSTUS AND GALLUS.

Veturius, commander of the army, persecutes the Christians.

End of the third cycle and beginning of the fourth.

DIOCLETIAN VI AND MAXIMIAN V.

CONSTANTIUS III AND MAXIMIAN III.

The Baths of Diocletian are built at Rome, and the Baths of Maximian at Carthage.

At Jerusalem, Hermon presided as the thirty-eighth bishop.

At Antioch, Tyrannus is appointed the nineteenth bishop.

In the Alexandrian church, after Theonas, Peter is ordained the sixteenth bishop; he later suffered martyrdom gloriously in the ninth year of the persecution.

TITIANUS AND NEPOTIANUS.

CONSTANTIUS IV AND MAXIMIAN IV.

The Augusti Diocletian and Maximian celebrated a triumph at Rome with great pomp. Their chariot was preceded by Narseus’s wife, his sisters, his children, and all the booty with which they had despoiled the Parthians.

DIOCLETIAN VII AND MAXIMIAN VI.

NINTH PERSECUTION. In Diocletian’s nineteenth year, in the month of March, during the days of Easter, the churches were overthrown.

DIOCLETIAN VIII AND MAXIMIAN VII.

In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down the purple.

GALERIUS, XXXV, held the empire alone for two years, and afterward jointly with another for six years.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] These words are absent from the manuscripts of the Eusebian Chronicle except for one Colbertine manuscript, which after this adds: “Galerius alone held the empire as Augustus for two years,” and soon afterward assigns him sixteen years. See Pontacus’s note above, volume XXVII, column 1115.]

CONSTANTIUS V AND MAXIMIAN V.

At Rome, EUSEBIUS is appointed the twenty-ninth bishop. After his seventh month, MELCHIADES holds the Church as the thirtieth bishop for three years.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] One Colbertine manuscript reads “four years”; another, together with Pontacus’s edition, “six years”; three others, “three years.”]

CONSTANTIUS VI AND MAXIMIAN VI.

During these consulships, Timothy suffered for Christ at Rome on the tenth day before the Kalends of July. Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by Galerius Maximian.

Constantius died in the sixteenth year of his reign in Britain, at Eboracum. After him, his son CONSTANTINE, born from the concubine Helena, seized the kingdom. At the beginning of his reign, the fourth year of the persecution was already under way.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] This word does not indicate that Helena was not the wife of Constantius Chlorus. Such a woman was otherwise called a concubine, whether she lacked a dowry or other insignia belonging to the mothers of families. Therefore, even if Helena was not of that rank, and although she was joined according to the laws to a husband descended from the imperial line of Vespasian and related by blood to the emperor Claudius II, it is nevertheless clear from ancient coins that she was united to Constantius Chlorus by a legitimate marriage bond—whatever certain rivals of Constantine’s glory, or even certain holy Fathers deceived by the rumors spread by slanderers, may appear to have asserted to the contrary.]

CONSTANTINE, XXXVI, reigned thirty years and ten months.

DIOCLETIAN IX AND CONSTANTINE.

Maxentius, the son of Herculius Maximian, is proclaimed Augustus at Rome by the praetorian soldiers.

Severus Caesar, sent by Galerius Maximian against Maxentius at Ravenna, is killed in the second year of his reign.

DIOCLETIAN X AND MAXIMIAN VII.

LICINIUS is made emperor by Galerius at Carnuntum.

Herculius Maximian, exposed by his daughter Fausta because he was plotting against Constantine, her husband, flees and is killed at Massilia.

AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF THE TENTH AND EIGHTH [CONSULS].

Quirinus, bishop of Siscia, is gloriously killed with his companions for Christ.

ALSO, IN THE SECOND YEAR AFTER THE TENTH AND EIGHTH CONSULSHIPS.

Galerius Maximian dies in the twenty-first year of his reign, part of which he spent as Caesar and part as Augustus.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] One Colbertine manuscript gives twenty years. The same manuscript assigns twenty-one years to the pontificate of Sylvester, whereas the others count twenty-two.]

At Rome, SILVESTER is ordained the thirty-first bishop and serves for twenty-two years.

MAXIMIAN VIII AND LICINIUS.

Maximinus, after persecuting the Christians and when he was already about to be punished by Licinius, dies at Tarsus in the sixth year of his reign.

CONSTANTINE II AND LICINIUS II.

CONSTANTINE III AND LICINIUS III.

At Alexandria, Achillas is ordained the seventeenth bishop.

Maxentius is defeated and killed by Constantine near the Milvian Bridge.

VOLUSIANUS AND ANIANUS.

At Jerusalem, Macharius is appointed the thirty-ninth bishop.

CONSTANTINE IV AND LICINIUS IV.

Peace was restored to us by Constantine.

Diocletian dies not far from Salona, at his villa in Spalatum.

SABINUS AND RUFINUS.

Crispus and Constantine, the sons of Constantine, and the young Licinius, son of Licinius Augustus by Constantine’s sister, are called Caesars. Lactantius educated Crispus; he was the most eloquent man of his time, but so poor in this life that he often lacked even the necessities.

GALLICANUS AND BASSUS.

LICINIUS V AND CRISPUS.

CONSTANTINE V AND LICINIUS CAESAR.

Licinius expels the Christians from his palace.

CONSTANTINE VI AND CONSTANTINE CAESAR.

Basileus, bishop of Amasea in Pontus, is crowned with martyrdom under Licinius.

At Alexandria, Alexander is ordained the eighteenth bishop.

CRISPUS II AND CONSTANTIUS II.

Arius, a presbyter expelled from the Alexandrian Church by Bishop Alexander, associates many with his impiety, preaching that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not of one and the same nature, or, more precisely, essence, since the Son is a creature; and that the Holy Spirit is a creature of a creature, that is, created by the Son himself. To refute this perfidy, a synod of 318 bishops assembled at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, overthrew all the devices of the heretics by its opposition to the *Homoousion*—the doctrine of consubstantiality.

[Note: [Col. 0575D] In the Appendix to volume I of Labbe’s New Manuscript Library: “Arius denied that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were of one nature—or, to speak more precisely, essence—so that the Son was regarded as inferior to the Father, and the Holy Spirit as even inferior to the Son. The rest is as above.”]

PROBIANUS AND JULIANUS.

SEVERUS AND RUFINUS.

Constantius, the son of Constantine, is made Caesar.

CRISPUS III AND CONSTANTINE III.

Licinius is killed at Thessalonica.

PAULINUS AND JULIANUS.

Crispus, the son of Constantine, and the younger Licinius, the son of Constantia, Constantine’s sister, and of the elder Licinius, are killed.

CONSTANTINE VII AND CONSTANTIUS.

Constantine’s twentieth-anniversary celebrations were held at Nicomedia and, in the following year, at Rome.

CONSTANTINE II AND MAXIMUS.

Thus far Eusebius, companion of the martyr Pamphilus, carried the history. After this, the authority of the presbyter Jerome takes over.

Constantine restored Drepanum, a city of Bithynia, in honor of the martyr Lucian, who was buried there, and named it Helenopolis after his mother.

JANUARIUS AND JUSTUS.

[Note: [Col. 0575D] 726. Appendix to volume I of Labbe’s New Manuscript Library: “Donatus is recognized as the one from whom the Donatists in Africa derive their name. Because of Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, since he had been ordained against their wishes, they divided into a schism, with Donatus as leader and author, bringing accusations against Caecilian—none of which they proved. Through their obstinacy they thereby also became heretics: they rebaptized those baptized in the Catholic Church, and, although they confessed one substance in the Trinity of the Godhead, they believed that the Son was not equal to the Father and that the Holy Spirit was inferior to the Son. Another Donatus, said to have been the third after him, is reported to have driven them into this impiety.”]

Donatus is recognized as the source of the Donatists in Africa. They first created a schism because Caecilian had been ordained bishop of the Church of Carthage against their will, bringing against him accusations that were not proved, especially the claim that he had been ordained by traditors—those who had handed over the divine Scriptures. But after the case had been investigated and settled, they passed through stubborn dissension into heresy. They declared that, because of Caecilian’s crimes—whether true or, as became more evident, false—the Church of Christ throughout the entire world had been extinguished by the contagion of communion and survived only in Donatus’s party. They even dared to rebaptize Catholics, although the Catholic Church had decided not to invalidate the common baptism even among heretics.

At Antioch, after Tyrannus, Vitalis is ordained the twentieth bishop; after him, Philogonus the twenty-first; his successor was Paulinus, the twenty-second; after him came Eustathius, the twenty-third. After Eustathius was driven into exile for the faith, the Arians held the Church down to the present day.

[Note: [Col. 0576D] Some manuscripts of Eusebius’s Chronicle read “Philogonius.”]

CONSTANTINE VIII AND CONSTANTINE CAESAR IV.

CONSTANTIUS III AND SYMMACHUS.

At Alexandria, Athanasius is ordained the nineteenth bishop.

BASSUS AND ABLABIUS.

Jerome is born.

PACATIANUS AND HILARIANUS.

At Rome, MARCUS is ordained the thirty-second bishop and serves for eight months.

After him, JULIUS is ordained the thirty-third bishop and serves for sixteen years and four months.

By Constantine’s edict, the temples of the Gentiles were overthrown.

The Romans defeated the Goths in the region of the Sarmatians.

Constans, the son of Constantine, is advanced to the government.

DALMATIUS AND XENOPHILUS.

OPTATUS AND PAULINUS.

CONSTANTIUS AND ALBINUS.

Constantine sends an honorably worded letter to Antony the monk together with his sons.

NEPOTIANUS AND FACUNDUS.

At Constantine’s thirtieth anniversary, Dalmatius is called Caesar.

Eunomia, the Christian virgin and daughter of Nazarius the rhetorician, equals her father in eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 0576D] In the most ancient Colbertine manuscript and in Pontacus’s edition, he is called “Eustathius.”]

Eustachius, a presbyter of Constantinople, becomes well known. Through his efforts, a *martyrium* was built at Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0576D] Understand “temple.” Why this temple, constructed in honor of the Savior’s most glorious tomb from among the five buildings that Constantine himself ordered to be erected at Jerusalem, was called the *Martyrium* is explained by Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 14: it was a testimony and memorial of Christ’s resurrection. It is called the Constantinian basilica in action 4 of the Second Council of Nicaea. Pontacus, in his notes on Eusebius’s Chronicle.]

[Note: [Col. 0576D] 727. The first part of this entry—that Constantine was baptized at the end of his life—is confirmed by the testimony of Socrates, book I, chapter 39; Sozomen, book II, chapter 34; Theodoret, book I, chapter 31; Freculf, book III, chapter 20; Marianus; and Eusebius, book IV of *The Life of Constantine*, chapters 24, 61, and 62; and afterward by Ambrose in his *Oration on the Death of Theodosius*. As for the second part, namely, that Constantine inclined toward the Arian doctrine, only Lucifer among the ancients seems to hold this view, in book I of *On the Apostolic Rule*. Perhaps he took the occasion for suspicion from the fact that Constantine sent Catholic bishops, such as Athanasius and others, into exile near the end of his life. But this action did not arise from corrupted faith; rather, he himself had been deceived by the devices and deceptions of the Eusebians, who, although they pretended to be Catholics, secretly favored the Arians. He believed that in this way Athanasius would be freed from the cruelty of those who were plotting against him, as Athanasius says in his letter to those living the solitary life. There he not only excuses Constantine for his exile but also defends him against this stain of heresy. Epiphanius does the same, *Heresy* 69; Hilary, book I *To Constantius*; and Theodoret, book II of the *History*, chapter 5. Add to this that sacred antiquity venerated Constantine as orthodox, and the Greek Church commemorates his memory on 21 May. These are a few of the many points discussed by the illustrious Pontacus in his notes. To support the reading of one manuscript, he adds some further remarks; that manuscript refers the entire sentence to Constantius. Finally, although he admits that it is difficult to see how Jerome could have understood this of Constantius, since all the books refer such statements to Constantine’s thirty-first year and in no way to the time of Constantius, he suspects that the Arians, from the beginning of the publication of the Chronicle, transferred to Constantine’s final year what had been said about Constantius. From all this he concludes that Baronius, after careful and mature judgment, excluded this paragraph in volume III of the *Annals*, p. 210, as spurious, inserted by another hand, and rejected and condemned by the consent and continuous practice of the whole Church. Nevertheless, because of the authority of both the manuscripts and the printed editions, he did not alter it.]

At the end of his life Constantine was baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and inclined toward the Arian doctrine.

FELICIANUS AND TITIANUS.

When Constantine was preparing for war against the Persians, he died at a public villa at Ancyrona near Nicomedia, in the sixty-sixth year of his life. After him, his three sons, formerly Caesars, were called Augusti.

CONSTANTINE, CONSTANTIUS, and CONSTANS, XXXVII, reigned twenty-four years, five months, and twelve days.

URSO AND POLEMius.

Dalmatius Caesar, whom his uncle Constantine had left as a partner in government together with his sons, was killed through the faction of his cousin Constantius.

James of Nisibis becomes known; at his prayers the city was often delivered from danger when it was being besieged by Shapur, king of the Persians.

CONSTANTIUS II AND CONSTANS.

From this time, the Arian impiety of the emperor Constantius, supported by his protection, persecuted first Athanasius and then all bishops who did not belong to his party through exiles, imprisonments, and various forms of affliction.

[Note: [Col. 0578C] One Colbertine manuscript reads “the impiety of Constantine.” All the others, together with Pontacus’s edition, read “of Constantius.”]

ACYNDINUS AND PROCULUS.

Constantine, making war against his brother, is killed near Aquileia, at the river Alsa, in the twenty-third year of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 0578C] We emend “Asia” to “Alsa” on the basis of five Colbertine manuscripts and Pontacus’s edition of Eusebius’s Chronicle. Aurelius’s *Epitome* establishes that Constantine was thrown into a river called Alsa, not far from Aquileia; and Rufinus, book I, chapter 15, says that Constantine was killed by soldiers near Aquileia at the river Alsa. In this sense Eusebius calls Aquileia “of Alsa,” that is, lying beside the river Alsa, as Pliny attests in book III, chapter 18. Pontacus, in his notes on Eusebius’s Chronicle.]

MARCELLINUS AND PROBINUS.

Audaeus becomes known in Syria; from him came the Audaean heresy and the Audaeans, whom they also call Anthropomorphites, because they believe that God is formed in the likeness of a human being. They are also criticized because they are said to celebrate the Christian Passover according to Jewish observance.

[Note: [Col. 0578D] In the Appendix to volume I of Labbe’s New Manuscript Library: “The Audaeans were named after a certain Audaeus,” etc., as above.]

CONSTANTIUS III AND CONSTANS II.

At Constantinople, Hermogenes, commander of the army, is dragged by the people because of Bishop Paul, whom he was expelling by the emperor’s command and through the faction of the Arians.

[Note: [Col. 0578D] The sense of these words is not that he was brought to Constantinople, but that, when the people attacked him, they dragged the captured and murdered man by a rope. So Socrates says in book I, chapter 13. Pontacus, in his notes.]

MACEDONIUS, an artisan in featherwork, is installed by the Arians as bishop in Paul’s place. From him came the Macedonian heresy, whose doctrine is to confess that the Father and the Son are of one divinity and the same substance, but to say that the Holy Spirit is a creature.

[Note: [Col. 0578D] Appendix of Labbe: “Macedonius was the author of the error of the Macedonians, whom the Greeks call Pneumatomachi, because they resist confessing the Holy Spirit as God. For they think rightly about the Father and the Son, that they are of one and the same substance; but they do not wish to believe this about the Holy Spirit, saying that he is a creature. Some call them Semi-Arians, because in this question they agree partly with the Arians and partly with us.”]

Paul is strangled through the cruelty of the prefect Philip—for he was a supporter of Macedonius’s party—and through the plots of the Arians.

PLACIDUS AND ROMULUS.

Maximinus was held in distinction as bishop of Trier. When Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, was being sought by Constantius for punishment, Maximinus received him honorably.

LEONTIUS AND SALUSTIUS.

Shapur, king of the Persians, persecutes the Christians.

CONSTANTIUS IV AND CONSTANS III.

In response to Constans’s letters, Athanasius returns to Alexandria.

AMANTIUS AND ALBINUS.

AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF AMANTIUS AND ALBINUS.

RUFINUS AND EUSEBIUS.

Maximus, the fortieth bishop of Jerusalem after Macarius, dies. After him, the Arians invade the Church.

PHILIPPUS AND SALIA.

LIBERIUS is ordained the thirty-fourth bishop of the Roman Church. When he was driven into exile for the faith in the ninth year of his episcopate, all the clergy swore that they would accept no other bishop. But when Felix had been substituted in the priesthood by the Arians, many perjured themselves; and when Liberius returned to the city after a year, they were expelled together with Felix.

LIMENIUS AND CATULINUS.

When Magnentius seized power at Augustodunum, Constans was killed not far from Spain, at a fort called Helena. Because the state was thereby thrown into confusion, Vetranio at Mursa and Nepotianus at Rome were made emperors.

SERGIUS AND NIGRIANUS.

Nepotianus’s head was carried through the city on a spear.

After Vetranio had been stripped of the royal insignia at Naissus by Constantius, Magnentius was decisively defeated at Mursa, with great disaster to the state.

AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF SERGIUS AND NIGRIANUS.

Gallus, also called Constantius, the cousin of Constantius, was made Caesar.

CONSTANTIUS V AND CONSTANTIUS CAESAR.

CONSTANTIUS VI AND CONSTANTIUS CAESAR II.

CONSTANTIUS VII AND CONSTANTIUS CAESAR III.

Magnentius killed himself with his own hand in the palace at Lyon, and his brother Decentius, whom he had sent as Caesar to hold Gaul, ended his life by hanging at Sens.

Gallus Caesar, summoned by his cousin Constantius, toward whom he had aroused suspicion because of his royal character, was killed in Istria.

[Note: [Col. 0579D] Pontacus’s edition and two Colbertine manuscripts read “because of his excellent character.” When it says above that he was “summoned by Constantius,” this means that Constantius drew Gallus to himself by various devices and finally arranged for his death, as Ammianus, Zosimus, Victor, Socrates, and others attest. Pontacus.]

Paulinus and Rhodonus, bishops of Gaul, were driven into exile for the faith.

Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli; Lucifer, of the Church of Cagliari; Dionysius, bishop of the Church of Milan; Pancratius, a Roman presbyter; and Hilary, a deacon, although separated from one another by distance, were condemned to exile by the Arians and Constantius.

ARBETIANUS AND LOLLIANUS.

Julian, the brother of Gallus, is proclaimed Caesar at Milan.

CONSTANTIUS VIII AND JULIAN CAESAR.

Antony the monk dies in the desert at the age of one hundred. He was accustomed to recount to the many who came to him a great deal about a certain Paul of Thebes, a man of extraordinary blessedness.

[Note: [Col. 0580D] Jerome’s Chronicle says “in his one hundred and fifth year.”]

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, driven into Phrygia by the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, and the other Arians who were with him, composed books about our religion.

The relics of Timothy the apostle are brought to Constantinople.

Sarmata, Amathas, and Macarius, disciples of Antony, are held in distinction.

Bishop Liberius of Rome is sent into exile.

CONSTANTIUS IX AND JULIAN CAESAR II.

The bones of the apostle Andrew and of Luke the evangelist are brought to Constantinople.

Paulinus, bishop of Trier, dies in exile in Phrygia.

DATIANUS AND CEREALIS.

A synod was held at Ariminum and Seleucia in Isauria. In it, the ancient faith of the Fathers was first condemned by the betrayal of the ten legates and afterward by that of all the others.

[Note: The printed column reference is [Col. 0580A]; the page marker “730” follows in the supplied text.]

EUSEBIUS AND HYPATIUS.

Gratian, who later became emperor, is born.

When Bishop Hilary had presented a book in his defense to Constantius at Constantinople, he returned to Gaul.

Almost all the churches throughout the world were polluted by association with the Arians under the name of peace and the emperor.

Through Hilary, Gaul condemns the deceitfulness of the Ariminian perfidy.

CONSTANTIUS X AND JULIAN III.

Constantius dies at Mopsucrenae, between Cilicia and Cappadocia.

JULIAN, XXXVIII, reigns two years and eight months.

[Note: [Col. 0580D] The manuscripts of Jerome’s Chronicle assign to him one year and eight months of reign, some one year and seven months.]

After Julian turned to the worship of idols, there was a mild persecution, enticing rather than forcing people to sacrifice. In it, many of our people fell of their own accord.

TAURUS AND FLORENTIUS.

After Georgius, who had been appointed in Athanasius’s place by the Arians, was burned by a popular uprising, Athanasius returned.

The bishops Eusebius and Lucifer return from exile. Lucifer, together with two other confessors, appoints Paulinus, a presbyter of Bishop Eustathius who had never defiled himself with the communion of heretics, as bishop of Antioch on the Catholic side.

The Athenian sophist Prohaeresius, when a law was issued forbidding Christians to be teachers of the liberal disciplines, voluntarily left his school, although Julian had expressly granted him permission to teach Christians.

MAMERTINUS AND NEVITTA.

Aemilianus is burned by the Vicar at Dorostorum because of the destruction of altars.

JULIAN III AND SALUSTIUS.

The churches of Antioch were closed, and the most serious storm of the impending persecution was calmed by God’s will. For Julian, having set out against the Persians, had vowed our blood to his gods after victory. He was led into the desert by a certain false deserter and, after losing a large part of his army through hunger and thirst, was killed.

JOVIAN, XXXIX, reigns six months, or, according to another reckoning, eight.

JOVIAN AND VARRONIANUS.

A synod was held at Antioch by Meletius and his supporters. Rejecting the *Homoousion* and the *Anomoean* doctrine, they vindicated the Macedonian doctrine, the middle position between these two, the *Homoiousion*.

[Note: [Col. 0581C] On this synod of Meletius and the mind of Saint Jerome here in the Chronicle, one may consult the learned men who have written about this difficulty and, meanwhile, the note of the illustrious bishop of Vasio on this passage of Jerome’s Chronicle in our volume XXVII. There he says much about restoring this text and adds several remarks about Meletius’s synod: some condemned it, while others considered it approved; among the latter he counts Saint Basil and most of the Fathers. Among them Meletius is repeatedly praised. Basil, in *Against the Arians*, book I, calls him “the Great,” as does Nicephorus the Confessor. Gregory of Nyssa, in his *Oration on the Funeral of Meletius*, and Theodoret, book II, chapter 31, call him divine and great. Even today he is venerated as a saint by the Greeks, and his feast is celebrated on the third day before the Ides of February. But since the issue concerns not so much the matter itself as Jerome’s mind and judgment, the following is clear from the manuscripts of this Chronicle and from his other books, in which he counts Meletius among the enemies of Christ. Nevertheless, the aforementioned commentator on Jerome’s Chronicle concludes that Meletius can still be defended or excused in various ways, so that one should not believe that what he did in this synod was done in a heretical spirit—especially since he was a most holy man and afterward was driven into exile for the faith a third time by Valens, as Sozomen says in book VI, chapter 7. [Col. 0581D]]

Jovian dies from indigestion, or from the smell of burning coals.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] The manuscripts of Jerome’s Chronicle add: “which he had ordered to be burned in excessive quantities.”]

After him, VALENTINIAN, a tribune of the imperial guard, is proclaimed Augustus at Nicaea and takes his brother Valens into partnership in the government at Constantinople.

VALENTINIAN and VALENS, XL, reigned fourteen years and five months.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] A Colbertine manuscript of older character gives thirty-four years, while the others, together with Pontacus’s edition, give thirteen, with the same number of months noted above.]

VALENTINIAN AND VALENS.

GRATIAN AND DAGALAIPHUS.

Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, composed writings on many aspects of our religion. Later he deviated from the Catholic faith and founded the heresy called by his name. Its error is that it asserts that Jesus assumed flesh alone, without a soul, or merely a vital soul and not a rational one, since the Word himself had supplied the power of the mind; and that the flesh was not assumed from Mary, but that something belonging to the Word had been changed into flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0582C] In the Appendix to volume I of Labbe’s New Manuscript Library: “Apollinaris’s perversity first went astray in this error: he said that the Lord Jesus Christ assumed human flesh without a soul, because the Godhead itself supplied life and direction to the body. After being refuted on this point, he confessed that the flesh did not lack a soul, but that the functions of the mind were completed by the power of the Word. Finally, he said that Christ’s flesh itself was a certain part of the Word, possessing the divine nature and not the maternal one.”]

Procopius, who had seized tyrannical power at Constantinople, was killed in Phrygia Salutaris, while many of his supporters were slain and proscribed.

At Rome, DAMASUS is ordained the thirty-fifth bishop and serves for eighteen years.

At this time there was a second schism, under the antipope Ursicinus. After he was expelled by a synod assembled at Rome, the schism lasted six months, in the year of the Lord 369.

[Note: This is taken from the margin of the book.]

Valens, baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, persecutes our people.

LUPICINUS AND JOVINUS.

Gratian, the son of Valentinian, is made emperor at Amiens.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, dies.

VALENTINIAN II AND VALENS II.

VALENTINIAN, N. P., AND VICTOR.

VALENTINIAN III AND VALENS III.

Athanaric, king of the Goths, begins a persecution against the Christians, kills very many, and drives them from their own homes into Roman territory.

Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, dies.

At Constantinople, the *martyrium* of the apostles is dedicated.

Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, dies. Along with Gregory, bishop of the Spaniards, and Philo of Libya, he never mingled with the Arian depravity. [Note: The illustrious commentator on the Vasatian Chronicle, explaining this passage of Jerome, says: “He means that they abstained from communion not only with the Arians, but also with those—whether bishops or others—who communicated with Arians, however penitent they might be; not that these alone, among all the bishops, were free from the Arian heresy. For in the West, apart from Auxentius, bishop of Milan, there were very few adherents of that impiety. Hence Basil, in Letter 70, which he addressed to the bishops of Italy and Gaul, says: ‘For this evil of heresy consumes everything, and there is danger that, once our churches have been devastated, it may spread to the sound part of the region you inhabit.’ Indeed, even in the East the greater part were Catholics, as Basil testifies in Letter 72: ‘Stand firm in the faith; look upon the whole world and see how small is the portion afflicted by this disease, while the entire remaining Church, which has received the Gospel from the ends of the earth to the ends of the earth, follows this sound and upright doctrine. We ask you not to fall away from communion with it.’”] But while he did not relax the rigor of justice toward the correction of those who had withdrawn, he himself withdrew from communion with his own people.

GRATIAN AND PROBUS.

MODESTUS AND ALINTHEUS.

Didymus of Alexandria, who after his fifth year was deprived of his sight and was also ignorant of the elements, dictates much concerning our doctrine to secretaries.

VALENTINIAN IV AND VALENS IV.

Eunomius, the disciple of Aetius, is recognized at Constantinople. From him came the Eunomian heresy, which says that the Son is not consubstantial with the Father but similar to him. His error is to assert that the Son is unlike the Father, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son.

GRATIAN III AND EQUITIUS.

[Column 0582C] AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF GRATIAN AND EQUITIUS.

Because the Sarmatians devastated Pannonia in the preceding year, the same consuls remained in office.

[Column 0583A] After the belated death of Auxentius, when Ambrose had been established as bishop at Milan, all Italy was converted to the true faith.

The clergy of Aquileia were regarded as a choir of the blessed.

Valentinian died at Brigetio from a sudden discharge of blood, which in Greek is called *apoplexia* (“apoplexy”).

After him, Gratian, having taken his brother Valentinian into the imperial government, reigned with his uncle Valens.

Valens issued a law that monks should serve as soldiers; those unwilling to do so were to be killed with clubs.

VALENS V AND VALENTINIAN.

Photinus dies in Galatia. From him the Photinian doctrine was introduced, having been conceived by Paul of Samosata and Artemon, of whom it was said above.

GRATIAN IV AND MEROBAUDES.

[Column 0584A] Many thousands of the Alemanni were slaughtered by Gratian’s army at Argentaria [733], a town of Gaul. [Note: The Colbert manuscripts have “about 30,000.” The highly learned André Schottus thinks the place of the battle was a town on the borders of the Lemovices, commonly called Argenton. Pontacus, however, considers it more probably the city situated on the Rhine, commonly called Strasbourg. Eusebius calls it Argentoratum around Olympiad 284, when he likewise mentions a similar slaughter of the Alemanni; so too does Marcellinus here. For it is rarely, or scarcely ever, established that the Alemanni penetrated as far as the Lemovices in the time of the earlier emperors.]

The nation of the Huns devastates the Goths, who rebel after being received by the Romans without laying down their arms.

VALENS VI AND VALENTINIAN II.

After defeating the Romans, the Goths pour into Thrace.

Valens, compelled to leave Antioch, recalls our people from exile in belated [734] repentance.

A lamentable war in Thrace: when the cavalry support abandoned them, the Roman legions were slaughtered by the Goths almost to annihilation. Valens himself, wounded by an arrow, fled; and because of his great pain he repeatedly slipped from his horse. He was carried to the hut of a certain farmstead. When the barbarians pursued them, the house was set on fire with him inside, and he was deprived even of burial.

## PART TWO: FROM THE DEATH OF THE EMPEROR VALENS TO THE DEATH OF VALENTINIAN III AND THE CAPTURE OF ROME BY THE VANDALS

[Column 0583]

[Column 0583B] Up to this point the presbyter Jerome has arranged the succession of the preceding years. We have taken care to add what followed.

Accordingly, after Valens was burned to death by the Goths in Thrace, Gratian reigned with his brother Valentinian, the forty-first Roman emperor, for six years.

AUSONIUS AND OLYBRIUS, CONSULS. [Note: The Colbert manuscript has “Musonius.” Pontacus restored “Ausonius” from the Cuspinian manuscripts in Cassiodorus, p. 513, and from Vasaeus in the *Chronicle of Spain*, p. 527. Joseph Scaliger and Onuphrius Panvinius, who identify this Ausonius as the distinguished poet Ausonius of Bordeaux, are not, he thinks, mistaken. This is demonstrated by Ausonius himself, who, writing about his consulship among the *Epigrams*, indicates that it fell in the third year of Olympiad 289.]

After the death of his uncle, Gratian takes Theodosius, the son of Theodosius, into partnership in the empire and grants him the rule of the East.

[Note: The following material, up to the section beginning with the words “At that time,” is absent from Labbe’s edition and from the Colbert manuscript; it is printed in Pontacus in italics, by which he intended to indicate additions to Prosper’s published Chronicle. It is also found in the 1677 Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers.] Theodosius defeats the Goths in many great battles with the greatest success and drives them out of Thrace.

[Column 0584B] The Lombards, departing in great numbers from the farthest borders of Germany, directly from the shores of the Ocean and the island of Scandia, and eager for new settlements, first defeated the Vandals under their leaders Iborea and Aio.

Sempronius is recognized as a man of outstanding learning.

At that time Priscillian, a bishop from Gallaecia, founded a heresy bearing his name from the doctrine of the Manichaeans and Gnostics. [Note: We emend the text to “from Gallaecia,” instead of “from Galatia,” as found in Labbe and the Lyon *Library of the Fathers of 1677*, or “from Gaul,” as found in the Augsburg manuscript and supported by the arguments of the illustrious Pontacus in his notes on Prosper’s Chronicle. It is certain that Priscillian was not from Galatia—that region of Asia near the Pontus Euxinus—on the testimony of Jerome, Letter 66; Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 6; and Augustine, *On Heresies*. That he was a bishop of Spain is clear from Sulpicius Severus and from Jerome himself in *On Illustrious Men*, who testify that he was bishop of Ávila, today called Avila. John Marianus, Book IV, chapter 20, *On the Affairs of Spain*, calls Priscillian bishop of Abula. Hence it is clear that Sulpicius’s text is corrupt where it reads “in the town of Labilensis” instead of “of Abilensis.” Elsewhere he was also corruptly called Priscianus; this has now been corrected, and it is recognized that it should be corrected from two Colbert manuscripts.]

GRATIAN V AND THEODOSIUS, CONSULS.

[Note: One Colbert manuscript and the Augsburg manuscript read “Ambrose the bishop wrote many elevated works in defense of the Catholic faith.” Pontacus omits the word “bishop.”] Ambrose writes many elevated works in defense of the Catholic faith.

[Note: This section and the two following it are absent from Labbe’s edition and from the Augsburg and Colbert manuscripts; Pontacus treats them as additions.] When Theodosius was ill at Thessalonica, [Note: Elsewhere: “by Basil.” This reading, according to Pontacus’s notes, could not agree with what is reported in the synodal letter of the Council of Constantinople and by Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 4; Socrates, Book V, chapter 6; Nicephorus, Book XII, chapter 16; and Cedrenus, who state that Theodosius was baptized by Ascholius, bishop of Thessalonica. Hence he judged that the books themselves gave him the option—since they say nothing about Prosper’s intention—of embracing the truth rather than adhering too scrupulously to an editors’ reading unsupported by witness or reason, since it is also plausible that this is merely a copyist’s error.] he received baptism from Ascholius, bishop of that same city.

[Note: [Column 0585] This note is printed at the foot of column 585, but its callout letter, c, does not appear in the text. The words in brackets are marked as additions in Pontacus’s edition and are absent from Labbe’s book. Although the statement agrees with the truth—for Jerome himself, in his letters to Pammachius, Rufinus, and Domnio, Letter 51, calls Gregory of Nazianzus his catechist, and in *Against Jovinianus* calls him his teacher, as also in *On Illustrious Men*, from which place these words seem to have been taken—the chronology in no way agrees with Jerome himself, since in *On Illustrious Men* he writes that Gregory died “nearly three years ago” under the emperor Theodosius. But since he also states there that he completed that work in the fourteenth year of Theodosius, it follows that Gregory of Nazianzus died in the eleventh year of Theodosius. Accordingly, Sigebertus appropriately assigns his death to that eleventh year in his Chronicle. Pontacus.]

Through Gratian’s efforts, because Theodosius [735] was ill, peace was established with the Goths.

A council of 180 Fathers was held at Constantinople against Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God. [Note: In Pontacus’s edition and elsewhere, only 150 are numbered. See the note concerning the year of this synod, which ought to be commended to every devout person, just as Gregory the Great regarded it as equivalent to the Gospel.]

[Note: Pontacus has “Evagrius and Eucherius”; others have “Eleutherius.”] SIAGRIUS AND EUCHERIUS, CONSULS.

Martin, bishop of Tours, a city of Gaul, is held in high renown.

Gregory of Nazianzus, the most eloquent man of his age and Jerome’s teacher, died.

[Note: One Colbert manuscript has “Antoninus and Siagrius”; others have “and Evagrius.” See Pontacus.] ANTONIUS AND SYAGRIUS, CONSULS.

Athanaric, king of the Goths, dies at Constantinople on the fifteenth day after he had been received there. [Note: In the margin of the Lyon edition one finds: “Read ‘he killed’ or ‘he died,’ according to the testimony of Marcellinus, Ammianus, Book XVII, Zosimus, Book IV, Themistius, Oration 6, Orosius, Book VII, chapter 34, Cassiodorus, and others.” Marcellinus and Sigebertus assign the event to the preceding year. See Pontacus.]

[Column 0585B] MEROBAUDES II AND SATURNINUS, CONSULS.

Arcadius, son of the emperor Theodosius, is called Augustus.

Petronius, bishop of Bologna, a man distinguished for learning and holiness, dies. [Note: This passage is also absent from several manuscripts and from Labbe’s edition. No one can doubt that Petronius was bishop of Bologna around this time, says Pontacus, since Gennadius, chapter 41, Ado, and others testify to it. But that he died during this consulship cannot be maintained, since Eusebius of Bologna was still living; Felix succeeded Eusebius, and Petronius succeeded Felix. It is therefore more credible that Gennadius is correct when he writes that Petronius died while Theodosius and the younger Valentinian were Augusti, followed by Ado. Hence this scholar, highly experienced in ecclesiastical history, concludes that this passage is not by Prosper.]

RICIMER AND CLEARCHUS, CONSULS.

Honorius, son of Theodosius, is born.

After Damasus, Siricius, the thirty-sixth bishop of the Roman Church, presided for fifteen years. [Note: In some manuscripts he is incorrectly called Ursinus; in one Colbert manuscript, Sericus. The Augsburg manuscript and one Colbert manuscript state that he presided for fourteen years, another for sixteen.]

In Britain, Maximus was made emperor through a military revolt. When he soon crossed over to Gaul, Gratian, defeated at Paris through the treachery of Merobaudes, the master of the soldiers, fled, was captured at Lyon, and killed. [Note: Elsewhere the reading is “when he transferred himself.”] [Column 0586A] [Note: The Augsburg manuscript reads “with Merobaudes as master of the soldiers.” Pontacus approves this reading, since Pacatus testifies that Merobaudes was killed by Maximus because he was Gratian’s close and intimate associate, and that Gratian was betrayed by the soldiers against Merobaudes’ wishes.]

Maximus makes his son Victor Caesar and associate in the government.

Valentinian, with Theodosius, the forty-second of the Romans, reigned for seven years. [Note: Pontacus, following the Ulrician manuscript—which he also calls the Augsburg manuscript because it belonged to the monastery of Saints Afra and Ulrich at Augsburg, according to Henry Canisius—gives eight years.]

ARCADIUS AND BAUTO, CONSULS.

At this time the presbyter Jerome, already [736] famous throughout the whole world, lives in Bethlehem, serving the universal Church with exceptional talent and devotion. [Note: Elsewhere: “with universal devotion.” This is absent from Labbe. The Colbert and Augsburg manuscripts read “of the whole Church”; another Colbert manuscript reads “with universal devotion.”]

Priscillian, realizing that he was to be condemned at the synod of Bordeaux, appealed to the emperor Maximus. After being heard at Trier by Evodius, the praetorian prefect, he was condemned by Maximus to the sword, together with Euchrocia, the wife of the rhetor Delphidius, and Latronianus and other associates in his error. [Note: One Colbert manuscript and the Lyon edition add “by Maximus”; it is absent from Labbe’s edition and from another Colbert manuscript. Pontacus defends the reading in his notes, p. 767, on the basis of Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, who writes that Priscillian was killed at Trier by the tyrant Maximus; Sulpicius, Book II, who reports that Evodius declared Priscillian guilty and, after the proceedings had been submitted to the emperor, that the emperor judged Priscillian and his associates deserving of capital punishment; and Isidore’s Chronicle, “Priscillian was struck down by the sword by the tyrant Maximus.”]

HONORIUS N. P. AND EVODIUS, CONSULS. [Note: One Colbert manuscript has “Honorius Nepos”; another “the emperor”; so too the Augsburg manuscript. Pontacus nevertheless observes in his notes, p. 768, that the letters N. P. do not mean *Nepos* but *nobilissimus puer*, “most noble boy.” Thus the Fasti read: “Flavius Honorius, son of the Augustus Theodosius, a most noble boy.” For when the consulship was conferred upon him, he was two years old, as Claudian teaches:

“Among your cradle beginnings  
you are advanced, marking the Fasti with your name inscribed.”]

At Bordeaux, a certain female disciple of Priscillian named Urbica was killed by stoning during a popular riot because of her obstinate impiety.

VALENTINIAN III AND EUTROPIUS, CONSULS.

THEODOSIUS II AND CYNEGIUS, CONSULS.

The tyrant Maximus is stripped of his royal garments by the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius at the third milestone from Aquileia, brought before them, and condemned to death. His son Victor was killed in Gaul that same year by the count Arbogast. [Note: The words “that same year” are added by two Colbert manuscripts and the Augsburg manuscript.]

TIMASIUS AND PROMOTUS, CONSULS.

The bishops Ithacius and Ursacius are deprived of communion with the Church because of the killing of Priscillian, whose accusers they had been.

[Note: Pontacus marks this section as an addition; it is absent from Labbe’s edition and the Colbert manuscripts. Pontacus indicates that it was taken from the Deacon, Book I, *On the Lombards*, chapter 10.] After the deaths of their leaders, the Lombards first created a king for themselves, Agelmund, son of Aio, who reigned for thirty-three years.

VALENTINIAN IV AND NEOTERIUS, CONSULS.

A sign appeared in the sky, like a hanging and burning column, for thirty days. [Note: It should be read “hanging column,” not “hanging dove,” according to Onuphrius, Canisius, Marcellinus, Sigebertus, and others.]

[Note: This passage too is designated as an addition. Nevertheless, Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 21; Cassiodorus, Book IX of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 43; and Sigebertus mention this translation, assigning it approximately to the year of Christ 392 and, with the author, to approximately the sixth year of Theodosius, as does Cedrenus. But if we trust Marcellinus, it must be assigned to the following year, since he says that Theodosius did not return to Constantinople before the following year. So Pontacus.]

Theodosius transported the venerable head of John the Baptist from the village of Coslai to Constantinople and deposited it, at the seventh milestone from the city, in the basilica [737] which he had built in his honor at great expense.

TATIAN AND SYMMACHUS, CONSULS.

[Note: This section is an addition. Pontacus believes that it should perhaps be entirely removed, since the same event is reported in the following year, and more accurately; for the Fasti and other writers place Eugenius’s rule after Valentinian’s death.] Eugenius, relying on the favor of Arbogast, usurped the empire for himself.

ARCADIUS II AND RUFINUS, CONSULS.

Valentinian, driven to disgust with life by the excessive harshness of Arbogast, the master of the soldiers, perished by a noose at Vienne. [Note: Whether Valentinian’s death was voluntary, as the author believes, together with Cassiodorus and Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 22, or was inflicted by another at Arbogast’s command, as Marcellinus, Orosius, Book VII, chapter 35, Socrates, Book V, chapter 25, and others think, was already doubtful at that time, as Rufinus testifies in Book II, chapter 31. One Colbert manuscript reads *audacitatem*, “boldness,” instead of *austeritatem*, “harshness.” Pontacus proves that the event should be assigned to this year.]

Arbogast, commander of the army, burdened by Valentinian’s death, makes Eugenius emperor in Gaul. [Note: This is how it is read in Labbe and in the Colbert and Augsburg manuscripts. Elsewhere: “whose army.”]

Theodosius, the forty-third of the Romans, after having already reigned for fourteen years, reigned with his sons Arcadius and Honorius for three years.

THEODOSIUS III AND ABUNDANTIUS, CONSULS.

[Column 0587C] [Note: These words are absent from the Colbert manuscripts and several others. They are found in Labbe’s edition. The bishop of Vasio suspects that the copyist borrowed the entire passage from Marcellinus, where it is found word for word, except that Marcellinus reads “at the seventh milestone from the city” instead of “the seventeenth”; this agrees with Socrates, Book V, chapter 25, and Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book IX, chapter 46. In the Chronicle the event is assigned to the preceding consulship.] Theodosius, his father, appointed Honorius ruler at the same place where he had also made his brother Arcadius Caesar—at the seventeenth milestone from the city—when darkness fell at the third hour.

ARCADIUS III AND HONORIUS II, CONSULS.

John, a celebrated monk and anchorite, is held in high regard. Endowed with the gift of prophecy, he predicted that Theodosius, who consulted him about the outcome of the war he was undertaking against Eugenius, would be victorious.

OLYBRIUS AND PROBINUS, CONSULS.

Theodosius defeats and kills the tyrant Eugenius.

Augustine, a disciple of blessed Ambrose, outstanding in eloquence and learning, is ordained bishop in the region of Hippo in Africa. [Note: See Pontacus’s note, where he proves that the reading in certain manuscripts, “in the region of Hippo in Africa,” is corrupt. He points out that there were two African cities bearing the name Hippo, one called Regius and the other Diarrhytus because of its watercourses, whereas it was unheard-of for Hippo to be the name of a region.]

At this time the distinguished poet Claudian is held in high regard.

The emperor Theodosius dies at Milan.

Arcadius, the forty-fourth of the Romans, after having [738] reigned for twelve years, reigns with his brother Honorius for thirteen years.

ARCADIUS IV AND HONORIUS III, CONSULS.

[Note: This is absent from Labbe’s codex and certain manuscripts, but appears word for word in Marcellinus; Ambrose also mentions it in his funeral oration for Theodosius. Pontacus.] There was an earthquake for many days, and the sky appeared to burn.

Orosius, a Spanish presbyter, a man eloquent and knowledgeable in history, is renowned. [Note: This is absent from several manuscripts and some printed editions, but Pontacus says that it is not contrary to the truth. The learned Nicolas le Fèvre preferred *conditor*, “founder,” to be read instead of *cognitor*, “knower,” but no manuscript supports this, and it conflicts with Gennadius’s catalogue, where *cognitor* is found.]

CAESARIUS AND ATTICUS, CONSULS.

[Note: This is absent from Labbe’s edition and the manuscripts, and seems to have been copied from Marcellinus. Cedrenus agrees with it, although elsewhere he calls her Flaccia and elsewhere Flavilla. Baronius, volume IV, p. 515, confirms the customary spelling. Pontacus.] Flacilla, daughter of Arcadius, was born. [Note: This too is missing from Labbe’s edition and many manuscripts. It is found in Gennadius’s catalogue, Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 23, and Cassiodorus, Book IX of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 1.]

Evagrius, a monk of incredible abstinence and learned in the sacred Scriptures, is renowned among the Egyptians.

[Note: This section is added from one Colbert manuscript and the Lyon edition, which follows the Augsburg manuscript.] The Council of Carthage, at which the decrees of the Council of Hippo were confirmed and incorporated.

HONORIUS IV AND EUTYCHIANUS, CONSULS.

[Column 0588C] Anastasius, the thirty-seventh bishop of the Roman Church, holds the episcopate for three years and twenty-one days.

[Column 0589A] [Note: That this consulship belongs here, and that it was previously misread as Manlius or Manilius and Theodorus, is discussed at length in Pontacus’s note, column 771 (our volume XXVII, column 1191). Among other witnesses he cites Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, at the end, and the same author, Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 2. Claudian also composed for him an exceedingly elegant panegyric on his consulship, where he declares that he alone was consul that year, saying: “You hold both summits.”] MANLIUS THEODORUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, CONSUL.

Eutropius the eunuch entered upon this consulship; soon afterward he was stripped of both office and life.

STILICHO AND AURELIAN, CONSULS.

The Goths entered Italy under the leadership of Alaric and Radagaisus.

VINCENTIUS AND [Note: Other manuscripts have “Flavita”; others, “Flavitus” or “Fabricius.”] FRAVITUS, CONSULS.

John of Constantinople [Note: John Chrysostom is meant. He had been ordained bishop of Constantinople during the consulship of Honorius and Eutychianus by Theophilus of Alexandria himself, as Socrates testifies in Book VI, chapter 2. Pontacus.] and Theophilus of Alexandria are regarded as illustrious bishops. But discord obscured both of them; it advanced so far that John, oppressed by Theophilus, was forced into exile in Pontus, although the greater part of the bishops, following the example of the Roman pontiff, maintained communion with him.

ARCADIUS V AND HONORIUS V, CONSULS.

[Column 0589B] [Note: Thus, after Pontacus’s correction, Labbe, the Colbert manuscript, the Augsburg manuscript, and others read it. One Colbert manuscript has: “A battle was fought against the Goths, with the defeat of both sides at either Pollentia.” The Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers* follows it, replacing *potentiae* with *Pollentiae*. Cassiodorus gives the same account somewhat differently. Pollentia is a city situated in the Cottian Alps, according to Ptolemy, among the cities of Liguria. Claudian, in his sixth consulship of Honorius, and Clarius, Book IV of *The Gothic War*, describe this event and testify that Alaric was defeated and left with few men. Cassiodorus and Jordanes, however, in *On Gothic Affairs*, say that Stilicho was defeated and put to flight. But according to the author, the victory seems rather to have been a Cadmean victory. Pontacus.] A fierce battle was fought against the Goths at Pollentia, with heavy losses on both sides.

Innocent, the thirty-eighth bishop presiding over the Roman Church, held office for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. [Note: Labbe’s Chronicle, together with the Colbert and Augsburg manuscripts, gives fourteen years. Some manuscripts give twenty-two days. See Baronius, *Annals*. Pontacus.]

739 THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS AND RUMORIDUS, CONSULS.

[Note: The first section of this consulship is added from a Colbert manuscript and Baronius; the second from Arn. Pontacus’s edition of the Chronicle, the Augsburg manuscript, and the Lyon edition. Both are absent from Labbe.] A council of Carthage was held concerning the Donatists.

A statue of Eudoxia, the wife of Arcadius, was placed upon a porphyry column.

HONORIUS VI AND ARISTENETUS, CONSULS.

[Note: This is absent from Labbe’s edition, the Colbert manuscripts, and several others. Marcellinus and Socrates place her death under the same consulship as the author. But how this can be reconciled with Nicephorus, Book XIII, chapter 38, and others, who report that Eudoxia outlived John Chrysostom, is left to the judgment of the learned reader. Pontacus, column 773.] Eudoxia, the wife of Arcadius, died.

STILICHO II AND ANTHEMIUS, CONSULS.

Radagaisus was defeated and captured in Tuscany, after many thousands of Goths had been slaughtered under the command of Stilicho.

[Column 0590A] ARCADIUS VI AND PROBUS, CONSULS.

The Vandals and Alans entered Gaul after crossing the Rhine on the day before the Kalends of January. [Note: One Colbert manuscript and the Augsburg manuscript read “on the third day before the Kalends.”]

HONORIUS VII AND THEODOSIUS II, CONSULS.

Constantine, rising from the lowest military rank merely because of the prestige of his name, emerged as a tyrant in Britain and crossed over into Gaul. [Note: These words are absent from Labbe’s edition, two Colbert manuscripts, and other witnesses cited by Pontacus; and not without reason, if we believe Sigebertus, who says in his Chronicle that this Constantine the tyrant—whom others call Constantius—was the brother of Aldroenus, king of Lesser Britain. Yet Orosius gives the very same words, and they are repeated by the Deacon and Bede in their *History of the English*. Pontacus.]

BASSUS AND PHILIPPUS, CONSULS.

The emperor Arcadius dies at Constantinople.

Honorius, with Theodosius, his brother’s son, the forty-fifth of the Romans, reigned for sixteen years.

HONORIUS VIII AND THEODOSIUS III, CONSULS.

The Vandals occupied Spain.

Attalus was made emperor at Rome. Soon deprived of his kingdom, he joined the Goths. [Note: This is how the Colbert manuscripts and Labbe’s edition read. In the commonly printed texts: “he yielded to the Goths.” Pontacus defends the former reading from Zosimus, Procopius, and Orosius, Book VII, chapter 42. He admits that the latter can be defended if it is understood that the Goths succeeded to his authority.]

[Column 0590B] FLAVIUS VARRO, VIR CLARISSIMUS, CONSUL. [Note: Some manuscripts erroneously add “Tertullus.” There were no ordinary consuls appointed on the Kalends of January that year; they were created later. Varro was appointed in the East by Honorius around the Kalends of February, while the other was appointed at Rome by Attalus around the Kalends of July. The latter was erased from the Fasti because he had been made consul by a tyrant. For this reason Orosius calls him a shadow-consul; he was also a pagan. Pontacus.]

[Note: This is omitted from Labbe’s edition, the Colbert manuscripts, and several others.] Rome, once victorious over the world, was captured by the Goths under the leadership of Alaric. For this reason there was only one consul from the Eastern regions, a practice observed in this and the following year.

IN THE FOURTH CONSULSHIP OF THE AUGUSTUS THEODOSIUS.

Constantine was defeated and captured near the town of Arles by the generals of Honorius, Constantius and Ulfilas. His son Constans, who had begun to reign in Spain, had been killed by the count Gerontius, who transferred the tyranny to a certain Maximus.

HONORIUS IX AND THEODOSIUS V, CONSULS.

After Maximus had been deprived of his kingdom in Spain, his life was spared, because the moderation and humility of a man who had assumed power did not deserve hatred.

The Goths entered Gaul under their king Athaulphus.

At the same time, the holy man Heros, a disciple of blessed Martin, while presiding as bishop over the town of Arles, was driven out by the people of that city [740], although innocent and liable to no accusation. Patroclus was ordained in his place, a friend and associate of Constantius, the master of the soldiers, whose favor he sought through him. This matter became the cause of great discord among the bishops of that region. [Note: Some books read: “although guilty of no accusation.”]

LUCIANUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, CONSUL.

His colleague in the consulship was Heraclianus, who, accused of revolutionary activity in Africa, lost both his office and his life.

The Burgundians occupied the part of Gaul near the Rhine.

[Note: Pontacus proves that this should be read “Jovinus,” instead of “Jovius.” Two Colbert manuscripts and other manuscripts cited by him support this. He also prefers *arrepto*, “having seized,” to *accepto*, “having received.” One Colbert manuscript has *abrepto*.] The brothers Jovinus and Sebastian, having seized the kingship in Gaul, were killed.

[Column 0591B] At this time Pelagius the Briton put forward the doctrine bearing his name against the grace of Christ, with Caelestius and Julian as his assistants, and drew many into his error. He taught that each person is directed toward righteousness by his own will and receives as much grace as he has deserved; that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and did not bind his descendants; that consequently it is possible for those who wish to be entirely without sin; and that all infants are born as innocent as the first human being was before the transgression. Therefore, he taught, they are not to be baptized so that they may be stripped of sin, but so that they may be honored by the sacrament of adoption.

[Note: Thus two Colbert manuscripts and other codices restored by Pontacus read, instead of “Constantine the consul.”] CONSTANTIUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, CONSUL.

With the counsel and assistance of the Goths, Attalus resumed the tyranny in Gaul.

HONORIUS X AND THEODOSIUS VI, CONSULS.

[Column 0591C] Attalus, abandoned by the Goths as they migrated to Spain and deprived of their support, is captured and presented alive to the patrician Constantius.

Athaulphus died after being wounded by one of his own men, and his kingdom was seized by Wallia, after those who were understood to desire the same thing had been killed.

THEODOSIUS VII AND PALLADIUS, CONSULS.

Wallia, seeking peace with Honorius, returns Placidia, the daughter of the emperor Theodosius, whom the Goths had captured at Rome and whom Athaulphus had taken as his wife; Constantius wins her marriage.

Zosimus, the thirty-ninth bishop of the Roman Church, assumes the episcopate for one year, nine months, and nine days. At this time the Pelagians, already condemned in advance by Pope Innocent, were resisted through the determination of the Africans [741] and especially through the learning of Bishop Augustine. [Note: One Colbert manuscript has *industria*, “zeal,” instead of *scientia*, “learning.” The same manuscript reads “by Pope Innocent,” along with others cited by Pontacus. Other books had: “Pelagius, already condemned in advance ... was resisted by the determination of the Africans,” and so forth.]

HONORIUS XI AND CONSTANTIUS II, CONSULS.

Honorius enters Rome in triumph, with Attalus preceding his chariot; he ordered Attalus to live in exile on Lipara. [Note: Labbe’s edition reads “he enters Rome with a triumph.”]

HONORIUS XII AND THEODOSIUS VIII, CONSULS.

At this time Constantius, a servant of Christ living in Rome as a vicarius, and resisting the Pelagians with the greatest devotion on behalf of God’s grace, suffered many things through their faction; these joined him to the holy confessors.

After a council of 214 bishops had been held at Carthage, the decrees of the synod were sent to Pope Zosimus. [Note: Labbe’s edition and the Colbert manuscripts read this way; one of them adds “and more.” Other codices have 217, and some 224. Pontacus says that 217 should rather be followed, since the author counts exactly that number in his book *Against the Collator*, and no more. Nevertheless, Marcellinus and the Continuator give the commonly transmitted number.] [Note: The Lyon edition notes in the margin that another reading is: “the decrees were delivered by Pope Zosimus.”] Once these decrees had been approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the entire world.

Valentinian, the son of Constantius and Placidia, was born on the sixth day before the Nones of July.

Boniface, the fortieth bishop of the Roman Church, held the episcopate for three years, eight months, and six days. [Note: Labbe, one Colbert manuscript, and the Augsburg manuscript give four years. Another manuscript and Pontacus give the figures above. Labbe, together with two Colbert manuscripts and the Augsburg codex, as well as others cited in Pontacus’s notes, assign this instead to the following consulship. Pontacus preferred the earlier reading, both because of Baronius’s authority and because of a letter from Symmachus, prefect of the city, to the emperor Honorius concerning Zosimus’s death and Boniface’s accession, dated in that same year on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.]

MONAXIUS AND PLINTA, CONSULS.

At this time there was a third schism. The antipope Eulalius was expelled by the emperor Honorius; the schism lasted two years.

The patrician Constantius made peace with Wallia, granting him Second Aquitaine as a place of residence, together with certain cities of the neighboring provinces. [Note: “Second” is added from one Colbert manuscript and other codices. That Aquitaine was divided into First and Second is shown by Sextus Rufus and the *Register of the Provinces*, when they discuss the bishops of First Aquitaine and Second Aquitaine and the seventeen provinces of Gaul, among which they count First Aquitaine and Second Aquitaine: the former extended from the river Garonne to the Loire, the latter from the Pyrenees to the Garonne. Pontacus.]

THEODOSIUS IX AND CONSTANTIUS III, CONSULS.

Constantius is taken into partnership in the government by Honorius.

[Column 0592C] The presbyter Jerome dies in the ninety-first year of his age, on the day before the Kalends of October. [Note: For the year of Jerome’s death and his age, see Arn. Pontacus’s note, columns 778–779 (our volume XXVII, column 1197).]

AGRICOLA AND EUSTATHIUS, CONSULS.

The emperor Constantius dies.

HONORIUS XIII AND THEODOSIUS X, CONSULS.

At this time an army was sent against the Vandals in Spain, commanded by Cassinus [742]. He turned the distinguished military leader Boniface away from joining the expedition by his foolish and insulting command. Boniface considered it dangerous and unworthy to follow a man whom he had found to be hostile and arrogant; he therefore quickly made his way to the city’s harbor and from there to Africa. This became the beginning of many hardships for the state.

MARINIANUS AND ASCLEPIODOTUS, CONSULS.

The Augusta Placidia, expelled by her brother Honorius, departed for the East with her sons Honorius and Valentinian.

Coelestine, the forty-first bishop presiding over the Roman Church, held office for nine years. [Note: The Colbert and Augsburg manuscripts read: “Coelestine assumed the episcopate of the Roman Church for nine years.” One adds ten months and seventeen days, as in Pontacus’s Chronicle.]

[Note: Pontacus notes that this passage is absent from several manuscripts, including two Colbert manuscripts, and that everything said about the Lombards in this Chronicle seems later in date and appended from another source, such as the Deacon, Book I, *On the Lombards*, chapters 10 and 11, where the figure named here Lamissus is called Lamission. Pontacus.] Lamissus, son of a prostitute, reigned as the eleventh king of the Lombards for three years.

Honorius dies, and John seizes his kingdom, with Castinus—who had served as master of the army—apparently conniving.

[Note: [Col. 0593C] One Colbertine manuscript and the Chronicle of Pontacus read: “Theodosius, forty-sixth [emperor], ruled the Romans for thirty years.”]

**THEODOSIUS, XLVI, holds the Roman Empire for thirty years.**

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF CASTINUS AND VICTOR.**

[Note: [Col. 0593D] Some manuscripts read *Victorinus*, among them one Colbertine manuscript.]

Theodosius makes Valentinian, the son of his aunt, Caesar, and sends him with his Augusta mother to receive the Western Empire. At that time John, while attempting by war to recover Africa, which Boniface held, was weakened in his efforts to defend himself.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS XII AND VALENTINIAN.**

[Note: [Col. 0593D] Some manuscripts, including that of Labbe, add “Caesar,” as do all the Fasti, Marcellinus, and Cassiodorus. Pontacus.]

Placidia Augusta and Valentinian Caesar, with remarkable success, overthrow the usurper John and, as victors, regain the kingdom. A pardon is granted to Aetius, because the Huns whom John had summoned through him [Note: [Col. 0593D] One Colbertine manuscript reads “had received.”] returned to their own country through his efforts.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] Although this passage is absent from many manuscripts and is regarded as an interpolation in the Chronicle of Pontacus, it is nevertheless supported by the testimony of the Deacon, Book IV, and the same account is confirmed by Augustine’s tenth letter in the appendix. The same writer, however, wishes it referred to the preceding consulship.]

Castinus, however, was driven into exile, because it appeared that John could not have assumed the kingdom without his connivance.

Valentinian is called Augustus by decree of Theodosius.

[Col. 0593C] [Note: [Col. 0593D] Labbe corrected this, following Pontacus’s Chronicle, in place of *Archillas*. Henry Canisius had also noted in the margin of his book that this should be read. Isidore’s Gothic Chronicle supports our reading. “Theodoricus,” he says, “king of the Goths, besieges Arelate, the most noble town of Gaul, but, as the power of Aetius, commander of the Roman forces, threatens him, he withdraws from the siege.” The Pithaean Chronicle likewise supports it. The town of Archilla is scarcely mentioned anywhere.]

Arelate, a noble town of Gaul, was attacked with great force by the Goths, until, when Aetius approached, they withdrew without escaping punishment.

**UNDER THE SECOND CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS XII AND VALENTINIAN.**

[Note: [Col. 0594C] Labbe’s edition adds “Augustus.” See Pontacus, p. 781 (Col. 1199 of our volume XXVII).]

[Col. 0594A] Patroclus, bishop of Arles, was mangled by many wounds and killed by a certain barbarian tribune. This crime was attributed to the secret command of Felix, master of the soldiers, through whose instigation Titus the deacon, a holy man who distributed money to the poor at Rome, was also believed to have been killed. [Note: Elsewhere: “is reported”; and below, “killed.” One Colbertine manuscript: “is believed … slain.”]

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF HIERIUS AND ARDABUR.**

Boniface, whose power and glory were increasing within Africa [Note: [Col. 0594C] Thus one Colbertine manuscript and several others. In others: “in Africa.”], was attacked in a war undertaken at Felix’s discretion, because he had refused to come to Italy [Note: [Col. 0594C] One Colbertine manuscript reads “might agree”; another, “was agreeing.” Labbe’s edition reads as above. This is more correct, since, according to the Deacon, Book XIV, the cause of the war against Boniface was that, although summoned by the emperor, he delayed coming. But what the author writes—that this war was undertaken at Felix’s discretion—the Deacon and Sigebert attribute to Aetius. Pontacus.], in the public name, under the command of Mavortius, Galbio, and Sinoce. Through the treachery of the latter, Mavortius and Galbio were killed while besieging Boniface; shortly afterward Sinoce himself, his treachery having been exposed by Boniface, [Note: [Col. 0594D] One Colbertine manuscript reads “detained.”] was killed.

From that time the sea became accessible to peoples who did not know how to use ships, when they were summoned to aid by the contending parties; and responsibility for the war begun against Boniface was transferred to Count Sigisvult.

The nation of the Vandals crosses from Spain into Africa. [Note: [Col. 0594D] One Colbertine manuscript and other codices read “from the Spains.”]

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF FELIX AND TAURUS.**

Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, attempts to introduce a new error into the Churches, preaching that Christ was born from Mary as man alone, [Note: [Col. 0594D] Other manuscripts add: “and not God.”] not also as God, and that divinity had been conferred upon him as a reward for merit. The chief diligence of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and the authority of Pope Celestine oppose this impiety.

A part of Gaul near the Rhine, which the Franks had occupied and taken possession of, is recovered by the arms of Count Aetius.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF FLORENTIUS AND DIONYSIUS.**

When Felix had been advanced to the rank of patrician, Aetius was made master of the soldiers. [Col. 0594C] [Note: [Col. 0594D] An error had entered the printed editions, where it was implied that Aetius had been made master of the soldiers after being a farmer; the manuscripts, including one Colbertine manuscript, also favored this error. But another Colbertine manuscript confirms the correction made by Pontacus and Labbe, as read above. For it had never been heard that Aetius was a farmer, and Prosper would have added this inappropriately here: since he had often mentioned Aetius earlier, he ought to have recorded his birth and status at the first mention. See more in Pontacus’s note, Col. 782 (in the place cited above).]

The Pelagian Agricola, son of Severianus, a Pelagian bishop, corrupted the Churches of Britain [Note: [Col. 0594D] This is the reading that should be adopted, not *Brastaniae* or *Hiberniae*, as is established by one Colbertine manuscript and several others, especially because Sigebert’s Chronicle makes clear that Germanus, bishop of Auxerre—whom Prosper mentions here—and Lupus, bishop of Troyes, sailed twice to Britain to refute the Pelagian heresy. Moreover, Prosper immediately adds “the Britons”; and it is more certain than needs proof that Pelagius scattered the seeds of his error there. Pontacus.] by insinuating his doctrine among them. But at the request of the deacon Palladius, Pope Celestine sends Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in his place [Col. 0595A] [Note: [Col. 0595C] Some books read “so that he may direct”; one Colbertine manuscript reads “he restored.”], and, after expelling the heretics, he directs the Britons to the Catholic faith.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS XIII AND VALENTINIAN III.**

Aetius killed Felix together with his wife Padusia and the deacon Grunnitus, when he discovered that they were plotting against him.

The most excellent bishop Augustine died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, during the attack of the besieging Vandals, replying to Julian’s books [Note: [Col. 0595C] One Colbertine manuscript reads “amid the attacks.” See Pontacus’s note on the year in which the death of so great a teacher occurred, Col. 783 (Col. 1201 of our volume XXVII).] at the very end of his days, and gloriously persevering in his confession of Christian grace.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF BASSUS AND ANTIOCHUS.**

A synod of more than two hundred priests is assembled at Ephesus. Nestorius is condemned, together with the heresy bearing his name and with many Pelagians who supported the doctrine, as being related to his own error [Note: [Col. 0595C] Some codices read “related to him.”].

Palladius is ordained by Pope Celestine for the Scots who believe in Christ and is sent as their first bishop.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF AETIUS AND VALERIUS.**

Xistus is placed in charge of the Roman Church as its forty-second bishop, for eight years and nineteen days, [Note: [Col. 0595C] In some codices the following words were separated from the preceding by punctuation and attached to what follows, as though they referred to Boniface rather than to Xistus. Pontacus and Labbe restored them from the manuscripts, replacing “of the city and confession” with “of the City and concord.”] with extraordinary peace and harmony throughout the entire City.

Boniface comes from Africa to Italy [Note: [Col. 0595C] Earlier: “arrives in Italy, in the City.” Pontacus defends another reading, followed by Labbe; it is preferred by two Colbertine manuscripts, by three others cited by Pontacus, [Col. 0595D] and by the Augustan codex, which Pontacus everywhere calls the Ulrician manuscript.], entering the City, after receiving the rank of master of the soldiers. After defeating Aetius, who resisted him, in battle, he died of illness a few days later.

But Aetius, having laid down his authority and living on his own estate, was there attacked by one of his enemies in a sudden assault [Note: [Col. 0595D] Labbe’s edition and one manuscript of Pontacus read: “and when some of his enemies had attempted to overwhelm him there by a sudden attack.”]. He fled to the City, [Col. 0596A] and from there to Dalmatia, then through Pannonia reached the Huns. Using their friendship and assistance, he obtained peace for the rulers [Note: [Col. 0595D] Pontacus and Labbe altered the text in this way, following several of the manuscripts cited earlier, which are supported by one Colbertine manuscript; another has “in place of authority.” The Deacon, Book XIV, recounting the whole sentence, writes: “Aetius obtained peace for the rulers through the recovery of his restored authority, and not long afterward he also acquired the dignity of patrician.” These words not only confirm our reading but explain it. Sigebert also records under A.D. 435 that Aetius withdrew to Ruga, king of the Huns, and returned with his aid [Col. 0596C] to Roman territory; and that in the following year Aetius was received back into favor. From this one understands how Aetius was restored to his former rank: according to Prosper, he defeated the king of the Burgundians, was made patrician and consul for the third time, and fought many battles, up to Valentinian’s thirtieth year, when he was killed by Valentinian’s own hand, as Prosper of Pithou and other writers report. Pontacus.] and the right to exercise restored authority.

**746 UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS XIV AND MAXIMUS.**

[Note: [Col. 0596C] This and the following entries, which are absent from the manuscripts of Pontacus and from two Colbertine manuscripts and are not found in Labbe’s edition, are assigned to the same consulship by Marcellinus and by Socrates, Book VII, chapter 39. By “the royal city,” understand the city of Constantinople. There is no doubt that John Cassian was then alive; his *Conferences of the Fathers* survive, and in Book VII of *On the Incarnation*, near the end, he testifies that he was a disciple of John Chrysostom, whom Prosper earlier called John of Constantinople. But, Pontacus says, it is not likely that Prosper would have mentioned him so honorifically when he had written against him as holding an unsound view of the faith together with the Pelagians, as Marcellinus notes under the consulship of Theodosius XVI [Col. 0596D] and as Cassian’s works testify. These are Pontacus’s notes. He adds a reckoning of the years from the creation of the world, etc., from the Lodève manuscript. Although it is not free from errors, it is nevertheless useful to some extent for confirming what appears in the printed edition, especially if several years are subtracted from certain portions. Since this material was added to Labbe’s edition of the Chronicle, with some variation in the three numbers, we have likewise thought it should not be omitted.]

Most of the northern part of the royal city was burned and collapsed for three consecutive days in the month of August.

John the Monk, surnamed Cassian, is regarded at Massilia as an eminent and eloquent writer.

All the years are collected up to the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus.

From the fifteenth year of Tiberius and the Passion of the Lord: 406 years.

From the restoration of the Temple under Darius: 954 years.

From the first Olympiad and the prophet Isaiah: 1,210 years.

[Col. 0596B] From Solomon and the first construction of the Temple: 1,466 years.

From Moses and Cecrops, king of Attica: 1,990 years.
