From Abraham, and from the reign of Ninus and Semiramis: 2,450 years.

From the Flood to Abraham: 1,071 years.

From Adam to the Flood: 2,242 years.

Thus, from Adam to the time of the consuls mentioned above, there are 5,362 years.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF ASPAR AND AREOBINDUS.**

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS XV AND VALENTINIAN IV.**

Peace was made with the Vandals, a portion of Africa being granted to them for habitation through Trigetius, at Hippo, on the third day before the Ides of February. [Note: [Col. 0596D] Pontacus corrected the passage in this form, followed by Labbe and supported by the Colbertine manuscripts and others. Previously it read: “given to them for habitation for three years in a place of Africa, Hippo, on the third day before the Ides of February.” One Colbertine manuscript and the Augustan, or Ulrician, codex read only: “a portion of Africa given to them for habitation.” See Pontacus’s note, Col. 786 (Col. 1203 of our volume XXVII).]

At the same time Aetius defeated in battle Gundicarius, king of the Burgundians living in Gaul [Col. 0597A] [Note: [Col. 0597D] This is the reading of one Colbertine manuscript, Labbe, and the Augustan codex. Others read “crushed him in battle.”], and granted peace to him when he begged for it, though he did not enjoy it for long. For the Huns [Note: [Col. 0597D] In different codices they are called *Hunni* or *Chunni*. Pontacus.] destroyed him together with his people and lineage.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF ISIDORE AND SENATOR.**

The Goths disturb the terms of peace and occupy many towns near their own settlements. They are especially hostile to the town of Narbonne, which, after suffering for a long time from siege and hunger, was freed from both dangers by Count Litorius. For, bringing in two measures of wheat for each horseman, he energetically both put the enemy to flight and filled the city with provisions [Note: [Col. 0597D] One Colbertine manuscript reads “he filled”; another, “he assisted”; the Augustan reads “he assisted.”].

**UNDER THE SECOND CONSULSHIP OF AETIUS AND SIGISVULT.**

War is waged against the Goths with the assistance of the Huns.

[Col. 0597B] In Africa, Geiseric, king of the Vandals, wishing within the boundaries of his settlement to overthrow the Catholic faith through Arian impiety, persecuted certain of our bishops—among whom Possidius, Novatus, and Severianus were the most distinguished [Col. 0597D] [Note: This has been added from Labbe’s edition and from the Lodève manuscript examined by Pontacus.]—to such an extent that he deprived them of the legal possession of their basilicas and even expelled them from their cities, although their steadfastness yielded to none of the threats of the most arrogant king.

Valentinian Augustus travels to Constantinople to the emperor Theodosius [Note: [Col. 0597D] Marcellinus gives the same account under the same consuls. Socrates, Book VII, chapter 44; Cassiodorus, Book XII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 13; and the Deacon, Book XIV, assign it instead to the preceding consulship. It is scarcely possible to determine which account should be preferred. This daughter was called Eudoxia, daughter of the other Eudoxia. Pontacus.], and takes his daughter in marriage.

In the same year deserters from the barbarian federates practiced piracy [Note: [Col. 0597D] Some codices read: “the barbarians practiced piracy.” This passage is absent from Labbe’s Chronicle.].

At about the same time four Spanish men—Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychius [Note: [Col. 0597D] Labbe has “Eutychianus.” He also adds *chari*, “dear,” [Col. 0598D] and later “into Arian perfidy.”—] had long been held in high esteem by Geiseric because of their deserved reputation for wisdom and faithful service. The king ordered them to pass over into the Arian sect, in order to make them more closely attached to himself. But they firmly rejected the deed. This aroused the barbarian to a raging fury: first they were proscribed, then driven into exile, then tortured with the most savage punishments; finally, killed by different forms of death, they met their end in a glorious and wondrous martyrdom.

A boy named Paulillus, the brother of Paschasius and Eutychius, was especially dear to the king because of the elegance of his appearance and intelligence. Since no threats could drive him from his profession and love of the Catholic faith, he was beaten for a long time with clubs and condemned to the lowest slavery [Note: [Col. 0598D] This is the reading of one Colbertine manuscript, the Augustan codex, and Labbe’s Chronicle. Others read “to infamous [servitude].”]. For this reason, it appears, he was not killed, lest even that age should glory in the defeat of the impious king’s savagery [Note: [Col. 0598D] Thus Labbe’s Chronicle, with two Colbertine manuscripts and the Augustan. Elsewhere: “and therefore, as appears, he was not killed.”].

[Col. 0598A] **UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS XVI AND FAUSTUS.**

In this year the same pirates devastated many islands, especially Sicily.

Some successes were achieved against the Goths in Gaul.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS XVII AND FESTUS.**

Litorius, who held the second position of authority after the patrician Aetius and commanded with Hunnic auxiliaries [Note: [Col. 0598D] Thus the text has been altered on the authority of many manuscripts, in place of “second in authority under Aetius the patrician.” Likewise, in place of “how useful that force of theirs which perished was.”], wishing to surpass Aetius’s glory and trusting in the responses of haruspices and the signs of demons, rashly engaged the Goths in battle. He thereby showed how useful the force that perished with him might have been if he had preferred to use better counsels than his own rashness. For he inflicted such a defeat on the enemy that, unless he had fallen into captivity through fighting recklessly, it would have been doubtful to which side the victory should be attributed.

At this time Julian of Eclanum [Note: [Col. 0598D] Other codices read “of Atellanum”; Pontacus and Labbe have “of Eclanum.” Eclanum was a city of Campania according to Antoninus and others, and Gennadius records that this Julian was a Campanian. On this matter consult the Preface to the books of the *Unfinished Work against Julian* in volume X of the works of Saint Augustine, the latest edition of the Benedictine Fathers, p. 865 and following.]—the most boastful defender of the Pelagian error, driven by an immoderate desire to recover the episcopate he had long ago lost—attempted by many deceptive devices, while holding out hope of correction, to creep back into communion with the Church. But Pope Xistus, vigilantly countering these snares at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no access to his deadly efforts. Thus he made all Catholics rejoice at the rejection of the deceitful beast, as though the apostolic sword had then for the first time cut down that most arrogant heresy.

At about the same time Vitricus was regarded as faithful to our state and distinguished by many proofs of military ability.

Peace was made with the Goths, after they had requested it more humbly than ever before, following the grievous experience of an inconclusive battle.

While Aetius was occupied with arranging affairs in Gaul, Geiseric, whose friendship was thought to pose no threat, invaded Carthage by treachery under the pretext of peace on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November. He converted all its wealth to his own possession after subjecting the citizens to various forms of torture, and did not refrain from plundering the churches. He emptied them of their sacred vessels, deprived them of the service of priests, and ordered them to be not places of divine worship but dwellings for his own people. He raged against the entire captive population, but was especially hostile to the nobility and religion, so that it could not be discerned whether he had waged war more against human beings or against God [Note: [Col. 0598D] This sentence is consistently found in Labbe’s Chronicle. In some manuscripts it is absent; in others a new entry begins here with the words: “Carthage was captured by the Vandals in the year 583 after Rome began to exist,” elsewhere 585. Pontacus does not think these words belong to the author. The earlier number corresponds very well to the third year of the 158th Olympiad, in which Eusebius recorded that Carthage had been captured by the Romans—provided that the present consulship, in which it was captured by the Vandals, is not included. Pontacus.].

[Col. 0599A] Carthage endured this captivity in the year 585 after Rome had begun to exist.

**748 UNDER THE FIFTH CONSULSHIP OF VALENTINIAN AUGUSTUS AND ANATOLIUS.**

After the death of Bishop Xistus, the Roman Church remained without a bishop for more than forty days, awaiting with remarkable peace and patience [Note: [Col. 0599C] Other codices read “awaiting the arrival.”] the presence of the deacon Leo, whom affairs in Gaul then detained while he was restoring friendship between Aetius and Albinus [Note: [Col. 0599C] Some books read: “friendship kept him detained so that it might be restored,” or “he was detained so that friendship might be restored.”]. It was as though his arrival had been delayed [Note: [Col. 0599C] Other codices read “as though the arrival were long”; one Colbertine manuscript reads “as though he had been brought farther away.” In others and in the Augustan codex these words are absent [Col. 0599D].] for the purpose of testing both the merit of the one elected and the judgment of those who elected him. Accordingly, the deacon LEO was summoned by an official embassy and presented to his rejoicing homeland, and was ordained the forty-third bishop of the Roman Church.

Geiseric, grievously afflicting Sicily, received news that Sebastian had crossed from Spain to Africa [Note: [Col. 0599D] Some codices read: “news of Sebastian crossing …”]. [Col. 0599B] [Note: [Col. 0599D] Sebastian was, as Victor says in Book II of *On the Vandal Persecution*, the son-in-law of the famous Count Boniface, sharp-minded and energetic in war. Geiseric both needed his counsels and feared his presence, and sought an opportunity to destroy him through religion. Sebastian had skillfully foiled Geiseric’s attempts to convert him from the Catholic faith to Arian perfidy by using the analogy of the finest wheat bread: if broken into pieces, soaked in water, and baked again, it becomes worse. Later Geiseric killed him by an argument of another kind. Victor relates this, but does not say by what means or kind of death Sebastian was destroyed. He had been regarded, through the envy of the commanders of the Roman army, as a traitor to the Roman Empire; for this reason he became an exile and went from Spain to Africa to Geiseric [Col. 0600C]. Spondanus, volume I of the *Epitome*, p. 647.]

He returned quickly to Carthage, believing that it would be dangerous for himself and his people if a man skilled in warfare were to devote himself to recovering Carthage. But Sebastian, wishing to appear more a friend than an enemy, found everything in the barbarian’s mind [Note: [Col. 0600C] The codices vary here: some read “among the barbarians,” others “in the barbarian,” and others “in the barbarian’s mind.” Meanwhile, it should be noted that in this entry and elsewhere Geiseric is written both *Geisericus* and *Gensericus* in the various books and authors listed by Pontacus.] quite different from what he had assumed. That hope became for him the chief cause both of his calamity and of his most wretched death.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF CYRUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS.**

The emperor Theodosius undertakes war against the Vandals, sending Areobindus, Anaxilla, and Germanus as commanders with a great fleet [Note: [Col. 0600C] Some manuscripts read “Alriovinda” and “Ausila,” or “Ansila,” “Ausilia,” and “Anaxilia.”]. By delaying the undertaking through long hesitation, they became more a burden to Sicily than a defense of Africa.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF DIOSCORUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, AND EUDOXIUS.**

While the Huns were devastating Thrace and Illyricum with savage destruction, the army that had been stationed in Sicily returned to defend the eastern regions [Note: [Col. 0600C] Some codices read “provinces.”].

Peace with Geiseric was confirmed by Valentinian Augustus, and Africa was divided between the two by fixed boundaries.

Certain nobles of Geiseric conspired against him while he was growing arrogant among his own people over the success of his affairs. But when the plot was discovered, he tortured and killed many of them with various punishments. When it seemed that others too might attempt the same thing, the king’s suspicion brought destruction upon many, so that through this concern for himself he lost more strength than he would have lost if he had been defeated in war.

**UNDER THE SECOND CONSULSHIP OF MAXIMUS AND PATERIUS.**

**749** At this time the diligence of Pope Leo revealed that very many Manichaeans were hiding within the City [Note: [Col. 0600D] Labbe, two Colbertine manuscripts, and the Augustan codex read “through diligence”; elsewhere, “through the diligence.” In the same Labbean Chronicle below: “their disgrace.”]. He had them dragged from their hiding places and exposed before the eyes of the whole Church, and made them both condemn and disclose all the disgracefulness of their doctrine. Their books were burned, great heaps of which had been seized [Col. 0600B]. This care, evidently inspired by God in the holy man, benefited not only the city of Rome but the entire world to a very great degree. For through the confessions of those captured in the City it was revealed who their teachers were, who their bishops or priests were, and in which provinces or cities they lived. Many priests of the eastern regions imitated the diligence of the apostolic ruler.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS XVIII AND ALBINUS.**

This year the Lord’s Pascha was celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, and no error was made. For the day of the Passion fell on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. Out of reverence for it, the birthday of the city of Rome passed without circus games.

[Col. 0600C] Attila, king of the Huns, kills his brother and fellow ruler Bleda and compels his peoples to obey him.

**UNDER THE SIXTH CONSULSHIP OF VALENTINIAN AND NOMO.**

[Note: [Col. 0600D] One Colbertine manuscript reads “Nomo.” Spondanus writes this way on p. 651 and does not allow “Nonio” to be read. Nevertheless, this is how it appears in Labbe’s Chronicle and in the old edition, although the Augustan codex prefers “Nomo.” Pontacus likewise defends our reading there from several manuscripts, the Sicilian Fasti, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, the Capitoline Fasti, Sigonius, and the first session of the Council of Chalcedon. After this point the old edition and one Colbertine manuscript end Prosper’s Chronicle with the words: “Here ends Prosper after Jerome.” Some further material is added in one of the Colbertine manuscripts—and in the Lodève manuscript read by Pontacus—up to the eighth consulship of Valentinian, his death, and the capture of the City by Geiseric. Among these additions are the same things that appear at the end of Prosper of Pithou, in nearly the same wording, beginning with the passage: “After Attila died in his own settlements, great struggles arose among his sons over obtaining the kingdom,” and so forth [Col. 0601C]. From this I conclude with complete certainty,” adds the most illustrious bishop of Vence, “that this codex is not only an authentic copy of Prosper’s Chronicle, since it contains everything that Gennadius formerly described—it begins with Adam and finally ends with Valentinian’s death and the capture of the City by Geiseric—but also that the work of Pithou belongs to another author, who copied certain passages from Prosper’s Chronicle. Our manuscript, or the Ulrician manuscript (which we called the Augustan), and similar manuscripts are for the most part indeed Prosper’s, but were enlarged by others—perhaps by Miletus or Melito, who likewise enlarged Isidore’s Chronicle, or by Tiro himself, whose name it bears—from which two sources Marianus says he made excerpts. This is especially clear in the places that, as we have noted, are absent by agreement from the books. Thus far Arnaldus Pontacus.]

**[Col. 0601A] UNDER THE THIRD CONSULSHIP OF AETIUS AND SYMMACHUS.**

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF CALLEPIUS AND ARDABUR.**

[Note: [Col. 0601D] This is how Labbe’s Chronicle names him. The Colbertine manuscript has “Alibius”; the Augustan codex, “Albius.” Spondanus, under the year 447, has “Alypius,” or “Callipius,” and Ardabur. The following entry is absent from Labbe’s Chronicle but is found in the Colbertine manuscripts and the Augustan.]

[Eutyches, the presbyter and arch-heresiarch of Constantinople, relying on the friendship of Theodosius Augustus, attempted to assert that Christ was not a perfect human being. Flavian, bishop of the same city, took action against him … and was condemned together with his priests, with Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, as the instigator. Against Dioscorus, Pope Leo of the City sent a bishop, a presbyter, and a deacon. Having suffered injury, they reported that Flavian had died in defense of the Catholic faith under the gravest wrongs.]

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF POSTHUMIANUS AND ZENO.**

The emperor Theodosius summons Pope Leo of the City to appear before him in defense of Eutyches. When Leo wished to go, he was prevented by the people, and he sent presbyters and deacons instead. [Col. 0601B]

[Note: [Col. 0601D] The words enclosed here by these two signs, [ ], are entirely absent from Labbe’s codex. They are read, however, in the Colbertine and Augustan manuscripts, with the same lacuna, which we have been unable to fill because of defects in the manuscripts. In Labbe they are represented only by the three consulships printed above, without any other narrative, apart from a fuller account of the Eutychian heresy, which is reported under the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.]

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF ASTURIUS AND PROTOGENES.**

[The Catholics were summoned again to be heard.]

At this time the Eutychian heresy arose, with a certain presbyter named Eutyches as its author. He presided over a very famous monastery at Constantinople and preached that Jesus Christ our Lord, the Son of the blessed Virgin Mary, possessed nothing of his mother’s substance, but that under the appearance of a human being there was in him only the nature of the Word of God. Because he refused to be corrected, he was condemned by Flavian, bishop of the same city. But relying on the royal friendship and the favor of the courtiers, he requested to be heard by a universal synod. The emperor Theodosius agreed and ordered all the bishops to assemble at Ephesus for the reconsideration of this case.

At that council Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, claiming primacy for himself, acquitted Eutyches and pronounced a sentence of condemnation against Flavian, bishop of Constantinople [Col. 0602A]. The Roman deacon Hilary protested; he had been sent by the Apostolic See in place of the holy Pope Leo, together with Julius, bishop of Pozzuoli [Note: [Col. 0601D] In addition to these, Renatus, a presbyter of the title of Saint Clement, had been sent; he died on the island of Delos while on the journey [Col. 0602C]. Dulcitius, Leo’s notary, a man of proven faith, was also attached to them.].

For when all the bishops assembled at the council were compelled by force and fear of the counts or soldiers whom the emperor had assigned to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, to give their assent to this heresy, the aforementioned deacon, placed amid so many dangers to his life, uttered a voice of protest. When they raged against him for this purpose, he secretly withdrew, leaving behind all his belongings, so that through his report he might reveal to the aforesaid pope and to the other priests of Italy how the Catholic faith had been violated there.

But the holy Flavian, in the hands of those by whom he was being led into exile, passed to Christ in a glorious death [Col. 0602B].

**UNDER THE SEVENTH CONSULSHIP OF VALENTINIAN AND AVIENUS.**

With Pope Leo again prevailing, presbyters and deacons were sent to the East to refute the heresy [Note: [Col. 0602C] In this year Saint Leo had sent to Theodosius his fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, and also the presbyters Basil and Senator, through whom, as he says in Letter 52, “you may graciously recognize what our form of faith is, once the instructions we sent have been made known.” That letter makes no mention of deacons. When these men arrived, they found Theodosius already dead.]. In the same year Theodosius Augustus died. [Note: [Col. 0602C]

The following material appears at this point in the Colbertine manuscript and the Augustan codex, while the events are narrated somewhat differently and more fully in Labbe:

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF ADELPHIUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS.**

Theodosius was escorted with great pomp by Placidia, Leo, and the entire senate, and was laid in the mausoleum at Saint Peter’s.

It was announced that, after Theodosius’s death, Marcian was reigning, and that his wife Pulcheria had been made Augusta. By him Eutyches and all his supporters were condemned. The Augustan codex reads: “his wife was made Augusta. By him he was condemned.” The Colbertine manuscript has:

**MARCian, having been made emperor at the age of forty-five, reigned for eight years.**

The Augustan codex reads: “And Marcian was made emperor at the age of forty-seven and reigned for eight years.”]

When the emperor Theodosius had died and the prefect Chrysaphius, who had misused the emperor’s friendship, had been killed, MARCIAN, a most serious man and indispensable not only to the state but also to the Church, assumed the kingdom with the consent of the entire army.

By his edicts, which followed the authority of the Apostolic See, the Ephesian synod was condemned, and it was decreed that an episcopal council should be held at Chalcedon, so that pardon might heal those who had been corrected and the obstinate might be expelled together with their heresy.

Placidia died on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF MARCIAN AUGUSTUS AND FLAVIUS ADELPHIUS.**

[Note: [Col. 0602D] The Colbertine manuscript and the Augustan codex have a shorter version: “A battle was fought in Gaul between Aetius and Attila, king of the Huns, with slaughter on both sides. Attila was driven into Upper Gaul.”]

After the death of his brother, Attila, enriched by the wealth of the man he had killed [Col. 0603A], gathered many thousands of the neighboring peoples into war. He declared that he was making war only on the Goths, as though he were protecting the Roman alliance. But after he crossed the Rhine and many Gallic cities experienced his savage attacks, both our people and the Goths quickly agreed that his fury should be resisted by united armies. Such was the foresight of the patrician Aetius that, having rapidly assembled fighting men from every direction, he met the opposing multitude with a force equal to it. In this conflict, although neither side gave way and immeasurable slaughter of the dying took place, it is nevertheless established that the Chunni were defeated, because those who survived, having lost confidence in battle, returned to their own country.

[Note: [Col. 0603C] The Colbertine manuscript and the Augustan codex read “under Honorius and Aspar.” In the margin of the Augustan edition: “under Herculianus and Asparatius,” or “Sporatius” [Col. 0603D]. The image of the emperor Marcian entered Rome on the third day before the Kalends of April.]

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF HERCULANUS AND SPORATIUS.**

Having restored the strength he had lost in Gaul, Attila intended to enter Italy through Pannonia [Col. 0603B]. Our commander Aetius made no provision according to the conduct of the earlier war, so that he did not even use the Alpine barriers by which the enemy could have been kept out. He thought that the only hope remaining for his people was to withdraw with the emperor from all Italy. But since this appeared full of disgrace and danger, shame restrained fear, and it was believed that the enemy’s savagery and greed had been satisfied by the vast devastation of so many noble provinces. Among all the counsels of the emperor, senate, and Roman people, nothing seemed more salutary than to seek peace from the most savage king through ambassadors.

**752** The blessed Pope Leo undertook this mission together with the consular Avienus and the former prefect Trigetius, relying on the help of God, whom he knew never to have failed the labors of the faithful. The outcome was no different from what faith had anticipated. For the king received the entire embassy graciously and rejoiced so much at the presence of the supreme priest that he ordered the war to cease and departed beyond the Danube after promising peace.

[Note: [Col. 0603D] The Colbertine manuscript and the Augustan codex read “under Opilio and Vincemalus”; in the margin, “Vincomalus, consul.” In the letters Saint Leo wrote that year he mentions only Opilio; both, however, are cited in Dissertation 1, *On the Life and Deeds of Saint Leo the Great*, p. 312, volume II of the new edition of his works.]

**UNDER THE CONSULSHIP OF OPILIO, VIR CLARISSIMUS.**

The Council of Chalcedon was completed, and Eutyches and Dioscorus were condemned. All who had withdrawn from them were received into communion, and the faith concerning the incarnation of the Word, preached by the holy Pope Leo according to evangelical and apostolic teaching, was universally confirmed.

[Col. 0604A] After Attila had died in his own dwelling, serious disputes first arose among his sons over securing the kingdom; then the defection of several peoples who had been subject to the Huns followed, providing causes and occasions for wars in which the fiercest peoples were to be crushed by mutual attacks.

Among the Goths settled within Gaul, disagreement arose between the sons of King Theodoric, whose eldest son Thorismodus had succeeded his father. And when the king was undertaking measures opposed both to Roman peace and to Gothic tranquillity, he was killed by his own brothers because he persisted unalterably in his harmful designs.

## Under the consulship of Aetius and Studio

[Note: [Col. 0603D] The same events are recorded in fewer words in the Colbertine manuscript and in the edition of the Augustan codex: “That year the patricians Aetius and Boethius were killed. At Carthage, Deogratias was ordained bishop in the Basilica of Faustus on Sunday, the eighth day before the Kalends of November.”]

Between the emperor Valentinian Augustus and the patrician Aetius, after the pledges of mutual fidelity and the agreement to unite their children in marriage, a dreadful enmity grew strong. What should have increased the favor of affection instead kindled the fuel of hatred, with the eunuch Heraclius—as was believed—as its instigator. He had so bound the emperor’s mind to himself through insincere service that he could easily drive him toward whatever he wished.

When Heraclius therefore persuaded the emperor that everything concerning Aetius was ominous, it was believed that the emperor’s safety could be served by forestalling the enemy’s schemes through his own action. Thus Aetius, while pressing his requests more insistently and pleading his son’s case with greater agitation, was cruelly cut down by the emperor’s hand and by the swords of those standing around him. Boethius, the praetorian prefect, who was closely attached to him by a long friendship, was killed at the same time.

[Note: [Col. 0603D] Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, and after him the author of the *Miscellany*, book XV, report that Aetius was killed by the emperor’s own hand and Boethius by those standing around him. Procopius, however, in *The Vandalic War*, book I, says that Aetius, although absent, was ordered to be killed. He relates at greater length that this happened because of the false accusation of Petronius Maximus, a Roman senator descended from that Maximus the tyrant whom the elder Theodosius had overthrown. After Valentinian had violated Maximus’s wife—of exceptional beauty and equally exceptional chastity—Maximus, considering revenge, first judged that Aetius, the bravest commander and the man in whom the Romans chiefly placed their hope, had to be removed. He therefore made Aetius suspect to the emperor Augustus by means of the imperial eunuchs, as though he were aspiring to the empire. What Maximus attempted against Valentinian himself after Aetius had been removed will be related in the following year. Spondanus, volume I of the *Epitome*, under the year of Christ 454, p. 674.]

## Under the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius

Aetius’s death was followed not long afterward by Valentinian’s death. Valentinian had failed to avoid it with sufficient prudence, since he had associated with himself Aetius’s friends and armed retainers. They secretly watched for an opportunity to carry out the crime they had conceived. When the emperor had gone outside the City and was occupied with the exercise of riding, they stabbed him with unexpected blows. Heraclius, who was close by, was killed at the same time, and no one from the imperial crowd was stirred to avenge so great a crime.

[Note: [Col. 0604D]

For all these events and those that follow, the Colbertine manuscript and the Lyon edition of the Augustan, or Ulrician, codex read:

“Valentinian himself was killed at the Two Laurels on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April. Petronius Maximus was raised up as emperor; he was killed on the seventy-second day and dragged through the City.

Geiseric entered Rome, carried off its spoils, and returned to Carthage. After several days Avitus was raised to the empire.”]

When this parricide had been committed, MAXIMUS, [Col. 0605A] a man who had held two consulships and possessed patrician rank, assumed the empire. Although he was believed to be capable of benefiting the endangered state in every respect, he soon demonstrated by his conduct what sort of mind he possessed. He not only failed to punish Valentinian’s murderers but also received them into his friendship; and he compelled Valentinian’s wife, who had been forbidden to mourn the loss of her husband, to enter his marriage within a very few days.

But he did not long enjoy this lack of restraint. For after the second month, when the arrival of King Geiseric from Africa was announced,

[Note: [Col. 0605B] Procopius, *The Vandalic War*, book I, relates that Eudoxia summoned Geiseric, wishing to avenge upon Maximus the death of her husband Valentinian.]

and when many nobles and commoners were fleeing from the City, Maximus himself also wished to depart in alarm after granting everyone permission to leave. On the seventy-seventh day after he had gained the empire, he was torn to pieces by imperial servants, thrown limb by limb into the Tiber, and [Col. 0605B] denied even burial.

After Maximus’s end, the Roman captivity, worthy of many tears, immediately followed. Genseric seized the City, which was entirely without defenses. Outside the gates, holy Bishop Leo met him; through Leo’s supplication, with God’s aid, he was so restrained that, although the city had been handed over to him and everything lay within his power, Genseric nevertheless refrained from fire, slaughter, and torture.

For fourteen days, therefore, Rome was emptied of all its possessions through secure and unrestricted plundering, and many thousands of captives were taken to Carthage, together with the queen and her daughters, according to the preferences of each captor with respect to age or skill.

That same year the Lord’s Pascha was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, through the persistent insistence of the bishop of Alexandria, with whom all the Easterners thought they ought to agree, although holy Pope Leo protested that it should rather be observed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Note: [Col. 0605B] Bucherius inserts the following in the *Paschal Cycle of Victorius*, chapter 3: “In which neither in the calculation of the full moon nor in the limit of the first month had there been any error.” Nevertheless, it would not be unreasonable to suppose that these words were a marginal note added by a learned annotator. For these words are not found in the manuscripts of Sirmond or Chifflet, from which Duchesne published that fuller version of the Chronicle. See Dissertation 1, *On the Life and Works of St. Leo*, pp. 326 ff., volume II of the new edition of the works of St. Leo the Great. There one will observe that on this occasion the Westerners first began to investigate the date of Easter and to calculate more carefully the movements of the sun and moon. Among the Latins, an emulation arose, and they were no longer willing to endure the Alexandrians’ imposing the date of Easter upon them as a law. Prosper of Aquitaine, who was then staying at Rome with Pope Leo, also composed his own cycle. His witnesses are Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 88, where he speaks of Victorius of Aquitaine, and Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 17—unless it had already been published by him for the year 444, when a similar difficulty had occurred. In any event, there is no doubt that Leo’s correspondence with him prompted its composition. That cycle has now perished. Certainly, since he writes somewhat more sharply about the Easter of this year 455, with which he closes his Chronicle, it appears that he himself argued for his position.]

Letters of that same pope to the most merciful emperor Marcian are extant. In them the reason for the disputed truth is clearly set forth, and the Catholic Church can learn from them that this practice was tolerated for the sake of unity and peace rather than approved, and that it must never afterward be imitated—so that what brought a destructive offense may forever lose all authority.

[Col. 0605]

# APPENDIX TO THE CHRONICLE OF PROSPER OF AQUITAINE (C)

## Note

755 Since, in the codex that we call the Augustan, but which Pithaeus cited in his notes on Eusebius’s *Chronicle* under the title “Ulrician,” certain materials are appended that are also found in manuscript 240 of the Colbertine Library, and since they extend beyond the limits assigned to Prosper’s *Chronicle* by Gennadius in his *Catalogue*, chapter 84, under Prosper—concerning which more is said in the admonition, which may be consulted if desired—we have thought that they should be printed here, though in smaller type. They present the condition of the Vandal kingdom for a number of years after the Vandals captured Rome. In these same books, however, three consulships are prefixed to them, following the final consulship of Valentinian VIII, which ended with his death.

## Under the consulship of Varane and John

## Under the consulship of Constantine and Rufus

## Under the consulship of Ardabur and Maximian

After the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus, Geiseric, king of the Vandals, entered Carthage [Col. 0605D] on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] In the Colbertine manuscript: “He ruled that same African city for twenty-seven years.”]

He ruled that same African city for thirty-eight years, three months, and six days.

After him his son Huneric ruled for seven years, ten months, [Note: [Col. 0606D] In the Colbertine manuscript: “twenty-eight days.”] and eighteen days. At the end of the seventh year of his reign, he persecuted the Catholic Church, closed all the churches, and sent all the Catholic priests of the Lord into exile, together with Eugenius, bishop of Carthage. By God’s judgment, he ended his life covered with worms.

After him ruled Guntamund, son of Gentunis, the brother of the same King Huneric, for eleven years, nine months, and eleven days.

[Note: [Col. 0606D] Elsewhere: “Gundabund, son of Gento,” or “son of Genzo.”]

In the third year of his reign, he ordered the cemetery of the holy martyr Agileus near Carthage to be given to the Catholics. Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, had already been recalled from exile by him. In the tenth year of his reign, he opened the Catholic churches and, at the request of Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, recalled all the priests of God from exile.

Those churches had been closed for eleven years, six months, and five days—that is, from the eighth year of Huneric, namely from the seventh day before the Ides of February, [Col. 0607A] until the tenth year of King Guntamund, on the fourth day before the Ides of August. At that point the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0607B] Perhaps “eleven years.”] ten years, six months, and five days were completed. The aforementioned King Guntamund afterward lived for two years and one month.

After him Trasamund, son of Gento, ruled for twenty-six years, eight months, and four days.

Therefore, from the beginning of Avitus’s reign until the twenty-seventh year of Trasamund, [Note: [Col. 0607B] This lacuna is not supplied from the Colbertine manuscript, which has the twenty-sixth year rather than the twenty-seventh somewhat earlier.] [lacuna] eighteen. From the fourteenth year of the reign and death of Valens until Trasamund’s twenty-fifth year, there are 118 years.

After him ruled Hildric, Huneric’s son, for [Col. 0607B] eight years and eight days. At the beginning of his reign he ordered Boniface to be ordained bishop at Carthage in the Church of Saint Agileus, and restored liberty to all Catholics.

While he was reigning, Geilamer seized his kingdom by usurpation and held it for three years and three months.

[Note: [Col. 0608B] The Colbertine manuscript reads: “He committed.”]

As a criminal, he committed so many murders that he did not even spare his own parents.

Thus, from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0608B] The Colbertine manuscript reads: “of King.”] of King Geiseric until the end of the Vandals, there were ninety-three years, ten months, and eleven days. From the death of Valens in the fourteenth year of his reign until the time mentioned above, there were 154 years. The total sum of all the years from Adam until the destruction of the Vandals is therefore 5,733 years.

# THE SECOND PART OF ALL THE WORKS OF SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITAINE, CONTAINING WORKS OF UNCERTAIN AUTHORITY ATTRIBUTED TO THE HOLY FATHER

## Confession

[Col. 0607]

## Admonition concerning the following short work

Concerning this short work, first published by Sirmond under the title *Confession of Prosper of Aquitaine*, and also found in the Joliensis manuscript among the other works of Saint Prosper, the often-mentioned Joseph Antelmius, priest and canon of Fréjus, expresses the following judgment in the book he titled *Critical Dissertations on the Genuine Works of the Holy Fathers Leo the Great and Prosper of Aquitaine*, Dissertation 7, “On Writings and Treatises Attributed to Saint Prosper,” p. 370:

“What remains, besides those works attributed to Prosper, is that I have not noticed any other writings of reputation or renown circulating under his name. There does indeed exist the *Confession of Prosper Tiro*, first published by Jacques Sirmond in 1619 from the Vatican Library, after the poems of Eugenius and Dracontius. Yet in it one can scarcely detect anything sufficiently similar to Prosper’s style or very consistent with his reputation—enough to justify spending much effort in defending its attribution to him.”

In this judgment Antelmius is entirely supported by the celebrated and learned author of the *New Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*, part II of volume III, which concerns the writers of the fifth century of the Church, p. 451, under Prosper. He calls that *Confession* “a work of no importance and unworthy of so great a Father.”

Another writer, highly skilled in ecclesiastical monuments, thought somewhat better of this little work and judged it to be written elegantly enough to be attributed to the great Prosper. Nevertheless, he reached no definite conclusion: he did not dare wholly to reject the authority of the following booklet, but he also refused to accept it as an indisputably genuine offspring of our Prosper.

Amid such divergent judgments by the wisest critics, we were even less permitted to make any definitive decision. It seemed safer, therefore, to count this composition among Prosper’s doubtful works, though not among those certainly spurious.

[Col. 0607]

# CONFESSION SAID TO BE BY SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITAINE (C, G, S)

[Col. 0607C] 769 Once I was born under the law of sin, and, having been made captive through the ordinary condition of death transmitted from my parents,

[Note: [Col. 0607C] The Joliensis manuscript reads: “of ordinary death.”]

so that I might not be held for long under the authority of my savage lord, at the very beginning of my life you, merciful and compassionate Lord, set me free. I found the tyrant-slayer before I had experienced the tyrant,

[Note: [Col. 0607C] The Joliensis manuscript adds: “before I had experienced the tyrant; and I obtained redemption before I understood servitude.”]

and I obtained redemption before I understood servitude.

Let those who wish complain about the speed of their salvation; let them plead their inexperienced age and thoughtless years as an excuse for their violated rebirth. For me, your swift favor and hastened mercy will always be worshiped. For I understand that, though I was unaware, this one thing benefited me: although I withdrew from your gifts, your gifts nevertheless remained in me.

Thus reborn in Christ Jesus through your Holy Spirit, enrolled as an heir and called a son, I received nothing less than the elder brother received. Indeed, once the burden of legal observance had been removed, initiated by grace, I became your Israel—not from Jacob, but from Esau.

Happy indeed would I have been if I had preserved the substance I received—not, I do not say increased, but at least kept whole—even through inactive innocence, if I could not do so through active virtue. But, alas, wretched me! I left my Father’s house and went away as a voluntary deserter into exile. Led by the multitude of all vices, and deceived by the downward paths of long journeys, I entered the innermost places of Egypt.

There, after the robe of beauty had been worn away and the garment of nobility corrupted, crafty companions and faithless friends sold me, poor and squanderer of my paternal goods, beneath the auctioneer’s spear of death and at the auction of sin to the most eager bidders.

Worn down under their long and heavy domination, I even passed under Babylonian rule. There, amid countless changes of savage dominations, while I served not with bodily submission but with the sweat of my soul, and while I was confounded by duties suited to me and daily disturbed by the worsening condition of my state, I withdrew, as far as my pressing masters allowed, into the hidden refuge of my spirit and heart.

I seized a volume of the Holy Scriptures and examined what hope might still remain for me. Bathed in a great shower of tears, I said: “How long will those who hate me dominate me? How long will I serve my enemies?”

I had indeed given myself to these people and received the price of my destruction through deadly pleasures; but I could not bargain away my own person by my own right. For I had a master, and I did not belong to myself. I know that I was redeemed by the blood of him to whom heavenly, earthly, and infernal things are subject.

What have these people to do with me, whose commerce is death? I will return to him who bought me for life.

And so that the opportunity to return might not be delayed, because I am in the midst of a foreign people and a barbarian guards the boundaries of his kingdom with arranged watch posts,

[Note: [Col. 0610B] The Joliensis manuscript reads: “guards.”]

it is well that those who hold my Redeemer, who holds all things, do not hold places. He is present in heaven and in the underworld; he is wholly in the abyss and wholly on earth. He is not to be approached by a journey or sought by sailing.

We left him in Jerusalem; we passed him by in Egypt; among the Babylonians we do not see him. But let us seek, and he will appear; let us knock, and he will open; let us ask, and he will grant.

But, alas, wretched me! I am ashamed because I am naked and have nothing with which to cover the indecency of my limbs. I am overwhelmed by the disgrace of shameful poverty. With what face, and with what conscience, shall I appear before the eyes of so great a household and of so great a Father?

As though judgment were more tolerable for those accused than for those who confess, for defiant defendants than for suppliants, for those who are displayed than for those who return! Let the shame of the cross have as many penances as it may; the fire of embarrassment will be lighter than that of Gehenna.

# Poem

[Col. 0609]

## Admonition concerning the poem “A Husband to His Wife”

It has already been observed by others that the Anacreontic poem to his wife, in which its author urges his wife to dedicate herself wholly to God, cannot be counted among works falsely attributed to Prosper under a spurious title, but neither can it be counted among his certain and indisputable works. We have therefore judged that it should be placed among the doubtful works.

There is certainly reason to doubt whether it is Prosper’s. Rosweydus, a man of uncommon learning, rejected this work from Prosper, under whose name it had previously been read, and attributed it to Saint Paulinus of Nola in his edition of Paulinus’s works, apparently after examining the evidence.

But the most recent editor and commentator of Paulinus’s works, no less learned than exact, strongly disagrees with him in volume II, Dissertation 6. Although he admits that this poem approaches the style of Paulinus of Nola and his language in several passages of his poems, he nevertheless, having made the reader judge, does not hesitate to assert that the poem, though excellent and most pleasing, flows more sweetly and freely than Paulinus’s other poems.

He then adds:

“But what can remove this poem from Paulinus is precisely that it describes the whole world amid that general upheaval and confusion of affairs which the empire of the West experienced in the year 407. At that time, however, it was not necessary for Paulinus to exhort himself and his wife to Christian living or to prescribe how they should use their possessions. Arbogastus caused great disturbances in the West when, on 15 May 392, he ordered the younger Valentinian to be strangled and placed the diadem upon Eugenius. But the poem gives no outline of this event.”

Thus far the commentator on Paulinus, who aptly observes that, given the times when the Roman Empire was oppressed and shaken by such great assaults, Paulinus would not have needed to urge his most holy wife Therasia toward similar things, since she had long before entered upon the path of Christian perfection as an imitator of her spouse—unless someone should say that it is not useless sometimes to admonish even one who is already running.

The same author also declares that he is prevented from attributing the poem to Paulinus because, as he says, it is assigned to Prosper in four manuscript codices and to Paulinus in none, and because its historical setting entirely fails to correspond to Paulinus. This consideration is so weighty that he does not dare recognize it as the offspring of Paulinus.

To the testimony of these four manuscripts, which Antelmius had not himself seen, he adds in Dissertation 9 on the works of Leo and Prosper a fifth manuscript, which he had in his hands. He judged it to have been written approximately eight hundred years earlier and to be of excellent quality. He testifies that it had been sent from the city of Marseille—where Prosper’s memory was more renowned and cherished—to Aix, where Antelmius was then living, and that it had been kept in the library of the distinguished senator Thomassinus. When he arrived there, it could not have remained unknown to him; indeed, he says that he obtained it from the owner of that extensive library, together with many other works and among numerous aids.

This codex contained nothing but Prosper’s epigrams, preceded by sayings excerpted from him. In that codex, after ninety-seven epigrams on restraining anger and related subjects, the text ended with this verse:

> Crescere non cupiens perdit adepta tepens,

“Lukewarm, unwilling to grow, he loses what he has gained.”

Immediately afterward came the Anacreontic meter, from the words “Come now, I beg, of my…” to “for whom it was a delight to seize souls.” Here the verses ended, and the page and the entire codex concluded with the words: “The book ends.”

Thus the hexameters interspersed with pentameters that others transmit, ingeniously joined to these iambics by a continuous sequence of ideas, are absent from this codex. Such a practice is not foreign to Prosper: he is known to have varied his extremely famous poem *Against the Ungrateful* through two series of verses, for he sang differently in the prologue and in the poem.

[Col. 0611] Moreover, what appears to the learned man entirely inconsistent with Paulinus’s history may perhaps fit Prosper’s person more suitably. The circumstances of time and events described in the poem under discussion could more appropriately belong to Prosper, since toward the end of the fourth century and the beginning of the following one the concerns of Christian piety may first have affected him deeply enough for him to urge his wife—if indeed he had ever lived as a married man—by the incentives of such sweet counsels.

Bede’s testimony at the end of his book *On the Art of Meter* also supports this attribution. He explicitly assigns the poem to Prosper Tiro:

> “The Anacreontic meter used by Prosper Tiro at the beginning of his exhortation to his wife, as follows: ‘Come now, I beg,’ and so forth.”

But, if the aforementioned most learned critic is to be believed, these poems are not entirely without Prosperian features. They are full of Prosper’s chaste sentiments, sincerely express his genuine feelings, and often display the same expressions. Yet, although he eagerly wishes to vindicate for Prosper every work that can be claimed for him with some foundation, he does not dare to make any definite judgment about this poem after the judgment of others has, as it were, restrained and suppressed the matter. He admits that his own mind still remains undecided.

For although the poem is recognized as somewhat more polished and elegant than Prosper’s other poetic writings, it nevertheless retains the circumstances of the period in which it must have been composed. Since it is evidently arranged at the beginning of his conversion, when our Aquitanian was less accustomed and devoted to heavenly things, his more youthful spirit, seeking art and elegance, could have pursued this refinement, which he might later, when more mature and holier, have rejected or neglected.

After weighing these considerations, while awaiting a better judgment from others who can examine the whole matter at greater leisure, he remains suspended and undecided. After this fluctuation among the learned, what could be safer for us, and more free from any charge of rashness, than to present this work neither among Prosper’s genuine works nor among the spurious works attributed to him, but among the doubtful ones?

[Col. 0611]

# POEM ON DIVINE PROVIDENCE

[Col. 0615]

## Admonition concerning the poem on divine providence
[Note: Since the poem *On Divine Providence* is not to be counted without reservation among the genuine works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, yet is not immediately to be numbered among the spurious, the differing judgments of learned men concerning it advise caution.]

Although it first appeared under the name of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine in the Lyon edition of 1539, it was for a long time published by other editors of Saint Prosper’s works with this qualification: it was to be carefully observed that this poem did not seem to be Prosper’s, but rather the work of someone who did not fully explain the grace of Christ. We read this observation in the older editions: the Louvain edition of 1565, prepared through the efforts of John Sotellus, alumnus of the Louvain theological college; then the Douai edition of 1576, completed by the labors of John Olivarius, which the Cologne edition of 1630 and those that followed copied word for word.

In that Douai edition, however, the most learned editor, in his letter to the reader, when he compiled a catalogue of the works he had corrected and was publishing and briefly stated his judgment concerning each, pronounced as follows concerning the work now before us:

> “We have judged that the poem *On the Providence of God* should be removed from the works of Prosper, because it is Pelagian in doctrine, whereas Prosper was that doctrine’s most determined enemy. For it teaches that the best person receives no more grace than the worst; that the holy fathers were good by the law of nature; that God’s help is preceded by our will; and many other things consonant with Pelagius’s error, which Saint Prosper never approved.
>
> “Nor is it a new occurrence”—he adds—“that works of heretics are inserted among the writings of great men. For among the books attributed to Jerome we find both Pelagius’s letter to Demetrias and brief commentaries on all Paul’s Epistles except the one to the Hebrews; likewise Celestius’s letter to his parent on knowledge of the divine law; also the letter concerning the two sons, the frugal and the prodigal—not the one addressed to Damasus, but the one beginning, ‘Of all things indeed from the Scriptures,’ and so forth—and many other works that need not be listed here.

“In the same way, among Augustine’s works there slipped in the book *Questions of the Old and New Testament*, which among other things asserts that Melchizedek was the Holy Spirit and the high priest; for this reason it was rightly rejected by Saint Jerome in his letter to Evagrius.

“By the same error”—he continues—“Gennadius’s book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* is attributed to Augustine. Since it is not sufficiently Catholic, some zealous person appended to it several chapters from Celestine’s first letter and the second Council of Orange, namely chapters 22, 29, and those that follow. Although these seem to belong to the same book, they are found omitted in some copies, both printed and manuscript; and they expressly contradict chapter 21 of that same book, so that anyone who gives the matter even a little consideration will immediately see that they were appended solely to refute it.

“For this reason”—he concludes—“the poem *On Providence* also seems to have been attached to the poem *Against the Ungrateful*, so that, if it were read separately and proved harmful, it would not lack an antidote.”

So he wrote.

Bellarminus agrees with the judgment of both men in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. In it that eminent and learned author judged that this work should be attributed to a semi-Pelagian rather than to Saint Prosper. The author of the new *Bibliotheca of Ecclesiastical Writers*, part II of volume III, likewise, while making nearly the same objections as those stated above against the parent poem, specifically notes that these are the very doctrines Prosper attacked both in his own poem *Against the Ungrateful* and in his other works. Even if one accepts, with the author of the *Dissertation on the Works of Saint Prosper*, that this writer sought certain advantages from Saint Augustine’s doctrine, he insists that it is scarcely credible that so great a man could have deviated so far as, having apparently forgotten his earlier writings, to defend here what elsewhere he had attacked with all his strength.

And so that readers might not remain unaware which passages in this work chiefly displeased the critics mentioned above, beginning with the Louvain edition they were marked in the margin by a double stroke as deserving correction; we have likewise decided to preserve that marking. Although, according to the more charitable judgment of some, these and similar passages scattered throughout the work *On the Providence of God* may at least in part be accommodated to the standard of Catholic doctrine, scarcely all of them can be consistently reduced to Prosperian ideas, according to Antelmius’s judgment (*Dissertation 9, On the True Works of the Holy Fathers Leo and Prosper*). For our Aquitanian saint sometimes took care to express his mind differently concerning the natural possibility of free choice and concerning the remnant of the seed of virtue after sin.

Hence some have sought another author for this work. Among them, Henry Noris, in book II, chapter 13 of his *Pelagian History*, suspected Hilary of Arles of having written the poem, since it is plainly semi-Pelagian. But if this were as obvious as that learned man thinks, his suspicion should be rejected all the more, since Hilary, on the contrary, cannot be proved by any sound testimony to have passed over to the side of the semi-Pelagians, as Antelmius demonstrated elsewhere in *The Secrets of the Lerins*.

As for investigating the author of this poem, nothing beyond this can be suspected in favor of Hilary from Gennadius, the chronicler of writers of his own time. For after saying of Hilary in chapter 69 of his *Catalogue*, “Without respect of persons, he inflicted correction upon all,”—as the manuscript codex of the Benedictine Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, written on parchment a thousand years ago, reads—whereas other printed and manuscript copies have, “Without exception or respect of persons, he inflicted upon all the corrected work of preaching,” which does not make the meaning so clear and agrees less well with what follows, after reporting these words, I say, the presbyter of Marseille reports that Hilary published only a few and minor works. Of these he mentions only the *Life of Saint Honoratus of Arles* as the principal one.

But the other Honoratus, namely Honoratus of Marseille, testifies in his *Life of Hilary* that, besides many excellent and copious monuments of his genius, Hilary also composed verses on the burning spring. The aforementioned Antelmius thinks that this praise can suitably be applied to these verses *On Providence*. “And perhaps,” he adds, “it would not be so easy to guess why Gennadius did not mention them, if he had clearly recognized both their meaning and their semi-Pelagian author.”

The same most learned critic nevertheless warns that these poems must be read cautiously in certain places; yet he considers them not unworthy of a pious and learned man, and one scarcely inferior to Hilary. Apart from these few points, he finds the author’s views like those of the anonymous Prosper: in this work he observes both ideas and words familiar to Prosper and expressions resembling Prosperian usage.

For this reason Labbeus, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, although the poem was attached to the *Against the Ungrateful* by John Hessels and John Olivarius—as has already been noted—not because it was originally thought to be Prosper’s, but so that an immediate remedy might be provided for the poison, nevertheless leans toward believing that, from the Prosperian features which he thinks he recognized in this work, the copyists were initially deceived and undoubtedly ascribed it to our Aquitanian. They did so with nearly the same carelessness by which they did not hesitate to attribute to him other treatises more opposed to that style, even though the work is said to have been recognized by Hincmar as Prosperian; and this indeed supports the older opinion.

The occasion for that opinion may have been that the writer flourished in Prosper’s age and, in scattered passages of his poem, touched upon the invasions of the Vandals and Getae, or Goths, into our land—events of which Saint Prosper was both witness and narrator in his *Chronicles*.

Considering all these matters more attentively, the aforementioned critic, and observing that at that time there was no writer of any reputation in Gaul—where these events chiefly occurred—suited to composing this poem, would readily attribute the work to our Prosper, were he not compelled from other evidence to acknowledge how greatly this poem differs from the most precise doctrines of Saint Prosper. Therefore, until a greater light emerges from the examination and judgment of more learned critics, he thought he should refrain from passing judgment on the matter. We too subscribe to his view in this respect.

But when our Gaul had groaned for ten full years beneath the calamities described here—calamities into which the barbarians had burst toward the end of the year 406—the author, who had previously been accustomed to exercise his poetic talent by writing poems, was delayed from writing because he bore no small part of the public misery. At last, apparently in the year 416, he again girded himself to the work so long interrupted. From this you may readily determine the age of the work.

[Col. 0617]

[Note: [Col. 0617C] Written around the year of Christ 416.]

# POEM ON DIVINE PROVIDENCE (C, G)

[Col. 0617A] 785

## CHAPTER I, OR PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 0617C] The author, delayed from writing verses by public calamities and compelled by complaining voices, undertakes to defend divine providence. What troubled people most was that even the innocent age and the sacred places themselves had felt the fury of the enemy. The author himself was brought under the power of the enemy while his city was burning. Even in peacetime the good groan and the wicked rejoice. Thus divine providence is assailed.]

Most of the year has already passed in months,

Since no page has been written in your verse.

What causes have brought you such prolonged silence?

What grief weighs down your sorrowful talent?

[5] Although poems are not absent even from grievous cares,

And sad hearts have their own modes of expression;

And if the world’s shattered wounds pierce you,

And the sea bears you, disturbed, upon a single vessel,

You ought to preserve an unconquered vigor for your studies.

[10] Why fear what is destined to endure, if falling things collapse?

O happy the one to whom, by God’s gift, such ability

Has been granted that he may act freely in such a time!

Who would not be shaken by the ruin of a neighboring disaster,

Unafraid amid flames and amid waters?

[15] But we, beneath so great a storm of evils,

Are struck down and fall, helpless everywhere.

When the image of our smoking homeland entered my mind,

And whatever is perishing everywhere stood before my eyes,

We are broken, and bathe our faces in excessive tears;

[20] And while we act as pious men, we are turned into complainers.

Some do not refrain from attacking the troubled mind;

They strike wounded hearts with the arrows of their tongues.

“Tell us,” they say, “the reasons, you who believe

That the hardships of things and men stand and are ruled

By the will of God:

[25] “What crime was committed, that so many cities perished together?

So many places, so many peoples—what evil had they deserved?”

[Col. 0617C] If Ocean had poured itself across all the fields of Gaul,

More water would have remained than is now there;

For surely cattle are lacking, and seeds of grain,

[30] And there is no place for vines or olive trees;

And the force of fire and rain has taken away the buildings of estates,

Of which it is more grievous to see some still standing empty.

If the stain of evil must be endured—alas!—after a decade of slaughter,

We have been laid low by Vandal and Gothic swords.

[35] Neither fortresses set upon rocks, nor towns placed upon high mountains,

Nor cities beside broad-flowing rivers,

Were able to overcome the barbarian treachery

And the weapons of their fury. We have endured the uttermost extremities.

Nor shall I complain that the common people were extinguished without distinction;

[40] Let death itself cease to be accused of envy toward the foremost.

Perhaps our elders and an age more wicked than ours

Bore what they deserved from an offended God.

But what of innocent children? What did the girls do,

Whom brief life had given no crimes?

[45] Why was it permitted that the temples of God be plundered by fire?

Why were the vessels of sacred service violated?

[Col. 0618B] The honor of unmarried women devoted to virginity

Did not protect them, nor the love of religious devotion protect widows.

Even those who had been accustomed to spend their lives in deserted caves,

Praising God night and day,

Suffered no different death from that of any unbeliever:

The same storm swept away the good and the wicked.

No reverence for the priests’ venerable name

Distinguished them from the punishments of the suffering people:

[55] Thus they were struck with harsh whips, thus burned by fire,

Thus their hands enclosed in chains groaned.

You too, amid the dust, wagons, and weapons of the Goths,

Were making your difficult journey, not without your burden,

When that holy old man, driven from the burned city,

[60] Like a shepherd in exile led forth the wounded sheep.

But let these events be silenced beneath the storm of war,

Since there was no order amid the confusion of evils.

Perhaps divine care may deign to look upon

The peaceful affairs of the world and the times of peace.

[65] If we recall all the years of our ancient ancestors

And everything that our own age has been able to see,

The greatest place in the world will be found to belong to the unjust,

While scarcely any portion remains for the oppressed good.

Whoever has been violent, savage, crafty, or greedy,

[70] Whose heart has cast faith aside and whose mouth has cast shame,

Everyone admires, loves, reveres, and honors him;

To him are given the highest offices, to him wealth.

But if someone is just and has preferred to lead

A chaste and blameless life with a different devotion,

[75] He lives dishonored and poor, hated by young and old,

An exile in every region of the world.

[Col. 0619B] 789 The impious rejoices, sound throughout his allotted years;

The terrible sores of the righteous never cease to be cut open.

Falsehoods prevail in the courts, while truths struggle;

Punishment pursues the innocent, and safety the guilty.

[80] The adulteress, unknown to the pious rites, mocks them;

The blasphemer safely approaches the threshold of the temple.

If God’s care looked down from its lofty citadel

And directed our affairs under its authority,

Either crimes deserving vengeance would not escape punishment,

[85] Or virtue alone would be found upon the earth.

When such things are easily scattered into the ears of the crowd,

How many uneducated people are harmed by a malicious tongue!

Nor is it such a great grief to be consumed by Scythian weapons

As it is for these things to be sown by faithless hearts.

[90] Therefore draw heavenly weapons from the holy quivers,

And strike down the enemy with healing wounds.

Perhaps some may escape the night of error

And, seeing the light, set their feet again upon the road.

But lest the speech suffer delay from an unequal verse,

Add the pentameter to the heroic meter.

## CHAPTER II

[Note: [Col. 0619D] All have always perceived that God exists and is the author of everything; that he arranged all things as he willed, but wisely.]

These matters would better be learned from books composed by divine authority,

Where, upon the open expanse of the law,

It would be easy to spread free sails before favorable winds.

[100] But since the uneducated fear entering the deep,

Let them first learn to run upon a shallow stream,

Where the land lies encircled by the outermost sea,

And where the human race is spread across the body of the world.

Whether you review our own years or ancient times,

[105] All have perceived that God exists; and nature, teaching the Author,

Has failed no one. Even if impious error

Lost him by assigning to many what was owed to one,

It is innate in all to recognize the true Father.

He remains the same, without an author and without beginning in time,

[110] Always; neither ages nor places enclose the immense one.

When no causes of the world yet existed, he alone,

Possessing within himself whatever he wished, when he saw fit,

Created all things as he willed, establishing forms,

Numbers, measures, kinds, lives, and the seeds of things.

[Col. 0620A] Whatever exists in heaven, whatever on earth or in the sea,

Whatever exists in any body, whether living

Or without life, hot, moist, cold, or dry,

All exists from the one Author, God. By his rich Word,

Which is God, the Craftsman brought forth

[120] The natures of things and the elements, attentive to the highest and the lowest alike.

But because created things struggle with opposing causes,

And one thing resists another, discordant opposition

Sustains all movement; and while one thing encounters another,

All things, driven into motion, receive vital vigor—

[125] Things that would otherwise perish through sluggish stagnation,

Through slippery downward falling, unstable motion,

Or stable torpor.

Thus soft things resist hard, dense things rare,

[Col. 0620B] Solid things liquid, swift things slow;

Bright contends with darkness, and bitter with sweet.

[130] Nor is it lawful for me to say that anything was created improperly,

Nor would I dare to criticize any part of the world,

Since that Sower of works holds the moments of his own creations

And adapts their various uses, portion by portion, into a whole.

In the end, whatever is harmful becomes beneficial,

[135] Either when its cause or its circumstance is changed;

And all things stand amid a twofold danger.

After suffering cold, one longs for the sun;

Burned by heat, another prefers to shiver amid northern frosts.

The traveler fears rain beneath his unjust burden,

While the farmer, whose field is thirsty, begs for it in his prayers.

[140] It is frightening for one to see blue serpents;

For another, an unafraid mind is burdened with roasted water-snakes.

But if perhaps you dislike wolves, lynxes, and bears as created things,

Look toward the princes of Scythia and the kings of the Goths;

For them, having rejected purple and Chinese wool,

[145] It is an exceptional adornment to bristle in the hides of wild beasts.

It would take too long to pursue each thing individually;

But through Christ’s gift we have learned that whatever the earth nourishes,

Whatever lives in the sea,

Whatever varies among trees and herbs,

[150] Exists by appointed causes to the praise of its Author.

And the very things that cause harm, when properly combined, heal.

## CHAPTER III

[Note: [Col. 0620D] God governs without weariness the world he created. One must not judge his government as one judges human government.

[Col. 0621D] 190. The Lyon edition reads, “Nor does it need obvious things to be taught for recognition.” Here *obvious* is used in place of *certain*, as earlier editions noted.]

God exists, therefore, and he is good; and whatever has been brought into being by him

Is entirely free from fault and complaint.

[Col. 0620D] He who created this entire mass of the world

Also governs it, so that nothing did not receive its origin from him;

[155] Thus there is nothing that can remain standing when its Maker is removed.

For those who give God sluggish leisure, I believe, fear

That vigilant care and strenuous labors will exhaust him,

And that one being could not at once unfold so many things.

O you submerged in darkness, empty of divine fire,

[160] Seeing more with bodily eyes than with the mind:

You dare to compare God with the nature and condition

Of your own being. And if you perversely add anything you desire to his praise,

You believe him blessed by your own goods,

Or liable to suffer any hardship.

[165] Is it because, when you hold great cities and peoples

Under your rule, it is miserable, amid sleeplessness and illness,

To divide the mind’s cares among many affairs?

And when weighty causes press upon you from every side,

Your defeated diligence cannot endure its urgent labors;

[170] And when anxiety has been driven away from troubled minds,

Rest, finding leisure, creates a soothing pleasure?

Is it pious to think this of the Lord, who always remains the same,

Whom nothing burdens and nothing occupies entirely?

Time flows away; things born and things begetting behold their end. He remains, holding at once what has been done and what is to be done,

Beyond the future and before the past;

Present to all, and alone creating times without being subject to time.

And just as he surpasses and transcends the spans and numbers of ages,

[Col. 0621B] 793 So the immeasurable one is contained by no boundary of places.

[180] Nothing is so great that a fixed limit does not restrain it;

Heaven, earth, and finally the entire world

Have a boundary; the heights have an end, and the depths have an end.

But God’s nature is to be nowhere absent: wholly present everywhere,

He freely penetrates and surrounds all the members of the world.

[185] This power alone, therefore, can distribute the controls of things

And persist amid the same peaceful cares;

It is not escaped by swift things, nor delayed by slow ones;

It is never ignorant, never distant, never approaching

By being transferred from one region to another,

[190] Nor does it need to be taught what is obvious in order to know it.

As the silent witness of events, let it hear and see what is hidden;

Let it give lives and take away those it has given;

Save what is perishing, raise up what has been cast down,

Press down what is lofty, prolong years,

And shorten them, change hearts, and forgive sins.

## CHAPTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0622D] God, who lacks no power, also possesses the will to care for human beings through his providence. The condition of the world after its creation. The creation of humanity.]

But those who grant omnipotence its power

May perhaps remove its will, and think that the one who governs great things

Has refused to care for human beings, born for brief lives

And abandoned amid changing storms.

Why do you willingly fall into this error,

And, forgetting your parent, pass over into the nature

[200] And lot of beasts?

The beginnings of our nature are unknown, or present circumstances disturb the hope set before us in Christ.

Do not, through unworthy fear, violate the sublime honors

Of the everlasting race; rather, having overcome heaven,

[205] Grasp the immortal dignity that was left to you.

The way is known, since Christ, our teacher, has opened it to all;

He calls us and will lead us with him and into himself.

And lest we seem to promise uncertain things with empty words,

Reason demands that we reveal from our first parents

[210] The origin of the human race and unfold the causes

Of the life that was lost and, by Christ’s gift, recovered.

When all things had been arranged, the Creator had already made

The entire world, and the world was blooming in beautiful beginnings.

The sun was already traveling through its measured courses of time,

[215] And the moon with the stars was providing light to the night;

The earth was already nourishing cattle, the sea fish,

And birds were swimming through the clear air with their wings.

But there was not yet upon the earth an animal capable

Of possessing divine reason. The most excellent Author gave this

[220] Special dignity to humanity, and although he created all things by his word,

He deigned to form this creature with his own hands,

So that it might possess more of its parent.

Two substances are joined, and opposites come together into one life.

For the soul, unlike other things, is generated from nothing;

It is free from destruction, except that, by the Lord alone,

[225] It can be subject to torment and, under the name of death,

Bear punishment; entering its earthly dwelling,

It grants its companion life with itself

And together they drink in the divine breath.

[Col. 0622C] 795 Nor, because the nature of the two things is unlike,

[230] Is their condition different: one end remains for both—

Whether the later is subjected to the right of the superior,

Or the weaker makes itself equal to the strength of the greater.

For it is possible for either to be conquered or to conquer,

To advance or diminish, to rule or lose its kingdom.

Not because one person brought more and another less

[235] At the origin of the cause of their birth,

Nor because any external force brought them forth created

And drove them unknowingly into moral dangers,

But because the human being is free and wise

And can distinguish right from wrong,

[240] Possessing within himself the distinctions among things

And the right of will by which the mind regulates choice.

Yet if, amid the blind battles of a precarious life,

He does not grow arrogant about himself, but is protected by modest prayers,

[Col. 0623A] Let him believe that he can accomplish everything from the source

From which he received both power and existence.

Thus the image of our native virtue is implanted in us;

[245] when it has been much cultivated by a long practice of justice,

it would, like a mirror, reflect the divine light it imitates.

And when he had passed his lifetime engaged in good pursuits,

victorious, he would possess the eternal citadel, destined to endure.

The whole work of God, once complete, would no longer enter

[250] Into battles, nor anxiously contend within itself,

Nor wish what it would soon not wish;

It would no longer know fear, ignorance, desire, or suffering,

Needing no growth through additions and subject to no losses.

And so that confidence in great promises might be present,

[255] And hope in the promised crown might not be uncertain,

Humanity receives, through the gift of the present life,

Proofs of the future and learns to trust what it is to receive

By what it has already attained.

To humanity are subjected the birds of heaven,

And all the animals of the earth,

And the fish nourished by sea and rivers.

[260] To humanity it was given to know the courses of sun and moon,

The stars of night, and to comprehend days and years by numbers;

To know the powers of herbs, to give names to things,

And to increase intelligence through various arts.

Humanity alone was made superior to all breathing creatures,

[265] Subject only to God, and appointed to rule the strongest

Not by bodily force but by the power of reason.

## CHAPTER V

[Note: [Col. 0623D] How human beings after the Fall differ from their first parent. The devil’s envy against the first human being. Some just persons in every age of the world. Examples of God’s providence toward human beings before the Law: Abel and Cain. What the translation of Enoch and Elijah teaches. Why Noah’s household was preserved in the flood. Abraham’s faith. Lot preserved. Joseph sold into Egypt. Moses leading the people out of slavery. God’s protection of the children of Israel in the wilderness.

[Col. 0624D] 288. Thus the Lyon edition; other editions read, “Which could.”

316. So other copies; and indeed with better sense than the reading in our editions, *immenso*.

327. That is, Elijah.

333. The Lyon and Louvain editions read *deducti*, contrary to the rules of the poem.]
