If anyone thinks that by these words I extend this condition to the whole human race

[Col. 0623C] And that he has not yet recognized himself in them,

Let him hear that the human race has differed from its first parents

[270] Through transgressions, corrupted by much moral rust,

With only a small seed of vigor remaining.

And so that he may learn the honor belonging to his nature alone,

Let him return to the highest head of the holy race

And consider himself as he was from the hands of the Lord,

Governed by his breath,

[275] Such as Adam was before he was condemned to this earth,

Free from guilt, and richly possessing the garden of paradise

With the fruit of cultivated virtues.

When God had bestowed upon him such great gifts,

The prince of the serpent race grew envious,

And, cast down from the lofty region of heaven—

[280] 797 For pure goodness alone can possess the highest things—

Conceived greater poisons for doing harm,

His heart changed and turned against what was good.

He knew that the possessor of such great delights

Had been excluded by command from one tree,

[285] And drove him to pluck an apple from the forbidden branches,

In which there was a greater knowledge of right and wrong,

Then under human control, since humanity had not yet received

[Col. 0624A] The power by which it could avoid what must be avoided

Without learning it at its own peril.

Brought about by these deceits, death subjected humanity,

[290] Born through this crime, with guilt flowing down to all descendants.

Once the ancient race had been driven from the citadel of virtue,

It was not entangled by the transmission of only one error from its parents;

Rather, as it grew among succeeding peoples,

It extended a manifold ruin through widespread destruction.

[295] “Yet although death, having been sent in, reigned over those whom it destroyed,

No age failed to produce people pleasing to the Lord,

And every generation had its own just persons.

Although, because of the merit of their lives, many good things awaited them,

Their corrupted nature nevertheless dragged them toward death,

[300] [Col. 0624B] Nor was it to be released from the bonds of the first parent

Until Christ, begotten in the very majesty of his undiminished nature,

Destroyed the causes and seeds of death.

It is easy to recognize, from examples drawn from the beginning,

That Christ’s perpetual care stands by all.

[305] The righteous Abel is not overlooked as he heaps the altars with holy sacrifices and, choosing the firstlings of his flock,

turns the Lord’s countenance toward his sincere gifts.

Nor does Cain deceive him by offering rejected gifts under the appearance of devoted religion,

while envy, kindled by bitter gall,

[310] boils within him against his brother.

Nor did the Lord refrain from recalling the savage man

With kindly speech; and however great the crime

He was preparing, God impressed it upon him

And gave him a form by which he might overcome himself

And prove stronger than his deranged anger.

[315] [Col. 0624C] But once conceived, impiety carried out its cruel deed,

Plunging the world’s beginnings into crime.

Yet could God not preserve the just man pleasing to him

From the wicked slaughter? Rather, the end of bitter life

And the life and crown that were to be bestowed

[320] Surpassed them in the immeasurable weight of eternal honor.

What of the time when he transferred Enoch alive from the earth?

Was God despising earthly things? No indeed;

For that example benefited everyone,

So that the terror of death might depart

And the substance of flesh might receive unshaken hope.

[325] Thus, many ages later, other generations deserved

To receive signs of the life promised in Christ,

When they saw Elijah, carried away through the air

By fiery horses, ascending heaven in a shining chariot.

Was God’s care absent then, when the human race,

[330] [Col. 0624D] 799 Having poured its sins everywhere and utterly abandoned piety,

Bore monstrous giants from forbidden unions,

Those unions foretelling the future destruction of the world?

He gave ample time in which mortals, brought back to better things,

Might cleanse the sequence of their crimes through virtue.

[335] But when wickedness persisted throughout the whole world,

[Col. 0625A] And the crimes could be erased only by a flood,

Only Noah’s household was preserved. With every pair

Of each species of living creature enclosed within it,

From which animals could be restored to the empty earth,

[340] The ark survived unharmed while the world perished.

Not because God could not have produced other peoples,

But because humanity, weakened by many diseases,

Was to come from that very seed, being born into Christ’s body;

And so that we might know that, with God as the just judge of merits,

[345] Rest is granted to the holy amid the destruction of the wicked.

Was the Lord’s love, even then, extending toward our race,

when believing Abram, made father of many peoples by faith’s fruitfulness,

reckoned the promised offspring among the innumerable stars?

[350] [Col. 0625B] Or when a fiery rain descended upon the Pentapolis,

Did not God’s wrath as Judge come only after much delay and examination?

He was ready to spare, but found no grounds for pardon;

And, among all of them, he found one man unlike the others

In the incestuous people of Sodom,

[355] Whom he rescued from the incestuous people of Sodom—Lot—and made him lord of a little town.

But when a dreadful famine held Egypt and the kingdoms of Canaan,

A famine to be endured for seven full years,

The reason for moving the patriarchs was certainly prepared,

And a household was established among foreigners

[360] That would kindly foster the growth of the future people,

While Joseph, who mysteriously revealed dreams,

Was sold by his brothers into slavery for a price,

And they deceived their father;

While the mistress’s lust condemned the chaste man to prison;

While the king, after the obscure dream had been explained,

[365] [Col. 0625C] Honored the liberated interpreter with the second place;

And while the Hebrew youth, led through pious stratagems,

Rejoiced to recognize in forgiveness the brother they had worshiped.

Although he endured many evils while innocent,

Could he have foolishly accused God in complaint,

As though God despised human affairs,

[370] Unless he knew that everything proceeded through deep causes

Under a just Judge?

Although such things commonly confuse faithless minds,

They cannot disturb the pious, because the virtue appointed for this time

Is that those who possess freedom endure the unjust

[375] For a brief span, while God himself endures them, his anger deferred.

If a people dear to God and suspect to a savage tyrant

Endured the unjust rule of a cruel king,

While the offspring of grieving mothers was slaughtered,

And they supplied the bricks ordered for the cities,

[380] 801 So that harsh labor and the mercilessness of savage death

Might consume all the years of that afflicted people,

These things were not inflicted upon the fathers with God removed;

God himself teaches that he cares for his own.

For he commands Moses, his chosen servant, to announce to Pharaoh

[385] That he must allow the Lord’s people to depart from Egypt.

[Col. 0626A] If he did not, his arrogance would be punished with many plagues;

He would feel the wrath aroused by him who holds the power of the kingdom.

Whenever he suffered the heavenly weapons,

[390] He yielded and pretended obedience; but when the disaster had been removed,

He hardened himself, God sparing him, and drew from that very source

The causes of his destruction by which he might have obtained salvation,

Until, overcome by force, the savage tyrant relaxed his harsh laws.

And Moses led forth the host, rich with barbarian spoils,

[395] A pillar marking the road through the wilderness with a notable furrow.

It changed its form according to the occasion,

So that it might provide the camps with fitting advantages in turn:

Covering them by day and guiding them by night,

The same thing fire and shadow,

[Col. 0626B] Dispelling darkness with flames and heat with cloud.

[400] Why should I speak of how, when the enemy pressed upon the terrified fathers,

The sea was divided, its waters bound in solid immobility

And standing like a mountain, yielding a passage through the empty depths;

And how, wherever the many thousands of the people had passed unharmed,

The Egyptian people were overwhelmed when the waters came together?

For all nature serves its mighty Author,

[405] And the same things that yield to aid also serve his anger.

But I have neither the leisure to pass through all the forms of virtue,

Nor a power of speech equal to the deeds.

For who could unfold the marvels of so many things?

The rain of manna, and every flavor in heaven’s bread,

[410] Water from a dry rock, and sweetness from a bitter spring,

Or how, through forty years in the wilderness,

Neither time harmed their bodies nor use wore out their clothing?

## CHAPTER VI

[Note: [Col. 0625D] Examples of God’s providence in the Law. The natural law innate in everyone. God’s providence was not manifested only among the Israelite people. The mind is a mirror cleansed by faith in Christ. The Law and the prophets announced that Christ would be born.

418. The Lyon, Louvain, and Douai editions read *perscripserit* (“had written out”); Cologne and the more recent editions read *praescripserit* (“had prescribed”).]

It is useful to turn to the Law as an example and ask those very people

[415] Who remove the Lord’s care whether, at some point, God began

To shape human minds for the covenant of life,

And, unmoved by the world’s vices through so many ages,

Then wrote down the just law.

Enter yourselves into the inner chambers of your mind,

[420] And look upon the letters engraved within,

The written volumes of your heart;

Recognize the law born together with you.

For who will be so foolish—not a beast of the field

Or a creature of the sea—as to delight

[Col. 0626D] In open vices to such a degree

That he himself would wish to suffer what he does?

The deceitful man condemns lies, the rapacious man thefts,

The savage man condemns frenzy,

The bloodstained murderer condemns bloodshed,

And the adulterer draws his sword against the adulterer.

[425] “For there is one father of all,

And no one lacks the seed of what is right;

Their origin produced them all alike.

For from where, before the law had been written down, were there

[430] [Col. 0627A] “Those who passed their age in peaceful moral conduct,

Ignorant neither of the supreme Father nor lacking justice?

803 Therefore we all came into life created with one law,

And we carry in our fibers what has been written in books.

Nor was concern for us new when the written law,

[435] Given to Moses, condemned crimes by present punishment.

But an additional safeguard was bestowed upon the holy race,

So that, mindful, it might remain steadfast in the honor

Of its ancestral faith and become heir to the Lord’s promises.

Yet since anyone whatever was permitted to enter under that sacred law,

[440] And the temple doors did not bar foreigners,

And since the prophets, at God’s command, sang of things to come,

They often also spoke many words to various peoples,

So the queen of the South, eager to hear,

[Col. 0627B] Received the word of the Lord from Solomon’s mouth

And reverently drew it into her ears.

Thus Nineveh, warned by Jonah at the time of its destruction,

Believed; and, fasting for three days in mourning,

Through the destruction of its evil ways, it deserved that its kingdom should endure.”

Truly, lest we delay too long in these matters,

which have been published here and there, in various ages:

[450] and lest anyone deny that what exists in part exists in the whole,

while divided concerns conceal the Lord’s undivided care

and nothing that appears rare is accepted—

say: what people, in what remote region of the world,

what human beings, of what race or condition,

[455] [Col. 0627C] has God neglected to save? Man, woman, slave,

free person, Jew, Greek, Scythian, barbarian—we are all one in Christ:

neither the person of the powerful,

nor of a master or king, takes precedence;

there is no difference in the one light,

unless the use of the one mirror differs.

[460] For the mind is like a mirror: the more it is polished,

as faith polishes it and directs it toward the rays above,

the more brightly it reflects the image of Christ confessed by it—

Christ who is always God with God the Father,

and, remaining in the Father’s majesty,

mingles with human condition;

[465] and the Word becomes flesh, and the Creator of all things

is born, and the Founder of time succeeds to years.

For this is what the Law, this is what the revered volumes of the prophets,

[Col. 0627D] this is what the undoubted hope of the patriarchs held:

when the final age was hastening toward the world’s end,

[470] God would come to earthly things, who, having destroyed death,

would release the laws of hell

and raise up the long ruin of the human race

through a better birth.

[Note: [Col. 0627D]

CHAPTER VII. Against Eutyches, concerning the Incarnation. No one has ever been saved without faith in Christ’s incarnation. The Law is easy to observe through the grace of Christ, who himself first did what he commanded. Against Nestorius.

478. Only the Lyon edition has *suscipias* (“receive”).]

But you, who see the two natures—of man and of God—

come together within the narrow limits of a single path,

[475] hold your steps firmly and cautiously, lest wandering error

drive you, as you tremble, to one side or the other:

[Col. 0628A] if, seeing the miracles of divine works,

you should suppose God to be without flesh;

or, while recognizing everything belonging to our body,

should believe a human being to be without the Godhead.

[480] For there is no life for me in being alone,

and death holds me in subjection; nor is there any way

by which I can conquer after being conquered,

unless the true power of God has been joined to me,

805 or the Savior has not assumed me in true flesh.

His majesty is not weakened by this,

[485] through which I am redeemed; nor is he diminished

while I am changed into him.

He enters into what is mortal in me, so that,

because life cannot be held by death,

death may perish for me, and I may no longer live in myself,

[Col. 0628B] but Christ may live, he who joined himself to me in himself.

For earthly Adam, having been conquered,

poured death into all human beings,

because all are born from him,

and the guilt of the transgressing father runs its course.

But a new human being, born from heaven through the womb of the holy Virgin,

[490] established in himself another, good beginning for mortals;

and, poured into all flesh,

by sharing in nature he brought forth those who had died,

and, by changing life, created the living.

And just as the grace of former times embraced only those

who saw Christ through faith,

so in our own age Christ renews no one

unless he is received into the heart.

[500] [Col. 0628C] Behold, human being, how great a power has been freely bestowed upon you:

if you wish, you can be a son of God.

The almighty Spirit created you,

overshadowed by the power of the Word.

Do not now regard yourself as born

from the bodily seed of your fathers;

let the beginnings of the flesh, which held you captive, perish.

[505] Join nothing old to what is new.

This world is not yours; this life is not yours;

nothing here has been given to you,

nor are you yourself your own.

For you have been bought,

and it is lawful for you to repay the price of yourself,

so that by paying you may become richer,

your gifts may increase,

and the Redeemer himself may become your portion.

[510] Nor does the difficult observance of the Law now command you

to go beneath a harsh yoke.

Let a free mind offer holy obedience with understanding,

which the gracious Spirit may write

[Col. 0628D] on the tablets of the heart with Christ’s blood.

He established by example everything

he conveyed to us in words,

making his commandments equal to his deeds.

[515] That king and lord of all things acted in the form of a poor man,

neither resplendent in clothing

nor proud in honor.

Strong toward the weak, a king toward servants,

rich toward the needy;

justice yielded to the unjust,

wisdom to the brutish.

[520] Struck by sacrilegious hands,

he does not prepare to return the blow;

he makes no reply to the insults of the eager tongue.

The judge is condemned;

the Word is silent;

light is spat upon;

he himself becomes the servant of his punishment.

He drinks gall and vinegar

[Col. 0629A] more sweetly than honeycombs.

The holy one becomes the curse of the Cross,

[525] and Christ dies while Barabbas lives.

Impious people, who dared such a monstrous crime,

do you already sense the fury of the world condemning you?

The sun flees from the world,

and night is made in the middle of day;

the earth, shaken, trembles,

and, while God undergoes death,

the bodies of the saints, raised from their tombs,

receive life.

The veil of the temple was also torn apart,

so that the unworthy people might no longer keep anything hidden

in the sacred inner sanctuaries,

and so that the holy things, offended, might flee the bloodstained priests.

[535] 807 And when you had trampled the darts of extinguished death

and brought back a new trophy from flesh through flesh,

on the third day, Jesus,

you gave light to your astonished disciples.

[Col. 0629B] Nor was it permitted to recognize the Lord

without unmistakable signs,

when faith received the proofs,

examining by sight and touch

the traces of the nails

and the wound of the spear;

and when, confirming your promises over forty days,

you were visible to many

and often tangible.

[540] Up to this point, Jesus, we have known you in our condition;

from here onward, our things pass into yours.

No longer are they different, but the two are one:

life in life, light in light,

with an increase—not an ending—of humanity.

When humanity has been glorified,

you are both human and God,

so that you are not one and another.

You command us to go upward to you

and to possess your light with you,

provided that we run along the same path,

taught that heaven cannot be attained

except from the Cross.

[550] [Note: [Col. 0629D]

CHAPTER XIV. The person who is ungrateful for divine providence and does not attribute his sins to himself is refuted, because he was created with free will and sins through it. What a person must avoid in the world if he wishes to cultivate virtue. The proper use of temporal things. All the saints were subject to the same temptations as we are; how they overcame them.

543. This must be accepted with a grain of salt, as the saying goes. Here the author seems to fall into the two errors of Nestorius and Eutyches, when he says that from the day of the Ascension Christ is human and God in such a way that he is not one and another, and that the two natures in him are no longer different but one. Yet a most learned man has wisely observed that, apart from the fact that it is easy to pardon a poet who touches in passing upon a very difficult matter if he is found to have spoken less precisely in technical terms, the author in this same passage acknowledges that Christ’s glorification occurred with an increase, not an ending, of humanity. This is especially so since shortly before he clearly declares that the two natures, human and divine, came together in Christ, and that there was no way in which he could conquer after being conquered unless the true power of God had been joined to human nature; see verses 473 and 480.

573. Thus in Lyon; but Leuven, Douai, Cologne, and later editions have *in aequore* (“on the level plain”).

694. The Cologne edition and later editions have *lenia* (“gentle”).]

Is the love of God now known,

and is his care, spread over all, evident?

Is salvation also known to everyone?

And yet, alas, once again, human being,

you stir up wars with complaining, babbling words,

and pierce your own vitals with your weapons.

Why am I not good? You do not want this.

Why am I bad? You want this.

[555] Why do I desire what is evil,

and why do I not desire what is good?

You are free;

but although you can distinguish what is right from what is crooked,

you choose what is worse

and cling heedlessly to what pleases you.

“I err,” you say,

“and I wish I were unable to err.”

This statement rests upon two desires:

for you wish either to be entirely without judgment

or to be without reason.

For error belongs to one who has departed from the boundary of what is right,

but who, with Christ leading, can return to the path.

But the person whom no line of a road has received

does not deviate anywhere

and fears no fall,

because he never stands.

[565] [Col. 0630A] Does God care about oxen?

Does the word of the Lord apply to any birds?

Are sea-monsters held by law?

When these creatures carry out the commands of the Almighty,

they do not know that they are doing so;

they assume the impulse to will,

and believe that what they do benefits themselves as well as others.

So too things without breath always remain in the form

in which they have been fashioned:

plains do not swell into hills,

nor do high mountains lie spread across the sea;

the Alps do not enter the sea,

nor the sea the fields;

rocks lie still,

rivers run down,

and marshes stand.

[575] Yet these things have no reward,

although without perception they offer to living beings

the uses assigned to them.

If nature seems to you to have made these things superior,

then you would already wish to be changed into an ox,

a rock, or a river.

“I would not wish to become worse;

I would have wished to become better.”

[580] 809 Did those who pleased the Lord by their gracious conduct

displease themselves?

Did we not all come from one seed,

or is the nature of good human beings different?

The rich person is born no differently from the poor;

there is one beginning for slaves and kings.

The best person received no more than the worst:

the Creator’s measure is equal,

for he illuminates everyone with one light.

But when we enter the world,

we are received amid various forms of things,

and whatever appears enters the mind

to be judged by human discernment.

Forms without number stand everywhere,

and all of them can be tested by looking.

Some also enter through open ears,

accompanied by the errors of ancient pursuits

and the empty doctrines of parents,

which display a certain coloring of truth.

Some come with measured sound,

some are light to the touch,

some are widely diffused through pleasing odors,

and others bring together various foods

in a thousand flavors.

[595] These things, therefore, must be discerned by human beings

at great risk,

lest, too fearful, one venture onto no sea at all,

or, wandering, be carried along

with reins let loose without law.

For there is a holy use of things:

by confining them within the limits of due measure

and the weight of proper proportion,

we shall render honor to the Lord alone for everything.

[Col. 0630D] He made all things very good,

not as incentives to vice,

but so that in them we might grasp what is above

and, having fought the contest of virtue,

win crowns.

[Col. 0631A] Do those heavenly men whom the world has produced

and continues to bear

not seem to you to have endured these same things

which we endure?

The movements of the mind,

rebellious passions,

and vices attacking from entrenched camps?

But with the sword of the Word

and the powerful shield of faith

they conquered the bows of darkness

and the darts of death.

When they saw this great and beautiful work of the world—

the sea, the sky, fire,

and the stars of heaven,

which they held beneath themselves

by number and by sight—

they did not look upon them as gods.

They worshiped one Author and Lord of all things,

with reason as their guide,

not the things that had been made.

But you, who would have wished

that you had been made more nobly,

would you not complain

that you had not been born among the angelic order?

For when that Lucifer,

cast down from the lofty heaven,

fell,

and a third part of the stars fell with him when he was struck down,

I ask in which part you would then have been.

Would you have remained the bright image

of God’s eternal goodness,

or would you have followed the camp of envy

and the ranks of night?

[Note: [Col. 0631D]

CHAPTER IX. Against those who attribute their sins to the stars. Free will alone is the cause of sin. A human being is not subject to the stars; rather, the stars were once subject to holy human beings: Joshua and Elijah. Empty and harmful predictions of human actions derived from the stars.]

But where is the revolving sphere rushing you headlong?

Do you wish to be good

without your own labor?

Do you believe this can happen

if the stars at your birth are changed,

whose course drives you into evil?

Why do you seek among the stars,

with the Chaldeans,

the empty refuges of an ancient error?

Although you approach the heavenly things

with anxious concern

and scrutinize thoroughly

the manifest causes of events,

[630] 811 you are no more unwilling to know God

than to know what nature he assigned to each element,

by what law he ordered the sea to move,

what power he accustomed the gentle winds to possess,

or at what times he created the fires of the stars.

Since he is the pure source of justice and goodness,

would he have imposed a merciless law

upon those subject to his commands,

if he himself had first bound human behavior to the stars?

For these things are opposed to one another

and conflict greatly:

to demand innocent conduct,

to punish crimes,

and to call everyone to the same promises,

while, on the other hand,

to fasten upon those who are born a violent star

that yields neither to human willing nor to human ability,

but from above drives everyone,

whether unaware, toward virtue or toward error.

[Col. 0631D] Therefore either the heavenly fires have no authority over us,

or, if they retain some authority over us,

they can lose it.

For when I am born for life,

the good Author entrusts the commands of salvation

to my heart and ears,

and calls me, as I run, with the promise of reward,

while terror makes me pause.

“Worship God alone,” he says,

“and remember to serve him alone;

despise foreign religions.

Pursue this work of goodness;

carefully flee this evil.

From the former, blessed life is born;

from the latter, death is produced.

Before you stand water, which saves,

and fire, which destroys.

Stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish;

an equal power of choice is open.”

What the Law instructs,

what the writings of the pious prophets teach,

and what God himself would proclaim through his own mouth

would all be pointless

if an external force held our free choice.

But if anything harms virtue

and holds back our spirits,

the heavenly fires do not produce it,

nor does it flow from the ether.

[660] Rather, it arises from our hearts;

and freedom itself wages the war,

while we are shaken by civil arms.

Soft pleasure embraces idleness

and refuses to go along the difficult road,

and those who have obtained the prize

are reluctant to attempt anything arduous

for the sake of a hope that still lies hidden.

When the crafty enemy saw these things

being carried on within us,

he drew strength from your pursuits.

To turn you away from the worship of the true Father,

he persuades you that fate is spun from the stars

and that human beings contend with the gods in vain.

From this, they purchase masters of life

under various forms of honor.

Away with error, away with error!

The inventions of ancient deceit

are sufficiently recognized:

through them the Almighty entangles us when he warns us,

and teaches us to avoid profane worship.

For we know at what great price

the star called Remphan was worshiped by some,

and the host of heaven revered,

and worship was offered to the Sun and Moon.

Nor is it hidden that commands expressed in human words

remained in force,

that the heavens obeyed the spoken command,

and that day grew during the periods

when night was driven back;

for the light did not know

any limit except the one victory established for it.

[680] We also know that conditions prescribed for heaven

once remained subject to the will of a holy prophet:

when the heavens, shut up for a fixed time,

were not permitted to send dew

upon the thirsty fields;

and when fire itself,

summoned from the regions above

to the sacred altars,

was made to mingle with profane things,

although he had given it to sacred purposes.

Its power would also have descended upon Christ’s disciples,

to exact punishment for a denied hospitality,

had the patient Lord not forestalled anger with pardon.

Therefore no authority over us

has been granted to the elements,

over which human beings possess authority.

Those things that receive a law

cannot establish a law.

God alone, the almighty King,

dispenses all the times of our life,

and he does not wish those whom he has placed above the stars

to serve the stars.

[Col. 0632D] For all whom the Holy Spirit has renewed

in his sacred stream,

born in Christ,

cut off from mortal stock,

already possess a heavenly dwelling.

Earthly descent does not bind those

who have been made into a temple

and transformed into the body of the Lord.

But if someone, after observing the course

and effects of the stars,

maintains that human nature and life

can be discerned through this art,

I ask what this art brings

to trembling mortals.

“This person,” he says,

“will be happy; that one will be wretched;

death will seize this one while still a child;

that one will surpass the years of Nestor in old age.”

Is this false or true?

If the predictions of the forecaster remain fixed,

then no hope is left for the wretched,

nor fear for the blessed.

And what reverence is due to fixed stars,

if, although they can carry out their decrees,

they cannot alter them?

Let everyone give himself over instead

to torrents of crimes:

let them deceive,

plunder,

slaughter,

and confuse what is lawful with what is unlawful.

The star will nevertheless persist,

since the fixed order of things is confirmed

by its effect.

Just as evils cannot be driven away

by holy integrity,

so good things due even to perverse conduct

will not flee.

But if the order of the predicted lot is changeable,

and what is to come can be avoided,

then the whole force of fate,

hanging upon uncertain chance,

is dissolved.

[Col. 0633B] Therefore, by investigating the movements of the stars—

that is, the work of this art—

one overturns the whole of religion,

whether by teaching mortals

to care for no god,

or by teaching that the elements

can be moved by prayers,

and by introducing to wretched people

an innumerable multitude of gods.

[Note: [Col. 0633D]

CHAPTER X. Against the Epicureans, who deny divine providence because the good suffer adversity here while the wicked experience every prosperity. Why the wicked ought not to be punished here, nor the good rewarded. God is patient because he is almighty and eternal.

[Col. 0634D] 760. Douai and Cologne, with later editions, have *successit* (“followed”).

778. Ancient editions have *Plectisset*; later editions, *Plexisset*.

[Col. 0635D] 804. The Lyon edition has *here*; others have *heri* (“yesterday”), whose final long syllable does not fit the verse’s required measure. That *here*, the adverb, has the same meaning as *heri* is clear from this pentameter of Martial:

“And nothing was set before us here except a boar.”

]

But since the snares of concealed deceit

have now been exposed,

and it has been discovered where error would lead those captured

by empty pursuits,

it remains to answer the complaints

that object that divine care withdraws from the affairs of the world,

since anxious toil often presses upon the good,

while the life of all the wicked flows peacefully.

Tell me: if you think human affairs proceed

without the reins of a governing Lord,

what departs from the order of nature?

What wars do the elements wage?

What anywhere disagrees

with the ancient covenant of things,

divided from its proper order?

[730] [Col. 0633C] Thus day is recalled to its rising

after the intervening night;

the return of the moon and stars is the same,

and the passing seasons retrace their marked boundaries.

The winds blow in the same way,

and so does rain from the clouds.

[735] 815 They deny no joy, but preserve their kind,

each seed pushing forth its own flowers.

The enduring order is not absent

from the origin of things;

all things persist through the same causes.

Unless the skillful prudence of the eternal King

established this

and sustained the whole mass

by breathing upon it,

all things would collapse

in sudden ruin,

to be reduced to nothing.

And since these things are carried on

by the Almighty’s ever-watchful care,

and move along a descending course

toward a fixed end,

who would deny that God distributes

his rights more particularly among our people,

to whom he has granted hope of eternal life,

lavishly giving the likeness of his own image?

But when you complain

that punishment is not presently restored to the unjust

nor rewards to the holy,

would you wish the judge’s avenging anger

to descend upon every guilt

throughout the whole world?

And how would the merciful patience

of the magnanimous King differ

from the savage cruelty

of a pitiless tyrant?

[750] [Col. 0634A] Or what part of humanity,

ignorant of sin,

would remain to possess the world?

What place would there be on earth

for holy virtue?

If present rewards flowed to virtue,

it would remain in heaven instead.

Thus the world’s appointed end

would have been hastened

by cutting short the ages,

and posterity would not have come

to be generated,

if promised honor or punishment

had equally removed the just and the guilty

from the world.

But now the deep succession of our race

is extended,

and a people succeeds through a double origin:

born from the members of its fathers,

and reborn from the fountain of Christ.

And while the pious patience of the Lord

spares the peoples,

we see many return to the light

from the deep darkness

and become renowned,

their stain of sin laid aside.

[765] One person, who once worshiped gods

through innumerable faces

and a thousand altars—

bearded and smooth,

young and old,

as people once did—

now, having cast away

the error of his ancestors,

humbly adores the Only-Begotten.

Another, having followed

the sophistic arts of the Greeks

and their empty doctrines,

now rejoices to know wisdom in Christ

and to become foolish to the world,

taught heavenly things

by apostolic instruction.

How many had the whirlwind of disgrace

carried far from the harbor of reason

into the deep;

tossed over the whole sea

and driven by excessively wandering errors—

how pleasing it now is

to receive them returning,

to warm them in a fatherly embrace,

and not to let them depart

from the anchorage of life.

If, amid their many former moral offenses,

the inexorable rigor of anger

had swiftly seized them,

the time of a better life

would have been cut short,

and the fallen would not have been allowed

to gather the strength to stand.

“I do not desire the death of the sinner,”

says the Lord,

“nor is there any profit in the destruction of one who is perishing.

Let him return,

and, changed, come back to the path he abandoned,

and enjoy life.”

And because he wishes those whom he has begotten

to be like him in virtue,

he says:

“Leave vengeance to me;

I shall repay what is worthy of my judgment.

Let room be given to anger.”

Thus, while the punishment of many wicked people

is postponed,

some are often recalled

to righteous conduct.

Each person becomes his own judge

and severe avenger,

destroying what he previously was

and rising again as another person.

But those who persist

in clinging to long-standing error,

although they grow old with impunity

amid many vices,

will come to a savage end.

There will be no hope of pardon there;

they will be summoned to punishment

for the smallest farthing.

[Col. 0635A] For whenever we are moved to action

by any cause,

we desire swift vengeance,

because our limited opportunity

does not allow those who have been injured

to let time pass without inflicting harm.

But nothing escapes eternity,

and everything is present,

safe with God.

For him nothing is late or early.

We should not think that what comes

is either delayed or hastened;

the times are changed according to our affairs.

For whatever is being done everywhere,

whatever has been done,

and whatever is to be done,

stands before the Lord’s eyes

in a single instant.

One day is always present to him,

and in it our tomorrow and our yesterday

are equally at hand.

[805] [Note: [Col. 0635D]

CHAPTER XI. Yet God often gives here the greatest proofs of his justice. Many things happen commonly to the good and the wicked in this life; in the next, things will by no means be so. No death is evil for the good. How unjustly the world judges happiness!

840. The Lyon edition has *et in ore parentum* (“and in the mouth of the parents”), that is, “and under the eyes of the parents.” The Leuven, Douai, Cologne, and other editions have *et more parentum* (“and according to the custom of the parents”), which perhaps means “and for the sins of their parents,” or “in the same manner as their parents.” The following words support this sense: “to die by another’s guilt.”

[Col. 0637D] 899. Thus the Lyon, Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editions. Later editions, however, have *in auras* (“into the breezes”).]

Although God reserves everything for that judgment

in which what now lies hidden

will be disclosed and made manifest,

he has nevertheless given the world,

through all the ages,

many proofs of the justice

of the One who governs all things,

shaking mighty kingdoms with wars,

often draining cities and powerful peoples

through disease,

burning them with fire,

and burying them beneath waters;

while enriching the poor,

raising up the fallen,

bringing down the exalted,

releasing prisoners,

and subduing the proud.

Nor should we think this happens

without great reason:

whenever the wicked experience anger,

the innocent seem to undergo

the punishments of the guilty.

Many things always remain common

to the worthy and the unworthy in this world:

the sun is the same for all,

the rain is the same,

cold and heat are endured alike.

[Col. 0635C] Just as water, light, and air

are undivided among everyone,

so the just must bear

the troubles of the unjust,

so that, while the innocent suffer many things

together with the wicked,

there may be people

whose merit causes the wicked peoples

to be spared,

and who lead the converted

by the image of virtue.

But when the unchangeable end

for those destined to destruction

draws near,

the same sentence does not fall upon the holy.

There are those whom the flood of the world

does not overwhelm,

and those who are allowed

to escape burning Sodom.

The angel who ravaged Egypt

recognized doorways marked

with the sign of the Cross

and removed the plague

from the sacred blood.

Nor was the woman deceived

by the shining fleece,

whose single house survived

when so great a city perished.

[Col. 0635D] The sea becomes a road through its swelling waters

for the holy;

a path is made through the river;

and through the empty air

there is a passage for the devout.

Food is supplied

by a bird that serves,

and the greedy reaper loses

the food he had gathered.

[835] And so that nothing may harm God’s servants,

the order of nature is changed.

Falling chains release prisoners;

the prison opens of its own accord,

and the bolt does not hold the doors shut.

Water fails in the streams,

heat fails in the fires,

and the lions’ rage—

[Col. 0636A] But there is no doubt that,

in the whirlwind of a great disaster,

tender years may be swept away

and, in the manner of their parents,

those free from crime may die

because of another’s guilt.

For when the sea covered human beings,

it is known that many thousands

of girls and boys

were destroyed throughout the world.

Yet their offspring does not seem

to have been unjustly removed from the earth,

for it would have increased the wicked.

Great honor was conferred upon it

in its very destruction,

because it died through the crime of its fathers

before its own harmful guilt had fallen upon it.

And if the punishment of the wicked

also embraced some just person,

do not doubt that this pleased God.

For no death is evil

for the good,

for whom, through varied and prolonged labor,

every exit lies open into rest.

The road gives life harshly;

it is not taken in a level field,

but at the end a crown is given.

But we, captivated by pleasing things

and offended by severe ones,

neither look at good things with sound judgment

nor truly recognize evil.

We undertake the concerns

that ought not to be ours,

and, leaving what belongs to us,

we find delight in what belongs to others.

We do not judge anyone wretched through vices

or blessed through virtue;

instead, we foolishly join

blame and honor to external things

and, though assigned to heaven,

cherish earthly things.

It is customary to call happy

those whom flattering power

has raised to the highest peaks

of swollen honors,

those whom great profits have enriched,

and for whom wealth spread throughout the world

has amassed abundant revenues.

Costly clothing and beautiful furnishings

are praised,

as are great houses,

countless servants,

and watchful clients,

and everything that is not ours,

which one day can give

just as one day can take away.

We embrace neither that distinctive good

which belongs to the human being

and fears no force,

nor those who lack these destructive things—

things that perish in a thousand ways—

but we regard them as wretched,

as though harsh labor oppressed justice,

or the pain of a sick body,

the deaths of children,

or shameful poverty.

We do not see how many victories

constant endurance produces,

nor where the brief struggle

is going to lead.

Fearing to taste the cup

of the Cross and of life,

we drink poisonous venom

coated with honey.

For sweet in taste

and beautiful in appearance

are the things that produce and nourish

the diseases and death of the soul,

and that, like a cancer,

consume the weakened organs.

[Col. 0637A] And when God deigns

to send healing care from heaven

and to cut away the rotten fibers

at their roots,

we accuse the tender remedy

and prefer to waste away in sickness

rather than endure

the power of the severe antidote.

Therefore the things we regard as evil

are not evil.

When the healing hand

does not spare terrible ulcers,

salvation must be embraced,

not sharpened by complaint.

Those whom God rebukes for sinning

he also loves even now

and wishes to correct

with a father’s scourge.

He joins me rather to these

than to those whom,

having withdrawn the scourge,

he has allowed to go

where their will leads

and to be carried along

by their own desire.

[Col. 0637B] These are the people

whom old age,

unpunished amid their crimes

and rich in the fruit of their wickedness,

has brought to the final borders

of a shameful life.

They have oppressed the just

with unjust hatred.

Because of them wars have been raised

against the devout,

and chastising blows

against those slow to heal.

[Note: [Col. 0637D]

CHAPTER XII. Affliction is punishment for crime to the wicked, but a crown of virtue to the good. The losses of the soul must be mourned more than external possessions. For the converted, endurance of affliction is beneficial. The devil is overcome even by those whom he had previously conquered, if they place their hope in Christ and ask Christ, who conquered the devil, for the power to conquer.

916. That is, “certain”; see above, verse 190.

944. Thus the old books of Lyon, Leuven, and Cologne; later editions have *inveximus orbi* (“we have brought upon the world”).]

For the same weapons assail all the faithful,

but for a double reason:

what torments the wicked

makes the holy grow,

and what brings punishment to the wicked

for their guilt

gives the holy a crown

for their virtue.

Finally, if you strip away

whatever is bitter

from the affairs of the world,

you will now see that

the servants of God

voluntarily anticipated all of it.

One man groans over the loss

of talents of silver and gold;

another, over household goods

carried off

and divided among Gothic daughters-in-law

the necklaces that cause grief.

Another is distressed

by stolen livestock,

burned houses,

and wine drunk by others,

by sorrowful children

and obscene servants.

But the wise servant of Christ

has lost none of these things

that he despised

and had previously transferred

and stored in heaven.

And if anything from the world’s storm

fell upon him as suffering,

he endured it without fear,

confident of the promised reward,

and eager to be released

once the contest had been won.

But you, who mourn

the barren fields,

the deserted halls,

and the ruined stages

of the burned estate,

could you not shed tears

more appropriately for your own losses

if you looked instead

at the devastated inner chambers

of your heart,

at the beauty covered

with much filth,

and at enemies

raging in the citadel

of your captive mind?

Unless it had surrendered

through every gate

and supplied fuel

for its own destruction,

even those things

made beautiful by human hands

would have remained

as testimonies to the merit

of a devoted people.

But now, lying prostrate

in ugly ruin,

they throw our disasters

and their own disasters

back in our faces.

Let us therefore mourn

these ashes of temples,

these tombs of the powerful,

which lie heaped up

in the hall of our ravaged heart,

with captive hands.

We are the once-shining vessels of God;

we are the gracious altars

and sanctuaries of Christ,

in which the silver of eloquence,

the gold of virtue,

the captured scepter of the Cross,

and the diadem of beauty

have been taken captive.

Nor should we provoke

just anger with furious complaints,

blaming God’s judgment,

which vastly surpasses

the office of mind and mouth

in the depths of the abyss.

Although, during this brief

and fleeting period of life,

the unjust swell with pride

and rejoice in the secure peace

of their own crimes;

although vineyard and field

do not deceive them,

and they inflict harm unharmed

and increase through crime,

let not perishing things seize us,

for we have everything in Christ.

We did not bring these things

with us when we were born,

nor shall we carry them out

when we depart this world.

But if any strength of spirit remains,

let us cast off

the servile yoke of sin

and, breaking our chains,

return to freedom

and the honor of our homeland.

Impious agreements

with the savage tyrant

will not harm us.

This covenant,

written by a captive hand,

can be dissolved by Christ,

who has the right

to overthrow it justly,

“recalling those who have turned away

and looking with favor upon those who have turned back.”

He is the lavish purchaser

who sought them with his own blood,

provided that a swift willingness

to seek the protector’s help

goes before it,

moving the Lord

through faithful tears.

For just as no one is saved

against his will

or while sunk in the sleep of deep repose,

and the person who has voluntarily withdrawn

is not compelled by force,

so the halls of life

stand open when those returning knock,

and heaven’s court receives

the citizens who have been saved.

Nourishing this hope of pardon

with steadfast hearts,

implore God,

brothers,

and abandon the conflicts

of words

and the disputes

arising from perverse opinions.

And because we fell,

scattered in the first battle,

let us not fear

to stand

and enter a second conflict.

Although the enemy may fill everything

with various terrors

and surround closed gates

with a vigilant army,

the war is nevertheless won

if, stripped of our old flesh,

we are renewed

into the body of Christ

and seek from the Victor

all the power by which we may conquer.

[Col. 0638D] He joined our things

to his own things

and his own things

to ours,

so that the human being,

trusting not in human strength,

may refer everything to him,

without whom those who seem to stand

do not stand,

and through whom those who have been scattered

are gathered together

and those who have fallen

rise again.

This will be enough

to have written

for the unlearned

in a small book:

once they have tasted

the pure liquid

from the living fountain,

they themselves will pour out

rivers from the depths

of the heart

and offer jars of living water

to their brothers.

# On the Calling of All Nations

[Col. 0639]

## Preface to the Books On the Calling of All Nations

For a long time the question has been asked

who was the author

of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*.

At first, on the testimony of certain manuscript codices,

they were attributed to Saint Ambrose.

But not long afterward

this opinion was abandoned,

when learned men observed

not only that these books cite the Pelagian heresy,

which arose after Ambrose had been taken up among the heavenly ones,

but also that they discuss

the controversy that arose in the Church

from the doctrine which Saint Augustine,

fighting vigorously against the Pelagian heresy,

had strongly defended.

Later, some attributed them to Prosper,

because they had read certain manuscripts

in which the books were written under the name

of Saint Prosper,

and because a considerable affinity

was observed between them

and the questions treated

in the works of that holy man,

the disciple and defender of Augustine.

But learned critics,

and not a few of them,

thought that this second opinion was also mistaken,

and that the books should not be acknowledged

as the genuine offspring

of that holy Father:

by some because of the difference in style,

by others because of the discrepancy in doctrine.

Since no manuscript codices remained

in which the books were assigned

to another parent,

the matter then came to conjectures.

Some, including Latius and Vossius,

believed that they should be attributed

to that Hilary

whose letter is said to have been sent

to Saint Augustine,

and whom some confused

with the bishop of that name at Arles.

Others, such as Erasmus,

suspected that they could be attributed

to Eucherius,

and judged that they sufficiently reflected

his character and genius.

Finally, Father Quesnel conceived the idea

that this work should be assigned entirely

to Leo the Great.

He asserted that he had recognized

Leo’s doctrine and style

completely in these two books.

His judgment on the matter

seemed sufficiently plausible,

so that many readily subscribed

to that final opinion.

But Joseph Antelmi,

a canon of Fréjus,

opposed himself to it

and, attempting to undermine the opinion

in a lengthy dissertation,

boasted that he had restored the other view—

namely, that these books

should be acknowledged as Prosper’s.

Among such diverse opinions concerning one matter, only two possess sufficient weight to deserve renewed examination: namely, the opinion that this work should be assigned to Saint Prosper, and that which assigns it to Saint Leo. For the others are found either to be manifestly false or to rest on no foundation. For how can a work be attributed to Ambrose in which questions are discussed that began to be treated only several years after Ambrose’s death? Nor is there such similarity of style between these books and the works of Saint Eucherius that they can be attributed to that author on this foundation alone. Still less is it credible that they were written by Hilary of Arles, since on the matter of grace he did not hold the same views as Augustine, but rather those of the men who are attacked in this work. Nor is it likely that they belong to Hilary of Syracuse, or to that Hilary, the companion of Saint Prosper—if indeed they were not one and the same—for the style of the letters they sent to Augustine is very far from the style of our author. But it is equally not acknowledged that this work belongs to Prosper of Orléans. He was so far from being capable of writing a treatise of the kind attributed to him here that, when he wished the life of Saint Anianus, his predecessor, to be written, he was compelled to approach Sidonius Apollinaris, since he himself did not dare undertake it, given the limitations of his talent. Nor can it belong, finally, to that Prosper who attended and signed the Council of Carpentras in 527 and that of Vaison in 529. For the work *On the Calling of the Gentiles* is read as cited without its author’s name by Pope Gelasius in his work against the Pelagians; Gelasius, however, died in 496. It is therefore wholly beyond the bounds of probability that it was cited by that author who was still alive in 529.

The whole question, then, turns on this: whether this work should be called Prosper’s, Leo the Great’s, or that of an author who has remained unknown until now. The following arguments are brought forward on both sides in support of the differing opinions.

In favor of Prosper, manuscript codices are first produced—indeed, quite a number of them—in which Prosper’s name is prefixed to this work. Hincmarus is also brought forward as a witness: in his book *On Predestination* he cites it under the name of Saint Prosper. It is likewise maintained that the doctrine of this work conforms to Saint Prosper’s doctrine, that its style is very similar, and that the same propositions are found in both. For example, Prosper says in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*:

> The seat of Peter, which, made the head  
> of pastoral honor for the world,  
> holds by religion whatever it does not possess by arms.

The same thought, in almost the same words, is read in the same author’s books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book II, chapter 16. Prosper also asserts in his *Response to the Objections of the Gauls* that “from the whole world the whole world is chosen”; a similar manner of expression occurs in book I of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 9, where “the whole world is acknowledged to have been delivered from the whole world.” In his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, Saint Prosper counts among various examples of God’s inscrutable judgments the differences found among human beings, even in natural gifts. The author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* employs the same comparison in book I, chapter 14. Finally, Saint Prosper and the author of the work that follows both use, to establish the same points, the examples of infants dying without baptism, unbelievers converted to God at the last breath of life, and many others.

Indeed, Joseph Antelmius, who undertook to defend this opinion, by then obsolete among critics, weighs and diligently amplifies such considerations, and adds others drawn from similarity of style and from the agreement of words and propositions. Distributing these into extensive tables, he establishes a long and almost wearisome parallel comparison. He then adduces the testimony of Photius, who, in codex 5 of his *Bibliotheca*, speaking of the Western bishops who rose up against the Pelagians, says:

> As time passed, when the men of this sect had been restored to the Church through their renunciation of their heresy, evil again took its beginning from them. Thus, when the same plague was being reborn under the seventh bishop, it had to be checked before it spread farther; letters were therefore sent to Leo, who at that time occupied the apostolic see at Rome. Leo fought against that impiety with fervent zeal. Not long afterward, when it had again begun shamelessly to arise and be reborn, as it were, from its evil root, certain men in Rome also spoke openly in favor of the heresy. The truly divine Prosper easily dispersed and extinguished them by publishing writings against them for the public, while the same Leo whom we have mentioned was still governing the Roman see.

What Photius says here cannot apply to Prosper’s other works written before the pontificate of Leo the Great. He was therefore speaking there of these books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*.

Those, however, who defend the view that these books must be separated from Prosper’s works say first of all that their style differs greatly from the style of Prosper’s writings. This was the judgment of the most learned critics of the present century. Thus Latius, Erasmus, Vossius, Grotius, and many other outstanding and exceptionally discerning critics judged. Indeed, the style of the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* is much more polished and harmonious than Prosper’s; the diction is more elegant, the periods more evenly proportioned, antitheses of ideas and clashes of words more frequent, figures of speech more abundantly used, and the whole discourse much more rhythmically modulated by the calculated recurrence of rhythmic patterns. This last point deserves particular attention, since it can have arisen only from deliberate planning and effort. Such patterns do not occur only when the discourse seems to run into them spontaneously—as one occasionally finds in Prosper—but also [Col. 0641] in other places where they could have been employed only intentionally.

**3.** The method of composition familiar to the anonymous author differs very greatly from Prosper’s manner. Prosper openly and publicly presents himself as the defender and champion of Saint Augustine; everywhere he vigorously and energetically defends every point of Augustine’s doctrine and carefully follows all his footsteps. Everywhere he breathes the mind, doctrine, and every thought of the holy Doctor. There is nothing of the sort in the two books. Not even the slightest mention of Saint Augustine appears, so that the author seems either not to know him at all—which no one will believe—or to have deliberately and for definite reasons withheld his name. When Prosper writes, he constantly proclaims and circulates the authority of the Roman Church, since, as some have thought, he was entering the arena in its name and under its commission. The other author brings forth his style from his own genius, less in the spirit of combat than of self-exercise, and appears more like an investigator than one defending certain doctrines already established and sanctioned. Prosper openly attacks the Semi-Pelagians and persecutes them as adversaries of Catholic doctrine. The other author attacks them less deliberately, as though engaged in something else, and does not do so with the force or zeal with which that disciple and defender of Augustine’s doctrine did.

**4.** Although it is certain that the little work was written some time before the period of Pope Gelasius, it is difficult to assign it to any period that suits Prosper. If one wishes to place its composition at the very beginning of the controversies, or shortly after they arose, one finds the author contradicting this in the opening of his book, where he explicitly asserts that these questions had already been disputed for a long time:

> “A great and difficult question has long stood between the defenders of free will and the proclaimers of God’s grace” (*On the Calling of All the Gentiles*, book I, chapter 1).

If, on the other hand, one concedes—as cannot be denied—that the controversy had long been raging between the Augustinians and the Semi-Pelagians when the author applied himself to writing, then he must have been someone other than Prosper. For as soon as the remnants of Pelagian poison began to be disseminated through the *Genoese Excerpts*, the *Chapters of the Gauls*, or the *Conferences of John Cassian*, Prosper immediately seized and sharpened his pen and attacked those novel expressions with all his strength.

The author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, by contrast, indicates that this is his first work on the subject, and one composed long after the questions had been raised:

> “A great and difficult question has long been under discussion . . . Concerning this conflict of opinions, therefore, I shall endeavor to inquire, insofar as the Lord assists me, with what measure and restraint it ought to be understood, exercising and testing the modest capacity of my ability in matters that, as I think, have soberly taken root in my heart.”

These are the words of someone writing after a long contest between those opinions, undertaking his first work and first attempt in this matter; of a man more concerned to investigate and exercise himself, and to examine the subject through his own study, than confidently to assert and defend it from the doctrine of the Fathers under a commission from the apostolic see. Indeed, he writes with considerable hesitation and uncertainty. Although he presented everything in agreement with Augustine’s doctrine as received in the Church, he was nevertheless introducing new modes of expression. He knew that new forms of speech are rightly regarded with suspicion in the Church, even when the ancient doctrine is preserved. Hence, after the words just quoted, he adds:

> “So that if the style should proceed according to rules containing nothing offensive and nothing perverse, it may prove useful not only to us but also to others that we have reached some limit which we ought not to exceed.”

Those who, in order not to deny the work to Prosper, have said that the difference might arise from the fact that Prosper wrote it at a time when he had not yet fully absorbed the streams of Augustine’s doctrine—especially when compared with the books he wrote later and toward the end of his life—are easily refuted by the fixed period of this writing established above.

Before the discussion proceeds farther, however, the arguments that Joseph Antelmius opposes to the considerations just presented must be examined. First, he says that the doctrine of Prosper is the same as that of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*. In this matter he claims Quesnellius as his supporter, since Quesnellius expressly refutes Norisius’s contrary opinion.

This is entirely true if one considers the doctrine of both works in itself. But we maintain that the anonymous author sometimes expressed his thought in a different manner of speaking from that which Prosper always used; no one can reasonably doubt this. We also admit that the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* sometimes uses the word “grace” in a sense not unlike that in which Prosper uses it, namely, for the true grace of Jesus Christ. But we maintain that this author sometimes understood natural gifts as well under the name of grace, and that in this sense he acknowledged grace as common to all human beings. No one will prove that Prosper ever used the word “grace” in any of his works in this sense.

Prosper teaches the same matter as the anonymous author: namely, that God has always cared for human beings and has called them either through the written law, through the natural light of reason, or through the preaching of the Gospel. But nowhere is Prosper found to have adorned such admonitions bestowed by God on humanity with the name of grace, nor has Antelmius produced any example of this. He proves only that Prosper taught that the natural light is common to all human beings and that God’s providence extends to everyone. But that is not the point at issue. He was required to prove that Saint Prosper gave the name of grace to such general helps of providence—that is, to the discipline of natural reason, the instruction of the law, the preaching of the Gospel, and so forth. Yet the learned critic does not bring forward a single passage from Prosper in which the word is shown to be used in this sense.

For the passage he produces on page 139 of his third dissertation, in which Saint Prosper speaks, in chapter 14 of his book *Against the Collator*, of the power of God’s grace and of the ways of knowing God through natural aids, proves nothing. Prosper did not give these external helps the name of grace; he teaches only in that passage that whatever external assistance God provides to a human being, it is always grace alone that draws the person inwardly to God.

Finally, the most learned critic admits, even against his will, that the author of the work *On the Calling of the Gentiles* entered by a somewhat different path from that taken by Saint Prosper in his other works when explaining questions concerning God’s grace. Yet he wants Prosper to have concealed himself in this work, to have published it anonymously, and to have disguised his views and thoughts to some extent—thereby withholding the name of his master Augustine so that he could defend Augustine’s doctrine more securely. He even claims that Prosper adopted a new approach in this work, and that this explains why he pretended never before to have written on the subject. He further maintains that Prosper sometimes spoke more cautiously in his other works, moderated Augustine’s principles, and, having at one point promised that he would write no further, was compelled to employ a different method of argument so that he would not be recognized. Finally, he supposes that Prosper changed and disguised his very style, and was driven to do so by the method of writing that he had decided to follow in this book.

Let the fair-minded reader judge what solidity these arguments contain. We assert only this: if conjectures of this kind are permitted to weaken arguments of such weight as those we have reviewed above, then no critic will ever again be able to produce an argument which, however powerful or effective it may be, could not be overturned by the same method.

How did Antelmius learn that Prosper intended to publish this work under the guise of a disguised and concealed person? From whom did he hear that no author’s name had been attached to these books? And if that happened, how will he prove that they are Prosper’s? For the manuscript codices he adduces for his cause, as though they were effective proofs, what further support do they provide him, when it is established that in Prosper’s own time this work was ordinarily read without an author’s name and remained so for a long period afterward, since it was cited by Pope Gelasius?

For what reason, then, would Prosper at some point have disguised his opinions? Why would he have ceased in this work to defend Saint Augustine’s [Col. 0643] doctrine with the freedom and constancy that were characteristic of him? Is it credible that he would then have been ashamed to pronounce the name of a man toward whom he had hitherto shown such reverence? For although Prosper carefully dissolved the perverse meanings that could be imposed upon the holy Doctor’s words, and expressed them in such a way as to leave no room for calumny, he nevertheless defended them openly and everywhere rose vigorously against Augustine’s adversaries, whom he most certainly charged with having fallen into error.

Even if he had wished to disguise his style, it is not likely that he could have done so with such success. For beyond doubt the style of the anonymous author is acknowledged to be more polished, more elegant, and more elevated than Prosper’s. Nor is anyone easily found who has changed his own style for the better. Whoever changes his persona declines toward the inferior; and whoever departs from his natural genius produces nothing that is not shapeless and imperfect. How difficult it would be for someone unaccustomed to it to invent so many rhythms and publish so many carefully balanced periods. Nor does the method by which this work is composed provide any indication that Prosper was compelled to change his style.

Finally, all the considerations that Antelmius opposes to the arguments proving that the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* are not Prosper’s rest on mere suppositions or on appearances of proof that are exceedingly weak.

It must now be examined whether the arguments by which these books are said to belong to Prosper are more effective. They are reduced entirely to three considerations: first, the authority of the manuscript codices; second, the testimony of Hincmarus; third, the similarity of doctrine and style.

As for the first, the only point on which we agree with the author of the dissertation, those manuscripts ought not to be considered more weighty for assigning this work to Prosper than other manuscripts in which the work of Julianus Pomerius, *On the Contemplative Life*, is said to have been attributed to Prosper. Nor does Hincmarus’s authority outweigh that of the councils of Gaul, in which, from the year 800, the books *On the Contemplative Life* have been cited under Prosper’s name.

Nor was it new or unusual for Hincmarus to assign certain works to holy Fathers whose authorship was nevertheless not acknowledged. He cites the *Hypomnesticon* under the name of Saint Augustine; he lists the book *On Predestination and Grace* under the same name; he attributes the book *On the Hardening of Pharaoh* to Jerome; the commentary of Hilary the deacon on Paul to Saint Ambrose; and he adduces the poem *On the Providence of God* as a testimony under the name of Saint Prosper.

As for the manuscript codices of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, of the five Vatican manuscripts, one of the oldest—believed to be more than a thousand years old—and another likewise extremely ancient bear the name of Saint Ambrose. The remaining three, none of which is more than eight hundred years old, are marked with Prosper’s name. Other manuscripts undoubtedly exist in which these books are presented under Ambrose’s name, since they are everywhere read as published under his name before the year 1566.

If, then, it were necessary to yield to the authority of the oldest manuscripts, the work would have to be assigned entirely to Saint Ambrose. Nor, I think, will Antelmius deny, given his own system, that the earliest manuscripts of this work appeared anonymously, since he intends Saint Prosper to have remained concealed. How will it be proved that the copyists who first prefixed Prosper’s name to the work knew, on the basis of certain arguments, that it was truly the offspring of our Prosper? Is it not more probable that, when they found the books anonymous, they were led by the similarity of their subject and doctrine to place Prosper’s name at the beginning? Other, less learned though more ancient, copyists gave the work the name of Ambrose with no greater success. From this diversity among the copyists it follows that the authority of the manuscripts cannot be relied upon here, and that the titles attached to these books arose solely from the rashness of copyists.

We have spoken above of the agreement of doctrine and have proved that, although the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* truly holds the same views as Saint Prosper, he nevertheless employs modes of expression different from his and uses qualifications that Saint Prosper would never have used. If the very few periods of each author are consulted, we shall rightly derive an extremely strong argument from the disparity of style, which will be apparent to readers at first glance.

Nor do the long tables prepared by Antelmius frighten us or move us from our opinion. In them, no conformity of style is often visible beyond certain words customarily used at that time. Nor are two authors easily found who treat the same subject and do not occasionally use the same words; still less is it surprising that they agree in their ideas and employ the same forms of expression.

If someone investigated Saint Augustine’s works with the same care with which Antelmius examined all of Saint Prosper’s works, it should not be considered hopeless that a comparison between Augustine’s works and the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* could be successfully undertaken. In fact, quite a few of the passages in Antelmius’s parallels are drawn from propositions excerpted by Prosper from Augustine, or are written in the same terms in the works of the holy Doctor.

But such a minute comparison would be entirely futile. Despite Antelmius’s excessively extensive parallels, the difference between the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* and Prosper’s works will reveal itself to the reader who examines and weighs the matter, on the basis of the arguments we have set forth.

It remains now to examine the conjectures by which Quesnellius assigned the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* to his Leo. His principal—indeed, his sole—argument rests on equality of style, which he asserts that he recognized between these books and the other works of Saint Leo the Pope.

> “For one who has repeatedly reread the writings of Saint Leo,” he says, “the Leonine phrase and the whole character of his expression became most familiar, and I recognized it in the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*. I immediately noticed that in them the same manner of expression, the calculated frequency of certain words, the same formation of periods, the same construction of speech, clashes of words, frequent antitheses, variety of diction, elegance, dignity, richness, and fiery vigor—in short, the entire appearance of the style—proclaim one and the same author.”

When he examined the matter more closely, the following points became clear.

**1.** The date of composition falls within Leo’s lifetime, since the author would have undertaken it when the disputes raised against Augustine’s doctrine had already been raging for a long time.

**2.** The author’s homeland points to Leo. He cannot easily be called an African, since he contains not even a word about Augustine; nor can he readily be proved a Gaul, since he was either unknown to Gennadius or omitted by him. He must therefore be pronounced an Italian on the basis of the elegance and polish of his style, and because of a particular passage in book II, chapter 33, where we read:

> “While certain barbarians were assisting the Romans, what they could not know in their own lands they learned in our regions, and they returned to their homes with the instruction of the Christian religion.”

These words indicate that Rome itself was the author’s homeland. Quesnellius adds that these books are never read as cited in the African Church, and in the Gallican Church not until the eighth century, whereas Pope Gelasius explicitly mentions them as a work known and approved at Rome.

**3.** This author agrees with Saint Leo in his citations of Scripture. Both use Jerome’s translation; both cite the same passages and employ them in a manner peculiar to themselves.

**4.** The doctrine of this work concerning the grace of Christ is entirely the same as Saint Leo’s doctrine. Since in the work there are certain ways of explaining and expressing this subject that at first sight seem to depart from Augustine’s position, the same ways are also frequently found in Leo.

Among these is the author’s repeated discussion of a certain general grace bestowed upon every age and every human being. He places this grace in the discordant harmony of the elements, in the structure, order, and, as it were, speech of earth, heaven, and all creatures, which proclaim the omnipotence, goodness, and wisdom of the Creator in an ineffable manner. Both authors call these elements pages and books in which the eternal law remains written.

**5.** [Col. 0645] Many other identical thoughts, concepts, and modes of expression also occur. Both speak in the same way about the foundation of the apostolic see in the city of Rome; about its election by God to hold primacy among all the Churches of the Christian world; and about God’s will that the Roman Empire should be extended to the ends of the world, so that the Christian religion might more easily spread to the places it has reached—places to which Roman rule had not extended.

One may compare Leo’s sermon 1 on Saints Peter and Paul, chapter 1, with book II, chapter 16, of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*. Both say the same things about Peter’s threefold denial and his swift repentance. One may also read sermon 3 *On the Passion* together with chapter 28 of book II of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*.

Both authors say that Peter drew solidity from Christ as from the principal rock:

> “Peter drew solidity of virtue and of name from the principal Rock,”

says Saint Leo; and our author, in the passage cited, says:

> “Who would doubt that the strongest rock received from that principal Rock a share both in strength and in name?”

Here there is the same thought, the same phrase, and entirely the same words.

**6.** The style of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* agrees in every respect with Saint Leo’s style. We have already observed in it an outstanding elegance and polish, frequent antitheses and rhythms, balanced periods divided into equal members. As we have noted, this too is a distinctive feature of the Leonine style.

**7.** Not only is the phraseology the same in both authors, but the words themselves are often the same, and are not frequently used by others. A long enumeration of them may be read on page 375 of volume II of Saint Leo, edited and illustrated by Quesnellius. Quesnellius also establishes parallels between many phrases common to both authors. From all this he considers it conclusively proved that this little work *On the Calling of the Gentiles* must be assigned to Leo the Great.

Quesnellius’s opponent undertakes to prove two points in order to appear to weaken the force of his arguments: first, that Quesnellius relies entirely on slight conjectures; second, that clear and effective arguments demonstrate that the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* must not be recognized as Leo’s work.

It would be futile to labor over the first point if the second should be correctly established; therefore we shall begin with the latter. According to Joseph Antelmius, the following considerations conclusively prove that the work must be denied to Leo.

First, he says, the special intimacy between Leo and Cassian stands in the way. Who could believe that Leo would have entrusted Cassian with the task of refuting Nestorius—which he most certainly did entrust to him—and would have held him in such high esteem if he had known him to be subject to error? Or would Leo have undertaken to refute Cassian’s doctrine in the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* if he believed that Cassian had already been recalled from error and had adopted sound views, as Quesnellius nevertheless asserted?

For my part, I do not think that evidence exists—or even that it is probable—that Cassian ever changed his mind. I admit that Leo must be counted among Cassian’s friends. But it does not follow that Leo held the same opinion as Cassian, nor can it be conclusively argued from this that Leo did not write the little books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*.

Ordinary experience makes it clear that friends write against friends when they differ in opinion.
