Friendship accomplishes only this: that one spares a friend as far as truth permits, does not attack him directly, and treats the matter in a gentle style, as one would treat a person whom one wishes more to instruct than to refute. The author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* does precisely this.

The disputes that then existed between Augustine’s disciples and those who opposed his doctrine were not yet regarded as introducing heresy. Saint Prosper, although an ardent disciple and defender of Augustine, calls those by whom he himself was attacked Catholics and acknowledges that they lived within the Church. The author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* speaks even more mildly of these controversies, calling the questions under debate difficult and saying that they were customarily debated among Catholics.

Cassian himself and his followers defended their views modestly, without obstinacy or abusive language. From this it follows that nothing prevents Saint Leo from having entrusted Cassian with the refutation of the Nestorians and afterward from having composed the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, in which he contradicts Cassian’s views concerning grace.

“But at least,” Antelmius adds, “if Leo had been indulgent toward Cassian and his disciples as friends, he would not have called their disputes ‘calumnious contests,’ nor accused them of making calumnious charges, of impiously denying the truth, or of presumption and ignorance; he would not have accused them of laying snares of deception or of making obstinate complaints, nor reproached them with malicious cunning and insolent presumption. Yet all these reproaches are scattered throughout the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* and are directed against those who did not follow the faith of perfect grace.”

Someone might perhaps answer that Leo showed sufficient indulgence toward Cassian when he spared Cassian’s name and did not undertake to refute him by name, but instead attacked generally those who attributed too much to free will. He treated the whole question as though he were choosing no side in it and were not openly declaring himself their adversary.

The harsh statements found in this work do not touch Cassian or his disciples specifically. They concern erroneous consequences that could easily be drawn from their principles. Moreover, it has not been proved that such expressions should be regarded as so insulting as they are represented to be.

Antelmius brings forward a third argument, which appears to him irresistible. He says that he has been completely convicted by it and easily persuades himself that everyone else will be convicted as well:

> If Leo, while still a deacon, had attacked the Semi-Pelagians so vigorously, who would believe that, after attaining the summit of the pontificate, he left those same men uncondemned throughout his entire pontificate? It would surely be unworthy and monstrous if he had established nothing against them, since such men nevertheless appear to have been loaded with honors and increased in dignities under Leo’s pontificate. Leo’s successor Hilary also wished their leader Faustus to preside over a Roman council.

If it is said that Leo assumed another face and silently tolerated such errors, then he is undeservedly called a sincere or fearless opponent of heretics and a steadfast defender of the truth. It is undeservedly that Leo is compared with the Lion of the tribe of Judah because of the ardent zeal with which he attacked the Pelagians. Why would he have neglected to rise against the Semi-Pelagians if he agreed with the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* in wanting to revoke the errors of Pelagius in them? Would Saint Prosper, Leo’s faithful secretary and confidant, an outstanding opponent of the Semi-Pelagians, not have inflamed his zeal against them?

It is difficult to accept all these excellent declamations as invincible and irresistible proofs. The author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* did not count the defenders of free will among the heretics; as a private individual, he refuted their opinions. Let us suppose, then, that the author of the books was Leo. Why would it have been necessary for him, once he had become pope and possessed the supreme authority he held in the Church, to condemn them as guilty of an unquestionable heresy?

Even if he had considered the opinions rejected in these books heretical, why would he have risen against quiet and silent men who had attempted neither to disseminate perverse doctrines nor to form a party? For it is not read that any dispute on this subject arose during the entire time he held the pontificate. That controversy revived only long after his death.

Let it therefore be stated on what occasion Saint Leo would have condemned the Semi-Pelagians. Were any of them brought before his tribunal? Was anything about them reported to him in writing? Under his pontificate did they defend their opinions in written works? All these points lack even the slightest proof.

“But their followers rose in honor,” it will be said; “they are read to have been elected abbots and bishops in Gaul. It was Leo’s responsibility to intervene on behalf of such men.” As though papal documents were then necessary for those elected to such dignities.

But Hilary, Leo’s successor, wished Faustus of Riez, the leader of the Semi-Pelagians, to preside over a Roman council. First, it must be understood what is meant here by “presiding over a council.” It does not mean presiding over it as its head, but merely attending it, as when one says, “with a numerous [Col. 0647] council of the brethren presiding.”

Will you therefore conclude that Leo was a supporter of the Semi-Pelagians? I do not think that conclusion follows for many reasons. When Faustus attended the Roman council, he had not yet written the book in which he attacked Saint Augustine’s doctrine. He wrote that book long afterward. Even if he had written it earlier, it would not follow that he attended the council at Hilary’s invitation, much less that he did so at the invitation of Leo, Hilary’s predecessor; nor can one conclude that Hilary had favored Faustus.

What is most astonishing is that Antelmius did not notice that all the examples he adduces are overturned by Prosper’s own example. For Prosper does not appear to have published anything against the Semi-Pelagians after his book *Against the Collator*, that is, Cassian, which he had published before Leo’s pontificate.

If those men attempted to introduce something new under Leo’s pontificate, why did Prosper remain silent, or why did he not openly and publicly attack them as before? Why did he not use the favor he enjoyed with the supreme pontiff against them? Why did he not bring the erring men before Leo? If someone pressed this kind of reasoning concerning Prosper as far as Antelmius presses it concerning Saint Leo, one would come close to concluding from it that Saint Prosper himself had never written anything against the Semi-Pelagians.

The argument drawn from the authority of Pope Gelasius—that he counts the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* among the Doctors of the Church, although he refrains from naming him—appears more plausible than the preceding arguments. If this work were Leo’s, how could Gelasius have been unaware of it? Or, if he was not unaware, why would he have suppressed Leo’s name?

Yet this argument proves only that the work appeared anonymously at that time, a point on which everyone agrees. The question therefore still remains whether Saint Leo himself may have published it without his name. Quesnellius adduces arguments that make this plausible.

Let us now turn to the replies made to those arguments, since it is already certain in our view that no argument conclusively proves that these books are not Saint Leo’s. Quesnellius’s opponent tries to prove only that Saint Prosper used Jerome’s translation in the same way as Saint Leo, and that Prosper also sometimes used the ancient version of Scripture. By this single point, he believes that he has answered his opponent’s very strongest argument.

I shall not undertake here to investigate which of them was right or wrong in this matter. I shall insist only on the argument drawn from similarity of style, a point on which Antelmius is known to agree with the opposing side. For Antelmius wishes the *Sermons* and *Letters* of Leo the Great to be attributed to Saint Prosper precisely because the style of those works agrees with the style of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*.

Nothing could advance Quesnellius’s cause more than this admission. For it is far more certain that the *Sermons* and *Letters* bearing Leo’s name are Leo’s work than that the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* are Saint Prosper’s offspring. If, then, the same parent of both collections must necessarily be acknowledged, the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* will be assigned to Leo with greater justice than the *Letters* and *Sermons* of Saint Leo will be assigned to Prosper.

Father Natalis Alexander and Father Olduin say that they recognized a difference in style and that there are not as many rhythms, figures, and similarly cadenced endings in Leo as in those books. But they do not appear to have considered the matter carefully. For if any difference is found, it will prove to be of exceedingly slight importance.

From what has thus far been argued concerning the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, the following points can be established:

1. This work first appeared anonymously.
2. It was written after the year 430 and before 496.
3. The work was known during the pontificate of Pope Gelasius, but was issued without the author’s name.
4. After that period, some manuscripts bore the name of Saint Ambrose, while others bore the name of Saint Prosper.
5. It certainly was not Ambrose’s.
6. Nor is it at all likely that it was Prosper’s.
7. Since its author remained unknown until now, it is difficult to determine who he ultimately was.
8. If a judgment is formed from the method of treatment and the conformity of style, there is grounds for conjecturing that the work is by Saint Leo.
9. It cannot in any way be proved that this work was not composed by Leo.

One thing remains: to establish with certainty that these books are the offspring of Saint Leo. We have not dared to affirm this on the basis of an argument founded solely upon similarity of style; nevertheless, we will not deny that the considerations brought forward by Quesnell have almost persuaded us.

We have not answered the proof which Antelmius derives from Photius’s testimony, because it contributes nothing to the matter under discussion. For this author appears to have had only a confused and superficial knowledge of the history of the Pelagians, and to have been entirely unfamiliar with the disputes that arose among Westerners after Augustine’s death concerning his teaching. On the basis of his own supposition, he says that Saint Prosper fought against the Pelagians during the pontificate of Saint Leo. He had heard that Prosper had written about grace; he therefore believed that Prosper had attacked the Pelagians. And when he had read in the letters of Septimius and Leo to Januarius of Aquileia that such men had arisen during this pontificate, he assumed that they had been attacked by Prosper at that very time—especially since he was not unaware that Prosper was then staying in Rome.

But it is plainly evident that Photius wrote all this on the basis of mere conjecture, speaking as a man separated from the relevant times and places, who lacked an exact knowledge of the history of events and invented everything from his own imagination. Even if we were to grant that Prosper exercised his pen against the Pelagians while Leo occupied the Roman See, the books *On the Calling of All Nations* are attributed to him on the basis of mere conjecture, although they are not directed against the Pelagians. From where, then, do we know that Photius was speaking of these books? Could Prosper not in the meantime have published some books against the Pelagians which have not come down to us? In the end, however, nothing certain can be established from this passage of Photius, who is demonstrably shown to have written all these things on the basis of mere conjecture.

From all this the impartial reader will readily conclude that nothing more satisfactory, and nothing more removed from any suspicion of rashness, could have been done by us than the following: although these books have been debated here and there by learned men with such vigorous contention that no certain judgment concerning their author can be reached, we should neither count them among the genuine works of Saint Prosper nor reject them altogether as spurious, until learned scholars have decided this great dispute. Nevertheless, from what has been said it may easily be conjectured that these books were written around the year 440 of Christ.

[Col. 0647]

# TWO BOOKS [Note: [Col. 0647A] Written around the year 440.] ON THE CALLING OF ALL NATIONS. (C, S)

## BOOK ONE

### 847 CHAPTER ONE. He proposes the subject to be treated in this book and shows that those who maintain that free choice is denied by the preaching of grace do not think correctly.

[Col. 0648A]

For a long time there has been a great and difficult dispute between the defenders of free choice and the preachers of God’s grace. [Note: [Col. 0649C] Our editions—Louvain, Douai, and Cologne—read *quaeritur quaestio* (“a question is asked”); we emend this from the edition of Saint Leo’s works made according to the Thuaneus manuscript, the Cambrai manuscript cited in the margin of our codices, and the Joliensis manuscript.] [Col. 0649A] The question is whether God wills all human beings to be saved; and since this cannot be denied, the question is asked why the will of the Almighty is not fulfilled. When this is said to happen according to human will, grace appears to be excluded; [Note: [Col. 0649C] Thus Leo’s edition, in agreement with the Thuaneus, Cambrai, and Joliensis manuscripts. Our editions elsewhere read, “to happen according to human wills.”] but if grace is given in return for merits, it is clear that grace is not a gift but a debt. Hence the question arises again why this gift, without which no one can be saved, is not bestowed upon all by the One who wills all to be saved. [Note: [Col. 0649C] The Cambrai manuscript and Leo’s edition read elsewhere, “can be saved.”]

Thus there is no end to the conflicting arguments, so long as what is manifest is not distinguished from what is hidden. Concerning this conflict of opinions, therefore, I shall endeavor to investigate, as far as the Lord assists me, with what measure and moderation one ought to think. I shall exercise and test the limited capacity of my ability in matters which, as I believe, have settled soberly in my heart, so that, if my style proceeds according to principles containing no offense and no perversity, it may be useful not only to us but also to others that we have reached some boundary which we ought not to cross.

First, then, we must discuss the movements and stages of the human will. Some people do not distinguish this properly from the grace of God, believing that free choice is denied by the preaching of grace. They do not notice that the same principle can be turned against them: they deny grace if they do not want it to be the guide of the human will but merely its companion. [Note: [Col. 0649C] So the Joliensis manuscript, to which the Cambrai and Thuaneus manuscripts come closer; yet where the text has *Si enim*, “For if,” they read *Sic enim*, “For thus,” as in the text. The Prosperian and Leonine editions read: “If the will is removed, where is the source of true virtues? If grace is removed, where is the cause of meritorious goods?”]

For if the will is removed, is it not itself the source of true virtues? If grace is removed, is it not itself the cause of meritorious goods? But now, with Christ’s help, let us begin the subject we have undertaken to treat.

### 849 CHAPTER II. That every human soul naturally possesses some kind of will, which is either sensual, animal, or spiritual.

So far as it is granted us to understand and experience, every human soul naturally possesses some kind of will, by which it desires what pleases it or turns away from what displeases it. [Note: [Col. 0649D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “either desires what pleases it, or turns away,” etc.] Insofar as this will belongs to a natural movement weakened by the fault of the first transgression, there are two kinds of it, according to which the human will is either sensual or animal. But when God’s grace is present, a third kind is added to it through the gift of the Spirit, so that it can become spiritual; and through this more excellent movement it judges all the affections arising from whatever source according to the law of heavenly reason.

### CHAPTER III. Concerning sensual will.

Sensual will, which we may also call carnal will, does not rise above the movement that arises from the bodily senses. [Note: [Col. 0649D] The edition of Leo’s works omits the preposition *in* (“in”).] Such is the condition of the minds of little children: although they use no judgment of reason, they nevertheless show that they want some things and do not want others. By seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, they love what delights them and hate what offends them. [Note: [Col. 0649D] The Cambrai manuscript reads, “For what is . . . and what is.” The Leonine edition and the Joliensis manuscript likewise have “and what is.”]

What, then, is loving except wanting? And what is hating except not wanting? They therefore also have their own will, although they are incapable of foresight and deliberation. [Note: [Col. 0649D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “which is incapable and ignorant.” The Cambrai manuscript and Leo’s edition read, “which is incapable and ignorant both of foreseeing and of taking counsel.”] Nevertheless, they take pleasure in doing what flatters the senses of the flesh, until the vigor of rational intelligence is awakened through the more mature functions of the body and begins to move the limbs that serve it, not by an alien impulse but according to its own law. [Note: [Col. 0649D] Thus the Cambrai, Thuaneus, and Joliensis manuscripts. Earlier editions read *alieno motu*, “by an alien impulse,” before this point.]

### 850 CHAPTER IV. Concerning animal will, by which nothing above the reward of temporal glory is acquired, even when a person possesses higher understanding in it through God’s gift.

From this sensual appetite, in which those whom we see to be senseless and foolish even in more advanced years remain, one rises to animal will. Before it is moved by the Spirit of God, this will may indeed raise itself above sensual movement; nevertheless, without participation in supreme love it remains occupied with earthly and perishable things. [Note: [Col. 0649D] Thus the Cambrai, Thuaneus, and Joliensis manuscripts. Earlier editions had *sine sui amoris*, “without love of self,” adding in the margin, “namely, of God.” The text defines grace as participation in the highest love, or supreme good. The same point is made below in chapter 8.]

Even those human intellects which do not shamefully serve bodily pleasure and restrain their desires according to the laws of justice and moral goodness acquire nothing beyond the reward of temporal glory. [Col. 0650A] Although they adorn the present life becomingly, they do not possess the reward of eternal blessedness, because they do not refer their upright actions and good pursuits to the praise and honor of the One from whom they received the ability to understand higher things and to shine more brilliantly than others. [Note: [Col. 0651D] The editions elsewhere read, “so that they might understand more highly in animal discernment itself.” We follow Leo’s edition, emended from the Cambrai and Thuaneus manuscripts, and the Joliensis manuscript consulted by us. The words “in animal discernment itself” have the appearance of a gloss that crept into the text from the margin of some scholar.] [Note: [Col. 0650C] This has been emended from the Cambrai and Thuaneus manuscripts in Leo, and here by us from the Joliensis manuscript. Earlier Prosperian and Leonine editions read: “Even in this human understanding, if bodily…” This weakens the force of the statement, by which the author asserts that those who do not refer their upright actions and good pursuits to the praise and honor of the One from whom they received higher understanding obtain only the reward of temporal glory and, as he says below in chapter 18, of empty praise, even though they restrain their desires according to the laws of justice and moral goodness. “Those who have received their reward in this life, empty as it is, will also receive their punishment in the next.” For, according to Augustine, *Against Julian*, book 4, chapter 3, when a person does something in which he does not appear to sin, if he does not do it for the reason for which he ought to do it—and true wisdom commands that he ought to do it—he is shown to be sinning. For although the deed itself may appear good in its function, it is nevertheless sinful because of its improper end. The author’s meaning becomes clearer from chapter 6, where he writes that the person lives badly who does not live for the glory of God, and from chapter 7, where he says that without the worship of God even what appears to be virtue is sin. It is also clear from this chapter itself: after saying that such people adorn the present life becomingly by these upright actions, he shortly afterward reproves them as people who, first, do not confess God to be the author of this upright action; second, glory not in God but in themselves; third, become futile in their reasoning; fourth, fall back into love of self; and fifth, corrupt God’s gifts within themselves. Prosper, *Poem Against the Ungrateful*, line 408, and the notes attached to it, may also be consulted.]

For when certain people have directed the attention of their minds not only toward the foundations of the most useful arts and the teachings of the liberal disciplines, but also toward the investigation of the supreme good, and have perceived the invisible things of God through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20), yet have not given thanks to God or confessed that he is the author of this ability, but have said that they were wise (ibid. 22)—that is, glorying not in God but in themselves, as though by their own studies and reasoning they had drawn near to the contemplation of truth—they became futile in their reasoning. What they had discovered through the illumination of God’s grace, they lost when pride blinded them. They fell back from the heavenly light into their own darkness, that is, from the unchangeable and eternal good to mutable and corruptible nature. [Note: [Col. 0652D] The editions read *ad tenebras suas*, “to their darkness”; the Joliensis manuscript and the Leonine edition read *in tenebras suas*, “into their darkness.”]

When such people therefore fall into love of themselves, and please themselves so greatly that they refer everything they judge praiseworthy in themselves not to God’s gifts but claim it for themselves and ascribe it to the exercise of their own will, they are banished far from that spiritual will. [Note: [Col. 0652D] *Exsulant*, “are banished,” is better, according to the Joliensis manuscript and the edition of Leo’s works, than *exsultant*, “exult,” which appears in the earlier editions.] They possess nothing by which they may advance to eternal life. Indeed, they begin to corrupt within themselves even those temporal gifts of God and to pass from their good use into the habit of countless vices.

### CHAPTER V. That all nations received legal precepts in the elements, so that they might be without excuse in idolatry.

Although it is written that, when the Most High distributed the nations, as he dispersed the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of God’s angels, and that the Lord’s portion became his people Jacob, and Israel the cord of his inheritance (Deuteronomy 32:8); and although it is written that the Lord says to Israel, “You shall be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy; I separated you from all the nations to be mine” (Leviticus 19:2); and although it is written in the book of Esther, where Mordecai says, “I give thanks to you, Lord, because you have made new signs and wonders such as have not been done among the nations, dividing the whole age into two portions: you chose one for yourself, your people, and left the other to the nations” (Esther 16, according to the Septuagint); and although Paul and Barnabas say, “We also are mortal human beings, like you, announcing to you that you should turn to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them, who in past generations allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways” (Acts 14:4); although, therefore, Scripture, which is truth, declares these and many similar things, nevertheless we believe and devoutly confess, in accordance with Scripture itself, that the care of divine providence [Note: [Col. 0652D] The Cambrai and Thuaneus manuscripts, and likewise the Joliensis manuscript, do not contain the words “in accordance with Scripture itself.”] was never absent from the human race as a whole. Although God directed a people reserved for himself toward piety through special institutions, he nevertheless withheld the gifts of his goodness from no nation of human beings. Thus they were shown to have received prophetic utterances and legal precepts through the services and testimonies of the elements. Hence they became without excuse, because they made gods for themselves out of God’s gifts and worshiped as objects of devotion those things that had been created for use.

### CHAPTER VI. That without divine grace the will approaches iniquity all the more quickly the more intensely it applies itself to action, because it does not live for the glory of God.

Even that nation which the Lord separated for himself from all the nations would have passed wholly into this impiety, had he not set before it the purpose of his mercy for the support of the falls of the elect. [Note: [Col. 0652D] The Joliensis manuscript reads *sustentantis*, “supporting.”] The pages of the Old Testament are full of accounts of Israel’s defection, so that it plainly appears always to have been by divine grace that not the whole people departed from the Lord.

Thus human nature, corrupted in the transgression of the first man, even amid God’s benefits, commandments, and assistance, is always inclined toward a worse will, and to entrust it to itself is nothing other than to abandon it. This will is wandering, uncertain, unstable, inexperienced, weak in accomplishment, bold in undertaking, blind in its desires, swollen in honors, anxious amid cares, restless amid suspicions, more eager for glory than for virtues, more attentive to reputation than to conscience, and throughout all its experience more wretched in possessing what it has desired than in lacking it. In its own powers it has nothing except an easy path to danger, because a changeable will that is not governed by an unchangeable will approaches iniquity all the more quickly the more intensely it applies itself to action. [Note: [Col. 0652D] The two words *instabilis, imperita*, “unstable, inexperienced,” are absent from Leo’s edition.]

As long, then, as a person is pleased by what displeases God, his will is animal. For even if he acts with good morals, he still lives badly if he does not live for the glory of God. This is the distinctive and chief characteristic of the pious: that they glory in the Lord and love themselves only in God. They love themselves rightly when they love God’s works in themselves. For God loves in us what he himself made, and he hates what he himself did not make.

If, then, we love God’s work in us, we rightly love a good will in ourselves. [Note: [Col. 0653D] The Thuaneus manuscript lacks the word *recte* (“rightly”).] Indeed, if it were not God’s work, it ought not to be loved. What person, except one of evil will, would not love in himself the good will [Note: [Col. 0653D] Here the editions insert “would be,” which is absent from the Joliensis and Cambrai manuscripts and from Leo’s edition. They also read “does not love,” as does Leo’s edition, where the Joliensis and Cambrai manuscripts read “loves.”] which is the first planting of the heavenly farmer? For since the Truth says, “Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matthew 13:13), whatever is not to be uprooted was plainly planted by the Father. A good will is the first germ of all virtues.

When it rests upon its own origin, in that eternal and unchangeable will, it becomes spiritual in truth. For “the one who clings to God is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17), since through the communion of the one who illuminates and the one who is illuminated, the one who justifies and the one who is justified, the one who rules and the one who is subject, every action is referred to one. And what is referred to one belongs to both. For what God has given cannot be alienated from God, nor what a human being has received from the human being.

### CHAPTER VII. That when a human being returns to piety, a different substance is not created in him, but the same substance that had been weakened is restored; nor is anything taken away from him except the fault, once his former will has been corrected.

Here it seems necessary to consider whether, when a human being begins to possess a good will, the will that was already in him is corrected, or whether another will is given to him which he did not previously have and which conflicts with the former. [Note: [Col. 0653D] The Cologne edition reads, “which he does not have.”] To make this clearer, let us not hesitate to investigate the matter more deeply.

All human beings were created without defect in the first man, and we all lost the soundness of our nature through that same man’s transgression. From this came mortality; from this, the manifold corruption of body and soul; [Note: [Col. 0653D] The Cambrai manuscript reads, “of soul as well.”] from this, ignorance and difficulty, useless cares, unlawful desires, sacrilegious errors, vain fear, harmful love, unjust joys, plans that must be regretted, and a multitude of miseries no less than of crimes. When these and other evils therefore invaded human nature, with faith lost, hope abandoned, understanding blinded, and the will enslaved, no one found within himself the means of restoration.

For even if there was someone who tried by natural understanding to resist vices, he adorned only the life of this present time fruitlessly; he did not advance to true virtues or eternal blessedness. Without the worship of the true God, even what appears to be virtue is sin, [Note: [Col. 0653D] The word *veri* (“true”) is absent from Leo’s edition, but is present in all our editions and in the Joliensis manuscript.] and no one can please God without God. But the one who does not please God—whom does he please except himself and the devil?

When a human being was stripped by the devil, he was deprived not of his will but of the soundness of his will, since he could not have been driven from the state of innocence unless he had sinned by his will. Thus the nature that was good became bad in quality; and that movement of the soul which can never exist without some love—that is, without some will—did not lose its appetite but changed its affection, receiving through desire what it ought to have rejected through judgment.

When, therefore, a human being returns to piety—of whom it was said, “A spirit goes forth and does not return” (Psalm 77:39), because unless God converts him he does not return—when he becomes a new work and a new creation, a different substance is not created in him, but the same substance that had been weakened is restored. Nor is anything else taken away from him except the fault which nature did not possess. [Note: [Col. 0653D] Thus the Thuaneus and Joliensis manuscripts and the Leonine edition. In their place, earlier editions read: “A new formation does not take place,” which is contrary both to the Apostle and to the mystery of baptism and justification.]

### CHAPTER VIII. That grace restores God’s work in such a way that it does not remove free choice but rather heals it through that very free choice.

For in Adam there was nature without fault, and through disobedience of the will he contracted many evils and transmitted them to his descendants, where they were multiplied more and more. [Note: [Col. 0654D] The Thuaneus and Joliensis manuscripts read *multiplicando*, “by multiplying them.”] These evils are overcome and reduced to nothing only by the grace of the Savior, who restores his work through his own work. [Note: [Col. 0654D] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read *non effecit* (“did not accomplish”); the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition more correctly read *efficit* (“accomplishes”).] For, as the apostle John says, “For this purpose the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8). He thus breaks the bonds of the captive, clothes the nakedness of the one who has been stripped, and heals the wounds of the injured, in such a way that what he does in the person is also accomplished through the person.

It is certainly not advantageous for that person to fight his enemy without a protector. [Note: [Col. 0654D] The word *suum* (“his own”) is absent from the Joliensis manuscript.] He is engaged in combat with the one by whom he was once defeated. Let him not therefore trust in his own strength, which did not stand even when it was unimpaired; but let him seek victory through the One who alone has not been defeated and who has conquered all things. And if he seeks, let him not doubt that he received from the One whom he seeks the desire to seek him.

Nor, because he is led by the Spirit of God (Romans 8:14), should he suppose that he does not possess free choice. He did not lose it even when by his will he surrendered himself to the devil, by whom the judgment of the will was corrupted, not taken away. What, therefore, was not killed by the one who inflicted the wound is not removed by the one who heals it: the wound is healed, but nature is not removed. What perished in nature is restored only by the author of nature, with whom what nature lost has not perished (Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 26). [Note: [Col. 0654D] The following passage to the end of the chapter is absent from the Louvain edition. It was formerly supplied in the Douai and subsequent editions from the Cambrai manuscript, and was later found in the Thuaneus and Joliensis manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0654D] All our editions read *non interfectum est*, “was not killed.” Perhaps *infectum*, “was not corrupted,” should be read instead. The Joliensis and Cambrai manuscripts and the edition of Leo’s works read *ereptum est*, “was taken away.”]

For wisdom is eternal, truth is eternal, goodness is eternal, justice is eternal; indeed, the light of every virtue is eternal, and everything that is virtue is God. If he does not work in us, we can participate in none of the virtues. Without this good, nothing is good; without this light, nothing is luminous; without this wisdom, nothing is sound; without this justice, nothing is right.

Through Isaiah the Lord says, “I am, I am God, and there is none besides me who saves” (Isaiah 43:11). And Jeremiah says, “I know, Lord, that a person’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to direct his path” (Jeremiah 10:23). A mortal human being, born carnally from an origin condemned in Adam, does not attain the spiritual dignity of a new kind unless he is ruled by the Holy Spirit.

Nor does anyone desire this dignity unless he has received from God the warmth of that desire. [Note: [Col. 0655D] The Joliensis manuscript omits “from God.”] Of this the Lord says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). This fire is the love of God, which the lover of the world cannot conceive with a captive heart. He is full of love for vanities. Even if he is able in some measure to avoid them, and, after passing beyond temporal and visible things, advances in understanding toward eternal and invisible things; even if he withdraws from worshiping images and ceases to venerate heaven and earth and all the elements of this world, [Note: [Col. 0655D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “bodily” in place of “temporal.”] he nevertheless will not grasp faith in and love for Christ. Disturbed by Christ’s very humility, he will not overcome by his own judgment the scandal of the Lord’s birth and death.

For because the wisdom of the world resists the wisdom of God, it pleased God, in order that the pride of those who presume upon themselves might be blinded, to save believers through the foolishness of preaching (1 Corinthians 1:21). Hence those who are puffed up by secular teachings consider the cross of Christ more worthy of ridicule than worship. And the more highly someone has climbed in the cultivation of human disciplines, the more he despises the lowliness and weakness of our preaching.

Nor is it surprising that pagan philosophy resists the Gospel of Christ’s cross, since even Jewish learning opposes it. [Note: [Col. 0655D] The Joliensis manuscript and the edition of Leo’s works add *gentilis* (“pagan”), to which “Jewish” corresponds.] Neither the educated nor the uneducated, whatever their origin or rank, are led to God by human reasoning. Every person who is converted to God is first moved by God’s grace. A person is not his own light, nor does he kindle his heart with the ray of his own light. [Note: [Col. 0655D] The Joliensis manuscript reads, “nor his course.”]

If blessed John, than whom no one born of human beings was greater, was not the light, because he did not shine with his own splendor but had received his light from that true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9), who is there who could by his own judgment alone break through so many struggles of opinion, so many bonds of habit, and so many prejudices of antiquity? And who could do so merely by using his own experience? [Note: [Col. 0655D] The Joliensis manuscript and the Leonine edition add *usus*, “by using,” which is absent from the other books.]

And who could, merely through the external sound of a teacher’s voice, receive from grace only what he heard, and receive everything from his own will that he believed?

If this were so, there would be no difference between grace and the law, nor would the Spirit give life to anyone through mercy if the killing letter remained. For the law commands what must or must not be done, but it does not provide that it be done or not done, since its severity is obeyed not through liberty but through fear.

But the Lord, so as not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17), made the command of the law effective through the aid of grace and, by multiplying mercy, removed punishment. Thus he punished sin not by exacting vengeance but by erasing it through forgiveness.

Accordingly, he delivered the adulterous woman, who according to the law’s decree ought to have been stoned, both through truth and through grace. The executors of the command, terrified by their consciences, left the trembling accused woman to the judgment of the One who had come to seek and save what had perished (Luke 19:10). Therefore, having bowed down—that is, having descended to the human condition and bent himself toward the work of our restoration—he wrote upon the ground with his finger (John 18:6), so that through the decrees of grace he might render void the law of commandments and show himself to be the One who had said, “I will give my laws in their understanding, and I will write them upon their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).

He does this every day, inserting his will into the hearts of those who are called. And with the pen of the Holy Spirit, whatever the devil in his envy falsified on the pages of the soul, truth rewrites in mercy. [Note: [Col. 0655D] These words were absent from Leo’s edition and had dropped out of the Cologne edition. They are found in the Cambrai and Joliensis manuscripts and in the Douai edition.]

When, therefore, the word of God is brought to the ears of the flesh through the ministry of preachers, the operation of divine power is mingled with the sound of a human voice, and the One who inspired the preacher’s ministry also established the hearer’s response. [Col. 0656C] [Note: [Col. 0656D] The Douai and Cologne editions read *firmavit*, “established.” The Joliensis manuscript and the Leonine edition read *formavit*, “formed.”]

The nourishment of the word becomes sweet to the soul, ancient darkness is driven away by new light, and the inner sight is stripped of the gloom of its former error. The mind passes from one will into another. Even if the will that is being driven away lingers for a while, the will that is being born nevertheless claims for itself the better things, so that the law of sin and the law of God have different and distinct dwellings in the same person. Although the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit also resists the desires of the flesh (Galatians 5:17), the tempter may indeed dare to lie in wait through external things, but the mind, fortified by God’s help, prevails. [Note: [Col. 0656D] The Joliensis and Douai manuscripts read *carnis autem*, “but of the flesh.” Others read *carnis etiam*, “also of the flesh.”]

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Pope Gelasius cites these words in his treatise against the Pelagians with this commendation: “As a certain teacher of the Church wisely taught, saying: ‘For the great benefit,’ etc.”]

The material of these struggles has been reserved for the great benefit of the faithful, so that holiness may not become proud while weakness is being assailed. Hence the Apostle also says: “So that I might not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me an angel of Satan to buffet me. For this I besought the Lord three times that he might depart from me; but he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7).

Let the Lord seek his image, and let the good shepherd find the wandering sheep. Let him not disdain to carry upon his shoulders the sick sheep, worn out for a long time in a trackless place, and to save it not merely by calling it back but also by carrying it. Let the Lord seek his image, and, after wiping away the accumulation of all the filth that has fallen upon it, let him clear the mirror of the human heart.

For it is written: “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” (Job 14:4). Let the Lord seek his image, so that in its renewal and justification the grace of the One who restores it may appear, [Note: [Col. 0657D] Thus the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Others read “in revelation” or “in lifting up.”] just as the Apostle Paul testifies that this happened in him when he says: “I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. They had heard only that the one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith which he had formerly attacked; and they glorified God in me” (Galatians 1:22). [Col. 0657B] [Note: [Col. 0657D] The Douai and Cologne editions read “the Lord.” The Joliensis manuscript and the Leonine edition read “God.”]

Thus the Christian people at that time had learned, and the people of the primitive Church, whose heart and soul were one (Acts 4:32), believed in this way: whenever they saw someone converted from error to the knowledge of the truth, they glorified God and confessed that the faith of the converted person was a divine gift. The Lord himself likewise taught his disciples, who were to be teachers of all nations, saying: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

### CHAPTER IX. [Note: [Col. 0657D] We begin this ninth chapter here on the authority of the Joliensis manuscript, which has the words with which this chapter elsewhere began written in continuous sequence with what precedes. It was not convenient to separate the passage from the name of the prophet cited, by giving it a new title, since the same passage was being presented as a testimony.]

That whether Scripture speaks of good or evil, of the elect or the reprobate, it remembers one part as though it omitted no human being.

[Col. 0657C] Therefore, with this faith fixed and immovably established in our hearts—by which we most salutarily believe that all good things, and especially those which advance us toward eternal life, are possessed by God’s gift, increased by God’s gift, and guarded by God’s gift—I think that a pious understanding ought not to be disturbed by the question that arises concerning the conversion of all human beings and of not all human beings, if we do not obscure what is clear by what is obscure, and, while we insist presumptuously on what is closed, are not shut out from what is open; for it ought to be sufficient that we walk in that to which we have attained.

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “and humbly.”] [Note: We add this from the Thuanensis and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition; it was absent from the printed editions.] [Note: The Thuanensis and Joliensis manuscripts read “conversion”; elsewhere, “conduct.”] [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “in that to which we have attained”; others, “to which we have attained.”]

For what wonder is it if some do not attain to the mysteries of life, when many who seemed to have arrived depart, of whom it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19)? [Note: These words are absent from our editions and from Leo’s; they are found in the Joliensis manuscript and seem altogether necessary before what follows.] Their likeness is found in those who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds (Titus 1:16).

For although it is written, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 7:21), the Lord nevertheless says of certain people: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21); and again: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will say to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, workers of iniquity’” (ibid., 22). [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has “will enter,” and a few lines later, “I never knew you.”]

Such people do not call upon the name of the Lord, because they do not possess the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). No one can say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3); and, “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14).

Those who come to God through God, and who desire to be saved, are altogether saved, because they conceive the very desire for salvation through God’s inspiration, and through the illumination of the One who calls they come to the knowledge of the truth. [Note: Thus the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition of the Works. Elsewhere: “to the Lord through the Lord.”]

858 For they are sons of promise, the reward of faith, the spiritual seed of Abraham, a chosen race, a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), foreknown and ordained beforehand for eternal life, as the Holy Spirit testifies through the prophet Jeremiah, saying:

[Alternative heading: CHAPTER IX.]

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant which I established with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them,” says the Lord. “For this is the covenant which I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will give my laws into their understanding, and I will write them upon their heart; and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And no one will teach his neighbor, nor each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all will know me, from the least of them to the greatest, because I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.” [Note: The Joliensis manuscript adds: “And again, and I will give …,” etc.]

“And I will give them another way and another heart, so that they may fear me all their days, for their own good and for that of their children after them; and I will establish for them an everlasting covenant, which I will not withdraw from them; and I will put my fear into their heart, so that they may not depart from me; and I will visit them, so as to make them good” (Jeremiah 31:31ff.).

Through Isaiah also the Lord foretells the same concerning his grace, by which he makes a new creation out of all human beings, saying:

“Behold, I will make the new things that will now arise, and you will know them; and I will make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the dry land. The beasts of the field, the sirens, and the daughters of ostriches will bless me, because I have given water in the wilderness and rivers in the dry land, to give drink to my chosen race, my people whom I acquired for myself, so that they may declare my mighty works” (Isaiah 43:19–20). [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has “he made a new creation.”] [Note: The Camberon manuscript and Leo’s edition have “which arise.”]

And again:

“By myself I swear: unless righteousness goes forth from my mouth, and my words shall not be turned back; for every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess God” (Isaiah 45:23–24). [Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition have: “By myself I swear: unless it goes forth.” Others have: “By myself I swear: unless it goes forth.”]

If, then, it is impossible for these things not to happen—for God’s foreknowledge is neither uncertain, nor his purpose mutable, nor his will ineffective, nor his promise false—all those of whom these things were foretold are saved without exception. For he gives his laws into their understanding and writes them upon their hearts with his own finger, so that they receive knowledge of God not through the work of human teaching but through the instruction of the supreme Teacher. For “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7). [Note: The Camberon manuscript and Leo’s edition have “into their understanding.”]

All these, from the least to the greatest, know God [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has “will know.”], because, in order to come to Christ, they have heard and learned from the Father; all, led out of error, are directed into the way of life. [Note: A learned man conjectured that one should read “all taught” (*omnes edocti*): “all are directed from error.”] 859 To all, once their heart has been changed, it is granted to think and desire what is right; in all, the fear by which they are instructed in God’s commandments is implanted. [Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts read “may be kept, and indeed rightly.”] A way is made in the wilderness [Note: The Joliensis manuscript adds “and the whole dry land.”], and the dry land is watered by rivers, so that those who previously did not open their mouths to confess God, and who had passed over into the savagery of beasts like mute and irrational animals (Isaiah 43:19), being cleansed by the fountains of the divine utterances [Col. 0659C] [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has “flooded.” The printed editions then have “they bless and praise”; the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s Works have “may they bless and praise.”], may bless and praise God, declaring the mighty works and wonders of his mercy—he who chose them, adopted them as sons, and made them heirs of the New Testament (Galatians 3:15).

But if, as the Apostle says, no one rejects or adds anything to a human testament once it has been confirmed, how can the divine promise be dissolved in any respect?

What the Lord promised to Abraham without condition and granted without law remains entirely in force and is fulfilled every day. For even if some to whom these things were foretold did not believe, their unbelief did not nullify God’s faithfulness. [Note: The Camberon manuscript has “these things foretold”; and below, “their unbelief nevertheless.”] “God is truthful, but every human being is a liar” (Romans 3:3).

Those who, after hearing the Gospel, refused to believe became more inexcusable than if they had heard no proclamation of the truth at all. But it is certain that, in God’s foreknowledge, they were not children of Abraham, nor numbered among the lot of those concerning whom it was said: “All the tribes of the earth will be blessed in your seed” (Genesis 26:31, 34). For he promised that they would believe when he said: “And no one will teach his neighbor, and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all will know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34).

He promised that they would be reconciled when he said: “I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more” (ibid.). [Note: The Joliensis manuscript adds “toward all.”]

He promised that they would obey when he said: “I will give them another way and another heart, so that they may fear me all their days” (ibid., 35).

He promised that they would persevere when he said: “I will put my fear into their heart, so that they may not depart from me; and I will visit them, so as to make them good” (ibid., 40–41).

Finally, he promised all without exception [Note: Perhaps “that they would obey him.”] when he said: “By myself I swear: unless righteousness goes forth from my mouth, and my words shall not be turned back; for every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess God” (Isaiah 45:23ff.).

If here we say that what God swore would happen does not happen, we ascribe—God forbid—falsehood to God and a lie to the Truth. But if, as piety and faith persuade us, God’s words do not fail and what he decreed is altogether brought about, how will the firmness of his truthful promise become evident to us, while many thousands of human beings still serve demons and bend the knee to idols?

Only if we recognize that such declarations of God were issued according to that immutable knowledge in which the whole human race has already been distinguished before him, and that, whether he speaks of the good or of the wicked, he mentions one part as though he omitted no human being. For when the Apostle says, “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:27), does he not seem to have said that all human beings have been renewed?

Or when he says, “For in him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things in him” (Colossians 2:19), does he not speak as though he wished no one to be understood as excluded from this reconciliation? [Note: The Joliensis manuscript lacks “does he not?” here. A little later it has “an exile” instead of “excluded.”]

Or when he says, “In these last days he has spoken to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things” (Hebrews 1:2), does the form of the statement signify anything other than that all human beings have been transferred by the Father into Christ’s inheritance, according to the prophecy of David: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8)?

[Note: Thus the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition; others read, “For when the Lord says.”]

And when the Lord says, “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32), does this not seem to promise the conversion of all?

Or when it is prophesied and said concerning the Church, “Every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be brought low, and the crooked places will become straight, and the rough ways smooth” (Isaiah 40:4), does any human being seem to have been omitted who has not been signified as destined to be subjected to Christ?

What of this: “And all flesh will come before me to worship in Jerusalem, says the Lord” (Isaiah 66:18)? Or this: “And it will be in those days: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28)? Or this: “The Lord raises up all who fall, and lifts up all who are bowed down” (Psalm 145:14)? Is it not pronounced as though no one were excluded from this gift of God?

The people of God therefore possess their fullness. And although a large part of humanity either rejects or neglects the grace that saves, yet among the elect and foreknown—who have been specially distinguished from all in general—a certain particular universality is reckoned, so that from the whole world the whole world appears to have been delivered, and from all human beings all human beings appear to have been taken up.

Likewise, when the divine style speaks of the wicked, it orders its expression so that what is said of a certain part appears to pertain to all human beings. Such is the statement of John the Baptist: “He who comes from heaven is above all; what he has seen and heard, he testifies, and no one accepts his testimony” (John 3:32).

Or that of the Apostle: “All seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21).

Or what David’s psalm sings: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13:3ff.).

By these and other proofs, which those who inquire can produce in still greater number, it is clearly demonstrated that sometimes “the whole earth” is named for a part of the earth, “the whole world” for a part of the world, and “all human beings” for a part of humanity. Yet Scripture usually soon reveals their distinction, [Note: The Joliensis manuscript lacks “soon.”] so that the reader’s understanding is transferred from the designation of the whole to the part that is intended.

Such is the Apostle’s statement: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Is Christ power to those for whom he is a stumbling block, or wisdom to those for whom he is foolishness? [Note: We add the substantive verb “is” from Leo’s edition.] But since some of them were justified by faith, while others were hardened by their own impiety, [Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition read: “some of them are justified by faith, while others are hardened . . .”; our printed editions differ.] he distinguished one class of believers and unbelievers under the designation “the called,” so that those whom he indicated as alien to the faith, although they had heard the Gospel, he might show to be strangers to the calling.

## CHAPTER X. How Scripture speaks of the elect and the reprobate of the same people as though they were the same persons

[Col. 0661D]

[Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition have: “This rule.”]

According to this rule, the divine utterance promises through Isaiah, saying:

“I will lead the blind by a way they do not know, and they will tread paths they do not know. And I will make darkness into light for them, and crooked things straight. I will do these things and will not abandon them” (Isaiah 42:26). [Note: Thus the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts. The printed editions elsewhere have: “I will bring forth … and cause darkness to shine.”]

But what follows—“They, however, turned backward”—must be referred to a certain part of their race, not to those of whom he says, “I will not abandon them.”

Again the Lord says to Jacob:

“Do not fear, for I am with you. From the east I will bring your seed, and from the west I will gather you. I will say to the north, ‘Bring them,’ and to the south, ‘Do not hinder’; bring my sons from a distant land and my daughters from the ends of the earth, all in whom my name has been called. For I have prepared him for my glory, and I formed and made him” (Isaiah 43:6–7). [Note: The Camberon manuscript has “Do not fear … and from the west.”]

But what follows—“And I brought forth a blind people, and their eyes are blind, and they have deaf ears”—cannot in any way apply to those whom he says he prepared for his glory. In all these words, which are spoken of one human race, the earlier statements apply to some persons and the later statements to others.

In the Apostle also, what is done in part of the people is narrated under the name of the whole people, and fullness is reckoned in the remnant. [Note: Thus the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts; the following apostolic citation appears to refer to this reading: “Even at this present time a remnant has been made according to the election of grace.” Our printed editions and Leo’s later edition read “in the rest.” That word perhaps refers instead to “I have left for myself,” etc.] When he was discussing the blindness of the Jews and demonstrating that some of them are saved by grace, he says:

“I ask, then: Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I myself am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Romans 11:1–2). [Note: The Camberon manuscript has “rejects” here and below.]

The foreknown people, the people not rejected, are those who have been justified in Christ. And what seems to be said of all Israel is shown to apply only to those whom the election of grace has made a remnant for itself, as the following words of the Apostle explain.

For he adds:

“Do you not know what Scripture says in Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my life.’ But what does the divine response say to him? ‘I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal.’ [Note: The Joliensis and Camberon manuscripts and Leo’s edition read “knees before Baal”; the printed editions read “the knee to Baal.” In the Apostle’s Greek: Τῇ Βάαλ, that is, before the image mentioned in 4 Kings 10.] Thus, he says, even at this present time a remnant has been made according to the election of grace. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript, in conformity with the Apostle’s Greek, omits “saved”; Leo’s later edition and the printed editions and Camberon manuscript retain it, where they read “through election” instead of “according to the election.”] But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (ibid., 2ff.).

Therefore not all Israel has been rejected, nor has all been chosen. Voluntary blindness turned away one part; free illumination reserved another part for itself. [Note: This word, “voluntary,” is absent from the Thuanensis, Camberon, and Joliensis manuscripts.] Yet the discourse concerning them is framed in such a way that no distinction of the whole race seems to have been made between those who perish and those who are saved.

For when we read, “According to the Gospel they are enemies for your sake, but according to God’s election they are beloved for the sake of the fathers” (ibid., 28) [Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo add “God’s”; the word is understood in the Apostle’s text but is not expressed.], the wording sounds as though it calls the same people beloved whom it called enemies. But the Apostle himself cleared away this obscurity by saying: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel,” so that we might understand one race to have been divided into two classes, and that “every human being,” “all fullness,” and “all Israel” do not always refer to the whole, but very often to a part.

## CHAPTER XI. How Scripture speaks of people of different periods as though they belonged to a generation of one and the same period

Among these forms of expression, we must also observe that usage in Scripture by which something pertaining to people of different periods is promised as though it were said of one generation of the same age. [Note: Thus the Camberon manuscript and Leo’s later edition; others read “is expressed,” less well.]

Thus the holy Apostle Peter, writing to peoples of his own time and of the future, says:

“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, so that you may proclaim the mighty works of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light; once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; you had not obtained mercy, but now you have obtained mercy” (1 Peter 2:9–10). [Note: The Joliensis manuscript alone has “not God’s people.”]

When these words were proclaimed, did those people whom God had earlier allowed in past generations to walk in their own ways (Acts 14:15) still remain alive? And were those same people who had previously been handed over to their own desires now being called from darkness into marvelous light? [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits “now.” Leo’s edition, while retaining it, has “are called” rather than “were called.”]

Had they not already perished in their ignorance, and were they not already absent from this world, with no return from error to truth available to those long dead? [Note: The words “in their ignorance,” added from the Thuanensis manuscript, already occur in Leo but were absent from the Camberon manuscript and the printed editions. The Joliensis manuscript has “in their disgrace,” which is not inappropriate if one considers the supreme dignity of the Christian people expressed shortly before in the Apostle Peter’s words.]

Nevertheless, the grace that operated many centuries later in the descendants of the wicked was expressed by this customary manner of speaking, so that those who had previously been abandoned appear to be chosen now. These statements do not concern the same people, but people of the same race. The calling that shone forth near the end of the world does not return to an earlier age.

Thus, in a certain respect, they are both the same and not the same people concerning whom, and to whom, these things are said: in one respect, particulars are not separated from generalities; in another, they are distinguished from what is common. [Note: Thus the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts. Elsewhere: “in some particular respect.”]

## CHAPTER XII. How the Apostle’s statement, “He wills all human beings to be saved,” is understood of every kind of human being

[Col. 0663D]

1. But when those who love contentious accusations read or hear these things, they will say that by such arguments we contradict the Apostle, who declares that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). [Note: The Camberon manuscript has “and to the knowledge” here and below.]

We accept this portion of the Apostle’s words so fully and completely that we subtract nothing from the preceding or following words belonging to it. For, even if we set aside the other testimonies of the divine utterances, this passage is sufficient both to annul what they maliciously object and to defend what they impiously deny.

Writing, therefore, to Timothy, the Apostle Paul says: [Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts add “teacher of the nations.”]

“I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before our Savior God, [Note: Our earlier printed editions read “saving”; the Camberon manuscript and Leo read “Savior”; the Thuanensis manuscript omits “God.”] who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (ibid., 1ff.).

Concerning this rule of apostolic teaching, by which the universal Church is instructed, let us inquire what the universal Church itself believes, so that we do not wander into a contrary interpretation according to our own judgment. For there can be no uncertainty in the command if obedience agrees in its practice. [Note: The Prosperian editions and the Joliensis manuscript insert the preposition “in,” which Leo’s edition lacks.]

The Apostle therefore commanded—or rather, through the Apostle, the Lord who spoke in the Apostle commanded—that supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all human beings, for kings, and for those who are in positions of authority. [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits “and,” which occurs in Prosper’s editions and in Leo. It also adds “and” before “for kings.”]

The devotion of all priests and all the faithful concordantly observes this law of supplication, so that there is no part of the world in which such prayers are not celebrated by Christian peoples. Everywhere, then, the Church supplicates God not only for the saints and for those already regenerated in Christ, but also for all unbelievers and enemies of the cross of Christ; for all worshipers of idols; for all who persecute Christ in his members [Note: The Camberon manuscript reads “in his own members.”]; for the Jews, upon whose blindness the light of the Gospel does not shine; and for heretics and schismatics, who are alienated from the unity of faith and charity.

What does she ask for these people except that, abandoning their errors, they may be converted to God, receive faith, receive charity, and, freed from the darkness of ignorance, come to the knowledge of the truth?

Since they cannot provide this for themselves, oppressed by the weight of evil custom and bound by the chains of the devil, nor can they overcome their deceptions, to which they have clung so obstinately that they love falsehood as much as truth ought to be loved, the merciful and just Lord wills that supplication be made for all human beings. Thus, when we see innumerable people rescued from such profound evils, we should not doubt that God has granted what he was entreated to grant. And while giving thanks for those who have been saved, we should also hope that those who have not yet been illuminated will, through the same work of divine grace, be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God before they depart this life. [Note: The Camberon manuscript has “not yet,” together with Leo. Others have “not yet.” A little later the same manuscript, with the Joliensis and Leo, has the wording of the text; the Prosperian editions have “so that they may be transferred into the kingdom of God before they depart this life.”]

865 ## CHAPTER XIII. The depth of that hidden dispensation by which the saving grace of God passes over some for whom the Church prays cannot be disclosed to us in this life

If, however, saving grace passes over some, as we see happening, and the Church’s prayer for them is not accepted, this must be referred to the hidden judgments of divine justice, and we must recognize that the depth of this secret cannot be disclosed to us in this life. [Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts omit “is,” as does Leo’s later edition.] “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9), and now “we see through a mirror in an enigma” (ibid., 12).

Nor are we wiser or more knowledgeable than the blessed Apostle, who, when discussing the power of grace and entering the secret of great mysteries, faltered before things that it was impossible to explain. [Note: The Camberon manuscript reads, “things that would be impossible to explain.”] For after saying:

“I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation: blindness has happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel will be saved; as it is written (Isaiah 59:20): ‘From Zion will come the one who delivers and turns away ungodliness from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins. According to the Gospel they are enemies for your sake, but according to election they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they too have now not believed because of the mercy shown to you, so that they themselves may obtain mercy. For God has enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Romans 11:25ff.). [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has, in agreement with the Greek text of Paul, “in unbelief.”] [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has “who delivers and turns away.”]

When he had poured forth, in an excess of his mind, the mysteries of the divine works—mysteries surpassing the measure of human understanding—he transferred the entire method of explanation into astonishment. [Note: The edition has “to astonishment”; the Joliensis manuscript and Leo have “into astonishment.”] And, marveling at what he had uttered, he exclaimed:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he should be repaid? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory forever” [Note: Leo omits “of ages” here, and it is absent from the Apostle’s passage; Prosper’s editions and the Joliensis manuscript include it]. “Amen” (Romans 11:33ff.).

The assertion that preceded this teaching opened the way to a many-sided question, so that the cause of the varied grace of God across so many peoples and ages might be sought. [Note: Leo’s edition reads “various”; the Joliensis manuscript omits “God’s” after “grace.”] Why, namely, in earlier ages were all the nations allowed to walk in their own ways (Acts 14:15), while only Israel was instructed in the divine utterances and chosen for knowledge of the truth—and why did its unbelief finally make room for the nations to be saved? Was it as though, if one people remained steadfast in the faith of its own race, the mercy of God could not extend itself to the other nations? [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “could extend itself to the rest.”]

Why, finally, are those whose diminution is the salvation of the nations not freed from their blindness before the fullness of the nations enters (Romans 11:12) [Note: Thus the Joliensis and Camberon manuscripts, following the Apostle’s text; elsewhere, “is of the nations.”]—as though those who are to be saved, after the adoption of all nations has taken place, could not be illuminated together with all?

Or how will all Israel be saved once its blindness has been removed, when an innumerable multitude of it, failing in its unbelief, does not reach the times promised for those who are to be saved? [Note: The Camberon manuscript has “to the times of salvation.”]

Or how is it said that the fullness of those very nations whose earlier calling did not previously take place is now entering, when many thousands of people of every age and condition in all the nations under heaven die without Christ’s justification? [Note: The Joliensis manuscript has “whose earlier calling,” and shortly afterward, together with the Camberon manuscript, “when there are so many.”]

But concerning the causes of these mysteries and judgments, the pious and learned teacher preferred to suspend them upon the height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge rather than rashly investigate the secret of the most just truth and most merciful goodness, which has been withheld from human knowledge—omitting nothing of what ought not to be unknown, and handling nothing of what may not be known.

## CHAPTER XIV. There are many things in the dispensation of divine works whose effects alone are shown while their causes remain hidden

1. For many things occur in the dispensation of divine works whose causes remain hidden while their effects alone are shown: what is done is evident, but why it is done is not evident; the matter is brought into the open, while the reasoning is withdrawn into concealment. Thus, in the same matter, presumption concerning what is inscrutable may be restrained, and falsehood concerning what is manifest refuted.

For if I do not know why one person is born Greek and another barbarian, one in wealth and another in poverty; why a strong and lofty bodily beauty elevates one person, while the contracted weakness of deficient limbs disfigures another; why one, born of Catholics, is nurtured in the cradle of truth, while another, the offspring of heretics, imbibes the poison of error with his mother’s milk; and, finally, if I cannot distinguish a thousand other differences in bodily appearance, in the qualities of souls, in the condition of times, and in the customs of regions, [Note: The Thuanensis, Camberon, and Joliensis manuscripts have “condition.” This is not inappropriate.]—do I therefore fail to know that God is the creator and disposer of all these things?

He certainly created the bodies and spirits of individual human beings in such a way that, apart from the voluntary diversity that would subsequently arise from each person’s choice, he varied the very beginnings of their condition through a countless multiplicity of differences.

But many opinions of empty talkers would disturb us and draw us in different directions. These people have presumptuously attempted to define what cannot be known in ways that are inconsistent, assigning these original inequalities to the fates—which are nothing—and to the stars. [Note: Thus the Thuanensis, Camberon, and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Other editions have “to arrive at inconsistencies.”]

This would be so unless we held with the most certain knowledge that God the Creator forms each vessel from the original elements as he wills, and, according to measures pleasing to himself, regulates one nature of souls and one nature of bodies. [Note: The Thuanensis and Joliensis manuscripts have “from the original elements”; the received texts and the Camberon manuscript have “from natural elements.”]

These works of God would not have been withheld from human understanding if they ought to have become known; and it would be revealed why each thing happened in this way, unless it were sufficient to know that it happened in this way. [Note: Thus the Joliensis and Camberon manuscripts and Leo. Other editions have “would be knowable.”]
