The Lord says to Moses: “Who gave a mouth to man, and who made him mute and deaf, seeing and blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?” (Exod. 4:21). And through Isaiah: “Is it not I who have made fruitful and barren?” says the Lord (Isa. 66:9).

**[Note: [Col. 0667D]** The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts read *secundam*, “a second time.”]

In the book of Ecclesiasticus it is written: “Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God” (Ecclus. 11:14). And Job says: **[Col. 0667C]** “The tents of the robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although he himself has given everything into their hands” (Job 12:6). And, discussing the advancement and decline of all human affairs, and referring all changes to God’s judgments, he says:

“With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding. If he destroys, no one can build; if he shuts a man in, no one can open.

**[Note: [Col. 0667D]** The Jol. manuscript reads: “and there is no one who.”]

If he holds back the waters, everything will dry up; if he lets them loose, they will overturn the earth. With him are strength and wisdom; he knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived. He brings counselors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment; he loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a rope. He leads priests without honor,

**[Note: [Col. 0667D]** Thus read the Camb. manuscript and Leo’s edition. Elsewhere: *ingloriosos*, “without honor.”]

and overthrows nobles, changing the speech of the truthful and taking away the instruction of the elders; pouring contempt upon princes and raising up those who had been oppressed.

**[Note: [Col. 0667D]** Thus read the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo. Others read *relevat*, “raises up.”]

He reveals the depths **[Col. 0668A]** from darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light. He multiplies nations and destroys them,

**[Note: [Col. 0667D]** Thus read the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts: *perdet eas* … *restituet* (“will destroy them” … “will restore”). Leo’s edition reads *perdit eas* … *restituet* (“destroys them” … “will restore”). Subsequently the Camb. manuscript and Leo read *decipiet*, “will deceive.”]

and restores the overthrown to wholeness. He changes the heart of the princes of the earth and deceives them, so that they wander vainly through a pathless place. They will grope as in darkness and not in light, and he will make them wander like drunkards” (ibid. 16 and following).

And again, saying that God’s will cannot be frustrated: “For he alone exists, and no one can turn aside his thought;

**[Note: [Col. 0668D]** The Camberon. manuscript reads *cogitationes*, “thoughts.” Some other codices read *cognitionem*, “knowledge.”]

and whatever his soul desires, that he does” (Job 23:13).

## 868 CHAPTER XV

### That the deliverance of part of humanity cannot be ascribed to the merits of their wills—as though grace had chosen the good and passed over the wicked

Part of humanity is delivered, while part perishes. If we wish to ascribe this to the merits of their wills, so that grace may seem to have neglected the wicked but chosen the good, the cause of innumerable peoples will resist us—peoples through so many ages to whom no proclamation of heavenly teaching shone forth.

**[Note: [Col. 0668D]** The Jol. manuscript, omitting *nulla*, reads: “the proclamation of heavenly teaching did not shine forth.”]

Nor can we say that their descendants were better than those of whom it is written: “The people of the nations who sat in darkness saw a great light; and for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. 9:1). And to them the apostle Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition, so that you may proclaim the mighty deeds of him who called you from darkness into his wondrous light; once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Pet. 2:9).

**[Note: [Col. 0668D]** Leo has *in admirabile*, “into wondrous,” omitting *tam*, “so,” which is found in the other printed editions and in the Jol. manuscript.]

Therefore what the greater did not deserve is not attributed to the merits of the lesser. The same impiety accused both fathers and sons, and the same blindness of ignorance plunged them all together into the same errors. But why God did not have mercy on those, yet had mercy on these—what knowledge can comprehend this? What wisdom can investigate it?

**[Note: [Col. 0668D]** Thus, more correctly, according to the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo than in the other printed editions: *ista ratio*, “this reason.”]

The reason for this distinction is hidden, but the distinction itself is not hidden. We do not understand the one who judges, but we see what he does. Why do we accuse hidden justice, when we owe thanks for manifest mercy?

**[Note: [Col. 0668D]** The Jol. manuscript alone reads: “Praise and venerate what is being done, because what is concealed from you is not yours to know.”]

Let us praise and venerate what is being done, because it is safe not to know what is concealed.

## CHAPTER XVI

### From the fact that, before the use of understanding, some equal infants depart to eternal life and others to eternal death, the inscrutability of divine judgments is shown

**[Col. 0668D]**

Consider also the entire multitude of infants, in whom—apart from that offense through which the human race is born into condemnation—neither past merits nor future merits can be reckoned. For all those of whom we are now speaking, before any use of understanding and before the free choice of the will, pass away: some, regenerated, to eternal blessedness; others, not regenerated, to everlasting misery.

If you acknowledge original guilt, the whole number is under guilt; if you seek moral innocence, **869** the entire number is without fault. Human justice finds nothing by which to make a distinction, but the unspeakable grace of God has something by which to choose. The plan is hidden, but the gift is not hidden; mercy extends its work, while power conceals the cause.

**[Note: [Col. 0669C]** Other printed editions read *opus erexit*, “raised up the work.” The manuscripts of Camb., Jol., and Leo read *opus exserit*, “extends the work.” In the Thu. manuscript: *opus excelsi*, “the work of the Most High.” In the same place, the manuscripts of Camb. and Jol. below read *ignotae*, “unknown,” where others and Leo have *incognitae*, “unrecognized.”]

Yet what is not seen is no less certain than what is seen, because confession of even unknown equity cannot be denied to the author of a manifest work.

## CHAPTER XVII

### From the impious who are converted and saved at the end of life, it is shown both that grace is given without merits and that God’s judgment is inscrutable

But if you direct the gaze of your mind also toward those

**[Note: [Col. 0669C]** The Jol. manuscript, omitting *et*, reads: “if you direct [your attention] toward those.”]

who, after spending a long life in crimes and wickedness, are renewed by Christ’s sacrament of baptism at the very end of life and, without any support from good works, are transferred into fellowship with the heavenly kingdom, by what understanding will you comprehend the divine judgment? You must surely recognize that God’s gifts are gratuitous. Just as no crimes are so detestable that they can repel the gift of grace, so no works can be so excellent that what is freely bestowed ought to be owed through a judgment of recompense.

**[Note: [Col. 0669D]** Thus read the Jol. manuscript and Leo’s edition. Other printed editions read *quae possunt*, “which can,” less appropriately.]

For the redemption by Christ’s blood would be cheapened, and the mercy of God would not yield to the priority of human works, if justification, which is effected by grace, were owed to preceding merits, so that it would be not the gift of the giver but the wage of the worker.

How could it be proved

**[Note: [Col. 0669D]** The Camb. manuscript and Leo’s edition read *possit*, “can be proved.” Our other codices read *posset*, “could be proved.”]

that no human effort was adequate to abolish original sin, unless even the impious and criminal were received into the kingdom through Christ’s washing? Then those who glory in their own righteousness would recognize how incapable they are of doing anything worthy of adoption as God’s children, if they have not attained the sacrament of regeneration—since they are held under the same condition as the most wicked sinners, destined to be equal in sanctification if regeneration is present, and destined to perish together if cleansing is absent.

**[Note: [Col. 0669D]** Thus read the Jol. manuscript and Leo’s edition. Others read *non perveniunt*, “do not attain.” The Camb. manuscript reads *non pervenerit*, “has not attained.”]

If, then, even among the most wicked, at the very end of life, grace finds **870** some whom it may adopt, while many who seem less harmful are excluded from this gift:

**[Note: [Col. 0669D]** The Jol. manuscript reads *alieni sint*, “are excluded.”]

who could say that this occurs either without God’s dispensation or that it is decreed without profound equity? It is not unjust because it is hidden; rather, it is just because there can be no doubt that it is God’s judgment.

For what depends upon his will—by what sentence it ought to be judged—is uncertain before it is judged. But when the matter has reached its end, no one is free to complain about the outcome, because it is entirely certain that God ought to have done nothing other than what he did.

He also confirmed the variety of the many forms of calling, all belonging to one grace, by that rule of comparison in the Gospel in which he shows the householder hiring laborers for his vineyard at different times under an agreement for a denarius (Matt. 20:1 and following).

**[Note: [Col. 0669D]** We have not omitted the words enclosed in these signs, “[ ],” because of the authority of Prosper’s printed editions and the Jol. manuscript. Nevertheless, it is useful not to pass over the note of Leo’s editor and commentator. “The printed copies,” he says, “immediately add: ‘By which the equality of eternal life is signified’; and in the following line, where we now have ‘joined to the laborers of the whole day,’ they have ‘made equal to the laborers of the whole day.’ The former seems to me corrupted, the latter added, in accordance with the view of the heretic Jovinian, who, as Saint Jerome teaches in Book XI Against Him, maintained that all the rewards of the blessed are equal. For the Camb. and Thuaneus manuscripts have nothing more than our edition—which omits these words—and certainly our author does not introduce this parable in order to assert the equality of the eternal reward from the equality of the parabolic denarius. Indeed, he says not a word about the reward to be paid to the elect in heaven; rather, his entire purpose is to commend from this parable the excellence of the grace that the supreme Householder bestows on some at the conclusion of life, and the variety of the many forms of calling belonging to the one grace of justification. Thus even those who labored in great toil and received no more than the last-comers may understand that they received the gift of grace, not the wage of works. In this passage he considers not equality of glory but the gratuitousness of grace.” That this is the genuine meaning of the parable and more consonant with the context is proved by Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ghent, in chapter 101 of his *Commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels*.]

[By which the equality of eternal life is signified.]

Without doubt, those admitted into the vineyard at the eleventh hour and joined to the laborers of the whole day present the lot of those of whom we are now speaking—those whom divine indulgence rewards, to commend the excellence of grace, at the decline of the day and the close of life. It does not pay a price for labor, but pours out the riches of its goodness upon those whom it has chosen without works.

**[Note: [Col. 0670D]** Other printed editions read *numeravit*, “counted.” The Camberon. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition read *muneratur*, “rewards.”]

**[Note: [Col. 0670C]** The Jol. manuscript alone adds *sine operibus legis*, “without works of the law.” All the others lack the word *legis*, “of the law.”]

Thus even those who labored in great toil and received no more than the last-comers may understand that they received the gift of grace, not the wage of works.

If we too murmur against the householder because those called last are made equal to the laborers of the whole day and, despite having performed many works, deserve no more than those who have performed almost none, the reply given to one of them will be addressed to us:

“Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. I wish to give to this last one as I give to you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is mine? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. 20:13 and following).

**[Note: [Col. 0671D]** The Jol. manuscript reads: “Or is your eye evil?”]

Certainly this generosity seemed unjust to that accuser; but what instruction did he receive from it? What reason did he learn? The justice of this dispensation

**[Note: [Col. 0671D]** The Jol. manuscript lacks the word *hujus*, “this.”]

was not revealed to him, nor was he admitted to behold the hidden secret **871**. Rather, so that he would refrain from examining God’s judgments, the goodness of the one who shows mercy and the power of the one who wills were set before him—as though the Apostle were saying to him as well:

“O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me this way?’” (Rom. 9:22).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Grace, without which good merits cannot exist, is received by no one except according to God’s will, without merits

**[Col. 0671B]**

For all human beings, of whatever nation and race,

**[Note: [Col. 0671D]** The Camberon. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition add: *gentis et*, “of nation and.”]

of whatever condition and age, the will of God is the cause by which grace is received. With him the reason for election is hidden; merits begin from that grace which they received without merits.

If they could be good without grace, it would not be said: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5); and: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). Rather, it would be said: “Unless someone is just and good, he cannot be blessed forever.”

Nor would it be necessary to be reborn through water and the Spirit if instruction through a commandment were sufficient. And the faith that believes all sins are forgiven through baptism would be emptied of meaning if grace were taught to be bestowed not upon the wicked and impious but upon the good and upright.

Therefore the origin of true life and true righteousness is established in the sacrament of regeneration, so that where a human being is reborn, there also the truth of those virtues may arise; and those who could scarcely attain the reward of temporal and empty praise may begin, through faith, to advance toward everlasting glory.

**[Note: [Col. 0671D]** Other Prosperian printed editions read *et incipiunt*, “and they begin.” The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts, together with Leo’s edition, read *et incipiant*, “and they may begin.” The same edition of Leo later has *quae vix*, “which scarcely,” with *intellige virtutis*, “understand, of virtue.” Our manuscripts, which have *qui vix*, “who scarcely,” evidently refer to human beings.]

For whether it is a Jew puffed up with knowledge of the law or a Greek inflated by the study of natural wisdom, before being justified through faith in Christ he is confined under sin. And if he persists in his unbelief,

**[Note: [Col. 0671D]** We correct this from the Camberon. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Elsewhere: *infelicitate*, “misfortune.”]

the wrath of God remains upon him—that wrath contracted in Adam’s transgression, of which the Apostle speaks:

“And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience,

**[Note: [Col. 0671D]** The Camberon. and Jol. manuscripts, following the Greek, read *in filiis*, “in the sons.” Others read, as the Vulgate, *in filios*, “into the sons.”]

among whom we also once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts; and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:1 and following).

And again:

“For at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the citizenship of Israel and strangers to the covenants, having no hope of the promise and without God in the world” (ibid. 12).

And again: **872**

“You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (ibid. 5:8).

And again:

“Giving thanks to the Father, who made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light, who rescued us from darkness and the power of darkness, and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 2:12 and following).

**[Note: [Col. 0672D]** These two words, *tenebris et*, “darkness and,” although they are found in all our books, are not read in either textual form of the Apostle’s Epistle.]

And again:

“For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, wandering, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared—not from works of righteousness that we ourselves had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior—so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:3 and following).

**[Note: [Col. 0672D]** The Camb. manuscript adds *renovationis*, “renewal,” here; that word is also not absent from the Apostle’s text.]

## CHAPTER XIX

### What human nature is like without grace

And so that the character of human nature without grace may be made clear as briefly as possible, let the apostle Jude say what is produced both by the ignorance of the unlearned and by the teaching of the wise:

“But these people blaspheme whatever they do not know; and whatever they know naturally, like mute animals,

**[Note: [Col. 0672D]** The Camberon. manuscript reads *velut bruta animalia*, “like brute animals.”]

in those things they are corrupted” (Jude 10).

**[Note: [Col. 0672D]** The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts read: “But let him also say.”]

Let the evangelist Luke also declare, in the words of Zechariah, through what night the human race wanders before the illumination of grace, and from what darkness of ignorance God’s people are delivered:

“And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people for the forgiveness of their sins, because of the tender mercies of our God, by which the Dawn from on high has visited us, to shine upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace” (Luke 1:76 and following).

## CHAPTER XX

### The Lord extends the tender mercies of his compassion for the salvation of all nations and saves all; yet it is also true that no one receives his testimony

**[Col. 0672D]**

The Lord extends these tender mercies of his compassion not merely for the redemption of one people but for the salvation of all nations, as the Evangelist says:

“Jesus was going to die for the nation—and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God” (John 11:52).

**[Note: [Col. 0672D]** Other printed editions read *mortuus erat*, “had died.” The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts, together with Leo, more correctly read *moriturus erat*, “was going to die,” in accordance with the Gospel text. Leo later adds *et non tantum*, “and not only.”]

For this is what that voice of the Lord does: resounding throughout the whole world **873** like a trumpet of compassion, it both invites and summons all human beings.

**[Note: [Col. 0673D]** Leo’s edition omits *omnes*, “all,” which Prosper’s manuscripts do not omit.]

For after he had said:

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, because this was well pleasing before you,”

he added:

“All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father,

**[Note: [Col. 0673D]** The Jol. manuscript reads *quisquam novit*, “anyone knows.”]

nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.”

Then he added:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:25 and following).

John the Baptist, in the Gospel of John, bears prophetic witness, saying:

“He who comes from heaven is above all. He testifies to what he has seen and heard, and no one receives his testimony. Whoever receives his testimony has certified that God is true” (John 3:31–33).

**[Note: [Col. 0673D]** The Duac. and Colon. editions read *significavit*, “has signified.”]

Therefore, so far as concerns the blindness of the human race, contracted through a long night of ignorance and pride, the Creator of the world came into this world, and the world did not recognize him (John 1:10); the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it (ibid. 5); he who is above all testifies to what he has seen and heard, and no one receives his testimony (John 3:31–32).

But because the Son of God did not come into the world without purpose, and gave himself for all, and died not only for the nation but also to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:52), and says to everyone, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened,” and, while reserving to himself the decision of inscrutable election, gives knowledge of himself and of his Father to those to whom he wishes to reveal him:

all the children of light, children of the promise, children of Abraham, children of God, a chosen race, a royal priesthood, true Israelites, foreknown and predestined for the kingdom of God—those whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the nations (Rom. 9:24)—receive the testimony of him who came from heaven; **874** they certify that God is true.

**[Note: [Col. 0673D]** This is the reading in Leo’s edition and above. In our printed editions the reading here is *significantes*, “signifying.” It is clear that the former is better, because *signantes*, “certifying,” is explicitly explained afterward by the phrase “signifying.”]

They certify that God is true—that is, they explicitly declare in their salvation that God is true, fulfilling and completing what he promised to Abraham, the father of all nations. When God promised that he would become heir of the world, he did not waver through unbelief but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God and being fully convinced that what he had promised he was also able to accomplish (Rom. 4:20).

But who is so alien to Abraham’s faith, who is so degenerate from the father of all nations, as to say either that God’s promise is not fulfilled or that it is fulfilled by someone other than the one who made the promise? Such a person will be a liar; but God is true. And everyone who receives his testimony certifies and declares this: that through the light which illuminates him he has been made seeing, made obedient, and made understanding.

**[Note: [Col. 0673D]** The printed editions read *factus est obediens, factus est intelligens*, “he has been made obedient, he has been made understanding.” The substantive verb is omitted in both places in the Jol. manuscript and in Leo.]

As the evangelist John testifies, saying:

“We know that the whole world lies in the evil one, and we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son” (John 5:19).

**[Note: [Col. 0674D]** The Jol. manuscript reads: “the whole world … and has given.”]

## CHAPTER XXI

### That one should not investigate why God chooses some and does not choose others, just as one should not investigate why previously, passing over all the nations, he chose Israel alone

**[Col. 0674B]**

But if it is asked why the Savior of all human beings did not give all of them this understanding, so that they might know the true God and be—that is, remain—in his true Son, although we believe that the help of grace was not wholly withdrawn from any human beings, a matter we shall discuss more fully

**[Note: [Col. 0674D]** The Jol. manuscript reads *in consequentibus*, “in what follows.”]

below, perhaps this has been veiled in the same way as that other matter has been hidden: why, previously, passing over all the nations, he set apart for himself one people to instruct in the knowledge of truth.

**[Note: [Col. 0674D]** The word *antea*, “previously,” is absent from the Jol. manuscript and Leo.]

If there is no complaint to be made about that judgment of God, much less should we murmur about this work that is now carried out in the election of all nations. What God has willed to remain hidden must not be investigated; what he has made manifest must not be neglected.

**[Note: [Col. 0674D]** The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts, together with Leo, read *negligenda*, “must not be neglected.” The others read *neganda*, “must not be denied.”]

Otherwise we may be found illicitly curious about the former and damnably ungrateful about the latter.

**[Note: [Col. 0674D]** The Jol. manuscript reads: “and about the latter.”]

We are not unaware that some are so thoughtlessly presumptuous and so arrogantly proud that they dare to profane with a doctrine falsely so called what the eminent teacher of the nations, instructed not by human beings or through a human being (Gal. 1:1) but by God, confessed to be far removed, above and beyond the measure of his knowledge. They wish nothing to be hidden or secret where the Apostle did not disclose what ought to be believed but showed what ought not to be investigated.

For no studies and no intellectual powers are permitted to discover by what judgment or counsel God—immutably good, immutably just, always foreknowing, always almighty—has confined all things in unbelief so that he might have mercy on all (Rom. 11:32).

**[Note: [Col. 0674D]** The Camberon. manuscript reads *dimiserit*, “has left.”]

And yet, in those ages when he was instructing Israel alone, he delayed illuminating innumerable peoples of the impious; and now he permits that same Israel to remain blinded until the full number of the nations enters, while it perishes among so many thousands who are born and die, and is saved **875** in those whom the end of the world will find.

Through this mystery, unfolded throughout the entire body of Scripture, it has indeed become known to us what has been done, what is being done, and what must be done; but why it pleased him that these things should happen in this way has been withdrawn from the contemplation of human understanding.

## CHAPTER XXII

### Those who refer the distinction by which God chooses some and does not choose others to the merits of the human will teach that no one is saved gratuitously but through recompense; and they are plainly refuted by the case of infants

But those who are ashamed to admit that they do not know something, and who use obscurity as an opportunity to spread traps of deception, refer every distinction by which God chooses some and does not choose others—for many are called,

**[Note: [Col. 0675D]** The Jol. manuscript reads: “For many are called.”]

but few are chosen (Matt. 20:16)—to the merits of the human will.

**[Note: [Col. 0675D]** The Duac. edition and the following editions write *elegit, alios non elegit*, “he chose, he did not choose,” in the margin as a variant reading.]

For they teach that no one is saved gratuitously but through recompense, since it is naturally implanted in everyone that, if they wish, they can share in the truth, and that grace flows abundantly to those by whom it has been sought.

This definition, leaving aside for the moment the truth of grace, seems to display some sort of reasoning concerning those who make use of free choice. But concerning infants, who, without any merit of a good will, share with the rest of mortals in the common condition of the original wound, no explanation can be offered by which it may be taught why some are saved through rebirth while others perish without rebirth, under the providence and omnipotence of him in whose hand is the soul of every living being and the spirit of all human flesh (Job 12:10), and to whom it is said: “The days of a human being are short; the number of his days is with you” (Job 14:5).

**[Note: [Col. 0675D]** The Jol. manuscript reads *afferre, qua doceat*, “to offer an explanation by which it may teach.”]

I do not think that these patrons of the wills of human beings will use their simplicity so shamelessly as either to say that these things happen by chance or to assert that those who are not reborn do not perish.

**[Note: [Col. 0675D]** The Camberon. and Jol. manuscripts read *fortuito*, “by chance.” Others read *fortuitu*, “by accident.”]

For they would plainly be convicted either of agreeing with the pagans about fate or of denying with the Pelagians that Adam’s sin was transmitted to his descendants. The Pelagians could not say that infants were not baptized by fate; but because they dared to profess that infants were free from sin, they deserved condemnation.

Since, then, the question concerns the distinction of all human beings, and infants cannot be separated from the whole of humanity, while the Truth has said concerning human beings of every age: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished” (Luke 19:10), those who establish the cause of election in the merits of those who are chosen attempt in vain to open the depth of inscrutable grace through free will.

And although they have produced many foolish and false claims about the will and judgment of adults, **876** they fail when confronted with the distinction among infants. They cannot boast that they have provided an account of that question which is treated with respect to all human beings but resolved with respect to none.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### Every good merit of a human being, from the beginning of faith to the completion of perseverance, is a divine gift; this is first shown concerning faith

**[Col. 0676A]**

The manifold character and greatness of divine grace prove that these people, even when they speak about the wills of adults, assert what is contrary to the truth, and that the testimonies of the divine utterances oppose their persuasion. If we wished to append all of them to our discourse, there would be no limit to our discussion.

**[Note: [Col. 0675D]** Thus read the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Other manuscripts read *disserendo*, “in discussing.”]

Nevertheless, those passages that present themselves to memory will not be omitted, so that it may be sufficiently made clear that a human being’s good merit, from the beginning of faith to the completion of perseverance, is a divine gift and work.

**[Note: [Col. 0676D]** The Jol. and Camb. manuscripts read: “Nevertheless, if they present themselves to memory, they will not be omitted.” Leo’s edition has the same reading.]

Let the apostle Paul explain from what source faith itself—which is the mother of good will and righteous action—is born. He gives thanks to God for the faith of the Romans, saying:

“First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. 1:8).

Writing also to the Ephesians, he says:

“Therefore I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation for the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart having been enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints” (Eph. 1:16 and following).

Likewise, giving thanks to God for the faith of the Colossians, he says:

“We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you, having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and the love that you have for all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven” (Col. 1:3–4 and following).

And, explaining what he asks for them so that they may receive other good things from the same author of good things, he says:

“For this reason we too, from the day on which we heard, do not cease praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in all things, bearing fruit in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God; strengthened with power according to the might of his glory, **877** in all endurance and patience with joy” (Col. 1:11).

**[Note: [Col. 0676D]** The Jol. manuscript reads *non cessavimus*, “we have not ceased.”]

**[Note: [Col. 0676D]** The Jol. manuscript supplies *per omnia*, “in all things,” which belongs to the sacred text but was absent from the other manuscripts of Prosper.]

**[Note: [Col. 0676D]** The Jol. manuscript reads *in omni sapientia*, “in all wisdom.”]

Likewise, to the Thessalonians, who were fervent in the spirit of faith and love, he says:

“We give thanks to God always for all of you, remembering you in our prayers without ceasing, mindful of the work of your faith and labor and love and endurance in the hope of our Lord Jesus Christ before our God and Father” (1 Thess. 1:2).

And below:

“For this reason we too give thanks to God without ceasing, because, when you received from us the word of the hearing of God, you received it not as the word of human beings but, as it truly is, the word of God, which works in you who have believed” (1 Thess. 2:13).

**[Note: [Col. 0676D]** The Jol. manuscript reads *verbum hominis*, “the word of a human being.”]

Could it have been demonstrated more fully or clearly that the faith of believers is God’s gift than by the fact that thanks were given to God because those to whom God’s word was preached through human beings did not doubt it as a human message, but believed as though God were speaking through human beings—he who worked within them so that they might believe?

In the second Epistle to the same Thessalonians, the Apostle speaks in this way of those who were progressing in faith in Christ:

“We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing greatly and the love of each one of you for one another is increasing, so that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God, for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and tribulations that you endure as an example of God’s just judgment, so that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer” (2 Thess. 1:3 and following).

**[Note: [Col. 0677D]** The Jol. manuscript reads *nosmetipsi*, “we ourselves.”]

**[Note: [Col. 0677D]** Our printed editions add *in*, “for,” here. It is absent from the Jol. manuscript, Leo’s edition, and the Apostle’s sacred text.]

The apostle Peter also teaches that faith is from God, writing:

“Knowing that you were redeemed not with corruptible things, gold or silver, from your vain way of life inherited from your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ Jesus, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world but manifested in the last times for your sake, who through him are faithful in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be in God” (1 Pet. 1:18 and following).

**[Note: [Col. 0677D]** Leo has *vestrae paternae traditionis*, “of your paternal tradition.”]

Likewise, in his second Epistle, he speaks in this way of receiving faith:

“Simon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a faith equal to ours through the righteousness of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Pet. 1:1).

**[Note: [Col. 0677D]** The Jol. manuscript adds *nostri*, “our,” in conformity with the sacred text. The other manuscripts had not added it.]

From where, then, the spirit of faith is obtained, the apostle John teaches most clearly, saying:

“Every spirit that confesses that Jesus has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the Antichrist” (1 John 4).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript adds “the same.”]

Likewise, the same apostle says that the Gospel is received from him in whom is the spirit of truth: “We are from God,” he says. “Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we recognize the spirit of truth and the spirit of error” (ibid., 6).

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, the apostle Peter, declaring that faith is through the Lord Jesus, says: “His name has strengthened this man, whom you see and know; and the faith that is through him has given him this complete healing in the presence of you all” (Acts 3:16).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits the word “is.”]

Concerning the faith of Lydia also, whose heart the Lord opened among the other women who were listening together to the Gospel, the same history relates:

“On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate beside the river, where there seemed to be a place of prayer; and sitting down, we spoke to the women who had gathered. And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, worshiping God, listened; the Lord opened her heart to attend to what was being spoken by Paul” (Acts 16:13–14).

[Note: Thus the Joliensis manuscript, together with Leo’s edition. Other copies have “of Thyatira.”]

That faith is not from human wisdom but from divine inspiration is confirmed by the voice of Truth himself. For when the Lord said to his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And Jesus, answering, said to him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:15 ff.).

The apostle Paul proclaims that this very faith is given according to the measure determined by the generosity of the giver:

“For I say, through the grace that has been given to me, to everyone among you, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, as God has allotted to each the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).

Likewise, commending the unity of right faith and agreement for the honor of God as coming from God, the same apostle says:

“Now may the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same mind toward one another, according to Jesus Christ, so that with one mind and one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 15:5–6).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “and confession.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “of patience and consolation,” as does the Vulgate.]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “so that with one mind and one mouth you may honor.”]

And below:

“May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope, in the power of the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 13).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “in hope and power.” Leo’s edition reads, “in hope, in power,” as do both apostolic texts. Prosper’s printed editions read, “that you may abound in hope, in power.”]

By this testimony we are taught that not only faith, but also joy, peace, and an abundance of hope are possessed only in the power of the Holy Spirit.

Writing to the Ephesians about the riches of grace, which repays evil with good, and about faith, which is not from ourselves but is possessed as God’s gift, the apostle says:

“But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his exceedingly great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—for by whose grace we have been saved—and raised us up together and seated us in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. For by grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift; not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Ephesians 2:4 ff.).

[Note: Leo’s edition adds “he says.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript does not explicitly have the preposition “us.”]

Therefore this is the characteristic of the new creation through grace: that those who are God’s workmanship, who are formed in Christ by a heavenly birth, should not grow sluggish through idleness or be weakened by laziness, but should advance from virtue to virtue by walking along the way of good works. For this is what it means to be fashioned; this is what it means to be made new from the old creation; this is what it means to be reformed from the image of the earthly man into the image of the heavenly man. All of this he begins, increases, and perfects, whether openly through the co-workers of grace or secretly through the ministration of the Spirit—he whose field, whose building, and whose workmanship we are.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Every good in a human being comes from grace, and faith is given without being requested, so that through its requests we may obtain the other good things.

[Column 0679A]

I believe that it has been sufficiently demonstrated by these testimonies—although other proofs could also have been assembled—that the faith by which the ungodly person is justified is possessed only as God’s gift, and is not bestowed on the basis of any preceding merits; rather, it is given so that it may be the beginning of merits.

[Note: Elsewhere, “so that, when it itself has been given.”]

And once it has been given without being requested, the other good things are then obtained through its requests.

[Note: Leo’s edition reads, “are bestowed.”]

Accordingly, some testimonies must be selected from among the many, which may display the generosity of grace in the variety of its gifts.

Thus the psalm of David sings that it comes from God both that a person chooses God’s way and that he rises from a fall:

“The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he wills his way. When he falls, he will not be crushed, because the Lord supports his hand” (Psalm 36:23).

Likewise, that one comes to God under God’s guidance:

“Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles” (Psalm 42:3).

Likewise, that human strength is in the Lord, and that God’s will precedes the one who is to be delivered:

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “is in God.”]

“I will guard my strength for you,” he says, “because God is my protector. My God, his will shall precede me” (Psalm 58:10).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits “he says.”]

[Note: The Camberon manuscript reads, “his mercy.”]

In Proverbs also we read concerning wisdom and understanding:

“For the Lord gives wisdom, and from his face come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 2:6).

Likewise, in the same book, concerning God’s ordering of wisdom, without which no actions are right, it is said:

“My counsel and my protection—I am prudence, and mine is strength. Through me kings reign, and through me tyrants possess the earth” (Proverbs 8:14).

Likewise elsewhere, that no one can walk rightly unless the Lord directs him:

“From the Lord a man’s steps are directed; but how can a mortal understand his ways?” (Proverbs 20:24).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “are directed.”]

Likewise elsewhere:

“Every man seems righteous to himself, but the Lord directs the hearts” (Proverbs 21:2).

And below:

“The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint).

Likewise in the same place, concerning thought and counsel:

“Many thoughts are in a man’s heart, but the Lord’s counsel prevails” (Proverbs 19:21).

In the book of Ecclesiastes it is written that both having necessities and using them well are gifts from God:

“There is no good for a man except what he has eaten and drunk and shown his soul as good in his labor. And indeed I saw this, that it is from the hand of God. For who can eat or who can provide nourishment without him?” (Ecclesiastes 5:17).

[Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts, and Leo’s edition, read: “There is no good for a man except what he has eaten and drunk and shown his soul as good in his labor.” Other copies read: “except that he should eat and drink and show his soul good.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “this I saw.”]

Likewise, in the same book it is read that the hearts and works of the righteous are in God’s hand, and that they advance in their pursuits only as much as he grants:

“However much a man may labor in seeking, he will not find; and whatever the wise man may say in order to know, he will not be able to find. Because I applied all this to my heart, and my heart saw all this: that both the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God” (Ecclesiastes 8:17; and chapter 9:1).

[Note: Leo’s edition reads, “he put into my heart.”]

In the book of Wisdom the same work of grace is described as follows:

“For he is both the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise. For in his hand are we, and our words, and all wisdom, and knowledge of works, and discipline” (Wisdom 7:15–16).

Concerning self-control also, that it is possessed as a gift from God, the same Scripture says:

“I knew that I could not otherwise be continent unless God gave it, and this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was” (Wisdom 8:21).

The teaching of the apostle Paul agrees with this statement. In his First Letter to the Corinthians he writes:

“I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (1 Corinthians 7:7).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “another, however, in that way.”]

The Lord is also reported in the Gospel according to Matthew to have indicated the gift of self-control in these words. When his disciples said to him, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry,” Jesus said to them:

“Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19:10–11).

[Note: Here Prosper’s books add “by my Father,” words found neither in the Joliensis manuscript, nor in Leo’s edition, nor in the Greek or Latin text of the Gospel. For this reason we have deleted them.]

Concerning the fear of God and wisdom, it is written in Ecclesiasticus:

“The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and both are gifts from God” (Ecclesiasticus 1:2).

Likewise in the same book:

“The fear of the Lord has set itself above everything; blessed is the one to whom it has been given to possess the fear of the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus 25:14).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “concerning the same.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript, omitting “itself,” reads “he has placed above”; afterward, “the fear of God.”]

Isaiah also speaks of spiritual riches, whose author is the Lord:

“In our treasures salvation has come, wisdom, piety, and discipline from the Lord; these are the treasures of righteousness” (Isaiah 25, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “Likewise concerning the height.”]

Likewise, concerning the height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, whose goodness is preceded by no one’s merit, he says:

“Who has measured the waters in his hand, and heaven with a span, and all the earth with a handful? Who has placed the mountains in a balance and the rocks in scales? Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor, to instruct him? Or whom has he consulted, and who instructed him? Or who showed him judgment, or who showed him the way of prudence? Or who first gave to him, and he shall be repaid?” (Isaiah 40:12 ff.).

From the same perspective, in the book of Job the words of the Lord are read as follows:

“Who has given to me first, that I may repay him? Everything under heaven is mine” (Job 41:2).

Jeremiah proclaims that true wisdom for a human being is from God:

“I know, Lord, that a man’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to direct his path” (Jeremiah 10:23).

[Note: Thus the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Other copies read, “right wisdom.”]

Likewise, that the turning of the heart toward God is from God, the Lord himself bears witness and says:

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “to the Lord.”]

“I will restore them to this land, and rebuild them, and not destroy them; and I will plant them, and not uproot them; and I will give them a heart to know me, because I am the Lord. And they shall be my people, and I shall be their God, because they shall turn to me with their whole heart” (Jeremiah 24:6 ff.).

[Note: Leo’s edition reads, “and I will build,” as in the Vulgate.]

[Note: Thus the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Other copies read, “Likewise, proclaiming the same.”]

Baruch also proclaims that the knowledge of God is from God:

“And they shall know that I am the Lord their God, and I will give them a heart to know me, and ears to hear” (Baruch 2:31).

That every good word and every holy work is a ministration of the Holy Spirit, without whom nothing is done rightly, the apostle Paul teaches in the First Letter to the Corinthians, saying:

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “is done.”]

“Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus.’ And no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit. There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:3 ff.).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “faith in one Spirit.” Below, the Colon edition reads, “to each individually as he wills.”]

The same apostle says to the Ephesians that each person possesses as much grace as the Lord has granted:

“One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in us all. But grace was given to each of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men’” (Ephesians 4:4 ff.).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “what God has granted.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript has, “and over all, and through all,” as in both apostolic texts.]

Likewise, in the Second Letter to the Corinthians he says that we are not capable even of thinking what is spiritual except through God’s grace:

“We have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as if from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of the new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:4 ff.).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, as in the apostle’s text, “our sufficiency.”]

And again in the same Letter, teaching that both the effect and the sufficiency of good works are supplied by God’s grace:

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “teaching . . . both the effect and the sufficiency.”]

“God is able,” he says, “to make every grace abound in you, so that, having sufficiency in all things and in every way, you may abound in every good work; as it is written: ‘He distributed; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever.’ Now he who supplies seed to the sower will also supply bread for eating, and will increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that in everything you may be enriched unto all simplicity” (Psalm 3:9).

[Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts read, “to make abundant.”]

Writing to the Ephesians, the apostle teaches that all good things by which God is pleased are God’s gifts, and that he should be asked to grant them to those who do not have them:

“For this reason,” he says, “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts; rooted and grounded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know also the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God. Now to him who is able to do all things far more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.”

[Note: Leo’s edition reads, as in the apostle’s text, “to be strengthened with power.”]

[Note: The words “and to know also” had fallen out of Prosper’s books. We restored them from the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition, since they are present in the apostle’s text.]

That God is the author of every good, whose gifts are neither uncertain nor changeable but come from an eternal will, the apostle James speaks as follows:

“Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration. For of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of first beginning of his creation” (James 1:16–17).

The prophet Zechariah also sings in harmony with him, saying:

“The Lord saved his people on that day like sheep, because holy stones are rolling over his land. For if anything is good, it is his; and if anything is excellent, it is from him” (Zechariah 9:16–17).

[Note: Leo’s edition, together with the Douay and Cologne editions, and the Joliensis and Louvain manuscripts, reads “he will save,” as in the text of Scripture, where in what follows they read “will roll,” not “are rolling,” which all our books prefer.]

In the Gospel according to Matthew, that knowledge and understanding are gifts of God, which he bestows on whomever he wishes, is stated as follows:

“Then his disciples came and said to him, ‘Why do you speak to them in parables?’ But he answered and said to them, ‘Because it has been given to you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given’” (Matthew 13:10–11).

[Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition read “knowledge”; others read “of knowledge.”]

The evangelist John also declares that no one has anything good except what he has received from above, saying:

“A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3:27).

In the same Gospel there is the teaching of Truth himself that no one comes to the Son unless drawn by the Father, because God makes a person come, understand, and obey:

“No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day. For it is written in the prophets: ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John 6:44 ff.).

And below:

“For this reason I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father” (ibid., 65).

[Column 0683B]

That progress and perseverance in faith and good works to the end are gifts and assistance from God is confirmed by the authority of the Holy Scriptures. For the apostle Paul, writing to the Philippians, says:

“I am confident of this very thing: that he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6).

Someone wishing to twist the force of this testimony toward the perversity of his own understanding wanted the words “he who began in you” to be understood as though they said “he who began from you,” so that both the beginning and the completion of the work would be attributed not to God but to the human being, who would have wished both to begin and to complete it.

But in the same Letter the outstanding preacher of grace strikes down this most insane pride, saying:

“In nothing be terrified by your adversaries, which is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation—and this is from God. For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (ibid., 28–29).

[Note: Thus the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Others read, “Because it is for you,” and so forth.]

And again:

“Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to act according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition read, “and to act.” Others read, “and to complete.”]

Likewise, in the First Letter to the Thessalonians he teaches that the beginning, progress, and completion of virtues are from God, saying:

“Now may God himself, our Father, and our Lord Jesus direct our way to you. And may the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love for one another and for all, just as we do for you, so that he may strengthen your hearts blameless in holiness before God our Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints” (1 Thessalonians 3:11 ff.).

[Note: Formerly the printed editions added “of life,” which are absent from the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition, and indeed from both texts of Saint Paul.]

Writing also to the Corinthians, and commending the perseverance that progresses in every virtue as a gift from God, he says:

“I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and knowledge; just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace, awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also confirm you to the end, without blame, on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:4 ff.).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, as in the apostle’s text, “on the day.” In Leo’s books this had formerly been the reading of the passage. The same manuscript also adds “our” near the end, after the apostle’s text.]

Likewise, in the Letter to the Romans, concerning the love of Christ by which he makes those whom he loves unconquerable—that is, persevering to the end. For what else is perseverance than not being overcome by temptation?

“Who,” he says, “will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us” (Romans 8:35 ff.).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “we are considered.”]

Likewise, to the Corinthians, concerning the victory that Christ brings to completion:

“The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:56–57).

Likewise, to the Thessalonians, concerning the perseverance that God grants:

“May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is he who called you; he will also do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:23–24).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “and complete,” as in the Greek text.]

[Note: Elsewhere Leo reads, “may he do it.”]

Likewise, to the Thessalonians, that all our good things, whether in doing or speaking, and perseverance in them, are gifts from God, he proclaims as follows:

“May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope by grace, exhort your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word. Finally, brothers, pray for us, so that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, as also among you, and that we may be delivered from troublesome and evil people. For not all have faith. But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from evil” (2 Thessalonians 2:16–17; 3:1, 3).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “the word of God.”]

[Note: Thus the Joliensis manuscript, as in the apostle. Other copies omit the second occurrence of “and.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “But God is faithful.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “But Peter,” and the same manuscript adds “Amen” after several words, as does Leo’s edition.]

Let us also hear the apostle Peter teaching from where the power of perseverance comes:

“The God of all grace, who called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after we have suffered a little, will himself perfect, strengthen, and establish you; to him be power and might forever and ever. Amen” (1 Peter 5:10–11).

The apostle John, saying that the victory of the saints is the work of God who dwells in the saints, speaks as follows:

“You are from God, little children, and you have conquered the world, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition read, “who is in us.”]

Likewise, the same apostle:

“Everything that is born of God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5:4).

In the Gospel according to Luke, that God grants perseverance in faith is promised as follows:

“Then Jesus said to Peter: ‘Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers, and pray that you may not enter into temptation’” (Luke 22:31 ff.).

[Note: The Cologne edition reads, “in virtue.” The Joliensis and Camberon manuscripts and Leo’s edition read “is stated,” in place of the word “is promised,” which appears in the others.]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “so that he might sift you.” All the others read “might see you.” The editors from Louvain onward have observed that *cernere* was then customarily used in the sense of “to separate” and “to sift”; Pliny also uses it in this same sense.]

[Note: Leo reads, “and pray.”]

In the Gospel of John, concerning Christ’s sheep, which no one can snatch from his hand, we read that Truth says:

“But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them from my hand” (John 10:26 ff.).

[Note: Thus the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Other copies read, “are snatched away.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition add “voice” after “I”; in the latter, instead of “I give them,” the marginal reading says, “I will give them.”]

Likewise, in the same Gospel, concerning those whom the Father gives to the Son, all of whom come to the Son and none of whom perishes, these words are spoken by the Lord himself:

“Everything that the Father gives me will come to me; and whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of the Father who sent me, so that I should lose nothing of everything he has given me, but raise it up on the last day” (John 6:37 ff.).

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “whoever has come.” This was formerly also read in Leo.]

## CHAPTER XXV. The question why one person receives grace rather than another is impenetrable and cannot be resolved by free will.

There are many other passages in the sequence of the canonical Scriptures that we pass over in order to avoid prolixity, since those we have selected are neither few nor obscure nor insignificant. They make it completely clear that everything pertaining to attaining eternal life can neither be begun, nor increased, nor completed without the grace of God.

Against every exaltation that boasts of free will, the apostle’s statement stands invincibly:

“For who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

[Note: The Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts, together with Leo’s edition, read “exaltation.” Others read “election.”]

Therefore the depth of that question, which in accordance with the apostle’s astonishment we confess to be impenetrable, is not resolved by the willing and refusing of free choice.

[Note: The Thuan, Camberon, and Joliensis manuscripts read, “willing and refusing.” The preference for the reading of the other copies is supported by what follows: “and this nature contracted through guilt,” which can refer only to willing evil.]

For although a refusal of good is present in a human being, he nevertheless does not possess the willing of good unless it has been given; and nature contracted the former through guilt, while it receives the latter through grace.

[Note: Prosper’s printed editions read, “the good gift of willing.” The word “gift” is better omitted, as in the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition.]

But what that is by which this same nature—guilty in all human beings before reconciliation, miserable in all, yet not justified in all—is, in some part of itself, distinguished from those who perish by him who came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10), cannot at all be investigated by human understanding.

However much the wickedness of the ungodly may be accused for resisting God’s grace, will it be proved that those to whom grace was granted had deserved it? Or could that power of grace, which subjected to itself those whom it wished, not convert those who remained unconvertible? Those who were drawn were of the same kind as those who were left in their hardness.

But to the former grace, astonishingly, granted what it willed; to the latter just truth repaid what was owed, so that God’s judgment is more inscrutable in the election of grace than in the recompense of justice.

[Note: Thus the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo. Prosper’s printed editions read, “grace repaid.”]

[Note: The Thuan manuscript reads, “in the repayment.”]

Nevertheless, lest that part of the faith by which we piously believe that God wills all human beings to be saved through the knowledge of the truth appear to be weakened by what is clearly demonstrated concerning the effects of grace, we must strive, with Christ’s help, to see the firmness of this definition.

But since the business of necessary inquiry requires no small effort, let us begin the discussion that follows from the beginning of another volume.

## BOOK TWO

[Column 0685]

887. ## CHAPTER I. Three things are certain in this question: that God wills all to be saved; that the knowledge of the truth and salvation are from grace; and that God’s judgments are impenetrable.

[Column 0685D]

When all the disputes produced by the contentiousness of intemperate argument have been removed and rejected, it is clear that there are three points to which one must adhere in this question with which we begin the second volume.

The first is that we must profess that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

[Note: Prosper’s printed editions read “that,” and below, “the second that,” and again, “the third that”; the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts, as well as Leo’s edition, read “by which.”]

The second is that there must be no doubt that everyone reaches the knowledge of the truth itself and the attainment of salvation not through personal merits but through the help and working of divine grace.

The third is that we must confess that the depth of God’s judgments cannot be penetrated by human understanding; and why he does not save all human beings, although he wills all human beings to be saved, ought not to be investigated.

[Note: Thus the Camberon and Joliensis manuscripts, together with Leo. The printed editions read, “who does not save all, although he wills all to be saved.”]

[Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads, “to be inquired into.”]

For if what cannot be known is not sought, no cause for conflict will remain between the first and second definitions; rather, both will be proclaimed and both believed with a secure and tranquil faith.

For God, with whom there is no iniquity (Romans 9:14), and whose ways altogether are mercy and truth (Psalm 24:10), is the good creator of all human beings and the just ordainer. He condemns no one undeservedly and liberates no one as a matter of debt; when he punishes the guilty, he imposes what is ours, and when he makes people righteous, he gives what is his:

“So that the mouth of those who speak iniquity may be stopped” (Psalm 62:12), and “God may be justified in his words and prevail when he is judged” (Psalm 50:6).

Neither is the complaint of the condemned just, nor is the arrogance of the justified truthful, if the former says that he did not deserve punishment or the latter asserts that he deserved grace.

888. ## CHAPTER II. Scripture teaches that God wills all human beings to be saved.

Just as the things that are brought forward from the divine utterances for the manifestation of grace cannot be violated by any art of argument, so that clear and harmonious statements might be dragged by a perverse interpretation into uncertainty amid such a great multitude of opinions [Note: [Col. 0687D] In the printed editions the word *ratione* (“by reasoning”) stood here. It is better omitted, as in the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and in Leo’s edition]; so too what is found in the same body of Scripture concerning the salvation of all human beings must not be rashly assailed by any contrary argument. Rather, the more difficult this very matter is to grasp intellectually, the more laudably it should be believed by faith. For great is the strength of agreement when authority is sufficient for following the truth, even while the reason remains hidden.

Let us therefore carefully consider what the Lord commands the preachers of the Gospel. According to Matthew, he says:

> All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age (Matt. XXVIII, 14 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0688D] The Joliensis manuscript reads: “Teach the nations, baptizing them.”]

According to Mark, however, he says to those same apostles:

> Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned (Mark XVI, 15).

Was any distinction made in this command among nations or among human beings? He excluded no one on the basis of merit, separated no one by race, distinguished no one by condition. The Gospel of Christ’s cross was sent absolutely to all human beings. And, lest the ministries of the preachers seem to be carried out merely by human effort, he says:

> Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

That is: when you enter like sheep into the midst of wolves (Matt. X, 16), do not tremble because of your weakness, but trust in my power. I will not abandon you in this entire work until the consummation of the age—not so that you will suffer nothing, but, which is far greater, so that no cruelty of those who rage against you will overcome you. You will preach by my power, and through me it will happen that, amid those who contradict and rage, children of Abraham will be raised up from stones (Matt. III, 9). I will make known what I have taught; I will accomplish what I have promised.

> For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will stand before kings and governors for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations. But when they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Brother will hand brother over to death, and father his son; children will rise up against their parents and put them to death; and you will be hated by all people because of my name. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved (Matt. X, 17–22).

Thus, as the Apostle says, the grace of God our Savior appeared to all human beings [Note: [Col. 0688D] So read the Camb. and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo. The printed editions read “the saving grace of God”] (Titus II, 11); and yet the ministers of grace were hated by all human beings. Although some were the haters and others were oppressed by the hatred of their persecutors, neither group was deprived of the designation “all human beings”: the rebellious portion indeed suffered the loss of its salvation, while the dignity of the faithful retained the full reckoning of that designation.

For the apostle John says:

> But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world (1 John II, 1).

## CHAPTER III. It is inscrutable why God judged that the calling of some should be delayed.

The mystery of a great and unspeakable sacrament is involved in the fact that the preachers to whom it was said, “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15), had first been told:

> Do not go along the road of the nations, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel (Matt. X, 5).

Although the Gospel was directed toward the calling of all human beings, and the Lord willed all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II, 4), he had not thereby taken away his authority over his dispensations, so that the order of his plan would proceed otherwise than he had determined by a hidden and righteous judgment. Hence the murmuring complaints of the obstinate have no place, because it is clear that what God willed to happen could not have happened otherwise than he willed.

At a later time, when the Lord Jesus was already seated in the glory of God the Father and the preachers were serving the task they had undertaken, the apostles desired to evangelize the word in Asia, but were forbidden by the Holy Spirit; and when they planned to go into Bithynia, they were prevented by the Spirit of Jesus (Acts XVI, 6–7). Grace was certainly not denied to those peoples, but, so far as appeared, was delayed. For afterward the Christian faith also grew strong among them [Note: [Col. 0689D] The printed editions read “afterward”; the Jol. and Camb. manuscripts and Leo read “later.”]

But what the reason for the delayed calling was is not clear. Nevertheless, the example of what happened teaches us that, among general promises, works, or commands, God knows how to arrange certain things apart from the common patterns by a more hidden rationale. I believe this is so that, when certain veils have been placed between us and them, the things that shine more secretly may become known more wonderfully; lest the eye grow careless because of the ease of seeing and, as it were, fall asleep through habit if it is not awakened by unusual things.

We know that these unknowable delays of illumination—during which many indeed fail through unbelief—occur not only among the more remote peoples of the impious, but also in the cities of the faithful, throughout many households and families, while even those who are destined to become Christians oppose the Christian faith. For many will love what they hate and preach what they do not accept.

And who, amid all this, will make known to the complaining or the curious why the Sun of righteousness (Mal. IV, 2) has not yet risen for certain nations, and why the truth, which must still be revealed to darkened hearts, even now withholds its rays from them (Wis. V, 6)? Why are those who must be corrected allowed to wander for so long, and why is what must be granted to the old at the end not bestowed throughout such a long lifetime? Why do parents not yet believe in Christ when their children already believe? And, again, why does wicked offspring disagree with devout parents?

Yet daily prayer is offered for everyone, according to God’s command, to him who grants both the beginnings of faith and its growth: so that, if he hears, the grace of his compassion may be recognized; and if he does not hear, the judgment of his truth may be understood [Note: [Col. 0689D] The printed editions read “even if he hears.” The reading of the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition, “if he hears,” is better.]

## CHAPTER IV. In past ages divine goodness always admonished human beings to worship God through the elements, just as it specially instructed the people of Israel through the law and the prophets.

But this same grace—which after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ has been diffused everywhere, and of which it is written, “Your flashes of lightning have shone upon the world” (Ps. LXXVI, 19)—was not absent from the world even in past ages.

Although it is clear that the Israelite people were chosen with God’s special care and favor, while all the other nations went along their own ways (Acts XIV, 15)—that is, were permitted to live according to their own will—the eternal goodness of the Creator did not therefore turn so far away from those peoples that it failed to admonish them, by any signs whatsoever, to know and fear him.
