For heaven and earth and the sea, and every creature that can be seen and understood, were arranged especially for the benefit of the human race, so that rational nature might be trained, through contemplation of so many forms, experience of so many goods, and reception of so many gifts, for the worship and love of its Creator, while the Spirit of God, in whom “we live and move and are” (Acts XVII, 28), fills all things.

For although salvation is far from sinners (Ps. CXVIII, 155), nothing is nevertheless empty of the presence and power of salvation itself. Thus, as the Prophet says, “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXXII, 5). This mercy has never been absent in any age or from any generation. He has always devoted that providence by which he administers and sustains the universe to governing and nourishing created natures, having determined from the eternity of his unchangeable plan what he would distribute at what times [Note: [Col. 0689D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “at the times appointed for each thing”; the Camb. manuscript reads “what, at what times”], as well as the inscrutable and unsearchable measures of his manifold grace, through which he varies his gifts and sacraments.

For just as this abundance of grace, which has recently flowed forth among all nations [Note: [Col. 0690D] The word “nations” had fallen out of the Duac. and Colon. editions. It is found in the Lovaniensis and Joliensis editions and manuscript, and in Leo], does not nullify the grace that once fell like dew upon Israel under the law [Note: [Col. 0690D] The Camb. and Thuan manuscripts read “which he distributed”], nor do present riches abolish the frugality of the past; so it must not be inferred from the special care of God that once presided over the children of the patriarchs that the governance of divine mercy was withdrawn from other human beings.

Compared with the elect, they may indeed seem cast aside, but they were never deprived of manifest or hidden benefits. For we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles Paul and Barnabas said to the Lycaonians:

> Men, why are you doing these things? We too are mortal human beings like you. We proclaim to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them, who in past generations allowed all nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without testimony, doing good, giving rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness (Acts XIV, 14 ff.).

What is this testimony, which has always served the Lord and has never been silent about his goodness, except the ineffable beauty of the whole world itself and the rich, ordered abundance of his ineffable benefits? Through these, certain tablets of the eternal law were offered to human hearts, so that, in the pages of the elements and the volumes of the ages, the common and public teaching of divine instruction could be read.

Heaven, therefore, and all heavenly things, the sea and the earth, and everything in them, proclaimed the glory of God by the harmonious concord of their beauty and order; and by their perpetual preaching they spoke of the majesty of their Creator. Yet the greatest number of human beings, who were permitted to walk in the ways of their own will [Note: [Col. 0691D] The Camb. manuscript reads “because they walked in the ways”; the Jol. manuscript, “because they walked by the ways”], did not understand and did not follow this law. The fragrance of life, which breathed toward life, became for them a fragrance of death toward death (2 Cor. II, 16), so that even through those visible testimonies it might be learned that “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (1 Cor. III, 6).

Therefore, what was being accomplished in Israel through the establishment of the law and the utterances of the prophets was always being accomplished among all the nations through the testimonies of the whole creation and the miracles of God’s goodness.

## CHAPTER V. Those among the nations who pleased God were distinguished by the spirit of faith and grace.

But since, in that people over whom both forms of instruction presided, no one was justified except by grace through the spirit of faith, who could doubt that those from whatever nations, at whatever times, who were able to please God were distinguished by the Spirit of God’s grace? Although that grace was formerly more sparing and more hidden, it nevertheless denied itself to no age: one in power, different in extent, unchangeable in purpose, and manifold in operation [Note: [Col. 0691D] The Camb. and Joliensis manuscripts read “directed”; others read “distinguished.”]

## CHAPTER VI. Even now grace is not conferred upon everyone in the same measure.

For even in these days, when the rivers of ineffable gifts water the whole world, the same mode and the same measure are not conferred upon everyone. Although the same truth is preached to all through the ministers of the word and of God’s grace, and the same exhortation is offered, it is nevertheless God’s field and God’s building; his power works invisibly so that what is built or cultivated may advance by growth.

As the apostle Paul testifies, saying:

> What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers through whom you came to believe, each as the Lord gave. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters are one. Each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building (1 Cor. III, 5 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0691D] The Jol. manuscript reads “What, then, is Paul?”]  
[Note: [Col. 0691D] Leo’s edition reads “minister.”]

Therefore, each person is an assistant, worker, and minister of this field and building to the extent that the Lord has given to each. Those who are cultivated through the labor of the ministers advance to the measure to which the author of growth has raised them.

For in the Lord’s field there is neither a uniform planting nor a single kind of plant. And although the structure of the whole temple is joined together in one beauty, the place and use of all the stones are not the same; just as in one body all the members do not have the same function (Rom. XII, 4). The Apostle says:

> But now God has placed the members, each one of them, as he willed (1 Cor. XII, 18).

[Note: [Col. 0691D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “therefore.”]

## CHAPTER VII. Since every good thing comes from God’s grace, the inequality of merits is neither to be attributed to free will nor made a subject of complaint.

But the same teacher explains from where these members are fitted, useful, and beautiful, saying:

> Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus”; and no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit. There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in the same Spirit; to another, workings of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues. But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. XII, 3 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0691D] This portion of the apostolic passage has been added from the Camb. and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition. It had fallen out of Prosper’s printed editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0692D] Elsewhere, “the working,” as in the Vulgate. The Jol. manuscript and Leo read “workings,” as in the Greek.]

Since the teacher of the nations proclaims these things with such great light and clarity [Note: [Col. 0692D] So read the Camb. and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Other printed editions read: “By what reasoning, by what cause should one doubt?”], what reason or cause is there for doubting that the seed of all virtues comes from God? Or who, unless utterly foolish, would complain about the difference among divine gifts, or suppose that what is not bestowed equally from heavenly generosity ought to be attributed to unequal merits? For if this distribution arose according to the merits of preceding works [Note: [Col. 0692D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “not the catalogue itself of the gifts.”], the Apostle would not have ended the catalogue of the gifts themselves with this conclusion:

> But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills (ibid., 11).

If he had wished the causes to be understood as merits, he would surely have said, “Distributing to each according as they merit,” just as he promised a reward for the devotion of those who plant and water, saying:

> Each will receive his own reward according to his own labor (1 Cor. III, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0692D] The Camb. and Joliensis manuscripts add “and those who water.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. Each person is given without merit the means by which to strive toward merit; and one who has already received grace is expected to increase what he has received through the one who gives the growth.

Each person, then, is given without merit the means by which to strive toward merit; and, before any labor, each is given the means by which he may receive a reward according to his labor.

This is also recognized from the teaching of evangelical truth, where it is said by way of comparison that a man going abroad called his servants and entrusted his property to them: to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability (Matt. XXV, 14 ff.) [Note: [Col. 0693D] In the Joliensis manuscript the words “to each according to his own ability” are absent, as are below the words “and natural”]; that is, according to his own natural capacity, not according to his own merit. For it is one thing to be able to act and another to act; one thing to be able to possess charity and another to possess charity; one thing to be capable of continence, justice, and wisdom, and another to be continent, just, and wise.

Therefore, not everyone who can be restored is restored, nor is everyone who can be healed healthy [Note: [Col. 0693D] So read the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts with Leo’s edition. Others read “has been healed”; later they likewise read “and to be healthy,” where others read “and to have been healed”]. To be capable of restoration and healing belongs to nature; to be restored and healthy belongs to grace [Note: [Col. 0693D] The Cologne edition reads “to the grace of God.”]

In short, the two servants who received different numbers of talents according to the measure of their capacity—which the distributor of the property had foreseen in them—received not the recompense of merit but the material for work. Through this work, the vigilant industry of the two servants is not only honored with glorious praise but is also commanded to enter into the eternal joys of their master (ibid., 20 and 23).

But the third servant’s lazy idleness and sluggish wickedness are punished in such a way that he is both disgraced by the reproach of condemnation and stripped of the portion he had received (ibid., 26 ff.). He was worthy to lose his useless faith because he had not exercised charity.

Accordingly, in the following discourse [Note: [Col. 0693D] The Joliensis manuscript reads: “in the following parable, the discourse in which,” etc.], in which the form of the future judgment is most clearly declared, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, after all the nations have been gathered before him [Note: [Col. 0693D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “before whom”; others read “before which.” The former reading is recommended by the evangelist’s words: “And all the nations will be gathered before him”], some are said to be placed on the right and others on the left [Note: [Col. 0693D] So read the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Other printed editions read “are led,” or, as more recent editions have it, “are led to be placed”]. The right-hand ones are praised for works of charity, while nothing else is charged against those on the left except the neglect of mercy and benevolence (Matt. XXV, 31 ff.).

These people, therefore, had also received faith, but they had not followed love; and they will be condemned not for a gift that was not preserved, but for one that was not increased. Although all good gifts are from God, some are nevertheless bestowed by God even without being requested, so that through the gifts already received people may seek those not yet bestowed [Note: [Col. 0693D] The Joliensis and Camb. manuscripts read “nevertheless, for this reason”].

For the seed cast into the earth is not sown so that it should remain alone, but so that, by producing fruit, it may become multiple and abundant (John XII, 24) [Note: [Col. 0694D] So reads the Joliensis manuscript with Leo. Others read “Qui quidem” (“who indeed”)]. Its growth comes from the one who gives the increase (1 Cor. III, 7); but the living and rational soil, already made fertile by the rain of grace [Note: [Col. 0694D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition add the words “and rational.” In these manuscripts, however, the phrase “and already made fertile by the rain of grace” is omitted, though it is retained in other books], has something to be expected from it: that it should increase what it has received.

## CHAPTER IX. The reason why grace has varied across different ages is not to be investigated by us.

Having, as I think, treated these matters rightly, insofar as the Lord has granted, let us return to the point from which the discussion digressed: namely, to the consideration of the differences by which the works and gifts of divine grace have varied.

For the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are inscrutable and whose ways are unsearchable (Rom. XI, 33), has always tempered his mercy and justice in such a way that, by the most secret will of his eternal plan, he did not wish the measures of his gifts to be equal in every age [Note: [Col. 0694D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts add “at all times,” a phrase that had fallen out of Prosper’s printed editions], among all generations, or among all human beings.

He helped in one way those whom the testimonies of heaven and earth summoned to know him [Note: [Col. 0694D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “by the testimony”;], and in another way those for whom he provided not only the service of the elements but also the teaching of the law, the oracles of the prophets, signs of miracles [Note: [Col. 0694D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “signs of wonders”], and the cooperation of angels.

And he declared his mercy to all human beings in a much greater way when the Son of God became the son of man, so that he might be found by those who were not seeking him and appear to those who were not asking about him (Isa. LXV, 1); and so that the honor of the Israelite race might not excel in one people alone [Note: [Col. 0694D] We have supplied the word “honor” from the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. The sentence requires it], but so that the multiplied offspring of Abraham might arise in every nation under heaven [Note: [Col. 0694D] Leo reads “in every kind of people”], and so that not children of the flesh but children of the promise might enter into the succession of the heirs (Acts XIV, 15).

At the same time, just as there had been such great abundance of grace in past ages among the other nations, so now there would be such great frugality of grace among the Jewish people; yet, when the fullness of the nations has entered (Rom. IX, 8), an overflowing of those same streams is promised even to their dryness.

Since the holy Scriptures do not speak of what causes these differences under the same grace, who will speak of them? And since the knowledge of the apostle Paul passes in this matter from discussion into astonishment (Rom. XI, 33), whose presumption would be so great as to think that these things should be disclosed by argument rather than admired in silence [Note: [Col. 0694D] The Camb. and Joliensis manuscripts read “should judge”]?

## CHAPTER X. In every age God’s mercy has nourished bodies and aided minds.

Let this secret, therefore, so remote from human knowledge [Note: [Col. 0695D] So read the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Our printed editions read “from human thought”], be patiently and calmly left unknown. Yet, because closed things cannot be penetrated, we must not therefore pass by the entrance to what has been opened [Note: [Col. 0696D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “because they cannot be penetrated”].

For many authoritative statements of the divine utterances have made this manifest, and the continuous experience of all ages has taught that God’s just mercy and merciful justice have never been absent either from nourishing human bodies or from teaching and aiding their minds.

For he has always sent rain upon the good and the wicked, always made his sun rise upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V, 45), always supplied life-giving breezes, always administered the alternations of day and night, and always bestowed abundance upon the fields, multiplication upon the seeds, and fertility upon human beings who are to be born [Note: [Col. 0696D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts read “he bestowed”].

And whenever he diminished any of these things, he chastised the turning away and negligence of those who used them badly by means of kindly corrections, so that in adversity they might seek his mercies, whose justice they had not feared in prosperity.

Finally, if we return to the very beginnings of the world, we shall find that the Spirit of God was the ruler of all the saints who preceded the flood. For this reason they were also called sons of God, since, as the Apostle says:

> Whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God (Rom. VIII, 14).

But when those same people, neglecting the observance of their ancestors, mingled themselves in unlawful unions with the reprobate, and on account of their abominable association were judged worthy of destruction, the Lord said:

> My Spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh (Gen. VI, 3).

From this it is apparent that this people, whose generations are set out in an ordered sequence together with the number of years, had previously been spiritual—spiritual, that is, by a will over which the Holy Spirit presided. The Spirit supplied the governance of its direction in such a way that it did not remove the power to turn toward vices. If this people did not use that power, it would neither abandon God nor be abandoned by God; and it would be the people of whom it is said:

> Blessed is the one who could transgress and did not transgress (Ecclus. XXXI, 10).

Therefore, as long as it remained with God, it remained by the will that God inspired and directed. For, as it is written, “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, according to the Septuagint).

## CHAPTER XI. What heavenly generosity has decreed to give human beings generally increases in them gradually and little by little.

But this preparation does not always have the same progress or the same measure. The works and gifts of grace vary in many ways and through innumerable differences; and within the individual kinds of gifts there are unequal degrees and different quantities.

For just as among the sprouts of herbs and trees that the earth produces there is not one species or one kind in all cases, but each is generated according to the form of its own seed and the quality of its own stock—and although they do not receive their full beauty as soon as they emerge, they advance through definite and ordered increases until, through successive growth, they reach the complete measure of their form—so too the seeds of spiritual gifts and the plants of virtues are not born in every field of the human heart already possessing all that they are destined to become. Maturity is not easily found at the beginning, nor perfection at the outset.

The powerful and merciful God frequently brings about these remarkable effects of his work, and in certain minds, without waiting for the expected delay of progress, he introduces all at once whatever he is going to bestow.

In the loins of Abraham, Levi is sanctified (Heb. VII, 10), and together with him the house of Aaron and the priestly order are blessed (Gen. XVII, 16). In Isaac, conceived according to the promise and born, contrary to hope, from aged and barren parents (Rom. IV, 18), the calling of all the nations and the whole form of Christ are prefigured. Jacob, with no merit lending support, is chosen as beloved before he is born (Mal. I, 3; Rom. IX, 13). To Jeremiah it is said:

> Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you (Jer. I, 5).

John, filled with the Holy Spirit within the womb of his mother Elizabeth, leaps for joy; and, so that no one among those born of women might be greater, he experiences the beginnings of grace before those of nature (Luke I, 44).

Although other examples of similar testimonies are not lacking, which we pass over for the sake of brevity, that portion of humanity is nevertheless much more common and much more numerous in which whatever heavenly generosity bestows increases little by little, so that the reasons for further gifts are produced from what has already been bestowed.

Some people, after receiving faith, are not free from doubt. The one who said, “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX, 24), certainly knew that doubt was present in him. Nor did those who said, “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 6) feel that it was entirely absent from their minds.

Some do not understand what they believe, and many remain for a long time within the measure of their simplicity. Many, however, soon receive the light of understanding. But understanding itself does not have the same vigor or a similar capacity in everyone.

And very many, although they seem adorned both with faith and with understanding, nevertheless suffer from a lack of charity and cannot cling to what they see by faith and understanding, because one cannot persevere in what one does not love with one’s whole heart.

The gift of charity itself is not always of such a kind that the recipient receives all that belongs to its fullness at once. There is a love that can be overcome by another love, and often the love of God grows weak through love of the world, unless it progresses, under the Spirit’s kindling, to that fervor which no cold can extinguish and no lukewarmness weaken.

Since this ineffable gift of God—the greatest of all gifts, and in a certain sense the life of all the virtues—is given so that the other gifts may be directed toward it, the faithful soul’s purpose has the means by which it may strive toward perfect charity. Because charity is not only from God but is also God (1 John IV, 8), it makes those whom it fills with the flood of its delight stable, persevering, and unconquerable.

But those who do not know the sweetness of these waters and still drink from the streams of this world—or who, even if they have tasted something of the fountain of life with the tips of their lips, nevertheless take pleasure in becoming drunk from Babylon’s golden cup (Rev. XIV, 8; XVI, 19)—are wholly deceived by their own judgment and slip through their own will. If they persist in this indolence, they themselves strip away the things they have received. For any good things can easily perish without charity, and without charity they cannot be beneficial (1 Cor. XIII, 4).

## CHAPTER XII. Our turning away from God is not the result of divine appointment but of our own will; therefore, if a person stands, it is a matter of merit, because he was able to fall.

These matters, touched upon briefly and in summary, should serve to make us certain that no faithful person who has not departed from God is abandoned by him, nor is anyone’s fall arranged by divine appointment. Rather, for many who already use the judgment of reason, it is free to depart for this reason: that not departing may be a reward; and so that what can happen only with the cooperation of God’s Spirit may be credited to the merits of the person by whose will it could have failed to happen [Note: [Col. 0697D] So read the Thuan, Camb., and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Prosper’s printed editions read “to the merits of those . . . whose.”]

In evil actions this will can be the sole cause; in good actions it cannot be the sole cause. For although it is natural for the will to be good [Note: [Col. 0697D] So read the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Prosper’s printed editions instead read: “Although according to nature it belongs to a human being to have a good will, yet the vice that rushes into nature through an evil will”]; nevertheless, the vice that, through an evil will, enters into nature is not overcome by the power of nature but by grace.

## CHAPTER XIII. Before the flood, God’s goodness was present not only to establish the holy but also to instruct the impious.

[Col. 0697C]

Therefore that first people of God were governed by the Spirit of God and, through the instruction of the Holy Spirit, abstained from the society and practices of the accursed and condemned people, maintaining their distinctness from the mingling of the carnal. God’s patience endured their wickedness for as long as the good could please him by not imitating them. But when the good too had been corrupted by imitating the wicked, and the whole community had conspired in the same wickedness through deliberate defection [Note: Our printed editions read *per voluntatis*; the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and the later edition of Leo read *per voluntarium*], then one impiety polluted them all, except Noah’s household, and one sentence destroyed them all [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads *conspirabat*, “was conspiring.”].

Yet God’s goodness was not absent even from that part which did not remain in charity [Col. 0697D] and which, from its beginning, swelled with the poison of the devil’s envy. For the Lord deigned to temper by paternal counsel the leader of the impious race, who envied the merits of his holy brother and was meditating his murder with a fratricidal heart [Col. 0698A], saying to Cain:

“Why are you sad? Why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be at peace. For its turning will be toward you, and you will rule over it” (Gen. 4:6).

He says: “Put away the sadness arising from jealous rivalry, and extinguish the flames of cruel hatred. Abel has done you no harm, nor has he injured you by pleasing me. I rejected your gifts by my own judgment, not at his desire. For you performed a good work negligently. Your offering would have been right if your discernment had been right. Knowing to whom you were offering, you ought to have known what you were vowing. You did not divide rightly between me and yourself, because you kept the better things for yourself. Therefore this error is yours, and this sin is yours. Be at peace, and do not turn against your innocent brother; rather, let your own guilt be recalled to you [Col. 0698B]. Do not give sin dominion over you; instead, take dominion over it yourself. For by repenting you will neither proceed to a greater crime nor remain unpurified from that in which you grieve that you displeased me.”

When God was speaking such words to Cain, is it at all doubtful that he wished—and, insofar as that method of healing was sufficient, acted—to bring Cain back from that frenzy of impiety? [Note: The word *illum*, “him,” is absent from the Thuaneus and Joliensis manuscripts and from all editions of Ambrose’s works in which the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* are included. In the Leuven edition of Prosper it is enclosed in parentheses as of doubtful authority. It appears in other books of Prosper and in the new edition of Leo. It is not easy to determine what difference this variation in reading makes to the meaning of the sentence.]

Yet his persistent wickedness became all the more inexcusable through the very circumstance by which it ought to have become more corrected. Certainly God knew beforehand to what end the conception of that madman would progress. But the deed of his will was not compelled to sin merely because divine knowledge could not be deceived. Abel’s safety could plainly have been preserved unharmed, both in intention and in result, unless God had chosen, with great praise of his own patience, that the impious man’s temporary frenzy should become the just man’s everlasting honor.

As for the descendants of that fratricide [Note: So the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Other printed editions read “of the fratricide”], although they lived according to the character of their ancestor, who would not readily perceive that they had never been denied divine goodness [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “that they had never denied God’s divine goodness”], if he considered how greatly the long patience of God, such an abundance of temporal goods, and the numerous propagation of multiplied fertility could have benefited them? Although these benefits brought neither remedy nor correction to the hardened, they nevertheless prove that their turning away resulted not from a divine decree but from their own will.

### CHAPTER XIV. In the Flood and afterward, up to Christ, the works of divine grace were revealed and the miracles of Christian grace foreshadowed, although the abundance of grace that now waters the world did not flow with equal generosity.

[Col. 0698D]

In the preservation of Noah, his sons, and his daughters-in-law (Gen. 7)—in whom the seedbed of all nations was being prepared—Holy Scripture reveals how many works of divine grace were made manifest. For while the ark of marvelous capacity received every kind of animal, insofar as was sufficient for restoration [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Other editions read “for instruction”], the Church, which was to gather to herself the whole human race, was prefigured. Through wood and water the redemption of Christ’s cross and the washing of regeneration were disclosed. In those who were saved from that devastation of the world, the fullness of all nations was blessed. The gift of fertility was renewed, and, with only the eating of strangled animals and blood forbidden, the freedom to eat whatever one wished was enlarged; and the assurance of salvation was consecrated in the testimony of the many-colored bow, that is, in the sign of manifold grace (Gen. 9).

These mysteries and sacraments were instructing not merely the few people of one family who were then alive, but all their descendants in them, so that what was devoted to the instruction of the parents might advance the knowledge of their children.

But when the increase of human propagation was rushing forward, and the very multitude of mortals was growing proud of its multiplication and, in keeping with the height of its arrogance, desired to join an enormous structure to heaven (Gen. 11), how remarkable was the judgment of divine justice for restraining this insolence! It confused the single language of those peoples, which had been mutually intelligible through familiar signs, into seventy-two varieties of language. Thus, while the concord of the workers perished amid discordant voices, the machinery of their insane undertaking was dismantled, and a timely dispersion gave the inhabited world inhabitants from that wicked assembly.

In this work of God’s providence, the miracles of Christian grace were preordained—miracles that were to fit all this dispersion together into the structure of that building in which every knee bows to God and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:10–11) [Note: So the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition. Earlier editions read “which was to be called.”].

This breadth of grace, to be revealed when the fullness of the appointed times had come, was already indicated by God’s promise to Abraham through clearer signs. His two lines of descent—the children of the flesh and the children of promise (Rom. 9:7)—were compared with the multitude of the sands and the stars. An aged man, cut off from hope of offspring because of his wife’s long-standing barrenness, believed with praiseworthy faith that through the offspring of one son he would become the father of the world, looking ahead to that one in his seed—or rather, beholding him—who said: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

When Abraham was justified by this faith, he had not yet received the commandment of circumcision. While he was still in natural uncircumcision, his faith was counted as righteousness (Rom. 4:10). And this same faith received the seal of circumcision in that member of the body through which the seed of procreation would reach the flesh in which the Son of God, God the Word, would become flesh without carnal seed and be born from Abraham’s daughter, the Virgin Mary. All were taken into fellowship with this birth who, having been regenerated in Christ through the Holy Spirit [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits “through the Holy Spirit”], believed what Abraham believed.

Before this seed came, of which it was said to Abraham, “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:3), this faith was confined within the people of one lineage, sustained among the true Israelites by the hope of our redemption. For although there were some foreigners whom the truth deigned to enlighten in the times of the Law, they were so few that it can scarcely be determined whether there were any [Note: Other printed editions read “whether they are known”; the Joliensis manuscript and Leo read “whether he is known”].

Nor are the nations excusable on this account [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “the nations are excusable”]: those who, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, without hope and without God in this world (Eph. 2:12), perished under the darkness of ignorance, because the abundance of grace that now waters the whole world did not earlier flow with equal generosity.

### CHAPTER XV. Better intellects did not arise now than before Christ’s coming; rather, at the time of Christ’s coming a more powerful wickedness was found, so that God’s grace might be manifested.

A certain measure of heavenly instruction was always offered to all human beings. Although it belonged to a more sparing and more hidden grace, it nevertheless sufficed, as the Lord judged, for some as a remedy and for all as a testimony. Thus it may plainly and evidently appear that, unless grace also superabounded where sin abounded, a similar impiety would blind the entire human race even now [Note: The Camb. manuscript reads “Before.”].

Or perhaps, as many chatter, better intellects than those of former generations have arisen in our times, and later ages have produced souls more suited to divine gifts [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “minds”?]? Even if that were so, it would have to be attributed to the goodness of the Creator, who, in calling peoples to eternal life, fashioned hearts that would not resist.

But nothing at all was changed in carnal generation, nor did a nobler succession arise from lesser ancestors. Rather, in the people of the time when the Redeemer of the world came, the slower the descent had become, the more powerful the wickedness was found to be. The impiety of Jewish fury proved this. How suitable that generation was for the Gospel of Christ was taught not only by the people but also by the hearts of the scribes, rulers, and priests.

It was not enough for them to rage against the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29)—against the testimony of the Law, the oracles of the prophets, and the evidence of divine powers—with seditions, insults, spitting, slaps, blows, stones, scourges, and finally the brutality of the cross. They also pursued the witnesses of his resurrection with the same madness.

When the Apostles were flogged by the high priests, they showed that this had been prophesied in David’s psalm, saying:

“Lord, you are the one who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them, who through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of our father David, your servant, said:

‘Why did the nations rage,  
and the peoples devise futile things?  
The kings of the earth stood by,  
and the rulers gathered together  
against the Lord and against his Christ.’

For truly in this city Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, to do whatever your hand and counsel had decreed should be done” (Acts 4:24ff.).

Therefore, in order to manifest the grace of God that, by his eternal and unchangeable counsel, had been prepared for the salvation of all nations, earlier times were not rejected as though they were incapable. Rather, these times were chosen, which produced peoples whose fierce and deliberate wickedness persisted in doing what God’s hand and counsel had decreed should be done—not from a desire to take counsel, but with an intention to rage.

Thus the grace and power of God would be more marvelous: from such hard souls, such dark minds, and such hostile hearts he made for himself a faithful, obedient, holy people. This people did not reach the light of God’s wisdom through the wisdom of this world, but through the gift of the one of whom the apostle John testifies, saying:

“We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son” (1 John 5:20).

The apostle Paul agrees with this testimony, saying:

“Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the darkness and from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:12).

And again the same Apostle says:

“For we too were once foolish, disobedient, wandering astray, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in wickedness and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared, he saved us—not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy—through the washing of regeneration by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:3ff.).

Could the merits of the people whom Christ found, the character he subjected to himself, and the hearts he converted to himself have been explained more fully, more brilliantly, or more truly, when he came to heal not the healthy but those who were ill, and to call not the righteous but sinners (Matt. 9:13)?

For the people of the nations who sat in darkness saw a great light, and for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, light arose (Isa. 9:2). The nations raged, the peoples grew angry, kings savagely opposed, powers resisted, superstitions and the errors of the whole world struggled against him.

But from those who resisted, raged, and persecuted, Christ increased his people. Through the bonds, punishments, and deaths of the saints, faith was strengthened, truth prevailed, and throughout the whole world the abundance of the Lord’s harvest multiplied [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Earlier editions read “the harvest of the Lord’s field.”].

Such constancy of faith, confidence of hope, and strength of endurance were supplied from above that the fire of love which the Holy Spirit had kindled in the hearts of the faithful could not in any way be extinguished by their oppressors. Those who were tortured burned more fiercely, while those who raged often conceived the very flame that they were persecuting.

With that fire the blessed apostle Paul was kindled, and he said boldly and fervently:

“Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand [Note: The Joliensis and Thuaneus manuscripts read “by faith”]. And we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. And not only that, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope. Hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:1ff.) [Note: This passage has been restored from Leo’s book in accordance with both Pauline texts. The Joliensis manuscript reads “to the Lord through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Earlier printed editions omitted “God through.”].

And again:

“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written, ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter’” (Ps. 43:24) [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “we have been counted.”].

“But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, nor powers, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:35ff.) [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “neither present things nor future things, neither angels nor principalities, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature.”].

This love, poured out through the Holy Spirit, caused the world of the faithful to conquer the world of the impious. It confounded the cruelty of Nero, the fury of Domitian, and the rage of many rulers after them in the glorious and innumerable deaths of the martyrs [Note: The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition add “rage”], while Christ granted his imitators eternal crowns as trophies from the persecutions of kings.

### CHAPTER XVI. That Christ died for all the impious.

There is therefore no reason to doubt that Jesus Christ our Lord died for the impious and sinners. If anyone has been found outside their number [Note: The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition add “if anyone”; the sentence depends on its absence in other books. The Leuven editors conjectured that the reading should be, with a new sense, “Did he not die for all?” so that the meaning of the passage would be complete], Christ did not die for all; rather, Christ died absolutely for all [Note: “Christ” is absent here from the Camb. and Joliensis manuscripts and Leo’s edition, although it appears in other copies]. Therefore, before the reconciliation accomplished through Christ’s blood, no human being was not either a sinner or impious.

The Apostle says:

“Why, when we were still weak, did Christ, at the appointed time, die for the impious? For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. But God demonstrates his love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Rom. 5:6ff.) [Note: Leo’s edition follows the Apostle’s text with “For if”; other copies read “If indeed.”].

The same Apostle says in the Second Letter to the Corinthians:

“For the love of Christ constrains us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them” (2 Cor. 5:14ff.).

Let us hear what he declares about himself:

“Faithful is the saying and worthy of complete acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I received mercy, so that in me first Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example for those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Tim. 1:15ff.).

Whether circumcision or uncircumcision, all were universally shut up under sin; one guilt bound everyone, and among the impious, whether more or less so, there was no one who could be saved without Christ’s redemption. This redemption presented itself to the whole world and became known indiscriminately to all human beings.

For on the fiftieth day after that Passover on which the true Lamb had offered himself to God as a sacrifice, when the Apostles and those who were of one mind with them were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke in the languages of all nations, a multitude of people of different kinds gathered, stirred by the miracle [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “aroused”], so that the whole world might hear the Gospel of Christ in those who were present.

For, as it is written, Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those inhabiting Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the regions of Libya around Cyrene, visiting Romans, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs—all heard the mighty works of God proclaimed in their own languages (Acts 2:9ff.). Their testimony would also spread far and wide among nations that were more remote.

For the accomplishment of this, we believe that the breadth of the Roman Empire was prepared by God’s providence, so that the nations destined to be called into the unity of Christ’s body might first be joined together under the law of one empire [Note: Earlier printed editions read “under the law of impiety”; the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition more correctly read “of empire.”]. Yet Christian grace is not content to have the same boundaries as Rome [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “the grace of Christ is now not content”]. It has already subjected to the scepter of Christ’s cross many peoples whom Rome has not subdued by her arms [Note: Earlier editions read “of peoples”; the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo read “peoples.”]. Rome, however, was made greater through the primacy of the apostolic priesthood, by the stronghold of religion rather than by the throne of power.

### CHAPTER XVII. The nations upon which the grace of the Savior has not yet shone are to be called to the Gospel at the appointed time.

If, then, just as we know that certain nations were not long ago adopted into the fellowship of the children of God [Note: This is how it reads in the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and in Leo’s edition. In Prosper’s printed editions: “which previously did not know, into the fellowship.” The Leuven, Douai, and Cologne editors indicated in the margin, by conjecture, “which do not wish.” They also note that in the time of Saints Leo and Prosper—the editor of Leo’s works adds Leo, while the others mention only Prosper—the Scots came to Christ through the efforts of Celestine, as is stated at the end of the book *Against the Collator*], so too we do not doubt that even now, in the remotest parts of the world, there are some nations upon which the grace of the Savior has not yet shone. For them also, by God’s hidden judgment, the time of calling has been appointed, when they will hear and receive the Gospel that they have not heard [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Other books of Prosper read “which they have not yet seen, they will hear and receive.”].

Nevertheless, that general measure of assistance which has always been supplied from above to all human beings is not denied to them. Yet human nature has been so grievously wounded that no one can be fully instructed in the knowledge of God by spontaneous contemplation, unless the true light disperses the darkness of the heart. God, just and good, has poured out this light according to his inscrutable judgment—not in former ages as he has poured it out in the last days.

Thus the blessed apostle Paul, writing to the Colossians, says:

“The mystery that was hidden from the ages and generations has now been revealed to his saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the nations [Note: The Leuven edition reads “among the nations.” Other copies omit the preposition *in*, although it appears in the Apostle’s text. In the Joliensis manuscript, as in that text, the reading is “in you,” instead of “in us,” as other copies have it], which is Christ in you” (Col. 1:26–27).

### CHAPTER XVIII. The grace of Christ was hidden from the nations in earlier ages, though not from the prophets.

Was this mystery also unknown to the prophets? And did those through whom the Holy Spirit spoke not know the things that were announced by them [Note: Other printed editions read “the announcements that were made”; the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition read as in our text]? I do not think it should be understood in that way. Rather, the mystery was hidden from the nations themselves, and the Lord revealed it when he wished and to whom he wished.

Concerning the calling of the nations, who were not God’s people, to whom he had previously shown no mercy but now shows mercy, it is said in Deuteronomy:

“The Lord saw, and he was jealous, and he was angered because of the anger of his sons and daughters. And he said, ‘I will turn my face away from them, and I will show what will happen in the end, because they are a perverse generation, children in whom there is no faith.’ They provoked me to jealousy with what is not God; they angered me with their idols. And I will provoke them to jealousy with those who were not a nation; I will anger them with a foolish nation” (Deut. 32:19ff.) [Note: So the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition. Other printed editions read “a perverse generation is among the children.” The Joliensis manuscript reads “in that which is not,” and below, “who were not nations.”].

David too prophesied these things concerning all nations that would worship God:

“All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord, and they shall glorify your name” (Ps. 85:9).

And again:

“All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:11) [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “shall magnify him” and omits the following testimony of the Psalmist].

And again:

“All the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him” (ibid. 11).

Isaiah likewise announces similar things, saying:

“For in the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God shall be at the summit of the mountains [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “the mountain of the Lord at the summit,” while the others omit this. The Vulgate reads “the mountain of the house of the Lord”], and it shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall come to it” (Isa. 2:2) [Note: The Joliensis manuscript omits “and,” and later omits “the same”; elsewhere it reads “he will make.”].

And again the same prophet says:

“And the Lord Sabaoth will make for all nations on this mountain: they shall drink wine in gladness; they shall be anointed with ointment on this mountain. He will hand all these things over to the nations, for this is the counsel concerning all nations” (Isa. 25:6, according to the Septuagint).

And again the same prophet:

“And the Lord will reveal his holy arm in the sight of all nations, and all the nations of the earth shall see the salvation that comes from the Lord” (Isa. 52:10) [Note: The Joliensis manuscript reads “The Lord revealed,” omitting “and.”].

And again:

“Behold, foreigners shall come to you through me, and they shall flee to you” (Isa. 54:15, according to the Septuagint).

And below:

“Nations that did not know you shall call upon you, and peoples who do not know you shall flee to you” (Isa. 55:5, according to the Septuagint).

Hosea too prophesies similar things, saying:

“And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people’; there they shall be called sons of the living God, and the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel shall be gathered together as one” (Hos. 1:10–11) [Note: The Joliensis manuscript and the older codices of Leo read “to it.”].

And again:

“I will have mercy on her who was not beloved, and I will say to the one who was not my people, ‘You are my people’; and he will say, ‘You are my God’” (Hos. 2:23–24).

In the time of the Apostles, when those who had believed in Christ from the circumcision considered that the Gentiles—who were called uncircumcision—could not share in the grace of justification, the blessed apostle Peter teaches how impartial God is toward both peoples if both come together in the unity of faith.

“When I had begun to speak,” he says, “the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as upon us in the beginning” [Note: Leo’s edition reads “in the Holy Spirit,” in accordance with the Greek text of Acts]. “Then I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ If, therefore, God gave them the same grace as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?”

When they heard these things, they were silent and glorified God, saying:

“Then God has also given repentance for life to the Gentiles” (Acts 11:15ff.).

The apostle James also speaks of this calling of the Gentiles (Acts 15:13ff.):

“Men and brothers, hear me. Simeon has related how God first visited the nations to take from them a people for his name. And the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:

‘After these things I will return and rebuild the fallen dwelling of David; I will rebuild its ruins and raise it up, so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, and all the nations upon which my name has been invoked,’ says the Lord who does these things. His work has been known from eternity to the Lord” (Amos 9:11).

Simeon too, who had received the answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he saw the Christ of the Lord, spoke these things concerning the salvation of all nations that was revealed in Christ:

“Now you release your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the nations and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2:29ff.) [Note: Leo’s edition follows the Gospel text; Prosper’s printed editions read “you dismiss.” The Joliensis manuscript reads “according to the face,” and afterward “for revelation … of your people Israel.”].

By these and other testimonies of Scripture it is unquestionably demonstrated that this exceedingly rich, powerful, and gracious grace—by which, at the end of the world, all nations are called into the kingdom of Christ—was hidden in God’s counsel during the earlier ages.

### CHAPTER XIX. God wills at all times that all human beings be saved, whether through general gifts or also through particular ones.

Why this manifestation, by which he is now made known to all nations, was not revealed earlier—no knowledge can comprehend it, no understanding penetrate it [Note: The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo add “rightly, knowledge”]. [Note: Supply from the preceding chapter: “it is unquestionably demonstrated by the testimonies of Scripture.”] Yet what is devoutly believed concerning God’s goodness—that he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4)—ought to be understood as perpetual and eternal, according to those measures by which God knows how to heap general gifts upon particular benefits. Thus those who have been deprived of grace may be convicted of their own wickedness, while those who have been illumined by its light may glory not in their own merit but in the Lord.

### CHAPTER XX. The objection from infants against the statement, “He wills all human beings to be saved.”

Along this narrow but nevertheless straight path of understanding, the consideration of infants presents no small difficulty. They use no judgment of reason by which, perceiving the benefits of their Creator, they might be able to approach the knowledge of truth. Nor do they seem justly blameworthy for neglecting assisting grace, since they are naturally established in that ignorance which unquestionably receives no knowledge and perceives no instruction.

Therefore, since God wills all human beings to be saved (1 Tim. 2:4), what are we to say about the fact that so great a multitude of infants is excluded from everlasting salvation, and that so many thousands of human beings at these ages are left outside eternal life—as though they had been created for this one purpose by him who created no one out of hatred: namely, that because they came into this world bearing the flesh of sin, they should fall into the bonds of an indissoluble guilt without liability from any action of their own [Note: Leo’s edition reads “should fall”; other copies have the same reading]? What could be deeper or more marvelous than this?

For it is not permissible to believe that those who have not attained the sacrament of regeneration [Note: The Camb. manuscript and Leo’s edition read “the sacraments”; other copies read “the sacrament”] belong to any fellowship of the blessed. And what is even more astonishing and more mysterious is that, where action does not offend, where choice does not resist, and where the same misery, similar weakness, and a common cause are present, the judgment is not the same for all in such equality: those whom rejection condemns are adopted by election.

### CHAPTER XXI. That justice is done with infants who perish, both in this age and in the age to come, on account of original sin.

Nevertheless, our humble heart will not be troubled by this height of God’s discernment if, with firm and steadfast faith, we believe that every judgment of God is just and do not desire to know what he has willed to remain secret. When it cannot be investigated why he judges in this way, it is enough to know who the judge is.

Yet this question is not so unknowable that we can acquire no instruction from it [Note: This is how it reads with the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s codex. In other copies of Prosper: “so that there is nothing concerning it from which we can acquire instruction”], if a calm gaze of sober heart is directed toward what can be seen.

When we consider how great a variety of infants perish among pagans, Jews, heretics, and even Catholic Christians—infants who, insofar as their own wills are concerned [Note: The Camb. and Joliensis manuscripts omit this phrase; other copies include it], are known to have done neither anything good nor anything evil [Note: The printed editions read “neither anything good nor anything evil.” In the second case they place “good” before “evil”; the Camb. manuscript and Leo’s edition read “good … evil”]—we learn that the sentence which the human race received in the transgression of its first parent Adam remains upon them [Note: Leo’s edition reads “received in Adam’s transgression”; the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts read “received in Adam’s transgression.” Prosper’s printed editions read “escaped the transgression of the first parent.”]. Since the severity of this sentence is not relaxed even with regard to such persons, how great that sin was is demonstrated.

No one would think that anyone is not born innocent unless it were also harmful to such persons not to be born again.

Concerning the untimeliness of death, there is no reason for complaint, since, once mortality entered our nature through sin, it made every day of our life subject to itself. For a human being could in some sense be called immortal if there were a period of time during which he could not die at all. But corruption never participates so fully in incorruption that what is destined to decline is not always liable to deterioration. The beginning of this life is the beginning of death; nor does our age begin to increase before it begins to diminish. Whatever span of time is added to it does not accrue so that it may remain, but passes away so that it may perish.

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Here we emend *quando* (“when”) from the Camb., Jol., and Leo manuscripts; in the other printed editions of Prosper, *quoniam* (“since”) is read.]

Therefore, whatever is mortal from the beginning of its existence, whenever it dies, does not perish contrary to the law of mortality; nor is it ever nearer to being able to live than to being able to fail. Although mortality arose from one cause for all human beings, corruptible nature is nevertheless dispersed into many forms of weakness. Whether through diseases, infirmities, or wounds, not only the years, months, and days of human life, but also every hour and every moment, are subject to them.

There is no kind of death, nor any manner of dying, that does not affect some portion of the whole body of mortals. For “a grievous yoke remains upon the sons of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Eccli. XL, 1).

**CHAPTER XXII. Divine justice ordains for each person the measure and limit of misery.**

Yet the burdens of this most bitter yoke did not fall upon Adam’s descendants in such a way that divine justice contributed nothing of its own proportion to them.

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Leo has *nihil ei*, “nothing to it,” referring to the yoke; the others have *nihil eis*, “nothing to them,” referring to the burdens.]

It subjected them to the laws of decline in such a way that, even as they were destined to decline, it did not withdraw from them the power of its own moderations.

[Note: [Col. 0708D] The Joliensis manuscript has *subegit*, “subjected.”]

[Note: [Col. 0708D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts, together with Leo, add *nec*, “nor.”]

Nor did all suffer every evil merely because, by their common condition, all were subject to all these things. Rather, by varying the general necessity, the Lord preserved for himself the causes both of mercy and of correction, so that in the one common debt there might be something that he would remit as merciful and demand as just.

Since, then, God’s just and omnipotent providence continually judges all things, and no one comes into this world or leaves it except by that birth and departure which the arbiter of all things determines according to his highest knowledge and wisdom, as it is written in the Book of Job: “Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things, in whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh?” (Job XII, 9). And again: “The days of a human being are short, and the number of his days is with you” (Job XIV, 5). Who would dare to investigate the causes of his works and counsels?

For it is unsearchable and deeply hidden why the human condition has been varied by such great differences.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The Joliensis manuscript has *decessu*, “departure,” instead of *ortu*, “birth”; later the Camb. manuscript has *quae*, “which.”]

One person is consumed from infancy into a long old age by lasting infirmity, and the appointed span of his life does not end amid continuing pains; another, vigorous in unimpaired strength, is sustained by an energy that lasts through many years.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The Joliensis manuscript has “into a long-lived old age.”]

For one, life ends in childhood; for another, in adolescence. One is not permitted to advance beyond youth; another cannot grow even to the beginnings of speech. Mortal humanity would experience these variously unequal limits of life as less bitter if it suffered only the losses of the present age, and if those who departed from here without the laver of regeneration did not fall into eternal miseries.

**CHAPTER XXIII. When little children perish, general grace is granted through its being given to their parents.**

But since the cause of the gifts bestowed by grace is still more inscrutable than that of the miseries deserved by nature, the very difficulty of understanding sends us back to our Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] Thus the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition; others have “the cause both of the gifts and of the miseries is inscrutable.”]

When we ask how he wills all human beings to be saved (I Tim. II, 4), although he does not grant everyone the time in which, through voluntary faith, they might become capable of receiving grace, I think it may rightly and reverently be believed and understood that these human beings of only a few days belong to that portion of grace which has always been bestowed upon all nations.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The Camb. manuscript has *impertitur*, “is granted.”]

If their parents used it well, they themselves too would be helped through them.

For the beginnings of all little children, and that entire initial stage of non-rational infancy, lie under the control of another’s will; nor can provision be made for them in any way except through others. Consequently, they belong to the company of those whose disposition—whether upright or perverse—directs them. For just as they believe through another’s confession, so through another’s unbelief or dissimulation they do not believe.

And since they themselves have desired neither the present life nor the future one, just as it was their lot to be born, so it comes about that they are not reborn [the Latin is elliptical here: *quam ipsorum factum est nasci, tam ipsorum efficitur non renasci*].

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The Joliensis manuscript has *habuerint*, “will have had” or “have had.”]

But just as, in the case of adults, beyond that general grace which touches the hearts of all people more sparingly and secretly, a special calling is exerted through a more excellent work, a more generous gift, and a more powerful virtue, so the same election is also manifested in the case of countless little children.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The Joliensis manuscript has “a more powerful justice.”]

This election was not absent from those who were not reborn, in their parents; rather, it was present among those who were reborn, in preference to their parents.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The Joliensis manuscript reads “neither in those ... but in those who.”]

Thus often, when the impiety of their own people abandoned many, the care of strangers served them, and through outsiders they came to regeneration—something that was not to be provided for them through their nearest relations.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] The Joliensis manuscript has *suorum pietas*, “the piety of their own people”; the contextual sense requires “the impiety of their own people.”]

**CHAPTER XXIV. The distinction among little children of equal condition is no just cause for complaint, but a great commendation of divine justice and Christ’s grace.**

[Note: [Col. 0710D] The Joliensis manuscript reads *atque inanissimus* (“and most empty-headed”) . . . *conquiratur* (“be sought”) . . . *simili providentia* (“with similar providence”).]

In this work of grace, who except the most arrogant and empty-headed person would complain of divine justice because it does not provide the same care for all little children, removing by power or forestalling by mercy all the dangers that can prevent the regeneration of those who are dying?

This would certainly be done for all, if it ought altogether to be done in that way.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] The printed editions have *ita fieret*, “it would be done in this way”; the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition omit *ita* here.]

Yet it is not hidden how much sloth would arise in the hearts of believers if, in the baptism of little children, there were nothing to fear from anyone’s negligence and nothing to fear from their death, since it could in no way happen that such children were deprived of baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] Some editions read *cordibus*, “in hearts,” without *in*; and after several words, *de ipsorum esset mortalitate*, “there would be concern about their mortality.” Our reading is taken from the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition.]

By such utterly inalienable happiness for infants, the opinion of that error would be greatly strengthened which dares to preach, against the Catholic faith, that God’s grace is given according to human merits. It would seem, with complete justice, that this should be owed to blameless innocence, so that adoption would pass over none of those whom no guilt bound. Nor would someone have spoken impiously about the baptism of little children when he said: “Grace has what it may adopt; water has nothing it may wash away.”

But all disciples of the truth understand that this was spoken detestably. From it, moreover, it is clear that those who are saved are liberated not by merit but by grace, because it is beyond doubt that those who die without baptism have perished. They would certainly not perish unless they were participants in a very grave sin. Thus, by God’s hidden yet just determination, both what grace bestows and what rebellious nature deserves are shown: pride is not raised up against the gift, nor diligence cease in the face of danger.

**CHAPTER XXV. Through general grace God wills at all times that all be saved; through particular grace, only some.**

Whether, then, we contemplate the final ages, or the earliest, or those in between, it is reasonably and devoutly believed that God wills, and has always willed, all human beings to be saved. This is demonstrated by nothing other than those benefits which God’s providence bestows commonly and without distinction upon all generations.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] Thus the Camb. manuscript and Leo’s edition; Prosper’s editions have “and that providence of God which ...”]

There were, and there are, gifts of this kind so general that, by their testimony, human beings could be helped to seek the true God.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The Joliensis manuscript has “these general gifts.”]

Through all the ages these gifts proclaim their author, while the abundance of special grace has been poured out above them.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition have “by their testimony”; other printed editions have “through the testimony of those persons themselves.”]

Although this grace is now supplied more abundantly than before, the Lord has kept the reasons for the distribution of his gifts within his knowledge and hidden them in the secrecy of his sovereign will. If these gifts flowed uniformly to all, they would not remain hidden; and just as there is no ambiguity concerning his general benevolence, so there would be nothing astonishing about his special mercy. In that case, the former would be grace, but the latter would not be.

Yet God was pleased both to grant the one to many and to remove the other from no one, so that from both it might be evident that what was bestowed upon a portion was not denied to the whole: in some, grace prevailed; in others, nature recoiled.

**CHAPTER XXVI. In every justification grace has the principal place, but the will is joined to it, because grace first prepares the will for itself as the receiver and servant of its gifts.**

We believe and experience this more abundant grace to be so powerful that we in no way judge it to be violent. Whatever is accomplished in the salvation of human beings is carried out solely by God’s will, even though little children themselves are helped through the service of another’s will.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The Thuan., Camb., and Jol. manuscripts read, “Thus we believe this grace to be benevolent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The Thuan. and Jol. manuscripts have *quod si quid*; the Camb. manuscript has *quo si quid*; Prosper’s editions have *quo quidquid*.]

The grace of God has the principal place in every justification: persuading through exhortations, moving through examples, terrifying through dangers, urging through miracles, giving understanding, inspiring counsel, illuminating the heart itself, and filling it with the affections of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The Jol. and Camb. manuscripts read, “That grace indeed principally prevails in every justification”; our printed editions have “The grace of God in all justifications”; Leo’s edition has “That grace of God in all justifications.”]

Yet the human will is also joined and united to it. Having been aroused by the aids just mentioned, the will cooperates in the divine work within it and begins to exercise toward merit what it conceived toward devotion from heavenly seed. If it fails, it has its mutability to blame; if it advances, it has the assistance of grace.

This assistance is applied to all in countless ways, whether hidden or manifest. The fact that it is rejected by many is due to their wickedness; the fact that it is received by many is due both to divine grace and to the human will. Whether, therefore, we consider the beginnings or the progress of believers, or perseverance to the end, no kind or form of virtue will be found that exists either without the gift of divine grace or without the consent of our will.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] Thus the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts, together with Leo; other editions have “when we consider the kind of those who persevere, no form ...”; they also later read *occurrit*, “appears.”]

For grace acts through every kind of healing and assistance to prepare, in the one whom it calls, the will as the first receiver and servant of its gifts. There is no virtue among the unwilling, nor can faith, hope, or charity be affirmed to exist in those whose consent is alienated from these goods.

**CHAPTER XXVII. The consent of the will is generated by grace not only through instruction and illumination, but also through terror and fear.**

This consent is generated not only by the exhortation of preachers and the incitements of instruction, but also by fear. Hence it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. IX, 10). However great the terrors by which it is imposed, it does nothing other than make the one whom it has made fearful also willing—and not merely willing, but wise.

Hence it is also written: “Blessed is the one to whom it has been granted to have the fear of God” (Eccli. XV, 18). For what is as blessed as this fear, which is the parent and teacher of wisdom?

In devotion to it, the will is also devoted; through the agency of grace, it advances by the same fear through which it began.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] The Joliensis manuscript has “which, through the agency of the same author, advances by the same fear”; the Camb. manuscript has “through which it advances by the same fear.”]

When, therefore, this fear is introduced through a certain force of great terror, reason is not extinguished there, nor understanding taken away. Rather, the darkness that had weighed upon the mind is dispersed, so that the will, previously perverted and captive, may become upright and free.

Thus, just as the mind receives no virtue unless it has received a ray of true light, so grace contributes nothing to the one whom it calls unless it has opened the eyes of the will within him. In many people, as was discussed above, this grace is enriched from its very beginning by most ardent, rapid, and great increases.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] Our printed editions previously had *sitis*, “thirst”; *citis*, “rapidly,” is better, on the basis of the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition, and corresponds to *statim*, “immediately,” in contrast with *tarde cunctanterque*, “slowly and hesitantly.”]

In many others, however, it advances slowly and hesitantly, scarcely reaching those increases that possess sufficient firmness for perseverance.

The Lord says: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI, 44). This was said so that we might know that the faith without which no one comes to Christ is possessed through the Father’s gift, in accordance with what is said to the apostle Peter:

[Note: [Col. 0712D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts, rightly, together with Leo, add *Petro*, “to Peter”; this word is absent from our printed editions.]

“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 17). In the hearts of those who are to be drawn, he brought about their believing; he brought about their willing. For there would be no basis on which they could be drawn if they were not followers in faith and will. Those who do not believe are not drawn at all, nor do they come; those who dissent do not approach but withdraw. Those, therefore, who come are led by love: they were loved, and they loved; they were sought, and they sought; and what God willed them to will, they willed.

**CHAPTER XXVIII. Those who believe in Christ through God’s grace can fail to believe, and those who persevere can depart from God.**

God grants the will to obey him in such a way that he does not even remove from those who will persevere that mutability by which they can refuse to will.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] The Camb. manuscript has *Quia*, “For.”]

Otherwise, no believer would ever have departed from the faith; no one would have been overcome by desire, cast down by grief, conquered by anger; no one’s charity would have grown cold, no one’s patience would have been broken, and no one would have neglected the grace bestowed upon him.

But because these things can happen, and because the descent into consent to such temptations is exceedingly easy and downhill, that saying of the Lord must never cease to sound in the ears of believers, the saying addressed to the apostles: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI, 41). If he had admonished the disciples only to watch, and not also to pray, he would seem to have exhorted merely the powers of free choice. But when he added “and pray,” he sufficiently taught that it would be a gift from above if, even while watching, the storm of temptation did not overcome them.

The same is true of what he said: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has asked that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers, and pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Luke XXI, 31).

[Note: [Col. 0713D] The Joliensis manuscript has “asked insistently that he might sift you”; the Camb. manuscript has “asked that he might sift you.” Concerning *cerneret*, “might see,” found in our printed editions and Leo’s, see above, p. 885, note C. The Camb. manuscript and Leo’s edition likewise have *rogate*, “pray,” instead of *roga*, “pray.”]

If, then, the faith of so great an apostle was going to fail unless Christ prayed for it,

[Note: [Col. 0713D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts have *nisi pro ea*, “unless he prayed for it.”]

there was undoubtedly in him a mutability that could waver in temptation; and he had not yet been so firmly established by the virtue of perseverance that he was immune to every danger.
