Indeed, such a grave disturbance shook him even after these events that, terrified in the house of Caiaphas by the questioning of a single maidservant, he was brought to a triple denial of Christ, although he had promised that he would die with him, when his constancy failed.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] The Joliensis manuscript has “of the one to whom”; other copies have “of the one who was to die”; Leo’s edition has “of the one with whom he was to die.”]

The one who then observed the apostle’s troubled heart not with human but with divine eyes, and by a powerful gaze moved him to abundant tears of repentance, could bestow this firmness of soul upon his foremost disciple, so that just as nothing deterred the Lord himself from completing his passion, so no fear would then overcome blessed Peter.

But this stability belonged only to him who alone truly and powerfully said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18).

[Note: [Col. 0713D] The Joliensis manuscript has “to take it up.”]

In other human beings, so long as the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V, 17), and so long as “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI, 41), unchangeable firmness of soul cannot be found. For the perfect and secure happiness of true peace belongs not to this life but to the next.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Thus the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition; our printed copies have “truly perfect.”]

In the uncertainty of the present struggle, where the whole of life is temptation (Job VII), and where even victory is not safe from ambushing pride,

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Prosper’s printed editions have “from ambushing pride”; the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo have the same reading.]

there is no escape from the danger of mutability. Although divine protection grants countless saints the virtue of persevering to the end, it does not remove from any of them what resists them from within themselves, so that in all their endeavors and efforts willing and unwilling are always in conflict.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] The Joliensis manuscript omits *sanctis*, “saints.”]

[Note: [Col. 0714D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts have *aufertur*, “is removed,” instead of *aufert*, “removes.”]

[Note: [Col. 0714D] Prosper’s printed editions have *decertet*, “may contend”; the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo have *decertent*, “contend.”]

That same most blessed Peter endured this conflict even at the completion of all his victories. For the Lord himself testified and said to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were young, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” He said this to signify by what death Peter would glorify God (John XXI, 18–19).

[Note: [Col. 0714D] Other printed copies have “the Lord himself”; the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo’s edition have “the Lord himself said.” The Joliensis manuscript has *dicebat*, “he was saying.”]

Who, then, could doubt or fail to know that this strongest of rocks, who received both virtue and name from communion with that principal Rock, always desired that he be granted steadfastness to die for Christ (Matt. XVI, 18)? Yet the struggle against trembling was so unavoidable that the man most eager for martyrdom was indeed promised victory in suffering, but not without the temptation of fear.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] The Joliensis manuscript has: “so that the victory of suffering was indeed announced to the man most eager for martyrdom, but not without the temptation of fear.”]

Rightly, therefore, not only beginners but also advanced saints uniformly beseech the Lord and say: “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI, 21).

[Note: [Col. 0714D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and the ancient editions of Leo have *inferas*, “lead”; other editions have *inducas*, “bring.”]

For all who remain in faith and love are granted by him not to be overcome in temptation, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31). He ascribes that victory itself to those to whom he grants it, so that although they stood by God’s help, since they had within themselves the means by which they could fall, the merit of standing belongs to them.

Therefore, just as those who have believed are helped to remain in the faith, so those who have not yet believed are helped to believe. And just as the former have it in their power to depart, so the latter have it in their power not to come. It is thus made clear that God wills all people to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II, 4), in diverse and countless ways; but those who come are guided by God’s help, while those who do not come resist through their own obstinacy.

**CHAPTER XXIX. The promise of the blessing of all nations is fulfilled daily, so that those who perish have no just excuse, nor those who are saved any ground for boasting in their own justice.**

Although many, loving their own darkness, do not receive the splendor of truth, and many who had been enlightened grow dark, nevertheless the word of God remains forever (Isa. XL, 8), and nothing falls away from the truth of the promise. Each day the foreknown and promised fullness of the nations enters, and in Abraham’s seed every nation, every tribe, and every tongue is blessed.

What the Father gave the Son, the Son does not lose, nor can anyone snatch from his hand what he has received (John VI, 39; X, 29).

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts have *rapere*, “snatch”; others have *eripere*, “take away.”]

“The firm foundation of God stands” (II Tim. II, 18), and the building of the temple that will remain forever does not totter, with God’s truth and mercy extended over all. From him, what is neither denied to anyone nor owed to anyone is brought about in those whom he promised. For he himself works all things in all people (I Cor. XII, 6), but unquestionably all things that are just and good. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

Just as he foreknew before the ages how great would be the multitude of people throughout the whole world who, whether using common gifts or helped by special aids, would nevertheless turn aside from the path of truth and life and enter the broad way of error and death, so he always had foreknown how great would be the number of the godly who, through the help of grace and the service of obedience, would belong to eternal blessedness.

Thus, with no one falling away from the fullness of those promised, he—who was neither to be deceived in their outcome nor to fail in assistance—would glorify before all others those whom he chose from among all.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] The Joliensis manuscript has *proventu*, “outcome,” in place of *provectu*, “progress”; it also has “by his assistance.”]

For, as we have abundantly proved, God’s manifold and ineffable goodness has always cared, and continues to care, for the whole human race, so that none of those who perish may have an excuse for having rejected the light of truth, nor may anyone have the liberty to boast of his own justice, since their own wickedness drags the former down to punishment, while God’s grace leads the latter to glory.

**918 CHAPTER XXX. Repetition of the first chapter of the second book.**

What we intimated at the beginning of this second volume we now commend once again: when the depth and height of grace are discussed, we should rely upon those three most salutary and truthful definitions.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] Leo’s edition has “those first definitions.”]

The first declares that it belongs eternally and properly to divine goodness to will all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II, 4). The second likewise proclaims that every person who is saved, and who comes to the knowledge of the truth, is helped and governed by God’s aid, and guarded so that he may remain in the faith that works through love (Gal. V, 6).

The third declares with moderation and sobriety that the reason for God’s will cannot be comprehended in its entirety, and that many causes of divine works are withdrawn from human understanding. Thus, when certain things are observed to have been done variously or remarkably in times, nations, families, little children, the unborn, and twins, we should not doubt that they belong among those things which the just and merciful God did not will to be known in this passing age.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] Thus the Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo. Other copies and the earlier books of Leo have “and those born.” The printed editions below have “we do not doubt,” where the manuscripts cited shortly afterward have “let us not doubt.” Farther below the Camb. manuscript has *transitorio*, “passing,” instead of *transituro*, “that is to pass.”]

This should be understood as arranged for our benefit: since “we were saved in hope” (Rom. VIII, 24), and since God has prepared for hope what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II, 9), just as we steadfastly believe that we shall see what we do not yet see, so let us patiently await understanding what we do not yet understand.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] The Joliensis manuscript has “we await.”]

If, then, treacherous malice ceases and insolent presumption grows quiet, once these matters have been rightly considered, there remains, as I think, no cause for dispute, nor is it any longer necessary for us to occupy ourselves with endless questions.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] The Joliensis manuscript has “reviewed.”]

**CHAPTER XXXI. God’s general goodness has been present to all people in every age, but particular grace belongs only to those who are to be saved.**

For, insofar as the Lord helped, it has been demonstrated that God’s grace was present to all human beings not only in the final days but also throughout all the ages that preceded them, with equal providence indeed and general goodness, but through manifold activity and differing measure.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] The Camb. manuscript has “with manifold and diverse measure”; this is also found elsewhere and in Leo.]

For whether secretly or openly, he is, as the Apostle says, “the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers” (I Tim. IV, 10). If this statement, which is of the most subtle brevity and strongest force, is considered with a tranquil gaze, it settles the whole controversy under discussion.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] The printed editions have “the controversy of which we have treated”; the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition have “the controversy which we are treating.”]

By saying “the Savior of all human beings,” he confirmed that God’s goodness is general over all people. By adding “especially of believers,” he showed that there is a portion of the human race which, through the merit of divinely inspired faith, is advanced to the highest and eternal salvation by special benefits.

This is accomplished without any injustice by the most just and merciful God, whose judgment in these arrangements should not be examined with arrogance but praised with trembling.

**CHAPTER XXXII. Among believers there are different degrees of God’s gifts; this is not based on their merits but on God’s just and hidden judgment.**

For even among the peoples of believers, as has already been shown above, not the same things or equal things are bestowed upon all; and before any consideration of human merits, the measure of divine gifts is profoundly unequal.

If we do not dare complain about the judgments of carnal parents, when they embrace some of their children with more indulgent affection before any examination of their conduct or any acts of filial devotion; if among masters also the disposition toward servants is free, and no one rightly reproves a master who, from a household of people having the same condition, chooses some whom he may honor more kindly and whom he may educate more generously,

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The Joliensis manuscript supplies *si*, “if,” which is also found in Leo.]

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The printed editions have *liberius*, “more freely”; this is corrected from the Joliensis manuscript and Leo.]

should we bring a charge against the most benevolent equity of the supreme Father and true Lord because everything in his great house is varied by innumerable distinctions?

Since no one possesses any good that he has not received from him, nevertheless not all shine with the same virtues or are enriched with the same endowment of spiritual gifts. Nor can we adapt this diversity of ranks to causes based on merits, since grace is the principal cause of every good merit, and whatever is found praiseworthy in individuals is drawn from its resources.

**CHAPTER XXXIII. No one perishes who ought not to perish; all the eternally elect are saved.**

Therefore, just as it is impious to conceive any complaint in one’s heart about the manifold works of the Holy Spirit within the Church, so one must not murmur in any way about that providence which presides over unbelievers. For the just and good judge is neither of an unjust will nor of an uncertain discernment, so that, under the immense mercy and justice of almighty God, we should think that anyone perishes who ought not to perish.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The Joliensis manuscript, omitting “of almighty God,” has “under his immense mercy.”]

No part of the world is without the Gospel of Christ. Although that general calling does not cease, this special calling too has already been made common to all. From every nation and every condition, thousands of old people, thousands of young people, and thousands of little children are adopted each day. Even the instruments by which the world is crushed serve the effects of Christian grace.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Duacensis and Coloniensis have *affectibus*, “affections”; others have *effectibus*, “effects.”]

For how many people who had been delaying to receive the sacrament of baptism in the tranquility of peace were driven by fear of imminent danger to flee to the water of regeneration? What quiet exhortation had long failed to persuade their slow and lukewarm minds, threatening terror suddenly extorted.

Some children of the Church, captured by enemies, made their masters subject to Christ’s Gospel; and those whom they served in the condition of war, they instructed as teachers of the faith.

Other barbarians, while aiding the Romans, learned in our regions what they could not have known in their own lands,

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition have *cognovere*, “they came to know”; others have *didicere*, “they learned.”]

and returned to their own homes with the instruction of the Christian religion.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The Joliensis manuscript has “with the justification of the Christian religion.”]

Thus nothing can obstruct divine grace from accomplishing what it wills: even conflicts draw people toward unity, and wounds are turned into remedies, so that from the very source where the Church feared danger, she receives increase.

Whatever outcome of human affairs our contemplation may turn toward, it will find that no age, no undertaking, no rise or decline of generations is free from the eternal and inscrutable judgments of God. All the conflicts of variations, and all the causes of dissimilar outcomes [Note: [Col. 0717D] Leo’s edition: “advancements” (*provectuum*). The others: “outcomes” (*proventuum*).]—which we are unable to investigate and discern—are at once known and at once distinguished within that eternal knowledge. Nor is anything there disordered, even with regard to the qualities of actions not yet existing. For in God there is no accidental movement, no new will, no temporal counsel; nor does his thought vary with the inequality of mutable things. Rather, he comprehends all times and temporal things together in an everlasting and steadfast vision, and has already repaid all things to all, [Note: [Col. 0718D] The Camberon manuscript: “whatever things are future.”] who has already made what is future.

Hence comes that saying of the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Ephesians:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love. He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0718D] The printed editions had added “our Lord” at this point; these words are absent from the Joliensis manuscript and from Leo’s edition, indeed also from the Apostle’s text in the Vulgate version.] according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace” (Ephesians 1:3 and following), 921 and so forth [Note: [Col. 0718D] Leo’s edition: “which are there.”]—things which he connects under the proclamation of the same meaning. He teaches that the gift and work of grace always remained in God’s eternal plan, and that all the children of adoption were chosen not only [Note: [Col. 0718D] The preposition *in* is not read in the Joliensis manuscript.] at the time when, already existing, they were called, but also before the world was established [Note: [Col. 0718D] Other printed editions: “was created.” The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts and Leo have the reading found in the text.].

In this election, whoever among humanity is not foreknown in Christ will in no way be joined to it. For all who are to come into the kingdom of God, from the calling of whatever age, have been marked out in this adoption, which preceded all ages. And just as no unbeliever is counted in this portion, so no godly person is separated from this blessing [Note: [Col. 0718D] The printed editions: “has been counted.” Later, the Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition read, “from this blessing,” while the others have, “from this portion.”].

For from the fullness of the members of Christ’s body, the foreknowledge of God—which cannot be deceived—loses nothing; nor can the foreknown total, chosen beforehand in Christ before the eternal ages, be diminished by any loss. As the Apostle writes to Timothy:

“Labor for the Gospel [Col. 0719A] according to the power of God, who delivered us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times” (2 Timothy 1:8–9).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. It is not useless to labor for the acquisition of the merits of good works or to persist in prayers, although God’s purpose concerning the salvation of the elect is unchangeable.

Against this most splendid light of unconquered truth, some people habitually say, without sound judgment, that laboring to acquire the merits of good works is superfluous, and that it is likewise futile to persist in prayers by which one hopes to entreat God, if the election of Christian grace rests upon his unchangeable purpose and nothing can proceed otherwise than as the will of the Almighty has ordained.

But those [Note: [Col. 0719D] Leo’s edition reads “*haec se ingeniose*”; the printed editions, “*se ingeniose hoc*”; the Joliensis manuscript has the word order printed above.] who cleverly imagine that they can set this objection against it do not understand that God’s knowledge, which embraces past, present, and future, is not held within time, and that things which must be done stand before him just as do things which are being done or have been done. Since this is most true, that power does not need time in order to see and distinguish what, by an everlasting and true vision, it sees simultaneously: what has been created and what is to be created, what has arisen and what is to arise, what has been done and what must be done. Whatever unfolds through the predetermined ages of the universe and is disclosed in manifold variations, it already comprehends entirely within that order which the end of this world will receive from his supreme and perfect judgment. 922

This eternal and always tranquil knowledge, however, compels us by no necessity to sin; nor does iniquity flow from the source from which justice comes. For since the good God made all things good, and there is no nature of evil at all [Note: [Col. 0719D] The Joliensis manuscript: “and there is no nature of evil whatsoever.”], transgression arose spontaneously from free wills—and it was certainly good that they should be made free. The mutable nature, whose safety depended upon the immutable essence, severed itself from the supreme good when it perversely delighted in what was its own [Note: [Col. 0719D] The Joliensis manuscript does not have *perverse* (“perversely”). Leo’s edition: “while delighting in its own things.”]; and God’s grace now heals that ruin.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Grace is given to the elect not so that they may be idle or be attacked by no enemy, but so that they may do good and conquer the enemy.

Therefore Jesus Christ came into this world “to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8). These works are destroyed in such a way that, even in their destruction, those who are helped labor as well, since this too is granted by the one who saves.

For this reason the blessed Apostle says:

“Not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5:3 and following).

Likewise, the same Apostle says to the Ephesians:

“By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Ephesians 2:8 and following).

Therefore God gives those whom he chose without merits [Note: [Col. 0719D] Earlier printed editions: “whom he chooses.” The Joliensis manuscript and Leo’s edition: “whom he chose.”] the means by which they may be adorned with merits as well. It is therefore said in vain that the elect have no reason to act, since they were chosen also for this purpose: that they should act [Note: [Col. 0719D] This must be the reading, not, as the printed editions formerly had it, “so that they might act in order to become elect.” The sequence of the context, the whole teaching of this book, and the Thuanus and Joliensis manuscripts establish this. The objection to which the author is replying arose from what he had taught earlier: “From the fullness of the members of Christ’s body, the foreknowledge of God, which cannot be deceived, loses nothing, nor can the foreknown total, chosen beforehand in Christ before the eternal ages, be diminished by any loss” (chapter 33). “If this is so,” they say, “the elect have no reason to act.” “On the contrary,” he replies, “they have the greatest reason to act, since they were chosen not only in order to be saved, but also in order to act.” This plainly agrees with the blessed Apostle’s words in Ephesians 2:10: “Created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them”; and with 1:4: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we should be holy.” From this Saint Augustine drew what he teaches frequently: predestination is the preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are saved are most certainly liberated; predestination is the preparation of grace; God predestined those whom he willed both for good works and for eternal rewards. Moreover, as our author adds, the gifts of virtues cannot be idle.].

For the gifts of the virtues cannot be idle. As the Truth says: “To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matthew 25:29).

Continence is not therefore given so that it may not resist desires. Nor is wisdom and understanding bestowed on anyone so that he may not meditate day and night on the law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0720D] The Joliensis manuscript: “in the law of God.”] (Psalm 1:2). What does the gift of love accomplish if the care of goodwill does not keep watch? What fruit is there in patience if strength has nothing to endure? Or how is it shown that someone lives devoutly in Christ (2 Timothy 3:1) [Note: [Col. 0720D] The Joliensis manuscript: “is believed to live devoutly.”] if he is assailed by no persecution? Or is the peace that comes from God and exists with God truly peaceful if it is not at odds with the world [Note: [Col. 0720D] The Joliensis manuscript: “if it does not depart from the world.”]? Or can the love of God [Note: [Col. 0720D] The printed editions: “can be obtained.”] be attained without the devil’s hostility?

God’s grace makes no one entirely beyond temptation. Nor is the Christian army armed with the protection of heavenly weapons on the right and on the left so that it may engage in conflict with no enemy, since it is more praiseworthy and more fortunate for one who fights not to have been defeated [Note: [Col. 0720D] The Camberon manuscript: “for the one who is certainly fighting,” omitting “more fortunate.”] than for one who is idle not to have been tempted.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Election does not remove the earnestness of prayer; rather, its effect is completed through prayer and good works.

That concern for prayers is not dissolved by the purpose of divine election I shall prove clearly by one testimony, omitting the rest for the sake of brevity.

In the Book of Tobit, therefore, the angel Raphael says to Tobit’s son Tobiah:

“Remember the commandments of your father, for he commanded you to take a wife from your father’s kindred. And now listen to me, brother: do not take account of that demon, but ask for her. And know that she will be given to you as a wife this night. When you enter the chamber, take the fish’s liver and place it upon the coals; its odor will spread, and the demon will smell it and flee, and it will never again appear around her at all. And when you begin to wish to be with her, first rise, both of you, and entreat the Lord of heaven to grant you mercy and healing. 924 And do not be afraid; for she was destined for you before the ages, and you will heal her” (Tobit 6:16 and following).

Although, therefore, what God has determined cannot in any way fail to occur, the earnestness of prayer is not removed, nor is the devotion of free will relaxed by the purpose of election. For the effect by which God’s will is to be fulfilled has been so foreordained that through the labor of works, the persistence of supplications [Note: [Col. 0721B] The Camberon manuscript: “of those who supplicate.”], and the practice of virtues, increases of merit come about; and those who have done good are crowned not only according to God’s purpose but also according to their own merits.

For this reason the determination of this election has been hidden in a secret most remote from human knowledge.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Before the end of this life, no one can be declared to be destined for the glory of the elect; and the restoration of no one who has fallen is to be despaired of.

Before a person’s own end, no one can be declared to be destined for the glory of the elect, so that useful fear may preserve the humility of one who perseveres, and “let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12) [Note: [Col. 0721B] The Camb. and Jol. manuscripts: “and if perhaps.”]. And if someone should perhaps fall after being overcome by temptation, let him not be swallowed up by grief, nor distrust the mercy of the one who raises up all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down (Psalm 144:14) [Note: [Col. 0722B] Other printed editions: “who fall.”].

As long as one lives in this body, the correction of no one is to be neglected [Note: [Col. 0722B] In the Joliensis manuscript, *est* is omitted here.], and the restoration of no one is to be despaired of. Therefore let the holy Church pray, and, giving thanks for those who have believed, let it ask that perseverance may grow in them; but for those who are outside the faith, let it ask that they may believe. Nor should it cease from supplications if it has not been heard on behalf of certain people. For God, who wills everyone to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4), cannot reject anyone without justice.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITAINE

[Col. 0721] [Note: [Col. 0721] This book, *On the Contemplative Life*, which highly learned men had attributed to Saint Prosper over a long period of time, appeared in all earlier editions. But since we have long since been able to identify its true author, and since in our universal Library each writer has his own assigned place and order, we shall arrange for this little work to be published at the same time as the works of Pomerius. —Editor.]

## [CANONS ON GRACE AND FREE WILL]

[Col. 0721]

# NOTICE ON THE CANONS OF THE SECOND COUNCIL OF ORANGE ON GRACE AND FREE WILL

The Second Council of Orange, comprising twenty-five canons, is usually appended to all the works of Saint Prosper. And rightly so. For the decrees of this council establish especially those doctrines which Augustine first defended against the Semipelagians, and afterward Saint Prosper, the vigorous defender and champion of Augustine’s teaching.

Indeed, they are noted as having been composed from the very words of both Fathers, since they were drawn from various books of Saint Augustine, and in particular excerpted from those passages which Saint Prosper had collected from Augustine’s works. They were taken not only from Augustine, but also from works written by Prosper himself after Augustine’s death—as is the case with canons 6, 7, and 8, which were excerpted from the book *Against the Collator*.

From this procedure of those bishops it is clear that the Fathers assembled at Orange approved both Augustine’s teaching and, specifically, the teaching of our Saint Prosper; indeed, this council was held under Felix IV, who was seated at Rome, urged them to celebrate it, and strengthened it by his authority.

The Fathers state the following in the Preface:

“It has come to our attention that there are some who wish to think about grace and free will less cautiously and not according to the simplicity of the Catholic faith. Therefore, according to the authority and admonition of the apostolic see, it seemed just and reasonable to us that we should present for observance by all, and subscribe with our own hands, a few chapters transmitted to us by the apostolic see concerning grace and free will, chapters which the ancient Fathers collected from the books of the holy Scriptures especially for this matter, in order to instruct those who thought otherwise than they ought.”

In some of their canons, especially the eighth, those Fathers explicitly reject the distinction which Cassian had devised in the thirteenth Conference: that there were two kinds of predestined people, some of whom preceded the gift of grace by certain merits, while others received grace from God without preceding merits. Saint Prosper had refuted this distinction at length in many chapters of his book *Against the Collator*.

Near the end of canon 25, the Fathers also reject, in a few words, various explanations of Scripture by this author, applied to individual clauses, establishing the following:

“We also salutarily profess and believe that in every good work we do not ourselves begin and are afterward assisted by God’s mercy; rather, he himself, without any preceding good merits, first inspires us with both faith and love of himself, so that we may faithfully seek the sacrament of baptism and, after baptism, with his help, be able to fulfill those things which are pleasing to him.”

Hence it must be believed most clearly that the remarkable faith of the thief whom the Lord restored to the homeland of paradise, of the centurion Cornelius to whom the Lord’s angel was sent, and of Zacchaeus, who was deemed worthy to receive the Lord himself, did not come from nature but was a gift of divine generosity.

This Second Synod met at Orange on the fifth day before the nones of July in the year of Christ 529, as James Sirmond observes, [Col. 0723] under Pope Felix IV, while Athalaric, son of Amalasuntha, was reigning in Italy, and the sons of Clovis in Gaul. Caesarius of Arles presided over the council. Pope Boniface II approved it in his letter to Caesarius himself, which Sirmond brought to light from ancient manuscripts.

At this synod, against the Semipelagians—who had become widespread in Gaul, especially in the second province of Narbonensis, through the principal proponents of this heresy, the men of outstanding intellect Cassian and Faustus—the necessity of Christ’s grace, even for the beginning of all faith and every godly life, was affirmed.

[Col. 0723]

# CANONS OF THE SECOND COUNCIL OF ORANGE ON GRACE AND FREE WILL

[Note: [Col. 0723C] In an old Lyon manuscript the title is: “Constitution of the bishops in the city of Orange, on grace and free will.” In the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions: “Canons of the other Council of Orange, around the time of Pope Leo I. On free will, or on various conditions, and on matters necessary to be requested by chapters.” Baronius first placed this council in the year 463, but later, in the additions to volume 10, he wished it transferred to the year 529. It is shown in various places that Caesarius, bishop of Arles, who presided over it, did not hold office in those earlier times. It is also established from the writers of his life that he lived until the year of Christ 544. Moreover, Spondanus, volume 2 of the *Epitome*, page 20, points out that the date of Liberius, prefect of the Gauls, who is found to have subscribed to this Council of Orange, was erroneous when it was assigned to the time of Leo the Great.] The Second Council of Orange, held at the dedication of the basilica constructed by the patrician Liberius, met on the fifth day before the nones of July, during the consulship of Decius the Younger, a man of consular rank—that is, in the year of Christ 525, in the third year of Pope Felix IV.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0723A]

When, with God’s favor, we had assembled for the dedication of the basilica which our most illustrious prefect and patrician, our son Liberius, had built in the city of Orange with the most faithful devotion, and when, at his invitation, a spiritual discussion had arisen among us concerning matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline, it came to our attention that there were some who wished to think about grace and free will less cautiously and not according to the rule of the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0724C] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions: “Therefore it also seemed to us.” This was changed in the Appendix to volume 10 of Augustine, as above. The same applies below to “from certain books of Scripture,” where Augustine’s edition now reads, “from the books of the holy Scriptures.”]

Therefore, according to the authority and admonition of the apostolic see, it seemed just and reasonable to us that we should present for observance by all, and subscribe with our own hands, a few chapters transmitted to us by the apostolic see, which the ancient Fathers collected from the books of the holy Scriptures especially for this matter, in order to instruct those who think otherwise than they ought. When these have been read, whoever has hitherto not believed concerning grace and free will as he ought should not delay to incline his mind toward what accords with the Catholic faith.

## That through Adam’s sin not only the body but also the soul was injured  
*(Augustine, Book 2 on Marriage and Concupiscence, chapter 34)*

[Col. 0723B]

**I.** If anyone says that, through Adam’s transgression, the human being was not wholly changed for the worse—that is, in body and soul—but believes that only the body was made subject to corruption while the soul’s freedom remained unharmed, he is deceived by Pelagius’s error and contradicts Scripture, which says: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20); and: “Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey?” (Romans 6:16); and: “By whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is also enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

## That Adam’s sin harmed not only him but also passed to his descendants  
*(Augustine, Book 4)*

**II.** If anyone asserts that Adam alone was harmed by his transgression, and not his descendants as well; or testifies that only bodily death, which is the punishment of sin, but not sin itself, which is the death of the soul, passed through one man into the whole human race, he makes God unjust, contradicting the Apostle, who says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12). [Note: [Col. 0724C] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions lack the words “and thus … death”; they were restored in the Appendix to volume 10 of Augustine.]

## That God’s grace is not given in response to invocation, but itself causes invocation

[Col. 0724A]

**III.** If anyone says that God’s grace can be conferred through human invocation, but does not confess that grace itself causes us to invoke it, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 65:1), or the Apostle, who says the same thing: “I was found by those who did not seek me; I openly appeared to those who did not ask about me” (Romans 10:20).

## That God does not await our will in order to cleanse us from sin, but prepares it

**IV.** If anyone contends that, in order that we may be cleansed from sin, God awaits our will, but does not confess that, through the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit in us, even the desire to be cleansed is brought about, he resists the Holy Spirit himself, who says through Solomon: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint); and the Apostle, who salutarily proclaims: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good will” (Philippians 2:13). [Note: [Col. 0724C] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions: “in us.”]

## That the beginning of faith is not from us but from God’s grace  
*(Augustine, Book on the Predestination of the Saints, chapters 1 through 9)*

[Col. 0724B]

**V.** If anyone says that not only the increase of faith but also its beginning, and the very affection of believing by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly and come to the regeneration of holy baptism [Note: [Col. 0724C] The edition of the council in the Appendix to volume 10 of Augustine adds here “sacred,” and below “and this,” before “not from yourselves.” These words are absent from the Prosperian manuscripts.], is naturally in us and does not come through the gift of grace—that is, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who turns our will from unbelief to faith and from impiety to godliness—he is shown to be an adversary of the apostolic teachings. For the blessed Paul says: “We are confident that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6); and: “It has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (ibid., 1:29); and: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves, for it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8).

For those who say that the faith by which we believe in God is natural thereby define, in a certain way, all who are alienated from the Church of Christ as believers.

## That mercy is not bestowed upon believers and petitioners without God’s grace, since grace itself causes us to believe and petition  
*(Augustine, Book on the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 23; Prosper, Against the Collator, chapter 6)*

[Col. 0724C]

**VI.** If anyone says that divine mercy is bestowed upon us without God’s grace when we believe, will, desire, strive, labor, keep watch, devote ourselves, ask, seek, and knock, but does not confess that through the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit in us we are enabled to believe, will, or perform all these things as we ought; and if he adds the help of grace to human humility or obedience, but does not agree that it is the gift of grace itself that makes us obedient and humble, he resists the Apostle, who says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7); and: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

## That without grace we cannot by the powers of nature think of or choose any good pertaining to the salvation of eternal life  
*(Augustine, Book on the Grace of Christ, chapter 26)*

**VII.** If anyone confirms that by the power of nature he can, as is fitting, think of or choose some good pertaining to the salvation of eternal life, or consent to the saving, that is, evangelical preaching—without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who gives sweetness to all in consenting to and believing the truth, he is deceived by a heretical spirit. He does not understand the voice of God in the Gospel, which says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); nor that of the Apostle: “Not that we are competent to think anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

## That no one can come to the grace of baptism through free will  
*(Prosper, Against the Collator, chapters 2, 7, and 18; and Response to Cassian’s Definition 6)*

**VIII.** If anyone contends that some can come to the grace of baptism through mercy, but others through free will—which is established to have been corrupted in all who were born from the transgression of the first human being—he is proved alien to the right faith.

For he either does not assert that everyone’s free will was weakened by the sin of the first human being, or else he thinks that it was injured in such a way that some are nevertheless able, without God’s revelation, to seek out the mystery of eternal salvation by themselves.

How contrary this is, the Lord himself proves, testifying that not some people but no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Likewise he says to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17); and the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus Christ,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). [Note: [Col. 0725D] The Appendix edition of volume 10 of Augustine reads “the Lord Jesus.” The Prosperian books add “Christ” to the sacred text.]

## On God’s help, by which we do good  
*(Prosper, Sentences 22)*

**IX.** It is a divine gift when we think rightly and restrain our feet from falsehood and injustice [Note: [Col. 0725D] This is the reading of Augustine’s edition and of the book of the *Sentences*. The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions here read “we hold fast.”]. For whenever we do good, God works in us and with us so that we may act.

## On always imploring God’s help  
*(Prosper, Against the Collator, chapter 24)*

**X.** God’s help must always be implored, even by those who have been reborn [Note: [Col. 0725D] Two manuscripts, namely the Lyon and Reims manuscripts: “and healed.”] and made holy, so that they may reach a good end or persevere in a good work.

## On the offering of vows  
*(Augustine, Book 17 of The City of God, chapter 4; Prosper, Sentences 54)*

**XI.** No one would rightly make a vow to the Lord unless he received from him what he was to vow, as it is written: “What we have received from your hand, we give to you” (1 Chronicles 29:14). [Note: [Col. 0725D] Corrected from volume 10 of Augustine’s Appendix and from Prosper’s *Sentences*. The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions here read *voverit* (“has vowed”), while omitting the remainder, “unless he received from him,” and so forth. The title has also been corrected from the *Sentences* printed above: *oblatione* (“offering”) replaces *obligatione* (“obligation”), which also slipped into Augustine’s Appendix.]

## The kind of people God loves  
*(Prosper, Sentences 56)*

**XII.** God loves us as the people we are going to be by his gift, not as the people we are by our merit.

## On the restoration of free will  
*(Augustine, Book 14 of The City of God, chapter 11; Prosper, Sentences 152)*

**XIII.** The will’s faculty [Note: [Col. 0726D] Some manuscripts: “the faculty of freedom.”] weakened in the first human being cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism. What was lost cannot be restored except by the one from whom it was able to be given. Hence the Truth himself says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:16).

## That we are preceded by God’s mercy so that we may be freed from misery  
*(Prosper, Sentences 211)*

**XIV.** No miserable person is freed from whatever misery except one who is preceded by God’s mercy, as the Psalmist says: “Let your mercy, O Lord, quickly come before us” (Psalm 78:8); and: “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Psalm 59:10).

## That through God’s grace the believer is changed for the better  
*(Augustine, Sermon on Psalm 68; Prosper, Sentences 225)*

**XV.** Adam was changed from what God had formed [Note: [Col. 0726D] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions: “is changed.”], but for the worse through his iniquity. The believer is changed from what iniquity had wrought, but for the better through God’s grace. The former change, therefore, belonged to the first transgressor; the latter, according to the Psalmist, is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 77:10).

## That one must not glory in what one has, since it is from God  
*(Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 28; Prosper, Sentences 260)*

**XVI.** Let no one glory in what he appears to have, as though he had not received it; nor let him think that he received it for this reason: that the letter appeared externally either to be read or sounded so as to be heard. For as the Apostle says: “If justification is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21).

But if he did not die for nothing: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4:8; Psalm 68:18). Whoever has anything has it from there. But whoever denies that he has it from there either truly does not have it, or what he has will be taken away from him (Matthew 25:29).

## On Christian fortitude  
*(Augustine, Book 1 of the Unfinished Work, section 83; Prosper, Sentences 297)*

**XVII.** Worldly desire produces the fortitude of the pagans, but the fortitude of Christians is produced by the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts not through the decision of the will but through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Romans 5:5), [Note: [Col. 0726D] These words occur at the end of canon 17 in the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne manuscripts of Prosper, but not in the edition of volume 10 of Saint Augustine’s works, nor in *Sentences* 295, nor in the *Unfinished Work against Julian*. Perhaps they have intruded here from the title of the following canon.] with no merits preceding grace.

## That grace is preceded by no merits  
*(Augustine, Book 1 of the Unfinished Work, section 133; Prosper, Sentences 299)*

**XVIII.** A reward is owed to good works if they are performed; but grace, which is not owed, precedes them so that they may be performed.

## That no one is saved except by God’s mercy  
*(Augustine, Letter 186, section 37; Prosper, Sentences 310)*

[Col. 0726D]

**XIX.** Human nature, even if it had remained in the integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. Therefore, since it cannot guard, without God’s grace, the salvation it received, how will it be able, without God’s grace, to restore what it lost [Note: [Col. 0727D] The printed Prosperian editions: “what he lost.” The correct reading, “what it lost,” is found in Augustine at the place cited in the margin, in the Appendix to volume 10, and in Prosper’s *Sentences*.]?

## That a human being can do no good without God  
*(Augustine, Book 2 against Two Letters of the Pelagians, chapter 8; Prosper, Sentences 314)*

**XX.** [Note: [Col. 0727D] This canon is read in this form in the Appendix to volume 10 of Augustine and in the Augustinian and Prosperian passages cited in the margin. In the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne edition of Prosper it reads: “Many good things are done in a human being.”] God does many good things in a human being which the human being does not do; but a human being does no good things which God does not grant that the human being may do.

## On nature and grace  
*(Augustine, Book on Grace and Free Will, chapter 13; Prosper, Sentences 317)*

**XXI.** Just as the Apostle says with complete truth to those who, wishing to be justified by the law, have fallen from grace, “If justification is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21), so it is said with complete truth to those who think that the grace which the faith of Christ commends and receives is nature: “If justification is through nature, then Christ died for nothing.”

For the law already existed here, and it did not justify; nature already existed here as well, and it did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing, so that through him the law might be fulfilled—he who said, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17)—and so that nature, lost through Adam, might be restored through him who said that he had come to seek and save what had perished (Luke 19:10).

## On those things which belong properly to human beings  
*(Augustine, Tractate 5 on John; Prosper, Sentences 325)*

**XXII.** No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin. [Note: [Col. 0727D] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions: “But if a human being has truth and righteousness.” Augustine’s Appendix to volume 10 and the passages cited in the margin have the reading found in the text.]

But if a human being has any truth or righteousness, it comes from that fountain for which we ought to thirst in this wilderness, so that, sprinkled from it as though by certain drops, we may not fail on the way.

## On the will of God and of the human being  
*(Augustine, Tractate 19 on John; Prosper, Sentences 340)*

**XXIII.** Human beings do their own will, not God’s, when they do what displeases God. But when they do what they will in such a way that they serve the divine will, although they willingly do what they do, it is nevertheless the will of the one by whom what they will is both prepared and commanded.

## On the vine and the branches of the vine  
*(Augustine, Tractate 81 on John; Prosper, Sentences 368)*

**XXIV.** The branches are in the vine in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine, but receive from it the source of their life. For the vine is in the branches in such a way that it supplies them with vital nourishment rather than receiving it from them. Therefore it benefits the disciples both to have Christ remaining in them and to remain in Christ—both of these benefit the disciples, not Christ [Note: [Col. 0727D] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne edition: “and not Christ.” The Appendix to volume 10 of Augustine and the passages marked in the margin have both readings, “not Christ.”]. For once a branch has been cut off, another may sprout from the living root; but the branch that has been cut off cannot live without the root.

## On the love with which we love God  
*(Augustine, Tractate 102 on John; Prosper, Sentences 372)*

**XXV.** It is entirely God’s gift to love God. He who loved while not loved gave that he might be loved [Note: [Col. 0727D] In Prosper’s Louvain, Douai, and Cologne manuscripts: “he loves … and below, “he poured out.” The Appendix to volume 10 of Augustine and Prosper’s *Sentences* have the reading found in the text.]. We were loved when we were displeasing, so that there might come to be in us that by which we would become pleasing.

For the Spirit of the Father and the Son pours love into our hearts, and with the Father and the Son we love him (Romans 5:5).

Accordingly, in accordance with the foregoing statements of the holy Scriptures and the definitions of the ancient Fathers, we ought, God being merciful, both to preach and to believe this: that through the sin of the first man free choice was so bent and weakened that thereafter no one could either love God as he ought, or believe in God, or perform for God what is good, unless grace and divine mercy had gone before him. Hence we believe that the illustrious faith of righteous Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the entire multitude of the ancient saints—which the Apostle Paul proclaims to their praise—was bestowed not through the good of nature previously given in Adam, but through the grace of God. We likewise know and believe that, even after the Lord’s coming, this grace is conferred upon all who desire to be baptized, not as something possessed in free choice, but as something bestowed simultaneously by Christ’s generosity.

[Note: The edition of the council in the appendix to volume X of Augustine, as well as the manuscripts examined, reads this way. The editions of Prosper at Louvain, Douai, and Cologne instead have “and Abraham . . .,” to their praise.]

This accords with what was already stated above and what the Apostle Paul proclaims: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29); and this: “God, who began a good work in you, will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 6).

[Note: The words “Jesus Christ” are absent from the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions of Prosper. They are found in the appendix to Augustine, volume X. In both texts of the Apostle, the two words “of our Lord” are absent.]

And this: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8); and what the Apostle says of himself: “I received mercy, so that I might be faithful” (1 Cor. 7:29). He did not say, “because I was faithful,” but “so that I might be.” And this: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). And this: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). And this: “No one has anything good unless it has been given to him from above” (John 3:27).

[Note: Prosper’s editions at Louvain, Douai, and Cologne read “unless that thing,” an addition that appears to be secondary and is absent from the appendix to Augustine, consistently with the sacred text.]

There are innumerable testimonies of the holy Scriptures that could be brought forward to prove grace, but they have been omitted for the sake of brevity; for, in truth, whoever is not satisfied with a few will not benefit from many.

[Col. 0728C] We also believe, in accordance with the Catholic faith, that once the grace received through baptism has been given, all baptized persons, with Christ helping and cooperating, can and ought—if they are willing to labor faithfully—to accomplish what pertains to salvation.

[Note: The Lyons manuscript adds: “after receiving the grace of baptism.”]

But we do not merely fail to believe that some have been predestined by divine power to evil; if there are people who wish to believe so great an evil, we pronounce anathema upon them with complete abhorrence.

We also salutarily profess and believe this: in every good work, it is not that we begin and are afterward helped by God’s mercy; rather, he himself, without any preceding good merits of ours, first inspires us with both faith in him and love for him, so that we may faithfully seek the sacraments of baptism and, after baptism, with his help, be able to fulfill what pleases him.

Therefore it must be believed most clearly that the extraordinary faith of the thief whom the Lord restored to the homeland of Paradise (Luke 23:43), of the centurion Cornelius to whom the Lord’s angel was sent (Acts 10:3), and of Zacchaeus, who was found worthy to receive the Lord himself (Luke 19:6), did not arise from nature, but was a gift bestowed by divine generosity.

[Note: The Lyons manuscript reads: “but was given by the generosity of grace.” The manuscripts of Rheims and Beauvais read: “but from the gift of divine generosity.” See above, Prosper, *Against Cassian*, chapter 7.]

And because we desire and wish the definition of the ancient Fathers, as well as our own definition written above, to be a remedy not only for religious persons but also for laypeople, it was decided that the illustrious and magnificent men who had gathered with us for the aforementioned festival should also subscribe to it with their own hands.

[Note: The editions of Prosper at Louvain and Douai read: “therefore it was decided that they too should.” The appendix to Augustine, volume X, reads as in the present text.]

CAESARIUS, bishop in the name of Christ, reread our constitution and, signing below, I subscribed, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the consulship of Decius the Younger, a man of highest distinction.

JULIANUS AMARTOLUS, bishop, reread it and I subscribed.

[Note: The word “Amartolus” is added in the edition of the appendix to Augustine, volume X; it is absent from Prosper’s printed books at Louvain, Douai, and Cologne. The same Augustinian edition also adds “in the name of Christ” and “I agreed.”]

CONSTANTIUS, bishop in the name of Christ, I agreed and I subscribed.

[Note: The edition of the appendix to Augustine, volume X, supplies this bishop’s name and subscription, which are absent from Prosper’s manuscripts.]

CYPRIANUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

EUCHERIUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

[Col. 0730A] Likewise EUCHERIUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

HERACLIUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

PRINCIPIUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

PHILAGRIUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

MAXIMUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

PRAETEXTATUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

ALETHIUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

LUPERCIANUS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

VINDEMIALIS [lacuna], bishop [lacuna], I subscribed.

[Note: In Prosper’s manuscripts the following was read: “Peter, Marcellinus, Felix, and Liberius, men of highest distinction and illustrious prefects of the praetorian prefecture of Gaul and patricians, agreeing, subscribed.” We have corrected this from the edition of the council as it appears in the appendix to Augustine, volume X, removing the commas and changing the plural to the singular. For Spondanus correctly observes in volume II of his *Epitome*, under the year 529, page 2, that it is falsely reported that four praetorian prefects were present at this council, as the corrupt text has it. For, as the Vatican manuscript shows, those four names belong to one person; and at the beginning of the synod only one prefect, Liberius the patrician, is named as having been present. Finally, it is clear that in the time of King Athalaric not four prefects governed Gaul, but this one Liberius, as appears from a letter of that king addressed to the same Liberius (Cassiodorus, book VIII, letter 6). This is the very Liberius to whom Theodoric, Athalaric’s predecessor, had earlier entrusted the fasces. Among other things, he is commended by Theodoric for his distinguished achievements in war and peace in Italy, Gaul, and elsewhere, and especially because he united the Italians with the Goths by granting them a third of the lands (ibid., book II, letter 15, to the Senate).]

PETRUS MARCELLINUS FELIX LIBERIUS, a man of highest distinction and illustrious prefect of the praetorian prefecture of Gaul and patrician, agreeing, I subscribed.

[Note: From the same edition, volume X of Augustine’s works, we change *subscribed*—which is read in Prosper’s manuscripts—to “I subscribed” here and in what follows.]

SYAGRIUS, an illustrious man, agreeing, I subscribed.

OPILIO, an illustrious man, agreeing, I subscribed.

PANTAGATHUS, an illustrious man, agreeing, I subscribed.

DEODATUS, an illustrious man, agreeing, I subscribed.

CARIATHTO, an illustrious man, agreeing, I subscribed.

MARCELLUS, an illustrious man, agreeing, I subscribed.

[Note: This name and subscription are added from Augustine, volume X, in the appendix, since they are absent from Prosper’s editions at Louvain, Douai, and Cologne. On its authority, in the six preceding subscriptions we have written “an illustrious man,” where previously “a man of highest distinction” appeared.]

NAMATIUS, an illustrious man, agreeing, I subscribed.

[ON THE PROMISES AND PREDICTIONS OF GOD]

[Col. 0729]

NOTICE CONCERNING THE BOOK ON THE PROMISES AND PREDICTIONS OF GOD

[Col. 0729]

Cassiodorus, in the first chapter of his book *Institutions of Divine Literature*, urges that the three books in which Saint Prosper gathered all the authorities of the divine word into 153 chapters be read constantly and attentively, after the pattern of the 153 fish which the evangelical nets drew from the stormy depths of this world. There is scarcely any room for doubt that he was speaking of this work, whose title is *On the Promises and Predictions of God*. For it is inferred that this was his intention from the fact that, in chapter 17 of the same book, while continuing his discussion of Christian historians, he speaks as follows of Prosper (chapter 84): “Saint Prosper also brought his *Chronicle* down from Adam to the time of Gaiseric and the plundering of the city of Rome.” By these words he sufficiently suggests that he considered the Prosper who wrote the *Chronicle* to be the same person whom he had previously stated to have composed three books encompassing the whole of divine authority; for both are regarded by him as saints. Everyone will understand that by that *Chronicle* Cassiodorus meant the work of our Prosper from the fact that Gennadius testifies in his *Catalogue* that he had seen a *Chronicle* bearing that title, from which Senator undoubtedly borrowed his information when, in the chapter just cited, he warmly commends the reading of this work.

This work is now preserved, as it came from its author, divided into five parts. Alluding to the 153 fish which the apostles are said in the Gospel to have caught with a single cast of the net after Christ’s resurrection (John 21:11), the author wished all the promises of the Lord Christ, dispersed throughout the entire field of sacred Scripture, to be contained under 153 headings, as Cassiodorus noted. He collected them into one work so as to demonstrate that they had truly been fulfilled by Christ, or would certainly and most surely be fulfilled in the future. Since those promises are found to have been made partly before the Law, partly under the Law, and finally fulfilled when grace was revealed to humanity, some people designated this work by the title *The Book before the Law, under the Law, and under Grace*. Cassiodorus, however, cites a passage taken from the third part as a saying of Saint Prosper.

The most learned author of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* likewise writes, under the year 444 of the Christian era, that Prosper was the author of the work *On the Promises and Predictions of God*. He then leads him on long journeys through Italy and Africa and attributes to him new battles against the Pelagians, all of which proceed from the same source. Many, without examining the matter more carefully, have entirely adopted the view of both the authors mentioned above. Yet I would not readily determine whether the name Prosper can rightly be assigned to the author of this work on the sole authority of those two writers. Some have not disapproved this conjecture, while others reject it entirely. Among the latter stands the eminent Cardinal Noris, who, in book II, chapter 14 of his *Pelagian History*, assuming the matter as probable, thinks that the author of the book may be recognized as Saint Prosper, bishop of Riez, distinct from Prosper of Aquitaine; for the very learned man does not believe that the latter was ever raised to episcopal dignity.

[Col. 0731] Whatever may be the truth concerning this conjecture, it would at least contribute this to our position: its authority could also confirm that our Prosper cannot in any way be called the author of the books under discussion, and that another author must necessarily be assigned to them. This is not difficult to establish both from the judgment of learned critics and from reading these books and appreciating their style. For, as Philip Labbe already noted very well in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and as the aforementioned Henry Noris observed still more precisely in book II, chapter 14 of his *Pelagian History*, the author himself testifies that he was not Aquitanian but African. Besides speaking among many heretics chiefly about the Donatists and Maximianists, and citing Ticonius, a celebrated man among the Donatists, he also brings forward as an eyewitness certain distinctive events that occurred in Africa.

He was still a young man living at Carthage when, in that city, the holy bishop Aurelius dedicated to Christ, the true heavenly King, the widely renowned temple of the goddess Caelestis. This is sufficiently indicated by his account in the third part, Promise 38, where he immediately adds: “I myself was present there with companions and friends.” And while, as is customary at the age of young men, he restlessly turned himself about in every direction, and while he was examining each detail curiously with his friends, something astonishing and incredible presented itself to his eyes: namely, an inscription written on the front of the temple in large bronze letters: “AURELIUS THE BISHOP DEDICATED IT.”

Since, according to this same African author’s testimony, the temple of Caelestis was consecrated to God a few lines later, on the occasion of the law enacted by Honorius, son of Theodosius the Younger, by which he transferred all temples, together with the spaces adjoining them, to the churches and at the same time permitted the images of the idols to be shattered, it follows that this deed occurred after the year 399, when this edict, along with others of the same kind, was issued or such permission was granted—and, as he observes, when the Easter solemnity was recurring.

While he was likewise living at Carthage, in the consulship of Aspar for the sixth time, if the reading of the manuscripts may be judged correct, a monstrous and diabolical sign occurred, as he says. “Who among the citizens of that region,” he writes, “is unaware of it?” (*On the Promises and Predictions*, latter half of the period, chapter 6). He then recounts it at greater length: a certain young woman of Arab nationality, seized by a demon as punishment for an immodest look, had been unable to take any food or drink for nearly seventy days. She was placed by a priest in a monastery of young women, where she remained for two weeks taking no food or drink. Finally, on the fifteenth day:

“When the priest ascended with us,” he says, “so that the morning sacrifice might be offered there, the superior brought the girl to the altar,” and so forth.

By these words he declares himself an eyewitness of the remarkable event, having been living at that time in the metropolis of Africa and perhaps having been honored among that clergy with some dignity or office; this seems to be suggested by the words of the account: “When the priest ascended with us,” and so forth. He was therefore living there in the sixth consulship of Aspar, that is, in the year 434, when the struggle against the invading Gaiseric was being waged fiercely with arms. In that same year Prosper, taking up his pen again against the Massilians, who were obstinately stirring up opposition to the teaching of Saint Augustine, had finally been compelled to strike at the writings of their champion Cassian with a vigorous response.

He also reports that, when he came to Carthage, he knew a certain man disguised as a monk who boasted that he performed various cures among the sick, whom he anointed with oil into which, I do not know whose, dead man’s bone had been infused. When he realized, however, that his fraud had been exposed, he immediately fled that city.

But if this writer, while still a young man around the year 400, lived at Carthage, and still maintained his established residence there in 434, it would be difficult to call him anything other than a Carthaginian, or at least an African. It would be even more difficult, given so long an interval, to deny that he—a man of no ordinary reputation—was personally known to Augustine, who was frequently staying both in that metropolis and in those regions on the occasion of provincial synods. Yet everyone up to the present has agreed that our Prosper was an Aquitanian, and by his own testimony he reveals that he was personally unknown to the bishop of Hippo. For, writing to him, he says: “Unknown to you in face, but already known to you to some extent, if you remember, in mind and speech,” and so forth (above, col. 67).

From this it is clear that the author who composed these books *On the Promises and Predictions of God* is entirely different from Saint Prosper of Aquitaine. We need not even mention that Gennadius, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, and other ecclesiastical writers who reviewed authors after him, nowhere attribute these treatises to Prosper.

Add to all this the unmistakable difference in style and manner of expression between the author of these books and Prosper of Aquitaine; anyone who judges the matter fairly will readily recognize it. The author’s discourse is humble, spare, and simple; Prosper’s manner of speaking is abundant, rich, vigorous in strength and sinew, and full of weighty thoughts.

It would be useless for anyone to say that this work was written by a younger Prosper, since it belongs to a man advanced in age, as the author himself testifies about himself and as is evident from many passages. He was writing during the reign of Valentinian III, but apparently after Placidia had died, and therefore after the year 450 and before 455. He frequently follows Augustine and repeatedly cites him.

Finally, the Louvain scholars who arranged for the works of Saint Prosper to be printed admit that this work appears to them inferior to Saint Prosper in style and learning, and that its text is corrupted and mutilated in many places. We have tried, insofar as possible, to remedy this defect with the aid of the Remigian-Rheims manuscript, eight hundred years old, and of the ancient editions.

It will not be burdensome now to examine with some care how it finally happened that this work was attributed to Prosper and included among his works. First, although the error could not have arisen from similarity of style—for the difference in style between the two authors is so great, quite apart from their wholly dissimilar turns of expression—the opportunity for the mistake could nevertheless have arisen from the fairly close similarity between their interests and studies.

For, besides revealing that he was thoroughly familiar with Augustine’s writings, whose words and authority he adopts in this little work just as Prosper does in his own, it must also be frankly acknowledged that this African writer seems in many other respects to have set Prosper’s genius before him as something to follow and imitate.

This is clear first from the opening line of the work, where he himself introduces, at the beginning of his preface, the statement from 1 Corinthians 3:7 so frequently praised by Prosper: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters,” and so forth. He then speaks of the cultivation of the heavenly and royal inheritance which the apostles cultivated, entirely in the spirit of Prosper, whose frequent use of such language is readily observed.

There are also other indications of this imitation. For, secondly, both in the preface to the entire work and in the following prologue, the prescribed method of arrangement breathes something of Prosper’s spirit, as is sufficiently clear from this expression: “Under manifest grace, which was always present in hidden things.” Here the hidden is set against the manifest, in the same way that these corresponding terms are repeatedly found in Prosper. Shortly afterward the author cites an Augustinian statement which Prosper is found to have previously excerpted and inserted among his own selections from Augustine.

Third, in many of the work’s headings, topics are taken up for treatment that Prosper had already addressed; at times even his words are reproduced. For this phrase in Part I, Prediction 3, is thoroughly Prosperian, where he says that those who do the devil’s will remain his. It is frequently used in the responses of our Prosper against the Gallic detractors. There are other headings of the same kind that follow.

From these and similar considerations, which can readily be found throughout these books, it is easy to believe that certain superficial scholars, misled by this agreement in subject matter, first began attributing to the Aquitanian—Augustine’s faithful disciple and most vigorous defender—the respectable work of an anonymous man devoted to Augustinian teaching. Thus that title also slipped into the collection of his works, along with other similarly spurious titles of treatises.

It is certainly easier to believe this than to admit another Prosper, one adorned with a reputation for holiness, of whom no memory survives and whose name, it is said, cannot be found in any record of those times.

[Col. 0733]

BOOK OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR ON THE PROMISES AND PREDICTIONS OF GOD, ATTRIBUTED BY SOME TO SAINT PROSPER (C, S)*

Preface

[Col. 0733]

[Col. 0733A] The Apostle Paul says: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters; but God, who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7). In this cultivation, therefore, of the heavenly and royal inheritance, which the apostles, patriarchs, and prophets cultivated, while I myself, like a little dog among the other dogs of the Lord, circle its boundaries, I have hunted down and assembled, with grace as my guide, 153 chapters from the divine Scriptures. In them are 103 promises of God and 50 predictions, distributed as follows.

The people before the Law had nineteen promises which they saw by believing and believed by seeing; six which they believed and left for the people after them to see; twelve predictions which they saw; and three which they believed.

The people under the Law had eighteen promises which they saw and believed by believing; one which, having been believed, they left for those after them to see; nineteen predictions which they saw; and two which they believed.

The people under grace had forty promises.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads *has*, and not without reason. All the printed editions read *had*.]

Of these, they saw thirty-two before us; we have seen and see seven fulfilled; and one concerns the end of the world, which we all believe.

For half a time, there are twelve predictions which are matters of faith, and two which we have seen. There are six promises which belong to faith and are to come at the end. Thirteen things concerning the glory of the saints are also matters of faith, because the saints alone will receive them once accomplished.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “Brothers, fulfill the promises.”]

There are eighty-four fulfilled promises and nineteen still to be fulfilled; thirty-five fulfilled predictions and fifteen still to be fulfilled.

Who, then, has so hard and iron-like a mind as to doubt that the few remaining things will be fulfilled, when he sees that so many have already been fulfilled?

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “still.”]

[Note: The Lyon edition does not have the word “iron”; the Remigian manuscript likewise lacks it.]

PART ONE. THE TIME BEFORE THE LAW

PROLOGUE

[Col. 0733B]

1. The whole structure of faith is enclosed by hope and love. For each person, by loving what he believes has been promised, lends his assent to faith until he obtains everything for which he hopes.

The Apostle Paul defined faith as the conviction of things that are not seen (Heb. 11:1). Through its dispensation, God, the Creator of all things, deigned to fashion everything from nothing—as holy Scripture says—from invisible matter (Gen. 1:2; Wis. 11:18), balancing the highest things with the middle and the middle with the lowest.

For, preferring certain invisible things to visible things, rational things to irrational, things perceived by the senses to things without sensation, and living things to those deprived of life, he arranged everything according to measure, number, and weight (ibid., 21). Assigning each thing its proper mode of existence, he set the rational creature, the human being, above earthly creatures, and granted free will to the one creature formed in the image and likeness of his divinity.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “attributed.”]

He also gave him a law by which he would live forever if he kept the commandments, but would die if he despised the precepts of his Creator (Gen. 1:26).

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “would die.”]

But through the serpent’s deceit, the devil—by the pride through which he himself had fallen with his companions—deceived the man (Gen. 3:1). When Adam, through disobedience, hurled himself and the entire stock of the human race into death (Rom. 5:12), the devil could not inflict prejudice upon the Creator’s well-formed nature.

Although he brought about death as the consequence of transgression, he did not destroy the essence of life, insofar as it exists, even in death. For the immortal soul, created for this stage of the world and corrupted by its pollution, overturned by the flood of the body and burdened by the weight of crimes, will live with the flesh in eternal punishment unless it is redeemed by the blood of the Savior and, washed by spiritual water, preserves, free from the contagion of the wound inflicted upon it, the beauty of the grace bestowed through inviolate faith.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “unviolated faith.”]

The evangelical faith announces this (Matt. 25; John 5:29). It established eternal life for the good and eternal punishment for the wicked by the authority through which it fulfilled everything that it had foretold from the beginning of the world.

2. But lest human and barren understanding prolong the lengthy preface of this book, the divine testimonies, gathered from every side and joined together, will fill out this book, divided into three and a half parts, with the help of him by whose gift we speak. We have undertaken to extract, chapter by chapter, from all the divine Scriptures whatever predictions and promises of God we encounter.

We mark three periods extending from the beginning of the world to its end, existing among different peoples: before the Law, under the Law, and under manifest grace, which was always present in what was hidden. Their threefold division is as follows.
