From the first creation of the first man until Moses is the time before the Law. From Moses, to whom the Law was given on Mount Sinai (Exod. 20:1 and following), until the coming of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is the time under the Law.

After he was revealed in the flesh, crucified, risen, and ascended into heaven, the time of grace continues until now and until the end of the world, including that brief period of the Antichrist.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “before that period.”]

During these three periods, the most just God, the Creator, ordered his rights and promises in accordance with his own governance, so that he did not commit everything merely to be believed by faith, but entrusted most things to be seen with the eyes; and those things which were hoped for as future were to be believed as destined to be fulfilled through those which were seen.

Accordingly, in each of the periods just mentioned, we shall assign one part of this book, as we promised. The chapters arranged in order will demonstrate what was promised, what was presented figuratively with reference to Christ and the Church, and what was left as something believed but destined to be seen in the future.

[Note: The Remigian-Rheims manuscript presents the whole passage as follows: “We have marked out: what promises are to be seen by those of the future, and what things have been figuratively presented with reference to Christ and the Church; the chapters arranged in order will demonstrate what has been left as something believed.”]

(Prosper, *Sentences* 214.)

CHAPTER I. [Note: In the Remigian manuscript the title is: “The promise from the book of Genesis, believed and seen.”] From the book of Genesis: creation in Adam and Eve, with reference to Christ and the Church.

[Col. 0735B]

3. In the beginning God made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that belongs to them: the shining things in heaven, those that walk upon the earth, those that fly in the air, and those that swim in the waters (Gen. 1). When these had been completed, God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (ibid., 26).

[Note: The Cologne edition reads “he created.”]

After forming him from the mud of the earth, he breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul (Gen. 2:1).

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “and, after forming him, he breathed into his face”; it adds the words “it was said.”]

And God said: “It is not good for man to be alone. Let us make for him a helper like him, a counselor” (ibid., 18).

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “a counselor like him.”]

And shortly afterward: “God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he fell asleep. And he took one of his ribs” (ibid., 21), and formed it into a woman; and he brought her to Adam so that he might see what he would call her (ibid., 22).

[Note: These words are not part of the sacred text in the Vulgate or in the Hebrew.]

And Adam said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called Woman, because she has been taken from her man” (ibid., 23).

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “woman.”]

“For this reason,” he says, “a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (ibid., 24).

[Col. 0735C] That this was done both as an actual event and as a figure is testified by the Apostle Paul. Explaining this passage in his Letter to the Ephesians, he says: “This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

Thus Adam saw the great mystery which he hoped had been promised, and saw joined to himself as wife the one whom he had believed in faith would signify the future Church, the mother of the living. He called her the mother of all the living (Gen. 3:20), for this reason: Eve, having been formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, prefigured the Church, as happened, to be formed from the side of Christ hanging upon the cross; and she truly is the mother of all the living.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “He marked out in faith the future Church, the mother of living men; for this reason Adam called that same woman his mother, the mother of all men. For this is that woman,” and so forth. The intervening material found in the printed manuscripts is omitted.]

For this is that woman who is protected for “a time and times and half a time” from the sight of the serpent, as is said in the Apocalypse concerning the Church (chapter 12, verse 14).

[Note: The Remigian manuscript adds: “and half a time, from the sight of the serpent.” The remainder is absent.]

CHAPTER II. [Note: In the Remigian manuscript the title is: “God foretold to Adam and his wife that death would follow if they touched the forbidden things”; then, beginning with the line “In Genesis, believed and seen,” chapter II begins: “From every tree,” and so forth.] Two deaths follow upon the despised commandment.

[Col. 0735D] 4. God foretold to Adam and his wife that death would follow if they touched the forbidden things, saying: “You shall eat from every tree of Paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat from it. On the day on which you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:16).

But, deceived by the devil, they despised the commandment and touched the forbidden thing (Gen. 3:6). While the man excuses this sin by blaming the woman, and the woman by blaming the serpent, they brought the foretold death not only upon themselves but also upon their descendants (Rom. 5:14).

All the human race has paid this debt, signifying another perpetual death from which everyone who keeps Christ’s commandments will be free (John 8:51); but the one who considers the salutary instructions of our Lord Jesus Christ unworthy of obedience will undoubtedly undergo it.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “which are not to be held.”]

“For blessed and holy,” says the Apostle John, “is the one who has a share in this first resurrection; over such the second death has no authority” (Rev. 20:6).

And the Lord says: “Whoever hears my words,” he says, “and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24).

[Note: The word “he says” is found in the Remigian manuscript but not in the printed editions.]

CHAPTER III. The sentence pronounced against the devil: those who do his will remain his. In Genesis, believed and seen.

[Col. 0736B]

5. There follows the sentence foretold and pronounced against the serpent, the devil. In it something fearful is found, for among other things this was said to him: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:14).

Souls that gape after earthly desires are compared to earth and are identified by the prophet David as impious, when he says in the first psalm: “They shall be like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4).

And the prophet Jeremiah says: “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. 17:13).

Job also says: “The earth has been handed over to the power of the wicked” (Job 9:24).

David likewise says: “Remember, Lord, that we are earth” (Ps. 102:14).

In another psalm he says that he is stripped of the earth which the serpent received to eat as the result of sin: “Save me from the mire, so that I may not cling to it” (Ps. 68:15).

Elsewhere also: “Our belly has clung to the earth; arise, Lord, help us, and redeem us for the sake of your name” (Ps. 43:25).

And elsewhere: “Do not hand me over, Lord, to the desire of the sinner” (Ps. 139:9).

For this reason divine mercy has judged that we should be admonished daily by priests to raise our hearts upward, and we profess that we have them directed toward the Lord—provided that our pledge is firm, so that what we utter with our words we may also complete in our deeds through continual grace.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “assisted by grace.”]

CHAPTER IV. In the woman’s curse, original sin follows. Original sin foretold. In Genesis, believed and seen.

6. And God said to the woman: “I will greatly multiply [Note: [Col. 0736D] Ms. Remig., “your groanings.”] your groanings and pains; in sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. III, 16). Thus the prophet David confirms that the children of transgressors are born: “In iniquities,” he says, “I was conceived, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Ps. L, 7). Solomon likewise bears witness to the same: “A grievous yoke,” he says, “is upon the sons of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. XL, 1). He himself also says: “And I, when born, received the common air, and fell upon the earth, made in the same manner; I uttered my first voice, like everyone else, crying; I was nurtured in swaddling clothes and in cares. For no king has had any other beginning of birth. There is one entrance into life for all, and the exit is alike” (Wis. VII, 3 ff.). And shortly afterward: “For the seed was accursed from the beginning” (ibid. XII, 11). Isaiah too says: “A wicked seed, sinful children, you have forsaken the Lord” (Isa. I, 4). Job likewise says: “No one is free from uncleanness, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day” (Job XIV, 4, according to the Septuagint). He himself also says: “Who can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed, except you, who alone are clean?” (ibid., according to the Vulgate). For the expiation of this accursed seed, legal sacrifices were instituted for the uncleanness of the woman giving birth and of the child (Lev. XII), until Christ reigned: he, by offering the sacrifice of his body, saves the little along with the great. For it is said: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 21). Yet these things that were foretold are seen to have been fulfilled in such a way that they are taught to remain in need of completion until the end of the world.

## CHAPTER V. In Adam, labor, sweat, and pain for all his descendants. The sentence foretold and transmitted. Believed and seen in Genesis.

7. But God said to Adam: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife, [Note: [Col. 0737D] These words, “more than to me,” are added from Ms. Remig.] rather than to me, and touched the tree from which alone I had commanded you not to eat, and you ate: cursed is the earth in your works; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you; in sorrow and groaning you shall eat the produce of your field; in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 17 ff.). The Apostle says that this punishment for sin, which Adam, the root of the human race, received as his sentence and transmitted to his descendants as branches [Note: [Col. 0737D] Ms. Remig., “poured into them.”], entered the world through one man, and thus passed into all human beings, “in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12). For the soil, which by the Creator’s command had previously produced fertile [Note: [Col. 0737D] The printed editions read “fruitful”; Ms. Remig., “fertile.”] and health-giving plants for humanity without any cultivation, afterward became filled with hardships and thorns, so that everyone must eat bread from it through sweat and labor until he returns in death. We have not merely been deemed worthy to hear these things foretold, but also to recognize them when proved. Hence David says: “Man goes forth to his work and to his labor until evening” (Ps. CIII, 23). And again: “You shall eat the labors of your hands” (Ps. CXXVII, 2). The Apostle likewise says: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (II Thess. III, 10). And the Lord sends laborers into the vineyard even until the eleventh hour (Matt. XX, 9).

## CHAPTER VI. In Cain and Abel, the two peoples, Christians and Jews. A figurative prophecy of the two peoples. Believed and seen in Genesis.

[Col. 0737D]

8. After the first human beings had already become mortal, two sons were born, both mortal: Cain, the elder, and Abel, the younger; one a shepherd of sheep, the other a farmer. While they inhabited the earth, which was now subject to labor by the judgment of the divine sentence, and sought to atone for their own sins and those of their parents, they offered sacrifices from the firstfruits of their crops. The sacrifice offered by the younger Abel from his sheep was accepted as pleasing; Cain’s was rejected (Gen. IV, 7), because the portion of earth was not rightly divided. From this envy arose. And the divinity, foreknowing the future, enjoined patience upon the enraged man, and said to Cain: “You have sinned; be quiet; its turning is toward you, and you shall rule it”—that is, he was to rule over his sin himself and not become sin’s slave, if he humbly obeyed the one giving the command. But Cain, defiant and unable to bear this, sprang upon Abel in the field and killed him. Oh, unspeakable crime! Are these, Cain, the bonds of brotherhood? Are these the beginnings of good nature? Is this the hope of a good disposition—that the father should know you as a murderer before he knows you as a son? Yet by these deeds Cain bound his crime with many additional knots [Note: [Col. 0737D] Ms. Remig., “with many bonds.”]. He became a despiser of the divine command, the head of pride, the author of envy, the originator of inflicted death, and the first parricide among human beings.

[Col. 0738B]

9. He established the beginnings of warfare, so that, guilty of shedding innocent blood [Note: [Col. 0737D] Ms. Remig., “pours out.”], filled with spite, he attacked another’s glory [Note: [Col. 0737D] Ms. Remig., “attains it”; this is not unsuitable if referred to what follows immediately: “From this, glorious martyrdoms shone forth, while,” etc.]. From this, glorious martyrdoms shone forth, while the righteous were killed by the wicked. But so that divine providence might show that everything that had happened would benefit us, it asked a brother about the brother whom it already knew had been killed [Note: [Col. 0737D] Ms. Remig., “who already knew that he had been killed.”]; and when he denied it, it convicted him, with the earth as witness: “The voice,” it says, “of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. IV, 10). No Christian now doubts that Cain prefigured the Jewish people, yearning after earthly desires, and Abel Christ, the shepherd of sheep, killed by that people. The whole earth now receiving his sacred blood cries out: “Amen”—which means “True”—so that, when the Jew denies having killed Christ, God may rightly say to him: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. IV, 25). In place of Abel, whom Cain killed, Seth was born; from him, through the succession of generations, came Enoch, who, because he pleased God, was taken away lest he taste death (ibid. 18, 22 and 24), to be joined with Elijah (IV Kings II, 11), so that the two suitable witnesses might be prepared for Christ’s second coming (Rev. XI, 3), [Note: [Col. 0738D] Ms. Remig., “for the refutation of Antichrist and in the glory.”] for the refutation of Antichrist and for the glory of the Son of God who judges. Of these we shall present testimonies in their proper place.

## CHAPTER VII. In the flood and the ark, which signified the Church. Prophecy: believed and seen in Genesis. The foretold flood.

10. When the sons of God abandoned their purpose of holiness [Note: [Col. 0738D] Ms. Remig., “fell away.”], God admonished the righteous Noah in this way: “The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is filled with their iniquity, and I will destroy them together with the earth. Make yourself an ark of squared timbers; you shall make the ark with three compartments, and you shall coat it with pitch inside and out; and this is how you shall make it. The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. You shall make a window in the ark, and you shall complete it within one cubit. You shall place the door of the ark in its side. Behold, I will bring a flood of water upon the earth, and I will destroy all flesh in which there is the breath of life under heaven” (Gen. VI, 13 ff.). While faith therefore lends its support and prepares the mind, believing that what it hopes for will come to pass, Noah obeyed the mystical command and construction. He built the ark in which he was to shelter himself with clean and unclean animals, as had been commanded: for its geometric proportion, it is said, extends six times as far as ours [Note: [Col. 0738D] The Lyon edition reads “than our [proportion].” Ms. Remig. reads: “for the geometric proportion, which, as is said, extends six times as far as ours.”].

[Col. 0739A]

11. Concerning these numbers [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ms. Remig., “however.”] that have been written down, I shall gather a few points as far as I am divinely assisted, and I shall introduce the judgment of our architect, the Apostle Paul (I Cor. III, 10). Referring the figurative construction of that ark, and all its spiritual structure, to the holy Church, he expressed in it the form of the cross. For he says in his Letter to the Ephesians: “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his grace, strength to have Christ dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the height, breadth, length, and depth, and also to know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. III, 14 ff.).

He spoke five sentences in five sections [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ms. Remig., “he spoke in five sections: ‘as I think, and these …’”], being the one who had said: “I desire to speak five [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ms. Remig., “my words in the Church.”] words with my mind in the Church” (I Cor. XIV, 19). These five sentences are therefore shown, for the following reason, to pertain to the measurements of the aforesaid ark. The number five, constituted from an even and an odd number, contains two and three: three from the Trinity, two from the two commandments which, joined together, form five. One is added to this because of the unity of the indivisible Trinity, and a perfect six results, corresponding to itself in every respect, in the first, third, and half. Many of the ancients have already spoken about this number. These two numbers, five and six, joined and multiplied together, extend to the fivefold measurements of the aforesaid ark.

For this reason God created on the fifth day all things that were created, except the human being [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ms. Remig., “he had made”; shortly afterward, Ms. Remig. reads “had been,” where the printed editions read “will have been.”]; and in the five books of Moses all the commandments of the law were written down; and, for the completion of the law, the Savior and Lord himself was handed over to the gallows on the fifth day of the week. The number six, however, contains this significance: the human being was formed on the sixth day; and in the sixth age of the world the Word of God assumed humanity for the redemption of the world; and on the sixth day of the week, hanging upon the cross, he poured out from his side our entire price, precious blood, as through the door of the ark. From this the dove, the Church (Gen. VIII, 8), endowed with such blood [Col. 0739C] came forth. [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ms. Remig., “Through which.”]

For this reason also the heretical raven, going out and shipwrecked through its desire for a human corpse, refused to return to the ark, the Church. Concerning it, the clean animals placed inside cry out: “It went out from us, but it was not of us; for if it had been of us, it would certainly have remained with us” (I John II, 19).

These two numbers, then, as I said, five and six, when multiplied together, complete thirty. For five times six, and six times five, produce the number thirty [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ms. Remig., “makes.”]. These are the thirty cubits which were commanded to be constructed in the height of the ark, pertaining to the exalted part of hope, in which the head of the Crucified was fixed on high. For all hope is in the head. For this reason also our head himself deigned to be crucified at the age of thirty.

Again, the number five is multiplied by the decade because of the ten commandments of the law. For ten times five, and five times ten, make fifty. These are placed in the breadth of the ark, which are marked out by the spaces of charity on the cross, on which the hands of the Crucified were fastened. [Col. 0739D] For the ten commandments are said to have been written by the finger of God [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ms. Remig., “are taught.”], and we ourselves are commanded to raise our hands in the sanctuary (Ps. CXXXIII, 2).

Again, the numbers five and six, multiplied by fifty, complete the length of the ark. For fifty times six, and sixty times five, produce three hundred, which are attributed to the length of our ark of patience, in which the body of the Crucified was stretched out. To him it is said: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II, 21). For “our old self was crucified together with him” (Rom. VI, 6), and we are commanded to be patient until the coming of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0739D] The word “Lord” is found in Ms. Remig.] (James V, 7). The depth, however, signifies the magnitude of the flood of the cross, by which both that ark and ours are carried. For “the judgments of God,” as it is written, “are like a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7).

12. But what is said—“You shall make it with three compartments” (Gen. VI, 14)—our aforesaid architect Paul expressed in this construction: “Faith, hope, and charity remain, these three” (I Cor. XIII, 13). For while in the first and second dwelling places the beasts, cattle, serpents, and birds remained in faith and hope, in the third Noah and his companions remained in charity—because “the greatest of all these is charity” (ibid.). He who remains in charity could not fear the flood, for he who remains in charity remains in God, and God remains in him [Note: [Col. 0739D] Ms. Remig., “remains.”], because “God is charity” (I John IV, 16).

We understand the window of the ark more suitably as a regard directed toward the salvation of souls, which are joined and bound together within and without by pitch in the unity of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0740D] In Ms. Remig. “Holy” is absent, in accordance with the Apostle’s text to which the author appears to allude.] and in the bond of peace (Eph. IV, 3). It was said that the ark was to be completed within one cubit; thus it was fitting for it to signify [Note: [Col. 0740D] Ms. Remig. adds: “the Church in unity”; perhaps the better reading is “to signify the unity of the Church.”] the unity of the Church. For “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4).

Hence that rich man in the Gospel, fearing the flood of this life [Note: [Col. 0740D] Ms. Remig., “of this life”; the printed editions, “of this kind.”], said to the Lord of all things: “Good Teacher, what must I do to obtain eternal life?” (Luke XVIII, 18). And the Lord, showing him the measurements of the aforesaid ark, said: “You know the commandments” (ibid. 20). When he had listed many of them according to their number, he, desiring to be joined to the ark as something square [Note: [Col. 0740D] Ms. Remig., “But he, as though squared.”], said: “I have kept all these commandments; what still remains for me?” (ibid., XXI). And the Lord, indicating that the perfection of our ark consists in one cubit, said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21). Since he could not do this, because he was not square on every side, he did not deserve to reach the cubit of the perfection of our ark [Note: [Col. 0740D] Ms. Remig. adds “our.”]. For he went away, as it is said, grieving (ibid., 22).

13. But the fact that the flood occurred upon the earth for forty days and forty nights (Gen. VII, 17) reveals not only the past in this number, but also the flood of souls in the present time, which are submerged upon the rocks of the world and in the whirlpool of crimes and of various pleasures by waves that cause shipwreck. [Note: [Col. 0740D] The printed editions read “because of which”; the remainder is supplied from Ms. Remig.] To show how these may be escaped, Moses is shown to have consecrated fasts for forty days (Exod. IV, 18), Elijah for forty days (III Kings XIX, 8), and the Savior himself for forty days and forty nights (Matt. IV, 2), according to this threefold pattern: as necessary in the three periods mentioned above—before the law, under the law, and under grace.

The end of the flood, completed in Noah’s six-hundred-and-first year (Gen. VIII, 13), signifies the end of the world after the six ages of the world, as has been said, and the brief period of Antichrist. For the life even of a long-lived human being is extended through so many ages, until it passes from infancy into old age.

Now the Church, or perhaps the ark, is recognized as carrying the good and the wicked, like the clean and unclean animals, until the aforesaid end. Concerning this our Lord and Savior testified in the Gospel, saying that his coming would be as it was in the days of Noah, when people were suddenly eating and drinking, buying and selling (Matt. XXIV, 37).

Noah therefore believed what he saw foretold in the ark. He believed what the Church, which was destined to be presented to us, would be: together with us he hopes for what will be revealed at the final judgment. [Note: [Col. 0741D] Ms. Remig., “what was destined to come … with us. And he hopes for what will ultimately be revealed at the judgment.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. In the three sons of Noah, the nations whom Christ the Lord found scattered and gathered together. The foretold nations: [Note: [Col. 0741D] We add this from Ms. Remigianus, in which Chapter VIII begins: “By these names, Shem, Ham, and Japheth,” etc.; perhaps, “By these men.”] from the three sons of Noah. Believed and seen in Genesis.

14. As the fecundity of mortals increased from Noah’s three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and from their equal number of wives, the root of sin, pride, could not itself perish when the world perished in the flood. A proud tower is built by the proud, whose top would reach to heaven (Gen. XI, 4). Its undertaking is brought to nothing by the true craftsman, God, through the confusion of languages. For thus it is written: “Behold, there is one language for all the earth, and they have begun to do this; and now nothing of all that they have undertaken to do will be beyond them” (ibid., 6). And God said: “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages there” (ibid., 7).

The Trinity God is speaking. God’s descending means observing human actions or drawing near to their understanding. These things, as they were foretold, were immediately fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0741D] In Ms. Remig., “These things that were foretold were immediately fulfilled.”]. For the confused languages were not only unable to complete what had been planned, but, being scattered throughout the world, they also distinguished the various nations by their own speech (ibid., 9) [Note: [Col. 0741D] Ms. Remig., “created them.”].

Nevertheless, when the Creator and Judge’s decree was fulfilled, charity, through the humility of Christ, gathered under one doctrine those whom proud impiety had wickedly scattered [Note: [Col. 0741D] “Wickedly” is added from Ms. Remig.; it is erroneous]. Therefore let every tongue now confess as one that the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the tower of strength, is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. II, 11).

When Ham, the son of Noah, mocked him as he lay drunk from the vine (Gen. IX, 21) and naked in his passion, he received a curse upon his son Canaan and handed him over to the nations. This curse Jesus the Lord removed, he who for us became a curse (Gal. III, 13).

## CHAPTER IX. In Heber, the Hebrew nation, which handed primacy over to the Christian people. The foretold Hebrew nation, from whom it arose, having primacy among all languages. [Note: [Col. 0741D] We add this on the authority of Ms. Remigianus.] Believed and seen in Genesis.

15. Among the others whom the confusion of languages divided among the nations, one was called Heber (Gen. XI, 14), in whom, as is said, the first language, Hebrew, remained; hence the Hebrew nation also received its name. That Hebrew was the first language is shown by that mystical title written by Pilate. For it was marked with three languages [Note: [Col. 0741D] Ms. Remig., “with these three.”]: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (John XIX, 20). These languages, retaining primacy over nearly all languages, were inscribed on the title for the same Creator, in that divine order in which the prophet David testified beforehand to what was to happen, saying: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title” (Ps. LVIII, 1).

For that judge had written: “The King of the Jews,” crucified (John XIX, 19). When the Hebrews read this in their own language [Note: [Col. 0742D] The printed editions read “Hebrew.”], which had been placed first, and requested that it be changed, Pilate, moved by divine providence, said: “What I have written, I have written” (ibid., 22). Thus both the integrity of the title remained inviolate, as had been promised, and the Hebrew language, under the testimony, was rightly marked as having the chief place, which it later lost.

From this Heber, then, the line of descent runs down to Abraham (Gen. XI, 17 ff.), from whom, as some say, the Abraei [perhaps *Abrahaei*, “Abrahamites”] were called, just as the Hebrews were called from Heber. That this people was the firstborn, although the Lord himself bears witness to it, saying, “Israel is my firstborn” (Exod. IV, 22), is shown more fully in the book of Deuteronomy: “When the Most High,” it says, “divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he fixed the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. And Jacob became his portion, Israel the line of his inheritance” (Deut. XXXII, 8, according to the Septuagint).

But let us retrace in order by what line this Jacob, who was called Israel, came, so that the promises made to Abraham, whose grandson he is, may be completed.

## CHAPTER X. In Abraham’s calling, the land of the living destined for the Christian people. A promise made and figured. [Note: [Col. 0742D] These words are supplied with the aid of Ms. Remigianus, which lacks the preceding title.] Believed and seen in Genesis.

16. From the seed of Shem, the son of Noah, Heber was born, whose son was Peleg (Gen. X, 25), under whom the languages were divided. Peleg begot Reu (Gen. XI, 18 ff.); Reu begot Serug; Serug begot Nahor; Nahor begot Terah; Terah begot Abram, who afterward was called Abraham [Note: [Col. 0742D] Thus we read in Ms. Remigianus. The printed editions lacked the words “Abram, who afterward was called Abraham”]; his grandson was Jacob.

Scripture testifies that Abraham [Note: [Col. 0742D] Ms. Remig., “Abram.”] was born among the Chaldeans (Gen. XI, 28). Called from that nation, when he first believed [Note: [Col. 0742D] Ms. Remig., “had believed.”], he deserved, by the grace of the one calling him, to be called the father of faith (Rom. IV, 11). The Chaldeans, devoted to astronomy, carefully examined the positions of the stars, but, greatly erring concerning divine worship and religion, and not seeking at all the true Creator of all things [Note: [Col. 0742D] Ms. Remig., “the protector of all things.”], became futile, as Paul says, in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened (Rom. I, 21).

From among them Abraham, inflamed not by crafty creation [Note: [Col. 0742D] Ms. Remig., “not by the cunning creature”; only the Lyon edition reads “not by a cunning creature.”], but by the fervor of divine worship, was separated from the foolish and senseless by the Lord’s gift. God said to him: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into whatever land I shall show you” (Gen. XII, 3). At the command of the one calling him, he left his first dwelling and kindred; through faith he believed what he had not seen, until he might deserve to see all that he believed.

Going out, therefore, from the land of the Chaldeans, he dwelt at Harran (Acts VII, 4), in which he was filled with every kind of wealth [Note: [Col. 0742D] Ms. Remig., “filled with riches, and also with the land.”]. He also received the inheritance of that land in hope of his future offspring. While, from an aged and barren wife, and while he himself was also advancing into old age, he awaited an heir through the promise [Col. 0742D] [Note: [Col. 0742D] Ms. Remig., “of the promise.”], this father of faith showed us that we need not fear the long course of our sojourn and that we must always hope in Christ the Lord. Through his grace we shall possess as an everlasting inheritance the land of the living [Note: [Col. 0743D] Ms. Remig., “we shall possess the everlasting inheritance of the land of the living.”], concerning which the prophet David says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13).

## CHAPTER XI. In the multiplication of Abraham’s seed like the stars, the Christian people. The promise of multiplying Abraham’s seed. Believed and seen in Genesis.

17. The word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision, saying: “Do not fear, Abraham; I protect you; your reward will be very great” (Gen. XV, 1 ff.). And Abraham said: “Lord, what will you give me? For I am without children, and the heir appointed over my household [Note: [Col. 0743D] Ms. Remig., “of my house.”] is this Damascus, Eliezer.” And Abraham said: “Because you have not given me offspring, my household servant will be my heir.” Immediately the word of the Lord came to him: “This man shall not be your heir; but the one who will come forth from your womb, him you shall have as your heir.” And he led him outside and said to him: “Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you can count them.” And he said: “So shall your seed be.” Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

The Apostle Paul confirms this [Note: [Col. 0743D] The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read “affirms.”], saying: “Therefore faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. X, 17). Isaiah also says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9, according to the Septuagint). Faith is the foundation of every future reality; its building’s summit has embraced earth and heaven in Christ Jesus, who is from the seed of Abraham.

## CHAPTER XII. In Abraham’s priesthood, the royal priesthood of the Church. The promise by which, when God demanded a sacrifice, Abraham is shown to be a priest. [Note: [Col. 0743D] Added from Ms. Remigianus, in which the preceding title is omitted.] Believed and seen in Genesis.

18. In the second oracle the Lord said to Abraham: “I am he who brought you out from the land of the Chaldeans, to give you this land, so that you might possess it.” But he said: “Lord, how can I know that I shall possess it?” And the Lord said: “Take a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram; also a turtledove and a pigeon.” [Note: [Col. 0743D] Ms. Remig., “And taking.”]

He took all these, divided them through the middle, and placed the two parts opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds. Birds of prey descended upon the divided carcasses, and Abraham drove them away. When the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abraham, and a great dark horror seized him. And it was said to him: “Know and foresee that your seed will be a sojourner in a land that is not its own; they will subject them to slavery, and they will afflict them for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation that they serve, says the Lord. After this they will go out with great possessions. But you shall go to your fathers, nourished in a good old age. In the fourth generation they will return here; for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Gen. XV, 6 ff.).

In this promise and in this threefold sacrifice—which was performed in the present in such a way as nevertheless to signify other future things—the spiritual reader should recognize the three periods mentioned above in these three animals: the three-year-old heifer, the people before the law, indulging itself without the yoke of the law; the three-year-old she-goat, the people under the law, which it ought to sacrifice for sin while transgressing the law; and the three-year-old ram, under grace, the perfect sacrifice. When Abraham offered it figuratively in place of his son, the altar of the cross received our three-year-old ram, Christ, proclaimed through the three periods, for the sin of the people [Col. 0744A] (see Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XVI, chapter 24). For, as Isaiah says: “Because of the iniquity of the people he was led to death, and by his bruising we were all healed” (Isa. LIII, 5 and 8).

19. But the fact that these animals were divided and placed opposite one another shows, as the Apostle Paul says, that divisions and schisms, which would attack one another, were to come: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI, 19). For even before the law, Cain’s sacrifice was rejected, as was that of the heretics (Gen. IV, 5); and under the law, when Korah, Dathan, and Abiram became the authors of heresies and schisms, the earth swallowed them alive (Num. XVI, 32).

Under grace also, Paul drives away the doctrines of many heresies, and the birds sitting around the divided carcasses of the dead, when he says: “Is Christ divided? [Note: [Col. 0743D] Ms. Remig. adds, “among you.”] Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (I Cor. I, 13).

Abraham was commanded in that sacrifice not to divide the chaste turtledove and the simple pigeon. For spiritual sons who are chaste, and virgins who are simple, while offering in charity the sacrifice of unblemished faith, cannot be divided at all.

That their seed would be a sojourner in this life is testified by David, who sings to his Lord: “I am a resident alien and a sojourner, like all my fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII, 13). [Note: [Col. 0744D] Thus in the manuscript; the printed editions read “as one afflicted.”] That they were afflicted in Egypt for four hundred years, while groaning and saying, “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX, 5), is sufficiently clear.

Their return to freedom in the fourth generation from this Egyptian servitude signifies our freedom, rescued from sin. When the three periods so often mentioned have been completed, may all our freedom arise in the fourth, which the Lord calls regeneration (Matt. XIX, 28), made manifest through the true resurrection, once the sins of the Amorites have been completed—that is, of those who do not believe the Gospel of God. For, as the Lord says, the one who does not believe “has already been judged” (John III, 18).

## CHAPTER XIII. In the perfection of the name by which Abraham is, through faith, the father of the nations. A figurative promise. Believed and seen in Genesis.

[Col. 0744C]

20. In the third oracle the divine promise is also confirmed in his name. Abram, previously so called, is named Abraham by the Lord the Creator, and the significance of this name is explained: “I have appointed you,” he says, “the father of many nations” (Gen. XVII, 5). Thus this promise was not to be understood as referring only to Abraham’s fleshly descent, from which the Jewish people came. Boasting of this in the Gospel, they said: “We have Abraham as our father” (Matt. III, 9; and Luke III, 8); but the one who had bestowed that title and that faith answered them: “Do not boast in this; for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Rom. IV, 18). Thus Abraham was to be the father of many nations in Christ through faith, though by birth he had belonged to only one nation.

## CHAPTER XIV. In circumcision, by which the Christian is circumcised in heart. A figurative prophecy.

[Col. 0744D]

21. After this Abraham had been called through faith, a covenant of circumcision was imposed upon him (Gen. XVII, 10 ff.), as a sign of the old covenant, which he and his descendants were commanded to observe; and every soul among the people that failed to practice circumcision was to perish (ibid., 14). Perhaps it may be asked why it pleased God that every male alone among those who had vowed themselves to obey God should be circumcised [Note: [Col. 0745D] Ms. Remig., “had pleased.”].

This matter was carried out with a great sacramental significance, looking back to the middle and past ages and forward to the future. For because of the first transgression, in that part of the body where the human being was struck by the serpent’s poison, burning with the heat of lust, he became ashamed of those parts that had not been created shameful; and he determined to cover with shame what had been naked without shame [Note: [Col. 0745D] We emend the passage from Ms. Remig. The other version reads “determined to submit to modesty.”].

Therefore God the Creator and Judge imposed the sign of circumcision upon that part of the body, moderating the disease of lust wrongly conceived through the due sexual union [Note: [Col. 0745D] Thus Ms. Remig.; the printed editions read “the debt.”], so that through the good of continence and the beauty of integrity he might restore what had been corrupted.

The circumcision of the heart, which shines forth in the New Testament, was figured in that sign, because there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of God (Matt. XIX, 14). And God reproves and rebukes the children of Israel as uncircumcised in heart (Jer. IX, 26).

## CHAPTER XV. In the birth of Isaac, whose name means “laughter,” what is shown in Christ. A figurative promise. [Note: [Col. 0745D] Supplied from Ms. Remigianus, in which the earlier title is read in mutilated form.] Believed and seen in Genesis.

[Col. 0745B]

22. Again, at the oak of Mamre, the divine majesty appeared to the same Abraham in the form of three men, bringing a promise concerning the son who was soon to be born and confirming what had been said above. Sarah his wife was also questioned by him (Gen. XVIII, 1 ff.). For God said to Abraham: “Where is Sarah your wife?” He said: “She is in the tent.” And the Lord said to him: “I will return to you at this favorable time, and Sarah will have a son.” When Sarah heard this, standing behind him at the entrance of the tent, she laughed within herself, saying: “As yet nothing has happened to me up to this time, and my lord is old.” The Lord said to Abraham: “Why did Sarah laugh within herself, saying: ‘Shall I truly give birth, now that I have grown old?’ Can anything be impossible for the word of God?” And again he confirms it: “I will return, then, to you at the favorable time, and Sarah will have a son” (ibid., 9 ff.).

[Col. 0745C] Because Sarah denied out of fear that she had laughed, she is convicted by the truth that she did laugh (ibid., 15). When she had conceived and given birth, his name was called Isaac, which is interpreted as “laughter” (Gen. XXI, 2). For this reason Sarah herself, when she was already carrying the little child in her arms, said: “God has made laughter for me.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] The Remigius manuscript reads “the Lord.”] Everyone who hears that an old and barren woman has given birth will rejoice with me in laughter” (ibid., 6).

[Note: [Col. 0745D] The Remigius manuscript reads “the laughter of offspring.”]

[Note: [Col. 0745D] The printed editions read “in whom.”]

The offspring of laughter was received, in whom Abraham received the promised blessing of all nations. [Note: [Col. 0745D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “who comes in the flesh through that succession.”]

[Note: [Col. 0745D] Perhaps *inrisum* (“into mockery”) should be read in place of *irrisum* (“mocked”).]

For the nations that now believe in Christ, who came in the flesh through that old man, confess their Savior, whom the Jews turned into mockery, and, glorifying him, acknowledge that his shameful passion is their true freedom.

# CHAPTER XVI. The day of the future judgment in Sodom and Gomorrah. A prediction made and foreshadowed. Believed and seen in Genesis.

23. The Lord showed the same faithful servant Abraham the foretold overthrow of the impious cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, saying: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sins are exceedingly great.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] The Remigius manuscript reads “hateful” (*invisa*) rather than “exceedingly great.”]

I will go down,” he says, “and see whether they have completed the cry that has come to me; and if not, I will know” (Gen. XVIII, 20 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0745D] The Remigius manuscript reads “whether they will complete.”]

[Col. 0746A] God “went down,” as it is said here, because he did not conceal his just judgment from his most beloved servant. Abraham, knowing that God rightly intended to destroy the cities foretold, sought to appease him through a kind of agreement that he, as a humble and suppliant intercessor, had obtained, saying: “Do not destroy the righteous together with the wicked. And shall the righteous be as the unrighteous? If there are fifty righteous in the city, will you destroy them? Will you not spare the whole place for the sake of the fifty righteous?” (ibid., 23–24).

[Note: [Col. 0746D] The Remigius manuscript adds “Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 0746D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “And when he had taken courage from the God who promised that he would not…”]

When God had promised that he would not destroy the places if he found fifty righteous there, Abraham then took courage to continue speaking. In pious words, confessing himself to be dust and clay, he gradually suspended God’s sentence from fifty-one down to ten, with remarkable serenity (ibid., 26–27 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0746D] The Remigius manuscript has this exact reading. In the printed editions, “forty-five” is added after “fifty righteous,” and the sequence is abruptly interrupted.]

It is said that he found none of that small number. When he rescued Lot, his wife, and his two daughters from the peoples and cities that he was about to consume with heavenly fire, he warned those whom he had delivered not to remain anywhere in that region and not to look back. But Lot’s wife, disregarding the command and looking back, was turned into a pillar of salt (Gen. XIX, 17 ff.). By her example she seasoned fools, showing that those who are advancing toward the holy purpose must not look back with harmful curiosity (Luke XVII, 32); nor can such people escape the punishments decreed. This woman demonstrated that she lost what she had escaped.

The Lord rebukes such people in the Gospel, saying: “It will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you” (Matt. X, 15; XI, 24). Those whom the grace of Christ delivers, he admonishes through the Apostle: “Come out from their midst and separate yourselves, says the Lord” (II Cor. VI, 17). Likewise he himself says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. III, 13). For no one who looks back and puts his hand to the plow is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke IX, 62). When the Lord said, “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVII, 32), he spoke thus.

Therefore those in whom the world has been crucified to the Lord’s cross, and they to the world, await the day of judgment without fear.

[Note: [Col. 0746D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “who, glorying in the Lord’s cross, have the world crucified to them,” and so forth.]

For the Lord terrified the hearts of the faithful, saying: “As it happened in the days of Lot, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Luke XVII, 28), lest that sudden day find them weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness (Luke XXI, 34). Of this the Apostle says: “For the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (I Thess. V, 2).

# CHAPTER XVII. The passion of Christ in Isaac’s sacrifice. A foreshadowed prediction. Believed and seen in Genesis.

[Note: [Col. 0746D] The Remigius manuscript reads “Promise.” It also adds: “Likewise, in Genesis…”]

24. “God tested Abraham,” saying: “Abraham, Abraham.” And he said: “Here I am.” And the Lord said: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the high land, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall tell you” (Gen. XXII, 1–2).

He commands that as a burnt offering to himself be offered the one through whom he himself had already divinely promised, in so many oracles, that Abraham’s seed would be multiplied like the stars of heaven and that the nations would be blessed in him. Yet the father does not hesitate to fulfill in his son what has been commanded, knowing, as Paul says, that the Lord could also raise him from the dead (Heb. XI, 19).

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “But the strength of faith granted to him who is tested in his son is not demonstrated so much…”]

But the strength of the faith granted to the one who is tested in his son is not merely demonstrated; it is also set before us for imitation, 

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “so that the authority of the new commandment might flow forth from the Gospel.”]

and so that the authority of the new commandment might endure from the Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37; Luke XIV, 26).

For although he knew that Isaac was not yet capable of offspring, Abraham nevertheless obeyed God’s command with the conviction that God was neither forgetful of his promises nor unaware of the mystical sacrament being enacted of the Lord’s future passion. He was looking toward that day of our redemption of which the Lord, rebuking the Jews in the Gospel, says: “Abraham your father desired to see my day; and he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII, 56).

Abraham saw, symbolized in his son, the day of the passion of the Son of God: that he did not spare his only son; that, as though approaching the altar of the cross, he went forth for three days with the innocent victim; that, suffering and voiceless, like a lamb before the one shearing him, the son offered his tender neck to the father to be struck;

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “like a lamb, the Son submitting to the Father who was striking him,” and so forth.]

that Isaac did not resist being hung upon the wood that he himself had carried; that the ram, caught by its horns in the thicket, appeared in place of Isaac, showing Christ crowned with thorns; and that Isaac was not sacrificed because resurrection was reserved for the Son of God.

Believing all these things, Abraham deserved to see through the figure what we recognize to have been fulfilled through grace.

# CHAPTER XVIII. The oath of God by which his seed is extended beyond number in Christ. The promise made to Abraham in symbolic form. Believed and seen in Genesis.

[Note: [Col. 0747D] This addition is found in the Remigius manuscript, in which the preceding title is missing.]

25. “By myself I have sworn,” says the Lord, “because you did not spare your beloved son for my sake: I will bless you, and I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea. And your seed shall possess the cities of its enemies, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. XXII, 16 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The printed editions read: “By me I have sworn.”]

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The printed editions read: “Therefore.”]

That Abraham’s seed was indeed multiplied and reached a great number is shown by the Book of Numbers; yet we do not know it to be innumerable. The promise of God, however, contains “like the stars of heaven” and “like the sand of the sea,” which cannot be counted. The whole course of events itself demonstrates that this promise was fulfilled in Christ through the faith of the nations, whose father Abraham is. At the same time, the oracles of the prophets testify through David and the others that Abraham’s children are called to an infinite number, not only from the seed of the flesh but also from faith.

“Through him,” it says, “all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed. All nations shall call him blessed” (Ps. LXXI, 17). Likewise: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him” (ibid., 11). And Isaiah: “There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to reign over the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Isa. XI, 10; Rom. XV, 12).

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “to rule … in him.”]

The Apostle Paul also says that the branches—the Jews—were broken off through unbelief, while the nations were grafted in, like a wild olive, into the faith of Abraham’s root (ibid., 19–20).

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “into the faith of the root.”]

Likewise he himself says: “The nations, however, glorify God for his mercy” (Rom. XV, 9)—the mercy by which, after removing their heart of stone as he had promised, he gave them a heart of flesh (Ezek. XI, 19; XXXVI, 26).

He calls those who worship stone gods “stones” when he says:

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “when he says to the Jews: ‘If you remain silent, the stones will cry out.’”]

“I tell you, if these remain silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke XIX, 48). In a wondrous manner, those who were stones, made sons through grace, cry out: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9); while those who were sons, having become stones, say: “Make gods for us to go before us” (Exod. XXXII, 1), because, abandoning the living God, they served Baal and the idols of the nations. The nations, on the contrary, rejecting idols, followed the living God.

These are the things we see being fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The two words “namely, those” are absent from the Remigius manuscript.]

Namely, the things that Abraham believed had been promised in his future seed through Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “which Abraham believed would be fulfilled through Christ, promised in his seed.”]

# CHAPTER XIX. That Christ would assume humanity from Abraham’s thigh. Believed and seen in Genesis.

The mystical action that follows shows that the flesh of Christ, previously foretold, would come from the thigh of Abraham.

26. Abraham calls the chief servant of his household and says to him: “Place your hand beneath my thigh and swear by the God of heaven that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of this land, among whom I dwell; but you shall take a wife for him from my tribe” (Gen. XXIV, 2–3).

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “placing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “upon.”]

This sequence shows that the God of heaven was in Abraham’s thigh: Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac, Jacob; Jacob, the twelve patriarchs; among them, Judah, from whose tribe came David; and from David, through the succession of generations, the virgin Mary, who bore Christ, who is the God of heaven, because through him all things were made (John I, 3).

# CHAPTER XX. The two peoples—Christians and Jews—in Rebecca’s twins. A promise made and foreshadowed. Believed and seen in Genesis.

27. When Isaac had taken Rebecca, his kinswoman, as his wife and, perceiving that she was barren, prayed to God for offspring, to whom he had promised multiplication, he received it as soon as he asked (Gen. XXV, 21).

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “he asks. For Rebecca, having conceived…”]

When Rebecca had conceived, twins struggled in her womb. But she, distressed, said: “If this was going to happen to me, why is this happening to me?” (ibid., 22).

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The Remigius manuscript has this reading. The printed editions instead read: “When she had reported this.” The manuscript then continues: “If this is beginning to happen to me, why…”]

Isaac went with her to inquire of the Lord, and received this answer: “Two peoples are in your womb, and two nations shall come forth from your belly; one people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (ibid., 23).

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The Remigius manuscript reads “shall come forth.”]

Isaac received the two promised sons, recognizing the two peoples who would exist by faith alone, whom that mystical action displayed to us as having been revealed. For while Esau first emerged from the womb, hairy, the hand of the younger Jacob came out after him and grasped his heel (ibid., 25), an event that presented a great and astonishing sign.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The printed editions here and below read “younger,” where the Remigius manuscript has “lesser.”]

That younger Jacob, gentle even in childhood, supplanted his elder brother by means of a red dish of lentils and took away his primacy (ibid., 30 ff.); nor could the sacrament of so great a mystery be without significance.

That gentle younger Jacob signified the gentle and meek Christian people, endowed with the gentleness by which pagan fury had believed the innocent to be destined for destruction.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] The Remigius manuscript reads “signified.”]

[Note: [Col. 0749D] The printed editions read “by Esau,” which appears to make no proper sense; the Remigius manuscript reads “for taking away,” perhaps for “destroying,” as the preceding word “fury” suggests.]

This gentle people, through the red dish—that is, the passion reddened with Christ’s blood—voluntarily offered itself to the devouring and savage Jewish people, whose figure Esau bore; he was also called Edom. The people that had possessed the primacy sold it, and this one received it. The Jew lost through desire what he had by birth; the Christian acquired through grace what he did not possess by nature.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] The word “red” comes from the Remigius manuscript.]

# CHAPTER XXI. What the same men did in symbolic form. A promise made and foreshadowed. Believed and seen in Genesis.

28. I shall attempt to explain briefly, as far as is fitting, how wondrous and how great were the things enacted in these two twins, and how completely all things were filled with sacraments in accordance with the promises of God.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] The Remigius manuscript adds “of God,” which is absent from the printed editions.]

Isaac their father, blinded in his outward eyes but shining with inward light, promised a blessing to Esau, his firstborn son, if the son would prepare for his father the desired food from his hunting (Gen. XXVII, 1 ff.). He went to fulfill what had been commanded (ibid., 5 ff.).

The mother, who had heard that the blessing had been promised to the elder son, moved by God so that it might come to the younger Jacob, prepares by prophetic skill a mystical stratagem.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] The Remigius manuscript reads “a stratagem.”]

She took the clothing of her firstborn, which she had in the house; with it she clothed the younger son, and upon his arms and bare neck she placed the skins of goats. [Note: [Col. 0749D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “and fitted him out … so that he could be seen,” perhaps for “be seen as.”]

She fitted him out so that he could be seen as what he was not, as though she were already showing us Christ in figure, who took not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. VIII, 3).

The Lord likewise received the law of the Old Testament as the clothing of the firstborn, saying that he had not come to abolish it but to fulfill it (Matt. V, 17).

[Note: [Col. 0749D] The printed editions lack “also” here.]

Thus disguised, that younger son Jacob, who had already taken the primacy from his brother, also usurps the blessing, offering his father the food prepared by his mother, and says: “Father.” But he says: “Who are you, my son?” He replies: “I am your firstborn son Esau. I have done as you told me” (Gen. XXVII, 18).

When the father recognized the younger son’s voice, he thought he should feel him with his hands and found that his limbs had the appearance of the elder.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “he found the appearance of the elder.”]

And, confused between the sons, he became, as someone has said (Virgil), “a welcome error to the parents.”

[Note: [Col. 0749D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Then, having been refreshed by the feast that the mother had prepared, the son offered it [or: was offering it], and the father willingly accepted it, giving this blessing…”]

After the son had offered the food that the mother had prepared, which the father willingly accepted, he gave the following blessing to the younger son:

“Behold,” he said, “the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field that the Lord has blessed. May God give you from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth an abundance of grain, wine, and oil. May nations serve you, and princes adore you; may you be lord of your brother, and may the sons of your father adore you.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads “shall serve you.”] Whoever blesses you shall be blessed, and whoever curses you shall be cursed” (Gen. XXVII, 27 ff.).

All these things apply to Christ the Lord; all the blessed nations gather after his fragrance.

29. After these events the firstborn son Esau came, already rejected because of the younger son’s grace. He too offered food to his father and said: “Let my father rise and eat from the game of his son, so that your soul may bless me.”

At this the father, terrified, said: “Who, then, is the one who hunted for me and brought it before you entered? I blessed him, and he is blessed” (ibid., 31 ff.).

The later people, the Christian people, already blessed, says to the Father: “You have given gladness to my heart”; “from the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil they have multiplied” (Ps. IV, 7–8).

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “He said.”]

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “From the time.”]

But to the elder people, the Jewish people, the Father says: “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. The sacrifice of praise will glorify me” (Ps. XLIX, 9, 23).

“For your brother came with deceit and received your blessing” (Gen. XXVII, 35). Because God loved Jacob but hated Esau (Mal. I, 3; Rom. IX, 13), therefore, when the time had been completed and the sacrifices of the Jews had been rejected, the whole Christian people now recognizes that a pure sacrifice, as was foretold (Mal. I, 11), is offered to his name; through grace it has taken from the Jew both the primacy and the blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “To this one.”]

For concerning this one it was said: “You shall be lord of your brother” (Gen. XXVII, 29).

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads “in those,” without “did not.”]

But this did not come to pass in those twins. For the younger also offered gifts to the elder, professed himself to be his servant, and humbly adored him (Gen. XXXIII, 3), so that what was then marked out through the letter might now be revealed to us in grace.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “might be revealed in grace.”]

# CHAPTER XXII. Esau, from whose seed came Job, and Christ among the nations through faith. A promise believed and seen in Genesis. Rewards promised to virtue and patience.

30. From the seed of Esau came the Idumaean people (Gen. XXXVI, 1), among whose leaders that most powerful athlete of God, Job, shone forth (Job I, 12). He was presented as an example of all patience, so that in an agonistic contest he might overcome the devil, the prince of the entire army, supported by God’s help.

For when he was a righteous man, blameless before God, and God deigned to show the devil what sort of man he was, God said to the devil: “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “my child.”]

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript does not have “anyone.”]

And the devil said: “Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not blessed his house and multiplied his livestock? But stretch out your hand and touch everything he has, and you will see whether he blesses you to your face.”

“Behold,” God said, “I give everything he has into your hands; only take care not to touch him” (ibid., 8 ff.).

A great contest takes place. The treacherous and apostate angel attacks God’s faithful servant and, since he possesses a fully self-generated wickedness, devastates, drives away, and destroys all the innocent man’s possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The word “good” is absent from the old printed edition.]

Together with the whole inheritance, he also consumed every heir.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “he confined [or: enclosed] him.”]

Yet after so many darts had been discharged, Job remains unharmed; and, as a soldier of God, with one blow he strikes down the devil.

“Naked I came out,” he says, “from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return to the earth. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (ibid., 21).

Defeated in this contest, the enemy announces another, greater one: “Stretch out your hand against him,” he says to God, “and touch his flesh and bones, and you will see whether he blesses you to your face” (Job II, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “to your face.”]

“Stretch out your hand” means nothing other than “give authority.” For the devil did not even have this authority over the pigs (Matt. VIII, 32), unless the one who, under this authority, also handed Job over to him had given it, so that he would not exceed the limit of the command.

“Behold,” God says, “I hand him over to you; only preserve his soul” (Job II, 6).

After Job was struck by a grievous wound, the structure of his whole body putrefying, all his limbs loosened, pus flowing, and worms boiling forth, while his spirit remained sound within his corrupted body, the devil perceived that the man whom he had considered weak outwardly was strong inwardly. He armed the man’s wife, whom he had left to him at that moment as necessary for himself, and through the wife attacked the strongest man from the side.

31. When the woman began to pour out the poisoned darts that she had received from the enemy, she said among other things: “Say some word against the Lord and die” (ibid., 9).

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The old editions read: “Say some word in the Lord.”]

Immediately recalling the downfall of the first man, and conquering a new Eve—and in her the enemy who was waging war—he said: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why do we not endure evil things?” (ibid., 10).

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The Remigius manuscript has this reading, whereas the printed editions read: “The enemy was struck down and, overcome through grace and through a human being, the perverse angel was humbled,” and so forth.]

Struck down by these divine darts, the enemy was overcome through grace; the perverse angel yielded to the devout man, and the humble piety of patience defeated every trouble caused by pride.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The Lyon edition and the Remigius manuscript read “through this man.”]

The footprints of Christ, who would pass through the righteous and powerful man into the nations, were already being signified. Concerning these David says in his person: “In Edom I will extend my sandal” (Ps. CVII, 10).

The Apostle James, likewise strengthening the hearts of believers by the example of patience, says: “You have heard of the patience of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord, because the Lord is compassionate and merciful” (James V, 11).

The victorious Job received double rewards.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The Remigius manuscript reads “a hundredfold.”]

To those who fight, and who conquer with his grace helping them, the Lord promises to give a hundredfold in this life (Matt. XIX, 29) and to grant eternal life in the age to come (Mark X, 30).

We see this fulfilled in Valentinian, the brother of Valens, who, while rejecting military service and the rank of tribune for Christ’s sake, gained the kingdom of this world and, as a true confessor of Christ, acquired eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] Perhaps “in Valentinian”; shortly afterward the Remigius manuscript reads “we have seen it fulfilled.”]

# CHAPTER XXIII. Jacob, to whom Christ the cornerstone was shown in a vision. A foreshadowed promise. Believed and seen in Genesis.

32. Jacob too, the son of Isaac and grandson of Abraham, received a promise through certain wondrous events enacted with him (Gen. XXVIII, 10 ff.).

Fleeing his brother’s ambush, he chose for his lodging a place reached by the course of the setting sun.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “with his own [head] placed there.”]

There, with a stone placed beneath his head, he relates that the following things were revealed to him in a dream: a ladder of extraordinary size, whose top extended as far as heaven, was shown to him; upon it were angels of God ascending and descending, and the Lord was leaning upon it and said to him: “I will give you the land on which you sleep, and to your seed after you” (ibid., 13).

When he awoke, he raised upright at a distance the stone that had been beneath his head as a sacramental sign, and, anointing it with oil, consecrated for us Christ as the cornerstone. Concerning him the prophet says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. CXVII, 22).

And Isaiah says: “Behold, I place in Zion a cornerstone, chosen and precious; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. XXVIII, 16).

This cornerstone, Christ, explained to Nathanael when he came to him the dream that Jacob had seen: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man” (John I, 51).

For the one who descended is Christ himself, and the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fulfill all things (Eph. IV, 10). He set forth the ladder as the narrow way that leads to life (Matt. VII, 14).

# CHAPTER XXIV. Jacob’s lameness, signifying that not all Jews would believe. A promise made and foreshadowed. Believed and seen in Genesis.

33. As Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia with his wives, sons, and servants, an angel also met him on the way. He engaged in a sacred struggle with him, and the angel allowed himself to be overcome by the man; then, though victorious, he demanded a blessing from the one he had defeated.

“I will not let you go,” he said, “unless you bless me.” And the angel said to him: “What is your name?” He answered: “Jacob.” “From now on,” he said, “you shall not be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, because you have prevailed with God, and you shall be powerful with men.”

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The Remigius manuscript adds “from now on,” here.]

The angel touched the breadth of his thigh, and Jacob became lame for all his days (Gen. XXXII, 26 ff.).

The lameness that arose from his thigh signifies the Hebrew people itself, limping.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The Remigius manuscript reads “of the Hebrews.”] To them the prophet Elijah says: “How long will you limp on both thighs? If the Lord is God, follow him” (III Kings XVIII, 21).

And David says: “The sons of strangers have grown old and have limped from their paths” (Ps. XVII, 46).

[Note: [Col. 0752D] This is the reading of the Remigius manuscript. The printed editions read “which.” The manuscript then has “was unwilling”; the printed editions read “was not willing.”]

Because that people was unwilling to follow Christ by the straight path, it limped through its errors and wandered along various paths. But the Christian people, seeing God—that is what “Israel” means—grasped him through grace (Gen. XXXII, 28).

# CHAPTER XXV. Jacob’s sons and Joseph, who prefigured Christ. A promise made and foreshadowed. Believed and seen in Genesis.

34. Jacob received twelve sons from his women, whom Scripture attests to have been the twelve patriarchs (Gen. XXXV).

[Note: [Col. 0752D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “not that it was lawful for a free and holy man to have many women, perhaps [meaning] that it was permitted for holy men to have many [women],” and so forth.]

This was not because it was permitted for free and holy men to have many women for the sake of desire, but because God granted permission for the multiplication of offspring—he who permitted one at that time and later at times forbade it.

For although he said in the Law: “Cursed is the man who has not raised up seed in Israel” (Deut. XXV, 9), through the prophet Solomon he set a limit to this permission: “A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing” (Eccles. III, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0752D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Among these, therefore, were the twelve patriarchs…”]

Among these twelve patriarchs was Judah, from whom came the Jews; Joseph and Benjamin were full brothers, born of Jacob and Rachel. Their action as a whole signifies Christ and the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “signifies the whole Church of Christ.”]

For it is said: “Jacob loved Joseph” (Gen. XXXVII, 3). And God says of the Son: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

“Jacob made Joseph a variegated tunic” (Gen. XXXVII, 3).

[Note: [Col. 0752D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “It will be said.”]

It is also said to this Joseph of ours, Christ: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed all around with variety” (Ps. XLIV, 10).

Joseph dreamed a dream and told it to his brothers: “I thought,” he said, “that we were binding sheaves in the field. My sheaf rose and stood upright; but your sheaves, turning, bowed down to my sheaf” (Gen. XXXVII, 5).

35. Jacob himself also showed that this would happen in Christ, in the blessing he had received from his father concerning Judah, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Jacob himself had received this in the blessing, saying: ‘They shall adore …’”] “The sons of your father shall adore you” (Gen. XLIX, 8).

For these are the ones who say: “Come, let us adore and fall prostrate before him” (Ps. XCIV, 6), and who now say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9).

And he himself says in the Gospel: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32).

Again he sees other sacraments in a dream and reported them to his brothers: “As though the sun and moon and eleven stars were adoring me” (Gen. XXXVII, 9).

The prophet also speaks of our Joseph, Christ the Lord: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light” (Ps. CXLVIII, 3); and, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII, 1); and Habakkuk: “The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. III, 11, according to the Septuagint).

The moon, the Church composed of mortals who pass away and succeed one another, after Christ the sun was exalted, rose again in complete order. It stood firm in the faith, while stars shone for him who numbers them.

To his disciples, whose number is definite, he said: “Let your works shine” (Matt. V, 16), “like lights in the world” (Phil. II, 15).

[Col. 0753B]

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “whose number is certain.” The printed editions read: “whose number is uncertain.” Below, the manuscript has “into the world.”]

# CHAPTER XXVI. Joseph, sent like Christ the Lord to visit the sheep. A foreshadowed promise. Believed and seen in Genesis.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The first title is not found in the Remigius manuscript. The second reads: “Joseph is sent by his father to visit his brothers and the sheep through a figurative promise: Believed and seen in Genesis.” Chapter 26 itself then begins with the words “He says,” and so forth.]

36. Joseph is sent by his father to visit his brothers and the sheep (Gen. XXXVII, 13).

Our Joseph, Christ the Lord, also says: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV, 24).

It is said: “Joseph’s brothers hated him because of his dreams” (Gen. XXXVII, 11). This Joseph of ours, Christ, also cries out concerning his Jewish brothers: “Because they hated me without cause” (Ps. XXIV, 19; John XV, 25).

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “When his brothers saw Joseph, they said of Joseph: ‘Behold…’”]

When Joseph was seen, his brothers said: “Behold, that dreamer is coming. Come, let us kill him and see what his dreams will be” (Gen. XXXVII, 19).

And in Solomon’s book the impious are reported to have said concerning our Joseph: “Come, let us kill the righteous man, because he is unpleasant to us” (Wis. II, 12).

It continues: “He claims to have knowledge of God and calls himself a son of God. Let us see whether his words are true, and let us test whether the things that are to happen to him will come to pass” (ibid., 13 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0753D] These two words, “whether they will follow,” are not found in the Remigius manuscript.]

The Lord himself also confirms these things in the Gospel concerning the son who was sent to the cultivators of the vineyard, and how they said: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXI, 38).

Joseph’s brothers took him, stripped him of that variegated tunic, and threw him into a pit (Gen. XXXVII, 23–24).

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The word “him” is found in the Lyon edition. The Remigius manuscript reads: “They stripped him of that variegated tunic and cast him into the pit.”]

Our Joseph also says through the prophet concerning his passion: “They cast me into the outer pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Ps. LXXXVII, 7).

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “They cast me.”]

37. The Gospel authority relates that the tunic was stripped off from above, yet woven throughout [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “stripped off from above, woven.”] (Matt. XXVII, 35)—a tunic which the soldiers likewise refused to divide (John XIX, 24), thereby affirming the unity of the Church, from whose lot heretics are excluded, since by lot it came about that one person—that is, unity—should possess it. “Taking,” he says, “a kid from the goats, Joseph’s brothers stained his tunic with blood” (Gen. XXXVII, 31), which they presented [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “would present.”] to their father under false testimony, claiming that an evil beast had devoured him.

Those three kinds of sacrifice which Abraham offered, in an altered order, observe their entire appointed sequence: a ram in place of Isaac; a kid from the goats in place of Joseph; and, for the prodigal son returning to his father (Luke XV, 23), a fattened calf from a young bull is slaughtered.
