“Come,” said one of the brothers, “let us sell Joseph and not kill him.” The Jews likewise said this concerning Christ, whom they delivered to Pilate to be put to death: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John XVIII, 31). And Joseph’s brothers sold him to the Ishmaelite merchants going down to Egypt for twenty pieces of gold [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “thirty pieces of gold.”] (Gen. XXXVII, 28). But the prophets Zechariah and Jeremiah bear witness to our Joseph, Christ, who was sold: “They gave the price of the one who was valued at thirty pieces of gold” [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “the appraised price, thirty pieces of silver.”] (Zech. II, 12). The Gospels likewise relate that Judas received this from the Jews (Matt. XXVII, 9; XXVI, 15; Mark XIV, 11; Luke XXII, 5), so that Christ, sold by the Jews, might pass over to the Gentiles. For Judas lost his life together with the price; the Jews lost both the price and Christ whom they had purchased [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “had bought.”]; but the Gentiles, by possessing the gain of grace, were themselves possessed by it.

**CHAPTER XXVII. In the same Joseph, in whom chastity is rewarded through suffering. The promise made and prefigured, by which Joseph, though afflicted, is not abandoned. Believed and seen in Genesis.**

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “the righteous” for “Joseph.”]

38. The Ishmaelites sold Joseph in Egypt to a certain official of Pharaoh’s cooks (Gen. XXXVII, 36).

[Note: In the Remigian manuscript, and in the Lyon edition, here and shortly afterward, *coquorum* (“of the cooks”) appears. The Louvain, Douai, and later editions, which believed Prosper to be the author of this book, note in the margin here that the author uses the reading of the Septuagint translators. This should be observed not only concerning this passage but also concerning several others in which the author cites Scripture differently from the way it is customarily read in our Vulgate.]

Nor is there no significance in the words “to the official of the cooks.” [Note: The Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions read: “For the cook indeed”; the Lyon edition: “For the cook indeed”; the Remigian manuscript: “That red cooking, here too, signifies the Passion of Christ.”] For that red garment of the cook signifies the Passion of Christ, through which, as has often been said, the later Christian people takes primacy away from the people that always knows how to sell but does not know how to purchase Christ by grace.

It is said: “The Lord was with Joseph” (Gen. XXXIX, 2); and our Joseph says: “I am not alone, because the Father who sent me is with me” (John VIII, 16).

His master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said to him: “Sleep with me” (Gen. XXXIX, 7). When he resisted, recounting the favor he had found with his master and fearing to offend through the holy fear of God with which he was filled [Note: The Remigian manuscript adds: “and the spirit of the fear of God.”], the woman, waiting for another suitable occasion, seized him by his clothing and said: “Come, sleep with me” (ibid. 12). But he left his clothing in her hands, fled, and went outside.

When her master—her husband—arrived, “it became known what a frenzied woman can do” [the author appears to allude to the opening of the fifth book of Virgil’s *Aeneid*: “And what a frenzied woman can do was known”]. She made wickedness serve her purpose: she asserted falsehoods as truths and claimed that she had suffered the violence which she herself had inflicted.

O shameless woman! “The wound feeds upon her veins, and she is consumed by a hidden fire” [Note: This entire verse is also inserted from the opening of the fourth book of the same *Aeneid*.]; she loves and pursues; she desires and rages. And because he did not consent to her adultery, she resolved that he should be slaughtered and sought the death of the man whom she loved [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “had loved.”].

I would rightly compare this shameless Egyptian woman with impious idolatry. For she too cast her eyes upon our Joseph; she saw him beautiful beyond the sons of men (Ps. XLIV, 3), and drew him by his clothing toward an unlawful consent.

39. What are the garments of our Joseph, Christ, except the holy martyrs? Concerning them he says through the prophet Isaiah to his body, the Church: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with all of them” (Isa. XLIX, 18); and in the Song of Songs: “How red are your garments!” (Song V, 10). Jacob too says in prophetic blessing: “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX, 11).

When Christians are seized so that, by sacrificing to idols, they may commit fornication in their souls, what else is being seized than Christ in his garments? “Let the Christians be held,” says that impious and shameless teaching, “or let them consent; otherwise prisons, exiles, swords, fires, beasts, and every other punishment shall be prepared for them.” In these things our Joseph, Christ, is seized by his garments.

But when he says to his own, “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. X, 28), and they answer him, “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Ps. XLIII, 22; Rom. VIII, 36), he left his garments in her hands.

What is meant by the statement, “He fled and went outside, leaving his garments” (Gen. XXXIX, 12), except that it reveals the soul set free, which cries out through David: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. CXXIII, 7)?

**CHAPTER XXVIII. In the same Joseph, the Passion of Christ is prefigured. The promise believed and seen in Genesis. The Passion of Christ promised through figures.**

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “The Passion promised to Christ, prefigured; believed and seen in Genesis.”]

40. Joseph is handed over to prison (Gen. XXXIX, 20). Our Joseph, Christ, as Isaiah says, “was numbered among the wicked” (Isa. LIII, 12). While the Wisdom of God governs the innocent one among the guilty, Wisdom—which descended with him, as it is written—“did not abandon him in his bonds” (Wis. X, 13). This our Joseph, Christ, cries out: “I have become like one without help, free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 5).

What follows—that he found the favor with which he was filled before the official of the prison, and that all the keys and the entire custody were entrusted to Joseph’s hands (Gen. XXXIX, 21)—must be understood as implying [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “to be supplied.”] that, just as heaven is subject to him in the sun, the stars, and the moon, and the earth in its sheaves, so also the lower regions of the prison were subjected to him, so that every knee might bow to our Joseph, Christ, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II, 10).

Nor do I think it unrelated to the mystery of the Lord’s Passion that two eunuchs of Pharaoh were thrust into prison with him during that Passion (Gen. XL, 3), so that in a certain manner the number of the three crucified might be completed (ibid., 21, 22). Of these, our Joseph, Christ, by revealing the mysteries, would punish one with the punishment he deserved and free the other through undeserved grace. These sacred actions were then enacted in prefigured events, so that everything to be revealed might be preserved for us.

**CHAPTER XXIX. In the same Joseph, the resurrection of Christ is prefigured. The promise believed and seen in Genesis. The resurrection promised through figures.**

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “The promise of the resurrection prefigured. In Genesis, etc.”]

41. After two years of days, at the beginning of the third, Joseph is brought out of prison (Gen. XLI, 1). And our Joseph, Christ the Lord, rose from the dead on the third day. He is presented to Pharaoh: the resurrection is proclaimed to the world.

Joseph explains Pharaoh’s dreams and, as a means of averting the future famine, wisely instructs that grain should be stored from the abundance of seven years, so that the storehouses may be filled. Our Joseph, Christ the Lord, likewise gave such counsel to the world as it runs toward its end through the number seven. For he says: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “much fruit.”] (John XII, 24). For “those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV, 5).

Pharaoh gave Joseph authority over all Egypt [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “throughout the whole land of Egypt”]. And our Joseph, Christ the Lord, says after his resurrection: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

Joseph sent his men throughout all Egypt and gathered an abundance of grain, like the sand of the sea (Gen. XLI, 47–49). Our Joseph, Christ the Lord, sent his own throughout the world, saying: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). And the number of believers was gathered beyond counting, like the sand of the sea.

Joseph established storehouses throughout all Egypt; and throughout the whole world Christ the Lord consecrated churches. Concerning him John says: “He will gather the grain into his barn” (Luke III, 17). Joseph opened the storehouses in the time of famine and supplied the peoples (Gen. XLI, 56). The same is said of our Joseph: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous”; and it follows: “To rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine” (Ps. XXXIII, 16).

The prophet Amos reveals the famine of the soul: “I will send upon them,” says the Lord, “a famine, not of bread and water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII, 11). And the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12).

To those placed in this famine, our Joseph, Christ the Lord, dispenses from his storehouses the divine nourishment of his body [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “he provides food”]. As we taste it, we see “how gracious the Lord is” (Ps. XXXIII, 9).

It is said that Joseph acquired all Egypt for Pharaoh (Gen. XLVII, 20). And it is said of our Joseph: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. V, 19).

**CHAPTER XXX. In the same Joseph, who, like Christ the Lord, loved his enemies. The promise believed and seen in Genesis. Greatness promised to those who have done good to their enemies.**

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads: “Greatness promised to those who have done good to their enemies. In Genesis, etc.”]

42. Joseph’s brothers, driven by famine, came to Egypt to purchase grain from the man whom they had sold (Gen. XLII, 3). They came to our Joseph, Christ the Lord, whom they had crucified, so that, nourished by his food, they might remove the famine by which their souls were afflicted. They worship him; these others worship him.

When Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but they did not recognize him (ibid., 8). This too was fulfilled in our case: his own brothers did not recognize him [Note: The Remigian manuscript omits “him.”]. “For if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. II, 8).

Joseph was separated from his brothers and said to them through an interpreter: “You are spies; you have come to examine the tracks of this land” [Note: This is the reading of the Septuagint translators.] (Gen. XLII, 2).

Our Joseph, Christ the Lord, likewise said through the interpreter Peter to his persecutors: “You denied the Holy and Righteous One and killed the Prince of eternal life” (Acts III, 14–15).

Joseph’s brothers repented of what they had done. They are told: “Repent” (ibid., 19). They say: “We are guilty concerning our brother” (Gen. XLII, 21). And Reuben says to them: “Did I not tell you, ‘Do not harm the boy’? And you did not listen to me. Behold, his blood is being required” (ibid., 22).

And the Jews who had said to Pilate, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25), say to the apostles: “What shall we do, men and brothers? Tell us” (Acts II, 37).

To prove that they were not spies, Joseph’s brothers testify that they are twelve sons of one father [the printed editions read “but sons”]. They affirm that one is no longer present, although he was the very man to whom they were recounting these things, and that another, the youngest, remains with their father.

When Joseph heard mention of his full brother and burned with desire for him, he said: “By this I shall test whether you are spies: if your younger brother comes with you.” Then he took Simeon from them, bound him before their eyes, and handed him over to custody (Gen. XLII, 15 ff.).

If you consider our Benjamin, the younger brother whom our Joseph seeks, he is that Paul who was formerly Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin, as he himself says (Phil. III, 5; Acts XIII, 21), and who calls himself “the least of the apostles” (1 Cor. XV, 9).

We might understand the bound Simeon—whom fear bound with the three bonds of denial and whom love released—as Peter. But we more correctly recognize that sins themselves are bound and released through him, to whom it was said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you release on earth will be released also in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19).

**CHAPTER XXXI. In the same Joseph, grace is prefigured. The promise made and prefigured. Believed and seen in Genesis.**

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “the promised grace under a figure,” perhaps for “under the figure.”]

43. Joseph ordered his brothers’ sacks to be filled with grain and the price each had brought to be returned (Gen. XLII, 25), so that the grace of our Christ might not be from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Rom. XI, 6).

The second time Joseph’s brothers come with Benjamin, as they had promised (Gen. XLIII, 2); the second time, three thousand from the Jews [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “five thousand.”] come to Christ (Acts II, 41), followed by Paul, the least of the apostles (1 Cor. XV, 9).

Joseph saw his brother Benjamin, born of the same mother, and wept (Gen. XLIII, 29–30). Jesus saw Paul raging against the mother Church and had mercy on him [the Remigian manuscript reads: “God saw”]. For Paul himself says that Jesus appeared to him “as to one untimely born” (1 Cor. XV, 8).

Benjamin was born through such a catastrophe that his mother was brought down into death; hence he was called “son of sorrow” (Gen. XXXV, 18). Our Benjamin, Paul, likewise says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. XV, 9).

Joseph said to the official of his house concerning his brothers [the Remigian manuscript reads: “to the steward”] (Gen. XLIII, 16): “Bring these men into the house, for they shall eat bread with me.” Our Joseph likewise says through the prophet to his brothers: “Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you” (Prov. IX, 5).

Joseph gave gifts to his brothers; and our Joseph, Christ, gave gifts to human beings (Ps. LXVII, 19), when he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples [the Remigian manuscript reads: “to his own people”].

Joseph gave Benjamin, his younger brother, greater gifts than he gave his brothers (Gen. XLV, 22). Our Benjamin, Paul, likewise proclaims this: “I labored more than all of them”—[the Remigian manuscript omits “them”]—“yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. XV, 10).

Again Joseph orders his brothers’ sacks to be filled with grain (Gen. XLIV, 1), and the prices to be returned. Our brothers likewise proclaim that they have received grace upon grace (John I, 16) [this pronoun, “they,” is absent from the printed editions but is found in the Remigian manuscript].

Joseph secretly ordered his cup to be placed in Benjamin’s sack. When it was sought and disturbed his brothers, the cup was found in Benjamin’s sack (Gen. XLIV, 2).

The cup of Christ’s Passion, secretly given through grace in Paul’s body, is recognized there. While proclaiming it, he disturbed the whole synagogue by his words, and he himself confesses that it was found in his own sack when he says: “I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ in my body” (Gal. VI, 17).

When Joseph now wished to make himself known to his brothers, he raised his voice and said: “I am Joseph, your brother. Is my father still alive?” (Gen. XLV, 3). Our Joseph, Christ, likewise said in the Psalms, in order to reveal himself to his brothers: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI, 23), whom he taught to say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9).

Joseph said to his brothers: “Do not be afraid; you did not send me here, but God” (Gen. XLV, 5) [the Remigian manuscript reads “Do not fear”]. Our apostle John likewise says concerning our Joseph: “For God sent his Son into the world for this purpose, that we might live through him” [Note: The Remigian manuscript and the Lyon edition add “also.”] (1 John IV, 9). And he himself says in the Gospel: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to enter into his glory” (Luke XXIV, 26).

**CHAPTER XXXII. Jacob’s descent into Egypt and that of Christ the Lord into the world. The promise made and prefigured. Believed and seen in Genesis.**

44. Jacob, visited at Luz, is commanded to descend into Egypt. For God appeared to him [Note: The Remigian manuscript adds “alone.”] and said: “Do not be afraid to descend into Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation, and your son Joseph shall place his fingers upon your eyes.”

Jacob descended into Egypt with seventy-five souls [the author follows the edition of the Septuagint translators and Stephen in Acts VII, 14. On this matter, see Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVI, chapter forty]. His son Joseph met him, and when Jacob saw him he said: “Now that I see you, my son, I shall gladly die” (Gen. XLVI, 1 ff.).

Something similar is found in our Joseph. For when that venerable old man Simeon—father by age, not by generation—saw Christ, on whose account he was being kept in this light, as in Egypt, until extreme old age, he said: “Now you release your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace. For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 29).

He descended in the number of seventy-five souls. The Davidic psalm also cries out: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV, 1). Since, therefore, “Israel” is interpreted as “seeing God,” it is necessary that everyone illuminated by grace, Jew and Greek, be freed from this Egyptian slavery, although he is oppressed under Pharaoh’s harsh yoke, the devil [the Remigian manuscript reads: “all those illuminated by grace, Jews and Greeks, must be freed”].

The book of Exodus says: “The people grew and multiplied in Egypt” (Exod. I, 7). This comes about through faith in the seed of Abraham, so that it may multiply in Christ, as was promised, like the sand of the sea (Gen. XXII, 17). Although Pharaoh, the raging devil, exacts punishments by which he may kill the innocent, who are to be put to death in the river, imagining that what he sees multiplying must be diminished lest the people increase (Exod. I, 22) [perhaps the text should read “whom he saw multiplying.” The Remigian manuscript immediately has “he saw”].

By God’s command the people are increased through dying, and the power of the raging one is frustrated. The same thing happened to our martyrs, and especially to the little ones who were killed for Christ by Herod (Matt. II, 16): while they were sown as precious grains, a rich harvest of faith sprang up for the Church.

**CHAPTER XXXIII. In Moses, who bore the role of the Mediator of Christ the Lord. The promise made and prefigured of the Mediator. Believed and seen in Exodus.**

45. At that time Moses was born, and he was acceptable to God; he was nourished for three months in his father’s house (Exod. II, 2; Acts VII, 21). These three months correspond to the three periods often mentioned.

When they could no longer conceal him, his mother took a basket, coated it on the outside with bitumen, placed the infant in it, and cast it into the river (Exod. II, 3). Figures follow figures, although all the events signify Christ and the Church.

We find three things enacted in this Moses which are to be compared with our Mediator: namely, the priest who was to come in the flesh, the river water in baptism, and the wood on which he hung upon the cross [the Remigian manuscript reads “we find”; the printed editions read “are found,” which fits less well with what follows; the word “namely” is absent from the manuscript].

Pharaoh’s daughter descended to bathe in the river [the Remigian manuscript reads “to wash”]. Our Moses had consecrated its waters through wood. She recognized that the child was one of the Hebrew infants [the Remigian manuscript reads “she recognized”], took him, and raised him as a son (ibid., 5 ff.).

When the learning of this world descended to Christ, it laid aside its pride, washed in spiritual water, and, receiving the little one as a grown woman through humble grace, was joined to the person of the Church, which, as Christ’s daughter, became a mother. Therefore it is written: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. XLIV, 17). Thus, while she undertook to instruct him, she herself was instructed.

For God chose the foolish things of the world in order to nullify the wisdom of the world (1 Cor. I, 27). All philosophy yielded to Christian teaching, which, in its useful conquest, destroyed its enemies with the weapons of its enemies. Just as Moses, instructed by the Egyptians, immediately conquered the Egyptians, so that all pride might be drowned in the Red Sea as in baptism (Exod. XIV, 22).

Through Moses the children of Israel were freed from the Egyptians (Exod. II, 11 ff.), and through Christ souls are freed from unclean spirits.

When Moses had grown up, he saw an Egyptian doing violence to one of his own people. He avenged him and defended him by killing the Egyptian and burying him in the sand.

Our Moses, the Mediator Christ, does the same: he rescues souls from the power of darkness amid that multitude of Abraham’s spiritual seed which grew like the sand of the sea [the Remigian manuscript reads “spiritual”]. He buried Egypt when the expelled demons cried out: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of David? Have you come to destroy us before the time?” (Matt. VIII, 29).

**CHAPTER XXXIV. In the same Moses, who, like Christ the Lord, brought peace to those who were quarreling. The prediction made and prefigured, by which we are commanded to be peacemakers with those who hate peace. Believed and seen in Genesis.**

[This heading is supplied from the Remigian manuscript.]

46. Moses saw the Hebrews quarreling among themselves on another day and began to reconcile them to peace, saying: “Men, brothers, why do you harm one another?” The man who was doing the wrong said: “Who appointed you ruler or judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” (Exod. II, 13; Acts VII, 26).

Our Moses, the Mediator Christ, cries out through David: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. CXIX, 7) [the Remigian manuscript reads: “They hated … they fought me without cause”]. And elsewhere: “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. XXXIV, 12).

Moses fled because of this speech and became an exile in the land of Midian (Exod. II, 15). Our Moses likewise says: “Behold, fleeing, I went far away and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. LIV, 8).

Moses took as his wife the daughter of Jethro, priest of Midian (Exod. II, 21), signifying that our Mediator took a wife, the Church, from the Gentiles.

“It was said” that Moses was pasturing the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law, in the wilderness (Exod. III, 1). Our Mediator Christ, pasturing the sheep, says: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X, 11).

Moved by a terrifying vision, Moses went to see why fire had descended upon the mountain without consuming the bush (Exod. III, 2). Our Mediator declares: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth,” and he rightly desires that it be kindled more intensely (Luke XXII, 49) [in the Remigian manuscript this passage appears very differently: after “without consuming,” it reads, “Our Mediator affirms that he has come to cast fire upon the earth, which he rightly wishes to be kindled more intensely”].

For he himself says: “I am fire, consuming vices, not human beings.”

When Moses was called and proceeded to climb the mountain, he was told: “Take off the sandals from your feet” (Exod. III, 5), so that the feet of the Mediator might be free and beautiful as they announce good things (Isa. LII, 7; Rom. X, 15) [the Remigian manuscript reads: “so that the free and beautiful feet of the Mediator announcing good things may be …”; the printed editions complete the sense with “announcing good things”].

47. Moses is commanded to go to the children of Israel and to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so that he might free the people of God—whose cry under harsh slavery had risen up—from his land and undertake the future mediation (Exod. XXXVII et seq.) [the Remigian manuscript reads: “undertake the role of the Mediator; he says …”].

Our Mediator says through Matthew: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV, 24).

Moses excuses himself, saying that he is impeded in speech and weak of voice [the Remigian manuscript reads: “slow of tongue and weak of voice”]. Our Mediator likewise says to the Jews: “My word does not take hold in you” (John VIII, 37).

Again, when God urges him to go, Moses excuses himself in every respect, saying: “Lord, provide another whom you may send” (Exod. IV, 13), so that the voice of our Mediator might be signified in the human weakness he assumed: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI, 39).

Moses is told to associate with himself Aaron, his brother: Moses is to undertake the things that concern God, Aaron those that concern the people. Signs and wonders are given to him in the hand and in the rod (Gen. IV, 14) [the wording is emended from the Remigian manuscript; the editions had “and what signs,” which makes less sense].

Our Mediator is likewise told: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession; you shall rule them with an iron rod” (Ps. II, 8).

We may understand that Paul, chosen to speak to the people, was signified by Aaron. Concerning him our Mediator, pointing him out to Ananias, says: “This man is a chosen instrument for me, to carry my name before the nations, kings, and the children of Israel” (Acts IX, 15).

Thus Moses and Aaron, preaching to the Hebrew people and affirming that they had been sent by God to rescue them from Egypt, strengthened them; and the people, hearing them, knelt and worshiped them and believed when they performed signs (Exod. IV, 30).

When Paul preached to the Gentiles and confidently promised salvation of souls through Christ to Jews, he converted the people with astonishing speed to the knowledge of God by performing signs, and rescued the kings from the future judgment of God [the Remigian manuscript reads “terrified them,” and not improperly, for the author may allude to Acts XXIV, 25: “As he discoursed about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became terrified and answered …”].

**CHAPTER XXXV. In the same Moses, who, like Christ the Lord, killed the devil. The prediction made and prefigured, by which the devil is conquered by God’s ministers. Believed and seen in Exodus.**

48. Moses and Aaron entered Pharaoh’s presence and, rather than merely recounting the words they had heard by divine command, displayed the signs that had been given (Exod. V, 1 ff.).

The rod that Moses carried in his hand was thrown down before Pharaoh and became a serpent. Pharaoh’s magicians too, so that they might be overcome by divine power, were permitted to perform such signs; they threw down their rods and themselves displayed forms of serpents [the Remigian manuscript reads “they too,” referring to the rods]. But Moses’ serpent swallowed the magicians’ serpents (Exod. VII, 10 ff.), signifying that the rod of our leader Christ’s teaching consumed, by divine power, all the doctrines of pagans and heretics [the Remigian manuscript reads “the rod and teaching”].

These things were not displayed merely to signify through this figurative action, but also so that the proclamations of the prophet David might resound, when he says: “The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies” (Ps. CIX, 2) [Note: The particle “so that” is absent from the older printed editions and from the Remigian manuscript, although it seems useful to the correct sense of the passage. That manuscript reads: “Not merely does this figurative action signify, but the proclamations of the prophet David also resound, saying …”].

Moses displayed another sign before the people: he placed his hand inside his breast, drew it out, and it became leprous like snow; then, when he put it back and drew it out again, it was restored to its own color (Exod. IV, 6).

The hand placed in the breast signifies prayer for sin, as David says: “My prayer returned into my breast” (Ps. XXXIV, 13). And when the hand drawn from the breast displayed snow, it signified that, through the prayer poured out by the Mediator Christ the Lord for us, our sins too are cleansed.

Thus he himself shows through Isaiah: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isa. I, 18) [the Remigian manuscript reads “like crimson”]. And the Church sings to him: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L, 9) [the Remigian manuscript reads “and to him”; the editions read “and what”].

For “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Lord, and he himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John II, 1).

**CHAPTER XXXVI. In the same Moses, when the devil is beaten with scourges like Pharaoh. The plagues already foretold are presented to hardened Pharaoh and his people, by which he is judged. Believed and seen in Exodus.**

[This title is absent from the Remigian manuscript, in which the preceding title reads: “The prediction made and prefigured, in which the devil is beaten with scourges like Pharaoh. Believed and seen in Exodus.” The final words are absent from the printed editions.]

49. As was promised to Abraham (Gen. XV, 14), the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians had held captive for a long time, at last reluctantly release them; and Pharaoh himself, soon destined to perish with his people in a fitting destruction and punishment, released them (Exod. VII ff.).

We have undertaken, with the Lord’s help, to demonstrate in this way that the ten plagues inflicted upon Egypt correspond to the ten commandments received by the people in the wilderness, so that their mutual correspondence may be established [the Douai edition reads “are confirmed”].

The first plague of the Egyptians was that, through Moses, the waters were changed into blood. The first commandment contains this: “Hear, Israel: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. You shall have no gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself any likeness” (Deut. VI, 4; Exod. XX, 2) [the Remigian manuscript reads “it contains”].

Those who, therefore, abandon the one true God and serve false gods wallow in flesh and blood; and “flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. XV, 50). For their corrupted morals deserved to possess a corrupted element of water.

The waters are therefore changed into blood because, sacrificing their sons and daughters to demons [the Remigian manuscript reads “to demons”], they poured out innocent blood (Ps. CV, 37–38), rejecting the true God Christ, the fountain of pure fluid. The woman healed through the flow of blood (Matt. IX, 22; Luke VIII, 44) demonstrated the soul rescued from the flow of idolatry by his grace.

[The Remigian manuscript inserts here: “Believed and seen in Exodus.”]

The second plague of the Egyptians was a multitude of frogs bursting forth, defiling all Egypt with foul filth (Exod. VIII, 3). The second commandment in the law is also: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. For the Lord will not cleanse such a person” (Exod. XX, 7) [the Remigian manuscript reads: “For the Lord God did not command such a thing.”]

50. Thus every heretic, perjurer, and sacrilegious person, while his tongue utters something other than the name of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0762D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “than is the name of the Lord God.”], cries out against God, like frogs, with the stench of his disputation. “With deceitful lips and with a double heart” (Ps. 11:3) they speak evil. Nor are those who do not wash away the filth accumulated in the pool of the rebaptized, but rather pile up sins, improperly compared with these creatures.

The THIRD PLAGUE OF THE EGYPTIANS IS gnats, vibrating throughout the air and also afflicting the Egyptians with their pestilential bite in the midst of the summer heat [Note: [Col. 0762D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “infecting.”]. In this plague every doctrine of the magicians failed; and they acknowledged that it was the finger of God, while they themselves too were afflicted [Note: [Col. 0762D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “they themselves also being afflicted.”]. Their cunning therefore remained empty and vain (Exod. 8:17–19).

The third commandment in the law is also that the soul which does not observe the Sabbath rest shall perish from its people (Exod. 20:9–10). The prophet David announces this rest in the person of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0762D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “declares,”] saying: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. 45:12). Those, therefore, who make a vow and offer themselves to God, devoting themselves to his word, observe a spiritual Sabbath, like Mary, who chose the better part (Luke 10:43). Turning away from this, they are injured by the pestilential bite of the aforesaid plague in the soul that is to be redeemed, when they become entangled in worldly cares through strangulation [Note: [Col. 0762D] The Remigius manuscript reads this instead of the printed text: “in the soul that is to be redeemed,”] by the leader Jesus, who is Lord of the Sabbath (Luke 6:5).

51. THE FOURTH PLAGUE OF THE EGYPTIANS IS cynomyia, that is, dog-flies, which inflict punishment by their bites even upon the hidden parts of the body (Exod. 8:24). The fourth commandment in the law is also that parents are to be honored (Exod. 20:12). This is the first commandment referred to human beings, since the preceding ones appear to have been assigned to the Divinity [Note: [Col. 0762D] The Remigius manuscript adds here: “the three preceding ones.”]. Those who do not honor their parents with the respect prescribed by the commandment, like dogs exercising the madness of their own foulness, cannot live long in the land [Note: [Col. 0762D] We emend from the Remigius manuscript. The printed editions had thus far: “far away.”]. Nor does the Lord say in the Gospel that what is holy should be given to such people (Matt. 7:6). From their company the Canaanite woman, cleansed by faith, obtained both grace for herself and healing for her daughter through a humble and devout barking, without any preceding merits (Matt. 15:27).

THE FIFTH PLAGUE OF THE EGYPTIANS IS the sudden death of all cattle and beasts of burden (Exod. 9:6). The fifth commandment of the law is also: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13). Therefore not only those who rage with the sword, but also those who rage with hatred, are murderers [Col. 0763A]. For the apostle John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). Such people fall like Egyptian animals in a sudden attack, because every murderer does not have abiding life within himself [Note: [Col. 0763D] The Remigius manuscript adds here the word “eternal.”] (ibid.).

THE SIXTH PLAGUE OF THE EGYPTIANS IS swelling blisters and oozing sores (Exod. 9:9). The sixth commandment of the law is also: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14). What adulterers suffer in their soul is shown by this closely joined plague. Unless the most shameful sores [Note: [Col. 0763D] The printed editions had “of the worst”; the Remigius manuscript has “of the most shameful.”] of love and swelling lust disturbed the mind’s reason, an adulterer would certainly not be one; nor, as it is written, would he acquire the destruction of his soul through lack of understanding (Prov. 6:32). Although people of this kind are also punished here by human laws, God will judge fornicators and adulterers as well, as our Paul says (Heb. 13:4) [Note: [Col. 0763D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “but God will judge …”].

THE SEVENTH PLAGUE OF THE EGYPTIANS IS hail mixed with fire, overturning not only every animal but also the trees and shrubs themselves (Exod. 9:23). The seventh commandment is: “You shall not steal” (Exod. 20:15). [Note: [Col. 0763D] The Remigius manuscript has a very different version: “For the thief is compared to hail; for he too, having secretly broken through walls, brings this upon houses … the thief is liable.”] The comparison is this: a thief brings upon other people’s walls and houses what raging hail brings upon the fields; and he is subject to the general law which says: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16).

52. THE EIGHTH PLAGUE OF THE EGYPTIANS IS a multitude of locusts, tormenting everything and destroying it from the roots (Exod. 10:13). The eighth commandment in the law is also: “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor” (Exod. 20:16) [Note: [Col. 0763D] So the Remigius manuscript reads. The printed editions have: “You shall not say”; more recent editions: “Do not say.”]. For the fabricator of falsehoods, inventing many varied things, gnaws away like a locust at another’s reputation, life, and actions, until he utterly destroys from the roots the person against whom he invents his falsehoods. But a false witness will not go unpunished (Prov. 19:5, 9).

THE NINTH PLAGUE OF THE EGYPTIANS IS the thickest darkness, filled with images and deadly terrors (Exod. 10:22). The ninth commandment of the law is also: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (ibid. 20:17). What is worse than evil desire, which so completely blinds the mind that, forgetting not only the fear of God but also the very penalties of the laws and a dishonorable death, no light remains in the adulterer, whom deadly darkness entirely occupies? [Note: [Col. 0763D] The Remigius manuscript omits the verb “is.”] But those whom grace frees from these things it admonishes and addresses through the Apostle: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Eph. 5:8). [Note: [Col. 0763D] So it is read in the Remigius manuscript. In the printed editions, however: “because deadly darkness does not entirely occupy them.”]

THE TENTH PLAGUE OF THE EGYPTIANS IS the death of all the firstborn (Exod. 12:19). The tenth commandment in the law is also: “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor” (ibid. 20:18). That evil desire is primal is shown by the case of Pharaoh the devil: he himself also coveted to be what he was not (Isa. 14:12) [Note: [Col. 0763D] Thus the Remigius manuscript reads. The printed codices instead have: “Pharaoh the devil showed through that”; except Lugdunensis, in which the particle “through” is absent. In others it appears as an addition, marked in different type or by two brackets.]. And Adam, through desire, cast himself into death (Gen. 3:5) [Note: [Col. 0764D] Thus the Remigius manuscript reads. Lugdunensis instead has: “who through desire rushed into death”; Duacensis and Coloniensis: “who through desire rushed,” omitting “himself.” Lugdunensis, however, has “who rushed desire into death.”].

But the vices of his angels, through whom death entered the world, our leader slew as the firstborn of the Egyptians in this world as though in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0764D] Thus the Remigius manuscript reads. Other printed editions have “in the primitive,” that is, “in the firstborn.”], while he teaches us to renounce the devil, his pomp and his angels [Note: [Col. 0764D] The Remigius manuscript lacks these words and reads: “the devil and his pomp.”], so that where sin abounded, grace might abound still more (Rom. 5:20).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The Passover figured, and Christ’s passage to the Father.

The promise made and figured. In Exodus believed and seen. [Note: [Col. 0764D] Thus the Remigius manuscript and the Lugdunensis edition. Other codices have: “the prediction.”]

[Col. 0764A]

53. Passover, which means passage, in which the whole action of our faith and the mystery of the Lord’s Passion is enacted, God commands Moses to arrange in this way: the Hebrews were to ask the Egyptians for vessels of gold and silver and clothing; having taken these, they were to strip the Egyptians, who were lending them under the pressure of necessity caused by the loss of their firstborn (Exod. 12:29). While fearing for themselves, the Egyptians drove out the Hebrews as quickly as possible, together with everything they had given them, so that, as the prophet says, “the recompense of their labors might be restored to the righteous” (Wis. 10:17). For the Hebrews had built two cities for the Egyptians, and therefore those spoils were not taken by theft, but were repayment of wages (Exod. 12:4 ff.).

The mystical passage itself was as follows: by divine command, a spotless year-old lamb was to be killed throughout the dwellings; the doorposts of the houses were to be smeared with its blood; none of its bones was to be broken; it was to be eaten with bitter herbs and unleavened bread, with the loins girded and in complete haste; and nothing of it was to be left until morning. How all these things, though figures, were fulfilled, the authority of the Gospel relates. It commands us to eat the flesh of the lamb until the morning that will have no evening—that is, until the Resurrection—not in the old leaven, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity [Note: [Col. 0764D] The Remigius manuscript adds: “and truth.”] (1 Cor. 5:8). The doorposts are marked with blood, and on their foreheads his cross shines forth [Note: [Col. 0764D] The Remigius manuscript omits the pronoun “his.”]. It was said “with bitter herbs” of those who pass their life mourning in bitterness. But blessed are they, for they shall be comforted (Matt. 5:5).

54. We understand that the Egyptians were stripped by our people for this reason: all worldly knowledge, with which they were puffed up and arrogantly exalted themselves above others, and moral wisdom passed over to Christ, so that he might possess it in humble and upright faith, while the people rightly proud of it might lose it.

The Hebrews, expelled, are led through the wilderness (Exod. 14:3), because for every Christian who renounces the world there is necessary the narrow and constricted way that leads to life (Matt. 7:14). A pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night showed this people the way (Exod. 13:21), because the steps of the Christian are directed by the Lord, and he will take pleasure in his ways [Note: [Col. 0764D] The Remigius manuscript reads in a different order: “The Christian’s steps are from the Lord … and he will delight in his way.”] (Ps. 34:23).

When the wilderness and the shore of the Red Sea received the people, Pharaoh hardened his heart and, in order that he might perish together with all his people, pursued the fugitives with his chariots and horsemen (Exod. 14:6). This is what the raging devil does with his vices and angels, pursuing our people as they flee from him. For everyone who renounces these things, hastening toward baptism as toward the Red Sea, flees from the enemy [Note: [Col. 0764D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “so that he may find the Savior.”], so that the Savior may find him.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. In baptism, as in the Red Sea.

The promise made and figured in baptism [Note: [Col. 0764D] These words, “made and,” are absent from the Remigius manuscript.]. In Exodus believed and seen.

[Col. 0765A]

55. The Lord said to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me? Tell the children of Israel to join together, and you lift up your staff over the sea and divide it, and let the children of Israel enter through the midst of the sea on dry ground. For I will harden the heart of Pharaoh and all the Egyptians, so that they may pursue them, and I will be glorified in Pharaoh and in all his army” (Exod. 14:15 ff.).

When this was done, the sea, carrying out the judgment of its Creator and King, fulfilled the commands of the divine sentence [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “the divine sentence”; perhaps it should be read as “the divine sentence commanded.”]. Then, in punishing the rebels, it provided a way for the innocent, cutting apart its waters and suspending its depths, so that they might walk over dry dust; and, drawing its waters back upon itself, it plunged the enemies into the depths (ibid. 22 ff.) [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Lugdunensis edition has: “Behold, the water as avenger.”].

And the avenging water, consecrated by the word, reddened by blood, and struck by the wood of the cross in the mystery of the staff, provided salvation to those coming to the Savior [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “to those coming.”]. It thrust sins, together with their author the devil, into the depths, just as it thrust the Egyptians into the depths with their king. This is our God, of whom the prophet Micah says: “He will again have compassion on us; he will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Mic. 7:19).

After harsh exiles [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “after harsh destructions.”], after the labors of the wilderness and the passage of the Red Sea (Exod. 15:17), the victorious palm received the people of God. Although the bitter water of Marah wearied the thirsty, when the wood cast into it made it sweet (ibid. 23), it showed that the Christian who is thirsty, as soon as he has drunk the bitter cup of suffering, is to be freed from all bitterness by the sweetness of the wood of the cross.

Hence Paul also says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “of my Lord.”] Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). The same place, which provided that people with rest at twelve springs of water (Exod. 15:17), was consecrated in our mysteries by seventy palm trees. For after baptism, the streams of the twelve apostles’ springs overflow with pure teaching to satisfy hearts, and the sacred psalm resounds: “Bless the Lord God in the churches, from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. 67:27).

In the seventy palm trees, the whole number of holy martyrs is signified in their thousands. They contend for the truth even unto death and receive the palm of the heavenly calling (Phil. 3:14). The Apocalypse of the apostle John also designates them, saying: “I saw a great multitude which no one could number, from every tribe and people and tongue. And they were clothed in white garments, and palms were in their hands” (Rev. 7:9)—the palms that Wisdom gave to those who conquered [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “the palm of wisdom.”], Wisdom which was exalted in Kadesh (Sir. 24:18).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The heavenly bread in the manna, which is Christ.

The manna promised from heaven. [Note: [Col. 0765D] Thus all the ancient editions read, although the word manna is now considered neuter in gender when it is used for heavenly bread.]

56. When the breads that they had brought with them from Egypt had been consumed, the people asked Moses for bread with murmuring, while also desiring the meat of Egypt (Exod. 16:2). But that mediator, Moses, quickly obtained from the Lord both bread and meat for them [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “so often.”]. The people were ordered to receive bread in the morning and meat in the evening (ibid. 8) [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “in the morning.”].

But these things were figures of our own. First the people received and ate that holy bread which descended from heaven; afterward, the flesh of Christ accomplished in the Passion, concerning which the Lord himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

The holy people ate manna according to a fixed daily measure. If anyone exceeded it, he threw it away, corrupted and putrefied by worms (Exod. 16:16), frustrated by his desire for greed and excess [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “to become infested.”]. The teacher of the nations, Paul, reproves such people, saying: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these; for those who wish to become rich fall into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction and perdition. For the root of all evils is greed” (1 Tim. 6:8–9) [Note: [Col. 0766D] The remaining words of the apostolic passage are taken from the Remigius manuscript; they are omitted in the printed editions.].

This is the rot and these are the worms of those who, while the world is perishing, desire their riches to increase and are not content with daily bread.

But the same people again murmured against Moses in the wilderness because they lacked water to drink. When Moses asked the Lord, he was told: “I will go before you,” he said, “at Horeb; and I will stand upon the rock, and you, coming, shall strike the rock, and water will come out, and my people will drink” (Exod. 17:6, according to the Septuagint) [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “and water will come out.”]. This happened. David bears witness: “He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink, as from the great abyss” (Ps. 77:15).

What this rock was, the apostle Paul explains, assigning to Christ the Lord everything that was then done in mystery: “Our fathers,” he says, “were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “They drank from the spiritual rock.”]. “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10 ff.).

This rock, which also satisfies us, says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst; but the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:13–14) [Note: [Col. 0766D] The word “I” is absent from the Remigius manuscript.]. This rock, struck on the cross, produced blood and water (John 19:34) [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript adds: “with which sacraments we are daily soberly inebriated.”], with which we are soberly inebriated.

## CHAPTER XL. To conquer enemies by the sign of the cross.

The promise figured, by which we are commanded to conquer all our adversaries by the sign of the cross. In Exodus believed and seen.

[Col. 0766C]

57. Amalek and every hostile people with its leader confronted this people, in whom all our figured action was enacted [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “was involved.”], declaring war against the inexperienced multitude, which it believed it could easily overcome (Exod. 17:8) [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “which it believed it could easily overcome.”].

When the battle was joined and the adversaries were prevailing greatly, Moses extended his hands toward God and expressed the likeness of one crucified. By this sign, when Moses’ hands drooped, the enemy was stronger and prevailed [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript adds: “while Moses’ hands remained steady, Aaron and Hur supported his hands and strengthened them with a certain firmness; when they fell …”]. But when Aaron and Hur supported Moses’ hands and made them steady with a certain firmness, Amalek fell and fled, and the whole of it was destroyed (ibid. 11 ff.).

If we understand here the sign of our Mediator, while we recall through David singing, “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2), and recall that in his Passion the sun and moon changed their appearance and course (Luke 23:44), what hostile spirit or inimical power could oppose this sign, and not rather flee altogether [Note: [Col. 0766D] The Remigius manuscript adds the word “all”]?

Provided, however, that the hope of the combatant depends upon the hands of the crucified one, through whom we are daily rescued [Note: [Col. 0767A] The Remigius manuscript reads: “we are rescued.”] from the power of darkness (Col. 1:13).

58. Now, returning through all the figured actions of the time before the law, when that people received all the things that happened as promises, so that it too, looking far ahead by faith, left for posterity things to be believed and seen [Note: [Col. 0767A] The older editions and the Remigius manuscript lack the word “far”; in place of “much farther” the manuscript reads “many things.”].

Since the people was led to Mount Sinai through definite predictions and promises, where Moses, receiving the law from the Lord, was to unfold heavenly ordinances for governing the tribes [Note: [Col. 0768A] The Remigius manuscript reads: “the law of the Lord”; and “the heavenly ordinances might be opened.”]—hence I think that they are now called Jews, as though they were “those bearing or following the law of God”—recognize, reader, that up to this point the time before the law has been concluded, like one day rising from the four cardinal points of the world: namely, from the patriarchal leaders Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, with the ray of the East shining through King and priest Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0768A] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Melchizedek the king and priest.”], within the twelvefold number of the hours.

Those descended from them are also called our patriarchs, so that another time, concluded toward evening under the law, may arise like another day beginning through the remaining numbers.

# PART TWO. THE TIME OF THE LAW.

[Col. 0767]

## CHAPTER I. The laws given on the mountain, and the commands of Christ the Lord on the mountain.

The prediction made and figured. In Exodus believed and seen.

[Col. 0767B]

1. Calling Moses to Mount Sinai, God gave him the law written on stone tablets, so that he might hand it over to the people, who, faithfully observing it, would receive the promised land (Exod. 19:20 and 34). But our Mediator, Jesus the Lord—whose figure Moses also bore—ascended the mountain with his disciples (Matt. 5:1), and wrote the law of how human beings would become blessed not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts, by the Spirit of God (2 Cor. 3:3). Through this law, those who keep his commands will possess not earth but heaven and eternal life [Note: [Col. 0767D] The Regius manuscript reads: “who … will possess not earth but heaven and eternal life.”].

But for the rest of the people, after the ten commandments had been set forth, Moses transmitted heavenly ordinances: concerning the succession of heirs; concerning the absence of an heir; that a faithful friend and member of the household should succeed in the place of an heir [Note: [Col. 0767D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “should succeed in the place of an heir.”]; concerning restitution fourfold for theft; concerning deposits or loans taken away by accident or by some act of violence; concerning the punishment of adulterers; concerning a violated virgin in the countryside or in the city; concerning a pregnant woman who is struck; “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,” and the other matters in which the authority of divine law is contained (Exod. 21 ff.) [Note: [Col. 0767D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “which are contained in that law.”].

The people received the law from Moses with this testimony, by which they promised that they would do everything. Moses therefore slaughtered a calf in sacrifice, took its blood as a testimony, and sprinkled both the people and the book with hyssop and scarlet wool, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded you” (Exod. 24:8; Heb. 9:19).

To this our Mediator, Christ the Lord, who did not abolish but fulfilled the law (Matt. 5:17), consecrated the New Testament with his own blood, not only for the free and powerful but also for the lowly and slaves who carry out his commandments, not without hyssop, which he drank mixed with vinegar in his Passion (Matt. 27:48; Mark 15:36; John 19:29) [Note: [Col. 0767D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “mixed with vinegar.”]. In this Testament there is no distinction of persons. For the apostle Paul says: “There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. 3:28), who is the undivided and everlasting inheritance of the faithful.

Through the same Apostle he commands that faith be kept toward one’s neighbor who lends or deposits something. “O Timothy,” he says, “guard the good deposit” (2 Tim. 1:14). And again: “Not each one looking to his own interests, but also to those of others” (1 Cor. 13:5; Phil. 2:4) [Note: [Col. 0768D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “but those things which are …”]. And through the prophet Solomon: “For the faithful person the whole world is wealth; but for the unfaithful, not even a penny.” Paul likewise says: “Let the one who used to steal steal no longer” (Eph. 4:28).

He also fears the serpent-like corruption of the devil for the chaste virgin (2 Cor. 11:3), when, conceiving her with devout affection, he declares himself to be pregnant in spirit, saying: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). He desires to bring them forth unharmed in every respect when he says: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15).

2. Our Mediator also added the commands of the new law, tempering the vengeance of the old Testament [Note: [Col. 0768D] The word “Testament” is absent from the Remigius manuscript.]. For although there he established that adulterers were to be punished (Lev. 20:10), here he frees the adulteress with the mercy by which he does not destroy the law, saying: “Go, and do not sin again” (John 8:11) [Note: [Col. 0768D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “he does not destroy it.”].

Not only is adultery forbidden, but one must not even consent to desire with the eyes (Matt. 5:27). Murder is not only something that must not be committed; whoever hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). An eye for an eye is in no way to be demanded; rather, evil is not to be repaid with evil. Whoever takes away a tunic is to be given the cloak as well. Whoever strikes the cheek is to be offered the other also. Whoever presses one into service is to be accompanied for twice the distance. Good is to be done to enemies [Note: [Col. 0768D] The Remigius manuscript adds: “by praying.”]. Prayer is to be made for persecutors (Matt. 5:38 ff.).

And the other commands imposed in the Gospel by the heavenly legislator himself are shown not to be contrary to the law by the fact that there it was commanded that, if an enemy’s animal fell on the road, it should be raised and not passed by; that one should not speak deceitfully with one’s neighbor; that a poor man’s pledge should not be retained until evening; that in the seventh year the crops sown should not be harvested, and all the produce of that year should be left for proselytes, widows, and orphans; and that in the same year Hebrew slaves should be given their freedom; that tithes of all produce and the first fruits should be brought into the house of the Lord; that, when the seventh year had been completed, a debt should not be reclaimed, with pledges also released; and that in the fiftieth year all estates that had been bound by the obligation of guarantees should be restored, without the money being recovered (Exod. 23:4–5 and following).

And when all the commands contained, as I have said, in the New and Old Testaments are examined, they are found to contradict one another in no respect, since in the New Testament also not insignificant and terrible examples of vengeance have occurred: when the proud person is handed over to the unclean spirit so that he may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim. 1:20); when adulterers are handed over to Satan for the eternal destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus (1 Cor. 5:5); when Ananias and Sapphira, deceivers and liars, are punished by sudden death (Acts 5:5, 9); when the person who lacks a wedding garment is thrown, bound hand and foot, into the outer darkness (Matt. 22:12)—the garment that is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1:5).

And whatever other matters from the ancient signs are known to have been fulfilled in the New Testament were consecrated, as has been said, together with the people themselves by the sacred blood of the Mediator.

## CHAPTER II. The house of God in the holy Church.

The promise made and figured. [Note: [Col. 0769D] The Remigius manuscript omits the first title and adds here: “the house of God.” It has the rest as the printed editions.] In Exodus believed and seen.

[Col. 0769B]

3. The following is said to the same Moses: “See that you make the tabernacle according to what was shown to you on the holy mountain” (Exod. 26:30). It is also prescribed from what offered materials that tabernacle should arise. “The children of Israel,” God says, “shall give as an offering blue wool, twisted linen, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet” (Exod. 25:3) [Note: [Col. 0769D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “as an offering.”]. From these, the tents of the tabernacle, and likewise the priestly vestment, were made with varied workmanship, so that all the mystical things might be revealed in the time of the future Church.

Divine authority also commands that coverings for the tabernacle be made of blue skins, other skins dyed red, and eleven curtains of goats’ hair (Exod. 26:1 ff.). The testimonies of the law itself resound that all these things were signs.

In the blue color there is a certain pallor joined with splendor, corresponding to fasts and almsgiving. Hence the holy archangel Raphael also says to Tobit: “Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving” (Tob. 12:8). In fasting pallor shines forth; in almsgiving, splendor, and these display the figure of blue [Note: [Col. 0769D] Thus the Remigius manuscript reads. All the printed editions have: “shows.”].

Fine linen, clean, as the Apocalypse says, is the righteous deeds of the saints (Rev. 19:8). That it is said to be twisted signifies: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

Purple is a royal garment, with which our King, Christ the Lord, was clothed in his Passion. In the twice-dyed scarlet the holy martyrdoms glow: they are dyed once in the baptism of Christ in blood and are dyed again in the blood of their own outpouring [Note: [Col. 0769D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “dyed again.”]. For the Lord himself was dyed once in the Jordan and again in his Passion, concerning which he says to his disciples: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and you do not know it” (Luke 12:50). The red and blue skins bear witness to this (Exod. 26:31).

The two sides of the tabernacle extend one hundred by one hundred cubits; the other two front sides, fifty by fifty—as though mercy and truth were meeting one another, and righteousness and peace were kissing one another (Ps. 84:11). The four joined sides, with their corners, display a tabernacle worthy of God [Note: [Col. 0769D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “demonstrate.”], the future temple of God, the Church, which in the hundredth and fiftieth number of psalms sings mercy and judgment to its Lord (Ps. 100:1).

4. Nor is it without mystery that the tabernacle is covered above with eleven curtains of goats’ hair (Exod. 26:14) [Note: [Col. 0769D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “not without this mystery.”]. This shows that the whole world is guilty before God and lives under repentance [Note: [Col. 0769D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “under penance.”]. For the number of the psalm begins: “Save me, O God, for the holy one has failed” (Ps. 11:2). And it explains why he has failed: “For the truths have been diminished among the children of men”; and for their salvation Truth itself descended from heaven [Note: [Col. 0769D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “descended from heaven,”] and deigned to dwell with human beings on earth.

The inner parts of the tabernacle are adorned with the following things. Twenty columns on each side, made of imperishable wood (Exod. 27:10), signify not only the holy apostles but also the teachers of the Churches. Paul also points them out, saying: “Peter and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship” (Gal. 2:9). For Barnabas was received into the apostolate in due order, when the Lord commanded and said: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).

In this work Wisdom herself, building her house, set up seven pillars (Prov. 9:1). When the earth had fallen away through invading sins, she herself strengthened her pillars (Ps. 74:4). The number of these pillars in the two sides of the tabernacle is forty [Note: [Col. 0769D] We emend with the aid of the Remigius–Remensis manuscript, and indeed in accordance with the text of Exodus 27:10–11. The printed editions had “eleven,” a reading contradicted by the author’s immediate application to the fortieth day of the Ascension.], signifying the fortieth day of the Lord’s Ascension, when he said to his disciples: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49) [Note: [Col. 0770D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “with strength.”].

The columns are joined by three bars each, because the teachers of the Churches are beneficially bound by the bond of the Trinity—faith, hope, and charity. They stand on silver bases and have golden capitals, as though in works of mercy [Note: [Col. 0770D] The Remigius manuscript does not have the word “mercy,” but reads: “in works and in holiness.”], so that all the beauty of the columns may arise from virginal holiness [Note: [Col. 0770D] “From bases of silver and golden capitals, as though in works of mercy” is the reading of the Remigius manuscript. The printed editions have “from vessels,” apparently corruptly, as seems to follow from Exodus.].

The Holy of Holies is in the interior of the tabernacle, possessing the ark of the covenant filled with mysteries (Heb. 9:3). Into it the priest enters once a year with the blood of another [Note: [Col. 0770D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “the priest enters”; the printed editions: “the priests enter.” See Heb. 9:7.]. From it, on receiving the divine response, that Word resounds which, assuming flesh for our redemption, consecrated the ark not of the old but of the New Testament: “In it are hidden all the treasures of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0770D] The Remigius manuscript adds: “and knowledge.”] and knowledge” (Col. 2:3).

The true high priest himself entered once into the holy places with his own blood (Heb. 9:12), since Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many (ibid. 28). To him the prophet says: “Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your holiness” (Ps. 131:8).

What else are we to understand in the table that was set out [Note: [Col. 0770D] Thus the Remigius manuscript reads. The printed editions have: “and the ark.”] and in the altar, which received the sacred flesh and the sacrifice of the one offering it, except the cross, on which our Lamb was sacrificed? He himself is priest and victim, establishing the consecrated bread—his sacred body—on his table.

A sevenfold lamp, kindled by the Spirit, shines upon the whole tabernacle. “Its lightning is like light” [Note: [Col. 0770D] The Remigius manuscript adds “is”; the same manuscript reads: “the hearts of the devout are,” where the printed editions have: “of the devout, namely.”]. The courts of this spiritual tabernacle, however, are the hearts of the devout who confess and praise God. The prophet David speaks of them: “His courts in hymns; confess to him” [Col. 0770D] (Ps. 99:4).

## CHAPTER III. Aaron’s priesthood figured in Christ.

The promise made and figured. In Exodus believed and seen.

[Col. 0771A]

5. The Lord commanded Moses to consecrate Aaron, his brother, to the priesthood, anointing him with sanctified oil (Exod. XXIX, 21); thus the very name of anointing would point to Christ the Lord, “anointed above his companions” [Note: [Col. 0771D] The Remigian manuscript adds “the high priest,” perhaps “of priests.”] (Ps. XLIV, 8). Aaron’s vestment too is described with mystical significance. “You shall clothe him,” he says, “with a full-length tunic of hyacinth-colored wool, and you shall place the ephod upon his shoulders” (Exod. XXVIII, 5). Two emerald stones [Note: [Col. 0771D] The Vulgate has “onyxes.” The Septuagint translators have “emeralds.”], each engraved with one of the names of the sons of Israel, from which little chains of the purest gold, running along the two ends of the ephod, should be attached (Ibid., 14 and 25) [Note: [Col. 0771D] The Remigian manuscript has “upon each shoulder, from which…”].

There was also a square breastpiece of varied colors and precious stones—twelve in number—to be placed upon the priest’s chest, binding together the two principal parts of the ephod. A belt was likewise to be given him around his loins, and at the hem of the full-length tunic they were commanded to place fifty golden bells, with an equal number of pomegranates among the bells, so that the entire garment, fashioned with varied workmanship from the materials mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0771D] The Remigian manuscript has “things.”], might shine.

These instructions were also given concerning his head: a turban of clean linen, and a headband from which a plate bearing an inscription, hanging as a title, would consecrate the priest’s head and forehead (Ibid., 16 ff.). Each of these things suits our Lord Christ the priest. For the turban of linen upon his head signifies, as we have said, the righteousness of the saints (Apoc. XIX, 8). Since Christ is the head of every man (I Cor. XI, 3), from him comes all righteousness.

The royal mitre indicates priesthood and spiritual marriage. The inscribed title is the one that Pilate placed upon our priest in his passion (John XIX, 19). The full-length tunic signifies the mercies of our God, of which the Apostle says: “Put on, as God’s elect, the mercies of compassion” (Coloss. III, 12).

The ephod, however, displays his sovereignty, of which Isaiah says: “A son has been given to you, and sovereignty has been placed upon his shoulders” (Isa. IX, 6). The two stones upon the shoulders are the two commandments concerning love of God and neighbor. Upon them are contained the engraved names of the twelve tribes, already designating in this number the twelve disciples, whom our Priest carried upon his shoulders in perfect love. “Having loved his disciples,” says the evangelist John, “he loved them to the end” (John XIII, 1). [Note: [Col. 0771D] The Remigian manuscript adds, “And from these.”]

The little chains bearing the bosses are the fruits of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Gal. V, 22).

The breastpiece upon the chest signifies that all the teaching of the high priest consists in precious conduct, so that he may have, as the Apostle says, “a reasonable service” (Rom. XII, 1).

The ninety-second Psalm shows our priest girded: “The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself” (Ps. XCII, 1).

The fifty bells and the equal number of pomegranates signify the tongues of the Churches, which, through the Holy Spirit, divided in the appearance of fire, settled upon the disciples on the day of Pentecost (Acts II, 3). The number itself also indicates this: through the pomegranates, the whole Church throughout the world, containing peoples joined together like seeds within them in the bond of peace (Ephes. IV, 3) and grace, covers them all with one garment of love [Note: [Col. 0771D] The Remigian manuscript has “covering.”].

As the apostles rang out in the bells, the pomegranates were immediately stirred, saying in the Acts of the Apostles: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans by birth?” (Acts II, 7). “And how do we each hear in our own language in which we were born?” And it follows: “For they were magnifying God in various languages” (Ibid., 4).

But all these things are moved by the steps of the free priest as he enters the Holy of Holies (Hebr. IX, 12), where our Mediator has now ascended on our behalf, to appear before the face of God.

## CHAPTER IV. The vengeance upon the peoples who transgressed and did not keep Christ’s commandments. A prediction made and figured. Believed and seen in Exodus.

6. While the things mentioned above were being commanded Moses to be made on Mount Sinai (Exod. XXX, 1), the people, having transgressed against God, incurred the crime of idolatry. Through Aaron he fashioned a calf from gold [Note: [Col. 0771D] So the Remigian manuscript reads. The printed editions have, “A calf is fashioned through Aaron”; but the reading of the manuscript seems more coherent.], and in insult to the true God offered it victims and sacrifices, saying: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Ibid., 4). “And they forgot God, who saved them, who did great things in Egypt, wondrous deeds in the land of Ham, and terrifying things at the Red Sea” (Ps. CV, 29).

Through our Priest, such apostate souls are also rebuked in the Gospel. For he says: “If I had not done among them signs which no one else has done, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV, 24).

Punishment follows the grave offense. The Lord said to Moses: “Go down quickly, for your people whom you brought out of Egypt have transgressed. They have made golden gods for themselves and said to them: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. And now leave me, so that I may destroy them and make you into a great nation, greater than this one” (Exod. XXXII, 7 ff.).

The merciful Lord grants time for intercession when he says, “Leave me.” For God did not depend upon the will of man; rather, man depended upon the will of God [Note: [Col. 0772D] The Remigian manuscript has “not from man.”].

When Moses entreated the Lord in many ways, offering himself for the people’s sin (Ibid., 11 ff.), he expressed our Mediator in figure, the one who gave his life for the ungodly. For Christ, as the Apostle says, died for the ungodly (Rom. V, 6).

7. Yet that very great sin does not go unpunished, since sin cannot be without punishment. When Moses descended from the mountain and saw the people running wild, he stood in the middle of the camp and said: “If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him come to me” (Exod. XXXII, 26) [Note: [Col. 0772D] The Remigian manuscript has “to the Lord.”].

When only one of the twelve tribes passed over to him, he gave them this command: “Thus says the Lord: Let each of you take his sword in his hand, pass from camp to camp, and let each one strike his father, brother, and son.” When they had done this without hesitation, Moses said: “You have filled your hands today for the Lord, each one against his son and brother” [Note: [Col. 0772D] The Remigian manuscript has “so that a blessing might be given to you.”], “so that a blessing might be bestowed upon you” (Ibid., 27 ff.).

In these people he displayed such disciples of our Mediator, to whom the Lord Jesus says [Note: [Col. 0772D] The Remigian manuscript adds “the Lord”]: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, brothers, children, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26). And again it is written: “He who says to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and who hated his own sons—they shall keep your covenant” (Deut. XXXIII, 9). [Note: [Col. 0772D] The Remigian manuscript has: “He who says to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you’; moreover, they hate even their own sons.”] This was done by the holy martyrs, called through grace and rewarded with everlasting happiness.

## CHAPTER V. Christ the Lord figured in all the sacrifices. A promise made and figured. Believed and seen in Exodus.

8. Moses was again commanded to ascend the mountain a second time (Exod. XXXIV, 2). He was instructed [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has “were commanded.”] concerning what animals and birds the people should offer in sacrifice, together with a prescribed measure of fine flour mixed with oil, for sin offerings, solemn offerings, votive offerings, or particular new moons and feast days (Ibid., 19 ff.).

The calf, it was said, was to be without blemish, pointing to Christ the Truth, in whom signs become realities. “The calf producing horns and hooves will please God” (Ps. LXVIII, 32).

The year-old lamb without blemish is himself the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John I, 29) [Note: [Col. 0773D] So the Remigian manuscript reads. The editions have “sin.”].

The ewe from the flock is likewise himself, of whom Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII, 7) [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has “he himself.”].

The ram from the flock is likewise Christ the Lord, who says through the prophet: “My horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn” (Ps. XCI, 11) [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has “in the hand.”]. And Habakkuk says: “Horns are in his hands” (Habac. III, 3, 4).

The young goat from the flock is Christ the Lord. Bearing not his own sins but those of others, he brought into his tabernacle the skins from which garments of penitence are woven [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has “they wove the skins…”]. Through David he also says: “I shall break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. LXXIV, 11).

In the turtledove and the pigeon we recognize the Church. For “the turtledove has found a nest for itself where it may place its young” (Ps. LXXXIII, 4). And he says that the pigeon is one: his bride, his chosen one (Cant. VI, 8). He commands her young to be offered in sacrifice when the Lord Jesus says: “Let the little children come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 14) [Note: [Col. 0773D] These words are added from the Remigian manuscript.]. For when the little ones are consecrated in his baptism, they are buried together with him in death, so that in them also the body of sin may be annulled (Rom. VI, 4, 6).

9. The distinction between sins of ignorance and sins committed knowingly, for which the sacrifice of a contrite heart is offered, like fine flour fried in oil (Levit.
