II, 3, 4 ff.), is also distinguished in our sacrifice, when the soul says: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. XXIV, 7).

Blessed Peter, insufficiently cautious, incurred these sins when, as the Lord foretold his passion, Peter, unaware that it had been promised through the Law and the Prophets, said: “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be gracious to you; this shall never happen” (Matt. XVI, 22). [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has, “And Christ said: Go back.”] And the Lord replied: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not understand the things of God, but those of men” (Mark VIII, 33) [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript adds “he said.”].

This sin of ignorance, together with the denial committed knowingly, and also the sin of youth—for in his presumption he had said to the Lord, “I will lay down my life for you” (John XIII, 37)—he washed away entirely by weeping, after reflection and contrition [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has “cleansed.”]. In him he taught the sinful and presumptuous person to say: “You turned your face away, and I was troubled” (Ps. XXIX, 8); “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL, 5).

As for the votive and solemn offerings that the people should offer to Christ the Lord [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has “or solemn offerings.”] [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has “to Christ the Lord.”], the Apostle Paul indicates them. “Let us offer,” he says, “a sacrifice of praise always to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. Do not forget acts of beneficence and fellowship; for with such sacrifices God is pleased” (Hebr. XIII, 15, 16) [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Remigian manuscript has “Let us offer,” and shortly afterward, “But do not forget to do good and to share.”].

## CHAPTER VI. The examination of leprosy prefigured various heretics. A prediction made and figured. Believed and seen in Leviticus.

10. God commands Moses that the examination and purification of leprosy be expiated through such sacrifices (Levit. XIII and XIV). A pair of hens is to be offered to the priest, one of which he is to offer and the other leave behind (Ibid., 4) [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript has “and leave the other.”]. The same applies to goats and other animals.

But our Priest, Jesus the Lord [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript has “Jesus Christ.”], clearly reveals these mysteries in the Gospel, saying: “Two will be in the field; one will be taken, and the other left; and two will be at the mill; one will be taken, and the other left” (Matt. XXIV, 40).

The difference between being taken and being left is shown by the pigeon and the raven sent out from the ark (Gen. VIII, 9). Noah received the pigeon back into the ark and kept it to be preserved for sacrifice; but he left the wandering and straying raven outside.

Thus he wished the sheep to be distinguished from the goats, and the wise virgins from the foolish (Matt. XXV, 2): namely, souls through grace. Purifying them with a worthy offering, the sacrifice of a contrite heart—which he signified by fine flour fried in oil—he brings them with himself into the homeland of the eternal Jerusalem, whose spiritual bridegroom he is [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript has “may he bring them in.”], while the heretics are rejected, because lepers are sent outside the camp (Levit. XIII, 46).

I do not think the very classification of leprosy should be passed over, since it may be possible to examine it to some extent. Leprosy on the head indicates the Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and their associates. Since Christ is the head of man, and God is the head of Christ (I Cor. XI, 3), when they set against God himself, the head, some unknown prince of darkness as his adversary, they deserved to be driven outside the camp, sprinkled with leprosy upon the head of their error.

Leprosy in the beard designates the Arians, Photinians, and Nestorians. By proclaiming our high priest Christ as lesser in divinity, or as merely a man and not God and man, and by thinking of Christ otherwise than the Catholic faith has handed down [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript has “and teaches.”], they assail him as lepers in the beard—the one whom the prophet David introduces in the likeness of Aaron, declaring him to be Christ the Lord, the true High Priest: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. It is like ointment upon the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. CXXXII, 1, 2) [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript has “upon the beard, the beard.”].

Those, therefore, who abandoned Catholic unity and judged that the ointment descending upon the beard of our high priest should be defiled by the doctrine of their error were found to be lepers in the beard and were themselves driven outside the camp.

Leprosy on the body signifies the Donatists, Maximianists, Luciferianists, and others wrapped in similar errors. By persecuting the body of Christ throughout the world, the Church of the Lord, with human slanders, they were expelled in the leprosy of their body [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript has “from leprosy.”]. Unless they are cleansed by Christ the true Priest through love [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript has “through the love of Christ.”], the camp of the people of God does not receive them.

11. The Pelagians, however, are disfigured by the stain of leprosy on every side, as they strive to pour the clouds of their perverse teaching over both head and body [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript has “their own.”].

Over the head, because they say that God made man mortal before sin: “He did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living; for he created all things that they might exist” (Wis. I, 13, 14).

Over the body, because they consider the grace of God unnecessary for man [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Remigian manuscript adds “for man.”], although one baptism has been consecrated for the remission of all sins.

Thus corrupted throughout by the stain of leprosy, they too were driven from the Lord’s camp. When our Priest examines these things and distinguishes the various wounds—whether the dark one among the Manichaeans, the red one among the Arians, or the white or variegated one among the Pelagians—this is because, as Paul says, “there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI, 19).

As long as souls are held in these various errors, as in the spots of leprosy, the Lord’s camp does not admit them, as has been said. When, moved by God’s grace, they return from all these heresies, desiring to be cleansed, they present themselves in a certain sense to our Priest as the ten lepers (Luke XVII, 21 ff.).

In accordance with the command of the Law, he sends them to the Jewish priest; but as they go on their way—that is, in this life—the power of the Word cleansed them. For their cleansing, that precious hen offered itself as a sacrifice, the one who says: “How often I wanted to gather your children, Jerusalem, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. XXIII, 37).

Indeed, she gathers even those unwilling ones [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Remigian manuscript has “although that Jerusalem was unwilling, namely…”] whom she recognizes as belonging to the members of her unity, because “the Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19).

One of the ten who had been cleansed returned and gave thanks to our High Priest (Luke XVII, 15), because unity knows that one must glory not in oneself but in the Lord (I Cor. I, 31); it refused to place its hope in man (Jerem. XVII, 5); it understood that good will is prepared by the Lord (Prov. XVI, according to the Septuagint) [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Remigian manuscript has “good will is prepared for the Lord.”]; and it truly wished to be free, because it recognized [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Remigian manuscript omits “also”; the editions have it.] that the Son had set it free (John VIII, 36).

But those who are ungrateful to the one cleansing them [Note: [Col. 0775D] The editions have “those who have been cleansed.” The Remigian manuscript has “to the one cleansing.”], or who persist in the leprous stains of their error, will not be received at all into the Lord’s camp. Against these, after excluding them and shutting the door, our High Priest will say [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Remigian manuscript has “Against whom, shutting [the door], he will say.”]: “I do not know you” (Luke XIII, 25), so that, dismissed from afar, they may remain outside—dogs, sorcerers, and all who practice and commit falsehood (Apoc. XXII, 16).

It was unnecessary to say much here, since Origen, examining each point in his work On Leviticus, committed to the Lord Christ everything that he understood according to the true faith.

## CHAPTER VII. In clean and unclean foods, all things are made clean through almsgiving. [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Remigian manuscript has “A promise.” It also lacks the preceding title.] A prediction made and figured. Believed and seen in Leviticus.

12. Among all the commandments that God gave Moses on Mount Sinai for the instruction of his people, after the order of sacrifices had been completed, clean and unclean animals that the people might take as food were marked out by this distinction [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Remigian manuscript lacks the word “distinction.”]. Those that chew the cud and have a divided hoof were to be considered clean and taken as food (Levit. XI, 3 ff.). These signify souls that chew the word of God and have a divided hoof, namely, the two commandments.

Specific commands were also given concerning birds and fish, identifying which the people should touch and which they should reject. The Lord testified in the Gospel that this law had been given on stone tablets according to the hardness of the Jews’ hearts (Matt. XIX, 8) [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Remigian manuscript has the word “these”; the editions omit it.].

But since our earlier fathers, to whom these matters were revealed, have written all the allegorical interpretations in extensive volumes and splendid style, what need is there to pursue every detail, since Christ died freely [that is, in vain] (Gal. II, 21), and since one baptism has flowed forth for the lesser and the greater alike? Our Mediator, Jesus the Lord, in whom all these things found their expression, rebuked the foolish Jews who followed the Law according to the letter and not the spirit, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint, cumin, and every herb, while cleansing the outside of the dish and the cup, although inwardly you are full of plunder and wickedness” (Matt. XXIII, 23, 25).

And he himself, passing by alone (Ps. CXL, 10), showed them the singular sacrifice, saying: “Nevertheless I say to you, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke XI, 41).

13. O how brief and compact a sacrifice, one that cleanses inwardly and outwardly, the whole person! Almsgiving delivers from death, and it itself purifies sins. [Note: [Col. 0775D] This section is added in the Remigian manuscript.] “Almsgiving does not permit one to walk in darkness” (Tob. IV, 11). Almsgiving is a good gift for all who practice it before the Most High God. It extinguishes everlasting fires; it resists sins; it feeds Christ, who is hungry in the poor; it clothes the naked; it visits the sick; it receives the stranger in hospitality [Note: [Col. 0776D] The editions have “receives.” The Remigian manuscript has “welcomes.”]; it removes every distress, even that of prison [Note: [Col. 0776D] The Remigian manuscript adds “even of prison.”] (Matt. XXV, 35); it ends every deprivation; it brings remedies to the rich; it obtains eternal life; it lends to God; it contains the kingdom of heaven.

It is what distinguishes the sheep from the goats (Ibid., 32); it places them at the Judge’s right hand (Ibid., 34); it joins them to the angels; it grants that slaves may become children of God.

Come, sinners of every kind; come, all of you leprous with vices and errors; come, all stained and unclean with whatever crime, repenting and making vows. Come to so great, compact, and useful a sacrifice, offering with complete joy. “For God loves a cheerful giver” (I Cor. IX, 7).

As each person possesses something to offer [Note: [Col. 0776D] The Remigian manuscript omits the words “that he offers.”], let him offer that gift. Our High Priest instituted this and commanded it to be accepted above all else [Note: [Col. 0776D] The Remigian manuscript has, “Our High Priest instituted this,” and adds below, “But do not forget to do good…”], so that he extended the measure of this sacrifice even to two small coins (Mark XII, 42) and a cup of cold water (Matt. X, 42), promising peace, even when these things are lacking, to people of good will (Luke II, 14).

These are the later things of God, which, when Moses could not see his face, were revealed to him by the prophetic Spirit (Exod. XXXIII, 20), in Christ Jesus the Lord, God and man, who is the eternal High Priest of all.

[Note: [Col. 0776D] These final words of the chapter are not found in the Remigian manuscript; they are added under the second title of the following chapter.]

These things are understood to have been supplied in Leviticus.

## CHAPTER VIII. In the foods desired from Egypt, Christ’s manna was rejected. A prediction made and figured. Believed and seen in the Book of Numbers.

14. In the Book of Numbers the people, with leaders appointed over them by Moses, are designated according to a fixed enumeration of their number (Num. I and XXVI). They are also found to have forgotten freedom [Note: [Col. 0776D] The Remigian manuscript has “and the Egyptian gratitude.” Perhaps this stands for “and, desiring Egyptian foods,” which follows.] and the Egyptian grace, desiring the same foods, and to have murmured against God and Moses (Num. XI, 1).

“Who will feed us meat?” they said. “For we remember the fish that we ate freely in Egypt, the cucumbers, leeks, garlic, and onions. But now,” they said, “our soul has dried up, and there is nothing before our eyes except manna” (Ibid. IV, 5, 6).

They reject sweet things and desire bitter ones. A dangerous and serious illness of the soul brings this about: that it wants to consume harmful things and despises and rejects what is useful and beneficial for salvation.

Thus they rejected Christ the manna, saying: “We know that God spoke with Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from” (John IX, 29). Rebuking them, he says: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me also [Note: [Col. 0777D] The word “certainly” is added from the Remigian manuscript.], for he wrote about me” (John V, 46). “For I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 51).

Did they not reject the holy manna when, while Pilate wished to release Jesus, they said: “Do not release him, but Barabbas” (John XVIII, 40)? Barabbas was a notorious robber. By asking that he be released, they confessed that they desired from the robber’s crimes the harsh and tearful Egyptian foods, like leeks, onions, and garlic [Note: [Col. 0777D] So the Remigian manuscript reads. The editions instead have “to have desired bitter tears,” without “Egyptian foods” and without the particle “to.”].

To those who murmured, divine majesty supplied meat—not meat that would restore them, but rather meat that would torment those who ate it (Num. XI, 33; Ps. LXXVII, 30).

Since the natural person does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit (I Cor. II, 14), and since everyone is sluggish in his desires (Prov. XXI, 25), the spiritual person rightly asked that the desires of the belly be removed from him (Eccli. XXIII, 6). It was shown to be wicked to desire or ask God for things harmful to the soul, especially when they are demanded with murmuring. [Note: [Col. 0777D] The Remigian manuscript has, “Let the soul flee such a desire … if it desires to see…”] Let the soul beware of offending God through such a desire, if it wishes to enter the promised land.

## CHAPTER IX. In Moses, Christ the Lord, and the Church, the brothers’ detraction. A prediction made [Note: [Col. 0777D] These words are supplied from the Remigian manuscript.] and figured. Believed and seen in the Book of Numbers.

15. “Moses,” says Scripture, “was the meekest of all the men who were upon the earth” (Num. XII, 3) [Note: [Col. 0777D] So the Remigian manuscript reads. The editions have “who are.”].

In this meekness our Mediator resounds, to whom David says: “You, Lord, are gentle and meek” (Ps. LXXXV, 5). And he himself says in the Gospel: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

Aaron and Miriam spoke against Moses, their brother, because he had taken an Ethiopian woman as his wife (Num. XII, 1). Our Lord’s own brothers also spoke against him because he ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke XV, 2).

When he said to them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. IX, 12), he showed that he had taken this Ethiopian woman from the Gentiles, the one who says: “I am dark but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Cant. I, 4).

Miriam, who had spoken against Moses, immediately received the punishment of leprosy as vengeance (Num. XII, 10)—a punishment that souls who speak against Christ and the Church ought to fear. For he says of such people through the prophet: “Instead of loving me, they spoke against me, but I prayed” (Ps. CVIII, 4).

Through Moses’ prayer, Miriam was cleansed and obtained forgiveness (Num. XII, 13), so that such a soul, with so great a High Priest interceding, might be healed from every fault.

Nevertheless, by divine command Moses sent twelve chosen men from the people to explore the land of the Canaanites. He instructed them not merely to inspect its cities and inhabitants, but also to bring back with them some of the land’s fruits. As they went and carried out what had been commanded, a certain valley received them. From it they cut down a cluster of grapes, placed it upon a pole because of its size, and returned to the camp carrying it together with pomegranates and figs, displaying the fruits and recounting what they had seen (Num. XIII, 3 ff.).

In these three fruits the mysteries of Christ the Lord and the Church resound.

The cluster of grapes signifies Christ, in the voice of the Church in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is a cluster of henna blossoms” (Cant. I, 13). Since it is carried upon wood, recognize the Crucified One. Since it is borne between the two explorers, recall the prophet Habakkuk: “In the midst of two living creatures you will be known” (Habac. III, 2, according to the Septuagint) [Note: [Col. 0777D] The Remigian manuscript has “Among these things.”].

Likewise, the Church says of herself in the same song: “The vine has blossomed; the pomegranates have blossomed” (Cant. VII, 12).

The figs, from whose leaves the first transgressors made themselves coverings (Gen. III, 7), display original sin, which is absolved through the pomegranates of the Church—the blood of the cluster—which was poured out for the remission of all sins.

16. Those who had gone up with the explorers, however, frightened the people by reporting that the inhabitants of the promised land were audacious men and great in stature, and that their cities were fortified. They also affirmed that they had seen giants there, in whose presence they themselves seemed like locusts upon the earth (Num. XIII, 28 ff.).

Struck by fear of these people, the people again murmured against Moses and decided to choose a leader who would take them back to Egypt (Num. XIV, 2 ff.). This is the evil of those who, liberated through baptism from fear of demons, look not forward but backward (Philipp. III, 13), forgetting God’s benefits and his wondrous deeds. Despairing that God’s promises will be fulfilled for them, they choose to return to the one whom they had already renounced, despising the one in whom they had believed and denying his power.

Rebuking them, he says: “They turned their back to me, and not their faces” (Jerem. II, 27) [Note: [Col. 0778D] The Remigian manuscript has “They turned.”].

The Apostle Peter likewise says: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them is expressed by the true proverb: A dog returns to its vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (II Peter II, 21; Prov. XXVIII, 11) [Note: [Col. 0778D] The Remigian manuscript has “to wallowing in the mud.”].

But Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh [Note: [Col. 0778D] The Remigian manuscript has “Jephunneh” in a different form, “Sephone.”], who had inspected the land, fell down together with Moses and Aaron the priests (Num. XIV, 5, 6). They perform acts of devotion and turn the people back from their resolve of despair, saying: “Do not fear the people of the land, for they are our food [Note: [Col. 0778D] The Remigian manuscript has “they are for us.”]. Their protection has departed from them, but the Lord is with us; do not fear them” (Ibid., 9, according to the Septuagint).

All these things also resound, through the overthrow of idols, among the Christian people, so that they may not be apostate from God—people who fear demons [Note: [Col. 0778D] The Remigian manuscript has “demons”; the editions have “men.”], from whom they have already been freed through God’s grace.

Describing their empty pomp, Jeremiah says: “Among other things, when you enter Babylon, you will see golden and silver gods being carried upon shoulders” (Baruch VI, 3 ff.). But they are handmade and empty; they can neither benefit nor harm, because they are nothing. Therefore, do not fear them. “Sanctify the Lord in your hearts, and he will be your fear,” as Isaiah says (Isa. VIII, 13; I Peter III, 15).

Writing about the worshipers of demons, Jeremiah says: “There were there those renowned giants, skilled in war. The Lord did not choose them, nor did he give them the way of knowledge. And they perished because they lacked wisdom” (Baruch III, 26 ff.). And Solomon says: “From the beginning, when the proud giants were perishing” (Wis. XIV, 6). Against their pride, the humble people of Christ rise victorious [Note: [Col. 0778D] The Remigian manuscript has “might rise.”].

17. But when the Hebrew people, angered, wished to stone those who were praying for them [Note: [Col. 0778D] So the Remigian manuscript reads. The editions have “on their behalf.”], the glory of the Lord appeared in the tabernacle (Num. XIV, 10). Thus the boldness of the wicked is always restrained by the presence of divine power.

When the Lord wished to destroy those who provoked him, that meek man, the meekest of all, Moses, found words of gracious intercession to utter: “The Egyptians will hear when you destroy this people, and they will say: Because he could not bring them into the land which he swore to give them, he slaughtered them in the wilderness. And now let your hand, Lord, be exalted, as you said: I am a patient God, very merciful and true” (Num. XIV, 13).

God was appeased by these prayers and moderated his anger, yet he nevertheless allowed fitting punishment to follow the sinners (Ibid., 20 ff.). He declared beforehand, as a testimony, that they themselves would not enter the rest of the promised land, except Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh [Note: [Col. 0779D] The Remigian manuscript has “Sephone.”]. All those who died in the wilderness (Ibid., 37) were excluded, while their obedient children received the inheritance that the rebellious had lost.

Thus our Mediator, Jesus the Lord, gave an eternal inheritance to the children of that same people, who had rebelled against him and had conferred with Herod concerning his death, while the Jews, rejected and dead—even in soul—in the wilderness of this life [Note: [Col. 0779D] The Remigian manuscript has “in the wilderness of this life”; the editions have “in this life.”], were passed over. The impious Herod had killed their children on his account (Matt. II, 16).

## CHAPTER X. In Aaron’s budding staff, confirmation of the priesthood of Christ the Lord. A prediction made and figured. Believed and seen in the Book of Numbers.

18. Korah, Dathan, and Abiron, despising their commandments and wishing to usurp the priestly office (Num. 16 and following), were being punished by the present judgment of God. In condemning them, he condemned all heretics, as we have already set forth above (Part I, ch. 12), and announced to Moses a sign confirming whom he had chosen as high priest. [Col. 0779D: The Remigius manuscript reads “foretells.”] [Col. 0779D: The Remigius manuscript reads “despising.”] The Lord said to Moses: [Col. 0779D: The Remigius manuscript reads “Say.”] “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: Let all their leaders, each one from their tribes, give their staffs” (Num. 17:2). [Col. 0779D: The printed editions read “in three.”]

Moses therefore took twelve staffs, including Aaron’s staff among theirs, placed them before the Lord, and brought them into the tabernacle of testimony. On the following day Moses and Aaron entered the tabernacle. And behold, Aaron’s staff, from the house of Levi, had blossomed: it had produced a bud and a flower, and had put forth almonds (ibid., 10). By this sign he commanded that the people should be quiet, saying: “Let their murmuring cease from me, and they shall not die” (ibid., 8). [Col. 0779D: The Remigius manuscript reads “will cease.”]

Heretics perish when they murmur against the Lord’s lawful priest. But the fact that Aaron’s blossoming staff produced almonds signifies our Lord Christ as Priest. Concerning him Isaiah says: “A staff shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). Whoever seeks this devoutly understands that in the almond the world and the Church in the world are represented. For, formed from two joined parts—as though within the vault of heaven and the spaces of the earth, like the four quarters of the world—peoples are contained within it. [Col. 0779D: The Remigius manuscript reads: “contained within, while the people are thin …”] It has a thin skin at its center, representing the seas spread through the various regions.

19. The mysteries of the Church are also present in this image: the two parts conceal the secrets of the Old and New Testaments; the four horns represent the cross, by which the world is redeemed; and water lies within it, representing baptism, through which the Church, ever green and fruitful, blossoms. [Col. 0779D]

The tree of this fruit, rising toward the heights, with shady branches scattered through slender, supple shoots, produces its fruits—either singly in unity, or in pairs according to the two commandments, or in threes according to the number of the Trinity, or joined in fours according to the four Gospels. Producing them in the manner of gems, it displays the beauty and wondrous works of its maker. [Col. 0780A]

The juice pressed from them, from their covering, gives a white color to something dyed in it and is applied as a remedy to irritated throats. [Col. 0779D: The Remigius manuscript adds after these words: “from the covering, it soothes those burning with fever,” omitting the remainder.] These coverings, clothed in the foliage of green groves, refresh those who are fevered, giving them rest beneath their leaves, and by their breath temper the fires of the sick. [Col. 0780D: The Remigius manuscript reads “of their children.”]

Nor without reason does the Lord command the prophet Jeremiah to make for himself an almondwood staff, or an almond-tree rod (Jer. 1:11). [Col. 0780D: The author alludes to Jer. 1:11: “I see an almondwood staff,” or “an almond-tree rod.”] In it the whole Church in the world, and the world within the Church, are sustained by Christ’s help and upheld by his grace. [Col. 0780D: The words “and the world within it” are omitted in the Remigius manuscript.] The Church sings in the Psalms: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:4).

## CHAPTER XI

### In the bronze serpent, Christ the Lord delivers from the bite of the devil. A prediction made and represented. Attested and seen in the Book of Numbers.

[Col. 0780B]

20. Again, when the people were thirsty in another part of the wilderness, they murmured against Moses and against the Lord (Num. 20:2). [Col. 0780D: A more recent edition reads “and from the rock.”] Moses, who had previously brought forth water from the rock, doubted that water could be produced from it again (Exod. 17:5), although he had already performed such signs, or even greater ones. He incurred offense because he had not glorified God before the children of Israel; and the divine sentence confirmed that he would not lead the people into the promised land (Num. 20:12). [Col. 0780D: The Cologne edition reads “because he had not glorified.”]

There Aaron died on Mount Hor and left Eleazar, his son and priest (ibid., 29). Moses was preserved for a little longer; in his place Joshua son of Nun succeeded. [Col. 0780D: The Remigius manuscript reads “Joshua son of Nun shall succeed … of the promise.”] He led the people into the promised land. It was fitting that the earthly inheritance should also be entrusted to this name, since the apostolic pronouncement has established that “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12; Phil. 2:10). This points to our leader, Christ Jesus the Lord, who distributes himself as an everlasting inheritance to his own; and those who receive him say: “The inheritance has fallen to me in a glorious place” (Ps. 16:6). [Col. 0780D: The Remigius manuscript reads “who receive it.”]

21. As that same people proceeded through the territories of certain nations whom the Lord had commanded them to destroy—nations whose guilt of idolatry had reached its appointed end—and grew weary on the journey, they murmured against the Lord and were afflicted in the wilderness by the bites of serpents. Repentant, they begged Moses to entreat the Lord on their behalf (Num. 21:5 and following).

But that ever-kind and merciful God, who, when judging, gives room for repentance (Wis. 12:10), provided a remedy through the exalted serpent on wood against the deadly bites of the serpents. Moses was commanded to form a bronze serpent and fasten it to a tall piece of wood. He was then to tell the people that if anyone felt himself wounded by the bite of any serpent, he should immediately look at the bronze serpent, and by looking at it he would be healed at once. [Col. 0780D: The Remigius manuscript reads “was healed.”]

Here too that serpent—the devil—is mocked, of whom David says: “The dragon whom you formed, to mock him” (Ps. 103:26). When, in the wilderness of this life, the devil has inflicted poisonous bites through various vices upon those already consecrated in baptism as in the Red Sea, let them immediately look upon Jesus the Lord exalted on the wood of the cross—that is, let them not withdraw from the heavenly physician—so that everyone who sees and believes in him, as he himself says in the Gospel, “may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:15).

## CHAPTER XII

### In those who despise their parents for Christ’s sake, a blessing is to come. A promise made and represented. Attested and seen in Numbers.

22. Balak, king of Moab, summoned Balaam, a prophet from the nations—although he was a seer of the one true God—and invited him to curse the people blessed by God, believing that by cursing them he would easily overcome them (Num. 22:5 and following).

But the prophet asked the Lord whether he should go or remain. The Lord forbade him to come, and he informed the king that he was forbidden to do so. [Col. 0781D: The Remigius manuscript reads: “Having been forbidden, he tells the king not to come, since it was forbidden to him.”] The king sent other messengers, promising greater gifts, and urged the prophet to come (ibid., 15 and following). [Col. 0781B]

Again Balaam, with a perverse heart, asked the one who had already forbidden him, testing whether permission to go might be granted. The Scripture rightly speaks to him: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:16; Matt. 4:7). Permission to go was therefore granted to him, though his mind was already wounded, on the condition that he say whatever the Lord placed in his mouth.

As he went, already taken captive in his heart by his greed, the angel who confronted him chose to reveal himself to the beast on which he rode rather than to the man himself (Num. 22:28). [Col. 0781D: The Remigius manuscript adds the word “journey.”] For “man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts, and became not merely like them but worse than they” (Ps. 48:21). The beast, responding with a human voice—as the apostle Peter says in his Epistle—restrained the prophet’s madness (2 Pet. 2:16). [Col. 0781D: The Remigius manuscript reads “on which he was being carried.”]

23. Then, when that prophet had been brought before the king and was thinking of cursing, he blessed instead (Num. 22:36; 23–24). He was numbered among those whom the prophet David describes, saying: “They will curse, and you will bless” (Ps. 108:28). [Col. 0781D: The Remigius manuscript reads “They curse him, and you bless.”] Elsewhere he says: “With their mouth they blessed” (Ps. 62:5). [Col. 0781D: The Remigius manuscript adds “and with their heart they blessed”; perhaps, “they were cursing.” The note continues only: “For this …”]

The later outcome made this clear. The prophetic blessing was fulfilled: through such a man, God was promising the nations the coming of his only Son from that people. [Col. 0781D: The Remigius manuscript and the Lyons edition read “which also.”] Moved by this prophecy, Balaam said among other things: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel, and shall shatter all the kingdoms of the earth” (Num. 24:17). The divine Gospels testify that these words were spoken of Christ the Lord (Matt. 2:2).

He who wished to curse, but could not, gave the king the counsel devised by the most wicked serpent. [Col. 0782D: The words “but could not” are supplied from the Remigius manuscript; they were absent from the older editions except the Lyons edition, which has “and was not able.”] He advised that the most beautiful women should be selected from his own people—women whose beauty and adornment would soften and weaken the strength of the men—and sent to the Hebrew people to arouse lust (Num. 24:14; 25:1; 31:16). [Col. 0782D: The Remigius manuscript reads “would soften”; the printed editions read “the Hebrew people.”]

Persuaded by desire for these women, the Israelites sacrificed to idols and ate what had been sacrificed. Having offended God, they led nearly the whole of Israel captive into death. Since a great multitude was struck down by the divine hand in the wilderness and nearly the entire synagogue had perished, Phinehas the priest alone appeased God’s anger by piercing the adulterers in mind and body with a sword (Num. 25:8). [Col. 0782D: The Remigius manuscript and the recent edition read “in this manner.”]

The apostle John is instructed in the Apocalypse to write to the angel—that is, to the ruler—of the Church of Pergamum that among his people there were some holding the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, so that they might eat sacrificial food and fornicate (Rev. 2:14; Num. 25:2). [Col. 0782D: The Remigius manuscript reads “before their eyes.”] He thus shows that such people still exist: either avenging wrath consumes them, or, when rebuked, the grace granted through the priest’s penitential discipline sets them free. [Col. 0782D: The Remigius manuscript reads “will consume them.”]

## CHAPTER XIII

### In Moses’ departure, Joshua is shown as signifying the Lord’s ruler. A prediction made and represented. Attested and seen in Deuteronomy.

24. Knowing that he was near burial, Moses recapitulated the whole law for the people. Through blessings and curses, and through that fearful song of Deuteronomy, he bound the whole synagogue to its obligation. He called heaven and earth as witnesses, declaring that he had concealed nothing of the Lord’s commandments and had taken every vigilant care that nothing harmful should arise for the people. He warned them not to depart from the Lord’s commandments or turn aside from him in anything, and warned them to fear prosperity, lest adversity follow it (Deut. 31:32). [Col. 0782D: The Remigius manuscript reads “prosperous things.”]

In a prophetic spirit he also disclosed what would happen to them in the future: after his death, they would abandon the true God and pursue the empty and harmful idols of the nations. [Col. 0782D: The Remigius manuscript adds “images.”] Weighed down by the burden of sins arising from their worship, they would be plunged into the depths. [Col. 0782D: The printed editions read “they are plunged.”] God would abandon them if they themselves abandoned God (Deut. 31:16).

After these words, marking all the tribes with a mystical blessing (Deut. 33:1 and following), and entrusting the people to Joshua son of Nun for governance (Deut. 31:7), Moses, now advanced in age, departed from this life to the Lord (Deut. 34:5).

Our Mediator, Jesus the Lord, likewise entrusted his faith and peace to his disciples as he passed from this world to the Father (John 14:2), teaching them while loving them to the end, as the evangelist John says (John 13:1). Through his apostle Paul he also entrusted to them this prophetic disclosure of the future: after his death, savage wolves would enter, not sparing the flock (Acts 20:29), and from among the disciples themselves false prophets would arise, speaking perverse things (Matt. 24:5). Concerning them he says in his Epistle: “Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the mutilation” (Phil. 3:2).

And after commending them all to God and to the word of his grace, Paul declares that they would no longer see his face (Acts 20:32). [Col. 0782D: The Remigius manuscript adds “all.”] He entrusted them to be governed by the Lord Jesus, who is with his own until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28:20).

## CHAPTER XIV

### In Joshua son of Nun he shows a figure of Jesus the Lord, conquering the earthly city. A promise made and represented. Attested and seen in Joshua son of Nun.

25. Joshua son of Nun, consecrated by God through the hand of Moses, became leader of the people (Deut. 31:7). For—as must often be said—it was not fitting that anyone other than the one who bore the mysteries and salvation signified by both his name and his work should lead God’s people into the promised land. [Col. 0782D: The Remigius manuscript adds “of the future.”]

He sent two spies into Jericho, which appeared to be the first of the cities of the promised land (Josh. 2:1). Our Jesus the Lord also sent two spies, who by preaching shook the land of his first coming: namely, Zechariah the priest and his son John. [Col. 0783D: The Remigius manuscript reads “to be preached.”] Concerning the latter, the same father and priest says to his son: “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76). Likewise the angel says of John: “He shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (ibid., 17).

Rahab the prostitute received the spies of that land; she hid them and rescued them from their pursuers (Josh. 2:1). Those whom the Lord Jesus sent were received by a sinful soul, which awaited salvation in the name of Jesus and was delivered from the prostitution of idolatry through the scarlet cord, the sign of his sacred blood. [Col. 0783D: The Remigius manuscript reads “our Jesus the Lord”; and “through his sacred blood.”]

26. Thamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, likewise marks these souls coming from prostitution in her twins. While her younger son began first to put out his hand from the womb and, after receiving the scarlet sign, was born later (Gen. 38:27), she represented in herself the people of the nations: wandering as they were, after first stretching out their hand toward the sacred things of idols, they later came to Christ, reborn in baptism through the sign of his blood. [Col. 0783D: This reading is emended with the aid of the Remigius manuscript; the other printed editions read *vehementer* (“violently”). The manuscript reads “in their crimes,” apparently less suitably, and “he should put out [his hand].”]

Rahab hid the spies beneath linen. The prophet Isaiah testifies that the spies of our Jesus the Lord were also hidden beneath linen, saying: “He shall not break a bruised reed, and he shall not quench smoking flax” (Isa. 42:3). [Col. 0783D: The Remigius manuscript reads “and our [spies].”] This signifies the Jewish people, which, like smoking flax in its sacrifices, concealed and hid the whole prophecy until Christ. It also signifies the forerunners of our Christ Jesus, by whom that prophecy was not extinguished but has been preserved to this day (Matt. 12:20), so that what still lies hidden within it may be revealed in the future. [Col. 0783D: The Remigius manuscript reads “covered and concealed.” The printed editions read “what is destined to be revealed in time”; the Remigius manuscript reads simply “what is hidden may be revealed in the future.”]

Through fear of Joshua the leader, that woman disclosed her terrified fellow citizens to the spies, so that this too might be fulfilled which was spoken of our Jesus the Lord: “At your presence the nations shall be troubled, when you perform wonders” (Isa. 64:2–3).

The spies returned to Joshua and reported everything they had done. Then, by divine command, he ordered the twelve tribes of Israel to break camp and all to cross the Jordan, with the ark going before them (Josh. 3:1). The ark already bore, in figure, all the mysteries of our leader Jesus. [Col. 0783D: The Remigius manuscript reads “in figure”; the printed editions omit this phrase. It also reads “all the mysteries.”]

27. While the ark remained in the middle of the river, the lower water flowed away in divided channels while the upper water stood still, and the riverbed itself offered dry ground to those crossing (ibid., 16). Immediately, at the Lord’s command, Joshua ordered twelve stones to be taken from the middle of the river, one from each tribe. By these, the twelve apostles of our Jesus were signified in the sacred number twelve (Josh. 4:1).

When the people had crossed and the service that the water had provided at God’s command had been completed, the river, returning into itself, once again made those who had crossed joyful (ibid., 18). Here too an image of baptism was displayed: those born in the wilderness who had not known the mysteries of the Red Sea were washed in the crossing of the Jordan and received circumcision with stone knives. [Col. 0784D: The Remigius manuscript reads “received [circumcision].”] Everyone consecrated in baptism under our Jesus is circumcised in heart from the rock, because all his strength is established upon the rock. That rock is Christ, as has already been shown above (1 Cor. 10:4). [Col. 0784D: The Remigius manuscript reads “we have shown.”]

## CHAPTER XV

### Through Jesus the Lord, souls are delivered from the prostitution of idols. A prediction made and represented. Attested and seen in Joshua son of Nun.

[Col. 0784A]

28. The people of God came with Joshua as leader to Jericho. Seeing the city fortified on every side, they surrounded it with a siege (Josh. 6:1 and following). A remarkable conflict appears to have been initiated there by the divine commands. [Col. 0784D: The printed editions read “there appeared to have been a power”; the correction follows the Remigius manuscript.] A kind of spiritual battle took place: for seven days, the sound of seven trumpets returned repeatedly; on the final day, when the trumpets resounded and everyone shouted for joy, the entire proud construction of the walls collapsed—not by human power but when shaken by the hand of God (ibid., 16).

When the city had been overthrown and burned with its people, Rahab alone, with her household, was able to be saved from it by the sign of the blood (ibid., 17). [Col. 0784D: The Remigius manuscript reads “from it.”]

At the command of Jesus the Lord, our army also fights with these trumpets and with this shouting of those who rejoice. For, when the sevenfold Spirit resounds—of wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and the fear of God (Isa. 11:2)—those who sing with trumpets and with the sound of the horn resound, while the people rejoice before the Lord the King (Ps. 97:6). Seven times a day they praise him for the judgments of his justice (Ps. 118:164), and all the earthly pride of the city of Jericho is conquered (Josh. 6:24). [Col. 0784D: The Remigius manuscript reads “the earthly [city].”] It is consumed by fire by him of whom it is said: “Fire shall go before him and burn up his enemies round about” (Ps. 96:3). [Col. 0784D: The Remigius manuscript reads “shall burn before him.”]

In that city hope of salvation is given to the repentant sinful soul. Delivered by the sign of the blood of Jesus the Lord, she hears the proud and swollen addressed: “Tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21:31).

Our Jesus the Lord found such souls both among the Jews and among the nations. To show by their example how a soul might pass from its prostitution to a lawful husband, the prophet Hosea was commanded to take a prostitute as a wife and beget children by her, so that she who had shortly before been a prostitute might now be a wife, and she who had sought not to have children might have children and serve no longer lust but the bearing of offspring (Hos. 1:2).

29. This is explained more clearly through the prophet Jeremiah, when the whole of Judea is rebuked: “If a woman has been defiled,” says the Lord, “will her husband return to her? Yet you have prostituted yourself with many shepherds; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. 3:1). And through Hosea: “I will call ‘my people’ her who was not my people, and ‘beloved’ her who was not beloved” (Hos. 1:10; 2:24; Rom. 9:25).

The apostle Paul also salutarily rebukes such souls, saying: “It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not found even among the nations” (1 Cor. 5:1). Yet when our Jesus the Lord receives such souls for salvation through his grace, he makes the prostitute a virgin by that divine power of his. Paul, acting as her bridal attendant, joins her to Christ in a chaste and spiritual marriage, saying: “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

Receiving from her children not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, he makes the Church a virgin mother, “nursing with the abundance of her children” (Ps. 112:9). [Col. 0784D: The older editions read “nursing”; the more recent editions read “rejoicing,” with the Remigius manuscript supporting the former.] The apostle John reminds these children along with her, saying: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3:2). [Col. 0784D: The source reads *quid evimus*, apparently corrupt; the older editions read *quod erimus*, “what we shall be.”] Paul adds: “If children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and joint-heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17).

## CHAPTER XVI

### Through Jesus the Lord, all vices are to be conquered. [Col. 0785D: The Remigius manuscript, the Cologne edition, and later editions read this; the older editions read “A prediction.”] A promise made and represented. Attested and seen in Joshua son of Nun.

30. Joshua son of Nun conquered the Canaanite, Hittite, Perizzite, and the other nations whose lands the Lord had promised to his people as an inheritance (Josh. 11:3 and following). Our Jesus the Lord likewise conquers idolatry, pride, envy, lust, and the other vices, so that he may prepare himself an everlasting inheritance among his own.

Joshua son of Nun divided the land among the victorious people with a measuring cord (Ps. 77:64). The people who triumph in Christ Jesus also say: “The measuring lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is glorious to me” (Ps. 15:6).

Because the daughters of Zelophehad had no male heir, the Lord commanded them to receive their father’s inheritance (Num. 27:6), signifying in them souls deprived of human assistance. [Col. 0785D: The Remigius manuscript adds “human.”] When God regards them, they say: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; you are the one who rest tues mihi [restores my inheritance to me]” (Ps. 15:5). The supplied reading *rest tues mihi* is corrupt; the intended sense is uncertain but evidently concerns restoring the inheritance.

Each tribe guards the boundaries assigned to it with inviolate faith. Our people too are told: “You shall not move the ancient boundaries which your fathers have established” (Prov. 22:28).

As Jesus was about to depart from the world, he delivered to the people the final words of his testimony, like Moses: they must not depart from the Lord’s commandments if they wished always to remain free and safe from the plots of their enemies; and he affirmed that he had taken nothing from them or harmed them in any way (Josh. 23).

As our Jesus the Lord departed, he bound his own by this covenant: “If you do what I command you, you are truly my disciples, and you shall know the truth, and the truth has set them free” (John 8:31). Having given them the power to perform miracles, he told them not to expect from anyone anything that they themselves had not given: “Freely give” (Matt. 10:8). [Col. 0785D: The Remigius manuscript reads: “He said, ‘Freely give.’”]

After Joshua’s departure, that people received not a leader but judges to govern them (Judg. 1:2). And when our Jesus the Lord passed from this world to the Father, he appointed rulers of his Church throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER XVII

### In the figure of the Church, Deborah overcame the enemy. [Col. 0785D: The Cologne edition and later editions read “A promise.”] A prediction made and represented. Attested and seen in the Book of Judges. [Col. 0785D: The Remigius manuscript and later editions add “book” here and in the titles of the following chapters; although omitted in the older editions, it is understood.]

31. Judah was the first among the other judges who judged Israel (Judg. 1:2). From this tribe, as we have often said, Christ the Lord was presented to this world in the flesh as Judge of all souls.

But after abandoning God, the people of Israel forgot the commandments of Moses and Joshua, the servants of God, and served the idols of the nations. [Col. 0785D: The Remigius manuscript adds “and followed him.”] As retribution, they were oppressed by neighboring enemies (Judg. 2:11 and following).

The same thing happens now, when the children of God, reborn through baptism, become entangled in empty superstitions and the cares of this age, and each person is bound by the chains of his own sins (Prov. 5:22).

The children of Israel cried to the Lord when they were suffering oppression: “And he delivered them from their distresses” (Ps. 106:6). Our Lord also says through the prophet: “It shall be that when you cry to me and say, ‘Father!’ I will hear you as a holy people” (Isa. 58:9). At its manifestation, the merciful Father in the Gospel receives the repentant prodigal son when he cries out to his father and returns (Luke 15:21). [Col. 0785D: The Remigius manuscript omits “repentant.”]

[Col. 0786D: In the Remigius manuscript the present chapter is divided before the word “Subsequent,” which is preceded by the title: “A prediction made and represented; attested and seen in Judges.”]

Subsequently, Deborah the prophetess, a mother, arose in Israel among the judges, and she judged the people for forty years (Judg. 4). [Col. 0786D: The Remigius manuscript reads “Deborah.”] In her time divine power delivered Sisera of King Jabin, who was rebelling against the Lord’s people, into the hand of a woman—he who was terrifying and feared because of his chariots, horsemen, and peoples. She did not kill him with iron; rather, a woman fastened the man to the wood, piercing his temples with a stake and a hammer (ibid., 21). [Col. 0786D: The Remigius manuscript reads “iron … wood.”]

She bore the likeness of our mother, the Church, which cries out in the Psalms: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will glory in the name of our God. Their feet were bound, and they fell; but we have risen and stand upright” (Ps. 19:8–9).

The holy Church sings these and other things as she conquers idols, the worshipers of idols, and also her neighboring enemies, the heretics. When they establish their camp against her, she says that her heart will not fear; and: “Though war arise against me, in this I will hope” (Ps. 26:3). In another psalm she says: “Often they have fought against me from my youth, yet they could not prevail against me” (Ps. 128:1, 4). For the just Lord has crushed the necks of sinners through the wood of the cross. [Col. 0786D: The Remigius manuscript reads “through the wood of the cross.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII

### In the figure of Gideon, he commends the grace of Christ the Lord. A promise made and represented. Attested and seen in the Book of Judges.

32. Again, because of the sin of idolatry, the people were afflicted, with Midian oppressing them (Judg. 6:1). An angel of the Lord was sent for their redemption, sending Gideon, son of Joash, one of the Hebrews, to judge and fight on behalf of the people, instructing him with these words: “The Lord is with you, mighty in valor.” Gideon replied: “If the Lord is with us, why have all these evils found us?” (ibid., 12–13).

And the angel said: “Go, for by your hand Israel shall be delivered from the hand of Midian” (ibid., 14). [Col. 0786D: The Remigius manuscript adds “he said.”]

When Gideon confessed before the Lord that he belonged to the least tribe in Israel, he was strengthened by him who exalts the humble and makes them sit with the leaders of his people (Ps. 112:8). Immediately he overthrew the altar of Baal, which the children of Israel had built.

For this deed the people pursued him, and he fled into his father’s house, where they surrounded him (Judg. 6:27 and following). When he had escaped their attack, his father Joash calmed the raging crowd with these words: “Are you going to plead Baal’s cause, or save him? Whoever brings charges against him shall die by morning. If he is a god, let him avenge himself” (ibid., 31). [Col. 0786D: The Remigius manuscript lacks “in”; it reads “who brings charges against him” and “until morning.”]

When the people had been pacified and departed, the Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon and, supporting him with power, sent him to battle. He granted a sign of victory according to Gideon’s request. Gideon asked for two signs, which were veiled in a great mystery until their appointed time:

“I ask, Lord, that the fleece which is on the threshing floor be filled with water, and that the threshing floor be dry” (Judg. 6:37).

And it happened. The threshing floor was dry, while all the dew descended upon the fleece; when it was squeezed, it filled a basin with water. [Col. 0787C: The Remigius manuscript adds “all”; for “basin” it reads “cauldron.”]

The fleece filled with dew while the threshing floor remained dry signifies the Synagogue [Col. 0787C: The Remigius manuscript instead reads: “we recognize the Church, then dry in the faith of the nations”]:  at that time the Church was dry with respect to the faith of the nations, receiving no rain of heavenly teaching, while the Synagogue, like the fleece, was filled with divine oracles and sacred mysteries. Our Lord Jesus Christ, the true power, squeezed this out into a basin to such an extent that, as his passion approached, he washed the feet of his disciples in it (John 13:5), emptying the whole glory of the Synagogue and leaving it empty, like a squeezed fleece, while ministering to the nations the grace of the New Testament. He clearly revealed this in the second sign:

“I ask, Lord, that the fleece be dry and that the whole threshing floor be drenched” (Judg. 6:39).

33. The prophet David confirms in the seventy-first Psalm that both things were accomplished and would be fulfilled in Christ and through Christ (v. 6), saying:

“He shall descend like rain upon the fleece”—which pertains to the Synagogue—“and like drops that distill upon the earth”—which pertains to the Church.

In Deuteronomy he likewise says: “Let my proclamation be received like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32:2). The dew upon the fleece then showed the Synagogue filled; the rain upon the threshing floor now shows the Church filled with grace.

The prophet Isaiah also says:

“As dew or rain descending does not depart until it has watered the earth, made it germinate, and given bread to those who cultivate it to eat, so the word that comes forth from my mouth shall not return until it accomplishes whatever I have willed” (Isa. 55:10–11).

[Col. 0787C: The Remigius manuscript adds “the prophet.” It then gives Isaiah’s passage in this form: “As dew or rain descends until … and gives …”] [Col. 0787D: It also reads: “so that the word, wherever it goes … does not return until it has accomplished what I willed.”]

Once all the mysteries had been fulfilled—mysteries that had been stored up and concealed in the fleece for others—the whole world now recognizes that the Synagogue of the Jews has remained empty. [Col. 0787D: The Remigius manuscript reads “will recognize.”] It also recognizes that the threshing floor, the Church, has been filled throughout all nations with grace and with the fruitfulness of believing peoples.

Yet Gideon was commanded, after gathering his army, to go forth to battle against the enemies of God’s people. [Col. 0787D: The Remigius manuscript reads “to go forth fighting.”] But because everything was concealed in mysteries, the army that had been led out was tested at the water. The Lord said to Gideon:

“Bring the people down to the water, for there are still many with you. Whoever laps with his tongue as a dog drinks, set him apart; dismiss the others from the camp” (Judg. 7:4).

[Col. 0787D: The Remigius manuscript reads “Bring [them].” It also reads: “when they have drunk as dogs drink.”]

Three hundred men were found. “You shall bring these with you,” says the Lord, “lest Israel say: ‘My own hand has saved me’” (ibid., 2). Thus divine providence acts while commending grace, so that no one may glory in himself but in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31). For “the strength of battle is not in the multitude of the army, but power comes from heaven from God” (1 Kings 14:6).

Additional apparatus: §19 [Col. 0779D], the Remigius manuscript reads *geminas* (“twin pairs”) for *binas* (“pairs”). §22 [Col. 0781D], it adds *sicut* (“as”). §28 [Col. 0784D], it adds *tubis* (“with trumpets”) to the description of the final day. §31 [Col. 0785D], it reads *eumque* (“and him”) rather than *eosque* (“and them”). §32 [Col. 0786D], the printed editions read *in minima* (“in the least”) for “from the least tribe.” §33 [Col. 0787C], the Remigius manuscript reads *confirmans dicit* (“confirming, he says”) for *confirmat, dicens* (“he confirms, saying”); [Col. 0787D], it reads *abscondita tangebantur* (“hidden things were touched upon”) for the reading concerning mysteries concealed in the fleece.

34. The soldiers of the Lord were furnished in this manner: girded about their loins and carrying jars in their hands (Judg. 7:16), and also carrying [Note: Ms. Remig. adds here, “carrying.”] lighted torches, aflame in mind and body, with this as the sign of victory: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon.” Accordingly, Gideon reconnoitered the camp of the opposing side during the night, and, perceiving by what dreams the Lord had terrified their adversaries, returned at dawn to his soldiers [Note: Ms. Remig. and the Lyon edition read, “returned to them and addressed them as those who had already obtained a certain victory.”], addressing them as those who had obtained a certain victory, and commanded the soldiers of God to throw their jars from their hands onto the ground and immediately to charge the enemy with complete confidence (ibid., 18). Thus also, under our Judge, the Lord Jesus, our army has conquered and is conquering. It is commanded: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning,” while carrying the two-edged sword, the word of God (Luke 12:35). The strong bodies of the martyrs, dashed upon the earth like jars [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “dashed upon the earth,” perhaps “smashed”], as they resounded—namely, those who fight for the truth unto death (Rev. 1:16)—put all their enemies to flight by their mighty sound. Their triumph echoes in a sweet song as they say: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” [Note: Ms. Remig. adds here, “hidden”], “so that the surpassing power may be God’s and not ours” (1 Cor. 4:7). Giving thanks to God, who gave them the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 15:57). For our own tested ones too passed through fire and water (Ps. 65:12), licking with their tongues like the Lord’s dogs; David recalls them, saying: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him” (Ps. 67:14). For these now bark on behalf of the one whom they once hated, and by their barking every adversary of Christ is put to flight.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### In Abimelech, the son of the concubine, heretics are signified. A prediction made and figured. [Note: These words are added from the manuscript of Remigius.] In Judges, believed and seen.

35. Abimelech, the son of a concubine, after the death of his father Gideon, killed Gideon’s seventy legitimate sons and, having won over the people, became judge in Israel (Judg. 9:1 ff.). One of the seventy escaped by hiding and, passing by, rebuked all Israel through a kind of parable (ibid., 7): the unfruitful wild trees, when they asked the vine and the fig tree to be king over them, had received the answer that fruitful trees could not abandon the fruitfulness of their fatness and go to reign over the trees. This figure [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “this presumed…”] displays the presumptuous audacity of heretics. For although they are not sons of the free woman but of the slave woman (Gal. 4:31), like wild things among wild things—that is, among unfruitful souls—they assert power, being overwhelmed by the thorns of sins, with the intention of killing, by rebaptizing them, the sons of the true King and Judge in the soul [Note: This is the reading of Ms. Remig. and the Lyon edition. The other editions read, “by baptizing.”]

Yet a woman killed this bold leader Abimelech by throwing a fragment of a millstone from the wall and crushing his head (Judg. 9:53) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “by throwing a fragment of a millstone from the wall”; the editions lacked the word “millstone.”]. Thus too it is fitting that heretics should perish: while they strive to assault our head, Christ the Lord, with an insulting disputation [Note: Ms. Remig. adds “while”; shortly afterward it reads “binding,” where the other editions have “assigning”; in this final point the Lyon edition alone agrees with the manuscript.], since the sons of the slave woman cannot be heirs, but the sons of the free woman can. The Church, like a woman from the nations, binds a millstone around their neck and plunges them into the depths (Matt. 18:6) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “having bound a millstone around their neck”; the editions omitted “millstone.”].

## CHAPTER XX  
### In Jephthah, the sacrifice of the virgin signifies the sacrifice of Christ’s sacrificed flesh. A promise made and figured. In Judges, believed and seen.

[Col. 0789A]

36. Jephthah too, following in due order, judged the people of God for six years (Judg. 11:6) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “Jephthah likewise, following in the succeeding order, judged the people of God.”]. While he was waging war against the Ammonites and saw that his adversaries were prevailing against him, he made a rash vow: if he should happen to conquer his enemies, whatever first came out to meet him from his house, he would offer as a sacrifice (ibid., 29). His rashness was corrected in this way: not an animal from any flock [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “an animal considered…”], but his only daughter, a virgin, came out to meet the triumphant victor and afflicted him grievously because of his promise. When he saw her, he said: “Alas for me, my daughter! You have wounded me. For I have opened my mouth in a vow to the Lord concerning you, and I cannot retract it.” And his daughter said to him: “If you have opened your mouth to the Lord concerning me, father, do to me as you promised, since the Lord has taken vengeance on your enemies” [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “what he had done … against your enemies.”] (ibid., 35).

She then asked her father for a period of respite, so that on the mountain she might mourn her virginity with her companions. When the appointed time had passed, Jephthah fulfilled his vows by means of her as his sacrifice [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “Jephthah fulfilled his vow by making her his sacrifice.”]. And, as has been said, she had not known a man (ibid., 39).

Perhaps it will be asked why God did not command him to spare his only daughter, just as he commanded Abraham to spare his only son (Gen. 22:12) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “to spare him.”]. Thus arises that famous and difficult question, which, with the Lord revealing it, I shall resolve in this way. First, God had not demanded this from Jephthah by testing him, as he had from Abraham [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “as from Abraham”]; rather, he vowed of his own accord—not, as I have said, tested by God, but himself in a certain sense testing God. Second, it was fitting [perhaps: “it was unfitting”] that, without designating the victim, he should sacrifice, as he had promised, the dog, pack animal, or any other unworthy beast that first met him [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “and indeed better, it seems, than the reading in the editions, ‘it was fitting.’ Then the manuscript reads, ‘to be sacrificed.’”]. Since, therefore, he wished to test God without having been tested, what met him was something that would prove the virtue, vow, and intention of the one making the promise [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “would provoke…”].

[Col. 0789C] 37. But the apostle Paul, in the Letter to the Hebrews (chap. 11:32), says that this Jephthah, among the others full of faith, performed righteousness precisely in this matter. He recalls Barak, Samson, Samuel, and our other heroes, lest the earthly city alone should exalt its citizens with the applause of vanity: if Torquatus killed his son for it, if Mucius extended his right hand into the flames, if Curtius, by throwing himself into the chasm, deprived himself of life for its savagery [Note: The older editions and Ms. Remig. read “for its savagery”; the more recent editions read “for its service”], while our citizens of Jerusalem, citizens of the great heavenly city, have accomplished things far loftier, numerous, and manifold [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “loftier.”].

Nevertheless, this deed of Jephthah’s righteousness admonishes us to seek the mysteries of the Lord’s action, as though it had been granted us to explain the secret of so great a matter [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “to explain the learned…”]. These figured mysteries, therefore, refer in such a way to our Judge and Leader, the Lord Jesus [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “in this way I shall refer them,” perhaps “interpret them”], that we recognize him as willing to take vengeance on our enemies for our redemption, and to have sacrificed his only virgin flesh, as a daughter [Note: The editions read “and her”; corrected from Ms. Remig.]. For he is said to have been formed by himself in the womb, through the prophet David: “Mother Zion will say: ‘A man and a man was born in her,’ and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 87:5).

This flesh came forward at the hour of the Passion, when its Creator publicly exposed the rulers and powers of this air, triumphing over them confidently in himself (Col. 2:15) [Note: That is, he “publicly displayed them and made them an object of derision”; this is what the Greek verb παραδειγματίζειν means.]. It came forward, I say, at the hour of which the Gospel says: “Father, what shall I say? Let this hour pass. But for this reason I have come to this hour” (John 12:29) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “so that he who had created it might sacrifice it.”], so that he who had created it might be sacrificed.

38. As for the fact that she asked for a respite in order to mourn her virginity on the mountain with her companions (Judg. 11:37), Jesus ascended the mountain with his companions as his Passion approached (Matt. 26:30) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “with his disciples … she praying.”]. There he prayed, as the Evangelist testifies, and sweated: drops of blood seemed to fall upon the ground instead of tears (Luke 22:44). He urged his companions to watch and pray, lest they enter into temptation, adding that his soul was sorrowful unto death (Matt. 26:38, 40).

Then, descending from the mountain, he offered to God the Father as a sacrifice this flesh that he had assumed for us, virgin and undefiled, which had not known a man. For here too he opened his mouth concerning his flesh, saying through the prophet: “What proceeds from my lips I will not reject” (Ps. 89:35) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “what proceeds … I will not nullify; I will not reject.”]. And he himself says in the Gospel: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 10:17). And again: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

For that flesh was not corrupted even in death. Of it he says in the psalm: “My flesh will rest in hope. For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 16:9–10) [Note: In Ms. Remig., “my flesh will rest … you will not abandon…”]. Therefore, the one who ends this life for God lives for God. “For me to live,” says the Apostle, “is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21).

## CHAPTER XXI  
### In Samson, the Lord Christ the Nazarite, strong in his head. A promise made and figured. [Note: The editions read, “In Judah.” Corrected with the help of Ms. Remig.] In Judges, believed and seen.

[Col. 0790C] 39. Manoah was named at the time when the judges of God governed the people, and his wife was barren (Judg. 13:2). The angel of the Lord appeared to her and promised that she would have such a son (ibid., 3). “No razor,” he said, “shall come upon his head, and he shall not drink wine or strong drink, for the boy shall be a Nazarite from the day of his birth until the end of his life.” Now “Nazarite” means “virtue in the head,” since “the head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3).

Thus that very strong Samson was born, full, as has been said, of strength from the hair of his head, and he judged Israel for twenty years. All his actions resound in figure of the Lord Christ. With God’s grace assisting me [Note: The word “thus” is absent from Ms. Remig.], I shall run through the order of his deeds in this way.

“Samson descended,” Scripture says, “to Taumatha” [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “to Tamna”], “and there he loved a foreign woman” (Judg. 14:1), and he asked his parents to obtain her as his wife. Our own mighty Nazarite also descended from heaven, of whom the angel says to Mary: “He will be called a Nazarene” (Matt. 2:23), in order to join to himself souls beloved from the nations and unite them in faith.

As Samson went to see his betrothed, a young lion came to meet him; filled with the Spirit, he tore it apart and scattered it limb by limb (Judg. 14:5–6) [Note: The Lyon edition reads “tore apart.” All the others, supported by Ms. Remig., read “scattered.” Yet from the scriptural text and what follows—where it says “he tore the people apart”—the former reading clearly ought to be placed first.].

Again, when he returned and turned aside from the road, he saw the carcass of the animal, found a honeycomb in the lion’s mouth, took it away, and, eating it, gave some of it to his parents, without telling them that it came from his deed (ibid., 8).

Our Nazarite too, Jesus the Lord, did this. He tore apart the Jewish people like a young lion and scattered them limb by limb [Note: The editions add “and the young lion.”]. Concerning him the gentile prophet Balaam says: “Israel is like a young lion, strongest on the road” (Num. 23:24) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads this way; the editions read “Judah.”]. David the prophet testifies that his members have been scattered throughout the world, saying to our strong Lord: “Scatter them by your power” (Ps. 59:12). [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “We believe this has happened as we see it.”] We do not merely believe that this has happened; we see it.

40. As for the honeycomb that he found in the mouth of this lion, understand, hearer, the spiritual law of his people: the patriarchs and prophets, constructing it like bees, poured into it the honey of divine speech. He took this from the mouth of the dead lion; having rejected the Jews, he also supplied that law to the nations. Eating it [Note: Ms. Remig. reads this way; the editions read, “And eating it … as he says.”], the body of our mighty Judge, Christ the Lord, he says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 119:103). Solomon also says: “Honeycombs are pleasant words” (Prov. 16:24).

He gave some of it, as has been said, to his parents—or to his disciples, when he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45)—or to those who passed from the Jews to faith in Christ, so that they too, tasting, might see how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 34:8).

Samson brought forward the enigma of this action at the wedding feast, under a definite pledge of thirty linen garments and an equal number of robes to the men who were present, if they could explain the riddle (Judg. 14:10). “Out of the eater,” he said, “came food, and out of the strong came something sweet” (ibid., 14) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “sweet.”].

When, as the day of its solution approached, they could not understand it, they compelled his wife by threats and terrors to investigate the man’s meaning [Note: Ms. Remig. reads this way; the Lyon and Louvain editions have “by excessive terrors,” while other manuscripts read “by great terrors.”]. Once they had learned the solution of the riddle through her, they disclosed it, saying: “What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?” To them he said: “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would never have understood my riddle” (ibid., 18) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “If you had not subdued my heifer, you would never have understood.”].

Great, therefore, is that mystery of the Lord’s piety which was veiled in the Law and hidden from the ages in God; through Christ it was revealed and manifested among the nations (Col. 1:26; 1 Tim. 3:16). Indeed, stripping those whom he had overthrown of their spoils, Samson promptly fulfilled the promise (Judg. 14:19), so that what had been said of our own would also be signified: “He will divide the spoils of the strong” (Isa. 53:12). Our own Lord healthfully kills his enemies when, in the flesh, he kills sin with sin (Rom. 8:3), fulfilling the promises of the spoils—not by repaying merits with merits, but by conferring good things on the wretched in place of evils.

41. When Samson went to the feast of the Hebrew people, so that he might celebrate with his companions, the parents of his wife gave her to another man (Judg. 15:1). This is what fickle and worthless souls do: refusing to preserve, with chaste and faithful hearts, the companionship of Christ, their only bridegroom, they surrender and join themselves to every kind of heretical teaching. The Apostle admonishes souls who belong to one bridegroom, Christ, and preserve the marriage bed with modest love: “See that no one deceives you in any way” (2 Thess. 2:3).

When Samson returned and learned that his wife had been joined to another man, he ambushed and destroyed that nation out of grief (Judg. 15:3). He therefore captured three hundred foxes, tied their tails together, placed burning torches on them [Note: These words—“and sent them through the fields of the Philistines, and burned all their crops with extraordinary efficiency”—which were found in Ms. Remig. and the Lyon edition, had dropped out of the later editions, to the detriment of the passage’s meaning], and sent them through the fields of the Philistines; with remarkable economy he burned all their crops.

Our strong Lord also speaks, signifying heretics: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song 2:15). Their torches are fires of error rather than of divine love. They are not in the head, but in the tail. For they burn with zeal and perverse teachings, by which they fan the ignorant—or rather, those destined to perish [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “those who will perish”—] with the scattering of their vapor, and consume them all like wild grass by fire [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “like field hay.”].

For in the sight of our Judge, Christ the Lord, fire will burn (Ps. 97:3), and, as the prophet says, all foreigners will be stubble; “the coming day will set them ablaze,” says the Lord (Mal. 4:1). That woman, however, who, abandoning so great a husband, believed she should join herself to another, is known to have been consumed by fire together with her parents by her own fellow citizens (Judg. 15:6), so that every heretical soul, together with its parents—that is, its teachers—may be burned by unquenchable fire, with its sins bringing it to judgment. For “their iniquities will lead them forth from the opposite side” (Wis. 4:20), when the Lord says to them: “Depart from me into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

## CHAPTER XXII  
### In the same Samson, Christ the Lord bound by the Jews and breaking all bonds. A prediction made and figured. [Note: The earlier title is supplied from Ms. Remig.] In Judges, believed and seen.

42. That same Samson loved another woman among that people. While he was going to take her, the ambushes of the enemies attacked him when he was alone on the road (Judg. 15:15). Divine strength immediately came to his aid. Taking up the jawbone of a donkey, he struck down a thousand men with it and put the rest to flight. When he grew weak from fighting because of thirst, he called upon God; water flowed from a fissure in the jawbone, restoring him when he had drunk, and, after he had overcome his adversaries, made him victorious.
