If you consider our mighty Lord carried by this animal, you will find that an equal and even greater number of enemies were struck down by him, since the prophet David says to him: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but they shall not come near you” (Ps. 91:7). For blood and water flowed from his side to his thirsting body as from a fissure (John 19:34), and every Christian soul, refreshed by this, says: “He led me beside waters of refreshment; he restored my soul” (Ps. 23:2).

After that marvelous battle, Samson joined to himself another woman whom he loved, named Delilah (Judg. 16:4). These two women, as the mystical action itself reveals when examined in many ways, I take to be the two cities that the prophet Ezekiel designated by these names, Oholah and Oholibah—namely, Samaria and Jerusalem (Ezek. 23:4): Samaria, which received the kingdom’s division into eleven parts, like that first woman who, abandoning her lawful husband, surrendered herself to heretics; and Jerusalem, like this Delilah, who brought the mysteries of the Passion of Christ the Lord to completion through the whole ordered action.

[Col. 0792D] 43. The events that occurred then proceed as follows. The Philistines said to Delilah: “Seduce your husband and find out where his strength lies, and we will each give you eleven hundred pieces of silver” (Judg. 16:5). Behold the threefold sale. Christ is sold in Joseph before the Law (Gen. 37:28), sold in Samson under the Law, and sold by Judas to the Jews under grace (Matt. 26:15).

Delilah seduces the man at their urging and says: “Tell me in what way your strength could be weakened” (Judg. 16:7). Samson, in a certain manner, opened his mouth in parables and said: “If I am bound with fresh sinews—that is, newly made ones—I shall be weakened and become like all men.” The strong man allows himself to be bound with these cords. While the adversaries lie in wait and his wife says to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson” [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “upon you”], he dissolves those bonds by his strength, as tow dissolves when it touches fire, and puts all the adversaries to flight.

Our strong Lord also permitted himself to be bound by such cords at Jerusalem. For the Pharisees bring to him a woman caught in adultery and, tempting him, say: “Teacher, we have just caught this woman. Moses commanded that such women be stoned; but what do you say about her?” (John 8:1 ff.). They thought that they had bound Jesus with cords as though from the Law, and especially with fresh ones when they said “just now” [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “which … and shortly afterward, ‘If anyone,’ he says.”]. Our strong one broke these bonds by this answer: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her” (ibid., 7). When they heard this, they went away one after another, so that the bond with which they had bound him might be loosed, just as the prophet said: “As wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. 68:3).

44. Again the Philistines set an ambush through the woman, and the woman says to Samson: “Tell me now in what way your strength can be weakened.” And Samson says: “If I am bound with new ropes, I shall be weakened and become like all men” (Judg. 16:11). When this had been done, she said, “The adversaries are upon you, Samson” [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “they say.”]. But he, filled with the Spirit, broke the ropes from his arms like a thread and scattered and put all the adversaries to flight [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “breaking … and scattering.”].

Our strong Lord also allows himself to be bound. A second time the Pharisees come to him and say: “Teacher, we know that you teach truthfully and do not show partiality. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. 22:16–18) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “our strong one, the second time: they come to him again.”]. In this temptation they bound our strong one with something like a two-headed noose. But, by the Spirit of strength, our strong one broke every knot with these words: “Why are you testing me, hypocrites? Show me the coin of the tax.” They brought him a denarius. And the Lord said: “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said, “Caesar’s.” The Lord said: “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (ibid., 18–21). With these words he swiftly broke those bonds—the man who had been taken up, who sings to his God in the psalms: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 116:16).

45. For the third time the woman presses the man [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “or, ‘How long … tell me now.’”]. “How long,” she says, “will you mock me? Tell me now in what way your strength can be weakened” (Judg. 16:13). The Jews spoke almost the same words to our Judge Christ: “How long,” they say, “will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John 10:24) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “you suspend.”].

But Samson permitted himself to be bound a third time in this way: “If the hairs of my head are fastened to a loom’s pin [the reading *paloor sorio* is uncertain], I shall be weakened and become like all men.” When the woman did this, she said, “The adversaries are upon you, Samson” [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “they say.”]. But he rose up, broke everything, and struck down his enemies after putting them to flight and wounding them.

A similar binding happens to our strong Jesus the Lord, as though the hairs were woven around a loom’s pin. The scribes and Pharisees say to Jesus: “Moses wrote for us that if someone’s brother dies without children, his brother should take the dead man’s wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were seven brothers. The second and the third took the wife of the brother, and they died without leaving children; afterward they all took her; and the woman also died childless. In the resurrection, they say, whose wife will she be?” (Matt. 22:24 ff.) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “one of them took a wife, and the second and third, and all died.”]

The more intensely they thought they had bound our strong one, the more swiftly he loosened the question they had posed. And truly he acted as one having authority (Matt. 7:29), for he could not be bound by these temptations unless he himself permitted it. “The sons of this age,” he says, “marry and are given in marriage; but those who are judged worthy to attain that age neither marry nor are given in marriage. For they cannot die anymore, because they are like angels and are sons of God” (Luke 20:34–36). After these words, his enemies, struck down by complete confusion, went away (ibid., 40).

And the hour of Samson’s death came. Our Lord also says: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (John 12:23). “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (ibid., 24).

46. When the woman persisted and deceitfully wept before him, Samson became fainthearted, Scripture says, even unto death, so that the figured action of our Lord might be fulfilled when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38) [Note: This is the reading of Ms. Remig. and the ancient editions; the more recent editions added here the word “Lord.”]. “If the hairs of my head are shaved,” Samson said, “I shall be weakened and become like all men” (Judg. 16:17).

Before this happened, the woman sent to the men, saying: “Bring the silver, for he has now told me everything truthfully.” A definite handing-over takes place, which Judas completed after receiving the silver; and what happened in our Lord Christ is fulfilled in Samson by way of figure [Note: Ms. Remig. has this in the accusative: “against our Lord Christ.”].

For when the woman received him and made him sleep in her lap, this signifies what our strong Lord says: “It is not fitting for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13:33). That she intoxicated him with a deadly drink signifies what our Lord also said: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 69:21).

That she used a razor to shave his head signifies that they crucified him at the place of Calvary. After Samson’s head was shaved, his strength departed. Our Lord, hanging upon the tree, cried out: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” And again: “Those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head” (Ps. 22:1; 69:4).

Samson’s enemies gouged out both his eyes. The two portions, like lights, namely, of the disciples, were poured out for a time—some by denying, others by fleeing [Note: These words, supplied from Ms. Remig., are absent from the other editions, which express the contrary.]. For them our strong one cries: “My eyes have failed while hoping in my God”; and again: “Give light to my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 69:4; 13:4). We know that this happened among the disciples when, after he had risen, their eyes were opened and they recognized him in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:31). The enemies took Samson and bound him with iron. These things indicate the nails of the Crucified One.

47. As for the things they did in mockery—striking him on the face with their palms, smearing him with spittle, and beating him with whips—the prophet Isaiah foretold them all (Isa. 50:6), and the holy Gospels testify that they were fulfilled in Christ the Lord (Matt. 27:29–30; Mark 15:17–19). There the Jews, as though mocking one who was blind, strike his head with a reed and say: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (Luke 22:63; Matt. 26:68).

At his death Samson performed one final miracle, which our Lord and strong one also fulfilled. When the hair of his head grew again, his strength grew with it. His enemies led him to the temple, where the entire people had gathered to offer praise and sacrifices to their gods because they had handed over their fiercest enemy to them. Once there, he ordered the boy who guided him to place Samson’s hands upon the pillars on which the whole building rested. Grasping them, one with each hand [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “each one with one hand”], and calling upon God, he asked that he might be strengthened once more. Then, by the force of the Spirit, he tore out the pillars, and the whole building fell together with the people. Samson killed more at his death than he had killed during his life (Judg. 16:22 ff.).

Our Lord also displayed more openly what Samson had done mystically: moving the two corners of the world—circumcision and uncircumcision—as though they were two pillars (Eph. 2:14 ff.), he overturned the whole worship of idols, dissolving hostility in his flesh so as to create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and reconciling both in one body to God through the Cross, killing hostility in himself [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “and to change both into one … in himself.”].

Up to this point, the events accomplished in Judges have appeared in figured form [Note: Ms. Remig. reads this way, with “books” understood; the editions read, “in judgments.”].

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Ruth, the Church from the nations, mocking the Jews. A prediction made and figured. In Ruth, believed and seen.

48. Ruth was named among that people. Although she was a foreigner—that is, coming from the Moabites—she was placed under the Law of God and among his people, and she performed deeds that bore the figure of the Church coming from the nations (Ruth 1:4). She offered herself in marriage to a certain man from the Hebrew people (ibid. 3:9, 12). But he, observing the commandments of the Law, neither drawn by the girl’s appearance nor captivated by the ardor of his youth, sent her to the man to whom, according to the Law, she was owed as the nearer kinsman (Deut. 25:5).

He who had been summoned by divine right refused her. The Law decreed that the man who was unwilling to take his female relative should be deprived of his sandal. Marked by this disgrace, he was succeeded by the man who had reserved the place for the nearer kinsman [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “who had reserved it for the kinsman.”] (Ruth 4:8, 10).

Thus the Church of the nations also offered herself in the faith of Christ the Lord to the people of Israel as to the nearer kinsman. Because Israel was unwilling to receive her, the glory of the Law that had been conferred upon it was rightly stripped from it, and it was branded with the mark of infamy, because it did not desire the blessing, and “it will be far from him” (Ps. 109:18).

As the Apostle says to that same people: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you have driven it away and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13:46) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “to announce … we turn to the nations.”].

The house of the man deprived of his sandal was marked among that people by this offense. But the people who later received her are those whose feet are shod “in the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:15). That Gospel announces that Boaz and Ruth begot Obed; through the succession of his offspring the line continued to Joseph and Mary, and finally to the birth of Christ the Lord (Matt. 1:5 ff.).

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### In Samuel, Christ the Lord, Leader, Priest, and Prophet, rebuking the priests. A promise made and figured. In the Books of Kings, believed and seen.

[Col. 0795D]

49. Anna, the wife of Elkanah, who was barren, made a vow to God that, if he gave her a son, he would belong from infancy to old age in the house of the Lord [Note: Ms. Remig., “of the Lord.”] (I Samuel 1:11ff.). [Col. 0796A] Samuel was given and born from her; when he had been weaned, she returned him to the Lord, as she had promised. While he was still a little child in the temple, he was so favored by grace that he received divine responses, and the Lord announced future things to him (I Samuel 3:4).

Yet he did not so much change the order of the priesthood in figure as that three things are found in him which must be attributed to Christ the Lord. For he became leader, priest, and prophet of the people. If you seek Christ as leader, the prophet Daniel speaks of him: “Leader of the heavenly army” (Daniel 9:25). If you seek Christ as priest, David says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4). If you seek Christ as prophet, he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Luke 4:24).

While the sons of the priest Eli were behaving wickedly, unjustly presuming to eat portions of the sacrificial meats that God had not assigned to them (I Samuel 2:12), claiming that these should be offered first to them and afterward to God, and harassing the women who came to the temple while committing outrages with them, God became angry when these crimes had been committed and sent the battle of a hostile people against them (I Samuel 4:1). [Col. 0796B] In it not only the people but also those very priests were slain. The ark of God itself was captured by the enemies.

For God becomes angry with sinful priests in such a way that he does not even spare his consecrated places and vessels. David says: “God rejected his tabernacle, in which he dwelt among human beings; and he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them” (Psalm 77:60–61). And again: “God rejected them from his sanctuary” (Psalm 88:40). Elsewhere also: “If the people sin, the priest will intercede for them; but if the priest [Note: Ms. Remig. adds the word “sins.”] sins, who will intercede for him?” (I Samuel 2:25).

50. [Note: The Cologne edition and Ms. Remig. read, “Alas for me.”] Alas for me! With a great groan and inexhaustible weeping I shall say—I shall say that, because of our sins and wicked conduct, these evils also come upon our own times.

The enemies who had captured the ark of God believed that it ought to be treated with such reverence that they thought it should be placed in the temple of their god Dagon (I Samuel 5:2). [Col. 0796C] Under its power, on the following day they saw their idol thrown down and lying prostrate. But attributing this to chance, they set it up again, fastening it with stronger and sturdier hooks (ibid., 5). On the next day, when they saw it broken and shattered before the ark, they could not understand what had happened (ibid., 6). The people themselves were struck by a more grievous and terrible plague, which the prophet David records with a certain sense of shame, saying: “He struck his enemies from behind; he gave them everlasting disgrace” (Psalm 77:66).

Nor could they escape the final punishment for this disgrace unless they returned the ark of God that they had captured, with gifts placed beside it [Note: Ms. Remig. reads *anis appositis*, “with asses added.”] (I Samuel 6:3). Let kings and nations see and fear—those who still keep captive among themselves the consecrated vessels of the almighty God and refuse to return them. For what evils do we believe await those who refused to honor in his sacred vessels that name which is above every name (Philippians 2:9), when divine History testifies that those who honored the ark of God were punished in this way (I Samuel 6:19), and that, because it was seen, God here too began to take vengeance on his enemies? [Col. 0796D]

51. That same obstinate Hebrew people, rejecting Samuel’s leadership, asked that a king be appointed over them (I Samuel 8:5). The Lord became angry and said to Samuel: “They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me” (ibid., 7). Thus was then signified what they later said to Pilate, rejecting the Lord Jesus as king: “We have no king except Caesar” (John 19:15). [Col. 0797A]

Nevertheless, the Lord gave them Saul as king, the son of Kish from the tribe of Benjamin (I Samuel 9:1), who oppressed them with royal power for forty years. Therefore every soul that rejects the law and yoke of Christ the Lord [Note: Ms. Remig., “the light yoke of Christ the Lord.”] deserves to be oppressed in this way; and while evil leaders, rulers, and priests dominate such people, they hear: “I gave you a king according to your heart” (I Samuel 12:13).

Let those who receive these powers also beware: whether they accept them from the desire to rule rather than from the will to serve and advise; whether they choose to be served rather than to serve. The Lord himself, and the prophet Hosea through him, rebukes this, saying: “Canaan has in his hand a balance of injustice” [Note: Ms. Remig., with the Lyon edition, “of justice”]—“for he chose domination” [Note: Ms. Remig., “he by no means chose”] (Hosea 12:7). And he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you shall be your servant; just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20:27–28).

## CHAPTER XXV

### In David, Christ the shepherd playing the harp. The promise made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

[Note: These words are added to this title, and to several others, with the aid of the Remigian–Remensis manuscript.]

[Col. 0797B]

52. When that same king Saul, seized by pride, despised God’s commands (I Samuel 15:1ff.), he was rejected by God. David—that is, “strong-handed”—although small among his brothers, received the sacrament of royal anointing (I Samuel 16:13). [Note: Ms. Remig., “the sacrament of royal anointing.”] He was truly a shepherd of sheep, signifying our shepherd, the anointed Christ the Lord, who says: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

David confesses that he rescued prey from the lion’s mouth (I Samuel 17:35). Our own “strong-handed” one, Christ, rescued from the mouth of the lion—the devil—both Peter, who denied him, and the repentant thief (Luke 22:61; 23:43; I Samuel 18:10).

By the sweet sound of his harp, David soothed not only the hearing of animals but also calmed the vexation of the evil spirit in Saul himself. [Note: Ms. Remig., “of the malicious spirit.”] If you consider the harp of our “strong-handed” one, Christ the Lord, resounding—the harp fitted to the wood of the cross by the strings of his flesh and limbs, while the plectrum of the Holy Spirit touched it—[Note: Ms. Remig., “which he fits to the wood of the cross … while the Holy Spirit touches it with the plectrum.”] filling every living creature with blessing (Psalm 144:16), he even drove the devil from the hearts of his enemies. For them, as he prayed on the cross, he uttered that sweet sound, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). [Col. 0797C]

Yet while David was pleasing to King Saul through his harp, and recognized that Saul was troubled by the messages concerning Goliath, who was challenging him to single combat under the condition of servitude, the little David opposed himself to that powerful man. “Let not my lord’s heart fall,” he said; “I shall go and fight this Philistine” (I Samuel 17:32). [Note: Ms. Remig., “I shall overcome this Philistine.”]

Saul said to him: “You cannot, for you are a boy, whereas he is a warrior from his youth.” David replied: “Your servant has killed both the lion and the bear. So this man also shall be like one of them” (ibid., 36)—signifying through his offspring, as had been promised, the one who was to come, who “trod upon the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90:13). [Col. 0798D]

53. When the battle had begun, David refused Saul’s armor, with which he had been clothed (I Samuel 17:39). Choosing five smooth stones from the stream, and taking the sling in his hand [Note: Ms. Remig., “taking the sling in his hand.”], the little shepherd overcame the great enemy—not a king in the appearance of a king, but a formidable adversary. [Col. 0797D]

Thus our shepherd, Christ the Lord, rejecting the wisdom of this world as though it were that armor, chose in the five stones the foolish things of the world, by which he might confound the strong (I Corinthians 1:27). For the whole terrifying display of the proud one was struck in the forehead by a single blow of the stone and thrown down; and he is recognized as having been beheaded with his own sword (I Samuel 17:49, 51). [Col. 0798A]

From the five books of the Law came the one foretold stone; speaking of the sling of the flesh, expressed by the strong-handed one, it struck down all the devil’s pride and killed him with his own sword, when death killed death. For “through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24). The innocent good Shepherd accepted this death, who laid down his life for his own (John 10:11), so that by his death he might defeat the devil.

When the enemy had been extinguished and thrown down, Saul unjustly conceived envy against David because of the victory (I Samuel 18:8): repaying good with evil, he drives away, hates, and persecutes the innocent. Our Lord also speaks of such people: “They repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love” (Psalms 34:12; 108:5). [Note: Ms. Remig., “But what then?”]

As David, while Saul pursued him, moved through mountain hiding places, caves, and deserts (I Samuel 20ff.), so our Lord, in the person of his body—that is, of his holy members, namely the martyrs—expressed persecutions in this figure. Of them the apostle Paul says: “The world was not worthy of them; they wandered through deserts, caves, and caverns of the earth” (Hebrews 11:38). [Col. 0798B]

54. David did not kill his persecutor Saul when Saul was delivered into his hands; instead, he cut off a piece of his cloak and spared the man who hated him (I Samuel 24:4). This is what our shepherd and king, Christ the Lord, does every day toward his haters and persecutors [Note: Thus Ms. Remig.; the printed editions read “and of things,” without sense.]:  while cutting away from them the great vice of pride, he also spares raging kings, because he does not desire the death of the wicked, but that they should turn back and live (Ezekiel 18:23). [Note: Ms. Remig., “provided only that they turn back and live.”]

This is what he did and does for all his enemies—the one who justifies the ungodly not on the basis of merits but freely (Romans 3:4). [Note: Ms. Remig. has “he” once; the printed editions have it twice.]

Again, when David withdrew from Saul’s ambushes, the Philistines received him (I Samuel 21:10). So our Christ the Lord, withdrawing from the raging Jews, gave himself to the nations. The Philistines betrayed to King Saul that David was hiding among them at Gath (I Samuel 26:1). The same prophet speaks of our betrayed king: “All my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evil” (Psalm 40:8). And again: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2:2). [Col. 0798C]

But when David realized that he had been betrayed, he performed certain things—or rather, future mysteries were performed through him—pretending to be deranged. His saliva ran down into his beard, and, as Scripture says, he was borne entirely “in his own hands” (I Samuel 21:13). [Note: Ms. Remig., “ran back.”] When the king of that people saw him in such a state, he dismissed him by having him thrown out, saying: “Why have you brought this madman to me?” (ibid., 14).

For nothing is said or done in the Law that can be empty or in any way unrelated to a figurative action. The enemies of our Lord, the Jews, also say to him: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John 8:48). They even spat upon him and drove him out of certain cities.

Jesus the Lord was also carried in his own hands, when, carrying his body in his own hands in the consecrated bread, he said: “This is my body, which will be given for you” (Luke 22:19; I Corinthians 11:24). Anyone who also wishes to know about those mysteries—how David danced naked before the ark in the presence of his male and female servants, thereby displaying Christ crucified before men and women—should consult the words of the bishop Augustine, of revered memory, in which he has treated these matters more fully and comprehended nearly everything (see Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 33, no. 5ff.). [Col. 0798D]

## CHAPTER XXVI

### In that same David, loving his enemies and restoring the fallen. The promise made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

[Col. 0799A]

55. As the order of the promise required, the anointed David received all Israel—not merely a part, as before—to govern, after Saul had been killed in battle (I Samuel 31:6). [Note: Ms. Remig. omits the word “in,” without harm.] He mourned deeply for the man who had been killed and even avenged him; and all Israel gathered to him (II Samuel 1:17ff.). [Col. 0799B]

This too is now taking place, when our king Christ the Lord loves his enemies exceedingly and avenges them; the whole world is gathered to him, as was promised: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8). And although he has already taken possession of almost all the nations, it remains that, when the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel destined for salvation may be saved, so that through it the whole world may be reconciled to God (Romans 11:25–26).

The deeds David performed when exalted in the kingdom refer to those who, having fallen through a certain presumptuous pride, are corrected through repentance and joined to the body of Christ, the second Church. [Perhaps, “secondarily.”] As someone has said, realities weary the minds of the wise. This David, once exalted, committed the two principal things forbidden by the Law: adultery and murder [Note: Ms. Remig. adds “at the same time.”] (II Samuel 11:1ff.).

When warned by the prophet Nathan, he undertook repentance, driven by great contrition of heart [Note: Ms. Remig., “touched”]—for sins cannot remain unpunished. Although he escaped immediate death, it is nevertheless clear that he was severely punished for what he had done (ibid., 12:1ff.). For he had already heard from the prophet’s mouth: “You acted in secret; you shall suffer in the open” (II Samuel 12:12).

By this sentence the whole condition of his household was disturbed in the following manner. One of his sons, seized by shameful desire, secretly assaulted and violated his sister, though she was by another mother. Absalom, the girl’s brother, killed the brother who had raped her (II Samuel 13:14). Struck by this deed, Absalom fled from the presence of his father (ibid., 34), stirred up all Israel, became a rebel, drove out his father (II Samuel 15:16), and pursued him, even criminally defiling his father’s bed with his concubines (II Samuel 16:22). [Col. 0799C]

David bore these things patiently, recognizing that, by the judgment of justice, he was being punished in himself for what he seemed to have committed secretly. [Note: The older editions read “openly”; the error does not appear corrected in Ms. Remig., but is emended in later editions.] As the divine Law recounts these deeds, it shows itself to be a mirror: it does not conceal even the deeds of their ancestors, and with the serenity of its splendor it reveals not only the beauties but also the foulness of all alike. [Note: “Also” is supplied from the Lyon edition.] It possesses that truth which both proves and punishes the guilt even of its own people, yet not without mercy—a mercy that covers everything and reveals everything [Note: The older editions read “did everything,” a reading not contrary to Ms. Remig.]: the fall of so great a man, the sentence of the just Judge, and the indulgence of the most merciful Father.

He was set here as an example [Note: Thus Ms. Remig.; older editions read “set, however, here,” and later ones “set indeed as an example.”] to sober souls, so that they may learn to fear prosperity more than to dread adversity. For in tribulation, as the prophet says, “we remember God” (Hosea 6:1). It is dangerous for the soul to be abandoned to its pleasures, since the Lord himself says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline” (Revelation 3:19). [Col. 0799D]

## CHAPTER XXVII

### In Abishag, souls fervent with the warmth of Christ’s grace. The prediction made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

56. When David himself had been worn out by old age, the virgin Abishag the Shunammite was brought to him to warm the king, without any purpose of intercourse; she was found still a virgin even after his death (I Kings 1:1ff.). [Note: Ms. Remig., “of desire.” The Remigian manuscript reads “when he had died”; all printed editions read “when he had failed/been exhausted.”]

This likeness [Note: The printed editions read “into a likeness”; a more recent edition, “in a likeness.”] signifies the soul inflamed by the warmth of God’s grace and chastity, which, through its own affection, kindles souls cold in faith as members of the great King. For it sings of itself in the Psalms: “You have tested me by fire, and iniquity was not found in me” (Psalm 16:3). Warming others by its breath, it says: “Come and hear, and I will tell all you who fear the Lord how great things he has done for my soul” (Psalm 65:16). [Col. 0800A]

When the king had died, Solomon succeeded his father David in the kingdom (I Kings 2:10, 12). Although many divine promises resound in his name, lest anyone attribute to his own person what had been represented—for he turned away from the Lord’s commandments and lost both life and wisdom in his old age (ibid., 11:4)—all those things that had been represented [Note: Ms. Remig., “marked.”] were reserved for Christ the Lord, the peaceful one, for “Solomon” is interpreted as “peaceful.”

I shall briefly recount what he did prophetically in the person of Christ the Lord and what was granted to him. [Col. 0800B]

57. At the beginning of his reign, the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: “Ask for whatever petition you wish” (I Kings 3:5). He desired nothing else but wisdom. Therefore he asked for Christ, because Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Corinthians 1:24).

“Give,” he said, “to your servant an understanding heart to judge and govern your people” (I Kings 3:9). When this petition pleased God—so that the gift of wisdom bestowed upon him might be made known to the whole people—two women appeared before the king. They lived together in one room and gave birth to sons at the same time (ibid., 16ff.).

One of them, while sleeping, accidentally smothered her little child and placed him beside her sleeping companion, claiming her companion’s living child for herself. [Note: The words “and claimed her living child for herself” are added from Ms. Remig., supported by the following words, “she whose living child had been stolen from her.”]

When the duties of night sleep had ended and the bright rising of the sun restored daylight to human eyes, all torpor having been dispelled, the woman who had lost her living child, believing that she should take him to her breasts, looked at the dead child and did not recognize him as her own. When she demanded the living child back from the thief, and the other fiercely denied that he had been taken, they both brought their dispute before the king. [Col. 0800C]

Since it could not be shown to whom the living child belonged, that Wisdom—Christ—which had been granted to the king ordered a sword to be brought, not in order to strike the child, but in order once more to reveal the mother’s womb that had given birth. “Divide,” the king said to his attendants, “the living child into two parts, and give half to this woman and half to that one” (ibid., 25).

The true mother, so that the child might live, yielded the whole child to her adversary; the false mother, so that the true mother might not possess him, demanded half.

Thus, under our King Christ, the souls of heretics are judged. While the true Catholic mother offers her living name whole to those who quarrel, they, wishing to separate, demand half. But our King, who came to cast a sword upon the earth (Matthew 10:34), removing the deceits of the heretics, restored the living state to the true mother who asked for life. “He asked for life,” says the prophet, “and you gave it to him” (Psalm 20:5).

The same undivided child, the son of the true Catholic mother, praises the judgment of the peaceful supreme King, Christ the Lord, and says: “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me” (Psalm 118:175). [Col. 0800D]

58. Solomon built for his Lord that same temple, large and constructed with marvelous magnificence, and dedicated it with every royal splendor (I Kings 6–8). His father had vowed to build it, but he was not permitted to fulfill the vow. For he had struck down many nations in war (II Samuel 7:5), and he was told that, because he had shed very much blood on the earth [Note: Ms. Remig., “because he had shed very much blood”], not he but his peaceful son should build a house for God (II Chronicles 22:8–9). [Note: Ms. Remig. lacks the word “that.”]

But since that temple signifies this spiritual building, it is written that “the Most High does not dwell in buildings made by human hands” (Acts 17:24). Therefore our King, true peace, Christ the Lord, building a spiritual house from living stones (I Peter 2:5), made the hearts of his faithful not merely individual temples in individuals, but one temple from them all. [Col. 0801A]

The Apostle says to them: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (I Corinthians 3:16). In it spiritual sacrifices are offered to God through the chief priest himself (I Peter 2:5). For he himself is our peace, who made both one (Ephesians 2:14).

The peaceful Solomon kept all his time quiet with the nations, peace being granted by the Lord. [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “Solomon the peaceful one had all his time peaceful with the nations: peace.”] When he had devoted himself entirely to wisdom, writing various ethical sayings—that is, moral sayings [Note: The printed text reads *et icas*, apparently for *ethicas*, “ethical”; it has *immortales*, “immortal,” where *mortales*, “mortal,” or more probably *morales*, “moral,” may have been intended]—and composing mystical riddles, the splendid fame of his kingdom was spread throughout the world. [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “The splendid fame of his kingdom was spread throughout the world to visit … to see.” The word “messengers,” or “by messengers,” is suspected to be superfluous; perhaps the reading should be, “the splendid fame of that kingdom was spread throughout the world.”] [Col. 0801B]

Therefore, to see such a man, the queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom (I Kings 10:1). When she marveled at his teaching, she presented gifts, placing his presence above praise, and departed from his sight. [Note: Ms. Remig., “to visit … to see.”]

59. From this deed our King Christ the Lord rebukes the Jews: the queen of the South, breaking through every delay and royal obligation, undeterred by the length of the journey, came with all haste to see and hear the wise man (Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31), whereas they themselves despised Wisdom itself, which came voluntarily to them. He rightly says that she will rise in judgment with that generation and condemn it.

But this queen displays our holy Church, of which it is said to our King: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Psalm 44:10). From the rising of the sun to its setting, she now hastens to hear Christ the Lord, Wisdom; praising the name of the Lord and offering gifts, because he has made all things sublime. [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “she now hastens to Christ the Lord”; perhaps the intended reading is, “to hear the wisdom of the Lord.”] [Col. 0801C]

Therefore what was said of Solomon, or prophetically done by him, is rightly attributed to Christ the Lord. As stated above, however, Solomon himself, exalted, committed fornication in old age [Note: The printed text reads *in semo*, evidently an OCR corruption for *in senio*, “in old age.”], in mind and body; and, when the Lord abandoned him, he died wickedly, leaving posterity a fearful example, lest, disturbed by the prosperity of this life, they abandon Christ, who is the eternal happiness of his own.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### In Rehoboam, the division of heresies, from which Christ gathers his sheep. The prediction made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

60. When Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, was reigning, and was bound by both his own sin and his father’s, and had almost entirely corrupted Israel through the worship of idols, the kingdom was torn from his hands (I Kings 12:16ff.). Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, also [Note: Ms. Remig., “also.”] received by divine judgment the larger portion of the kingdom among eleven tribes [Note: Ms. Remig., “among twelve tribes”; perhaps “among ten tribes” was intended]. [Col. 0802A]

Through this division, Samaria and Jerusalem preserved the succession and order of their kings of Judah and Israel. But this displays, as has often been said, a figure of heretics and schismatics, until he who creates and loves unity brings, by the illumination of his grace, the other sheep that he has outside his fold, so that, as he deigned to promise, there may be “one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

For the sake of brevity, and to avoid burdening the reader, we shall not now review all the kings in order, but only those in whose times certain deeds or sayings occurred that announced the coming of our Redeemer.

61. When the very wicked king Ahab was reigning (I Kings 16:30), the prophet Elijah was sent to rebuke the king and the people because they had abandoned God and followed Baal (I Kings 18:1ff.). When Jezebel, the wife of King Ahab, had killed the Lord’s prophets by that inscrutable judgment of God by which power is given to the wicked, Elijah, praying for sterility, hid himself from the king’s presence (I Kings 19:1ff.). [Note: Ms. Remig., “having imposed sterility,” that is, after he had prophesied the sterility that was soon to come.] [Col. 0802B]

When three years and six months had been completed, and a savage famine afflicted all Judea, Elijah was ordered to present himself to the king. When he had told the Lord that, after all the prophets had been killed, he alone remained, he received this divine response: “I have left seven thousand men for myself who have not bent the knee before Baal” (I Kings 19:18; Romans 11:4).

Here too [Note: Ms. Remig., “for here.”] the pride of the saints is restrained, lest anyone think that God needs him for any good work, since God fulfills all his work through whomever he wishes, for “all things serve him” (Psalm 118:91). [Note: Ms. Remig., “for every time.”] Human beings are shown to need God, not God human beings. Hence that holy prophet says: “I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Psalm 15:2).

Elijah completed what had been divinely commanded before king and people through that mystical evening sacrifice, obtaining fire from heaven by prayer (I Kings 18:36). By this figure our sacrificed calf extinguished all the priests of idolatry, together with the error of Baal, as Elijah did (ibid., 38), filling the earth with the rain of grace by which the famine of the faithful soul might be driven away. [Note: Ms. Remig., “with grace and rain.”] [Col. 0802C]

62. When Elijah was living in the wilderness, ravens, by divine command, brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening (I Kings 17:6), a figure of the whole body of the Lord was displayed. [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “which”; perhaps “by which.”] First, in the commandments, the Jews, like ravens, supplied bread to the nations; afterward they supplied the flesh of the Lord’s passion, dark in color, harsh and croaking in voice, foul-smelling, and horrible in appearance. [Note: Ms. Remig., “with a flesh-sounding voice.”]

Like these birds, the Jews, preparing for the nations the flesh of the cross cooked from wood, cried out to Pilate with one hoarse and croaking voice: “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6). Those who hear him saying, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” eat this flesh (John 6:54). [Note: The printed editions read “his.”]

Yet here too the three times and half a time—three years and six months, as we mentioned above—are represented: by the high judgment of God, heavenly rain is withheld from those who neither eat his flesh nor have been redeemed by drinking his blood, and are found alienated from his body. [Col. 0802D]

## CHAPTER XXIX

### In Elijah, Christ; and in the widow, the primacy of mercy. The prediction made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

63. The Lord said to Elijah: “Go to Zarephath of Sidon; for behold, I have commanded a widow there to feed you” (I Kings 17ff.). Here too the spiritual reader recognizes mystical actions. [Note: Ms. Remig., “recognizes.”] For the Almighty was not unable to feed his prophet through the same birds for as long as he wished. Yet he knew that the prophet was necessary for the widow, for whom he wished, through his servant and by the power of his word, to prepare abundance in the midst of famine.

Seeing this widow gathering two small pieces of wood in the field as the two commandments, Elijah, moved also by the burning of spiritual thirst, asked the woman for water. While she went to fetch it, the prophet also asked her for a little bread.

She testified that she had only a small amount of flour in a jar and a little oil in a vessel: food for one day for herself and her children, after which they would die. [Note: Ms. Remig., “and very little”; perhaps “very little.”] [Note: Ms. Remig., “in a day.”] [Note: Ms. Remig., “for after consuming it she would die.”] [Col. 0803A]

The prophet therefore ordered that some of it first be offered to him and then prepared for herself and her sons [Note: Ms. Remig. adds “afterward”], so that mercy might take the first place—mercy which Scripture testifies to have gone before the face of God (Psalm 88:5). [Note: Ms. Remig., “For from it the whole household was filled.”]

“From him indeed comes all abundance.”

“For thus says the Lord,” Elijah said: “The jar of flour shall not fail, and the vessel of oil shall not diminish, until the day when the Lord gives rain upon the earth” (I Kings 17:14). [Col. 0803B]

Thus the merciful soul lends to God; thus, while giving in time of need, it provides for its own salvation. Thus the soul is filled: when it departs from the body, loving the Lord who disciplines it, it preserves faithfully, in chaste love, the fidelity of one marriage bed, fortified by the sacrament of flour and the anointing of oil; confidently awaiting the gracious rain, when the Lord says to it: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21). [Note: Ms. Remig., “the rain of grace.”]

In her likeness, the woman who put two small coins into the treasury is also praised by the Lord (Luke 21:2ff.). He who saw it said that she had put in more than all the others, because she left nothing for herself. [Note: Ms. Remig., “he who gave.”] [Col. 0803C]

## CHAPTER XXX

### In Elisha, the disciples of Christ receiving a double portion of the Spirit. The promise made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

64. Elijah left behind the disciple Elisha. Knowing, through the Lord’s revelation, that the time of his assumption had come, he said to his disciple: [Note: Ms. Remig.: “who, recognizing that the time … had come, said to his disciple.”] “Ask for whatever petition you wish before I am taken from you.”

He replied: “I wish that the spirit which is in you may be double in me.” Elijah said to him: “You have asked for a difficult thing; nevertheless, if you look upon me when I am taken from you, it shall be granted to you” (II Kings 2:9–10). [Note: The older editions and Ms. Remig. read “double”; the more recent editions read “twofold.”]

Strengthened by this promise, Elisha, so that he might obtain his desired petition in every respect [Note: Ms. Remig., “into the eagerness of his petition.”], clung to his master so closely that no necessity could separate him from him. When the prophet wished to test the disciple’s devotion, he ordered him to follow him through the byways and difficult places, enduring the journey. But he replied: “As the Lord lives and as your soul lives, I will not leave you, wherever you go” (ibid., 2, 4, and 6). [Col. 0804A]

This continued until they reached the place where Elijah, received into a fiery chariot, was carried as though even to heaven. The disciple’s attention remained so watchful that, when his master was snatched away, he followed him with weeping and a loud voice, saying: “My father, Elijah, my father, chariot of Israel!” (ibid., 12).

Struck by these words, Elijah left him his little cloak as a spiritual provision for the journey and a pledge of the gift that was his. [Note: Ms. Remig., “his mantle.”] Having received it, Elisha rent [materially uncertain: the printed text does not clearly state the object] and struck the Jordan River with it. With the help of the cloak he crossed the river, which he had not been able to cross by himself (ibid., 14). Therefore the sons of the prophets said: “The spirit of the Lord has rested upon Elisha” (ibid., 15). [Note: Ms. Remig., “The Spirit of the Lord rested upon Elisha.”] [Col. 0804D]

65. In this mystical action there is also a likeness of the Lord and our teacher Jesus Christ. For when he had said to his disciples, “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do” (John 14:12), wishing to show that Christ had given a twofold gift, he added: “And he will do greater works than these.” But this applies to those who cling to him and turn aside from him in no respect, whom he instructed, saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also” [Col. 0804B]. [Note: [Col. 0804D] We supply from the authority of the Remigian–Remensis manuscript the words from “to him, and turn aside” through “there my servant will be also.”]

In this way he infused them with a double spirit: first, after the resurrection, when he breathed upon their faces, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained in heaven” (John 20:22–23); and second, when he was received into the cloud, borne by angels, while the disciples themselves watched him depart [Note: [Col. 0804D] Ms. Remig.: “as they raised their eyes,” perhaps “raising their eyes”; and, twelve lines below, the same manuscript reads “and to them.”], and he said: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). On the day of Pentecost he sent the gift of the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire (Acts 2:4).

We must not understand two Spirits here, since the Holy Spirit is one; rather, the one and same Spirit distributes the gifts of grace, being variously bestowed by the undivided Trinity, so that within it there are not two Spirits but one. For, as the apostle Paul says: “One God, one faith, one baptism, one Spirit” (Ephesians 4:5).

Therefore Elisha did not say to his teacher, “May the two spirits that are in you be in me,” but, “May there be a double portion in me.” [Note: [Col. 0804D] We restore this passage from the Remigian manuscript: it formerly read, “May two spirits be in me,” but the correct reading is “a double Spirit.” This is what he expounded. In the Lyons edition the text is “he said to his teacher, Spirit.” The words enclosed in parentheses were added as doubtful by the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions and by later editions.] The Lord explained this double portion when he said, “Until you are clothed with power from on high,” so that he might accomplish greater things through them than he had accomplished through himself. He healed the woman suffering from a flow of blood by the touch of his garment’s fringe (Matthew 9:20) [Note: [Col. 0805D] Thus Ms. Remig.; the printed editions read, “For by the touch”]; but the disciples healed every sickness by their shadow (Acts 3:15).

Even when he had risen, the disciples themselves scarcely believed as they touched and saw him [Note: Ms. Remig., “touching and seeing.”]; but when he ascended into heaven, while they preached him, the whole world believed in him whom it had not seen.

Finally, it is a greater work to justify an impious person than to raise a dead man. All these things the same Lord accomplished through his disciples, to whom he granted this power, saying: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

## CHAPTER XXXI

In the same Elisha, when the Lord Christ raised the dead by grace. A prophecy made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

66. The same Elisha, while traveling through various places and proclaiming the word of the Lord, was received as a guest by a certain Shunammite woman (2 Kings 4:8). As a reward, after removing her barrenness, he obtained a son for her from the Lord (2 Kings 4:16 and following). She received and nourished the child. When he had grown up and was going to his father in the field, he was struck by the heat of the sun; he returned home and, burning with fever in his mother’s arms, gave up his spirit.

At once the woman returned to the man of God. Falling at his feet on Carmel, she announced that the son whom she had received through his grace had died [Note: Ms. Remig., “announcing.”]. The prophet marvels that this had been concealed from him by the Lord, so that he might complete the whole figure of our Lord Jesus: the prophet, who knows everything, pretends not to know something [Note: The printed editions read “prophecy” instead of “the prophet.” Ms. Remig. reads, more appropriately, “knows something.”].

Thus, in the case of Lazarus: “Where have you laid him?” (John 11:34). And: “No one knows the day or the hour, neither the angels nor the Son” (Mark 13:31), although the Son himself will come on that day and at that hour. Likewise, when two disciples told him about his passion and said to him, “Do you not know what happened in Jerusalem three days ago?” (Luke 24:18–19), he himself, in whom these events had occurred, pretending not to know, said, “What things?”

But what is concealed is either done within a great mystery, or the heart’s attention is extended toward God, so that, insofar as it does not comprehend, it may seek knowledge more eagerly; and when it does not understand what it has sought, it may fear more deeply, knowing that whatever mortals have been denied knowledge of is divine and profound.

67. Elisha performs the sacramental signs of the Lord’s actions (2 Kings 4:29). He sends his staff through his servant, so that, placed upon the lifeless body, it might restore the dead to life. The Lord likewise sent the law through his servant Moses; but, like that staff, it could not give life to the dead world. For, as the Apostle says, “If a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be through the law” (Galatians 3:21), because “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

Afterward Elisha himself descended [Note: These same words are found in Augustine, Sermon 26 on the Words of Psalm 94 and in the Apostle’s Letter to the Galatians 3, p. 141 of the new edition; the same meaning is also found in Sermon 136 on the Words of the Gospel of John 9, p. 663 of the new edition.]—the great to the small, the savior to the one to be saved, the living to the dead. Our Lord also descended. “The one who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fulfill all things” (Ephesians 4:10).

What are all these things? [Note: [Col. 0805D] The words “What are all these things?” are added by Ms. Remig.] Those which Elisha performed mystically. In order to raise the small dead child, he fitted his youthful limbs to the child’s body (2 Kings 4:34) [Note: Ms. Remig., “contracted.”]. The Lord Jesus likewise “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7); he adapted himself, small, to that small one, so that he might make “this body of our humiliation conformable to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:21).

Lying beneath him, he kindled the cold body with his own warmth (2 Kings 4:34). Similarly, our Lord and Savior—“from whose heat no one can now hide himself” (Psalm 18:7)—breathed upon him as he lay there three times, so that a threefold confession might be infused into the believer [Note: [Col. 0805D] The word “Savior” is absent from Ms. Remig. Ms. Remig. reads: “upon him … so that by a threefold confession.”]. Thus the dead man was raised when the impious man was justified from everlasting death.

68. The Spirit of the Lord performed many and varied signs through Elisha, as the same history of the Books of Kings relates. It would be lengthy to pursue them all. I shall nevertheless examine a few, since all these signs are figures of future things and must be adapted to Christ the Lord, who says through Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me. He has sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to release the oppressed into rest, to restore freedom to captives, and sight to the blind” (Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18).

Elisha crossed the Jordan through the working of that Spirit (2 Kings 2:14), through which our Lord Jesus consecrated the same river in his baptism (Matthew 3:13). The prophet handed over to beasts the children who mocked him (2 Kings 2:24). And our Lord Jesus says through Paul concerning children: “Do not become children in your minds” (1 Corinthians 14:20) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads, “our Lord Jesus says through Paul,” and does not contain the words “concerning children.”]. Some of them he handed over to beasts—that is, to unclean spirits [Note: These words, “that is, to unclean spirits,” are added by Ms. Remig.]—so that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20).

The king of Israel sent fifty men, three times, with their commanders, to kill Elijah; the prophet consumed them with heavenly fire (2 Kings 1:9, 11, 13). It is also said of our prophet and Lord: “Fire will go before him and burn his enemies round about” (Psalm 96:3).

Afterward, when the king himself had surrounded him with his whole army in a siege, Elisha struck the enemies with a certain blindness and led them captive into Samaria (2 Kings 6:18). When their sight had been restored, he also obtained their pardon for them (ibid., 22).

Although these things are represented in many persons, the Lord displayed them more clearly in Paul and in those who were persecuting the Church with him [Note: The printed editions read “were pursuing.” Ms. Remig. reads more appropriately, “were persecuting.”]. For when he had been blinded and thrown down on the road, having become God’s captive, his sight was restored; the former persecutor became a preacher (Acts 9:8). In him God displayed all his patience, as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life (1 Timothy 1:16).

69. Naaman the Syrian, a friend of the king, was sent to the king of Israel so that he might be cleansed by Elisha from the mark of leprosy. When the man of God saw him, he ordered him, if he wished the marks on his body to be removed, to bathe seven times in the Jordan [Note: [Col. 0806D] Ms. Remig. adds “seven times,” which was absent from the printed editions.]. When he did so, he was cleansed (2 Kings 5:1 and following).

He believed that gifts should be offered to the man of God (ibid., 16); but Elisha rightly refused them according to divine law, prefiguring the grace of our Lord Christ, freely given, which he commended to his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “You received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10:8).

The soul’s cleansing from the vices by which the inner and outer person are polluted is also demonstrated by the sevenfold Spirit and by the water in which those consecrated in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are baptized (Matthew 28:19).

Gehazi, the prophet’s servant, followed Naaman the Syrian and, with a fabricated lie, tried to sell what the prophet had given freely. He was struck with the same mark of leprosy from which Naaman had been cleansed (2 Kings 5:20 and following). He represents heretics, who, driven by the blindness of their greed, sell to their followers what they call, as it were, expiations for sins; and they too are marked by the stains with which those others had been covered. They rightly hear from the Lord: “I do not know you. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7:23).

## CHAPTER XXXII

In Hezekiah, through whom Christ teaches his own not to become proud in good works. A prophecy made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

70. As the kings of Israel took turns—some becoming entangled in errors by departing from the ways of the Lord, others walking faithfully in the Lord’s way—the narrative reaches King Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:1 and following) [Note: The older editions, together with Ms. Remig., read “taking turns.” The more recent editions read “alternating.”].

He destroyed all the idols and overthrew every form of idolatrous worship, converting almost the whole erring Israel to the Lord (ibid., 4). He received a divine message that he should order and arrange his household, because he was already going to die (2 Kings 20:1). When he prayed with tears, saying, “Remember, Lord, how I have walked in your way” (ibid., 3 and 6), fifteen years were added to his life as a sign [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “fifteen.” The Vulgate has only ten.].

The sun descended twelve steps by the course through which it had ascended (2 Kings 20:12). When neighboring kings noticed that this had happened wondrously, they sent messengers to Hezekiah asking what the sign might mean. But, lifted up by his success, he told them not only what had happened for his sake; out of boastfulness he also showed them all the treasures of his royal house and his vessels (ibid., 13).

The Lord became angry and rebuked the king through the prophet Isaiah, declaring that days would come when all the things he had shown them would be carried captive to Babylon together with the people (ibid., 16).

Not without reason does our King likewise admonish us through the apostle John in the Apocalypse, saying: “Hold fast what you have, so that no one else may take your crown” (Revelation 3:11). Elsewhere: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and preserves his garments, lest he walk naked” (ibid., 16, 15). And in the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6:3). He warns that in good works, which are God’s gifts, one must glory not in oneself but in the Lord, lest the proud lose what the humble receive [Note: Ms. Remig., “receives.”].

## CHAPTER XXXIII

In the sinful kings who lead the people with themselves into captivity. A prophecy made and represented. Believed and seen in the Books of Kings.

71. When Josiah and his son Zedekiah were reigning (2 Kings 22:1 and 13), the whole people of Israel broke the bonds of the law by which they were governed and, through many grave sins [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “faults”; the printed editions read “causes.”], provoked God, the author of all piety, to great anger.

The Lord sent the prophet Jeremiah to rebuke and correct the king and the people (Jeremiah 22:2 and following), declaring that if they turned back and kept the commandments of the law, they would always remain unharmed in their own land; but if they despised him who warned them, they would be led captive to Babylon.

Thus, when both the commandments and the words of the preacher had been spurned, and king and people were oppressed by their sins and driven onward by evil undertakings, Jeremiah expressed the divine sentence to the already captive people and to the kings in a letter, saying: “Because of the sins that you have committed before God, you will be led to Babylon, and there you will remain for a long time, for seven generations” (Baruch 4:1–2).

Therefore King Nebuchadnezzar seized the kings of Judah and carried all Israel away into captivity in Babylon, having the eyes of King Zedekiah put out on the way (5 Kings 21:1 and following), so that what two prophets had foretold concerning the same king might be fulfilled.

Jeremiah said that the king would see Babylon (Jeremiah 24:3); Ezekiel, that he would not see it (Ezekiel 12:13). Although they seemed to contradict one another, both prophecies appear to have been fulfilled in this way: when Zedekiah was brought to Babylon after his eyes had been removed, he saw it because he arrived there, and did not see it because he lost his eyes on the way.

Our Lord admonishes his own by this example and says: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:3). The same Lord also says in the Gospel that even kings who despise his commandments are blind: “The blind are guides of the blind. And when the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14) [Note: [Col. 0807D] Ms. Remig.: “when the blind leads the blind.”]. This is the harsh captivity of the unrepentant soul, concerning which it is said: “I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent” (Revelation 2:21).

Thus, until the measure of seventy years had been completed, that people remained captive in Babylon.

72. The same King Nebuchadnezzar carried off all the vessels of the temple of God through his servants (2 Kings 25:13–15). Woe to the sins of humanity, when, because of them, the sacrifices themselves—which had always served as remedies for salvation—are trampled by foreigners.

Jeremiah’s Lamentations show with what groaning, with what most bitter tears, and with what anguish of soul he described these things: the Lord’s tabernacle had been polluted; the feast day had been forgotten; all the Sabbaths and solemn observances had been abolished; and of the priests and princes, the children, the old men, the young men, and the virgins, some had been consumed by the sword and some had remained captive (Lamentations 1:1 and following) [Note: Ms. Remig. adds the word “portion.”].

Behold the wounds of our sorrows; behold the reproach of our mourning; behold the great sins whose consequences have also deservedly allowed us to witness these things, yet we refuse to have the greater wound of punishment healed. Though crushed, we believe that we still stand; although expelled and exiled as we deserved, we do not grieve. There is no satisfaction, no sorrow; anger remains, and we do not ask forgiveness [Note: Ms. Remig. reads: “No sorrow remains; anger remains, and we do not ask forgiveness.”].

“Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners” (ibid., 5:2). Though chastised in this way, we do not mourn; though corrected in this way, we refuse to accept discipline. Let us withdraw from the evils by which we offended the Lord; let us repent of the things by which we inflicted insult upon his holy ones. Let our pride be healed by humility. Let us not despise the time granted for remedies [Note: Ms. Remig., “for the remedy.”], lest he whose gentle and mild mercy we have experienced impose eternal anger and a penal sentence upon those who do not repent [Note: Ms. Remig. reads: “so that he whom we have experienced as gentle and mild may not impose eternal anger and a penal sentence upon those who do not repent.”].

For that Lord is ready to forgive who says: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zechariah 1:3), provided that the merciful Father recognizes the voice of his son returning with repentance (Luke 15:18).

73. In the same captivity [Note: [Col. 0808D] This passage is corrected from Ms. Remig.; the printed editions read, “into the same captivity.”], the history relates that Daniel and Ezekiel prophesied. Daniel, the man of desires—called Balthasar by the king—had three friends from his own nation: Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael (Daniel 10:11; 1:7).

Although all his prophecy is full of mysteries (Daniel 9:25), one part of it nevertheless shines so brightly that it even marked the time when the Savior and Lord himself would come. Since his prophetic visions are twelve in number, ten are found in the Hebrew text. With the Lord’s help, I shall go through these twelve with a precise comparison.

In the first, he defended Susanna’s chastity against the shameless elders (Daniel 13:51). The Lord Jesus does the same when, against the crimes of the heretics, he protects the integrity of his Church, which they strive to corrupt through their perverse arguments. He also marks them through the apostle Paul, saying: “Among them are those who creep into households and take captive little women burdened with sins and led by various desires” (2 Timothy 3:6).

In the second, Daniel himself and his friends resolved, while observing the commandments of their law, not to defile themselves with the food from the king’s table on which their other companions fed (Daniel 1:8). Our Teacher and Lord was not merely undefiled by the desires of this world; he also forbade his friends to indulge them, saying: “Do not love the world or the things in the world. For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (1 John 2:15–16). He showed that all these things must be rejected like those royal foods.

And through the apostle Paul he gives the clearer command: “Food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians 6:13), so that the Savior himself may be the soul’s one food, offering it various and differing flavors.

74. In the third, Daniel revealed to the king the sacrament of the divine plan that had been shown to him and that he had forgotten [Note: The printed editions read “offered”; but Ms. Remig. more appropriately reads “forgotten.”]. He did so not by the human teaching with which Daniel had been instructed, but because the Lord revealed it: he recounted both the dream and its interpretation to the king (Daniel 2:1 and following).

Four kingdoms were to arise in the world, represented by the four metals from which the statue standing before him had been fashioned [Note: The printed editions read “was present”; Ms. Remig. reads “stood.”]: the golden head was Babylon, in the East; its silver chest and arms were Macedonia, in the North; its bronze belly and thighs were Carthage, in the South; and its iron legs and feet, partly iron and partly clay, were the final kingdom, namely Rome, in the West, as the very learned historian Orosius also set forth.

That kingdom, like iron, crushed everything and subdued it. Daniel also adds the kingdom of Christ in the stone cut from the mountain without the hands of those who cut it down, signifying, as it were, God—uncontained by hands—made man and born of the Virgin (Daniel 2:44–45). When this stone struck the statue, it reduced all its parts to dust, and the wind carried them away, so that no place for them was found. But the stone that struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole face of the earth.

When all the kingdoms have been emptied, the kingdom of Christ the Lord will arise; it will not be handed over to any other people, because it will endure forever (ibid., 35). The whole Church now asks for this when she prays: “Your kingdom come” (Luke 11:2).

In the fourth, when the three friends of Daniel refused to worship the statue and image of Nebuchadnezzar that he had set up for worship, they were thrown into the furnace. There God displayed a wondrous act: when the fire was driven away, the ravenous flame consumed the ministers of the royal command instead. The three men, unharmed, sang a hymn to the true King in the midst of the furnace and were counted worthy to have the Son of God with them.

When grace revealed him, the king himself recognized him. He leads his true worshipers—those who despise the emptiest images—from the flames of the present age to heavenly glory in triumph (Daniel 3).

## CHAPTER XXXIV

In Daniel, who proclaimed Christ the Lord through his visions. A prophecy made and represented. Believed and seen in Daniel.

75. The fifth vision contains the dream of the same king, which Daniel interpreted as follows (Daniel 6:2 and following): the magnificent tree he had seen, beneath whose branches all the beasts, cattle, and birds dwelt, represented the king himself. When the Lord ordered it to be cut down, only its root was to be preserved; his kingdom was to be taken from him, and he himself was to remain with the beasts (ibid., 17 and following). His hair was to grow like a woman’s and his nails like an eagle’s; he was to eat grass like an ox, until the seven divinely appointed periods had been completed. Daniel advised the king that he should redeem his sins by almsgiving.

When he neglected to do this, all the things foretold came upon the king. Once the appointed measure of time had been completed, he recovered the kingdom he had lost (ibid., 31). Thus presumptuous people are cut down; thus the proud are chastised by the one who “feeds them with tears by measure” (Psalm 80:5), because his judgments are gracious (Psalm 119:39). [The source reads “makes [them] drink tears, by measure,” not “feeds them with tears.”]

Thus, when the apostle Peter denied him, the Lord restored him to the place that his presumption had caused him to lose, when he saw him weeping after that look (Luke 22:61). Thus, to those who shed his sacred blood, for whom he prayed, he offered that same blood to drink, so that they might receive royal dignity [Note: [Col. 0809D] We restore from Ms. Remig. the words “those who shed it, for whom he prayed, that same blood.” That manuscript, however, shortly afterward reads “he might receive,” not “they might receive,” as do the printed editions.].

Thus our King daily restores the fallen, preserving for them afterward the gift of the heavenly kingdom that has been bestowed through grace.

In the sixth, from the four beasts that appeared to him, he confirms the kingdoms of the four regions of the world (Daniel 7:4 and following) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “those four aforesaid beasts.”]. The same prophet testifies that the fourth beast was greater and more terrifying: it had ten horns, and from among them another small horn arose; three of the horns were torn out before it, until the Ancient of Days sat in judgment.

But these matters have been explained in the manner of those four successive kingdoms [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “are explained.”]. The fourth beast, which surpassed all the kingdoms, conquered and subjected the whole earth (ibid., 23). After it, ten kings will arise at one time; and after them, the one who will bear the name of his own destruction—that is, Antichrist. In its proper place, as already promised, divine testimonies concerning him will be produced.

In the seventh, from the ram and the goat, he describes the battles revealed to him between the Persians and the Greeks (Daniel 8:3 and following). Under the figure of Antichrist also, who, when he exalts himself in his heart, will corrupt many through deceit (ibid., 25), this continues until Jesus the Lord comes, who is to come and will not delay (Habakkuk 2:3).

76. In the eighth vision (Daniel 5:1 and following), the same man of desires, Daniel, indicates the provident justice of God judging proud kings in the following manner. King Belshazzar was holding a banquet for his nobles. The vessels of the temple of God, which his father Nebuchadnezzar had carried away, were brought out [The printed editions read “taken away”], and he drank from them with his concubines and nobles, praising his gods of gold and silver, wood and stone. Immediately the fingers of a human hand appeared in his sight and wrote on the wall of the royal palace (ibid., 5).

Disturbed by this vision, the king summoned Daniel, since all the wise men he possessed had been unable to read the writing. Daniel declared that this had happened because of the vessels of the house of God. Rebuking the king firmly, he also read the writing: “Mene, Tekel, Parsin.” He interpreted it as follows:

“Mene: God has numbered your kingdom and brought it to an end.

“Tekel: You have been weighed in the balance and found wanting” [Note: Ms. Remig. reads: “You have been weighed in the balance and found wanting.”].

“Parsin: Your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians” (ibid., 23).

When the king had bestowed upon the prophet the promised gifts which Daniel had refused, the course of his life was completed; as had been foretold, he left the kingdom to the Medes and Persians.

Let proud kings look—yes, let them look! When, by the presumption of their minds, they seize the vessels of the house of God, which he justly handed over to sinful ministers, and handle them without reverence, they seem to inflict insults upon God, whose name consecrated them. Their end is certainly death, which has no end.

## CHAPTER XXXV

In the same Daniel, when he rescued him from the lions’ den, as Christ the Lord from the Jews. A prophecy made and represented. Believed and seen in Daniel.

77. In the ninth vision, Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom. When he appointed one hundred and twenty satraps over his kingdom, he established three superintendents over them (Daniel 6:1 and following). Daniel was one of the three and enjoyed favor in the king’s eyes.

The envious sought a scheme against God’s servant and persuaded the king that for thirty days no petition should be made to any god or human being except the king alone. A penalty was attached to the decree: whoever disregarded the king’s command was to be thrown into the den of lions and given as food to them (ibid., 7 and following).

When the prophet discovered that this decree had been issued, he prayed to his Lord at the customary three times of the day. They seized him as a transgressor and brought him before the king. Since the king could not rescue him from the envious, he released the prophet to his God with this confession: only God could rescue him from the danger of death.

And so it happened. Overcome by this grief, the king neither ate nor slept; at dawn he went himself to see Daniel. When he found him alive and unharmed, he gave glory to the true God and ordered him brought out of the den. He then threw into the den those who had accused Daniel, and they were immediately devoured in his sight.

In these events also the prophecy was fulfilled: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it; and whoever sets a snare for his neighbor will perish in it” (Sirach 27:29) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads: “falls into it … sets it … will perish.”].

Our own Jesus the Lord, in whom all these things were represented, says through the Prophet: “They dug a pit before my face, and they fell into it” (Psalm 57:7). And again: “The Lord sent his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul from among the lions’ cubs” (ibid., 4).

78. In the tenth vision (Daniel 9:2), as the end of the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation drew near—the desolation that the Lord had foretold through the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10)—Daniel poured out a prayer with complete weeping and fasting for himself and for the sins of his people, imploring the Lord’s mercy.

The archangel Gabriel stood beside him as he prayed and revealed future mysteries to him: that seventy weeks had been shortened for his people and for the holy city, so that sins might be completed and transgressions sealed, iniquity brought to an end, and everlasting righteousness introduced (ibid., 21) [The printed editions read: “for the holy city, so that sins might be completed and transgressions sealed.”]. He also revealed that the visions of the prophets would be fulfilled and that the Holy of Holies would be anointed from the issuing of the word in reply.

“Jerusalem will again be built, until Christ the prince: seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks.” Again the street and the walls will be rebuilt in the distress of the times. “After the seventy-two weeks, the anointed one will perish, and judgment will not be in him”; or, according to the Hebrew interpreter: “Christ will be killed, and there will be no people of his who will deny him.”

“And the people of the coming prince will destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end will be devastation; and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed. He will confirm a covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will fail; and in the temple there will be the abomination of desolation, and desolation will endure until the consummation and the end” (ibid., 26) [Note: Ms. Remig. reads: “for a long time … and in the middle of the week.”].

Daniel wrote that these things had been revealed to him to refute the error of the Jews. Those, therefore, who still await Christ’s coming will believe in Antichrist. For the Lord Jesus rebukes them in the Gospel, saying: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not believe me; another will come in his own name, and him you will believe” (John 5:43).

79. Through great labor and ingenuity, Jerome, of blessed memory [Note: See Jerome’s exposition of the seventy-two weeks in his Commentary on the Prophet Daniel, chapter 9.], extended the seventy weeks, by calculating the years of the kings of Babylon, to four hundred and ninety years, reaching to the birth of Christ the Lord, our Redeemer.
