He separated seven weeks for the restoration of the temple, sixty-two up to the Lord’s birth and then to his passion, and one for the devastation carried out by the commander Vespasian or by his son Titus [Note: Ms. Remig. reads: “but joining … seventy-two.”].

The enemies of the Lord, the Jews, deceive themselves when, although many things have been prophesied about Christ, they strive to refer them to the persons of each of their kings. Whether they wish it or not, they bow their necks to the prophet Daniel, who not only recorded all the signs written above but also marked the very times of the Lord’s coming.

The whole world now recognizes that all these things have been fulfilled with the clearest light [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “will recognize.”]. Yet the Jews still refuse to believe in the glory of Christ the Lord spread among the nations and in his being worshiped by the whole earth, as it is written (Psalm 66:4), though they see with us that everything foretold in the oracles of the prophets is being fulfilled.

80. In the eleventh vision (Daniel 11:1 and following), the deeds of Antichrist himself, the afflictions of the final age, and also the resurrection of the dead—how the impious and how the holy will rise—were revealed to the same prophet under the figure of warring kings. These things were also shown to Isaiah (Isaiah 6:11 and following; 13:9, 16) and to Ezekiel (Ezekiel 38–39), in the manner confirmed by the authority of the Gospel in their sayings.

81. In the twelfth vision (Daniel 14:2 and following), Daniel presented a most joyful spectacle, not only to the king but also to spiritual minds.

The idol Bel, which all the Babylonians, together with the king, worshiped, appeared to consume great royal provisions every day. In fact, the priests and their families entered secretly through a hidden door and consumed them. Daniel exposed their fraud by a subtle device: he ordered ashes to be spread on the floor of the temple [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “to be strewn.”].

After the doors had been sealed with the king’s ring, the footprints of men and women appearing on the following day showed that the provisions had not been consumed by the image. The priests’ confession also disclosed the hidden door through which they entered and devoured everything.

Then, by royal command, the image was smashed (ibid., 22 and following). Daniel also killed the dragon, which they likewise regarded as divine, without sword or club, in the way he knew that what is corruptible could be corrupted. He taught and demonstrated that the one and only true God must be worshiped, while vain superstitions were abandoned—superstitions by which the prophet saw not only the Babylonians but also the whole world held captive under the power of demons [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “from whose dominion”; understand “from the dominion of these superstitions.”].

He also indicated in his proclamation that the world would in the future be freed from their dominion by the grace of Christ the Lord [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “future times.”].

But, as someone says, “Truth produces hatred.” Hence our Paul also says: “Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?” (Galatians 4:16). In return for the true religion he had revealed, the Babylonians cast the prophet into the lions’ den to be devoured.

But divine power was not absent. It provided him with his customary protection and supplied him with food through his companion while he was shut in [Note: Ms. Remig. reads “a solid protection.”]. Through the merit of this grace, it changed the savage attacks of the lions into the gentleness of sheep.

When Daniel was brought out and the king marveled that he was unharmed, his enemies were given as food to the lions and perished (Daniel 14:30 and following).

These events did not occur without a sign of that Lord who prays for his own, saying: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you” (Psalm 74:19). For that roaring lion, the devil, who prowls about seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8), consumes the enemies of our prophet, Christ the Lord, whenever he finds them, having received the power to do so.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

In Ezekiel, the manifest resurrection through Christ the Lord. A promise made and represented. Believed and seen in Ezekiel.

82. The prophet Ezekiel, too, among the other things he wrote, concealed in mysteries, made known in this way the resurrection of the dead that had been shown to him. He saw himself brought into a certain field that was full of the bones of the dead (Ezek. XXXVII. 1 ff.). There, by the power of the word of God, he saw each bone joined to its proper parts, flesh, sinews, and skin rising over them, and vital breath being breathed into them by that Spirit through whom we hope for and believe in the future resurrection.

[Col. 0812D] In addition, while recounting many things under the figure of the king of Tyre concerning the Antichrist, he also describes the city gathered from the nations out of living stones, the heavenly Jerusalem (Ezek. XXVIII, 2, etc.). He always presents its eastern gate as closed, saying: “This gate shall be closed; only the high priest shall pass through it, and it shall remain closed to the prince” (Ezek. XLIV, 2). This signifies Mary’s virginal womb, which, remaining forever wholly intact, brought forth the Savior. For Christ the Lord alone, as Bishop Augustine of blessed memory says, brought forth the limbs of an infant through the inviolate virginal organs of his mother, and after the resurrection brought in the limbs of a young man through closed doors; he alone, without sin, had no sin at the beginning of infancy and had no sin in the maturity of age, as he himself says: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

83. During this Babylonian captivity, Ezra was also a priest and prophet. He was held in favor before the king, and when the king saw him weeping and asked him why he was sad, he affirmed that the customary rites of his religion and people were normally being celebrated at that time, and he declared that he was separated from them (II Esdr. II, 1, etc.). The king gave him permission to depart and ordered the temple of God to be restored. When Ezra also came to Jerusalem, inflamed with zeal for the law, he first resolved that the people should be cleansed from their vices. For, as the Prophet says, “A wise king is the stability of his people” (Wis. VI, 26).

Having found the book of Moses, he showed, among other things, that the anger of God had also been kindled because the people, contrary to God’s command, had taken wives for themselves from foreigners (I Esdr. X, 1, etc.). By the authority he possessed, he persuaded each man to cast out the women, together with their children. Thus, held back by no carnal affection, and desiring God to be favorable to them, they promptly did what had been commanded, so that he might display a figure of the Christian people. The chief of all priests admonishes them, saying: “If anyone has left house, or field, or wife, or children for the sake of my name, he shall receive many times as much and shall obtain eternal life” (Matt. XIX, 29).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. In Ezra: the restoration of the house of God, that is, through Christ the Lord. The prediction made and represented. Believed and seen in Ezra.

[Col. 0813C]

84. While Ezra was restoring the temple of God (I Esdr. IV, 1, etc.), certain wicked men who wished to be partners in the building but not partners in religion maliciously informed the king that, because Ezra would not accept them as uncircumcised men, work on the temple had ceased until the reign of Cyrus (ibid., 24). Moved by divine command, after the completion of the seventy years that Jeremiah had foretold from the mouth of the Lord (Jer. XXV, 12; XXIX, 10), Cyrus sent the entire people, together with the vessels of the house of God, from the Babylonian captivity back to Jerusalem. The king also added gifts, from which he ordered the temple’s construction to rise.

The work begun under Darius continued for forty-six years until its completion, which Cyrus both ordered and assisted (I Esdr. V, 13). The Jews, when the Lord promised the restoration of his body and said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19), did not understand the mystery of that saying. They replied: “It was built in forty-six years” (ibid., 20); and how, they asked, does he say, “In three days I will raise it up”? It was built by Solomon with the same speed with which he found everything prepared by his father David. Therefore, the Jews were not speaking of the time spent on Solomon’s construction, but of Ezra’s, whose work had been forbidden to reach completion.

85. Once the temple and wall of Jerusalem had been restored, the periods established according to Daniel’s times—while the people remained in Jerusalem, with him and Zechariah praying—ran through the seventy weeks until the birth of Christ the Lord, as we said above (chap. 3). Through his forgiveness, even now souls are freed from the captivity of this age by grace and mercy, when the measure granted amid contrition of heart has been completed. “They rejoice,” says the Psalm, “for the days in which they were humbled, for the years in which they saw evil, until the Lord looks upon his servants and upon his works” (Ps. LXXXIX, 15–16).

Let us therefore serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in him with trembling (Ps. II, 11), until we are brought back to the city that our King and Priest restores, the heavenly Jerusalem, so that in the temple of his body, which he raised in three days, we may continually offer him a sacrifice of praise.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. In the same book, when he unfolds a parable in the figure of the Church. The prediction made and represented. Believed and seen in Ezra.

[Col. 0814B]

86. When Artaxerxes, king of Babylon, wished to test his captives, he chose three wise Jews, whose opinions Ezra the priest recorded (III Esdr. III, 4, etc.). One preferred wine to everything; another, the king; the third, Zerubbabel, preferred women and, above all, truth. When they had stated their opinions, Zerubbabel was judged wiser than all, because he had established that women were superior, and truth above everything.

And truly, what is stronger than a woman, who first so enticed Adam, the man (Gen. III, 6), that he despised God’s commands? What is stronger than a woman whose beauty exalts itself above every desire? What is stronger than a woman who softens both royal strength and the man? What, even in goodness, is stronger than a woman who believed that she would give birth to Christ, the whole truth (Luke I, 45)? What is stronger than a woman who, while the disciples were fleeing, looked upon the mysteries of the cross itself, undaunted and full of confidence (John XIX, 25)? What is stronger than a woman who, running ahead of all the men, was the first to deserve to see the risen Lord (Mark XVI, 9)?

After Ezra had written these things as a type of the Church, the represented action followed as well. Esther, who had been raised as a daughter by Mordecai (Esth. II, 7), was brought by God, who exalts the humble, to royal dignity while Mordecai was attending to the royal court. When she understood that her people had been given over to death through the agency of the king’s friend Haman, because of Mordecai, and that a sword hung over their necks, Esther, offering her life for her people, invoked divine assistance and entered the king’s inner chamber (Esth. V, 1, etc.), although an un summoned woman was not permitted to approach there.

When the king looked upon her in anger, she too melted away with shame. “God,” as it is said, “turned his heart to gentleness” (ibid. XV, 11). The king promised her many benefits and, while seeking to restore her safety, did not refuse her request that he come to a banquet with Haman. There, when she recounted what had happened to her and her people, the king ordered Haman to be crucified on the very wood on which Haman had planned to hang the innocent Mordecai (ibid. VII, 3, etc.), “so that the evil he had plotted,” as the Prophet says, “might turn back upon himself.”

87. Thus the holy Church destroys her enemies by the wood of the cross. Thus she exposes herself to the dangers of this world on behalf of her own. Thus, by giving herself over to death and conferring life through her labors, she ministers to them—as a queen who is admonished by her King, Bridegroom, and Lord, and to whom it is said: “Rescue those who are being led away to death, and redeem those who are being slaughtered” (Prov. XXIV, 11).

Even her enemies themselves seek refuge in her benefits. In a comparable place, holy Judith is also set down in the succeeding order; she too assumes the figure and person of the holy Church. For when Holofernes, commander of the Babylonian king’s army, had surrounded Bethulia with a siege and, after cutting off the water, afflicted the entire city with thirst, its leaders resolved to surrender it to Holofernes (Judith VII, 10, etc.).

88. Judith opposed this plan, asking for a few days’ delay (Judith VIII, 1, etc.). During that time she humbly entreated the King of kings and Lord of lords with fasts and prayers (ibid. IX, 1, etc.). Having removed her widow’s clothing, she composed herself in every respect—in mind, body, and conduct—and displayed herself as marvelous to all (ibid. X, 3, etc.). She followed the plan by which, with God as her guardian, she believed that she could destroy the enemy once he had been captivated by her beauty, while the one who gives and guards chastity preserved her modesty.

When she herself, unharmed, brought back the enemy’s head, the woman restored to her homeland the liberty that the men had not been able to secure (Judith XIII, 10). If you recognize our Church, of which she bore the figure, you see how, after her husband Christ the Lord had suffered, risen, and ascended into heaven, she too, casting off all sorrow as though it were widow’s clothing, was afterward clothed in beauty by him of whom the prophet Isaiah says: “He clothed me with the garment of salvation and wrapped me in the robe of joy, like a bride adorned with her jewels” (Isa. LXI, 10).

She too was sent against the wound of the enemies’ head, since she is the body of him who crushed the head of the great dragon. She did not spare her life, as Judith did not spare hers, because she is the one who says through the apostle John: “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we also ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (I John III, 10). It is clear that this was done in the holy martyrs, who are blessed before almighty God.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. In Tobit: through the fish, Christ; demons are driven away and the blind are illuminated. The prediction made and represented.

89. Tobit was also a captive at Nineveh, endowed with such patient endurance in his religion that he knew the Lord’s anger must be borne with equanimity (Tob. I, 1, etc.). Satisfying God through worthy deeds and confessions, he also instructed his son in holy conduct. He commanded him not to fear either the scarcity of poverty (Tob. IV, 23) or the labors of prolonged exile, provided that, persevering in the Lord’s commandments, he departed from every iniquity and acted well.

While he was blind in body but, through the radiance of interior righteousness, showing his son the right paths, Raphael the archangel, sent by God (Tob. V, 1, etc.), supplied those who prayed with not only comfort in captivity but also heavenly benefits. He guided the son in recovering the money and gave him Raguel’s daughter as a wife (Tob. VI, 12). From her he drove out the most wicked demon Asmodeus, who had already killed seven husbands for her (Tob. VIII, 3).

The son returned wealthy with his wife and, using the fish’s liver—the same with which he had driven out the demon—removed the spots from Tobit’s eyes and restored his former sight (Tob. XI, 13). He admonished them always to glorify God and to persevere in good works.

This Tobit prophesied Christ the Lord among his other praises, saying: “Many nations shall come from far away, inhabitants from the remotest parts of the earth, to the name of the Lord God, bringing their gifts in their hands; they shall offer them with joy to the King of heaven” (Tob. XIV, 14). We now see this being fulfilled.

The mystical meaning of this action is that, from the fish’s inner organs, the demon was driven away and Tobit was illuminated.

90. This was accomplished by the great fish, Christ, through his passion, cleansing Mary, from whom he expelled seven demons (Luke VIII, 2; Matt. XII, 45). He removes the despair of the soul thus held captive. When seven more wicked spirits have tormented it, it must likewise be cleansed and healed by the liver of our fish, if, returning in repentance, it understands that the evil spirits are driven out from her and guards against them as enemies.

For the evil spirit is the spirit of pride; worse than it is the pretense of humility. The evil spirit is the spirit of envy; worse than it is the pretense of charity. The evil spirit is the spirit of falsehood; worse than it is the pretense of truth. The evil spirit is the spirit of lust; worse than it is the pretense of chastity. The evil spirit is the spirit of greed; worse than it is the pretense of mercy. The evil spirit is the spirit of excess; worse than it is the pretense of frugality. The evil spirit is the spirit of error; worse than it is the pretense of religion.

When a soul is possessed by these, and its latter condition is worse than its former, it is freed by the medicine of our fish, because “where sin abounded, grace abounded even more” (Rom. V, 20). He paid the tribute for himself and for Peter (Matt. XVII, 26), restored light to Paul after he had been blinded (Acts IX, 18), satisfied his disciples from himself on the shore (John XXI, 13), and offered himself to the whole world as a fish—ἰχθὺν. For our forefathers interpreted the word for “fish” in the sacred writings in Latin by gathering from the Sibylline verses the meaning: Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior, the fish cooked in his passion, from whose inner organs we are daily illuminated and nourished.

## CHAPTER XL. In the Maccabees: those who received both martyrdoms and Christ himself, born as king. The prediction made and represented. Believed and seen in the Maccabees.

91. After liberty had been restored from the Babylonian captivity, the Maccabees provided leadership to the Hebrew people (II Macc. I, 1, etc.). Their valor shone so brightly that not only the Macedonians and Ptolemy, king of Egypt, but the Romans themselves also invited them into treaties of friendship (I Macc. X; II Macc. XI).

There, among the Jews, in a region that the Romans had already captured, while Antiochus was reigning, that illustrious woman, the mother of the Maccabees, in hope of eternal life and in fidelity to her lawful observances, so that her sons would not touch the forbidden flesh of swine, gave seven martyrs to God in a single day (II Macc. VII, 1, etc.). Having despised the earth, she bore them not for this world but for heaven itself. By her example she admonished us to despise perishing things, to seek eternal things, and to finish more swiftly what must soon end, so that, striving and conquering, they might seize what has no end.

Since she herself was immediately to follow them (II Macc. VII, 41), she sent her sons ahead to life—the true life, which she knew to be without every fear—and acquired it for herself and her sons by her faithful testimony. For this reason Judas Maccabeus also sent twelve thousand talents to Jerusalem to offer a sacrifice for those who had died in battle (II Macc. XII, 43), thinking rightly and most appropriately about the resurrection.

Through this holy exhortation the Church directs her children: impressing contempt for death upon them, she compels them to pass over to true life, so that she herself may be perfected in the kingdom of God with her children, who say to her: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?” (Rom. VIII, 35).

92. In the Maccabean period, the last commander and high priest was Hyrcanus (I Macc. XVI, 24). Pompey, a magistrate of the Roman people, sent his brother Aristobulus, bound together with his children, to Rome while he was storming Jerusalem, as Josephus relates in his History.

Nevertheless, the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob was fulfilled: “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes to whom all things have been reserved, and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. IX, 10).

[Note: The Remigius manuscript adds: “Let us observe the succession of the kings who rest.”]

We observe that the succession of the kings of Judah and Israel, or the Levitical priesthood, had ceased, when Herod, a foreign king, ruled over the Hebrew people. The anointing also ceased, which the prophet Daniel had foretold would cease, so that the people would not follow anointed kings or priests, [the Remigius manuscript reads this way; the printed editions, especially: “when the King was already coming,” etc.] since the eternal King and Priest, Christ, who is the expectation of the nations, was already present.

Herod—whose father Josephus says was from Idumea and whose mother was from Arabia—received from Caesar Augustus the authority over that people assigned to him at the very time when Caesar ordered a registration to be made by an edict throughout the whole pacified world (Luke II, 1). Thus, in that year of the census conducted when Quirinius governed Syria, Christ the Lord was born; Paul too came within that registration.

For this is how we should understand what he said to the tribune Lysias: “But I was born a Roman” (Acts XXII, 28). Everyone purchased the dignity of this name for a price; but when this Jew said that he had been born a Roman, he showed more clearly that he had come within that registration. John the forerunner and herald of the true King and Judge had already been born, and from him the time of grace took its beginning.

93. Up to this point, with the Lord’s help, I have been able to collect, as was granted me, the figurative promises and predictions under the Law. Here too, the second age—like the second day rising from the four quarters of the world—takes shape from the succession of the prophetic fathers, with Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel established in the eastern region; and, with the twelve minor prophets, as though corresponding to the number of the hours, it closes the second day as toward evening. Thus, with the chapters assigned to it, the third part of the book begins: the third age of manifested grace together with the eternal day itself. Amen.

# PART THREE. THE AGE OF GRACE

## PROLOGUE

1. Since the world, illuminated by the radiant grace of Christ the Lord, has now shone forth in splendor, I do not think that in this third part I should, as was done above, set down the figurative promises or predictions under prefixed chapters while examining them. Especially since the whole Law and prophecy proclaimed Christ the Lord and the Church.

The heralds of every spirit announced the coming of this heavenly King and Judge in such an order that the truth would be proclaimed even through the tongues of his enemies. For demons also believe and tremble (Jas. I, 19), and, confessing him when he was present, they said: “We know who you are, and why you have come—to torture us before the time” (Luke IV, 24).

Therefore, with the Lord’s help, I have decided to insert into this work not only the prophecies of those who were moved by the Spirit of God, but also those who, deceived by the seduction of erring spirits, knew God but did not glorify him as God (Rom. I, 21). Considering a few things from among many, and adding certain appropriate sayings of the Sibyl or of others concerning Christ the Lord, I shall first introduce John, the herald and forerunner of that unique King and true Judge. Truth itself bore witness to him, saying that among those born of women no one had arisen greater than John the Baptist (Matt. XI, 11); in him the whole Law and prophecy ceased (ibid. 13).

## CHAPTER I. Concerning John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ. The promise believed and seen.

2. The prophet Isaiah says: “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way for the Lord; make straight the paths of our God. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be humbled. The crooked places shall become straight, and the rough places, smooth roads. And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. XL, 3, etc.).

The evangelist John confirms this, saying: “This is John’s testimony concerning Christ, when the chief priests sent men to him asking whether he was the Christ. And he confessed and did not deny, saying: ‘I am not.’ They asked him: ‘Are you Elijah?’ And he said: ‘No.’ ‘Who then are you?’ they said. ‘Tell us, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?’ He said: ‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way for the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah says” (John I, 19, etc.).

Peter also bears witness in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XIII, 24), saying: “When his course was being fulfilled, John said: ‘I am not the one you suppose me to be, but behold, after me comes one whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie.’”

The Erythraean Sibyl also confesses, saying:

> The sign of judgment: the earth shall grow wet with sweat.  
> Now the mountains are made level with the plains, and the dark-blue waters of the sea.

Explaining herself, she added:

> There shall be nothing lofty or high among human affairs.

We know and see that this has been fulfilled through Christ the Lord.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Christ the King and Judge who is to come from heaven. The promise believed and seen.

3. The prophet David says: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven.” And again: “Your kingdom is a kingdom throughout all ages” (Ps. XVIII, 7; CXLIV, 13). He himself also says: “The Lord has reigned over all the nations” (Ps. XLVI, 9).

And Isaiah says: “You shall see the King in his glory.” Again: “Behold, your King comes,” he says, “sitting upon a light cloud” (Isa. XXXIII, 17; XIX, 1), that is, flesh bearing no weight of sin.

The Gospel of Matthew confirms this, saying: “Magi came from the East, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?’” (Matt. II, 1). Paul also bears witness: “To the King of the ages,” he says. And again: “The blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords will display him” (I Tim. I, 17; VI, 15).

The Sibyl also confesses:

> From heaven the King shall come, destined to endure throughout the ages.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the Word, God and man. The promise believed and seen.

4. The prophet David says: “He sent his Word and healed them” (Ps. CVI, 20). And Jeremiah says: “This is our God, and there is no other beside him. He found the whole way of prudence and gave it to Jacob, his chosen one. After this he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 36, etc.).

The prophet Habakkuk says: “The Word walked and went forth into the fields” (Hab. II, 3, according to the Septuagint). The evangelist John confirms this, saying: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

Paul also bears witness: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being.”

The Sibyl also confesses:

> Certainly present in the flesh, so that he may judge the world.

[Note: This is how it is read in Augustine at the place cited above. The Lyon edition reads, “certainly present in the flesh, and may judge the world”; Louvain, Douai, Cologne, and later editions read, “certainly present in the flesh, and may judge the world.” The Remigius manuscript reads, “certainly present as flesh, and may judge the world.”]

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Christ born from a Virgin. The promise believed and seen.

5. The prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14), which is interpreted as “God with us.”

The evangelist Luke confirms this, saying: “The angel Gabriel was sent to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, and her name was Mary. He entered and greeted her in this way: ‘Hail,’ he said, ‘full of grace; the Lord is with you.’” And a little later: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (ibid. 35).

Paul also bears witness, saying: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. IV, 4), following the Hebrew expression, which calls all females “women.”

The Sibyl also confesses:

> The unbelieving and the faithful shall behold God.

Maro says:

> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven;  
> Now the Virgin returns.

She said “returns” because the virgin Eve, remaining a virgin, brought death into the world, while the returning Virgin Mary brought forth the Savior.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Christ placed in the manger. The promise believed and seen.

6. The prophet Isaiah says: “The ox knows his owner, and the donkey his master’s manger” (Isa. I, 3). And Habakkuk says: “You shall be known in the midst of two animals” (Hab. III, 2, according to the Septuagint).

The evangelist Luke confirms this, saying: “When the days of Mary were completed, she gave birth to a son, wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and placed him in a manger, because there was no room in the lodging” (Luke II, 6–7). And the angel said to the shepherds: “Christ the Lord has been born for you in the city of David, and this shall be the sign for you: you shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger” (ibid. 11).

Paul also bears witness, saying: “Although he was rich, he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (I Cor. VIII, 9).

The Sibyl also confesses:

> While the world lies uncultivated amid dense thorns.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the sign of the star. The promise believed and seen.

7. Balaam, a prophet from the nations, says: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel, and he shall shatter all the kingdoms of the earth” (Num. XXIV, 17).

And the prophet Isaiah says: “The people of the nations, sitting in darkness, saw a great light” (Isa. VII, 2).

David said: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents” (Ps. LXXI, 10). Isaiah likewise says: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold, frankincense, and precious stone; they shall proclaim well the salvation of the Lord” (Isa. LX, 6).

The evangelist Matthew confirms this, saying: “Behold, the star that the Magi had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood above the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with very great joy. They entered and found the child and his mother. Opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, as to a King; frankincense, as to a Priest; and myrrh, as to one who would die for us” (Matt. II, 9, etc.).

Paul also bears witness: “God,” he says, “who commanded light to shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the glory of his knowledge in the face of Christ Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 6).

The Sibyl also confesses, saying:

> Fire shall consume the lands, the sea, and the sky.

Maro also says something appropriate (Aeneid II, lines 694, 700):

> A star, leading a torch with abundant light, ran across the sky;  
> They heap up gifts and worship the holy star.

[Note: The first part of this verse is not found in Virgil.]

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the peace and salvation of his Nativity. The promise believed and seen.

8. Through the prophet Isaiah: “A son,” he says, “has been given to us” (Isa. IX, 6). And a little later: “I shall bring peace upon his leadership; his peace and salvation shall be great, and there shall be no end to his power and peace” (ibid. 7).

The evangelist Luke confirms this, saying: “Immediately there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising and saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will’” (Luke II, 13).

And he himself says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV, 27).

The apostle Paul also bears witness, saying: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II, 14).

Maro also confesses (Eclogue 4, line 17):

> And he shall rule a peaceful world with the virtues of his fathers.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the flight into Egypt. The promise believed and seen.

9. Through the prophet Hosea: “From Egypt,” he says, “I called my Son” (Hos. XI, 1).

The evangelist Matthew confirms this: “An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: ‘Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt. For Herod is going to seek the child in order to destroy him’” (Matt. II, 15).

For this reason Christ was brought into Egypt: so that, as the apostle Paul says, “where sin abounded” (Rom. V, 20), grace might abound even more.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the infants killed for Christ. The promise fulfilled.

10. In the prophet Jeremiah: “A voice,” he says, “was heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning: Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are no more” (Jer. XXXI, 15).

And through David: “The innocent and upright have clung to me” (Ps. XXIV, 21). Elsewhere also: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. VIII, 4).

The evangelist Matthew confirms this. “When Herod,” he says, “saw that he had been deceived by the Magi, he was very angry, and he sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its districts, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the Magi” (Matt. II, 18).

John also bears witness in the Apocalypse: “These,” it was said, “are those who came out of the great tribulation, and they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. VII, 14). Their number was shown from every tribe of Israel: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed (ibid. 4). Christ also joined to their number those whom Jerusalem, unwillingly, had produced, because, as Paul says: “Those whom he predestined, he also called” (Rom. VIII, 30).

Maro says (Aeneid VI, line 426):

> And the souls of infants, weeping at the very threshold.

Again (Eclogue 4, line 23):

> The cradle itself shall pour forth gentle flowers for you.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the child Jesus, who convicted the elders of the Jews in the temple from the prophet Isaiah. The promise fulfilled.

Editorial and textual notes from the supplied text:

- 82, [Col. 0812D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “made known” (*intimavit*); the printed editions read “initiated” (*initiavit*). The printed editions read “among the nations, and from stones,” in place of “from the nations, out of living stones.” The Remigius manuscript reads “has passed through it” (*transiit*) for “shall pass through it.” Augustine’s comparison is found in his Letter to Volusianus (formerly no. 3, now no. 137), ch. 2, p. 405 of the new edition, and in *Against Julian*, book V, ch. 15, p. 656, no. 57, likewise in the new edition.
- 83, [Col. 0813D]: The printed editions read “of the region” (*regionis*) for “of his religion,” “he said” (*dicebat*) for “he declared,” “to restore” (*restaurare*) for “to be restored,” and “held” (*tenenti*) for “held back.”
- 84, [Cols. 0813D–0814A]: The Remigius manuscript reads “while promising and saying”; the printed editions have the equivalent participial construction. The printed editions read “But Solomon … who”; the Remigius manuscript reads “the times” where the printed editions read “the former [times].”
- 85, [Col. 0814D]: The printed editions read “ran together” (*concurrerunt*); the Remigius manuscript reads “ran” (*cucurrerunt*). It reads “in contrition” for “amid contrition of heart,” and “when the measure of grace has been completed, they are freed” for the corresponding clause. It adds “years” after “those days,” and later reads “restore,” as do the later printed editions.
- Chapter XXXVIII title, [Col. 0814D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “Promise.”
- 86, [Col. 0814D]: The Remigius, Douai, and Cologne texts read “desire” (*cupiditate*) for “every desire.” The Remigius manuscript adds “steadfastly” (*constanter*) to the woman’s beholding of the cross, and reads “had written” (*scripserat*). It reads “given over” (*donatum*) for “condemned”; the printed editions read “condemned” (*damnatum*). The printed editions read “had kept silent” (*tacuisset*), while the Remigius manuscript reads “had melted away with shame” (*pudore tabuisset*).
- 86–87, [Col. 0815D]: The Remigius manuscript and printed editions read: “so that those who devise wicked things against me, as the Prophet says, might be turned back upon themselves.” For “dangers of this world,” the Remigius manuscript reads “dangers of this kind.”
- 87, [Col. 0815D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “figures the holy Church and assumes its person”; Cologne and later editions read “signifies the figure and person of the holy Church.”
- 88, [Cols. 0815D–0816D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “if you recognize [it]” (*si agnoscis*). It reads “the saving garment, and a robe” for “the garment of salvation and the robe.” It reads singular “life” (*animam*) where the text has “lives.”
- Chapter XXXIX title, [Col. 0816D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “Promise.”
- 89, [Cols. 0815D–0816D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “endowed with that power of his religion”; the Cologne and later editions read “with that patient endurance in his religion.” It reads “The son, returned wealthy …” at the beginning of the sentence concerning Tobit’s restored sight.
- 90, [Col. 0816D]: The printed editions read “does” (*agit*) for “was accomplished” (*egit*).
- Chapter XL title, [Col. 0816D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “Promise.” In the reference to Ptolemy, the Lyon edition prints “Ptolemy” (*Ptolemaeus*).
- 92, [Cols. 0817B–0818B]: Josephus narrates this matter at length in *Antiquities*, book XIV, ch. 8. The Remigius manuscript reads “Let us observe the succession of the kings at rest.” It preserves the wording “especially when the King was already coming,” whereas the printed editions continue across the column break, “especially when the King ….” Josephus states that Herod’s father was Idumaean and his mother Arabian in *Antiquities*, book XIV, ch. 12, at the end. The Remigius manuscript adds “John” before “the forerunner and herald”; the printed editions read “the Lord, [the] King” for “the true King.”
- 93, [Col. 0818B]: The Remigius manuscript reads “noble fathers” (*procerum patrum*) for “prophetic fathers.”
- Prologue, [Col. 0817D]: The printed editions read that the demons “confessed: ‘… you who have come …’” (*fassique … qui advenisti*) in the cited saying.
- Chapter I title, [Col. 0817D]: The words “Promise believed and seen” are added to this title and to a few following titles from the Remigius-Reims manuscript; they are absent from the printed editions. The Remigius manuscript reads “John’s” in the citation from Acts. On the Sibylline sayings cited here and in the following chapters, see Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, ch. 23.
- Chapter II title, [Col. 0818D]: The Remigius manuscript has: “Of Christ the King and Judge who is to come from heaven. Believed and seen.”
- Chapter III title and text, [Col. 0819D]: The Remigius manuscript title is simply “The Word of God assumed a human being”; the Lyon and Louvain editions read “Concerning the Word of God and man.” The Remigius manuscript reads “his chosen one” for “his chosen [one].” It also inserts: “Isaiah the prophet likewise says: ‘The heart is grievous above all things; and he is a man, and who shall know him?’” Since these words are not found in Isaiah, they perhaps allude to Jeremiah 17:9: “The heart of all is perverse and inscrutable; who shall know it?”
- Chapter III, Sibylline verse, [Col. 0819D]: Augustine reads “Certainly present in the flesh, that he may judge the world”; Lyon reads “certainly present in the flesh, and may judge the world”; Louvain, Douai, Cologne, and later editions read “certainly present into flesh, and may judge the world”; the Remigius manuscript reads “certainly present as flesh, and may judge the world.”
- Chapter IV, [Col. 0819D]: The Remigius manuscript title is simply “Born of a Virgin.” The printed editions read “interpreted,” perhaps to be corrected to “is interpreted,” as at Matthew 1:23. The Remigius manuscript reads “brought forth life” for “brought forth the Savior.”
- Chapter V, [Col. 0820D]: The Remigius manuscript title reads “Placed in a manger.” All older editions read “of two animals” (*duum animalium*); the Remigius manuscript and later editions read “of two [animals]” (*duorum*). The Remigius manuscript reads “for us” in the angelic announcement. The Remigius manuscript and Augustine’s *City of God* read “amid dense thorns”; the printed editions read “amid brambles.”
- Chapter VI, [Col. 0820D]: The Remigius manuscript title reads “Made manifest through a star, etc.” It reads “a great light.” For the myrrh, it reads “for the Lord’s burial.” The words “in the face” are supplied from the Remigius manuscript. The text corrects the Sibylline line from “the sea and the people” to “the sea and the sky,” on the authority of Augustine’s *City of God* and the same verse below in Promise 14 of the Remigius manuscript. The first half of the purported Virgilian verse, “They heap up gifts,” is not found in Virgil.
- Chapter VII title, [Col. 0820D]: The Remigius manuscript reads: “Promise fulfilled: the salvation and peace bestowed upon us, etc.” It reads “to you” for “to us,” and “I leave you my peace” for the same clause.
- Chapter VIII title, [Col. 0821D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “How, while still a child, he was led into Egypt.”
- Chapter IX, [Col. 0821D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “there” for “elsewhere”; it and the Lyon edition add “he says” after “Herod.”
- Chapter X title, [Col. 0821D]: The Remigius manuscript reads “How the child [was] in the temple.”

[Col. 0821D]

11. The prophet Isaiah, speaking in the person of Christ the Lord:

> “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “is upon me. Therefore he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to preach release to captives, and sight to the blind” (Isaiah 61:11).

The Gospel of Luke confirms this, saying:

> “Jesus came into the temple and received the book of Isaiah” (Luke 4:16). [Col. 0822A]

When he had read the words set out above, he said to them:

> “Truly I tell you, today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

And all who were in the temple marveled, saying:

> “How does this man read, who has not learned letters?” (John 7:15).

The apostle Peter bears witness:

> “For prophecy never came by human will, but men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

Paul also says:

> “You have been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20).

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0821D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “On Christ the Anointed,” etc.

On Christ’s being anointed by the dove after John baptized him in the Jordan. The promise fulfilled.

12. The prophet Isaiah: [Col. 0821D]

> “The deserts of the Jordan,” he says, “will be exalted” (Isaiah 26:44, according to the Septuagint).

The author appears to be alluding to Isaiah 44:26 according to the Septuagint, although there the subject is the deserts of Idumea, not the Jordan. See the Greek text. [Col. 0822D]

And it follows:

> “My people shall see the height of God and the glory of the Lord.” [Col. 0822B]

David also says:

> “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45:5).

Again, he himself says:

> “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

The Gospel of Matthew confirms this, saying:

> “Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to be baptized by John. But John tried to prevent him, saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?’ Jesus answered him: ‘Let it be so for now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.’”

Then he immersed him. And when Jesus had been immersed, he immediately came up from the water, and the heavens were opened to him; and he saw the Holy Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and remaining upon him. And a voice came from heaven, saying:

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:13ff.).

[Col. 0822D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Immediately when he came up from the water, the heavens were opened.”

The apostle Peter bears witness to this, saying:

> “And we heard this voice brought from heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain” (2 Peter 1:18).

For this voice sounded from heaven three times, as those who read or hear the Gospels attentively know.

[Col. 0822D] The Remigius manuscript reads “who read attentively”; the printed editions read “who understand.”

By the dove he understands the anointing, since one who knows the account understands that after the Flood the dove carried an olive branch to the ark (Genesis 8:11).

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0822D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “How Christ chose fishermen as disciples.”

On the choosing of the disciples. The promise fulfilled.

[Col. 0822C]

13. Through the prophet Jeremiah:

> “I will send fishermen to them,” he says, “and they shall fish for them; and hunters, and they shall hunt them” (Jeremiah 16:16).

The Gospel of Mark confirms this:

> “Jesus found Simon Peter and Andrew his brother beside the Sea of Galilee, casting their nets, and said to them: ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men’” (Mark 1:16).

[Col. 0822D] The Remigius manuscript reads *venantibus* (“for those hunting”), corresponding to the following *piscantibus vero* (“but for those fishing”). The printed editions read *venientibus* (“for those coming”).

For the hunters he gave mountains exceedingly high for the deer, and the rock as a refuge for the hedgehogs and the hares (Psalm 103:18); but for the fishermen, the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, which travel the paths of the sea (Psalm 8:9).

David briefly explains this, saying:

> “The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham” (Psalm 46:10).

The Sibyl also acknowledges:

> “The Most High [is] with the holy ones, now at the very end of the age.”

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0822D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “On the miracles that Jesus performed,” etc.

On Christ’s miracles. The promise believed and seen.

[Col. 0822D]

14. The prophet Isaiah:

> “Encourage,” he says, “those who are fainthearted; take courage, and no longer be afraid. For behold, our God will render judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. Then the lame man shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear” (Isaiah 35:4ff.).

The Gospel of Mark confirms this, saying:

> “The disciples of John, sent by him, came to Jesus and said to him: ‘The teacher says this: Are you the one who was to come, or are we to expect another?’ Jesus answered them: ‘Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, the poor receive good news, and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me’” (Matthew 11:2ff.). [Col. 0823A]

[Col. 0823D] The wording “the Gospel of Mark” may perhaps need to be read as “the Gospel of Matthew.” These words are not found in Mark but in Matthew, chapter 11 and following. Since no manuscript or printed edition supports the correction, we have not attempted to emend the error.

Peter also bears witness in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Jesus,” he says, “who went about doing good and healing every sickness among the people, because God was in him” (Acts 10:38).

To this Virgil also speaks (*Eclogue* 4.15):

> “He himself shall receive the life of a god.”

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0823D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “How Christ walked upon the sea,” etc.

On Christ’s walking upon the sea. The promise believed and seen.

[Col. 0823B]

15. The prophet David:

> “Your way was in the sea, and your paths in many waters” (Psalm 76:20).

Habakkuk also says:

> “Scattering the waters of his path, the abyss gave forth its voice” (Habakkuk 3:10).

[Col. 0823D] The Remigius manuscript reads “by his tread.”

The Gospel of Matthew confirms this, saying:

> “In the fourth watch of the night Jesus came to his disciples, walking upon the sea. When the disciples saw him, they were afraid, saying: ‘It is a phantom.’ But Jesus approached them and said: ‘It is I; do not be afraid’” (Matthew 14:25ff.).

Solomon also says:

> “You gave a way through the sea and a most secure path among the waves, showing that you can save even those who cross the sea without a boat” (Wisdom 14:3).

Jesus is also known to have done this in the case of Peter (Matthew 14:3).

Paul also bears witness that Jesus stood by him during the shipwreck, saying:

> “Do not be afraid, Paul; for behold, God has granted you all those who are sailing with you” (Acts 27:24).

Of these, no human being perished, but only the ship.

The Sibyl mentioned above responds to both matters:

> “Fire shall consume the lands, and the sea and the pole.”

[Col. 0823D] The Lyons edition reads “stated above.” The Remigius manuscript reads “the sea and the pole”; the printed editions read “the sea and the people.” See the note above on this same verse, in promise 6.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “How Jesus miraculously fed the people,” etc.

On Jesus’ miraculously feeding the people in the wilderness. The promise believed and seen.

[Col. 0823C]

16. The prophet David:

> “He satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things” (Psalm 106:9).

Isaiah says:

> “He will feed you upon the inheritance of your father Jacob” (Isaiah 58:14).

[Col. 0824D] The Lyons edition reads “He will feed you”; the Remigius manuscript reads “as an inheritance.”

The evangelists confirm this: Jesus ordered his disciples to have the people sit down in groups of fifty upon the grass; and from five loaves and two fish he fed five thousand people in the wilderness, and twelve baskets were filled with the leftovers.

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “The Evangelist confirms this.”

Paul also bears witness:

> “For we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

And again:

> “All things are sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Timothy 4:5).

The Sibyl mentioned above also resounds in harmony with this sign.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “How Jesus was carried upon an ass,” etc.

On Jesus’ being carried upon an ass. The promise believed and seen.

[Col. 0823D]

17. The prophet Zechariah says to the daughter of Zion:

> “Behold, your King comes to you, righteous and saving; he is gentle, sitting upon a burden-bearing she-ass and a young colt” (Zechariah 9:9).

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads “Savior.”

All the evangelists confirm that Jesus sat upon the colt of an ass and that the people spread their garments before him (Matthew 21:5; Mark 11:7; Luke 19:35; John 12:14). [Col. 0824A]

In this act Jesus revealed Cornelius, who was to come from the Gentiles to the faith, and in whom the grace of the one who calls took its seat (Acts 10:1ff.).

For in that dish the Lord showed Peter the Gentiles cleansed, with Cornelius believing (Acts 10:15).

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “How Jesus drove them from the temple,” etc.

On Jesus’ expelling the merchants from the temple of God [or: sinners]. The promise believed and seen.

[Col. 0824C]

18. Through the prophet David he himself says:

> “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68:10),

because my enemies have forgotten your words (Psalm 118:139).

Again in the same place:

> “Because I have not known commerce, I shall enter into the power of the Lord” (Psalm 70:15).

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads “trade”; the printed editions read “learning.”

The evangelists also confirm this: the Lord Jesus drove from the temple, with a whip of cords, those buying and selling doves (Matthew 21:12; John 2:15); and he overturned the tables of the money-changers, saying:

> “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matthew 21:13). [Col. 0824B]

Paul bears witness:

> “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

And again:

> “These things were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

In this passage he also marks, among others, lovers of money and traitors, who, by betraying the innocent, traffic in them as in doves.

Hence also Virgil’s lines (*Aeneid* 8.325):

> “Gradually the age grew dark,  
> and the madness of war and the love of acquiring took its place.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “How Christ the Lord revealed his betrayer.”

On Christ the Lord, who revealed his betrayer. The promise believed and seen.

[Col. 0824C]

19. Through the prophet David he himself says:

> “The one who ate my bread has magnified his heel against me” (Psalm 40:10).

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads “enlarged.”

Again in the same place:

> “He went outside and spoke in the same way: all my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evil” (Psalm 40:7).

And again:

> “If an enemy had cursed me, I could certainly have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken a great word against me, I would certainly have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food” (Psalm 54:13).

And more openly:

> “I have been handed over,” he says, “and I did not go out” (Psalm 87:9).

He also says through Zechariah:

> “They set my wages at thirty pieces of silver” (Zechariah 11:12).

All the evangelists confirm this: while the disciples were reclining at table, the Lord Jesus said to them:

> “You know that one of you will betray me” (Matthew 27:9)?

[Col. 0824D] The Remigius manuscript reads “will betray.”

When each one said, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” he said:

> “The one to whom I give the morsel after dipping it is he” (John 13:26).

When Judas said, “Surely it is not I, Teacher?” Jesus said to him:

> “You have said so.”

And immediately, when he had received the morsel, Satan entered into him. He went away and went out, in order to betray him to the Jews.

And again Judas went away and returned the silver to the chief priests, saying:

> “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Mark 14:18; Luke 22:21; Matthew 27:4).

Paul also bears witness:

> “The Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread” (1 Corinthians 11:23), [Col. 0825A]

and the other things that were done up to the betrayal.

The Sibyl also acknowledges:

> “He shall be handed over; eternal flame shall burn the guilty.”

[Col. 0825D] We emend this from Augustine’s *City of God* 18.22. The Prosperian manuscripts had “eternal,” contrary to the laws of the verse.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0825D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “The promise made, prefigured, and fulfilled concerning the insults directed against Jesus.”

On the insults directed against Jesus. The promise fulfilled.

20. Through the prophet Isaiah:

> “I gave my back,” he says, “to scourging, and my cheeks to blows; I did not turn my face away from the disgrace of spitting” (Isaiah 50:6).

Jeremiah also says:

> “He will give his cheek to the one striking him; he will be filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3:30).

[Col. 0825D] The Remigius manuscript reads “he will be satisfied.”

All the evangelists confirm this: Pilate handed Jesus over to them, after he had been scourged, to be crucified; and they struck him with blows and slaps, saying:

> “Prophesy to us, Christ; who is it that struck you?” (Matthew 26:67).

The apostle Peter also bears witness to these things, saying:

> “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten; but he entrusted himself to the one judging justly” (1 Peter 2:21ff.). [Col. 0825B]

[Col. 0825D] The Remigius manuscript reads “to the one judging justly,” which better suits the word “entrusted” and agrees with the Greek text. The older printed editions instead read “but he entrusted himself to the one judging him unjustly”; a more recent edition has “but he commended himself to the one judging him unjustly.”

Another Sibylline passage acknowledges:

> “Afterward he shall come into the hands of the impious. They shall strike God with unholy hands and spit poisonous spittle upon him with an impure mouth. He himself shall give his holy back to blows; and, receiving slaps, he shall remain silent, so that no one may recognize that he is the Word, or from where he comes.”

[Col. 0825D] Augustine quotes these same Sibylline words more fully in the cited book 18 of *The City of God*, chapter 22, section 2, presenting them as drawn from Lactantius’s first book, chapter 6. “Lactantius,” says the holy doctor, “also inserted into his work certain prophecies of the Sibyl concerning Christ, although he does not identify which Sibyl; but the passages that he set out separately I judged should be joined together, as though they formed one extended passage, although he had mentioned them as several brief passages.” [Col. 0826D]

All these things were fulfilled in Christ the Lord, as the whole world now recognizes.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0826D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “That Christ was crowned with thorns.”

On Christ crowned with thorns. The promise fulfilled.

21. Through David he himself says:

> “I was turned into misery when a thorn was driven in” (Psalm 31:4).

[Col. 0826D] The printed editions read *ipsum* (“him”); more appropriately, the Remigius manuscript reads *ipse* (“he himself”), namely Christ, who then was pierced.

The evangelists also confirm this: they placed a crown of thorns upon his head, and he went out carrying his cross (Matthew 27:29; Mark 15:17; John 19:18).

[Col. 0826D] The words “they placed it upon his head” are absent from the Remigius manuscript, not without reason.

This was also signified by that ram which, caught by its horns in the thorns, was sacrificed in place of Isaac (Genesis 22:13). [Col. 0825C]

The Sibyl also acknowledges:

> “So that he may speak to the dead below and be crowned with a crown of thorns” (as quoted in Augustine, the same work, book 18, chapter 22). [Col. 0826D]

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0826D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Of the cross and wounds.”

On Christ’s cross and wounds. The promise fulfilled.

22. The prophet Isaiah:

> “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before the one shearing it, so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

And again:

> “For the iniquity of my people he was led to death” (Isaiah 53:8).

Through David he also says:

> “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones” (Psalm 21:17).

Jeremiah also says:

> “Before our face Christ the Lord was seized into their corruption” (Lamentations 4:20).

Again he himself says:

> “Come, let us cast wood into his bread” (Jeremiah 11:19).

All the evangelists confirm this: when they came to the place called Golgotha, which is the Place of the Skull, they crucified him there (Matthew 27:33). [Col. 0826A]

[Col. 0826D] The Remigius manuscript does not have the phrase “which is called,” nor the word “place.”

The apostle Peter bears witness to this, saying:

> “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood” (1 Peter 2:24).

Paul also says:

> “Although he was crucified in weakness, he lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

## CHAPTER XXII

That Christ was crucified between criminals. The promise fulfilled.

23. The prophet Isaiah:

> “He was counted among the criminals,” he says; “he committed no sin, and by his bruise we have all been healed” (Isaiah 53:12, 5; 1 Corinthians 15:3).

The Gospel of John confirms this, saying:

> “They crucified two others with him, one on either side, and Jesus in the middle” (John 19:18).

The apostle Peter says in addition:

> “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a slanderer; but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify the Lord in this name” (1 Peter 4:15–16). [Col. 0826B]

## CHAPTER XXIII

That his garments were divided and that they cast lots for his tunic. The promise fulfilled.

24. Through the prophet David:

> “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Psalm 21:19).

The evangelist John confirms this:

> “The soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts. Likewise the tunic, which was woven from above throughout, they said: ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be’” (John 19:23–24).

The apostle Paul shows that this tunic is the one Catholic Church, saying:

> “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water in the word, so that he might present the glorious Church to himself, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but that she might be holy and immaculate” (Ephesians 5:25ff.). [Col. 0826C]

[Col. 0826D] The Remigius manuscript reads “that it is one,” namely one Church.

## CHAPTER XXIV

On Christ, who was given gall and vinegar to drink. The promise fulfilled.

25. Through the prophet David he himself says:

> “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68:22).

All the evangelists also confirm this.

John says:

> “Knowing that all things had been completed, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, Jesus said: ‘I thirst.’ A vessel was placed there, full of vinegar, and a sponge full of vinegar; placing it around hyssop, they offered it to his mouth. When Jesus had therefore received the vinegar full of gall, he said: ‘It is completed.’ And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John 19:28ff.).

[Col. 0826D] Thus the Remigius manuscript reads. The printed editions, however, read: “full of vinegar: placing a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop…”

Through David he did not leave this herb unmentioned, saying:

> “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Psalm 50:9).

The Sibyl also acknowledges:

> “For food they gave him gall, and for thirst they gave him vinegar; they shall display this table of inhospitality.”

[Col. 0826D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “They displayed this inhospitality.” [Col. 0827A]

[Col. 0827D] The Remigius manuscript has: “To this also … [lacuna] It shall perish … [lacuna] It shall perish.”

To this also responds that Virgilian line (*Eclogue* 4.44):

It shall perish: for then the devil was defeated.

[Col. 0827D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “On the piercing of his side with a lance.”

On Christ’s being pierced with a lance, and blood and water flowing from his side. The promise fulfilled.

The apostle John also says:

[Col. 0827D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “There are three who give testimony.”

[Col. 0827D] In Augustine’s text: “with the minds of mortals and with thorns”; the Remigius manuscript reads “but with thorns”; the printed editions read “with the senses of mortals and with thorns.”

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0827D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “On the darkening of the sun during the Passion.”

That the sun and moon were darkened in Christ’s Passion. The promise fulfilled.

[Col. 0827D] The Remigius manuscript reads this way, and more correctly than the printed editions, which have “Isaiah.” This passage is expressed more fully and explicitly in Joel than in Isaiah.

[Col. 0827D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “When you have crossed over.”

On the burial of Christ the Lord. The promise fulfilled.

28. Through the prophet David he himself says:

> “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead, and like the wounded who lie cast down in the tombs” (Psalm 87:5–6).

[Col. 0827D] The Remigius manuscript reads “among the dead” and “in the tombs”; the printed editions read “in the tomb.”

Again in the same psalm:

The Sibyl also acknowledges:

> “He shall die by death for three days, having taken on sleep.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0828D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “On the bodies of the saints being raised.”

That at Christ’s death the bodies of the saints rose. The promise fulfilled.

29. The prophet Isaiah says:

[Col. 0828D] The Remigius manuscript reads “shall be raised”; and “and those things that are upon the earth shall rejoice.”

The evangelist Matthew confirms this, saying:

[Col. 0828D] The Remigius manuscript reads “and the cold [gates].”

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 0828D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “On the third day of the Resurrection.”

That he rose from the dead on the third day. The promise fulfilled.

30. The prophet Hosea says:

> “After two days he will heal us. On the third day we shall rise, and before dawn we shall find him prepared” (Hosea 6:3).

[Col. 0828D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “He healed … we shall rise.”

Through David he also says:

> “I shall rise before dawn” (Psalm 62:2). [Col. 0828C]

Again in the same place:

> “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome by wine” (Psalm 77:65).

[Col. 0828D] The Remigius manuscript and the more recent editions read “mighty”; the older editions read “drinking.”

Matthew and the other evangelists confirm this: the chief priests came to Pilate and said:

> “Lord, we remember that while that deceiver was still alive he said: ‘After three days I shall rise.’ Therefore command the tomb to be guarded” (Matthew 27:62ff.).

For he had said to them:

> “This generation is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man must be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:39–40).

[Col. 0828D] The words “three days and three nights” are absent from the Remigius manuscript.

But in the evening of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled away the stone, and sat upon it. His appearance was terrifying, and his clothing was like snow. At his fear the guards trembled and became like dead men. [Col. 0829A]

[Col. 0828D] The Remigius manuscript reads “and he came … and sat”; “his appearance was glorious.”

But the angel said to the women:

The question arises why he is called the firstfruits, since he himself raised the dead, and Elijah and Elisha also raised the dead.

The answer is that those who were raised died again, and now rest among those who sleep; but the apostle Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who sleep because, having risen from the dead, he dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him (Romans 6:9).

[Col. 0829D] The Remigius manuscript reads “raised again”; the printed editions read “raised,” perhaps for “raised again.”

The Sibyl also acknowledges:

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0829D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “How he rebuked the unbelieving disciples.”

On the rebuking of the unbelieving disciples. The promise fulfilled.

[Col. 0829B]

Again:

Virgil also says (*Eclogue* 4.13–14):

[Col. 0829D] The Remigius manuscript has only: “The Ascension of the Lord.”

[Col. 0829D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Our assumption, and of the Holy One of Israel, our King.”

And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind being carried along, and it filled the entire place where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, and it rested upon each one of them; and they spoke in various tongues, as the Spirit gave them to utter” (Acts 1:1ff.). [Col. 0830B]

[Col. 0829D] The Remigius manuscript reads “as they were sitting”; the printed editions read “as they were believing.”

> “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “sent from heaven, whom he poured out most abundantly upon us and upon all believers” (1 Peter 1:12; Titus 3:6).

## CHAPTER XXXII

On the origin of the Church. The promise fulfilled.

33. The prophet David says:

> “He makes the barren woman dwell in the house as a joyful mother of children” (Psalm 112:9).

And Isaiah:

> “Rejoice,” he says, “you barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1; Galatians 4:27).

And how this woman gives birth, the Lord himself shows in the Gospel attributed here to Mark:

> “Go,” he says to the disciples, “baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

[Col. 0829D] These words of Christ, prescribing the form of baptism, are found in Matthew, not in Mark. The source of this error—whether the fault of copyists or the author’s own lapse of memory—cannot be determined because of the defective state of several manuscripts. [Col. 0830D]

[Col. 0830D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “Baptize all nations”; the printed editions read: “Baptizing in the name,” etc.

[Col. 0830D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “throughout all Judea.” [Col. 0830C]

Peter also says:

[Col. 0830D] The Remigius manuscript reads “rational”; the Douai, Cologne, and later editions read “desiring”; the Remigius manuscript, together with the Lyons and Louvain editions, reads “desire.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0830D] The Remigius manuscript reads: “On the New Testament, etc., as in the printed editions.”

On the New Testament, the new song, and the new human being. The promise fulfilled.

### 34. Jeremiah the prophet:

“Behold, the days are coming,” says the Lord, “and I will establish over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant, [Note: These words, “not according to the covenant,” are supplied by the Remigian manuscript.] not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers” (Jer. 31:31; Heb. 8:8). [Note: The Remigian manuscript adds, “And the apostle Paul.” The Apostle partly cites this prophetic passage at Heb. 10:16.]

And shortly afterward:

“This is the covenant that I will establish with them: putting my laws into their minds, and upon their hearts I will write them; [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “I will know.”] and each one will no longer teach his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all will know me, from the greatest to the least of them” (Jer. 31:33–34).

And through Isaiah:

“Behold, I am making new things, which shall now arise” (Isa. 43:19).

And again:

“But for those who serve me, a new name shall be named” (Isa. 62:2).

This is plainly understood as “Christian,” a name that has taken possession of the world.

David also says:

“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95:1).

Who but one blind in heart could fail to see that these things have been fulfilled?

The Lord confirms this in the Gospel of Matthew. He says:

“Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of God is like a man bringing forth from his treasures new things and old” (Matt. 13:52). [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “from his own treasure.”]

And again:

“That which is born from the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). [Note: The Remigian manuscript inserts here: “That which is born from the flesh is flesh; that which is born…” These words are omitted by all the printed editions.]

Paul also bears witness:

“The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also put on the image of him who is from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47, 49). [Note: This word is found in the Remigian manuscript and in the more recent printed editions, but not in the older editions of Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne.]

And again:

“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind,” he says, “and put on the new man, [Note: The Remigian manuscript lacks the word “him.”] the one who was created according to God” (Eph. 4:23–24). [Note: The printed text cited appears to contain an OCR or typographical error: the Latin has *Ephes. IV, 28*, but the quotation corresponds to Eph. 4:23–24.]

Likewise:

“If there is any new creation in Christ,” he says, “the old things have passed away, and behold, new things have come to be” (2 Cor. 5:17).

Maro also says (Eclogue 4.8–9):

> When iron first  
> Ceases, and a golden race rises throughout the world.

### CHAPTER XXXIV

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “On the Martyrs.”]

#### On the Martyrs. The Promise Fulfilled

### 35.

Through the prophet David they say:

“For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43:22).

And again:

“You gave us like sheep for food” (ibid., 12).

Likewise, in the same psalm:

“Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:6).

The Lord himself confirms these things in the Gospel, saying:

“Behold, I am sending you like sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10:16).

And again:

“He who loses his life for my sake will preserve it for eternal life” (ibid., 29).

Likewise:

“But you will be handed over by brothers, relatives, and friends, and they will put some of you to death; and you will be hated by all because of my name. But whoever endures to the end will be saved” (Luke 21:16).

And in John:

“Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

The apostle John also bears witness, saying:

“Just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (1 John 3:16).

Paul also says:

“For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels, [Note: The printed editions read “an angel.”] nor principalities, nor things present nor things future”—and he concludes—“nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38–39).

To this may be added the following passage of Maro (Eclogue 4.15–16):

[Note: In Virgil the passage reads:

> And he will see heroes mingled with the gods,  
> and he himself will be seen by them.]

> And he will see heroes mingled with the gods,  
> and he himself will be seen by them.

### 36.

The historian Orosius wrote that there were ten persecutions, from Nero to Diocletian and Maximian, like the ten plagues of Egypt. Blessed Augustine inserted many others into his writings. [Note: See chapter 52 of book 18 of *The City of God*, where Saint Augustine discusses at length whether, after the ten preceding persecutions had been completed, none remained except the one that is to occur in the time of Antichrist.] [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, uncertainly owing to corruption: “which, as the people feels them far from others, and to us [in] its memory.”]

He both experienced and witnessed persecutions not far removed from our own time, and handed down to us memories consecrated and worthy of veneration of his martyrdom, himself also believing in the growth of the Church, whose fulfillment we see.

We know, moreover, that in our own times a persecution took place among the Persians, under Arcadius, a devout and Christian ruler [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads “glorious”], who waged war against the Persians so that he would not surrender the Armenians who had fled to him for refuge. As a sign of this, before he had gained the victory, when the soldiers were already assembling for battle, aerial crosses appeared upon their garments. Therefore, after his victory, he also ordered a gold coin to be made with the same sign of the cross, [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “which was in circulation.”] and it remains in circulation throughout the entire world, especially in Asia, even today.

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “The Bringing of the Nations.”]

The prophet David said:

“Many nations will marvel at him, and kings will shut their mouths. Those to whom nothing was announced [Note: The printed editions read, “by God.”] about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand” (Isa. 52:14–15).

Likewise:

“They will proclaim his powers in the islands” (Isa. 42:12).

Again Isaiah says: [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “himself.”]

And again:

“The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 18:45).

The Lord confirms these things in the Gospel:

“Many will come from east and west, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 3:11). [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “of my Father.”]

Peter also bears witness:

“Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God” (1 Pet. 2:10).

Paul also says:

“I speak to you Gentiles: inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “I will honor [it], if at some time …”] I will glorify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to rivalry and save some of them” (Rom. 11:13).

And again:

“Blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel may be saved” (ibid., 25). [Note: The printed editions read, “will be saved.”]

“Everyone who is written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. 13:8).

### CHAPTER XXXVI

[Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “How kings … are brought in.”]

#### That Kings Who Persecuted Christ in the Church Will Be Brought to Her in Humility. The Promise Fulfilled

### 38.

In the prophet David:

“All the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. 72:11).

And the prophet Isaiah:

“Nations and kings who have not served you will perish” (Isa. 60:12).

And again:

“Behold,” says the Lord, “I raise my hand over the nations, and I lift up my sign over the islands; and they will bring your sons in their bosom, while they will lift your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings will be your foster fathers, and their princesses your singing women. They will worship you with their faces toward the earth, and they will lick the dust of your feet” (Isa. 49:22 and following). [Note: The Remigian manuscript reads, “they will carry them.”]

The Lord confirms these things in the Gospel, saying:
