The prophet Malachi says: “He entered like a refiner’s fire, and he will sit refining and purifying like silver and gold, and he purified the sons of Levi” (Mal. 3:2 ff.).

In the Gospel Matthew confirms these things about the Lord, saying: “He is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire, holding a winnowing fork in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor. He will gather the grain into his granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3:11–12).

Again the Lord himself says: “Before heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law without being fulfilled” (Matt. 5:18).

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads: “until all things are fulfilled.”]

The apostle Peter also says: “The heavens that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment” (2 Pet. 3:7). And shortly afterward: “You are hastening toward the coming of the Lord, because of which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the heat of fire” (ibid. 12).

Paul says: “Creation itself will be set free from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:21).

The Sibyl also acknowledges this, saying:

All things will cease; the shattered earth will perish.

Thus likewise the springs will burn, and the rivers in fire.

When these things have been accomplished, the wicked will look upon the righteous and say: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We foolishly considered their life madness and their end dishonorable. How have they been counted among the children of God, and how is their lot among the saints?” (Wis. 5:3 ff.).

Then they will practice fruitless repentance, since it is written: “But in the underworld, who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6). When the wicked have been consigned to outer darkness, where there will be no light and no day, and that terrible and fearful voice has sounded: “Let the wicked be taken away, and let him not see the glory of the Lord of the saints” (Isa. 26:10), then the eminent and glorious glory will follow, which must be set forth in other chapters.

# PART FIVE: ON THE GLORY AND KINGDOM OF THE SAINTS

## CHAPTER I. On the New Heaven and the New Earth

[Note: In the Remigius manuscript, the titles of all thirteen following chapters consist of these two words: “The promise to be fulfilled.”]

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled and Believed**

1. The Apocalypse of John says: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Apoc. 21:1). Peter also bears witness: “We await new heavens and a new earth according to his promises, in which righteousness dwells” (2 Pet. 3:13). David says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). The wicked will not see these things.

## CHAPTER II. On the Transformation of the Saints

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled, and First to Be Believed**

2. The apostle Paul says: “Until we all come to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13). Into this state the saints of every age and both sexes will pass, with this glory, into the thirty-year-old maturity in which Christ the Lord suffered, and they will pass with their King, whom the wicked will not see.

## CHAPTER III. On the New Jerusalem

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled and First to Be Believed**

3. The Apocalypse says: “I saw the new Jerusalem descending from God, prepared and adorned like a bride for her husband” (Apoc. 21:2).

[Note: Later editions read “as a bride.”]

Paul also says: “The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26). In this city there will be no night, nor will there be need of the light of a lamp; there will be neither mourning nor death nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away (Apoc. 22:5; 20:4).

[Note: All the printed editions read “deceit” rather than “pain.”]

The wicked will not see the glory of this homeland.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Saints’ Shining Like the Sun

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled and Believed**

4. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the presence of their Father” (Matt. 13:43), because they will be equal to the angels of the Lord (Luke 20:36). The wicked will not see this glory.

## CHAPTER V. On the Difference among the Saints in Glory, Like That among the Stars

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled and Believed**

5. The apostle Paul says: “Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:41–42). Some will shine with different honors and without envy because of the confession of martyrdom, others because of virginal integrity, others because of widowly continence, and others because of marital chastity. The wicked will not see them.

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads “because of confession”; the printed editions read “because of agreement.”]

## CHAPTER VI. On the Virginity of the Saints

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled and Believed**

6. The Apocalypse of John says: “These are the ones who did not defile themselves with women, for they remained virgins. These are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Apoc. 14:4). Where the virgins follow him, and where non-virgins cannot follow him, the wicked will not see.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Inexpressible Gift of the Saints

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled and Believed**

7. The apostle Paul says: “What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). When the saints have received these things, the wicked will not see them.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Seeing God Face to Face

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled**

8. The apostle Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). How the saints will see God the Trinity—the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit both in the Father and in the Son—the wicked will not see.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Unveiled Face of the Saints

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled**

9. The apostle Paul says: “With unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. And the wicked will not see these things” (2 Cor. 3:18).

## CHAPTER X. On the Son’s Handing Over the Kingdom to God the Father

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled**

10. How the Son will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, as the apostle Paul says (1 Cor. 15:24), the wicked will not see.

[Note: The printed editions read “handed over”; the Remigius manuscript reads “will hand over.”]

## CHAPTER XI. On the Unceasing Song of Alleluia

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled**

11. How, in an unceasing song, as the Apocalypse says, the saints will sing Alleluia without interruption and without end (Apoc. 19:1, 3, 4, 6), the wicked will neither hear nor see.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Renewal of All Things

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled**

12. How all things will be renewed, as the prophet Isaiah and the Apocalypse say, and will remain forever (Isa. 43:19; Apoc. 21:5); and how the saints will take food from the tree of life, or from corruption [the printed reading is uncertain], and drink from the fountain that is Christ (Apoc. 22:14), not from necessity but from power—the wicked will not see.

## CHAPTER XIII. That God Will Be All in All

**The Promise to Be Fulfilled**

13. How God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), as the apostle Paul says, the wicked will not see, because only the saints and the redeemed will enjoy these heavenly pleasures and delights. This is our city, our strength, and our salvation. This is the everlasting heavenly Jerusalem. With the saints established in it, the true God is King.

He sets no limits to things, nor any span of time;

He has granted rule without end.

(*Aeneid* 1.85, 286.)

14. These are the ones who reign with Christ the King, of whom Daniel says: “His kingdom will not be left to another people” (Dan. 2:44; 3:100), because he will reign for infinite ages, and his kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:33).

## CHAPTER XIV. Conclusion

[Note: “The Final Address of Saint Prosper and the Conclusion of This Most Faithful and Useful Book of His.” The Remigius–Rheims manuscript contains no mention of Prosper here; it occurs only in the printed editions. Whether this work can be attributed to someone of this name, although it certainly should not be attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine, see the preliminary notice to this book.]

15. With the help of God’s grace, I have brought this book to a conclusion by noting forty chapters in each of its first three parts, like the forty days during which Moses, Elijah, and the Lord Jesus observed fasts in the course of this life. For three times forty makes one hundred and twenty. Twenty more are added, corresponding to the half-period of the world’s end, making one hundred and forty. Thirteen are added in the glory of the saints, completing one hundred and fifty-three.

It was with this number that those sacred fish were caught in the uncorrupted net of truth after the Lord’s resurrection (John 21:11). They signify the number of the saints, whom the Lord gathers from every nation, tribe, and language throughout all time and consecrates to himself—an infinite number known to him.

You have here the first pleasure of fishing, if you are a lover of this pursuit, spiritual reader, especially since, as I think, you will find in this book every pleasure and every affection.

“Enter here, young man, and be invited here; play here, and exercise your conceptions” (Sir. 32:15).

For if perhaps the game board attracts you, you have in a single die the numbers two and three, five and six, by which the measurements of the ark are raised (Gen. 6:15), rolling the dice of threefold unity; and you move counters that are white in good works and purple in passion, while he looks on who says: “To the one who conquers I will give a counter, and upon the counter a new name, which no one knows except the one who receives it” (Apoc. 2:17).

On ivory counters the names of proconsuls were written at Carthage and proclaimed in the forum before the people by the presiding judge under fixed designations; and the proclamation of the white counters was a solemn day. Those who had overcome greed and administered the republic faithfully, without bribes or favors, were honored even in their absence. But those whom rapacity had conquered were marked by the people with insults and jeers.

16. You therefore know what you must conquer, you who, while governing the republic, play in this world. Conquer greed, which is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10); and let not earthly powers, which slip away by one means or another, but heavenly and eternal powers attract you.

If you are drawn to hunting, you have the highest mountains, through which the swift-running sayings of the apostles and prophets range. You also have in the fields the rock, a refuge for hedgehogs and rabbits (Ps. 103:18), whom Christ the Lord hunts through his hounds, in simplicity of heart, so that they may be free from the thorns of sins.

If the pleasure is that of watching spectacles, here you have the spiritual charioteer, Christ, and Elijah, who was carried in a fiery chariot to the turning-posts of heaven (2 Kings 2:11), as well as Pharaoh’s chariots submerged in the deep (Exod. 14:2).

As a contest, you have the holy Daniel, who conquered the lion not with iron but with prayer (Dan. 6:22), and the bears that attacked those who had insulted the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 2:24).

In this holy spectacle you also have not shameful enemies but virgins consecrated to Christ. You have, in place of the horse-racers—

[Note: The Lyon and Louvain editions read *Cadalistarum*, but *Caballistarum* is better, as found in the Remigius manuscript and the Douai and Cologne editions. By *Caballistae* the author seems to mean those who competed in the arena by driving and racing horses.]

—Rebecca’s twins, mystically playing (Gen. 25:22). You have David dancing before the ark (2 Sam. 6:5), and Christ, stripped in his Passion before his male and female servants, presenting that very history. Finally, you have the laments and mournful songs of Jeremiah, sung not with tragic art but with prophetic art.

17. If there is a desire to build, you have the structure of the world, the measurements of the ark (Gen. 6:14), the circuit of the tabernacle (Exod. 26:1 ff.), the height of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:1 ff.), and the members of the Church throughout the world, which all those things prefigured.

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads “its own.”]

If there is a delight in feasting, here you have Wisdom’s table prepared (Prov. 9:1–2), at which there is angelic bread and the fatted calf, and a cup of salvation that intoxicates soberly. Nor are holy flowers lacking at this banquet: lilies of virgins, violets of the continent, and rose-crowns of martyrs.

[Note: The printed editions read “of continence”; the Remigius manuscript reads “of the continent.”]

The pleasure of music, I think, remains. Here you have an organ made from the various pipes of the holy apostles and all the teachers of the churches, fitted with certain accents—grave, acute, and circumflex. The Spirit of God, that musician, touches, fills, and makes it resound through the Word.

[Note: The printed editions read “which”; the Remigius manuscript reads “that,” referring to the organ.]

You have David’s key, which shuts and no one opens, and opens and no one shuts (Apoc. 3:7), consecrating and adorning all things with the oil of chrism and the water of baptism.

To the organ’s most pleasant and sweetest voices the princes joined those who were singing in the midst of young women playing tambourines (Ps. 67:26). What these are follows: “Bless the Lord in the churches.” These young women are the churches; while they strike the tambourine—that is, stretched skin of a dead creature on wood—they preach Christ crucified. The great sound of this tambourine now delights the hearing of the whole world.

18. Nor is the psaltery of ten strings (Ps. 143:9) absent from this banquet, while, at the conclusion of the one hundred and fifty psalms, the saints praise the Lord with the sound of the trumpet, with psaltery and lyre, with tambourine and chorus, with strings and organ, with well-sounding cymbals and cymbals of jubilation (Ps. 150:3 ff.), because every spirit praises the Lord (Ps. 28:9).

As I look upon these things in the temple of my God, in which each person says, “Glory,” I consider that the passions which arise through the law are still at work in our members (Rom. 7:5), so that they may bear fruit for death. Entangled in many vices, we are held in this life, which is wholly a testing (Job 7:1).

I have vowed in this book and sacrificed upon the altar of a contrite heart a sacrifice from the fat of calves—the patriarchs and prophets—and from the fat of goats and rams—the apostles, leaders of the flock—for the sin of my soul and the cleansing of my whole person, not without the incense of the prayers of all the saints (Apoc. 8:4). Through these I trust that I can be cleansed from every sin.

Let the envious reader be quiet, lest, as Cain struck with iron (Gen. 4:8), this one strike with tooth or tongue. “The teeth of the children of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5).

If anything displeases him, let him correct it in mercy, if he is devout, and reprove it with gentleness (Ps. 140:5), and let him pray for us, so that together we may be found in the ark among the clean animals, joined together in the cubit of its perfection, and, under the guidance of grace, may all follow the love of the Lord, the unity of the Trinity’s majesty, the way that surpasses all else (1 Cor. 12:31).

[Note: We have corrected this from the Remigius manuscript; the printed editions read “through the eminent way.”]

May he remain in us and we in him, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, who is God, blessed forever. Amen (Rom. 1:25; 11:36).

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads “forever and ever. Amen.”]

[Additional editorial notes omitted above:

- Col. 0849D. A note printed at the foot of column 849 states that its callout letter, *e*, does not appear in the text; the Remigius manuscript reads “In the Passion.”
- Col. 0850D. On Ps. 101:27–28, the Remigius manuscript reads “like garments … and like coverings.” On Ps. 65:10, it reads “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested.”
- Col. 0852D. Later editions read “will enter”; the printed editions read “will purify,” while the Remigius manuscript reads “purified.” The Remigius manuscript reads “into barns” and, on Rom. 8:21, “from the slavery of destruction into freedom.”
- Col. 0853D. The Remigius manuscript reads, concerning Wis. 5:3, “in laughter and in the likeness of reproach.” It also reads: “There follows … what must be communicated in other chapters”; the printed editions read “must be communicated in another chapter.”
- Col. 0855D. The Remigius manuscript’s heading reads: “By God’s grace I have concluded [this work] in 150 chapters.” It reads “pleasures” in place of “desires”; “looking on” in place of the corrupt printed “awaiting”; and “without votes” in place of “without disgraceful practices and favors.” The Lyon and Louvain editions, with the Remigius manuscript, read “on one *as*”; the Douai and Cologne editions read “in one being,” less well.
- Col. 0856D. The Remigius manuscript reads “attraction” in the heading on building, and “in the conclusion” in place of “at the conclusion.”]

[CHRONICON ALTERUM, OR PSEUDO-CHRONICON]

[Col. 0857]

## NOTICE ON THE CHRONICLE THAT FOLLOWS
Besides that Chronicle of Saint Prosper which we have presented at the end of his twofold works, and which everyone—except a very few—willingly attributes to Prosper of Aquitaine, the disciple of Saint Augustine, another Chronicle also appeared under the name of Tiro Prosper, first published by the most learned Pierre Pithou from a manuscript codex of the library of Saint Victor in Paris. Like Saint Prosper’s ordinary Chronicle, it begins in the year 379 and extends to the year 455. Pithou assigned the name Prosper to the author of this work (Duchesne, vol. I of the *History of France*, p. 196), relying on the authority of the manuscripts of Sigebert and Marianus. But he adds on his own authority that this is the true Chronicle of Prosper, whose character, he argues, it reflects so closely that he thinks it may rightly be regarded as a section of that more extensive work which, under Prosper’s name, Gennadius of Massilia, a priest, attests that he had read—from the creation of the world to Rome’s capture by the Vandals. He also wonders how it happened that another Chronicle—namely, the one previously published—arranged by consuls, had until then been appended under Prosper’s name in all editions of Jerome’s Chronicle. Although that work shares quite a few things with this one, since both concern the history of the same period, anyone who reads both more attentively will easily understand that they are of a different kind.

Indeed, we shall readily admit to Pithou that these two Chronicles cannot be called the offspring of one and the same author. Otherwise, as Bucherius says (*Cycl.*, p. 212; Nori, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 15, p. 218), we would have to concede that, as the saying goes, hot and cold breath could issue simultaneously from one and the same mouth. Yet it is altogether astonishing that such a man should have been led to this opinion: for although he himself willingly acknowledges that this Chronicle is very confused and disordered, it is nonetheless filled with errors in its chronological arrangement; scarcely anything is touched upon concerning the Pelagians; and the only observation it makes about Augustine is that he discussed many matters in countless books. Finally, it says that the heresy of the Predestinarians arose from Augustine—something Saint Prosper most certainly did not know, since he is nowhere reported to have attacked or refuted such a heresy. It is astonishing, I say, that such a work should be judged more worthy of Prosper, and more representative of his character, than the other Chronicle, which is plainly clearer and arranged in better order; from which the greatest light is shed upon the entire history of Saint Augustine and the Pelagian heresy; and in which, finally, Saint Augustine and Saint Leo are praised with the greatest testimony of reverence—both of whom may rightly and deservedly be called Saint Prosper’s teachers. For this reason Jacobus Sirmondus wholly disagrees with Pithou’s opinion (*On Predestination*, chapter 5, p. 31), and does not allow this new Chronicle to be numbered among the works of the great Prosper.

Pithou, however, convinced of the contrary, designated the author of his Chronicle by the name Tiro Prosper, although the handwritten codices from which he had drawn this little work bore only the name Prosper. Sirmondus rightly acknowledged that Pithou had done this without justification (*ibid.*). Hence this name Tiro is not found in the editions prepared by Dunhest or Scaliger. But since the name Prosper, without any further addition, appears to have been consecrated to the designation of the most holy defender of the grace of Christ, the author of Pithou’s Chronicle is commonly identified by the name Tiro Prosper, so that he will not be thought to be confused with the other Prosper.

Yet Pithou made his greatest mistake in the passage concerning the Predestinarians. For although in the two manuscripts he had in hand the reading was:

> “The heresy of the Predestinarians, which is said to have received its beginning **from Augustine**, began in these times to spread”;

and in only one of the two this alternative reading had been added:

> “**from Augustine’s books, wrongly understood**”;

and the same wording was found in the Chronicle of Sigebert—by which single argument it was sufficiently demonstrated that the author of the work ought not to be recognized as Prosper, but as some adversary of Saint Augustine, and that anyone who said that a heresy had arisen from Augustine was wholly unworthy of belief—Pithou nevertheless, disregarding the manuscripts, substituted Sigebert’s reading. Although that reading is less offensive to the writer, it nevertheless could in no way have proceeded from Saint Prosper.

Hence even Sirmondus, whose interest it was to undertake Pithou’s defense, so that he might preserve unimpaired the credibility of the man whom he had adopted as the principal witness of the Predestinarian heresy, was compelled to blame Pithou on this point. He confessed that Pithou ought to have written in his Chronicle, “from Augustine,” as it was later published by Philippe Labbe in the *New Library of Manuscripts* (Labbe, *New Library*, vol. I, pp. 58–59; likewise *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 260). Yet Sirmondus still doubts—something no one will easily believe unless he has read him—whether this Chronicle should not be acknowledged as a work of Prosper.

[Note: The same reading is found in a manuscript codex perhaps five hundred years old, which had belonged to the distinguished Claudius Joli, precentor and canon of the metropolitan church of Paris; later, through his gift, it became the property of the venerable chapter of that same church. In this manuscript the first hand reads “from Augustine”; a later hand, in more recent script, substituted “from Augustine’s books, wrongly understood.” The same wording was also noted almost as a correction in the margin of the manuscript of Saint Victor examined by us; and Philippe Labbe likewise notes that it was substituted by a later hand in the Oysel manuscript, in the *New Library of Manuscripts*.]

Nor are there lacking those who think that this work was falsely attributed to Prosper (Maignan, vol. II, p. 519), so that both he himself and Saint Augustine might thereby be brought into contempt and hatred. This conjecture does not seem to rest upon solid foundations or adequate proofs. For Hincmar, whom they observe to have been silent about this Chronicle, either did not know it or certainly did not wish to use it for other reasons.

It is therefore more natural to believe either that it was composed by a certain Prosper, a rival of Saint Prosper, the defender of grace; or that, since the earliest copies lacked the name of any author, the name of Saint Prosper was later imposed upon it because he was publicly known to have written a Chronicle of the same period; or, finally, that it was arbitrarily altered, abridged, or interpolated by some Semi-Pelagian from Provence, in whose possession was the genuine Chronicle of Saint Prosper—although perhaps that man never intended to publish it. Both Joseph Antelmius, in the eighth dissertation *On the True Works of the Holy Fathers Leo and Prosper*, and the most learned author of the *Library of Ecclesiastical Authors* (Dupin), volume IV, under Prosper, adopted this last opinion. We too readily believe that their judgment should be followed.

[Col. 0859]

## THE SECOND CHRONICLE PUBLISHED UNDER THE NAME OF TIRO PROSPER

This is called by some the **Pseudo-Chronicle**. From the death of the emperor Valens to the capture of the City by Genseric; very different from the work hitherto appended to the Chronicle of Blessed Jerome; from Pithou’s edition. (C)

[Col. 0859A] **I.** [Note: [Col. 0859C] In the Joli manuscript the following is prefixed: “Thus far Jerome the priest has arranged the sequence of the preceding years. What follows Prosper has arranged.”] Accordingly, after Valens had been burned by the Goths in Thrace, Gratian reigned for six years with his brother Valentinian. Since he had his little brother as a partner in the kingdom, he associated with them in rule Theodosius, a man of mature age and proven character. This Gratian was very favorable to religion and in every respect zealous for the churches.

Martin, bishop of Tours, was regarded as distinguished for apostolic virtues.

**II.** Theodosius restored the exhausted commonwealth in the eastern regions.

**III.** Maximus was proclaimed emperor in Britain by the soldiers.

**IV.** Maximus vigorously defeated the invading Picts and Scots.

A certain Priam reigns in France, as far as we have been able to gather from more remote sources.

**V.** Ambrose wrote most brilliant books against the perfidy of the Arians to Gratian Augustus.

**VI.** Maximus crossed into Gaul and, after engaging Gratian in battle, killed him at Lyons while Gratian was fleeing.

Theodosius, eleven years.

**I.** Fearing Theodosius, ruler of the Eastern Empire, Maximus entered into a treaty with Valentinian.

At Trier, the Manichaeans who had been discovered were exterminated through Maximus’s greatest efforts.

**II.** Justina, the mother of Valentinian, favoring the Arians, heaped various kinds of injuries upon Ambrose and the entire Church of Milan.

The relics of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius were first discovered at Milan by Ambrose.

[Note: The word “martyrs” was absent from Pithou’s edition.]

The hymns of Ambrose were composed; previously they had never been sung in the Latin churches with musical melodies.

**III.** Maximus, judging it unworthy that action should be taken against the position of the Church, found an opportunity to break the treaty he had made with Valentinian. Valentinian, fearing the tyrant who was already threatening his neck, fled to Theodosius.

[Col. 0859C] [Note: The material enclosed in brackets is thought to have been transferred from the margin.]

> Honorius and Arcadius, 32, 400.  
> Theodosius and Joannes, 25 and 22.  
> Valentinian and Marcian, 3, 400, 25.

Augustine, teaching rhetoric with great distinction at Milan, abandoned the schools and was converted to the true faith, having previously been a Manichaean.

**IV.** Theodosius crossed into Italy with an army, killed Maximus, and restored Valentinian to his own kingdom.

Justina, who had harassed the churches, was overtaken by death before she could recover the kingdom with her son.

The devout emperor washed away the monstrous crime committed at Thessalonica—the slaughter of the people—by an outstanding example of repentance.

**V.** The heresy of the Apollinarists began with Apollinaris.

The Arians, who had defiled almost the whole East [Note: These words, “and the West,” are absent from the Victor manuscript.] and the West, were deprived by an edict of the glorious prince of the churches assigned to the Catholics.

**VI.** John the Egyptian, a monk who, on account of the purity of his life, earned from the Lord the grace of prophecy, was regarded as distinguished.

After Damasus, Siricius assumed the governance of the Roman Church for thirty-six years. [Note: Both the Victor and Joli manuscripts read “undertook.”]

**VII.** At Alexandria, after Peter’s death, Timothy, and after him Theophilus, were appointed bishops.

At Jerusalem, after Cyril, John took over the Church.

At Antioch, after Meletius’s death, Flavian was appointed in his place.

A great dispute arose among our people: namely, that the bishops who had been driven out by the heretics did not want other priests substituted for them after those whom the emperor had expelled.

A terrifying sign appeared in heaven, entirely resembling a column.

**VIII.** At Alexandria the temples were destroyed, including the ancient and famous temple of Serapis, which, like a kind of column, supported the collapsing idolatry.

**IX–X.** Valentinian was killed at Vienne by his count Arbogast, in whose place Eugenius seized the tyranny.

**XI.** To avenge Valentinian’s death and crush the tyranny of Eugenius, Theodosius crossed into Italy, the elements conspiring toward the same end through the manifest favor of God.

After Eugenius had been defeated, Theodosius died in the eleventh year of his reign. [Note: The Victor manuscript reads, “he died on that day.”]

Arcadius and Honorius, thirty-two years.

[Col. 0860C] **I.** Constantinople, fearing the eminent wrath of God, terrifyingly manifested in a fire flashing above the clouds, turned with its whole heart to repentance and escaped.

Rufinus of Bosporus, having risen to the highest military rank and unable to endure Stilicho’s being preferred to him, was killed by Stilicho after the Huns, whose support he relied upon, had been defeated. [Note: We have restored the passage from the Victor and Joli manuscripts. Pithou previously read “after the support of the Huns had been overcome.”]

**II.** The poet Claudian was regarded as worthy of admiration.

[Note: [Col. 0860C] In Philippe Labbe’s manuscript library, the reading is not “Gildo the African,” but “Africa.”]

Gildo the African, after rebellion had broken out, withheld the customary Roman pay.

Our lyric poet Prudentius, a Spaniard by birth, of distinguished lineage, exercised the strength of his talent. [Note: The Joli manuscript reads, “a Spaniard by birth, illustrious in the strength of his talent,” and so does Labbe’s *Library*.]

[Col. 0861A] **III.** Stilicho, master of the soldiers, killed Gildo of Mauretania, and Africa was restored to its former status.

Innocent held the chair of the Roman Church as its thirty-seventh bishop.

**IV.** Throughout the Roman world, the temples of ancient superstition were destroyed.

Paulinus, later bishop of Nola, while the owner of countless estates, sold everything and chose religion in a state of freedom from worldly burdens, setting an admirable example.

**V.** John, bishop of Constantinople, became renowned in word and deed.

Martin, after living an outstanding life, departed from the body.

**VI.** The madman Pelagius attempted to defile the churches with his execrable doctrine.

**VII.** A dispute arising from Origen’s teaching stirred up a synod at Alexandria. Its decision was that anyone who approved the works of the aforementioned man should be excluded from the Church.

[Col. 0861B] **VIII.** An eclipse of the sun occurred.

Augustine discusses very many matters in countless books. [Note: Two manuscripts, Victor and Joli, read “innumerable books.”]

**IX.** Severus, following the discipline of Saint Martin, set forth his life in three books.

**X.** A savage storm of barbarian upheaval descended upon Italy. For Radagaisus, king of the Goths, crossed over intending to lay waste to the frontier of Italy. From this time the Arians, who had previously been driven far from the Roman world, began to be strengthened by the support of the barbarian nations to which they had fled. [Note: The word “previously” was absent from Pithou’s edition.]

**XI.** After many cities had first been devastated, Radagaisus perished. His army, divided among three commanders, opened some opportunity for resistance to the Romans. In a distinguished victory, Stilicho, with the auxiliary forces of the Huns brought around them, destroyed the army of the third division of the enemy to the point of annihilation.

**XII.** Arcadius, governing the Eastern Empire, completed his life and left as his successor to the empire his very young son Theodosius.

Coelestine governed the Roman Church as its thirty-eighth bishop.

[Col. 0861C] **XIII.** The fury of various peoples began to tear Gaul apart, chiefly through the instigation of Stilicho, who was indignant that the kingdom had been denied to his son.

**XIV.** At Utica, in Trajan’s forum, the earth bellowed for seven days.

Among other measures, the death of Stilicho benefited the commonwealth greatly, since he was plotting against the emperor’s safety.

Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, turned to the heresy that separates God in Christ from the human being.

John, count of Africa, was killed by the people.

**XV.** Proculus, bishop of Marseille, was regarded as distinguished. With his consent, a major inquiry was conducted into the suspected adultery of Bishop Remedius.

At this time, through the weakness of the Romans [Note: The manuscript reads “through the strength of the Romans.” Perhaps the intended reading is “through the illness”], the strength of Britain was utterly weakened.

**XVI.** The Vandals and Alans devastated the part of Gaul that had been laid waste by the Saxon invasion; what remained was held under siege by the tyrant Constantine.

[Col. 0861D] The Suebi occupied most of the Spanish provinces.

Finally, Rome itself, the head of the world, lay shamefully open to plunder by the Goths.

**XVII.** The tyrant Constantine was killed.

**XVIII.** Once again another plundering of Gaul occurred, when the Goths who had captured Rome under the leadership of Alaric crossed the Alps.

[Col. 0862A] **XIX.** After Constantine, Jovinus seized the tyranny through the energetic action of Dardanus, a vigorous man who alone did not submit to the tyrant. [Note: Labbe’s manuscript library immediately adds after this line: “Through the enterprise of that vigorous man, who alone did not yield to the tyrant, Dardanus; Atawulf, who afterward…”] [Note: Consult Philippe Labbe’s notes on Olympiodorus.]

Atawulf, who ruled the Goths after Alaric, was turned away from the alliance of Jovinus.

Sallustius and Sebastianus were also killed.

Valentia, the most noble city of Gaul, was stormed by the Goths; Jovinus had fled there and taken refuge.

**XX.** A great famine occurred in Gaul.

Aquitaine was handed over to the Goths.

Patroclus, bishop of Arles, dared to sell priestly offices by a disgraceful bargain.

Heraclianus, count of Africa, who had displayed energetic service in restoring the city of Rome, was killed after undertaking certain new schemes.

**XXI.** Placidia, the emperor’s sister, long held captive and afterward also the wife of the king, was joined in marriage to Constantius after the king had been removed through treachery. [Note: In Labbe’s *Library of Manuscripts*, here and in the following section, the reading is “Constantius.”]

**XXII.** When the Goths again took up arms after Atawulf had been killed, they were repelled by Constantius’s arrival.

[Col. 0862B] **XXIII.** The heresy of the Predestinarians, which is said to have received its beginning from Augustine, began to spread in these times. [Note: For these words Pithou had written “from Augustine’s books, wrongly understood.” See the preliminary admonition to this work.]

**XXIV.** Xystus, the thirty-ninth bishop, governed the Roman Church.

**XXV.** An eclipse of the sun occurred this year.

**XXVI.** Pharamund reigned in France.

**XXVII.** A remarkable sign appeared in the sky.

The tyrant Maximus obtained dominion over Spain by force.

**XXVIII.** Honoratus, Minervius, Castor, and Jovian flourished in Gaul as fathers of their respective monasteries.

**XXIX.** The dignity of the empire was voluntarily transferred from Honorius to Constantius. After enjoying it for scarcely eight months, Constantius died, leaving behind Valentinian, his eight-year-old son. [Note: Labbe writes in the margin, “not eight.”]

**XXX.** The tyrant Maximus was driven from the kingdom and brought to Ravenna, where he provided Honorius with the splendid spectacle of the thirtieth-anniversary celebrations.

**XXXI.** Placidia, when she was discovered to have been plotting against her brother, was banished from Rome into exile. [Note: Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts* reads, “from Rome into exile.”]

**XXXII.** Honorius died at Ravenna.

John, owing the throne to no legal right, seized it from the chief secretary of the notaries; he left the empire wounded by many disasters.

Theodosius, twenty-seven years.

**I.** Placidia sent to Theodosius to ask for assistance.

Sigisvultus hastened to Africa against Boniface.

**II.** In Gaul, the prefect Exuperantius was killed by the soldiers.

Carthage was surrounded by a wall. From the time when that ancient city had been destroyed, the Romans had not permitted it to be fortified with walls, lest it become a center of rebellion.

After John had been defeated and killed by the army of the East, Ravenna was devastated by plunder.

[Col. 0862D] Aetius, son of Count Gaudentius, who had been killed by the soldiers in Gaul, entered Italy with the Huns to bring aid to John.

**III.** Valentinian was made emperor at Rome.

**IV.** Arles was liberated from the Goths by Aetius.

**V.** Placidia at last entered upon the kingdom she desired.

Clodius reigned in France.

**VI.** Cassian set forth, in books issued to very many readers, the lives, teachings, and rules of the Fathers which he had discovered in Egypt. [Note: The Victor manuscript reads this way. Pithou’s edition instead has “the paths of the Fathers …”]

**VII.** Aetius sought to destroy the people of the Juthungi. [Note: The Victor manuscript reads “intended to destroy.”]

**VIII.** Nearly twenty thousand soldiers fighting against the Vandals in Spain were killed. The Vandals crossed over into Africa and, after the whole province had been torn apart, inflicted an immense disaster upon the Romans.

**IX.** After Aetius had been appointed consul, he withdrew from Boniface, who had been summoned from Africa by the queen, and went up to more strongly fortified positions. [Note: The Victor and Joli manuscripts read “Boniface” here and in other places. They likewise later read “he mounted.”]

The severity of excessive cold also proved fatal to the safety of very many.

After engaging Aetius in battle, Boniface was struck down; although victorious, he withdrew as a dying man. [Note: The Joli manuscript and Labbe’s *Library* read “wounded.”]

**X.** When Aetius had withdrawn to the people of the Huns, over whom Rugila then ruled, after the battle, he obtained assistance and returned to Roman territory. [Note: This is the reading of the Victor and Joli manuscripts. The printed editions read “he returned.”]

The Goths were summoned by the Romans to bring assistance.

Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, became renowned for his virtues and strictness of life.

**XI.** Aetius was restored to favor.

Rugila, king of the Huns, with whom peace had been established, died; Bleda succeeded him.

**XII.** Further Gaul, following Tibatto, the leader of the rebellion, withdrew from the Roman alliance. From this beginning, almost all the slaves of Gaul conspired in the Bagaudian movement.

**XIII.** A memorable war broke out against the Burgundian people, in which almost the entire nation, together with its king Peretius, was destroyed. [Note: Labbe’s manuscript library reads “by Aetius.”]

**XIV.** After Tibatto had been captured and the other leaders of the rebellion had been partly bound and partly killed, the uprising of the Bagaudae subsided.

**XV.** The Theodosian Code, containing in one collection all the laws of the legitimate emperors, was published for the first time this year.

Silvius, a man of greatly disturbed mind, after having served in the palace, wrote something concerning religion. [Note: The Joli manuscript reads, “after having completed his duties”; Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts* agrees.]

[Col. 0863C] **XVI.** Leo assumed the leadership of the Roman Church as its fortieth bishop.

**XVII.** After the disturbances in Gaul had been pacified, Aetius returned to Italy.

The abandoned fields of the city of Valence were given to the Alans, under the leadership of Sambida, to be divided among them.

**XVIII.** Britain, torn apart by various disasters and events up to this time, was brought under Saxon rule.

**XIX.** The Alans, to whom the patrician Aetius had entrusted the lands of further Gaul to be divided together with their inhabitants, subdued the inhabitants by force of arms, expelled the rightful owners, and took possession of the land by violence.

**XX.** Savoy was given to the remnants of the Burgundians to be divided with the native inhabitants.

**XXI.** Carthage was captured by the Vandals, and together with all Africa, through a disastrous calamity and a blow to the empire, it brought down Roman power. From that time it has been possessed by the Vandals.

[Col. 0863D] **XXII.** Thrace was shaken by an invasion of the Huns.

**XXIII.** Bleda, king of the Huns, was struck down through the treachery of his brother Attila. Attila himself succeeded him.

**XXIV.** A new ruin again arose in the East: no fewer than seventy cities were devastated by the plundering of the Huns, since no assistance was being provided by the Westerners.

**XXV.** Merovech reigned in France.

[Col. 0864A] Eudoxius, a physician by profession, of wicked but practiced intellect, having been accused at the time of the Bagaudian uprising, fled to the Huns.

**XXVI.** Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, and Hilary, bishop of Arles, completed their outstanding lives by death. [Note: The word “Hilary” is absent from Pithou’s edition.]

**XXVII.** A detestable heresy was stirred up by a certain archimandrite, whom Theodosius favored; Theodosius then died after completing twenty-seven years in the empire. Marcianus was substituted in his place.

Placidia also completed her life this year after an irreproachable way of life, while her son was completing his twenty-fifth year in the empire. [Note: The Joli manuscript reads “conversion.”] [Note: Pithou’s edition reads “in that very year.”]

Valentinian and Marcian.

**I.** At this time the condition of the commonwealth appeared exceedingly miserable, since not even one province was without a barbarian cultivator; and the unspeakable Arian heresy, which had mingled with the barbarian nations, presumed to usurp the name of the Catholic faith, which had spread throughout the whole world. [Note: The Joli manuscript reads, “spread throughout the whole world.” Labbe notes the same reading in the margin of the *Library of Manuscripts*.]

Attila entered Gaul and demanded a wife as though she were owed to him by right. After suffering and inflicting a severe defeat, he withdrew to his own territory.

**II.** Very many signs appeared this year.

After receiving the unexpected disaster in Gaul [Note: Pithou’s edition reads, “the unexpected disaster in Gaul”], Attila, driven mad, attacked Italy, whose inhabitants, terrified by fear alone, stripped it of its defenses.

**III.** The Council of Chalcedon was held. After Eutyches and Dioscorus had been condemned, all who had withdrawn from them were received into communion. The faith concerning the incarnation of the Word, which Saint Pope Leo had preached according to evangelical and apostolic teaching, was universally confirmed.

After Attila had died in his own quarters, a great struggle first arose among his sons over possession of the kingdom. Then defections followed among several peoples who had obeyed the Huns; these supplied causes and occasions for wars in which the fiercest peoples were worn down by mutual attacks.

[Col. 0864C] **IV.** After mutual oaths of pledged loyalty and an agreement concerning the union of their children, bitter enmity grew between Valentinian Augustus and the patrician Aetius. What should have increased the favor of affection instead kindled the fuel of hatred, through the instigation, as was believed, of Heraclius the eunuch, who had so bound the emperor’s mind to himself by sincere service that he could easily drive him toward whatever he wished.

When Aetius therefore pressed his requests more insistently and pursued the cause of their common son [Note: The Joli manuscript reads, “conducted the matter face to face.” Labbe, in the margin of the *Library of Manuscripts*, reads “face to face,” or alternatively “with greater agitation”], he was cruelly cut down by the emperor’s hand and by the swords of those standing around him. Boetius, prefect of the praetorium, who had been closely attached to him in great friendship, was killed at the same time. [Note: The Victor manuscript reads “had been joined to him.”]

**V.** Valentinian’s death followed not long afterward upon Aetius’s death. He failed to avoid it with such imprudence that he associated with himself the armed retainers and friends of Aetius, whom he had killed. Secretly watching for an opportunity to carry out the crime they had conceived, they stabbed the emperor with unexpected blows as he went outside the City, intent upon an exercise ride. Heraclius, who was close by, was killed at the same time, and no one among the imperial crowd was moved to avenge so great a crime.

Once this parricide had been committed, Maximus, a man of two consulships and patrician rank, assumed the empire. Although he was universally thought likely to benefit the endangered commonwealth, he soon demonstrated what sort of mind he possessed: he not only failed to punish Valentinian’s murderers [Note: The particle “not” is absent from Pithou’s edition, evidently through an obvious error], but even received them into his friendship. He also forbade Valentinian’s wife to mourn the loss of her Augustus-husband and compelled her, within a very few days, to enter his own marriage.

But he did not long enjoy this license. For after two months, when the arrival of King Genseric had been announced from Africa and many nobles and common people were fleeing the City, he too, having granted everyone permission to depart, wished to withdraw in panic. But he was torn apart by the queen’s servants and thrown limb by limb into the Tiber; he was denied even burial.

[Col. 0866A] After Maximus’s death came immediately the Roman captivity, deserving of many tears. [Note: The Victor manuscript and Pithou’s edition read “Roman captivity”; the Joli manuscript reads “the captivity of Rome.”] Genseric seized the City, which was entirely without defenses, while Saint Leo, its bishop, went out to meet him beyond the gates. His supplication, through God’s agency, so softened Genseric that, although everything had been placed in his power once the City was surrendered, he nevertheless refrained from fire, slaughter, and torture.

For fourteen days, therefore, Rome was emptied of all its wealth by a secure and unrestricted search; and many thousands of captives, according as each person’s age or skill pleased the captors, were carried away to Carthage with the queen and her daughters. [Note: These words, “according as each person’s age or skill pleased the captors,” are not found in the Victor manuscript.] [Note: The Victor manuscript reads “were carried away.”]

[Note: At the end of this work, the Joli manuscript adds the following in red letters, whether by the author himself or by a copyist:

“Thus far extends Prosper’s Chronicle. We have not noted the years of the Lord’s Incarnation because in the following Chronicle nearly the same events, and more besides, are related by the monk Sigebert under the years of the Lord, beginning with the year 381 of the Lord’s Incarnation, at which point Jerome the priest had brought his Chronicle to an end. In both manuscripts, the Joli and the Victor, the Chronicle of Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, follows.”]

[Col. 0865]

## LIST OF PRINTED AND MANUSCRIPT CODICES

According to which the works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine—both certain and doubtful, or hitherto attributed to him—were newly examined and corrected.

### Letter of Saint Prosper to Saint Augustine concerning the remnants of the Pelagian heresy arising in Gaul, and concerning the complaints of such people against the doctrine of predestination and grace, explained in Augustine’s works, especially in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*.

[Col. 0865B]

In this new edition it was examined and corrected against the following editions:

- **Lov.**, or **Lovan.**, that is, the Louvain edition of 1565, prepared by Joannes Sotellus of Louvain;
- **Duac.**, that is, the Douai edition, enlarged and corrected through the efforts of Joannes Olivarius in 1577;
- **Col.**, or **Colon.**, that is, the Cologne edition, reprinted at Cologne in 1630 after the model of the Douai edition.

We also consulted the Paris edition of the works of Saint Augustine, prepared by the Reverend Fathers, monks of the Order of Saint Benedict of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, from 1679 to 1690. There the same letter is presented both in volume II and in volume X.

Also two manuscripts from the library of the Most Christian King, and another manuscript from the Colbert Library.

### Saint Prosper’s Letter to Rufinus on Grace and Free Will

It was corrected against the **Ven.**, or **Venet.**, edition—that is, the edition printed at Venice in 1538—of several of Saint Prosper’s little works on grace and free will.

Also against the **Lugd.**, or **Lugdun.**, edition—that is, the Lyons edition, the oldest of all the complete editions of Prosper’s works, printed at Lyons in 1539 by the printer Sebastian Gryphius and under his supervision.

Also against the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, and against the latest edition of Saint Augustine’s works, in which this letter is found in the appendix to volume X.

Also against the **Remig.** manuscript, that is, the Remigian–Rheims manuscript, namely that of the abbey of Saint Remigius at Rheims, of the Order of Saint Benedict. From there one of the most pious and learned inhabitants of that monastery, out of his kindness toward us, sent us its variant readings.

[Col. 0865D] Also against the **Jol.**, or **Joliens.**, manuscript, that is, the manuscript which had formerly belonged to the most distinguished and learned Claudius Joli, precentor and canon of the metropolitan church of Paris; later, through his bequest, it became the property of the venerable chapter of that same church. Through the very faithful keeper of that library of the Paris church, we were granted the opportunity to read and collate it from beginning to end.

### Saint Prosper’s poem *Against the Ungrateful*, with its preface

It was corrected, insofar as possible, against the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions listed above, as well as the Lyons edition.

It was also collated with the edition in which the same poem appeared at Paris in 1646, translated into French both in verse and in prose.

Furthermore, it was collated with the version published at Louvain by Martin Steyaert, doctor of Louvain, with miscellaneous notes, in the third volume of his little works, published in 1703.

### Both epigrams against a detractor of Saint Augustine, and the epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies

These were reviewed against the same books as the aforementioned poem *Against the Ungrateful*.

### Saint Prosper’s replies on behalf of Augustine to the chapters of objections raised by the Gallic calumniators

[Col. 0866C]

In correcting these, besides the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, and the edition of the appendix to volume X of the works of Saint Augustine in the new edition, we consulted one Royal manuscript, the Joli manuscript, and the variant readings of the Remigian–Rheims manuscript.

### Saint Prosper’s replies on behalf of Augustine’s doctrine to the chapters of the Vincentian objections

We corrected this work according to the editions noted in the preceding entry, and also according to the Joli manuscript and the variant readings of the Remigian–Rheims manuscript.

### Replies on behalf of Augustine to the excerpts sent from the city of Genoa

We collated these with the Venetian edition of 1538 of certain little works of Saint Prosper; with the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions listed above; and with the readings of the Joli manuscript and the Remigian–Rheims manuscript.

### Authorities of bishops of the Apostolic See in former times concerning the grace of God and the free choice of the will

We reviewed these according to the aforementioned Venetian, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, and the Mainz edition of 1524.

[Col. 0867A] Also according to the appendix to volume X of the works of the same Saint Augustine in the new edition, and the latest edition of the works of Saint Leo, corrected and illustrated by Quesnel at Paris in 1675.

### *On the Grace of God and Free Will*, a book against the *Collator*

It was reviewed against the Mainz edition of this book from 1524, the Venetian edition from 1538, and the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions of Saint Prosper’s works.

Also against the edition of the same book in the appendix to volume X of Saint Augustine’s works.

The Joli manuscript, which we collated ourselves, and the variant readings of the Remigian–Rheims manuscript sent to us were also of assistance.

### Exposition of Psalms 100 through 150

[Col. 0867B] It was corrected, insofar as permitted, on the authority of the Lyons, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne codices.

Since we lacked manuscripts, we set forth several conjectures at particular passages, drawn from Saint Augustine’s work itself, which our author had before his eyes.

### One book of Sentences excerpted from the works of Saint Augustine

It was checked against the Cologne edition of 1531, the Lyons and Louvain editions, the Douai edition, and the Cologne edition of 1630. It was also checked against the same book as it appears in the appendix to volume X of Saint Augustine’s works in the new edition.

Nor did we omit the Joli manuscript and the variant readings of the Remigian–Rheims manuscript.

### One book of epigrams drawn from the Sentences of Saint Augustine

We collated it with the Venetian edition of 1538 of certain little works of Saint Prosper; with the Lyons and Louvain editions of all his works; with the Douai edition; and with the Cologne edition of 1630.

We likewise consulted one Regius manuscript; three Colbertine manuscripts: the Jolian manuscript and the Theodoricensian manuscript (so designated: *Theodor.* or *Theodoric.*), that is, of the monastery of Saint-Thierry near Reims, whose variant readings were sent to us through the kindness of one of that monastery’s monks; and the Douai edition of 1577, collated by the same monk.

## The Complete Chronicle of Saint Prosper, Divided into Two Parts

We edited it from volume I of the *New Library of Manuscripts* by Rev. Father Philippe Labbe, of the Society of Jesus. We collated it with the same work as found in volume VIII of the Lyon edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers* of 1677, and with the edition of the Chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper, corrected and supplied with notes in 1604 by the most illustrious Arnaldus Pontacus, bishop of Bazas.

We also collated it with five manuscripts of the Colbert Library. In two of them, Prosper’s genuine Chronicle is appended to the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, in the form in which we have published it in this work; in the other three, a spurious Chronicle is appended to the same works, which we present in the appendix under the title of the *Pseudo-Chronicle*.

## The Confession Called That of Prosper of Aquitaine

It was published from volume VIII of the Lyon *Library of the Holy Fathers*, and collated with the Jolian manuscript.

## The Poem of a Husband to His Wife

It was printed as it is read in the Venetian editions of certain little works of Saint Prosper of 1538, and in the Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, and was compared with those same manuscripts that contain the *Epigrams*, to which this poem had previously been everywhere appended.

## On Divine Providence, a Poem by an Uncertain Author

[Col. 0868B] Since the manuscripts were lacking, the Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions of 1630 provided assistance in correcting it.

## On the Calling of All Nations, Two Books by an Unknown Author

It was corrected with the aid of the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions of Prosper’s works, as well as the new edition of the works of Pope Leo, published under the care of Father Quesnel.

The Jolian manuscript was added; nor did we entirely disregard the variant readings which the Douai editors, and those who followed them, had placed in the margin, as had Quesnel in his edition of Leo, drawing on the Camberon and Thuane manuscripts.

## The Second Council of Orange, on Grace and Free Will

It was collated with the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions, and with the appendix to volume X of the new edition of Saint Augustine’s works.

## A Book by an Uncertain Author on the Promises and Predictions of God

[Col. 0868C] It was corrected according to the Lyon, Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions of Prosper’s works, with the addition of variant readings which a very religious man from the monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims most courteously sent us. He had excerpted them from a manuscript which, as he testified, was more than eight hundred years old, although it appears to have been written in the ninth century through the work of the monks Leutbert and Adelold.

## Another Chronicle, Also Called the *Pseudo-Chronicle*

It is presented as it appears in the Pithoean edition, volume VIII of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, 1677, and in Labbe, volume I of the *New Library of Manuscripts*, p. 56 and following.

Nor did we neglect to consult the Victorine manuscript, from which Pithoeus had drawn his text, and the Jolian manuscript.

# In the Year of Our Lord 460. Idatius [Note: [Col. 0869] Once the works of Saint Prosper had been completed, since only a few quires remained for the volume to be filled out, we wished to place Idatius and Marcellinus a few years ahead of their proper order, confidently hoping for pardon for this chronological offense because, from the little works of those Fathers, not only would this volume be brought to its proper size, but an appendix, so to speak, would also be added to Prosper’s Chronicle. Editor.] Bishop of Aquae Flaviae

*(From Galland’s* Maximus Library of the Ancient Fathers, *vol. X.)*

# Prolegomena

[Col. 0869A] We learn from the author himself [Note: [Col. 0869C] Idatius, preface to the Chronicle below.] that Idatius was born in the city of Lemica in the province of Gallaecia. Floresius [Note: [Col. 0869C] Floresius, *Sacred Spain*, vol. IV, p. 300.] places his birth about the year 388. He arranged the deeds of Idatius with considerable diligence in his learned work entitled *Sacred Spain*, issued at Madrid in four volumes in the years 1744–1749.

Idatius, having gone to the East while still a very young child, testifies that there, among other distinguished men, he saw the greatest teacher [Note: [Col. 0869C] Idatius, preface to the Chronicle below.] in the third year of the 216th Olympiad, A.D. 407. He undertook an embassy to the general Aetius on behalf of the Gallaecians when he was already a bishop [Note: [Col. 0869C] Idatius, *Chronicle* below.] in the third year of the 302nd Olympiad, A.D. 431; hence he must have been raised to this dignity around the year 427 or 428.

Idatius was indeed made chief bishop in the city of Lemica, as he himself seems to indicate in the preface [Note: [Col. 0869C] Idatius, cited passage below.]. But it does not therefore follow that he should be considered bishop of Lemica, as Sigebert of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0869C] Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 18.] and Trithemius [Note: [Col. 0869C] Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 140.] did, together with other more recent writers who followed both of them—namely Miraeus [Note: [Col. 0869C] Miraeus, *Supplement on Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 97.], Vossius [Note: [Col. 0869C] Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, book II, ch. 17, p. 230; on p. 225 he incorrectly says that the inscription reads “Idacius Lemovicensis.”], Pagius [Note: [Col. 0869C] Pagius, on the year 431, §61.], Ruinart [Note: [Col. 0869C] Ruinart, on Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, part II, ch. 2, p. 413, Paris edition, 1694.], Fabricius [Note: [Col. 0869C] Fabricius, *Ecclesiastical Library*, under “Booklet by an Uncertain Author,” p. 70, and *Medieval Latin Library*, vol. IV, p. 79, Hamburg edition.], and others.

For the author himself reports that in the second year of the 310th Olympiad, A.D. 462, he was captured by the Goths in the Church of Aquae Flaviae on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, and that, after completing three months of captivity, he returned to Flavia in November [Note: [Col. 0869C] Idatius, *Chronicle* below.]. From this it is rightly understood that Idatius was bishop of that same Church of Aquae Flaviae.

Cave [Note: [Col. 0869C] Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, p. 438.], Floresius [Note: [Col. 0870C] Floresius, cited work, p. 306.], and the most recent editors of the works of Saint Leo [Note: [Col. 0870C] Ballerini, vol. II, p. 1366, edition of Saint Leo’s works.] adopted this view. Accordingly, Basnage’s remark must plainly be rejected [Note: [Col. 0870C] Basnage, on Canisius’s *Thesaurus*, vol. II, p. 150, §4.], where he says that learned men doubt Idatius’s episcopate because he himself does not identify his see.

I would also have you add that Saint Leo remembered our bishop Idatius near the end of his letter to Turribius, bishop of Astorga [Note: [Col. 0870C] Leo, letter 15, vol. I, p. 711, Ballerini edition.]. From this learned men infer [Note: [Col. 0870C] Ballerini, on vol. I of the edition of Leo, p. 1475.] not only that Idatius was older than the bishop Turribius—for that reason he places himself before Turribius around the year 445 [Note: [Col. 0870C] Idatius, *Chronicle* below.]—but also that he was held in great esteem by Pope Leo himself, who evidently considered him worthy of contributing a more effective and useful service to the younger bishop Turribius, so that a synod might be convened in the province of Gallaecia against the Priscillianists.

These, then, are the principal events in the life of Idatius. In what year he subsequently died is by no means entirely established. The anonymous author of the booklet *On Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, which is usually appended to Isidore and Ildefonsus [Note: [Col. 0870C] Anonymous, *On Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 8, in Fabricius, *Ecclesiastical Library*, p. 69.], says: “He died under the emperor Leo, already almost at the end of an extremely advanced old age, as the indication in his own preface likewise shows.”

On this matter I would like to bring forward the opinion of Cangius, drawn from the *Idatian Fasti*. He writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0870C] Cangius, preface to the *Paschal Chronicle*, §40, p. 31.]:

> “These Fasti,” he says, “continue as far as the second consulship of Anthemius—that is, to the period in which Idatius lived, since he is said to have died under Leo the Great. The second consulship of Anthemius falls in the common reckoning of the Christian era in the year 468, and in that year, or certainly the following one, the Chronicle of Idatius also ends.”

Thus far Cangius, whom Floresius follows very closely [Note: [Col. 0870C] Floresius, cited work, p. 305.]. Pagius, however, from what Idatius writes [Note: [Col. 0870C] Idatius, *Chronicle* below.] about Aspar’s degradation and the killing of his son—events which occurred in the year 471—concludes that these matters were reported to the author in that very year, or perhaps later, and were then added by him to his Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0870C] Pagius, on the year 469, §5, and on the year 470, §2.]. He therefore concludes that Idatius lived on longer, contrary to the opinion of the others.

## II

As for the Chronicle of Idatius, the author had initially decided to compose it from the first year of Theodosius to the third year of Valentinian, the son of the empress Placidia, as we understand from the author himself [Note: [Col. 0870C] Idatius, preface to the Chronicle below.]. We learn either from Idatius himself [Note: [Col. 0870C] Idatius, *Chronicle* below.] or from the anonymous writer just mentioned [Note: [Col. 0870C] Anonymous, *On Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 8.] that he later extended it to the eighth year of the emperor Leo.

Nor should Sigebert be heeded when he records that our bishop extended this little work to A.D. 490 [Note: [Col. 0871D] Sigebert, *Chronicle*, on the year 490.], as Sirmond [Note: [Col. 0871D] Sirmond, preface to Idatius, in *Ancient Testimonies*.], Vossius [Note: [Col. 0871D] Vossius, cited work, p. 230.], and Pagius [Note: [Col. 0871D] Pagius, on the year 469, §6.] observed after him.

Sirmond explains the value of this Chronicle of Idatius as follows [Note: [Col. 0871D] Sirmond, cited work.]:

> “How valuable this little book deservedly is, you, reader, will immediately recognize. For you will understand that the material found in Isidore and other writers concerning the affairs of the Goths, Suevi, and other peoples who during that period acted in Spain and Gaul was drawn from this source, and is contained there in almost no words other than those of this Chronicle. Moreover, many additional matters, both sacred and civil, are taught here—matters which, since they remain untouched by all the other surviving writers, we too would be forced to ignore if Idatius had not disclosed them.”

In this respect Sirmond is rightly judged; but Pagius takes a different view of Idatius’s chronological computation [Note: [Col. 0871D] Pagius, on the year 463, §6.]. Cointius discusses the matter more fully [Note: [Col. 0871D] Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, on the year 468, §1, vol. I, p. 103.], and it will be useful to consult him.

## III

The consular Fasti follow the Chronicle. Sirmond writes of them [Note: [Col. 0871D] Sirmond, preface to Idatius.]:

> “We have already mentioned the Idatian consular Fasti which I appended to the Chronicle—not so much because they were appended to the same Chronicle in the Metz manuscript which we used in editing it, as because the affinity and relationship of subject and wording in the two works, together with their equal observance of epochs and periods, sufficiently show that they had the same author, even though the inscription contains no author’s name. It is there worded as follows: ‘List of the consuls from the time when they were first appointed.’
>
> “Although in our copy these Fasti continued to the second consulship of Anthemius—that is, to the period at which Idatius’s Chronicle ends—and, beginning with the earliest consuls, reckoned all the pairs of consuls from then to that year, we nevertheless thought it preferable for the present, until a different plan might be put forward, to publish only that portion which had been less corrupted by the antiquarians and which seemed likely to be more welcome and pleasing to readers because of the variety and usefulness of its memorable events.”

Thus far Sirmond.

## IV

“But as for the fact,” Labbeus adds [Note: [Col. 0871D] Labbe, *Syllabary of Writers*, vol. I of the *New Library of Manuscripts*, book, p. 2.], “that that great man refused to publish them until his death, I, pressed by the requests and almost the reproaches of many, undertook to make them public. I reproduced the complete Idatian Fasti, mutilated at head and foot, for readers from our manuscript, adding in the margin of each column the years from the foundation of the City according to Varro’s computation, and correcting many errors of antiquarians or copyists.

“I also added, in a different type from the rest, the two consuls sometimes omitted by those same antiquarians—more through their fault than through that of Idatius—because both the nature of the subject and the greater convenience of readers seemed to demand this.”

Thus far Labbe. Baunius, the editor of Sirmond’s works, adds [Note: [Col. 0871D] Baunius, preface to vol. II of Sirmond’s works, §2.]:

> “In order that these same Fasti might emerge from our hands somewhat more splendid, besides supplying what Labbe had omitted, and besides the corrections or variant readings he himself added, we likewise wrote in the margins of both columns many additional items of the same kind, collected from Cicero’s books and other monuments of antiquity. We also interwove several brief observations in which we noted certain errors in Idatius’s account—especially since others had already performed this task accurately, among them Emmanuel Schelestratius and Antonius Pagius, from whom learned dissertations on the entire subject have recently appeared.”

Thus far the distinguished Baunius. We have followed his Sirmondian edition of both Idatius’s Chronicle and Fasti, enlarged in several places by a few of our own observations at the edges of the pages.

## V

One point, however, must not be passed over here. Floresius, whom we mentioned above, does not acknowledge Idatius as the author of the Fasti [Note: [Col. 0872D] Floresius, cited work, p. 454.], contrary to the unanimous judgment of the learned men who followed Sirmond, among them the distinguished Cangius [Note: [Col. 0872D] Cangius, preface to the *Paschal Chronicle*, §40, p. 31.].

Cangius also collated these Fasti anew with the very manuscript used by Labbe, and corrected many things from it that had previously been copied with an unreliable or inaccurate hand. He published this restored edition of the Fasti among selected materials for the illustration of the *Paschal Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 0872D] Cangius, on the *Paschal Chronicle*, §12, pp. 344 ff.].

You will find some further corrections to the same Idatian Fasti in Dodwell [Note: [Col. 0872D] Dodwell, on the posthumous works of Pearson, in *Single Dissertation*, ch. 7, §10, pp. 101 ff.].

We should also mention that the celebrated Floresius published from a manuscript once owned by Juan de Mariana, collated with the Complutensian and Toletan manuscripts, the shorter Chronicle of Idatius, previously unpublished [Note: [Col. 0872D] Floresius, cited work, p. 403.].

## VI

At this point it will finally be worthwhile to bring forward Sirmond’s observation concerning the numerical signs affixed to the margins of the Chronicle and Fasti. He writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0872D] Sirmond, preface to Idatius.]:

> “In Idatius’s Chronicle, besides the Olympiads and the years of the individual emperors, which are arranged in order, two principal numbers are noted. One is larger, and its beginning is reckoned from Abraham, that is, from the beginning of Eusebius’s Chronicle. Since Idatius continued the Chronicle of Eusebius, it followed that he would also follow its chronological eras. This first number, therefore, is the Eusebian number.
>
> “The other is the Spanish Era, which he also added in the Fasti as customary and familiar to the Spaniards. This precedes the birth of Christ by only thirty-eight years, whereas the Eusebian number precedes it by 2,015 years. Therefore, if one wishes to determine the Christian year from the assigned Era, thirty-eight years must be subtracted from the Era.
>
> “For example, in the Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0872D] Idatius, *Chronicle* below.] and in the Fasti [Note: [Col. 0872D] Idatius, *Fasti* below.] he records that the barbarians entered Spain in Era 447. Subtract thirty-eight years; the remainder is 409. That, then, was the Christian year when the barbarians penetrated into Spain. The other chronological indicators recorded there together confirm this. The Olympiad is 297, the second consulship of Honorius VIII, and the third of Theodosius, and Tuesday, the fourth day before the Kalends of October: all coincide in the year 409.
>
> “Again, he reports in the Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0872D] Idatius, *Chronicle* below.] that certain prodigies were seen in Gallaecia on the sixth day before the Nones of March, and that it was a Friday, in Era 500. If thirty-eight are subtracted from five hundred, 462 remains. It was therefore the Christian year 462, to which both that weekday and the second year of the emperor Severus Augustus, who succeeded Majorian, also correspond.
>
> “In this way one may reason in all the other cases, unless the numbers have sometimes been displaced from their proper places through the fault of the antiquarians, eluding the industry and efforts of those who investigate them.”

Thus far he. As for the reckoning and origin of the Spanish Era, it is preferable to consult Juan de Mariana [Note: [Col. 0872D] Mariana, *History of the Affairs of Spain*, book III, ch. 23, vol. I, pp. 101 ff., The Hague edition, 1733.]. But enough of this.

[Col. 0873]

# Chronicle of Bishop Idatius (C, S)

## Preface

Idatius, servant of our Lord Jesus Christ, sends greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ to all the faithful and to those who serve him in truth.

[Col. 0873A] The endeavors of men approved above all others, whom the affirmation of divine worship teaches to be witnesses of the truth, especially in Catholic faith and perfect conduct, are adorned by the beauty of their words and commended by the honor of their merits; thus they attain remarkable steadfastness in all their work.

But Idatius, born in the province of Gallaecia in the city of Lemica, was created, more by divine gift than by his own merit, to the office of chief bishop. As remote in region as he was near the end of life, he had been formed by very little secular learning and was still less instructed by the salutary volume of sacred reading. In his earlier work he followed, according to the capacity of his own understanding or expression, the model displayed by the most learned holy Fathers.

The first of these was Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, who wrote ecclesiastical histories in books of his own arrangement. Beginning with the reign of Ninus, king of the Assyrians, and with the patriarch Abraham among the Hebrews, and covering the intervening years of the kings contemporary with them, he concluded the history of his Greek chronography in the twentieth year of Constantine Augustus.

After him, the accomplished successor in writing, Jerome the presbyter—himself called Eusebius, interpreter of this work from Greek into Latin—continued the history from the twentieth year of the aforementioned emperor to the fourteenth year of Valens Augustus.

Let it be that, while he lived in the holy places of Jerusalem, he added many things concerning events that followed, extending from the aforementioned year of Valens to the time during which he remained in the present life, since he never ceased, for as long as he was able, from the various labors of his pen. I am certain that I saw him, while still a very young child, during one of my own journeys in the regions mentioned above. After some years he remained blessed in body as he was.

Whether he later added anything to the work he appended is certainly and fully known to those to whom the whole or the greater part of his writings has come. But since it is clear that in one of his writings he said that, with the barbarians already raging through Roman territory, everything had become mixed and confused, we suppose from this statement that he himself added nothing to the following volume of years concerning the succession of times.

Nevertheless, since the account of the years, as the preceding reading shows, had flowed down to the course of our own time, when the care of this history fell to one inexperienced, the mind of the unskilled man admonished him to follow, concerning known matters, however unequal his progress in every respect, in the footsteps of his predecessors.

Receiving these matters with the faithful attention of our heart, we added what follows: partly from the study of written works, partly from the reliable report of certain persons, and partly from the knowledge which the already lamentable period of my own life has revealed.

You who read will distinguish the contents of these events and periods as follows. From the first year of Theodosius Augustus to the third year of Valentinian Augustus, son of the empress Placidia, what we have written derives either from the style of written authors or from reports of informants.

After that, having been undeservedly summoned to the office of bishop, and not ignorant of the miseries of that unhappy age, we set down the boundaries of the Roman Empire, closed in by straits and destined to collapse; and, more grievously still, within Gallaecia, the remotest region of the whole world, we recorded the disfigured condition of ecclesiastical order, the destruction of honorable liberty through indiscriminate appointments, and the almost complete decline of religion under divine discipline, amid the disorder of savage nations exercising dominion.

These matters have now been inserted; but we have left them for posterity to complete in the periods in which they shall have occurred.

# Chronicle

[Col. 0873]

## Roman Year 39: Theodosius

Theodosius, taken by Gratian into partnership in the rule, reigns with him and with the younger Valentinian for seventeen years.

### I

Theodosius, a Spaniard by birth, from the province of Gallaecia and the city of Cauca, is proclaimed Augustus by Gratian.

Many battles are fought between the Romans and the Goths.

### II

Theodosius enters Constantinople in his first consulship, which he held together with Gratian Augustus.

In Alexandria, Theophilus, a most learned and distinguished man, is the twenty-first bishop. Beginning with the first consulship of Theodosius Augustus, he composed a calendar arranged for one hundred years concerning the observance of Easter.

### III. Olympiad 290

Athanaric, king of the Goths, died at Constantinople on the fifteenth day after he had been received by Theodosius.

### IV. Spanish Era 490

The Goths submit to the Romans under an unreliable peace.

Ambrose, bishop at Milan in Italy, and Martin, bishop at Tours in Gaul, are regarded as distinguished both for the merits of their lives and for the miracles they performed.

### V

Theodosius proclaimed his son Arcadius Augustus and made him his partner in the kingdom.

### VI. Eusebian Year 2400

Honorius, son of Theodosius, is born.

Persian envoys come to Theodosius at Constantinople.

### VII. Olympiad 291
