The nation of the Greuthungi is defeated by Theodosius.

Priscillian, declining into the heresy of the Gnostics, is ordained bishop of Ávila by bishops whom he had gathered to himself in the same perversity. After being heard by several councils of bishops, he goes to Italy and Rome. There, not even being admitted to the sight of the holy bishops Damasus and Ambrose, he returns to Gaul with those who had gone with him.

There, likewise judged a heretic by Saint Martin the bishop and by other bishops, he appeals to the emperor, because in those days the tyrant Maximus held imperial power in Gaul.

### VIII

The quinquennial celebration of Arcadius is held.

Siricius is the thirty-sixth bishop of the Roman Church.

### IX

Priscillian, removed from the episcopate because of the heresy mentioned above, and with him the layman Latronianus and several of his followers, are put to death at Trier under the tyrant Maximus. From that time the heresy of the Priscillianists spread through Gallaecia.

### X

The tyrant Maximus is killed by Theodosius at the third milestone from Aquileia, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. At the same time, or in that same year, in Gaul, Maximus’s son Victor is killed by the count Arbogast [Manuscript: Arvagast].

Cynegius, prefect of Theodosius, is held in distinction. Endowed with notable achievements and advancing even as far as Egypt, he overturned the images of the nations.

### XI. Olympiad 292

Theodosius enters Rome with his son Honorius.

### XII

### XIII

### XIV

The younger Valentinian is murdered at Vienna through the crime of the count Arbogast [Manuscript: Arvagast], and Eugenius becomes tyrant.

### XV. Olympiad 293; Spanish Era 430

### XVI. Eusebian Year 2410

Eugenius is defeated and killed by Theodosius Augustus.

### XVII

Theodosius died at Milan from dropsy in the seventeenth year of his reign. This year, which is itself the seventeenth of Theodosius, is the first year of Arcadius and Honorius at the beginning of their reign. This is indicated so that the addition might not disturb the five-year Olympiad; it is inserted here only because it concerns the reigning emperors [Note: [Col. 0875D] Cangius, in the preface to the *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 29, §27, reads *principium*—“beginning”—from the manuscript, rather than *principum*—“of the emperors”—as it appears in the edition.]

[Col. 0876A]

## Roman Year 40: Arcadius and Honorius

Arcadius and Honorius, sons of Theodosius, reign for thirty years after their father’s death.

### I

### II. Olympiad 294

### III

[The thirty-seventh bishop of the Roman Church is Anastasius.]

### IV

### V

In the province of Carthage, in the city of Toledo, a synod of bishops is convened. In it, as the acts contain, Symphosius and Dictinius, together with other bishops of the province of Gallaecia, condemn the heresy of Priscillian and its blasphemous teaching, subscribing to the condemnation with the same profession of faith.

Certain matters are also established for observance concerning the discipline of the Church. The bishop Ortigius participates in the same council; he had been ordained at Celenis but, driven into exile by the factions of the Priscillianists because of the Catholic faith, was living in exile.

### VI. Olympiad 295

### VII

### VIII

An eclipse of the sun occurs on the third day before the Ides of November, on a Monday.

In the Roman Church, Innocent is recognized as the thirty-eighth bishop [Manuscript: thirty-seventh].

### IX. Eusebian Year 2420

Theodosius, son of Arcadius, is born.

### X. Olympiad 296

At Constantinople, John is proclaimed bishop, a distinguished man who suffers intense hostility from Eudoxia, the Arian wife of Arcadius, because of the Catholic faith.

### XI

### XII

At Jerusalem, John; at Caesarea, Eulogius; in Cyprus, Epiphanius; and in Alexandria, the aforementioned Theophilus are recognized as distinguished bishops.

Jerome, a presbyter residing at Bethlehem, near Judea, is regarded as preeminent in all things.

### XIII

After the Arians mentioned above, who had been bishops at Jerusalem before John, Idatius, who writes this, was unable to know who they were. He saw this holy man together with the saints Eulogius, Theophilus, and Jerome, both as a very young child and as an orphan.

### XIV. Olympiad 297

### XV

The Alans, Vandals, and Suevi entered Spain in Spanish Era 447. Some report that this occurred on the fourth day before the Kalends, others on the third day before the Ides of October, on a Tuesday, during the consulships of Honorius VIII and Theodosius, son of Arcadius, III.

Alaric, king of the Goths, entered Rome. While slaughter was being carried on inside and outside the city, everyone who fled to the thresholds of the saints was granted immunity.

Placidia, daughter of Theodosius and sister of the emperor Honorius, was captured by the Goths in the city.

Alaric died, and Ataulf succeeded him in the kingdom.

The barbarians who had entered Spain ravaged it with hostile slaughter. Pestilence did its work no less vigorously.

### XVI

While the barbarians raged throughout Spain and the evil of pestilence was likewise raging, a tyrannical tax collector plundered wealth and property stored in the cities, and the soldier drained them [Manuscript: “the soldiers”]. A dreadful famine spread, so that human beings, under the force of hunger, devoured human flesh; mothers too were nourished by the bodies of their children, whom they had killed or cooked themselves.

Wild beasts, accustomed to the corpses of those killed by the sword, hunger, or pestilence, attack the stronger among the human beings wherever they find them, feed on their flesh, and roam everywhere for the destruction of the human race.

And so, with the four scourges—the sword, famine, pestilence, and wild beasts—raging everywhere throughout the whole world, the announcements foretold by the Lord through his prophets are fulfilled.

### XVII

After the provinces of Spain had been overthrown by the ravaging of the scourges just mentioned, the barbarians, converted to the making of peace by the Lord’s mercy, divide the regions of the provinces among themselves by lot for habitation.

The Vandals and Suevi occupy Gallaecia, situated at the western extremity of the Ocean Sea. The Alans receive Lusitania and the provinces of Carthage, while the Vandals called Silingi receive Baetica.

The Spaniards who remain in the cities and fortresses after the scourges submit themselves to the slavery of the barbarians ruling through the provinces.

After three years of usurped tyranny, Constantine is killed within Gaul by the general Constantius acting for Honorius.

### XVIII. Olympiad 293

Jovinus and Sebastianus, brothers, within Gaul, and Heraclianus in Africa, are puffed up with the same madness of tyranny.

Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius, is regarded as distinguished. Among his magnificent labors, the well-attested testimony of the authors shows that the Donatists were defeated by him with God’s help.

### XIX. Eusebian Year 2430

Jovinus and Sebastianus, defeated by the generals of Honorius, are killed at Narbonne.

The Goths enter Narbonne during the vintage season.

Heraclianus, moving an army from Africa against Honorius, is defeated in battle at Utriculi in Italy and flees to Africa; fifty thousand armed men are killed at the place mentioned. He himself is later killed at Carthage in the Memorial Church, after Honorius sent men to strike him down.

### XX

Ataulf married Placidia at Narbonne. In this, people think that Daniel’s prophecy was fulfilled, in which he says that the daughter of the king of the South will be joined to the king of the North, though no offspring of his by her remained.

### XXI

At Jerusalem, while John, the bishop mentioned above, was presiding, Saint Stephen, the first martyr after the Lord Christ, was revealed.

Jerome, who was mentioned above as preeminent in all things, was also exceedingly skilled in the Hebrew language. Constantly meditating day and night on the law of the Lord, as it is written, he left innumerable works as the fruits of his labor.

Finally, with the adamantine hammer of truth, he crushed the sect of the Pelagians [Manuscript: Pelagian], together with its author. His most highly approved writings against them and against other heretics are extant.

### XXII. Olympiad 299

Ataulf, driven by the patrician Constantius to leave Narbonne and seek Spain, is murdered near Barcelona [Manuscript: Barcinona] by a Goth during familiar conversation among his companions.

Wallia succeeds him in the kingdom. Peace was soon made with the patrician Constantius, and Wallia opposed the Alans and the Vandals called Silingi, who were settled in Lusitania and Baetica.

While writing this, I did not know who presided over the Church of Alexandria after Theophilus.

Constantius took Placidia as his wife.

(Fredibal, king of the Vandal people, was captured by ingenuity without any battle and sent to the emperor Honorius.)

### XXIII

Wallia, king of the Goths, caused great slaughter of the barbarians within Spain for the sake of the Roman name.

### XXIV

An eclipse of the sun occurred on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, which was a Thursday.

Zosimus presides as the thirty-ninth bishop of the Roman Church [Manuscript: Eulalius].

During the episcopate of the bishop mentioned above, the holy places in Jerusalem and other places were shaken by an extremely severe earthquake, as the written acts of that same bishop make clear.

All the Vandals called Silingi were destroyed in Baetica by Wallia, king of the Goths.

The Alans, who had held dominion over the Vandals and Suevi, were so thoroughly slaughtered by the Goths that, after their king Ataces [Addaces] had been killed, the few survivors, abandoning the name of their kingdom, submitted themselves to the protection of Gunderic, king of the Vandals, who had settled in Gallaecia.

The Goths, interrupting the conflict in which they were engaged, were recalled by Constantius to Gaul and received settlements in Aquitaine, from Toulouse to the Ocean.

After Wallia, their king, died, Theodoric succeeded to the kingdom.

### XXV

A conflict arose between Gunderic, king of the Vandals, and Hermeric, king of the Suevi. The Suevi were blockaded by the Vandals in the Nervasian Mountains [Manuscript: Nerbasis].

Valentinian, son of Constantius and Placidia, is born.

In the Gallic region, in the city of Béziers, many terrifying signs occurred, as the letter of Paulinus, bishop of that city, sent everywhere, recounts.

### XXVI. Olympiad 300

The Vandals, abandoning the siege of the Suevi at the approach of Asterius, count of Spain, and under the deputy Maurocella, killed several men of Braga during their departure, left Gallaecia, and crossed into Baetica.

Boniface presides as the fortieth bishop of the Roman Church.

Honorius at Ravenna makes Constantius his partner in the kingdom.

### XXVII

Constantius, emperor at Ravenna, dies in his third consulship.

### XXVIII

Castinus, master of the soldiers, with a large force and Gothic auxiliaries, brings war against the Vandals in Baetica. When he had pressed them so severely by the force of the siege that they were already preparing to surrender, he imprudently engaged them in open battle and, deceived by the treachery of the auxiliaries, fled defeated toward Tarragona [Manuscript: Terracona].

Boniface, abandoning the palace, invades Africa.

### XXIX. Eusebian Year 2411

### XXX. Olympiad 301

Honorius died at Ravenna after completing his thirtieth-anniversary celebrations.

Paulinus, a man of the highest nobility and eloquence, made still nobler by his conversion to God, an apostolic man and bishop of Nola in Campania, is regarded as distinguished. Therasia, transformed from wife into sister, equals him in the testimony and merit of a blessed life. His outstanding works remain worthy of praise.

## Roman Year 41: Theodosius

Theodosius, son of Arcadius, who had reigned for several years in the eastern regions and whose father had died, holds the sole rule of the empire after the death of his uncle Honorius, at the age of twenty-six.

John seizes the tyranny.

### I

Theodosius makes Valentinian, the son of his paternal aunt Placidia, Caesar at Constantinople and sends him against John. Under him, John is killed at Ravenna in the first year after he seized the tyranny by the generals whom Theodosius had sent with Valentinian, and the patrician Felix is appointed from the mastership of the soldiers [Manuscript: “and master of the soldiers”].

Valentinian, who had been Caesar, is proclaimed Augustus at Rome.

The Vandals ravage the Balearic Islands. Then, after Carthage Spartaria and Hispalis had been overthrown and Spain had been ravaged, they invade Mauretania.

### II

Coelestine presides as the forty-first bishop of the Roman Church [Manuscript: fortieth].

### III
### IV. (Olympiad 302)

Gunderic, king of the Vandals, after capturing Seville, impiously exalted himself and stretched out his hands against the church [Col. 0879C] of that city. Immediately, by God’s judgment, he was seized by a demon and died. His brother Gaiseric succeeded him in the kingdom. According to the report of some, he became an apostate and is said to have passed from the Catholic faith into the impiety of Arianism.

### V.

Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, crossed from the coast of the province of Baetica to Mauretania and Africa in the month of May, together with all the Vandals and their families, after abandoning Spain. Before he crossed, he was informed that Hermigarius the Sueve was plundering the neighboring provinces along his route. Turning back with some of his men, he caught up with the plunderer in Lusitania. Not far from Mérida—which Hermigarius had insulted by scorning the holy martyr Eulalia, and where Gaiseric had slain many—he seized some of those who were with him and, taking what he thought was a swift means of escape in the form of a rushing current, was hurled into the river Anas by the arm of God and perished [Col. 0879D]. Once he had thus been destroyed, Gaiseric soon continued his voyage from the point at which he had begun.

### IV.

The Sueves under their king Hermeric, while plundering the central regions of Gallaecia, restore the peace they had broken by returning the families held captive, after the people who retained the safer hill-forts had inflicted slaughter on some of their men and taken others captive.

Through the count Aetius, not far from Arles, a band of Goths is destroyed, their chief Anaulf being captured. The Juthungi are likewise defeated by him, as are the Norici.

Felix, who was called Patricius, is killed at Ravenna in a military uprising.

[Col. 0880A] ### VII.

Aetius, commander of both armies, subdues the rebellious Norici. Again the Sueves disturb the peace they had made with the Gallaecians, having seized an opportunity for themselves. Because of their depredations, Bishop Idatius undertakes an embassy to the commander Aetius, who was conducting a campaign in Gaul. Vetto, who had deceitfully come from the Goths to Gallaecia, returns to the Goths without accomplishing anything.

### VIII. (Olympiad 303)

After Aetius has defeated the Franks in battle and received them into peace, Count Censorius is sent as envoy to the Sueves, with the aforementioned Idatius returning with him.

Boniface, summoned from Africa to Italy and to the palace by Placidia in rivalry with Aetius, returns. After expelling Aetius and succeeding him in his position, he enters into conflict with Aetius a few months later; he dies from the wound he received [Col. 0880B]. His son-in-law Sebastian is appointed in his place, but Aetius defeats him and drives him from the palace.

### IX. (Eusebius 450)

When Censorius has returned to the palace, Hermeric restores peace with the Gallaecians whom he had continually plundered, under episcopal mediation and after receiving hostages from them.

Bishop Symphosius, sent by him as an envoy to the imperial court, accomplishes nothing and is frustrated in the matters he had undertaken.

At a council held at Lugo, against the will of Agrestius, bishop of Lugo, Pastor and Syagrius are ordained bishops.

Aetius, commander of both armies, is called Patricius.

### X.

Sebastian, having become an exile and fugitive, sails to the palace in the East.

[Col. 0880C] Xystus is recorded as bishop of the Roman Church, the forty-second [Ms. forty-first].

### XI.

We have learned from the report of the priest Germanus, who came from the region of Arabia to Gallaecia, and from that of other Greeks, that Juvenal presides as bishop in Jerusalem. They add that he was summoned to Constantinople together with the bishops of the province of Palestine and of the East, and that, in the presence of the emperor Theodosius, he took part in a council convened to destroy the heresy of the Ebionites, which Nestorius [Ms., Atticus], bishop of that same city, was reviving through the perverse ingenuity of a most foolish sect.

But the report of those relating these matters did not state when the holy John, Jerome, and the others mentioned above died, or who succeeded John before Juvenal; nor did it identify the older man known to have done likewise in a brief account [Col. 0880D].

### XII. (Olympiad 304)

The Goths begin to besiege Narbonne.

The Burgundians who had rebelled are defeated by the Romans under the command of Aetius.

A letter from Cyril himself to Nestorius shows that at one and the same time Cyril presided as bishop in Alexandria and the heretical Ebionite Nestorius in Constantinople; the letter both destroys the heresy and sets forth the rule of faith. This, together with other material, is reported here.

### XIII.

The siege of Narbonne is lifted under the command and military leadership of Aetius. Twenty thousand Burgundians are slain.

[Col. 0881A] Again Censorius and Fretimund are sent as envoys to the Sueves.

### XIV.

Eight thousand Goths are slain under the command of Aetius.

The Sueves confirm the rights of peace with that part of the Gallaecian population against which they had been hostile.

King Hermeric, overcome by illness, appoints his son Rechila to the kingdom. Rechila defeated Andevotus and the force he possessed in open battle at the river Singilio in Baetica, seizing his great stores of gold and silver.

### XV.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, Carthage having been deceived by treachery, King Gaiseric invades all Africa.

In the Gothic war under King Theodoric, the Roman commander Litorius, acting too rashly with an auxiliary force of Huns, is defeated and slain; he himself is wounded, captured, and killed a few days later [Col. 0881B].

Peace is established between the Romans and the Goths.

Gaiseric, impiously exalted, expels the bishop and clergy of Carthage from the city and, in accordance with the prophecy of Daniel, changing the ministries of the holy ones, hands the Catholic churches over to the Arians [Ms., handed them over].

Rechila, king of the Sueves, enters Mérida.

### XVI. (Olympiad 305)

After plundering Sicily, Gaiseric besieges Palermo for a long time. At the instigation of Maximinus, the Arian leader in Sicily, who had been condemned by the Catholic bishops, he is driven against the Catholics, that he might compel them by whatever means into Arian impiety. Some gave way; others, persevering in the Catholic faith, attained martyrdom.

[Col. 0881C] Count Censorius, who had been sent as envoy to the Sueves, remaining at Myrtilis [Martyli], surrenders himself to Rechila when besieged, under the terms of peace.

### XVII.

Hermeric, king of the Sueves, afflicted by a long illness lasting seven years, dies.

King Rechila, having taken Seville, brings the provinces of Baetica and Carthaginensis under his power.

[Bishop Leo presides over the Roman Church, the forty-third.]

After Bishop Sabinus is expelled from Seville by a faction, Epiphanius is ordained in his place through fraud, not lawfully.

Asturius, commander of both armies, sent to Spain, slaughters a multitude of Bacaudae in the region of Tarragona.

### XVIII.

A comet begins to appear in the month of December. Seen for several months, it served as an omen announcing the plague that followed and was spread through almost the whole world [Col. 0881D].

After Nestorius is expelled, Flavian presides as bishop over the church of Constantinople.

### XIX. (Eusebius 460)

Asturius’s son-in-law Merobaudes, noble by birth and comparable to the ancients in eloquence, especially in the cultivation of poetry, is sent as his successor in the office of commander of both armies. He is also advanced by the testimony of statues. In the brief period of his authority he breaks the insolence of the Bacaudae of Aracellium. Soon, pressed by the hostility of certain people, he is recalled to the city of Rome by an imperial command.

### XX. (Olympiad 306)

Sebastian, having been discovered at the place to which he had fled plotting against him, flees from Constantinople after receiving a warning [Col. 0882A]. Coming to Theodoric, king of the Goths, he enters Barcelona as an enemy, having sought it for himself by whatever means he could.

### XXI.

In the city of Asturica in Gallaecia, certain Manichaeans who had remained hidden for some years are exposed through episcopal proceedings. These proceedings, conducted by Bishops Idatius and Turibius, who had heard them, are sent to Antoninus, bishop of Mérida.

Vandals, suddenly arriving by ship at Turonio on the coast of Gallaecia, seize the families of many people.

Sebastian, driven from Barcelona, goes over to the Vandals.

The proceedings against the Manichaeans are circulated through the provinces by the bishop then presiding at Rome.

### XXII.

Vitus, appointed commander of both armies, is sent to Spain. Supported by a considerable force, he harasses the Carthaginienses and the Baeticians. When the Sueves arrive there with their king, and after the Goths who had come to help him plunder them are defeated in an encounter, he is terrified by a pitiable fear and flees. Thereafter the Sueves devastate those provinces with great plundering.

### XXIII.

Leo presides as bishop of the Roman Church, the forty-third [Ms. forty-second]. His writings against the Priscillianists are carried to the Spanish bishops by Pervincus, the deacon of Bishop Turibius. Among them is a full treatise addressed to Bishop Turibius on the observance of the Catholic faith and on the blasphemies of the heresies; certain Gallaecians accept it with deceitful judgment.

[Col. 0882C] An eclipse of the sun occurs on the ninth day before the Kalends of January, which was a Tuesday.

### XXIV. (Olympiad 307)

Rechila, king of the Sueves, a pagan, dies at Mérida in the month of August. His Catholic son Rechiarius immediately succeeds him in the kingdom, although some of his own people secretly rival him. Once he has obtained the kingdom, he invades the farther regions without delay for the sake of plunder.

Antoninus, bishop of Mérida, captures a certain Pascentius, a citizen of Rome who had fled from Asturica and was a Manichaean, and, after examining him, also has him expelled from the province of Lusitania.

Censorius is put to death at Seville by Agiulfus.

### XXV.

Rechiarius, having taken the daughter of King Theodoric as his wife, inaugurates his reign by plundering the Vascones in the month of February [Col. 0882D].

Basil, in testimony to his outstanding boldness, gathers the Bacaudae in the church at Tyriasson and kills those allied with them. There Bishop Leo of that church also dies there from wounds inflicted by the same men who had been present with Basil.

In the month of July Rechiarius sets out to visit his father-in-law Theodoric. On his return, he plunders the region of Zaragoza together with Basil. The city of Lleida is entered by treachery, and a considerable number of people are taken captive.

### XXVI.

Asturius, an illustrious man, is advanced to the honor of the consulship.

Sebastian, having become an exile, flees to the power of Gaiseric, disastrous to himself, as later events showed [Col. 0883A]. A short time after his arrival, Gaiseric orders him to be killed.

Letters are brought from Gaul: those of Bishop Flavian sent to Bishop Leo, together with writings of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to Nestorius of Constantinople concerning Eutyches, the heretical Ebionite, and Bishop Leo’s replies to the same man. These are circulated through the churches together with the acts and writings of other bishops.

### XXVII.

The emperor Theodosius dies at Constantinople in the forty-eighth year of his age.

Immediately afterward, in Constantinople, Marcianus is made emperor by the soldiers and army, at the urging of Theodosius’s sister, Queen Pulcheria. He takes her as his wife and reigns in the East.

[Col. 0883B] ### XXVIII. (Olympiad 308)

Placidia, mother of the emperor Valentinian, dies at Rome.

In Gallaecia there are continual earthquakes, and many signs appear in the sky. For on the day before the Nones of April, a Tuesday, after sunset, the sky in the northern region becomes red like fire or blood. Brighter lines, formed amid the fiery redness in the shape of shining spears, disfigure it. From the close of day until nearly the third hour of the night, the appearance of the sign lasts; it is soon shown to have announced a great outcome.

The nation of the Huns, having broken the peace, plunders the provinces of Gaul. Many cities are breached. On the Catalaunian plains, not far from the city they had breached, they engage in open battle with the commander Aetius and King Theodoric, with whom they had been in alliance; they are defeated, by divine assistance, and slaughtered. Deep night brought the battle to an end. King Theodoric falls and dies there; it is reported that nearly three hundred thousand men perished in that battle.

Many signs occur during the year. On the fifth day before the Kalends of October, the moon is darkened in the eastern region. Certain phenomena seen in the sky over the regions of Gaul during the days following Easter are clearly described in a letter from Euphronius, bishop of Autun, to Count Agrippinus. A comet begins to appear on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. On the third day before the Kalends, it is seen at dawn in the east and soon afterward, after sunset, in the western region. On the Kalends of August it appears in the western region.

After Theodoric is killed, his son Thorismund succeeds him in the kingdom [Col. 0883D].

The Huns, with their king Attila, leave Gaul after the battle and make for Italy.

### XXIX. (Eusebius 461)

In the second year of the reign of the emperor Marcian, the Huns who were plundering Italy, after breaching several cities as well, are struck by divine means, partly by famine and partly by some disease sent through heavenly scourges. They are also defeated by auxiliaries sent by the emperor Marcian under the command of Aetius. Likewise, both in their own settlements and through heavenly scourges, they are subdued by Marcian’s army. Thus subjugated, they make peace with the Romans and all return to their own settlements; their king Attila soon returns there and dies.

Count Mansuetus of the Spanish provinces and Count Fronto are sent as envoys to the Sueves concerning peace, and they obtain the conditions imposed.

Thorismund, king of the Goths, harboring hostile intentions against the brothers Theodoric and Frederic, is killed by them. Theodoric succeeds him in the kingdom.

### XXX.

In the third year of the reign of the emperor Marcian, Queen Pulcheria dies in the month of July.

The Tarraconian Bacaudae are slaughtered by Frederic, brother of King Theodoric, by Roman authority.

In Gallaecia there is an earthquake, and a sign is seen in the sun at its rising, as though another sun were contending with it.

Aetius, commander and patrician, is deceitfully summoned alone into the palace and killed by the hand of the emperor Valentinian himself. Together with him, several distinguished men who had been admitted separately are slaughtered by the emperor’s sword-bearer [Col. 0884B].

After these events Valentinian sends envoys to the nations; Justinian comes from them to the Sueves.

### XXXI.

In the fourth year of the reign of the emperor Marcian, Valentinian, emperor at Rome, is killed in a field by two barbarians who had been retainers of Aetius, with the army surrounding him, in the thirty-sixth year of his age and the thirty-first of his reign. Immediately afterward Maximus, one of the former consuls, is proclaimed Augustus at Rome, the forty-third [consul]. After becoming emperor, he takes Valentinian’s widow as his wife and gives Valentinian’s daughter in marriage to his son Palladius, whom he had made Caesar. Distorted by the upheaval of the great disturbances he feared, and because he had contributed to the criminal plans carried out both in Valentinian’s killings and in Valentinian’s own death through his ambition for the throne, he wishes to abandon the empire and Rome. Yet, scarcely four months of his reign having been completed, he is killed in the city itself by a popular uprising and military sedition.

In the same year in Gaul, Avitus, a Gallic citizen, is first proclaimed Augustus at Toulouse and then at Arles by the Gallic army and distinguished men. He proceeds to Rome and is received.

The dynasty of Theodosius held the principate down to Valentinian.

Of the Romans, Marcianus, already in the fourth year of his reign, holds the imperial monarchy.

### I. (Olympiad 309)

Through Avitus, who had been both summoned and accepted as emperor by the Romans, envoys are sent to Marcian for the sake of unity in the empire.

[Col. 0884D] Gaiseric, incited by Valentinian’s widow, as malicious report spreads it, enters Rome before Avitus became Augustus. After plundering the wealth of the Romans, he returns to Carthage, taking with him Valentinian’s widow and two daughters, as well as Aetius’s son, named Gaudentius.

The Sueves plunder the Carthaginian regions they had returned to the Romans.

Marcian and Avitus rule the Roman empire in concord.

Through the emperor Avitus, Count Fronto is sent as envoy to the Sueves. Likewise, King Theodoric of the Goths, because he was loyal to the Roman empire, sends envoys to them, so that, since they were joined with the Roman empire by a single treaty of peace, they might keep the promises of their sworn alliance both with him and with the Roman empire. After the envoys of both sides have been sent back and every legal obligation violated, the Sueves invade the province of Tarragona, which served the Roman empire.

About four hundred lightly armed men of the Eruli, brought by seven ships to the coast of Lugo, are attacked by a gathered multitude. Only two of their number escape, after the others are killed. Returning to their own settlements, they plunder the coastal regions of Cantabria and Vardulia with extreme cruelty.

The envoys of the Goths again come to the Sueves. After their arrival, the Sueve king Rechiarius invades the regions of the province of Tarragona with a great multitude of his people, carrying out plunder there and leading a great number of captives into Gallaecia [Col. 0885B].

Soon the Gothic king Theodoric enters Spain with his enormous army, with the consent and under the arrangements of the emperor Avitus. King Rechiarius, meeting him with a multitude of Sueves, is defeated in battle twelve miles from Asturica, at a river called the Urbicus, on the third day before the Nones of October, a Friday. His forces are slaughtered, some are captured, and many are put to flight; he himself, wounded, scarcely escapes to the farthest regions of Gallaecia as a fugitive.

When King Theodoric with his army reached Bracara, the farthest city of Gallaecia, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, a Sunday, the plundering of that city, although bloodless, was nevertheless sufficiently sorrowful and tearful. A great multitude of Romans is led into captivity. The basilicas of the saints are breached; the altars are removed and shattered; the virgins of God are indeed led away, but their chastity is preserved; the clergy are stripped even to the point of nakedness; people of both sexes, together with children, are dragged from the holy places of refuge; the sacred place is filled with the horror of beasts of burden, sheep, and camels. This recalled, in part, the examples of heavenly wrath recorded concerning Jerusalem.

### II.

Rechiarius is brought as a fugitive and captive to King Theodoric at a place called Portucale. After he is placed under guard, the remaining Sueves who had survived the earlier battle surrender themselves. Nevertheless, some are killed, and the kingdom of the Sueves is destroyed and brought to an end.

In those same days it is reported to King Theodoric that, through the ambush of Count Rechimer, a great multitude of Vandals who had set out from Carthage with sixty ships for Gaul or Italy had been killed by Avitus [Col. 0885D].

The tribune Hesychius, sent as an envoy to Theodoric with imperial gifts, comes to Gallaecia and announces to him what has been stated above: that a multitude of Vandals was slaughtered in Corsica and that Avitus had succeeded in Italy, at Arles, as emperor of Gaul. He reports that Eastern ships arriving at Seville were destroyed by Marcian’s army.

After Rechiarius is killed in the month of December, King Theodoric succeeds from Gallaecia to Lusitania.

In a part of the district of Bracara, plundering is carried out by brigands.

[Col. 0886A] Aiulfus abandons the Goths and remains in Gallaecia.

The Sueves who remained in the farthest part of Gallaecia appoint Maldras, son of Massilia, as their king.

Theodoric, wishing to plunder Mérida, is terrified by manifestations associated with the blessed martyr Eulalia.

### III.

Avitus, in the third year after he had been made emperor by the Gauls and the Goths, loses the empire, deprived of the promised assistance of the Goths, and loses his life as well.

In the East, Marcian dies in the seventh year of his reign.

Of the Romans, Majorian is proclaimed Augustus in Italy and Leo at Constantinople.

### I.

Theodoric, terrified by adverse reports, leaves Mérida soon after Easter, which fell on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. Returning to Gaul, he sends part of the mixed multitude he possessed, together with its commanders, toward the plains of Gallaecia [Col. 0886B]. Equipped with deceit and perjury, as they had been ordered, they enter Asturica, which his own plunderers had already entered under the guise of Roman authority, pretending to the Sueves who had remained there that the expedition had been ordered for them. They enter under a counterfeit peace, following their customary art of treachery.

Without delay, a multitude of people of every kind found there is slaughtered. The holy churches are broken open; the altars are plundered and demolished; all sacred ornaments and furnishings are taken away. Two bishops found there, together with all the clergy, are led into captivity. A pitiable captivity is inflicted on the weaker people of both sexes. After the remaining empty houses of the city are set on fire, the countryside is devastated [Col. 0886C].

The city of Palencia perishes through a similar destruction at the hands of the Goths. The single fortress of Coviacum, thirty miles from Asturica, is exhausted by a long struggle with the Goths but, with God’s help, resists and prevails against the enemy. After many of their forces are killed, the rest return to Gaul.

Aiulfus, while aspiring to the kingdom of the Sueves, dies at Portucale in the month of June.

The Sueves, divided into factions, seek peace in Gallaecia. One faction calls Frantanes king, another calls Maldras king. Following their customary treachery, the faction of the Sueves that follows Maldras plunders Lusitania. After slaughtering Romans there and gathering booty, they enter the city of Lisbon under the guise of peace.

Frantanes dies between Easter and Pentecost. At the command of Maldras, the Sueves, reverting to their customary treachery, plunder the region of Gallaecia adjoining the river Douro. On the fifth day before the Ides of June, a Wednesday, from the fourth hour to the sixth, the sun appeared diminished in its light, taking on the appearance of a fifth- or sixth-day moon.

### II. (Olympiad 310)

The Gothic army, under its commander Cyrila, sent by King Theodoric to Spain, arrives in Baetica in the month of July. Envoys of the Goths and Vandals alike come to the Sueves and return.

### III.

Theodoric sends part of his army under his commander Suniericus to Baetica. Cyrila is recalled to Gaul. Nevertheless, some Sueves, together with Maldras, plunder parts of Lusitania, while others, together with Rechimundus, plunder Gallaecia [Col. 0887A].

The Eruli invade several coastal districts of the district of Lugo with extreme cruelty, proceeding toward Baetica.

Maldras kills his own brother and, as an enemy, invades the fortress of Portucale.

After several distinguished men by birth are killed among the Sueves and Gallaecians, hostile evil is stirred up between them.

Envoys sent by Nepotianus, commander of the army, and by the count Suniericus come to the Gallaecians, announcing that the emperor Majorian and King Theodoric had established the firmest terms of peace between them after the Goths had been defeated in a certain battle.

### IV. (Eusebius 480)

Maldras is deservedly killed by a violent death at the end of the month of February.

[Col. 0887B] During the days of Easter, several Romans living at Lugo, together with their distinguished governor, are suddenly killed by an attack of the Sueves, who show no reverence for the holy days.

In the month of May the emperor Majorian enters Spain. As he proceeds toward the province of Carthaginensis, the Vandals, warned by traitors, seize from the Carthaginian coast several ships he had prepared for the crossing against the Vandals. Thus frustrated in his arrangements, Majorian returns to Italy.

Part of the Gothic army, sent by the counts Suniericus and Nepotianus toward Gallaecia, plunders the Sueves at Lugo. This report is brought back to its own people by the informers Dictinius [Ms.: “plunders the Sueves living at Lugo; this report …”], Spinio [Col. 0887C], and Ascan, who spread the poisons of their own treachery to cause terror. Soon, under the impulse of the same informers mentioned above, Frumarius, with the Sueve force he possessed, captures Bishop Idatius on the seventh day before the Kalends of August in the church of Aquae Flaviae and brings great destruction upon the same district.

Rechimundus ravages the nearby territories of the Auregensians as well as the coastal districts of Lugo.

Dissension over royal power arises between Frumarius and Rechimundus.

A kind of shadow of peace is established between the Gallaecians and the Sueves.

Envoys from Theodoric come to the Sueves and return.

[Col. 0887D] Suniericus obtains the city of Scallabis, which had opposed him.

Idatius, mentioned above, after completing three months of captivity, returns to Flaviae in the month of November, by the merciful grace of God, contrary to the wish and arrangements of the informers mentioned above.

Envoys of the treacherous nation return from King Theodoric.

King Gaiseric asks the emperor Majorian for peace through envoys.

### V.

When Majorian was returning from Gaul to Rome and arranging what was necessary for the Roman empire and name, Rechimer, inflamed by envy and supported by the counsel of envious men, deceitfully surrounds and kills him.

[Col. 0888A] Of the Romans, Severus is proclaimed Augustus by the Senate at Rome in the fifth year of the reign of Leo.

### VI. I. (Olympiad 311)

Suniericus returns to Gaul. By arrangement of Theodoric, Nepotianus receives Arborius as his successor.

Various signs of prodigies are seen in the province of Gallaecia. In the year 500, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, at the crowing of the chickens, the full moon turns to blood from sunset. That day was also a Friday.

Antioch the Greater of Isauria [Perhaps: “the Greater of Syria”], disobedient to salutary warnings, is swallowed up when the earth opens. Only some inhabitants of the city, who had obeyed and followed the fear of the Lord, are saved from destruction; even the tops of the towers alone remain above the ground [Col. 0888B].

Gaiseric sends Valentinian’s widow back to Constantinople. One of her daughters is joined in lawful marriage to Gaiseric’s son Gento, the other to Olybrius, a senator of Rome.

Agrippinus, a Gaul, both count and citizen, hostile to Count Aegidius, an illustrious man, hands Narbonne over to Theodoric in order to obtain the assistance of the Goths.

Against Count Aegidius, commander of both armies, a man whom report commends as pleasing to God through good works, Fretiricus, brother of King Theodoric, rises in the province of Armorica. He is defeated and killed together with those who had been with him.

When Palegorius, a distinguished man of Gallaecia who had been an envoy to the aforementioned King Cyrila, comes to Gallaecia, he meets envoys of Rechimundus who were going to that same king [Col. 0888C]. After quickly returning, they receive Cyrila as he returns in the city of Lugo. Soon after he leaves Gallaecia, the Sueves, always false and treacherous in their promises, plunder various places in unhappy Gallaecia according to their customary practice.

Through Theodoric, Remismundus and Cyrila, together with some Goths who had previously come, are sent back to the Sueves. While Cyrila remains in Gallaecia, Remismundus soon returns to the king, and undisciplined disorder dominates between the Gallaecians and the Sueves.

Bishop Hilary presides over the Roman Church, the forty-fourth [Ms. forty-third].

### VII. II.

Nepotianus dies.

After Frumarius dies, Rechimundus recalls all the Sueves under his royal authority and restores the peace that had lapsed [Col. 0888D].

In the month of May, envoys of the aforementioned Aegidius cross the Ocean to the Vandals; they return to their own people by the same route in the month of September.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, a Monday, the sun is seen diminished in its light, taking on the appearance of a fifth-day moon, from the third hour until the sixth.

Remismundus sends envoys to Theodoric. Theodoric likewise sends his own to Remismundus, together with arms and gifts, and a wife for him to have.

The Vandals, defeated by Marcellinus, are driven from Sicily.

Aegidius dies; some say by ambush, others deceived by poison [Col. 0889A]. After his death, the Goths soon invade the regions he had defended for the Roman name.

The Sueves deceitfully enter Coimbra, strip the noble household of Cantabria, and lead away the mother with her children as captives.

In the same year, envoys are sent twice by the king of the Sueves to King Theodoric; Arborius also proceeds to him after being summoned.

### [VIII. III.]

The returning envoys of the Sueves report that Severus died in the fourth year of his reign. They are sent back to Coimbra.

Ajax, a Galatian by nation, having become an apostate and an Arian elder, emerges with the aid of his king among the Sueves as an enemy of the Catholic faith and of the divine Trinity. This poisonous venom of the hostile man is brought to the Gothic settlement in Gaul [Col. 0889B].

The Sueves rage against the people of Aunona. For this reason envoys are sent by Theodoric to Remismundus, but without effect; Remismundus rejects them, and they soon return.

From Constantinople, Anthemius, brother of Procopius, is sent by the emperor Leo to Italy by God’s providence, together with Marcellinus and other chosen counts, and with a vast multitude of a well-equipped army.

Of the Romans, Anthemius is proclaimed Augustus eight miles from Rome in the eighth year of the emperor Leo’s reign, in the month of August.

### IX. I.

The expedition organized against the Vandals in Africa is recalled because of the exchange of transport ships and the unfavorable conditions for sailing.

[Col. 0889C] Theodoric sends Salla as envoy to Remismundus, king of the Sueves. When Salla returns to Gaul, he finds that Theodoric has been killed by his brother Euricus [Ms. Euvericus].

Euricus succeeds to the kingdom with the same criminality as his brother. Advanced both by honor and by crime, he sends envoys to the king of the Sueves. Remismundus sends them back without delay, and envoys of that same king are sent: some to the emperor, others to the Vandals, and others to the Goths.

Opilio returns from the people of Aunona, against whom the Sueves had been hostile, together with the men who had set out with him from the king and with some others who had been sent with him.

The Goths who had been sent to the Vandals, terrified by the report of the aforementioned expedition, return quickly [Col. 0889D]. Likewise, the Sueves who, after the envoys’ departure, had been scattered in various places for plunder according to their custom are recalled. But a few months later the king of the Sueves himself crosses into Lusitania.

### II. (Olympiad 312)

Coimbra, deceived by an appearance of peace, is plundered. Houses are destroyed together with part of the walls; the inhabitants are captured and scattered; the region is laid waste and the city destroyed [Col. 0890A].

The envoys returning from the Goths report various portents seen in Gaul: in the presence … a second sun seemed to appear immediately beside the first … at sunset. On a certain day, when the Goths had gathered for one of their councils, the weapons they held in their hands changed and for some time did not possess the natural appearance of iron: in the portion of the iron or blade, some were green, some rose-colored, some saffron-colored, and others black. In the middle of the city of Toulouse, during those same days, blood is said to have burst from the earth and flowed throughout the entire day.

### III.

A Gothic force pursuing the return of the Sueve envoys proceeds toward Mérida.

Lisbon is occupied by the Sueves, after its own citizen Lusidius, who was in charge there, hands it over. When the Goths who had come learn of this, they invade and plunder the Sueves, and likewise the Romans serving them in the regions of Lusitania.

The envoys who had been sent to the emperor return, announcing that, in their presence, a very large army with three chosen commanders had marched out against the Vandals from the emperor Leo. Marcellinus had also been sent with a large force joined to him by the emperor Anthemius. Rechimer, the emperor Anthemius’s son-in-law, had been made patrician; Aspar had been degraded to private life, and his son killed, because they were found to be advising the Vandals against the Roman empire.

After Hilary’s death, when he had completed six years of his priesthood, Simplicius is ordained bishop of the Roman Church, the forty-fifth.

[Col. 0890C] The people of Aunona make peace with the king of the Sueves, who also invades and plunders certain places in Lusitania and in the district of Asturica.

The Goths rage with equal hostility around that same district and also plunder parts of Lusitania.

Lusidius is sent by Remismundus, together with his own men and Sueves, as an envoy to the emperor.

At this same time an extraordinarily harsh year of winter, spring, summer, and autumn is spread through the air, together with a change in all the fruits.

Several signs and prodigies are also clearly seen in the regions of Gallaecia. In the river Minho, about five miles from the municipality of Lais, four fish new in appearance and form are caught. Those who caught them, Christians and devout men, reported that they were marked with Hebrew and Greek letters, but with Latin numbers [Col. 0890D], and that they contained a cycle of 365 years, with an equal interval of months. Not far from the municipality mentioned above, something shaped like a lentil, full of grains of a very green color, like grass, and of great bitterness, flowed down from the sky. There were many other portents, the recounting of which would be lengthy.

[Col. 0891]
