# MARCELLINUS COMES, V. C.

*(From Gallandi’s* Bibliotheca Maxima Veterum Patrum, *vol. X.)*

[Col. 0913]

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0913D] **I.** Very little concerning the deeds of Marcellinus Comes, a man of illustrious rank, is readily available. The Anonymous of Melk records that he was Roman by nationality.[^c0090-1] From Cassiodorus we learn that he served as Comes of Illyricum and as chancellor to Justinian while the latter was still a patrician.[^c0090-2] At the beginning of the sixth century he became famous through various literary works, one of which Cassiodorus, among earlier writers, mentions in these words:[^c0090-3] “Marcellinus, composing four books on the character of times and the positions of places with exceptionally fine precision, traversed the course of his journey with distinction.” Elsewhere he says:[^c0090-4] “Marcellinus should be read with equal care: he described the city of Constantinople and the city of Jerusalem in an extremely detailed narrative.”

Yet both of these mentioned works of our Comes have either entirely perished or still lie hidden somewhere. Senator continues:[^c0090-5] “Eusebius wrote in Greek the *Chronicle*, which consists of brief images and very concise recollections of history; Jerome translated it into Latin and carried it down admirably to his own times. The aforementioned Marcellinus of Illyricum followed him. He is said still to have been serving as chancellor to the patrician Justinian; but, being devoted under more favorable circumstances, with the Lord’s help he carried his work from the time of the emperor Theodosius to the threshold of the empire of the triumphant Augustus Justinian—that is, from the first year of the elder Theodosius to Justinian’s fourth consulship, which is the eighth year of his reign, A.D. 434—completing, as he himself testifies in his preface, a period of 156 years.”[^c0090-6]

**II.** Marcellinus’s *Chronicle*, which appeared several times after the first edition by Antonius Schonhovius, canon of Bruges, was published in the most carefully corrected form of all at Paris by Sirmond in 1619. He says the following about it:[^c0090-7]

“You must be warned, reader, concerning the author of this *Chronicle*: the contents of it do not belong entirely to Marcellinus. For in his preface Marcellinus testifies that he carried his work from the beginning of the reign of Theodosius to the consulship of Magnus over 140 years; thereafter he added only another 16 years, from the first consulship of Justin to the fourth consulship of Justinian Augustus—that is, to A.D. 434. Marcellinus therefore did not proceed beyond that year, nor, indeed, was there anything more than this in the edition of Antonius Schonhovius, who first brought this *Chronicle* to light.

“What follows thereafter, down to the end of the reign of Justinian, was added later by someone else and was first published by Panvinio, and afterward by others, without distinction, as material belonging to Marcellinus. From the most ancient manuscript of the Tilius library, we are publishing both all of Marcellinus, much more accurately corrected than hitherto, and an appendix—which itself also belongs to a very ancient writer—in a substantially enlarged form. We would publish it complete if the mutilated copy had not failed us in the seventh year after the consulship of Basil. For this reason it was necessary, in the remaining portions down to the end, to follow the Panvinian edition, except for the calculations of years at the end. We judged these should be omitted because it was not clear that they belonged either to Marcellinus’s *Chronicle* or to its Appendix.”

Thus far Sirmond.

**III.** We think it worthwhile to add to what has just been reported what the editor of Sirmond’s works, Baunius, recorded in writing concerning the same work. He writes as follows:[^c0090-8]

“We compared Marcellinus Comes’s *Chronicle* once again with two manuscripts, one belonging to our Parisian college and the other to the Victorine library. From them we noted several variant readings, as well as some readings from the papers of the learned man Peter Francis Chifflet, who was exceptionally experienced in reviewing the writings of the ancients and had compared Sirmond’s edition of Marcellinus’s *Chronicle* with an old Bruges manuscript. Besides these and the other readings that we indicated in their proper places, further new readings of the same *Chronicle* subsequently appeared to us in Chifflet’s papers; we shall immediately provide a list of them.”

These later readings, which Baunius was unable to append to his Sirmondian edition because they were discovered too late, we have inserted in their respective places. Since the aforementioned Baunius also published longer observations on this same *Chronicle* in his preface, we have thought it more appropriate to present them here, arranged in a more suitable order. They are as follows:

**IV.** “That the year 381 is headed ‘the consulships of Eucherius [or Eucharius] and Evagrius’ is certainly erroneous; in place of Evagrius, Syagrius should be written. This is clear both from the *Fasti* of Hydatius and from other ancient writers. But because of the similarity of the writing, it happened that first in Socrates Εὐάγριος (*Euagrios*) was written in place of Συάγριος (*Syagrios*), and afterward in Marcellinus *Evagrio* in place of *Syagrio*, as the very learned Johannes Harduinus observed.”[^c0090-9]

“In the year 397, during the consulships of Caesarius and Atticus, where Flaccilla is said to have been born to Arcadius; and likewise in the year 431, during the consulships of Antiochus and Bassus, where Flaccilla is called the daughter of Theodosius Augustus, Petrus Lambecius maintains that *Placilla* should be written in both places.[^c0090-10] He likewise wishes the passages of Saint Ambrose, Claudian, Paul the Deacon, and Prosper to be corrected wherever, as he thinks, *Flaccilla* is named instead of *Placilla*. For he argues that the daughter of Theodosius was undoubtedly called Placilla, after the name of Placidia, or Placilla, daughter of Antonius and first wife of Theodosius; and that this name subsequently passed also to Arcadius’s daughter, Theodosius’s granddaughter.

“Socrates indeed calls the first wife of Theodosius Πλακίδην (*Plakidēn*), but the daughter of Theodosius and Galla Πλακιδίαν (*Plakidian*);[^c0090-11] and Sozomen calls the former Πλακίλλαν (*Plakillan*). Yet Henri Valois observes that Epiphanius Scholasticus calls her Flaccilla, and more correctly, since this is how she is named on ancient coins. He then adds:[^c0090-12] ‘But it is strange that the Greeks are almost always mistaken in this name. For above we observed that Socrates uses Πλάκιτον (*Plakiton*) for Flaccillus, who was bishop of Antioch.’

“Finally, Johannes Harduinus very appropriately remarks that, however the Greeks may have written the name, greater credence ought to be given concerning the name of the Latin empress to Ambrose and the other Latins, who call the elder Theodosius’s wife Flaccilla.”

“For the year 525, during the consulships of Philoxenus and Probus, where the text reads: ‘John, pope of the Roman Church, the fifty-first; in the year from Peter … 475,’ Chifflet places 485, though he cites no manuscript. Later Schelestratius, in the *Dissertations by Which the Antiquity of the Church Is Illustrated*, wrote the following for that year: ‘Peter entered upon the Roman pontificate, according to our chronology, in the twelfth year after Christ’s death. From that point to the aforesaid consulship there are 485 years; hence ten years are missing in Marcellinus—perhaps through the carelessness of scribes, who wrote 475 instead of 485.’

“Finally, for the year 547, after the sixth consulship of Basil, Chifflet observes that in the royal manuscript 1690 Marcellinus’s *Chronicle* ends there, specifically after the words ‘he received the command of the Praesental army.’ Peter Lambecius likewise attests this concerning an old imperial manuscript that once belonged to Matthias Corvinus, king of Hungary.[^c0090-13] In it, after the words just mentioned, the following is added in the manner of a heading: ‘Collection of all the years’; then below: ‘All the years of this *Chronicle* are collected down to the sixth consulship of Valens,’ and so forth.”

Thus far the distinguished Baunius, whose revised Sirmondian edition we have set in type. But enough on these matters.

[Col. 0917]

# THE CHRONICLE OF MARCELLINUS COMES, V. C. (C)

## Preface

[Col. 0917B] After the remarkable work in which Eusebius of Caesarea, from the creation of the world to the emperor Constantine, recorded in Greek the origin, times, years, kingdoms, and virtues of mortals, the inventors of various arts, and the monuments of almost all the provinces of this age, our Jerome translated the whole into Latin and extended it in Roman eloquence to the emperor Valens.

Accordingly, each author of this work calculated, with astonishing ingenuity, that this world would then have existed for 5,579 years. I, however, following only the Eastern empire by a simple calculation, counted 140 years through the indictions and consuls written below, beginning with the seventh indiction and the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius—under whose consulship Theodosius the Great was also made emperor—and gathering them up to the consulship of Magnus in the eleventh indiction. I appended these years to the work of the same authors. I then supplied another 16 years, from the first consulship of Justin Augustus to the fourth consulship of Justinian Augustus: that is, 156 years altogether, and I added my rustic work.

# THE CHRONICLE BEGINS

[Col. 0917]

**A.D. 379.** Indiction VII; the consulships of Ausonius and Olybrius.

[Col. 0917B]

Theodosius, a Spaniard from Italica, the city of the deified Trajan, was made emperor by Augustus Gratian at Sirmium, on the thirty-ninth day after the death of Valens, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. He was to govern only the Eastern state. He was a most religious man and promoter of the Catholic Church, and should be preferred to all the Eastern emperors—except that he had Marcian, the third emperor after him, as an imitator. He defeated the Alans, Huns, Goths, and Scythian peoples in great and numerous battles.

**A.D. 380.** Indiction VIII; the consulships of Gratian Augustus for the fifth time and Theodosius Augustus.

Gregory of Nazianzus, a most eloquent priest of Christ and the teacher of our Jerome, while our church at Byzantium was occupied by the Arians, daily kept the Catholic people steadfast through Catholic exhortation in the oratory of the blessed Anastasia. He was often attacked by the insults of wicked men; but, endowed with Christ’s grace, he resisted the perfidious Arians until the time when that same church was restored to our people by his presence.[Col. 0917D] For under these consuls, after Theodosius the Great had triumphed over the Scythian peoples, he immediately expelled the Arians from the church of the orthodox. They had held it for nearly forty years under Arian emperors. In December the orthodox emperor restored it to our Catholic people.

**A.D. 381.** Indiction IX; the consulships of Eucherius and Evagrius [perhaps Syagrius].

[Col. 0918C] With 150 holy Fathers assembled in the imperial city against Macedonius, who was shipwrecked concerning the Holy Spirit, the holy synod was confirmed by those same bishops: Damasus was occupying the see of blessed Peter; at Constantinople the proceedings were represented by Timothy of Alexandria, Meletius of Antioch, and Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem; Nectarius, immediately baptized from paganism, was ordained bishop in the aforesaid synod. Athanaric, king of the Goths, with whom the emperor Theodosius had made a treaty, came to Constantinople in January and died of illness in that same month.

**A.D. 382.** Indiction X; the consulships of Antonius and Syagrius.

The emperor Theodosius brought back from Italy the body [variant: upon the body] of the deified Valentinian the Great and placed it in a tomb at the imperial residence [variant: when it had been brought back]. In the same year, after their king Athanaric had died, the entire Gothic people surrendered themselves to the Roman empire in October. Damasus, the thirty-fifth bishop of the Roman Church—apart from Liberius and Felix—rested in the Lord in the eighteenth year of his pontificate.

**A.D. 383.** Indiction XI; the second consulship of Merobaudes and the consulship of Saturninus.

Siricius was made the thirty-sixth bishop of the Roman Church and lived fifteen years. Arcadius was crowned as co-ruler with his father, the emperor Theodosius, at the seventh milestone from the City. The emperor Gratian was killed through the treachery of the tyrant Maximus at Lugdunum on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

**A.D. 384.** Indiction XII; the consulships of Richomer and Clearchus.

Persian envoys arrived at Constantinople, requesting peace from the emperor Theodosius. At the same time, another son, Honorius, was born to Theodosius in September.

**A.D. 385.** Indiction XIII; the consulships of Arcadius and Bauto.

[Col. 0919B] The emperor Theodosius, through his envoys, subjected several Eastern peoples—[variant: savage peoples]—to his own empire, as was proper.

**A.D. 386.** Indiction XIV; the consulships of Honorius Caesar and Evodius.

The emperor Theodosius recovered Thrace, which had been invaded by enemies; victorious, he entered the City with his son Arcadius. Galla, the second wife of King Theodosius, came to Constantinople during these consulships.

**A.D. 387.** Indiction XV; the consulships of Valentinian III and Eutropius.

Caesar Arcadius celebrated his quinquennalia with his father Theodosius. Theodosius the Great advanced into Italy to fight the tyrant Maximus.

**A.D. 388.** Indiction I; the second consulship of Theodosius Augustus and the consulship of Cynegius.

Valentinian, the brother of Gratian, and the emperor Theodosius defeated the tyrant Maximus and his son Victor, who were rebelling at Aquileia. When the death of Maximus became known, the comes Andragathius threw himself headlong from a ship into the waves and drowned.

**A.D. 389.** Indiction II; the consulships of Timasius and Promotus.

The emperor Theodosius entered Rome with his son Honorius in June, granted a distribution to the Roman people, and left the City on the Kalends of September. During the same period, hail fell with a rattling sound instead of rain for two continuous days, destroying livestock and trees. A star rose in the north at cockcrow and appeared burning rather than shining, like Lucifer; on the twenty-third day [variant: the twentieth day] it ceased to be visible. The temple of Serapis at Alexandria was dismantled by decree of the emperor Theodosius.

**A.D. 390.** Indiction III; the fourth consulship of Valentinian Augustus and the consulship of Neoterius.

[Col. 0919D] A sign appeared in the sky, like a hanging and burning column, for thirty days. Galla, the wife of Theodosius, was expelled by her stepson Arcadius. An obelisk was erected in the circus; a column was set up not far from the church, bearing a silver statue of Theodosius the Great, which remains visible to this day.

**A.D. 391.** Indiction IV; the consulships of Tatian and Symmachus.

The emperor Theodosius, departing from Italy, returned to Constantinople. The emperor Valentinian was strangled through the treachery of Arbogast at Vienne and died on the Ides of March. Eugenius, relying on the support of Arbogast, usurped the empire for himself.

**A.D. 392.** Indiction V; the second consulship of Arcadius and the consulship of Rufinus.

[Col. 0920A] After the emperor Valentinian had been destroyed and Eugenius made Caesar, Arbogast gathered countless and unconquered forces from everywhere into Gaul, intending to claim the Western empire for himself. He was a barbarian excessive in spirit, judgment, strength, audacity, and power. He gathered countless forces from every quarter, relying in some places on Roman garrisons, in others on barbarian auxiliaries, here on authority and there on kinship.

Up to this nineteenth year of Theodosius’s reign, the blessed Jerome, beginning with the apostle Peter after the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ and ending with himself, described the ecclesiastical works of 135 illustrious men. He lived at Bethlehem, where he founded a monastery for himself and wrote many other works, having also been instructed in the Hebrew letters.[Col. 0920B] He brought his life to an end at a very advanced age and was buried there. To Catholics he was an impregnable tower of the Church; to all heretics, an indefatigable enemy, fighting both through the principles of his life and through the affirmations of the books he published.

**A.D. 393.** Indiction VI; the third consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of Abundantius.

Theodosius made Honorius Caesar in the same place where he had made his brother Arcadius Caesar, namely, at the seventh milestone from the imperial city. At that time darkness occurred at the third hour of the day.

**A.D. 394.** Indiction VII; the third consulship of Arcadius and the second consulship of Honorius.

Theodosius Augustus, taking Caesar Honorius, his son, with him, again hastened against Arbogast, who had dared to make the tyrant Eugenius emperor.[Col. 0920C] When battle was joined, Eugenius was defeated, captured, and killed; Arbogast struck himself with his own hand. Because an earthquake continued from September into November, several regions of Europe were shaken. The Baths of Arcadius received their name from their founder.

**A.D. 395.** Indiction VIII; the consulships of Olybrius and Probinus.

Theodosius the Great died at Milan. He had ruled for seventeen years. His body was brought to Constantinople and buried in the same year. The brothers Arcadius and Honorius began to hold the two empires, dividing them only by their seats of residence. The patrician Rufinus, plotting against the emperor Arcadius, secretly sent money to Alaric, king of the Goths, made him hostile to the state, and sent him into Greece. When his treachery was discovered, Rufinus was deservedly slaughtered before the city gates by Italian soldiers who had previously been sent to Arcadius with the comes Gainas [variant: *olim* is absent]. His head and right hand were displayed throughout Constantinople.

**A.D. 396.** Indiction IX; the fourth consulship of Arcadius and the third consulship of Honorius.

Rufinus’s wife and daughter went into exile. Eutropius, chamberlain of the sacred palace, seized all the wealth and exceeded the limits of avarice. An earthquake lasted for many days, and the sky seemed to burn.

**A.D. 397.** Indiction X; the consulships of Caesarius and Atticus.

Under these consuls, Flaccilla, a daughter of Arcadius, was born.

**A.D. 398.** Indiction XI; the fourth consulship of Honorius and the consulship of Eutychianus.

Anastasius was ordained the thirty-seventh bishop of the Roman Church and lived four years. Ambrose of Milan, a bishop of virtues, a fortress of faith, and a Catholic orator, departed to Christ the Lord.

John, born at Antioch and ordained a reader of the church there by Meletius, bishop and confessor of that city, advanced through each rank of ecclesiastical office. After serving continuously for five years as a deacon, he published many divine books; after becoming a presbyter, he composed still more over twelve years. Thereafter, having deservedly gained such a reputation everywhere, he was appointed bishop at Constantinople in place of Nectarius. There he added many sweet works on the divine Scriptures to his Catholic writings [variant: to his Catholic works]. He had as enemies these bishops: Theophilus of Alexandria, Epiphanius of Cyprus, Acacius of Beroea, Antiochus of Ptolemais,[Col. 0921B] Severianus of Gabala, and Severus of Chalcedon.

The comes Gildo, also a pagan, who governed Africa after the death of the emperor Theodosius, became jealous while Arcadius and Honorius were still ruling as boys and strove to seize Africa. His brother Mascezel, learning of his madness and leaving two sons in Africa, returned to Italy. Gildo treacherously killed both of his brother’s sons. When Mascezel learned of his brother’s crime, he advanced against Gildo, who confronted him with 70,000 armed men, with five thousand of his own. He drove out Gildo the parricide through his fasts and prayers, aided—or rather, through the dream-warning of the blessed Ambrose, aided [variant: *suis*, “his,” is absent]. Gildo, fleeing, strangled himself with his own hand. Thus Mascezel won victory without battle and vengeance without slaughter.

**A.D. 399.** Indiction XII; the consulships of Theodorus and Eutropius the eunuch.

[Col. 0921C] This Eutropius was the first and last of all eunuchs to be consul. Concerning him the poet Claudian wrote:

> All monsters yielded to a eunuch consul.

Pulcheria, another daughter, was born to Arcadius. The comes Gainas secretly urged his barbarians at Constantinople to prepare a civil war. Pretending illness, he himself left the city. When battle began against the Byzantines, many of the enemy fell; the rest, fleeing, entered our church. There, after the roof of the church had been uncovered and stones thrown down from above, they were buried beneath them [variant: “after the roof had been discovered”].

**A.D. 400.** Indiction XIII; the consulships of Stilicho and Aurelian.

[Col. 0921D] A naval battle was fought against the tyrant Gainas between the Chersonese and the Hellespont. Many thousands of Goths were killed or drowned. The comes Gainas escaped by fleeing from that battle; nevertheless, he was killed in the same year, in February [perhaps December].

**A.D. 401.** Indiction XIV; the consulships of Vincentius and Fravita [Chifflet: Fravitus].

The head of Gainas, fixed upon a spear, was brought to Constantinople. The surface of the Pontic Sea was so restrained by ice that, after thirty days, the ice finally broke up and flowed over the Propontis like mountains. Theodosius the Younger was born to his father Arcadius on the third day before the Ides of April [variant: the fourth day before the Ides].

**A.D. 402.** Indiction XV; the fifth consulship of Arcadius and the fifth consulship of Honorius.

[Col. 0922A] Innocent was made the thirty-eighth bishop of the Roman Church and lived fifteen years. Theodosius the Younger was made Caesar in the place where his father and paternal uncle had been made Caesars. There was a great earthquake at Constantinople.

**A.D. 403.** Indiction I; the consulships of Theodosius the Younger and Rumoridus.

Marina was born to Arcadius on the third day before the Ides of February. A silver statue of Eudoxia, the wife of Arcadius, erected on a porphyry column beside the church, still stands to this day.

They conspired against John, bishop of the city of Constantinople, against whom the six bishops mentioned above had been rivals in vain, and against thirty other bishops; against the will of the emperor Arcadius, they sent him into exile at Cucusus, a town of Armenia. After one year they banished him from exile into exile again, to a villa called Comana in the region of Pontus.[Col. 0922B] When he died there, the devout orthodox people, warned in a dream by the martyr himself, reburied him in a new tomb that had soon been found, in the atrium of the holy bishop Basiliscus, who was likewise a martyr.

**A.D. 404.** Indiction II; the consulships of Honorius VI and Aristaenetus.

The church of Constantinople, which had formerly been burned by a fire that had arisen from the throne of the blessed John, once a bishop, suddenly burned down; the fire also spread and consumed the neighboring façade of the city church. Eudoxia, the wife of Arcadius, died.

**A.D. 405.** Indiction III; the second consulship of Stilicho and the consulship of Anthemius.

The Isaurians, roaming through Mount Taurus, inflicted a great loss on the state,[Col. 0922C] and the envoy Narbazaicus immediately repaid them with a greater disaster.

**A.D. 406.** Indiction IV; the sixth consulship of Arcadius and the consulship of Probus.

Theodosius the Younger celebrated his quinquennalia. Radagaisus, a pagan and a Scythian, flooded all Italy with 200,000 of his people. Huldin and Sarus, kings of the Huns and Goths [Chifflet: Saurus], immediately defeated Radagaisus, cut off his head, and sold his captives for one gold coin each.

**A.D. 407.** Indiction V; the seventh consulship of Honorius and the second consulship of Theodosius the Younger.

A very large cistern was constructed beside the porphyry column of the emperor Constantine, in his forum, beneath the passage of the street.[Col. 0922D]

**A.D. 408.** Indiction VI; the consulships of Bassus and Philippus.

The comes Stilicho, whose two daughters, Maria and Thermantia, had each been wives of the emperor Honorius, though both died virgins, despised Honorius and longed for his kingdom. He incited the peoples of the Alans, Suebi, and Vandals against Honorius’s kingdom by enticing them with gifts and money. He wished to make his pagan son Eucherius Caesar, who was plotting against the Christians. When his treachery was discovered, Stilicho was killed together with that same Eucherius. At Rome, in the Forum of Peace, the earth gave forth a roar for seven days. The emperor Arcadius died; after the death of his father Theodosius, he had reigned thirteen years.

**A.D. 409.** Indiction VII; the eighth consulship of Honorius and the third consulship of Theodosius the Younger.

[Col. 0923A] A great popular revolt broke out at Constantinople, as a shortage of bread pressed upon the people.

**A.D. 410.** Indiction VIII; the sole consulship of Varanes.

Alaric invaded the trembling city of Rome and burned part of it in a fire. On the sixth day after entering it, he left the plundered city, carrying away Placidia, the sister of the emperor Honorius; afterward he gave her in marriage to his kinsman Ataulf.

**A.D. 411.** Indiction IX; the ninth consulship of Honorius and the fourth consulship of Theodosius the Younger [variant: Theodosius IV alone].

Theodosius the Younger celebrated his decennalia, and Honorius celebrated his vicennalia at Rome. Constantine invaded the empire in Gaul and made his son Caesar after taking him from a monastery.[Col. 0923B] Constantine himself was killed at the city of Arelate; his son Constans was beheaded at Vienne.

**A.D. 412.** Indiction X; the sole consulship of the emperor Theodosius V [variant: the ninth consulship of Honorius and the fifth consulship of Theodosius].

Jovinus and Sebastianus, attempting a tyranny in Gaul, were killed. Attalus was captured at sea, brought before Honorius, and left alive after his hand had been cut off.

**A.D. 413.** Indiction XI; the sole consulship of Lucius.

Heraclianus [Chifflet: Heraclius], comes of Africa, advanced toward the city with 700 ships and 3,000 soldiers. Soon he set out for the city of Rome, but was terrified by the approach of the comes Marinus and put to flight. Seizing a ship, he alone returned to Carthage, where he was immediately killed.

**A.D. 414.** Indiction XII; the consulships of Constantius and Constans.

[Col. 0923C] Pulcheria, the sister of Theodosius, was called Augusta. Valia, king of the Goths, having made peace with the emperor Honorius, returned his sister Placidia to him as a widow.

**A.D. 415.** Indiction XIII; the tenth consulship of Honorius and the sixth consulship of Theodosius.

The church of Constantinople, long before burned by fire, was restored and dedicated under these consuls, with the bishop Atticus governing that same church. The holy presbyter Lucian, to whom God revealed during these consulships the location of the tomb and relics of the body of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, wrote the revelation itself in Greek for the persons of all the churches.

**A.D. 416.** Indiction XIV; the seventh consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of Palladius.

[Col. 0923D] Orosius, a presbyter of Spanish origin, composed seven books of *Histories*. Sent by the bishop Augustine to the presbyter Jerome to learn about the nature of the soul, Orosius, on his return, was the first to bring to the West the relics of the blessed Stephen, which had then recently been discovered. Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, wrote to the empresses, the daughters of the emperor Arcadius, a highly distinguished book on Faith and Virginity, in which he anticipated and opposed the Nestorian doctrine.

**A.D. 417.** Indiction XV; the eleventh consulship of Honorius and the second consulship of Constantius.

Darkness occurred during the day. The city of Cybera in Asia, and several estates, were submerged by an earthquake. Zosimus was ordained the thirty-ninth bishop of the Roman Church and lived three years.

**A.D. 418.** Indiction I; the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth consulship of Theodosius.

The comes Plinta, likewise the author of the rebellion in the province of Palestine, was destroyed. An eclipse of the sun occurred. A star appeared rising and burning in the east for seven months.

**A.D. 419.** Indiction II; the consulships of Monaxius and Plinta.

Valentinian the Younger was born at Ravenna to his father Constantius and his mother Placidia on the fifth day before the Nones of July. Many cities and villages of Palestine collapsed in an earthquake. Our Lord Jesus Christ, ever present everywhere [variant: wholly present], manifested himself from a cloud above the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem.[Col. 0924B] Many peoples of the neighboring nations, of both sexes, terrified and convinced by what they saw and heard, were then washed in the sacred font of Christ. On the tunics of all who were baptized, the cross of Christ the Savior immediately shone forth, impressed by the will of the divine power.

**A.D. 420.** Indiction III; the ninth consulship of Theodosius and the third consulship of Constantius.

Boniface was ordained the fortieth bishop of the Roman Church and lived three years. In the East, the soldiers stirred up a revolt and killed their commander, Maximinus by name. Persecution raged against Christians in Persia.

**A.D. 421.** Indiction IV; the consulships of Eustathius and Agricola.

The emperor Theodosius took Eudoxia of Athens as his wife.[Col. 0924C] In the forum named after his father Arcadius, upon an enormous column, that same Theodosius dedicated a huge statue to him. The Baths of Aetius were constructed. The Romans fought with the Persians.

**A.D. 422.** Indiction V; the thirteenth consulship of Honorius and the tenth consulship of Theodosius.

The emperor Theodosius fathered a daughter, Eudoxia. At the thirtieth anniversary of Honorius’s reign, the tyrant Maximus and Jovinus, defeated by the sword, were brought from Spain and killed. The Huns devastated Thrace. The Persians made peace with the Romans.

**A.D. 423.** Indiction VI; the consulships of Asclepiodotus and Marinianus.

Coelestinus was made the forty-first bishop of the Roman Church[Col. 0924D] and lived nine years. Evagrius wrote the *Debate of the Jew Simon and the Christian Theophilus*, which is known to almost everyone. There was an earthquake in many places, followed by a scarcity of provisions. The philosophers Philippus and Sallustius died of illness. After a star had often appeared with a fiery tail, the emperor Honorius fulfilled his destined end.

**A.D. 424.** Indiction VII; the consulships of Victor and Castinus.

Placidia, the mother of Valentinian, was called Augusta. Valentinian was made Caesar, and Eudoxia, the daughter of the emperor Theodosius, was betrothed to him. After the death of Honorius, John seized the Western empire.

**A.D. 425.** Indiction VIII; the consulships of Theodosius XI and Valentinian Caesar.

The aforementioned John was killed through the treachery of Ardabur and Aspar rather than by force of arms.[Col. 0925A] Valentinian the Younger was made emperor at Ravenna.

**A.D. 426.** Indiction IX; the twelfth consulship of Theodosius and the second consulship of Valentinian.

Sisinnius, a man of holy simplicity and simple holiness, was made bishop of Constantinople.

**A.D. 427.** Indiction X; the consulships of Hierius and Ardabur.

The provinces of Pannonia, which had been held by the Huns for fifty years [Chifflet: sixty years], were recovered by the Romans. The Baths of Theodosius were dedicated.

**A.D. 428.** Indiction XI; the consulships of Felix and Taurus.

Nestorius, born at Antioch, a man possessing considerable eloquence but little wisdom, was ordained bishop from the presbyterate, with the Constantinopolitans exerting themselves vigorously on his behalf. The commemoration of the most blessed bishop John, who had earlier been exiled through the envy of evil bishops,[Col. 0925B] began to be celebrated at the imperial residence on September 26 [Chifflet: September 25].

**A.D. 429.** Indiction XII; the consulships of Florentinus and Dionysius.

Our orthodox people took possession of the church of the Macedonians, located outside the city walls, because those same Macedonians had killed Antoninus, Catholic bishop of Germis [or Germia]. The most blessed Augustine, the exceptionally eloquent priest of Christ of the Church of Hippo and a preeminent teacher, rested in peaceful death.

**A.D. 430.** Indiction XIII; the thirteenth consulship of Theodosius and the third consulship of Valentinian.

The emperor Theodosius celebrated his tricennalia. Felix was killed at Ravenna. Coelestinus, bishop of the Roman see, announced by letter to Nestorius, a bishop of depravity, after granting him a delay of ten days, either pardon if he repented or condemnation if he dissented.[Col. 0925C] That same Nestorius, the perfidious bishop of the Church of Constantinople, from whom the Nestorian perfidy also sprang, was condemned at Ephesus by the judgment of 200 holy Fathers in synod, with Coelestinus appointing Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, as his temporary representative. Maximian was substituted as bishop in place of Nestorius.

**A.D. 431.** Indiction XIV; the consulships of Antiochus and Bassus.

Flacilla, daughter of the emperor Theodosius Augustus, breathed her last. Barbarians raised in the imperial city flocked to our church with hostile intent. As they hurled fire into the church to burn the altar, they slaughtered one another, God resisting them.[Col. 0925D] At this time, while Theodosius was conducting a public procession to the state granaries because a shortage of grain had fallen upon the populace, the emperor was attacked with stones by the starving people.

**A.D. 432.** Indiction XV; the consulships of Valerius and Aetius.

Xystus was ordained the forty-second bishop of the Roman Church and lived eight years. At the instigation of Placidia, the mother of the emperor Valentinian, a great war was fought between the patricians Boniface and Aetius. Aetius, using a longer weapon that he had prepared for himself the day before, wounded Boniface when he engaged him, without himself being injured. In the third month Boniface died from the wound he had received, urging his very wealthy wife Pelagia to marry no one except Aetius.

**A.D. 433.** Indiction I; the fourteenth consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of Maximus.

[Col. 0926A] The greater northern part of the imperial city burned continuously for three days and collapsed in August.

**A.D. 434.** Indiction II; the consulships of Ariobindus and Aspar.

Honoria, the sister of the emperor Valentinian, was violated by her steward Eugenius and conceived. Expelled from the palace and sent from Italy to the emperor Theodosius, she incited Attila against the Western state [some manuscripts read *transmissa*, “sent”; for “she was plotting against the Western state” is erroneous].

**A.D. 435.** Indiction III; the fifteenth consulship of Theodosius and the fourth consulship of Valentinian.

The forum of the emperor Theodosius was built in the place called the Heliana. Sebastian, once the son-in-law of the patrician Boniface,[Col. 0926B] fled from the imperial city and was killed in Africa.

**A.D. 436.** Indiction IV; the consulships of Isidore and Senator.

The emperor Theodosius traveled by ship to the city of Cyzicus, showed great generosity toward that city, and sailed back to the imperial city.

**A.D. 437.** Indiction V; the second consulship of Aetius and the consulship of Sigisvultus.

The emperor Valentinian departed from Rome and arrived at Constantinople to marry Eudoxia, the daughter of the emperor Theodosius, to whom he had long been betrothed. After she married him, he spent the winter near Thessalonica while returning to Italy.

**A.D. 438.** Indiction VI; the sixteenth consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of Faustus.

[Col. 0926C] The pirate Cotradis [Chifflet: Contradis], together with his pirates and companions, was captured and killed. The relics of the most blessed John, once bishop of the imperial city, were returned to that same city and buried there on January 28. The emperor Valentinian entered Ravenna with his wife Eudoxia.

**A.D. 439.** Indiction VII; the seventeenth consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of Festus.
