[^c0090-2]: [Col. 0913D] Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Letters*, ch. 17.
[^c0090-3]: [Col. 0914D] Cassiodorus, ibid.
[^c0090-4]: [Col. 0915D] Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Letters*, ch. 25.
[^c0090-5]: [Col. 0915D] Cassiodorus, ibid., ch. 17.
[^c0090-6]: [Col. 0915D] Marcellinus, preface to the *Chronicle*, below.
[^c0090-7]: [Col. 0915D] Sirmond, preface to Marcellinus’s *Chronicle*.
[^c0090-8]: [Col. 0915D] Baunius, preface to vol. II of Sirmond’s *Works*, §3.
[^c0090-9]: [Col. 0916D] Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, V.8; Harduinus, notes on Themistius, Oration 16.
[^c0090-10]: [Col. 0916D] Lambecius, *Bibliotheca Caesarea*, II, p. 585.
[^c0090-11]: [Col. 0916D] Socrates, IV.31.
[^c0090-12]: [Col. 0916D] Valois, annotations on Socrates, IV.31.
[^c0090-13]: [Col. 0917A] Lambecius, *Bibliotheca Caesarea*, II, p. 874.

The emperor Theodosius celebrated his eighth quinquennial festival. Eudoxia, wife of the emperor Theodosius, returned from Jerusalem to the royal city, bringing with her the relics of the blessed Stephen, the first martyr, which are venerated after being placed in the basilica of Saint Laurence. At this time Genseric, king of the Vandals, occupied the cities of Africa and the metropolis Carthage with his satellites, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November [23 October].

(A.D. 440.) Indiction VIII, in the consulship of Valentinian V and Anatolius.

[Column 0926D]

Paulinus, master of the offices, was killed at Caesarea in Cappadocia at the command of the emperor Theodosius. Leo was made pope of the Roman Church, the forty-third; he lived twenty-one years.

(A.D. 441.) Indiction IX, Cyrus being sole consul.

The Persians, Saracens, Tzanni [another reading: Zanni], Isaurians, and Huns, having left their own territories, ravaged only those of the Romans. Anatolius and Aspar, masters of the soldiers, were sent against them and made a one-year peace with them. John, a Vandal by birth and also master of the soldiers, was killed in Thrace through the treachery of Arnegisclus [other readings: Arnitisclus; in Corb.: Argenislus]. The kings of the Huns invaded Illyricum with many thousands of their men; they destroyed Naissus, Singidunum, and many other cities and strongholds of Illyricum.

(A.D. 442.) Indiction X, in the consulship of Eudoxius and Dioscorus.

A star called “the long-haired one” appeared blazing for a very long time. Bleda and Attila, brothers and kings of many peoples, devastated Illyricum and Thrace.

(A.D. 443.) Indiction XI, in the consulship of Maximus II and Paterius [or Paternus].

During these consuls so much snow fell that it could scarcely melt for six months. Many thousands of human beings and animals perished, overcome by the severity of the cold. The emperor Theodosius returned to the city from his expedition in Asia. The inauguration of the baths called the Achillean Baths was celebrated.

(A.D. 444.) Indiction XII, in the consulship of Theodosius XVIII and Albertus.

[Column 0927B]

The emperor Theodosius celebrated his ninth quinquennial festival. Arcadia, the sister of Theodosius, died. Several towns and estates of Bithynia collapsed and perished because of the prolonged force of the rains and the flooding of swollen rivers. Saturninus, count of the household troops, sent by the emperor Theodosius, killed the presbyter Severus and the deacon John, who were serving Queen Eudoxia at the city of Aelia. Eudoxia, stirred by some unknown grief, immediately beheaded Saturninus; then, by the command of her husband the emperor, she was stripped of her royal attendants and remained at the city of Aelia to die.

(A.D. 445.) Indiction XIII, in the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nomo [or Nonnius].

[Column 0927C]

Bleda, king of the Huns, was killed through the plots of his brother Attila. At Byzantium, when a popular uprising arose in the circus, many people killed one another, and many bodies of men and animals perished from an internal [Chiffl.: external] disease.

(A.D. 446.) Indiction XIV, in the consulship of Aetius III and Symmachus [another reading: Valentinian VII and Aetius III].

During these consuls a great famine invaded Constantinople, and a pestilence immediately followed. The temple of the royal city was consumed by fire.

(A.D. 447.) Indiction XV, in the consulship of Ardabur and Callepius [another reading: Calippius].

[Column 0927D]

When a great earthquake threatened various places, most of the walls of the imperial city, recently rebuilt, collapsed together with fifty-seven towers. Huge stones that had long been set one upon another in a building in the Forum of Taurus also fell, as did many statues, evidently without injuring anyone. Nevertheless, many cities collapsed. Famine and the pestilential stench of the air destroyed many thousands of people and beasts of burden. Attila, king of the Huns, inflicted a huge war upon our people, greater than the previous one; by destroying and invading cities and fortresses, he ravaged almost the whole of Europe. In the same year, the walls of the imperial city that had formerly collapsed in the earthquake were rebuilt within three months, under the direction of Constantine, prefect of the praetorian guard. King Attila arrived as an enemy as far as Thermopylae. Arnegisclus [Chiffl.: Argenislus], master of the soldiers in Riparian Dacia, was killed near the river Utus by King Attila while fighting bravely and killing many of the enemy.

(A.D. 448.) Indiction I, in the consulship of Zeno and Postumianus.

The province of India sent the emperor Theodosius a tamed tiger as a gift. A sudden fire consumed both Trojan porticoes and both gate towers. Their ruins were immediately cleared, and Antiochus, prefect of the praetorian guard, restored them to their former appearance, while Attila’s envoys demanded from Theodosius the sums formerly rejected [another reading: agreed upon].

(A.D. 449.) Indiction II, in the consulship of Protogenes and Asturius.

Marina, sister of King Theodosius, fulfilled the debt of fate. Bishop Flavian was exiled to Epipus [Chiffl.: also] at the second synod at Ephesus, through the violence of Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, and the eunuch Saturninus. The patricians Areobindus and Taurus died in the same year.

(A.D. 450.) Indiction III, in the consulship of Valentinian VII and Abienus.

The emperor Theodosius died. After the death of his father Arcadius, he had reigned forty-two years. Marcian assumed the empire in his place. The eunuch Chrysaphius was killed, through the command of Pulcheria, the sister of Theodosius, together with his avarice.

(A.D. 451.) Indiction IV, in the consulship of the emperor Marcian Augustus and Adelphius.

While Leo was governing the see of blessed Peter, the holy and universal synod of six hundred and thirty Fathers was confirmed at Chalcedon, in the basilica of Saint Euphemia, against Eutyches, the most wicked leader of the monks. Only Dioscorus, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, dissented; he was immediately deposed from the priesthood by those same Catholic Fathers.

(A.D. 452.) Indiction V, in the consulship of Sporacius and Herculanus.

By his decrees, Augustus Marcian established that those who wished to become consuls should distribute no bronze money among the people, but should pay the prescribed sum for repairing the city’s aqueduct. At this time three great stones fell from heaven in Thrace. The city of Aquileia was destroyed by Attila, king of the Huns.

(A.D. 453.) Indiction VI, in the consulship of Vincomalus and Opilio.

John, the Lord’s forerunner and baptizer, revealed to two Eastern monks, who had entered Jerusalem to worship the resurrection of Christ the Lord, that his head—which the impious and wicked Herodias had once demanded to be cut from his shoulders and placed on a dish—had been buried far from his mutilated body. He revealed this so that, when they approached the dwelling of the former King Herod, they might be warned to search for it and faithfully raise it from the earth.

Accordingly, when this head had been found by faith and concealed in their hairy leather bag, as they were returning to their own dwellings, a potter from the city of Emesa, fleeing the long-standing poverty that threatened him, presented himself to them as a companion. While unknowingly carrying the bag entrusted to him, he was warned at night by the one whose head he was carrying. He abandoned both his companions in flight and immediately entered the city of Emesa with the holy and light burden. There, as long as he lived, he venerated the head of Christ’s forerunner; when he was dying, he entrusted it in a sealed vessel to his sister, who knew nothing of its contents, to be preserved [possibly: venerated]. She in turn left it to her successor, deposited and sealed as it was.

Afterward Eustochius, a certain secret presbyter of the Arian perfidy, unworthily obtained so great a treasure. The grace that Christ the Lord bestowed through John the Baptist upon the infirm people, he spread among the populace as though it were exclusively his own. Once his depravity had been exposed, he was expelled from the city of Emesa.

Later, certain monks began to use as their dwelling the cave in which the head of the blessed John had been placed in an urn and buried underground. At last the presbyter Marcellus, superior of the entire monastery, while living an irreproachable life in that same cave, saw the blessed John himself, Christ’s forerunner, appear to him and show him his own head; he made known that it had been buried there, shining forth with many miracles.

Thus this venerable head was found, under Uranius, the aforementioned bishop of the city, by the presbyter Marcellus, in the consulship of Vincomalus and Opilio, on 24 February, in the middle week of the paschal fasts, while the emperors Valentinian and Marcian were reigning. Pulcheria Augusta, wife of the emperor Marcian, completed the atrium of blessed Laurence with incomparable workmanship and died a blessed death.

(A.D. 454.) Indiction VII, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius.

Attila, king of the Huns and the despoiler of the provinces of Europe, was stabbed at night by a woman’s hand and a knife. Some, however, report that he died by vomiting blood. The patrician Aetius, the great salvation of the Western state and the terror of King Attila, was slaughtered by the emperor Valentinian in the palace together with his friend Boethius. With him the Western kingdom fell, and to this day it has not been able to recover.

(A.D. 455.) Indiction VIII, in the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius.

The emperor Valentinian, through the treachery of the patrician Maximus, by whose fraud Aetius had also perished, was beheaded in the Campus Martius by Optila [Chiffl.: Ostila] and Traustila, Aetius’s retainers, after the eunuch Heraclius had already been struck down. The same Maximus seized the empire; in the third month of his tyranny he was dragged through Rome by the Romans, torn apart limb from limb, and killed [another reading: torn apart]. Genseric, king of the Vandals, invited by letters from Eudoxia, the wife of Valentinian, entered Rome from Africa. After stripping that city of all its possessions, he took Eudoxia herself and her two daughters with him on his return.

(A.D. 456.) Indiction IX, in the consulship of Varanes and John.

During these consuls countless swarms of locusts devastated the fruit of Phrygia. Eucherius, bishop of the Church of Lyon, wrote much that was necessary both for ecclesiastical and monastic studies.

(A.D. 457.) Indiction X, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

The emperor Marcian, comparable to the good emperors, lost the breath of life. He had ruled six years and six months. Leo succeeded him after his death; by Leo’s will Majorian was appointed Caesar at Ravenna.

(A.D. 458.) Indiction XI, in the consulship of Leo Augustus and Majorian [another reading adds: Augustus].

The emperor Leo sent throughout the world to each orthodox bishop individual letters agreeing with one another concerning the Tome of Chalcedon, asking that each indicate in a written reply what he thought about that Tome. He received replies from all these bishops so concordant that one might have thought they had been dictated at the same time in the eloquence of a single man.

(A.D. 459.) Indiction XII, in the consulship of Patricius and Ricimer.

Isaac, a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, wrote much in the Syriac language, especially against the Nestorians and Eutychians. He lamented the destruction of Antioch in an elegiac poem, just as the deacon Ephraem lamented the fall of Nicomedia.

(A.D. 460.) Indiction XIII, in the consulship of Apollonius and Magnus.

The city of Cyzicus, shaken by an earthquake and its circuit of walls broken, lamented itself and its inhabitants for a long time.

(A.D. 461.) Indiction XIV, in the consulship of Dagalaiphus and Severinus.

Hilarus was made the forty-fourth pontiff of the Roman Church; he lived six years. Majorian Caesar was killed near Dertona, beside the river called the Hyra. Severus seized his position.

(A.D. 462.) Indiction XV, Leo Augustus II being sole consul [Cassiodorus and Severus Augustus].

[Column 0930C]

Jacobus, an Achaean by birth and a pagan in religion, was highly distinguished both in talent and in learning through his expertise in the medical art. Having been summoned to the sacred palace chamber to treat Leo Augustus, who was exhausted by fever, he entered and immediately sat down without any command from the Augustus on a chair placed beside the imperial bed; thus he applied his medical hands. At midday, when he returned to the same sacred couch, he immediately understood that the seat on which he had sat that morning had been removed on account of his position beside the throne. Without hesitation he sat on the royal side of the bed and explained to the sick emperor that, instructed by the precepts of the discoveries of his ancient study, he had acted in this way deliberately and not rashly.

(A.D. 463.) Indiction I, in the consulship of Vivianus and Felix.

Prosper, a man of Aquitanian origin, scholarly in language and forceful in argument, is said to have composed many works. The letters of Pope Leo against Eutyches concerning the true Incarnation of Christ are also believed to have been dictated by him.

(A.D. 464.) Indiction II, in the consulship of Rusticius and Olybrius.

Beorgor, king of the Alans, was killed by King Ricimer.

(A.D. 465.) Indiction III, in the consulship of Basiliscus and Herminericus.

Constantinople, seized by a great fire and disfigured in appearance, lamented itself. Severus, who had seized the principate of the West, died at Rome.

(A.D. 466.) Indiction IV, Leo Augustus III being sole consul.

Theodoret, bishop of the city of Cyrus, wrote concerning the Incarnation of the Lord against the presbyter Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, who deny that Christ possessed human flesh.

(A.D. 467.) Indiction V, in the consulship of Puseus and John.

The emperor Leo sent the patrician Anthemius to Rome and appointed him emperor. Simplicius was made the forty-fifth pontiff of the Roman Church; he lived fifteen years. An earthquake terrified the city of Ravenna.

(A.D. 468.) Indiction VI, Anthemius Augustus II being sole consul.

Marcellinus, patrician of the West and also a pagan, while bringing aid and assistance to the Romans fighting against the Vandals near Carthage, was treacherously stabbed by those for whom he had openly come to fight.

(A.D. 469.) Indiction VII, in the consulship of Zeno and Marcian.

[Column 0931B]

In these consulships the head of Denzic, son of Attila, king of the Huns, was brought to Constantinople.

(A.D. 470.) Indiction VIII, in the consulship of Jordanes and Severus.

Gennadius, pontiff of the Church of Constantinople, expounded the prophet Daniel completely and word for word, composed many homilies, and explained all the Epistles of Paul.

(A.D. 471.) Indiction IX, in the consulship of Leo Augustus IV and Probienus.

Aspar, the foremost of the patricians, perished after being wounded in the palace by the swords of eunuchs, together with his sons Ardabur and Patriciolus—the former once a patrician, the latter called Caesar and son-in-law of the emperor Leo. He was an Arian, as was his Arian offspring.

(A.D. 472.) Indiction X, in the consulship of Marcian and Festus.

[Column 0931C]

Mount Vesuvius in Campania, burning and seething with inward fires, vomited out its scorched entrails; while night-like darkness descended upon the day, it covered the entire face of Europe with fine ash. The Byzantines annually commemorate the memory of this terrifying ash on 8 November. The emperor Anthemius was killed at Rome by his son-in-law Ricimer. Olybrius was substituted in his place and died in the seventh month of his reign. In Asia several cities or towns collapsed in an earthquake.

(A.D. 473.) Indiction XI, Leo Augustus V being sole consul.

Glycerius was made Caesar at Ravenna more by presumption than by election. When an uprising arose in the circus at Constantinople, many Isaurians were killed by the people.

(A.D. 474.) Indiction XII, Leo the Younger being sole consul.

The elder emperor Leo died of illness after having already appointed Leo the Younger Caesar. Counting both the years of his own empire and the months of this Leo’s reign, he had ruled seventeen years and six months. Leo the Younger, himself both emperor and son, appointed Zeno as ruler of the kingdom. Glycerius, holding the imperial power at Rome as Caesar, was expelled from the empire by Nepos, son of the sister of the former patrician Marcellinus; he was ordained bishop at the port of Rome after becoming Caesar and died.

(A.D. 475.) Indiction XIII, Zeno Augustus II being sole consul.

The emperor Zeno, surrounded by the plots of his mother-in-law Verina and her brother Basiliscus, fled with his wife Ariadne toward Isauria. The tyrant Basiliscus seized the kingdom from Zeno. Nepos, who had driven Glycerius from the kingdom, was elevated as emperor at Rome. After immediately driving out Nepos, Orestes placed his own son Augustulus in the imperial office.

(A.D. 476.) Indiction XIV, in the consulship of Basiliscus and Armatus.

The tyrant Basiliscus made his son Marcus Caesar. While, swelling with Nestorian impiety [rather: Eutychian], he attempted to rise against the Catholic faith, he burst before he could stand repentant. Basiliscus, together with his son and his wife Zenonida, was sent into exile after Zeno had returned to the former empire; he was thrust into a little town called Lemini in the province of Cappadocia and wasted away from hunger.

Odoacer, king of the Goths, seized Rome. Odoacer immediately slaughtered Orestes. He condemned Augustulus, the son of Orestes, to exile in the fortress of Lucullanum in Campania. The Western empire of the Roman people, which Augustus Octavian first began to hold in the seven hundred and ninth year [Chiffl.: seven hundred and eighth] from the founding of the City, perished with this Augustulus, in the five hundred and twenty-second year reckoned from the reigns of the emperors who had preceded him, with Gothic kings thereafter holding Rome.

(A.D. 477.) Indiction XV, without consuls.

King Odoacer killed the count Bracila at Ravenna.

(A.D. 478.) Indiction I, Illus being sole consul.

[Column 0932C]

The presbyter Theodulus wrote much in Coelesyria and is held in high renown.

(A.D. 479.) Indiction II, Zeno Augustus III being consul.

Sabinianus was appointed commander of both Illyrian military forces. He sustained the fragile curia and the rightful revenues of the state, whether threatened beforehand or already collapsing, and protected them while they were failing. Moreover, he was such an excellent trainer and disciplinarian of military discipline that he is compared with the ancient Roman commanders. The same Sabinianus deterred Theodoric, who was raging through Greece, more by intelligence than by valor.

(A.D. 480.) Indiction III, Basil being sole consul [that is, Basil the Younger].

The royal city was shaken for forty continuous days by constant earthquakes; greatly afflicted, it lamented itself. Both Trojan porticoes collapsed; several churches were either split apart or fell. The statue of Theodosius the Great, placed in the Forum of Taurus upon a spiral column, fell when two of its arches collapsed. The Byzantines commemorate this terrifying day on 24 September. During these consulships, Nepos—whom Orestes had formerly deposed from the empire—was killed not far from Salona, in his own villa, by the plots of his counts Viator and Ovida [Chiffl.: Ovila].

(A.D. 481.) Indiction IV, Placidus being sole consul.

Theodoric, son of Triarius and king of the Goths, having gathered his men, arrived armed as far as Anaplus, at the fourth milestone from the City. Yet, harming none of the Romans, he immediately returned. As he hurried toward Illyricum, while moving among the wagons in motion, he died after being pierced and transfixed by the point of a weapon lying on a cart, driven there by the movement of his frightened horse. Death, which deservedly threatens this sinful world, took Sabinianus Magnus before he could become a complete support for the exhausted state.

(A.D. 482.) Indiction V, in the consulship of Trocondus and Severinus [that is, Severinus the Younger].

Felix was ordained the forty-sixth bishop of the Roman Church; he lived twelve years. Theodoric, surnamed Valamer, devastated both Macedonias and Thessaly and also plundered Larissa, the metropolis.

(A.D. 483.) Indiction VI, Faustus being sole consul.

[Column 0933B]

The same Theodoric, king of the Goths, having been nearly pacified by the benefactions of Zeno Augustus and made master of the present army, was also designated consul. With his satellites he held for the time being the portion of Riparian Dacia and Lower Moesia entrusted to him.

(A.D. 484.) Indiction VII, in the consulship of Theodoric and Venantius.

Illus, an Isaurian by birth and master of the offices in rank, having had part of his ear cut off at court, invaded the East as an enemy of Zeno. Later he seized the tyranny together with Leontius.

A cruel persecution by Huneric, king of the Vandals, was brought throughout Africa against our Catholics. More than three hundred and thirty-four [Chiffl.: three hundred and thirty-three] orthodox bishops were exiled and driven away, their churches were closed, and the faithful people, subjected to various tortures, completed a blessed contest.

At that time King Huneric ordered the tongue of a certain Catholic youth, who from his birth had lived without speaking a word, to be cut out. Though mute, having believed in Christ without human hearing and learned through faith, immediately after his tongue had been cut out he spoke and gave glory to God at the beginning of his speech. Finally, from this company of the faithful I myself saw at Byzantium several most devout men, with their tongues cut out and their hands severed, speaking with an unimpaired voice. This cruelty of the Arians began to be inflicted upon the devout worshipers of Christ in the February of the above-mentioned consulships.

(A.D. 485.) Indiction VIII, Symmachus being sole consul.

[Column 0933D]

Longinus, brother of Zeno Augustus, came to his brother at Constantinople after the ten-year confinement that Illus had inflicted upon him in Isauria.

(A.D. 486.) Indiction IX, Longinus being sole consul [another reading: in the consulship of Decius also].

John, formerly a grammarian and now a presbyter of the Antiochene district, wrote against those who assert that Christ is to be worshiped as possessing only one substance and who do not agree that two natures must be confessed in Christ.

(A.D. 487.) Indiction X, Boethius being sole consul.

King Theodoric of the Goths, never satisfied with the benefits of Zeno Augustus, advanced as an enemy with a great force of his people as far as the royal city and the town of Melentiada. After burning many places, he returned to Novae, a city of Moesia, from which he had come.

(A.D. 488.) Indiction XI, in the consulship of Dinamius and Siphidius.

Meanwhile King Leontius and the tyrant Illus were captured in the fortress of Papyrius in Isauria and beheaded. Their heads were brought to Constantinople, fixed upon poles, and left to decay. In the same year King Theodoric, gathering all his multitude of Goths, set out for Italy.

(A.D. 489.) Indiction XII, in the consulship of Eusebius and Probinus.

The same Theodoric, king of the Goths, seized the Italy he had desired. Odoacer, likewise king of the Goths, terrified by fear of Theodoric, entered Ravenna; afterward, having been lured by Theodoric through perjuries, he was killed.

(A.D. 490.) Indiction XIII, in the consulship of Longinus II and Faustus.

The emperor Zeno ordered Pelagius’s throat to be broken by a noose on the island called Panormus.

(A.D. 491.) Indiction XIV, Olybrius being sole consul.

Zeno Augustus died, counting both the years of his own empire and the months of the tyranny of Basiliscus: seventeen years and six months. Anastasius, formerly a silentiary, was made emperor. A plebeian war arose among the Byzantines, and a large part of the city and the circus was burned by fire.

(A.D. 492.) Indiction XV, in the consulship of Anastasius Augustus and Rufus.

While the Isaurian war was being prepared, and while the Isaurians were trying to claim the empire for themselves, they gathered from every side in Phrygia near the city of Cotiaeum. There Lilingis—slow on foot but extremely fierce as a cavalryman in war—was the first to be killed in battle by the Romans. All the Isaurians then gave themselves to flight and returned to Isauria through mountainous and rugged regions. This Isaurian war lasted six years.

(A.D. 493.) Indiction I, in the consulship of Eusebius II and Albinus.

Civil wars were waged against the reign of Anastasius at Constantinople. Statues of the king and queen were tied with ropes and dragged through the city. Julian, master of the soldiers, fighting in a nocturnal battle, was pierced by a Scythian weapon in Thrace and died.

(A.D. 494.) Indiction II, in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius.

[Column 0934D]

The emperor Anastasius began to stir up internal battles against the majesty of the orthodox faith. He first revealed the perfidy of his impious deed against Euphemius, bishop of the city, who was courageously resisting him on behalf of the orthodox faith, through a profane stratagem. Laodicea, Hierapolis, Tripolis, and Agathicum collapsed at the same time in a single earthquake. Gelasius was ordained the forty-seventh bishop of the Roman Church; he lived four years [Chiffl.: three].

(A.D. 495.) Indiction III, Viator being sole consul.

Euphemius, bishop of the imperial city, whom we mentioned above, was falsely accused and condemned by the emperor Anastasius and led into exile. Macedonius occupied the place of Euphemius.

(A.D. 496.) Indiction IV, Paulus being sole consul.

[Column 0935A]

After Anastasius had earlier granted his customary military payment to the soldiers, he also gave a donative in this year, when his brother was consul. India sent the emperor Anastasius an elephant, which our poet Plautus calls by the name “Lucabus” [that is, *Lucam bovem*, “the Lucan ox”], and two giraffes as a gift.

(A.D. 497.) Indiction V, Anastasius Augustus [another reading: II] being sole consul.

An eclipse of the sun appeared, and the Isaurian war was settled in its sixth year. Athenodorus, the first of the Isaurians, was captured and beheaded in Isauria. His head was brought to the city of Tarsus, fixed upon a pole before the gates, and left to decay.

(A.D. 498.) Indiction VI, in the consulship of John the Scythian and Paulinus.

Anastasius was ordained the forty-eighth pontiff of the Roman Church; he lived two years. Longinus the Isaurian, surnamed Selinunteus, was captured near Antioch in Isauria by the count Priscus, sent to Constantinople, and, bound in chains, paraded by an agent before the emperor Anastasius and the people as a great spectacle. He was afterward worn down by various tortures at Nicaea in Bithynia. By issuing coins stamped with his own name, which the Romans call Terentians [perhaps *Teruntii* or *Teruntiani*] and the Greeks *follares*, the emperor Anastasius introduced for the people a favorable [another reading: conciliatory] exchange.

(A.D. 499.) Indiction VII, John Gibbus being sole consul.

Aristus, commander of the Illyrian forces, set out against the Bulgars, who were devastating Thrace, with fifteen thousand armed men and five hundred and twenty wagons loaded with weapons necessary for battle. Battle was joined near the river Zurta, where more than four thousand of our men were killed, either in flight or by falling from the riverbank. There the military valor of Illyricum perished, as the counts Nicostratus, Innocentius, and Aquilinus were killed. In this year a great earthquake shook the province of Pontus.

(A.D. 500.) Indiction VIII, in the consulship of Patricius and Hypatius.

Symmachus was made the forty-ninth bishop of the Roman Church; he lived fifteen years. The emperor Anastasius sent a donative to the Illyrian soldiers, to be distributed by Paulus, tribune of the notaries.

(A.D. 501.) Indiction IX, in the consulship of Pompeius and Avienus.

While Constantius, prefect of the city, was watching theatrical games at midday, the faction of Cerealis prepared a hidden ambush for the opposing Blue faction [Sirm.: incorrectly, “the grain faction in a different way”]. They placed swords and stones enclosed in earthen vessels beneath the theater’s portico, in the manner of vendors, and piled various fruits over the weapons. While Constantius sat there and the customary voices of the citizens resounded, weapons were drawn out before they were seen or heard; stones were hurled like rain upon the unsuspecting citizens, and flashing swords, stained with the blood of friends and neighbors, raged together with their wielders.

The theater’s seating swayed and groaned; trampled under the feet of those fleeing this way and that, and stained with the blood of the slain, it lamented. The imperial city mourned the loss of more than three thousand citizens to stones, swords, crushings, and the waters before the stage.

(A.D. 502.) Indiction X, in the consulship of Probus and Avienus.

The Bulgars, a people accustomed to plundering Thrace repeatedly, devastated it again, with no Roman soldier resisting. Choades, king of the Persians, broke into Amida, a most wealthy city betrayed through the stratagem of its monks, in the fifth month after he had begun to besiege it, and beheaded the monks who had betrayed it.

(A.D. 503.) Indiction XI, in the consulship of Dexicrates and Volusianus.

Three Roman commanders—Patricius, Hypatius, and Areobindus—who had formerly been sent against the Persians with fifteen thousand armed men, engaged the same Persians near the fortress of Syficum without courage. Many military commanders were then killed while fleeing from the battle. Afterward, when an immense weight of gold had been given to the enemy, these same commanders bought back the city of Amida, which had been captured and stripped of its possessions; Celer, master of the offices, had already been sent to them in support with two thousand fighters.

(A.D. 504.) Indiction XII, Cethegus being sole consul.

Meanwhile Celer, master of the offices, led armed soldiers through Callinicum, a city of Mesopotamia, and ranged about to devastate the Persian countryside. He slaughtered many peasants engaged in rural labor like beasts; he carried away shepherds with numerous animals of various kinds; he attacked fortresses built of brick and mud; and, devastating everything, advanced as far as the bridge called the Iron Bridge. Having obtained all the booty, he returned to the common camp with his soldiers enriched. Thereafter he deliberated about striking a treaty with the Persians, sending for Armonius, a secretary, who had come to him to negotiate the treaty.

(A.D. 505.) Indiction XIII, in the consulship of Sabinianus and Theodorus.

The same Sabinianus, son of Sabinianus Magnus and commander of the army, was appointed to take up arms against Mundon the Getan. He advanced to fight, taking with him ten thousand armed men whom he had gathered and wagons loaded with weapons and provisions. When battle was joined at Horrea Margi [perhaps: the granaries of Margus], after losing many of his soldiers in the encounter and many more drowned in the river Margus, and after also losing the wagons, he fled with a few men into the fortress called Nato. So great was the army’s hope that fell in this lamentable war that it could in no way be restored among mortals.

(A.D. 506.) Indiction XIV, in the consulship of Areobindus and Messala.

During these consulships, a statue of the emperor Anastasius was erected upon an enormous column in the Forum of Taurus, in the same place where the statue of Theodosius the Great had formerly stood.

(A.D. 507.) Indiction XV, Anastasius Augustus III [Cassiodorus and Venantius] being consul.

A popular uprising took place in the circus; the soldiers, armed, resisted it. The steps of the northern circus, with their own structure, were set on fire and collapsed while Caesar Anastasius was staying in the processional avenues.

(A.D. 508.) Indiction I, in the consulship of Celer and Venantius.

Romanus, count of the household troops, and Rusticus, count of the scholae, set out with one hundred armed ships and an equal number of dromons, carrying eight thousand armed soldiers. They proceeded to devastate the shores of Italy and attacked as far as Tarentum, a very ancient city. Having crossed the sea again, they brought back to Caesar Anastasius a dishonorable victory, which Romans had seized from Romans by pirate audacity.

(A.D. 509.) Indiction II, Opportunus [or Importunus] being sole consul.

After a fire arose in the imperial city, it reduced both porticoes, from the Forum of Constantine as far as the very slender statue of Perdiccas, to ashes. The harbor of Julian, previously drained of its waters by wheel-machines and cleared by removing the mud, was cleaned.

(A.D. 510.) Indiction III, Boethius being sole consul.

A bronze image seated upon an arch in the Forum of Strategius and holding the horn of Fortune’s abundance was set ablaze by the fire and lost the arm that had been burned away; the sculptors immediately repaired it. The patrician Appius was exiled. Constantine, formerly master of the soldiers, was ordained bishop of Laodicea.

(A.D. 511.) Indiction IV, in the consulship of Secundinus and Felix.

Macedonius, bishop of the imperial city, although he had formerly been surrounded by the deceits and falsehoods of the emperor Anastasius and accused before that Caesar by the testimony of evil men, was sent by the same emperor into exile at Euchaita because he had delayed giving him the Tome of the holy Fathers, formerly ratified at Chalcedon by a holy subscription. Timothy, who had been ordained bishop by Caesar Anastasius at midday, seized the place of Macedonius.

(A.D. 512.) Indiction V, in the consulship of Paulus and Muscianus.

The sky was often seen to burn in the northern quarter. On Sunday, while Caesar Anastasius ordered, through Marinus and Plato standing in the church pulpit, that the fourfold Deipassian addition be made to the hymn of the Trinity, many orthodox believers, singing with the traditional voice and denouncing the impious heralds with shouts, were beaten within that same church and led away to prison, where they perished. On the following day, in the atrium of Saint Theodore [Chiffl.: Theodosius], Catholics were likewise struck down in an even greater slaughter for the sake of the one faith.

Therefore, on the next day, that is, 6 November—the day on which the Byzantines commemorate the memory of the ash that formerly covered all Europe—crowds of orthodox believers converged from every direction upon the Forum of Constantine. Some of them, while the rest sang the hymn of the Trinity to Christ God throughout the city day and night, killed with sword and fire those who flattered Caesar Anastasius in monastic dress. Others carried the keys of the gates and all the military standards to the forum where they had established their religious camp. There, while Caesar Anastasius was present in the processional avenues, they loudly demanded that Areobindus be made emperor.

After throwing the images and statues of Anastasius to the ground, they drove back the senators Celer and Patricius, who had been sent to them to ask for mercy or to give satisfaction, by hurling stones like rain. After burning the houses of Marinus and Pompeius, they came to Anastasius in the circus and stood before his throne, singing the hymn of the Trinity according to Catholic custom and carrying the shining Gospel and the cross of Christ. Many came from the forum, shouting that Marinus and Plato, the authors of his depravity, should be handed over to the wild beasts.

Caesar Anastasius, by his customary perjuries and feigned words, promised that he would do everything and, on the third day after they had come to the forum, made them return to their homes without accomplishing anything.

Then Anastasius, having renewed his depravity, ordered an infamous and laughable synod to be held in the city of Sidon—whose name is prefixed to names in jest—with nearly eighty perfidious bishops assembled against the orthodox bishop [another reading: bishops]. Flavian, the Catholic patriarch of Antioch, and John, bishop of the town of Paltus, were sent into exile in the fortress called Petra because they had opposed this sacrilegious assembly.

There Flavian, the confessor of Christ, rested in the Lord. Justin Augustus, soon after becoming emperor, recalled John. At approximately the same time an eclipse of the sun occurred. At the command of Caesar Anastasius, the people of the Heruli were brought into the lands and cities of the Romans.

(A.D. 513.) Indiction VI, in the consulship of Clementinus and Probus.

Severus, a devotee of Eutyches’ perfidy, at the wish of the emperor Anastasius, occupied the see of Bishop Flavian, having been made a bishop from a monk. Dorotheus, the venerable bishop of the city of Ancyra, who was continually opposed to Emperor Anastasius on account of the one orthodox faith, met the end of life which he himself had foretold would come to him at the hands of the imperial officer sent against him by Caesar, at the very time he had predicted. [Col. 0938C]

**A.D. 514. Indiction VII, Senator being sole consul.**

Vitalian the Scythian, having gathered in three days more than sixty thousand armed Roman cavalry and infantry, arrived at a place called Septimius and there pitched camp. Having drawn up his forces in ranks from sea to sea, he himself advanced as far as the gate called the Golden Gate without suffering any loss, declaring that he had come to Constantinople on behalf of the orthodox faith and of Macedonius, bishop of the city, who had been unjustly exiled by Emperor Anastasius. But, enticed and deceived by Anastasius’s pretences and perjuries through the intermediary Theodore, he returned on the eighth day after reaching the city. From there Vitalian entered by night, through cunning, the city of Odessus in Moesia. Vitalian found Cyril, more a procurer than a vigorous military commander, asleep between two mistresses; he dragged him away and soon cut his throat with a Getic knife, openly and plainly declaring himself an enemy of Emperor Anastasius.

**A.D. 515. Indiction VIII, Anthemius and Florentius being consuls.**

Hormisdas was ordained the fiftieth [L] bishop of the Roman Church; he lived nine years. The same Vitalian became a more ferocious enemy of the emperor Anastasius. Having sent ahead his cavalry and having armed boats run along the shore on his left, he himself, surrounded by infantry armed for battle, entered the estate of Systhenes and took the palace of the entire district as his residence. Senators were sent by Caesar to Vitalian to establish terms of peace with him. At that time he accepted ninety pounds of gold, apart from royal gifts, as the price of Hypatius, whom his own men had offered him at Sozopolis together with Uranius, a captive, for one thousand one hundred pounds of gold. Vitalian was made master of the soldiers in Thrace. He returned Hypatius, whom he had held captive and chained at the fortress of Acres, to his uncle. At that time the Huns, having crossed Armenia and ravaging all Cappadocia, advanced as far as Lycaonia. The Augusta Ariadne died after spending sixty years in the palace.

**A.D. 516. Indiction IX, Peter being sole consul.**

Emperor Anastasius, having changed his faith, succeeded Vitalian and appointed Rufinus as his successor. Elias, bishop of the city of Jerusalem, died in the village called Haila, to which the same emperor had banished him. Anastasius also ordered Lawrence of Lychnidus, Domnion of Sardica, Alcissus of Nicopolis, Gaianus of Naissus, and Evangelus of Pautalia, the Catholic priests of Illyricum, to be brought into his presence. The bishops Alcissus and Gaianus died at Byzantium and were buried in a single tomb. Domnion and Evangelus were immediately sent back to their own sees because of fear of the Catholic soldiers of Illyricum. Lawrence alone, repeatedly convicting Emperor Anastasius in the palace on behalf of the Catholic faith, was detained at court as though banished into exile, and thereafter became more agile in body than he had been when he came to Constantinople. For, in the seventh year of his illness, that same Lawrence was healed, by his faith but [Onuphrius: “and”] by Christ’s grace, in the atrium of Cosmas and Damian; he was enabled to stand on his own feet and to be strengthened so that he could walk. He was then safely restored to his native country, where he rests after reaching more than eighty years of age.

**A.D. 517. Indiction X, Anastasius and Agapitus being consuls.**

That pot which, in the prophet Jeremiah, is often kindled against us and our sins from the north forged fiery weapons and wounded a very large part of Illyricum with those same arrows. The two Macedonias and Thessaly were then laid waste, and Gothic cavalry plundered as far as Thermopylae and ancient Epirus. At that time Emperor Anastasius sent one thousand pounds of gold in denarii through Paul to John, prefect of Illyricum, for the redemption of Roman captives. When the payment proved insufficient, the Roman captives were either held shut up with their little houses or slaughtered before the walls of the besieged cities. [Col. 0939D]

**A.D. 518. Indiction XI, Magnus being sole consul [or: and Florentius; or: and Agapetus II].**

In the province of Dardania, twenty-four fortresses collapsed in a single instant through a continual earthquake. Of these, two were swallowed up together with their inhabitants; four were destroyed after losing half of their buildings and people; eleven were thrown down with the loss of a third of their houses and an equal proportion of their population; seven were crushed with a quarter of their roofs and so great a portion of the populace. The neighboring places, fearing the ruins, were abandoned [Onuphrius: “the neighboring places were neglected through fear of the ruins”]. [Col. 0940A] Scupus, the metropolis, although without the slaughter of its citizens who had fled from the enemy, nevertheless collapsed completely. In one fortress of the region of Canisa, called Sarnunto, the veins of the earth then burst open; the earth, seething like a fiery furnace, vomited forth a long-lasting, boiling rain on either side. Many mountains throughout the province were split by this earthquake; rocks were torn from their joints, and a line of fallen trees extending for thirty thousand paces and gaping to a width of twelve feet opened a deep chasm, making ready a profound abyss for the inhabitants, the ruins of fortresses and rocks, and those still fleeing the incursions of the enemy. Emperor Anastasius, overtaken by sudden death, died at more than eighty years of age. He had reigned twenty-seven years, eleven months, and twenty-nine days.

**A.D. 519. Indiction XII, Justin Augustus and Eutharicus being consuls.**

Justin was elected emperor by the Senate and immediately appointed. Amantius, prefect of the palace; Andreas, Misael, and Ardabur, chamberlains; supporters of the Manichaeans and traitors to Justin Augustus, were discovered. Two of them, Amantius and Andreas, were slain by the sword; Misael and Ardabur were sent into exile at Sardica. Theocritus, an accomplice of Amantius, whom Amantius, the prefect, had secretly prepared to seize the throne, was arrested and died in prison, battered with great stones. His body lay in a briny pool, and he was denied burial as well as the empire for which he had yearned. Vitalian the Scythian, recalled to public service through the piety of Emperor Justin, entered Constantinople and on the seventh day after his reception was appointed master of the soldiers.

**A.D. 520. Indiction XIII, Vitalian and Rusticus being consuls.**

[Col. 0940C]

Vitalian, consul VII, was stabbed with wounds in the sixteenth month of his consulship and killed in the palace together with his attendants Celerianus and Paulus.

**A.D. 521. Indiction XIV, Justinian and Valerius being consuls.**

Justinian made this most famous consulship, evidently more munificent than all the consulships of the East, illustrious by these acts of generosity. For he distributed 288,000 solidi among the people and for the spectacles or the apparatus of the spectacles; he displayed twenty lions and thirty leopards in the amphitheater at the same time, besides other wild beasts. Moreover, he bestowed numerous horses, adorned with trappings, even upon charioteers who had already received gifts, denying the frenzied crowd only the final and last napkin. [Col. 0940D]

**A.D. 522. Indiction XV, Symmachus and Boethius being consuls.**

**A.D. 523. Indiction I, Maximus being sole consul.**

Most of the stone-throwers, murderers, and despoilers of the city, having been discovered on account of their crimes, were punished by sword, fire, and hanging, providing a pleasing spectacle for good citizens.

**A.D. 524. Indiction II, Justin Augustus for the second time and Opilio being consuls.**

During these consulships, a shortage of oil brought great want upon the people.

**A.D. 525. Indiction III, Philoxenus and Probus being consuls.**

John, the fifty-first [LI] pope of the Roman Church from Peter, chief of the apostles and bishops, in the 475th year of his see, while King Theodoric was laboring to restore the ceremonies of his Arians, came alone of all the Romans who had preceded him from the city to Constantinople, and was received with extraordinary honor. He occupied the right-hand seat in the church and celebrated the day of the resurrection of our Lord with a full-voiced Roman prayer. [Col. 0941A]

**A.D. 526. Indiction IV, Olybrius being sole consul.**

A sudden earthquake struck the whole city of Antioch in Syria during dinner. Otherwise, the western part of the city suffered a great and twofold fiery destruction: violent winds immediately blew from every side, and the flames then raging in the kitchens were mingled with the collapsing buildings. It also overwhelmed Euphrasius, bishop of the whole city [Onuphrius: “of this part of the city”], burying him in his tomb after his head had been removed and the tomb itself burned, when the circus obelisk had been overturned and buried in the ground. [Col. 0941B]

**A.D. 527. Indiction V, Mavortius [or Mavortius] being sole consul.**

In the year 197 from the founding of the royal City, Emperor Justin, on the Kalends of April, made Justinian, his nephew through his sister, whom he had long before designated as a most noble man, also a partner in his kingdom and his successor. He himself died four months after this, in the ninth year of his reign and the second month.

**A.D. 528. Indiction VI, Justinian Augustus being sole consul.**

In the year 198 from the founding of the royal City, the victorious Emperor Justinian restored, higher and brighter than it had been, the royal vestibule and the ancient throne within it, built for viewing and judging the contests in the circus, as well as the two porticoes where the senators customarily watched, with his customary magnanimity, indicating a reward for good charioteers but severity for the lazy. [Col. 0941C]

**A.D. 529. Indiction VII, Decius being sole consul.**

When the Parthians took up arms, the Roman army prepared for war and, in rebellion, defended its own frontiers. This expedition occupied our forces for nearly five years; then, departing from the East, it turned toward Africa, where it was to fight successfully against the Vandals.

**A.D. 530. Indiction VIII, Lampadius and Orestes being consuls.**

Mundus, commander of both Illyrian armies, was the first of all Roman commanders to attack the Goths, who had long been roaming through Illyricum, and drove them into flight after killing not a few of them. During the same consulships, that commander, following up his boldness with a second exploit, also hastened into Thrace and, in a more successful battle, struck down the Bulgars who were plundering it, killing five hundred of them in the battle.

**A.D. 531. Indiction IX, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes.**

During this year the Justinian Code [Chiffl.: “the Code of Justinian”] was promulgated to the world.

**A.D. 532. Indiction X, likewise after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes.**

Hypatius, Pompeius, and Probus, cousins by birth and nephews of the blessed Anastasius, attempted by stratagem to seize the empire, which each of them ardently desired through unworthy ambition. On the Ides of January, after most of the nobles had conspired and the entire mob of seditionists had been enticed by the distribution of weapons and gifts, they roamed through the royal city for five continuous days, plundering it and laying it waste with sword and fire through criminal citizens, without any settled ruler, while themselves pretending in the palace to be loyal to the state, with hostile impiety. On the fifth day of this unspeakable crime, as Hypatius, crowned with a golden torque by the hands of his criminal companions, and his companion Pompeius, wearing a cuirass beneath his clothing, were ascending from the forum to seize the palace, both were captured before the palace gates. Immediately, at the command of our most pious emperor, they were chained and slain, paying the penalty before they had possessed the empire they sought. Countless people were slaughtered throughout the circus, and the tyrants’ associates were immediately proscribed. The church, having then been burned, soon began to be rebuilt by the same Augustus. [Col. 0942A–B]

**A.D. 533. Indiction XI, Justinian Augustus for the third time being consul.**

After the Romans had endured prolonged and terrible labor and exertion against the Medes, peace was at last arranged with the Parthians through the patrician Rufinus and Hermogenes, master of the offices, both sent as ambassadors by our emperor. The exchange of gifts between the two emperors, sent to one another in token of concord, followed the pledge of the treaty that had been struck.

**A.D. 534. Indiction XII, Justinian Augustus for the fourth time and Paulinus being consuls.**

The province of Africa, which most people place as the third part in the division of the world’s lands, was recovered by the will of God. Carthage also, in the ninety-sixth year after its destruction, was recovered during the fourth consulship of Emperor Justinian and restored, under his direction, more securely than before, after the Vandals had been driven out and defeated, their king Gelimer captured and sent to Constantinople. At that time King Theodahad killed Queen Amalasuntha, his foster-mother, who had been driven from the kingdom, on an island in Lake Bolsena. Emperor Justinian grieved over her death as much as he avenged it [Scaliger: “and so he avenged it”]. [Up to this point, Marcellinus Comes.]

**A.D. 535. Indiction XIII, Belisarius being sole consul.**

After Carthage and Libya had been subjected, together with their king Selimer, by Belisarius, the emperor deliberated about Rome and Italy. An expedition was again prepared, and again a fleet; the same commander, who was also elected consul, sailed directly toward Sicily and without delay overran Catania and Syracuse—indeed, the whole of Trinacria. There, learning that civil war had broken out in Africa and that the army had risen against its own commander, he hastened to Africa with a few men and aided Solomon, who was in command. He served the interests of the state by partly winning over the army with persuasion, partly punishing it, and driving away the hostile tyrant. Then, sailing back, he returned to Trinacria. Agapitus, bishop of the city of Rome, sent on an embassy by King Theodahad of the Goths, came to Constantinople. The patrician Tzitta, engaging the Bulgars in battle in Moesia, was found superior at Latrus [reading uncertain]. Bishop Epiphanius of the royal city died before the arrival of the Roman prelate; Anthimus, abandoning the Church of Trebizond, seized his bishopric contrary to the canons. [Col. 0942D–0943A]

**A.D. 536. Indiction XIV, after the consulship of Belisarius.**

Ebremud, a kinsman of Theodahad, abandoning the royal army in Bruttium, flew to Belisarius in Sicily. In Africa, when Solomon likewise became estranged from the army, Germanus succeeded him, sending Solomon back to the emperor. Belisarius, crossing Campania, laid waste to Naples. The Gothic army, suspecting King Theodahad, chose Witigis as king; he soon seized the kingship in the Barbarian Plain. When the expedition had been concluded, he entered Rome. There, after Agapitus had died at Constantinople, King Theodahad had substituted Silverius in the bishopric. Remaining there, Witigis directed his forces toward Ravenna and killed Theodahad at a place called Quintus, beside the river Santernus. He himself then followed through Tuscany, plundering all the wealth that Theodahad had gathered on the island and at Orvieto. Entering Ravenna, he joined Matasuntha, the granddaughter of Theodoric, to himself as his partner in the kingdom more by force than by love. Belisarius entered with the Lord’s favor. Germanus administered Africa successfully. Agapitus, bishop of Rome, arriving at Constantinople, as we have said, soon expelled Anthimus from the Church, declaring him, according to ecclesiastical regulation, an adulterer because he had abandoned his own Church and sought another. In his place he ordained the presbyter Menna as bishop, and himself died in the Lord. Nevertheless, he held no opinion contrary to the faith, as the emperor accused him of doing. In that same year, because of excessive drought, pasture was unavailable in Persia; approximately fifteen thousand Saracens, led by Alamundarus together with the phylarchs Chabo and Hezidus, entered the frontier district of the Euphrates. There the commander Batzas kept them at peace, partly by persuasion and partly by coercion [or: strict enforcement], and restrained them from desiring battle. [Col. 0943B–C]

**A.D. 537. Indiction XV, again after the consulship of Belisarius.**

The tyrant Witigis, having gathered an army, besieged Rome. Belisarius removed Pope Silverius, who at that time favored Witigis, from the episcopate and ordained in his place the deacon Vigilius. While Witigis continued the long siege of Rome, Belisarius, suffering inside from hunger and sleepless watches, requested aid from the emperor. Martinus and Valerianus, both masters of the soldiers, were sent to him; nevertheless Witigis did not abandon the siege. In Africa, Germanus drove off rebellious soldiers while fighting the tyrant Stotzas among the deserts of the Moors. In the East also, John Cottistis seized the tyranny, but before he could attempt anything against his opponents, he was killed at Dara. The Great Church at Constantinople, built by the emperor Justinian as a singular work in the world, was dedicated on the sixth day before the Kalends of January. [Col. 0943D]

**A.D. 538. Indiction I, John being sole consul [or: Volusianus and John].**

While Witigis still remained in the siege of Rome, John, master of the soldiers, with Batza, Conon, Paulus, and Remus, illustrious men, hastened to Italy with a great army, set up camp at the Roman harbor, and came to the aid of Rome in its distress. Seeing their arrival, Witigis confirmed the agreement of three months that he had made with Belisarius and sent his ambassadors to the emperor. Under this peace Belisarius returned to Campania to bring a supply of grain into Rome. After returning from Campania, he removed from his path the patrician Constantine. John, however, abandoning the camp he had established at the harbor, entered the territory of the Samnites and, after storming the town of Aternum, defeated and crushed Tremon, a Gothic commander, together with his men. He similarly attacked Ortona; plundering Picenum, he occupied Ariminum. When Witigis heard this, he abandoned the siege of the City, where he had still been staying after the peace had been disrupted, and left Rome. He crossed the Apennines by the Clodian road and through the grain-producing Tuscany, pitched camp on the bank of the river Rubicon, and besieged Ariminum. Driven from there by Narses, who came from Constantinople, and by Belisarius, who came from Rome, he fled to Ravenna. His nephew Oraius, meanwhile, wore down Milan by a long famine, besieging Mundilas and Paulus, commanders stationed there, together with their soldiers. Narses remaining at Ariminum, Belisarius approached Rome to spend the winter and, after its surrender, took possession of Urbino, Orvieto, and the island in Lake Bolsena. [Col. 0944A–B]

**A.D. 539. Indiction II, Appio being sole consul.**

Narses returned to Constantinople. Belisarius, besieging Auximum, entered it in the seventh month, and likewise Fiesole. The Goths entered Milan, tore down its walls, took the booty, and killed all the Romans. They carried the commanders Mundilas and Paulus away to Ravenna. Theudibert, king of the Franks, arriving with a great army, plundered all Liguria and Emilia. He destroyed and plundered Genoa, a town situated on the shore of the Tyrrhenian Sea. When his army subsequently suffered from disease, he made an agreement with Belisarius in order to receive assistance and returned to Gaul. Germanus was summoned from Africa to Constantinople. Solomon was sent there again. Calluc, master of the soldiers, fought successfully against the Gepids the first time but fell disastrously in the second engagement.

**A.D. 540. Indiction III, Justin the Younger being sole consul.**

The Parthians entered Syria and overthrew many cities. Germanus took up arms against them, bringing with him Justin, his son and also consul, in the very insignia of office. Great Antioch was plundered and destroyed by the Persians. Belisarius entered Ravenna, took King Witigis, the queen, all their wealth, and the more noble Goths, and returned to the emperor, having been summoned by the count Marcellus. Solomon fought successfully in Africa and drove off the rebels. The Goths living beyond the Po, led by Oraius, the nephew of Witigis, and by Heldibadus, decided to revolt after hearing that King Witigis, the queen, the palace wealth, and the Goths had been expelled from their homes and carried east by Belisarius. They set up Heldibadus as their king. Against him, preparing to fight, the patrician Bessas came from Ravenna and ascended upon Placentia. Constantine was sent by the emperor from Dalmatia to Ravenna to command the army. [Col. 0944D–0945A]

**A.D. 541. Indiction IV, Basil being sole consul.**

While the Parthians continued as enemies, Belisarius undertook the eastern expedition, Germanus having returned to the royal city. After Heldibadus was killed, the Goths appointed Erarius as their king. Solomon was killed in Africa; Sergius succeeded him as commander of the war and governor of the province.

**A.D. 542. Indiction V, after the consulship of Basil.**

Soldiers secretly entered Verona, but while they were quarreling over the booty in their eagerness for gain, the Goths emerged from hiding places and drove them from the city in disgrace. The Goths killed King Erarius and installed Totila as king. He soon crossed the Po to the detriment of Italy and defeated the Roman army at Faventia, a city of Emilia; he drove off the commanders and occupied Cesena, Urbino, Montefeltro, and Petra Pertusa, roaming here and there and laying Italy waste. Again in grain-producing Tuscany, at Mucella, he defeated the Roman army through his commanders Ruderit, Viliarid, and Bleda. In that battle the patrician Bessas escaped wounded; the others were saved by fleeing in every direction. [Col. 0945A–B]

**A.D. 543. Indiction VI, the second year after the consulship of Basil.**

Totila devastated Campania and, destroying its walled cities, besieged Tibur through his men. A great mortality devastated the soil of Italy, while the East and Illyricum had already been almost equally exhausted. In the East, while the Persians still maintained the conflict against our forces, Sergius was troubled in Africa by rebellions involving Stotzas and the Moors.

**A.D. 544. Indiction VII, the third year after the consulship of Basil.**

Totila besieged Firmum and Asculum, and, having invaded, laid waste Naples and Tibur. Rome was besieged from a distance; John, master of the soldiers, was in command there. While Belisarius was stationed in the East, John, an ex-consul, ordinary patrician, and prefect of the praetorium, was exiled, and his house was given to Belisarius.

**A.D. 545. Indiction VIII, the fourth year after the consulship of Basil.**

Totila entered Firmum and Asculum under oath. After dismissing the Roman soldiers with their possessions, he exercised his cruelty against the Romans, stripping and killing them all. In Africa, John attacked the tyrant Stotzas and killed him, but was himself killed by one of Stotzas’s guards. During that tyranny a certain John, chosen to succeed him, was called Stotzas the Younger. Belisarius was summoned from the East, incurred grave danger and disfavour, and became subject to envy; he was sent back to Italy. On arriving, he sent Bessas to Rome and John to the emperor. Totila, having devastated Picenum and fought at Auximum, was victorious. From there, roaming through Tuscany, he destroyed Spoleto, occupied the towns of Assisi and Clusium, and besieged Perusia. [Col. 0945C–D]

**A.D. 546. Indiction IX, the fifth year after the consulship of Basil.**

Pope Vigilius, the fifty-ninth [perhaps sixtieth] from the apostle Peter, summoned by the emperor, left Rome and came to Sicily. Totila, having occupied Lucania and Bruttium, destroyed Naples and besieged Rome. Sergius was summoned from Africa, and Areobindus was sent there as judge after receiving the emperor’s niece in marriage. In the East, a treaty was made with the Parthians through Constantianus, master of the soldiers, and the army returned to Constantinople.

**A.D. 547. Indiction X, the sixth year after the consulship of Basil.**

The Goths sent an embassy to the emperor through Aventius, bishop of the city of Asisium. John, master of the soldiers, hastened to Italy. Belisarius left Ravenna and came to Dyrrachium; from there John was sent directly to Calabria, while Belisarius himself proceeded through Sicily to Rome. Pope Vigilius entered Constantinople on the eighth day before the Kalends of February. Totila entered Rome through a stratagem involving the Isaurians on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, destroyed the walls, burned a number of houses, and took all the Romans’ possessions as booty. He led these Romans themselves away as captives into Campania. After this devastation Rome remained so deserted for forty or more days that no human beings, but only beasts, lived there. Belisarius then came and restored part of the walls; when Totila came to battle, he resisted him. In the same year the emperor’s niece returned from Africa as a widow, Areobindus having been killed by the tyrant Guntharis, who, acting in concert with Stotzas the Younger, had killed him. Artabanes, however, arrested both of them, killed Guntharis, and sent John, that same Stotzas the Younger, bound, to the emperor. After some days John was sent to Africa, and Artabanes, having been summoned, received the command of the imperial guard. [Col. 0946A–B]

**A.D. 548. Indiction XI, the seventh year after the consulship of Basil.**

John, master of the soldiers, while plundering the Goths in Campania, freed several senators. Later he suffered a nocturnal attack by Totila through the treachery of his Bulgars [lacuna].

**A.D. 549. Indiction XII, the eighth year after the consulship of Basil.**

**A.D. 550. Indiction XIII, the ninth year after the consulship of Basil.**

**A.D. 551. Indiction XIV, the tenth year after the consulship of Basil.**

During these times the Moors in Africa were subdued by John the patrician.

**A.D. 552. Indiction XV, the eleventh year after the consulship of Basil.**

At this time Emperor Justinian made the eunuch Narses, his chartulary and chamberlain, commander-in-chief and sent him to Italy. After joining battle, he killed Totila by God’s grace and, with the assistance also of the Lombards, exterminated the Gothic nation in Italy. During these years, when Count Buccelinus, sent long before by Theudibert, king of the Franks, with his companions, had been ravaging Italy and Sicily for several years and had often defeated the Roman army, his army was eventually weakened by a flux of the bowels. It was defeated and routed in battle by Narses, and the commander himself was killed. Not long afterward his associate, the commander Omnirugus, was killed together with the remaining Goths who had joined him.

**A.D. 553. Indiction I, the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

Theudebald, king of the Franks, died, and King Chlothar, his father Theudibert’s paternal uncle, who had already reigned for forty-four years, took possession of his kingdom and his wife, Vanderada. In that same year Chlothar himself subdued the rebellious Saxons beside the river Weser with great slaughter and devastated Thuringia, which he had overrun. [Col. 0946D–0947A]

**A.D. 554. Indiction II, the thirteenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

Pope Vigilius, at last released from exile by the Roman emperors and by Narses, had begun to return to Rome when he died in Sicily from a stone disease. His body was soon carried to Rome and buried at Saint Marcellus on the Via Salaria. Pelagius was ordained pope in his place, the sixty-second [perhaps sixty-first] from Peter; he held the office for eleven years and ten months. Accused by the Roman people of being part of the faction against Vigilius, he celebrated litanies together with Narses, mounted the ambo at Saint Peter’s, placed the Gospel upon his head, and cleared himself by oath of the charge.

**A.D. 555. Indiction III, the fourteenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

At this time the Saxons again rebelled against Chlothar. When he attacked them and they offered him half of their possessions as satisfaction, the splendid Frankish army fought them despite Chlothar’s opposition, but was crushed by them with great slaughter and sought safety in flight. [Col. 0947A–B]

**A.D. 556. Indiction IV, the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

In these days Hramnus rebelled against his father Chlothar, with the approval of his uncle Childebert, and disturbed the kingdom of the Franks by sedition. The Saxons, through the faction of Childebert, carried out raids in Francia. Childebert ravaged the Reman Campania. [Col. 0947B–0948A]

**A.D. 557. Indiction V, the sixteenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

In Britain, Bridus became king of the Picts. About this time Childebert, king of the Franks, died and was buried in the Basilica of Saint Vincent, which he himself had built at Paris. His brother Chlothar assumed his kingdom and obtained the monarchy of the entire paternal realm.

**A.D. 558. Indiction VI, the seventeenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

Hramous, who had offended his father Chlothar by many wrongs, fled to Britain at this time. Chlothar pursued him there; Hramous was defeated and captured in battle with King Gonobor, and he was burned alive together with his wife and daughters. At the same time, the Basilica of Saint Martin at Tours was burned by fire, because rebels had fled to it.

**A.D. 559. Indiction VII, the eighteenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

**A.D. 560. Indiction VIII, the nineteenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

**A.D. 561. Indiction IX, the twentieth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

**A.D. 562. Indiction X, the twenty-first year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

**A.D. 563. Indiction XI, the twenty-second year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

**A.D. 564. Indiction XII, the twenty-third year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**

**A.D. 565. Indiction XIII, the twenty-fourth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus.**
