The effect of baptism is the remission of every kind of sin, 206. Even in those who relapse, sins are cleansed, ibid. and 219. The origin of true life and true righteousness is in baptism, 871. Through baptism divisions of things are made; it is compared with the Red Sea, 493. The power and form of baptism are distinguished, ibid. The necessity of baptism, 329. How the baptized should live, 592. All the baptized, if they wish, can—with Christ helping and cooperating—fulfill what pertains to salvation, 766.

BARACH and Deborah. See DEBORAH. The apostles and martyrs are signified by the beard, 485. Barbarians embrace the faith among the Romans, 920.

BARCOCHEBAS became leader of the rebellion among the Jews, 711. He was defeated, and thereafter the Jews were deprived of permission to enter Jerusalem, ibid.

BARDESANES, heretic, 714. Bashan means “confusion,” 488. BASILEUS, bishop of Amasia in Pontus, martyr, 725. BASILIDES, heretic, 710. His errors, ibid.

The blessed life is joy in truth, 569. What true blessedness is, 552. A right will that has not obtained what it desires is closer to blessedness than a perverse will that has obtained what it craved, 552, 649, epigram 63. The blessedness of the righteous begins with fear and advances into desire for God’s commandments, 461. Whoever desires the same things as the apostles shares in their blessedness, 475. The blessedness of the saints comes both from the gift of mercy and from the recompense of justice, 460, 547. Those who die to this world before the separation of the soul from the flesh, and are not found in desires that only love of God overcomes, attain blessedness, 600. All things were created for heavenly blessedness and undertook the office of remaining in the praise of God, 529. How unjust is the world’s judgment concerning blessedness, 819, verse 855 and following. Who are blessed, 435. Full of vanity and empty of faith, people call him blessed who possesses temporal goods, 517. It is an impious opinion to think that the person to whom God has given nothing is happier than the person to whom he has granted everything, 360.

The Trojan War, 690. War in Gaul against the Goths, 746. The war undertaken against the Vandals turns out badly through delay, 478. The Servile War in Sicily, 697. The civil war between Caesar and Pompey, 699.

Persevering blessing involves no forgetfulness of God’s rewards, 379. The blessing that the Jews refused passed to the nations, 412. All prophets, apostles, and saints blessed those who live well in the name of the Lord, not in their own, 478.

BENEVENTUM was built, 695. It is characteristic of a kind person not only not to arouse or increase enmities but to extinguish them, 569. The Lord’s kindness toward his people, 531. Two works of kindness—remitting sins and bestowing benefits—make a person acceptable to God and contain every work of piety, 421.

BERILLUS, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, a distinguished writer, 717.

BOETHIUS, prefect of the praetorium, was killed with his friend Aetius, 752, 753.

Count BONIFACIUS, provoked by Cassinus, withdrew to Africa, 742. War was declared against Boniface, 743. Boniface defeated Aetius and died, 744. BONIFACIUS XL was placed in charge of the Roman Church, 741. Pope Boniface used the emperors’ edicts against the Pelagians, 362, 363. Although Pope Boniface was highly learned, he nevertheless sought the responses of the blessed bishop Augustine concerning the books of the Pelagians, 362, 363. BONIFACIUS was ordained bishop of Carthage, 756.

How far true goodness extends, 555, 661, epigram 79. The good are hidden, 571. God instructs the good through the wicked, 577. No one is good through himself, except by participation in him who alone is good, 272. No one becomes good except from being evil, 565. No one is good through himself, 272. What the highest good and the highest evil are, 565. From where our good comes, and what is to be rewarded, 560. Nothing is better than that good by which a person becomes good, 457. All good things, especially those that advance salvation, come from God, 857. God does many good things in a person that the person does not do; no good thing is done by a person that God does not do, 590, 764. All good things, great and small, come from God, 606. The evil of losing a higher good is not felt while the lower good that is loved is possessed, 585. All good things arise from God’s eternal will, 882. All good things are present through Christ’s working, not from merit but toward merit, 106, verses 9 and 10. The soul sins by loving a certain good because that good has been ordered below the soul, 608, 609. We can neither desire nor complete any good without God’s help, 287. God alone is the author of the fruit of goodness, 892. Every good thing comes from God, 876, 879 and following; 882 and following; 950 and following. All good things by which God is pleased are God’s gifts and must be sought from him, 882. All good things are God’s gifts, 883. The things that are corrupted are good, but they are not the highest good, 568. Temporal goods are God’s gifts, 517. How one should use goods, 779, verse 108. Temporal goods are gifts of God; yet he does not specifically promise these to the saints, since he commonly bestows them even on the reprobate, 476. To do good truly means to do it not from fear of bodily evil but from delight in spiritual good, 52. God alone is the creator of the creature’s good, 562. Every good belongs both to God and to humanity, 852. One who seeks future goods, not present ones, is not disturbed by the prosperity of the wicked, 422. Good should be done with joy, 559. Good should not be done unwillingly or from fear, 567, 568. Goods that unwilling people do not lose, 572, 669, epigram 94. Mortal life should receive consolation from present gifts and patiently await the future goods of eternity, 448. The Greek schools and Roman eloquence achieved nothing by laboring to discover the highest good, because they used themselves as guides for knowing the truth, 337, 338.

BURGUNDIONES occupied part of Gaul, 740.

## C
CAECILIUS, comic poet, 696. CAESAR Augustus, from whom the Augusti were named, 699. CAESARIUS subscribes to the Second Council of Orange, 766. CAIN: God did not refrain from turning him back from the crime he was contemplating, 799, verse 311. Cain admonished by God after the sin, 899. Although his posterity imitated his character, divine goodness did not deny itself to them, 900. Cain warned by God, 899. Guilty of negligence in a good work, ibid. What sufficient means of healing was offered to him, 899, 900. Why Cain’s offering was displeasing to God, 899. Cain did not deceive God by a false appearance of religion, 797, verse 308 and following. The posterity of Cain the fratricide was not counted among God’s people, 686.

CAIUS Caesar Caligula reigns for four years, 703. Caligula orders his statue to be erected at Jerusalem and elsewhere, and altars to be consecrated to him as a god, 703. He kills very many, ibid. He is killed, ibid.

CAIUS, twenty-seventh bishop of Rome, 722.

The golden cup of Babylon, 398.

CALLISTUS, fifteenth bishop of Rome, 717.

CAMILLUS defeats the Gauls, 694.

CAMILLUS, a presbyter of Genoa, together with Theodore, likewise a presbyter in the same city, sends Prosper certain excerpts from books *On Predestination* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, 241.

The CANTABRIANS are subdued, 700.

There is one song of all the saints, both of those who have escaped the dangers of tribulations and of those who are still worn down by them, 470. What the new song is, 516. Singing is perfected in charity, ibid. What the new and old song are, 555. They sing the new song who live not in the oldness of the flesh but in the newness of the spirit, 530. Rational singing, whose entire melody consists in faith and charity, 530. How one should use the psaltery and the tambourine, ibid.

CAPYS SYLVIUS, king of the Latins, 691.

The Capitol is built, 707.

The captivity of the Israelite kingdom, 692.

CARAUSIUS invades Britain, 722.

The coals of fire that enlighten the faithful and punish sinners, 505. Spiritual coals that beneficially lay waste, 465.

The prison of distress and the dwelling in the body, 511. David desired to be led out, not from the body but from the corruption of the body, when he said: “Bring my soul out of prison,” 511.

CARIATHO, an illustrious man, attends and subscribes to the Second Council of Orange, 768.

To whom Christ’s flesh is life, 596. Who eats Christ’s flesh and drinks his blood, 6. None of the reborn faithful is excluded from eating the flesh, 493. Why the Wisdom of God came to human beings through flesh, 580. The desires of the flesh must be chastened, not fulfilled, with the sure hope of eternal recompense, whose pledge is found in Christ’s glorification: he brings about the fulfillment of what he commanded through the prevenient help of grace, 675, epigram 102.

Certain poems appropriate to sadness, 785, verse 5.

CARTHAGE was founded by the Tyrians, 690. Carthage is brought under Roman rule, 697. Carthage is invaded by Geiseric, 747. The Council of Carthage, 733.

CARUS reigns for thirty-two years with his sons, 722. Their death, 722.

CASSIANUS, a presbyter, author of the Thirteenth *Collation* against the grace of God, 311. The disciples of evangelical and apostolic teaching shudder at Cassian’s views on grace and free will, 356. Why Saint Prosper chiefly attacks Cassian’s definitions, 310. Cassian agrees fully neither with the Catholics nor with the Pelagians, 314 and following. He is shown to fall, even against his will, into the condemned proposition: “The grace of God is given according to our merits,” 314.

Cassian’s first definition is Catholic: it acknowledges that the grace of God is the beginning of all good things, and teaches that free will is not taken away by it, 311 and following, 312. In what sense Cassian called divine providence the companion of human beings, 312. Cassian is unstable in his position, 313. Forgetting his first definition, Cassian teaches and insists that holy thoughts, conceived without any inspiration from God, can arise from natural wisdom, 335, 336. The passage he adduces is defended against its perverse interpretation, 336 and following.

Cassian’s deception: at the beginning of the dispute he proclaims the Catholic position concerning grace, and afterward attacks that same position, 345. He gradually descends toward Pelagian precipices, 345, 346 and following.

Cassian argues in doubt whether free will depends on grace or grace on free will, 291, 292 and following. He adduces examples that support both sides, 292 and following. How he reconciles grace with free will, 292. He introduces various callings, 299. He teaches that grace is bestowed according to each person’s capacity, 299 and following. Yet Cassian professes that he condemns the giving of grace according to merits, 300 and following.

Cassian’s definition is that free will and grace must be received equally—that is, in such a way that they are believed to contribute equally to salvation, 225. He attributed victory over temptation to free will, not to grace, 297, 298. What role he assigns to God in victory over temptations, 298. He tries to establish his view by examples of God’s providence toward the Israelites and of a nurse toward her infant, 298.

Cassian did not wish all the merits of the saints to be referred to God in such a way that nothing except what is evil would be attributed to human nature, 294 and following. What he thought concerning the natural seeds of the virtues, 294. How he teaches that God works all things in all, 303. Yet how this can be reconciled fully with free will cannot be comprehended, 304.

Cassian’s error: that some are saved through grace, while others are justified through law and nature, 315. Cassian is at once hostile to free will and ungrateful toward grace, 327. According to Cassian, God provides the salvation of the human race in different ways: he helps some who are willing and compels others against their will, 301, 302. Christ is Savior to the former and helper to the latter, ibid. He acknowledges that the sum of salvation must be attributed not to the merit of works but to heavenly grace, 302.

Cassian proves that God gives more than is asked, 300 and following, 301. Confusing contradictory definitions, Cassian tries to give his intention the appearance of validity by examples: that some can accomplish through free will what others cannot accomplish except with God’s cooperation, 322, 323.

Cassian, teaching that two contrary positions must be accepted together—both that good will arises from grace and that grace depends on good will—is refuted from the supreme pontiffs and the councils, 317–320. Cassian’s error, that the beginnings of good wills sometimes arise from the goodness of nature, is refuted from his own first definition and from the Apostle, 316, 317. Cassian’s teaching assigns merit to free will, by which grace is anticipated, 327. This was condemned in the synod of the bishops of Palestine, 328.

According to Cassian, sometimes grace precedes the will and sometimes the will precedes grace, 295 and following. Nevertheless, grace always remained gratuitous, 295, 296. Cassian removes free will from one part of the human race and establishes it in another part, 325. If Cassian’s distinction is accepted, we must receive from the Pelagians what they teach, and the Pelagians must receive what we teach; in this way they will not so much be Catholics as we will be Pelagians, 355.

Cassian accuses the Pelagians and the Catholics alike of error, 318, 319. How he perversely attempts to reconcile the two, 318. Cassian defines that human nature must not be credited with only what is evil. He is refuted, 334, 335. Cassian attributes to human beings before grace as much as it is most fruitful for them to possess through grace, 344. He undertakes to demonstrate the strength of free will, 344.

Cassian wishes human beings to be entrusted to their own discernment in such a way that they have no more protection from God than danger from the devil, 342. According to Cassian, Matthew’s conversion was compelled, while the faith of Zacchaeus and the thief was voluntary, 346. Cassian’s error: that Job possessed the power to resist through free will, not through grace, 349. How he would have spoken more correctly, so that Job’s patience might be attributed both to God’s help and to human free will, 349. According to Cassian, in Job’s conflict with the devil God was not a co-worker but merely a spectator, 349.

How easily Cassian’s opinion leads to the conclusion that in lighter temptations grace is given so that what could have been fulfilled without it may be fulfilled more easily through grace, 350. Cassian attempts to combine incompatible things and divides the faithful into two classes, applying contrary positions to them, 354. He defines God as Savior to some and merely protector to others, 354, 355. He goes before some and helps others, ibid. According to Cassian, God was a witness to Job’s patience, not his helper, 360.

Cassian, contrary to himself, assists those who say, “The grace of God is given according to our merits,” although he professes that such people hold a profane opinion, 352, 333 and following. Cassian almost confirms the whole Pelagian doctrine in a single statement, saying: “There would be no praise or merit if Christ had preferred in the centurion what he himself had bestowed,” 350. Cassian gathers the weapons of [an uncertain reading: *elisarum*] arguments, 321.

Saint Prosper recapitulates twelve of Cassian’s definitions, so that it may become clear what those who opposed the defenders of grace and disturbed the peace of the Church thought concerning grace, 357 and following.

CASSIUS captures Judea and plunders the Temple, 699.

The chastisement of the righteous is not cruelty but medicine, 507.

CASTINUS, sent as commander against the Vandals, exasperates the count Boniface, 142. Castinus is punished with exile, 742.

The falls of the righteous and of the impious differ, 520.

Among all the virtues, chastity most greatly needs God’s help, 286.

CATANA is founded, 692.

The error of the Cataphrygians, 713. Why they were so called, 714. What their character was, ibid.

When the crimes of CATILINE occurred, 698.

CECROPS, king in Attica, 689.

CELADION, eighth bishop of Alexandria, 712.

A census is conducted in Judea by Quirinius, 701.

The faith of the centurion was given and praised by Christ, 350. Cassian teaches that the centurion’s faith was tested and praised by Christ but was not a gift of God, 297. He holds the same opinion concerning Abraham, ibid.

The flooding of the river Cephissus, 709.

CERDO, bishop of Alexandria, 708.

CERDO, a heresiarch, and his doctrines, 711, 712.

The neck of sinners is pride, 477.

The Council of Chalcedon condemns Eutyches and confirms the Catholic faith concerning the Incarnation, 752.

The Chaldeans conjectured the future from the stars, 800, verse 627 and following.

Perfect and imperfect charity, 898 and following. Charity makes people unconquerable, 884, 898. Its connection with humility, 949. Without it the other virtues are of no benefit, 948 and following. Without it they perish, 898. It is a part of humility, and humility likewise a part of it, 949.

Without charity, according to the Apostle, the other virtues are of no benefit, 92, 93. Without charity they possess the appearance, but not the reality, of piety, 93. No one was found worthy of the gift of charity, ibid. Any good things may perish without charity; without charity they cannot benefit, 398. Charity is the greatest of all gifts and, in a certain sense, the life of the virtues, 398. The other virtues are referred to it, ibid. Without charity, which does not seek its own interests, nothing is beneficial, 948 and following. Without charity no good is beneficial; through charity every sin is destroyed, 951.

The perfect efficacy of charity, 398. Without charity all good things are of no benefit, 343. Charity is the fulfillment of the law, 574. Imperfect charity is sometimes found together with faith and strength of understanding, 898. Charity is from God and is God, 398. The commandment of charity is above all books; every language and every teaching of the saints serves it, 383. The two commandments of charity are the two wings by which souls rise toward God, 384.

When God pours into our hearts the charity with which we love, 384. Charity alone is the proper and distinctive virtue of the devout and the saints, 383, 544, 619, epigram 7. The charity of God conquered the world of the impious, 904. The charity of Scripture is higher than heaven; nothing is more exalted than it in the divine utterances and commandments, 283.

He is worthy to lose the faith that is useless if he has not practiced charity: this is illustrated by the servant from whom the talent uselessly preserved was taken away, 894. Charity and faith are gifts of God, 92 and following. Charity is breadth, 444. The capacity for charity grows through use, 556. The charity with which God loved us is greater than our love for him, 384. Not only the Law but, even more, the Gospel is contained in the commandments of charity, 582. Charity is a gift from God, 343. The necessity of charity, 593. Charity is the seed of God; it does not commit sin, 951.

CHELCIAS, high priest, 693.

By the name “choir” the harmony of those praising is signified, 530.

CHRYSAPHIUS is killed, 751.

Why a Christian is so called, 596. The Christian people are the true Israel, 424. When God promised Abraham an innumerable offspring, he was thinking of Christians, 799, verse 346 and following. Spiritual Christians sit beside the rivers of the world and are not carried away by their current, 494.

Christians are happier the fewer things they have that are their own and the more things they have that belong to God, 356. The entire Christian people is priestly. More fully, however, this applies to the rulers of the people, who represent the high priest and mediator in a more particular way, 484. What is said about the departure of the people of Israel from Egypt applies even more aptly to the freedom of Christians, 424 and following.

The name CHRIST is derived from *chrisma*, that is, anointing, 596.

Christ is equal to the Father and less than the Father; Christ is one, God and human being, 597. In Christ there are two forms or natures, 413. The Father helps the Son insofar as God helps the human being, because of the form of a servant, 413. How the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ, 587.

Christ, according to his divinity, is Lord and creator of David; according to the flesh, he is the son of David—not two persons but one Christ, 517. Christ is Son and Lord of David, 415 and following. After the resurrection and ascension, precisely in that by which he had become the son of David, he also became Lord of David, 415. All will be subjected to Christ either through condemnation or through correction, 416.

Both natures must be confessed in Christ, divine and human, 803, verse 473 and following. Both are necessary for human salvation, ibid., verse 480. When Christ’s Incarnation was completed, 902. Christ, remaining God, becomes human, 803, verse 463 and following.

Christ is the fruit of the womb because, according to the flesh, he is the son of the Virgin Mother, conceived not through intercourse with a man but through the Holy Spirit, 483. Christ came to fulfill the Law of the Old Testament through the new law of evangelical truth, 479.

From the ineffable humility of God, by which he deigned to become human and wretched in order to redeem humanity, the captive human being should recognize in what prison he was confined and by what disease he was afflicted, 181, verse 889 and following. Only by the death of the physician could help be brought to the one needing rescue, ibid., 903, 904.

Christ must be confessed not only as God but also as human being; what danger is involved in denying this, 600. Born of the Virgin, Christ made a new beginning for human beings, 805, verse 492 and following. Christ’s Incarnation and Passion were for humanity, and were not useful to God but to humanity, 777, verse 79 and following.

By descending to us through us, Christ made an ascent to himself through himself, 486. The patriarchs confidently hoped for Christ’s future Incarnation, and the prophets announced it, 803, verse 468 and following. Christ was truly incarnate, 633, epigram 66. Christ became poor and a beggar, 412. The time of Christ’s coming was when sinners had dispersed the law of God, 457.

Christ is born, 701. The true and greatest praise of Christ is that he is proclaimed to be what he is: the only-begotten Son of God, 408. Christ our head sometimes speaks in himself and sometimes in his body, because the two are one flesh, 501. How Christ left God the Father and the synagogue as mother, 593. Christ, according to his divinity, is the creator of David and of all things; according to the flesh, he is the son of David, 503.

Christ, poor, clothed himself in our poverty, 373. Christ prays in the Psalms in the person of his members, 373. And he groans, 374. Christ is one rock; the many words of God are many rocks, from which those whose disputations harmonize with the testimonies of Scripture give voice, 387.

For whom Christ’s birth or death is beneficial, 213, 214. Christ is priest as a human being, not as God; his priesthood does not end, 417. He is so according to the order of Melchizedek—that is, according to the mysteries declared through him, 417. Christ alone could say, “Iniquity has not been found in me,” 512.

How Christ was begotten from the womb before the morning star, both from the Father and from the Virgin Mother, 417. Christ chose the hour of his birth and death, 604. Why Christ came after so long a time, 33, 34. The errors of the Manichaeans, Photinians, and Apollinarians concerning Christ’s Incarnation, 81. What must be believed concerning Christ, 81.

The Son of God was predestined, 40. And he is the most splendid light of predestination, ibid. In Christ there is one person, 81. No one comes to Christ unless it has been given to him; and this is given to the predestined, 67. To believe in Christ is a gift of God, 32. Christ and the Church are one body, 57. Christ in his entirety, together with his members, exists for the sake of the Church, ibid. The martyrdom of Christians for Christ is the best end, 52.

Christ is the arm of God, 516. Christ preaches, 701, 702. The necessity of confessing Christ as true God and human being, 597. What Christ did or suffered for our salvation, 805, verse 516 and following.

Although Christ’s Passion was voluntary, the crime of the persecutors was nevertheless immense, because they repaid good with evil, 409. Christ prayed both for the apostles before the Passion and for those crucifying him on the cross, 409. Christ’s sadness belonged to our nature, 512. Christ died for all the impious, 904.

Although it can be said in a certain sense that Christ was crucified for those alone whom his death benefited, Christ was crucified for the redemption of the whole world, 213, 214 and following, 215, 230, 231. Christ died for all, 904, 905 and following.

In giving an example of suffering, Christ bestowed a gift, 430. On the cross Christ taught patience toward enemies, 409. Christ’s side was pierced by a lance so that the sacraments might flow forth by which the Church is formed, 573.

Christ asks help from the Father both for himself, because of the form of a servant, and for his body, because of his servants, 414. Christ alone, without sin, underwent the punishment of sin, 590. Christ is the door of those entering the kingdom of God, 475. Those who contradict the preaching of truth are kept from entering through it, 475. No one comes to Christ unless he is drawn, 325.

What Christ teaches by writing with his finger on the ground, 855, 856. The impious persecuting Christ, not knowing what they were doing, made him sweeter, 432. How Christ had no companions in his Passion, 509.

Christ’s descent, ascension, and kingdom, 381. Christ became the cornerstone through his death—not through those by whom he suffered but through the Lord, 434. Christ is the true David, 511. Christ, the spiritual rock, made his teaching, which previously seemed hard and rigid, drinkable by sending the Holy Spirit, 425.

Christ is the refuge of both the spiritual and the simple, 388. Christ is priest and victim, atoner and atonement, 484. Christ suffered and died willingly, 388. In Christ there are the altar of propitiation, the ark of sacrifice, and the ark of doctrine, 482.

Christ alone can say, “Let those who fear you turn to me,” etc., 449. The enemies hated Christ without cause in two ways, 409. How Christ took vengeance on his persecutors, 432. Christ is Truth, and all things in Christ are true, 593. Christ’s sitting and exaltation, 499. Christ is the salvation of God, 398.

Christ is the head of the Church; its prayer is not separated from the head, which causes the Church to pray, 506. Christ asks for his body, which is the Church, and in that same body suffers need through what is necessary for his members, 448.

Christ’s love toward those who love him is twofold: now, so that we may believe; then, so that we may see and receive the vision itself as the reward of faith, ibid. As the vine supplies life to its branches and does not receive it from them, so it benefits the disciples to remain in Christ, not Christ to remain in them, 601, 602, 765.

Christ must be confessed as life, light, and righteousness, 92. From the beginning of the human race Christ has not ceased to be preached, 33. Christ and the Church are one human being, one Christ, 476. Christ is the way to God, 580. Christ is the Savior of all who are saved, 355, 356.

CICERO is born, 697. Cicero is killed, 699.

The CIMMERI near the Rhône are defeated by Gaius Marius and Catulus, 697.

Why circumcision was commanded and what it signified; why on the eighth day, 587, 588. Why circumcision was commanded to Abraham, 901. It was commanded because of Christ, ibid. The commandment of circumcision was given to Abraham, 687. Until Christ it was the bodily sign of the promise, ibid. It passed into the spiritual sign of true circumcision of the heart, ibid. Christian and spiritual circumcision is a gift of God, 286.

What makes citizens of the earthly and heavenly cities, 565. One city consists of angels and human beings striving toward the same fellowship, 530. The eternal joys of the eternal city, 476, 549, 635, epigram 37.

The cry of the heart is great intensity of thought, 459. A cry to God is the fervor of love, 557.

CLAUDIANUS, poet, 737.

CLAUDIUS reigns for five years, 703. Claudius dies, 704.

CLAUDUS reigns for twenty-eight years, 720. His victories, ibid. And his death, ibid.

CLEMENS, third bishop of Rome, 707.

CLEMENS of Alexandria, presbyter, 715. He writes much, 716.

CLEOPATRA reigns, 698. Cleopatra enters the city, 699. The death of Cleopatra and Antony, 700.

The clergy of Aquileia are of outstanding virtue, 732. The Roman clergy, guilty of perjury together with the antipope Felix, are expelled, 728.

CLETUS, second bishop of the Roman Church, 706.

CLODIUS ALBINUS, who had made himself Caesar, is killed, 716.

Cnossus is founded, 689.

COELESTINUS, forty-first bishop of Rome, 742. Pope Coelestine had received many gifts of grace for the protection of the Church, 363. When Coelestius sought a hearing, he ordered him to be expelled from the whole of Italy, ibid. He freed Britain from the Pelagian error by ordaining Palladius, ibid. He freed the Eastern Churches from the Pelagian and Nestorian plague, ibid. He restrained within Gaul the critics of Saint Augustine, ibid. With what eulogy he honored both Augustine and his teaching, ibid. The quibbling of certain persons against Coelestine’s testimony is refuted, 364 and following.

Coelestine sends Germanus of Auxerre to Britain against the Pelagians, 744. Coelestine ordains Palladius the first bishop of the Scots, 744. Coelestine resists Nestorius, 743. A letter of Pope Coelestine I to the bishops of Gaul on behalf of Prosper and Hilary, 259 and following.

The beauty of heaven and earth is like certain pages that do not keep their author silent, 939. They speak in vain unless God himself works, 940. How the heavens were made in the intellect, 492. How heaven and earth are understood in the Lord’s Prayer, 54. Heaven and earth will grow old and perish—not so that they cease to exist, but so that they may exist differently, 378. That heaven which is the dwelling of God is not what is seen, but Jerusalem, which is built in the glorification of the holy angels and human beings, 469.

What the thought of God is, 565. A good thought is a gift of God, 882. Thoughts cannot be upright unless they have been implanted by God, 950. That a salutary thought and assent to evangelical preaching do not occur without the inspiration of the Holy Spirit is a matter of faith, 761, 762. Pious thoughts do not arise from free will without God’s inspiration, 336. Good thoughts are a voice directed to God, and do not produce evil works, 555. All works, whether good or evil, proceed from thought, 455. Human thoughts perish with death, 522.

To know: not to know is not to approve, 372. Knowledge of God is from God, 881. Knowledge of God is the salvation of the one who knows him, 509. He does not know the person in whom he does not find his works and gifts, ibid. Who approach the knowledge of God and who are driven away from it, 524, 525.

Cassian’s *Collations* contradict Augustine, 90. They must be refuted by hundreds of Augustine’s volumes, ibid.

The Colossus of Rhodes, shaken, falls, 696.

The pillar of fire and cloud is the guide of the people of Israel traveling through the wilderness by day and night, 801, verse 395 and following.

COMMODUS becomes co-ruler, 714. His victory with his father, 714, 715. Commodus reigns for fifteen years, 715. The vanity and cruelty of Commodus, 715. He is killed, ibid.

The sharing of good works among the faithful through charity, 480.

COMPARTUS SYLVIUS, king of the Latins, 691.

Contrition of heart because of sin does not befit Christ in himself but in his members, 412.

The Council of Nicaea decrees that the Photinians should be baptized, 720. African councils concerning grace, 319. African councils against the Pelagians, 125, verse 76 and following; see the notes there. The letter of the council of 214 bishops to Pope Zosimus concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, 320. The Council of Carthage concerning the Donatists, 739. The Council of Carthage against the Pelagians, 741. The Council of Ephesus condemns Nestorius together with many Pelagians, 744. The Council convened at Ephesus in the case of Eutyches, 750. Everything there is thrown into confusion by the faction of Dioscorus of Alexandria, ibid. The Council of Chalcedon convened in the case of Eutyches, 751. The Second Council of Orange concerning grace and free will, 759 and following. The definitions of the Second Council of Orange are useful even to laypeople, 766. For this reason they were subscribed by illustrious men and laypeople, 766.

The evil desires are illnesses of the soul, 379. It is requested that the desire of the flesh against the spirit may be diminished and the spirit against the flesh increased, 449. Desire is quieted by heavenly overshadowing, lest one fall into the snare of an evil will, 505. The essence of desire is to take pleasure in sin, 556. There must be not peace but war with it, ibid. Desire has been left for struggle and humiliation, 856. From the one by whom victory over desire and pleasure comes, strength for patience also comes, 456. Because of rebellious desire, God is not yet all in all in this life, 950.

Condescension toward the weak, 591.

How necessary is the mutual forgiveness of sins, 599, 600. It is a gracious condition: by forgiving the sins of others, one wipes away one’s own, 600.

There is confession of sins and confession of praise, 418. Confession not by penitents but by those who praise, 431. How the confession of truth is not wholly removed, 443. The confession of sins is the glory of those who act rightly, 382. The confession of sins and justification are the work of the Lord, 419. We acknowledge from Christ’s own words that confession of sins is always necessary, 507. A kind of confession of divine praise, not of human iniquity, 497. Confession of sins praises God, 397. When confession of sin is beneficial, 557.

Through humble confession a human being reveals himself to God, who knows; and God reveals him to a human being, who does not know, 391. Those who through obstinate pride have lost the remedies of confession and repentance descend into the pit of eternal misery, 513. The fruit of confession, 577.

In married couples it is not only the flesh that is the same, but also the mind and spirit, 779, verse 121, 122. The spiritual marriage by which the Church is joined to Christ is designated by many names, 476.

The greatest punishment of an evil conscience is, 570.

CONSTANS is advanced to the throne, 726. The death of Constans and the disturbances that arose from it, 728.

CONSTANS, son of the tyrant Constantine, is killed by Gerontius, 739.

CONSTANTINE reigns for thirty-six years, 724. Peace is restored to the Church by Constantine, 724. Constantine writes to Antonius, 726. Constantine’s baptism, 727. Whether he inclined toward the Arians, ibid., note. Constantine’s death, 727.

CONSTANTINE, son of Constantine, is made Caesar, 725. Constantine, Constantius, and Constans reign for thirty-seven years, 727. The death of the younger Constantine, 727.

CONSTANTINE the tyrant, 739. Constantine is defeated and captured, 739.

The burning of Constantinople, 745.

The Council of Constantinople against Macedonius, 735.

CONSTANTIUS and Galerius Maximianus are taken into the imperial government by Diocletian and are joined to him and to Herculius by marriage alliance, 722. Constantius dies, 724.

CONSTANTIUS, son of Constantine, is made Caesar, 725. Constantius, favoring the Arians, harasses the Catholics, 727. Constantius dies, 730.

CONSTANTIUS is taken by Honorius into partnership in the imperial government, 741. Constantius dies, 741. Constantius suffers much at the hands of the Pelagians, 741. CONSTANTIUS, bishop, subscribes to the Second Council of Orange, 767.

Continence is a gift of God, 880.

Christ’s disturbance was voluntary, 512.

Conversion must not be postponed, 553, 657, epigram 74. When a human being is converted to God, this change should be attributed to God’s grace as its principle rather than to free will, 183, verse 911 and following. The power of conversion comes from God, 429. God brings about the conversion both of those who obey without hesitation and of those who resist for a long time, 322. Although human conversion does not occur without the human being, it does not begin from the human being, 338. Conversion of the heart is a gift of God, 881. What takes place in the human heart when it is converted to God, 856. The beginning of conversion is to return to the heart and read the Scriptures, 770. When a human being is converted, no other substance is created; the same substance is restored, and nothing is taken away from him except vice, 853, 854. Every conversion begins from God, 855.

Among the Romans, consuls succeed kings, 693.

Two things chiefly beat upon the human heart: love and fear. Through these twin movements the soul is either opened or closed, whether to the devil or to God, 509. One migrates in the heart when one changes one’s affection, 596. It is little to have Christ in the heart unless what we believe in the heart we confess with the mouth, 443. The expansion of the heart is love of truth, so that God may be served not through fear but through love, 441. The inclination of the heart is at once a divine gift and an act of one’s own will, 454. How the heart becomes pure through the grace of God, 449. A pure heart is a place suited to prayer and a temple of God, where God hears because he dwells there, 594. How one ought to have the heart lifted upward, 564. A heart upright with God, 577. The perfection of the heart is a divine gift, 302.

CORNELIUS prayed and gave alms not without some faith, 30. The example of the centurion Cornelius is cited by the Semi-Pelagians, 91. All Cornelius’s preparation was bestowed through the grace of God, 91. God was evidently at work in the beginning of his new calling through the signs of his preceding zeal, 91.

CORNELIUS, twentieth bishop of Rome, dies a martyr, 719.

CORNELIUS, fourth bishop of Antioch, 710.

The body, previously our adornment, afterward became our fetters, 554. The body can be changed into another body, but never into a rational soul, since God does not overturn his established order, 385. In this life there is no one whose soul is not weighed down by a corruptible body, 440, 546, 625, epigram 18.

One reaches the structure of Christ’s body only through humility and prayer, through groans and tears, 376. The body is absent in place, while the soul is a pilgrim in affection, 466. Our bodies do not perish to God, 573. The horn signifies height, 484.

Correction: God deprives no one of the way of correction, nor strips anyone of the possibility of good; but the sinner has deprived himself both of the will and of the ability to do good, 238.

The corruptibility of the body and concupiscence are not human nature but punishment, 589.

Corinth is founded, formerly called Ephyre, 689.

Quail is granted by God at the request of the chosen, to suppress the murmuring of the carnal, 397.

CRASSUS, consul, is captured, 698.

CRATINUS, comic poet, 694.

CREATION of those who will be good and of those who will be evil, 586. Why those who will not share in eternal life are created, 216, 217 and following. There is no fault in the Creator, ibid. That such beings adorn the world and serve the progress of the saints, ibid. This is proved from the death of Christ, from the martyrs, and from the Apostle, ibid., 222.

Why God created an angel or human being whom he foreknew would become evil, 562. God alone is Creator—not the angels, even though they apply their activity to things generated in the world, 563. By cleaving to the Creator, a creature becomes greater and better; the Creator does not, 552.

Three things about the condition of creatures had to be made known: by whom, through what, and why they were made, 562. From considering creatures the author of the universe is understood, so that from things it is possible to see, in which there is so much material for wonder, things that cannot be seen may be estimated, 518.

God made all creatures to serve our salvation, not our destruction, 209, verse 603 and following. How the saints used them in order to worship the one God, ibid., verses 606 and following. That creature is better which no unlawful thing delights; even that creature is good which can restrain unlawful pleasure and rejoice in that restraint, 586.

One must not cling to creatures, but ascend through them to the Creator, 554. Christians are properly God’s creatures, 389.

To believe is merit; to see is reward, 601.

CRESCENS, a Cynic, persecutor and accuser of Justin, 712.

CRISPUS and CONSTANTINE, sons of Constantine, are called Caesars, 725. Crispus and Licinius are killed, 725.

The cross of Christ is foolishness to the wise of the world; the more they swell with secular teachings, 855. It was also rejected by the Jews learned in the Law, ibid.

The worship of God: God must be worshiped with supreme love, 577. The Scriptures teach that God is to be worshiped gratuitously, 442. What it means to worship God gratuitously, ibid., 546, 627, epigram 20.

Guilt: guilt is evident where punishment is not hidden, and complicity in sin is proved by sharing in the penalty, 320.

Desire and charity, 558.

Desires are the gates of hell, 561.

Anxieties: what one who wishes not to be entangled in unworthy anxieties should avoid and pursue, 677, epigram 107.

The CURETES and CORYBANTES, 689. They found Cnossus and devised a certain kind of dance, ibid.

The guardianship of God around us must not be understood carnally, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit guard us together, 604, 605. The Lord guards the little ones whom he wishes to become perfect, 429.

The beginning of the first cycle, 703. The end of the first cycle and the beginning of the next, 710. The end of the second cycle and the beginning of the third, 717. The end of the third cycle and the beginning of the fourth, 723.

CYRILLUS, twenty-second bishop of Antioch, 722.

CYRILLUS of Alexandria resists Nestorius, 743.

CYPRIAN, bishop and martyr, 719. Cyprian’s book *On Mortality* is commendably known to many, indeed almost all, who love ecclesiastical writings, 37. His treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer*, 53. The letters of Saint Cyprian to Lucius and Stephen, Roman pontiffs, 719.

CYPRIAN, bishop, subscribes to the Second Council of Orange, 767.

CYZICUS is founded, 690.

D
### D

**DEMONS**, rulers of darkness—that is, of human beings subjected to the devil, 432. Demons can inflict no harm unless God permits it, 389. By God’s judgment a person is handed over to his enemies either for punishment or for testing, 389. Although demons incite the minds of the impious to persecute Christians, they do not dare to rage against the Church, but are restrained within the hearts of unbelievers, 389. Even if the malice of many human beings is like that of demons, there is this difference between them: if God shows mercy, reconciliation remains possible for human beings; no conversion has been reserved for demons, 233–234.

**DALMATIUS** is made Caesar, 726. Dalmatius is killed, 727.

**DAMASUS**, thirty-fifth bishop of the Roman Church, 731.

The cause of condemnation in infants who die without baptism is original sin, not the deeds they would have committed had they lived, 60–61.

**DANIEL and his companions**, 693.

**DARIUS**, king of the Persians, 693. **DARIUS NOTHUS**, 694. **DARIUS**, son of Arsames, 694.

**DAVID**, king, 691. Christ and the Church in the person of David, 483. David was most observant of meekness, 481. A figure of Christ and the Church, 481. In this there is a fervor of faith, ibid. When the prophet David desired to build the temple, he was not unaware that the true and perfect temple was to be founded by Christ, 336. Why David was not chosen for the construction of the temple, but David’s son was, 336. David’s desire came from God, and Solomon’s accomplishment of it likewise came from God, 336. By this example it is proved that God sometimes wills that something not happen which human beings, with God’s will, have desired, 337.

Who can walk in the breadth of the soul, 371.

Christ restored our debts, although he owed nothing, 498.

**DEBORAH and BARAK**: from which tribe they came, and for how many years they ruled the people, 889–890.

**DECENTIUS**, the brother of Magnentius, dies by hanging, 729.

**DECIUS**, twenty-fourth emperor, reigns, 718. He is killed, 719.

The martyr-shrine of the apostles is dedicated at Constantinople, 772.

The dedication of the basilica built by the patrician Liberius, 759. The bishops celebrating the dedication hold a spiritual conference at Orange, 759. They present the chapters transmitted by the Apostolic See and subscribe them, ibid. In these chapters they define, according to the Catholic faith, what is to be held concerning grace and free will, ibid.

A good kind of deficiency is the desire for a good not yet attained but ardently sought, 449. Whatever form remains in a thing whose form is failing derives from that form which does not know failure, and it does not allow the movements of failing things to exceed the laws of their numbers, 606.

**Defense.** In defense of a particular definition, one must bring forward arguments that do not yield to another understanding and do not abandon the rule to which they have been adapted, 90.

The enjoyment of the good is a great gift of God, 446. Who takes delight in Christ, 437. The danger when there is no delight either in reading or in prayer, 405, 545.

Temporal pleasures and tribulations: how they are to be despised or endured, 575.

**DEMETRIAS**, a virgin, asks the author of the letter addressed to her to write to her about perfection, 933. She belonged to the Anician family and to the nobility of the Trabeates, 934. She was praised by the most distinguished teachers of the Church, ibid. She consecrates her virginity to God, ibid. Demetrias needed greater humility because of the purity of her virginity and the splendor of her family, 947.

**DEMETRIANUS**, bishop of Alexandria, 515. **DEMETRIANUS**, fourteenth bishop of Antioch, 719.

**DEMOSTHENES** is renowned, 694.

**DEODATUS**, an illustrious man, attended and subscribed the Second Council of Orange, 768.

The lowering of the eyes through the shedding of tears signifies the humility of the penitent, 458.

The desire for the good comes from God, 854. The good desire itself is stirred by God, 520. Where and for whom the fulfillment of righteous desires will occur, 600. Whoever is overcome by the heat of desire is handed over to the sinner and subjected to an adverse power, 505.

The misery of one who despairs of God and presumes upon himself, 555.

The Jews’ reviling of Christ was worse than his killing, 409.

That God exists and is the author of all things has always been known to everyone; and that he wisely arranged all things as he willed, 789, verse 104 and following.

God alone truly exists, and one must cling to him, 621, epigram 11. God is what he possesses, 602. What ought to be thought about God, 675, epigram 103. If God is sought according to what he is, this is possible for few; he must be sought according to his wonders and benefits, 392–393. All principles are eternal and unchangeable in God, 920. God alone is truly eternal, 569. How God is all that is rightly desired, 594.

God’s excellence surpasses all things not only in speech but also in every understanding; nevertheless, he is usefully praised by human beings, 649, epigram 61. In God, essence and knowledge are one, 602. No bodily form is to be perceived in the nature of the Godhead, 448. Whoever thinks that what he understands about God is sufficient has an inadequate conception of God, 518. God alone is truly simple, 602. God is ineffable and incomprehensible, 552. He is known not a little if one knows what he is not, 552, 649, epigram 61.

God is good, not as other good things are, but above them, 486. For this reason he is called the only good, ibid. All other good things come from him, ibid. God beholds all things simultaneously, 921.

God is unchangeable, 378. By God’s omnipotence all things are preserved and continue to exist, 583. God alone is greatest and omnipotent, 524. God knows all things from eternity, 349, 637, epigram 40. Nothing is new to God’s eternal wisdom, 551, 647, epigram 57. God is merciful and just, 519.

How God is in heaven, 426. By God’s presence a human being is enlightened, 585. No place is without God, 500, 576. God is merciful and just in retribution, 421.

His will concerns the salvation of all, 863. The Apostle’s statement about this must be understood fully, ibid. Why he has withheld certain matters from human knowledge, 866. His eternal will is the cause of every good, 882. He leaves none of the faithful who have not departed from him, 898. He has ordained the ruin of no one, ibid. His foreknowledge embraces all times but is contained by none, 921. It does not compel the will, 922.

For God no good is impossible and no evil incurable, 389. God dispenses all things for his glory, 647, epigram 58. How great a good God is appears from the fact that no one who departs from him fares well: every pleasure is disturbed by fear; and if it is not felt, that is a greater misery, 586.

To remember his word is for God to fulfill his promise, 444. God is patient because he is omnipotent and eternal, 817, verse 795 and following. God’s knowledge embraces past, present, and future, 921. No necessity compels us to sin, 922.

God’s mercy is not to be criticized either by those to whom it has not been granted or by those to whom it has been granted, 165, verse 678 and following. It is criticized only by those who, as far as they can, undermine grace by attributing the primary distinction between the good and the wicked to free will, ibid., verse 684.

God knows when he makes something known to others, 499. To those who are not watchful, God seems to sleep, 466. God is affected neither by leisure nor by work, 563. God provides for the earth through heaven, and for the little ones through their elders, 427. How God is called our mercy, 515. How God is asked to remember, 381.

God is to be praised in all things, 779, verses 113 and 144. God himself accomplishes what he promises, 550, 641, epigram 45. God alone is infinite and eternal, 791, verse 175 and following. How memory and forgetfulness are spoken of with reference to God, 558. God, who is everywhere, can be found in every place by one who seeks him, 770.

God chastises in order to spare, 521. To whom God is near and from whom he is far away, 498. God’s marvelous goodness and love toward human beings, 515. All things are present to God, 512. God makes good use of the evil works of human beings, when human beings turn God’s good works into instruments of their own malice, 394.

God’s magnificence is shown in the free remission of sins, 419. God governs the world he created without weariness, 791, verse 151 and following. It is not to be judged in the same way as the government of human beings, ibid., verse 159 and following.

God is the glory of his people, 400. God has assumed toward us the role of a father and therefore arranges all things mercifully, 390. God is the creator of all, 499. God is to be seen through faith, so that afterward he may be seen in direct vision, 466. God’s first and later things, 466. How God is refuge, protector, and deliverer, 515.

God condemns no one unjustly and frees no one deservedly, 887. Nothing is done in God by a new disposition, 402. One departs from God not by intervals of place but by turning away of the will, 385. How great God’s patience is and toward what end it tends, 380, 543, 617, epigram 4.

God repays good for evil, 430. A person ought to thirst for God with his whole being, because God nourishes and made the whole person, 573–574. No one who does not depart from God is abandoned, nor is anyone’s ruin due to God’s decree, 898.

God’s goodness was not absent from the impious before the flood, 899. God sought grounds for pardon for the inhabitants of the Pentapolis before destroying them, but found none, 799, verse 350 and following. The causes of God’s works are unknown, though they can be known to some extent, 567, 667, epigram 91. God tolerates the wicked for the sake of the good, 899. The more subject one is to God, the more perfect one is, 952. God is all in all, 950.

His judgments are inscrutable, 863, 865, 868, 889 and following. God made all things by command and will, 487. God is properly the God of the righteous, although he is also the God of the wicked, 504. One must flee from God to God, 576. God’s counsels are hidden, 866.

How and with what fruit God is to be sought, 392, 544–545, 612, epigram 9. One approaches God not by places but by conduct, 560. Contemplation of all God’s works reveals the eternity of God’s goodness and mercy, 491. All God’s works, both natural and spiritual, are wondrous, 389. Both kinds were made in Christ, ibid. All God’s works are testimonies to his majesty and goodness, 457.

God shakes the earth when he converts sluggish and inert hearts, 425. Why God is angry temporally, 380, 544, 619, epigram 5. We are near to or far from God not by places but by our actions, 556, 663, epigram 82. How God turned the hearts of the Egyptians so that they hated his people, 395. How God is said to lead astray, 407. The tranquility of God’s vengeance, 409, 545, 623, epigram 12.

God the Father is Father and Lord to Christ: Father according to the form of God, Lord according to the form of a servant, 499. Before anyone deserts God, God does not desert him; and he often converts many deserters, 234–235. The name “gods,” when used positively, is to be understood according to grace, not according to nature, 491.

The right hand of a human being signifies love of God and desire for the things that unite one to God; the hand of this right hand signifies the power God gave believers to become children of God, 466. The right hand signifies iniquity for those who rejoice in unjust things and delight in perverse things as though they were right, 516. The right-hand things are those belonging to God and leading to God’s promises, 510. The right hand performs whatever is done for eternal life; the left signifies whatever is done for transient joys, 495. For each person, whether in good or evil, that which he places above everything else will become his right hand, 405.

The devil must be fled, not followed, 561. It is more useful to have him as an enemy than as a ruler, ibid. The devil is a dragon; although he desires to harm, he cannot inflict more temptations on anyone than he is permitted to do, 390. His food is those devoted to earthly desires and actions, 390. The devil is conquered even by those whom he had previously conquered if they place their hope in Christ and ask Christ—the one who conquered the devil—for the power to conquer, [Col. 0964] 823, verse 965 and following.

The devil’s envy against the first human being, 795, verse 279. The devil observes the movements of minds in order to tempt them from that point, 819, verse 668 and following. The devil’s pride destroyed humanity; Christ’s humility restored humanity, 552, 649, epigram 62. The devil devours those who think according to the flesh, 400.

Although the devil himself delights in crimes, he does not impose the force of crimes, 235–236. In disgraceful acts he is an assistant of enticements, not the creator of wills, 236. What is taken away from the devil is not his own but another’s, 575. The devil is the ruler of the wicked; Christ is the ruler of the faithful, 511. The devil remains to persecute the body of Christ, and Judas is not absent among false brothers, 512. What does every adversary intend? 512.

**DIDYMUS**, the Alexandrian blind man and author, 732.

The day of a human being, 428. The day of Christ’s power properly signifies eternity, 416.

The cause of the differences that exist among human beings is hidden, 910–911.

**Difficulties of doing good.** Why God does not prevent the difficulties suffered by the faithful in doing good, 404.

Love of God often withers through love of the world, 898. What is to be loved, and how, 568. Nothing is to be loved except what is from God, 947. This is the true purity of the soul, ibid. and 948. Love that clings to God will itself be the voice of eternal praise, not a noise of words, 435.

When Christ commended his love to those for whom he was about to give an undeserved life, he willed to suffer an undeserved death for them, 591. Since three things are to be loved, why are there only two commandments of charity? 566. How love of eternal things differs from love of temporal things, 581.

To love God is God’s gift: he who was not loved first loved, 623, 765. Whoever loves God does not go astray in loving himself, and advises his neighbor to love God, 566. How wicked people are to be loved, 372, 543, 618. Our love toward God is twofold: now by believing, then by seeing what we believed, 601. What is to be loved and not loved, and how, 580. What true love is, 599. God loves his gifts in us, 551, 645, epigram 56. The person truly loves himself who, in order to love God, does not love himself, 605. What kind of people God loves, 763. He loved first so that he might be loved, 458. Love of truth makes one steadfast, 464. What is rightly loved, 580. Perfect love of God, 503.

How long the flood was delayed and when it finally occurred, 899. For which sins of human beings the flood was brought, 896. The flood because of the marriage of most of the good with foreigners, 686. God did not fail the impious before the flood, 899 and following. Before the flood God warned human beings to repent, 799, verse 329 and following. Before the flood the people of God were ruled by the Spirit of God, 899.

**DIOCLETIANUS**, thirty-fourth emperor, reigns, 722. He takes Herculius Maximianus as his colleague, ibid. Diocletian’s pride, 722. Diocletian and Maximian triumph over the Parthians, 723. They lay aside the purple, ibid. Diocletian’s death, 725.

**DIOGENES’** opinion was not very modest, 286.

**DIONYSIUS**, thirteenth bishop of Alexandria, 718. **DIONYSIUS**, twenty-fourth bishop of the Roman Church, 720. **DIONYSIUS**, tyrant of Sicily, 694. **DIONYSIUS**, bishop of Corinth, 713.

**DIOSCORUS**, bishop of Alexandria, throws everything into confusion at the Council of Ephesus, absolves Eutyches, and condemns Flavian, 450.

A *diplois* is a double cloak, 414.

**Learning.** It is safer to learn than to teach, because of the temptation of vainglory, 599. We are necessarily led to learning by authority and reason, 609. In time, authority comes first; in the matter itself, reason comes first, 610.

Why the disciples did not obtain fire from heaven against the city that refused to receive Christ, 813, verse 686 and following.

It is shown that the distinction among human beings is not to be attributed to merits, 868. That God converts certain criminals at the very end of life while leaving behind others who are less evil is inscrutable, 870. It is contrary to reason that those who have been liberated solely by God’s kindness should accuse him because he has not shown the same kindness equally to all the guilty, 166, verse 167 and following.

Considering the just abandonment of unbelievers, pious and faithful servants of God are stirred to seek their liberation and mercy by humble prayer, since the sinners themselves do not seek it and even take pleasure in their misery, 166, verse 672 and following.

The cause and reason for the distinction between the elect and the non-elect is sought above the capacity of human knowledge and is unknown without diminishing faith, 95. One must not investigate why, from the whole human race, one part is chosen and the other rejected, although the same cause involves everyone, 167, verse 703 and following. Why ignorance of this does no harm, ibid., verse 709 and following. Just as formerly it did no harm not to know that all nations would be called to life, 167, verses 712 and following. Nor does it now do harm not to know when the world will end, ibid., verses 718 and following. Nor does it do harm not to know the cause of such great variety within the human race, so that although all have the same nature, one rules and another serves, etc., ibid., verses 721 and following. Although the causes of so many evident variations remain hidden, no one nevertheless accuses God, their author, on account of them, [Col. 0965] 169, verse 740 and following.

The cause of God’s distinction is not to be investigated, 874. What God wished to remain hidden is not to be investigated; what he made manifest is not to be neglected, 874. The hidden reason for this inequality, 895. In distinguishing the good from the wicked, God’s justice does not err, 571.

To those asking about God’s distinction, the answer is given in the Gospel concerning the laborers in the vineyard and in the Apostle, Romans 9:22, 870–871. Why God exempts certain things from common causes, 890. The cause of the distinction among infants is a profound mystery, 908–909. How it can be known to some extent, 909. What instruction can be drawn from this judgment concerning infants, 909.

The distinction between the good and the wicked belongs to God alone, 571. Among the faithful there are various degrees of God’s gifts, not according to merits but according to God’s hidden and just judgment, 919. The inscrutability of the distinction between the good and the wicked, 886. The distinction among infants is not a just cause for complaint but a great commendation of divine justice and grace, 912. Why God has mercy on some and not on others is hidden, 868. The reason for the distinction is hidden; the distinction itself is not hidden, 868.

The rich are stewards of the poor, 938. Who the Christian rich are and what riches they seek, 576. The rich of this world are not accused because of their wealth but because of their perverse love of perishable things, 517. Who is the rich poor person? 578. The riches of iniquity make people needy; where true riches are found, 555, 659, epigram 78. When contempt for riches is perfect, 591–592. Here arrogance must be avoided, ibid. Earthly wealth is better retained than proudly abandoned, 592.

**Teaching.** Why the Father does not teach everyone to come to Christ, 31. The school of God the Father is very hidden, 31. Although grace is freely given, exhortation is nevertheless necessary, 73. It has been granted to very few to receive the teaching of salvation without the ministry of any human being, 73.

God teaches through the incarnate Word, 595. God teaches us to do his will when, through grace, he fulfills it in us, 514. God’s teaching not only commands what is to be done but assists so that it may be done, 464. Spiritual teaching is distinguished from the transgression of the teacher, 473. All teaching of this age passes away, 386.

A certain measure of teaching has always been applied to all human beings, 901. Although this teaching is more sparing and hidden in grace, it is sufficient for some as a remedy and for others as a testimony, ibid. and 902. Apostolic teaching is suited to instructing everyone, 386, 544, 621, epigram 8.

The deception by which the Egyptians were deceived by the Hebrews is to be referred not to God’s command but to his permission; although it may be thought to have contained something of justice, 396. The snares of the wicked are called “ropes,” 504.

To know the Lord belongs to few, 439, 546. The true God and Lord commands nothing that benefits himself, 549, 637, epigram 39. Who is truly lord of his own things? 571. Like a good physician, the Lord refreshes his servants at the proper time with health-giving food, whether he judges that harsh or gentle treatment should be applied, 520.

**DOMITIANUS**, ninth emperor, reigns, 706. His wife is Augusta, ibid. He forbids the making of eunuchs, ibid. He expels astrologers from Rome and sends many senators into exile, 707. He triumphs over the Dacians and Germans, 707. Domitian forbids vines to be planted in cities, 707. Domitian’s pride, 707. His cruelty, ibid. Domitian orders himself to be called Lord and God, 707. Domitian’s fury is confounded by the glorious end of the martyrs, 904. All Domitian’s decrees are annulled by the senate, 768.

**DOMNUS**, fourteenth bishop of Antioch, 720.

The inner house of God, 434–435. The house of God is built and guarded by the Spirit of God, 474, 549. Those inhabit the house of God who persevere in the Lord, 482.

**DONATUS**, from whom the Donatists derive their name, at first a schismatic and later a heretic, 726. They rebaptize Catholics, ibid.

**Gifts of God.** The measures of God’s gifts have not at all times been equal among all generations or human beings, 895. The cause of every gift is God’s mercy, 514. The good use of natural gifts is God’s gift, 880. The withdrawal of natural gifts serves to correct those who use them badly, 896. At the judgment those will be condemned who have not increased God’s gift, although they preserved it, 894.

**DRUSUS’** death, 702.

The beginning of the Twelve Tables, 694.

**THE CHURCH**, the whole house of David, 468. In the Church is the spiritual seed of Abraham, 406. The Church will remain until the end of the age, 377. The Church is gathered not only from the Jews but also from the nations, 215. It is to be spread throughout the whole world, 221. The Church is founded upon Christ, 384.

The Church is Jerusalem: in the union of all the saints, one house, one temple, and one city, built by the Lord until the end of the world, 474. The Church is to be covered by an abyss of persecutions, so that the oppression of the persecutors may be raised even above the most eminent of the saints, 385. The Church is in the light throughout the whole world, 389. Each day the Church grows into the temple of God, 376.

There is such peace in the Church that it can be nothing other than what belongs to all, since it has been possessed by individuals, 938. In Noah’s ark and in the sheet appearing in Peter’s vision, every kind of human being is shown to be gathered into the unity of the Church, 386. The Church is the body of Christ and the mother of all the fathers and all the children, 378. The Church is not diminished in the elect but in the reprobate, 407, 545, 621, epigram 11.

The Church is the body of Christ and one human being, with one heart and one soul in one faith, 382. With God granting victory, the Church grew through its sufferings, 464. Amid the storms and waves of the world, with Christ at the helm, the course of the Churches is safe, 390. The whole Church, composed of people of different ranks, has one body and one subject of praise for God, 529–530.

All the children of the Church recognize themselves in the present life as bound by a kind of captivity and receive consolation from the hope of future freedom, 526. Outside the Church there is neither blessing nor sanctification, 526. Christ made one thing out of many in the Church, 486. Christ protected the Church amid persecutions, 433.

The Church is Zion; Zion is the heavenly Jerusalem and the city of God, whose better part has always remained with its author and awaits the other part, 483. The perpetuity of the Church, 451. The Church arose from the beginning of the human race and was absent from no generation, 461. In the Church, the person who does not labor for its progress but seeks his own honor is diminished, 469.

Christ is present in the Church until the end of the age, 414. How he praises God in the midst of many, ibid. The whole Church with Christ is one human being, whose special task at every time is to bless the Lord, 378. One people from Jews and nations, coming together into one flock under one shepherd, 432. How much God loves the Church, and how freely he loves it, 483.

The Church recalls the Babylonian dispersion into its own unity, 901. Its prayers for all, according to apostolic tradition, 275. The growth of the Church is prophesied in the Psalms, 427. The Church, like Eve from the side of sleeping Adam, comes forth from Christ after his death, 593.

The Church, attacked by the impious from the beginning, has never been conquered; through the sufferings and deaths of its members, its crowns and triumphs have increased, 477. The Pelagians taught that in the present age the Church exists only in the righteous, 55. The universal Church is shaken by every innovation, 262. The Church bears the form of a widow, 483.

Those who despise God’s commandments hate the Church, 477. In the Church there are stones and dust, 376. The Church is the earth of God, the field of God, and the Church of God, 411. The virtue of the Church is charity; by this it is great and from this it grows, 468.

The Church awaits the day of Christ’s coming, 450. There is no place of worship except in the Catholic Church, 482. The Church still fears, but hopes, 448. The Church is to be spread throughout the whole world, 96. The Church’s various enemies exercise its patience or wisdom and its benevolence, 565.

The Church of Saint Agileus, 756.

**ELEAZAR**, high priest of the Hebrews, 680. **ELEAZAR**, brother of Samon, becomes high priest, 695.

All the elect—Jacob and Israel—learn that all God’s judgments are just, 528. The name “elect” is used of the good and the wicked, 507.

We were chosen and predestined not because we were going to be holy, but so that we might be holy, 43. God chose the righteous not because he foresaw that they would become such by themselves, but because he predestined them to become such, 43. God works so that we may exist for the praise of God’s glory, 44. How God chose the rich in faith, 42.

The other peoples, in comparison with the elect, appear rejected, but they have never been deprived of manifest and hidden benefits, 891. This is demonstrated from the passage in Acts, ibid. The manner of God’s working in the elect, since they were chosen even for the purpose of working, 922.

No one would say that God’s promise concerning the elect is either unfulfilled or fulfilled by someone other than the one who made the promise, 873. The promises made to all and to the whole people concern the elect alone, 861 and following. They signify God as truthful, 851. The fullness and universality of the elect, 860 and following.

The election of the good is from God, 879. God’s election does not waver, 917 and following. It does not remove the diligence of prayer and action, 921 and following. The future election of the nations was once hidden and later became known, 97. Neither faith itself precedes election and calling, 44. Predestination and election proceed from God’s good pleasure, 43. The calling of the elect proceeds from God’s purpose, 44.

God elected before the foundation of the world those whom he predestined, 43. Election from the world, or calling, presupposes election before the foundation of the world, 42. It is manifest in infants that the election of those who are to be saved cannot be traced back to the merits of the human will, 875. Nor can it be attributed to chance, ibid.

No one is secure concerning his election before the end of life, and no one’s restoration is to be despaired of, 924. The election of those who are to be saved was made from eternity, 921.

The fruit of almsgiving is eternal, 473. The only thing not lost is what is spent on a work of piety, 556. [Col. 0967]

**ELIACHIM**, or Eliasib, high priest, 694.

**ELIJAH** withheld the rain and caused fire to descend from heaven, 819, verse 68 and following.

Eloquence without wisdom is to be avoided, 580. God’s utterance becomes established in the heart when what is commanded is done, 442. The utterance of our tongue is Jerusalem’s song, 495.

**EMPEDOCLES**, philosopher, 694.

The error of the Encratites, 714. From whom it arose, ibid.

**ENNIUS**, poet, 696. He dies and is honorably buried, 697.

The pseudo-synod of Ephesus is condemned, 751.

The Epicureans, who deny providence because the good suffer adversity here while the wicked experience every prosperity, are refuted, 813, verse 721 and following.

**EPIDAURUS**, founded, 688.

The duty of bishops is to teach, 260–261. Certain bishops are censured who, having been elevated too quickly from the lay state, do not know their rights and duties, 261. Letter of the African bishops to Zosimus, 320. How they reconcile freedom with the assistance of grace, 320–321. Pelagian bishops are expelled from the episcopate and excommunicated, 309.

**Epitaph.** An epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies, 197. The Nestorian heresy is the daughter and yet the mother of the Pelagian heresy, ibid. Both are condemned by the same judgment, 199. Whoever contends that grace was given to Christ according to merits or is given to Christians according to merits is guilty of both, 199.

**ERISICHTHON** builds the temple of Apollo at Delphi, 689.

**ERON**, bishop of Antioch after Ignatius, 708.

**Error.** Error does so much harm that it is advantageous to err, 165, verses 675–676. It matters how much and in what things one errs, and how readily one corrects oneself or with what obstinacy one attempts to defend one’s error, 76. The errors contained in Cassian’s definitions are collected in summary, 362 and following.

**ESAU**, also called Edom, from whom the Idumeans derive their name, 688.

**ESBON**, judge, 690.

Who receive the food of life, 596.

**ESDRAS**, priest, 694.

To be with God, 552, 651, epigram 64.

Daily reception of the Eucharist, 55. Separation from the Eucharist when a more serious offense intervenes, ibid.

**EUCROCIA** is punished as guilty of Priscillian’s error, 736.

A statue of **EUDOXIA**, 739. Eudoxia dies, ibid.

**EUFRATES**, philosopher, 707.

**EUNOMIUS**, from whom the Eunomian heresy derives its name, 732.

**EURIPIDES** is renowned, 693.

**EUSEBIUS**, bishop of Laodicea, 721. **EUSEBIUS**, companion of Pamphilus, and how far he carried his history, 725. **EUSEBIUS**, twenty-ninth bishop of Rome, 723. **EUSEBIUS**, bishop of Vercelli, 727. The return of Eusebius from exile, 730. Eusebius of Vercelli dies, 732.

**EUSTATHIUS**, twenty-third bishop of Antioch, 726. He is driven into exile by the Arians, ibid. **EUSTATHIUS**, presbyter of Constantinople, 726.

**EUTYCHIANUS**, twenty-sixth bishop of Rome, 722.

**EUTYCHIUS**, a Spaniard and martyr for the faith, 746.

**EUTROPIUS**, consul, is soon deprived of both honor and life, 738.

**EVAGRIUS**, a monk distinguished for holiness, 738.

The Gospel was to be heard by all nations, 96. The Gospel of Christ’s cross was sent to all human beings without exception, 888. The Gospel of truth cannot be overcome by any persecution, 508. Everything that ends and passes away is small, 377.
