## F

**FABIANUS**, nineteenth bishop of Rome, 718. Fabianus is crowned with martyrdom, 719. **FABIUS** succeeds Babylas at Antioch, 719. The foundation of the earthly and heavenly structure is different, 557, 558. Fables of vain opinions narrated by the wicked, 450. Yet there is nothing useful in them, as there is in the law of the Lord, 450. “Face” is used for “presence,” 392. The price of a good reputation, 580. Famine, the destructive condition caused by starvation, 394. How it is called by God, ibid. Fate has been rejected even by many non-Christians, 205. Nor did the Pelagians say that infants are baptized by fate, 875. Nothing happens by fate, but everything by God’s judgment, 98. Flaccilla, daughter of Arcadius, 738. Happiness is never secure, 571. Neither the happiness of this age makes us blessed, nor adversity makes us wretched, if we love the true goods, 581. Why the wicked are thought happy, and are permitted to be such, 596. Nothing is more wretched than the happiness of sinners, 549, 639, epigram 42. **FELIX**, twenty-fifth bishop of Rome, 721. **FELIX**, antipope, is substituted for Liberius by the Arians, 728. **FELIX**, master of the soldiers, 743. At his command Patroclus and the deacon Titus are killed, ibid. Felix becomes a patrician, 743. Felix is killed by Aetius together with his wife and the deacon Grunnitus, 744. The times of Pope Felix IV, 759. Scripture also calls hay “standing crops,” 396. Iron signifies the tribulation of harsh necessity, 394. **FESTUS**, successor of Felix, before whom Paul gives an account and is sent bound to Rome, 704.

Faith is a gift of God, 34, 35, 44. God works our faith in our hearts, 26. Faith is from the grace of God, 32. That faith and perseverance are gifts of God is attested by the whole Church in its prayers, 79, 80. Both faith and the salvation promised to faith are gifts of God, 35. The beginning of faith is a gift of God, 24, 25, 26, 45, 74, 75, 76 and following. No one is sufficient for himself either to begin or to perfect faith, 26. It is pride to attribute the beginning of faith to a human being, 26. A person could claim the whole work of salvation for himself, 26. When Augustine recognized that the beginning of faith is a gift of God, 75. Not only the beginning of faith but also its growth is a gift of God, 46, 52. Both perfect faith and faith in its beginning are from God’s gift, 28. Between the beginning of faith and the perfection of perseverance stand those things by which we live rightly; even these, the Semi-Pelagians agree, are granted to us by God when faith obtains them, 77, 80. Grace is not given freely if the beginning of faith comes from a human being but its increase from God, 26. Whatever precedes faith, accompanies faith, or follows faith must be attributed to God, 31. Why the gift of faith is not given to everyone, 32. The merit of faith comes from mercy, 27. Faith begins merit, but the merit of faith itself is also a gift of God, 27. Both our willing and our believing belong to us and are at the same time God’s gift, 27. From what does a person become worthy of faith? 34. Those to whom faith was not announced were foreknown as not going to believe, 34. Why the Apostle said that we are justified by faith rather than by works, 30. How the Apostle distinguishes faith from works, 30. To very few it has been granted to receive faith from the Lord or through angels, without any human preaching, 73. It is safer to entrust one’s faith, hope, and love to God’s will than to one’s own, 35. Faith is the beginning of the Christian person; martyrdom for Christ is the best end, 52. Faith is entirely a gratuitous gift: it is not from merit, since all merit comes from it, 147, verse 410 and following. This is proved by the fact that Christ came to heal the sick, not the healthy, and because baptism, received by many previously most wicked people when death was imminent, sent them to heaven, 147, verse 415 and following; 149, verses 426 and following. The only thing that can rightly be attributed to such people is that they desired baptism; but this desire arose from faith, and faith from grace, 149, verses 441 and following. Faith, which is the root of all merits, cannot itself be from merit: what is not done through it is not done well, 149, verses 445 and following. He overturns grace from its foundations who thinks that any merit can exist before faith, or that faith arises from free will rather than from God’s sheer gift, ibid., verses 452 and following. The advocates of these errors attribute to God no other beginning of human restoration than that, through the law and preachers, he suggests to the human will what it ought to do, 149, verses 459 and following. But according to this view, the will comes before grace, and grace is like a maidservant; it does not function as grace but as the law, commanding only and not giving what it commands, 151, verses 470 and following. How strongly this teaching reinforces the Pelagian heresy by teaching that the beginning of salvation, or the will to believe, arises from the natural freedom of choice, ibid., verses 479 and following. It follows from that teaching that grace is nothing other than law and teaching, and that free choice was not injured by sin, 151, verses 483 and following. And likewise whatever else Pelagius taught, such as that a person can attain salvation by his own righteousness and merit heaven, ibid., verses 493 and following. That many people pleased God by their own power from the beginning of the world without God’s grace; that the law was given when human morals had become more corrupt, so that fear alone might convert them; and that through the law what is accomplished through grace was accomplished, 153, verses 498 and following. As vices grew stronger, grace was added to the law—not because nature could not attain salvation without it, but so that it might do so more easily, 505 and following. That infants are innocent and are washed in baptism in body, not in mind, ibid., verses 513 and following.

No one believes except the one who has heard from the Father, and everyone who has heard and learned comes, 31. To believe the Gospel is a gift of God, 32. Both believing and doing good are given through the Holy Spirit, and at the same time belong to us, 27. Why it was given to some to believe and not given to others is an inscrutable judgment of God, 68. Whether a person can or cannot believe is neither beneficial nor harmful unless predestination is taken into account, 66, 67. Even if some are naturally suited to believe if certain words or deeds were presented to them, they are nevertheless not presented if they are not among the predestined, 66. It did not benefit the Tyrians that they could believe, because they were not predestined; it would not have harmed the Jews that they could not believe, if they had been predestined, 66, 67. Since it had not been given to the Tyrians to believe, even the means by which they might believe was denied them, 66. It did not benefit the Tyrians that they were able to believe, because they were not predestined by him whose judgments are inscrutable and whose ways are unsearchable, 66. Even if the Tyrians would have repented had the miracles performed in Chorazin and Bethsaida been performed among them, they will nevertheless be punished on the day of judgment, though more leniently than those cities, 60.

Faith is a gift of God because the Church prays for those who do not believe, 247. The Apostle also gives thanks to God for those who received the Gospel, ibid. And he joins peace and love to faith; consequently heretics are convicted of claiming to possess these from themselves, ibid. The remaining lesser goods as well, 248. Those who have faith have received it; those who do not have it have not received it, 248. Faith is a gift of God, 877. To be able to possess faith and love belongs to nature; to possess them belongs to gratuitous grace, whose dispensation is unsearchable, 591. Faith is God’s gift, 223. Faith is God’s gift and the foundation of the heavenly building, 251. What absurdities follow from attributing faith to free choice, 251. Those who wish to begin the building of salvation from themselves place their entire election upon shifting sand and crumbling ash, 251. Faith, from which all good merits begin, is a gift of God, lest grace cease to be grace if something precedes it for which it is bestowed, 244. The beginning of faith and the inclination to believe come through the gift of grace and are not naturally present in us, 761. If faith were possessed naturally, all who are outside the Church would be believers, ibid. What the faith of Christ is, and by whom it is not apprehended, 598. Faith is the mother of good will and righteous action, 876. The faith of Abraham, 901. Unless faith itself is from God’s gift, there will be no difference between law and grace, 855. The vigor of the Christian faith is begun through Christ’s passion, resurrection, and ascension, 572. Pelagius does not want faith to be given, so that he may persuade people that grace is owed, 245. Faith is the beginning of all merit, 879. It is itself possessed through God’s gift, ibid. It is given without being requested, so that the remaining gifts may be obtained through its requests, ibid. Faith is the beginning of prayer and merit, 344. Faith in things that are not seen, 601. Through one faith both peoples received justification, 376, 377, 378. What we heard in the books of the Jews is made manifest in the faith of the nations, 482. We must walk by faith in order to arrive at vision, 600. Faith precedes vision, 598. Faith is believing what you do not see, 598. If Adam had not lost faith, he would not have been deprived of the other goods, 244. The faith lost in Adam is not recovered except through God’s grace, 244. The Church lives by faith, 1. Faith cleanses the mind so that it may shine with the image of Christ, 803, verse 460 and following. Human reason is insufficient for faith and love of God, 854, 855 and following. Faith and truth are victorious in the holy martyrs, 903. This arose from the love that the Holy Spirit had kindled, which often converted the persecutors themselves, 903. Paul’s faith was recognized by the early teachers of the Church as a gift of God, 856, 857. Those who did not believe after hearing the Gospel became more inexcusable; nevertheless, in God’s foreknowledge they were not sons of Abraham, 859. Faith is not from human wisdom but from divine inspiration, 878. The unity and harmony of right faith are from God, 878. Faith and conversion are from God, 92. Faith, works, and perseverance in them are from God, 218. Faith is a gift of grace in all the saints, both in those who lived before Christ’s coming and in those who lived afterward, 765. This is proved from Scripture, 766. Faith is from God, 876. It is the mother of good will and good action, ibid. It must not be attributed to diversity of intellect, 901, 902. The faith by which one comes to Christ is inspired by God, 914. Faith is the foundation of the holy building, 49. Persecutors sought to overturn it, ibid. Faith is the beginning of good, 871. Faith is shown to be from grace, 353. Before faith everyone is under sin and a child of wrath, 81, 872. From where the spirit of faith comes in a person, 877. Faith is given according to measure, at the discretion of the giver, 878. Initial faith is imperfect in some, 897. The increase of faith and grace must be requested, 438. Those who are in the faith of the holy fathers throughout the world are counted in the honor of heirs, 483. Captives draw their masters to the faith, 920.

**Fidelis.** Few believers among the Gentiles in the time of the old law; unbelievers are without excuse, 901. To the faithful, earth is despised and heaven lies open, 777, verse 62 and following. The whole salvation and entire endurance of the faithful must be referred to God, from whom they come, 470, 548, 633, epigram 33. The confidence of those who hope rests on the mercy of God, who denies none of his gifts to those who have been corrected, 479, 480. Confidence in God alone, even when he gives help through angels or human beings, 432.

The Son of God, begotten by the Father and consubstantial with the Father, does everything with the Father, 677, epigram 105. The Son has life as the Father does, not by participation but by being born, 595, 677, epigram 105. To say that the Son was taught by the Father means the same as to say that he was begotten, 452, 598. He is more readily understood to have learned from the Father according to the form of a servant, 452. The Son, and not the Father, is said to judge because he alone will appear to all in human form, 595. Why he says to the Son in Psalm 108, “Deal with me,” and why no more should be added, 413. How the Son will also be subject to the Father in the future, 606. The sons of Abraham, the sons of promise, throughout the world, 393. The sons of promise, the reward of faith and the spiritual seed of Abraham, are altogether saved, 857, 858. Scriptural testimonies concerning them, 858 and following. They receive knowledge of the supreme God through the instruction of the teacher, ibid. The sons of the Church conceived in the womb of faith, 474. The elect and the reprobate in the Church, to be distinguished after death, 474. It is not in human power but in God’s power that people receive the power to become sons of God, 59. The sons of those put to death, the sons of martyrs who, 377. The sons of the righteous, who are better understood, 381.

The end of good and evil, 565. The end of human life in this life is to merit eternal life, 775, verse 41 and following. Christ is the end of the faithful, 572. God’s scourges do not remove hope but increase it, 443. What benefit God’s scourges provide, and why both the righteous and the unrighteous are scourged by God, 582. The exile of Flavia Domitilla, 707. Flavianus, bishop of Constantinople, killed by the Eutychians, 749. Flavianus, driven into exile by the Eutychians, is killed on the way, 750. **Flere.** The time of weeping is the time of sowing, 473. **FLORIANUS**, thirty-first emperor, 721. He is killed, ibid. A decree of alliance between the Romans and Athenians with the Jews is sent, 699. Fortitude is from God, 879. In God are strength and praise, lest we fall, 433. True strength of spirit in hardships, 551, 645, epigram 52. Flight during persecutions is permitted, 510. Flight perishes in the person who prefers to endure every cruelty rather than yield, 510. **GEMINUS**, Alexandrian presbyter, 717. The groaning of spiritual people living among the carnal, 465. The groaning of every faithful person concerning the earthly dwelling, 494. Even in time of peace the good groan while the wicked prevail, 787, verse 60 and following; 788, verse 77 and following. “Generation and generation” signifies the whole human race, 518. The repetition of “generation” indicates both the present age and the future one, 520. One human generation is that in which people are born into the world; another is that in which they are reborn to God, 489. In both, under the supreme judgment of God, the work of nature and the work of grace are fulfilled, ibid.

The nations are often indicated in Scripture by the name of beasts, 386. The promise of blessing all nations is fulfilled daily in such a way that neither those who perish have a just excuse nor those who are saved have grounds to boast of their own righteousness, 917. The minds of the nations are like forests, 482. The alternation of illumination or abandonment among the nations and the Jews is inscrutable, 874, 875. Concerning Gentiles who do what belongs to the law without the law, 332. From all the nations one people understands that it is delivered from eternal destruction not by its own merits but by God’s grace, 528.

After **GEORGE** is killed by the people, Athanasius is restored to his see, 730. **GERMANUS**, bishop of Antissiodorum, defeats the Pelagians in Britain, 744. The sword of truth strikes the whole world, 493. A sword that is kind and one that is evil, 516.

**Boasting.** We must boast not in merits but in God, 38, 943. Whoever does not boast in the Lord, I do not hesitate to say, possesses whatever else he has in vain, 80. The Lord’s Prayer itself shows that one must boast in God alone, 57. Whatever praiseworthy thing is found in a creature returns to the glory of him who works all things in all, 518. Since everything is possessed from God, one must boast in nothing except God, 579, 763.

The Gnostics: from where they received their name, 710. They were called “Cœnosi” and “Borboritae” because of their shamefulness, ibid. **GOLIATH** represents the devil, and David represents Christ, including in his body, which is the Church, 514, 516.

**Grace.** The Catholic position on grace, 38. What must be held concerning grace, 80. Whether it teaches everyone or not, 31, 32. What God promises that human beings will do, he himself causes them to do, 34. The power and efficacy of divine grace, 31. From where the force and effectiveness of grace arise, 32, 45. We will, but God works willing in us; we act, but God works in us both the willing and the acting, 65. Grace is rejected by no hardened heart, 13. It is given precisely so that hardness of heart may be removed, ibid. Grace removes the heart of stone—that is, the will made utterly hard and inflexible against God, 31. The grace of God properly distinguishes the good from the evil, 29. The nature and force of grace are recognized from prayer, 38. Now it belongs solely to God’s grace that we approach God and do not depart from him, 57. True grace of God could be defended even if, as Pelagius wished, there were no original sin, 63. When grace is at issue, everything must be attributed to God, 56, 57. We live more securely if we give everything to God rather than entrusting ourselves partly to him and partly to ourselves, 56.

Pelagius also condemned the giving of grace according to merits at the Palestinian synod, denying that grace is given according to merits, 25, 64. At the Palestinian episcopal judgment Pelagius was compelled to condemn those who say that grace is given according to merits, lest he himself be condemned, 76. Some think they are restrained from every pursuit of piety unless they assign to themselves something that they first give so that it may be repaid to them, 36. Grace is given freely, 58. Grace is not given according to merits, 39, 65, 77, 79. Grace for beginning and for persevering to the end is not given according to merits, 65. Grace is the effect of God’s mercy, not the reward of the human will, 61. Merits do not precede grace, 27. To say that grace is given according to merits is to deny grace, 75. Grace is defended without merits even if there were no original sin, 63. From infants it is most aptly inferred both that grace is not given according to merits and that no one is punished except for his own merits, 62. By the same grace through which Christ was made, the Christian person is made, 40. There are outstanding examples of grace and predestination in infants and in Christ, 36. How hidden grace is and how far removed from the senses, 31. Why grace is not given to all, 32. Why, if grace is given freely, it is not given to all, 63. It does not happen by fate that some infants are helped and others are not, 64. God’s judgments in the distribution of grace are inscrutable, 38, 63, 64. It is inscrutable why God frees or punishes one rather than another, 58. God is not unjust when he does not give grace to all, or gives it to one rather than another, 58. Grace is given according to the good pleasure of God’s will, 63.

Before Pelagius, interpreters of Scripture touched only briefly on the difficult questions concerning grace, 58. Why Augustine did not deal with grace, predestination, and so forth in his books On Free Choice, 62. Augustine is wrongly challenged in the question of grace by appeal to the books On Free Choice, 64. Augustine himself answers the objection drawn from those books, 64. Grace works not merely by teaching but by effectively changing the mind, ibid., verses 335 and following. This cannot be accomplished by law, preaching, or nature left to itself, ibid., verses 334 and following. Grace causes faith to take root in hearts, to sprout, grow, mature, be preserved, and persevere to the end, ibid., verse 347 and following.

The Son of Man did not come to choose the righteous but to save sinners and the ungodly, 527. God’s grace is so powerful that it can make even the long-standing ice of hearts grow warm through heavenly fire, 527. The example is Paul, who was made a preacher of the Gospel from a persecutor, ibid. God’s prevenient grace does not remove freedom but heals it, 276. Thanksgiving for all people proves that all good works are divine works, 275, 276. If anything praiseworthy or joyful is done by a human being, it is God’s work and the gift of his grace, 391. Whoever praises God in the saints confesses grace, because they are holy through his sanctification, 532. In those things that are done throughout the body of the world by God’s command and will, one must understand what he works in human beings themselves, 487. Every holy thought and movement of a pious will is from God, through whom we can do some good and without whom we can do nothing; this is proved from a passage of Pope Zosimus, 274.

Grace is oil, 387. Works of righteousness come not from nature but from grace, 213. Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to Christ, 32. Christ gave the law through a servant, while he himself descended with grace, 592. In the created human being there was the power not to depart from God, 57. Now it belongs solely to God’s grace that we approach God and do not depart from him, 957. The helps of divine grace are supports of the human will, 356. From the example of the farmer, whose entire labor is useless unless God helps, it follows that the beginning of all acts and thoughts is from God, 284, 285. It is an unjust complaint against God that he does not free everyone through grace from the destruction so universally deserved that he could justly have freed no one, 163, verse 159.

Authorities supporting the necessity of grace, 91. There is nothing in a human being worthy of love that is not from God, 647, epigram 56. The virtue of the pious should not be valued less because they receive it entirely from Christ, just as the heavenly glory of the saints should not be valued less because they possess it entirely from God, who is all things in all of them, 185, verse 954 and following. Much less should we be troubled to acknowledge that in this valley of tears we can do nothing good except through grace; this does not remove freedom but restores and redeems it, so that whatever a person does rightly is attributed not to that person but to the grace of Christ, 187, verses 973 and following.

Grace is entirely gratuitous, especially as revealed in infants who die after baptism, 94, 95. God’s grace is wholly rejected unless it is wholly received, 939. In what sense what the Holy Spirit works in us is ours, 945 and following. The preaching of grace does not dissolve the pursuit of virtue, as the Semi-Pelagians objected. On the contrary, without grace there is no work of virtue; by grace alone human minds are made capable of and inflamed for right living, 187, verses 986 and following. Enemies of grace are those who want what is given freely to belong to injustice unless it is referred to retribution, 247. Grace has been withdrawn in no age, 892. The necessity of grace for all good things, 213. This follows from the decree of the bishops, which the whole world embraced, 213. It is wrongly objected that free choice is destroyed by God’s grace, 97 and following.

Cassian began to introduce the definition that many come to grace without grace, 313. The necessity of grace for overcoming temptations, 272. With God’s help we conquer; without him we are conquered, 273. Grace generates the affection of believing and willing in free choice, 91. How greatly faithful men must beware of the enemies of grace, 171, verse 767 and following. Initial grace is identified by the Semi-Pelagians with nature itself, 4. Whoever maintains that some can come to the grace of baptism through free choice is alien from the right faith, 762. Every day what some lose through merit others receive through the gift of grace, 489. Innumerable testimonies of Scripture prove grace, 766. God’s first grace is to teach us humility, 557. Two gifts or functions of grace, 561. Right thought and good action are God’s gift, 445, 547, 629, epigram 22, 762. Grace is not given in response to invocation; rather, it causes invocation, 760. Through grace God bestows not only the fruit of good works but also the will and thought to perform them, and the entire sequence of a pious life, 187, verses 982 and following.

In past ages grace drew a few from the whole world; now it saves countless people from the entire human race, 249. Grace acts so that God’s commandments may be fulfilled through love, though they could not be fulfilled through fear, 477. The Apostle attributes the reason for the diversity of God’s grace to the depth of God’s riches and wisdom, 865, 866. Those who think they do not need to be reformed by grace have gone mad; but if they are children of the promise, they will be healed, 322. God’s grace is effective both for the remission of past sins and for help against committing future sins, 274. It is given not only so that we may know what to do but also so that we may love doing it, 274. Without God’s grace we can do nothing, much less do anything more easily, 275. Grace makes the unwilling willing, 314. The effects of grace in the soul without injury to freedom, 314. God works in us the willing and the doing of good, so that we may be fellow workers with his grace, 276.

Some who boasted of the Catholic name, although they condemned Pelagius and Coelestius, accused the holy teachers who defended grace of excess, 271. Through the grace of Christ we do not lose but recover the original honor of nature; that grace is the beginning of merits in us, and our merits increase the more as we receive grace more humbly and increase it by receiving it, 161, verse 607 and following. God’s grace is to be recognized from the quality of good works, 313. God gives constancy to the fearful and restores confidence to the terrified, 430. Leaving to God the knowledge of his secrets, we should acknowledge him alone as the author of all good, down to the smallest beginning of good will, 169, verse 754 and following. We owe it to Christ alone if we think or will anything rightly, 165, verse 694 and following. Justifying grace does not make the good better but makes the good out of the evil, 93. That grace is not given according to merits is shown by the ungodly who are converted and saved at the end of life, 869. What is sufficient for desiring is not sufficient for obeying unless it is increased, 438. The cause of every grace is God’s will, 871. The passages of Scripture brought forward to manifest grace cannot be evaded by any artifice, 888. Those who do not confess Christ working in them are separated from Christ, 944. When the Apostle was discussing the power of grace, he was overcome by the things that were impossible to explain, 865 and following. God subjects to himself through his grace those whom he wills, 886. The occasion of error concerning grace is dread of fixed and gratuitous predestination, 94. To deny the fixed number of the predestined is impious and contrary to grace, 94. Scripture declares both God’s grace and the freedom of our choice, 290 and following.

Grace is given to the elect not so that they may be idle or struck by no enemy, but so that they may work well and conquer the enemy, 922, 923. Without God’s grace nothing pertaining to eternal life can be begun, increased, or perfected, 886. Every good thought and action is God’s gift, 879, 880. The happier and more closely joined to God a person is, the more divine grace there is in that person than human action, 952. Grace is neither law nor nature; through grace the law is fulfilled and nature restored, 591, 764. The first gift of grace is to attribute no good to oneself but to grace, 939. The difference of grace according to different times, 891. Understanding and knowledge, a good word and a holy work, are from God, 943. In no matter is the operation of grace preceded by the human will, 945 and following. Grace is the glory of God, 332. Grace is altogether gratuitous, since no one acts well except the one to whom God grants the ability to act well; indeed, no one can even desire it unless grace makes itself desired, 157, verses 557 and following.

The conversions of Matthew and Paul, and likewise of Zacchaeus and the thief on the cross, are equally from grace, 323, 324, 766. Nor can the desire for healing exist without grace, 316. The necessity of grace, to which the diligence of free choice must be joined, 210. The Apostle expresses how much grace accomplishes for wills through the word “are moved,” 590. Whatever good is born in the field of the heart comes from the work and gift of the heavenly farmer, 487. The necessity of grace, 852. What grace provides for free choice, 97, 98. God’s grace, drawing daily, must be followed with humility, 285. “You did not choose me, but I chose you” applies to everyone, 355. Other passages of Scripture concerning the prevenience of grace, 355 and following. Irrefutable testimonies of Scripture prove that no human being can do anything good without grace, 944. The Semi-Pelagians’ confession of grace is feigned and insincere when they say that grace is given according to merits, 942. They are refuted, ibid.

Whatever truth and love the saints possess in this life, they possess from God; and whatever they will possess in heaven will also be from him: from him comes their portion, from whom their fullness will come, 950 and following. Gratuitous grace is proved when the ungodly are justified while the less guilty but proud are excluded from the gift of justification, 869, 870. Some try in vain to open the inscrutable depth of grace through free choice, 875. Without the help of Christ working in us we can do nothing good; free choice is not thereby removed but helped, 944 and following. If grace came from merits, the redemption by Christ’s blood would be cheapened, and the prerogative of God’s mercy would yield to human works, 869. Grace does not remove the mutability of the will, 915 and following. Hence the Lord commanded vigilance and prayer, ibid. Why both are necessary, ibid. Whoever says that grace accompanies the human will rather than leads it denies grace, 848.

General grace is given for recognizing the true God, 913. Special grace is not common to all, ibid. Although it is now bestowed more abundantly than before, its causes are known to God alone, ibid. General grace is given to all; special grace is given to the elect, 918, 919. To die for the truth is a gift of grace, 454. God’s grace precedes every human merit, 605. Grace is given so that through it new gifts may be obtained, 895. The special grace of evangelical preaching is now common to all, 920. God’s grace makes the human will spiritual, 849. The various progressions of grace, 914. Divine authorities concerning grace, 325, 326. The efficacy of grace in subjecting rebels to itself, 903. Special grace beyond general grace, both in adults and in infants, 911. Those who discuss the depth of grace must rely on three definitions, 918. The function and efficacy of grace, 913. The will is subordinated and joined to it, ibid. The will is the receiver and servant of grace, 914. God’s grace was revealed to the prophets but hidden from the nations, 906, 907 and 908. Grace heals a person even through that person, 854. The beginning of good will is from grace, 328. The gifts and works of grace vary innumerably, 897. Grace is the beginning of every merit, 871. What grace confers on a human being, 879. It is not given so that we may be idle but so that we may advance from virtue to virtue, ibid. Human diligence and cooperation are also God’s gift, 949. Grace is the principal cause of merit, 919.

The prayers of the Catholic Church to God resound with Christ’s grace, 275. The help of grace is necessary for keeping the commandments, 436. It is always necessary, ibid. One does not reach God’s promises without his help, 255. Grace does not abandon a person before the person abandons it, 220. Sound teaching concerning the complete necessity of grace, 519. Whoever asks to be heard according to God’s righteousness expresses grace, 511. Whatever help comes through ministers belongs to God, 471. Grace does not remove the power to turn toward vices, 896. Even now the same measure of grace is not bestowed on everyone, 892. It is wrongly objected that the preaching of grace denies free choice, 848. God’s grace is more manifest the harder those are whom it subjects to itself, 902. The first seeds of grace are sometimes perfect, 897. The measure of grace, 881.

**Pelagian grace**, 88. It acts toward all as teacher and substitute for the law, so that those who wish may be justified by the merit of their will, ibid. If grace is repaid according to merits and is not itself the creator of good things, it is called grace in vain, 88. What grace the Pelagians would preach, 244. Grace for satisfying the trees of the field and the cedars of Lebanon—that is, the humble and the exalted, 388.

Thanksgiving is a testimony to grace, 53. Thanksgiving is mockery if thanks are given to God for something he neither gave nor did, ibid. If one human being gave thanks to another for something that he either thought the other had not provided or knew the other had not provided, it would be called flattery or mockery rather than thanksgiving, 44. Thanksgiving for all good things is owed to God, 531. Thanksgivings are testimonies of grace, 352.

**GRATIANUS**, his birth, 739. Gratianus becomes emperor, 731. Gratianus defeats the Alamanni, 732. Gratianus reigns with Valentinian, 732. Gratianus reigns with his brother Valentinian, the forty-first emperor, 733. Gratianus is defeated and killed, 735. **GREGORIUS NAZIANZENUS**, 74. Gregory of Nazianzus dies, 735. **GORDIANUS**, twenty-third emperor, 718. He is killed by Philip, ibid.

The Goths, devastated by the Huns and received by the Romans, rebel, 733. They defeat the Romans and invade Thrace, ibid. When battle is again joined with the Romans, the Romans are slaughtered, and Valens, wounded by an arrow, is carried into a hut and burned with it, 733, 734. The Goths enter Italy, 738. The Goths enter Gaul, 739. The Goths, not keeping the peace, are attacked with the aid of the Huns, 746. Peace is again made with the Goths, 747. **GOTHOLIA** reigns, 691. **GOTHONIEL**, judge of the Hebrews, 689. For how many years, ibid. **GUNDICARIUS**, king of the Burgundians, defeated by Aetius; afterward he and his line are destroyed by the Huns, 745. **GUNTAMUNDUS**, king of the Vandals, 755. He favors the Catholics, ibid. and 756.

## H
HABITATION OF GOD in Jerusalem, that is, in the hearts of the faithful, 496. HAEMON, king in Thessaly, 688. What good heresies bring to the Church by occasion, [Col. 0975] 75. The heresies of Arius and Sabellius are cut down with two words, when Christ says: “I and the Father are one,” 597. Heretics, having become like idols, have lost all the duties of rational life, 490. They are changed daily by them, ibid. Heretics and schismatics rejected by the Church because they wished to be leaders, 407. Heretics and schismatics are struck down in the faith, which, when it separates from the charity of the Church, is extinguished, 488. Hallelujah, “Praise the Lord,” 392. HANNIBAL defects from the Romans, 696. HEBER: the confusion of languages occurred in his time because of the building of the tower of Babylon, 687. The departure of the Hebrews: at what time it was a cause of rejoicing for the Egyptians, 396. When the Hebrews were departing from Egypt, none was physically infirm, 396. The division of the kingdom of the Hebrews, 691. The rape of HELEN, 690. HELENA, Constantine’s mother: in what sense she is called the concubine of Constantius by Jerome and Prosper, 724 n. HELENOPOLIS, formerly called Drepana, restored by Constantine, 725. ELI, the priest, 690. HELVIUS PERTINAX reigns XVI, already an old man, 715. HERACLAS, XII bishop of Alexandria, 717. HERACLIUS, the eunuch who had bound Valentinian’s mind to himself, 752. He stirs him up to the murder of Aetius, ibid. Enmity between Valentinian and Aetius, instigated by Heraclius the eunuch, 752. Heraclius is killed together with Valentinian, 753. HERACLIUS, bishop, subscribes to the Second Council of Orange, 767. HERACLIANUS deprived of his consulship and of his life, 740. HERACLITUS, the philosopher, 694. HERCULES overcomes Antaeus, 689. The age of Hercules, 690. HERCULIUS MAXIMIAN, Diocletian’s imperial colleague, suppresses the Bagaudae and restores peace to Gaul, 722. He is killed, 724. HERMOGENES is killed by the people at Constantinople, 727. Hermon: when the river is exalted, Christ is understood, 485. HERMON, XXXVIII bishop of Jerusalem, 723. HEROD, a foreigner, assumes the rule of the Jews, 699. The prophecies of Jacob and Daniel are fulfilled, ibid. Herod founds Tiberias and Libiada, 701. Herod builds Sebaste and Panion, and calls the Tower of Strato Caesarea, 700. Herod kills Hyrcanus and others, 700, 701. Herod kills the infants and, two years later, dies miserably but deservedly, 701. HERODOTUS, the historian, 694. HEROS V, bishop of Antioch, 712. HEROS, bishop of Arles, driven from his see, 739. JEROME is born, 726. His books against Pelagius, 121, verse 55 and following. “Graceful in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin speech,” ibid., verse 54. Jerome wrote the books of the Dialogues against the Pelagians, 121, verse 58. Jerome the presbyter continued the history of Eusebius, 725. Jerome withdraws to Bethlehem, 735, 736. Jerome dies, 741. HILARY of Poitiers, bishop, driven by the Arians into Phrygia, 729. He composes books on religion, ibid. Hilary returns to Gaul, 730. Gaul condemns Arian impiety through Hilary’s efforts, 730. Hilary dies, 731. HILARY of Arles, bishop, 8. HILARY the Gaul who sent a letter to Augustine indicates that he is a layman and a disciple of Augustine, 18. He requests books of Retractions and the book On Grace and Free Will, 18. Hilary preserved the respect due to certain people of Massilia and did not cease to contend for the truth as far as he was able, 18. HILARY, a deacon exiled for the faith, 729. Hilary the deacon, legate of Pope Leo to the Ephesian synod, 450. He contradicts all the bishops who had assented to the heresy and flees, ibid. HILDRIC, king of the Vandals, 756. He favors the Catholics, ibid. HIPPOCRATES, the physician, 694. HIPPOLYTUS, a distinguished writer, 717. Historical actions narrated in the Psalms are forms of spiritual realities, 514. HOMER, the poet, 691. HUMAN BEING, the image of God but subject to vanity, 557. God’s work is not only the first human being, but also each individual human being every day, 448, 583. The first human being was created without fault and, if he had wished, able to persevere in the good; by free choice he departed from the good, 328. The first human being is Adam, and how Christ is called the second, 588. What was disclosed in the first and second human beings, 578. The creation of humanity is good, although humanity is born subject to sin, 589. The dignity of the human being is great, 515. How human beings after the fall differ from their first parent, 795, verse 267 and following. For what purpose the human being is sufficient to himself, 559. Nature does not distinguish one human being from another, but grace distinguishes the faithful from the unbeliever, [Col. 0976] 246. The voluntary diversity of human beings arises from each person’s pursuit, and another diversity from condition, 857. It must not be ascribed to fate or the stars, but to God’s will, who did not wish the cause of this matter to become known because it was not fitting, ibid. This is proved from the Scriptures, ibid. The carnal human being is foreign soil, incapable of sacred seed, 495. What the human being possesses from himself and what from God, 592, 764. The miserable human being amid both the prosperity and the adversities of the world: adversity oppresses, prosperity deceives, 428. Humanity lost natural possibility through Adam, 271. All things were created for the sake of humanity, but humanity itself for God, 795, verse 258 and following. How little the things remaining to humanity after the fall are to be valued, 181, verse 905 and following. Whence and how far humanity has been cast down through sin, 608. God orders the original differences among human beings by a hidden judgment, 866. The creation of humanity, 793, verse 218 and following. Humanity must neither become proud nor despair, 381. Since one belongs to another, a human being cannot bargain concerning himself, 770. The honor due to authorities, 471, 472. Provided that they do not turn people away from the worship of God, ibid. Mutual honor strengthens love, 935.

HONORIUS is born, 735. Honorius is appointed ruler, 737. Honorius reigns XLV with Theodosius, 739. The triumph of Honorius over Attalus, 741. Honorius dies, 742. The hour of the Lord’s Passion came not by fate but by God’s ordination, 604. HORACE FLACCUS is born, 698.

The excellence of human nature consists in the fact that it can cleave to God, and that apart from him it can fare only badly, 585. The excellence of human nature is to be assessed from the state in which Adam was before sin, 795, verse 267 and following.

HUMBLE. The truly humble despise worldly glory and riches, 936. The humble advance in wisdom and understanding, 936. What true humility is, 555. Humility is never without the fountain of grace, 385. Humility is the drink of maternal milk, 480. How necessary it is, ibid. Great happiness lies in true humility, to which God is everything and in which there is participation in future blessedness, 950. Humility is the virtue that joins together, 938. On humility: a letter to Demetrias, 913 and following. The rich are not excluded from humility, 937 and following. Those who do not cease to be exalted do not cease to be destroyed, 418. But those who are humbled through Christ are restored, ibid. Description of humility and its first degree, 935. The progress of humility, 936. Humility heals what pride wounded, 524. Humility is beautiful in outward things and much more splendid in the inward parts, 935. Not every form of humility is to be praised, ibid. But voluntary humility is, ibid. True humility consists in a complete and unbroken confession of grace, 939. The first good of humility is to preserve love and concord among human beings, 935. The faithful soul rejoices not in its own strength but in God’s help, 471. Humility is the unconquerable strength of all the virtues, 947. How true humility is distinguished from false, ibid. Not only the poor but also the rich can be adorned with Christian humility, 937. The matter is established by examples, ibid. The dignity of humility is to refer everything to God, 944. Through humility the human being is truly subjected and united to God, 947. Christ crushes the heads when he makes the humble out of the proud, 418. He makes all the saints, although differing in other matters as children of the Church, equal in humility, 938. Those who have been humbled and have spent the time of their present life in tears of tribulation are to be exalted, 474. Through confession of humility, the one who does not fail in tribulation becomes powerful, 509. Through humility there is a stairway to sublime things, 610. How God teaches the just to humble themselves, 390, 391. The usefulness of humility, 407, 408. Christ is the model of descent for all the faithful, 465. Humility is to be pursued in all the virtues, 480. Through humility one reaches glory, 474. Punitive humility is prepared for the proud, 488.

HUNERIC, king of the Vandals, 755. His persecution of the Catholics, ibid. The Huns are defeated in the East, 748. HYGINUS presides over the Roman Church VIII, 711. HYMENAEUS, XXXVII bishop of Jerusalem, 720. Hyperbolical statements, 396. A hymn is a song by which God is praised, 530. All the saints who are the true Israel use this, ibid. HYRCANUS, going to Ptolemy, is honorably received, 696. What occasioned great calamities for the Jews, ibid. Hyrcanus is appointed high priest of the Jews by Gnaeus Pompey, 698.

## I

Those who worship idols are like ravens, 525. The young ravens call upon God; when their parents do not call upon God, posterity believed what antiquity had not known, 526. Worshipers of idols are like dreamers, 573. All who do not know the true God and resist the Gospel of Christ are worshipers of idols, 489. IGNATIUS II, bishop of Antioch, 705. The martyrdom of Ignatius of Antioch, 708. [Col. 0977] The fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth is the love of God, 854. Ignorance and difficulty belong to the misery of just condemnation, 62. Even if ignorance and difficulty were humanity’s natural beginnings, God would still not be blameworthy but praiseworthy, 63. Although it has been granted, by way of supposition, to the Manichaeans that ignorance and difficulty are not punishments of nature, faith concerning original sin must nevertheless be defended against the Pelagians, 63. Ignorance is either sin or the punishment of sin, 590. How ignorance does not excuse sin, 590. ILIUM, founded by Ilus, 690. The image of God in the human mind, 595. In what the imitation of Christ is to be pursued, 558. Those who give counsel command; those who are advised obey, 566. It is impious to think that anyone is rescued by his own merits from the power of darkness, 249. The multitude of the ungodly is neither unbecoming to the world nor useless to God’s kingdom, 222. The impunity of sinners is the gravest punishment, even when delayed, 555, 561, 661, epigr. 80.

INACHUS, king of the Argives, 688. His daughter Io, or Isis, ibid. The incarnation of the Word is ineffable, 40. The mystery and fruit of the incarnation of the Word, 552, 651, epigr. 65. The necessity and fruit of Christ’s incarnation, 446. How much Christ’s incarnation promises to humanity, 793.

REBUKE. God’s power in the sea is called a rebuke, 399. How ineffable things are to be narrated, 519. Why infants before the use of reason are involved in public calamities, 787, verse 43–44. Why sacred things themselves and holy men do not escape public calamities, 787, verse 45 and following. Infants and fools, without any exercise of their own will, either receive or lose God’s grace, 342.

UNHAPPINESS. Whom does unhappiness not break? 578. Unbelievers held the elements as law, 851. Providence was not lacking to them either, ibid. The whole life of unbelievers is sin, and their virtue is false, 557, 663, epigr. 83. What the works of unbelievers are like, 853 and following, 871 and following.

WEAKNESS. Why the strong are often permitted to become weak, 443. TALENT. What good talents seek in the words of those who discuss, 580.

The ungrateful are proud and ungrateful adversaries of grace, 103. Whom Saint Prosper designates by the name “the ungrateful,” *Poem against the Ungrateful*, 303 n. The subject of the *Poem against the Ungrateful*: whence good will and faith arise, 103. The reason for writing the *Poem against the Ungrateful*, 115, verse 1 and following. The only enemies of the good are the wicked; why they are permitted: why we should pray for them, 572. How the perfect are at peace with the enemies of peace, 466, 547, 548, 631, epigr. 29. The enemies to be guarded against are the devil and his angels, 513. The more treacherous enemy is the one who carries good things on his lips but hides evil in the inner chambers of the soul, 504. He is compared with serpents, ibid.

Iniquity is not a substance but a defect of nature desiring what is not its proper order, 671, epigr. 97. Open iniquity is less harmful than hidden iniquity, 504. The depth of iniquity is the defense of sin, 575. All iniquity and impiety has an end, 556. No iniquity need be feared by one who approaches God, provided that he approaches with his whole heart and ceases to do and will evil, 480. The wicked find justice hateful, 568. Injustice makes bad use of evil and good things; justice makes good use of good and evil things, 564. The unjust person is first injured by his own iniquity, 561. It is more fitting for the unjust person to grieve in punishment than he rejoiced in sin, 566.

DISOBEDIENCE. What humanity lost through disobedience, 579. The innocent person is not innocent if, although he harms no one else, he harms himself in any way, 503. What true innocence is, 371, 543, 613. INNOCENTIUS XXXVIII presides over the Roman Church, 738. Praise of Pope Innocent I and his testimony concerning grace and free will, 319. Letter of Innocent I to the Council of Carthage, 272. To the Council of Milevis, 273.

Understanding is not something other than the soul, but a certain hidden vision of the soul, 594. Understanding is to be sought, so that one may understand how contemptible is what can be taken away from one who hopes for eternal life, 459. Human understanding, corrupted by sin and to be restored by the gift of grace, 448. Scripture reproves understanding and memory, 398. Faith opens the way to understanding; unbelief closes it, 560. How the prophet asks that understanding be given to him, 448. Good understanding: to do what one has understood, 420, 445, 623, epigr. 13. The poverty of human understanding, 569. Natural understanding, or the use of God’s benefits, is sufficient for eternal life neither to the ancients nor to us, [Col. 0978] 94. He understood beyond the teachers whom the Father taught, 452. There is always something remaining that can be understood and known, even by those who understand and are learned, 456, 547, 631, epigr. 27. An intention is not right in good works when they are performed not out of love for the highest good but for present advantage and praise, 442. No one knows a person’s intention except God, 510. Envy is hatred of another’s happiness, 586. Envy is born from pride, not pride from envy, 586, 587. Cain’s envy caused God to reject his brother’s gifts, 797, verse 308–309. Envy is never anything but malicious and is not satisfied with another’s misfortunes, 372. What it means to call upon God in truth, 521. If human beings desire what the just and good God commands, God is wholly near to the affections which he inspired, ibid.

Io, or Isis, daughter of Inachus, whom the Egyptians worshiped with divine honor, 688. IPHITUS, founder of the Olympiads, 692. Anger must quickly be restrained lest it turn into hatred, 592, 673, epigr. 100. When the anger of the sinner is late and fruitless, 422. How anger is understood in God, 402, 565. Certain words of the Psalms seem to belong to anger and hatred, although they express the chief charity, 391. No one escapes God’s anger except the one who flees to the angry God, 500, 576. IRENAEUS of Lyons, bishop, flourishes, 715. The rainbow, a sign of manifold grace, 900. ISAAC begets Esau and Jacob, 688. Isaac dies, 688. Isaac is a figure of Christ and of the calling of the nations, 897. ISAIAH, the prophet, 692. ISHMAEL, son of Abraham by a slave woman, from whom came the Ishmaelites, also called Hagarenes and later Saracens, 687.

ISRAEL means “seeing God,” 466, 472. Israel is the same as Jacob, 395. Why the Israelites were called christs before the use of chrism, 394. Why the people of Israel are said to have been redeemed from the hand of their enemies, 399. This was a figure of baptism, in which we are redeemed by the price of Christ’s blood, ibid. The Israelites desired present goods more than future goods, although from God’s many benefits toward them they ought to have understood that they were being called to some blessedness without end, 399. The Israelites and Jerusalem signify all the nations and peoples who through imitation of faith became children of Abraham, 431. Unless God’s mercy had come to the aid of the Israelites themselves, they would have passed into the same impiety as the other nations, 851. God reserved to himself the care of the Israelite nation and assigned the other nations to angels, 487. Not the whole Israelite race perished because of the crimes of the wicked, 482. For from it came the apostles, from it the teachers, from it so many martyrs and the firstborn of the whole adoption, ibid. For these Christ prayed on the cross, ibid. ITHACIUS, bishop and accuser of Priscillian, excommunicated, 736.

## J

JACOB, son of Isaac and also called Israel, from whom came the Israelites, now called Jews, 688. Jacob descends into Mesopotamia and serves for seven years, 688. He begets Joseph, ibid. Jacob enters Egypt, 688. Jacob dies, 688. Prophesying about Christ and the calling of the nations, ibid. Jacob represents all the children of promise, while under the name Esau is figured the entire part of the unbelieving, 496. There is perpetual struggle between the two, ibid. In Jacob it was shown what would be given to humanity; in Esau, what would be owed, 244.

JAMES, first bishop of Jerusalem, 703. James, the brother of the Lord, is stoned by the Jews, 704. JAMES of Nisibis, 727. His holiness, ibid. JADDUS, high priest of the Jews, 694. JAIR, judge, 690. JANNAEUS ALEXANDER, king and high priest, rules the Jews with extreme cruelty, 698. JECHONIAH, king of Judah, 693. His captivity, ibid. JEPHTHAH, judge, 690. JEREMIAH, the prophet, 693. JEROBOAM, king in Samaria, 691.

JERUSALEM means “vision of peace,” 431, 472. The heavenly Jerusalem is the mother of all the saints, 467. Her children rejoice in future goods because of their firm hope in them, 467. The heavenly Jerusalem rises not through a mass of stones but through the solidity of virtues and the fellowship of the saints, 467. Nothing carnal ought to be understood concerning the building of the eternal Jerusalem, 468. The one who confesses that his ascent is not the work of his own power but God’s gift ascends to fellowship with the heavenly Jerusalem, 468, 518, 633, epigr. 31. Jerusalem is both mother and daughter, 497.

At Jerusalem 1,100,000 perish, and another 100,000 captives are publicly sold, 705. How so great a multitude was found at Jerusalem, 705. After Philip, the bishops of Jerusalem were: X, Seneca; XI, Justus; XII, Levi; XIII, Ephres; XIV, Joseph; XV and last from the circumcision before Jerusalem was overthrown by Hadrian, Judas, [Col. 0979] 710. Then XVI, Marcus; XVII, Cassianus; XVIII, Publius; XIX, Maximus; XX, Julianus; XXI, Grajanus; XXII, Symmachus; XXIII, Carus; XXIV, Julianus; XXV, Capito, 712, 713. XXVI, Mormius; XXVII, Antoninus; XXVIII, Valens; XXIX, Dachianus; XXX, Narcissus; XXXI, Dius; XXXII, Germanio; XXXIII, Gordius; XXXIV, another Narcissus, 715. XXXV, Alexander, while Narcissus was still living, 716.

JESUS, son of Josedech, high priest, 693. JESUS, son of Sirach, author of the Book of Wisdom, 696. JOAHAZ, king of Judah, 693. JOACHIM, also called Eliakim, 693. In his thirtieth year Judaea is captured by Nebuchadnezzar, and Joachim becomes tributary, ibid.

JOHN first perceives the beginnings of grace before those of nature, 897. John preaches, 702. JOHN the apostle is exiled to Patmos, 707. Saint John’s return from exile to Ephesus, 708. JOHN HYRCANUS: whence he received this name, 697. A friend of the Romans, ibid. He levels Samaria to the ground, ibid. JOHN, bishop of Constantinople, oppressed by Theophilus, 738. JOHN CASSIAN flourishes, 745. See Cassian. JOHN, monk and prophet, 737. JOHN seizes the imperial power, 742. He demands Africa but, having become weaker, ibid. He is overthrown by Placidia and Valentinian, 742.

JOASH, king, 691. JOTHAM, king, 692. Among the triumphs of the saints nothing is more illustrious than Job’s patience, 347. The Lord did in holy Job what he promised he would do in his apostles and martyrs, 348. The Lord had not abandoned Job but was caring for and purifying him, 348. Job prophesied concerning the incarnation and resurrection of Christ, and the hope of redemption laid up in him for all the saints, 348. Cassianus claims that Job conquered the devil by his own strength, not by God’s help, except insofar as God did not give the tempter greater power than he knew Job possessed, 344, 345. Cassianus thinks that Job conquered in the conflict with the devil by his own strength, 347. Cassianus teaches that Job engaged the demon by his own strength, not protected solely by the grace of God, 295, 297. It is proved that Job conquered with God’s help, 347, 348.

JOLADA: how many years he lived, 691. JONADAB, son of Rechab, 691. JONAH, the prophet, 692. JONATHAN, high priest of the Jews, is killed, 697. JEHORAM, king, 691. JEHOSHAPHAT, king of Judah, 691. JOSEPH: in what year of his father’s life he was born, 688. Joseph is sold by his brothers, 688. Joseph, so great a man and worshiper of the one true God, provided not only for feeding the bodies of the Egyptians but also for educating their souls, 395. Joseph, governor of Egypt, 688. He dies, ibid. In everything that happened to him, Joseph considered God’s providence, which orders all things justly, 799, verse 356 and following.

JOSEPHUS, a noble man among the Jews, is sent as an envoy to King Ptolemy and honored by him, 695, 696. JOSIAH, king of Judah, 693. He is killed, ibid. JOSHUA, successor of Moses, 689. JOVIAN XXXIX reigns, 730. He dies, 731. JOVINUS and SEBASTIAN, tyrants, are killed, 740.

TO COMMAND. God causes human beings to do what he commands to be done, 35. See Commands, Precepts. JUBILATION: what it is, 532, 533.

Why the Jews could not believe, 66. The Jews, after Jerusalem was captured, became tributaries of the Romans, 698. The Jews are hostile to Christians in many places, 709. Those rebelling at Alexandria are suppressed, ibid. The Jews destroy Salamis, 709. The madness of the Jews who crucified Christ, 902. They also persecuted the witnesses of his resurrection, 902. The Jews’ obstinacy at Christ’s coming, 902. What is said about Judas in Psalm 108 is also understood as prophesied about the Jewish people, 410 and following. The kingdom of the Jews did not last long after Christ’s crucifixion, 411. The Jews receive remission for no sin because they rejected him in whom alone there is abolition of sins, 411. They have no one to pity them—not for temporal life but for eternal life, 411. Deprived of the sacraments and sacrifice, the Jews passed into the humility of the nations, 406. The Jews rage in Palestine and are suppressed, 710. The Jews think that the prophecy of Psalm 105 refers to their visible kingdom and are therefore to be deceived by Antichrist, 403.

JUDAS MACCABEUS, leader and high priest of the Jews, 697. He makes a treaty with the Romans, expels the commanders of Antiochus from Judaea, and cleanses the temple, ibid. He is killed, ibid. JUDAS THE GALILEAN, 701. How Judas was punished for the sin of his father and mother, 410. Not everything in Psalm 108 is to be understood of Judas the betrayer alone: some things refer to the whole class of Christ’s enemies, and some specifically to Judas himself, 408. [Col. 0980]

God’s judgment is more inscrutable in the election of grace than in the retribution of justice, 886. God’s judgment is inscrutable in the distinction made among infants, 868, 869. Human justice finds nothing in them by which to distinguish one from another, but God’s unspeakable grace has what it may choose, 869. The Semi-Pelagians were compelled to say that infants are judged according to what they were foreknown to have done if they had lived, 64. Those who think that each person is judged according to foreknown merits oppose the Catholic teaching concerning original sin, 37. They favor the Pelagians, 37. It is absurd to say that anyone is judged according to merits he would have had if he had lived longer, 36, 60. The Pelagians themselves saw that it is false for a person to be judged according to foreknown merits, 37. God does not judge anyone for what he would have done if he had lived longer, but only for deeds actually done, 36, 39, 61. God’s judgment has already been carried out upon the Jewish people, 489. The just were separated from them, while the unjust remained, ibid. Among all the nations there will be people of Israelite dignity, while the Jews, for the most part, will be ungodly and enemies of the truth, 489. How inscrutable God’s judgments are, 38. Examples of God’s inscrutable judgments, 59 and following. God’s judgments bring consolation, 444. God’s judgment can neither be spoken nor comprehended, 821, verse 937 and following. God’s judgments must be distinguished from his works, 589. God’s judgment cannot be unjust, although it is hidden, since all possess a deservingness for death, even from original sin alone, while no one possesses a claim to life except what grace has granted, 171, verse 763 and following. God’s judgments of justice are those by which eternal life is pronounced for the just and punishment for the wicked, 462. The secrets of God’s judgments, or the riches of God’s wisdom, are clear to no one, 528. God’s judgments are always just and must not be compared with human judgments, 588, 673, epigr. 99. God’s judgments are not disclosed to the proud and transgressors, 500. God’s judgment will not be without mercy toward the just, 461.

RASH JUDGMENT. The hidden things of another’s heart must not be judged rashly, 442, 546, 627, epigr. 21. Christ’s yoke seems heavy to the proud and light to the humble, 775, verse 45 and following. JUGURTHA is defeated and captured by the Romans, 697.

JULIAN is called Caesar, 729. Julian XXXVIII reigns, 730. He becomes an idolater and deceitfully persecutes Christians, 730. Julian forbids Christians to be teachers of the liberal arts, 730. Julian’s death, 730. JULIAN, the jurist whose crime caused Pertinax to be killed, is himself killed by Severus, 715. JULIAN X, bishop of Alexandria, 715. JULIAN the Pelagian, attempting by deceit to enter the lost see and communion of the Church, is repelled by Xistus at the urging of Leo, the deacon, 747. JULIAN AMARTOLUS, bishop, subscribes to the Second Council of Orange, 767.

GAIUS JULIUS CAESAR is the first to exercise sole imperial power among the Romans; from him came the Caesars, 698. He devastates the Germans and subdues the Gauls, ibid. He is killed, 699. JULIUS XXXIII, bishop of Rome, 726. JULIUS of Puteoli, bishop and legate of Saint Leo at Ephesus, 750.

In Scripture, beasts and cattle are said to represent those who walk simply in the Church, usefully though not very learnedly, but full of faith, 406, 407. Anyone who is renewed through repentance at any age is considered young, 437. An oath is called what the mind establishes even without a sacrament, because the mind ought to be fixed in keeping God’s commandments, 453. An oath in God is an unchangeable establishment of truth, 482.

A just punishment awaits the one who willingly lost what he ought to have loved, so that he may lose with grief what he loved, 585. The one justified by a free gift acquires merit by that same gift, 210. If a just person turns away from the justice in which he lived for a long time and dies in the impiety in which he lived—not for one year but for one day—he will go into the punishments owed to the wicked, and his former justice will profit him nothing, 37. The person who lacks grace or has been puffed up by pride is not just, 439. The just are nourished not only by the fruits of their labor but also by the labor itself, through which they strive toward the fruit: as the love of endurance becomes for them a share in future delight, 475, 476. At every time, the just—both from the people of Israel and from whatever nations have pleased God—are distinguished by the Spirit of God’s grace, 892. Venial sins do not prevent the just from eternal life, nor do any good works of the wicked benefit them for eternal salvation, 550, 641, epigr. 46. No one among the just is without labors and troubles in this life, 526. The Lord loves the just because he himself is their justice, 523. Some just people existed in every age of the world, 797, verse 265 and following. Many just people either had no children, or those who had children did not glory in all of them or in every respect, 381. The just are more excellent than the visible heaven, 427. The hearts and works of the just are in God’s hand, 880. The birth of the just comes from being reborn from God, 588. What the just will do eternally, 521. God does not abandon the just even in adversity, 556. The just are always free; the wicked are always slaves, 551, 615, epigr. 5. God is the portion of the just, 472. Who is considered excessively just, 602. The just who rule serve those over whom they seem to rule, 566. For the just person who loves God, the beloved himself is the reward, 452.

JUSTIN, the philosopher and martyr, dies, 712. Justin the philosopher’s *Apology for the Christians*, 712. Justice and judgment are similar, and either term is used in place of the other, 398. Nevertheless, they differ to some extent, ibid. In God’s great justice, punishment is decreed for the sinner, and justification is not denied to the penitent, 458. In what justice consists, 556. It must be preserved amid adversities, ibid. True human justice exists only through Christ, 92. Past justice, even if long-lasting, profits nothing if someone dies in impiety, even after one day, 37. The justice of this life, although real, consists more in the remission of sins than in the perfection of virtues, 567, 667, epigr. 90. The justice of this life, even when perfect, is small in comparison with the great justice of the other life, 590. The lesser justice produces merit; the greater produces reward, 590. What true and perfect justice is, 590. The justice of unbelievers is false, 92. Even in this world God displays the clearest proofs of his justice, 817, verse 805 and following. Although God is not the evil author of these things, he is a just avenger, 607. The punishment of the soul that abandons justice, 574.

JUSTUS of Tiberias, a Jewish writer, 708. JUSTUS succeeds Simon in the bishopric of Jerusalem, 708.

LABDON, judge of Israel, 690. Lips that are wicked and deceitful, turning one back from a holy purpose, 465. The labor of the godly is exercise, not condemnation; and it ought not to disturb those who know that Christ suffered greater things, 582. The end of labor is to love what cannot be taken away, 561, 665 epigr. 87.

**LAC.** The same thing may be food for both infants and adults, namely milk, 69.

LACTANTIUS, tutor of Crispus; and his eulogy, 725.

The joy of God’s people is not apart from him, 398.

LAMISSUS, king of the Lombards, 742.

The war of the Lapiths and Centaurs, 690.

The snare of the hunters will be broken when all the allurements of present vanities are destroyed, 471.

LATINUS SYLVIUS, king of the Latins, 690.

The thief on the cross, drawn in together with all believers, is taught from his own confession, 324. Earlier he blasphemed Christ on his own account, but afterward believed in the Holy Spirit, 324.

LATRONIANUS, a Priscillianist, is executed, 736.

When praise of God is acceptable to God, 530. What true praise of God is, 381, 544, 619 epigr. 6. To praise God and sing psalms to the glory of God, not merely with the voice, but much more through the harmony of a rational life, 523. God must be praised in all things, because he makes people praiseworthy, 398. The whole life of the righteous praises God: by his teaching and gift one lives in such a way that no action is unworthy of God’s praise, 523. What the soul, weakened by corruptible flesh, can do toward praising God is little; therefore it longs to advance toward perfect and eternal praise, 521, 522. One who praises God joins himself in devotion to the heavenly beings, so that according to his measure he may already do what he will do without end, 529. Praise of God properly belongs to two kinds of creatures, the angelic and the human, 528. How the others praise him, ibid. God does not need human praise, 486. The praise of God, however, benefits human beings, ibid. What those who praise God ought to be like, ibid. The fullness of praise of God is expressed when he is called good, ibid. How all God’s works, even those lacking understanding, praise God by giving their immense usefulness and beauty as material to those who praise him, 519. They seem to praise, because they are praiseworthy: although they cannot speak, they cause themselves not to be silent, ibid. In continual praise of God, the hope of eternity is received, 518. Works must not be discordant with the voice, nor the voice with works; and praise uttered by the voice should proceed from a good conscience, 524. All God’s works are praised by true worshipers, and they marvel at all that has been made in such a way that the maker himself is more marvelous, 518. Even all irrational things and those without sensation, although they cannot praise God by a personal confession, proclaim through their nature the power of their author, 528. God must always be praised, because he is always greater than all praise, 518. God’s mercy and justice, the eternal kingdom, and everlasting fire must be proclaimed, 519, 553, 657 epigr. 73. God’s praise truly continues if one lives well without ceasing, 382. Whatever is uttered by the mouth and whatever is done in action must be spoken and done to the praise of God, 398. God is praised in this age, and will be praised much more in the age to come, 518. Whatever is praiseworthy in the universe is praise of its author, [Col. 0982] 530. The praise of God must be continued in the present time, for it will remain in eternity, 517. God must be praised whether the day is spent joyfully amid prosperity or sadly amid adversity, 518. False praisers of Christ conspired for his death, 375. God praises himself without danger, and not for his own benefit but ours, 599. God, who is life, must always be praised, 554. Why those above are urged by those below to praise God, 529. God rules everywhere; therefore he must be praised everywhere, 381, 382. Praise ought always to precede invocation, 392. The praise and reward of faith, 579, 580. False praise is not to be loved, 507.

LEO, the deacon, restores friendship between Aetius and Albinus, 748. Leo XLIII, bishop of the Roman Church, 748. Pope Leo sends legates against Eutyches, who suffer an injury, 749. Leo, summoned by Theodosius in the case of Eutyches, is prevented by the people from going, but sends legates, 749, 750. Pope Leo goes to Attila for the sake of peace and successfully accomplishes the matter, 752.

LEONIDES, father of Origen, a martyr, 716.

LEONTIUS, the deacon, carries letters from Prosper to Augustine and from Augustine to Prosper, 1, 18.

LISBON founded, 689.

The Law and the Prophets announced Christ, 803 vers. 467 and following. The difference between law and grace, 315, 592. No one penetrates the height and depth of the Law except one who has received understanding; but the person who carries it out understands the Law, and the person who has charity possesses perfect knowledge of the Law, 441. The Law of God is bread, 374. The Law is easy to observe through the grace of Christ, who first himself did what he commanded, 803, vers. 510 and following. The Law, as pedagogue, leads one to ask for chaste fear, 456. The great mystery revealed to Moses and to true Israelites: the Law was given so that transgression might abound, in order that grace might abound still more, 380. The Law, which could not give life, was given so that grace might be sought, 457. This secret of grace is disclosed only to the humble and weak, ibid. The Law, given in paradise, implanted by nature and promulgated in writing, made people transgressors, 455. The Law is written by the Holy Spirit in hearts with Christ’s blood, 805, vers. 512 and following. God writes the Law in the heart so that we may fear him not like slaves, without love, but love him like sons with chaste affection, 452. The law of faith, which works through love, obtains grace, 451. The Law is fixed immovably, so that everyone who exalts himself may be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself may be exalted, 461. The Law does not assist the will, 855. The Law is fulfilled through charity, not fear, 574. The proof of the natural law is that no one wishes to suffer what he does to another, 801, vers. 422 and following. God is the portion of the one who keeps his Law, 445. How the Law becomes natural, 579. How the Law is not a stumbling block to one who loves it, 463. Charity, which is the fullness of the Law, is to be kept perpetually; when the other commandments cease, it alone remains forever, 443. To disperse the Law is not to preserve its integrity through the iniquity of transgression, 457. The law of works and the law of faith, 440. The ends of law and grace are different, 550, 639, epigr. 44. The Law was not unfulfilled through any fault of its own, 550. Whoever loves the Law honors even what he does not understand in it, 463. Nor does he make it depend upon the changeable customs of human beings, ibid. Even if holy people abandon their purpose, the justice of the Law endures, ibid. The New Law is the perfection of charity, 479, 549, 645, epigr. 38. Without grace the Law cannot be fulfilled, 855. The Law of God is more marvelous than all his works, 457. In what sense Christ is the end of the Law, 570. Meditation on the Law nourishes and strengthens the desire for Christ’s coming, 494. The Law is truth, through which knowledge of sin comes and which bears witness to God’s justice, 459. The uselessness of the Law if grace is absent, 549, 639, epigr. 43. What the Law accomplishes without grace, 579.

What it means to be freed from the body of death, 590.

LIBERIUS, the thirty-fourth bishop of Rome, 728. He is driven into exile on account of the faith and afterward restored, ibid. Liberius is exiled, 729.

Free will is the sole cause of sin, 811, vers. 651 and following. Whether freedom, in itself, stands equally disposed toward good or evil, 342, 343 and following. What the freedom of the will possessed in the excellence of that first condition is apparent in the angels who stood firm, 57. By free will a human being could fall, but could not rise again in the same way, 62. Freedom from sin, 39. The purpose of the books on free will, and against whom they were written, 62 and following. No one serves unless with some freedom, and no one is free except with some servitude, 331. Bad freedom arises from a defect of the will; good freedom comes only from the help of grace, 331. The will remains free after the fall, but not good. Wherever it is carried, it rushes and slips, 159, vers. 388 and following. The harmony between divine inspiration and freedom, 273. Free will deceived the first human being, 273. Freedom under grace, 898. Free will, 795, vers. 238 and following. Let it humbly acknowledge that all its ability comes from God, ibid. Through sin, unless grace comes first, free will is sufficient for no good, [Col. 0983] 765. A human being does not lose free will when he is moved by the Spirit of God, nor when he has voluntarily given himself to the devil, 854. Free will drank the poison of all vices and drenched the whole nature of humanity with the drunkenness of its intemperance, 329. As it could fall when God did not impel it, so it cannot rise when God does not raise it, 330. Free will wounded by sin, 330. It is not as sound in Adam’s descendants as it was in Adam before sin, ibid. It is absurd to say that free will is taken away when it is healed and liberated by grace, 161, vers. 593 and following. This thought arises from the same pride that destroyed Adam, ibid. vers. 596 and following. Free will cannot be healed by the power of free will, but by the grace of Christ, which is the tree of life, and so forth, ibid. vers. 600 and following. The fact that a human being attributes too much to free will proceeds from that pride which the devil inspired into our first parents, 183, vers. 915 and following. From this many errors arise, ibid. vers. 929. All the godly ought to reject them, ibid. vers. 932 and following. Since they are members of Christ, they draw all their power from their head, 185, vers. 959 and following. Free will is not destroyed but reborn, 97. What it can accomplish by itself, ibid. It ought to place its hope in the physician, 97. A human being is good and evil in free will, but evil through himself and good through God, ibid. Free will exists, but before faith it acts in darkness, 209. What it is before grace, and how grace heals it, 209, 210. Free will is not taken away by the grace of God, but formed, governed, and ordered, 321. They are foolish who think they can solve, through the willing and unwilling of free will, the question inscrutable even to Paul himself: why some rather than others are liberated by grace, 169, vers. 757 and following. Saint James describes the character of free will when it is directed by the human spirit and when it is governed by God, chapter III, 14, 98. Against all exaltation that boasts of free will stands the Apostle’s statement: “For who distinguishes you?” and so forth, 886. The foolish complaint of the proud that free will is taken away if its beginnings, progress, and perseverance in good unto the end are all said to be gifts of God, 356. The fall of free will and its impotence resulting from the fall, according to Innocent, 319. Free will has neither the will nor the ability to do good except through grace, 334. After grace, free will remains in nature, but with its quality and condition changed through Christ, 356, 557. To refer everything to God does not destroy free will, 944. Free will is not wholly erased, but fallen and bound to evil, 159, vers. 586 and following. No one uses free will well without grace, 273. The difficulty concerning grace is not solved by its willing and unwilling, 886. Free will and its weakness according to the Scriptures, 291 and following. Free will without grace is in no way fit to choose good, 329. Free will is corrupted in all respects, 762. Free will is the spontaneous appetite for something pleasing to oneself, 329. How much power Cassian attributes to free will, 347. What free will is without God or with God, 93.

How many years the five books of Moses contain, 689.

The Book of the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, called *Panareton*, 696. The Massilians reject the Book of Wisdom, 15, 37. The Book of Wisdom possesses the authority of canonical Scripture, 38, 39. Great and learned men who treated the divine utterances long before Augustine used the authority of the Book of Wisdom, 70.

The Shepherd, cited by Cassian, 294. The Shepherd is of no authority, 342.

The subject of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*: how God’s will concerning the salvation of all human beings is fulfilled, 847.

LICINIUS becomes emperor, 724. Licinius drives out the Christians, 725. Licinius is killed, 725.
