The confusion of languages at Babel, 901. The confusion of languages, 904. From one language seventy-two were made, 900. By what design of God’s mercy, 901.

A talkative person does not grasp knowledge of the truth, 506.

LINUS, Peter’s successor in the Roman see, 705.

LITTORIUS, imprudently engaging the Goths in battle, is captured, 746, 747.

A higher position, although it ought to be administered as is fitting, is sought improperly, 566, 567.

Locusts and grasshoppers are one plague, because one is the parent and the other the offspring, 396. The faithful are called locusts because of their multitude, or because they moved from place to place, 413.

Longevity comes from God and is not a cause of sin, 207, 220. It is not sinful to live long, but to live badly, ibid.

The LOMBARDS, after leaving their settlements, defeat the Vandals, 733.

Long. Even what is brief for one who is helping seems long to one who is desiring help, 450.

Unlearned loquacity prefers teaching to learning, 506. [Col. 0984]

LOT alone is preserved while five cities perish, because he alone was found righteous, 799, vers. 353 and following.

LUCIFER of Cagliari, 729. Lucifer, returning from exile, appoints Paulinus bishop of Antioch, 730. The death of Lucifer of Cagliari, 732. Judgment concerning him, ibid.

Lycia and other provinces subdued, 706.

## M

MACEDONIUS, from whom the Macedonian heresy arose, is substituted by the Arians for Paul in the see of Constantinople, 728.

The history of the Maccabees: from it the Greeks reckon their kingdom, 695. The books of the Maccabees are not received by the Hebrews, ibid.

MACHARIUS, the thirty-ninth bishop of Jerusalem, 724.

MACHARIUS, disciple of Saint Antony, 729.

MACRINUS, the nineteenth emperor, reigns, 717. He is killed, ibid.

MAGNENTIUS, after seizing the empire, is defeated, 728, 729. Magnentius kills himself, 729.

The great moderate their speech for the sake of the little ones, 434.

In comparison with God, nothing is truly called great, nothing truly powerful; in him alone are true greatness and great power, 524.

To magnify. How God is magnified, 382.

The greatness of God is to be proclaimed, 519.

MALACHI, the prophet, 693.

**Curse.** The empty curse of human beings; but when God blesses, he brings about what he says, 414.

The wicked are assigned for the uses of the good, 562. The intention of the wicked is to make the good like themselves; when they do not accomplish this, they burden them with accusations, 477. It belongs to the perfect patiently to endure such people to the end and not yield, 477. God uses the wicked for the correction of the good, like a good father, 433. All wicked people must be carefully fled and avoided, 504. Why neither the wicked ought to be punished here nor the good rewarded here, 815, vers. 746 and following. The wicked are to be tolerated by the righteous in this life, however violently they may rage, 556, 557. The whole time of the wicked is brief, 556. The wickedness of the unrighteous benefits the good, 559. The more obvious is the wickedness of one who openly displays himself as evil, 412. All evil is in something good, because every nature is good insofar as it is nature, 587, 588. There is no nature of evil, because every nature was made through the Word, whereas iniquity was not made through him, 671, epigr. 97. Evil has no substance, 568. There is no substance of evil, 608. How God guards against every evil, 467, 548, 631, epigr. 30. The unrighteous perish through evils, 506. The evils of this life are just punishments and must be endured patiently as salutary, 667, epigr. 95. From two evils one good cannot be made; two vices do not generate one virtue, and two falsehoods do not make one truth, 318. The evil from which we ask to be liberated, 503.

MANASSEH, king of Judah, 692.

MANASSEH, high priest of the Jews, 695.

When God’s commandment is rightly carried out, 579. God’s commandments are loved more than gold and topaz when, in observing them, one seeks not a temporal reward but justice, 457. God’s commandments are to be searched out so that they may be known by more perfect practice, 447, 547, 629, epigr. 24. How one may not forget God’s commandments, 381. God’s commandments are the paths of the righteous, 504. Those who add plausible things to truths place a stumbling block beside them, 504. The Gospel commandments are not difficult for faith but possible, 775, vers. 59 and following. God’s commandments are hidden from almost no one and can be known even by the ungodly, 439. How the prophet asks that they not be hidden from him, 439. How a human being is not repelled from God’s commandments, 437. God’s commandments are to be searched out in tranquility, 454, 547, 629, epigr. 26. God’s commandments are emphatically enjoined and must be carefully kept, 436. God himself causes people to do what he has commanded, 34. One learns God’s commandments by doing them and grasps knowledge of them through practice, 437. Those who despise God’s commandments commonly become enemies of those who keep them, 463. Why commandments are imposed upon a human being when he does not find the ability to fulfill them in his nature, 334. The very broad commandment is charity, 451.

MANES, founder of the Manichaean heresy. Their errors and disgraceful practices, 721, 722. The Manichaeans do not receive the books of the Old Testament, and accept of the New only those they choose, 62. The Manichaeans do not accept the Old Testament and assert that the New Testament has been corrupted, 63. The Manichaean error concerning Christ’s incarnation, 81. The Manichaeans think that the nature of evil is coeternal with God, 82. The Manichaeans hiding in the City are discovered and condemned by Leo, [Col. 0985] 749. The same action is carried out by many eastern bishops, ibid.

MANLIUS TORQUATUS strikes down his victorious son, 694.

Manna, the bread of heaven, 397.

Many dwelling places in one eternal life according to the variety of merits; nevertheless, God is all in all, 600.

The hands signify the fullness of a work; the fingers, the division of labors, 514. The hand of the Lord is the power of God, 447. The hand of God is power and wisdom, and Christ is both, 448. The hand of God is the Son and the Holy Spirit, ibid. The hand of the Lord is Christ, 390, 414.

MARCELLINUS, the twenty-eighth bishop of Rome, 723.

MARCELLUS, an illustrious man, agrees with and subscribes to the Council of Orange, 768.

MARCIANUS becomes emperor, the forty-fifth, 750. His outstanding qualities, ibid.

MARCION, a heresiarch, and his errors, 712.

MARK the evangelist preaches at Alexandria, 703.

MARK I, bishop of Jerusalem, from the Gentiles, 711.

MARK VII, bishop of Alexandria, 712.

MARK XXXII presides over the Roman Church, 726.

The sea signifies the age, 425.

C. MARIUS defeats the Cimbri and celebrates a triumph with Catulus, 697.

MARTIN of Tours flourishes, 735.

The martyrs were not terrified by the threatening words or punishments of earthly kings, but by the words of Christ, 462. Through the blood and groans of the martyrs, liberty was granted to the Church and the conversion of unbelievers, 377. The martyrs contended against their persecutors through love; therefore the latter failed by killing, while the former conquered by dying, 439, 440. The martyrs, assisted by God’s mercy, conquered by dying for the truth, 450. The earth was thickened by the blood of the martyrs, and the world was made fruitful, 508. The whole world is made illustrious by the examples of the martyrs, yet they attribute their victory not to themselves but to God, 461. The voice of the martyrs who tremble and do not presume upon themselves, 430. Christ alone is the strength of the martyrs, 509. The sufferings of the martyrs are preserved in writing, 713. Christ is everywhere the glory of the martyrs, 433. Martyrs in Gaul, 713. Unbaptized martyrs are justified, 564, 665, epigr. 89. Very many of the guards of the martyrs believed, 462. Martyrdom without charity is of no benefit, 463.

**Masses.** There are not two masses but one mass, 98. If no one were liberated from the condemned mass, no one could justly criticize God’s judgment, 31. We are liberated from the condemned mass by mercy alone, not by merits, 389.

MASSILIA founded, 693.

The Massilians, offended because they did not understand Augustine’s books, 1. Some became more discerning after reading the book *On Correction and Grace*, 2. The opinion of the Massilians is partly Catholic and partly Pelagian, 3. The extent to which the Massilians withdrew from the Pelagians, 24. How dangerous these remnants of the Pelagian heresy are, 6. The opinion of the Massilians and certain others in Gaul concerning predestination and calling, 13 and following. And concerning the gift of perseverance, 15. Among the Massilians were many outstanding in the pursuit of virtue, 2. Certain bishops, 6. Many to whom, by ecclesiastical custom, it was necessary to show the highest reverence as laymen, 18. Few dared oppose them, 6. Concerning the remainder of their doctrine, see Faith, Grace, Predestination, Perseverance, and the letters of Prosper and Hilary, 1 and following. With certain exceptions, the Massilians admire Augustine in all his actions and statements, 18. The Massilians think contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and the ecclesiastical understanding whatever Augustine disputed in his books against the Pelagians concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose, 1. The Massilians reject the testimony and the Book of Wisdom as noncanonical, 15. The Massilian opinion concerning original sin and the grace of regeneration, 3, 13. Concerning predestination, 3, 14, 15. Concerning the interpretation of the blessed Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, 3, 4. Concerning the purpose of the grace that calls, 4, 13. Concerning the will to save all, 4, 17. Concerning human freedom to do good and evil, 4. Concerning election from foreseen goods or evils that infants would have committed if they had lived longer, 4, 5. Concerning Christ’s death for the whole human race, 5. Concerning the number of the predestined, 6, 14, 15, 16, 17. Concerning the two things by which human salvation is accomplished, grace and human obedience, 6. Concerning the insufficiency of the human being to begin and complete a good work, 13. Concerning the beginning of good will, ibid., 14. Concerning preaching being made to some and not to others, and at some times and not at others, 14 and following. Concerning perseverance, 15. Prosper declares himself unequal to acting against the Massilians, 6. He asks Augustine to respond, ibid. He proposes questions to which he wants answers, 7. In the remnants of Pelagian depravity a vein of no slight virulence is nourished, 6. The Massilians wanted the beginning of faith and good will to begin from the will, so that the rest might follow as a merited consequence, 13. They acknowledged that a work could neither be begun nor completed without grace, [Col. 0986] 13. They did not think that any nature was so corrupted that it could not wish to be healed; nor did they want grace thereby to be denied, 13. From what source they wished the cause of the elect and the rejected to be sought, 14. They suspended every distinction upon foreknowledge, 14 and following. They tried to support this from Augustine’s words, ibid., 17. The Massilians seem to have doubted whether infants were snatched from the power of darkness through baptism, 63.

The Church’s morning office, 460.

MAXENTIUS is called Augustus, 724. Maxentius is killed, ibid.

MAXIMINUS XXII reigns, 718. He begins the sixth persecution, ibid. He is killed by Pupienus, ibid.

MAXIMINUS and Severus are made Caesars, 724. Maximinus dies, ibid.

MAXIMINUS, bishop of Trier, honorably receives Athanasius while he is fleeing, 728.

MAXIMUS XIV, bishop of Alexandria, 720.

MAXIMUS XL, bishop of Jerusalem, 728.

MAXIMUS becomes emperor, 735. He associates his son Victor with him in the kingdom, ibid.

MAXIMUS assumes the empire, 753. He does not punish Valentinian’s assassins but receives them into friendship and compels Valentinian’s wife to marry him. He is killed shortly afterward, ibid. and 754.

MAXIMUS, after receiving and soon losing the tyranny, is allowed to live, 739.

The tyrant Maximus is condemned to death, 736. So also is his son Victor, ibid.

MAXIMUS, bishop, subscribes to the Second Council of Orange, 767.

MAZABANUS, successor of Alexander in the Jerusalem see, 719.

MEDEA of Colchis, 699.

Our physician grants this also to the sick: that they desire true health, 338. The supreme Physician mercifully and skillfully applies different remedies, because one treatment cannot cure many kinds of wounds, 524.

Meditation is perseverance in action so as not to forget; for this God’s help must be requested, 438. What meditation on the Law is useful, 449, 547.

MELCHIADES, the thirtieth bishop of Rome, 723.

MELITO, an Asian bishop, delivers a defense of the faith to Antoninus, 713.

The members of Christ are an ark of sanctification, whether through the truth of the incarnation or through the election of grace, 482.

God’s memorial, because he brings to complete fulfillment whatever he has promised, 489.

Falsehood is laborious, truth is not so, 553, 653, epigr. 68. The enemies of truth protect themselves by falsehood, 505. It is better to be silent than to lie, 581. Falsehood assumes the appearance of truth in order to insinuate itself more easily, 488. Concerning the ease of lying, 578. Not everyone who conceals the truth lies, ibid.

MENELAUS, 690.

The mind is the highest part of the soul, 521.

The mind is a mirror that faith cleanses, 803, vers. 460.

The Lord’s table consists of the sacraments and doctrine, 476.

The measure of each person’s miseries is ordained by God, 910.

The month Quintilis is called July by decree of Antoninus, 699. Two months, September and October, are called Germanicus and Domitianus, 707. The month of September is called Commodus after Commodus, 715.

A reward is owed to good works if they are performed; grace, which is unowed, is given so that they may be performed, 587, 764.

Whence merit comes to a human being, 916. It is a gift of God, 276. Each person is given, without merit, the means by which he may advance toward merit, 894. Something is given before any labor from which each person may receive a reward according to his labor, ibid. This is proved from the Gospel parable, Matthew XXV, 14–15, ibid. Grace produces merits, 29. Merits are not acquired except through the time of the body, 36. Concerning foreknowledge of future merits, 37. If the dead are not judged according to the works they would have done, grace is not given according to merits, 65. It is shown that every good merit is a divine gift, 876 and following; first concerning faith, ibid.; then concerning the other gifts, 878, 879. The differences of merits must be referred back to God, and no complaint should be made about their inequality, 893. To those whom he chose without merits, God gives the means by which they may be adorned with merits, 922. There are no good merits without grace, 871. If, as Cassian wishes, the person whom God has always helped is without merit, it will follow that there is no merit among God’s gifts—or at least that merits can be acquired by one’s own ability—and that we are therefore helped in certain matters so that through grace what was not impossible by nature may become more possible, 335. Praise and merit may be attributed to faith and good works without prejudice to grace, 351. Praise and merit are not taken away by grace, 351. Those have neither praise nor merit in whom are not found the things that cannot be possessed unless the Lord gives them, 351. Those are to be cast far away who think that the saints lose the reason for obtaining the crown unless human merits are found in them, 185, vers. 945 and following. Every cause of praise and merit is in God, 352. All the merit of the saints must be referred to God, 532. Our merits are God’s gifts, and for them we receive eternal rewards, 276. There is no place for merits before grace, 314. Human merits are nothing except from grace, 334. All the merits of the saints are gifts of God, 273. Without the love of God there is no true merit, 859. Every merit is from God, 514.

MESSALA CORVINUS, the orator, 701.

MESSANA founded, 688.

The sweating turning-post is erected, 707.

A thousand generations on behalf of all, 393. It is clear that this number cannot be completed from Adam to the end of the world, ibid.

The fable of the Minotaur, 690.

MINUTIUS FUNDANUS, proconsul of Asia, 710. He receives a letter from Hadrian that Christians should not be condemned rashly, ibid.

The wonders performed by God alone, 491, 492. Nevertheless, the Father did nothing without the Son and the Holy Spirit, 492. Some things are performed through angels or human beings, 492. Those to whom they are beneficial see God’s wonders, 558. God’s daily miracles, although great, are not marveled at because of familiarity; therefore through unusual and new things human attention is awakened and useful fear is nourished, 741. Visible and invisible miracles, 561. One must pass from visible to invisible things, ibid. Miracles are not contrary to nature, even though they may appear so to us, 584. Miracles of grace are a cause of joy and fear, 501. Why Christ’s miracles were not performed among those who would believe but were performed among those who would not believe is inscrutable, 252 and following.

Human miseries arise not from the Creator’s institution but from the Judge’s retribution, 320. Whether the miseries of living descendants belong as punishment to one who has died, 410. God’s mercy and truth must be proclaimed, because there are no other roads by which it comes to us or by which it raises us to itself, 497. Mercy and truth are undivided in the saints alone; in everyone else they are more easily distinguished, 460, 547, 631, epigr. 28. To the pride of the Pelagians, God’s mercy and judgments seem penetrable, so that they think God’s plan is not hidden if grace, like wrath, arises from merit, 247. Mercy and truth are almost always joined in the Scriptures, 426. They will be revealed at the last, 426. Through the same mercy by which merits were given, crowns of merits are bestowed, 379. Each of the faithful is a minister of God’s mercy toward others, 528. The dispensation of God’s mercy extends not only to the Israelite race but also to the propagation of all nations, 525. Mercy precedes judgment, 460. Causes of vengeance would abound even against the righteous unless God tempered his justice with mercy, 528. God’s mercy is not bestowed upon those who pray and believe merely because they pray and believe, and so forth; rather, it is bestowed through grace so that we may pray and believe, and so forth, 761. Who are worthy and who unworthy of mercy, 607. God looks upon the earth when he grants his mercy to human beings, 377. Mercy is gratuitous, whereas judgment is owed, 37. No merit precedes mercy; judgment presupposes merits, 30. Unbelievers count the Savior’s mercy as a reproach, saying that hope of forgiveness is fuel for sinning, 375. How God’s mercy is eternal toward the saints, 491. What mercy is to be sought, 498. God’s mercy has always been present for helping bodies and souls, 896. The Lord’s compassion extends toward the salvation of all nations, 872, 873. Yet God gives knowledge of himself to whom he wills, ibid. God brings those whom he wills to faith, 873. God’s mercy has never failed in any age or among any generation, 891. God’s mercy is greater toward the Gentiles after Christ’s coming and lesser toward the Jews, 895. Through God’s preceding mercy, a human being is liberated from every misery, 763. Mercy and truth must not be separated in judgments, 558.

The sending of the Word, his appearance and incarnation: these must be believed by faith, because they are not quickly understood, 597.

MONTANUS, founder of the Cataphrygian error, 713.

The mountains signify the prophets, apostles, and all preachers of truth, from whom every spiritual person receives food and rest, 386. The same mountains and valleys have different meanings, 385. The mountains themselves are watered by divine grace, 387. The mountains are the apostles and evangelists and leaders of the flocks; the hills are those governed by them, 425. The mountains, the preachers of truth, receive from above and spread into lower regions, 471. The higher mountains, 525. The swollen mountains confess when touched by God’s grace, 516.

It is a great labor to tolerate perverse customs; whoever is not offended by them makes little progress, 559.

Death was introduced through the sin of the first human being and increased as human crimes multiplied, 797, vers. 288 and following. Death comes to no one earlier or later than God wills, 207. Death and all evils arise from sin, 233. Why a human being is liable to death at every moment, 909. The various causes of death, and why it comes at different ages, are unknown, 910 and following. God did not make death, yet death is from God: how this is to be understood, 588, 589. The first and second death of the body, 563. How the first and second deaths differ and in what they agree, 567. [Col. 0988]

Christ’s death is a powerful and unique remedy for sin, 229. In what sense all have been redeemed by it, and with whom the particular possession of redemption lies, 230. The death of the Lord and of servants: it benefits the servants, not the Lord, 430. The death of the first humans was the punishment of sin, yet it was good for them, 563, 564. However death may come to the saints, it is never evil, 550, 643 epigr. 50. The death of the saints is precious because it was bought with Christ’s blood, 430. Death is not merely unprofitable but even beneficial to the faithful, according to Cyprian, 37, 39. The dead are not judged according to the deeds they would have done if they had lived, 60, 61. It is absurd to say that the dead are to be judged for sins they would have committed if they had lived, 60. The soul is exempt from death even when surrounded by mortal flesh, 429. Meditation on death is useful for restraining every form of boasting, 610. One who confesses the truth, even if he meets death, does not perish, 451. Bodily mortifications and other spiritual exercises, if they are not supported by human praise, are sustained by the grace of God alone, 287.

MOSES is sent by God to Pharaoh so that he may release the people, 801 vers. 385 and following. Moses leads the people of Israel out of Egypt and gives them the Law, 689. Moses demonstrates how much the intercession of the saints avails with the Lord on behalf of the wicked, 400. Moses did not maintain the confidence he ought to have had and struck the rock hesitantly, 401. Therefore he was punished by deprivation of the earthly inheritance, but not of the eternal one, ibid.

The beauty of the world everywhere bears witness to the wisdom and virtue of its maker, but especially the renewed creation in Christ, 389.

The condition of the world immediately after its creation, 793 vers. 212 and following.

Although the whole world is divided against itself in both hatred and love, we are commanded both to hate it and to love it, 599. From the whole world the whole world is chosen, and from all human beings all human beings are adopted, 221. Love of the world is hostile to charity, 898. What a human being must avoid in the world if he wishes to cultivate virtue, 809 vers. 587 and following. The word “world” signifies two classes of human beings, 599. The world does not judge well concerning the good and the wicked, 811 vers. 851 and following. Amid the world’s scandals, those who do not depart from the Lord are compared with Mount Zion, 471.

Every musical instrument sounds either by striking or by blowing, 532. Musical instruments signify various affections of the soul, 532.

MUSONIUS, the philosopher, 705.

## N
NAMATINUS, an illustrious man, agrees with and subscribes to the Second Council of Orange, 768. The city of NARBONNE, besieged by the Goths, is liberated by Litorius, 745, 746. NARCISSUS, bishop of Jerusalem, 716. Two births of human beings, each unique, 593, 594. Nature precedes vice, and vice is contrary to nature, 562. All nature is good: for nothing in vice displeases except what corrupts what is pleasing in nature, 608. Vices of nature arose from Adam’s sin, 853. All nature serves God’s omnipotence, 801, verse 405. Human nature can never exist without some love, 853. What remained to nature is not sufficient for it unless it receives from its restorer what it lost, 448. If the power in nature were the same as that which was in Adam, each person could reconcile himself to God, and therefore Christ would have died in vain, 181, verses 880 and following. To be able to possess virtue belongs to nature; actually to possess it belongs to grace, 894. Likewise, to be capable of being restored and healed, but not to be restored and healthy, ibid. Why we are called by nature children of wrath, 375. All natures, insofar as they are natures, are good, 563. Human nature, submerged in profound evil by Adam’s fall, 329. There is a nature in which no evil can exist, and none in which no good exists, 566. Human nature can be restored by its Maker, 339. Good will is according to nature, 898. Yet vice is overcome not by the power of nature but by grace, ibid. Human nature, although evil because it has been corrupted, is not itself evil, because it is nature, 588, 764. Grace alone heals nature, 853. What nature is like without grace, 872. For God, nature is what he has made, 584. Nature before grace is under condemnation, 359. Nature is defiled without grace, 92. For simple being and knowing, it is not one thing and another but the same thing, 598.

The use of ships was established among certain peoples, 743. What it means to perform a good work negligently, 899. NEHEMIAH restores Jerusalem, 694. NEPOTIANUS, having seized imperial power, is punished, 728, 729. NERO VI reigns, 704. Nero contends with the lyre, etc., 704, 705. A thunderbolt falls before his table, 704. Nero sets Rome on fire, 705. Nero’s cruelty is overwhelmed by the glorious end of the martyrs, 904. Nero’s extravagance, 704. He kills his mother and his father’s sister, ibid. Nero kills himself, 705. NERVA X rules, 708. He dies, ibid. He is enrolled among the gods, ibid. [Col. 0989] NESTORIUS, arch-heresiarch, 743. Cyril and Celestine resist him, ibid. The Council of NICAEA against Arius, 725. Part of NICOMEDIA and Nicaea collapses in an earthquake; they are restored by Hadrian, 710. “Very much” (*nimis*), not because it is more than ought to be, but meaning “exceedingly,” 436. The NINEVITES, doing penance, deserved the preservation of their kingdom through a change of conduct, 803, verses 445 and following. NIOBE, from whom came Apis, or Serapis, 688. Snow and mists serve to enrich the earth, 527. Snow hardened in ancient times is changed into crystal, 527. What they signify, ibid. The desire to harm comes from human beings, but the power comes from God—and this is a deep and hidden justice, 586. Things that seem in some respect to cause harm benefit in another, 791, verse 134 and following. NOAH begot three sons in the five-hundredth year of his life, and was six hundred years old when the Flood occurred, 686. Noah, the just man, was preserved with his wife, three sons, and the same number of daughters-in-law for the restoration of the human race, 686. Why Noah was preserved with his family, 900. In Noah’s family all their descendants were instructed, 900. How the name of God has been magnified above all, 497. NOVATUS, an African bishop, 746. He suffers persecution from Geiseric, ibid. The schism and heresy of Novatus, 719. The NOVATIANS called themselves “Cathars” after Novatus; in what they were mistaken, 719. The manifold night of this life, in which a person ought to be mindful of the Lord’s name, 445. It benefits those who are healthfully exercised in it, 445. Night as adversity. In it one must devote oneself to the work of holiness, 485. Midnight as profound tribulation, 446. NUMA POMPILIUS, king of the Romans, 692. The silver coin is first struck, 695.

HARDENING and abandonment by God arise from God’s judgment, as he justly punishes sins, 215, 216, 222. Hardening is dissolved by the word of evangelical preaching, and, when the Holy Spirit breathes, the warmth of charity is released, 528. Obedience is a gift of God, 447. The goodness of obedience appeared in paradise, 576. Obedience and humility do not precede grace but are themselves gifts of grace, 761. To obey God when he commands is always useful to a person; not to obey is always disastrous, 585. What seemed harsh to those who turned away becomes pleasant to those who obey, 531. The priestly supplications handed down by the apostles and celebrated throughout the whole world proclaim that grace is necessary for the beginning of faith and righteousness and for all other good things, 275. Hidden things are not to be investigated, since we are granted to know and possess all things in Christ, 667, epigram 91. The eyes of the body see vanities even unwillingly, 442. How the eyes of the heart must be turned away so that they may not be intent on vanity, 442. The inner eyes are from God, 398. The eyes fail while awaiting God’s salvation, not because the longing person’s intention has been defeated and collapsed, but because it has passed over with the full ardor of the mind into expectation of God’s grace, 456. To have something before one’s eyes means to love it, 371. Perfect hatred, 503, 552, 533. With what hatred the wicked are to be hated, ibid., 552, 653, epigram 67. The world’s hatreds are to be patiently endured for the love of God, 599. With what hatred the wicked are to be hated, 454, 547, 552, 629, epigram 25, 653, epigram 67. Offense. We must be without offense toward everyone, 259. Through the duties of ordinary life God is won over, and human society is bound together, 935. OG, conclusion, 488. OLDA, prophetess, 693. Oil flowing from a shop of prostitution signifies Christ’s grace coming from the nations, 699. Oil as spiritual grace, 413. The first Olympic games, instituted by Iphitus, 692. How “all” and “everything” are understood in Scripture, 857, 861 and following, 889. In what sense God wills all to be saved, 863 and following, 872 and following, 888. Whether Scripture speaks of the good or the wicked, the elect or the reprobate, it mentions one part as though it omitted no human being, 857, 858, 859, 860, 861. It speaks of the elect and the reprobate of the same people as though they were the same persons, 861, 869 and following. It speaks of people of different times as though they belonged to the same time, 862, 863. According to nature all are from the truth, but not according to grace, 605. Why it was not said, “Everyone who hears my voice is from the truth,” but, “Everyone who is from the truth hears my voice,” 506. In what sense it is rightly said that all are to be taught so that they may come, 31. Whether God absolutely wills everyone to be saved, 211 and following, 231. God saves all whom he wills to be saved, 95. Scripture speaks of a part as though it were the whole, 859, 860 and following. Elsewhere it explains itself, 861. [Col. 0990]

ONIAS, son of Jaddi, high priest, 695. ONIAS, son of Simon the Just, high priest, 695. By failing to pay tribute to Ptolemy, he provokes him to anger, ibid. But peace is obtained through Joseph as envoy, ibid.

Good works are performed from faith and love, 574, 575. Good works are to be attributed to God, evil works to those who sin, 207. It is not useless to labor to acquire the merits of good works or to persist in prayers, although God’s purpose concerning the salvation of the elect is unchangeable, 921, 922. The effect and sufficiency of good works come from God, 882. Every good work begins not from us but from grace, which freely inspires what is good, 766. God is to be praised for good works, so that we may glory in them in the Lord, 381. It is very difficult to find the life of even the worst person entirely without some good works, 550, 641, epigram 46. In our works we must be praiseworthy in such a way that God is praised in us, 392. At the judgment, nothing is said to be praised except works of charity; nothing is condemned except the neglect of mercy and benevolence, 894. How greatly pride in good works must be avoided, since it corrupts everything, 946 and following. How this danger is to be met, ibid. Works of mercy are the seed of the future harvest, 421. God is perceived to dwell in those who act rightly, 371. We are the works of God’s hands, both as human beings and as justified persons, 498. The causes of divine works are hidden; their effects are evident, 866. The laborers sent into the vineyard at different hours establish the variety of the many forms of calling that belong to one grace: those sent at the eleventh hour represent those whom God rewards at the end of life in order to commend the excellence of grace, 870. OPILIO, an illustrious man, took part in and subscribed to the Second Council of Orange, 768.

Prayer. For whom and for what the Church prays, 864. Right prayer is a gift of God, 449. We have confidence that we will be heard by God because he did not spare his own Son for us, 428. Prayer that is not made through Christ cannot destroy sin; indeed, it itself becomes sin, 410. Why God wished that things which he could also give to those who do not pray should be requested from him, 57. Although God knows what is necessary for us, we must nevertheless pray, 69. How we should ask for what we have received, 54. To pray to God is a gift of spiritual grace, 79. The just God often does not grant what he gave us to ask for, 337. However much progress one makes, one must always ask God for the gift of greater progress, until joy is perfected without danger of losing it, 441, 442. The proper place for prayer is a pure heart, 594. Prayer is a gift of God, 373. We must always pray, even when God has heard us, 506. God must be prayed to without ceasing; he is helper and witness to the one who prays, 509. He who desires what God has taught to be asked petitions to be heard quickly, 497. The prayers of the saints are the fragrance of incense rising to God, 507. Whoever prays in the secrecy of the heart prays in the sight of God, 509. A person who would use wrongly what he asks for does not receive it through God’s mercy, 601. We must fear that God, in anger, may give what in his mercy he could withhold, 601. God mercifully hears—and does not hear—those who plead for the necessities of this life; those who ask for what he commands or promises, he always hears, 573, 669, epigram 95. One ought to ask God for what pleases him, 882. The Church prays for everyone, 864. God wills that prayer be made for everyone, ibid. The failure of the Church’s prayers to be heard for everyone must be referred to God’s hidden judgments, 865 and following. There is no good in us, since not even right prayer comes from us, 949, 950. What those who do not do God’s will ask against themselves when they say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Your will be done,” 239, 240. In accordance with God’s command, supplication is made daily to God for everyone, 890. The certainty of predestination does not abolish prayer, 923. When God becomes angry with one who asks for evil things, 578. Prayer must be made for everyone in the Church, and supplications must never cease, 924. Prayers are quickly obtained when they ask for what the one being petitioned wills, 373. Christ’s prayer on the cross is the evening sacrifice, 506, 507. The prayer Christ taught and with which he intercedes for us daily, 508. Christ, speaking in the person of his members, asks for many things that are not appropriate to his own person, 507. ORIGEN is prominent, 717. He mixes certain perverse teachings into his books, ibid. and 718. OROSIUS, the historian, is prominent, 738. ORPHEUS the Thracian, 690. The mouth of the heart, from which the words themselves take their beginning, is heard, 497. The invisible mouth of the inner person is [his] affection, 473. The mouth that speaks carnal things is mute, because it takes pleasure in what brings it shame, 496. HOSEA, the prophet, 692. OSIAS reigns, 691. Why bones are said to be stronger in Christ’s body, 374. The bones of Andrew and Luke, 729. The bony strength and invincible patience of the saints amid prosperity and adversity, 501. OTHO seizes imperial power and kills himself, 705. Let love of truth seek holy leisure, and let the necessity of love undertake just activity, 567. In leisure one must meditate on God, so that one may be able to think of him in action, 574. OVID is born, 699. Christ’s sheep, found in part, are still being sought, 464. The sheep to be gathered by Christ come not only from Israel but also from the nations, 403.

## P
PACUVIUS, the tragedian, is distinguished, 697. How repentance may be attributed to God, 402. Repentance in God means a change of decision, 482. Everything calls to repentance, since God cares for the elect through scourges, 619 epigr. 4. It does not follow that, to those whom God has not granted repentance, he has taken away the capacity to recover their senses, 238.

PAEONIUS, martyr, 713.

PALLADIUS is ordained the first bishop of the Scots, 363, 744.

What the bread is that strengthens the heart, 388. A human being, not yet made equal to the angels, would not eat the bread of angels unless the bread of angels deigned to become equal to human beings, 607.

PANCRATIUS, Roman presbyter, 729.

PANTAENUS, Christian philosopher, 716.

The Pantheon is built, 707.

The parable of the talents is expounded, 894.

PARTHIA: Arsaces reigns first, from whom the Arsacids derive their name, 696.

PARMENIDES, philosopher, 694.

Little children are subject to the devil because of original guilt, 232. Little children dying without baptism are rejected, 908. Their eternal misery, 911. What grace is bestowed upon them, 911 and following. How the guilt of parents can be said to bring about their destruction, ibid. Their faith and unbelief lie with their parents, ibid. Why God permits this, 612 and following. Why unbaptized children cannot possess eternal life, 37. The eternal misery of children dying without baptism, 911. From children who die immediately after baptism it is most clearly seen that grace is not given according to the desires of the human will but according to God’s good pleasure, 161, verse 616 and following. Their salvation is not to be attributed to the merits of their parents, nor their condemnation to their parents’ demerits, 163, verse 629 and following. This is especially evident in twins, one of whom is baptized while the other dies without baptism, Christ’s mercy alone distinguishing between them, 163, verse 637 and following. By the same mercy faith is granted to others, so that they may do good works and increase in merit to the end, ibid., verse 643 and following. The reason for the premature death of children, 909, 910.

Easter celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, 749. Easter celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May by Leo, through his desire for peace, and through the persistent intention of the bishop of Alexandria and the Eastern bishops, 754. Leo’s letters to Marcian on this matter, by which the truth was disclosed, ibid. The question of the date of Easter arises, 716. Those who wrote about it, ibid. The beginning of the eighty-four-year Paschal cycle, 704.

PASCHASIUS, a Spanish martyr for the faith, 746.

The sparrows signify the humble among the faithful, 471.

The Father is a principle and the Son a principle, not two principles, 416. Just as there are not two gods, but one God, ibid. How the Father acts toward the Son and through the Son, 605. How the Father gave life to the Son, 602. How the Father taught the Son by begetting him, 598. By begetting, the Father gave all things to the Son, 604.

Patience. No one can suffer for Christ without great love, 92. God helps patience to endure to the end, 426. Perseverance is also to be given by God to those of greater spiritual stature, 426. For our instruction in patience, the Savior said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” etc., 520. God wills his people to be patient and gentle, 379.

With what disposition heads of households should command, 566.

PAULILLUS, a boy condemned to slavery for the faith, 746.

PAULINUS, bishop of Gaul, exiled for the sake of the faith, 729.

PAULINUS XXII, bishop of Antioch, 726.

PAUL, a most ardent soldier and an unconquered defender of grace, 45. The apostle Paul pleads before Felix, 704. Paul carries the doctrine of grace to the point of astonishment, 865, 874. PAUL OF SAMOSATA, fifteenth bishop of Antioch, 720.

The heresy of Paul of Samosata, 720.

The poor and beggar are humble before God, 407. The poor are humble and sigh with holy longing, 506. Voluntary poor people are received by wealthy Christians and assisted with necessary support, 388. They follow Christ the Rock, 388.

Poverty is not to be feared, nor riches to be valued, 779, verse 109 and following. The name “poverty” is one, but the mind of the poor is not the same, 935.

Peace with the Goths, 735. The peace that comes from God is not truly tranquil if it is not at odds with the world, 923. Peace rests upon the one who always pleases God and disagrees with his will in nothing, 472. The perfect peace of the heavenly city, 527. There is no need there, where the food of justice is served at the banquet, the food that here existed as desire, 527. Why the perpetual rewards of justice are expressed under the name of peace, 476, 477, 549. Where domestic peace consists, 566. The peace of Christ is the perfection of every pious intention and action, 603. Full peace does not exist in this life, 567. How peace is to be sought from God, 569.

Sin. It lies within the power of evil beings to sin; but that this particular evil or that one should do this or that lies in God’s power alone, 41. Some things are sins in such a way that they are also punishments for sins, 34. Sin has no substance, 471. To impel someone into sin is the work not of God but of the devil, 215. Sins are works of the devil, 478. God does not predestine sins, but the punishments owed to sins, 235, 236, 237. God is not the author of sin but of nature; sin, however, is against nature, 233. Sin itself is evil, not the substance that is loved in sinning, 609. How every sin is called a lie, 564. Sin is not nature but a fault of nature, and alone was not made through the Word, 575, 671 epigr. 97. Sin is a fault of nature that desires what is not in its proper order, 575. Every sin must necessarily be punished, 573. We were all taken captive by the devil through the first transgression and redeemed by Christ, 495. The part that willingly serves its captors offers itself as a minister for attacking the redeemed, 495. The transmission of original sin and death, 769. The misery of the human race is a sure proof of original sin, 582, 583. Some parents aggravate original sin, some lessen it; Christ alone removes it, 589. Just as baptism does, so also the law of circumcision proves that all are born liable to condemnation in Adam, 942. Original sin and its punishments, 374. What remained in humanity after sin, 339. An excellent description of the fall of humanity: the transmission of original sin and the blindness of the mind, 159, verse 575 and following. The effects of original sin, 853 and following. Through Adam’s sin not only the body but also the freedom of the soul was injured, 759. What remains to human beings after the mortal transgression can make their earthly life honorable but cannot confer eternal life, 337. Original sin belongs to the period of bodily existence, 36. Adam’s sin harmed not himself alone but transmitted sin and death to his descendants, 760. How a baptized person can transmit original sin, from which he is free, 588. Before Christ’s reconciliation, no one was anything but a sinner and an impious person, 905. All born in sin are alienated from salvation unless they are reborn in Christ, 942. The Manichaeans deny original sin, 62. Original sin was also acknowledged by some heretics, 36. When original sin is not removed by God’s judgment, or is removed by God’s grace, infants die either passing from evil to good by the merit of regeneration, or from evil to evil by the merit of their origin, 36. There would be no justice of God in the grievous yoke of the misery of little children if innocence were present in them, 894. The descendants can be understood in two ways as having sinned with their ancestors, who were so much older than they, 398. All are under sin, and the redemption by Christ’s blood has been made known to all, 905. No one before the reconciliation accomplished through Christ’s blood is not a sinner or an impious person, 904, 905. No one in this life is without sin, 512. Throughout the world this supplication gains strength: “Forgive us our debts,” etc., 508. How it is true that no one is without sin, and how the one born of God does not sin, 951. Those marked by the name of hedgehogs signify people bristling with petty sins, 388. They too are received by Christ, ibid. All sins, however great, are forgiven in baptism, 570. Sins are to be avoided out of love, not fear, 559. Whoever does not sin out of fear is guilty only in his will, ibid. Those who forgive the sins of their neighbors release their own sins, 637, epigr. 38. Sins are to be confessed, not excused or attributed to the necessity of nature, 507. Some defend their sins with greater learning and boast of such a defense, 507. Those who attribute their sins to the influence of the stars are refuted, 809, verse 624 and following. Those who attribute their sins to divine providence rather than to themselves are refuted, 807, verse 550 and following. With what caution past sins should be recalled, 572. Who are usually understood by the name “sinners,” although even the just do not consider that name foreign to themselves, 477. Although the just are not without sin, Scripture nevertheless is accustomed to call people by this name when they are not guilty of merely trivial faults, 400. God will destroy no sinners except those who persevere in their sins, 521. Every sinner is without excuse, 589. Every sinner is justly punished, because he has carried out not God’s will but his own, 235. No one is a sinner except through transgression, for even one whom the letter does not condemn is convicted by conscience, 455. Why God allows sinners to labor in their own ways, [Col. 0993] 499. We must not despair of sinners, 569, 667, epigr. 92.

The origin, associates, and errors of PELAGIUS, 470. Pelagius was compelled at the council of Eastern bishops to condemn those who said, “The grace of God is given according to our merits,” 319. Pelagius would have led innumerable people astray if he had coated the cup of his teaching with some honey; for, because at first he concealed his errors less, their very deformity deterred most people from them, 175, verse 806 and following. Pelagius is called the British serpent, 115, verse 2. The teachings of Pelagius, 115, verse 1 and following. What Pelagius thought concerning the mortality of the first human beings, 116, verse 3. Concerning original sin, ibid., verse 9 and following. That Adam harmed his descendants through imitation, not propagation, ibid., verse 12. That a human being, if willing, can ascend to the summit of virtue, ibid., verse 13. That a human being can do this through the powers of nature alone, 118, verse 15 and following. What he taught concerning the effect of baptism, ibid., verse 24 and following. That grace is offered to everyone provided they wish to be baptized, and that the innocence voluntarily lost by sinning is recovered and preserved by freedom, 119, verse 29. How strongly the Church rejected Pelagius’s teaching, 119, verse 33 and following. How the apostolic see first cut down this plague, ibid., verse 39, note. The Eastern bishops, ibid., verse 42. Although the Palestinian Synod was perhaps more lenient toward Pelagius, it nevertheless compelled him to condemn his errors, 119, verse 44 and following. Pelagius denied his errors with a feigned heart, 121, verse 51 and following. Pelagius could not endure the words, “Give what you command, and command what you will,” 75. Out of fear of his condemnation, Pelagius condemned the teaching that grace is given according to merits, 64. The teachings of Pelagius, 941, 942. The Pelagian doctrine, 912. The Pelagian interpretation of Saint Paul’s passage, “He who began a good work in you,” Philippians 1:6, 883. It is refuted from the Apostle himself, ibid. Many years earlier, Cyprian had prepared an antidote against the poisons that were to become the Pelagians’ doctrine, 53. The Pelagians deny original sin, 875. The teachings of the Pelagians, 942. Against the Pelagians condemned by Innocent, Augustine’s learning especially offered resistance, 740, 741. The Pelagians are expelled from Ephesus, 121, verse 68. They are driven from Sicily, ibid., verse 69. The Pelagian heresy is chiefly overthrown through the efforts of the African bishops, 123, verse 72 and following. The two African councils at which the Pelagians were condemned and all their devices examined, 123, verse 77 and following. The prayer of the Pelagians, in which they ask that judgment be passed upon them in such a way that either they may be received into the Church and be permitted to teach what the Semipelagians teach, or that those men too may be expelled together with them, 133, verse 196 and following. The chief point of the Pelagian heresy is that grace is given according to merits; even when it confesses that grace is necessary, it weakens grace by attributing it to the merits of the human will, 244, 245. The entire Pelagian heresy is renewed from its smallest part, 131, verse 287 and following. If the Pelagian error is admitted even in its smallest part, it rises again in its entirety, 365. The most wicked and subtle of all the Pelagians’ errors is that grace is given according to merits, 87. The first Pelagian error was to deny grace, and then craftily to confess it, 87, 88. The cunning of the Pelagians detected and defeated, 19. The Pelagian error that the just are free from every sin, 55. The three principal heads of the Pelagian heresy, 53. The objections of the Pelagians arose for the most part from their refusal to confess original sin, 232, 233.

The wings of the soul are the two supports of love, 500.

Who is a pilgrim, 438.

One must always add to the perfection of this life, 557. Nothing more perfect can be requested than that one should increase in virtue, 496. Even the perfect must endure the labors of old age in this life, 557. The perfect desire mercy rather than vengeance for those who have injured them, 380. How the Apostle spoke of the perfect and the imperfect, 590.

The martyrdom of PERPETUA and FELICITY, 716.

The first persecution, under Nero, 705. The second persecution, under Domitian, 707. He is killed, 707. The third persecution, under Trajan, 708. The fourth persecution, 713. The fifth persecution, 716. The sixth persecution, under Maximinus, 718. The seventh persecution, under Decius, 719. The eighth persecution, under Valerian, 719. The ninth persecution, 723. The final persecution at the end of the world, 389. The Church increased through persecutions, not destroyed, 433. During persecutions by slanderers, patience is to be requested from God, 458. What must be avoided during persecutions, 510. Persecutions and dangers cannot be avoided in this life, 390. One must beware lest they creep in, and must not withdraw from the wood of the cross, 390. God has set a measure and an end to persecutions, 385. What the persecutions of kings accomplished for those who imitate Christ, 904. The soul is saved from persecutors if it does not consent to evil with them; but it does not consent when the Lord stands by it, 415. What constitutes a good persecution, 372. The living are swallowed up when, through fear of persecution, they associate with the impious or, while retaining faith inwardly, acquiesce in the worship of idols, 470. The promises of persecutors were snares, and the examples of those who fell were stumbling blocks, 508. Amid persecutions, love among the godly does not grow cold and does not cease practicing God’s commandments, [Col. 0994] 449. The cruelty of persecutors could take away neither the hope nor the joy of the saints, because they could not conquer their patience, 433. The persecutions of the world are not to be compared with the goods for which we hope; they can either be overcome or can hasten our attainment of the reward, 582. The persecutors of God’s people wished to overthrow their faith through savage devastation, 496. Christ endures in himself and in his own people the persecution of false brothers and false children, 511. What the members of Christ suffer is inflicted upon Christ, 511.

Perseverance is a gift of God, 210. It is mercifully given to some and justly withheld from others, 210, 211. Perseverance is given only to the predestined, 58. No one fails to persevere once perseverance has been granted to him, 55. When God’s gift has been granted, no saint is such that he does not hold fast to perseverance in holiness to the end, lest he be led into temptation, 55. No one ceases to persevere unless he is first led into temptation, 56. Whether someone has received perseverance remains uncertain as long as he lives, 51. Why God mingles those who will not persevere with those who will persevere, 65. The perseverance of martyrs is more difficult, 53. The perseverance that is God’s gift is perseverance to the end, 51, 52. Perseverance is requested in the Lord’s Prayer, 53. The saints ask for perseverance, 54. The gift of perseverance can be obtained by prayers, but once given it cannot be lost, 56. Whether perseverance can be lost, 56. Whether perseverance can therefore be lost because someone voluntarily abandons God, so that he may deservedly be abandoned, 56, 59. Perseverance is God’s gift, 51, 52, 53 and following; 70, 72, 74, 76. Cyprian recognized this before Augustine, 76. To give perseverance belongs to faith in God, 53. The perseverance debated among theologians, 52. Perseverance in good works is always to be requested from God by the saints, 762. Perseverance in good comes from Christ, 377. Perseverance is God’s gift, 93. Perseverance is a gift of God, 916. It is also to be requested by those who are more advanced, ibid. Perseverance comes from God, 883. What it is, 884. Perseverance in good comes from God, 884, 885. To persevere means not to be overcome by temptation, 884. One cannot persevere in what one does not love with one’s whole heart, 898.

The modesty of PERTINAX, 715. He is killed, ibid.

PETRONIUS dies, 735.

PETER, the foremost disciple, 915. Even changeable in the Passion, 915 and following. From the principal Rock he received a share in virtue and in name, ibid. Peter’s most ardent faith would have failed in temptations unless the Lord had prayed for him, 93. In Peter it is demonstrated that free will can do nothing without grace, 93. Although Peter was most eager for martyrdom, he is nevertheless told that he will attain victory in suffering only after the temptation of fear, 916. Peter’s threefold denial, 915. Christ encountered Peter’s heart not with human but with divine eyes, ibid. Peter’s faith would have failed unless Christ had prayed for him, 915. PHARAOH: destruction, 488.

PHAEDRA and Hippolytus, 690.

The Photinian error concerning Christ’s incarnation, [Col. 0995] 81.

Where true piety consists, 852. The duties of piety in this life, 587, 671, epigr. 96. With respect to piety, we are not capable of thinking anything as though it came from ourselves, 65. All the godly are despised by the impious as fools; this contempt will eventually be turned back upon the impious themselves, 469, 548, 633, epigr. 32.

PINYTUS of Crete, a most eloquent man, 713.

PIUS IX, bishop of Rome, 712.

The **SEMipelagians** are more dangerously deceptive because they appear to condemn Pelagius while acknowledging original sin and also the necessity of baptism, even in the case of infants, so that they may be freed from sins, 175, verse 817 and following.

Yet they agree with Pelagius when they say that nature can be carried toward the good by its own powers, as before sin, as though it had not been wounded by original sin, etc., 275, verse 823 and following.

The Semipelagians deceived the Church under the appearance of virtue, 127, verse 120. They took the occasion of their error from this, 127, verse 122 and following.

That they do not differ from the Pelagians and therefore ought to enter into public peace with them, ibid., verse 132 and following.

The Pelagians are introduced with complaining words, addressing the Semipelagians so that they may be received back into favor by them, since they approve their opinion, ibid., verses 147 and following.

Those who hold these views cannot refuse association with the Pelagians unless they change their opinion; nor can they embrace it unless they openly dissent from the Church, 131, verse 173 and following.

The Pelagians would readily concede everything else, provided that human freedom is acknowledged, 131, verse 159 and following.

The Pelagians could make the same complaints before the rulers of the Church, 131, verse 184 and following.

The principal tenets of the Pelagian heresy which, by the admission of the Semipelagians themselves, have been condemned by the Church, 135, verse 126 and following. Among them: that grace is given according to merits, 137, verse 239 and following.

The doctrine of the Semipelagians: grace invites everyone, but each person obeys the one calling by his own judgment; grace helps and enlightens those who wish to be helped and enlightened, 137, verse 249 and following.

In these people, with the Lord’s help, the pursuits of virtue subsequently grow, so that everyone has the capacity to persevere, 139, verse 263 and following.

Yet it happens through free judgment that one perseveres and another does not, ibid., verse 267 and following.

Saint Prosper refutes these positions. First, that there is no one to whom Christ’s grace is not given, and so forth, using as an example those who received nothing concerning the mysteries of faith, 139, verse 271 and following.

Response of the Semipelagians: those to whom faith is not announced were not suitable to receive the gifts of salvation because the light of nature had been overwhelmed by vices, 139, verse 287 and following.

Those who say this fall into two Pelagian heresies: that human nature was not wounded and that grace is given according to merits, 141, verse 296 and following.

Concerning God’s will regarding the salvation of all, 141, verse 309 and following.

Not all are saved or come to faith, although whatever God wills is fulfilled, ibid.

Prosper refutes the Semipelagians, who attribute to free judgment the fact that some wish to be saved and others do not, ibid., verse 317 and following.

By examples he proves that, through God’s grace and power, the hearts of the worst people have been converted at every time, ibid., verse 323 and following.

The Semipelagians falsely acknowledge that a person cannot by himself attain either righteousness or salvation or persevere, but maintain that he assents to God’s call by his own freedom, and that God follows and perfects this effort, 143, verse 334 and following.

They are refuted: by this doctrine true grace is overturned, because it is placed outside the human soul, as though it merely knocked at the door of the heart but did not open it, ibid., verse 365 and following.

By this arrangement grace does not truly act, but free judgment does; this is proved by the example of things that are read or heard, ibid., verse 373 and following.

On the contrary, grace bends the will wherever it wishes, with utterly powerful force, and no obstacle delays it, ibid., verse 382 and following.

It is not the minister who plants or waters externally by preaching who accomplishes anything, but God, who gives the increase within, 147, verse 389 and following.

The marvelous effects of grace in human minds, ibid., verse 390 and following.

The inclination to will the good, by which the heart approaches God, cannot be given by one human being to another, nor by a human being to himself, nor through natural wisdom, ibid., verse 395 and following.

Their opinion concerning the gift of perseverance, 15. They did not admit that the saying, “What do you have that you did not receive?” was spoken concerning faith, ibid.

They did not admit a distinction between the grace now given and that given to innocent Adam, 16.

In what respect they wished the nature of all human beings to differ from that of the first man, 16.

They did not want the number of the predestined to be defined, 17.

What meaning they rejected in the words, “He wills all human beings to be saved,” and what meaning they admitted, 17.

The Semipelagians glory in the Catholic name, 271. They are infected with the condemned opinions of heretics, ibid. They accuse teachers of grace of excess, ibid. Yet they profess to follow the decrees of the Apostolic See, ibid.

The errors of the Semipelagians are to be avoided by all who are truly devout, whose entire righteousness is Christ’s, and who acknowledge that human nature was so wounded by the injury of the first parent that it cannot even spontaneously raise the eyes of the mind on high and recognize its misery, 177, verse 847 and following.

Objection of the Semipelagians: by this preaching of grace free judgment is taken away; nor are punishments or rewards owed to anyone if nature, left to itself, wills only evil, while good works must be attributed not to us but to grace, 157, verse 565 and following.

They reason in this way with Pelagius because, like him, they do not truly acknowledge the fall of the whole nature in the first man, 159, verse 571 and following.

The Semipelagians condemn the Pelagians only in words, while retaining the most subtle poison of that heresy, 175, verse 801 and following.

The heresy extinguished among the Pelagians by the Church began to revive among the Semipelagians, 127, verse 114.

Objection of the Semipelagians: if grace is altogether necessary for doing good, and is not given to everyone, those to whom the ability to act well was not given will not be guilty of sin, 163, verse 647 and following.

By this argument original sin is denied; by original sin alone human beings are guilty of death, even if they have added no personal sin, ibid., verse 652 and following.

The remnants of the Pelagians: what Pelagian doctrines the Semipelagians preserved, 942.

The remnants of the Semipelagians: what they retained from them, 942.

They denied original sin, ibid.

Scriptural authorities which the Semipelagians misuse, 90, 91 and following.

If the Semipelagians do not dare to defend Pelagian doctrines, they must also abandon their own errors, 153, verse 522 and following.

They must confess that nature has been so wounded that it can never rise by free judgment to perform righteousness, ibid.

If they refuse to confess this, they cannot deny that they are on equal terms with the Pelagians, with whom in fact they agree, 155, verse 534.

For they differ only in words, while they are forced to say that through Adam’s sin our body was made subject to death, but that the soul was not corrupted by sin; this is to attribute injustice to God and to absolve human beings entirely, 155, verse 540 and following.

God, however, is not unjust, since according to the Apostle all fell in one, and afterward no one could rise to life except by Christ’s grace—not even the righteous who lived before Christ, ibid., verses 549 and following.

The second is the difficulty of desires, from which one is delivered through the ability to act rightly given by grace, ibid. The third temptation concerns the word of God, 405. ## Notice on St. Prosper’s Letter to St. Augustine

63 **LETTER TO AUGUSTINE.**—On the remnants of the Pelagian heresy springing up in Gaul, and on the complaints of such men against the doctrines of predestination and grace, explained in Augustine’s short works. 67

Notice on the Letter to Rufinus. 73

**LETTER TO RUFINUS.**—On grace and free will. 77

Notice on the *Poem against the Ungrateful*. 89

**POEM AGAINST THE UNGRATEFUL.** 91

**Preface.** Ibid.

**PART ONE.**—St. Prosper declares that he intends by this poem to ward off the impending danger to the Church from the hidden enemies of grace. He then discloses what Pelagius’s doctrine was, with what zeal it was rejected by the bishops of the Church, condemned by the authority of councils and the Apostolic See, and refuted by the holy doctors—above all by St. Augustine, whose diligence and illumination in this struggle, as well as whose possession of more abundant gifts of grace from God, shone forth above all others. 93

**PART TWO.**—He reviews the principal doctrines of Pelagius condemned by the Church. He then sets forth their doctrine, which has two parts. One is that grace is offered by God to all human beings; the other, that free will is the reason why one person embraces grace and another rejects it, because the latter has failed to obtain the help of grace for himself—something which all can do, since enough strength supposedly remains in human nature from the remnants of its original integrity to desire and seek God’s help. Both parts are refuted in accordance with Catholic teaching. 107

**PART THREE.**—The arguments and complaints of the Semipelagians are driven back. They chiefly advanced two objections: first, that free will is abolished, and that neither punishment is due to vices nor rewards to virtue if either nature, corrupted by sin, wills nothing but evil, or if everything a person does well is the work of grace—indeed of that grace which gives both willing and running. St. Prosper replies that this objection overturns faith in Original Sin, through which the freedom granted to us in Adam was destroyed, and we were subjected to the yoke of concupiscence, by which we are always dragged toward evil, even when we do what we desire. Our will cannot be freed from that servitude except insofar as it is freed by Christ’s saving grace; through that grace, our former freedom is not removed but restored, and so forth. 123

**PART FOUR.**—He compares the doctrine of the Semipelagians with the Pelagian heresy, showing that they establish a more dangerous form of Pelagian doctrine. He especially destroys their foundation concerning the remnants of original integrity which they thought remained in human nature, and teaches that, as regards the desire for true good, nothing sound has remained in nature. 135

**CHAPTER VI.**—That every holy thought and movement of a devout will is from God. 208

**CHAPTER VII.**—That God’s grace not only forgives sins but also helps prevent them from being committed, and enables the law to be fulfilled—not, as Pelagius says, easily, as though without God’s grace it could only be fulfilled with greater difficulty. Ibid.

**CHAPTER VIII.**—That, apart from the decrees of the Apostolic See, all the prayers of the Church echo the grace of Christ, by which the human race is restored from eternal damnation. 209

**CHAPTER IX.**—That the established purification of those to be baptized also bears witness to God’s grace, since unclean spirits are driven from them by exorcisms and breathings. 210

**CHAPTER X.**—That deeper questions should neither be disregarded nor asserted absolutely. 211

Notice on the book *Against the Collator*. Ibid.

**BOOK AGAINST THE COLLATOR.** 213

**CHAPTER I.**—The slanderers of St. Augustine’s teaching go so far as to make it seem that the enemies of grace were unjustly condemned by the Church. Hence arises the greater necessity of refuting them. 215

**CHAPTER II.**—Why he attacks chiefly the definitions of Cassian alone. Cassian’s first definition is Catholic. A definition is then introduced which teaches that many come to grace without grace. 217

**CHAPTER III.**—Cassian agrees fully neither with the Pelagians nor with Catholics when he asserts that some are justified by grace, others by law and nature. Cassian’s third definition: That a person possesses the desire for virtues from himself. 221

**CHAPTER IV.**—It is proved against Cassian that the desire for healing is not possessed without grace. Cassian’s fourth definition: That, through the good of nature, beginnings of good wills sometimes arise. This is refuted. 223

**CHAPTER V.**—Cassian’s fifth definition: That contrary propositions must be accepted together—both the proposition that a good will is born from grace and the proposition that grace depends upon a good will. Refutation. 225

**CHAPTER VI.**—Since the question concerning the origin of holy wills has been clearly defined against the Pelagians, Cassian acts wrongly when, gathering weapons from the adversaries, he argues that free will is taken away by grace. 228

**CHAPTER VII.**—Cassian, confusing contrary definitions, attempts to lend color by examples to what he intends: that some things can be done by certain people through free will without God’s help, while others cannot be done except with God’s cooperation. He is refuted. 229

**CHAPTER VIII.**—Cassian’s sixth definition: That free will and grace ought to be received together—that is, in such a way that they are believed to contribute equally to salvation. Divine authorities concerning grace are brought forward, and the reason is given why the will is not removed by grace. 233

**CHAPTER IX.**—It is proved against Cassian that the beginning of a good will comes from grace. Cassian’s seventh definition is refuted, namely: That Adam, after his transgression, received knowledge of evil but did not lose knowledge of good. 235

**CHAPTER X.**—The Apostle’s passage, Romans 2:14, concerning Gentiles who do by nature what belongs to the law, is explained and defended. A certain wisdom exists among unbelievers from the remnants of the nature created by God; but no movement of a good will exists except from the Holy Spirit. 240

**CHAPTER XI.**—Free will possesses neither the will nor the ability for good except through grace. Why human beings are commanded to do what they do not find the ability to do in their own nature. Cassian’s eighth definition: That not only what is evil should be attributed to human nature; that no human merits exist except by grace. 242

**CHAPTER XII.**—Cassian’s view is demonstrated more fully: that pious thoughts and holy counsels, conceived without God’s inspiration, can arise from natural wisdom. It is refuted. 243

**CHAPTER XIII.**—Cassian’s ninth definition: That the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator. It is refuted because it overturns Original Sin. True virtues do not exist in the ungodly. There are no beginnings of virtues or merits in us before grace. Although there are many things worthy of praise in the abilities of the ungodly, they are not true virtues. He refutes what the Collator had attempted to prove from the apocryphal book of *The Shepherd*: that even before grace a human being is equally disposed toward good and evil. 247

**CHAPTER XIV.**—Cassian’s tenth definition: That Job overcame the devil by his own powers, not with the help of grace, except insofar as God did not give the tempter greater power than the virtue he knew Job possessed. Cassian’s deception: at the beginning of his discussion he professes the Catholic view of grace, intending afterward to overthrow it. 252

**CHAPTER XV.**—How much Cassian attributed to free will. He thinks that Job overcame the devil in the conflict by his own virtue. It is proved against him that Job overcame by God’s help. The strength of endurance comes only from God’s grace. Cassian’s error was to hold that Job possessed the virtue of resistance from free will, not from grace. 253

**CHAPTER XVI.**—What Cassian had taught above, he attempts to confirm by the example of the Gospel centurion. His eleventh definition is this: That there would be no praise or merit if Christ had preferred in him what he himself had bestowed. Refutation. 259

**CHAPTER XVII.**—How much Cassian, in the points refuted above, assists the Pelagians. Salvation cannot come to the whole world except through faith. 261

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—Cassian attempts to mix incompatible things and divides the faithful into two classes, to which he adapts contrary propositions. Cassian’s twelfth definition: That God is savior to some in the matter of salvation, but merely receiver to others. Refutation. 262

**CHAPTER XIX.**—Recapitulation of Cassian’s twelve definitions. 265

**CHAPTER XX.**—The errors contained in Cassian’s definitions are collected in summary. 269

**CHAPTER XXI.**—He returns to the defense of Augustine undertaken at the beginning, whom the Semipelagians especially attacked. The Church must therefore oppose them with the same weapons. Augustine’s teaching is shown to be everywhere of the same character. 270

**CHAPTER XXII.**—Conclusion of the work. Although Augustine’s critics have been sufficiently convicted, they must nevertheless be tolerated, and one must not despair of their correction. Meanwhile, they should always be loved, but avoided. 274
