Notice on the books *On the Calling of All Nations*. 639

**ON THE CALLING OF ALL NATIONS. BOOK ONE.** 647

**CHAPTER ONE.**—He proposes the subject to be treated in this book and teaches that those who contend that free will is denied by the preaching of grace do not think rightly. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—That every human soul naturally possesses some kind of will, which is either sensual, animal, or spiritual. 649

**CHAPTER III.**—On the sensual will. 650

**CHAPTER IV.**—On the animal will, by which nothing beyond the reward of temporal glory is acquired, even if something higher is understood in it by God’s gift. Ibid.

**CHAPTER V.**—That all nations received legal precepts through the elements, so that they are without excuse in idolatry. 651

**CHAPTER VI.**—That without divine grace the will approaches iniquity all the more quickly the more intensely it is directed toward action, because it does not live for the glory of God. 652

**CHAPTER VII.**—When a human being returns to piety, it is not another created substance that is restored, but the same substance that had been weakened; nothing is removed from it except vice, while the former will is corrected. 653

**CHAPTER VIII.**—That grace so restores God’s work that it does not take away free will but rather heals it through free will itself. 654

**CHAPTER IX.**—That Scripture, whether it speaks of the good or the evil, of the elect or the reprobate, remembers one side in such a way as though it had omitted no human being. 657

**CHAPTER X.**—That Scripture speaks of the elect and reprobate of the same people as though they were the same persons. 661

**CHAPTER XI.**—That Scripture speaks of people of different periods as though they belonged to the generation of the same period. 663

**CHAPTER XII.**—That the Apostle’s statement, “He wishes all human beings to be saved,” is understood of every kind of human being. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XIII.**—The depth of that hidden mystery by which the grace of God the Savior passes over some for whom the Church prays cannot be revealed to us in this life. 665

**CHAPTER XIV.**—There are many things in the administration of divine works whose causes remain hidden while only their effects are shown. 666

**CHAPTER XV.**—The fact that some human beings are delivered cannot be attributed to the merits of their wills, as though grace chose the good and passed over the evil. 668

**CHAPTER XVI.**—The inscrutability of divine judgments is shown by the fact that, before attaining understanding, some equal infants depart from this life to eternal life and others to eternal death. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XVII.**—The conversion and salvation of ungodly people at the end of life shows both that grace is given without merits and that God’s judgment is inscrutable. 669

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—Grace, without which good merits cannot exist, is received by no one except through God’s will, without merits. 671

**CHAPTER XIX.**—What nature is without grace. 672

**CHAPTER XX.**—The Lord extends the bowels of mercy toward the salvation of all nations and saves everyone; yet it is also true that no one receives his testimony. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XXI.**—One must not investigate why God chooses some and does not choose others, just as one must not investigate why, after passing over all the nations, he formerly chose Israel alone. 674

**CHAPTER XXII.**—Those who refer the distinction by which God chose some to the merits of the human will teach that no one is saved freely, but by recompense; they are openly refuted by the case of infants. 675

**CHAPTER XXIII.**—Every good merit of a human being, from the beginning of faith to the completion of perseverance, is a divine gift. 676

**CHAPTER XXIV.**—Everything good in a human being is from grace, and faith is given without being requested, so that through its petitions we may obtain the other good things. 679

**CHAPTER XXV.**—Why one person rather than another receives grace is impenetrable and cannot be resolved by free will. 685

**BOOK TWO.** Ibid.

**CHAPTER I.**—Three things are certain in this question: that God wishes all to be saved; that knowledge of the truth and salvation are from grace; and that God’s judgments are impenetrable. 685

**CHAPTER II.**—Scripture teaches that God wishes all human beings to be saved. 687

**CHAPTER III.**—It is inscrutable why God judged that the calling of certain people should be postponed. 688

**CHAPTER IV.**—In former ages divine goodness always admonished human beings to worship God through the elements. 689

**CHAPTER V.**—Those among the nations who pleased God were distinguished by the spirit of faith and grace. 691

**CHAPTER VI.**—Even now, the same measure of grace is not bestowed on all. Ibid.

**CHAPTER VII.**—Since every good thing is from God’s grace, inequality of merits must neither be attributed to free will nor made a matter of complaint. 692

**CHAPTER VIII.**—To each person, without merit, is given the means by which he may strive toward merit; and grace already bestowed expects him to increase what he has received through him who gives the increase. Ibid.

**CHAPTER IX.**—The reason for the variation of grace through different periods is not to be investigated by us. 694

**CHAPTER X.**—In every age God’s mercy has nourished bodies and aided minds. 695

**CHAPTER XI.**—What the heavenly generosity has decreed to give human beings generally increases gradually and in portions. 695

**CHAPTER XII.**—Our turning away from God is not part of the divine constitution, but belongs to our own will. 697

**CHAPTER XIII.**—Before the Flood, God’s goodness was present not only for the saints but also for the ungodly [the printed reading is uncertain]. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XIV.**—In the Flood and afterward up to Christ, the works of divine grace were revealed, and the miracles of Christian grace were foreshadowed. 698

**CHAPTER XV.**—Better abilities are not born now than before Christ’s coming. At the time of Christ’s coming, iniquity was found to be stronger, so that God’s grace might be manifested. 700

**CHAPTER XVI.**—Christ died for all. 702

**CHAPTER XVII.**—The nations on which the Savior’s grace has not yet shone are to be called to the Gospel at the appointed time. 704

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—The grace of Christ was hidden from the Gentiles in earlier ages, but not the prophecy. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XIX.**—For all time God wishes all human beings to be saved. 706

**CHAPTER XX.**—An objection from infants against the statement, “He wishes all human beings to be saved.” 707

**CHAPTER XXI.**—God deals justly with infants who perish, both in this age and in the future, on account of Original Sin. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XXII.**—Divine justice assigns to each person the measure and degree of misery. 708

**CHAPTER XXIII.**—Infants who perish receive general grace, since it is given to their parents. 709

**CHAPTER XXIX.**—The distinction between equal infants is not a just cause of complaint, but a great commendation of divine justice and the grace of Christ. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XXV.**—By general grace God always wishes all to be saved; but by particular grace he wishes only some to be saved. 710

**CHAPTER XXVI.**—In every justification grace indeed takes precedence principally, but the will is joined to it, because grace first prepares the will for itself, as the receiver and servant of its gifts. 711

**CHAPTER XXVII.**—The will’s consent is produced by grace not only through teaching and illumination but also through terror and fear. 712

**CHAPTER XXVIII.**—Those who believe in Christ through God’s grace can fail to believe, and those who persevere can depart from God. 713

**CHAPTER XXIV.**—The promise of the blessing of all nations is fulfilled daily in such a way that those who perish have no just excuse, and those who are saved have no ground for boasting of their salvation. 715

**CHAPTER XXX.**—Repetition of the first chapter of Book Two. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XXXI.**—In every age the general goodness of God has been present to all human beings, but particular grace only to those who are to be saved. 716

**CHAPTER XXXII.**—Among the faithful there are various degrees of God’s gifts; this is due not to their merits but to God’s just and hidden judgment. 717

**CHAPTER XXXIII.**—No one perishes who ought not to perish; but all who were chosen from eternity are saved. 717

**CHAPTER XXXIV.**—It is not futile to labor to acquire the merits of good works or to persist in prayers, although God’s purpose concerning the salvation of the elect is unchangeable. 719

**CHAPTER XXXV.**—Grace is given to the elect not so that they may remain idle or be attacked by no enemy, but so that they may do good works and overcome the enemy. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XXXVI.**—Election does not remove the zeal for prayer, but its effect is completed through prayer and good works. 720

**CHAPTER XXXVII.**—Before the end of this life, it cannot be declared of anyone that he will be destined for the glory of the elect. 722
